en: Preface to the Second Assembly of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra,
composed by the Śramaṇa Xuánzé.
Contemplating how the profound realization of the Middle Way unfolds its sublime course across the boundless, and how the flow of appreciation returns to a single source, surging forth...
Within the realm of the mundane world, how could there ever be a time when one does not first ground oneself in reality to draw forth awakening, and rely on concrete facts to dispel doubt?

As doubts proliferate, instruction naturally expands; as initial awakening begins, inquiry becomes increasingly earnest. This is why [the sages] repeatedly pointed toward Vulture Peak and Āṭavī, and twice struck upon the assembly of the Dragon King.

When the community of those with wisdom gathered, Subhūti presided over the school; when the assembly of those with the patience of the Dharma convened, Vimalakīrti led the group. Thereupon, he shook the region to issue a warning and opened up the world to reveal his majesty; his tongue covered the great trichiliocosm and his body spanned billions of realms. His light spread like a compassionate shadow, moistening the harmony of the six destinies; his voice raised the words of the Dharma, sending forth tidings to the ten directions. Having been startled by these extraordinary sights, they then hoped for his secret instructions.
Some might say that because his traces are lofty, he appears to be eccentric; and because their own minds are clouded, they wait expectantly for an analysis. Thus, it has been said:
"To pursue the observations of a tube peering through a keyhole is to suffer from an inability to grasp the profound and sublime."
To cling to the brevity of a cicada’s life or a mushroom’s existence is ultimately to deceive the cycles of years.
For even with shallow resolve and subtle arts, one may still command the five supernatural powers;
through small virtues and a few words, one truly responds across a thousand li.
How much more so when it gives birth to and nurtures all categories of beings, and exerts sovereign control over all spirits;
when the myriad kalpas meet in a single assembly, exhausting the depths of darkness and reaching the furthest reaches.

This causes lands as numerous as motes of dust to travel without moving, and Buddhas as vast as the sands of the Ganges to realize enlightenment without consultation. Were it not for the ultimate profundity of Prajñā, who could bring this about?

Thus, by means of the ten voids one polishes and dries [the mind], and through the seven suchnesses one listens with clarity; although the realms of affliction are dense and chaotic, and the shore of tranquility is tiered and remote, they are all alike in being like the opening and falling of illusory blossoms—neither extinguished nor born—and comparable to the beauty or ugliness of elephants in a dream—neither defiled nor pure.

When an echo is cast into a rushing valley, praise and slander dissolve together; when the moon bathes the pond with its light, both object and self fade away. The phrasing is elegant and the principles reach their ultimate point, evoking a resonance that leads to eternal awakening.

In total, there are eighty-five chapters and seventy-eight fascicles, comprising the old *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (*Dapin*), the *Prabhāsa-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (*Guangzan*), and the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (*Fangguang*).

Now, as for the *Dapin* compared to the *Guangzan*, its wording is twice as abundant and more beautiful; likewise, this portion [of the *Fangguang*] compared to the *Dapin* has even more complete texts and is increasingly correct. When these radiant splendors are gathered and these treasures are compared, how magnificent they are!
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 413.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Part Two: Chapter One, "The Originating Conditions" (Nidāna-parivarta). Chapter One.

Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of five thousand bhikṣus. All were arhats whose outflows were exhausted and who were free from further afflictions; they had attained true mastery, being well-liberated in mind and well-liberated in wisdom. They were like well-trained thoroughbred horses and like great dragons; having done what was to be done and accomplished what was to be accomplished, they had laid down their heavy burdens and achieved their own welfare. Having exhausted all fetters of existence, they were liberated through right knowledge, having reached the heart of mastery and the supreme consummation—with the sole exception of Ānanda, who remained alone on the stage of training as a stream-enterer. The venerable Subhūti was the leader of the assembly.
Furthermore, there was a community of five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, all of whom were arhats, with the Venerable Yaśodharā as their leader.
There were also immeasurable upāsakas and upāsikās who had all realized the truths.
Furthermore, there was an immeasurable and incalculable assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all of whom had attained various dhāraṇīs and samādhis;
they constantly dwelt in emptiness, practiced within the realm of signlessness, maintained non-conceptual vows ever present before them,
possessed the patience of equality regarding the nature of all phenomena, and had attained unimpeded eloquence without regression.
With supernormal powers, their conduct was pure and lofty, diligent and tireless;
they expounded the True Dharma without seeking anything for themselves, responding to principles and adapting to capacities while remaining free from all deceit and hypocrisy.

Having reached the ultimate goal through profound patience regarding the Dharma, they severed all fears, subdued the various Māras, extinguished all delusions, and crushed all karmic obstructions with wisdom and eloquence.
Fully endowed with skillful means, having been adorned by great vows for countless eons, he speaks first with a smile, with a relaxed countenance and a gentle gaze;
his praise is exquisite and his eloquence inexhaustible; majestic and dignified, he dwells among the assembly without fear;
his temperament is serene and refined, his deportment is appropriate, and he explains the teachings with flowing artistry that remains undiminished through many eons.

He skillfully contemplates that all phenomena are identical to illusions, mirages, dreams, the moon reflected in water, and echoes; they are like flowers in the sky, reflections in a mirror, and shadows of light, and equal to magical transformations and the city of the gandharvas—knowing them all to be without reality and appearing only as semblances of existence.
His mind is neither inferior nor timid, but remains composed and fearless; he is able to penetrate and enter all dharma-gates.
Regarding the inclinations, mental activities, and the destinies of sentient beings, he attains unimpeded mastery and delivers them.
Having attained supreme forbearance and thoroughly understood the true nature of reality, they embrace great vows and infinite Buddha-fields;
toward the countless Buddhas throughout the ten directions, they maintain equanimity and right mindfulness so that those Buddhas are always present before them;
and in order to deliver sentient beings, they serve all Buddhas through successive lifetimes, exhorting them to remain long in the world and turn the wheel of the True Dharma.

They have extinguished all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), views, and the stains of the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*); they sport in hundreds of thousands of immeasurable samādhis and bring forth boundless, preeminent wholesome dharmas.
This assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possesses such immeasurable merits, their names being:
the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, the Bodhisattva Ratnākara, the Bodhisattva Śāstṛ, and the Bodhisattva Varadatta.
The Bodhisattva Jyotisprabha, the Bodhisattva Nityapradatta, the Bodhisattva Guṇakośa, the Bodhisattva Uttaramati,
the Bodhisattva Ratnakośa, the Bodhisattva Vijayamati, the Bodhisattva Vardhamānamati,
the Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin, the Bodhisattva Suprasthita, the Bodhisattva Suvikrāntavikrāmin, and the Bodhisattva Nityodyukta.
The Bodhisattva Constantly Engaged in Application, the Bodhisattva Never-Relinquishing-the-Yoke,
the Bodhisattva Sūryagarbha, the Bodhisattva Peerless Wisdom, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta,
the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva Vajramati, the Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāhasta, the Bodhisattva Nityotkṣiptahasta, and the Bodhisattva Maitreya.
The Bodhisattva Śrī and other such immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas were all Dharma-princes,
capable of succeeding to the noble position, serving as their leaders.

At that time, the World-Honored One, upon the lion throne, spread out his own sitting mat and sat cross-legged. With body upright and resolve correct, he dwelt in mindfulness directed toward the object before him and entered the sublime samādhi known as the King of Samādhis. All other samādhis were subsumed within this samādhi, for they are its outflow.

At that time, the World-Honored One, with perfect knowledge and mindfulness, arose calmly from the Samādhirāja-samādhi. With his pure divine eye, he surveyed the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; his entire body was filled with joy, and from the thousand-spoked wheel marks on the soles of both feet, he emitted sixty hundred-thousand *koṭi-nayuta* rays of light each.
From the ten toes of his feet, both insteps, both heels, the four ankles, both calves, both shins, both knees,

both thighs, both hips, the waist and ribs, the abdomen and back, the navel, the area above the heart, the *bhadra* mark on the chest, both breasts, both armpits, both shoulders, both upper arms, both elbows, both forearms, both wrists, both hands, the ten fingers of the palms, the nape of the neck, the chin and jaw, the cheeks and forehead, the crown of the head, both eyebrows, both eyes, both ears, both nostrils, the four teeth of the mouth, the forty teeth, and the *ūrṇā-kośa* between the brows— from each of these individual parts of the body, he emitted sixty hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* rays of light.

Each of these individual rays of light individually illuminates a trichiliocosm, and from there they spread successively until they pervasively illuminate as many Buddha-worlds in the ten directions as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River; any sentient beings who encounter this light will certainly attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

At that time, every pore of the Blessed One’s body became radiant with joy, each emitting sixty hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* rays of light. Each of these individual rays illuminated a trichiliocosm, and from there they spread successively until they pervaded the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Any sentient being who encountered this light would inevitably attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted from his body a constant light that illuminated this trichiliocosm; from there it spread successively until it pervasively illumined Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions. Any sentient beings who encountered this light would inevitably attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One extended his broad and long tongue from his mouth, completely covering the trichiliocosm, and smiled with serene joy.

Furthermore, from his tongue-mark he emitted immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of light rays; these rays were of various colors, and from each of these multicolored rays there appeared precious lotus flowers, each with a thousand petals, all of true golden color and adorned with various jewels.
Thus, these lights and flowers pervaded the trichiliocosm, and from there they circulated successively throughout the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Within each flower pedestal was a transformation Buddha, seated in the full lotus posture and expounding the sounds of the sublime Dharma; every such sound of the Dharma taught teachings corresponding to the six *pāramitās*, so that any sentient being who heard them would surely attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

At that time, the World-Honored One, without rising from his seat, again entered the samādhi called "Lion’s Play" and manifested supernatural powers, causing this trichiliocosm to undergo six kinds of movement:

namely, shaking, intense shaking, and universal intense shaking; leaping, intense leaping, and universal intense leaping; quaking, intense quaking, and universal intense quaking; crashing, intense crashing, and universal intense crashing; roaring, intense roaring, and universal intense roaring; and bursting, intense bursting, and universal intense bursting.

Furthermore, he caused this world-system to rise in the east and sink in the west, rise in the west and sink in the east, rise in the south and sink in the north, rise in the north and sink in the south, rise in the center and sink at the edges, and rise at the edges and sink in the center.
The ground was pure, radiant, fine, and soft, bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.

At that time, all sentient beings within the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, and other perilous pits of the unfortunate states throughout this trichiliocosm were freed from their suffering and hardships. Having passed away from those realms, they were reborn among humans and the six heavens of the desire realm; all of them remembered their past lives and, filled with joy and exultation, went together to the place where the Buddha was, prostrating at his feet with profound purity of mind.

From there, it spread successively throughout the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, with six kinds of miraculous transformations through the Buddha’s spiritual power.

At that time, all sentient beings in the evil realms and elsewhere in those worlds were freed from suffering and hardship; they passed away from those states and were reborn among humans and in the six heavens of the desire realm. Remembering their past lives, they leaped for joy and each went from their own realm to the place where the Buddha was, prostrating at his feet.

At that time, the sentient beings in this trichiliocosm and in other worlds throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, were such that the blind could see, the deaf could hear, the mute could speak, the insane regained their mindfulness, the distracted attained concentration, the poor became wealthy, the naked obtained clothing, the hungry received food, the thirsty received drink, the sick were healed, the ugly became handsome, those with physical deformities became complete, those with impaired faculties became whole, the bewildered and dazed became alert, and the weary and exhausted found peace and comfort.

At that time, all sentient beings turned their hearts toward one another, regarding each other as fathers and mothers, elder and younger brothers, elder and younger sisters, friends, and kin. They abandoned wrong speech, action, and livelihood, cultivating right speech, action, and livelihood; they abandoned the ten paths of unwholesome action and cultivated the ten paths of wholesome action; they abandoned evil thoughts and cultivated wholesome thoughts; they abandoned non-celibacy and cultivated pure celibacy. Delighting in purity and discarding filth, finding joy in stillness and abandoning clamor, their bodies and minds became serene, suddenly giving rise to sublime bliss, like a practitioner entering the third dhyāna.
Furthermore, supreme wisdom suddenly manifested before them, and they all thought:

"Generosity, self-discipline, patience, diligence, tranquility, and discernment; being free from negligence, practicing the holy life, and maintaining loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity toward all sentient beings without causing mutual disturbance—how excellent this is!"

At that time, the World-Honored One sat upon the lion throne; his radiance was extraordinary and his majestic virtue was so sublime that it eclipsed the great trichiliocosm as well as the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Mount Sumeru, the Cakravāḍa mountains, and all other palaces of nāgas, devas, and even those of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens were entirely obscured and no longer appeared.

He was like the full autumn moon outshining the host of stars, like the summer sun’s orb overwhelming all colors with its light, or like the Great King of Mountains composed of four jewels, whose majesty causes all other mountains to lose their luster.
By means of his supernatural power, the Buddha manifested his original physical body, causing all sentient beings throughout this trichiliocosm to behold it.
At that time, the immeasurable and innumerable devas of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens,
down to the Cāturmahārājika devas of the desire realm, as well as all others— both humans and non-humans— saw him.
The Tathāgata sat upon the lion throne, his majestic radiance shining like a great mountain of gold;
filled with joy and leaping for gladness, they marveled at this unprecedented occurrence, each holding various kinds of exquisite flower garlands,
powdered and incense perfumes, robes, necklaces, jeweled banners, pennants, canopies, music, and all manner of rare treasures, as well as immeasurable...
They brought various celestial blue lotuses, celestial red lotuses, celestial white lotuses, celestial fragrant lotuses,
celestial yellow lotuses, celestial crimson lotuses, celestial *dīnāra* tree flowers, and fragrant leaf flowers,
as well as countless other flowers born of water and land, and went to the place where the Buddha was to scatter them over him in offering.

By the Buddha’s spiritual power, the various flower garlands and other offerings revolved upward and merged to form a flower pedestal, equal in size to the trichiliocosm; it was adorned with hanging celestial canopies, jeweled bells, and pearl banners, their exquisite decorations so profuse and magnificent as to be most delightful.
At that time, this buddha-field was exquisitely adorned, just like the Western World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).

The Buddha’s radiance illuminated the myriad things of the trichiliocosm, and the entire void became the color of gold; likewise, it was so in all the buddha-worlds of the ten directions, each as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.

At that time, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, throughout this great trichiliocosm, every god and human saw the Buddha sitting directly before them, each thinking, "The Tathāgata is preaching the Dharma for me alone."

At that time, the World-Honored One did not rise from his seat; with a serene smile, he emitted a great radiance from the gate of his face, which illuminated the trichiliocosm Buddha-field as well as the worlds of the Ganges-sand number of Buddhas in the other ten directions.

At that time, all sentient beings within this trichiliocosm, following the Buddha’s radiance, universally beheld in the ten directions all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas—equal in number to the sands of the Ganges River—surrounded by assemblies of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, as well as all other categories of sentient and insentient beings.

At that time, all sentient beings in the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, following the Buddha’s light, also beheld this land and Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, surrounded by an assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, as well as all other categories of sentient and insentient beings.

At that time, in the eastern direction, throughout as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, the final world was named Prabhūtaratna; its Buddha was named Ratnagotra, who was currently teaching the Great Prajñāpāramitā to bodhisattvas.

There was a bodhisattva there named Samantaprabha; seeing this great radiance, the trembling of the earth, and the marks of the Buddha’s body, he felt uncertainty in his mind and approached the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"For what cause and for what reason has this auspicious omen appeared?
At that time, the Buddha Ratnagotra addressed Samantaprabha, saying:

"From this western direction, passing through as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, there is a final world named Sahā, where the Buddha is named Śākyamuni. He is about to preach the Great Prajñāpāramitā to the bodhisattvas; it is by the spiritual power of that Buddha that this auspicious omen has been manifested."
Having heard this, Samantaraśmi was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, saying to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
I now request permission to go to the Sahā world to behold, pay homage to, and make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha and the assembly of bodhisattvas; I only pray that you will grant me leave!"
At that time, the Buddha Ratnagotra said to Samantaprabha:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Go as you please.
He then took a thousand-stalked golden lotus flower, its thousand petals adorned with various jewels, and handed it to Samantaraśmi, instructing him:
"Take this flower to the presence of Śākyamuni Buddha and speak these words on my behalf:"
“Tathāgata Ratnagotra sends his greetings to you in measureless numbers:
Are you free from illness and affliction? Is your daily life light and easy? Are your physical strength and energy well-balanced? Do you dwell in peace and happiness?”
"Are the affairs of the world bearable?
Are sentient beings easy to deliver?
Take this lotus flower and entrust it to the World-Honored One as a Buddhist service."
"When you arrive in that realm, you should abide in right mindfulness; do not, out of pride, look upon that Buddha-field and its great assembly, lest you bring harm upon yourself. Why is this?"
"The majestic power of those bodhisattvas is difficult to equal; with compassion and vows permeating their hearts, they have been born in that land through great causes and conditions.

Bodhisattva Samantaprabha accepted the flowers and received the command, then, together with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of bodhisattvas, as well as countless hundreds of thousands of boys and girls, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and took their leave. Each carrying immeasurable, most excellent offerings, they set out and proceeded, and in every Buddha-world they passed through in the eastern direction, they made offerings, paid homage, showed respect, and offered praise to each Buddha, never passing by any without doing so.
Arriving at the place where the Buddha was, they prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, and then withdrew to stand to one side.
The Bodhisattva Samantaprabha came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
From here, extending eastward through worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, there is a final world named Prabhūtaratna; its Buddha is named Ratnagotra.

He sends his greetings to the World-Honored One, inquiring whether you have little illness and little affliction, whether your daily life is light and easy, whether your physical strength is harmonious and balanced, and whether you dwell in peace and happiness.
"Are the affairs of the world endurable?
Are sentient beings easy to deliver?
I hold these thousand-stalked golden lotuses to entrust to the World-Honored One as a Buddha-activity."
Then, Śākyamuni Buddha accepted these lotuses and scattered them throughout the worlds of the Buddhas in the eastern direction.

By the Buddha’s spiritual power, these lotuses pervaded all those Buddha-fields; within each flower calyx, there was a transformation Buddha sitting cross-legged, preaching the Great Prajñāpāramitā to the bodhisattvas. Any sentient beings who heard it would surely attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

At that time, when Samantaprabha and his retinue saw this event, they leaped for joy and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence. Each, according to their own roots of goodness and the extent of their offerings, made offerings, paid homage, showed respect, and praised the Buddha and the bodhisattvas; having done so, they withdrew and sat to one side.
It was likewise in all other realms of the eastern direction.

At that time, in the southern direction, there were worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River; the final world among them was named Free from All Sorrow, where the Buddha, named Virtue Free from Sorrow, was currently teaching the Great Prajñāpāramitā to a bodhisattva.

In that place there was a bodhisattva named Vigatāśoka. Seeing this great radiance, the trembling of the earth, and the marks of the Buddha’s body, he felt uncertainty in his mind and approached the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"For what cause and for what reason has this auspicious omen appeared?
At that time, the Buddha Aśoka-guṇa said to Vigataśoka:

"To the north of here, passing through as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, there is a final world named Sahā. Its Buddha is named Śākyamuni, who is about to preach the Great Prajñāpāramitā to the bodhisattvas; it is by the spiritual power of that Buddha that this auspicious omen has been manifested."
Having heard this, Vigatāśoka was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, saying to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
I now request to go to the Sahā world to behold, pay homage to, and make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha and the assembly of bodhisattvas; I only pray that you will grant me permission!”
At that time, the Buddha Aśokaguna said to Vigataśoka:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Go as you please.
He then took a thousand-stalked golden lotus, its thousand petals adorned with various jewels, and gave it to Vigataśoka, instructing him:
"Take these flowers to the presence of Śākyamuni Buddha and speak these words on my behalf:"
"Buddha Aśoka-guṇa sends his greetings to you in measureless number:
Are you free from illness and affliction? Is your daily life light and easy? Are your physical strength and energy well-balanced? Do you dwell in peace and happiness?"
"Are the affairs of the world endurable?
Are sentient beings easy to deliver?
I hold this lotus flower to entrust it to the World-Honored One as a Buddhist service."
"When you arrive in that realm, you should abide in right mindfulness; do not, out of pride, look upon that Buddha-field and the great assembly, lest you bring harm upon yourself. Why is this? "
"The majestic power of those bodhisattvas is difficult to equal; with compassion and vows perfuming their hearts, they have been born in that land for the sake of great causes and conditions.

Bodhisattva Vigataśoka accepted the flowers and received his instructions. Together with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of bodhisattvas, as well as countless hundreds of thousands of boys and girls, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and took his leave. Each carrying immeasurable, supreme, and wonderful offerings, he set out and traveled toward the south. In every buddha-field he passed through, he made offerings, paid homage, showed respect, and offered praise to each buddha, never passing by any without doing so.
Arriving at the Buddha’s dwelling, they prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, and then withdrew to stand to one side.
The Bodhisattva Vigataśoka came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

From here, proceeding southward through as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, there is a final world named Free from All Sorrow. The Buddha there is named Virtue of Freedom from Sorrow.

He sends his greetings to the World-Honored One, inquiring whether you have little illness and little affliction, whether your daily life is light and easy, whether your physical strength is harmonious and balanced, and whether you dwell in peace and happiness.
"Are the affairs of the world endurable?
Are sentient beings easy to deliver?
I hold these thousand-stalked golden lotuses to entrust to the World-Honored One as a Buddhist service."
Then, Śākyamuni Buddha accepted these lotuses and scattered them back toward the worlds of the Buddhas in the southern direction.

By the spiritual power of the Buddha, these lotuses pervaded all those Buddha-fields; within each flower calyx, there was a transformation Buddha sitting cross-legged, preaching the Great Prajñāpāramitā to the bodhisattvas. Any sentient beings who heard it would certainly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

At that time, having witnessed this event, Vītarāga and his retinue were filled with joy and leaped for gladness, exclaiming in wonder at such an unprecedented occurrence. Each, according to their own roots of goodness and the extent of their offerings, made offerings, paid homage, showed respect, and praised the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas; thereafter, they withdrew and sat to one side.
It was likewise in all other realms of the southern direction.

At that time, in the western direction, throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a final world named Upaśānta, where the Buddha was named Ratnajvāla; he was currently teaching the Great Prajñāpāramitā to a bodhisattva.

In that place there was a bodhisattva named Cāritramati. Seeing this great light, the trembling of the great earth, and the marks of the Buddha’s body, his mind was filled with uncertainty; he approached the Buddha and said:
“World-Honored One!
"For what cause and for what reason has this auspicious omen appeared?
At that time, the Buddha Ratnajvāla said to Cāritramati:

"From this eastern direction, passing through as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, there is a final world named Sahā. The Buddha there is named Śākyamuni; he is about to preach the Great Prajñāpāramitā to the bodhisattvas, and it is by the supernatural power of that Buddha that this auspicious omen has been manifested."
Having heard this, Gaṅgottarā rejoiced and leaped for joy, saying to the World-Honored One:
“World-Honored One!
I now request permission to go to the Sahā world to behold, pay homage to, and make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha and the assembly of bodhisattvas; I only pray that you will grant me leave!”
At that time, the Buddha Ratnārcis said to Cāritramati,
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Go as you wish.
He then took a thousand-stalked golden lotus flower, its petals numbering a thousand and adorned with various jewels, and bestowed it upon Cāritramati, instructing him:
"Take this flower to the presence of Śākyamuni Buddha and speak these words on my behalf:"
“Tathāgata Ratnārcis sends his greetings to you in immeasurable measure:
Are you free from illness and affliction? Is your daily life light and easy? Are your physical strength and vital energy harmonious? Do you dwell in peace and happiness?”
"Are the affairs of the world endurable?
Are sentient beings easy to deliver?
I hold this lotus flower to entrust it to the World-Honored One as a Buddhist service."
"When you arrive in that realm, you should abide in right mindfulness; do not, out of pride, look upon that Buddha-field and the great assembly, lest you bring harm upon yourself. Why is this? "
"The majestic power of those bodhisattvas is difficult to equal; with compassion and vows permeating their hearts, they have been born in that land for the sake of great causes and conditions.

Bodhisattva Cāritramati accepted the flowers and, in accordance with the command, set out together with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of bodhisattvas, as well as countless hundreds of thousands of boys and girls. At that time, in all the worlds above, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a final world named Joyful, where the Buddha was named Virtue of Joy; he was currently teaching the Great Prajñāpāramitā to the bodhisattvas.

In that realm there was a bodhisattva named Priyadatta. Seeing this great radiance, the trembling of the earth, and the marks of the Buddha’s body, he felt uncertainty in his mind and approached the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“For what cause and for what reason has this auspicious omen appeared?
At that time, the Buddha Priyaguna said to Priyadatta:

“From this lower direction, passing through worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is a final world named Sahā, where the Buddha is named Śākyamuni. He is about to preach the Great Prajñāpāramitā to the bodhisattvas; it is by the spiritual power of that Buddha that this auspicious omen has been manifested.”
Having heard this, Hṣi-shou (Pramudita-datta) was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, saying to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
I now request permission to go to the Sahā world to behold, pay homage to, and make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha and the assembly of bodhisattvas; I only pray that you will grant me leave!”
At that time, the Buddha Priyaguna said to Priyadatta:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Go as you please.
He then took a thousand-stalked golden lotus flower, its petals numbering a thousand and adorned with various jewels, and presented it to Nandadatta, instructing him:
"Take this flower to the presence of Śākyamuni Buddha and speak these words on my behalf:"
"May the Tathāgata Priyaguṇa inquire after you with boundless concern:
Are you free from illness and affliction? Is your daily life light and easy? Are your physical strength and vital energy harmonious? Do you dwell in peace and happiness?"
"Are the affairs of the world endurable?
Are sentient beings easy to deliver?
I hold this lotus flower to entrust it to the World-Honored One as a Buddhist service."
"When you arrive in that realm, you should abide in right mindfulness; do not, out of pride, look upon that Buddha-land and its great assembly and thereby bring harm upon yourself. Why is this?"
"The power and majesty of those bodhisattvas are difficult to equal; with compassion and vows perfuming their hearts, they have been born in that land due to great causal conditions.

Having received the flowers and accepted the command, the Bodhisattva Xishou, together with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of bodhisattvas, as well as countless hundreds of thousands of boys and girls, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and took their leave. Each carrying immeasurable, most excellent offerings, they set out and traveled through the various Buddha-worlds of the upper direction, making offerings, paying respect, honoring, and praising each Buddha without fail at every station.
Arriving at the Buddha’s dwelling, they prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, and then withdrew to stand to one side.
The Bodhisattva Xishou stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

From this point upward, through worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is a final world named *Ānanda* (Joy). There, a Buddha named *Priyaguṇa* (Virtue of Joy) inquires after the World-Honored One with boundless concern:
Are you free from illness and affliction? Is your daily life light and easy? Is your physical strength harmonious? Do you dwell in peace and happiness?
"Are the affairs of the world endurable?
Are sentient beings easy to deliver?
I hold these thousand-stalked golden lotuses to entrust to the World-Honored One as a Buddhist service."
Then, Śākyamuni Buddha accepted these lotuses and scattered them back toward the worlds of the Buddhas in the upper directions.

By the Buddha’s spiritual power, these lotuses pervaded all the Buddha-fields; within each flower calyx, there was a transformation Buddha sitting cross-legged, preaching the Great Prajñāpāramitā to the bodhisattvas, such that any sentient beings who heard it would surely attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

At that time, having witnessed this event, Nandadatta and his retinue were filled with joy and leaped for gladness, exclaiming in wonder at such an unprecedented occurrence. Each, according to their own roots of goodness and the extent of their offerings, made offerings, paid homage, showed respect, and praised the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas; having done so, they withdrew and sat to one side.
All other realms above were likewise so.

At that time, this Sahā world-system of three thousandfold worlds was filled with various jewels; exquisite fragrant flowers were strewn across its ground, and jeweled banners, pennants, and canopies were arrayed everywhere. Flower trees, fruit trees, incense trees, garland trees, clothing trees, jewel trees, and various ornamental trees surrounded it in magnificent adornment, making it exceedingly delightful—like the pure land of the Tathāgata Samantakusuma in the world-system Padmāvatī, or the original lands where the youth Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva Supratiṣṭhitamati, and other immeasurable Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas of great majestic power once dwelt.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 412. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Order.
Chapter Two: The Chapter on Joy (Prāmodya-varga), Part Two.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that all those in the various worlds who had a karmic connection with him had assembled—including devas, māras, brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, gandharvas, asuras, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, non-humans, and the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwelling in their final bodies who were destined for the rank of the Honored One—addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
“If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to attain complete awakening to all phenomena in all their aspects, they should train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).”

At that time, Śāriputra, filled with joy and elation, rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, bared his left shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully awaken to all phenomena in all their aspects train in the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha addressed the venerable Śāriputra, saying:

“All bodhisattva mahāsattvas should, by means of non-abiding as their skillful method, dwell in the perfection of wisdom, because neither that which is dwelt upon nor that which dwells can be apprehended.”
One should fulfill the perfection of generosity by means of non-renunciation, because the giver, the recipient, and the gift cannot be apprehended;
one should fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline by means of non-protection, because the characteristics of transgression and non-transgression cannot be apprehended;
one should fulfill the perfection of patience by means of non-appropriation, because the characteristics of agitation and non-agitation cannot be apprehended.
One should fulfill the perfection of diligence through the means of non-exertion, because physical and mental exertion and indolence are unapprehendable;
one should fulfill the perfection of meditative concentration through the means of non-conceptualization, because the presence or absence of relish is unapprehendable;
and one should fulfill the perfection of wisdom through the means of non-attachment, because the nature and characteristics of all phenomena are unapprehendable.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, bodhisattva mahāsattvas dwelling in the perfection of wisdom should, by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method, cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path, because these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are unapprehendable;

by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method, they should cultivate the concentration on emptiness, the concentration on signlessness, and the concentration on wishlessness, because these three samādhis are unapprehendable."

Taking non-apprehension as the means, one should cultivate the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments, because the dhyānas, immeasurables, and formless attainments are unapprehendable;

taking non-apprehension as the means, one should cultivate the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities, because the liberations, bases of mastery, meditative equipoises, and totalities are unapprehendable;

taking non-apprehension as the means, one should cultivate the nine perceptions—namely, the perception of bloatedness, the perception of festering, the perception of discolored, the perception of livid, the perception of being devoured, the perception of scattered, the perception of skeletons, the perception of burning, and the perception of dissolution—because such perceptions are unapprehendable.

Taking non-apprehension as the means, one should cultivate the ten recollections (*daśa-anusmṛti*): namely, recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dharma, recollection of the Saṃgha, recollection of ethical discipline (*śīla*), recollection of renunciation (*tyāga*), recollection of the devas, recollection of inhalation and exhalation, recollection of disenchantment, recollection of death, and recollection of the body; for these various recollections are unapprehendable. Taking non-apprehension as the means, one should cultivate the ten perceptions (*daśa-saṃjñā*):

namely, the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering, the perception of non-self, the perception of impurity, the perception of death, the perception that all worlds are not worth delighting in, the perception of revulsion toward food, the perception of abandonment, the perception of detachment, and the perception of cessation; for these various perceptions are likewise unapprehendable.

Taking non-apprehension as the means, one should cultivate the eleven knowledges: namely, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, the knowledge of cessation, the knowledge of the path, the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, the knowledge of phenomena, the subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, the knowledge of others' minds, and the knowledge of how things truly are; for such knowledges are unapprehendable.

Taking non-apprehension as the means, one should cultivate the concentration with directed thought and sustained evaluation, the concentration without directed thought and with only sustained evaluation, and the concentration without directed thought and without sustained evaluation;

for these three concentrations are unapprehendable. Taking non-apprehension as the means, one should cultivate the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known"; for these three untainted faculties are unapprehendable.
Taking non-apprehension as the skillful means, one should cultivate the contemplation of the impure,
the contemplation of the pervasive, the knowledge of all modes, śamatha, vipaśyanā, the four means of attraction, the four sublime abodes,
the three clarities, the five eyes, the six superknowledges, and the six perfections.
The seven noble riches, the eight awakenings of a great being, the knowledge of the nine abodes of sentient beings,
the doors of dhāraṇī, the doors of samādhi, the ten stages, the ten practices, the ten patiences, the twenty superior intentions,
the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
The common dharmas, the thirty-two marks of a great man, the eighty secondary signs, the quality of non-forgetfulness,
the state of constant equanimity, all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*),
the subtle knowledge of all aspects, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity, as well as other [qualities].
The immeasurable qualities of a Buddha are such that these various dharmas cannot be apprehended. "Furthermore, Śāriputra,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes, they should study the perfection of wisdom."

Those who wish to swiftly fulfill all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), should study the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Those who wish to swiftly fulfill the knowledge of the mental activities of all sentient beings and the subtle knowledge of all aspects, should study the perfection of wisdom.
Those who wish to uproot all afflictions and their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), should study the perfection of wisdom.
Those who wish to enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth should study the perfection of wisdom;
those who wish to transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas should study the perfection of wisdom;
those who wish to abide in the bodhisattva stage of non-retrogression should study the perfection of wisdom.
Those who wish to attain the six kinds of sublime supernormal powers should study the *prajñāpāramitā*;
those who wish to know the distinctions in the mental activities and inclinations of all sentient beings should study the *prajñāpāramitā*;
and those who wish to surpass the wisdom and functional capacities of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
If one wishes to attain all dharani-doors and samadhi-doors, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā;
if one wishes, with a single thought of sympathetic joy, to surpass all the generosity of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā;
if one wishes, with a single thought of sympathetic joy, to surpass all the pure ethical discipline of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If one wishes, with a single thought of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā-citta*), to surpass all the concentrations, wisdom, liberations, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.

If one wishes, with a single thought of sympathetic joy, to surpass all the dhyānas, liberations, meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), attainments (*samāpatti*), and other wholesome dharmas of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.

If one wishes, by means of the wholesome dharmas cultivated in a single thought, to surpass all the wholesome dharmas of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.

If one wishes to practice even a small portion of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; if one wishes to employ skillful means for the sake of all sentient beings and dedicate [these merits] toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, thereby attaining immeasurable and boundless merit—one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to cause the practices of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom to be free from all obstacles and swiftly reach fulfillment, they should study the perfection of wisdom.

If they wish to see the Buddhas in every birth, constantly hear the true Dharma, attain the awakening of a Buddha, and receive the Buddhas' mindfulness, instructions, and exhortations, they should study the perfection of wisdom."
If one wishes to attain the Buddha-body, fully endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man and adorned with the eighty secondary characteristics, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.

If one wishes to remember past lives in every birth, never forget the mind of great enlightenment (*mahābodhicitta*), distance oneself from evil friends and associate with virtuous friends, and constantly cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
If one wishes to possess great power in every birth, to crush the hosts of Māra and enemies, and to subdue all non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
If you wish to be born life after life far removed from all afflictions and karmic obstructions, and to penetrate all phenomena with a mind free of hindrance, you should study the Prajñāpāramitā;
if you wish to be born life after life with a continuous succession of virtuous minds, virtuous vows, and virtuous deeds, never faltering or ceasing, you should study the Prajñāpāramitā;

if you wish to be born into the family of the Buddhas, enter the stage of the youthful truth (kumārabhūmi), and never be separated from the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, you should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If one wishes to be born again and again endowed with all the marks and signs of physical excellence, as majestic and sublime as a Buddha, so that all sentient beings who see them rejoice, and if one wishes to give rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and swiftly accomplish the merits of the Buddha-ground, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.

If one wishes to use the power of various supreme and wholesome roots to draw forth, at will, the most excellent offerings to honor, revere, respect, and praise all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, thereby causing all wholesome roots to be swiftly perfected, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.

If one wishes to fulfill all the needs of sentient beings—providing them with food and drink, clothing, beds and couches, bedding, medicinal requisites for illness, various flowers and incense, lamps and lights, vehicles, gardens and groves, houses and dwellings, wealth and grain, precious jewels, ornaments, music, and other various kinds of excellent and sublime articles of pleasure—one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to skillfully establish all sentient beings throughout the entirety of the realm of space, the dharma-realm, and all worlds, causing them all to abide in the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, they should study the perfection of wisdom;

if they wish to cause the merit obtained from generating a single thought of goodness to remain inexhaustible until the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should study the perfection of wisdom."
If one wishes to be praised together by all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and Bodhisattvas throughout the worlds of the ten directions, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā;

if one wishes that upon a single arousal of the mind one may reach as many worlds in each of the ten directions as there are sands in the Ganges to make offerings to the Buddhas and bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā;

if one wishes that with a single utterance of sound one may pervade as many worlds in each of the ten directions as there are sands in the Ganges to praise the Buddhas and instruct sentient beings, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If one wishes, in a single moment of thought, to establish all sentient beings in as many Buddha-worlds of the ten directions as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, causing them all to practice and study the path of the ten wholesome actions, to receive the three refuges and uphold the prohibitive precepts, to cultivate the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments, and to obtain the five supernormal powers—one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.

If one wishes, in a single moment of thought, to establish all sentient beings in as many Buddha-worlds of the ten directions as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, causing them to abide in the Mahāyāna, to cultivate the bodhisattva practices, and not to disparage other vehicles—one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.

If one wishes to succeed to the lineage of the Buddhas so that it is never severed, to protect the family of bodhisattvas so they do not regress, and to adorn and purify Buddha-fields so they are swiftly accomplished—one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to dwell in internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, endless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, emptiness of self-characteristic, emptiness of common characteristic, emptiness of all phenomena, emptiness of the unapprehendable, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of intrinsic nature, and emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, they should train in the perfection of wisdom."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to dwell securely in the suchness of all phenomena, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-illusory nature, the unchanging nature, the state of equality, the nature of being free from birth, the fixedness of dharma, the stability of dharma, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm, they should study the perfection of wisdom.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to awaken to and know the exhaustiveness and suchness of all phenomena—without error and without conceptual differentiation—they should train in the perfection of wisdom.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to awaken to and know that the nature of all phenomena as causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*), objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is non-existent and unapprehendable, they should study the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to awaken to and know that all phenomena are like illusions, like dreams, like echoes, like reflections, like shadows, like mirages, like flowers in the sky, like cities of Gandharvas, and like magical transformations—all being manifestations of the mind alone, their nature and characteristics being entirely empty—they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to know the most minute particles of the great earth, space, mountains, great oceans, rivers, ponds, mountain torrents, valleys, marshes, lakes, and the elements of earth, water, fire, and wind throughout the trichiliocosm worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to split a single hair into a hundred parts and, taking one part of that hair, lift up all the waters within the great oceans, rivers, ponds, mountain torrents, and lakes of the trichiliocosm and cast them away into other boundless worlds, yet without harming the sentient beings therein, they should train in the *prajñāpāramitā*.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees the fire kalpa arise, burning throughout the trichiliocosm so that heaven and earth are ablaze, and wishes to blow it out all at once with a single breath, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees the onset of the wind kalpa, when the wind-circle upon which the trichiliocosm rests surges upward with violent force, threatening to blow away all things within the great trichiliocosm—including Mount Sumeru and the Cakravāḍa mountains—reducing them to fragments like chaff and husks, and if he wishes to obstruct that wind-force with a single finger so that it subsides and does not arise, he should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to fill the entirety of space while sitting in a single cross-legged posture within a trichiliocosm, they should study the perfection of wisdom.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to take all things within the Great Trichiliocosm—the King of Mountains Sumeru, the Cakravāḍa mountains, and so forth—with a single hair-noose and cast them beyond immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless worlds in other directions, without harming the sentient beings therein, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to fully satisfy all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their assemblies of disciples throughout as many worlds in each of the ten directions as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River—by offering a single meal, a single flower, a single incense, or a single banner and parasol—and wishes to honor, revere, respect, and praise them, they should train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to establish all sentient beings throughout each of the worlds of the ten directions—as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—in the aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; or wishes to establish them in the fruit of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship, or in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; or even wishes to lead them into the realm of nirvana without remainder, they should train in the perfection of wisdom.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are able to know, as it truly is, that such giving yields great fruit and retribution; that is to say, they know as it truly is that such giving leads to birth in a great kṣatriya clan, or birth in a great brāhmaṇa clan, or birth in a great householder clan, or birth in a great merchant clan;

and that such giving leads to birth among the gods of the Four Great Kings, or birth in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, or birth in the Yāma Heaven, or birth in the Tuṣita Heaven, or birth in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, or birth in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven."
By means of this generosity, one attains the first dhyāna, or the second dhyāna, or the third dhyāna, or the fourth dhyāna;

by means of this generosity, one attains the concentration of the sphere of infinite space, or the concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness, or the concentration of the sphere of nothingness, or the concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;

by means of this generosity, one gives rise to the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, and attains the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship, or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, or unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
To know these pure ethical disciplines, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom as they truly are, and thereby to attain their great fruits and rewards, is likewise so.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are able to know as it truly is that such skillful means in giving can fulfill the perfection of giving;
such skillful means in giving can fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline; such skillful means in giving...
Through skillful means in such giving, one is able to fulfill the perfection of patience; through skillful means in such giving, one is able to fulfill the perfection of diligence;
through skillful means in such giving, one is able to fulfill the perfection of meditative concentration;
and through skillful means in such giving, one is able to fulfill the perfection of wisdom.
In this way, pure ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom— through skillful means—
are all able to bring the six pāramitās to fulfillment.
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) know, as it truly is, such skillful means (upāyakauśalya) of giving that can fulfill the perfections from giving up to wisdom; and how does he know such skillful means of ethical discipline up to wisdom that can fulfill the perfections from ethical discipline up to meditative concentration (dhyāna-pāramitā)?”
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!

By taking non-apprehension as the skillful means, that is to say, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving, because they thoroughly understand that the characteristics of the giver, the recipient, and the gift given are all unapprehendable, they are able to fulfill the perfection of giving.”
Because the characteristics of transgression and non-transgression cannot be apprehended, one is able to fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*);
because the characteristics of movement and non-movement cannot be apprehended, one is able to fulfill the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*);
and because the characteristics of diligence and indolence of body and mind cannot be apprehended, one is able to fulfill the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
Because distraction and non-distraction cannot be apprehended, one is able to fulfill the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*);
because the nature and characteristics of all phenomena cannot be apprehended, one is able to fulfill the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing generosity, employs skillful means to fulfill the six perfections.

Likewise, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices ethical discipline, they employ skillful means to fulfill the six perfections; and so on, up until when they practice wisdom, they employ skillful means to fulfill the six perfections.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain the merits of all buddhas of the past, future, and present, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to reach the further shore of all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to penetrate the suchness (tathatā), the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), non-arising (anutpāda), and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) of all phenomena of the past, future, and present, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to exhaustively fathom the limits of birth and non-birth throughout the past, future, and present, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to be the leader of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to be the personal attendant of all Tathāgatas, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to become an inner retinue to all Tathāgatas, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to obtain a great retinue, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to have bodhisattvas as their constant retinue, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to digest all the offerings of donors, they should study the perfection of wisdom.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to subdue the mind of stinginess and greed, not give rise to the mind of violating the precepts, eliminate the mind of anger, cast aside the mind of laziness, quiet the mind of distraction, and distance themselves from the mind of wrong wisdom, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to establish all sentient beings in the meritorious action consisting of giving, the meritorious action consisting of ethical discipline, the meritorious action consisting of cultivation, the meritorious action consisting of service, and the meritorious action based on material things, they should study the perfection of wisdom.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain the five eyes—namely, the flesh eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the dharma eye, and the buddha eye—they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes, by means of the divine eye, to see all the Buddhas in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes, by means of the divine ear, to hear entirely all the essential teachings of the Dharma spoken by the Buddhas in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to know, as they truly are, the minds and mental factors of all Buddhas in each of the worlds of the ten directions—as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to hear universally the Dharma teachings of all Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions, continuing without interruption until reaching unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to see all the buddha-fields of the ten directions in the past, future, and present, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to receive, uphold, and master to the ultimate degree all the sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, gāthās, udānas, nidānas, itivṛttakas, jātakas, vaipulyas, adbhutadharmas, avadānas, and upadeśas spoken by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present throughout the ten directions—teachings that have never been heard before by the śrāvakas and others—they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to personally receive, uphold, and thoroughly master the Dharma-gates taught by all the Buddhas of the past, future, and present throughout the ten directions, and furthermore wishes to be able to explain them extensively and according to reality for others, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to practice, in accordance with reality, the dharma-gates taught by all the Buddhas of the past, future, and present throughout the ten directions, and furthermore wishes to encourage others to practice them in accordance with reality, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to provide illumination in the dark worlds of the ten directions—equal in number to the sands of the Ganges—or in the intervals between worlds where the sun and moon do not shine, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to transform and enlighten the sentient beings within immeasurable worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions—beings who have accomplished false views and have not heard the names of the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha—and desires to cause them to give rise to right view and hear the names of the Triple Gem, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes, by means of their own power, to cause the sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions to see if they are blind, hear if they are deaf, speak if they are mute, regain mindfulness if they are insane, attain concentration if they are distracted, obtain wealth if they are poor, obtain clothing if they are naked, obtain food if they are hungry, obtain drink if they are thirsty, be cured of illness if they are sick, become handsome and dignified if they are ugly, become physically complete if they are deformed, become fully endowed with faculties if they are deficient, and awaken from confusion if they are bewildered; and if they wish for all sentient beings to regard one another with equal minds—as father and mother, as elder and younger brother, as elder and younger sister, as friend and relative—they should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes, by means of their own power, to cause all sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions who are in the evil realms to be reborn in the happy realms, they should study the perfection of wisdom.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes, by means of their own power, to cause all sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions who have practiced unwholesome deeds to instead cultivate wholesome deeds, they should train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes, by means of their own power, to cause the sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions to all abide in the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*), those who have not attained meditative concentration to all abide in the aggregate of concentration (*samādhiskandha*), those with faulty wisdom to all abide in the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñāskandha*), those without liberation to all abide in the aggregate of liberation (*vimuktiskandha*), and those without the knowledge and vision of liberation to all abide in the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśanaskandha*); or if they wish for those who have not yet seen the truths to attain the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship; or if they wish for them to attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, or to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttarasamyaksambodhi*), they should train in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to train in the sublime deportment of all Buddhas—so that sentient beings never tire of beholding it, and so as to cause all evil to cease and all goodness to arise—they should train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they reflect thus:
'When shall I attain the majestic bearing and gaze of an elephant king while preaching the Dharma to the assembly?'"
"To accomplish this matter, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, they reflect thus:
'When shall I attain the complete purity of body, speech, and mental actions, such that they proceed in accordance with wisdom?'"
"To accomplish this matter, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, they reflect thus:
'When shall I attain the power to walk freely without my feet touching the ground, at a height of four finger-breadths?'"
"To accomplish this matter, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, they reflect thus:

'When shall I be attended by hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of gods from the Cāturmahārājika heaven up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven, who will make offerings, pay homage, respect, and praise me as they escort and surround me to the Bodhi tree?'"
"To accomplish this matter, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, they reflect thus:

'When shall I obtain immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of gods from the Cāturmahārājika Heaven up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, who will provide me with celestial robes as a seat beneath the Bodhi tree?'"
"To accomplish this matter, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, they reflect thus:

'When shall I sit cross-legged beneath the Bodhi tree and, with my hands adorned by all manner of wondrous marks, stroke the great earth, causing the Earth Goddess and her retinue to appear simultaneously?"
"To accomplish this matter, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, they reflect thus:
'When shall I sit beneath the Bodhi tree, subdue the hosts of Māras, and realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?'"
"To accomplish this matter, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he reflects thus:
'When shall I attain perfect enlightenment, such that wherever I walk, stand, sit, or lie down, every location shall become adamantine?'"
"To accomplish this matter, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, they reflect thus: 'When shall I renounce my kingdom and go forth into homelessness?

On that very day, may I attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; on that same day, may I turn the sublime wheel of Dharma; and on that very day, may I cause immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings to distance themselves from dust and leave behind defilement, giving rise to the pure Dharma-eye; furthermore, may I cause immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings to forever exhaust all outflows, attaining liberation through mind and wisdom; and likewise, may I cause immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings to attain non-retrogression in unexcelled bodhi?'"
"To accomplish this matter, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, they reflect thus:

'When shall I attain unsurpassed enlightenment, having immeasurable and innumerable śrāvakas and bodhisattvas as my assembly of disciples; and at the time of a single teaching of the Dharma, cause immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings to attain the fruit of arhatship without rising from their seats, and further cause immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings to attain non-retrogression from unsurpassed enlightenment without rising from their seats?'"
"To accomplish this matter, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*. When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, he reflects thus:

'When shall I attain an inexhaustible lifespan and boundless radiance, adorned with the marks and signs such that those who behold me never tire; such that even when walking, a thousand-petaled lotus supports each foot, causing a thousand-spoked wheel to appear upon the ground as I step and walk, yet without disturbing the sentient beings dwelling on the earth; such that when I wish to look back, my entire body turns along with me; and such that wherever my feet tread, reaching even to the limits of the vajra-ground, the earth itself revolves there like the circumference of a chariot wheel? "
"To accomplish this matter, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, they reflect thus:

'When shall I attain the state where all my limbs and joints emit radiance, illuminating the boundless worlds of the ten directions, and wherever that light reaches, bring great benefit to all sentient beings?'"
"To accomplish this matter, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, they reflect thus:

'When I attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, may there not be even the names of any greed, hatred, or delusion in the land where I dwell; may the sentient beings therein achieve sublime wisdom, and by the power of that wisdom, quickly think as follows:'"

Practicing generosity, self-discipline, patience, diligence, tranquility, and discernment; remaining free from negligence and cultivating the holy life; and maintaining loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity without harming sentient beings—how excellent this would be, just like other Buddha-fields!
"To fulfill this vow, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, they reflect thus:

'When I attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, once my work of transformation is finished and after I have entered parinirvāṇa, may the True Dharma never come to an end, and may it constantly bring great benefit and happiness to sentient beings.'"
"To fulfill this aspiration, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, they reflect thus:

'When I attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may all sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions who hear my name necessarily attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.'"
"To fulfill this aspiration, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Śāriputra, if bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to accomplish these immeasurable and boundless merits, they should study the *prajñāpāramitā*."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom and is able to accomplish such merits as these, at that time the Four Great Kings of the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system will all rejoice greatly and think:
'We should now offer four alms bowls to this bodhisattva, just as the heavenly kings of old offered bowls to the previous Buddhas.'"
At that time, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmitavaśavartin heavens within this trichiliocosm were all greatly rejoiced, and they all thought:
"We shall all serve and make offerings to such a bodhisattva, so that the wicked factions of the asuras may diminish and the retinues of the devas may increase."

At that time, the gods of the Brahma assembly, the Brahma ministers, the Brahma peers, the Great Brahmas, the Light-sphere gods, the Limited Light gods, the Infinite Light gods, the Utmost Purity of Light gods, the Pure gods, the Limited Purity gods, the Infinite Purity gods, the Universal Purity gods, the Vast gods, the Limited Vast gods, the Infinite Vast gods, the Vast Fruit gods, the Untroubled gods, the Heatless gods, the Well-Appearing gods, the Well-Seeing gods, and the Akaniṣṭha gods of the form realm, filled with joy and celebration, all thought:
"We should entreat such a bodhisattva to quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, and turn the sublime wheel of Dharma for the benefit and happiness of all."

“Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom and causes the six perfections to increase, all the sons and daughters of good family in that world will be filled with great joy and will all think:
‘We shall act as parents, brothers, wives, children, kinsmen, acquaintances, and friends to such a bodhisattva.’”
At that time, the gods from the Realm of the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven in the Form Realm were filled with joy and celebration, and they all thought:

"We shall employ every kind of skillful means to cause this bodhisattva to remain free from unchaste conduct, so that from his first resolution until his attainment of Buddhahood, he may constantly practice pure conduct."
Why is this? If even the arising of stained sensual desire in the Brahma-heaven can act as an obstacle, how much more so for attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment!
