All those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of wisdom should be honored, revered, respected, and praised by all the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras.”
At that time, the Buddha addressed the great disciples and the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, saying: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.
All those in the world—gods, humans, and asuras alike—should offer worship, reverence, respect, and praise to all bodhisattva mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of wisdom.

Why is this? It is because of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that humans and devas appear in the world; that is to say, great clans of kṣatriyas, great clans of brahmins, great clans of householders, great clans of laymen, universal monarchs (cakravartin kings), and the devas from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Control over Others' Emanations; from the Heaven of Brahmā’s Retinue up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven; and from the Heaven of Infinite Space up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception appear in the world.
It is because of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that there appear in the world the stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and all buddhas.

It is because of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that various means of livelihood and articles of enjoyment appear in the world; that is to say, food and drink, clothing, bedding, dwellings, lamps, and treasures such as mani-jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, jade, coral, gold, and silver appear in the world.
In brief, all the pleasures of humans, the pleasures of devas, and supramundane pleasures in the entire world do not exist without such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

Why is this? Because these Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having practiced giving themselves, teach others to give; having maintained ethical discipline themselves, they teach others to maintain it; having practiced patience themselves, they teach others to practice it; having exerted diligence themselves, they teach others to exert it; having cultivated meditative concentration themselves, they teach others to cultivate it; and having trained in wisdom themselves, they teach others to train in it. Therefore, by virtue of these Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, all sentient beings obtain such benefit and happiness.
Chapter Five: The Characteristics of the Tongue Faculty, Part Two. At that time, the World-Honored One manifested the characteristic of his tongue faculty, its extent equal to the trichiliocosm.

From this tongue-mark, there again issued forth countless rays of light of various colors, which illuminated throughout the worlds of the Buddhas in the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

At that time, within each of the Buddha-lands in the east, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there were immeasurable and innumerable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, seeing this great light, felt doubt in their hearts. Each of them went to the presence of the Buddha in their own realm, prostrated with reverence, and said:
"World-Honored One!..."
"By whose power and for what reason does this great light illuminate all these Buddha-fields?
At that time, each of those Buddhas replied individually:

"In this western direction there is a Buddha-field named Sahā. Its Buddha is called Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Worthy, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān. He is now proclaiming the Prajñāpāramitā to a multitude of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, manifesting the mark of his tongue-root, which is equal in measure to a trichiliocosm."

From that mark of the tongue, there further issued forth countless rays of light of various colors, which universally illumined the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The light now being seen is precisely what is manifested from the mark of that Buddha’s tongue.

At that time, in those various realms, immeasurable and innumerable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having heard this matter, were filled with joy and leaped for gladness, exclaiming in wonder at such an unprecedented event. Each addressed the Buddha, saying:

“We wish to go to the Sahā world to behold, pay homage to, and make offerings to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni, as well as the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and to hear the Prajñāpāramitā. We only pray that the World-Honored One will compassionately grant us permission!”
Then, each of those Buddhas replied, "Now is the very time; go according to your wish.

Having received this permission, the assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas prostrated at the feet of the Buddhas and circumambulated them seven times to the right. Carrying forth immeasurable jeweled banners, pennants, canopies, robes, necklaces, fragrant garlands, rare treasures, flowers of gold and silver, and playing various kinds of sublime music, they arrived at the presence of this Buddha in an instant. After making offerings, paying homage, showing respect, and praising the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas, they circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, prostrated at his two feet, and withdrew to sit at one side.

In each of the Buddha-fields of the Ganges-sand number of worlds in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below, there are likewise immeasurable and innumerable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, each one being just like this.
At that time, there were the gods of the Realm of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven,
the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the Brahmakāyika Heaven, the Brahmapurohita Heaven, the Mahābrahmā Heaven,
the Mahābrahmā Heaven, the Ābhāsvara Heaven, the Parīttābha Heaven, and the Apramāṇābha Heaven.
The gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven;
the Ābhāsvara Heaven, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, the Parīttaśubha Heaven, the Apramāṇaśubha Heaven, and the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven;

the Bṛhatphala Heaven, the Parīttaśubha Heaven, the Apramāṇaśubha Heaven, and the Bṛhatphala Heaven; the Avṛha Heaven, the Atapa Heaven, the Sudṛśa Heaven, the Sudarśana Heaven, and the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
Each held immeasurable varieties of incense garlands, namely: liquid incense, powdered incense, burning incense, tree incense, leaf incense, and various blended incenses;
pleasing flower garlands, garlands of living beings, garlands of nāga-money, and immeasurable kinds of diverse flower garlands; as well as holding immeasurable supreme and exquisite [garments].
Celestial flowers— *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, *puṇḍarīka*, *sugandhika*, *mahāsugandhika*,
and other immeasurable, exquisite celestial fragrant flowers— came to where the Buddha was;
having made offerings, paid homage, revered, and praised the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, they circumambulated them.
Having circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, they prostrated at his feet and withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, the various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had come from the ten directions, as well as the immeasurable devas of the desire and form realms, offered various jeweled banners, streamers, canopies, robes, necklaces, precious gems, fragrant flowers, and musical instruments. Through the Buddha’s spiritual power, these rose into the air and merged to form a tiered canopy and pavilion, equal in size to a trichiliocosm. At each of the four corners of the pavilion’s summit were jeweled banners; the canopy, the banners, and all the necklaces hung down, adorned with exquisite pennants, wonderful silks, and rare flower garlands, creating a magnificent array most delightful to behold.
At that time, hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of beings in the assembly all rose from their seats, joined their palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"In the future, we vow to become Buddhas, with the marks and signs, the majestic virtue,
the adornment of our lands, the assemblies of śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, humans, and devas, and the turning of the wheel of Dharma, all exactly like those of the World-Honored One now."

At that time, the World-Honored One, having known their mental aspirations, realized the patience of non-arising regarding all phenomena; thoroughly comprehending that all things are neither born nor extinguished, unconditioned and uncreated, he immediately smiled, and from his face issued forth rays of light of various colors.
Then, Ānanda rose from his seat, joined his palms in reverence, and said:
"World-Honored One,
for what cause and for what reason do you manifest this smile?"
"The Buddhas manifest a smile for no reason other than a specific cause and condition!
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"These hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of beings who have risen from their seats have already realized the patience of the non-arising of all phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), fully comprehending that all things are neither born nor extinguished, unconditioned and uncreated."

In the future, after diligently practicing the bodhisattva path for sixty-eight *koṭi* great kalpas, they shall all attain buddhahood during the Kalpa of the Lotus of the Sublime Dharma (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-kalpa*), each bearing the same name: Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Worthy One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān—namely, the Tathāgata Bodhyaṅgapuṣpa.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 405; The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 406.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Six: Subhūti, Part One of the Second Section.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Subhūti:

"By means of your eloquence, you should proclaim for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas the Dharma associated with the *prajñāpāramitā*, instructing and training those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas so that they may all achieve accomplishment in the *prajñāpāramitā*."
At that time, the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the great śrāvakas, the devas, humans, and others all had this thought:

"Will the Venerable Subhūti, by means of his own eloquence, proclaim for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas the Dharma associated with the *prajñāpāramitā*, instructing and teaching the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas so that they may all achieve accomplishment in the *prajñāpāramitā*?"
"Is this because we rely upon the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power?
The Venerable Subhūti, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the great śrāvakas, the devas, humans, and others, addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"Whatever is spoken by the disciples of the Buddhas, all of it relies upon the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power."
Why is this? Śāriputra!

When the Tathāgata proclaims the essential Dharma for others, it never contradicts the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*). The disciples of the Buddhas, relying on the Dharma thus taught, practice with diligence and realize the true nature of phenomena. Because of this, whatever he proclaims for others is never inconsistent with the nature of phenomena; therefore, the words of the Buddha are like a lamp that transmits its light.

Śāriputra! Relying upon the majestic spiritual power and empowerment of the Buddha, I shall proclaim for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas the Dharma associated with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), instructing and exhorting these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas so that they may all achieve accomplishment in the perfection of wisdom; it is not by my own independent eloquence that I am able to perform this task.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is not the domain of any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding the bodhisattva mahāsattvas spoken of by the Buddha, what dharma herein is designated as a ‘bodhisattva mahāsattva’?”
"Bhagavān! I do not see a single dharma that can be called 'bodhisattva-mahāsattva,' nor do I see a single dharma that can be called 'prajñāpāramitā'; thus, I do not even see these two names."

How may I proclaim for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas the Dharma associated with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), instructing and advising the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas so that they may all achieve accomplishment in the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva exists as a mere name; the perfection of wisdom exists as a mere name; and these two names likewise exist as mere names.”

"Subhūti! These three names are neither produced nor extinguished; they are merely provisional designations. They do not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between the two, for they cannot be apprehended."

“Subhūti, you should know that just as the ‘self’ in the world exists only as a mere designation, so too this name ‘designation’ is neither born nor extinguished; it is merely a conventional designation that we call ‘self.’”

In this way, sentient beings, life-principles, those who are born, those who nourish, persons, individuals, mind-born ones, young scholars, agents, experiencers, knowers, and seers are also merely conventional designations. Thus, these names as designations are neither produced nor extinguished; it is only through conventional designation that they are called "sentient beings" up to "seers."
All these are merely conventional designations; these conventional designations do not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between the two, for they cannot be apprehended.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

Whether it be a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), or these two names—all are merely conventional dharmas. Such conventional dharmas are neither born nor extinguished; they are merely provisional designations. They do not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between the two, because they are unapprehendable.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! Just as internal forms are merely conventional dharmas, so too these conventional dharmas are neither produced nor extinguished; it is merely through conventional designation that they are called 'form.

Likewise, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also merely conventional dharmas; such conventional dharmas are neither produced nor extinguished, and it is merely through conventional designation that they are called 'feeling,' 'perception,' 'mental formations,' and 'consciousness.'"

All these are merely conventional designations; these conventional designations do not exist internally, nor do they exist externally, nor do they exist in between the two, because they cannot be apprehended.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

Whether it be a bodhisattva mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), or these two names—these are all conventional dharmas (*prajñapti-dharma*). Such conventional dharmas are neither born nor extinguished; they are merely provisional designations. They do not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between the two, for they are ungraspable.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! For example, the sense base of the eye is merely a conventional dharma; likewise, this conventional dharma is neither born nor extinguished, yet it is conventionally designated as the 'sense base of the eye.

In the same way, the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are also merely conventional dharmas; likewise, these conventional dharmas are neither born nor extinguished, yet they are conventionally designated as the 'sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.'"
All these are merely conventional designations; these conventional designations do not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between the two, because they are unapprehendable.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

Whether it be a bodhisattva mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), or the names of these two—all are merely conventional dharmas (*prajñapti-dharma*). Such conventional dharmas are neither born nor extinguished; they are merely provisional designations. They do not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between the two, because they are ungraspable.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! For example, the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) is merely a conventional phenomenon (*prajñaptidharma*); likewise, this conventional phenomenon is neither born nor extinguished, and it is only through conventional designation that it is called the 'sense-base of form.

In the same way, the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) are also merely conventional phenomena; likewise, these conventional phenomena are neither born nor extinguished, and it is only through conventional designation that they are called the 'sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental objects.'"
All these are merely conventional designations; these conventional designations do not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between the two, because they are unapprehendable.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

Whether it be a bodhisattva mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), or the names of these two—all are merely conventional dharmas (*prajñapti-dharma*). Such conventional dharmas are neither born nor extinguished; they are merely provisional designations. They do not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between the two, because they are ungraspable.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! For example, the eye constituent (*cakṣurdhātu*), the form constituent (*rūpadhātu*), and the eye-consciousness constituent (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) are merely conventional phenomena (*prajñaptidharma*). Such conventional phenomena are neither born nor extinguished; they are merely designated by convention as the 'eye constituent,' 'form constituent,' and 'eye-consciousness constituent.

Likewise, the ear constituent, sound constituent, and ear-consciousness constituent; the nose constituent, odor constituent, and nose-consciousness constituent; the tongue constituent, taste constituent, and tongue-consciousness constituent; the body constituent, tangibility constituent, and body-consciousness constituent; and the mind constituent, mental-object constituent, and mind-consciousness constituent—all these are also merely conventional phenomena. Such conventional phenomena are neither born nor extinguished; they are merely designated by convention as the 'ear constituent,' 'sound constituent,' and 'ear-consciousness constituent,' up to and including the 'mind constituent,' 'mental-object constituent,' and 'mind-consciousness constituent.'"
All these are merely provisional designations; these provisional designations do not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between the two, because they cannot be apprehended.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

Whether it be a bodhisattva mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), or these two names—these are all conventional dharmas (*prajñapti-dharma*). Such conventional dharmas are neither born nor extinguished; they are merely provisional designations. They do not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between the two, for they are ungraspable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

For example, all that exists within the body—the head, neck, shoulders, upper arms, hands, forearms, abdomen, back, chest, ribs, waist, spine, thighs, knees, calves, shins, and feet—consists merely of skin, flesh, bone, and marrow, which have only a provisional name. Thus, these names are merely provisional and are neither born nor extinguished; it is only through provisional designation that we speak of 'internal body' or objects such as the head and neck."
All these are merely conventional designations; these conventional designations do not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between the two, because they are unapprehendable.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

Whether it be a bodhisattva mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), or these two names—these are all conventional dharmas (*prajñapti-dharma*). Such conventional dharmas are neither born nor extinguished; they are merely provisional designations. They do not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between the two, for they are ungraspable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

For example, all external things—such as grasses, trees, roots, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits—exist only as provisional designations (*prajñapti*). Thus, these names as designations are neither born nor extinguished; it is merely through provisional designation that they are called 'external things,' such as grasses, trees, roots, and so forth."
All these are merely provisional designations; these provisional designations do not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between the two, because they cannot be apprehended.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

Whether it be the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), or these two names—these are all dharmas that are merely provisional. Such provisional dharmas are neither born nor extinguished; they are merely conventional designations. They do not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between the two, because they are unobtainable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

For example, just as the past and future Buddhas exist only as mere designations, so too these names as designations are neither produced nor extinguished; it is merely through conventional designation that they are called 'past and future Buddhas.'"
All these are merely conventional designations; these conventional designations do not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between the two, because they are unapprehendable.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

Whether it be a bodhisattva mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), or these two names—all are conventional phenomena (prajñapti-dharma). Such conventional phenomena are neither born nor extinguished; they are merely provisional designations. They do not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between the two, for they cannot be apprehended.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

For example, just as dream-objects, echoes, reflections, illusions, mirages, the moon in water, and transformations exist only as provisional designations, so too these names are merely provisional and neither arise nor cease; it is only through provisional designation that they are called 'dream-objects' up to 'transformations.'"
All these are merely provisional designations; these provisional designations do not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between the two, because they cannot be apprehended.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

Whether it be a bodhisattva mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), or these two names—all are merely conventional dharmas. Such conventional dharmas are neither born nor extinguished; they are merely provisional designations. They do not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between the two, for they cannot be apprehended.

"In this way, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should correctly train themselves in the conventional designation of names, the conventional designation of phenomena, and the conventional designation of skillful means regarding all dharmas."
Why is that? Subhūti!

When practicing the perfection of wisdom, bodhisattva mahāsattvas should not regard the designation of form as either permanent or impermanent; they should not regard the designations of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either permanent or impermanent.
One should not contemplate form as being either pleasant or painful; one should not contemplate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as being either pleasant or painful.
One should not contemplate form as being either self or non-self; one should not contemplate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as being either self or non-self.
One should not contemplate form as being either pure or impure; one should not contemplate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as being either pure or impure.

One should not contemplate the designation of form as either empty or non-empty; one should not contemplate the designations of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either empty or non-empty.

One should not contemplate the designation of form as either with signs or signless; one should not contemplate the designations of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either with signs or signless.

One should not contemplate the designation of form as either with aspiration or without aspiration; one should not contemplate the designations of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either with aspiration or without aspiration.

One should not contemplate whether the designation "form" is tranquil or not tranquil; one should not contemplate whether the designations "feeling," "perception," "volitional formations," or "consciousness" are tranquil or not tranquil.

One should not contemplate whether the designation "form" is detached or not detached; one should not contemplate whether the designations "feeling," "perception," "volitional formations," or "consciousness" are detached or not detached.

One should not contemplate whether the designation "form" is defiled or purified; one should not contemplate whether the designations "feeling," "perception," "volitional formations," or "consciousness" are defiled or purified.
One should not contemplate the designation of form as arising or ceasing; one should not contemplate the designations of feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness as arising or ceasing.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When practicing the perfection of wisdom, bodhisattva mahāsattvas should not contemplate the eye-base as either permanent or impermanent; they should not contemplate the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-base as either permanent or impermanent.
They should not contemplate the eye-base as either pleasant or painful; they should not contemplate the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-base as either pleasant or painful.
They should not contemplate the eye-base as either self or non-self; they should not contemplate the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-base as either self or non-self.
One should not contemplate the eye-base as either pure or impure; one should not contemplate the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-base as either pure or impure.
One should not contemplate the eye-base as either empty or non-empty; one should not contemplate the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-base as either empty or non-empty.
One should not contemplate the eye-base as either having marks or being markless; one should not contemplate the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-base as either having marks or being markless.

One should not contemplate the designation of the eye-base as being either with aspiration or without aspiration; one should not contemplate the designations of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-bases as being either with aspiration or without aspiration.

One should not contemplate the designation of the eye-base as being either tranquil or untranquil; one should not contemplate the designations of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-bases as being either tranquil or untranquil.

One should not contemplate the designation of the eye-base as being either secluded or unsecluded; one should not contemplate the designations of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-bases as being either secluded or unsecluded.

One should not contemplate the designation of the eye-base as either defiled or pure; one should not contemplate the designations of the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-base as either defiled or pure.

One should not contemplate the designation of the eye-base as either arising or ceasing; one should not contemplate the designations of the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-base as either arising or ceasing.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When practicing the perfection of wisdom, bodhisattva mahāsattvas should not regard the designation of the sense-base of form as either permanent or impermanent; they should not regard the designations of the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena as either permanent or impermanent.

They should not regard the designation of the sense-base of form as either pleasant or painful; they should not regard the designations of the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena as either pleasant or painful."

One should not contemplate the sphere of form as being either "self" or "non-self"; one should not contemplate the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena as being either "self" or "non-self.

One should not contemplate the sphere of form as being either "pure" or "impure"; one should not contemplate the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena as being either "pure" or "impure.

One should not contemplate the sphere of form as being either "empty" or "not empty"; one should not contemplate the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena as being either "empty" or "not empty."

One should not contemplate the designation of the sphere of visible forms as being with signs or signless; one should not contemplate the designations of the spheres of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as being with signs or signless.

One should not contemplate the designation of the sphere of visible forms as being with aspiration or without aspiration; one should not contemplate the designations of the spheres of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as being with aspiration or without aspiration.

One should not contemplate the designation of the sphere of visible forms as being tranquil or untranquil; one should not contemplate the designations of the spheres of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as being tranquil or untranquil.

One should not contemplate the designation of the sphere of form as being either secluded or not secluded; one should not contemplate the designations of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena as being either secluded or not secluded.

One should not contemplate the designation of the sphere of form as being either defiled or pure; one should not contemplate the designations of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena as being either defiled or pure.

One should not contemplate the designation of the sphere of form as being either arising or ceasing; one should not contemplate the designations of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena as being either arising or ceasing.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When practicing the perfection of wisdom, bodhisattva mahāsattvas should not regard the eye constituent as either permanent or impermanent; they should not regard the form constituent, the eye-consciousness constituent, eye-contact, or the various feelings produced with eye-contact as conditions as either permanent or impermanent.

They should not regard the eye constituent as either pleasant or painful; they should not regard the form constituent, up to and including the various feelings produced with eye-contact as conditions, as either pleasant or painful."

One should not contemplate the eye-element as being either self or non-self; one should not contemplate the form-element, up to and including those sensations produced with eye-contact as condition, as being either self or non-self.

One should not contemplate the eye-element as being either pure or impure; one should not contemplate the form-element, up to and including those sensations produced with eye-contact as condition, as being either pure or impure.

One should not contemplate the eye-element as being either empty or non-empty; one should not contemplate the form-element, up to and including those sensations produced with eye-contact as condition, as being either empty or non-empty.

One should not contemplate the designation of the eye-element as having marks or being markless; one should not contemplate the designations of the form-element, up to and including those sensations produced with eye-contact as condition, as having marks or being markless.

One should not contemplate the designation of the eye-element as having aspirations or being aspirationless; one should not contemplate the designations of the form-element, up to and including those sensations produced with eye-contact as condition, as having aspirations or being aspirationless.

One should not contemplate the designation of the eye-element as being tranquil or untranquil; one should not contemplate the designations of the form-element, up to and including those sensations produced with eye-contact as condition, as being tranquil or untranquil.

One should not observe the name of the eye-element as being either detached or non-detached; one should not observe the names of the form-element, up to and including those feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, as being either detached or non-detached.

One should not observe the name of the eye-element as being either defiled or pure; one should not observe the names of the form-element, up to and including those feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, as being either defiled or pure.

One should not observe the name of the eye-element as being either arising or ceasing; one should not observe the names of the form-element, up to and including those feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, as being either arising or ceasing.

"One should not contemplate the ear element as either permanent or impermanent; one should not contemplate the sound element, the ear-consciousness element, ear-contact, or the various feelings produced with ear-contact as condition as either permanent or impermanent.

One should not contemplate the ear element as either pleasant or painful; one should not contemplate the sound element, up to and including the various feelings produced with ear-contact as condition, as either pleasant or painful.

One should not contemplate the ear element as either self or non-self; one should not contemplate the sound element, up to and including the various feelings produced with ear-contact as condition, as either self or non-self."

One should not contemplate the ear-element as pure or impure; one should not contemplate the sound-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition, as pure or impure.

One should not contemplate the ear-element as empty or non-empty; one should not contemplate the sound-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition, as empty or non-empty.

One should not contemplate the ear-element as having marks or being markless; one should not contemplate the sound-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition, as having marks or being markless.

One should not contemplate the ear-element as being either with aspiration or without aspiration; one should not contemplate the sound-element, up to and including those sensations produced with the ear-contact as condition, as being either with aspiration or without aspiration.

One should not contemplate the ear-element as being either tranquil or untranquil; one should not contemplate the sound-element, up to and including those sensations produced with the ear-contact as condition, as being either tranquil or untranquil.

One should not contemplate the ear-element as being either detached or undetached; one should not contemplate the sound-element, up to and including those sensations produced with the ear-contact as condition, as being either detached or undetached.

One should not contemplate the ear element as being either defiled or pure; one should not contemplate the sound element, up to and including the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition, as being either defiled or pure.

One should not contemplate the ear element as being either arising or ceasing; one should not contemplate the sound element, up to and including the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition, as being either arising or ceasing.

"One should not contemplate the nose element as either permanent or impermanent; one should not contemplate the odor element, the nose-consciousness element, nose-contact, or the various feelings arising with nose-contact as condition as either permanent or impermanent.

One should not contemplate the nose element as either pleasant or painful; one should not contemplate the odor element, up to and including the various feelings arising with nose-contact as condition, as either pleasant or painful.

One should not contemplate the nose element as either self or non-self; one should not contemplate the odor element, up to and including the various feelings arising with nose-contact as condition, as either self or non-self."

One should not contemplate the nose element as pure or impure; one should not contemplate the fragrance element, up to and including the various feelings produced with nose-contact as condition, as pure or impure.

One should not contemplate the nose element as empty or non-empty; one should not contemplate the fragrance element, up to and including the various feelings produced with nose-contact as condition, as empty or non-empty.

One should not contemplate the nose element as having marks or being markless; one should not contemplate the fragrance element, up to and including the various feelings produced with nose-contact as condition, as having marks or being markless.

One should not contemplate the nose element as being with aspiration or without aspiration; one should not contemplate the odor element, up to and including those feelings produced with nose-contact as condition, as being with aspiration or without aspiration.

One should not contemplate the nose element as being peaceful or not peaceful; one should not contemplate the odor element, up to and including those feelings produced with nose-contact as condition, as being peaceful or not peaceful.

One should not contemplate the nose element as being detached or not detached; one should not contemplate the odor element, up to and including those feelings produced with nose-contact as condition, as being detached or not detached.

One should not contemplate the nose element as being either defiled or pure; one should not contemplate the odor element, up to and including the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, as being either defiled or pure.

One should not contemplate the nose element as being either arising or ceasing; one should not contemplate the odor element, up to and including the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, as being either arising or ceasing.

"One should not contemplate the tongue element as either permanent or impermanent; one should not contemplate the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, tongue-contact, or the various feelings arising with tongue-contact as condition as either permanent or impermanent.

One should not contemplate the tongue element as either pleasant or painful; one should not contemplate the taste element, up to and including the various feelings arising with tongue-contact as condition, as either pleasant or painful.

One should not contemplate the tongue element as either self or non-self; one should not contemplate the taste element, up to and including the various feelings arising with tongue-contact as condition, as either self or non-self."

One should not contemplate the tongue element as pure or impure; one should not contemplate the taste element, up to and including the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, as pure or impure.

One should not contemplate the tongue element as empty or non-empty; one should not contemplate the taste element, up to and including the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, as empty or non-empty.

One should not contemplate the tongue element as having marks or being markless; one should not contemplate the taste element, up to and including the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, as having marks or being markless.

One should not regard the tongue element as being either with aspiration or without aspiration; one should not regard the taste element, up to and including the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, as being either with aspiration or without aspiration.

One should not regard the tongue element as being either tranquil or untranquil; one should not regard the taste element, up to and including the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, as being either tranquil or untranquil.

One should not regard the tongue element as being either detached or undetached; one should not regard the taste element, up to and including the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, as being either detached or undetached.

One should not contemplate the tongue element as being either defiled or pure; one should not contemplate the taste element, up to and including the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as condition, as being either defiled or pure.

One should not contemplate the tongue element as being subject to arising or ceasing; one should not contemplate the taste element, up to and including the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as condition, as being subject to arising or ceasing.

"One should not contemplate the body element as either permanent or impermanent; one should not contemplate the tangible object element, the body-consciousness element, body-contact, or the various feelings arising with body-contact as condition as either permanent or impermanent.

One should not contemplate the body element as either pleasant or painful; one should not contemplate the tangible object element, up to and including the various feelings arising with body-contact as condition, as either pleasant or painful.

One should not contemplate the body element as either self or non-self; one should not contemplate the tangible object element, up to and including the various feelings arising with body-contact as condition, as either self or non-self."

One should not contemplate the body element as pure or impure; one should not contemplate the tangible element, up to and including the various feelings produced with body-contact as condition, as pure or impure.

One should not contemplate the body element as empty or non-empty; one should not contemplate the tangible element, up to and including the various feelings produced with body-contact as condition, as empty or non-empty.

One should not contemplate the body element as having signs or being signless; one should not contemplate the tangible element, up to and including the various feelings produced with body-contact as condition, as having signs or being signless.

One should not contemplate the body element as being either with aspiration or without aspiration; one should not contemplate the tangible element, up to and including the various feelings produced with body-contact as condition, as being either with aspiration or without aspiration.

One should not contemplate the body element as being either tranquil or untranquil; one should not contemplate the tangible element, up to and including the various feelings produced with body-contact as condition, as being either tranquil or untranquil.

One should not contemplate the body element as being either detached or undetached; one should not contemplate the tangible element, up to and including the various feelings produced with body-contact as condition, as being either detached or undetached.

One should not contemplate the body element as being either defiled or pure; one should not contemplate the tangible element, up to and including the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition, as being either defiled or pure.

One should not contemplate the body element as being either arising or ceasing; one should not contemplate the tangible element, up to and including the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition, as being either arising or ceasing.

"One should not contemplate the mind-element (*manodhātu*) as either permanent or impermanent; one should not contemplate the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*), mental contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*), or the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with mental contact as their condition as either permanent or impermanent.

One should not contemplate the mind-element as either pleasant or painful; one should not contemplate the dharma-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with mental contact as their condition, as either pleasant or painful.

One should not contemplate the mind-element as either self or non-self; one should not contemplate the dharma-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with mental contact as their condition, as either self or non-self."

One should not contemplate the mind-element (*manodhātu*) as pure or impure; one should not contemplate the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), up to and including the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition, as pure or impure.

One should not contemplate the mind-element as empty or non-empty; one should not contemplate the dharma-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition, as empty or non-empty.

One should not contemplate the mind-element as having marks or being markless; one should not contemplate the dharma-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition, as having marks or being markless.

One should not contemplate the mental faculty (*manodhātu*) as being either with aspiration or without aspiration; one should not contemplate the phenomena (*dharmadhātu*)—up to and including the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with the mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśa*) as condition—as being either with aspiration or without aspiration.

One should not contemplate the mental faculty as being either tranquil or untranquil; one should not contemplate the phenomena—up to and including the various feelings produced with the mental contact as condition—as being either tranquil or untranquil.

One should not contemplate the mental faculty as being either detached or undetached; one should not contemplate the phenomena—up to and including the various feelings produced with the mental contact as condition—as being either detached or undetached.

One should not contemplate the mental faculty (*manodhātu*) as being either defiled or pure; one should not contemplate the phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) up to the feelings produced with mental contact as a condition as being either defiled or pure.

One should not contemplate the mental faculty as being either arising or ceasing; one should not contemplate the phenomena up to the feelings produced with mental contact as a condition as being either arising or ceasing.
"Why is this so? Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, whether it be the bodhisattva mahāsattva, the name 'bodhisattva mahāsattva,' the perfection of wisdom, or the name 'perfection of wisdom,' none of these are seen to exist within the realm of the conditioned (saṃskṛtadhātu), nor are they seen to exist within the realm of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛtadhātu)."
Why is this? Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not form conceptual distinctions regarding any phenomena, nor do they form any differentiated conceptualizations.

“Subhūti! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, abiding in the non-conceptuality of all phenomena, he does not perceive a bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor does he perceive the name ‘bodhisattva mahāsattva’; he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive the name ‘perfection of wisdom.’”

“Subhūti! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he is able to practice the perfection of generosity, and is also able to practice the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom;

he is able to abide in internal emptiness, and is also able to abide in external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, endless emptiness, dispersion emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.”

They are able to abide in suchness, and they are also able to abide in the dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, non-illusory nature, unchanging nature, equality, the nature of freedom from birth, the fixed nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of empty space, and the inconceivable realm;

they are able to cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness, and they are also able to cultivate the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;
they are able to abide in the noble truth of suffering, and they are also able to abide in the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path.
They are able to cultivate the four dhyānas, and are also able to cultivate the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments;
they are able to cultivate the eight liberations, and are also able to cultivate the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities;
they are able to cultivate the gate of liberation of emptiness, and are also able to cultivate the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.
They are able to cultivate all doors of dhāraṇī, and also able to cultivate all doors of samādhi;
they are able to cultivate the five eyes, and also able to cultivate the six supernormal powers;

they are able to cultivate the ten powers of a Buddha, and also able to cultivate the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

"At that time, this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive a bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor does he perceive the name 'bodhisattva mahāsattva'; he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), nor does he perceive the name 'perfection of wisdom'."
Why is this? Subhūti!

It is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, has thoroughly realized the true reality of all phenomena, having thoroughly realized that within them there are neither defiled phenomena nor purified phenomena.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they realize that all phenomena are merely provisional designations of names and provisional designations of dharmas.
“Subhūti! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva has awakened to names and dharmas as they truly are, he does not cling to form; he does not cling to feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness;
he does not cling to the eye base, nor does he cling to the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind bases.”
They do not cling to the sphere of forms, nor do they cling to the spheres of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena;

they do not cling to the eye element, the form element, the eye-consciousness element, and eye-contact, nor to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition; and so on, up to not clinging to the mind element, the mental-phenomena element, the mind-consciousness element, and mind-contact, nor to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition;
they do not cling to the conditioned realm, nor do they cling to the unconditioned realm.
One does not cling to the perfection of generosity; one does not cling to the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom.

One does not cling to the primary and secondary marks of a Buddha; one does not cling to the body of a bodhisattva; one does not cling to anything from the fleshly eye up to the Buddha-eye. One does not cling to the perfection of knowledge or the perfection of supernormal powers. One does not cling to anything from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature. One does not cling to the maturation of sentient beings; one does not cling to the purification of buddha-fields; one does not cling to skillful means.
Why is this? Subhūti! Because all phenomena are non-existent;
for the one who clings, the object of clinging, the locus of clinging, and the time of clinging are all unapprehendable.

"So it is, Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom without attachment to any phenomena, they augment the perfection of generosity, and they augment the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom. They enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth, they enter the bodhisattva’s stage of non-retrogression, and they perfect the bodhisattva’s sublime supernormal powers."

Having thus attained the perfection of these sublime supernormal powers, the bodhisattva proceeds from one buddha-field to another in order to bring sentient beings to maturity, to purify his own buddha-field, and to behold the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; and having beheld them, he makes offerings, pays homage, respects, and praises them, so that all his roots of virtue may grow and flourish.
Once these roots of goodness have grown, they will be able to hear and receive all the true Dharma of the Buddhas according to their inclinations.
Having heard and received it, they shall not forget or lose it until they attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, and they will achieve mastery over all doors of dhāraṇī and samādhi.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they realize and know, as they truly are, that both the designation of persons and the designation of phenomena are without any basis for attachment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Regarding what is called a 'bodhisattva mahāsattva,' what do you think?
Is form itself the bodhisattva mahāsattva?"
"No, World-Honored One! Is it that very feeling,
perception, mental formations, and consciousness which is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?"
"No, World-Honored One! Is there a bodhisattva-mahāsattva apart from form?"
“No, World-Honored One!
Is there a bodhisattva mahāsattva apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?”
“No, World-Honored One! Is the eye-base itself the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?”
“No, World-Honored One! Are the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?”
"No, World-Honored One! Is there a bodhisattva-mahāsattva apart from the sense-base of the eye?"
"No, World-Honored One!
Is there a bodhisattva mahāsattva apart from the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind?"
"No, World-Honored One! Is the sense-base of form itself the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?"
"No, World-Honored One!
Are the sense bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena the bodhisattva mahāsattva?"
“No, World-Honored One! Is there a bodhisattva mahāsattva apart from the sphere of form?”
"No, World-Honored One!
Is there a bodhisattva mahāsattva apart from the spheres of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena?"
"No, World-Honored One! Is the eye-element itself the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?"
"No, World-Honored One! Is the form element,
the eye-consciousness element, and eye-contact, as well as the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?"
"No, World-Honored One! Is there a bodhisattva mahāsattva apart from the eye-element?"
“No, World-Honored One!
Is there a bodhisattva mahāsattva apart from the realm of form, the realm of eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition?”
"No, World-Honored One! Is the ear-element itself the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?"
“No, World-Honored One! Are the sound element,
the ear-consciousness element, and ear-contact, as well as all feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?”
"No, World-Honored One! Is there a bodhisattva mahāsattva apart from the ear-element?"
"No, World-Honored One!
Is there a bodhisattva mahāsattva apart from the sphere of sound, the sphere of ear-consciousness, ear-contact, and the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition?"
"No, World-Honored One! Is the nose-element itself the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?"
“No, World-Honored One! Are the fragrance element,
the nose-consciousness element, nose-contact, and all feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?”
"No, World-Honored One! Is there a bodhisattva mahāsattva apart from the nose-element?"
"No, World-Honored One!
Is there a bodhisattva mahāsattva apart from the fragrance element, the nose-consciousness element, nose-contact, and the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition?"
"No, World-Honored One! Is the tongue-element itself the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?"
"No, World-Honored One! Are the taste-element,
the tongue-consciousness-element, tongue-contact, and all feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?"
"No, World-Honored One! Is there a bodhisattva-mahāsattva apart from the tongue-element?"
“No, World-Honored One!
Is there a bodhisattva mahāsattva apart from the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, tongue-contact, and the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition?”
“No, World-Honored One! Is the body-element itself the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?”
"No, World-Honored One! Are the tangible-object element,
the body-consciousness element, and body-contact, as well as all feelings produced with body-contact as a condition, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?"
"No, World-Honored One! Is there a bodhisattva mahāsattva apart from the body-element?"
"No, World-Honored One!
Is there a bodhisattva mahāsattva apart from the element of tangibility, the element of body-consciousness, body-contact, and the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition?"
"No, World-Honored One! Is the mind-element itself the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?"
“No, World-Honored One! Are the dharma-element,
the mind-consciousness-element, mental contact, and the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?”
"No, World-Honored One! Is there a bodhisattva mahāsattva apart from the mind-element?"
"No, World-Honored One!
Is there a bodhisattva mahāsattva apart from the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness element, mental contact, and the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition?"
"No, World-Honored One! Is the earth element itself the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?"
"No, World-Honored One!
Are the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?"
“No, World-Honored One! Is there a bodhisattva mahāsattva apart from the earth element?”
"No, World-Honored One!
Is there a bodhisattva mahāsattva apart from the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness?"
"No, World-Honored One! Is ignorance itself the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?"
"No, World-Honored One!

Are form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva? Is volitional formation, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age and death the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva?"
"No, World-Honored One! Is there a bodhisattva mahāsattva apart from ignorance?"
"No, World-Honored One!
Is there a bodhisattva mahāsattva apart from conditioned formations, up to and including old age and death?"
"No, World-Honored One! At that time,
the Buddha addressed the Venerable Subhūti:
“What meaning do you perceive that leads you to say:
‘Form and the other dharmas are not the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, yet apart from form and the other dharmas there is no bodhisattva-mahāsattva’?”
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If awakening, the bodhisattva, or dharmas such as form are ultimately unobtainable because their nature does not exist, how much less could there be a bodhisattva-mahāsattva!”
Since this does not exist, how can it be said that the dharmas such as form are themselves the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, or that there is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva apart from the dharmas such as form?
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “Excellent! Excellent!”
So it is! So it is! It is just as you have said.
Subhūti! Because awakening, the bodhisattva, or dharmas such as form cannot be apprehended, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas likewise cannot be apprehended.
Because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are unapprehendable, the perfection of wisdom they practice is also unapprehendable. Subhūti,
when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should train themselves in this manner.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Regarding what is called a 'bodhisattva mahāsattva,' what do you think?
Is the suchness of form the bodhisattva mahāsattva?"
"No, World-Honored One! Is the suchness of feeling,
perception, mental formations, and consciousness the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?"
"No, World-Honored One! Is there any bodhisattva-mahāsattva apart from the *tathatā* (suchness) of form?"
"No, World-Honored One!
Is there a bodhisattva mahāsattva apart from the *tathatā* (suchness) of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?"
“No, World-Honored One! Is the suchness of the eye-base itself the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?”
“No, World-Honored One! Is the suchness of the spheres of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?”
"No, World-Honored One! Is there a bodhisattva mahāsattva apart from the suchness of the eye-base?"
"No, World-Honored One!
Is there a bodhisattva-mahāsattva apart from the suchness of the spheres of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind?"
“No, World-Honored One! Is the suchness of the sphere of form the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?”
“No, World-Honored One!
Is the suchness of the sense bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena the bodhisattva mahāsattva?”
"No, World-Honored One! Is there a bodhisattva-mahāsattva apart from the *tathatā* (suchness) of the sphere of form?"
"No, World-Honored One!
Is there a bodhisattva-mahāsattva apart from the suchness of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena?"
"No, World-Honored One! Is the suchness of the eye-element the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?"
"No, World-Honored One!
Is the suchness of the form element, the eye-consciousness element, eye-contact, and all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?"
"No, World-Honored One! Is there any bodhisattva-mahāsattva apart from the *tathatā* (suchness) of the eye-element?"
“No, World-Honored One!

Is there any bodhisattva-mahāsattva who exists apart from the realm of form, the realm of eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, within their *tathatā* (suchness)?"
“No, World-Honored One! Is the suchness of the ear-element the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?”
"No, World-Honored One! Is the suchness of the sphere of sound,

"No, World-Honored One! At that time,
the Buddha addressed the Venerable Subhūti:
“What meaning do you perceive that leads you to say this:
that the suchness of dharmas such as form is not the bodhisattva mahāsattva, and that apart from the suchness of dharmas such as form there is no bodhisattva mahāsattva?”
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since even phenomena such as form are ultimately unattainable because their nature does not exist, how much less so could there be the true suchness (tathatā) of phenomena such as form!”

Since this suchness is neither existent nor non-existent, how can it be said that the suchness of dharmas such as form is the bodhisattva mahāsattva, or that there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva apart from the suchness of dharmas such as form?
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “Excellent! Excellent!”
So it is! So it is! It is just as you have said.

Subhūti! Because dharmas such as form are unapprehendable, the true suchness (*tathatā*) of dharmas such as form is also unapprehendable; and because dharmas such as form and their true suchness are unapprehendable, bodhisattva mahāsattvas are also unapprehendable.
Because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are unapprehendable, the perfection of wisdom they practice is also unapprehendable. Subhūti,
when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should train in this manner.

“No, World-Honored One! At that time,
the Buddha addressed the Venerable Subhūti:
"What meaning do you perceive that leads you to say:
'The designations for phenomena such as form are not the bodhisattva-mahāsattva'?
Furthermore, what meaning do you perceive that leads you to say this?"

Are the designations for phenomena such as form—whether they be permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, empty or not empty, with signs or signless, with aspirations or aspirationless, tranquil or not tranquil, detached or not detached, defiled or purified, or arising or ceasing—are these also not the bodhisattva mahāsattva?
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since even phenomena such as form are ultimately unobtainable because their nature does not exist, how much less so could there be a designation for phenomena such as form!”
Since this designation (*adhivacana*) does not exist, how can it be said that the designation of phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) is a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
"World-Honored One,
since phenomena such as form are ultimately and absolutely unobtainable because their nature does not exist, how much less could there be impermanent phenomena such as form!"

Since even the permanence or impermanence of phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) is ultimately unfindable, how much more so the designation (*adhivacana*) "permanence or impermanence of form and so forth"?
Since this designation does not exist, how can it be said that the designation "permanence or impermanence of form and so forth" is a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
“World-Honored One!
Since even the pleasure of dharmas such as form is ultimately unobtainable because its nature does not exist, how much less could there be suffering in dharmas such as form?
Since even the pleasure and suffering of dharmas such as form are ultimately unobtainable, how much less could there be a designation for the pleasure and suffering of dharmas such as form?”
Since this designation does not exist, how can it be said that the designation of pleasure, suffering, and so forth regarding phenomena such as form is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?
“World-Honored One!
Since even a self regarding phenomena such as form is ultimately unobtainable because its nature does not exist, how much less could there be a selflessness of phenomena such as form!”
Since the self and non-self of phenomena such as form are ultimately unfindable, how much more so is there any designation (*adhivacana*) for the self or non-self of phenomena such as form!
Since this designation does not exist, how can it be said that the designation of the self or non-self of phenomena such as form is a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
“World-Honored One!
Since even the purity of phenomena such as form is ultimately unobtainable because their nature does not exist, how much less so is there impurity in phenomena such as form!
Since even the purity and impurity of phenomena such as form are ultimately unobtainable, how much less so is there a designation for the purity or impurity of phenomena such as form!”
Since this designation does not exist, how can it be said that the designations of "pure" or "impure" regarding phenomena such as form constitute a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
“World-Honored One! [he asked.]
Since even non-empty phenomena such as form are ultimately unobtainable because their nature does not exist, how much more so is there emptiness of form and other phenomena!

Since even the emptiness and non-emptiness of form and other phenomena are ultimately unobtainable, how much more so is there a designation for the emptiness and non-emptiness of form and other phenomena!
Since this designation does not exist, how can it be said that the designation of the emptiness or non-emptiness of dharmas such as form is a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
“World-Honored One! [he asked.]

Since even the existence of characteristics in phenomena such as form is ultimately unattainable—because their intrinsic nature does not exist—how much less so the non-existence of characteristics in phenomena such as form!

Since even the existence or non-existence of characteristics in phenomena such as form is ultimately unattainable, how much less so the designation "existence or non-existence of characteristics" for phenomena such as form!
Since this designation does not exist, how can it be said that the designations "with marks" and "without marks" regarding dharmas such as form constitute a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
“World-Honored One! [How can this be so?]”

Since even the existence of aspiration regarding phenomena such as form is ultimately unattainable—because their nature is non-existent—how much less so is the non-existence of aspiration regarding phenomena such as form?

Since even the existence or non-existence of aspiration regarding phenomena such as form is ultimately unattainable, how much less so is the designation "existence or non-existence of aspiration" regarding phenomena such as form!
Since this designation does not exist, how can it be said that the designations "with aspiration" and "without aspiration" regarding phenomena such as form constitute a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
“World-Honored One! [he asked.]
Since even the quiescence of phenomena such as form is ultimately unapprehendable because their nature does not exist, how much less could there be non-quiescent phenomena such as form!

Since even the quiescence and non-quiescence of phenomena such as form are ultimately unapprehendable, how much less could there be a designation for the quiescence and non-quiescence of phenomena such as form!
Since this designation does not exist, how can it be said that the designation "the tranquility or non-tranquility of dharmas such as form" is a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
"World-Honored One!"
Since even the remoteness of dharmas such as form is ultimately unobtainable because their nature does not exist, how much less so is there any non-remoteness of dharmas such as form!

Since even the remoteness and non-remoteness of dharmas such as form are ultimately unobtainable, how much less so is there any designation (*adhivacana*) for the remoteness or non-remoteness of dharmas such as form!
Since this designation does not exist, how can it be said that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is one for whom designations such as "form" and so forth are either distant or not distant?
"World-Honored One!"
Since even the defilement of phenomena such as form is ultimately unfindable because their nature does not exist, how much less could there be purity of phenomena such as form!
Since even the defilement and purity of phenomena such as form are ultimately unfindable, how much less could there be a designation for the defilement and purity of phenomena such as form!
Since this designation does not exist, how can it be said that the designation for the defilement and purification of dharmas such as form is the bodhisattva mahāsattva?
“World-Honored One!”
Since the arising of phenomena such as form is ultimately unattainable because their nature does not exist, how much less so is there the cessation of phenomena such as form!
Since the arising and cessation of phenomena such as form are ultimately unattainable, how much less so is there even a designation for the arising and cessation of phenomena such as form!
“Since this designation does not exist, how can it be said that the designation for the arising and ceasing of phenomena such as form is a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin! [It cannot.]”
Excellent! Excellent! It is so!
"So it is! It is just as you have said, Subhūti."

Because phenomena such as form, as well as [attributes] such as permanence and impermanence, are unapprehendable, the designations for phenomena such as form, as well as the designations for permanence and impermanence, are also unapprehendable. Because both phenomena and their designations are unapprehendable, bodhisattva mahāsattvas are also unapprehendable. Because bodhisattva mahāsattvas are unapprehendable, the *prajñāpāramitā* they practice is also unapprehendable.
"Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should train in this way.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"
"As for what you previously said— that 'I do not see even a single dharma that can be named a bodhisattva-mahāsattva'— it is so! It is so!"
It is as you have said. "Subhūti!

All phenomena do not perceive all phenomena; all phenomena do not perceive the dharma-realm; the dharma-realm does not perceive all phenomena; and the dharma-realm does not perceive the dharma-realm."
“Subhūti! The dharma-realm does not perceive the form-realm, and the form-realm does not perceive the dharma-realm;

the dharma-realm does not perceive the realms of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, and the realms of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness do not perceive the dharma-realm.”
“Subhūti! The dharma-realm does not perceive the eye-base, and the eye-base does not perceive the dharma-realm;
the dharma-realm does not perceive the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-base, and the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-base does not perceive the dharma-realm.”
“Subhūti! The dharma-realm does not perceive the sphere of form, nor does the sphere of form perceive the dharma-realm;

the dharma-realm does not perceive the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena, nor do the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena perceive the dharma-realm.”
“Subhūti! The dharma-realm does not perceive the eye-element, nor does the eye-element perceive the dharma-realm;
the dharma-realm does not perceive the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-element, nor do the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-elements perceive the dharma-realm.”
“Subhūti! The dharma-realm does not perceive the form-realm, and the form-realm does not perceive the dharma-realm;
the dharma-realm does not perceive sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or the dharma-realm, and sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and the dharma-realm do not perceive the dharma-realm.”
“Subhūti! The dharma-realm does not perceive the eye-consciousness realm, and the eye-consciousness realm does not perceive the dharma-realm;
the dharma-realm does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-consciousness realms, and the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-consciousness realms do not perceive the dharma-realm.”
“Subhūti! The dharma-realm does not perceive the earth-element, and the earth-element does not perceive the dharma-realm;
the dharma-realm does not perceive the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness-elements, and the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness-elements do not perceive the dharma-realm.”
“Subhūti! The dharma-realm does not perceive ignorance, nor does ignorance perceive the dharma-realm;

the dharma-realm does not perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death, nor do volitional formations through to aging-and-death perceive the dharma-realm.”
“Subhūti! The conditioned realm does not perceive the unconditioned realm, and the unconditioned realm does not perceive the conditioned realm. Subhūti!”
"The unconditioned is not designated apart from the conditioned, nor is the conditioned designated apart from the unconditioned.

'In this way, Subhūti, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive any phenomena at all. Because they perceive nothing, their minds are not startled, terrified, or frightened; regarding all phenomena, their minds neither sink nor feel regret.'"
Why is this? Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom in this manner, they do not perceive form, nor do they perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
They do not perceive the sense-base of the eye, nor do they perceive the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind;
they do not perceive the sense-base of forms, nor do they perceive the sense-bases of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena;
they do not perceive the eye-element, nor do they perceive the elements of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
One does not perceive the realm of form; one does not perceive the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena.
One does not perceive the realm of eye-consciousness; one does not perceive the realms of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness.
One does not perceive the earth element; one does not perceive the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness.

One does not perceive ignorance; one does not perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, existence, birth, or aging-and-death.
One does not perceive desire-attachment; one does not perceive hatred or delusion.

One does not perceive a self; one does not perceive a sentient being, a life-principle, a living being, a nourisher, a spirit, a person, an individual, a mind-born, a youth, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, or a viewer.
One does not perceive the desire realm, nor does one perceive the form or formless realms;

one does not perceive śrāvakas or the dharmas of śrāvakas, nor does one perceive pratyekabuddhas or the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, nor does one perceive bodhisattvas or the dharmas of bodhisattvas, nor does one perceive the Buddhas or the dharmas of the Buddhas, nor does one perceive unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not perceive any phenomena at all; because they perceive nothing, their minds are not startled, not terrified, and not afraid; regarding all phenomena, their minds neither sink nor feel regret.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
by what further causes and conditions do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, have minds that neither sink nor feel regret regarding all phenomena?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
