"When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they neither obtain nor perceive any mind or mental factors whatsoever. By virtue of this cause and condition, their minds do not sink into despondency nor do they feel regret regarding any phenomena."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
for what causes and conditions does the mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva not tremble, not fear, and not dread when practicing the perfection of wisdom regarding all phenomena?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they do not apprehend nor do they perceive any mind or the sphere of mind."
Thus it is, Subhūti!
When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, their minds are not startled, not terrified, and not afraid regarding all phenomena.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
All bodhisattva mahāsattvas, having nothing whatsoever to apprehend regarding all phenomena, should practice the perfection of wisdom."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, at all places and at all times, they do not apprehend the perfection of wisdom, nor do they apprehend the name 'perfection of wisdom';
they do not apprehend the bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor do they apprehend the name 'bodhisattva mahāsattva,' nor do they apprehend the mind of the bodhisattva mahāsattva."
"Subhūti! You should instruct and advise the bodhisattva mahāsattvas in this way, so that they may fully accomplish the perfection of wisdom."
Chapter Seven: Entering the State Beyond Error. Part Two. Chapter Seven: Entering the State Beyond Error. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to fulfill the perfection of generosity, they should train in the perfection of wisdom;
if they wish to fulfill the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, they should train in the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to fully know form, they should study the perfection of wisdom;
if they wish to fully know feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to fully know the sense base of the eye, they should study the perfection of wisdom;
if they wish to fully know the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to fully know the sphere of form, they should study the perfection of wisdom;
if they wish to fully know the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to fully know the eye constituent, they should study the perfection of wisdom;
if they wish to fully know the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind constituents, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to fully know the realm of form, they should study the perfection of wisdom;
if they wish to fully know the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to fully know the eye-consciousness element, they should study the perfection of wisdom;
if they wish to fully know the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness elements, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to fully know eye-contact, they should study the perfection of wisdom;
if they wish to fully know ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to fully know all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, they should study the perfection of wisdom;
if they wish to fully know all feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as condition, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to fully know the earth element, they should study the perfection of wisdom;
if they wish to fully know the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to fully know ignorance, they should study the perfection of wisdom;

if they wish to fully know volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age and death, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
“If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to permanently sever desire, hatred, and delusion, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to permanently sever the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), attachment to precepts and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa), doubt (vicikitsā), sensual desire, and hatred, they should study the perfection of wisdom.”

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to eternally sever attachment to the realm of form, attachment to the formless realm, ignorance, pride, and restlessness, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to forever sever all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and fetters (*paryavasthāna*), they should study the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to forever sever the four kinds of nutriment (*āhāra*), they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to permanently sever the four floods, yokes, graspings, bodily fetters, and inversions, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to distance themselves from the ten unwholesome paths of action, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to undertake and practice the ten wholesome paths of action, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to practice the four dhyānas, they should study the perfection of wisdom;
if they wish to practice the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions, they should study the perfection of wisdom."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to practice the four foundations of mindfulness, they should study the perfection of wisdom;

if they wish to practice the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain the ten powers of a Buddha, they should study the perfection of wisdom;

if they wish to attain the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to enter the bodhyaṅga-samādhi with mastery, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to sport with mastery in the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā), they should study the perfection of wisdom.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain mastery over the successive transcendence of the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, and the attainment of cessation, whether in forward or reverse order, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain mastery over all dhāraṇī-doors and samādhi-doors, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain mastery in entering and emerging from all the *siṃhavikrīḍita* samādhis, up to and including the *siṃhavijṛmbhita* samādhi, they should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to enter the *kṣepaṇa* (swift-walking) samādhi, the *ratnamudrā* (jewel-seal) samādhi, the *sudarśana* (wondrous moon) samādhi,
the *candradhvajaketu* (moon-banner-sign) samādhi, the *sarvadharmamudrā* (seal of all phenomena) samādhi,
the *mudrādarśana* (contemplation of the seal) samādhi, the *dharmadhātuniyata* (certainty of the dharma-realm) samādhi, and the *niyatadhvaja* (determined banner) [samādhi]...
The samādhi of signs, the vajra-like samādhi, the samādhi of entering the gateway of all dharmas,
the king of samādhis, the royal seal samādhi, the power-purifying samādhi,
the jewel casket samādhi, and the samādhi of definitive entry into the terminology of all dharmas.
The samādhi of entering the designations of all phenomena, the samādhi of observing the ten directions,
the samādhi of the seal of the dhāraṇī-gate of all phenomena, the samādhi of non-forgetfulness regarding all phenomena,
the samādhi of the seal of the signs of the equal course of all phenomena, and the samādhi of abiding in the realm of space.
One who wishes to attain mastery over the samādhi of the purity of the three wheels, the samādhi of non-retrogressive supernormal powers,
the samādhi of the surging vessel, the samādhi of the banner-mark of supreme concentration,
and all other immeasurable, supreme samādhis, should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to fulfill the aspirations of all sentient beings, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to fulfill such sublime roots of virtue (kuśalamūla), and because these roots of virtue are brought to completion, they do not fall into the evil destinies, are not born into lowly families, do not fall into the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, and never regress from the summit of the bodhisattva path, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti,
“What is meant by the ‘summit-fall’ of a bodhisattva? Subhūti replied:

"If bodhisattvas practice the six pāramitās without skillful means and dwell in the three gates of liberation without skillful means, they fall back into the level of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas and do not enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth; this is called the 'falling from the summit' of a bodhisattva."
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti, "What is called 'arising'? Subhūti replied:
"Birth refers to craving for dharmas.
Śāriputra asked, "What is meant by craving for dharmas?"

Subhūti replied: "If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, dwells upon the emptiness of form and gives rise to conceptual attachment; dwells upon the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness and gives rise to conceptual attachment;

dwells upon the signlessness of form and gives rise to conceptual attachment; dwells upon the signlessness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness and gives rise to conceptual attachment;"
Abiding in the wishlessness of form, they give rise to conceptualizations; abiding in the wishlessness of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, they give rise to conceptualizations.
Abiding in the tranquility of form, they give rise to conceptualizations; abiding in the tranquility of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, they give rise to conceptualizations.
Abiding in the detachment from form, they give rise to conceptualizations; abiding in the detachment from feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, they give rise to conceptualizations.

They dwell upon the impermanence of form and give rise to conceptual attachment; they dwell upon the impermanence of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness and give rise to conceptual attachment.

They dwell upon the suffering of form and give rise to conceptual attachment; they dwell upon the suffering of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness and give rise to conceptual attachment.

They dwell upon the selflessness of form and give rise to conceptual attachment; they dwell upon the selflessness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness and give rise to conceptual attachment.

Abiding in the impurity of form, they give rise to conceptual attachments; abiding in the impurity of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, they give rise to conceptual attachments. Śāriputra!
This is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s compliance with the craving for dharmas; this very craving for dharmas is what is called "birth.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva forms such a thought:
"This form should be abandoned; this feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness should be abandoned.
By means of this, form should be abandoned; by means of this, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness should be abandoned."
"This suffering should be fully understood; for this reason, suffering should be fully understood.
This origin should be permanently abandoned; for this reason, the origin should be permanently abandoned.
This cessation should be realized; for this reason, cessation should be realized."
This path should be cultivated; for this reason, the path should be cultivated.
This is affliction; this is purification.
This should be approached; this should not be approached.
"This should be practiced; this should not be practiced.
This is the path; this is not the path.
This is to be studied; this is not to be studied."
"This is the perfection of generosity; this is not the perfection of generosity.

This is the perfection of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; this is not the perfection of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom."
"This is skillful means; this is not skillful means.
This is the birth of a bodhisattva; this is the bodhisattva’s departure from birth. Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, dwells in these various dharma-gates and gives rise to conceptual attachment, this constitutes the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s compliance with craving for dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*). This very craving for dharmas is called "birth," just as the digestion of last night's food can give rise to affliction.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra asked the Venerable Subhūti:
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva enter into the state of certainty of rightness?"
Subhūti replied, “Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive internal emptiness, nor do they rely on internal emptiness to contemplate external emptiness.”
One does not perceive external emptiness; one does not, relying on external emptiness, contemplate internal emptiness, nor, relying on external emptiness, contemplate internal-and-external emptiness.

One does not perceive internal-and-external emptiness; one does not, relying on internal-and-external emptiness, contemplate external emptiness, nor, relying on internal-and-external emptiness, contemplate the emptiness of emptiness.

One does not perceive the emptiness of emptiness; one does not, relying on the emptiness of emptiness, contemplate internal-and-external emptiness, nor, relying on the emptiness of emptiness, contemplate great emptiness.

One does not perceive the great emptiness, nor does one, relying on the great emptiness, contemplate the emptiness of emptiness; nor, relying on the great emptiness, does one contemplate the emptiness of the ultimate.

One does not perceive the emptiness of the ultimate, nor does one, relying on the emptiness of the ultimate, contemplate the great emptiness; nor, relying on the emptiness of the ultimate, does one contemplate the emptiness of the conditioned.

One does not perceive the emptiness of the conditioned, nor does one, relying on the emptiness of the conditioned, contemplate the emptiness of the ultimate; nor, relying on the emptiness of the conditioned, does one contemplate the emptiness of the unconditioned.

One does not perceive the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*); one does not, relying on the emptiness of the unconditioned, contemplate the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*); nor does one, relying on the emptiness of the unconditioned, contemplate ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).

One does not perceive ultimate emptiness; one does not, relying on ultimate emptiness, contemplate the emptiness of the unconditioned; nor does one, relying on ultimate emptiness, contemplate the emptiness of the boundless (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*).

One does not perceive the emptiness of the boundless; one does not, relying on the emptiness of the boundless, contemplate ultimate emptiness; nor does one, relying on the emptiness of the boundless, contemplate the emptiness of the non-dispersal of dispersion (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*).

One does not perceive the emptiness of dispersion and non-dispersion; one does not, relying on the emptiness of dispersion and non-dispersion, contemplate the emptiness of the limitless, nor, relying on the emptiness of dispersion and non-dispersion, contemplate the emptiness of intrinsic nature.

One does not perceive the emptiness of intrinsic nature; one does not, relying on the emptiness of intrinsic nature, contemplate the emptiness of dispersion and non-dispersion, nor, relying on the emptiness of intrinsic nature, contemplate the emptiness of self-characteristics and common characteristics.

One does not perceive the emptiness of self-characteristics and common characteristics; one does not, relying on the emptiness of self-characteristics and common characteristics, contemplate the emptiness of intrinsic nature, nor, relying on the emptiness of self-characteristics and common characteristics, contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena.

One does not perceive the emptiness of all phenomena; one does not, relying on the emptiness of all phenomena, contemplate the emptiness of specific and general characteristics; nor does one, relying on the emptiness of all phenomena, contemplate the emptiness of non-apprehensibility. One does not perceive the emptiness of non-apprehensibility;

one does not, relying on the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena; nor does one, relying on the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, contemplate the emptiness of the absence of intrinsic nature. One does not perceive the emptiness of the absence of intrinsic nature;

one does not, relying on the emptiness of the absence of intrinsic nature, contemplate the emptiness of non-apprehensibility; nor does one, relying on the emptiness of the absence of intrinsic nature, contemplate the emptiness of intrinsic nature.

One does not perceive the emptiness of intrinsic nature; one does not, relying on the emptiness of intrinsic nature, perceive the emptiness of non-existence, nor, relying on the emptiness of intrinsic nature, perceive the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.

One does not perceive the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; one does not, relying on the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, perceive the emptiness of intrinsic nature.

Śāriputra! When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they engage in such contemplation as this, which is called "entering the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth" (samyaktvaniyāma).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should train in this way:
they should know form as it truly is and not grasp it; they should know feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as they truly are and not grasp them."
One should know the eye-base as it truly is and not grasp it; one should know the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases as they truly are and not grasp them.
One should know the form-base as it truly is and not grasp it; one should know the sound, odor, taste, tangible, and mental-object bases as they truly are and not grasp them.
One should know the eye-element as it truly is and not grasp it; one should know the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements as they truly are and not grasp them.

One should know, as it truly is, that the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) should not be clung to; one should know, as it truly is, that the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) should not be clung to.

One should know, as it truly is, that the eye-consciousness realm (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) should not be clung to; one should know, as it truly is, that the realms of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness (*manovijñānadhātu*) should not be clung to.

One should know, as it truly is, that the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) should not be clung to; one should know, as it truly is, that the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom (*śīla-kṣānti-vīrya-dhyāna-prajñāpāramitā*) should not be clung to.
One should know the four dhyānas as they truly are and not cling to them; one should know the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, as they truly are and not cling to them;

one should know the four foundations of mindfulness as they truly are and not cling to them; one should know the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path as they truly are and not cling to them;

one should know the ten powers of a Buddha as they truly are and not cling to them; one should know the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as they truly are and not cling to them.

"In this way, Śāriputra, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they are able to know as it truly is that the mind of awakening (bodhicitta) should not be grasped, the unequaled mind should not be grasped, and the vast mind should not be grasped."
Why is this? Śāriputra,
this mind is no-mind, because its intrinsic nature is pure.
Then, Śāriputra asked Subhūti: "In what way is the intrinsic nature of the mind pure? Subhūti replied:

“The nature of this mind is neither associated nor dissociated with greed; it is neither associated nor dissociated with hatred; it is neither associated nor dissociated with delusion; it is neither associated nor dissociated with the fetters, the secondary afflictions, nor the latent tendencies; it is neither associated nor dissociated with various views, outflows, and so forth; and it is likewise neither associated nor dissociated with the minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.”
“Śāriputra! All bodhisattva mahāsattvas know that the mind is thus pure by nature.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed Subhūti, saying:
"Does this mind possess a nature that is not the nature of mind?
Subhūti questioned, saying:
"Within the nature that is not the nature of mind, can existence or non-existence be apprehended?"
Śāriputra said: "No, Subhūti!"
Subhūti replied: "If neither existence nor non-existence can be apprehended within the nature of mind, how can one ask whether this mind exists as the nature of mind or not?"
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"What is meant by 'the nature of non-mind'? Subhūti replied:
"In all phenomena there is no alteration and no conceptual differentiation; this is called the 'non-mind nature'. Śāriputra asked:

"Is it only that the mind has no alteration and no conceptual differentiation, or do form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness likewise have no alteration and no conceptual differentiation?"
Subhūti replied:

"Just as the mind is without alteration and without conceptual differentiation, so too are form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness without alteration and without conceptual differentiation; and likewise, even up to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas, it is without alteration and without conceptual differentiation."
At that time, Śāriputra praised Subhūti, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
It is exactly as you have said.

You are a true son of the Buddha, born from the mind of the Buddha, born from the mouth of the Buddha, born from the Dharma of the Buddha, and born through transformation from the Dharma; you have received a portion of the Buddha’s Dharma rather than a portion of material wealth. Among all phenomena, you have personally realized them through your own body and, seeing them with the eye of wisdom, are able to give rise to this teaching.

The Buddha has always declared that among my assembly of śrāvakas, you are the foremost in abiding in the concentration of non-contention (*araṇāsamādhi*); what the Buddha has said is true and not false.
Subhūti! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should train in the profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) in this manner.

Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can train in the profound perfection of wisdom in this way, you should know that they already abide on the stage of non-retrogression and are never separated from the perfection of wisdom.

“Subhūti! If sons or daughters of good family wish to train in the stage of the śrāvaka, they should diligently listen to, study, read, recite, receive, uphold, and reflect upon this profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) according to the principle, bringing it to ultimate completion.

Those who wish to train in the stage of the pratyekabuddha should likewise diligently listen to, study, read, recite, receive, uphold, and reflect upon this profound perfection of wisdom according to the principle, bringing it to ultimate completion.”

Those who wish to study the bodhisattva stages should likewise diligently listen to, study, read, recite, receive, and uphold this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, reflecting upon it according to reason, so as to bring it to ultimate completion.
Why is this? Subhūti!
Because within this profound sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā, the three vehicles of the Dharma are extensively explained and revealed.
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to study the perfection of wisdom, they will have studied all the dharmas of the three vehicles and attained skillfulness in them all.
Chapter Eight: The Chapter on the Victorious Army (Śūraṅgama), Part Two, Section One. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

Since I neither know nor perceive either the bodhisattva mahāsattvas or the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), how can I instruct and admonish the bodhisattva mahāsattvas with dharmas corresponding to the perfection of wisdom?
“World-Honored One!

Regarding all dharmas, I neither know nor perceive any increase or decrease. If I were to instruct or admonish the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas by means of these dharmas, I would surely have cause for regret.”
“World-Honored One!
Regarding all dharmas, I neither know nor perceive any increase or decrease; how, then, can it be said:
‘This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva,’ or ‘This is called the prajñāpāramitā’?”
“World-Honored One!
The names of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the name of the prajñāpāramitā are both non-abiding and yet not non-abiding. Why is this?
Because these two kinds of meanings do not exist, these two kinds of names abide nowhere at all, nor do they not abide.
"World-Honored One!
Regarding form up to consciousness, I neither know nor perceive any increase or decrease; how then can it be said that 'this is form' up to 'this is consciousness'?"
These names such as "form" and so forth neither abide anywhere nor do they not abide.

Why is this? Because the referents of these names—form and so forth—do not exist; therefore, these names for form and so forth have no place of abiding whatsoever, yet they are not non-abiding either.
“World-Honored One!

Regarding the sense bases from the eye base up to the mind base, I neither know nor perceive any increase or decrease; how, then, can it be said that ‘this is the eye base’ up to ‘this is the mind base’?”
Names such as "the sense base of the eye" neither abide anywhere nor do they not abide.
Why is this? Because the referents of "the sense base of the eye" and so forth do not exist, names such as "the sense base of the eye" have no abode whatsoever, nor do they not abide.
“World-Honored One!

Regarding the sphere of form up to the sphere of mental phenomena, I neither know nor perceive any increase or decrease; how, then, could it be said that ‘this is the sphere of form’ up to ‘this is the sphere of mental phenomena’?”
Names such as "the sphere of form" (rūpāyatana) neither abide anywhere nor do they not abide.
Why is this? Because the referents of "the sphere of form" and so forth do not exist, names such as "the sphere of form" have no place of abiding whatsoever, nor do they not abide.
“World-Honored One!
Regarding the eye-element up to the mind-element, I neither know nor perceive any increase or decrease; how, then, can it be said that ‘this is the eye-element’ up to ‘this is the mind-element’?”
The names such as "eye-element" (cakṣurdhātu) and so forth neither abide anywhere, nor do they not abide. Why is this?
Because the referents of the eye-element and so forth do not exist; therefore, the names of the eye-element and so forth have no place of abiding whatsoever, nor do they not abide.
“World-Honored One!

Regarding the realm of form up to the realm of phenomena, I neither know nor perceive any increase or decrease; how then can it be said that ‘this is the realm of form’ up to ‘this is the realm of phenomena’?”
The names "form realm" and so forth neither abide anywhere nor do they not abide.
Why is this? Because the referents of "form realm" and so forth do not exist, the names "form realm" and so forth have no place of abiding whatsoever, yet they are not non-abiding either.
“World-Honored One!

Regarding the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element, I neither know nor perceive any increase or decrease; how, then, can it be said that ‘this is the eye-consciousness element’ up to ‘this is the mind-consciousness element’?”
The names such as the "eye-consciousness element" and so forth neither abide anywhere, nor do they not abide.

Why is this? Because the referents of the eye-consciousness element and so forth are non-existent, the names of the eye-consciousness element and so forth have no place of abiding whatsoever, nor do they not abide.
“World-Honored One!
Regarding eye-contact up to mind-contact, I neither know nor perceive any increase or decrease; how, then, can it be said that ‘this is eye-contact’ up to ‘this is mind-contact’?”
Names such as "eye-contact" and so forth neither abide anywhere, nor do they not abide.
Why is this? Because the referents of "eye-contact" and so forth are non-existent, names such as "eye-contact" have no place of abiding whatsoever, nor do they not abide.
“World-Honored One!

Regarding the various feelings arising with eye-contact as condition, up to the various feelings arising with mind-contact as condition, I neither know nor perceive their increase or decrease; how then can it be said that ‘these are the various feelings arising with eye-contact as condition,’ up to ‘these are the various feelings arising with mind-contact as condition’?”
The names for all feelings and so forth produced with eye-contact as a condition neither abide anywhere, nor do they not abide.

Why is this? Because the referent objects (artha) of all feelings and so forth produced with eye-contact as a condition do not exist; therefore, the names for all feelings and so forth produced with eye-contact as a condition have no abode whatsoever, nor do they not abide.
“World-Honored One!
Since I neither know nor perceive whether there is an increase or decrease from ignorance up to old age and death, how can it be said that ‘this is ignorance’ up to ‘this is old age and death’?”
Names such as "ignorance" (avidyā) and so forth neither abide anywhere, nor do they not abide. Why is this?
Because the referents of ignorance and so forth do not exist, names such as "ignorance" have no abode whatsoever, nor do they not abide.
“World-Honored One!

Regarding the cessation of ignorance up to the cessation of old age and death, if I neither know nor realize whether they increase or decrease, how can it be said that ‘this is the cessation of ignorance’ up to ‘this is the cessation of old age and death’?”
Names such as "the cessation of ignorance" and so forth neither abide anywhere, nor do they not abide.
Why is this? Because the meaning of the cessation of ignorance and so forth is non-existent; therefore, names such as "the cessation of ignorance" have no abode whatsoever, nor do they not abide.
“World-Honored One!

Regarding greed, hatred, delusion, as well as the various fetters, latent tendencies, and views—whether they increase or decrease—I neither know nor perceive them. How, then, can it be said that ‘this is greed’ and so forth?”
These names for greed and so forth neither abide anywhere, nor do they not abide.
Why is this? Because the referents of greed and so forth do not exist; therefore, these names for greed and so forth have no place of abiding whatsoever, nor do they not abide.

“Bhagavān, regarding the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, I neither know nor perceive any increase or decrease; how then can it be said that ‘this is the perfection of generosity’ up to ‘this is the perfection of wisdom’?”
The names such as "perfection of generosity" (dānapāramitā) neither abide anywhere nor do they not abide. Why is this?
Because the referents of "perfection of generosity" and so forth do not exist, the names "perfection of generosity" and so forth have no abode whatsoever, nor do they not abide.
“World-Honored One!

Regarding this self, up to and including the viewer, I neither know nor perceive whether there is an increase or a decrease; how, then, could it be said that ‘this is my self,’ up to and including ‘this is the viewer’?”
Our names abide nowhere, nor do they not abide.
Why is this? Because the referents of "we" do not exist, our names abide nowhere and yet do not not abide.
“World-Honored One!

Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, I neither know nor perceive any increase or decrease; how then can it be said that ‘these are the four foundations of mindfulness’ up to ‘these are the eightfold noble path’?”
The names of the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth neither abide anywhere, nor do they not abide.

Why is this? Because the referents of the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth are non-existent, the names of the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth do not abide at all, nor do they not abide.
“World-Honored One!

Regarding the gate of liberation of emptiness up to the gate of liberation of wishlessness, I neither know nor perceive any increase or decrease; how then can it be said that ‘this is the gate of liberation of emptiness’ up to ‘this is the gate of liberation of wishlessness’?”
The names of the gateways to liberation such as emptiness neither abide anywhere nor do they not abide.

Why is this? Because the referents of the gateways to liberation such as emptiness are non-existent, the names of the gateways to liberation such as emptiness have no place of abiding whatsoever, nor do they not abide.
“World-Honored One!

Regarding the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments, I neither know nor perceive their increase or decrease; how, then, can it be said that these are the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments?”
The names of the four dhyānas and so forth neither abide anywhere nor do they not abide.

Why is this? Because the referents of the four dhyānas and so forth are non-existent, the names of the four dhyānas and so forth have no place of abiding whatsoever, yet they are also not non-abiding.
“World-Honored One!

Regarding my mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Saṅgha, mindfulness of ethical discipline, mindfulness of relinquishment, mindfulness of the devas, mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation, and mindfulness of death—I do not know nor do I perceive their increase or decrease. How, then, can it be said that these are ‘mindfulness of the Buddha’ up to ‘mindfulness of death’?”
Names such as "recollection of the Buddha" (buddhānusmṛti) neither abide anywhere nor do they not abide. Why is this?
Because the referents of "recollection of the Buddha" and so forth do not exist; therefore, names such as "recollection of the Buddha" have no abode whatsoever, nor do they not abide.
“World-Honored One!

Regarding the Buddha’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, I neither know nor perceive any increase or decrease in them; how, then, could it be said that ‘these are the Buddha’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha’?”
The names of the Buddha’s ten powers and so forth neither abide anywhere, nor do they not abide.

Why is this? Because the referents of the Buddha’s ten powers and so forth are non-existent; therefore, the names of the Buddha’s ten powers and so forth have no place of abiding whatsoever, yet they are not non-abiding either.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle Four Hundred and Eight.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle Four Hundred and Nine.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.
The Second Part of the Eighth Chapter, "The Superior Army," Section Two:
"World-Honored One!

Regarding the five aggregates—which are like a dream, like an echo, like a reflection in light, like a mirage, like an image, like a magical illusion, and like a transformation—I neither know nor perceive any increase or decrease in them. How, then, can it be said that 'these are the five aggregates like a dream,' up to 'the five aggregates like a transformation'?"
Names such as the five aggregates, which are like a dream, abide nowhere, nor do they not abide.

Why is this? Because the referents of the five aggregates, which are like a dream, do not exist; therefore, names such as the five aggregates, which are like a dream, abide nowhere, nor do they not abide.
“World-Honored One!

Regarding that which is secluded, tranquil, without arising or ceasing, without defilement or purity, free from all conceptual proliferation—namely, suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the reality-limit, equality, the nature of transcendence, the fixedness of dharmas, and the stability of dharmas—I neither know nor perceive any increase or decrease therein. How, then, could it be said that ‘this is seclusion’ up to ‘this is the stability of dharmas’?”
Terms such as "detachment" and so forth neither abide anywhere nor do they not abide.
Why is this? Because the meaning of detachment and so forth is non-existent, terms such as "detachment" have no place of abiding whatsoever, nor do they not abide.
“World-Honored One!

Regarding dharmas such as wholesome or unwholesome, conditioned or unconditioned, with outflows or without outflows, mundane or supramundane, I neither know nor perceive any increase or decrease; how then can it be said that ‘this is wholesome’ or ‘this is unwholesome,’ and so forth?”
The names of phenomena such as wholesome and unwholesome neither abide anywhere, nor do they not abide.

Why is this? Because the referents of phenomena such as wholesome and unwholesome do not exist; therefore, the names of phenomena such as wholesome and unwholesome have no place of abiding whatsoever, nor do they not abide.
“World-Honored One!

Regarding dharmas of the past, future, and present, as well as dharmas that are neither past, nor future, nor present, I neither know nor perceive any increase or decrease therein. How, then, can it be said that ‘this is a dharma of the past, etc. or ‘this is not a dharma of the past, etc.’?”
The names of phenomena such as the past and the names of phenomena that are not the past, etc., neither abide anywhere nor do they not abide.

Why is this? Because the referents of phenomena such as the past and the referents of phenomena that are not the past, etc., are non-existent; therefore, the names of phenomena such as the past and the names of phenomena that are not the past, etc., have no abode whatsoever, nor do they not abide.
World-Honored One!
What is called the dharma that is neither past, nor future, nor present?
World-Honored One!
"It refers to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*),
World-Honored One!
Unconditioned phenomena refer to those dharmas that are without arising, without abiding, and without cessation."
“World-Honored One!

Regarding all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as well as the Bodhisattvas and the Saṅgha of Śrāvakas, in all the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I neither know nor perceive any increase or decrease. How, then, can it be said that these are all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as well as the Bodhisattvas and the Saṅgha of Śrāvakas, in the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges?”
Thus, all these names neither abide anywhere nor do they not abide.
Why is this? Because such referents do not exist, these names likewise have no place of abiding whatsoever, nor do they not abide.
“World-Honored One!
Regarding all the dharmas mentioned above, I neither know nor perceive any increase or decrease; how then can it be said that ‘this is a bodhisattva mahāsattva’ and ‘this is the prajñāpāramitā’?”
“Blessed One!

Since I neither know nor apprehend either the bodhisattva mahāsattvas or the perfection of wisdom, how am I to instruct and admonish the bodhisattva mahāsattvas with dharmas associated with the perfection of wisdom?”
“World-Honored One!
The names of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the name of the prajñāpāramitā are both without any place of abiding, nor are they non-abiding. Why is this?
Because these two meanings do not exist, these two names abide nowhere at all, nor are they non-abiding.
"World-Honored One!
Thus, through the combination of causes and conditions of all dharmas, there is the provisional name 'Bodhisattva Mahāsattva' and the provisional name 'Prajñāpāramitā'."
These two conventional designations cannot be expressed within the aggregates, bases, and elements; they cannot be expressed even among the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
They cannot be expressed within the five aggregates that are like a dream, nor can they be expressed even within the five aggregates that are like a magical creation.

They cannot be expressed within suchness, seclusion, tranquility, and so forth; they cannot be expressed even among all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as well as the Bodhisattvas and the Saṅgha of Śrāvakas, throughout as many Buddha-worlds in the ten directions as there are sands in the Ganges.
Why is this? Because, as previously stated, the increase or decrease of all dharmas is neither knowable nor obtainable.
"World-Honored One! [he said.]

As has been explained above, the names of the five aggregates and so forth cannot be designated as having any location; likewise, the name "Bodhisattva Mahāsattva" and the name "Prajñāpāramitā" also cannot be designated as having any location.

In this way, names such as "dream" and so forth cannot be designated anywhere; names such as "space" cannot be designated anywhere; names such as "earth, water, fire, and wind" cannot be designated anywhere; names such as "morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation" cannot be designated anywhere; names such as "stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, arhat, pratyekabuddha, and Tathāgata," as well as their respective dharmas, cannot be designated anywhere; names such as "wholesome and unwholesome," "permanent and impermanent," "pleasure and suffering," "self and non-self," "detachment and non-detachment," "quiescence and non-quiescence," and so forth—whether existent or non-existent—all such names cannot be designated anywhere. Likewise, the name "bodhisattva-mahāsattva" and the name "prajñāpāramitā" also cannot be designated anywhere.
Why is this so? Because all such names neither abide anywhere, nor do they not abide. Why is that?
Since these various meanings do not exist, these various names have no place of abiding whatsoever, nor are they non-abiding.
"World-Honored One!

Based on this meaning, I say that regarding the dharmas, neither increase nor decrease can be known or attained. How then can it be said, 'this is named a bodhisattva-mahāsattva' or 'this is named the prajñāpāramitā'?"

“Blessed One! Since I neither know nor have attained either the meaning or the names of these two, how am I to instruct and admonish the bodhisattva mahāsattvas with dharmas associated with the perfection of wisdom?”
"For this reason, if I were to instruct and admonish the bodhisattva mahāsattvas with such a teaching, I would feel regret.
World-Honored One!

If, when hearing the *prajñāpāramitā* being proclaimed through such characteristics, a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s mind does not sink, nor does it feel sorrow or regret; if their mind is not startled, alarmed, or terrified, one should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has certainly already dwelt in the stage of non-retrogression, dwelling by means of the skillful means of non-dwelling."

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they should not abide in form (*rūpa*) up to consciousness (*vijñāna*); they should not abide in the sense-base of the eye (*cakṣur-āyatana*) up to the sense-base of the mind (*mano-āyatana*); they should not abide in the sense-base of forms (*rūpa-āyatana*) up to the sense-base of phenomena (*dharma-āyatana*); they should not abide in the element of the eye (*cakṣurdhātu*) up to the element of the mind (*manodhātu*); they should not abide in the element of forms (*rūpadhātu*) up to the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); they should not abide in the element of eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) up to the element of mind-consciousness (*manovijñānadhātu*); they should not abide in eye-contact (*cakṣuḥsaṃsparśa*) up to mind-contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*); they should not abide in the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition; they should not abide in the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*) up to the consciousness element (*vijñānadhātu*); and they should not abide in ignorance (*avidyā*) up to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*)."
Why is this? World-Honored One!
Form is empty of the nature of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

World-Honored One! This form is not form, it is empty; this emptiness of form is not form. Form is not separate from emptiness, and emptiness is not separate from form. Form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself form. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.

For this reason, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should not abide in form, nor even in consciousness; it should be understood that the same applies up to old age and death.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,

when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they should not abide in the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha."
Why is this? World-Honored One!
The four foundations of mindfulness are empty of the intrinsic nature of the four foundations of mindfulness.
World-Honored One!

These four foundations of mindfulness are empty of the four foundations of mindfulness; this emptiness of the four foundations of mindfulness is not the four foundations of mindfulness. The four foundations of mindfulness are not separate from emptiness, and emptiness is not separate from the four foundations of mindfulness. The four foundations of mindfulness are themselves emptiness, and emptiness is itself the four foundations of mindfulness.

For this reason, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they should not abide in the four foundations of mindfulness; one should know that the same applies up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should not abide in the perfection of giving, up to and including the perfection of wisdom."
Why is this? World-Honored One!
The perfection of giving is empty of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of giving.

"Bhagavān! This perfection of giving is not empty of the perfection of giving; the emptiness of the perfection of giving is not the perfection of giving. The perfection of giving is not separate from emptiness, and emptiness is not separate from the perfection of giving. The perfection of giving is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself the perfection of giving."

For this reason, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should not abide in the perfection of generosity; it should be understood that the same applies up to the perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,

when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they should not abide in syllables, nor should they abide in that which is conveyed by syllables— whether conveyed by a single word, conveyed by two words, or conveyed by many words— and they should not abide in sublime supernormal powers (abhijñā)."
Why is this? World-Honored One!
All syllables are empty of the intrinsic nature of syllables.
World-Honored One!

These syllables are not distinct from the emptiness of the syllables; the emptiness of the syllables is not distinct from the syllables themselves. The syllables do not depart from emptiness, and emptiness does not depart from the syllables. The syllables are themselves emptiness, and emptiness is itself the syllables.

For this reason, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they should not abide in syllables; it should be understood that the same applies to the sublime supernormal powers (abhijñā) induced by those syllables.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,

when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should not abide in any phenomena as being either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, empty or non-empty, tranquil or non-tranquil, or secluded or non-secluded."
Why is this? World-Honored One!
All phenomena, whether permanent or impermanent, are empty of the nature of permanence and impermanence.
“World-Honored One!

These dharmas—both permanent and impermanent—are empty of being both permanent and impermanent; this emptiness of these dharmas as being both permanent and impermanent is not itself the state of being both permanent and impermanent. Dharmas that are both permanent and impermanent do not depart from emptiness, and emptiness does not depart from dharmas that are both permanent and impermanent. Dharmas that are both permanent and impermanent are themselves emptiness, and emptiness is itself dharmas that are both permanent and impermanent.”

For this reason, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they should not abide in any phenomena as being either permanent or impermanent; it should be understood that the same applies even to whether phenomena are detached or non-detached.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,

when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should not abide in the suchness of all phenomena, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, equality, the nature of transcendence from birth, or the limit of reality."
Why is this? World-Honored One!
The suchness of all dharmas is empty of the nature of suchness.
World-Honored One!

This suchness is empty of non-suchness; this emptiness of suchness is not suchness itself. Suchness does not depart from emptiness, and emptiness does not depart from suchness. Suchness is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself suchness.

For this reason, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should not abide in the true suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena; it should be understood that the same applies up to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they should not abide in any of the gateways of dhāraṇī or the gateways of samādhi."
For what reason?
World-Honored One,
the nature of all dharani-gates is empty of the nature of dharani-gates.
“World-Honored One!

This dharani-gate is empty of the dharani-gate; this emptiness of the dharani-gate is not the dharani-gate. The dharani-gate does not depart from emptiness, and emptiness does not depart from the dharani-gate. The dharani-gate is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself the dharani-gate.”

For this reason, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they should not abide in any of the gateways of dhāraṇī; it should be known that the same applies to the gateways of samādhi.

“Bhagavān! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom without skillful means, because they are entangled by the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self, their mind dwells upon form, and dwells upon feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.”
Because they dwell in this way, they apply effort toward form, and they apply effort toward feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

Due to this application of effort, they are unable to embrace the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, unable to train in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, unable to bring the profound *prajñāpāramitā* to fulfillment, and unable to accomplish the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*).

“Bhagavān! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom without skillful means, because they are entangled by the grasping for ‘I’ and ‘mine,’ their mind may even come to abide in all the doors of dhāraṇī and abide in all the doors of samādhi.”
Because they abide in this way, they apply themselves to all the gateways of dhāraṇī and apply themselves to all the gateways of samādhi.

Yet, due to such application, they are unable to embrace the profound perfection of wisdom, unable to train in the profound perfection of wisdom, unable to bring the profound perfection of wisdom to fulfillment, and unable to accomplish the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).
"Why is this? World-Honored One!
Form should not be grasped; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness should not be grasped."

Because form should not be grasped, it is therefore not form; because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness should not be grasped, they are therefore not feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Why is this? Because form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are all empty by their very nature,
World-Honored One.
One should not grasp at any of the gateways of dhāraṇī, nor should one grasp at any of the gateways of samādhi;

because one does not grasp at any of the gateways of dhāraṇī, they are not the gateways of dhāraṇī, and because one does not grasp at any of the gateways of samādhi, they are not the gateways of samādhi.
Why is this? Because all doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of samādhi are by their very nature empty.
World-Honored One!

That which is grasped as the complete cultivation and study of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* should likewise not be grasped; because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* should not be grasped, it would then no longer be the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is empty.

Thus, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should contemplate all phenomena through the emptiness of intrinsic nature. When contemplating in this way, the mind has no place of activity; this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s samādhi of non-appropriation.

This samādhi is subtle, sublime, vast, and immeasurable; it can gather infinite and unimpeded functions that are not shared with any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Even the omniscient wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*) it accomplishes should not be grasped; because such omniscient wisdom should not be grasped, it would not be omniscient wisdom.

Why is this? Because of internal emptiness, and because of external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the limitless, the emptiness of dispersion and non-dispersion, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of self-characteristics and common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.
Why is this? World-Honored One!
This knowledge of all modes is not attained through cultivation by grasping at signs.
Why is this so? All grasping at signs is affliction.
What are these signs?

That is to say: the characteristics of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; and so on, up to the characteristics of all dharani-doors and the characteristics of all samadhi-doors.
To grasp at these various signs is called affliction.

Therefore, one should not cultivate the attainment of the knowledge of all modes by grasping at signs; if one were to cultivate the attainment of the knowledge of all modes by grasping at signs, the brahmin Jayasena would not have had faith and understanding in the knowledge of all modes.
What is called the characteristic of that resolute belief?

It is to generate profound pure faith in the *prajñāpāramitā* and, by the power of superior understanding (*adhimukti*), to contemplate and examine the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*). This is done neither by taking signs (*nimitta*) as a means, nor by taking the absence of signs as a means, because both signs and the absence of signs are ungraspable.

"Although this brahmin Jayasena has turned toward the Buddha-dharma through the power of faith and understanding and is thus called a 'follower by faith,' he is nevertheless able to enter into the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) by means of the emptiness of intrinsic nature."

Having thus entered into realization, one does not grasp at the marks of form, nor grasp at the marks of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; indeed, one does not grasp at the marks of any of the *dhāraṇī* gates or the marks of any of the *samādhi* gates.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are empty of their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), and both the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*) are unapprehendable. Why is that so?

In this way, O Brahmin, one does not contemplate the knowledge of all modes by means of an internal realization; one does not contemplate the knowledge of all modes by means of an external realization; one does not contemplate the knowledge of all modes by means of an internal-and-external realization; one does not contemplate the knowledge of all modes by means of a realization through non-knowledge; one does not contemplate the knowledge of all modes by means of a realization through anything else; nor does one contemplate the knowledge of all modes by means of a realization through non-attainment.

Why is this? Because this brahmin Jayasena does not see the omniscient wisdom that is observed, nor does he see the prajñā that observes, nor does he see the observer, the basis upon which observation depends, or the time at which observation arises.

“Venerable Jitendriya, this brahmin does not contemplate the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) by means of internal form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; he does not contemplate the knowledge of all modes by means of external form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; he does not contemplate the knowledge of all modes by means of both internal and external form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; nor does he contemplate the knowledge of all modes apart from form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.”

Furthermore, one does not contemplate all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna) within all dharanī-doors and samādhi-doors; nor does one contemplate all-knowledge outside all dharanī-doors and samādhi-doors; nor does one contemplate all-knowledge both within and outside all dharanī-doors and samādhi-doors; nor does one contemplate all-knowledge apart from all dharanī-doors and samādhi-doors.
Why is this? Because whether internal, external, both internal and external, or apart from the internal and external, all are empty and cannot be apprehended.
Thus, through such gateways of detachment as these, the brahmin Jayasena conceived deep faith and understanding in the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (sarvajñajñāna).
Through this faith and understanding, one has no grasping or attachment toward any phenomena, because the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena cannot be apprehended.

Thus, O Brahmin, having attained faith and understanding in the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*) by means of the gateway of signlessness, one does not grasp at signs regarding any phenomena, nor does one contemplate signless phenomena, because both sign and signless phenomena are unapprehendable.
Thus, by the power of his resolute conviction, that brahmin neither grasps nor rejects any phenomena, for within the reality of the true nature of phenomena there is no grasping or rejecting.
At that time, that brahmin did not even cling to his own conviction, up to and including nirvāṇa itself.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are by their very nature empty and cannot be grasped.
"World-Honored One!..."
The prajñāpāramitā attained by all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is likewise: it has no grasping or attachment toward any phenomena, for it enables one to go from this shore to the other shore;
if there were even the slightest grasping or attachment toward phenomena, one would not be able to reach that other shore.

Therefore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do not grasp at any form, nor do they grasp at any feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are ungraspable.
This extends to not grasping any dharani-doors and not grasping any samadhi-doors.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are ungraspable.

Although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, with respect to all form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including all dhāraṇī-doors and samādhi-doors—whether collectively or individually—take nothing at all;

However, because the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path practiced through his original vows have not yet been perfected, and because the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha realized through his original vows have not yet been accomplished, he does not enter parinirvāṇa during that interval by means of non-apprehension of all signs.

“Although this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to fulfill the four applications of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path, and is able to accomplish the ten powers of a buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, they do not perceive the four applications of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path, nor do they perceive the ten powers of a buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.”

Why is this? Because these four foundations of mindfulness are not the four foundations of mindfulness, and so on up to the eight branches of the noble path which are not the eight branches of the noble path; and because the ten powers of a Buddha are not the ten powers of a Buddha, and so on up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha which are not the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, for all dharmas are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas.

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, although they do not grasp at or adhere to form, nor grasp at or adhere to feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, and so on up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, they are nonetheless able to accomplish all activities.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they should examine and contemplate with thorough discernment as follows:
'What is this perfection of wisdom?'"
For what reason is it called *prajñāpāramitā*? Whose *prajñāpāramitā* is it?
For what purpose is this *prajñāpāramitā* employed?
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they scrutinize and observe:
"If dharmas are non-existent and unapprehendable, then within this non-existence and unapprehensibility, what is there for the perfection of wisdom to investigate or interrogate?"
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"In this context, what dharma is called 'non-existent' and 'unobtainable'? Subhūti replied:

"It is because the dharma of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is non-existent and unobtainable, up to and including the dharma of the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā), which is non-existent and unobtainable; this is due to internal emptiness (adhyātma-śūnyatā), up to and including the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence (abhāvasvabhāva-śūnyatā)."
“Śāriputra! The dharma of form does not exist and cannot be apprehended; the dharmas of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not exist and cannot be apprehended.

The dharma of internal emptiness does not exist and cannot be apprehended, up to and including the dharma of the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, which does not exist and cannot be apprehended.”
The dharmas of the four foundations of mindfulness are non-existent and unapprehendable; likewise, up to the dharmas of the eight branches of the noble path are non-existent and unapprehendable;
the dharmas of the ten powers of a Buddha are non-existent and unapprehendable; likewise, up to the dharmas of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are non-existent and unapprehendable;
the dharmas of the six supernormal knowledges are non-existent and unapprehendable.
The dharma of suchness is non-existent and unobtainable; even up to the dharma of the limit of reality, it is non-existent and unobtainable.
The dharma of the stream-enterer is non-existent and unobtainable; the dharmas of the once-returner, the non-returner, the arhat, and the pratyekabuddha are non-existent and unobtainable.
The dharma of the bodhisattva is non-existent and unobtainable; the dharmas of all buddhas are non-existent and unobtainable.
The dharma of the knowledge of all modes is non-existent and unattainable,
because of internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence. “Śāriputra!...”

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom is able to conduct such thorough and discerning observation that when all phenomena are found to be non-existent and unobtainable, their mind does not sink, nor do they feel regret; and their mind is neither startled, terrified, nor afraid—then it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is never able to abandon the perfection of wisdom.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"By what reason do you know that these bodhisattva mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of wisdom are able to never abandon the perfection of wisdom?"

Subhūti replied: "When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he knows, as it truly is, that form is devoid of the intrinsic nature of form; that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are devoid of the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;

and he knows, as it truly is, that the perfection of generosity is devoid of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of generosity, up to and including the perfection of wisdom, which is devoid of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom."

...up to knowing, as it truly is, that the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are devoid of the intrinsic nature of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; up to knowing, as it truly is, that the limit of reality is devoid of the intrinsic nature of the limit of reality.
Śāriputra! By this you should know that those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of wisdom are able to never abandon the perfection of wisdom.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"What is the intrinsic nature of form?
What is the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?"
“...up to: what is the intrinsic nature of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)? Subhūti replied:

“The absence of intrinsic nature is the intrinsic nature of form; the absence of intrinsic nature is the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; up to: the absence of intrinsic nature is the intrinsic nature of the limit of reality.”

Śāriputra! By this you should know that form is devoid of the intrinsic nature of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are devoid of the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; and so on, up to the limit of reality, which is devoid of the intrinsic nature of the limit of reality.

Śāriputra! Form is also detached from the characteristic of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also detached from the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; even the limit of reality is detached from the characteristic of the limit of reality.

"Śāriputra! Self-nature is also free from self-nature; characteristics are also free from characteristics; self-nature is also free from characteristics; and characteristics are also free from self-nature.
At that time, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this, they will swiftly be able to accomplish the knowledge of all modes. Subhūti replied, "So it is!"
So it is! It is exactly as you have said.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this, they will swiftly be able to accomplish all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna).
Why is this? Śāriputra,
it is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas know that all phenomena are without arising or formation.
Śāriputra asked: "For what reason are all phenomena unborn and unestablished? Subhūti replied:
"Because form is empty, both its arising and its accomplishment cannot be apprehended;

because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, both their arising and their accomplishment cannot be apprehended; and so on, up to: because the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) is empty, both its arising and its accomplishment cannot be apprehended."

Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can train in the perfection of wisdom in this manner, they will gradually draw near to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*). Just as they gradually draw near to the knowledge of all modes, so too do they attain purity of body, purity of speech, purity of mind, and purity of marks.

As they thus attain these four kinds of purity—of body, speech, mind, and marks—so too do they not give rise to thoughts associated with greed, hatred, delusion, pride, flattery, deceit, stinginess, or dogmatic views.

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva never gives rise to thoughts of greed and the like, they ultimately do not fall into a woman’s womb; they always undergo miraculous birth and remain free from the perilous evil realms, except when it is for the sake of bringing benefit and happiness to sentient beings.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva travels from one buddha-field to another, making offerings to, revering, honoring, and praising the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; maturing sentient beings and purifying buddha-fields, until they realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek, never being separated from a Buddha.
Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain such meritorious benefits and advantages, they should study the perfection of wisdom and never abandon it for even a moment.
Chapter Nine: Modes of Activity (Ākārakāraṇa), Part One. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom without skillful means, if they practice with respect to form, they are practicing its signs; if they practice with respect to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, they are practicing their signs.

If they practice with respect to the permanence or impermanence of form, they are practicing its signs; if they practice with respect to the permanence or impermanence of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, they are practicing their signs.

If they practice with respect to the pleasure or suffering of form, they are practicing its signs; if they practice with respect to the pleasure or suffering of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, they are practicing their signs.

If one practices with the thought that form is "self" or "not-self," one is practicing its characteristic mark; if one practices with the thought that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness are "self" or "not-self," one is practicing their characteristic marks.

If one practices with the thought that form is "pure" or "impure," one is practicing its characteristic mark; if one practices with the thought that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness are "pure" or "impure," one is practicing their characteristic marks.

If one practices with the thought that form is "detached" or "not detached," one is practicing its characteristic mark; if one practices with the thought that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness are "detached" or "not detached," one is practicing their characteristic marks.

If one practices the tranquility or non-tranquility of form, one is practicing its characteristic; if one practices the tranquility or non-tranquility of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, one is practicing their characteristics;

if one practices the four foundations of mindfulness, one is practicing their characteristics, and so on, up to if one practices the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, one is practicing their characteristics.
If one forms the thought,
"I am practicing the perfection of wisdom," because there is something apprehended, this is practicing its signs.
If one forms the thought,
"I am a bodhisattva," because there is something apprehended, this is practicing its characteristic mark.
If one should think:
"There is one who is able to practice the perfection of wisdom in this manner; this is a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom."
"Because there is something apprehended, this is practicing its signs.
World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva makes such various distinctions as these, because they lack skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) in practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they are not practicing the perfection of wisdom."
Then, the Venerable Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom without skillful means, and if they dwell upon a conceptual conviction regarding form, they apply effort toward form;
if they dwell upon a conceptual conviction regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, they apply effort toward feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.”
Due to such application, one cannot be liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, grief, despair, and the suffering of future lives.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom without skillful means, and dwells upon the conceptual resolution of the sense base of the eye up to the sense base of the mind, then they apply themselves to the sense base of the eye up to the sense base of the mind;
if they dwell upon the conceptual resolution of the sense base of forms up to the sense base of phenomena, then they apply themselves to the sense base of forms up to the sense base of phenomena.
Because of such application, one cannot be liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, grief, despair, and the sufferings of future lives.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom without skillful means, and dwells in conceptualization and conviction regarding the eye-element up to the feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, then they apply themselves to the eye-element up to the feelings produced with eye-contact as condition; and likewise, if they dwell in conceptualization and conviction regarding the mind-element up to the feelings produced with mind-contact as condition, then they apply themselves to the mind-element up to the feelings produced with mind-contact as condition.
Due to such application, one cannot be liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, grief, despair, and the suffering of future lives.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom without skillful means, and dwells in conceptualization and conviction regarding the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, they then apply themselves to the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; likewise, if they dwell in conceptualization and conviction regarding the ten powers of a buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, they then apply themselves to the ten powers of a buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.
Due to their application [of effort], they are unable to be liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, grief, despair, and the suffering of future lives. "Śāriputra!

Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas lack skillful means when practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they cannot even realize the stages inhabited by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, much less realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment!"
Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in such a manner as this, you should know that he is one lacking skillful means;
because he has failed to accomplish various forms of skillful means, everything he undertakes cannot be successfully accomplished.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"How should one know that bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom with skillful means?"

Subhūti replied: "When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, because they possess skillful means, they do not engage with form, nor do they engage with the characteristics of form;
