they do not engage with feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor do they engage with the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness."
One does not practice regarding form as permanent or impermanent, nor does one practice regarding the mark of form as permanent or impermanent;

one does not practice regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as permanent or impermanent, nor does one practice regarding the marks of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as permanent or impermanent.
One does not practice the pleasure or suffering of form, nor does one practice the characteristic of pleasure or suffering in form;

one does not practice the pleasure or suffering of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does one practice the characteristic of pleasure or suffering in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
One does not practice with respect to form as "self" or "non-self," nor does one practice with respect to the characteristic of form as "self" or "non-self";

one does not practice with respect to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as "self" or "non-self," nor does one practice with respect to the characteristic of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as "self" or "non-self."
One does not practice regarding form as pure or impure, nor does one practice regarding the marks of form as pure or impure;

one does not practice regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as pure or impure, nor does one practice regarding the marks of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as pure or impure.
One does not practice the emptiness or non-emptiness of form, nor does one practice the mark of the emptiness or non-emptiness of form;

one does not practice the emptiness or non-emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does one practice the mark of the emptiness or non-emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
One does not practice with regard to form as having marks or being markless, nor does one practice with regard to the mark of form as having marks or being markless;

one does not practice with regard to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as having marks or being markless, nor does one practice with regard to the mark of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as having marks or being markless.
One does not practice with regard to form as having a wish or being wishless, nor does one practice with regard to the characteristic of form as having a wish or being wishless;

one does not practice with regard to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as having a wish or being wishless, nor does one practice with regard to the characteristic of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as having a wish or being wishless.
One does not practice with regard to the tranquility or non-tranquility of form, nor does one practice with regard to the characteristic of the tranquility or non-tranquility of form;

one does not practice with regard to the tranquility or non-tranquility of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does one practice with regard to the characteristic of the tranquility or non-tranquility of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
One does not practice the separation or non-separation of form, nor does one practice the characteristic of the separation or non-separation of form;

one does not practice the separation or non-separation of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does one practice the characteristic of the separation or non-separation of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
one does not practice the four foundations of mindfulness, nor does one practice the characteristics of the four foundations of mindfulness.
...up to and including not practicing the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, nor practicing the characteristics of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
"Śāriputra, you should know that it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom through skillful means."

Why is this? Śāriputra, this form is not empty of form; this emptiness of form is not form. Form is not separate from emptiness, and emptiness is not separate from form; form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself form. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this. This extends even to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), which are not empty of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; this emptiness of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha is not the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. The eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are not separate from emptiness, and emptiness is not separate from the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are themselves emptiness, and emptiness is itself the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Śāriputra! It is because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of wisdom possess skillful means that they are able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Śāriputra! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not grasp at practicing the perfection of wisdom, nor do they grasp at not practicing it; they do not grasp at both practicing and not practicing, nor do they grasp at neither practicing nor not practicing; they do not even grasp at this non-grasping.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"For what reason and by what causal conditions does this bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, not grasp at anything whatsoever within the perfection of wisdom?"
Subhūti replied: “Because the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom cannot be apprehended. Why is that? Because...”
Śāriputra! This is because the perfection of wisdom has non-existence as its intrinsic nature. Śāriputra!
For this reason, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing prajñā takes up or does not take up [phenomena], none of these constitute practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

Why is this? Śāriputra, because all dharmas take non-existence as their intrinsic nature, there is nothing at all to be grasped and nothing to which one may be attached; this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s samādhi of non-grasping and non-attachment toward all dharmas.
This samādhi is subtle, sublime, vast, and immeasurable; it can gather boundless and unimpeded functions, which are not shared by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can constantly abide in and never forsake such a sublime samādhi, they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"Do all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by constantly abiding in and never relinquishing only this one samādhi, or are there other samādhis as well?"

Subhūti replied, “It is not only by constantly dwelling in and never relinquishing this single samādhi that bodhisattvas swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening; there are, moreover, other samādhis as well.”
Śāriputra asked, "What are those other samādhis? Subhūti replied:
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess the *suvikrāntavikrāmin* samādhi,
the *ratnamudrā* samādhi, the *siṃhavikrīḍita* samādhi, the *candraprabha* samādhi, the *candraketudhvaja* samādhi,
the *sarvadharmasāgara* samādhi, the *mūrdhadarśana* samādhi, and the *dharmadhātuniyata* [samādhi].”
The *mudrā* samādhi, the *niyata-dhvaja-lakṣaṇa* samādhi, the *vajropama* samādhi,
the *sarva-dharma-mudrā-praveśa* samādhi, the *samādhirāja* samādhi, the *susthu-pratiṣṭhita* samādhi,
the *rāja-mudrā* samādhi, the *vīryabala* samādhi, and the *samantāvabhāsa* samādhi.
The samādhi of entering the words, the samādhi of entering the designations, the samādhi of observing the directions,
the samādhi of the seal of dhāraṇī, the samādhi of non-forgetfulness, the samādhi of the ocean-seal of the equal course of all phenomena,
the samādhi of pervading space, and the samādhi of the vajra-wheel.
The Samādhi of the Mark of the Victorious Banner, the Samādhi of the Mark of the Imperial Banner, the Samādhi of Accordance with the Luminous Treasury,
the Samādhi of the Lion’s Boundless Prowess, the Samādhi of Supreme Manifestation, the Samādhi of the Jewel Nature,
the Samādhi of Universal Illumination, the Samādhi of the Unblinking Eye, and the Samādhi of Abiding in the Signless.
...the samādhi of certainty, the samādhi of the stainless lamp, the samādhi of boundless light, the samādhi of emitting light,
the samādhi of producing brilliance, the samādhi of the pure seat, the samādhi of stainless radiance,
the samādhi of generating affection, the samādhi of the lightning lamp, and the samādhi of no...
The samādhi of exhaustion, the samādhi of possessing majestic radiance, the samādhi of being free from exhaustion,
the samādhi of subduing, the samādhi of dispelling, the sun-lamp samādhi, the moon-lamp samādhi,
the pure-light samādhi, the luminous-nature samādhi, and the wondrous-nature samādhi.
The Samādhi of the Mark of Wisdom, the Samādhi of Abiding Mind, the Samādhi of Universal Radiance, the Samādhi of Excellent Abiding,
the Samādhi of Jewel Accumulation, the Samādhi of the Seal of the Sublime Dharma, the Samādhi of the Equality of All Phenomena,
the Samādhi of Abandoning Dust and Affection, the Samādhi of Entering the Pinnacle of the Dharma, and the Samādhi of Drifting...
The Samādhi of Dispersion, the Samādhi of Discerning the Dharma-phrases, the Samādhi of the Equal Character of Syllables,
the Samādhi of Detachment from the Characteristics of Syllables, the Samādhi of Severing the Object of Cognition, the Samādhi of Non-alteration,
the Samādhi of Entering the Determined Character of Names, the Samādhi of Practicing Signlessness, and the Samādhi of Being Free from Obscuration.
The Samādhi of Darkness, the Samādhi of Endowed Practice, the Samādhi of Immovability, the Samādhi of Transcending Objects,
the Samādhi of Accumulating All Merits, the Samādhi of Resolute Abiding, the Samādhi of Pure and Wondrous Flowers,
the Samādhi of Endowed with Factors of Enlightenment, the Samādhi of Boundless Eloquence, and the Samādhi of No...
...the Samādhi of Waiting, the Samādhi that Transcends All, the Samādhi that Generates Sublime Contemplation,
the Samādhi that Dispels Doubt, the Samādhi of Non-abiding, the Samādhi of Equanimity toward the Single Characteristic,
the Samādhi that Induces Modes of Activity, the Samādhi of the Single Mode of Activity, and the Samādhi Free from All Characteristics.
the *mudrā* samādhi, the *nirupadhiśeṣa-sarvatraidhātuka-vivikta* samādhi,
the *sarvaprajñapti-vākpraveśa* samādhi, the *vimukta-ghoṣa-vyañjana* samādhi, the *jvalanolkā* samādhi,
the *viśuddhanetra* samādhi, the *animitta* samādhi, and the *sarvanimittapraveśa* samādhi.
The *mudrā*, the *samādhi* that does not delight in any suffering or pleasure, the *samādhi* of inexhaustible modes of activity,
the *samādhi* endowed with *dhāraṇī*, the *samādhi* that subdues all correct and erroneous natures,
the *samādhi* that enters into the silence of all speech, the *samādhi* free from opposition and compliance, and the stainless [samādhi].
The samādhi of clarity, the samādhi of possessing firmness, the samādhi of the pure light of the full moon,
the samādhi of great adornment, the samādhi of emitting all radiance, the samādhi of the equality of meditative concentration,
the samādhi of the principle of equality between the dustless and the dusty, and the samādhi of equality between the non-contentious and the contentious.
The samādhi of the principle of equality, the samādhi of being without a nest, without signs, and without attachment,
the samādhi of dwelling decisively in suchness, the samādhi of destroying misconduct of body,
the samādhi of destroying misconduct of speech, the samādhi of destroying misconduct of mind, and the samādhi like space.
The "Space-like Unstained and Unattached Samādhi.
Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly dwells in and does not abandon such samādhis as these, they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Śāriputra! Furthermore, there are other immeasurable and innumerable gates of samādhi and gates of dhāraṇī; if a bodhisattva mahāsattva can constantly and skillfully train in them, they will also swiftly realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek.
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in these samādhis, you should know that they have already received the prophecy of enlightenment from the Buddhas of the past, and they also receive the prophecy from the Buddhas of the ten directions in the present."
Śāriputra! Although this bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in these samādhis, he does not perceive these samādhis, nor does he become attached to them. Furthermore, he does not think:
"I have entered these samādhis," "I am now entering these samādhis," or "I shall enter these samādhis; it is only I who can enter them, and not others."
"In this way, all such discursive thoughts and conceptualizations do not arise for him.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"Is it certain that there are distinct bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who abide in these samādhis and have already received the prediction of enlightenment from the Buddhas of the past and present?"
Subhūti replied, "No, Śāriputra!"
Why is this? Śāriputra,
the perfection of wisdom is not different from samādhi, and samādhi is not different from the perfection of wisdom.
The bodhisattva mahāsattva is not different from the perfection of wisdom and samādhi, and the perfection of wisdom and samādhi are not different from the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
The perfection of wisdom is itself samādhi, and samādhi is itself the perfection of wisdom.
The bodhisattva mahāsattva is himself the perfection of wisdom and samādhi, and the perfection of wisdom and samādhi are themselves the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Why is this? Because the nature of all phenomena is equal.
*The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll 409.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle Four Hundred Thirteen.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.
The Second Part of Chapter Nine: The Analysis of Characteristics. At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

"If samādhi is not different from the bodhisattva mahāsattva, and the bodhisattva mahāsattva is not different from samādhi—if samādhi is itself the bodhisattva mahāsattva, and the bodhisattva mahāsattva is himself samādhi—and if it is likewise with respect to the prajñāpāramitā, how then do the bodhisattva mahāsattvas truly understand all phenomena as they really are and enter into samādhi?"
Subhūti replied, "When a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters into various meditative concentrations, he does not form this thought:
'Relying upon the equality of all phenomena, I have realized such and such a samādhi.'"

For this reason, although bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter into such and such samādhis by relying on the equality of all phenomena, they do not form conceptualizations or interpretations regarding the equality of all phenomena or those samādhis themselves.

Why is this? Śāriputra, because all phenomena, all meditative concentrations, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, and the prajñāpāramitā are all non-existent; within that which is non-existent, there is no possibility for conceptualization or understanding to arise.
At that time, the Bhagavat praised Subhūti, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
It is as you have said.

Therefore, I declare that among the assembly of śrāvakas who dwell in the concentration of non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*), you are the foremost; for this reason, my statement is consistent with the meaning, as there is no conflict within the state of equality.

"Subhūti! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) should train in this way; those who wish to train in the perfections of meditative concentration (dhyāna), diligence (vīrya), patience (kṣānti), ethical discipline (śīla), and generosity (dāna) should train in this way; those who wish to train in the four applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) up to the eightfold noble path (āryāṣṭāṅgamārga) should train in this way; and likewise, those who wish to train in the ten powers of a Buddha (buddhabala) up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇikabuddhadharma) should train in this way."
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, is he training correctly in the perfection of wisdom?”
“...and even for the sake of correctly training in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha? The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!”

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they are training correctly in the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension; and so on, up to training correctly in the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha by means of non-apprehension.
Then, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, does he train in the perfection of wisdom by taking non-apprehension as his skillful means?"
“...up to and including training in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method?
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!...”

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they train in the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, and so on, up to training in the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method.
Śāriputra said: "Regarding 'that which is unobtainable,' what is it that cannot be obtained?
The Buddha said:
“Śāriputra! The self is unapprehendable, up to and including the seer, because they are ultimately pure;
the aggregates, sense bases, and elements are unapprehendable, because they are ultimately pure.”
Ignorance is unapprehendable, up to and including old age and death, because they are ultimately pure;
the Four Noble Truths are unapprehendable, because they are ultimately pure;
the realms of desire, form, and formlessness are unapprehendable, because they are ultimately pure.
The four foundations of mindfulness are unapprehendable, up to and including the eight branches of the noble path, because they are ultimately pure;
the ten powers of a Buddha are unapprehendable, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, because they are ultimately pure;
the perfection of generosity is unapprehendable, up to and including the perfection of wisdom, because they are ultimately pure.
The stream-enterer is unapprehendable, up to and including the arhat, because they are ultimately pure;
the pratyekabuddha is unapprehendable, because he is ultimately pure;
the bodhisattva is unapprehendable, and the Tathāgata is unapprehendable, because they are ultimately pure.
Śāriputra said: “World-Honored One,
what is the meaning of that which you have described as ultimate purity?”
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!

That all dharmas are neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, neither emerging nor submerging, and neither attained nor conditioned— this is what is called the meaning of ultimate purity.”
Then, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, in what dharma is he training?
The Buddha said:
“Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they train in nothing at all regarding any phenomena. Why is that?
"Śāriputra! All phenomena do not exist in the manner that foolish, ordinary worldlings grasp them; one should train within this. Śāriputra said:
“If that is so, how do all phenomena exist?
The Buddha said:
“All phenomena exist in the manner of non-existence; if one cannot thoroughly comprehend such phenomena as being non-existent, this is called ignorance.”
Śāriputra asked: "What dharma is non-existent, such that failing to comprehend it is called ignorance?
The Buddha said:
“Śāriputra! Form does not exist;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not exist, because of internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.

In this same way, up to the four foundations of mindfulness do not exist, and even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha do not exist, because of internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.”
Śāriputra! If foolish ordinary beings cannot penetrate such dharmas that are non-existent, this is called ignorance (*avidyā*).

Driven by the power of ignorance and craving, they conceptually cling to the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism; consequently, failing to know or see the non-existent nature of all dharmas, they differentiate among those dharmas.

Due to conceptualization, one becomes attached to form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, up to and including attachment to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. Because of this attachment, one conceptualizes all phenomena as having a nature of non-existence; consequently, one neither knows nor sees these phenomena.
Śāriputra asked: "Regarding what dharmas is there no knowing and no seeing?
The Buddha said:

"To not know and not see form; to not know and not see feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; and so on, up to not knowing and not seeing the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha."
"Because they neither know nor see all phenomena, they fall among the ranks of foolish commoners and are unable to escape.
Śāriputra asked: "From what are they unable to escape?"
The Buddha said:
"They will be unable to transcend the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm.

Because they cannot transcend the three realms, they will not accomplish the Dharma of the śrāvakas, they will not accomplish the Dharma of the pratyekabuddhas, they will not accomplish the Dharma of the bodhisattvas, and they will not accomplish the Dharmas of the Buddhas."
"Because the three vehicles cannot be accomplished, they are unable to have faith and acceptance toward all phenomena.
Śāriputra asked: "In what phenomena are they unable to have faith and acceptance?"
The Buddha said:

"They cannot believe in or accept the emptiness of form; they cannot believe in or accept the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; and so on, up to the emptiness of the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha. Because they do not believe in or accept them, they are unable to abide [in them]."
Śāriputra asked, "In what dharmas does he not abide?
The Buddha said:
"Śāriputra! They cannot abide in the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom; they cannot abide in the stage of non-retrogression up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha."
"For this reason they are called foolish ordinary beings (*bāla-pṛthagjana*), because they cling to all phenomena as having intrinsic nature. Śāriputra asked:
"To what phenomena do they cling as having intrinsic nature?"
The Buddha said:
"They cling to form as having an inherent nature; they cling to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as having an inherent nature;
they cling to the eye-base as having an inherent nature, and so on, up to clinging to the mind-base as having an inherent nature."
They cling to the nature of existence in the sphere of form, and so on, up to clinging to the nature of existence in the sphere of mental phenomena;
they cling to the nature of existence in the eye-element, and so on, up to clinging to the nature of existence in the mind-element;
they cling to the nature of existence in greed, hatred, and delusion, and they cling to the nature of existence in all various views.
"One clings to the intrinsic nature of the four applications of mindfulness, and so on, up to clinging to the intrinsic nature of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Is there any bodhisattva mahāsattva who, training in this manner, does not train in the perfection of wisdom and thus fails to accomplish the knowledge of all modes?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who train in this manner; they are not training in the perfection of wisdom and cannot accomplish the knowledge of all modes.”
Śāriputra asked, "What is this like? The Buddha said:

“Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva lacks skillful means and discriminatively clings to the perfection of wisdom, discriminatively clings to the perfections of meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity;
and discriminatively clings to the four applications of mindfulness, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.”

Due to this attachment, one also gives rise to attachment toward all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

For this reason, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who train in such a manner; they are not training in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and cannot accomplish the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā-jñāna*).
Śāriputra said: "When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, is it not certain that they are not training in the perfection of wisdom and cannot accomplish the knowledge of all aspects?"
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they are certainly not training in the perfection of wisdom and will be unable to accomplish the knowledge of all modes.”
Then, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice and study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), such that by studying this perfection of wisdom, when training in this manner, they are able to accomplish the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna)?”
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and studies the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor do they perceive anything up to and including all-aspect omniscience (sarvākārajñatā). When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and studies the perfection of wisdom in this way, this is the study of the perfection of wisdom; studying in this manner, they are able to accomplish the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).”
Why is this? Śāriputra, it is because they take non-apprehension as their means.
Śāriputra asked: "By means of the non-apprehension of what phenomena does this bodhisattva mahāsattva practice?
The Buddha said:

“Śāriputra! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of generosity, he takes non-apprehension of the perfection of generosity as his means; likewise, when practicing up to the perfection of wisdom, he takes non-apprehension of the perfection of wisdom as his means; even when seeking awakening, he takes non-apprehension of awakening as his means; and even when seeking the knowledge of all aspects, he takes non-apprehension of the knowledge of all aspects as his means.”

Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva thus trains in the perfection of wisdom, this is training in the perfection of wisdom; when training in this manner, they are able to accomplish the knowledge of all modes.
Śāriputra asked: "When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by means of what non-apprehension does he employ skillful means?"
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and studies the perfection of wisdom, they do so by means of the non-apprehension of internal emptiness, and so on, up to the non-apprehension of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.”
"By means of these causes and conditions, one will swiftly be able to accomplish the knowledge of all modes.
Chapter Ten: The Parable of Illusion (The Second Part) At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Suppose someone were to ask:

"If there were a phantom being who could study the perfection of wisdom, up to and including the ability to study the perfection of generosity, would that being be able to accomplish the knowledge of all modes?"

If there were a phantom being who could train in the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including training in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, would that being be able to accomplish the knowledge of all modes?
"If I were to receive this question, how should I answer it?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"I shall now question you; answer as you see fit."
"Subhūti! What do you think?
Is form different from an illusion?"
“Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness different from an illusion? Subhūti replied, “No!”
“World-Honored One!
“Sudhana! What do you think?”
Is the eye-base different from an illusion?
And so on, up to: is the mind-base different from an illusion?
Is the form-base different from an illusion?
“...up to: Is the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana) different from an illusion? Subhūti replied, “No!”
“World-Honored One!
“Subhūti! What do you think?”
Is the eye-element different from an illusion?
And so on, up to: is the mind-element different from an illusion?
Is the form-element different from an illusion?
"Is the dharma-dhātu different from an illusion?
Is the eye-consciousness-element different from an illusion?
And so on, up to: is the mind-consciousness-element different from an illusion?"
Is eye-contact different from an illusion?
And so on, up to: Is mind-contact different from an illusion?
Are the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition different from an illusion?
"Is there any difference between the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition and an illusion? Subhūti replied, "No!"
“World-Honored One!
“Sudhana! What do you think?”
"Are the four applications of mindfulness different from an illusion?
And so on, up to: are the eight branches of the noble path different from an illusion? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! " "Suvikrāntavikrāmin!"
What do you think?
Is the gate of liberation of emptiness different from illusion?
Are the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness different from illusion?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
“Subhūti, what do you think? Is the perfection of generosity different from an illusion?”
“...up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—
are these different from an illusion? Subhūti replied, “No!”
“World-Honored One!
“Sudhana! What do you think?”
"Is the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas different from an illusion? Subhūti replied, "No!"
World-Honored One!
For what reason?
World-Honored One!

Form is not different from illusion, and illusion is not different from form; form is itself illusion, and illusion is itself form. In this same way, up to and including the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas, that is not different from illusion, and illusion is not different from the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas; the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas is itself illusion, and illusion is itself the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas.
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin, what do you think?”
"Is there defilement or purification in that which is like an illusion? Subhūti replied, "No!"
“World-Honored One!
“Sudhana! What do you think?”
“Does an illusion have arising or cessation? Subhūti replied, “No!”
“World-Honored One!
“Sudhana! What do you think?”
If a phenomenon is neither defiled nor purified, and neither arises nor ceases, can such a phenomenon study the perfection of wisdom and accomplish the knowledge of all modes?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does one give rise to a notion,
a conceptualization, a designation, a verbal expression, or a conventional name for a bodhisattva mahāsattva within the five aggregates?”
Subhūti replied, “So it is, World-Honored One!”
“Subhūti, what do you think? Regarding that which arises as a perception,
a conceptualization, a designation, a verbal expression, or a conventional establishment within the five aggregates— does it have arising and ceasing, or does it have affliction and purification?”
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
“Subhūti, what do you think? If a dharma is without perception,

without conceptualization, without designation, without verbal expression, without conventional names, without body or bodily action, without speech or vocal action, without mind or mental action, without affliction or purification, and without arising or ceasing— could such a dharma study the perfection of wisdom and accomplish the knowledge of all aspects?”
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, employing the method of non-apprehension, trains in this profound perfection of wisdom, they will swiftly be able to accomplish all-knowledge.”
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should constantly train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) like an illusory person.”
For what reason?
World-Honored One!
You should know that the illusory person is none other than the five aggregates.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Can the five aggregates, which are like an illusion, study the perfection of wisdom and thereby accomplish the knowledge of all modes?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
Why is this? World-Honored One!
The five aggregates, which are like an illusion, have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, because an intrinsic nature of non-existence cannot be apprehended.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Can the five aggregates, when they are like a dream, study the perfection of wisdom and thereby accomplish the knowledge of all modes?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
Why is this? World-Honored One!
The five aggregates, like a dream, have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, because an intrinsic nature of non-existence cannot be apprehended.
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin, what do you think?”

If the five aggregates are like an echo, like a reflection in light, like an image, like a mirage, like a flower in the sky, like a magical transformation, and like a city of Gandharvas, can one who trains in the perfection of wisdom attain the realization of the knowledge of all modes?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
Why is this so? World-Honored One!
Because the five aggregates—from an echo up to a city of Gandharvas—have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, and that intrinsic nature of non-existence cannot be apprehended.
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin, what do you think?”
“Are the five aggregates, such as the illusory one,
each distinct in nature? Subhūti replied, “No!”
World-Honored One!
For what reason?
World-Honored One!
Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that are like illusions are precisely form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that are like dreams.

The five aggregates that are like illusions are precisely the six sense bases that are like illusions; the six sense bases that are like illusions are precisely the five aggregates that are like illusions.
"All these are likewise unapprehendable because of internal emptiness, and so on, up to being unapprehendable because of the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have newly set out in the Mahāyāna hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, will their minds not be startled, terrified, or afraid?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have newly set out in the Great Vehicle practice the perfection of wisdom, if they lack skillful means and are not sustained by virtuous friends, their minds will be startled, terrified, and frightened upon hearing this profound perfection of wisdom being taught.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Which bodhisattva mahāsattvas, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, possess skillful means such that, upon hearing this teaching of the profound perfection of wisdom, their minds are not startled, not terrified, and not afraid?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, with a mind directed toward the knowledge of all modes, they observe that the mark of impermanence in form is unapprehendable, and they observe that the marks of impermanence in feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also unapprehendable;

they observe that the mark of suffering in form is unapprehendable, and they observe that the marks of suffering in feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also unapprehendable."

One contemplates that the characteristic of selflessness in form is also unapprehendable; one contemplates that the characteristic of selflessness in feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness is also unapprehendable.

One contemplates that the characteristic of impurity in form is also unapprehendable; one contemplates that the characteristic of impurity in feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness is also unapprehendable.

One contemplates that the characteristic of emptiness in form is also unapprehendable; one contemplates that the characteristic of emptiness in feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness is also unapprehendable.

One contemplates form as signless, yet even the sign of signlessness cannot be apprehended; one contemplates feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as signless, yet even the sign of signlessness cannot be apprehended.

One contemplates form as wishless, yet even the sign of wishlessness cannot be apprehended; one contemplates feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as wishless, yet even the sign of wishlessness cannot be apprehended.

One contemplates form as quiescent, yet even the sign of quiescence cannot be apprehended; one contemplates feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as quiescent, yet even the sign of quiescence cannot be apprehended.
One cannot apprehend even the characteristic of detachment in form; one cannot apprehend even the characteristic of detachment in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Subhūti!

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses skillful means when practicing the perfection of wisdom, upon hearing such a profound teaching on the perfection of wisdom, their mind is not startled, not terrified, and not afraid.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having made this contemplation, further thinks:

'I shall, by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, for the sake of all sentient beings, teach that these five aggregates have the characteristic of impermanence which is also unapprehendable; likewise, the characteristics of suffering, non-self, impurity, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, tranquility, and detachment are also unapprehendable.'"
"Subhūti! This is the unattached perfection of giving practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when cultivating the perfection of wisdom."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they remain far removed from mental orientations associated with śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. They contemplate the characteristic of impermanence of the five aggregates, yet even that is unapprehendable; likewise, the characteristics of suffering, non-self, impurity, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, tranquility, and detachment are also unapprehendable, by means of the expedient of non-apprehension."
"Subhūti! This is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s unattached perfection of ethical discipline while practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, employing the skillful means of non-apprehension, they observe that such dharmas—namely, the characteristic of impermanence—are unapprehendable; likewise, the characteristics of suffering, selflessness, impurity, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, tranquility, and detachment are also unapprehendable. Being able to endure and find delight therein, their mind is neither startled, nor terrified, nor afraid.
"Subhūti! This is the perfection of patient endurance (kṣānti-pāramitā) without attachment for a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā).
Furthermore, Subhūti!"

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, with a mind directed toward the knowledge of all modes, they constantly contemplate that the five aggregates have the characteristic of impermanence, yet this too is unapprehendable; likewise, the characteristics of suffering, selflessness, impurity, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, tranquility, and detachment are also unapprehendable.

Although they take non-apprehension as their skillful means, they never abandon the mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes, and they constantly cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
"Subhūti! This is the unattached perfection of vigor of a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not employ mental orientations associated with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; they contemplate that the characteristic of impermanence regarding the five aggregates is unapprehendable, and likewise, the characteristics of suffering, non-self, impurity, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, tranquility, and detachment are also unapprehendable.

By taking non-apprehension as the means, one does not give rise therein to mental orientations associated with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor to other unwholesome, distracted states of mind that would obstruct unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Subhūti! This is the perfection of meditative concentration without attachment for a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they observe according to reality:
it is not because form is empty that form is empty; rather, form itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is form. It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
It is not because the eye-base is empty that the eye-base is empty; rather, the eye-base itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is the eye-base. This extends likewise up to the mind-base.
It is not that the sphere of form is empty because it is separate from emptiness; rather, the sphere of form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself the sphere of form.

This applies likewise up to the sphere of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*). It is not that the eye-sphere is empty because it is separate from emptiness; rather, the eye-sphere is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself the eye-sphere.

This applies likewise up to the mind-sphere (*manodhātu*). It is not that the form-sphere is empty because it is separate from emptiness; rather, the form-sphere is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself the form-sphere. This applies likewise up to the sphere of mental phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).

It is not because the eye-consciousness element is empty that the eye-consciousness element is empty; rather, the eye-consciousness element itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is the eye-consciousness element.

This applies likewise up to the mind-consciousness element. It is not because eye-contact is empty that eye-contact is empty; rather, eye-contact itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is eye-contact. This applies likewise up to mind-contact.

It is not because the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are empty that the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are empty; rather, the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition themselves are emptiness, and emptiness itself is the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition. This applies likewise up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition.

Because the four foundations of mindfulness are not empty, the four foundations of mindfulness are empty; the four foundations of mindfulness are themselves emptiness, and emptiness itself is the four foundations of mindfulness.

Thus it continues up to: because the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are not empty, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are empty; the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are themselves emptiness, and emptiness itself is the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
"Subhūti! This is the unattached prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti!"

In this way, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, because they possess skillful means, their mind is not startled, terrified, or frightened upon hearing such a profound teaching on the perfection of wisdom.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,

how is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, being sustained by virtuous friends, their mind is not startled, not terrified, and not afraid upon hearing this teaching of the profound perfection of wisdom?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Those who are good friends to the bodhisattva mahāsattvas are those who, employing the skillful means of non-apprehension, teach that the characteristic of impermanence in form is also unapprehendable, and teach that the characteristics of impermanence in feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also unapprehendable;

they teach that the characteristic of suffering in form is also unapprehendable, and teach that the characteristics of suffering in feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also unapprehendable."

To speak of the characteristic of selflessness in form is also unattainable; to speak of the characteristic of selflessness in feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is also unattainable.
To speak of the characteristic of impurity in form is also unattainable; to speak of the characteristic of impurity in feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is also unattainable.

To speak of the characteristic of emptiness in form is also unattainable; to speak of the characteristic of emptiness in feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is also unattainable.

It is taught that the mark of form being signless is also unapprehendable; it is taught that the marks of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness being signless are also unapprehendable.

It is taught that the mark of form being wishless is also unapprehendable; it is taught that the marks of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness being wishless are also unapprehendable.

It is taught that the mark of form being tranquil is also unapprehendable; it is taught that the marks of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness being tranquil are also unapprehendable.

It is said that even the characteristic of the detachment of form cannot be apprehended, nor can the characteristic of the detachment of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness be apprehended; furthermore, one is exhorted to diligently cultivate roots of goodness based upon this, not directing them toward the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but solely to seek the attainment of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
“Subhūti! This is what constitutes a virtuous friend for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!”

The spiritual friends of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are those who, employing the method of non-apprehension, teach that the characteristics of impermanence from the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) up to the mind-base (*mano-āyatana*) are also unapprehendable; and they teach that the characteristics of suffering, selflessness, impurity, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, tranquility, and detachment are also unapprehendable.

They likewise teach that the characteristics of impermanence from the form-base (*rūpa-āyatana*) up to the phenomena-base (*dharma-āyatana*) are unapprehendable, and that the characteristics of suffering, selflessness, impurity, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, tranquility, and detachment are also unapprehendable; furthermore, they encourage reliance upon these to diligently cultivate roots of goodness, ensuring they are not dedicated toward the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but only directed toward the attainment of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
"Subhūti! These are the virtuous friends of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"

The good friends of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are those who, employing the skillful means of non-apprehension, teach that from the eye-element up to the mind-element, the characteristic of impermanence is likewise unapprehendable; and they teach that the characteristics of suffering, selflessness, impurity, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, tranquility, and detachment are likewise unapprehendable.

They also teach that from the form-element up to the dharma-element, the characteristic of impermanence is likewise unapprehendable; and they teach that the characteristics of suffering, selflessness, impurity, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, tranquility, and detachment are likewise unapprehendable.

It is taught that even the characteristic of impermanence cannot be apprehended in the eye-consciousness element, up to and including the mind-consciousness element; likewise, the characteristics of suffering, non-self, impurity, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, tranquility, and detachment cannot be apprehended.

It is taught that even the characteristic of impermanence cannot be apprehended in eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact; likewise, the characteristics of suffering, non-self, impurity, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, tranquility, and detachment cannot be apprehended.

He teaches that the impermanent nature of all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including those produced with mind-contact as a condition, cannot be apprehended; nor can their nature of suffering, selflessness, impurity, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, tranquility, or detachment be apprehended. Furthermore, he exhorts them to diligently cultivate roots of goodness based upon these, not directing them toward the level of a Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha, but solely to seek the attainment of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
"Subhūti! This is what constitutes a good friend for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"

The spiritual friends of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas are those who, employing the skillful means of non-apprehension, teach that although the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path is unapprehendable; although the cultivation of the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—is unapprehendable; although the cultivation of the Buddha’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha is unapprehendable; and although the cultivation of all-knowledge up to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is unapprehendable—they nevertheless exhort one to diligently cultivate roots of goodness based upon these, not allowing them to be dedicated toward the level of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, but only directing one to seek the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
“Subhūti! These are the virtuous friends of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), is sustained by such virtuous friends, then upon hearing this profound perfection of wisdom being taught, their mind will not be startled, terrified, or frightened.”
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One,

how is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, due to a lack of skillful means, their mind becomes startled, terrified, and afraid upon hearing this teaching of the profound perfection of wisdom?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, employs the method of apprehending something as real, thereby departing from the mental attention directed toward omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), and practices the perfection of wisdom while having gain and reliance regarding that practice of the perfection of wisdom;

and if, employing the method of apprehending something as real, they depart from the mental attention directed toward omniscience and practice the perfections of meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity, while having gain and reliance regarding the practice of meditative concentration up to the perfection of generosity;”

Because they employ the method of apprehending something as an attainment, they depart from the mental engagement of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), and while contemplating the internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, emptiness of limits, emptiness of dispersion and non-dispersion, essential emptiness, the emptiness of self-characteristics and common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehension, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature within form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, they nevertheless find something to grasp and rely upon in their contemplation of the emptiness of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.

Because they employ the method of apprehending something as real, they depart from the mental attention directed toward the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*). They contemplate the emptiness of the eye-base up to the mind-base, and the emptiness of internal phenomena up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature;

yet, in contemplating the emptiness of the eye-base up to the mind-base, they have apprehension and reliance. Because they employ the method of apprehending something as real, they depart from the mental attention directed toward the knowledge of all modes. They contemplate the emptiness of the form-base up to the phenomena-base, and the emptiness of internal phenomena up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature;

yet, in contemplating the emptiness of the form-base up to the phenomena-base, they have apprehension and reliance. Because they employ the method of apprehending something as real, they depart from the mental attention directed toward the knowledge of all modes. They contemplate the emptiness of the eye-element up to the mind-element, and the emptiness of internal phenomena up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature; yet, in contemplating the emptiness of the eye-element up to the mind-element, they have apprehension and reliance.

Because they employ the method of apprehending something as an object, they depart from the mental attention directed toward the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*). They contemplate the emptiness of the form realm up to the dharma-realm, and even the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature (*abhāvasvabhāvaśūnyatā*);

yet, in contemplating the emptiness of the form realm up to the dharma-realm, they have apprehension and reliance. Because they employ the method of apprehending something as an object, they depart from the mental attention directed toward the knowledge of all modes. They contemplate the emptiness of the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element, and even the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature; yet, in contemplating the emptiness of the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element, they have apprehension and reliance.

Because they employ the method of apprehending something as an objective reality, they depart from the mental attention directed toward the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), and while contemplating the emptiness of eye-contact through to mind-contact, and the emptiness of internal nature through to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature, they find something to grasp and rely upon within that contemplation of the emptiness of eye-contact through to mind-contact;

because they employ the method of apprehending something as an objective reality, they depart from the mental attention directed toward the knowledge of all modes, and while contemplating the emptiness of internal nature through to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature regarding all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition through to all feelings produced with mind-contact as condition, they find something to grasp and rely upon within that contemplation of the emptiness of feelings produced with eye-contact as condition through to feelings produced with mind-contact as condition.

Because they employ the method of "attainment," they depart from the mental attention directed toward the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), yet they practice the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; in so doing, they have attainment regarding the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and they harbor self-reliance therein.

"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this way, because they lack skillful means, their mind becomes startled, terrified, and frightened upon hearing this teaching of the profound perfection of wisdom."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, why is it that, because they have been influenced by evil associates, their mind becomes startled, terrified, and frightened upon hearing this profound perfection of wisdom being taught?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"The evil friends of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are those who teach one to become weary of and recoil from the perfection of wisdom, or who teach one to become weary of and recoil from the perfections of meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity, saying: 'Alas!'"
"O men! You should not train yourselves in this. Why is that? Because—"

These six kinds of pāramitās were not spoken by the Buddha; they are fabrications created by those who compose verses. Therefore, you should not listen to them, nor should you master them, nor should you recite them, nor should you contemplate them, nor should you investigate them, nor should you explain or reveal them to others.
"Subhūti! This is what constitutes an evil friend for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"

The evil friends of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are those who do not explain the deeds of Māra or the faults of Māra; that is to say, there is an evil Māra who assumes the form of a Buddha and comes to instruct a bodhisattva to become weary of and detached from the six perfections, saying:
"O son of good family!..."
"Why do you cultivate these six perfections? Subhūti!
If one does not explain such matters as these to bring about awakening, you should know that this person is an evil friend to a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

As for the evil friends of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, they are those who do not explain the deeds of Māra or the faults of Māra—namely, when an evil Māra assumes the form of a Buddha and comes to preach and reveal to the bodhisattva the teachings associated with śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, such as the sūtras up to the *upadeśa*, analyzing and clarifying them so that [the bodhisattva] may focus exclusively on practicing and studying them."
“Subhūti! If one does not explain such matters as these to bring about awakening, you should know that this person is an evil friend of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!”

Regarding the evil friends of a bodhisattva mahāsattva: they are those who do not explain the deeds of Māra or the faults of Māra; that is to say, there is an evil Māra who assumes the form of a Buddha and approaches the bodhisattva, speaking these words:

"You are not a bodhisattva; you lack the mind of awakening (bodhicitta); you cannot abide in the stage of non-retrogression, nor can you realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) that you seek."
“Subhūti! If one does not explain such matters as these to cause awakening, you should know that this is an evil friend of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!”

The evil friends of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva are those who do not explain the deeds and faults of Māra; that is to say, there is an evil Māra who assumes the form of a Buddha and comes to speak to the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, saying:
"You should know this!..."
Form is empty, devoid of self and what belongs to self; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, devoid of self and what belongs to self.
The eye-base is empty, devoid of self and what belongs to self, and so on up to the mind-base, which is empty, devoid of self and what belongs to self.
The form-base is empty, devoid of self and what belongs to self, and so on up to the phenomena-base, which is empty, devoid of self and what belongs to self.
The eye-element is empty of self and what belongs to self, up to and including the mind-element, which is empty of self and what belongs to self;
the form-element is empty of self and what belongs to self, up to and including the phenomena-element, which is empty of self and what belongs to self;
the eye-consciousness-element is empty of self and what belongs to self, up to and including the mind-consciousness-element, which is empty of self and what belongs to self.
Eye-contact is empty and devoid of self and what belongs to self; likewise, up to mind-contact, it is empty and devoid of self and what belongs to self.

The various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition are empty and devoid of self and what belongs to self; likewise, up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition, they are empty and devoid of self and what belongs to self.

The four foundations of mindfulness are empty and devoid of self and what belongs to self; likewise, up to the eight factors of the noble path, they are empty and devoid of self and what belongs to self.
The perfection of generosity is empty of self and what belongs to self; even the perfection of wisdom is empty of self and what belongs to self.
The gate of liberation of emptiness is empty of self and what belongs to self; the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are empty of self and what belongs to self.
The ten powers of a Buddha are empty of self and what belongs to self; even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are empty of self and what belongs to self.
"What is the use of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Subhūti!
If one does not explain such matters to cause awakening, you should know that this person is a bad friend to a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

As for the evil friend of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, it is one who does not describe the deeds of Māra or the faults of Māra; that is, an evil Māra takes the form of a pratyekabuddha, comes to where the bodhisattva is, and speaks these words: 'Ho!'"

“Good son! In the worlds of the ten directions—east, west, south, north, the four intermediate points, above, and below—all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, śrāvakas, and bodhisattvas are utterly non-existent. You should have deep faith and acceptance in this matter; do not exert yourself in seeking to make offerings, but rather listen to the True Dharma and practice according to what you have heard.”
"Subhūti! If one does not explain such matters as these to cause awakening, you should know that this is an evil friend of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"

Regarding the evil friends of a bodhisattva mahāsattva: they are those who do not explain the deeds of Māra or the faults of Māra; that is to say, there are evil Māras who take the form of śrāvakas and come to where the bodhisattva is, causing [the bodhisattva] to feel deep revulsion for the mental engagement associated with omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), and causing [him] to take extreme delight in the mental engagement associated with śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
"Subhūti! If one does not explain such matters as these to bring about awakening, you should know that this person is a bad friend to a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"

The evil friend of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is one who does not explain the deeds of Māra or the faults of Māra; that is, an evil Māra may manifest in the form of a preceptor or a teacher and come to the bodhisattva’s dwelling, causing [the bodhisattva] to feel deep revulsion for the sublime practices of a bodhisattva—namely, from the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom—and further causing [them] to feel revulsion for the knowledge of all modes, namely, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

They are taught only to cultivate the three gates of liberation so as to swiftly realize the stage of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, rather than proceeding toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Subhūti!
If one does not explain such matters as these to cause awakening, you should know that this person is an evil friend of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

Regarding the evil friends of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva: they are those who do not explain the works of Māra or the faults of Māra; that is, there are evil Māras who assume the forms of parents and come to where the bodhisattva is, saying:
"Child!..."

"Son! You should diligently strive to realize the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship; this is sufficient to bring about your eternal departure from the great suffering of birth and death and to swiftly realize the ultimate peace and bliss of nirvana. Why then do you seek the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas?"

Those who seek bodhi must pass through immeasurable and innumerable great kalpas, circulating through birth and death to transform sentient beings; they give up their lives, sacrifice their bodies, and sever their limbs and joints—laboring in vain for themselves, who will bear your kindness? Whether you realize the sought-after bodhi or not!
"Subhūti! If one does not explain such matters as these to cause awakening, you should know that this is an evil friend of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"

The evil friend of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is one who does not explain the works of Māra or the faults of Māra; that is, an evil Māra appearing in the form of a bhikṣu comes to where the bodhisattva is and, using the attainment of something as a means, says that the characteristic of impermanence in form is truly existent and can be attained; he says that the characteristics of impermanence in feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are truly existent and can be attained.

He says that the characteristics of suffering, non-self, impurity, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, tranquility, and detachment in form are truly existent and can be attained; he says that the characteristics of suffering, non-self, impurity, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, tranquility, and detachment in feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are truly existent and can be attained.

Using the attainment of something as a means, they teach that the sense bases from the eye base up to the mind base possess the characteristics of impermanence, suffering, non-self, impurity, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, tranquility, and detachment, as if these were truly existent and obtainable;

using the attainment of something as a means, they teach that the sense bases from the form base up to the mental-object base possess the characteristics of impermanence, suffering, non-self, impurity, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, tranquility, and detachment, as if these were truly existent and obtainable.

Using the attainment of something as a means, they teach that the eye-element up to the mind-element possess the characteristics of impermanence, suffering, non-self, impurity, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, tranquility, and detachment as truly existent and obtainable;

using the attainment of something as a means, they teach that the form-element up to the dharma-element possess the characteristics of impermanence, suffering, non-self, impurity, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, tranquility, and detachment as truly existent and obtainable.

Using the approach of apprehending something as real, they teach that the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element possess the characteristics of impermanence, suffering, non-self, impurity, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, tranquility, and detachment as truly existent and obtainable;

using the approach of apprehending something as real, they teach that eye-contact up to mind-contact possess the characteristics of impermanence, suffering, non-self, impurity, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, tranquility, and detachment as truly existent and obtainable.

Using the approach of apprehending something as real, they teach that the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, possess the characteristics of impermanence, suffering, non-self, impurity, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, tranquility, and detachment, as things truly existent and obtainable;

using the approach of apprehending something as real, they teach that the four foundations of mindfulness, up to the eightfold noble path, are truly existent and obtainable, and cause others to train in them;

using the approach of apprehending something as real, they teach that the perfection of generosity, up to the perfection of wisdom, are truly existent and obtainable, and cause others to train in them.

Using the attainment of something as a skillful means, they teach that the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are truly obtainable, so that beings may practice and learn them;
using the attainment of something as a skillful means, they teach that the gates of dhāraṇī and the gates of samādhi are truly obtainable, so that beings may practice and learn them;
using the attainment of something as a skillful means, they teach that the five eyes and the six supernormal powers are truly obtainable, so that beings may practice and learn them.

Using the attainment of something as a skillful means, they teach that the Buddha’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha truly exist and can be attained, so that others may practice and study them.
"Subhūti! If one does not explain such matters as these to bring about awakening, you should know that this is an evil friend of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, is influenced by such an evil friend, their mind will be startled, terrified, and afraid upon hearing this profound perfection of wisdom explained."
Therefore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should carefully examine and skillfully distance themselves from all evil associates.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 410; The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra,
Fascicle 411.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Eleven: Similes, Part Two, Chapter Eleven: Similes. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is the meaning of the term 'bodhisattva'?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"The meaning of the term 'bodhisattva' is that it has no meaning."
Why is this? Subhūti!

Since both "enlightenment" (bodhi) and "being" (sattva) are non-arisen, and since even the principle of a linguistic term does not exist therein, the meaning of the absence of terms is the meaning of the term "bodhisattva."
“Subhūti, you should know this:
for example, just as the referent of the term ‘bird-tracks in the sky’ truly does not exist, so too the referent of the term ‘bodhisattva’ truly does not exist.

For example, just as the referents of the terms ‘dream-objects,’ ‘illusory phenomena,’ ‘mirages,’ ‘reflected light,’ ‘the moon in water,’ ‘echoes,’ ‘flowers in the sky,’ and ‘magical transformations’ truly do not exist, so too the referent of the term ‘bodhisattva’ truly does not exist.”
“Subhūti, you should know this:
just as the referential meaning of the *tathatā* (suchness) of all phenomena is in reality non-existent, so too is the referential meaning of ‘bodhisattva’ in reality non-existent.

Just as the referential meanings of the *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm), *dharmatā* (dharma-nature), non-falsity, immutability, *dharmatā*, *dharmaniyāmatā* (stability of phenomena), and *bhūtakoṭi* (limit of reality) of all phenomena are in reality non-existent, so too is the referential meaning of ‘bodhisattva’ in reality non-existent.”
“Subhūti, you should know this:
just as the referential meaning of the term ‘form’ for a phantom person does not exist in reality, so too the referential meaning of the term ‘bodhisattva’ does not exist in reality;

just as the referential meanings of the terms ‘feeling,’ ‘perception,’ ‘volitional formations,’ and ‘consciousness’ for a phantom person do not exist in reality, so too the referential meaning of the term ‘bodhisattva’ does not exist in reality.”
“Subhūti, you should know this:
just as the referential meaning of the sense-base of the eye of a phantom person does not exist in reality, so too the referential meaning of ‘bodhisattva’ does not exist in reality;

just as the referential meanings of the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind of a phantom person do not exist in reality, so too the referential meaning of ‘bodhisattva’ does not exist in reality.”
"Subhūti, you should know this:
just as the referential meaning of the term 'form' for a phantom person does not exist in reality, so too the referential meaning of the term 'bodhisattva' does not exist in reality;

just as the referential meanings of the terms for sound, odor, taste, tangibles, and mental phenomena for a phantom person do not exist in reality, so too the referential meaning of the term 'bodhisattva' does not exist in reality."
"Subhūti, you should know this:

just as the referential meaning of the term 'eye-element' for an illusory person is in reality non-existent, so too the referential meaning of the term 'bodhisattva' is likewise in reality non-existent;

just as the referential meanings of the terms 'ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-element' for an illusory person are in reality non-existent, so too the referential meaning of the term 'bodhisattva' is likewise in reality non-existent."
"Subhūti, you should know this:
just as the referential meaning of the term 'form-realm' for an illusory person does not exist in reality, so too the referential meaning of the term 'bodhisattva' does not exist in reality;

just as the referential meanings of the terms 'sound,' 'odor,' 'taste,' 'tangible object,' and 'dharma-realm' for an illusory person do not exist in reality, so too the referential meaning of the term 'bodhisattva' does not exist in reality."
“Subhūti, you should know this:
just as the referential meaning of the term ‘eye-consciousness element’ for a phantom person is truly non-existent, so too the referential meaning of the term ‘bodhisattva’ is truly non-existent;

just as the referential meaning of the terms for the ‘ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements’ for a phantom person is truly non-existent, so too the referential meaning of the term ‘bodhisattva’ is truly non-existent.”
“Subhūti, you should know this:
just as the referential meaning of the eye-contact of an illusory person is truly non-existent, so too is the referential meaning of a bodhisattva truly non-existent;
just as the referential meanings of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact of an illusory person are truly non-existent, so too is the referential meaning of a bodhisattva truly non-existent.”
"Subhūti, you should know this:

just as the referential meaning of the various sensations produced with eye-contact as a condition for an illusory person does not exist in reality, so too the referential meaning of a bodhisattva does not exist in reality;

just as the referential meaning of the various sensations produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact as conditions for an illusory person does not exist in reality, so too the referential meaning of a bodhisattva does not exist in reality."
“Subhūti, you should know this:
just as the referential meaning of a phantom person’s ignorance is truly non-existent, so too is the referential meaning of a bodhisattva truly non-existent;

just as the referential meanings of a phantom person’s volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age and death are truly non-existent, so too is the referential meaning of a bodhisattva truly non-existent.”
“Subhūti, you should know this:
just as the meaning of the term ‘inner emptiness’ practiced by an illusory person is in reality non-existent, so too is the meaning of the term ‘bodhisattva’ in reality non-existent.

Just as the meanings of the terms ‘outer emptiness,’ ‘inner-and-outer emptiness,’ ‘emptiness of emptiness,’ ‘great emptiness,’ ‘emptiness of the ultimate truth,’ ‘emptiness of conditioned phenomena,’ ‘emptiness of unconditioned phenomena,’ ‘absolute emptiness,’ ‘emptiness of the limitless,’ ‘emptiness of dispersion,’ ‘emptiness of non-alteration,’ ‘emptiness of intrinsic nature,’ ‘emptiness of self-characteristics and common characteristics,’ ‘emptiness of all phenomena,’ ‘emptiness of the unapprehendable,’ ‘emptiness of non-existence,’ ‘emptiness of intrinsic nature,’ and ‘emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence’ practiced by an illusory person are in reality non-existent, so too is the meaning of the term ‘bodhisattva’ in reality non-existent.”
"Subhūti, you should know this:

just as the meaning of the terms for a phantom person practicing the four foundations of mindfulness is truly non-existent, so too the meaning of the term 'bodhisattva' is likewise truly non-existent.
