Just as the meaning of the terms for a phantom person practicing the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path is truly non-existent, so too the meaning of the term 'bodhisattva' is likewise truly non-existent."
"Subhūti, you should know this:

just as the referential meaning of the ten powers of a Buddha—even down to the activities of an illusory person—is in reality non-existent, so too is the referential meaning of a bodhisattva in reality non-existent.

Just as the referential meaning of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—even down to the activities of an illusory person—is in reality non-existent, so too is the referential meaning of a bodhisattva in reality non-existent."
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Just as the referent of the term 'Buddha' does not exist in reality, so too the referent of the term 'bodhisattva' does not exist in reality;

just as the referents of the terms 'feeling,' 'perception,' 'formative predispositions,' and 'consciousness' do not exist in reality, so too the referent of the term 'bodhisattva' does not exist in reality."
Just as the referential meaning of the Buddha’s sense bases (*āyatana*) is in reality non-existent, so too is the referential meaning of a bodhisattva in reality non-existent;
just as the referential meaning of the Buddha’s ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind bases is in reality non-existent, so too is the referential meaning of a bodhisattva in reality non-existent.
Just as the referential meaning of the Buddha’s sense-base of form is in reality non-existent, so too is the referential meaning of the Bodhisattva in reality non-existent;

just as the referential meanings of the Buddha’s sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are in reality non-existent, so too is the referential meaning of the Bodhisattva in reality non-existent.
Just as the referential meaning of the Buddha’s eye-element is in reality non-existent, so too is the referential meaning of the bodhisattva non-existent;
just as the referential meanings of the Buddha’s ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements are in reality non-existent, so too is the referential meaning of the bodhisattva non-existent.
Just as the referent of the term "Buddha" in the realm of form does not exist in reality, so too the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist in reality;

just as the referents of the terms for the Buddha’s realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena do not exist in reality, so too the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist in reality.
Just as the referential meaning of the Buddha’s eye-consciousness element is in reality non-existent, so too is the referential meaning of "bodhisattva" in reality non-existent;

just as the referential meanings of the Buddha’s ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness elements are in reality non-existent, so too is the referential meaning of "bodhisattva" in reality non-existent.
Just as the referential meaning of the Buddha’s eye-contact is truly non-existent, so too is the referential meaning of the bodhisattva truly non-existent;
just as the referential meanings of the Buddha’s ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact are truly non-existent, so too is the referential meaning of the bodhisattva truly non-existent.

Just as the referential meaning of the various feelings produced with the eye-contact of a Buddha as their condition does not exist in reality, so too the referential meaning of a bodhisattva does not exist in reality;

just as the referential meaning of the various feelings produced with the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact of a Buddha as their conditions does not exist in reality, so too the referential meaning of a bodhisattva does not exist in reality.
Just as the meaning of the term "Buddha" is in reality non-existent, so too is the meaning of the term "bodhisattva" in reality non-existent;

just as the meanings of the terms for the Buddha's practice, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, sensation, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age and death are in reality non-existent, so too is the meaning of the term "bodhisattva" in reality non-existent.
Just as the meaning of the term "Buddha" when practicing the emptiness of the internal is truly non-existent, so too is the meaning of the term "bodhisattva" truly non-existent.

Just as the meaning of the terms for the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, the absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the limitless, the emptiness of dispersion and non-dispersion, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of self-characteristics and common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature are truly non-existent, so too is the meaning of the term "bodhisattva" truly non-existent.
Just as the meaning of the terms for the Buddha’s practice of the four foundations of mindfulness is truly non-existent, so too is the meaning of the term "bodhisattva" truly non-existent;

just as the meaning of the terms for the Buddha’s practice of the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path is truly non-existent, so too is the meaning of the term "bodhisattva" truly non-existent.
Even as the meaning of the phrases regarding the Buddha’s practice of the ten powers is ultimately non-existent, so too is the meaning of the phrase "bodhisattva" ultimately non-existent;

even as the meaning of the phrases regarding the Buddha’s practice of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha is ultimately non-existent, so too is the meaning of the phrase "bodhisattva" ultimately non-existent.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Just as within the realm of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtadhātu*) the referential meaning of the 'unconditioned realm' (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*) is truly non-existent, and within the unconditioned realm the referential meaning of the 'conditioned realm' is likewise truly non-existent, so too is the referential meaning of 'bodhisattva' truly non-existent.

Just as the referential meanings of 'non-arising and non-ceasing,' 'non-activity and unconditioned,' 'non-formation and non-destruction,' 'non-attainment and non-abandonment,' and 'non-defilement and non-purity' are truly non-existent, so too is the referential meaning of 'bodhisattva' truly non-existent."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,

how is it that while the meaning of the phrases ‘non-arising and non-ceasing,’ ‘unconditioned and uncreated,’ ‘neither formed nor disintegrated,’ ‘neither attained nor abandoned,’ and ‘neither defiled nor pure’ truly have no existence, the meaning of the phrase ‘bodhisattva’ is likewise truly non-existent?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Just as form, up to and including consciousness, has no birth and no cessation, no activity and no conditioning, no formation and no destruction, no attainment and no relinquishment, and no defilement and no purification—such that the meaning of these terms truly does not exist—the meaning of the term 'bodhisattva' is likewise truly non-existent.

Just as the eye-base, up to and including the mind-base, has no birth and no cessation, no activity and no conditioning, no formation and no destruction, no attainment and no relinquishment, and no defilement and no purification—such that the meaning of these terms truly does not exist—the meaning of the term 'bodhisattva' is likewise truly non-existent."

Just as the bases of form up to the base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) are without arising and without cessation, unconditioned and uncreated, without formation and without destruction, without acquisition and without relinquishment, and without defilement or purification—such that their meaning and reality are non-existent—the meaning and reality of the bodhisattva are likewise non-existent.

Just as the eye-element up to the mind-element are without arising and without cessation, unconditioned and uncreated, without formation and without destruction, without acquisition and without relinquishment, and without defilement or purification—such that their meaning and reality are non-existent—the meaning and reality of the bodhisattva are likewise non-existent.

Just as the realms of form up to the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) are without arising or cessation, unconditioned and uncreated, without formation or destruction, without gain or loss, and without defilement or purity—such that the meaning of these terms is truly non-existent—the meaning of the term "bodhisattva" is likewise truly non-existent.

Just as the eye-consciousness realm up to the mind-consciousness realm are without arising or cessation, unconditioned and uncreated, without formation or destruction, without gain or loss, and without defilement or purity—such that the meaning of these terms is truly non-existent—the meaning of the term "bodhisattva" is likewise truly non-existent.

Just as the term and meaning of eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact, are without arising and without cessation, without action and without conditioning, without formation and without disintegration, without acquisition and without relinquishment, and without defilement and without purification—being in reality non-existent—the term and meaning of a bodhisattva are likewise in reality non-existent.

Just as the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, are without arising and without cessation, without action and without conditioning, without formation and without disintegration, without acquisition and without relinquishment, and without defilement and without purification—being in reality non-existent—the term and meaning of a bodhisattva are likewise in reality non-existent.

Just as from ignorance up to old age and death, there is no arising and no cessation, no conditioned activity and no unconditioned state, no formation and no destruction, no attainment and no relinquishment, and no defilement and no purification—such that the meaning of these terms is truly non-existent—the meaning of the term "Bodhisattva" is likewise truly non-existent.

Just as from the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, there is no arising and no cessation, no conditioned activity and no unconditioned state, no formation and no destruction, no attainment and no relinquishment, and no defilement and no purification—such that the meaning of these terms is truly non-existent—the meaning of the term "Bodhisattva" is likewise truly non-existent.

In this way, up to and including the ten powers of a Buddha and even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, their phrase-meanings are without arising or cessation, without action or formation, without accomplishment or destruction, without acquisition or relinquishment, and without defilement or purity; they truly do not exist at all. The phrase-meaning of "bodhisattva" is likewise truly non-existent.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! Just as the ultimate purity of the meaning of the terms for the four applications of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path does not exist in reality, so too the term 'bodhisattva' does not exist in reality.

Likewise, up to the ultimate purity of the meaning of the terms for the Buddha’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, which do not exist in reality, so too the term 'bodhisattva' does not exist in reality."

Just as the referential meaning of [the terms] from "self" up to "seer" does not exist in reality because there is no possibility for them to exist, so too the referential meaning of "bodhisattva" does not exist in reality;
just as at the time of sunrise the referential meaning of "darkness" does not exist in reality, so too the referential meaning of "bodhisattva" does not exist in reality;
just as at the end of an eon the referential meaning of "conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskāra*) does not exist in reality, so too the referential meaning of "bodhisattva" does not exist in reality.

Just as within the aggregate of pure ethical discipline of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, the referent of the term "immoral conduct" does not exist at all, so too the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist at all;

just as within the aggregate of tranquil concentration of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, the referent of the term "distracted mind" does not exist at all, so too the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist at all;

just as within the aggregate of clear wisdom of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, the referent of the term "wrong wisdom" does not exist at all, so too the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist at all.

Just as the referent of the term "bondage" does not exist at all within the aggregate of liberation of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, so too the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist at all;

just as the referent of the term "non-liberation-wisdom-and-vision" does not exist at all within the aggregate of liberation-wisdom-and-vision of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, so too the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist at all;
just as the referent of the term "darkness" does not exist at all within the great radiance of the sun, moon, and so forth, so too the referent of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist at all.

Just as within the light of the Buddha there is truly no such thing as the light of the sun, moon, stars, jewels, fire, medicinal herbs, or the various devas, so too the referent of the term "bodhisattva" is likewise truly non-existent.
"Why is this? Subhūti!

Whether it be awakening (bodhi), whether it be a sentient being (sattva), or the meaning of the term 'bodhisattva'—all these are neither associated nor dissociated; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness."

"Subhūti! Regarding all phenomena, bodhisattva mahāsattvas should diligently train themselves in the fact that they are not truly existent, being without attachment and without obstruction; they should realize this through perfect awakening."
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In regard to which all dharmas, which are not truly existent, should Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas diligently train themselves so as to be without attachment and without obstruction?"
“How should bodhisattva-mahāsattvas correctly awaken to all dharmas?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“All dharmas refer to wholesome dharmas and unwholesome dharmas; determinate dharmas and indeterminate dharmas; mundane dharmas and supramundane dharmas; outflowing dharmas and non-outflowing dharmas; conditioned dharmas and unconditioned dharmas; common dharmas and uncommon dharmas.”
"Subhūti! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should diligently train themselves in non-attachment and non-obstruction regarding the nature of all such phenomena;
bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should correctly realize that in reality, all phenomena are non-existent."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What are called the worldly wholesome dharmas?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Worldly wholesome dharmas refer to: filial piety toward one's parents; making offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas;
honoring and serving teachers and elders; meritorious actions consisting of giving; meritorious actions consisting of ethical discipline;
meritorious actions consisting of cultivation; merit performed together with nursing the sick; and merit performed together with skillful means."

The ten paths of wholesome action in the world; the perception of bloatedness, the perception of festering, the perception of lividness, the perception of bloody disfigurement, the perception of disintegration, the perception of being devoured, the perception of scattering, the perception of skeletons, and the perception of burning;
as well as the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments in the world.
They are: mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Saṅgha, mindfulness of ethical discipline, mindfulness of relinquishment,
mindfulness of the devas, mindfulness of peace, mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation, mindfulness of the body, and mindfulness of death.
“Subhūti! These are called the mundane wholesome dharmas.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“What are called unwholesome dharmas?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Unwholesome dharmas refer to killing living beings, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct; false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech; covetousness, ill will, and wrong view; as well as anger and resentment, concealment and vexation, guile and deceit, hypocrisy and harmfulness, envy, stinginess, pride, and so forth.”
“Subhūti! These are called unwholesome dharmas.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What are the determinate dharmas?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“All wholesome dharmas and unwholesome dharmas are called determinate dharmas.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What are called the indeterminate dharmas?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

That is to say: indeterminate bodily action, indeterminate verbal action, indeterminate mental action; the indeterminate four great elements; the indeterminate five faculties; the indeterminate five aggregates; the indeterminate twelve bases; the indeterminate eighteen elements; and indeterminate resultant phenomena.
"Subhūti! These are called the indeterminate dharmas.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“What are called the worldly dharmas?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“They are the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the ten paths of action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the twelve-linked dependent origination.”
"Subhūti! These are called worldly dharmas.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What are called the supramundane dharmas?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“They are the supramundane four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, and the five faculties.”
The five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eight branches of the noble path; the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known";

and the concentration with directed thought and sustained investigation, the concentration without directed thought and with only sustained investigation, and the concentration without directed thought and without sustained investigation.
The stages, whether they be clarity, liberation, mindfulness, correct awareness, or appropriate mental attention; whether they be the eight liberations,
the nine successive attainments, or internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness,
great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, the emptiness of the conditioned, and the emptiness of the unconditioned.
Emptiness, ultimate emptiness, boundless emptiness, emptiness of the non-dispersal of the dispersed, emptiness of intrinsic nature, emptiness of self and common characteristics,
emptiness of all phenomena, emptiness of the unapprehendable, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of intrinsic nature,
and emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; as well as the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four [grounds of self-confidence]...
The analytical knowledges and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Subhūti! These are called supramundane dharmas.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What are called ‘contaminated phenomena’ (sāsrava-dharma)?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"It refers to falling into the three realms—whether as the five aggregates, the twelve bases, or the eighteen elements; or as the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments."
“Subhūti! These are called the phenomena with outflows (sāsrava-dharma).
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What are called the untainted phenomena (anāsrava-dharma)?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“They are the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.”
"Subhūti! These are called the untainted dharmas.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“What are called conditioned phenomena?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“They are the phenomena bound to the three realms; namely, the five aggregates; or the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; or the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.”
"Subhūti! These are called conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"What are called unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Those phenomena that are without arising, without cessation, without abiding, and without alteration; the exhaustion of greed, the exhaustion of hatred, and the exhaustion of delusion; as well as suchness (*tathatā*), the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), non-falsity, immutability, equality, the nature of being free from birth, the fixed nature of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)."
“Subhūti! These are called unconditioned phenomena.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“What are called the shared dharmas?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“They are the four worldly dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers.”
"Subhūti! These are called 'shared dharmas,' because they are shared with ordinary worldlings.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“What are called the unique qualities?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“They are the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.”
"Subhūti! These are called the unshared dharmas, because they are not shared with ordinary beings. Subhūti!"

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should not cling to such phenomena that are empty of their own characteristics, because all phenomena are without conceptual differentiation.
"Subhūti! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should correctly awaken to all phenomena by means of non-duality, because all phenomena are entirely immovable."

"Subhūti! That all dharmas are non-dual and immovable is the meaning of the term 'bodhisattva'; that they are without conceptual differentiation and without attachment is the meaning of the term 'bodhisattva'."
"For this reason, the absence of a referent is the referent of a bodhisattva.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"For what reason is a bodhisattva further called a mahāsattva?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Because this bodhisattva shall become the foremost among the great assembly of sentient beings, he is further called a mahāsattva."
Subhūti said to the Buddha,
“What is called the ‘great multitude of sentient beings’ among whom the bodhisattva shall become the leader?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Those who abide in the lineage, the eighth-rank practitioner, the stream-enterer, the once-returner, the non-returner, the arhat, the pratyekabuddha, and the bodhisattva mahāsattvas from the first generation of the mind of awakening up to the stage of non-retrogression—all such as these are called the great assembly of sentient beings."
“Because a bodhisattva shall be the leader among this great assembly of sentient beings, they are further called a ‘mahāsattva.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“For what reason is it that such a bodhisattva is able to be the leader among this great assembly of sentient beings?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Because this bodhisattva has already generated a firm, vajra-like mind that is certain not to regress or be destroyed, he shall be able to act as the leader among the great multitude of sentient beings."
Subhūti spoke again:
"What is meant by the 'vajra-like mind' of a bodhisattva?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought:
'I shall now don the great armor of merit; within the vast wilderness of boundless birth and death, I shall destroy all enemies that are the afflictions for the sake of all sentient beings.'"
I shall universally dry up the boundless great ocean of birth and death for the sake of all sentient beings.
I shall relinquish all my bodies and possessions to bring great benefit to all sentient beings.
I shall, with an impartial mind, bring benefit, welfare, and happiness to all sentient beings.
I shall cause all classes of sentient beings to travel upon the paths of the three vehicles and proceed toward parinirvāṇa.
Although I shall deliver all sentient beings by means of the three vehicles, I shall not perceive even a single sentient being who attains extinction.
I shall realize that the nature of all phenomena is without arising and without ceasing, without purity and without defilement.
I shall practice the six perfections with a mental orientation associated solely with the knowledge of all modes.
I shall train in all phenomena to attain ultimate penetration and enter into sublime wisdom.
I shall penetrate the gateway of the single principle of all phenomena;
I shall penetrate the gateway of the dual principles of all phenomena;
I shall penetrate the gateway of the manifold principles of all phenomena.
"I shall cultivate and study various sublime wisdoms to penetrate the nature of all phenomena and bring forth supreme merits. Subhūti!
This is called the diamond-like mind of a bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in this mind by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method, they will certainly be able to become the foremost among the great assembly of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas give rise to this thought:

'Whatever sufferings and afflictions are experienced by all sentient beings within the realms of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and gods, I shall undergo them in their stead so as to bring them peace and happiness.'"
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas give rise to such a thought:

"For the sake of benefiting even a single sentient being, I shall undergo various kinds of heavy sufferings in the hells for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas, and through countless skillful means, I shall teach and transform them so that they attain nirvāṇa without remainder."

In this manner, proceeding in succession for the universal benefit of all sentient beings, he shall undergo various kinds of heavy sufferings in the hells for each and every one of them throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas; and for each one, he shall employ countless skillful means to teach and transform them, causing them to attain nirvana without remainder.

Having performed these deeds, they plant roots of goodness for themselves and, after further passing through immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas, fully cultivate and accumulate the provisions for awakening; only then do they realize the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
"Subhūti! Such a vow is also called the 'diamond-like mind' (*vajropamacitta*) of a bodhisattva.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in this mind by means of the skillful method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), they will certainly be able to become the foremost among the great multitude of sentient beings."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constantly give rise to the superior mind and the great mind; by virtue of this mind, they are certain to become leaders among the great assembly of sentient beings."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by the bodhisattva’s superior mind and great mind?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should give rise to this thought:

‘From the first production of the thought of enlightenment until the attainment of the knowledge of all aspects, I shall certainly not give rise to thoughts of desire, hatred, delusion, anger, resentment, concealment, vexation, flattery, deceit, envy, parsimony, hypocrisy, harmfulness, views, or pride; nor shall I certainly give rise to thoughts that seek the levels of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.’”
This is the superior mind and great mind of a bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in this mind by means of the expedient of non-apprehension, they will certainly be able to become a leader among the great assembly of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas give rise to a mind that is resolute and unshakable; by virtue of this mind, they will certainly become leaders among the great assembly of sentient beings."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by a bodhisattva’s unshakable mind?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should give rise to this thought:

‘I should always rely upon the mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), practicing and initiating all cultivated deeds and undertakings without arrogance or indolence.’”
"Subhūti! This is called the unshakable mind of a bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in this mind by means of non-apprehension as a skillful method, they will certainly be able to become the leader among the great assembly of sentient beings."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas universally give rise to a mind of genuine benefit and happiness toward all sentient beings. By virtue of this mind, they will certainly be able to become the foremost among the great assembly of sentient beings."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by a bodhisattva’s mind of genuine benefit and happiness?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should give rise to this thought:
‘I shall resolutely continue until the end of the future to benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings, acting as their refuge, island, and dwelling, never abandoning them.’”
"Subhūti! This is called the bodhisattva’s mind of true benefit and happiness.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in this mind by means of the skillful method of non-apprehension, they will certainly be able to become the foremost among the great multitude of sentient beings."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they are constantly diligent and energetic, loving the Dharma, delighting in the Dharma, rejoicing in the Dharma, and finding joy in the Dharma. By virtue of these causes and conditions, they will certainly become leaders among the great assembly of sentient beings."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
what is this 'dharma'?"
“How is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, always loves, delights in, and rejoices in this Dharma?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“As for what is called ‘Dharma,’ it refers to the fact that both form and non-form lack intrinsic nature; they are entirely unapprehendable, indestructible, and undifferentiable—this is what is called ‘Dharma.’”
To speak of "loving the Dharma" means to give rise to desire and aspiration for this Dharma;
to speak of "delighting in the Dharma" means to praise its merits;
to speak of "rejoicing in the Dharma" means to receive it with joy and faith.
"Delighting in the Dharma" means that regarding this Dharma, one yearns for it, practices it extensively, draws near to it, and cherishes it with affection. Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by employing the method of non-apprehension, they are always able to thus love the Dharma, delight in the Dharma, rejoice in the Dharma, and take pleasure in the Dharma without becoming conceited or arrogant; they will certainly become a leader among the great assembly of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, abiding in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, and cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will certainly be able to become the foremost among the great assembly of sentient beings."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, abiding in the vajra-like samādhi, and even abiding in the samādhi of liberation that is unattached, unconditioned, untainted, and like space—by virtue of these causes and conditions, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will certainly become a leader among the great assembly of sentient beings."

“Subhūti! By means of these and various other such causes and conditions, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas will certainly be able to become the leaders among the great assembly of sentient beings; for this reason, a bodhisattva is further named a mahāsattva.”
Chapter Twelve: Severing All Views, Part Two. At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"I, too, delight in using wisdom and eloquence to explain why these bodhisattvas are called 'mahāsattvas' on account of this meaning.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra, "Speak as you wish."
Śāriputra said: “World-Honored One!

Because bodhisattvas, through their skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), are able to proclaim the essential teachings of the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, causing them to sever the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-principle, the view of a living being, the view of a nourisher, the view of a person, the view of a *pudgala*, the view of a mind-born being, the view of a youth, the view of an agent, the view of an experiencer, the view of a knower, and the view of a seer—for this reason, they are called ‘Great Beings’ (*mahāsattva*).”
“World-Honored One!

Because bodhisattvas, through their skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), are able to proclaim the essential teachings of the Dharma for sentient beings, causing them to sever the views of permanence and annihilation, the view of non-existence, and the view of existence—it is by virtue of this meaning that they are called ‘Great Beings’ (*mahāsattva*).”
“World-Honored One!

Because bodhisattvas, through their skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), are able to proclaim the essentials of the Dharma for sentient beings, causing them to sever views regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), views regarding the bases (*āyatana*), views regarding the elements (*dhātu*), views regarding the truths (*satya*), and views regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), they are called ‘Great Beings’ (*mahāsattva*) by virtue of this meaning.”
“World-Honored One!

Because bodhisattvas, through their skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), are able to proclaim the essential teachings for the sake of sentient beings, causing them to sever views regarding the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), they are for this reason called ‘Great Beings’ (*mahāsattva*).”

Because bodhisattvas, through their skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), are able to proclaim the essential teachings for the sake of sentient beings, causing them to sever the views of maturing sentient beings, purifying buddha-fields, bodhisattvas, tathāgatas, awakening (*bodhi*), nirvāṇa, and turning the wheel of Dharma; for this reason, they are called *mahāsattvas*.
“World-Honored One!

Because bodhisattvas possess skillful means, they are able to teach sentient beings—using the method of non-apprehension—to permanently sever all views regarding phenomena; for this reason, they are called ‘mahāsattvas.’”
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti asked Śāriputra:

"If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able, for the sake of sentient beings, to proclaim the essential Dharma for the permanent severance of all views by employing the method of non-apprehension, for what cause and for what reason do some bodhisattvas, employing the method of apprehension, give rise to views of the aggregates, views of the sense bases, views of the elements, views of the truths, views of dependent origination, and even views of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; as well as views of maturing sentient beings, views of purifying buddha-fields, views of bodhisattvas, views of Tathāgatas, views of enlightenment, views of nirvāṇa, and views of turning the wheel of Dharma?"

Śāriputra said: “If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, lacks skillful means and takes ‘attainment’ as their means, giving rise to views regarding the aggregates up to the view regarding the turning of the wheel of Dharma—because that bodhisattva mahāsattva lacks skillful means, they will certainly be unable to take ‘non-attainment’ as their means to proclaim to all sentient beings the essential Dharma for the permanent severance of all views.”

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, possesses skillful means, they are able to teach sentient beings the essential dharma for permanently severing all views by employing the method of non-apprehension; such a bodhisattva mahāsattva will certainly not give rise to views regarding the aggregates and so forth.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I too would like to use my wisdom and eloquence to explain why bodhisattvas are called 'mahāsattvas' based on this meaning."
The Buddha said to Subhūti, "Speak as you wish. Subhūti replied:
“World-Honored One!

Because bodhisattvas, desiring to realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), give rise to the mind of enlightenment, the unequaled mind, and the mind not shared with śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—and yet do not even grasp at such a mind—it is for this reason that they are called ‘mahāsattvas.’”
Why is this? World-Honored One!

Because the mind of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) is truly without outflows (anāsrava) and does not fall within the triple world; the mind that seeks the knowledge of all modes is likewise without outflows and does not fall within the triple world. One should not grasp or cling to such a mind; for this reason, a bodhisattva is called a mahāsattva.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"In what way does a bodhisattva mahāsattva possess a mind that is unequaled and not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas?"

Subhūti replied, “From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, bodhisattva mahāsattvas do not perceive even the slightest phenomenon as having arising or ceasing, decreasing or increasing, or being defiled or purified.”

Śāriputra! If one does not perceive even the slightest dharma as having arising or ceasing, decreasing or increasing, being defiled or purified, nor does one perceive a śrāvaka-mind, a pratyekabuddha-mind, a bodhisattva-mind, or a tathāgata-mind.
Śāriputra! This is called the peerless mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, a mind not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; yet, bodhisattva mahāsattvas do not even grasp at or cling to such a mind.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not become attached to such a mind, then they should also not become attached to the minds of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and ordinary beings; nor should they become attached to the minds of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, up to and including the minds of the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha."
"Why is this? Because these various minds lack the nature of mind. Subhūti replied:
"So it is! So it is! It is exactly as you have said."
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

"If all minds, because they lack the nature of mind, should not be grasped or clung to, then form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness likewise lack the nature of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness and should not be grasped or clung to; and so on, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, which likewise lack the nature of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha and should not be grasped or clung to."
Subhūti replied, “So it is! So it is!”
"It is exactly as you have said. Śāriputra said:

"If the mind of omniscience is truly untainted and does not fall within the three realms, then the minds of all foolish ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and so forth, should also be truly untainted and not fall within the three realms."
"Why is this? Because all such minds are empty by their very nature. Subhūti replied:
"So it is! So it is! It is exactly as you have said."

Śāriputra said: "If it is because the intrinsic nature of such a mind is empty that it is truly untainted and does not fall within the three realms, then form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—even up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—should likewise be truly untainted and not fall within the three realms."
"Why is this? Because all such phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature. Subhūti replied:
"So it is! So it is! It is exactly as you have said."
Śāriputra said: "If phenomena such as mind and form should not be grasped because they lack the intrinsic nature of mind and form, then all phenomena must be equal and entirely without distinction."
Subhūti replied: “So it is! So it is!”
"It is exactly as you have said. Śāriputra asked:
"If all dharmas are equal and without distinction, why does the Tathāgata speak of various differences such as mind and form?"
Subhūti replied, “This is the Tathāgata speaking in accordance with worldly convention, not in accordance with the ultimate truth. Śāriputra said:

"If the mental and physical phenomena (*nāmarūpa*) of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas were all untainted (*anāsrava*) and did not fall within the three realms (*tridhātu*), then there would be no distinction between ordinary beings and noble ones, nor between bodhisattvas and tathāgatas."
Subhūti replied, “So it is! So it is!”
"It is exactly as you have said. Śāriputra asked:

"If there is no distinction between ordinary beings and sages, bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas, why has the Buddha taught that there are various differences among ordinary beings and sages, and among the great and the small?"
Subhūti replied, “This too is spoken by the Tathāgata according to worldly convention, not according to the ultimate truth (paramārtha), Śāriputra.”

When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), by means of the expedient of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), they neither rely upon nor cling to the great bodhicitta they have generated—the mind that is unequaled and not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. They neither grasp nor adhere to form or the formless, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*). For this reason, they are called mahāsattvas.
Chapter Thirteen: The Six Perfections, Part Two, Chapter Thirteen, Section One. At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I, too, would delight in using wisdom and eloquence to explain why it is for these reasons that bodhisattvas are called 'mahāsattvas' (great beings).
The Buddha said to Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra,
"Speak according to your own inclination."
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:
“World-Honored One!

Because all bodhisattvas universally seek to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, don the great armor of merit, set out upon the Great Vehicle, and ride the Great Vehicle, they are called ‘mahāsattvas.’”
At that time, Śāriputra asked Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva don the great armor of merit for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings?"
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said: “Śāriputra!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of generosity, they do not practice the perfection of generosity for the sake of benefiting or bringing happiness to only a few sentient beings; rather, they practice the perfection of generosity for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings.”

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of ethical discipline, they do not practice the perfection of ethical discipline for the sake of benefiting or bringing happiness to only a small portion of sentient beings; rather, they practice the perfection of ethical discipline for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings.

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of patience, they do not practice the perfection of patience for the sake of benefiting or bringing happiness to only a small portion of sentient beings; rather, they practice the perfection of patience for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings.

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of diligence, they do not practice the perfection of diligence for the sake of the benefit and happiness of only a few sentient beings; rather, they practice the perfection of diligence for the sake of universally benefiting and gladdening all sentient beings.

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of meditative concentration, they do not practice the perfection of meditative concentration for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to only a few sentient beings; rather, they practice the perfection of meditative concentration for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings.

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they do not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of benefiting or bringing happiness to a limited number of sentient beings; rather, they practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings.
"Śāriputra! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva dons the great armor of merit for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas don the great armor of merit; their aim to benefit and bring happiness to sentient beings knows no limits, and they do not form such thoughts as:
"I shall rescue this many sentient beings and cause them to enter the realm of nirvana without remainder, but I shall not cause that many sentient beings to enter;
I shall rescue this many sentient beings and cause them to abide in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, but I shall not cause that many sentient beings to abide therein."

Nevertheless, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas universally act to deliver all sentient beings, causing them to enter the realm of nirvana without remainder and to abide in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Śāriputra! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva dons the great armor of merit for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
The bodhisattva mahāsattvas form this thought:
"I shall personally fulfill the perfection of generosity, and I shall also cause all sentient beings to fulfill the perfection of generosity."
I shall personally fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline, and I shall also cause all sentient beings to fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline.
I shall personally fulfill the perfection of patience, and I shall also cause all sentient beings to fulfill the perfection of patience.
I shall personally fulfill the perfection of diligence and also cause all sentient beings to fulfill the perfection of diligence.
I shall personally fulfill the perfection of meditative concentration and also cause all sentient beings to fulfill the perfection of meditative concentration.
"I shall personally fulfill the perfection of wisdom, and I shall also cause all sentient beings to fulfill the perfection of wisdom.
Thus do the bodhisattva mahāsattvas reflect:

"Relying upon these six perfections, I shall personally abide in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, and practice the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha."

Furthermore, they cause all sentient beings to rely upon these six perfections to dwell in the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, and to practice the four applications of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattvas form this thought:
"Relying upon these six perfections myself, I shall swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and enter the realm of nirvana without remainder."
Furthermore, may all sentient beings, by relying on these six perfections, swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and enter the realm of nirvana without remainder.
"Śāriputra! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva dons the great armor of merit for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings.

*The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Fascicle 411, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Second Division, Chapter Thirteen on the Six Pāramitās (Part Two): "Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of generosity, they do so by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes.

Taking these roots of goodness as a basis, employing the method of non-apprehension, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience; at the time of giving, they harbor no stinginess whatsoever.
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of generosity donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of generosity.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of generosity, they do so by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes."

Taking these roots of goodness as the basis, employing the method of non-apprehension, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience; while practicing generosity, they do not give rise to the mental orientations of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of ethical discipline donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of generosity.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of generosity, they do so by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes."

Taking these roots of goodness as the basis, employing the method of non-apprehension, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience; while practicing generosity, they cultivate the dharma of giving with faith, patience, aspiration, and delight.
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of patience donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of generosity.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of generosity, they do so by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes."

Taking these roots of goodness as a basis, employing the skillful means of non-apprehension, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience; and while practicing generosity, they apply themselves with diligent vigor, never relinquishing their application.
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of diligence donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of generosity.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of generosity, they do so by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes."

Taking these roots of goodness as the basis, employing the method of non-apprehension, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience. At the time of giving, they direct their single-minded attention toward omniscience, ultimately seeking the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, without intermingling the mental orientations of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of meditative concentration donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of generosity.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of generosity, they do so by means of mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes."

Taking these roots of goodness as the basis, employing the method of non-apprehension, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience. At the time of giving, they abide in the realization that things are like illusions, perceiving neither the giver, nor the recipient, nor the gift, nor the fruit obtained from the giving.
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of wisdom donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of generosity.
“Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of generosity in this manner, they are fully armored with the great armor of the six perfections.”

Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of generosity with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes, and does not apprehend or acquire the characteristics of the six perfections, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has donned the great armor of merit.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), they do so by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).”

Taking these roots of goodness as a basis, employing the method of non-apprehension, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience; when practicing pure ethical discipline, they are entirely free from stinginess regarding all things.
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of generosity donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of ethical discipline.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), they do so by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).”

Taking these roots of goodness as a basis, using the method of non-apprehension, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). When practicing pure ethical discipline, they do not even seek the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, much less the stage of ordinary worldlings!
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of ethical discipline donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of ethical discipline.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā), they do so with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna)."

Taking these roots of goodness as a basis, employing the skillful means of non-apprehension, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience; when practicing pure ethical discipline, they maintain faith, patience, aspiration, and delight in the dharma of pure ethical discipline.
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of patience donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of ethical discipline.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of ethical discipline, they do so by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes."

Taking these roots of goodness as a basis, employing the skillful means of non-apprehension, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience; while practicing pure ethical discipline, they exert themselves with heroic vigor and do not abandon their application.
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of diligence donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of ethical discipline.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), they do so by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).”

Taking these roots of goodness as a basis, employing the method of non-apprehension, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*). When practicing pure ethical discipline, they take great compassion as their primary guide; they do not even allow themselves to be interspersed with the mental orientations of the two vehicles, much less the minds of ordinary worldlings!
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of meditative concentration donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of ethical discipline.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā), they do so by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna)."

Taking these roots of goodness as the means through non-apprehension, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience. When practicing pure ethical discipline, they abide in the view that all phenomena are like illusions; regarding the practice of pure ethical discipline, they have no reliance and no attainment, because its intrinsic nature is empty.
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of wisdom donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of ethical discipline.
“Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline in this manner, they are fully armored with the great armor of the six perfections.”

Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes, practices the perfection of ethical discipline while not grasping at or apprehending the characteristics of the six perfections, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has donned the great armor of merit.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of patience, they do so by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes, while practicing the perfection of patience."

Taking these roots of goodness as the basis, employing the method of non-apprehension, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience; when practicing patience, they have no attachment to their bodies, lives, or anything else in order to perfect that patience.
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of generosity donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of patience.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of patience, they do so by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes, while practicing the perfection of patience."

Taking these roots of goodness as the basis, employing the method of non-apprehension, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience; while practicing patience, they do not allow themselves to be mixed with the inferior mental orientations of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of ethical discipline donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of patience.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of patience, they do so by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes, while practicing the perfection of patience."

Taking these roots of goodness as a basis, employing the method of non-apprehension, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience. When practicing patience, they have faith, acceptance, desire, and delight in the dharma of patience.
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of patience donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of patience.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of patience, they do so by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes."

Taking these roots of virtue as a basis, employing the skillful means of non-apprehension, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience; while practicing patience, they exert themselves with heroic vigor and do not abandon their application.
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of diligence donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of patience.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of patience, they do so by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes."

Taking these roots of goodness as the basis, employing the method of non-apprehension, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience; when practicing patience, they concentrate their minds on a single object, so that even when encountering manifold sufferings, their minds remain undisturbed.
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of meditative concentration donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of patience.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), they do so by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā)."

Taking these roots of goodness as the basis, employing the method of non-apprehension, one should dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). When practicing patience, one should abide in the realization that things are like illusions; for the sake of gathering the Buddha-dharmas and maturing sentient beings, one contemplates the emptiness of all phenomena and does not cling to hostility or harm.
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of wisdom donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of patience.
“Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of patience in this way, they are fully armored with the great armor of the six perfections.”

Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of patience with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes, and does not apprehend or acquire the characteristics of the six perfections, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has donned the great armor of merit.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of diligence, they do so by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) while practicing the perfection of diligence."

Taking these roots of goodness as the basis, employing the method of non-apprehension, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience; when practicing diligence, they are able to zealously train in the practice of difficult acts of giving.
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of generosity donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of diligence.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of diligence, they do so by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes."

Taking these roots of goodness as a basis, employing the method of non-apprehension, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience; while practicing diligence, they zealously guard pure ethical discipline, never violating it.
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of ethical discipline donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of diligence.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of diligence, they do so by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes."

Taking these roots of goodness as a basis, employing the method of non-apprehension, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience; while practicing diligence, they are able to assiduously train in the difficult practice of patience.
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of patience donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of diligence.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of diligence, they do so by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes."

Taking these roots of goodness as the basis, employing the method of non-apprehension, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience; when practicing diligence, they are able to zealously cultivate and train in beneficial ascetic practices.
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of diligence donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of diligence.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of diligence, they do so by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes."

Taking these roots of goodness as a basis, employing the method of non-apprehension, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience; while practicing diligence, they are able to ardently cultivate and train in meditative concentrations and attainments.
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of meditative concentration donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of diligence.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of diligence, they do so by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes."

Taking these roots of goodness as the basis, employing the method of non-apprehension, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience; when practicing diligence, they are able to assiduously train in wisdom free from grasping.
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of wisdom donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of diligence.
“Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of diligence in this manner, they are fully armored with the great armor of the six perfections.”

Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of diligence with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes, and does not grasp at or cling to the characteristics of the six perfections, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has donned the great armor of merit.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of meditative concentration, they do so by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes."

Taking these roots of goodness as a basis, employing the method of non-apprehension, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience. When practicing meditative concentration, they practice giving with a tranquil mind; thus, a distracted mind or stinginess no longer manifest.
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of generosity donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of meditative concentration.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of meditative concentration, they do so by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes."

Taking these roots of goodness as a basis, employing the skillful means of non-apprehension, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience. When practicing meditative concentration, they maintain their precepts with a settled mind, ensuring that no unwholesome precepts manifest again.
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of ethical discipline donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of meditative concentration.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of meditative concentration, they practice the perfection of meditative concentration by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes."

Taking these roots of goodness as a basis, employing the method of non-apprehension, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience (*sarvajñājñāna*). When practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they abide in the samādhi of loving-kindness and compassion, cultivating patience (*kṣānti*) so as not to afflict sentient beings.
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of patience donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of meditative concentration.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of meditative concentration, they do so by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes."

Taking these roots of goodness as a basis, employing the method of non-apprehension, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience. When practicing meditative concentration, they abide in pure samādhi, diligently cultivating merit, and remain free from all indolence.
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of diligence donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of meditative concentration.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā), they do so by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).”

Taking these roots of virtue as the basis, employing the method of non-apprehension, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*). When practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they rely on such concentrations to induce superior absorptions and remain free from a distracted mind.
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of meditative concentration donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of meditative concentration.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of meditative concentration, they do so by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes."

Taking these roots of goodness as a basis, employing the method of non-apprehension, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience. When practicing meditative concentration, they rely on such concentration and other factors to induce superior wisdom, thereby abandoning the mind of unwholesome wisdom.
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of wisdom donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of meditative concentration.
“Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā) in this manner, they are fully armored with the great armor of the six perfections.”

Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes, practices the perfection of meditative concentration while neither grasping nor apprehending the characteristics of the six perfections, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has donned the great armor of merit.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they do so by means of mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes."

Taking these roots of goodness as the basis, employing the method of non-apprehension, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience. When practicing prajñā, although they give everything, they are able to not perceive the gift, the recipient, or the object.
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of generosity donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they do so by means of mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes."

Taking these roots of goodness as the basis, employing the method of non-apprehension, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience. When practicing *prajñā*, although they maintain pure precepts, they do not perceive any distinction between upholding and violating them.
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of ethical discipline donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they do so by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes, thereby practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Taking these roots of goodness as a basis, employing the method of non-apprehension, one dedicates them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*). When practicing *prajñā*, one cultivates patience (*kṣānti*) by relying on the superior wisdom of emptiness, without perceiving such things as the one who endures, the object endured, or the act of enduring itself.
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of patience donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they do so by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes."

Taking these roots of virtue as a basis, employing the method of non-apprehension, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience (*sarvajñājñāna*). When practicing *prajñā*, although they contemplate that all phenomena are ultimately empty, they diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas out of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of diligence donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of wisdom.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they do so with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*). Taking these roots of goodness as their basis, they employ the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) to dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward the knowledge of all modes."
When practicing *prajñā*, although one cultivates sublime meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), one contemplates that the objects of those concentrations are all ultimately empty. Śāriputra!
This is the great armor of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*) donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they do so by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes, while practicing the perfection of wisdom."
Taking these roots of goodness as the basis, employing the method of non-apprehension, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience.

When practicing *prajñā*, they contemplate all phenomena, all sentient beings, and all conditioned activities as being like illusions and the like, thereby cultivating various forms of wisdom free from grasping and attachment.
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of wisdom donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of wisdom.
“Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this manner, they are fully armored with the great armor of the six perfections.”

Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes, does not apprehend or acquire the characteristics of the six perfections, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is clad in the great armor of merit.
“Śāriputra! This is called the donning of the great armor of merit by all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings. Śāriputra!”
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in each individual pāramitā, they cultivate all six pāramitās to bring them to perfection; for this reason, they are said to be "donning the armor of great merit."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, although bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*), they do not relish them, nor do they take birth under their influence, nor are they led away by their power."
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of wisdom and skillful means donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of meditative concentration.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, although bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), they dwell in the vision of seclusion, the vision of tranquility, and the vision of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, yet they do not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). They do not enter the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but surpass all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of wisdom through skillful means donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of meditative concentration.
"Śāriputra! Because these bodhisattvas universally don such armor of great merit for the sake of the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, they are further named Mahāsattvas."

“Śāriputra! Thus, for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to sentient beings, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have donned the great armor of merit are universally praised with joy by all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas in Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions, amidst their great assemblies, who speak thus:
