The ultimate refers to nirvāṇa.
It should be understood that herein nirvāṇa is empty of nirvāṇa, being neither permanent nor subject to destruction."
Why is this? Because such is its intrinsic nature, Subhūti!
This is the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
What is the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*)?
The conditioned refers to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

It should be understood that herein the desire realm is empty of the desire realm, being neither permanent nor subject to destruction; the form and formless realms are empty of the form and formless realms, being neither permanent nor subject to destruction.
Why is this? Because such is their intrinsic nature, Subhūti!
This is the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*).
What is the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*)?
The unconditioned refers to that which is without arising, without cessation, without abiding, and without change.
One should know that herein, the unconditioned is empty of the unconditioned, being neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why?
Because such is its intrinsic nature.
"Subhūti! This is the emptiness of the unconditioned.
What is the emptiness of the ultimate?"
"Ultimate" refers to those phenomena that are ultimately unfindable.
One should know that herein, the ultimate is empty of the ultimate; it is neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because it is such by its very nature, Subhūti,
this is called ultimate emptiness.
"What is the emptiness of the limitless (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*)?
'Limitless' refers to the fact that no beginning or end can be apprehended.
One should know that herein, the limitless is empty of the limitless, being neither permanent nor subject to destruction."
Why is this? Because such is their intrinsic nature, Subhūti!
This is the emptiness of the limitless (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*).
What is the emptiness of dispersion and non-dispersion (*anavakāra-anavakāra-śūnyatā*)?
"Dispersion" refers to that which can be found as being released, abandoned, or relinquished; "non-dispersion" refers to that which cannot be found as being released, abandoned, or relinquished.
It should be known that herein, dispersion and non-dispersion are empty by virtue of dispersion and non-dispersion; they are neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because such is their intrinsic nature.
"Subhūti! This is the emptiness of dispersion and non-dispersion.
What is the emptiness of intrinsic nature?

Intrinsic nature refers to the nature of conditioned phenomena or the nature of unconditioned phenomena; all such things are not created by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or tathāgatas, nor are they created by anyone else, and for this reason it is called intrinsic nature.
It should be understood that herein, intrinsic nature is empty of intrinsic nature; it is neither permanent nor subject to destruction.
Why? Because such is the nature of intrinsic nature.
"Subhūti! This is intrinsic emptiness (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).
What is the emptiness of self-characteristics and common characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*)?"

"Specific characteristics" refers to the specific characteristics of all phenomena (*dharma*). For example, resistance and obstruction are the specific characteristic of form (*rūpa*); experiencing is the specific characteristic of sensation (*vedanā*); grasping signs is the specific characteristic of perception (*saṃjñā*); volitional activity is the specific characteristic of formations (*saṃskāra*); and discernment is the specific characteristic of consciousness (*vijñāna*). Such as these, whether they be the specific characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) or the specific characteristics of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), are what constitute "specific characteristics."

The "common characteristics" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) refer to those characteristics shared by all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*). For example, suffering is the common characteristic of all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*); impermanence is the common characteristic of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*); emptiness and selflessness are the common characteristics of all phenomena. In this way, there are immeasurable such common characteristics.
It should be understood that herein, specific and general characteristics are empty of specific and general characteristics; they are neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because such is their intrinsic nature.
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
This is the emptiness of specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇasāmānyalakṣaṇaśūnyatā*). What is the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmaśūnyatā*)?”

"All dharmas" refers to the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements; those with form and those without form; those visible and those invisible; those with resistance and those without resistance; those with outflows and those without outflows; and those conditioned and those unconditioned—these are called all dharmas.
It should be understood that herein all phenomena are empty of all phenomena, being neither permanent nor subject to destruction.
Why is this? Because such is their intrinsic nature.
"Subhūti! This is the emptiness of all dharmas.
What is the emptiness of the unapprehendable?
"Unobtainable" means that when one seeks all phenomena herein, they are unobtainable.
One should know that this unobtainability therein is due to the emptiness of the unobtainable, which is neither permanent nor subject to destruction.
Why is this? Because such is their intrinsic nature, Subhūti!
This is the emptiness of the unapprehendable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*). What is the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*)?
"Non-existence" refers to the fact that within this, not even the slightest existence can be apprehended.
One should know that herein, the absence of nature is empty of the absence of nature, being neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because such is its intrinsic nature.
"Subhūti! This is the emptiness of non-existence.
What is the emptiness of intrinsic nature?
Intrinsic nature refers to the intrinsic nature by which all phenomena are able to coalesce.
It should be understood that herein, intrinsic nature is empty of intrinsic nature; it is neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why is this so?
Because it is its very nature,
Subhūti; this is what is meant by emptiness of intrinsic nature.
"What is the emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence?

The 'self-nature of non-existence' refers to the fact that among all phenomena there is no nature of an agent capable of bringing about a combination, nor is there a self-nature of that which is so combined."
It should be understood that herein, the nature of non-existence is empty of the nature of non-existence; it is neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why?
Because its intrinsic nature is such.
"Subhūti! This is the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence. Furthermore, Subhūti!"
Existence is empty of existence; non-existence is empty of non-existence; intrinsic nature is empty of intrinsic nature; and other-nature is empty of other-nature.
"In what way is existence empty of existence?"
"Existence" refers to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*); this existence is empty of existence.
"How is non-existence empty of non-existence?
Non-existence refers to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*); this non-existence is empty of non-existence.
"What is meant by 'intrinsic nature is empty of intrinsic nature'?

It means that all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature; this emptiness is not produced by wisdom, not produced by views, nor produced by anything else. This is called 'intrinsic nature being empty of intrinsic nature.'"
"What is meant by 'other-nature is empty of other-nature'?

It refers to all phenomena—whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear—which abide as the fixed nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the equality of phenomena (*dharma-samatā*), the nature of phenomena free from arising (*dharma-anutpāda-dharmatā*), suchness (*tathatā*), non-falsity (*avitathatā*), non-alteration (*ananyathatā*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). All these are empty because they are other-nature; this is called 'other-nature being empty of other-nature.'"
“Subhūti, you should know that this is the characteristic of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 413, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Second Division, Chapter Sixteen on Samādhi, Part Two. “Furthermore, Subhūti!”
The characteristic of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva consists of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of unsurpassed and subtle samādhis,
namely: the *Vīradatta* (Heroic Progress) samādhi, the *Ratnamudrā* (Jewel Seal) samādhi, the *Siṃhavikrīḍita* (Lion’s Play) samādhi,
the *Sucandra* (Excellent Moon) samādhi, the *Candradhvajaketu* (Moon Banner Sign) samādhi, and all...
The *Dharmodgata* samādhi, the *Cūḍāvalokana* samādhi, the *Dharmadhātuniyata* samādhi, the *Niyatadhvajalakṣaṇa* samādhi,
the *Vajropama* samādhi, the *Dharmamudrāpraveśa* samādhi, the *Rasmi-pramuñcanāsaṃpramoṣa* samādhi,
the *Susthitavimānarāja* samādhi, and the *Rasmi-pramuñcana*... [samādhi].
The *Ālokasamādhi*, the *Vīryabalasamādhi*, the *Samudgatāsamādhi*, the *Sarvavākpathanirdeśapraveśasamādhi*, the *Niruktisamavasaraṇasamādhi*, the *Diṅmukhaprekṣaṇasamādhi*,
the *Dhāraṇīmudrāsamādhi*, the *Asammoṣasamādhi*, and the *Sarvadharmasamādhi*.
The samādhi of proceeding to the ocean-seal, the samādhi of pervading space, the samādhi of the vajra-wheel,
the samādhi of freedom from dust, the samādhi of universal illumination, the samādhi of the unblinking eye,
the samādhi of abiding in signlessness, the samādhi of non-mentation, and the samādhi of the stainless lamp.
the Samādhi of Boundless Light, the Samādhi of Radiating Light, the Samādhi of Universal Illumination,
the Samādhi of Pure and Firm Stability, the Samādhi of Stainless Light, the Samādhi of Emanating Sublime Bliss,
the Samādhi of the Lightning Lamp, the Samādhi of the Inexhaustible, and the Samādhi of Possessing Majestic Splendor.
The samādhi of detachment from exhaustion, the immovable samādhi, the flawlessly clear samādhi,
the sun-lamp samādhi, the pure moon samādhi, the pure light samādhi, the illuminating samādhi,
the samādhi of performing what is to be done, the wisdom-banner-mark samādhi, and the vajra [samādhi].
The Mālā-samādhi, the Citta-sthiti-samādhi, the Samantāloka-samādhi, the Supratiṣṭhita-samādhi,
the Ratnakūṭa-samādhi, the Dharmamudrā-samādhi, the Sarvadharmasamatā-samādhi, the Priyaviprahīṇa-samādhi, and the Dharmakūṭāvatāra-samādhi.
The Samādhi of Dispersion, the Samādhi of Discerning the Phrases of Dharma, the Samādhi of the Equality of Letter-Marks,
the Samādhi of Detachment from the Marks of Letters, the Samādhi of Severing the Object of Cognition,
the Samādhi of Non-Transformation, the Samādhi of Absence of Categories, the Samādhi of Practice Without Characteristics, and the Samādhi of Freedom from Obscuration.
The samādhi of darkness, the samādhi of endowed practice, the samādhi of immovability, the samādhi of transcending realms,
the samādhi of gathering all merits, the samādhi of abiding in certainty,
the samādhi of abiding without mind, the samādhi of pure exquisite flowers, and the samādhi of endowed factors of enlightenment.
The earth-samādhi, the samādhi of boundless lamps, the samādhi of boundless eloquence, the samādhi of the unequaled,
the samādhi that transcends all phenomena, the samādhi that definitively discerns all phenomena,
the samādhi that disperses the net of doubt, the samādhi of non-abiding, and the samādhi of the adornment of the single mark.
...the samādhi that induces mental formations, the samādhi of a single mental formation, the samādhi free from mental formations,
the samādhi of sublime mental formations, the samādhi that reaches the depths of all existences and shatters them,
the samādhi of entering conventional designations and language, the samādhi of liberation from sounds and letters, and the torch...
The Samādhi of Blazing Radiance, the Samādhi of Adorned Purity, the Samādhi of Signlessness,
the Samādhi Endowed with All Sublime Marks, the Samādhi of Indifference Toward All Suffering and Pleasure,
the Samādhi of Exhaustless Phenomenal Aspects, the Samādhi Endowed with Dhāraṇī, and the Samādhi that Subdues All Correct [Views].
The samādhi of the nature of non-evil, the samādhi of the pacification of all that is discordant or concordant, the samādhi of freedom from hatred and love,
the samādhi of stainless clarity, the samādhi of possessing firmness, the samādhi of the pure light of the full moon,
the samādhi of great adornment, and the samādhi that illuminates all worlds.
The samādhi of the equality of the stages and meditative concentrations; the samādhi of the principle of equality regarding contention and non-contention;
the samādhi of being without a nest, without signs, and without craving; the samādhi of definitive abiding in suchness;
the samādhi of being free from the defilements of body; and the samādhi of being free from the defilements of speech.
The samādhi of being free from mental defilement, the samādhi like space, and the samādhi of non-attachment like space—
there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of such samādhis; these constitute the characteristics of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
“Subhūti! What is called the ‘Heroic Progress’ (śūraṅgama) samādhi?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is able to experience the objects of all samādhis, is able to accomplish boundless and sublime heroic progress, and is able to serve as the leader of all meditative concentrations (samādhi); therefore, it is named the ‘Heroic Progress’ samādhi.”
"What is called the 'Jewel Seal Samādhi'?
It is because this samādhi can seal all meditative concentrations; therefore, it is named the Jewel Seal Samādhi."
"What is called the 'Lion’s Play Samādhi'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one sports with mastery over all supreme concentrations; therefore, it is named the Lion’s Play Samādhi."
"What is called the 'Exquisite Moon Samādhi'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, it universally illuminates all meditative concentrations like the pure, full moon; therefore, it is named the Exquisite Moon Samādhi."
"What is called the Moon Banner Mark Samādhi?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is universally able to sustain the supreme marks of all meditative concentrations; therefore, it is named the Moon Banner Mark Samādhi."
"What is called the 'Samādhi of the Surge of All Dharmas'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is able to universally surge forth all supreme concentrations; therefore, it is named the 'Samādhi of the Surge of All Dharmas.'"
"What is called the Samādhi of Contemplating the Summit?
It means that when one abides in this samādhi, one is able to universally contemplate the summit of all meditative concentrations; therefore, it is named the Samādhi of Contemplating the Summit."
"What is called the 'Samādhi of Certainty in the Dharma-realm'?
It means that when one abides in this samādhi, one is able to definitively illuminate and realize the dharma-realm; therefore, it is named the Samādhi of Certainty in the Dharma-realm."
"What is called the samādhi of the definitive banner-mark?
It means that when one abides in this samādhi, one is able to definitively uphold the banner-marks of all concentrations; therefore, it is named the samādhi of the definitive banner-mark."
"What is called the 'Vajra-like Samādhi'?
It refers to when one abides in this samādhi, being able to shatter all other meditative concentrations and not being subdued by them; therefore, it is named the Vajra-like Samādhi."
"What is called the 'Samādhi of Entering the Seal of Dharmas'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is universally able to realize and enter all seals of dharmas; therefore, it is named the 'Samādhi of Entering the Seal of Dharmas'."
"What is called the 'Samādhi of Radiating Light and Non-forgetfulness'?

It means that when one abides in this samādhi, one radiates the light of supreme concentration upon sentient beings, causing them to recollect the teachings they have previously received; therefore, it is named the 'Samādhi of Radiating Light and Non-forgetfulness'."
"What is called the 'Samādhi of the King of Well-Established Concentration'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is well able to establish oneself among all the kings of concentration; therefore, it is named the 'Samādhi of the King of Well-Established Concentration'."
"What is called the 'Emission of Light' samādhi?
It refers to when, while abiding in this samādhi, one is able to universally manifest all the lights of meditative concentration; therefore, it is named the 'Emission of Light' samādhi."
"What is called the *vīryabalasamādhi*?
It refers to when, while abiding in this samādhi, one is able to exert the power of diligence toward all meditative concentrations; therefore, it is named the *vīryabalasamādhi*."
"What is called the 'Samādhi of Equal Surging'?
It means that when one abides in this samādhi, all meditative concentrations (samādhis) surge forth equally; therefore, it is named the Samādhi of Equal Surging."
"What is called the samādhi of entering the certainty of all verbal expressions?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one definitively awakens to and enters into all verbal expressions; therefore, it is named the samādhi of entering the certainty of all verbal expressions."
"What is called the samādhi of equal entry into designations (*adhivacana*)?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is able to universally penetrate the principles of etymological interpretation regarding the names of all meditative concentrations; therefore, it is called the samādhi of equal entry into designations."
"What is called the samādhi of observing the directions?

It refers to when, while abiding in this samādhi, one is able to universally observe and illuminate all the directions of meditative concentration; therefore, it is named the samādhi of observing the directions."
"What is called the 'Samādhi of the Seal of Total Retention' (dhāraṇīmudrā-samādhi)?

It means that when one abides in this samādhi, one is able to universally maintain and uphold the sublime seals of all meditative concentrations; therefore, it is named the Samādhi of the Seal of Total Retention."
"What is called the 'samādhi of non-forgetfulness'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one does not forget any of the characteristics of meditative concentration; therefore, it is called the 'samādhi of non-forgetfulness'."
"What is called the 'Samādhi of the Ocean Seal in Which All Dharmas Equally Converge'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, it causes all supreme concentrations to enter [into it], just as the ocean seal receives and gathers all streams; therefore, it is named the 'Samādhi of the Ocean Seal in Which All Dharmas Equally Converge'."
"What is called the 'Samādhi that Pervades and Covers Space'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is able to universally protect and cover all meditative absorptions (samādhis) without making any distinctions, just like the great void of space; therefore, it is named the 'Samādhi that Pervades and Covers Space.'"
"What is called the Vajracakra Samādhi?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is universally able to sustain all supreme concentrations, preventing them from being dispersed or destroyed, just like a vajra-wheel; therefore, it is named the Vajracakra Samādhi."
"What is called the 'Dust-Free Samādhi'?
It means that when one abides in this samādhi, one is able to extinguish all afflictions, fetters, and impurities; therefore, it is named the Dust-Free Samādhi."
"What is called the Samādhi of Universal Illumination?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, it universally illuminates all meditative concentrations, making them radiant; therefore, it is named the Samādhi of Universal Illumination."
"What is called the 'Unblinking Samādhi'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one no longer seeks after other concentrations or other dharmas; therefore, it is named the Unblinking Samādhi."
"What is called the 'samādhi of dwelling in the signless'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one does not perceive even the slightest dharma within any meditative concentration in which one could dwell; therefore, it is called the 'samādhi of dwelling in the signless'."
"What is called the 'non-contemplative samādhi'?
It refers to when one dwells in this samādhi, all inferior states of mind and mental factors cease to arise; therefore, it is called the non-contemplative samādhi."
"What is called the 'Stainless Lamp Samādhi'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, it is like holding a pure lamp to illuminate all meditative concentrations; therefore, it is named the Stainless Lamp Samādhi."
"What is called the 'Infinite Light Samādhi'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one can emit a great light that illuminates without limit; therefore, it is called the Infinite Light Samādhi."
"What is called the 'Radiant' samādhi?
It means that if one dwells in this meditative concentration without interruption, one is able to emit the light of all supreme concentrations; therefore, it is named the Radiant Samādhi."
"What is called the Samādhi of Universal Illumination?

It means that if one attains this meditative concentration (*samādhi*), immediately thereafter one is able to universally illuminate all gateways to superior concentrations; therefore, it is named the Samādhi of Universal Illumination."
"What is called the 'samādhi of pure firmness'?
It refers to when, while abiding in this samādhi, one attains the pure state of equality of all samādhis; therefore, it is called the 'samādhi of pure firmness'."
"What is called the 'Stainless Light Samādhi'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is able to universally eliminate all defilements of meditative concentration; therefore, it is named the Stainless Light Samādhi."
"What is called the 'Emission of Wondrous Bliss' samādhi?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one experiences the wondrous bliss of all meditative concentrations; therefore, it is named the 'Emission of Wondrous Bliss' samādhi."
"What is called the 'Lightning Lamp' samādhi?
It refers to when one dwells in this samādhi, illuminating all meditative absorptions like the flash of lightning; therefore, it is named the 'Lightning Lamp' samādhi."
"What is called the 'Inexhaustible Samādhi'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one brings forth the inexhaustible merit of all meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), yet does not perceive any characteristic of exhaustion or non-exhaustion therein; therefore, it is named the 'Inexhaustible Samādhi'."
"What is called the 'Samādhi Endowed with Majestic Splendor'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, the majestic splendor among all meditative concentrations is uniquely magnificent; therefore, it is called the 'Samādhi Endowed with Majestic Splendor'."
"What is called the 'samādhi free from exhaustion'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one perceives all meditative concentrations as entirely inexhaustible, yet does not perceive any characteristic of exhaustion or non-exhaustion; therefore, it is called the 'samādhi free from exhaustion'."
"What is called the 'Immovable Samādhi'?

It refers to when one abides in this samādhi, causing all meditative concentrations to be immovable, without agitation, and free from conceptual proliferation; therefore, it is named the Immovable Samādhi."
"What is called the 'Flawless' (*nirañjana*) samādhi?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, it causes all meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) to appear without flaw or gap; therefore, it is named the 'Flawless' samādhi."
"What is called the 'Sun-Lamp Samādhi'?
It refers to when one dwells in this samādhi, causing all gateways of concentration to emit light and shine everywhere; therefore, it is named the Sun-Lamp Samādhi."
"What is called the 'Pure Moon Samādhi'?
It refers to when one dwells in this samādhi, causing all meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) to dispel darkness like the moon; therefore, it is named the Pure Moon Samādhi."
"What is called the 'Samādhi of Pure Light'?

It refers to when, while abiding in this samādhi, one attains the four types of unimpeded analytical knowledge (pratisaṃvid) regarding all meditative concentrations; therefore, it is named the Samādhi of Pure Light."
“What is called the ‘Illumination-Producing’ samādhi?
It means that when one abides in this samādhi, it causes all gateways of concentration to produce illumination and shine everywhere; therefore, it is named the ‘Illumination-Producing’ samādhi.”
"What is called the 'samādhi that performs what is to be performed'?

It means that when one abides in this samādhi, one accomplishes all the tasks that the various meditative concentrations (samādhis) ought to perform, and furthermore, causes the functions of all concentrations to be successfully fulfilled; therefore, it is named the 'samādhi that performs what is to be performed.'"
"What is called the samādhi of the mark of the banner of wisdom?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one perceives the marks of the sublime banner of wisdom of all samādhis; therefore, it is named the samādhi of the mark of the banner of wisdom."
"What is called the Vajramālā Samādhi?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, although one can penetrate all dharmas, one does not perceive any characteristic of penetration; therefore, it is called the Vajramālā Samādhi."
"What is called the 'Samādhi of Abiding Mind'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, the mind does not waver, does not shift, does not illuminate, nor does it diminish; one does not even think of there being a mind. Therefore, it is called the Samādhi of Abiding Mind."
"What is called the Samādhi of Universal Radiance?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is able to universally observe and illuminate all meditative concentrations; therefore, it is named the Samādhi of Universal Radiance."
"What is called the 'Samādhi of Good Abiding'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is well able to abide securely within all meditative concentrations; therefore, it is named the Samādhi of Good Abiding."
"What is called the Jewel-Heap Samādhi?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one contemplates all meditative concentrations as being like a heap of jewels; therefore, it is named the Jewel-Heap Samādhi."
"What is called the 'Samādhi of the Seal of the Sublime Dharma'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is able to seal all meditative concentrations (samādhis) by means of the 'seal of no-seal'; therefore, it is named the Samādhi of the Seal of the Sublime Dharma."
"What is called the 'samādhi of the equality of all phenomena'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one does not perceive any phenomenon that is apart from the nature of equality; therefore, it is named the 'samādhi of the equality of all phenomena.'"
“What is called the samādhi of relinquishing attachment and delight?
It refers to when, while abiding in this samādhi, one relinquishes all attachment and delight toward all phenomena; therefore, it is called the samādhi of relinquishing attachment and delight.”
"What is called the 'Samādhi of Entering the Summit of Dharma'?

It means that when one abides in this samādhi, one is able to eliminate the obscuration of darkness regarding all phenomena and also serves as the foremost among all meditative concentrations; therefore, it is called the 'Samādhi of Entering the Summit of Dharma'."
"What is called the 'Scattering Samādhi'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, all attachment to meditative concentration and attachment to phenomena are scattered away; therefore, it is named the Scattering Samādhi."
"What is called the 'Discrimination of Dharma-Phrases' samādhi?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is well able to discriminate the dharma-phrases of all meditative concentrations; therefore, it is named the 'Discrimination of Dharma-Phrases' samādhi."
"What is called the samādhi of the mark of equal letters?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one attains the mark of equal letters of all samādhis; therefore, it is called the samādhi of the mark of equal letters."
"What is called the 'samādhi of being free from the marks of letters'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, not a single letter can be apprehended among all meditative concentrations; therefore, it is called the 'samādhi of being free from the marks of letters.'"
"What is called the 'samādhi that severs the object of focus'?

It means that when one abides in this samādhi, all signs of the objects of focus of various meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) are severed; therefore, it is called the 'samādhi that severs the object of focus.'"
"What is called the 'unchanging samādhi'?
It means that when one abides in this samādhi, one does not perceive the characteristics of change in any phenomena; therefore, it is called the unchanging samādhi."
"What is called the 'non-categorical samādhi'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one does not perceive the distinct characteristics of the categories of all phenomena; therefore, it is called the non-categorical samādhi."
"What is called the 'samādhi of signless practice'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, no signs of any meditative concentrations whatsoever are apprehended; therefore, it is called the 'samādhi of signless practice'."
"What is called the 'Samādhi Free from Obscuration and Darkness'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, all obscurations and darkness within the various meditative concentrations are eliminated without exception; therefore, it is named the 'Samādhi Free from Obscuration and Darkness.'"
"What is called the 'Samādhi Endowed with Practice'?

It refers to when one dwells in this samādhi, there is no grasping or attachment whatsoever toward the practices of any meditative concentrations; therefore, it is called the 'Samādhi Endowed with Practice'."
"What is called the 'Unwavering Samādhi'?
It refers to when one dwells in this samādhi, one perceives no wavering among all samādhis; therefore, it is named the Unwavering Samādhi."
"What is called the 'Samādhi that Transcends Objects'?
It refers to when one dwells in this samādhi, one transcends the objects of focus of all other meditative concentrations; therefore, it is named the 'Samādhi that Transcends Objects'."
"What is called the 'Samādhi that Accumulates All Meritorious Qualities'?

It refers to when, while abiding in this samādhi, one is able to accumulate all the meritorious qualities inherent in various concentrations, yet maintains no perception of accumulation regarding any phenomena; therefore, it is named the 'Samādhi that Accumulates All Meritorious Qualities.'"
"What is called the 'Samādhi of Decisive Abiding'?

It means that when one abides in this samādhi, although the mind remains decisively settled within all meditative concentrations, one knows that its characteristics are utterly unapprehendable; therefore, it is called the Samādhi of Decisive Abiding."
"What is called the 'samādhi of dwelling without mind'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, the mind neither shifts nor falls away among any meditative concentrations; therefore, it is called the 'samādhi of dwelling without mind'."
"What is called the 'Pure and Wondrous Flower Samādhi'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, it causes all meditative absorptions (*samādhis*) to become pure, adorned and radiant like a wondrous flower; therefore, it is named the Pure and Wondrous Flower Samādhi."
"What is called the 'Samādhi Endowed with the Factors of Enlightenment'?

It refers to when, while abiding in this samādhi, one causes the cultivation of the seven factors of enlightenment within all meditative concentrations to be swiftly perfected; therefore, it is named the 'Samādhi Endowed with the Factors of Enlightenment'."
"What is called the 'Infinite Lamp Samādhi'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is able to illuminate and comprehend all phenomena, just like a bright lamp; therefore, it is called the Infinite Lamp Samādhi."
"What is called the 'Infinite Eloquence Samādhi'?
It refers to when, while dwelling in this samādhi, one attains infinite eloquence regarding all phenomena; therefore, it is named the Infinite Eloquence Samādhi."
"What is called the 'Samādhi of the Unequaled' (Asamasama-samādhi)?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one attains the state of equality regarding all meditative concentrations (samādhis), and also causes all these concentrations to become unequaled; therefore, it is named the 'Samādhi of the Unequaled.'"
"What is called the 'Samādhi that Transcends All Phenomena'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is universally able to transcend all phenomena of the three realms; therefore, it is named the 'Samādhi that Transcends All Phenomena.'"
"What is called the 'Samādhi that Decisively Discerns All Dharmas'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is able to decisively discern all supreme concentrations and all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings according to reality; therefore, it is named the 'Samādhi that Decisively Discerns All Dharmas'."
“What is called the *vikiraṇa-saṃśaya-jāla* samādhi?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, all nets of doubt regarding all meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and all phenomena (*dharma*) are completely dispersed; therefore, it is named the *vikiraṇa-saṃśaya-jāla* samādhi.”
"What is called the 'Samādhi of Non-Abiding'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one does not perceive any place where phenomena abide; therefore, it is called the 'Samādhi of Non-Abiding'."
"What is called the 'Samādhi Adorned with the Single Characteristic'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one does not perceive any dual characteristics of phenomena to be grasped; therefore, it is named the 'Samādhi Adorned with the Single Characteristic'."
“What is called the samādhi of manifesting various aspects?

It refers to when, while abiding in this samādhi, although one can manifest various aspects regarding all meditative concentrations and all phenomena, one does not perceive at all any agent who manifests them; therefore, it is called the samādhi of manifesting various aspects.”
“What is called the ‘single-aspect samādhi’?
It refers to when, while abiding in this samādhi, one perceives all meditative concentrations as having no dual aspects; therefore, it is called the single-aspect samādhi.”
"What is called the samādhi of being free from mental formations?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one perceives that all meditative absorptions (samādhis) are entirely devoid of mental formations; therefore, it is called the samādhi of being free from mental formations."
"What is called the 'Samādhi of the Aspect of Sublime Conduct'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, it causes all meditative concentrations (samādhis) to give rise to the aspect of sublime conduct; therefore, it is named the 'Samādhi of the Aspect of Sublime Conduct'."
"What is called the 'samādhi that penetrates the depths of all existences and scatters them'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one attains the wisdom of penetration regarding all meditative concentrations and all phenomena, entering into them as they truly are. Having entered therein, one penetrates and scatters all phenomena of existence so that none remain; therefore, it is called the 'samādhi that penetrates the depths of all existences and scatters them.'"
"What is called the samādhi of entering into designations and linguistic expressions?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one penetrates all dharmas of samādhi, such that designations and linguistic expressions are without attachment or obstruction; therefore, it is named the samādhi of entering into designations and linguistic expressions."
"What is called the 'Samādhi of Liberation from Sound, Voice, and Syllables'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one perceives all meditative absorptions as liberated from all sounds, voices, and syllables, with all their manifold characteristics extinguished; therefore, it is named the 'Samādhi of Liberation from Sound, Voice, and Syllables.'"
"What is called the 'Blazing Torch Samādhi'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, it radiates brilliant light upon all meditative concentrations; therefore, it is named the Blazing Torch Samādhi."
"What is called the 'Samādhi of Purifying Characteristics'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is able to purify the characteristics of all meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), which is to say, one is able to eliminate all characteristics; therefore, it is called the 'Samādhi of Purifying Characteristics'."
“What is called the signless samādhi?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one perceives no signs within any meditative concentrations; therefore, it is called the signless samādhi.”
"What is called the 'Samādhi Endowed with All Sublime Characteristics'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, there are no sublime characteristics of any meditative concentrations that are not fully possessed; therefore, it is named the 'Samādhi Endowed with All Sublime Characteristics.'"
"What is called the 'samādhi of not delighting in any suffering or pleasure'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one does not take pleasure in observing the characteristics of suffering or pleasure within any meditative absorptions; therefore, it is called the 'samādhi of not delighting in any suffering or pleasure.'"
"What is called the 'Samādhi of the Aspect of Inexhaustibility'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one does not perceive any aspect of the various meditative absorptions as being exhaustible; therefore, it is named the 'Samādhi of the Aspect of Inexhaustibility'."
"What is called the samādhi endowed with dhāraṇī?

It refers to when, while abiding in this samādhi, one is able to universally sustain the preeminent qualities of all meditative concentrations; therefore, it is named the samādhi endowed with dhāraṇī."
"What is called the samādhi that subdues all right and wrong natures?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, regarding the right and wrong natures of all meditative concentrations, it subdues all views so that they do not arise; therefore, it is called the samādhi that subdues all right and wrong natures."
"What is called the 'Samādhi that Quells All Adverse and Favorable Conditions'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, regarding all meditative concentrations and all phenomena, one perceives no signs whatsoever of either adverse or favorable conditions; therefore, it is called the 'Samādhi that Quells All Adverse and Favorable Conditions.'"
"What is called the 'samādhi free from aversion and attachment'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, regarding all meditative concentrations and all phenomena, one perceives no signs of aversion or attachment whatsoever; therefore, it is called the 'samādhi free from aversion and attachment'."
"What is called the 'Stainless Radiance Samādhi'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one perceives neither the mark of radiance nor the mark of defilement within any meditative concentrations; therefore, it is called the Stainless Radiance Samādhi."
"What is called the Samādhi Endowed with Firmness?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, it causes all meditative concentrations (samādhis) to become firm; therefore, it is named the Samādhi Endowed with Firmness."
“What is called the ‘Samādhi of the Pure Light of the Full Moon’?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, the merits of all meditative concentrations (samādhis) are increased, just as the pure light of the full moon increases the waters of the ocean; therefore, it is named the ‘Samādhi of the Pure Light of the Full Moon.’”
"What is called the 'Great Adornment Samādhi'?

It refers to when one dwells in this samādhi, causing all meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) to accomplish various subtle, wondrous, and rare great adornments; therefore, it is named the Great Adornment Samādhi."
"What is called the 'Samādhi that Illuminates All Worlds'?

It refers to when one abides in this samādhi, illuminating all meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and all phenomena (*dharma*), causing all classes of sentient beings to attain clear understanding; therefore, it is named the 'Samādhi that Illuminates All Worlds.'"
"What is called the samādhi of the equality of concentration?

It means that when one abides in this samādhi, one does not perceive any distinction between meditative equipoise and distraction; therefore, it is called the samādhi of the equality of concentration."
"What is called the samādhi of the principle of equality between the contentious and the non-contentious?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one does not perceive any distinction in the characteristics of the contentious or non-contentious nature of all phenomena or all meditative concentrations; therefore, it is named the samādhi of the principle of equality between the contentious and the non-contentious."
"What is called the 'samādhi without nesting place, without signs, and without attachment'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one destroys all nesting places, abandons all signs, and severs all attachments so that there is no grasping; therefore, it is called the samādhi without nesting place, without signs, and without attachment."
"What is called the 'samādhi of definitive abiding in suchness'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, with respect to all meditative concentrations and all phenomena, one never abandons the true reality of suchness; therefore, it is called the 'samādhi of definitive abiding in suchness'."
"What is called the 'samādhi that is free from bodily defilement'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, it causes all meditative concentrations to destroy the view of a self-existent body; therefore, it is called the 'samādhi that is free from bodily defilement.'"
"What is called the 'samādhi that is free from verbal corruption'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, it causes all meditative absorptions (samādhis) to destroy the evil karma of speech; therefore, it is called the 'samādhi that is free from verbal corruption.'"
"What is called the 'samādhi that removes mental corruption'?
It refers to when one dwells in this samādhi, it causes all meditative concentrations to destroy the evil karma of the mind; therefore, it is named the 'samādhi that removes mental corruption'."
"What is called the 'space-like samādhi'?
It refers to when one dwells in this samādhi, one is able to universally benefit all sentient beings, and the mind is as impartial as the great void; therefore, it is called the space-like samādhi."
"What is called the 'Space-like Samādhi Free from Attachment'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one contemplates all phenomena as being utterly non-existent, like the pure sky which is neither defiled nor attached; therefore, it is called the Space-like Samādhi Free from Attachment."
"Subhūti! Such immeasurable hundreds of thousands of subtle, marvelous, and supreme samādhis should be known as the characteristics of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas."

17. Chapter on the Foundations of Mindfulness, Part Two, Section One: "Furthermore, Subhūti, the characteristic of the Great Vehicle of a bodhisattva mahāsattva consists of the four foundations of mindfulness."
What are the four? First, the foundation of mindfulness on the body.
Second, the foundation of mindfulness on feelings.
3. Mindfulness of the mind. 4. Mindfulness of phenomena. Regarding "mindfulness of the body":

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, employing the method of non-apprehension, they dwell observing the body internally, or dwell observing the body externally, or dwell observing the body both internally and externally; yet they never give rise to discursive thoughts associated with the body. With ardent diligence, correct knowledge, and full mindfulness, they subdue greed and sorrow.

“Regarding the application of mindfulness to feelings (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*): when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), employing the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), although they dwell observing feelings internally, or dwell observing feelings externally, or dwell observing feelings both internally and externally, they never give rise to discursive thoughts associated with feeling. With ardent diligence, correct knowledge, and full mindfulness, they subdue greed and sorrow.”

"Regarding the application of mindfulness to the mind: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, employing the method of non-apprehension, although they abide in the observation of the mind internally, or abide in the observation of the mind externally, or abide in the observation of the mind both internally and externally, they never give rise to discursive thoughts associated with the mind; they exert fervent diligence, possess correct knowledge and full mindfulness, and subdue greed and sorrow."

"Regarding the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*): when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), employing the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), although they dwell in the contemplation of phenomena regarding internal phenomena, or dwell in the contemplation of phenomena regarding external phenomena, or dwell in the contemplation of phenomena regarding both internal and external phenomena, they never give rise to discursive thoughts associated with phenomena; they exert fervent diligence, possess correct knowledge and mindfulness, and subdue greed and sorrow."

"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, dwell observing the body within the body by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, ardent in vigor, clearly comprehending and possessed of mindfulness, having subdued covetousness and dejection?"

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, taking non-apprehension as the means, they carefully observe their own body: when walking, they know they are walking; when standing, they know they are standing; when sitting, they know they are sitting; when lying down, they know they are lying down. In whatever way their bodily postures differ, in that very way they exert ardent diligence, possessing right mindfulness and clear comprehension, and subdue greed and sorrow.”

This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, dwells observing the body within the body by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, ardent in vigor, clearly comprehending and fully mindful, having subdued covetousness and dejection.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, they clearly observe their own body: they are clearly aware of coming and going; clearly aware of looking ahead and looking back; clearly aware of bending and stretching; clearly aware of wearing the saṃghāṭī robe and holding the robes and bowl; whether eating or drinking, reclining or walking, sitting or rising, receiving guests, waking or sleeping, speaking or remaining silent, and entering or emerging from various meditative concentrations—they are in every case mindful and clearly aware."

This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, dwells observing the body within the body by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, ardent in vigor, clearly comprehending and fully mindful, having subdued covetousness and dejection.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, employing the method of non-apprehension, he carefully observes his own body: when breathing in, he is mindful that he is breathing in; when breathing out, he is mindful that he is breathing out; when breathing in long, he is mindful that he is breathing in long; and when breathing out short, he is mindful that he is breathing out short."

Just as a wheelwright or his apprentice knows when the momentum of a wheel is long that the momentum of the wheel is long, and knows when the momentum of the wheel is short that the momentum of the wheel is short;
so too it is with this bodhisattva mahāsattva, who mindfully knows the distinctions of length in all breaths, whether entering or exiting.

This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, dwells contemplating the body within the body by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, ardent in vigor, clearly comprehending and possessed of mindfulness, having subdued covetousness and dejection.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, they carefully examine the distinctions among the elements of their own body, namely: the earth element, the water, fire, and wind elements."

Just as a skilled butcher or his apprentice, having taken the life of an ox, uses a sharp knife to dissect its body and divide it into four quarters, whether sitting or standing, observes and knows it as it truly is.
In the same way, this bodhisattva mahāsattva observes the distinctions between the four elements of his own body—earth, water, fire, and air.

This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, dwells in the contemplation of the body within the internal body by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, ardent in vigor, clearly comprehending and mindful, having subdued covetousness and dejection.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, employing the method of non-apprehension, he carefully contemplates his own body from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head as being filled with various kinds of impurities, externally enveloped by a thin skin. That is to say, this body consists only of various hairs of the head and body, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, blood, sinews, veins, bones, and marrow; heart, liver, lungs, kidneys, spleen, gallbladder, bladder, stomach, large intestine, small intestine, excrement, urine, mucus, saliva, spittle, tears, filth, and sweat; phlegm, pus, fat, grease, brain, membranes, and lymph. Thus, the body is filled with such impurities."

It is like a farmer or a householder whose granary is filled to the brim with various kinds of grain, such as rice, hemp, millet, beans, and wheat. A person with clear vision, opening the granary and looking within, is able to know exactly that there are only these various grains, such as rice, hemp, and millet.

In the same way, this bodhisattva mahāsattva carefully contemplates his own body from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head as being filled with impurities, such that it is not to be craved or delighted in.

This is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s dwelling in the contemplation of the body within the internal body while practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), employing the skillful means of non-apprehension, with ardent diligence, correct knowledge, and full mindfulness, thereby subduing greed and sorrow.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, employing the method of non-apprehension, he goes to a charnel ground to observe a discarded corpse that has been dead for one day, or two days, or even up to seven days; its body is bloated, its color has turned bluish-black, it is putrid and rotting with the skin pierced, and pus and blood are flowing out."
Having seen this, he reflects: "My own body possesses such a nature and is endowed with such qualities; until liberation is attained, it will ultimately end in this same way.

This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, dwells observing the body within the body by means of non-apprehension as a skillful method, ardent in diligence, clearly comprehending and possessed of mindfulness, having subdued greed and sorrow.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, employing the method of non-apprehension, he goes to a charnel ground to observe a discarded corpse that has been dead for one day, or two days, or even up to seven days, being pecked at or clawed by various birds and beasts such as vultures, eagles, crows, magpies, hawks, owls, tigers, leopards, foxes, wolves, jackals, and dogs, with its flesh and bones strewn about as they tear and devour it."
Having seen this, he reflects: "My own body possesses such a nature and is endowed with such dharmas; until liberation is attained, it will ultimately end in this same way.

This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, dwells in the contemplation of the body within the internal body by means of non-apprehension as a skillful method—ardently diligent, clearly comprehending, and fully mindful, having subdued greed and sorrow.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, employing the method of non-apprehension, he goes to a charnel ground and observes a discarded corpse that has been devoured by birds and beasts, becoming impure and putrid, with pus and blood flowing away, from which countless kinds of maggots emerge, its foul stench and filthiness exceeding even that of a dead dog."
Having seen this, he reflects: "My own body possesses such a nature and is endowed with such qualities; until liberation is attained, it will ultimately end in this same way.

This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, dwells contemplating the body within the body by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, ardent in vigor, clearly comprehending and mindful, having subdued covetousness and dejection.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, employing the method of non-apprehension, he goes to a charnel ground and observes a discarded corpse: its flesh has been devoured by worms and maggots until the bones are exposed; the limbs and joints remain connected, bound by sinews and smeared with blood, yet still with some putrid flesh remaining."
Having seen this, he reflects: "My own body possesses such a nature and is endowed with such qualities; until liberation is attained, it will ultimately end in this same way.

This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), dwells in the contemplation of the body within the internal body by means of non-apprehension as a skillful method, ardent in vigor, clearly comprehending and mindful, having subdued covetousness and dejection.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, employing the method of non-apprehension, they go to a charnel ground and observe a discarded corpse that has become a skeleton, with all flesh and blood gone, remaining only as bones joined by sinews.
Having seen this, he reflects: "My own body possesses such a nature and is endowed with such qualities; until liberation is attained, it will ultimately end in this same way.

This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, dwells in contemplation of the body within the internal body by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method—ardent in vigor, clearly comprehending and possessed of mindfulness, having subdued greed and sorrow.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, employing the method of non-apprehension, he goes to a charnel ground and observes a discarded corpse that remains as nothing but a collection of bones; these bones are white like jade or snow, with all tendons rotted away and the joints separated."
Having seen this, he reflects: "My own body possesses such a nature and is endowed with such qualities; until liberation is attained, it will ultimately end in this same way.

This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, dwells observing the body within the body by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, ardent in vigor, clearly comprehending and mindful, having subdued greed and sorrow.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, employing the method of non-apprehension, he goes to a charnel ground and observes a discarded corpse that has become white bones, with its limbs and joints scattered and fallen apart in different directions."
Having seen this, he reflects: "My own body possesses such a nature and is endowed with such phenomena; until liberation is attained, it will ultimately end in this same way.

This is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of the perfection of wisdom when, employing the skillful means of non-apprehension, he dwells in the contemplation of the body within the internal body, ardent in diligence, clearly comprehending and possessed of mindfulness, having subdued greed and sorrow.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, employing the method of non-apprehension, he goes to a charnel ground and observes discarded corpses whose bones are separated and scattered in various places: the bones of the feet in one place, the bones of the calves in another, the bones of the knees in another, the bones of the thighs in another, the bones of the hips in another, the bones of the spine in another, the bones of the ribs in another, the bones of the chest in another, the bones of the shoulders in another, the bones of the upper arms in another, the bones of the hands in another, the bones of the neck in another, the bones of the jaw in another, the bones of the cheeks in another, and the skull bones likewise in another place."
Having seen this, he reflects: "My own body possesses such a nature and is endowed with such qualities; until liberation is attained, it will ultimately end in this same way.

This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), dwells in contemplation of the body within the internal body by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, ardent in vigor, clearly comprehending and mindful, having subdued covetousness and dejection.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, employing the method of non-apprehension, he goes to a charnel ground to observe discarded corpses. The skeletal remains lie scattered, blown by the wind, scorched by the sun, drenched by rain, and encrusted with frost for many years, until their color becomes like white jade or snow."
Having seen this, he reflects: "My own body possesses such a nature and is endowed with such qualities; until liberation is attained, it will ultimately end in this same way.

This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, dwells observing the body within the body by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, ardent in vigor, clearly comprehending and possessed of mindfulness, having subdued covetousness and dejection.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, employing the method of non-apprehension, they go to a charnel ground to observe a discarded corpse: other bones scattered upon the ground for many hundreds or many thousands of years, their appearance having turned blue-green like the color of a pigeon, or some being decayed and reduced to powder like dust, mixed with the earth such that they can hardly be distinguished from it."
Having seen this, he reflects: "My own body possesses such a nature and is endowed with such qualities; until liberation is attained, it will ultimately end in this same way.

This is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of the perfection of wisdom when, by means of non-apprehension as a skillful method, he dwells in the contemplation of the body within the internal body, ardent in vigor, clearly comprehending and mindful, having subdued covetousness and dejection.

“Subhūti! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they do so by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method. Just as they dwell observing the body in its internal aspects with such distinctions—ardently diligent, clearly comprehending, possessed of mindfulness, and having subdued greed and sorrow—they likewise dwell observing the body in its external aspects, and they dwell observing the body in its internal and external aspects, being ardently diligent, clearly comprehending, possessed of mindfulness, and having subdued greed and sorrow; it is also thus according to what is appropriate for each case.”

“Subhūti! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they take non-apprehension as their skillful means and dwell in the contemplation of feelings, the mind, and dharmas—both internally, externally, and both internally and externally—with ardent diligence, clear comprehension, and full mindfulness, subduing greed and sorrow; all this should be explained in detail according to what is appropriate.”

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this way, employing the method of non-apprehension, they abide in the internal body, feelings, mind, and phenomena, as well as the external and both internal-and-external body, feelings, mind, and phenomena. While contemplating the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena, although they perform this contemplation, they apprehend nothing.”
"Subhūti, you should know that this is the mark of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The characteristics of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas refer to the four right endeavors (*samyakprahāṇa*).
What are the four? Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, employing the method of non-apprehension, they generate desire, exert effort, arouse right diligence, and apply themselves with mental uplift and mental sustenance so that unarisen evil and unwholesome states do not arise; this is the first [basis of power].

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, employing the method of non-apprehension, they generate desire, exert effort, arouse right diligence, and apply themselves with mental uplift and mental sustenance for the sake of the permanent abandonment of all evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen; this is the second [basis of power].

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, employing the method of non-apprehension, they generate desire, exert effort, arouse right diligence, and apply themselves with mental exertion and mental maintenance so that wholesome dharmas not yet arisen may arise; this is the third [basis of power].

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, employing the method of non-apprehension, they generate desire, exert themselves, arouse right effort, and apply themselves with mental uplift and mental maintenance, so that wholesome dharmas already arisen may remain stable, not be forgotten, and be further increased, practiced repeatedly, and brought to fulfillment; this is the fourth [basis of psychic power].
"Subhūti, you should know that this is the characteristic of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas.

*The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Fascicle 414, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Second Division, Chapter Seventeen on the Foundations of Mindfulness, Part Two. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The characteristics of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas refer to the four bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*).
What are the four? Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, employing the method of non-apprehension, they cultivate the basis for psychic power consisting of concentration of desire and the formations of abandonment; this is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment—this is the first.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, by means of non-apprehension as a skillful method, cultivates the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration through exertion and the accomplishment of the formative forces of abandonment, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and culminating in relinquishment—this is the second.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, they cultivate the basis of psychic power consisting in concentration of mind and the volitional formations of abandonment; this is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment—this is the third.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, they cultivate the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration through the cultivation of insight and the accomplishment of the formations of abandonment; relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and resulting in relinquishment—this is the fourth.
"Subhūti, you should know that this is the characteristic of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas. Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The characteristics of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas refer to the five faculties.
What are these five? Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they cultivate the faculty of faith, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method.
"Subhūti, you should know that this is the characteristic of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas. Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The characteristic of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva refers to the five powers. What are the five? Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they cultivate the power of faith, the power of diligence, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method.
"Subhūti, you should know that this is the mark of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!"
Subhūti, the characteristics of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva refer to the seven factors of enlightenment.
What are these seven? Subhūti, they are as follows:

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, employing the method of non-apprehension, they cultivate the awakening factor of mindfulness, the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena, the awakening factor of energy, the awakening factor of joy, the awakening factor of tranquility, the awakening factor of concentration, and the awakening factor of equanimity; these are based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and result in relinquishment.
"Subhūti, you should know that this is the characteristic of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas. Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The characteristic of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva refers to the eight branches of the noble path.
What are these eight? Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, employing the method of non-apprehension, they cultivate right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and dedicating them toward relinquishment.
"Subhūti, you should know that this is the characteristic of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas. Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The characteristics of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva refer to the three samādhis.
What are these three? Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, they contemplate that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty; their mind abides securely therein, which is called the gate of liberation of emptiness and also called the samādhi of emptiness—this is the first.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by means of non-apprehension as a skillful method, they contemplate that all phenomena are signless because their own-characteristics are empty; with the mind thus dwelling in peace, this is called the gate of liberation of signlessness, and it is also called the samādhi of signlessness—this is the second.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by means of non-apprehension as a skillful means, they observe that all phenomena are empty of intrinsic characteristics and thus have no object of aspiration; their mind abides peacefully therein, which is called the gate of liberation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*) and is also called the samādhi of wishlessness; this is the third.
"Subhūti, you should know that this is the characteristic of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The characteristics of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva consist of eleven knowledges.
What are the eleven? They are:

the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), knowledge of the origin (*samudayajñāna*), knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), and knowledge according to what has been taught (*yathārutajñāna*).
"What is the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)? Subhūti!
If a knowledge, by means of non-apprehension as its expedient, knows the distinct characteristics of the five aggregates, this is called the knowledge of phenomena."
"What is subsequent knowledge? Subhūti,
if one employs the method of non-apprehension and knows that from the eye up to the mind, and from forms up to phenomena, all are impermanent— this is called subsequent knowledge."
“What is the knowledge of others’ minds?

Subhūti, it is the knowledge that, by means of non-apprehension as its expedient, knows the minds and mental factors of other sentient beings without any doubt or obstruction; this is called the knowledge of others’ minds.”
"What is conventional knowledge? Subhūti!
If, by means of non-apprehension as a skillful method, one knows the differences in the practices of all sentient beings, this is called conventional knowledge."
"What is the knowledge of suffering? Subhūti!
If, by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, one knows that suffering should not arise, this is the knowledge of suffering."
"What is the knowledge of origination? Subhūti!
If, by means of non-apprehension as the expedient, one knows that origination should be eternally abandoned, this is called the knowledge of origination."
"What is the knowledge of cessation? Subhūti,
if one employs the method of non-apprehension to know that cessation is to be realized, this is the knowledge of cessation."
"What is the knowledge of the path? Subhūti,
if one employs the method of non-apprehension to know that the path should be cultivated, this is the knowledge of the path."
"What is the knowledge of exhaustion? Subhūti!
If, by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, one knows that greed, hatred, and delusion are exhausted, this is the knowledge of exhaustion."
“What is the knowledge of non-arising? Subhūti!
If, by means of the expedient of non-apprehension, one knows that the various realms of existence will never again arise, this is the knowledge of non-arising.”
“What is the knowledge that accords with what was taught? Subhūti,
all the knowledge of all aspects possessed by the Tathāgata is the knowledge that accords with what was taught.”
“Subhūti, you should know that this is the characteristic of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!”
The characteristics of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas consist of three faculties:
first, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"; second, the faculty of "knowing"; and third, the faculty of "one who has fully known."
"What is the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown'?

Subhūti, it refers to the faculties of faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom possessed by those individuals in training who have not yet realized the noble truths; this is called the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown'."
“What is the faculty of one who has already known?

Subhūti, it refers to whatever faculties of faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom belong to those individuals in training (śaikṣa) who have already attained clear realization (abhisamaya) regarding the noble truths; this is called the faculty of one who has already known.”
“What is the faculty of one who has fully known?

Subhūti, it refers to the faculties of faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom possessed by those individuals beyond training—whether they be arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas established in the ten stages, or Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas. These are called the faculty of one who has fully known.”
“Subhūti! If these three faculties are practiced with non-apprehension as the means, you should know that this is the mark of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
the characteristics of the Great Vehicle of a bodhisattva mahāsattva consist of the three samādhis.
What are these three?
1. Samādhi with vitarka and vicāra; 2. Samādhi without vitarka and with only vicāra;
3. Samādhi without vitarka and without vicāra.
“What is the concentration with directed thought and evaluation? Subhūti!

If, having detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, one enters and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by directed thought and evaluation and possesses the joy and happiness born of seclusion—this is called the concentration with directed thought and evaluation.”
"What is the samādhi without vitarka and with only vicāra?
Subhūti, it is the intermediate concentration between the first dhyāna and the second dhyāna; this is called the samādhi without vitarka and with only vicāra."
“What is the concentration without applied thought and sustained thought? Subhūti!
If it is the second dhyāna up to the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, this is called the concentration without applied thought and sustained thought.”
“Subhūti! If these three kinds [of phenomena] are practiced by means of non-apprehension, you should know that this is the characteristic of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
the mark of the Great Vehicle of a bodhisattva mahāsattva consists of the ten recollections. What are the ten?

That is to say: recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dharma, recollection of the Sangha, recollection of ethical discipline, recollection of relinquishment, recollection of the devas, recollection of tranquility, recollection of inhalation and exhalation, recollection of the body, and recollection of death.
"Subhūti! If these ten kinds [of practices] are undertaken with non-apprehension as the means, you should know that this is the characteristic of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

The mark of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva consists of all wholesome dharmas, such as the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the eight liberations, and the nine successive attainments, when practiced by means of non-apprehension. You should know that this is the mark of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
the characteristic of the Great Vehicle of a bodhisattva mahāsattva refers to the ten powers of a Tathāgata. What are these ten?

"Subhūti! To take non-apprehension as the skillful means and, in accordance with reality, to thoroughly understand the characteristics of what is possible and what is impossible regarding phenomena such as cause and effect—this is the foremost."

“Subhūti! To know, by means of non-apprehension as a skillful means, the distinct characteristics of the causes and effects of the various karmas, dharmas, and experiences of all sentient beings in the past, future, and present—this is the second.”
"If, by means of non-apprehension as a skillful method, one knows as it truly is that the world consists of various and manifold realms—this is the third.
If, by means of non-apprehension as a skillful method, one knows as it truly is that sentient beings possess various and manifold inclinations—this is the fourth."
"If one employs the skillful means of non-apprehension to understand, as they truly are, the superior and inferior faculties of all classes of sentient beings, this is the fifth.
If one employs the skillful means of non-apprehension to understand, as they truly are, the characteristics of pervasive conduct, this is the sixth."

"If one takes non-apprehension as the skillful means and, in accordance with reality, thoroughly understands the differences among sentient beings regarding their faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, liberations, meditative absorptions, concentrations, attainments, and their states of defilement and purity—this is the seventh."
"If, by means of non-apprehension as a skillful method, one understands as they truly are the immeasurable varieties of the past lives of sentient beings, this is the eighth."
"If one takes non-apprehension as the skillful means and, in accordance with reality, thoroughly understands the immeasurable varieties of death and birth among sentient beings, this is the ninth."

"If, by means of non-apprehension as a skillful method, one understands as it truly is the permanent exhaustion of all taints, attains the untainted liberation of mind, attains the untainted liberation of wisdom, and in this very life realizes for oneself and dwells in its fulfillment, being able to correctly know: 'Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence'—this is the tenth."
