the sense base of the eye does not arise, nor do the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body,
or mind arise. Why is this?
Because their intrinsic nature is empty, the sphere of form is not produced; the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are likewise not produced. Why is this?
Because their intrinsic nature is empty, the eye-element does not arise; nor do the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-elements arise. Why is this?
Because their intrinsic nature is empty, the realm of form does not arise; nor do the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena arise. Why is this?
Because their intrinsic nature is empty, the eye-consciousness element does not arise; nor do the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-consciousness elements arise. Why is this?
Because their intrinsic nature is empty, eye-contact does not arise; ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact likewise do not arise. Why is this?

Because their intrinsic nature is empty, the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition do not arise; likewise, the various feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as conditions do not arise either.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is empty.
The earth element is not produced; the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are likewise not produced.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is empty.
Thus, bodily formations do not arise, nor do vocal or mental formations arise.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is empty.
The perfection of generosity does not arise, and so on, up to the knowledge of all aspects, which also does not arise.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is empty, Śāriputra!
For this reason, regarding phenomena that are non-arising, one utters the word "non-arising"; both these phenomena and this word are devoid of the meaning of arising.
Śāriputra, whether it be the phenomenon spoken, the words by which it is spoken, the speaker, or the listener—all are devoid of the meaning of arising.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra praised Subhūti, saying:
"Among those who preach the Dharma, you are foremost; none can equal you except for the Buddha, the World-Honored One."
"Why is this? Because regarding whatever various Dharma-gates one may inquire about or challenge, he is able to provide answers without any obstruction. Subhūti replied:

"Those disciples of the Buddhas who are without dependence or attachment regarding all phenomena are, by the very nature of things, able to provide individual responses to every question and inquiry with mastery and fearlessness."
"Why is this? Because all dharmas have nothing upon which they rely. Śāriputra said:
"How is it that all phenomena have no basis whatsoever? Subhūti replied, "Śāriputra!..."
Because the intrinsic nature of form is empty, it does not rely on the internal, nor on the external, nor on that which lies between the two;

because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise empty of intrinsic nature, they do not rely on the internal, nor on the external, nor on that which lies between the two.
“Śāriputra! Because the sense-base of the eye is empty of intrinsic nature, it does not rely on the internal, it does not rely on the external, and it does not rely on that which is between the two;

the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise empty of intrinsic nature, and thus they do not rely on the internal, they do not rely on the external, and they do not rely on that which is between the two.”
“Śāriputra! Because the sphere of form is empty of intrinsic nature, it does not rely on the internal, nor does it rely on the external, nor does it rely on that which is between the two;

because the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are also empty of intrinsic nature, they do not rely on the internal, nor do they rely on the external, nor do they rely on that which is between the two.”
“Śāriputra! Because the nature of the eye-element is empty, it does not rely on the internal, it does not rely on the external, and it does not rely on that which is between the two;

because the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements are also by nature empty, they do not rely on the internal, they do not rely on the external, and they do not rely on that which is between the two.”
“Śāriputra! Because the nature of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is emptiness, it does not rely on the internal, nor on the external, nor on that which is between the two;
because the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, and phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) are also by nature empty, they do not rely on the internal, nor on the external, nor on that which is between the two.”
“Śāriputra! Because the eye-consciousness element is empty of intrinsic nature, it does not rely on the internal, nor does it rely on the external, nor does it rely on that which is between the two;

the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements are likewise empty of intrinsic nature, and thus they do not rely on the internal, nor do they rely on the external, nor do they rely on that which is between the two.”
“Śāriputra! Because the intrinsic nature of eye-contact is empty, it does not rely on the internal, nor on the external, nor on that which is between the two;
because the intrinsic natures of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact are likewise empty, they do not rely on the internal, nor on the external, nor on that which is between the two.”

“Śāriputra! Because the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are empty of intrinsic nature, they do not rely on the internal, they do not rely on the external, and they do not rely on that which is between the two.

Because the various feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as conditions are likewise empty of intrinsic nature, they do not rely on the internal, they do not rely on the external, and they do not rely on that which is between the two.”
"Śāriputra! Because the nature of the perfection of generosity is emptiness, it does not rely on the internal, nor on the external, nor on that which is between the two;
and so on, up to the perfection of wisdom, because its nature is also emptiness, it does not rely on the internal, nor on the external, nor on that which is between the two."
“Śāriputra! Because the emptiness of the internal is empty of its own intrinsic nature, it does not rely on the internal, nor on the external, nor on that which lies between them;

and so on, up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, which, being empty of its own intrinsic nature, does not rely on the internal, nor on the external, nor on that which lies between them.”
“Śāriputra! Because the four foundations of mindfulness are empty of intrinsic nature, they do not rely on the internal, nor on the external, nor on that which lies between the two;
and so on, up to the eightfold noble path, which, because it is empty of intrinsic nature, does not rely on the internal, nor on the external, nor on that which lies between the two.”

“Śāriputra! Because even the ten powers of a Buddha are empty of intrinsic nature, they do not rely on the internal, they do not rely on the external, nor do they rely on that which is between the two;

because even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are empty of intrinsic nature, they do not rely on the internal, they do not rely on the external, nor do they rely on that which is between the two.”

"Śāriputra! Because the intrinsic nature of even all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is empty, it does not rely on the internal, nor does it rely on the external, nor does it rely on that which is between the two;

because the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are also empty of intrinsic nature, they do not rely on the internal, nor do they rely on the external, nor do they rely on that which is between the two."
“Śāriputra! For this reason, because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, I say they have no basis whatsoever. Furthermore, Śāriputra!”

they should purify the eye constituent up to the mind constituent; they should purify the form constituent up to the phenomena constituent. They should...

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva purify the path to enlightenment while practicing the six perfections?”
Subhūti replied, "Śāriputra, each of the six pāramitās has two kinds."
"The first is the mundane;
the second is the supramundane. Śāriputra asked:
“What is the mundane perfection of generosity?
What is the supramundane perfection of generosity? Subhūti replied:

“Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva acts as a great donor, he is able to give to all śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the poor, the sick, the orphaned, the destitute, and those who beg on the road: food to those who need food, drink to those who need drink, vehicles to those who need vehicles, clothing to those who need clothing, incense and flowers to those who need incense and flowers, ornaments to those who need ornaments, houses to those who need houses, medicine to those who need medicine, lamps to those who need lamps, and bedding to those who need bedding; in this way, he gives away all such other requisites for life according to their needs.”

Furthermore, if there should come those who beg for a son, he gives a son; those who beg for a daughter, he gives a daughter; those who beg for a wife or concubine, he gives a wife or concubine; those who beg for official rank, he gives official rank; those who beg for a kingdom or city, he gives a kingdom or city; those who beg for the throne, he gives the throne; those who beg for his head or eyes, he gives his head or eyes; those who beg for his ears or nose, he gives his ears or nose; those who beg for his hands or feet, he gives his hands or feet; those who beg for his limbs and joints, he gives his limbs and joints; those who beg for his flesh or blood, he gives his flesh or blood; those who beg for his marrow or bones, he gives his marrow or bones; those who beg for his servants, he gives his servants; and those who beg for living beings, he gives living beings. In all such cases, according to their requests, he bestows everything, both internal and external.
Although one performs such giving, there remains a basis for it, namely the thought:

"I am the giver and he is the recipient; I am the donor; I am not stingy or greedy; I am able to relinquish everything in accordance with the Buddha's teaching; I am practicing the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā)."

When he practices giving, he employs the skillful means of perceiving objects as attainable, sharing [the merit] equally with all sentient beings, and dedicating it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Again, he forms this thought:
"I dedicate this merit to all sentient beings, so that they may obtain peace and happiness in this life and future lives, even unto the realization of nirvana without remainder."
He practices giving while attached to the three spheres.
What are these three?
They are the notion of self, the notion of another, and the notion of giving.
Because one practices giving while attached to these three wheels, it is called the mundane perfection of generosity (*laukikī dānapāramitā*).
For what reason is this generosity called mundane?
Because it functions in common with the world, and because it neither moves nor transcends worldly phenomena; for these reasons, it is called the mundane perfection of generosity.
“Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices generosity, the three spheres are pure.
What are these three?
First, not grasping at oneself as the giver;
second, not grasping at the other as the recipient;
third, not being attached to the gift or the fruit of giving.
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving, the three spheres are pure.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, taking great compassion as the foremost, dedicates the merit of the practice of giving universally to all sentient beings, perceiving no sentient being whatsoever; and although they share it equally with sentient beings and dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they do not perceive even the slightest mark therein. Because they practice giving without any grasping at all, it is called the supramundane perfection of giving.
For what reason is this giving called supramundane?

Because it does not function in common with the mundane world, and because it can move and transcend mundane phenomena; for these reasons, it is called the supramundane perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
Śāriputra said: "What are the mundane perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom?"
"What, then, are the supramundane perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration,

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, if there is a basis for these practices due to attachment to the three spheres, they are called mundane pāramitās; this is because they proceed in common with the world and do not move beyond or transcend worldly phenomena.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, because they are without basis and possess the purity of the three spheres, these are called supramundane pāramitās; for they do not function in common with the mundane world and are capable of shaking and transcending mundane phenomena.
“Śāriputra! In this way, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six perfections, they purify the path to enlightenment.
At that time, the venerable Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

The path to enlightenment for a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva consists of inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence;
it consists of suchness, the dharma-realm, the reality-limit, the inconceivable realm, and so forth;
it consists of all doors of samādhi and all dhāraṇīs.

The doors of liberation are the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s path to enlightenment; the ten powers of a buddha, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, are the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s path to enlightenment.

Because internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature is empty, one should know that this dwelling and this mental attention are also empty.
Because internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature is detached, one should know that this dwelling and this mental attention are also detached.
Because internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, is quiescent, one should know that this dwelling and mental attention are likewise quiescent.

Because internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, is devoid of cognition, one should know that this dwelling and mental attention are likewise devoid of cognition.
"Śāriputra! Because the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path do not exist, you should know that this dwelling and mental attention likewise do not exist."

Because the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path lack substantial reality, one should know that these states of abiding and mental attentions likewise lack substantial reality.
Because the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path lack intrinsic nature, one should know that these states of abiding and mental attentions likewise lack intrinsic nature.
Because the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path are empty, one should know that these states of abiding and mental attentions are also empty.
Because the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path are detached, one should know that these states of abiding and mental attentions are also detached.
Because the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path are quiescent, one should know that this dwelling and mental attention are likewise quiescent.

Because the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path are without cognitive awareness, one should know that this dwelling and mental attention are likewise without cognitive awareness.

“Śāriputra! In this way, because even the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha do not exist, you should know that such a dwelling and such mental attention also do not exist.”
Because the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha lack substantial reality, one should know that such dwelling and mental attention likewise lack substantial reality.
Because the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha lack intrinsic nature, one should know that such dwelling and mental attention likewise lack intrinsic nature.
Because the ten powers of a Buddha, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are empty, one should know that this dwelling and this mental attention are also empty.
Because the ten powers of a Buddha, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are detached, one should know that this dwelling and this mental attention are also detached.
Because the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are quiescent, one should know that this dwelling and this mental attention are also quiescent.
Because the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are without cognition, one should know that this dwelling and this mental attention are also without cognition.
“Śāriputra! Because all doors of samādhi and all doors of dhāraṇī do not exist, you should know that such dwelling and mental attention likewise do not exist.”
Because all doors of samādhi and all doors of dhāraṇī are without reality, one should know that such dwelling and mental attention are likewise without reality.
Because all doors of samādhi and all doors of dhāraṇī are without intrinsic nature, one should know that such dwelling and mental attention are likewise without intrinsic nature.
Because all doors of samādhi and all doors of dhāraṇī are empty, one should know that this dwelling and mental attention are also empty.
Because all doors of samādhi and all doors of dhāraṇī are detached, one should know that this dwelling and mental attention are also detached.
Because all gateways of samādhi and all gateways of dhāraṇī are quiescent, one should know that such abiding and mental attention are also quiescent.
Because all gateways of samādhi and all gateways of dhāraṇī are devoid of cognitive awareness, one should know that such abiding and mental attention are also devoid of cognitive awareness.

“Śāriputra! Because omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) do not exist, you should know that this dwelling and this mental attention (*manasikāra*) likewise do not exist.”

Because all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) lack substantial reality, one should know that such abiding and mental attention (*manasikāra*) likewise lack substantial reality.

Because all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), one should know that such abiding and mental attention likewise lack intrinsic nature.

Because all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are empty, one should know that this dwelling and this mental attention (*manasikāra*) are also empty.
Because all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects are detached, one should know that this dwelling and this mental attention are also detached.

Because all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are quiescent, one should know that such dwelling and mental attention (*manasikāra*) are also quiescent.

Because all-knowledge, knowledge of the paths, and knowledge of all aspects are devoid of cognitive apprehension (*anupalambha*), one should know that such dwelling and mental attention are also devoid of cognitive apprehension.

“Śāriputra! Because the enlightenment of śrāvakas, the enlightenment of pratyekabuddhas, and unsurpassed enlightenment do not exist, you should know that such dwelling and mental attention also do not exist.”

Because the enlightenment of the śrāvakas, the enlightenment of the pratyekabuddhas, and the unsurpassed enlightenment lack substantial reality, one should know that such dwelling and mental attention likewise lack substantial reality.

Because the enlightenment of the śrāvakas, the enlightenment of the pratyekabuddhas, and unsurpassed enlightenment lack intrinsic nature, one should know that such dwelling and mental attention likewise lack intrinsic nature.
Because the enlightenment of śrāvakas, the enlightenment of pratyekabuddhas, and unsurpassed enlightenment are empty, one should know that such dwelling and mental attention are also empty.
Because the enlightenment of śrāvakas, the enlightenment of pratyekabuddhas, and unsurpassed enlightenment are detached, one should know that such dwelling and mental attention are also detached.

Because the enlightenment of the śrāvakas, the enlightenment of the pratyekabuddhas, and unsurpassed enlightenment are quiescent, one should know that this dwelling and mental attention are likewise quiescent.

Because the enlightenment of the śrāvakas, the enlightenment of the pratyekabuddhas, and unsurpassed enlightenment are devoid of cognitive apprehension, one should know that such dwelling and mental engagement are likewise devoid of cognitive apprehension.

“Śāriputra! For this reason, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas never abandon such dwelling and such mental attention, for they are no different from all sentient beings, because all phenomena are without differentiation.”
At that time, the Blessed One praised Subhūti, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"You have skillfully expounded the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; this is entirely through the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata.
Anyone who wishes to expound the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should do so exactly as you have expounded it."
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they should all train according to what you have said.

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train in the perfection of wisdom according to what you have said, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) and turn the sublime wheel of Dharma to deliver immeasurable multitudes of beings.

When the Venerable Subhūti was thus proclaiming this profound *prajñāpāramitā* for the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas, this trichiliocosm shook in six ways: that is to say, it moved, moved intensely, and moved most intensely; it surged, surged intensely, and surged most intensely; it quaked, quaked intensely, and quaked most intensely; it rattled, rattled intensely, and rattled most intensely; it roared, roared intensely, and roared most intensely; it crashed, crashed intensely, and crashed most intensely.

Furthermore, this trichiliocosm rose in the east and sank in the west, rose in the west and sank in the east, rose in the south and sank in the north, rose in the north and sank in the south, rose in the center and sank at the periphery, and rose at the periphery and sank in the center.
At that time, the Blessed One smiled. The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what cause and for what reason do you manifest this smile?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Just as I now, within this trichiliocosm, proclaim the *prajñāpāramitā* for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, so too, in the immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless worlds of the eastern direction, there are Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas who likewise proclaim the *prajñāpāramitā* for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;

and in the immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless worlds of the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir, there are likewise Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas who proclaim the *prajñāpāramitā* for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."

Just as now, because I proclaim the Prajñāpāramitā in this trichiliocosm, twelve nayutas of devas, humans, asuras, and others have attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).

Now, in the immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless worlds of the ten directions, there likewise dwell Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas who proclaim the Prajñāpāramitā; and in each of those worlds, immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings likewise give rise to the mind set on unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and attain great benefit and happiness.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 424; The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra,
Fascicle 425.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Chapter 25: Śakra, Part Two. Chapter 25, Section One: At that time, in this Sahā world-system of three thousand great thousandfold worlds, all the Four Great Heavenly Kings, each with their [retinues]...
Countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of devaputras from the Cāturmahārājakāyika heavens all came together in assembly;
all the Śakras, each accompanied by countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of devaputras from the Trāyastriṃśa heavens, all came together in assembly;
and all the Suyāma kings, each accompanied by countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis...
The hosts of devaputras from the Yāma Heaven all came together for the assembly;
all the Śakradevendra kings of the Tuṣita Heaven each came together with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of devaputras from the Tuṣita Heaven;
and all the Sunirmitadevaputra kings each [came] with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of devas from the Nirmāṇarati Heaven.

The hosts of devaputras all gathered together; all the sovereign kings of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven each came with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of devaputras from the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven;
all the Great Brahmā kings each came with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Brahmā assemblies.
All the gods of the Ābhāsvara Heaven each came together with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of gods of the second dhyāna;
all the gods of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven each came together with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of gods of the third dhyāna;
and all the gods of the Bṛhatphala Heaven each [came together] with immeasurable hundreds of thousands...
The hosts of gods from the fourth dhyāna heaven, numbering in the hundreds of millions (koṭi), all came together in assembly;
likewise, all those from the Akaniṣṭha heaven, each accompanied by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Śuddhāvāsa gods, came together in assembly.

The radiance of the bodies resulting from the maturation of pure karma belonging to the hosts of the Four Great Kings up to the hosts of the Śuddhāvāsa deities does not equal even one hundredth part, nor one thousandth part, nor one hundred-thousandth part, nor one koṭi-th part, nor one hundred-koṭi-th part, nor one thousand-koṭi-th part, nor one hundred-thousand-koṭi-th part of the constant light manifested from the body of the Tathāgata; indeed, it does not equal even a fractional part, a calculable part, a countable part, a comparable part, or even an upaniṣad-part thereof.

Why is this? Because the constant radiance manifested from the body of the Tathāgata blazes with such intense brilliance that it is the most honored, the most excellent, the highest, the most sublime, peerless, unequaled, and the foremost of all lights; it eclipses the radiance of all devas so that they no longer appear, just as a charred wick is outshone by Jambūnada gold.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:

"All the gods from the Cāturmahārājakāyika realm up to the Śuddhāvāsa realms have now assembled here, desiring to hear the Venerable One proclaim the Prajñāpāramitā. We pray that the Venerable One will deign to speak at this opportune moment."
Venerable One!
What is the prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva?
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva abide in the prajñāpāramitā?
"How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva train in the perfection of wisdom?
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed Śakra, the Lord of Devas, saying: "Kauśika!..."
You hosts of devas, listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well!

I shall, by receiving the Buddha’s power of majestic spiritual authority and in accordance with the Tathāgata’s intention, proclaim the Prajñāpāramitā for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, so that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may dwell therein in this manner and train therein in this manner.
Kauśika! All you gods who have not yet resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta should now all do so. Kauśika!
Those who have already entered the fixed course of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas are no longer able to give rise to the mind of great enlightenment.
Why is this, Kauśika?
Because they have already established a boundary around birth and death,
if there are any among them who can resolve their minds toward and set out for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, I likewise rejoice in that.
Why is this? Kauśika!
All superior persons should seek the supreme Dharma; I shall never obstruct the excellent qualities of others.
“Kauśika! As for your question, ‘What is the prajñāpāramitā of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?’, listen attentively!
I shall explain it for you.
"Kauśika! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva generates a mind associated with the knowledge of all modes, by way of non-apprehension..."
And as a skillful means, one contemplates form up to consciousness as impermanent, or as suffering, or as non-self, or as empty,
or as like a disease, or as like an abscess, or as like an arrow, or as like a wound,
or as feverish affliction, or as oppression, or as decay, or as decrepitude, or as fluctuation.

Whether it be subject to swift destruction, or fearsome, or loathsome, or fraught with calamity, or involving untimely death, or involving pestilence, or involving epidemics, or lacking in peace and security, or being unreliable—contemplate the sense-base of the eye up to the sense-base of the mind;
contemplate the sense-base of forms up to the sense-base of mental phenomena. Contemplate...
One contemplates the eye-element up to the mind-element; one contemplates the form-element up to the mental-object-element;
one contemplates the eye-consciousness-element up to the mind-consciousness-element; one contemplates eye-contact up to mind-contact;
one contemplates all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition up to all feelings produced with mind-contact as condition; one contemplates earth.
It is the same for the element of space up to the element of consciousness. Kausika,
this is called the Prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Kauśika! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva generates a mind associated with the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna),
and by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, contemplates form up to consciousness as either tranquil, or detached, or..."
Contemplating the sense base of the eye up to the sense base of the mind;
contemplating the sense base of forms up to the sense base of mental phenomena; contemplating the eye element up to the mind element;
contemplating the form element up to the phenomenon element—[whether it be] non-arising, or non-ceasing, or non-defilement, or non-purity, or non-action, or the unconditioned.
It is the same when one contemplates the visual consciousness element up to the mental consciousness element; when one contemplates visual contact up to mental contact;
when one contemplates all feelings produced with visual contact as condition up to all feelings produced with mental contact as condition;
and when one contemplates the earth element up to the consciousness element. It is likewise so.
Kauśika! This is called the Prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to a mind associated with the knowledge of all modes, employing the method of non-apprehension, they contemplate that ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions grasping; grasping conditions becoming; becoming conditions birth; and birth conditions old age and death, up to the entire great mass of suffering that arises.

Using non-apprehension as the skillful means, one contemplates that because ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease; because volitional formations cease, consciousness ceases; because consciousness ceases, name-and-form ceases; because name-and-form ceases, the six sense bases cease; because the six sense bases cease, contact ceases; because contact ceases, feeling ceases; because feeling ceases, craving ceases; because craving ceases, clinging ceases; because clinging ceases, existence ceases; because existence ceases, birth ceases; and because birth ceases, aging and death, and even the entire great mass of suffering, cease.
Kauśika! This is called the Prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to a mind associated with the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), employing the method of non-apprehension, they abide in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, and they abide in suchness (tathatā), the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), the inconceivable realm, the realm of peace, and so forth.
Kauśika! This is called the Prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva generates a mind associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), taking non-apprehension as the means (*upāya*), they cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; they cultivate the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; they cultivate the ten powers of a buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha; they cultivate all gateways of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and dhāraṇīs; and they cultivate all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Kauśika! This is called the Prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva generates a mind associated with the knowledge of all modes and, employing the method of non-apprehension, practices the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Kauśika! This is called the Prajñāpāramitā of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Furthermore, Kauśika!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they contemplate in this way:
"Only all phenomena mutually moisten, mutually increase, and mutually perfect one another; one contemplates and calculates that there is no self or what belongs to a self."
Furthermore, he forms this contemplation:

"The mind of dedication of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas does not merge with the mind of enlightenment, nor does the mind of enlightenment merge with the mind of dedication. This means that within the mind of enlightenment, the mind of dedication of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is non-existent and unobtainable; likewise, within the mind of dedication, the mind of enlightenment is also non-existent and unobtainable."
"Although the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas contemplate all dharmas as they truly are, they do not see anything at all within those dharmas. Kausika,
this is called the prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Then, Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, asked Subhūti:
"In what way is the mind of dedication of a bodhisattva mahāsattva not conjoined with the mind of enlightenment, and the mind of enlightenment likewise not conjoined with the mind of dedication?"

How is it that the mind of dedication is non-existent and unobtainable within the mind of enlightenment, and the mind of enlightenment is likewise non-existent and unobtainable within the mind of dedication?
Subhūti replied, “Kauśika!
The mind of dedication of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas is not a mind, and the mind of awakening is also not a mind.”
One should not dedicate a non-mind to a non-mind, nor should a mind dedicate itself to a non-mind;
one should not dedicate a non-mind to a mind, nor should a mind dedicate itself to a mind.
Why is this? Kausika!

That which is non-mind is itself the inconceivable; the inconceivable is itself non-mind. Thus, these two kinds are both non-existent; within that which is non-existent, there is no meaning of dedication.
Kauśika! The mind has no intrinsic nature; because the nature of the mind does not exist, mental factors also do not exist.
Since both the mind and mental factors lack intrinsic nature, the mind also lacks the sense of "dedicating" the mind.
"Kauśika! To practice such contemplation is called the Prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Subhūti, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!

You have skillfully expounded the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and you have skillfully encouraged the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to give rise to joy and diligently cultivate the Prajñāpāramitā.”
The Venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One:
“World-Honored One!
Since I recognize your kindness, I ought not to fail to repay it.”

Why is this? Because the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, along with their disciples, proclaimed the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) for the sake of the assembly of Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas; they demonstrated, instructed, exhorted, gladdened, comforted, and established them, causing them to attain the ultimate goal.

“World-Honored One, at that time you were also training therein; now you have realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and turned the sublime wheel of Dharma to bring benefit and happiness to us. Therefore, I should now follow the Buddha’s teaching and proclaim the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—showing, instructing, encouraging, and gladdening them; comforting and establishing them so they may attain the ultimate and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. This is what is called repaying his debt of gratitude.”
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed Śakra, the Lord of Devas, saying: "Kauśika!
You ask, 'How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwell in the perfection of wisdom?'"
"Listen attentively! I shall explain for you the characteristics of how bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should and should not abide within the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)."

“Kauśika! Form is empty of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; and the bodhisattva is empty of the bodhisattva.”

Whether it be the emptiness of form, or the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, or the emptiness of the bodhisattva—all such things are non-dual and have no state of duality.
Kauśika! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should dwell in the perfection of wisdom in this manner. "Kauśika!"
The eye-base is empty of the eye-base, and so on up to the mind-base being empty of the mind-base; the bodhisattva is empty of the bodhisattva.
Whether it be the emptiness of the eye-base, up to the emptiness of the mind-base, or the emptiness of the bodhisattva—all such things are non-dual and have no state of duality.
Kauśika! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should abide in the perfection of wisdom in this manner. Kauśika!
The sphere of form is empty of the sphere of form, and so on up to the sphere of phenomena being empty of the sphere of phenomena; the bodhisattva is empty of the bodhisattva.
Whether it be the emptiness of the sphere of form, up to the emptiness of the sphere of phenomena, or the emptiness of the bodhisattva—all such things are non-dual and have no state of duality.
Kauśika! All bodhisattva mahāsattvas should abide in the perfection of wisdom in this manner. Kauśika!
The eye-element is empty of the eye-element, and so on up to the mind-element being empty of the mind-element, and the bodhisattva being empty of the bodhisattva.
Whether it be the emptiness of the eye-element, up to the emptiness of the mind-element, or the emptiness of the bodhisattva—all such things are non-dual and have no state of duality.
Kauśika! All bodhisattva mahāsattvas should abide in the perfection of wisdom in this manner. "Kauśika!"
The realm of form is empty of the realm of form, up to and including the realm of phenomena being empty of the realm of phenomena, and the bodhisattva being empty of the bodhisattva.
Whether it be the emptiness of the realm of form, up to the emptiness of the realm of phenomena, or the emptiness of the bodhisattva—all such things are non-dual and have no state of duality.
Kauśika! All bodhisattva mahāsattvas should abide in the perfection of wisdom in this manner. "Kauśika!"

The eye-consciousness element is empty of the eye-consciousness element, and so on up to the mind-consciousness element being empty of the mind-consciousness element; the bodhisattva is empty of the bodhisattva.

Whether it be the emptiness of the eye-consciousness element, up to the emptiness of the mind-consciousness element, or the emptiness of the bodhisattva—all such things are non-dual and have no state of duality.
"Kauśika! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should abide in the perfection of wisdom in this manner. Kauśika!"
Eye-contact is empty of eye-contact, and so on up to mind-contact, which is empty of mind-contact; the bodhisattva is empty of bodhisattva.
Whether it be the emptiness of eye-contact, up to the emptiness of mind-contact, or the emptiness of the bodhisattva—all such things are non-dual and have no place of duality.
Kauśika! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should abide in the perfection of wisdom in this manner. "Kauśika!"

The various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are empty of the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition; likewise, up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition are empty of the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition; and the bodhisattva is empty of the bodhisattva.

If the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are empty, and so on up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition are empty, and if the bodhisattva is empty—all such things are non-dual and have no state of duality.
Kauśika! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should abide in the perfection of wisdom in this manner. "Kauśika!"
The earth element is empty of the earth element, and so on up to the consciousness element being empty of the consciousness element; the bodhisattva is empty of the bodhisattva.
Whether it be the emptiness of the earth element, up to the emptiness of the consciousness element, or the emptiness of the bodhisattva—all such things are non-dual and have no state of duality.
Kauśika! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should dwell in the perfection of wisdom in this manner. "Kauśika!"
Ignorance is empty of ignorance, and so on up to old age and death, which are empty of old age and death; the bodhisattva is empty of the bodhisattva.
Whether it be the emptiness of ignorance, up to the emptiness of old age and death, or the emptiness of the bodhisattva—all such things are non-dual and have no state of duality.
Kauśika! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should abide in the perfection of wisdom in this manner. "Kauśika!"

The cessation of ignorance is the emptiness of the cessation of ignorance, and so on up to the cessation of old age and death being the emptiness of the cessation of old age and death, and the Bodhisattva being the emptiness of the Bodhisattva.

Whether it be the emptiness of the cessation of ignorance, up to the emptiness of the cessation of old age and death, or the emptiness of the Bodhisattva—all such things are non-dual and have no state of duality.
Kauśika! All bodhisattva mahāsattvas should abide in the perfection of wisdom in this manner. "Kauśika!"

The perfection of generosity is empty of the perfection of generosity; up to and including the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of wisdom is empty of the perfection of wisdom; and the bodhisattva is empty of the bodhisattva.

Whether it be the emptiness of the perfection of giving, up to and including the emptiness of the perfection of wisdom, or the emptiness of the bodhisattva—all such things are non-dual and have no state of duality.
Kauśika! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should abide in the perfection of wisdom in this manner. "Kauśika!"

The emptiness of the internal is empty of the emptiness of the internal, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature is empty of the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, and the bodhisattva is empty of the bodhisattva.

Whether it be the emptiness of the internal, up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, or the emptiness of the bodhisattva—all such things are non-dual and have no state of duality.
Kauśika! All bodhisattva mahāsattvas should abide in the perfection of wisdom in this manner. "Kauśika!"

The four foundations of mindfulness are empty of the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha being empty of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the bodhisattva being empty of the bodhisattva.

Whether it be the emptiness of the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including the emptiness of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or the emptiness of the bodhisattva—all such things are non-dual and have no state of duality.
Kauśika! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should abide in the perfection of wisdom in this manner. "Kauśika!"
All gates of samādhi are empty of all gates of samādhi; all gates of dhāraṇī are empty of all gates of dhāraṇī; a bodhisattva is empty of a bodhisattva.
Whether it be the emptiness of all samādhi-doors, the emptiness of all dhāraṇī-doors, or the emptiness of the bodhisattva—all such things are non-dual and have no place of duality.
Kauśika! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should abide in the perfection of wisdom in this manner. "Kauśika!"

The Śrāvaka vehicle is empty of the Śrāvaka vehicle; the Pratyekabuddha vehicle and the Unsurpassed Vehicle are empty of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle and the Unsurpassed Vehicle; the Bodhisattva is empty of the Bodhisattva.

Whether it be the emptiness of the Śrāvaka vehicle, the emptiness of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle or the Unsurpassed Vehicle, or the emptiness of the Bodhisattva—all such things are non-dual and have no place of duality.
Kauśika! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should abide in the perfection of wisdom in this manner. "Kauśika!"
The stream-enterer is empty of the stream-enterer, up to and including the Tathāgata who is empty of the Tathāgata, and the bodhisattva who is empty of the bodhisattva.
Whether it be the emptiness of the stream-enterer, up to the emptiness of the Tathāgata, or the emptiness of the bodhisattva—all such things are non-dual and have no basis for duality.
Kauśika! All bodhisattva mahāsattvas should abide in the perfection of wisdom in this manner. Kauśika!

All-knowledge is empty of all-knowledge; the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects are empty of the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects; the bodhisattva is empty of the bodhisattva.

Whether it be the emptiness of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the emptiness of the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), or the emptiness of the bodhisattva—all such things are non-dual and have no duality.
“Kauśika! All bodhisattva mahāsattvas should abide in the perfection of wisdom in this manner.
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed Subhūti, saying:
“How is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not abide when practicing the perfection of wisdom? Subhūti replied, “Kauśika!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should not abide in form; they should not abide in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
they should not abide in the sense-base of the eye, up to and including the sense-base of the mind;
they should not abide in the sense-base of forms, up to and including the sense-base of phenomena.
One should not dwell on the eye-element, up to and including the mind-element;
one should not dwell on the form-element, up to and including the phenomena-element;
one should not dwell on the eye-consciousness-element, up to and including the mind-consciousness-element.
One should not dwell on eye-contact, nor should one dwell on anything up to mind-contact;
one should not dwell on the various sensations produced with eye-contact as condition, nor should one dwell on the various sensations produced with anything up to mind-contact as condition;
one should not dwell on the earth element, nor should one dwell on anything up to the consciousness element.
One should not dwell on ignorance, nor even on old age and death;
one should not dwell on the cessation of ignorance, nor even on the cessation of old age and death;
one should not dwell on the perfection of generosity, nor even on the perfection of wisdom.
One should not dwell in internal emptiness, nor even in the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;
one should not dwell in the four foundations of mindfulness, nor even in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
one should not dwell in any gateways of samādhi, nor should one dwell in any gateways of dhāraṇī.
One should not dwell in the Śrāvaka vehicle; one should not dwell in the Pratyekabuddha vehicle or the Unsurpassed Vehicle;
one should not dwell in the stage of Stream-enterer, up to and including the stage of Tathāgata;
one should not dwell in omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), nor should one dwell in the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Why is this? Kauśika!
Because one who dwells in such a manner has something to be apprehended.
"Furthermore, Kauśika, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should not dwell on the thought that 'this is form,' up to and including 'this is consciousness';
they should not dwell on the thought that 'this is the eye base,' up to and including 'this is the mind base.'"
One should not dwell on the notion that "this is the sense-field of form," up to "this is the sense-field of mental phenomena";
one should not dwell on the notion that "this is the eye-element," up to "this is the mind-element";
one should not dwell on the notion that "this is the form-element," up to "this is the mental-phenomena-element."
One should not dwell on the thought, "This is the eye-consciousness element," up to and including, "This is the mind-consciousness element";
one should not dwell on the thought, "This is eye-contact," up to and including, "This is mind-contact";

one should not dwell on the thought, "These are the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition," up to and including, "These are the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition."
One should not dwell on the thought that "this is the earth element," up to and including "this is the consciousness element";
one should not dwell on the thought that "this is ignorance," up to and including "this is old age and death";
nor should one dwell on the thought that "this is the cessation of ignorance," up to and including "this is the cessation of old age and death."
One should not dwell on the thought that "this is the perfection of generosity," up to and including "this is the perfection of wisdom";
one should not dwell on the thought that "this is internal emptiness," up to and including "this is the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature";
and one should not dwell on the thought that "this is the four applications of mindfulness," up to and including "these are the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha."
One should not dwell on the thought that "this is all the gateways of samādhi" or "this is all the gateways of dhāraṇī";
one should not dwell on the thought that "this is the Śrāvaka vehicle," "this is the Pratyekabuddha vehicle," or "this is the Unsurpassed Vehicle";
nor should one dwell on the thought that "this is a Stream-enterer," up to and including "this is a Tathāgata."
One should not dwell on the thought that "this is all-knowledge," or "this is the knowledge of the aspects of the path," or "this is the knowledge of all aspects.
Why is this so, Kauśika?
One who abides in such a manner does so because they have something to apprehend.

Furthermore, Kausika, when bodhisattva mahasattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should not abide in form, nor up to consciousness, as either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, empty or non-empty, tranquil or non-tranquil, or detached or non-detached.
One should not dwell on the sense-base of the eye, up to and including the sense-base of the mind, whether as permanent or impermanent, or even as detached or non-detached;
one should not dwell on the sense-base of forms, up to and including the sense-base of mental phenomena, whether as permanent or impermanent, or even as detached or non-detached;
one should not dwell on the element of the eye, up to and including the element of the mind, whether as permanent or impermanent, or even as detached or non-detached.
One should not dwell upon the realm of form, up to and including the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), whether as permanent or impermanent, up to and including as detached or non-detached;
one should not dwell upon the realm of eye-consciousness, up to and including the realm of mind-consciousness, whether as permanent or impermanent, up to and including as detached or non-detached;
one should not dwell upon eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact, whether as permanent or impermanent, up to and including as detached or non-detached.

One should not dwell on any feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, up to and including those produced with mind-contact as condition, whether they are permanent or impermanent, or even whether they are detached or non-detached;
one should not dwell on the earth element, up to and including the consciousness element, whether they are permanent or impermanent, or even whether they are detached or non-detached;
one should not dwell on ignorance, up to and including old age and death, whether they are permanent or impermanent, or even whether they are detached or non-detached.
One should not dwell on the cessation of ignorance up to the cessation of old age and death, whether as permanent or impermanent, and so forth, up to as detached or non-detached;
one should not dwell on the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, whether as permanent or impermanent, and so forth, up to as detached or non-detached;
one should not dwell on inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, whether as permanent or impermanent, and so forth, up to as detached or non-detached.
One should not dwell upon the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, whether as permanent or impermanent, or even as detached or non-detached;
one should not dwell upon any of the doors of samādhi or any of the doors of dhāraṇī, whether as permanent or impermanent, or even as detached or non-detached;
one should not dwell upon the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, or the unsurpassed vehicle, whether as permanent or impermanent, or even as detached or non-detached.
One should not dwell on the stream-enterer up to the Tathāgata as being either permanent or impermanent, up to being either detached or non-detached;

nor should one dwell on omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) as being either permanent or impermanent, up to being either detached or non-detached.
Why is this? Kauśika!
Because one who abides in such a manner has something to be apprehended.

"Furthermore, Kauśika, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should not dwell upon the fruit of a stream-enterer—whether manifested as conditioned or unconditioned; nor should they dwell upon the fruits of a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat; nor should they dwell upon the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha or the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas—whether manifested as conditioned or unconditioned."
Why is this? Kausika,
it is because one who dwells in such a manner has something to be apprehended.

"Furthermore, Kauśika, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should not abide in the notion that a stream-enterer is a field of merit; nor should they abide in the notion that a once-returner, a non-returner, an arhat, a pratyekabuddha, a bodhisattva, or a Tathāgata is a field of merit."
Why is this? Kauśika!
Because one who dwells in such a manner has something to be apprehended.
"Furthermore, Kauśika, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should not abide in the first stage, nor indeed should they abide in any stage up to the tenth."
Why is this? Kauśika,
it is because one who dwells in such a manner has something to apprehend.
Why is this? Because one who dwells in such a manner is subject to movement and change. Furthermore, Kausika!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should not, upon first generating the mind of enlightenment, dwell in the thought:
"I shall fulfill the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom."
One should not, having already resolved upon the initial aspiration, dwell on the thought:
"I shall practice the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path.
One should not, having already resolved upon the initial aspiration, dwell on such thoughts.

One should not dwell on the thought: "I shall practice the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha," nor should one dwell on the thought:
"Once my preparatory practices are perfected, I shall enter the Bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth."
One should not dwell on the thought:
"I have already entered the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma) and shall abide in the stage of non-retrogression of a bodhisattva.
One should not dwell on such a thought.
One should not dwell on the thought: "I shall fulfill the five supernormal powers of a bodhisattva," nor should one dwell on the thought:

"Abiding in the fulfillment of the five supernormal powers of a bodhisattva, I shall constantly travel through immeasurable and innumerable buddha-fields to pay homage, gaze upon, make offerings to, and serve the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; I shall hear the True Dharma, contemplate it according to principle, and extensively explain it to others."
Why is this? Kauśika, it is because one who abides in such a manner has something to be apprehended.
"Furthermore, Kauśika, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they should not dwell upon or form the thought:
'I shall adorn and purify a buddha-field such as those in which the Buddhas of the ten directions reside.'"
One should not dwell upon the thought:
"I shall manifest a transformation-body pure land such as those inhabited by the Buddhas of the ten directions.
One should not dwell upon this thought:

One should not dwell upon the thought: "I shall bring all sentient beings to maturity, causing them to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, or parinirvāṇa, or the happiness of humans and devas.
Nor should one dwell upon the thought:

"I shall travel to immeasurable and incalculable Buddha-fields to offer worship, respect, honor, and praise to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; furthermore, I shall make offerings with boundless flowers, incense, necklaces, precious banners, pennants, canopies, robes, bedding, food, drink, lamps, hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of celestial musical instruments, and immeasurable kinds of supreme and exquisite treasures."
One should not dwell on the thought:
"I shall establish immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings, causing them to attain non-retrogression in unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Why is this? Kauśika! Because one who abides in such a manner has something to be apprehended.
"Furthermore, Kauśika, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should not dwell upon the thought:
'I shall accomplish the pure fleshly eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the Dharma eye, and the Buddha eye.'"
One should not dwell upon the thought:
"I shall accomplish all gateways of meditative concentration (samādhi) and sport with mastery in all meditative concentrations.
One should not dwell upon such thoughts.
"One should not dwell on the thought: 'I shall accomplish all the gates of dhāraṇī and attain mastery over all dhāraṇīs.
Nor should one dwell on the thought:

'I shall accomplish the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.'"
One should not dwell upon the thought:

"I shall accomplish a body adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary signs, so that all sentient beings who see it will behold it with joy and never grow weary, thereby attaining benefit and happiness."
Why is this? Kauśika! Because one who dwells in such a manner has something to be attained.

"Furthermore, Kauśika! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should not dwell on the thought: 'This is the eighth person; this is one who follows by faith; this is one who follows by dharma'; nor should they dwell on the thought:
'This is a stream-enterer who will be reborn at most seven times; this is one who goes from family to family; this is one who has only one interval.'"
One should not dwell on the thought that this is a "level-headed" (*samaśīrṣaka*) person for whom afflictions are only exhausted at the end of their lifespan;

nor should one dwell on the thought that this is a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) fixed in the state of non-falling; nor should one dwell on the thought that this is a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) who, having come to this world, will reach the end of suffering;

nor should one dwell on the thought that this is a candidate for the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmi-patipanna*), or that this is a non-returner (*anāgāmi*) who attains parinirvāṇa upon reaching that [other] realm.
One should not dwell on the thought: "This is an Arhat who has forever exhausted future existence and will certainly enter nirvana without remainder in the present";
one should not dwell on the thought: "This is a Pratyekabuddha";
one should not dwell on the thought: "This is a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
"One should not dwell upon the thought:
'I have transcended the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas and now abide in the stage of a Bodhisattva.
One should not dwell upon such a thought."

"I shall fulfill all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); having awakened to all phenomena in all their aspects, I shall forever sever all afflictions, fetters, latent tendencies, and their continuities."
One should not dwell upon the thought:

"I shall realize the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; I shall become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; I shall turn the sublime wheel of Dharma and perform the deeds of a Buddha; I shall deliver immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings, causing them to attain the ultimate peace and happiness of nirvāṇa."
One should not dwell upon this thought:

"Having well cultivated the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), I shall abide in such a sublime meditative concentration (*samādhi*); by the predominant power of this concentration, may my lifespan remain for as many great eons (*mahākalpa*) as there are grains of sand in the Ganges."
One should not dwell upon the thought:
"I shall attain an infinite lifespan.
One should not dwell upon such a thought.
One should not dwell on the thought: "I shall accomplish the thirty-two marks, each of these marks being adorned by a hundred merits.
Nor should one dwell on the thought:
"I shall accomplish the eighty secondary characteristics, each of these characteristics possessing immeasurable, rare, and supreme qualities."
"One should not dwell upon this thought:
'I shall abide in a single adorned and purified land, a land as vast in the ten directions as the extent of worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.'"
One should not dwell on the thought:
"I shall sit peacefully upon a single vajra-throne, a throne so vast in extent that it is equal to the trichiliocosm."
One should not dwell upon the thought:

"I shall reside beneath the Great Bodhi Tree, which is lofty and vast, adorned with various jewels, and from which emanates a sublime fragrance; when sentient beings smell it, their mental afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion will all be eliminated, and their immeasurable and boundless physical ailments will also be healed."
"Whoever hears the fragrance of this Bodhi tree will abandon the mental orientations of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas and will certainly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
One should not dwell on the thought:

"May I obtain a purified Buddha-field, a field so pure that even the names of the aggregate of form do not exist there, nor the names of the aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness;"
The absence of the sense-base of the eye is called "sound"; the absence of the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind is called "sound.
The absence of the sense-base of form is called "sound"; the absence of the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena is called "sound.
The absence of the eye-element is called "sound"; the absence of the elements of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind is called "sound."
The name "formless realm" does not exist; the names of the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena do not exist;
the name of the eye-consciousness realm does not exist, nor do the names of the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness realms exist;
the name of eye-contact does not exist, nor do the names of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact exist.
There is no sound of the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition; there is no sound of the various feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-contact as condition;
there is no sound of the earth element; there is no sound of the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements;

there is no sound of ignorance; and there is no sound of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, or old age and death.
There is only the renown of the perfection of giving, up to and including only the renown of the perfection of wisdom;
there is only the renown of internal emptiness, up to and including only the renown of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence;
there is only the renown of suchness, up to and including only the renown of the inconceivable realm.
There is only the designation "four foundations of mindfulness," and so on, up to the designation "eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha";

within this, there is no designation whatsoever for stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, or ordinary beings, but only the designations "bodhisattva mahāsattva" and "Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
Why is this? Kauśika! Because one who abides in such a manner has something apprehended.
Why is this? When all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they awaken to the fact that all phenomena are utterly non-existent;
likewise, when the assembly of all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwells on the stage of non-retrogression, they also perceive that all phenomena are utterly non-existent.
“Kauśika! This is the characteristic of how a bodhisattva mahāsattva should and should not abide in the perfection of wisdom. Kauśika!”

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, regarding the characteristics of how they should or should not abide in the profound perfection of wisdom, should train in this manner by taking non-apprehension as their skillful means.
At that time, Śāriputra had this thought:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), should not abide in any phenomena, how then should they abide in the perfection of wisdom?"
The Venerable Subhūti, knowing what was in the mind of Śāriputra, said to him:
"What do you think? In what does the mind of the Tathāgatas abide?"
Śāriputra said: “The minds of all Tathāgatas abide nowhere. Why is this? Because...”
"Subhūti! The mind of the Tathāgata does not dwell in form; it does not dwell in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
it does not dwell in the sense base of the eye, nor does it dwell in the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind."
He does not abide in the sphere of form; he does not abide in the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena.
He does not abide in the eye-element; he does not abide in the elements of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
He does not abide in the element of form; he does not abide in the elements of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena.
They do not dwell in the eye-consciousness element, nor do they dwell in the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-consciousness elements;
they do not dwell in eye-contact, nor in ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-contact;
they do not dwell in the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, nor in the various feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-contact as a condition.
They do not abide in the conditioned realm, nor do they abide in the unconditioned realm;
they do not abide in the four foundations of mindfulness, and so on, up to and including not abiding in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they do not abide in all-knowledge, nor do they abide in the knowledge of the paths, nor in the knowledge of all aspects.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are unattainable.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
"The mind of the Tathāgata does not abide in any phenomena whatsoever, nor does it not abide.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti said to Śāriputra:

"When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, it is likewise so; although they abide in the perfection of wisdom, they are just like the Tathāgata, who does not abide in any phenomena whatsoever, nor does he not abide."

Why is that? Śāriputra, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, although they abide in the perfection of wisdom, they neither abide nor do they not abide in form; and so on, up to the knowledge of all aspects, wherein they neither abide nor do they not abide.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
it is because dharmas such as form possess no dual characteristics.

Śāriputra! Regarding the profound perfection of wisdom, bodhisattva mahāsattvas should train in this manner by means of non-apprehension, in accordance with this characteristic of neither abiding nor not abiding.
At that time, there were among the assembly certain sons of the gods who thought to themselves:
"Although the words and incantations of the yakṣas and others are indeed obscure, we are still able to understand them;
yet although the Venerable Subhūti has displayed this Prajñāpāramitā through various expressions, we are ultimately unable to comprehend it!"
The Venerable Subhūti, knowing what was in the minds of those devaputras, addressed them, saying:
"Do you, O devaputras, not understand what I have said?"
The devaputras said: “So it is! So it is!”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed him, saying:
"I have not uttered a single syllable regarding the meaning associated with this profound perfection of wisdom; you likewise have heard nothing—what, then, is there to be understood?"
Why is this? O sons of the gods!

Because within the meaning associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, all letters and verbal expressions are utterly transcended; therefore, within it, neither speaker, listener, nor one who understands can be apprehended. It is likewise with the subtle and profound unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment realized by all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
“O sons of the gods!
Just as the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas manifest emanated bodies, so too do these emanated bodies manifest the fourfold assembly, which gather together for them to preach the Dharma.”
"What do you think?
Is there herein anyone who truly can speak, listen, or understand?
The sons of the gods replied:
"No, Venerable One! Subhūti replied.
"In this way, O sons of the gods!

Because all phenomena are like magical illusions, within this profound meaning associated with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), neither the speaker, the listener, nor the one who understands can be apprehended."
“O sons of the gods!
Suppose a person, while dreaming, sees a Buddha preaching the true Dharma to a great assembly. What do you think?
Is there therein anyone who truly speaks, anyone who truly listens, or anyone who truly understands?”
The devaputras replied, "No, Venerable One!"
Subhūti replied: "It is so, O devaputras!

Because all phenomena are like dreams, within this profound meaning associated with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), neither a speaker, nor a listener, nor one who can understand is to be found."
“O sons of the gods!

Suppose there were two people in a single mountain valley, each staying on one side praising the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and they both produced sounds at the same time. What do you think?”
"Can these two echoes hear each other or understand each other?
The sons of the gods replied, "No!"
"Venerable One!
Subhūti replied, "So it is!"
O sons of the gods!
Since all phenomena are like echoes, within this profound meaning associated with the *prajñāpāramitā*, neither speaker, listener, nor understander can be apprehended at all.
“O sons of the gods!

Suppose a skilled illusionist or his apprentice were to create at a crossroads an illusory assembly of the four groups and a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. That illusory Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha would then proclaim the True Dharma for the illusory assembly of the four groups. What do you think?”
"In this, is there anyone who truly speaks, anyone who listens,
or anyone who can understand? The sons of the gods replied, "No!"
"Virtuous One!
The Subhūti replied, "It is so, O sons of the gods!"
Since all phenomena are like illusions, within this profound meaning associated with the Prajñāpāramitā, neither the speaker, the listener, nor the one who understands can be apprehended.
“O sons of the gods!
For this reason, I have not uttered a single word regarding the meaning associated with this profound perfection of wisdom; you likewise have heard nothing—what, then, could there be to understand?”

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 425. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Second Division, Chapter on Śakra, Part Two, Number Twenty-five. At that time, the sons of the gods again had this thought:

"Although the Venerable Subhūti has used various skillful means to explain this Prajñāpāramitā so that it may be easily understood, its underlying meaning becomes increasingly profound and subtle, difficult to fathom."
The Venerable Subhūti, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the devaputras, addressed them, saying: "Devaputras!
From form up to consciousness, none are profound or subtle; from the intrinsic nature of form up to the intrinsic nature of consciousness, none are profound or subtle."

The sense base of the eye, up to and including the sense base of the mind, is neither deep nor subtle; the intrinsic nature of the sense base of the eye, up to and including the intrinsic nature of the sense base of the mind, is also neither deep nor subtle.

The sense base of form, up to and including the sense base of mental phenomena, is neither deep nor subtle; the intrinsic nature of the sense base of form, up to and including the intrinsic nature of the sense base of mental phenomena, is also neither deep nor subtle.

The eye constituent, up to and including the mind constituent, is neither deep nor subtle; the intrinsic nature of the eye constituent, up to and including the intrinsic nature of the mind constituent, is also neither deep nor subtle.

The realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) up to the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) is neither deep nor subtle; the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the realm of form up to the intrinsic nature of the realm of phenomena is also neither deep nor subtle.

The realm of eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) up to the realm of mind-consciousness (*manovijñānadhātu*) is neither deep nor subtle; the intrinsic nature of the realm of eye-consciousness up to the intrinsic nature of the realm of mind-consciousness is also neither deep nor subtle.

Eye-contact (*cakṣuḥsaṃsparśa*) up to mind-contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*) is neither deep nor subtle; the intrinsic nature of eye-contact up to the intrinsic nature of mind-contact is also neither deep nor subtle.

The various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, up to and including those produced with mind-contact as condition, are neither profound nor subtle; the intrinsic nature of the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, up to and including the intrinsic nature of those produced with mind-contact as condition, is also neither profound nor subtle.

The perfection of generosity, up to and including the perfection of wisdom, is neither profound nor subtle; the intrinsic nature of the perfection of generosity, up to and including the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom, is also neither profound nor subtle.
