Inner emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature, is neither profound nor subtle; the intrinsic nature of inner emptiness, up to and including the intrinsic nature of the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature, is also neither profound nor subtle.

The four applications of mindfulness, explained at length up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are neither deep nor subtle; the intrinsic nature of the four applications of mindfulness, explained at length up to the intrinsic nature of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, is also neither deep nor subtle.

All doors of samādhi and all doors of dhāraṇī are neither deep nor subtle; the intrinsic nature of all doors of samādhi and the intrinsic nature of all doors of dhāraṇī are also neither deep nor subtle.

Up to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and all-aspect knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), these are neither deep nor subtle; the intrinsic nature of all-knowledge, the intrinsic nature of knowledge of the paths, and the intrinsic nature of all-aspect knowledge are also neither deep nor subtle.
Then, those sons of the gods again had this thought:
"In the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, there is no designation of form up to consciousness;
there is no designation of the eye-base up to the mind-base; there is no designation of the form-base up to the phenomena-base."
One may designate the eye-element up to the mind-element, but one does not designate the form-element up to the phenomena-element;
one does not designate the eye-consciousness-element up to the mind-consciousness-element; one does not designate eye-contact up to mind-contact;
nor does one designate the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition.
In feeling, one does not designate the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
one does not designate inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature;
one does not designate the four applications of mindfulness, and so forth, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; nor does one designate any gateways of meditative concentration.
Within all the gateways of dhāraṇī, one does not designate omniscience, the knowledge of the paths, or the knowledge of all aspects;
one does not designate the stream-enterer or the fruit of stream-entry, up to and including the arhat or the fruit of arhatship;
one does not designate the pratyekabuddha or the awakening of a pratyekabuddha; nor does one designate...
One may establish the bodhisattva and the bodhisattva stages, yet one does not establish the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, nor samyaksaṃbodhi,
nor does one establish written characters or verbal expressions.
The Venerable Subhūti, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the devaputras, addressed them, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have conceived:

from form and all other phenomena up to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, all are devoid of words and entirely ineffable; therefore, in the Prajñāpāramitā, there is nothing spoken, nothing heard, and no one who understands.
Therefore, among all phenomena, you should cultivate profound and firm patience (*adhimātra-dṛḍha-kṣānti*) in accordance with what has been taught.

Those who wish to abide in or realize the fruits of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*), once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), non-returning (*anāgāmin*), or arhatship (*arhattva*) can only abide in and realize them through this patience.
Likewise, those who wish to abide in or realize the enlightenment (*bodhi*) attained by a pratyekabuddha can only abide in and realize it through this patience.
All those who wish to abide in and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment must rely on this patience in order to abide in and realize it.
Thus, O sons of the gods!

From the first generation of the mind of awakening until the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should constantly and diligently train in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, which is without speaker, without listener, and without understanding.
Chapter 26: Acceptance with Faith. Part Two, Chapter Twenty-Six: Acceptance with Faith. At that time, the sons of the gods again had this thought:
"What kind of sentient beings does the Venerable Sudarśana now wish to address, and what Dharma does he intend to preach?"
The Venerable Subhūti, knowing their thoughts, addressed them, saying:
"O sons of the gods!
I now wish to joyfully expound for those sentient beings who are like illusions, like transformations, and like dreams, the Dharma that is like illusions, transformations, and dreams."
Why is this? O sons of the gods!
For those who listen in such a manner, there is nothing heard, nothing understood, and nothing realized within what has been spoken.
Then, the sons of the gods immediately asked again:
"Are the speaker, the listener, and the Dharma taught all like an illusion, like a transformation, and like a dream?"
Subhūti replied, “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said:

illusory sentient beings teach illusory dharmas to illusory beings; emanated sentient beings teach emanated dharmas to emanated beings; and dream-like sentient beings teach dream-like dharmas to dream-like beings.
O sons of the gods!
From the self up to the perceiver, they are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream;
from form up to consciousness, they are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream; from the eye up to the mind, they are like an illusion, like a transformation.
...like what is seen in a dream; from form (*rūpa*) up to phenomena (*dharma*), they are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream;
from eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) up to mind-consciousness (*manovijñāna*), they are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream;

from eye-contact (*cakṣuḥsaṃsparśa*) up to mind-contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*), they are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream; and the feeling (*vedanā*) produced by eye-contact [is likewise].
Even the feeling born of mental contact is like an illusion, like a magical creation, like what is seen in a dream;
the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom is like an illusion, like a magical creation, like what is seen in a dream;
and inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature is like an illusion, like a magical creation, like a dream.
That which is seen—the four applications of mindfulness, and so forth, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—is like a magical illusion, like a transformation, like a dream;
likewise, even the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship is like a magical illusion, like a transformation, like a dream;
and the awakening of a pratyekabuddha as well as unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening [are likewise].
“Awakening is like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream.
At that time, the sons of the gods asked Subhūti:

“Does the Venerable One now say only that we, and form and so forth, up to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream; or does he also say that nirvāṇa is like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream?”
Subhūti replied, "O sons of the gods!

I do not merely say that 'self,' 'form,' and so forth, up to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream; I also say that nirvāṇa is like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream."
"O sons of the gods!
Even if there were another dharma superior to nirvāṇa, I would likewise say that it is like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream. Why is this so?"
"O sons of the gods!
Illusion, transformation, and dream-phenomena are entirely non-dual with all dharmas, up to and including nirvāṇa, because there is no distinction between them.

At that time, the great śrāvakas—Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākauṣṭhila, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Mahākātyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, and others—as well as immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, addressed the venerable Subhūti, saying:

“This Prajñāpāramitā that has been taught is thus profound, thus difficult to see, thus difficult to realize, thus tranquil, thus subtle, thus deep-seated, and thus sublime; who is able to believe and accept it?”
At that time, having heard those words, Ānanda addressed the great śrāvakas and the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, saying:

"There are non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are able to have deep faith and acceptance in this profound, difficult to see, difficult to realize, tranquil, subtle, profound, and exquisite Prajñāpāramitā thus taught."

Furthermore, there are immeasurable numbers who have already seen the noble truths and are able to fathom the very source of all profound dharmas; these arhats, whose aspirations are fulfilled, are also able to believe and accept this most profound, difficult to see, difficult to realize, tranquil, subtle, secret, and exquisite Prajñāpāramitā as it is here taught.

Furthermore, there are immeasurable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, having already approached and made offerings to many koṭis of buddhas in the past, have given rise to great vows and planted the roots of all virtues; they are likewise able to believe in and accept this profound, difficult to see, difficult to realize, tranquil, subtle, deep-seated, and exquisite Prajñāpāramitā as it is here taught.

Furthermore, there are immeasurable sons and daughters of good family who, having already made great vows and planted various roots of goodness under countless Buddhas in the past, being of sharp faculties and wisdom and sustained by virtuous friends, are also able to believe and accept this profound, difficult to see, difficult to realize, tranquil, subtle, deep-seated, and exquisite Prajñāpāramitā as it is here taught.
Why is this? Because such persons do not, by means of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, non-cessation, tranquility, or detachment, conceptualize form through to consciousness;
nor do they, by means of form through to consciousness, conceptualize emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, non-cessation, tranquility, or detachment.
In this way, one does not, by means of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, non-ceasing, tranquility, or detachment, differentiate the eye up to the mind;
forms up to mental objects; eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness; eye-contact up to mind-contact;
or the feeling produced with eye-contact as a condition up to [feeling produced with] mind-contact.
Feeling produced with contact as its condition; the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature;
the four foundations of mindfulness, and so forth, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; all doors of samādhi and all doors of dhāraṇī.
The fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship, the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, all the practices of bodhisattva mahāsattvas,
the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment of all buddhas, all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*),
as well as the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛtadhātu*) and the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*).
Nor does one, by means of the eye up to the unconditioned realm, discriminate emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, non-ceasing, tranquility, or detachment.

By virtue of these causes and conditions, such persons as these are able to have faith in and accept this Prajñāpāramitā, which is thus described as profound, difficult to see, difficult to realize, tranquil, subtle, profound, and sublime.
Then, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the devaputras, saying:

"This profound Prajñāpāramitā that has been described—difficult to see, difficult to realize, tranquil, subtle, deep, and exquisite—is not an object of discursive thought; it transcends the sphere of discursive thought, and therein there is truly no one capable of believing and accepting it."
Why is this? O sons of the gods!
Within this there is no dharma that can be manifested or shown; since there is truly no dharma that can be manifested or shown, one who could believe and accept it is truly unobtainable.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

"Is it not the case that within this profound teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā, the dharmas corresponding to the three vehicles are extensively explained—namely, the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Unsurpassed Vehicle?"

Why does he extensively explain the bodhisattva-mahāsattva path that encompasses all bodhisattvas from their initial generation of the mind up to the tenth stage—namely, the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*) through to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*), the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) extensively explained through to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), and all doors of samādhi and all doors of dhāraṇī?
This extensively explains the supreme matters of the supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) acquired by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; that is to say,
because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas diligently practice this *prajñāpāramitā*, they are always born through transformation (*upapāduka*) in whatever place they are reborn,
never regressing from their supernatural powers as they sport with mastery, and are able to skillfully penetrate immeasurable dharma-gates.
From one buddha-field to another buddha-field, they shall offer worship, respect, reverence, and praise to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones;
they shall be able to cultivate and accumulate all various roots of goodness according to their aspirations and joys until they swiftly attain fulfillment;
and in the presence of all Buddhas, they shall hear and uphold the True Dharma, never forgetting it until they reach unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Having lost [these], how is it that you now constantly abide in supreme meditative concentration, free from a distracted mind, and by virtue of this as a condition,
have attained unimpeded eloquence, inexhaustible eloquence, appropriate eloquence, rapid eloquence, flawless eloquence,
eloquence rich in meaning and flavor in all that is expounded, and the most excellent and sublime eloquence in all the world?
Subhūti replied, “So it is! So it is!”
It is exactly as you have said.

Within this profound teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā, by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method (*upāya*), the dharmas corresponding to the three vehicles are extensively taught, up to and including the extensive teaching on the superior matters of the supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) that sustain bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and even up to the attainment of the most excellent and wondrous eloquence in all the world; yet, regarding that which takes non-apprehension as its skillful method, in what dharma does it take non-apprehension as its skillful method?
That is to say: employing the method of non-apprehension of a self up to a viewer; employing the method of non-apprehension of form up to consciousness;
employing the method of non-apprehension of the eye up to the mind; employing the method of non-apprehension of forms up to mental objects;
and employing the method of non-apprehension of visual consciousness up to mental consciousness.
Taking non-apprehension as the means, one takes non-apprehension of everything from eye-contact up to mind-contact as the means;
taking non-apprehension of everything from the feelings produced with eye-contact as their condition up to the feelings produced with mind-contact as their condition as the means;
and taking non-apprehension of everything from the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom as the means.
Using skillful means, one takes non-apprehension as the skillful means regarding everything from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the nature of non-existence;

using skillful means, one takes non-apprehension as the skillful means regarding everything from the four foundations of mindfulness, as explained at length, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
and likewise, up to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
"Attainment is the means. Then, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"For what reason, within this profound teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā, is the Dharma corresponding to the three vehicles extensively explained by taking non-attainment as the means?"

For what reason, within this profound teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā*, does it employ "non-apprehension" as the skillful means, and so forth, extensively explaining the superior matters of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) that sustain bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, up to causing them to attain the most excellent and wondrous eloquence in all the world?
Subhūti replied, “Śāriputra!

Because of internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, within this profound teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā, one extensively expounds the dharmas corresponding to the three vehicles by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method.”

Śāriputra! Because of the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of the nature of non-existence, within this profound teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā, by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, [the Buddha] extensively explains everything from the inclusion of the superior matters of the supernormal powers of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, up to enabling them to attain the most excellent and wondrous eloquence of all the world.

Chapter 27: The Chapter on Scattering Flowers, Part One. At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and all the gods from the Cāturmahārājakāyika realm up to the Akaniṣṭha realm within this trichiliocosm, all had this thought:

"Now, the Venerable Subhūti, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic power, is raining down the great rain of Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings. It would not be well if we were each to magically create exquisite celestial *mandārava* flowers to scatter as an offering to Śākyamuni Tathāgata, the assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, the community of Bhikṣus, and the Venerable Subhūti, and likewise to scatter them as an offering to the profound Prajñāpāramitā?"

Then, having formed this thought, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the host of devas each manifested a celestial *divyagandhapuṣpa* flower; holding these, they scattered them as an offering over the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, the community of bhikṣus, the Venerable Subhūti, and the profound Prajñāpāramitā.

At that time, this trichiliocosm, the world-system of the Buddha, was completely filled with flowers; through the Buddha’s supernormal power, these flowers combined in the void to form a flower pedestal, exquisitely adorned and equal in size to the trichiliocosm.
At that time, having witnessed this event, Subhūti thought to himself:

"The flowers now scattered have never been seen before among the realms of the devas; these flowers are so subtle and wondrous that they certainly were not produced from grass, trees, water, or land. They must have been emanated from the minds of the devas for the purpose of making offerings."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knowing the thoughts in Subhūti’s mind, said to him:
“These flowers that have been scattered are truly not produced from grass, trees, water, or land; nor are they actually emanated from the mind; they are merely a magical manifestation.”
At that time, Subhūti said to Śakra: “Kauśika!

As for what you have said—that these flowers were not actually produced from grass, trees, water, or land, nor were they truly emanated from the mind—and since they are not phenomena produced by birth, they cannot be called ‘flowers.’”
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked Subhūti:
"Venerable One,
is it only these flowers that are non-arisen, or is it the same for other dharmas as well?"
Subhūti replied, "It is not only these flowers that are unarisen; other dharmas as well have no meaning of arising.
What does this mean?"
Kauśika! Form (*rūpa*) is also unarisen; since it is unarisen, it is not form.

Feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are also unarisen; since they are unarisen, they are not feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness.

The same applies to the eye up to the mind; to forms up to mental phenomena; to eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness; to eye-contact up to mind-contact; and to the feelings produced with eye-contact as condition up to the feelings produced with mind-contact as condition.
Kauśika! The perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) is also unarisen; since it is unarisen, it is not the perfection of generosity.

The perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are also unarisen; since they are unarisen, they are not the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom.

From internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature; from the four foundations of mindfulness, explained at length, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha; and likewise, from all-knowledge, knowledge of the paths, and all-aspect knowledge—all are also thus.
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, had this thought to himself:
"The Venerable Subhūti possesses profound wisdom; he teaches the nature of phenomena without contradicting conventional designations."
The Buddha, knowing his thought, addressed him, saying:
"Kauśika, just as you have conceived in your mind, the Venerable Subhūti possesses profound wisdom; he teaches the nature of phenomena without contradicting conventional designations."
Then, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In what manner does the Venerable Subhūti teach the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) without contradicting conventional designations?
The Buddha said:
“Kauśika! Form is merely a provisional designation; the Venerable Subhūti does not contradict the provisional designation of form when he speaks of the dharma-nature of form.

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are merely provisional designations; the Venerable Subhūti does not contradict the provisional designations of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness when he speaks of the dharma-nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.”
Why is this? Because the dharma-nature of form and so forth is neither contrary nor conformable, what Subhūti has spoken is likewise neither contrary nor conformable.

This is also true for the eye up to the mind; for forms up to dharmas; for eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness; for eye-contact up to mind-contact; and for the feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition up to the feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition. It is thus in all these cases.

“Kauśika! The perfection of generosity is merely a provisional designation; the Venerable Subhūti does not contradict the provisional designation of the perfection of generosity when he speaks of the dharma-nature of the perfection of generosity.

The perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are merely provisional designations; the Venerable Subhūti does not contradict the provisional designations of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom when he speaks of the dharma-nature of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.”

Why is this so? Because the dharmic nature (*dharmatā*) of the *pāramitās* such as generosity is free from both opposition and compliance, what Subhūti has spoken is likewise free from both opposition and compliance. This applies to everything from internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of non-existence and intrinsic nature (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*);

from the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), explained at length, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*); and likewise for everything from the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) up to the fruit of arhatship, the awakening of a solitary buddha (*pratyekabuddha-bodhi*), and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*); and for omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); and for everything from stream-enterers up to arhats, solitary buddhas, bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas—it is all likewise so.
“Kauśika! The Venerable Subhūti teaches the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) without contradicting conventional designations.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed Śakra, the Lord of Devas, saying:
“Kauśika! So it is! So it is!”
As the Buddha has taught, there are no phenomena whatsoever that are not merely provisional designations. Kausika!
Having realized that all phenomena are but provisional designations, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Kauśika! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train in this manner, they do not train in form, nor do they train in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Why is this? Kauśika!

It is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive form as something in which one can train, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as something in which one can train.

The same applies to the eye up to the mind; to forms up to mental phenomena (*dharma*); to eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness; to eye-contact up to mind-contact; and also to the feelings produced with eye-contact as condition up to the feelings produced with mind-contact as condition.

“Kauśika! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas train in this manner, they do not train in the perfection of giving; they do not train in the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom.”
Why is this? Kauśika!

It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not perceive a perfection of giving in which they may train, nor do they perceive a perfection of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom in which they may train.

From internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature; from the four foundations of mindfulness, explained at length, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and likewise from the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship, pratyekabuddha enlightenment, and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment; and all-encompassing wisdom, wisdom of the aspects of the path, and all-aspect wisdom—all are also thus.
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, asked Subhūti:
"For what reason do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas not perceive form, nor even perceive the knowledge of all aspects?"
Subhūti replied: "Kauśika!
Form is empty of form, and so on, up to: the knowledge of all aspects is empty of the knowledge of all aspects."
Kauśika! By virtue of this causal condition, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not perceive form, nor even up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Kauśika!

Because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not perceive form, they do not train in form; and so on, up to: because they do not perceive all-aspect-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), they do not train in all-aspect-knowledge.
Why is this? Kausika!

One cannot perceive the emptiness of form as the emptiness of form, nor can one perceive the emptiness of the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) as the emptiness of the knowledge of all aspects; furthermore, one cannot train in the emptiness of form by means of the emptiness of form, nor can one train in the emptiness of the knowledge of all aspects by means of the emptiness of the knowledge of all aspects.
“Kauśika! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not train in emptiness, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is training in emptiness. Why is this?
Because they are non-dual, Kauśika!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not train in the emptiness of form as being for the sake of training in the emptiness of form, because they are non-dual; and so on, up to: they do not train in the emptiness of all-aspect-knowledge as being for the sake of training in the emptiness of all-aspect-knowledge, because they are non-dual.
Kauśika! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of non-duality as the skillful method, trains in the emptiness of form, and so on,
up to training in the emptiness of all-aspect omniscience by means of non-duality as the skillful method, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to...
By means of non-duality as a skillful method, they study the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
by means of non-duality as a skillful method, they study inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence;
and by means of non-duality as a skillful method, they study the four foundations of mindfulness, and so forth, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Dharma: in this way, up to and including, one can train by means of non-duality in the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship;
one can train by means of non-duality in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment up to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
and one can train by means of non-duality in all-knowledge and the knowledge of the aspects of the path.
...and the knowledge of all aspects. Kausika!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can train in the perfection of giving up to the knowledge of all aspects by means of non-duality, that bodhisattva mahāsattva can, by means of non-duality, train in the immeasurable, innumerable, boundless, and inconceivable pure qualities of a Buddha.

“Kauśika! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to train in the immeasurable, innumerable, boundless, and inconceivable pure Buddha-dharmas, this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not train for the sake of increasing form, nor does he train for the sake of decreasing form; and so on, up to not training for the sake of increasing all-aspect-knowledge, nor training for the sake of decreasing all-aspect-knowledge.”

Kauśika! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not train for the sake of increasing form, nor does he train for the sake of decreasing form, and so on up to not training for the sake of increasing the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), nor training for the sake of decreasing the knowledge of all aspects; this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not train for the sake of grasping form, nor does he train for the sake of destroying form, and so on up to not training for the sake of grasping the knowledge of all aspects, nor training for the sake of destroying the knowledge of all aspects.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

"When bodhisattva mahāsattvas train in this manner, do they not train for the sake of grasping form, nor do they train for the sake of destroying form; and so on, up to: do they not train for the sake of grasping the knowledge of all aspects, nor do they train for the sake of destroying the knowledge of all aspects?"
Subhūti replied: “So it is! So it is!”

Śāriputra! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train in this manner, they do not train for the sake of grasping form, nor do they train for the sake of destroying form; and so on, up to: they do not train for the sake of grasping all-aspect omniscience, nor do they train for the sake of destroying all-aspect omniscience.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

"For what reason do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas not train for the sake of grasping form, nor do they train for the sake of destroying form; and so on, up to why they do not train for the sake of grasping all-aspect knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), nor do they train for the sake of destroying all-aspect knowledge?"
Subhūti replied:

"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not perceive that form is something to be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy form; this extends even to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), which they do not perceive as something to be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy the knowledge of all aspects."
Why is this? Śāriputra, it is because dharmas such as form—
whether as subject or object— are empty of both internal and external [self-nature].

Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding all phenomena, perceives neither that which can be grasped nor that which can be destroyed, and likewise perceives no one who can grasp or destroy, yet trains in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to accomplish the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñājñāna).
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"Can bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who train in the perfection of wisdom in this manner accomplish all-knowledge?"
Subhūti replied, “Śāriputra!
When bodhisattva mahāsattvas train in the perfection of wisdom in this way, they are able to accomplish all-knowledge because they employ the means of neither grasping nor destroying any phenomena.”
Śāriputra said: “If a bodhisattva mahāsattva employs as a skillful means neither the grasping nor the destruction of any phenomena, how can they accomplish the knowledge of all modes?”
Subhūti replied, “Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive form as arising or ceasing, as being grasped or relinquished, as being defiled or purified, or as increasing or decreasing; and so on, up to not perceiving the knowledge of all aspects as arising or ceasing, as being grasped or relinquished, as being defiled or purified, or as increasing or decreasing.”
Why is this? Because from form up to the knowledge of all aspects, they are all non-existent by nature and cannot be apprehended.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!

When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do not perceive in any phenomena arising or ceasing, grasping or relinquishing, defilement or purity, increase or decrease. By taking as their skillful means the state of having nothing to learn and nothing to accomplish, they train in the perfection of wisdom and are thus able to accomplish the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñājñāna).
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, asked Śāriputra: "Venerable One,
where should one seek the perfection of wisdom in which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas train?"
Śāriputra said: “Kauśika!
The perfection of wisdom in which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas train should be sought within what Subhūti has spoken.”
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to Subhūti:
"Is it by relying upon the power of your great virtue, O Venerable One, that you have caused Śāriputra to speak thus?"
Subhūti replied: "Kauśika,
it is not by relying on my own spiritual power that Śāriputra has made such a statement."
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked:

"This is sustained by the supernatural power of the Buddha as its support.

"All dharmas are without support; how can it be said that they have the Buddha’s spiritual power as their support?
Subhūti replied, "Kauśika!..."
So it is! So it is! It is just as you have said.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle Four Hundred Twenty-Six. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Chapter Two: The Distribution of Flowers, Part Twenty-Seven, Section Two. "Furthermore, Kauśika!
Regarding what you previously asked, "Where should one seek the perfection of wisdom in which all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train?", Kausika!

The perfection of wisdom in which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas train should not be sought within form, nor should it be sought apart from form; it should not be sought within feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor should it be sought apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

In this way, one should not seek it within all-knowledge, nor should one seek it apart from all-knowledge; one should not seek it within the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects, nor should one seek it apart from the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects.
Why is this? Kauśika!

Whether it be the perfection of wisdom, or seeking, or form—and so on, as extensively explained, up to all-aspect omniscience—all such things are neither associated nor dissociated; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and of a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.

Why is this so? "The perfection of wisdom in which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas train is not form, yet it is not separate from form; it is not feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, yet it is not separate from feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

In this way, it extends even to being neither all-knowledge nor separate from all-knowledge, and neither the knowledge of the paths nor the knowledge of all aspects, yet not separate from the knowledge of the paths nor the knowledge of all aspects."

The suchness of form is not [separate from] form; it is not separate from the suchness of form. The suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is not [separate from] feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; it is not separate from the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

In this way, up to and including: the suchness of all-knowledge is not [separate from] all-knowledge; it is not separate from the suchness of all-knowledge. The suchness of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects is not [separate from] the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects; it is not separate from the suchness of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects.

It is not the dharma-nature of form, yet it is not separate from the dharma-nature of form; it is not the dharma-nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, yet it is not separate from the dharma-nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

Thus, up to and including: it is not the dharma-nature of all-knowledge, yet it is not separate from the dharma-nature of all-knowledge; it is not the dharma-nature of the knowledge of the paths or the knowledge of all aspects, yet it is not separate from the dharma-nature of the knowledge of the paths or the knowledge of all aspects.
Why is this so? Kauśika! All such dharmas are non-existent and entirely unobtainable.

Because they are non-existent and unapprehendable, the perfection of wisdom in which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas train is not form, yet it is not separate from form; as explained at length, it is not up to and including all-aspect-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), yet it is not separate from all-aspect-knowledge.

It is not the suchness (*tathatā*) of form, yet it is not separate from the suchness of form; as explained at length, it is not the suchness of up to and including all-aspect-knowledge, yet it is not separate from the suchness of all-aspect-knowledge.

It is not the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) of form, yet it is not separate from the dharma-nature of form; as explained at length, it is not the dharma-nature of up to and including all-aspect-knowledge, yet it is not separate from the dharma-nature of all-aspect-knowledge.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to Subhūti:
"Venerable One!
The perfection of wisdom in which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas train is a great perfection, an immeasurable perfection, and a boundless perfection."

Those who are stream-enterers attain the fruit of stream-entry by training in this; those who are once-returners attain the fruit of once-returning by training in this; those who are non-returners attain the fruit of non-returning by training in this; those who are arhats attain the fruit of arhatship by training in this; those who are pratyekabuddhas attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha by training in this; and bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by training in this, mature immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of sentient beings, establishing them in the three vehicles as appropriate, purifying various buddha-fields, and realizing unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti replied: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is as you have said,
Kauśika! Because form (rūpa) is great, the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) in which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas train is also great."
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are great, the perfection of wisdom in which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas train is also great.
Thus, up to and including because omniscience is great, the perfection of wisdom in which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas train is also great;
and because the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects are great, the perfection of wisdom in which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas train is also great.
Why is this? Kauśika!

Because form, up to and including the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), cannot be apprehended in the past, future, or present limits, it is called "great. Because of that greatness, the *prajñāpāramitā* in which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas train is also called "great."
For this reason, Kausika, the perfection of wisdom practiced by bodhisattva mahasattvas should be called the "Great Perfection. Kausika!

Because form is immeasurable, the perfection of wisdom in which bodhisattva mahāsattvas train is also immeasurable; because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are immeasurable, the perfection of wisdom in which bodhisattva mahāsattvas train is also immeasurable.
In this way, because all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is immeasurable, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) in which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas train is also immeasurable;

because the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are immeasurable, the perfection of wisdom in which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas train is also immeasurable.
Why is this? Kausika!

Because the measure of form, up to and including the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), cannot be apprehended; just as the measure of space cannot be apprehended, so it is with form and the others. Therefore, they are said to be immeasurable.
“Kauśika! Because space is immeasurable, form and the other aggregates are also immeasurable;
because form and the other aggregates are immeasurable, the perfection of wisdom in which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas train is also immeasurable.”
For this reason, the perfection of wisdom practiced by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should be described as the immeasurable perfection.
“Kauśika! Because form is limitless, the perfection of wisdom in which bodhisattva mahāsattvas train is also limitless;
because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are limitless, the perfection of wisdom in which bodhisattva mahāsattvas train is also limitless.”
In this way, because all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is boundless, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) in which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas train is also boundless;

because the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are boundless, the perfection of wisdom in which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas train is also boundless.
Why is this? Kauśika!
Because the limit of form, up to and including all-aspect omniscience, cannot be apprehended.
For example, just as the limits of space cannot be apprehended, so it is with form and the other aggregates; therefore, they are said to be "boundless. "Kauśika!
Because space is boundless, form and the others are also boundless."
Because form and the other aggregates are boundless, the perfection of wisdom in which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas train is also boundless. "Furthermore, Kauśika!
“Because the objects of focus are boundless, the perfection of wisdom in which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas train is also boundless.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked:
“In what way, because the objects of focus are boundless, is the perfection of wisdom in which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas train also boundless?”
Subhūti replied, “Because the objective referent of the knowledge of all modes is limitless, the perfection of wisdom in which bodhisattva mahāsattvas train is also limitless.”
"Furthermore, Kauśika, because the objective referent of the dharma-realm is boundless, the perfection of wisdom in which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas train is also boundless."
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked:
"In what way is it that because the objective sphere of the dharma-realm is boundless, the perfection of wisdom in which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas train is also boundless?"
Subhūti replied, “Because the dharma-realm is boundless, its objects of cognition are also boundless; because its objects of cognition are boundless, the dharma-realm is also boundless.”
Because the objective sphere of the dharma-realm is boundless, the perfection of wisdom in which the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train is likewise boundless. "Furthermore, Kauśika!
"Because the object of focus, suchness, is boundless, the perfection of wisdom in which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas train is also boundless.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked:
"In what way is it that because the object of focus, suchness, is boundless, the perfection of wisdom in which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas train is also boundless?"
Subhūti replied: “Because true thusness is limitless, its object of focus is also limitless; because its object of focus is limitless, true thusness is also limitless.”
Because the object of focus, suchness, is boundless, the perfection of wisdom in which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas train is also boundless. "Furthermore, Kausika!
“Because sentient beings are infinite, the perfection of wisdom in which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas train is also infinite.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked:
“In what way, because sentient beings are infinite, is the perfection of wisdom in which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas train also infinite?”
Subhūti replied: "What do you think?
Regarding the term 'sentient being,' what dharma is this designation for?"
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:

"To speak of 'sentient beings,' the term 'sentient being' is not a designation for what exists, nor is it a designation for what does not exist; rather, it is comprised of adventitious designations, comprised of designations for non-entities, and comprised of designations for the objectless."
Subhūti spoke again: "What do you think?
Within this profound *prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, is there any indication that there exists a real sentient being?"
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said: "No,
Venerable Sir!"

Subhūti replied: "In this profound *prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, since no real sentient beings are demonstrated, they are said to be 'boundless,' because neither a middle nor an extreme can be apprehended therein."
“Kauśika! What do you think?

If all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas were to remain for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River and speak the names of sentient beings, would there, in that regard, be any sentient beings who are born or who perish?”
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said: "No,
Venerable Sir!"
"Why is this? Because all sentient beings are pure by nature, and they have been non-existent from the very beginning. Subhūti replied:
"For this reason, I say that because sentient beings are limitless, the perfection of wisdom in which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas train is also limitless, Kauśika!"
"For this reason, the *prajñāpāramitā* studied by the bodhisattva mahāsattvas should be called 'boundless. **Chapter 28:

The Chapter on Prophecy (The Second Part of the Second Division)** At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the other devas of the Desire Realm; Brahmā, King of the Gods, and the other devas of the Form Realm; as well as Īśāna, the ṛṣis, and the celestial maidens—all simultaneously praised the Venerable Subhūti for what he had said three times, saying:

"Venerable Subhūti, sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power, has skillfully analyzed and revealed for us the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the unsurpassed essential Dharma that is the cause for the appearance of a Buddha in the world."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to practice this profound perfection of wisdom as it has been taught and does not depart from it, we shall honor and serve them as we do the Buddha.

Why is this so? It is because in this profound *prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, no dharma can be apprehended; that is to say, herein there is no form (*rūpa*) to be apprehended, no feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*) to be apprehended. In this way, up to and including, there is no omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) to be apprehended, and no knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) or knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) to be apprehended.

Although no such dharmas can be apprehended, there is the provisional establishment of the holy teachings of the three vehicles, namely: the teachings of the Śrāvaka, the Pratyekabuddha, and the Anuttara-yāna.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the devas and others, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.
Although within this profound *prajñāpāramitā* sūtra no phenomena such as form can be apprehended, there is nevertheless the provisional establishment of the holy teachings of the three vehicles.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding this perfection of wisdom, practices as it has been taught through the skillful means of non-apprehension and does not depart from it, you gods and others should always honor and serve them just as you would the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
Why is this? O devas!

Although within this profound *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtra the holy teachings of the three vehicles are extensively expounded, the Tathāgata cannot be apprehended as being identical to the *dānapāramitā*, nor can the Tathāgata be apprehended as being separate from the *dānapāramitā*; and so on, up to: the Tathāgata cannot be apprehended as being identical to the *prajñāpāramitā*, nor can the Tathāgata be apprehended as being separate from the *prajñāpāramitā*.

The Tathāgata cannot be apprehended as being identical with internal emptiness, nor can he be apprehended as being separate from internal emptiness; this extends up to: the Tathāgata cannot be apprehended as being identical with the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, nor can he be apprehended as being separate from the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.

The Tathāgata cannot be apprehended as being identical with the four foundations of mindfulness, nor can he be apprehended as being separate from the four foundations of mindfulness; this is explained at length up to: the Tathāgata cannot be apprehended as being identical with the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, nor can he be apprehended as being separate from the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

Likewise, up to: the Tathāgata cannot be apprehended as being identical with all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), nor can he be apprehended as being separate from all-knowledge; the Tathāgata cannot be apprehended as being identical with the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), nor can he be apprehended as being separate from the knowledge of the paths or the knowledge of all aspects.

"O devas! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding all phenomena, employs the method of non-apprehension to diligently train in this perfection of giving—and as extensively explained, up to and including the knowledge of all aspects—then that bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to correctly practice this perfection of wisdom and remains never apart from it. Therefore, you should honor and serve that bodhisattva mahāsattva as you would the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas."
"O devas and others, you should know!

In the past, at the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, at the crossroads of the city of Saṃkusumitarājadhānī, I beheld Dīpaṃkara Buddha, offered him five lotus flowers, spread my hair to cover the mud, and heard the sublime and wondrous Dharma. By means of this..."
Because they have attained skillful means, they are not separated from the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
they are not separated from inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;
they are not separated from the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; and they are not separated from the four dhyānas and the four immeasurables.
The four formless absorptions do not depart from all gateways of samādhi and all gateways of dhāraṇī;

they do not depart from the Buddha’s ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; nor do they depart from any other [qualities].
At that time, when the immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless Buddha-dharmas were [attained],
Dīpaṃkara Buddha immediately bestowed upon me the prediction of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
saying: "O son of good family!..."

In a future age, after incalculable eons have passed, you shall become a Buddha within this very world-system during the Bhadrakalpa, known as Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; you shall proclaim the Prajñāpāramitā and deliver immeasurable multitudes.
At that time, all the devas addressed the Buddha, saying: "How rare!
World-Honored One!"
"How marvelous!
Well-gone One!

This *prajñāpāramitā* is most marvelous, for it enables the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas to swiftly grasp the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*). By taking non-apprehension as the means, they neither grasp nor reject any form; they neither grasp nor reject feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness; and so on, up to neither grasping nor rejecting the knowledge of all modes, nor grasping nor rejecting the knowledge of the aspects of the path, nor grasping nor rejecting the knowledge of all aspects."

At that time, the Buddha surveyed the fourfold assembly—namely the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—as well as the multitude of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the deities from the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, all of whom had gathered together to serve as witnesses. Thereupon, he looked toward Śakra, the Lord of Devas, and addressed him: “Kauśika!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, or a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, or upāsikā, or any sons or daughters of gods, or any sons or daughters of good family, do not depart from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), and by means of the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), respectfully hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently practice, reflect upon according to the principle, expound to others, and widely disseminate this *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that none of these individuals can be harmed or disturbed by any evil Māras or the armies of Māra.
Why is this? Kauśika!

These sons and daughters of good family dwell well in the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness of form; they dwell well in the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

In this way, they abide well in the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), and they abide well in the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness of the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and all-aspect knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
One cannot afflict emptiness with emptiness, one cannot afflict signlessness with signlessness, and one cannot afflict wishlessness with wishlessness. Why is this so?
In this way, all these phenomena lack intrinsic nature; neither the agent nor the object of harm can be apprehended.
"Furthermore, Kausika, these sons and daughters of good family cannot be harmed by humans or non-humans."
Why is this? Kauśika!

It is because these sons and daughters of good family, employing the skillful means of non-apprehension, have well cultivated the minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity toward all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Kauśika! These sons and daughters of good family shall never be afflicted or harmed by various perilous and evil conditions, nor shall they die an untimely death."
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because these sons and daughters of good family practice the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) in order to properly nourish and sustain all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

Among all those in this trichiliocosm, from the gods of the Four Great Kings up to the gods of the Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala), who have already resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta—if they have not yet heard, received, upheld, recited, diligently practiced, or correctly contemplated this Prajñāpāramitā—they should now, without departing from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), and employing the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), listen with a sincere heart to this Prajñāpāramitā, receive it, uphold it, recite it, diligently practice it, and correctly contemplate it."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If sons or daughters of good family, not departing from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), employ the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) to wholeheartedly hear, receive, uphold, recite, diligently study, and reflect upon this Prajñāpāramitā according to the truth, then these sons or daughters of good family—whether in an empty house, in the wilderness, on a perilous path, or in a place of danger—will never experience fear, alarm, or horripilation."
Why is this? Kauśika!

It is because these sons and daughters of good family do not depart from the mind of omniscience, and by employing the method of non-apprehension, they skillfully cultivate inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.

At that time, all those from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven within this Sahā world-system of three thousand great thousandfold worlds, joined their palms in reverence and addressed the Buddha in unison:
“World-Honored One!

If sons or daughters of good family do not depart from the mind set on omniscience, and by means of the practice of non-apprehension, are able at all times to wholeheartedly hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently study, reflect upon according to principle, transcribe, explain, and widely disseminate this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, we devas and others shall constantly follow and protect them, ensuring that no calamities or afflictions may invade or distress them.
Why is this? World-Honored One!
It is because these sons and daughters of good family are themselves bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
“World-Honored One!

It is because of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that all sentient beings are enabled to forever sever the various perilous and evil destinies, such as those of the hells, animals, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the asuras.”
“World-Honored One!

Because of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all devas, humans, yakṣas, nāgas, and others shall forever be freed from all calamities, epidemics, poverty, hunger and thirst, cold and heat, and other such sufferings.”
“World-Honored One!

Because of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all devas, humans, asuras, and others shall forever be free from various unfavorable conditions; wherever they dwell, the clash of weapons shall forever cease, and all sentient beings shall regard one another with hearts of loving-kindness.”

“World-Honored One! It is because of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that there exist in the world the ten paths of wholesome action; the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; the perfection of giving up to the perfection of wisdom; internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature; the four foundations of mindfulness, and so forth, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha; and even all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects.”
“World-Honored One!

It is because of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that there exist in the world great clans of kṣatriyas, great clans of brahmins, great clans of householders, and great clans of laymen, as well as minor kings, wheel-turning sage-kings, and their attendant ministers and officials.”
“World-Honored One!

It is because of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that there exist in the world the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations; the Heaven of Brahma’s Retinue up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven; and the Heaven of Infinite Space up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception.”
“World-Honored One!

It is because of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that there exist in the world the stream-enterer and the fruit of stream-entry, up to and including the arhat and the fruit of arhatship, as well as the pratyekabuddha and the awakening of a pratyekabuddha.”
“World-Honored One!

It is because of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that there exist in the world various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who bring sentient beings to maturity, adorn and purify buddha-fields, realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and turn the wondrous wheel of Dharma to deliver immeasurable multitudes.”
“World-Honored One!

It is because of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that there exist in the world the Jewel of the Buddha, the Jewel of the Dharma, and the Jewel of the Bhikṣu Saṃgha, which bring benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings.”
“World-Honored One!

For this reason, we—the hosts of devas, asuras, nāgas, yakṣas, and humans and non-humans of great power—should always follow, revere, and protect these bodhisattva mahāsattvas, ensuring that no calamities or afflictions may harm them, and that their activities of hearing, receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, practicing, reflecting according to principle, and transcribing the Prajñāpāramitā shall never be interrupted.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the other devas, nāgas, asuras, and so forth: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.

It is because of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that all sentient beings are brought to forever sever the evil destinies, and even until the appearance of the Three Jewels in the world, they bring great benefit to all sentient beings.

Therefore, you gods, nāgas, spirits, and those of great power—whether human or non-human—should constantly follow this bodhisattva mahāsattva, making offerings, showing reverence, honoring, and praising him, while diligently protecting him so that no calamities or afflictions may harm him.

If you are able to make offerings to, revere, respect, praise, and diligently protect these bodhisattva mahāsattvas, you should know that you are thereby making offerings to, revering, respecting, praising, and diligently protecting me and all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the ten directions.

Therefore, you all should constantly follow this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, making offerings, honoring, respecting, and praising him, and diligently protecting him without ever abandoning him for even a moment.
“Devas and others, you should know!

Suppose the great trichiliocosm of the Buddha’s world were filled with śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as densely packed as a grove of sugarcane, reeds, bamboo, rice, hemp, or thickets, with no space between them.

Suppose there are sons or daughters of good family who, toward that field of merit, provide offerings, pay homage, show respect, and offer praise with immeasurable kinds of supreme and exquisite articles of enjoyment for as long as their lives last.

Furthermore, if there were another person who, for even a brief moment, made offerings to, honored, revered, and praised a single bodhisattva mahāsattva who has first resolved their mind upon awakening and does not depart from the six pāramitās, the former mass of merit would not equal even a hundredth part of this accumulation of merit; it would not equal a thousandth part, nor even a *upaniṣad* (infinitesimal) part.
Why is this? It is not because of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas appear in the world;
rather, it is because of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that there exist in the world śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

Therefore, all you devas, nāgas, asuras, humans, non-humans, and others should constantly protect, make offerings to, revere, honor, respect, and praise these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, so that no calamities or afflictions may harm them.

By virtue of the mass of merit you have thereby acquired, you shall always enjoy peace and happiness among humans and devas; until you attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, this merit you have gained shall never be exhausted.
Chapter 29: On Gathering and Sustaining (Saṃgraha-parivarta), Part Two, Chapter Twenty-nine, Section One. At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How truly marvelous and extraordinary are these bodhisattva mahāsattvas!
With sincere hearts, they hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently practice, reflect upon according to the principle, transcribe, explain, and widely disseminate this Prajñāpāramitā;

they embrace such rare and wondrous benefits and merits in the present life, ripen sentient beings, purify buddha-fields, and travel from one buddha-field to another to attend upon and serve the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

Regarding all roots of goodness, according to whatever one delights in, by making offerings, showing respect, honoring, and praising the Buddhas, one is able to cause them to grow and swiftly bring them to fulfillment;
from the time of hearing and receiving the true Dharma from the Buddhas until reaching unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, one never forgets it in the interim;

and one is swiftly able to acquire the perfection of lineage, the perfection of the birth mother, the perfection of the physical body, the perfection of the retinue, the perfection of the marks and signs, the perfection of radiance, the perfection of the supreme eye, the perfection of the supreme ear, the perfection of the voice, the perfection of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and the perfection of dhāraṇī.

Furthermore, by the power of skillful means, they transform their own bodies into the likeness of the Buddha, traveling from one world-system to another. They go to buddhaless lands to praise and expound the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); they praise and expound inner emptiness (*adhyātmaśūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature (*abhāvasvabhāvaśūnyatā*); they praise and expound the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*); and they praise and expound the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) at length, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*).

Furthermore, by the power of skillful means, they proclaim the essentials of the Dharma for all sentient beings, establishing them appropriately within the vehicles of the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*), causing them to be forever liberated from birth, old age, sickness, and death, and to realize the realm of nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣanirvāṇadhātu*).
Or again, they rescue others from the sufferings of the evil realms, causing them to experience various sublime pleasures among gods and humans.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again addressed the Buddha: “This Prajñāpāramitā is truly marvelous and rare!

If one can embrace such Prajñāpāramitā, then one fully embraces all six pāramitās; as has been explained at length, one even fully embraces the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. Furthermore, one fully embraces the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship; the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas; and all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).”
At that time, the Buddha said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.
If one can embrace this perfection of wisdom, then one fully embraces all six perfections, and so forth, up to and including the full embrace of the knowledge of all aspects.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If sons and daughters of good family can, with a sincere heart, hear, receive and uphold, read and recite, diligently practice and study, reflect upon according to the principle, write down, explain, and widely disseminate this Prajñāpāramitā, these sons and daughters of good family will acquire various meritorious benefits and advantages both in the present life and in the future."
"You should listen attentively!
Pay careful heed, and I shall analyze and explain it for you.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:
"Indeed! Great Sage!
We pray that you will explain this at once; we long to hear it."
The Buddha told Kauśika:

"If there are various classes of non-Buddhist practitioners, or the Māras who are lords of the desire realm along with their retinues, or others who are violent, evil, and arrogant, who wish to initiate various harmful acts against such sons and daughters of good family—seeking to cause them to distance themselves from, oppose, harm, reject, or slander the *prajñāpāramitā*—as soon as they give rise to such thoughts, they will swiftly encounter calamity and misfortune; they shall naturally be extinguished and fail to achieve their purpose."
Why is this? Kausika!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva has long practiced the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom. If sentient beings, due to stinginess and greed, engage in strife for a long night, this bodhisattva mahāsattva relinquishes all internal and external phenomena and employs skillful means to cause them to abide in the perfection of generosity.

If there are sentient beings who have long been transgressing the precepts, this bodhisattva mahāsattva relinquishes all internal and external things and, through skillful means, causes them to abide securely in the perfection of ethical discipline.

If there are sentient beings who have long been prone to anger and resentment, this bodhisattva mahāsattva relinquishes all internal and external phenomena and employs skillful means to establish them in the perfection of patience.

If there are sentient beings who have been indolent throughout the long night, this bodhisattva mahāsattva relinquishes all internal and external phenomena and employs skillful means to establish them in the perfection of diligence.

If sentient beings have been distracted throughout the long night, this bodhisattva mahāsattva relinquishes all internal and external phenomena and employs skillful means to establish them in the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).

If there are sentient beings who have been deluded throughout the long night, this bodhisattva mahāsattva relinquishes all internal and external phenomena and employs skillful means to establish them in the perfection of wisdom.
If sentient beings wander through birth and death, their minds being constantly disturbed by the stains of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) such as greed,
hatred, and delusion throughout the long night, thereby committing various harmful deeds; this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva,
through his skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), causes them to sever and extinguish those underlying tendencies of greed, hatred, and delusion.
They cause those who are bound by the afflictions to dwell securely in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions;
or they cause them to dwell in the four foundations of mindfulness, and so forth, up to the eightfold noble path;
or they cause them to dwell in the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; or they cause them to dwell in the fruit of stream-entry, and so forth...
They cause them to abide in the fruit of arhatship, or cause them to abide in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha,
or cause them to abide in the ten stages of a bodhisattva, or cause them to abide in the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas.

Kauśika! These are called the benefits and merits of the present life that are embraced by Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, with a sincere mind, hear, receive and uphold, read and recite, diligently practice and study, reflect according to the principle, transcribe, explain, and cause this Prajñāpāramitā to be widely disseminated.

“Kauśika! By virtue of these causes and conditions, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in a future life; he will turn the sublime wheel of Dharma to transform immeasurable multitudes, establishing them through skillful means according to their original vows, leading them to ultimate mastery in the training of the three vehicles, and even enabling them to realize nirvana without remainder.”

Kauśika! These are called the future merits and benefits that Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas will acquire by listening to this Prajñāpāramitā with a sincere mind, receiving and upholding it, reading and reciting it, diligently practicing and studying it, reflecting upon it according to the principle, copying it, explaining it, and causing it to be widely disseminated.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters, with sincere hearts, hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently practice, reflect upon according to principle, transcribe, explain, and widely disseminate this Prajñāpāramitā, then in that place, whether there be evil Māras and their retinues, various kinds of followers of external paths, or other violent and arrogant persons who harbor hatred and envy for the Prajñāpāramitā, desiring to create obstacles, destroy it, or cause its disappearance, and who employ means to reproach, insult, and resist it—even with such intentions, they shall ultimately be unable to succeed."

Because they have briefly heard the sound of the Prajñāpāramitā, their various evils gradually perish and their merits gradually arise; subsequently, by relying on one of the three vehicles, they will reach the end of suffering, or escape the evil realms to be born among gods and humans.
Kauśika! It is like a wondrous medicine called Mākṣī; by its majestic power, it can dissolve all poisons.
Wherever this wondrous medicine is located, various venomous insects cannot approach it.

There was a large venomous snake that, hungry, went about seeking food; encountering a living being, it sought to sting and devour it. That creature, terrified of death, fled toward a potent medicinal herb. Upon smelling the scent of the medicine, the snake immediately retreated and fled.
Why is this? Kausika!
Just as such a wondrous medicine possesses great majestic power, able to benefit life and suppress all poisons, you should know that the Prajñāpāramitā likewise possesses great majestic power.

If sons or daughters of good family listen with a sincere mind, receive and uphold, read and recite, diligently practice and study, reflect according to the principle, transcribe, explain, and widely disseminate [this], then whatever evil deeds the various Māras intend to commit against these Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas shall, by the majestic power of this Prajñāpāramitā, be naturally extinguished in their respective places so that they can do nothing at all.
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because this Prajñāpāramitā possesses great power, being able to destroy all evils and increase wholesome dharmas.
“Kauśika! How is it that the perfection of wisdom can destroy all evils and increase all virtues? Kauśika!”

In this way, the *prajñāpāramitā* can extinguish desire, hatred, and delusion; from ignorance up to the entire mass of suffering; the hindrances, latent tendencies, entanglements, impurities, and fetters; the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a person, the view of annihilation, the view of permanence, the view of existence, the view of non-existence, and even the various inclinations toward all manner of evil views; as well as avarice, immorality, anger, indolence, distraction, and delusion; the notions of permanence, pleasure, self, and purity; and all other forms of greed, hatred, delusion, pride, doubt, and the activities of [wrong] views.
Kauśika!

In this way, the perfection of wisdom can extinguish attachment to form, up to and including attachment to consciousness; it can extinguish attachment to the eye, up to and including attachment to the mind; it can extinguish attachment to forms, up to and including attachment to phenomena; it can extinguish attachment to eye-consciousness, up to and including attachment to mind-consciousness; it can extinguish attachment to eye-contact, up to and including attachment to mind-contact; it can extinguish attachment to the feelings produced by eye-contact, up to and including attachment to the feelings produced by mind-contact; it can extinguish attachment to the perfection of generosity, up to and including attachment to the perfection of wisdom; it can extinguish attachment to internal emptiness, up to and including attachment to the emptiness of non-existence and self-nature; it can extinguish attachment to the four applications of mindfulness, and so forth, up to and including attachment to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; it can extinguish attachment to all-knowledge, path-knowledge, and all-aspect knowledge; and it can extinguish attachment to awakening and nirvana.

Kauśika! This Prajñāpāramitā is able to extinguish all such unwholesome dharmas and is able to increase their respective antidotes; therefore, the Prajñāpāramitā possesses great majestic power and is most honored and supreme.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
