Kauśika! Thus, this prajñāpāramitā does not bestow the qualities of a Buddha, nor the qualities of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor the qualities of a pratyekabuddha, nor the qualities of a śrāvaka; yet it does not abandon the qualities of ordinary beings.
Then Śakra, the Lord of Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the Great Pāramitā; it is the Unsurpassed Pāramitā; it is the Peerless Pāramitā.”
When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice these pāramitās in this manner, although they know the distinctions among the mental activities and spheres of all sentient beings,
they do not apprehend a self, nor do they apprehend sentient beings,
nor even an agent who knows or a perceiver; they do not apprehend form through to consciousness, nor do they apprehend the eye through to [the mind].
With a focused mind, one does not apprehend form, up to and including mental phenomena (*dharma*); one does not apprehend eye-consciousness, up to and including mind-consciousness;

one does not apprehend eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact; one does not apprehend the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, up to and including the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition;
one does not apprehend the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*), up to and including [the perfection of wisdom].
If the perfections do not apprehend inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence;
if they do not apprehend the four applications of mindfulness, and so on, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
if they do not apprehend awakening, nor nirvana, nor the Buddhas and their dharmas.
Why is this? World-Honored One!
It is because this Prajñāpāramitā does not appear by relying on the apprehension of any phenomena.

Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) whatsoever; it neither exists nor can it be apprehended. This is because both the grasper and the grasped, as well as their two bases, are empty of essential characteristics and cannot be found.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of Devas, saying: “So it is! So it is!”
"It is as you have said,
Kauśika! Even though bodhisattva mahāsattvas have practiced and studied the profound *prajñāpāramitā* for a long night, they do not even apprehend awakening, much less the dharmas of a bodhisattva!"
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice only the perfection of wisdom, or do they also practice the other five perfections?”
The Buddha said,
“Kauśika! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the six perfections by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method.”
This means that when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), they do not apprehend the perfection of giving, nor do they apprehend the giver or the recipient;

when they practice the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), they do not apprehend the perfection of ethical discipline, nor do they apprehend the one who maintains the precepts or the one who violates them;

and so on, until when they practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*), they do not apprehend the perfection of wisdom, nor do they apprehend those who possess sublime wisdom or those who possess inferior wisdom.

"Furthermore, Kauśika, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas is the sovereign and the guide; by practicing it, they cause all the *pāramitās* to be swiftly brought to fulfillment."

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices generosity, the profound perfection of wisdom serves as their honor and guide; thus, the perfection of generosity they cultivate is free from attachment and is swiftly brought to fulfillment.

This continues until, when practicing wisdom, the profound perfection of wisdom serves as their honor and guide; thus, the perfection of wisdom they cultivate is free from attachment and is swiftly brought to fulfillment.

"Furthermore, Kauśika! Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension regarding all phenomena, they are without attachment, and thus cause their practice to be swiftly brought to fulfillment;
that is to say, they take non-apprehension as the means with respect to form, and so on, up to taking non-apprehension as the means with respect to the knowledge of all aspects."
Kauśika! Just as all the trees in Jambudvīpa—whether their branches, twigs, trunks, flowers, leaves, or fruits differ in their various forms and colors—their shadows are entirely without distinction.

Thus, although these first five pāramitās each have their own distinct characteristics, because they are embraced by the prajñāpāramitā and dedicated toward the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), and because they employ the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), none of their differentiated characteristics can be apprehended at all.
Then, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One! This Prajñāpāramitā accomplishes vast and sublime merit; it accomplishes all sublime merits; it accomplishes perfect and sublime merits; it accomplishes immeasurable sublime merits; it accomplishes incalculable sublime merits; it accomplishes boundless sublime merits; it accomplishes incomparable sublime merits.”

"Bhagavān! If sons or daughters of good family were to write down and uphold this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, adorn it with various jewels, and honor, revere, respect, and praise it with immeasurable kinds of supreme and exquisite offerings, and reflect upon it according to reason as taught in this sūtra."
There may be sons of good family or daughters of good family who write down this profound perfection of wisdom, bestow it upon others, uphold it, and cause it to be widely disseminated.
"Between these two accumulations of merit,
which is greater? The Buddha said, "Kauśika!..."
I shall ask you further; answer as you see fit.

Suppose a son or daughter of good family were to receive from another the relics of a Buddha, place them in a precious casket, and set them in a high and eminent location, and furthermore offer worship, honor, respect, and praise with immeasurable, supreme, and exquisite flower garlands, up to and including lamps and illuminations.

If there are sons or daughters of good family who receive from others the relics of the Buddha and distribute even as much as a mustard seed to another, causing them to respectfully accept and enshrine them according to the Dharma, and further to offer various kinds of exquisite flower garlands, up to lamps and lights, with worship, reverence, respect, and praise.
"What do you think?
Of these two accumulations of merit, which is superior?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied:
“As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, of these two accumulations of merit, the latter is superior.

Why is this? Because the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, observing those classes of sentient beings who are to be liberated by making offerings and showing reverence to the *śarīra* (relics) of the Buddhas, at the time of their parinirvāṇa, employ the power of the *vajropama-samādhi* (diamond-like concentration) to shatter their diamond-like bodies into pieces the size of mustard seeds. Furthermore, through the power of their profound and vast great compassion, they empower these *śarīra* so that after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, anyone who obtains even a single grain the size of a mustard seed and makes offerings or shows it reverence shall obtain boundless merit; such a person will experience abundant wealth and happiness among gods and humans, until finally reaching the end of suffering. Therefore, the merit of giving [the relics] to others is superior.”
At that time, the Buddha praised Śakra, the Lord of Devas, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"It is as you have said, Kauśika!
It is likewise with this Prajñāpāramitā: between one who personally upholds it and one who bestows it upon others for their circulation, the latter accumulation of merit is greater."
Why is this? Because by giving to others, one enables immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to attain the joy of the Dharma. "Furthermore, Kauśika!

If there is one who, regarding the meaning and intent of this profound Prajñāpāramitā, correctly analyzes and explains it to others so that they attain right understanding, the mass of merit obtained by them is hundreds of thousands of times greater than the merit of bestowing [material gifts] and causing them to be circulated.

“Kauśika! You should revere this Dharma-preacher as you would revere a Buddha, and likewise honor this fellow practitioner of the holy life who possesses great wisdom as if he were the Buddha himself. Why is this?
Kauśika! You should know that the perfection of wisdom is itself the Buddhas, and you should know that the Buddhas are themselves the perfection of wisdom;
you should know that the perfection of wisdom is not different from the Buddhas, and you should know that the Buddhas are not different from the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? All Buddhas of the three periods of time, by diligently practicing and studying the *prajñāpāramitā*, have realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment;

likewise, those of the lineage of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who practice the holy life, by diligently practicing and studying the *prajñāpāramitā*, attain the fruit of a śrāvaka and the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.

A person belonging to the bodhisattva lineage also diligently trains in the perfection of wisdom, transcends the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, enters the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth, gradually practices all the bodhisattva deeds, and attains the stage of the bodhisattva’s non-retrogression.
For this reason, Kauśika,

if any son of good family or daughter of good family wishes to personally make offerings, show reverence, honor, and praise to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, they should write down this profound Prajñāpāramitā and make offerings, show reverence, honor, and praise it.
“Kauśika! Contemplating this meaning, when I first attained Buddhahood, I reflected thus:
‘Upon whom shall I rely for my dwelling?’”
"Who is worthy to receive my offerings and respect?
While he was reflecting thus, he did not see anyone among the gods, Māras, Brahmās, or other worldly humans and non-humans who was his equal, let alone his superior.
He further reflected:

"Relying upon this Dharma, I have already realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. This Dharma is profound, subtle, and tranquil; I shall dwell in reliance upon this very Dharma, making offerings and paying homage to what is called the Prajñāpāramitā."

“Kauśika! Even though I have already attained Buddhahood, I still rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā for making offerings and showing reverence; how much more so should sons and daughters of good family who seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment not rely upon this profound Prajñāpāramitā to practice with diligence, making offerings, showing reverence, honoring, and praising it!”
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is able to give birth to that which has already been born.
For this reason, Kauśika, whether they belong to the bodhisattva vehicle,

the pratyekabuddha vehicle, or the śrāvaka vehicle, all sons and daughters of good family should diligently study and train in the *prajñāpāramitā*, honoring, revering, respecting, and praising it with offerings of immeasurable kinds of exquisite flower garlands, up to and including lamps.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 430; The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra,
Fascicle 431.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter 36: The Text of the Sūtra, Part Two, Section Thirty-Six, Part One. At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of Devas, saying: "Kauśika!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to instruct all sentient beings throughout Jambudvīpa, causing them all to abide in the ten paths of wholesome action—what do you think?
"Would these sons and daughters of good family, by reason of this cause and condition, acquire much merit?
Śakra, Lord of Devas, replied: "Very much!"
"World-Honored One!
It is very much so! Sugata!"
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters transcribe such profound *prajñāpāramitā* and bestow it upon others for recitation, or if they transcribe it further and cause it to circulate widely, the mass of merit obtained by these good sons and good daughters will be far greater than the former.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
Within this secret treasury of the Prajñāpāramitā, all untainted dharmas are extensively expounded; therein, sons and daughters of good family have studied, are studying, and shall study.

There are some who have entered, are now entering, or will enter the state of correctness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*) within the vehicle of the śrāvakas, gradually attaining, are now attaining, or will attain the fruit of arhatship;

there are some who have entered, are now entering, or will enter the state of correctness and departure from birth within the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, gradually realizing, are now realizing, or will realize the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;

and there are some who have entered, are now entering, or will enter the state of correctness and departure from birth within the vehicle of the bodhisattvas, gradually practicing the various bodhisattva deeds, having realized, are now realizing, or will realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
“Kauśika! What are called the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*)? They are: the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;

the knowledge of the four noble truths; the three gates of liberation; internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*); the ten powers of a Tathāgata; the four fearlessnesses; the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*); great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity; the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), and all other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas—all these are the untainted dharmas spoken of herein.”

“Kauśika! If a son or daughter of good family were to instruct a single sentient being to abide in the fruit of a stream-enterer, the mass of merit obtained would be far superior to that of instructing all the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa and causing them all to abide in the ten paths of wholesome action.”
Why is this? Kauśika!

Those who abide in the ten paths of wholesome action are not exempt from the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts; however, those who abide in the fruit of a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) attain permanent liberation from the three evil destinies. How much more so, then, would the mass of merit obtained by teaching others to abide in the fruits of a once-returner, a non-returner, an arhat, or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha not surpass that [merit]?

Kauśika! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to instruct all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa so that they all abide in the fruit of a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, an arhat, or in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, it would not be as meritorious as someone instructing a single sentient being to set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
For what reason? Kauśika!
If one instructs sentient beings to incline toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, then one ensures that the Buddha-eye in the world shall not be severed.

Why is this? It is because it is due to the existence of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that there are the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship, as well as the awakening of a pratyekabuddha;
and it is because it is due to the existence of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that there are Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas who turn the sublime wheel of Dharma to deliver immeasurable multitudes.
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas achieve their accomplishment by relying upon the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). For this reason, Kauśika,

if a son of good family or a daughter of good family writes down this profound perfection of wisdom and gives it to others to read and recite, or transcribes it and causes it to be widely circulated, the mass of merit they obtain will be infinitely and boundlessly superior to the previous mass of merit.
Why is this so, Kauśika?

Because within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, all the supreme and wondrous wholesome dharmas of both the mundane and supramundane realms are extensively taught. Based upon these wholesome dharmas, there come to be in the world the great clans of kṣatriyas, the great clans of brāhmaṇas, the great clans of householders, and the great clans of laymen; likewise, from the gods of the Four Great Kings up to the gods of the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception. Furthermore, there come to be the designations for the four foundations of mindfulness, and so on extensively up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); and there also come to be the designations for stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

"Furthermore, Kauśika! Setting aside the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa, suppose a son or daughter of good family were to instruct all the sentient beings of the four great continents, causing them all to abide in the ten paths of wholesome action. What do you think?"
"Would these sons and daughters of good family, by reason of this cause and condition, acquire much merit?
Śakra, Lord of Devas, replied: "Very much!"
"World-Honored One!
It is very much so! Sugata!"
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!

Setting aside these sentient beings in each of the worlds throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—suppose a son or daughter of good family were to teach and transform all sentient beings in all the worlds of the ten directions, causing them all to dwell securely in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers. The Buddha said, “Kauśika!

"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters should listen to this Prajñāpāramitā with a sincere mind, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, diligently practice and study it, and contemplate it according to the principle, the mass of merit obtained by these good sons and good daughters surpasses that of one who teaches all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa, causing them all to abide in the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers;

it also surpasses that of one who teaches all sentient beings in the four great continents, causing them all to abide in the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers."

It is also superior to teaching and transforming all sentient beings in a small thousand-world system, causing them all to dwell securely in the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless absorptions, and the five supernormal powers;

it is also superior to teaching and transforming all sentient beings in a medium thousand-world system, causing them all to dwell securely in the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless absorptions, and the five supernormal powers;

and it is also superior to teaching and transforming all sentient beings in a great trichiliocosm, causing them all to dwell securely in the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless absorptions, and the five supernormal powers.

It is even more superior than teaching and transforming all sentient beings in as many worlds in each of the ten directions as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, causing them all to dwell securely in the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers;

it is also more superior than teaching and transforming all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions, causing them all to dwell securely in the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers.

Kauśika! In this context, "correct reflection" refers to reflecting upon the *prajñāpāramitā* up to the *dānapāramitā* by means of a practice that is neither dual nor non-dual, for the sake of seeking unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;

or if one reflects upon internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāvaśūnyatā*) by means of a practice that is neither dual nor non-dual, for the sake of seeking unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

If, by means of a practice that is neither dual nor non-dual, one seeks unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, one contemplates the four foundations of mindfulness, and so forth, up to the knowledge of all aspects.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to extensively teach this *prajñāpāramitā* to others through immeasurable gateways—proclaiming, revealing, expounding, clarifying, explaining, and analyzing its meaning and intent so that it may be easily understood—the mass of merit they would obtain would be infinitely greater than the merit obtained by oneself merely hearing, receiving, upholding, reciting, diligently practicing, and reflecting upon this *prajñāpāramitā* in accordance with the truth."

Kauśika! Regarding the meaning and intent of this *prajñāpāramitā*, the meaning and intent of this *prajñāpāramitā* should not be viewed through dualistic characteristics, nor should it be viewed through non-dualistic characteristics. It is neither with characteristics nor without characteristics; neither entering nor exiting; neither increasing nor decreasing; neither defiled nor pure; neither arising nor ceasing; neither grasping nor relinquishing; neither clinging nor non-clinging; neither abiding nor non-abiding; neither real nor unreal; neither associated nor dissociated; neither conjoined nor dispersed; neither causal nor non-causal; neither dharma nor non-dharma; neither suchness (*tathatā*) nor non-suchness; neither the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) nor non-limit-of-reality. Such meanings and intents have immeasurable gateways.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters, with sincere hearts, listen to, receive and uphold, read and recite, diligently study, and reflect upon the Prajñāpāramitā according to the truth; and if they extensively explain it for others through immeasurable gateways—proclaiming, expounding, clarifying, interpreting, analyzing its meaning and intent so that it may be easily understood—the mass of merit obtained by these good sons and good daughters shall exceed the previous mass of merit, being immeasurable and boundless."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
All sons and daughters of good family should, by means of various skillful words and meanings, expound the profound *prajñāpāramitā* for others.”
The Buddha said,
“Kauśika, it is so! It is thus!”
"So it is! It is just as you have said.
All sons and daughters of good family should expound this profound Prajñāpāramitā to others using various skillful words and meanings."

Kauśika! If sons or daughters of good family can expound the profound *prajñāpāramitā* for others using various skillful words and meanings, these sons and daughters of good family will achieve an immeasurable, incalculable, boundless, and inconceivable mass of great merit.

“Kauśika! If good sons and good daughters, for as long as their lives last, were to provide offerings, honor, respect, veneration, and praise to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas—each as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in each of the ten directions—using immeasurable varieties of supreme and exquisite articles of pleasure, clothing, food and drink, requisites for illness, and medicines;”

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, with sincere hearts, hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently study, and reflect upon the Prajñāpāramitā according to the principle, and furthermore, relying on its various skillful words and meanings, extensively expound it to others through immeasurable approaches—proclaiming, revealing, elucidating, clarifying, explaining, analyzing the significance, and making it easy to understand—the mass of merit obtained by these sons or daughters of good family is far greater than the former.
Why is this so? Kauśika!

It is because in each of the ten directions, in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas have all diligently studied and trained in the Prajñāpāramitā, thereby realizing unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"Furthermore, Kauśika! If good sons and good daughters, for immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless great kalpas, practice the perfections from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom by means of the apprehension of a [real] object; [their merit would be less than that of one who practices with non-apprehension]."

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, regarding this Prajñāpāramitā, by means of the method of non-apprehension, listen with a sincere heart, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, diligently practice and study it, and reflect upon it according to the principle; and furthermore, using various skillful words and meanings, for even a brief moment explain it to others, proclaiming, expounding, clarifying, and interpreting it, analyzing its significance and making it easy to understand—the mass of merit they obtain is far greater than the former.
Kauśika! Those who have grasping at attainment refer to good men and good women and others who, when practicing generosity, form such thoughts as:
"I am the one who bestows; he is the recipient; this is the fruit of giving; and these are the act of giving and the objects given."
"When he practices giving, it is called abiding in generosity, but it is not called the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā).
When practicing pure ethical discipline, he forms this thought:
'I am able to maintain the precepts in order to protect that [giving]; this is the fruit of the precepts and the precepts themselves that are maintained.'"
"When he practices ethical discipline, it is called abiding in pure discipline, but it is not called the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
When practicing patience, he forms this thought:
'I am able to practice patience for the sake of protecting others'; this is the fruit of patience as well as the intrinsic nature of patience."
"When he practices patience, it is called abiding in patience, but it is not yet called the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
When he practices diligence, he forms this thought:
'I am able to exert diligence in order to cultivate abandonment; this is the fruit of diligence and the intrinsic nature of diligence.'"
"When he practices diligence, it is called abiding in diligence, but it is not called the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā).
When he cultivates meditative concentration (dhyāna), he forms this thought:
'I am able to cultivate concentration; that is the object of concentration, and this is the fruit of concentration as well as its intrinsic nature.'"
"When he practices meditative concentration, it is called 'abiding in dhyāna,' but it is not called the 'dhyāna-pāramitā.
When he practices wisdom (prajñā), he forms this thought:
'I am able to cultivate wisdom; that is the object of wisdom, and this is the fruit of wisdom as well as the intrinsic nature of wisdom.'"
"When they cultivate wisdom at that time, it is called abiding in *prajñā*, but it is not called *prajñāpāramitā*. Kausika!

Because these sons and daughters of good family employ the means of apprehending something as an object, they are unable to bring to fulfillment the *pāramitās* of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom."
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice so as to be able to fulfill the pāramitās of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom?"
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices generosity, he does not apprehend the giver, the recipient, the fruit of giving, the act of giving, or the objects given; because he employs the method of non-apprehension, he is able to fulfill the perfection of generosity.”

When practicing pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), one does not apprehend the practitioner, the fruit of the protected discipline, nor the discipline itself; because one employs the method of non-apprehension, one is able to fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).

When practicing patience (*kṣānti*), one does not apprehend the one who is patient, the fruit of the protected patience, nor the intrinsic nature of patience; because one employs the method of non-apprehension, one is able to fulfill the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*).

When practicing diligence (*vīrya*), one does not apprehend the diligent one, the fruit of the exertion performed, nor the intrinsic nature of diligence; because one employs the method of non-apprehension, one is able to fulfill the perfection of diligence (*vīryapāramitā*).

When practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one does not apprehend the practitioner, the object of concentration, the fruit of concentration, or the intrinsic nature of concentration; because one employs the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), one is able to fulfill the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).

When practicing wisdom (*prajñā*), one does not apprehend the practitioner, the object of wisdom, the fruit of wisdom, or the intrinsic nature of wisdom; because one employs the method of non-apprehension, one is able to fulfill the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

Kauśika! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should, by means of such wisdom of non-apprehension as well as various skillful expressions and meanings, proclaim the *prajñāpāramitā* and so forth, up to the *dānapāramitā*.
Why is this? Kauśika!
In future ages, there will be sons of good family and daughters of good family who, for the sake of others, shall proclaim a counterfeit *prajñāpāramitā*, even down to the *dānapāramitā*.

Those who have first resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, upon hearing those teachings on semblance-prajñā up to the perfection of generosity, may become confused and fall away from the Middle Way. Therefore, one should teach the prajñā up to the perfection of generosity to those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta by means of the wisdom of non-apprehension and through various skillful expressions and meanings.
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
what is meant by the teaching of counterfeit *prajñāpāramitā*, *dhyāna*, *vīrya*, *kṣānti*, *śīla*, and *dāna*?”
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!

If sons or daughters of good family speak of the prajñāpāramitā up to the dānapāramitā as having something to be attained, this is called proclaiming counterfeit prajñā, dhyāna, vīrya, kṣānti, śīla, and dāna pāramitās.”
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Why is it that when good sons and good daughters speak of the prajñāpāramitā up to the dānapāramitā as having something to be attained, it is called speaking of a semblance of the prajñāpāramitā up to the dānapāramitā?”
The Buddha said,
“Kauśika! If good sons and good daughters, for the sake of generating the mind set on unsurpassed bodhi, practice the six pāramitās...”
"Perfection" (Maitrī) refers to teaching that form up to consciousness are impermanent, suffering, and non-self;
teaching that the eye base up to the mind base are impermanent, suffering, and non-self; teaching that the form base up to the phenomena base are impermanent, suffering, and non-self;
and teaching that the eye element up to the mind element are impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
I teach that the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) up to the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) are impermanent, suffering, and non-self;
I teach that the eye-consciousness realm up to the mind-consciousness realm are impermanent, suffering, and non-self;

I teach that eye-contact up to mind-contact are impermanent, suffering, and non-self; and I teach all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, up to [feelings produced with mind-contact as condition]...
He says that all feelings produced with mental contact as a condition are impermanent, suffering, and non-self;
he says that the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions are impermanent, suffering, and non-self;
and he says that the four foundations of mindfulness up to the knowledge of all aspects are impermanent, suffering, and non-self, speaking thus:

"If there are those who are able to practice from the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity by relying on such dharmas as these, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity."
Furthermore, it is said:
"One who practices the perfection of wisdom, up to the perfection of generosity, should seek the impermanence, suffering, and non-self of form, up to the knowledge of all aspects."

If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice from the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity, this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity.

“Kauśika! If there are those who seek form up to the knowledge of all aspects as impermanent, suffering, and non-self, and who practice the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity based on these dharmas, I say that they are practicing a semblance of the perfections of wisdom up to generosity, which is characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.”
Kauśika! If it is as previously described, you should know that all these are merely discourses on a semblance of prajñāpāramitā up to dānapāramitā that involve apprehension.

"Furthermore, Kauśika! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family should proclaim the perfection of wisdom, up to the perfection of generosity, to those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, saying: 'Come!'"
"O son of good family!
I shall instruct you in the practice of the *pāramitās*, from the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) down to the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*).
If you practice according to my instructions, you shall swiftly become established in the bodhisattva stages, from the first through the tenth."

"Kauśika! Because they employ signs and the apprehension of objects as their means, and rely on the notion of accumulation to teach the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity, this is called teaching counterfeit perfections of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity."

"Furthermore, Kauśika! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family should proclaim the *prajñāpāramitā* and even the *dānapāramitā* to those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, saying: 'Come!'"
“Son of good family!
I shall instruct you in the cultivation and study of the perfections from prajñāpāramitā down to dānapāramitā.
If you practice according to my instructions, you will swiftly transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.”

"Kauśika! Because they employ signs and the apprehension of objects as their means, and rely on the perception of accumulation to teach the cultivation of the *prajñāpāramitā* up to the *dānapāramitā*, this is called the teaching of counterfeit *prajñāpāramitā* up to the *dānapāramitā*."
"Furthermore, Kauśika! If a son or daughter of good family should proclaim the *prajñāpāramitā* and even the *dānapāramitā* to those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, saying: 'Come!'"
"Good son! I shall instruct you in the cultivation and study of the *pāramitās*, from *prajñā* down to *dāna*.
If you cultivate and study according to my instructions, you will swiftly enter the bodhisattva’s state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*)."

Having entered the bodhisattva’s state of right determination free from birth, they immediately attain the bodhisattva’s forbearance regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Having attained the bodhisattva’s forbearance regarding the non-arising of phenomena, they immediately attain the bodhisattva’s sublime supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

Having attained the sublime supernormal powers of a bodhisattva, they are able to travel to all buddha-fields throughout the ten directions, proceeding from one buddha-field to another, making offerings, paying respect, honoring, and praising all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; by means of this, they are able to swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

“Kauśika! Because they employ signs and the apprehension of objects as their means, and rely on the notion of accumulation to teach the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity, this is called the teaching of counterfeit perfections of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity.”
"Furthermore, Kauśika! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family should say to those belonging to the lineage of the Bodhisattva vehicle:

'If one listens with a sincere mind to the Prajñāpāramitā, receives and maintains it, reads and recites it, diligently practices and studies it, and reflects upon it according to the principle, one will certainly obtain immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless merit.'"

“Kauśika! Because they employ signs and the apprehension of objects as their means, they speak in such a manner; this is called proclaiming a counterfeit *prajñāpāramitā*, up to and including the *dānapāramitā*.”

"Kauśika! Because they employ signs and the apprehension of objects as their means, they speak in this manner; this is called teaching a counterfeit *prajñāpāramitā*, and so forth, up to the *dānapāramitā*."
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by proclaiming the true and correct perfections of wisdom, meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity?”
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!

If sons and daughters of good family teach the *prajñāpāramitā* up to the *dānapāramitā* as being without anything to be attained, this is called proclaiming the true and correct *prajñā*, *dhyāna*, *vīrya*, *kṣānti*, *śīla*, and *dāna* pāramitās.”
Then, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

How is it that when good sons and good daughters speak of the non-apprehension of the *prajñāpāramitā* up to the *dānapāramitā*, it is called speaking of the true and correct *prajñāpāramitā* up to the *dānapāramitā*?”
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!
If good sons and good daughters proclaim the *prajñāpāramitā* and even the *dānapāramitā* for those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, speaking as follows:”
"Come, son of good family!
You should cultivate the perfection of wisdom, up to and including the perfection of generosity."

When you practice correctly, you should not contemplate form as either permanent or impermanent, as either pleasant or painful, or as either self or non-self; you should not contemplate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either permanent or impermanent, as either pleasant or painful, or as either self or non-self.

In this way, one should not contemplate the sense base of the eye up to the sense base of the mind; the sense base of forms up to the sense base of phenomena; the eye element up to the mind element; the form element up to the phenomenon element; the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element; eye-contact up to mind-contact; the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition; nor should one contemplate the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, or the four foundations of mindfulness up to the knowledge of all aspects, as either permanent or impermanent, as either pleasant or painful, as either self or non-self.
Why is this? Good son! Form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form, and so on, up to the knowledge of all aspects, which is empty of the intrinsic nature of the knowledge of all aspects.

The intrinsic nature of form is itself the absence of intrinsic nature; likewise, the intrinsic nature of everything up to the knowledge of all aspects is itself the absence of intrinsic nature. That which is the absence of intrinsic nature is itself the perfection of wisdom, and so on, up to the perfection of generosity.

In this Prajñāpāramitā, and even up to the Dānapāramitā, form is unapprehendable; its permanence or impermanence, pleasure or suffering, self or non-self is likewise unapprehendable. Even up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), it is unapprehendable; its permanence or impermanence, pleasure or suffering, self or non-self is likewise unapprehendable.

Why is this? Because herein even form and the other aggregates cannot be apprehended; how much less could there be the apprehension of such things as permanence or impermanence, pleasure or suffering, self or non-self!
"Good son! If you can cultivate such perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity."
"Kauśika! When these sons and daughters of good family speak in this manner, it is called proclaiming the true and correct Prajñāpāramitā, up to and including the Dānapāramitā."
"Furthermore, Kauśika! If good sons or good daughters proclaim the *prajñāpāramitā* and even the *dānapāramitā* to those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, saying: 'Come!'"
"Good son! I shall instruct you in the practice and study of the *pāramitās*, from *prajñā* down to *dāna*.

When you practice and study, do not observe any phenomenon as having even the slightest thing that can be dwelled in, transcended, entered, attained, realized, or heard; nor [observe] any merit obtained that could be rejoiced in and dedicated toward enlightenment."
Why is this? Son of good family!

Within this *prajñāpāramitā* and even up to the *dānapāramitā*, there is ultimately not the slightest dharma that can be dwelled in, transcended, entered, attained, realized, or heard; nor is there any merit to be acquired that can be rejoiced in or dedicated toward enlightenment.

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is empty; if their intrinsic nature is empty, then they are non-existent. That which is non-existent is precisely the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and so forth, up to the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).

Within this Prajñāpāramitā, and even up to the Dānapāramitā, there is ultimately not the slightest dharma that can be apprehended as entering or exiting, arising or ceasing, being annihilated or permanent, being one or different, or coming or going.

“Kauśika! When these sons and daughters of good family speak in this manner, they are entirely contrary to all that belongs to the dark category; this is the teaching of the true perfection of wisdom, meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity.”

For this reason, Kauśika, all sons and daughters of good family should, regarding the Prajñāpāramitā, by means of the method of non-apprehension, listen with a sincere heart, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, diligently practice and study it, and contemplate it according to the principle. "Come! [Listen!]"

“Good son! You should, with a sincere mind, hear, receive, uphold, read, and recite this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, making it thoroughly mastered and reflecting upon it according to the principle. You should correctly believe and understand the Dharma-gates taught in accordance with this *prajñāpāramitā*; if you correctly believe and understand them, you will be able to practice and study such *prajñāpāramitā*. If you can practice and study such *prajñāpāramitā*, you will be able to realize the dharma of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). If you can realize the dharma of omniscience, then your cultivation of *prajñāpāramitā* will increase and become perfected. If your cultivation of *prajñāpāramitā* increases and becomes perfected, you will then realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).”
"Kauśika! The merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family is far greater than that mentioned before. Furthermore, Kauśika!"

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to instruct all sentient beings throughout Jambudvīpa so that they all attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and furthermore were to extensively expound the *Prajñāpāramitā* for them through immeasurable methods and skillful words and meanings—proclaiming, revealing, elucidating, explaining, analyzing the significance, and making it easy to understand; [the latter would generate far more merit than the former].

If there are sons or daughters of good family who instruct a single sentient being to attain non-retrogression in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and furthermore extensively explain the *Prajñāpāramitā* to them through immeasurable methods and skillful words and meanings—proclaiming, revealing, expounding, clarifying, interpreting, and analyzing its significance so that it may be easily understood; [this latter person generates greater merit].
Kauśika! The merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family is far greater than that mentioned before. Furthermore, Kauśika!

Setting aside the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa, suppose a son or daughter of good family were to instruct all sentient beings of the four great continents, or all sentient beings of a small thousandfold world system, or all sentient beings of a medium thousandfold world system, or all sentient beings of this trichiliocosm, or even all sentient beings in worlds throughout the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, causing them all to aspire to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and furthermore, were to extensively teach them the *Prajñāpāramitā* through immeasurable methods, using skillful phrasing and meanings, proclaiming, expounding, clarifying, explaining, analyzing its significance, and making it easy for them to understand.

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to instruct a single sentient being, causing them to attain non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and furthermore were to extensively explain the *Prajñāpāramitā* to them through immeasurable methods of skillful phrasing and meaning—proclaiming, revealing, expounding, clarifying, interpreting, and analyzing its significance so that it may be easily understood; [this would generate a greater merit than the former].
Kauśika! The merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family is far greater than that mentioned before. Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to instruct all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa so that they all attain non-retrogression from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and furthermore, were to extensively expound the Prajñāpāramitā for them through immeasurable approaches with skillful phrasing and meaning—proclaiming, revealing, elucidating, clarifying, explaining, and analyzing its significance and intent to make it easy to understand; [this would be even more meritorious].
If a single sentient being were to speak these words:
"I now joyfully aspire to swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, in order to rescue sentient beings from the sufferings of the various evil realms."

There are sons and daughters of good family who, for the sake of accomplishing that task, extensively expound the Prajñāpāramitā through immeasurable gateways of skillful phrasing and meaning; they proclaim, reveal, elucidate, manifest, explain, analyze the significance, and make it easy to understand.
Kauśika! The merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family is far greater than that mentioned before. Why is this?

Kauśika! Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwelling on the stage of non-retrogression do not depend extensively upon the teachings they have heard, because they are certain to advance toward great enlightenment, and because they will inevitably never retreat from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; whereas those who aspire to quickly realize great enlightenment must depend extensively upon the teachings they have heard, because they seek to quickly realize unexcelled awakening, and because they contemplate the suffering of birth and death for all sentient beings and stir a heart of great compassion that is most poignant.

"Furthermore, Kauśika! Setting aside the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa, suppose a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to instruct all sentient beings of the four great continents, or all sentient beings of a small thousandfold world system, or all sentient beings of a medium thousandfold world system, or all sentient beings of this trichiliocosm, or even all sentient beings in as many worlds in each of the ten directions as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, causing them all to attain non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and furthermore, were they to extensively expound the Prajñāpāramitā for them through immeasurable methods, using skillful phrasing and meanings, proclaiming, revealing, elucidating, clarifying, explaining, and analyzing its significance so that it may be easily understood."
If a single sentient being were to speak thus:
"I now joyfully aspire to swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, in order to rescue sentient beings from the sufferings of the three evil realms."

There are sons and daughters of good family who, for the sake of accomplishing that task, extensively expound the Prajñāpāramitā through immeasurable methods with skillful words and meanings; they proclaim, reveal, elaborate, manifest, explain, analyze the significance, and clarify it so that it may be easily understood.
Kauśika! The merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family is far greater than that mentioned before. Why is this?

Kauśika! Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling on the stage of non-retrogression does not rely excessively upon the teachings spoken, because they are certain to advance toward great enlightenment, and because they will inevitably never retreat from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

Those who joyfully seek to swiftly realize great enlightenment must rely extensively upon the teachings that have been expounded; for they seek swift realization of unsurpassed awakening, and because they contemplate the suffering of birth and death, they stir a heart of great compassion toward all sentient beings with the utmost intensity.
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One!

As a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws closer to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, they should be instructed and exhorted accordingly with the perfection of giving up to the perfection of wisdom; they should be instructed and exhorted with inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature; they should be instructed and exhorted with the four applications of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; and so on, up to being instructed and exhorted with the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. Furthermore, they should be honored and sustained by providing them with exquisite robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites, as well as various other necessities according to their requirements.”

"Bhagavān! If good sons or good daughters can provide such offerings of Dharma-gifts, material gifts, instructions, and teachings to sustain those Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the merit obtained by these good sons and good daughters will be far greater than the former."
Why is this? World-Honored One!

It is because those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas must, through such offerings of the Dharma, material wealth, instructions, teachings, and supportive care, swiftly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"

Kauśika! That you are able to exhort those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, further able to sustain those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and also able to protect and assist those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—you have now performed what should be done by a noble disciple of the Buddha.
Why is this? Kauśika!

All Tathāgatas and their noble disciples, desiring to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, skillfully exhort and encourage those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to swiftly proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. By means of the gift of Dharma, the gift of material wealth, instruction, admonition, offerings, gathering, and diligent protection and assistance, they cause those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Why is this? Because all the supreme worldly phenomena of the Tathāgatas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas appear by virtue of those Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Why is this? "Kauśika!

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas did not give rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, then there would be no bodhisattva-mahāsattvas capable of training in the six pāramitās, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha."

If there were no bodhisattva mahāsattvas training in the six pāramitās up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, then there would be no bodhisattva mahāsattvas who realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas did not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, then there would be no such superior worldly phenomena as the Tathāgatas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.

Kauśika! Because there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who give rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, there are then bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are able to train in the six pāramitās, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.

Because there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who train in the six pāramitās up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, there are consequently bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Because there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening and turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, they are able to sever the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts;
they are also able to diminish the hosts of asuras and increase the numbers of devas and humans. Consequently, there arise great kṣatriya clans, great brāhmaṇa clans, and long...

Great clans and great families of householders appear in the world; likewise, the gods of the Four Great Kings up to the gods of the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception appear in the world.
Furthermore, the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, and inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, appear in the world.
The four foundations of mindfulness, and so forth, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, appear in the world;
furthermore, the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, and the vehicle of the perfectly awakened ones appear in the world.
Chapter 37: Dedication through Rejoicing, Part One. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:
"Virtuous One!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of non-apprehension as a skillful method, rejoices in all the meritorious qualities and various meritorious deeds associated with the joy of all sentient beings;

and if that bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of non-apprehension as a skillful method, takes these meritorious deeds associated with joy and, sharing them equally with all sentient beings, dedicates them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
and if other sentient beings likewise rejoice in and dedicate their various meritorious deeds;

Whatever meritorious deeds there may be of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas—namely, the three types of meritorious deeds consisting of giving, ethical discipline, and cultivation; or the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; or the three gates of liberation, the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, the four analytical knowledges, the six supernormal powers, and other such meritorious deeds.

All the merit of this bodhisattva mahāsattva’s rejoicing and dedication is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the highest, the most sublime, the most exquisite, the most superior, and the unsurpassed—equal to the unequaled—compared to all the meritorious deeds of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.
Why is this so, Venerable One?

Because when ordinary beings cultivate meritorious deeds, they do so only for their own sovereignty, ease, and happiness; when Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas cultivate meritorious deeds, they do so only for their own self-discipline, their own tranquility, and their own nirvāṇa. However, all the merit of the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas that consists of sympathetic joy and dedication is universally for the sake of disciplining, tranquilizing, and bringing all sentient beings to parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti asked the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya: "Great Being!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva’s mind of sympathetic joy and dedication universally takes as its object the countless, immeasurable, and boundless worlds of the ten directions. Within each world, regarding all the Buddhas who have already entered parinirvāṇa—from their first generation of the mind of awakening until they attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and continuing thus through their successive entry into the realm of nirvana without remainder until the extinction of the Dharma—all the roots of virtue associated with the six pāramitās therein, as well as the roots of virtue associated with the countless, immeasurable, and boundless Buddha-dharmas, whether shared or unshared, belonging to śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and all sentient beings."
Whatever meritorious deeds consisting of giving, morality, and cultivation belong to those ordinary disciples;
whatever untainted roots of virtue belonging to the stages of training and beyond-training belong to those śrāvaka disciples;

and whatever aggregates of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation achieved by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas—including the immeasurable, limitless, and boundless Buddha-dharmas of great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity for the sake of benefiting and gladdening all sentient beings, as well as the True Dharma taught by those Buddhas.

If, by diligently training in those dharmas, one attains the fruit of a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat; or attains the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; or enters the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth, as well as the other practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Thus, all these roots of goodness, as well as the roots of goodness planted by other sentient beings toward the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their assemblies of Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas—whether they currently abide in the world or have entered parinirvāṇa—I now rejoice in them all collectively and with full presence of mind.

Having thus rejoiced, he further dedicates all these meritorious deeds accompanied by such rejoicing to be shared equally with all sentient beings for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, saying:
"By means of these roots of virtue, may I, together with all sentient beings, jointly realize unsurpassed enlightenment."

"This rejoicing and dedication thus generated is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the most exalted, the most wondrous, the most subtle, the highest, and the unsurpassed—equal to the unequaled—among all other meritorious deeds that have been generated."
What do you think,
Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva?

Does that Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, when giving rise to a mind of sympathetic joy and dedication based on such an object, actually have such an object of focus as it is grasped by the marks perceived by that Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya replied to the Venerable Subhūti: "Venerable One!

When those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy and dedication based on such objects, there is in reality no such object as exists for the marks grasped by those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti said to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya: "O Great Being!

If there were no objective referent corresponding to the marks as they are grasped, then how could that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s mind of sympathetic joy and dedication—employing the grasping of marks as its means—universally take as its object the countless, immeasurable, and boundless worlds of the ten directions; and within each world, all the roots of virtue of the Buddhas who have already entered parinirvāṇa, from their first generation of the mind until the extinction of the Dharma, as well as all the roots of virtue of their disciples and others, and having gathered them all together before him, rejoice in them and dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
Is this arising of sympathetic joy and dedication not, then, a perversion?

Just as to regard the impermanent as permanent, suffering as pleasure, the non-self as self, and the impure as pure constitutes a perversion of perception, a perversion of mind, and a perversion of view—so too should it be with this, which grasps at signs where there are no signs.
"O Mahāsattva!

Just as the objects of focus are in reality non-existent, so too is the mind of sympathetic joy and dedication; so too are all roots of virtue; so too is unsurpassed enlightenment; so too are the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; and so on, in detail, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha."
"O Mahāsattva!

If the reality of the object of focus is non-existent, and if the mind of sympathetic joy and dedication is likewise, and if all roots of goodness are likewise, and if unsurpassed enlightenment is likewise, and if the six pāramitās are likewise, and even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are likewise—then what is that which is the object of focus?"
What is this matter?
What is the mind of sympathetic joy and dedication?
And what are these various roots of goodness?
What is this unsurpassed enlightenment?
What are these six perfections up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha,
such that those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, taking these things as their object, give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy and dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya replied to the Venerable Subhūti: "Virtuous One!

If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has long practiced the six pāramitās, has already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, has planted roots of goodness in past lives and long since made great vows, is sustained by virtuous friends, and has well studied the meaning of the emptiness of the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) of all phenomena—such a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is able, regarding the object of focus, the mind of sympathetic joy and dedication, the various roots of goodness, unsurpassed enlightenment, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and all dharmas, to not grasp at their marks (*nimitta*), yet is able to give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy and dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

The rejoicing and dedication thus performed employ as their means that which is neither dual nor non-dual; they employ as their means that which is neither characterized by marks nor markless; they employ as their means that which is neither attainment nor non-attainment; they employ as their means that which is neither defiled nor pure; they employ as their means that which is neither arising nor ceasing. Regarding the objects of focus, up to and including unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they are able to refrain from grasping at marks. Because they do not grasp at marks, they are not subsumed under perversion.

If there are bodhisattvas who have not long practiced the six pāramitās, who have never made offerings to immeasurable buddhas, who have not planted roots of goodness in the past, who have not long since generated the great vows, who have not been sustained by many spiritual friends, and who have not well studied the self-characteristic emptiness of all phenomena—such bodhisattvas, regarding the objects of focus, the bases, the rejoicing and dedication, the various roots of goodness, unsurpassed enlightenment, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and all phenomena, still grasp at their signs and give rise to a mind of rejoicing, dedicating [the merit] toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Such rejoicing and dedication that arise, because they involve grasping at signs, are still subsumed under perversion; they are not true rejoicing and dedication toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"Furthermore, Venerable Sir, one should not proclaim the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity, the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature, the four foundations of mindfulness— expounded at length— up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, nor the meaning of the self-characteristic emptiness of all phenomena, before those bodhisattvas who have newly begun their training in the Mahāyāna."
Why is this? Venerable One!

Although those bodhisattvas who have newly begun their training in the Mahāyāna possess a small measure of faith, respect, and delight toward such teachings, as soon as they hear them, they forget them all; they become startled, terrified, and doubtful, and thus give rise to slander.

If there are irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas in the past, planted roots of goodness, long since made great vows, and are sustained by many virtuous friends, one should, in their presence, extensively explain, analyze, and reveal for them everything from the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity; from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature; from the four foundations of mindfulness, as extensively explained, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and the meaning of the self-characteristic emptiness of all phenomena.
Why is this so? Venerable One!

Because those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are non-retrogressive, who have made offerings to immeasurable buddhas in the past, who have planted roots of goodness over many lifetimes, who have long since made great vows, and who are sustained by many virtuous friends—if they hear this Dharma, they are all able to receive and uphold it without ever forgetting it; nor will they be startled, terrified, doubtful, or disparaging toward it.
"Venerable One!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should dedicate these meritorious deeds accompanied by such sympathetic joy toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, saying:

"O Great Being! All Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should dedicate these meritorious deeds accompanied by such sympathetic joy toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. This is because the mental state used for sympathetic joy and dedication is itself subject to exhaustion, cessation, detachment, and transformation; likewise, the objects of focus and all those roots of virtue are also like that mental state, subject to exhaustion, cessation, detachment, and transformation."
In this context, what is the mind that is employed?
Furthermore, by means of what objects of focus and what roots of goodness does one speak of sympathetic joy and dedication toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?

This mind, with respect to the nature of mind, should not have rejoicing or dedication, because two minds cannot arise simultaneously; nor can the mind rejoice in or dedicate itself, because it is the self-nature of mind.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are able to know in this way that all perfections of wisdom are non-existent, up to and including the perfection of generosity; that form is non-existent, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-existent; and even unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is non-existent. This bodhisattva mahāsattva, knowing that all phenomena are entirely non-existent, is nevertheless able to dedicate to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment those meritorious deeds associated with sympathetic joy.
"Such a mind of sympathetic joy and dedication is not comprised within perversion, because it employs non-apprehension as its means.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:
"Venerable One!"
When the newly initiated bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have set out in the Mahāyāna hear such a teaching as this, will their minds not become terrified or filled with doubt?
Venerable sir,
how can the newly initiated bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have set out in the Mahāyāna dedicate the roots of goodness they have cultivated toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
"Venerable Sir!

How should newly initiated bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have set out in the Mahāyāna embrace and take up those meritorious deeds accompanied by sympathetic joy, and dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
The Venerable Subhūti, sustained by the majestic power and empowerment of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, addressed Śakra, the Lord of the Devas: “Kauśika!

If bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have newly set out in the Great Vehicle cultivate the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity, they should embrace these perfections from the perfection of wisdom down to the perfection of generosity by means of non-apprehension as their expedient and signlessness as their expedient.”

By virtue of these causes and conditions, this bodhisattva mahāsattva extensively believes in and understands internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, and extensively believes in and understands the four applications of mindfulness, as explained at length, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.

They are constantly sustained by spiritual friends, who, through immeasurable methods and with skillful words and meanings, extensively explain for them the dharmas associated with the perfections of wisdom, meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity; by instructing and training them in these dharmas, they cause them to eventually enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth.

Until they have entered the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*), they are also never separated from the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) up to the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), from internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*), and from the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*)—as explained at length—up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*).
He also extensively explains various demonic activities so that, having heard them, their minds will neither increase nor decrease in regard to those demonic deeds.
Why is this? Because the nature of all demonic activities is non-existent and cannot be apprehended.

He also instructs and exhorts them with this Dharma, causing them to eventually enter the Bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*), never being separated from the Buddhas. Having planted various roots of goodness in the presence of the Buddhas, and because they are sustained by those roots of goodness, they are always born into the family of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas; until they reach unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), they shall never be separated from these roots of goodness.

Kauśika! If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have newly set out in the Mahāyāna are able to embrace all merits by means of non-apprehension and signlessness, and if they possess deep faith and understanding regarding these merits, are constantly sustained by virtuous friends, and hear such a Dharma without being startled, terrified, or doubtful—[they shall not fall back].

"Furthermore, Kauśika! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have newly set out in the Mahāyāna practice and accumulate the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom; when they abide in inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature; and when they practice and accumulate the four foundations of mindfulness, as extensively explained, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, as well as other immeasurable and boundless buddha-dharmas—they should, by means of non-apprehension and by means of signlessness, dedicate all these together with all sentient beings equally toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Furthermore, Kauśika! For all those newly trained bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the Great Vehicle throughout the countless, immeasurable, and boundless worlds of the ten directions,
all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have severed the paths of existence and cut them off.
One who has played out the path of conceptual proliferation, laid down the heavy burdens, pulled out the thorns of the village, exhausted the fetters of existence,
is fully endowed with right knowledge, whose mind is well-liberated, and who is skilled in expounding the Dharma;
as well as the aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, and liberation accomplished by the disciples of that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
The aggregate of liberation, the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation, and all other various merits performed,
as well as the roots of goodness planted in this place— namely, the roots of goodness planted among the great clans of kṣatriyas,
the great clans of brahmins, the great clans of householders, and the great clans of laymen, or among the gods of the Four Great Kings— [all these are dedicated].

The roots of goodness planted by the gods up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, and those planted by the gods from the Brahmakāyika Heaven up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven— all these are gathered together, weighed,

and brought before one’s mind to give rise to a heart of sympathetic joy that is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the highest, the most sublime, the most exquisite, the unsurpassed, the peerless, and equal to the unequaled compared to all other roots of goodness. Furthermore, with these meritorious deeds accompanied by such sympathetic joy, one dedicates them equally and in common with all sentient beings toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya asked the Venerable Subhūti:
"Venerable One!..."

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are newly training in the Mahāyāna recollect all the merits of the Buddhas and their assemblies of disciples, as well as the roots of goodness planted by humans, devas, and others—collecting, weighing, and bringing all such things before them—they give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy that, compared to other roots of goodness, is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the highest, the most wondrous, the most subtle, the most superior, the unsurpassed, the unequaled, and the equal to the unequaled. Furthermore, they share these roots of goodness born of sympathetic joy equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. How is it that these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not fall into perversion of perception, perversion of mind, or perversion of view?
Then, the Venerable Subhūti replied to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya:

"Great Being! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding all the virtues of the Buddhas and their assemblies of disciples whom they recollect, does not give rise to the conceptualization of 'the virtues of the Buddhas and their assemblies of disciples';"
Regarding the roots of goodness planted among humans, devas, and others, they do not give rise to the notion of "humans, devas, and others" as the planters of those roots of goodness;

nor, regarding the mind of sympathetic joy and dedication toward great enlightenment that they have generated, do they give rise to the notion of "sympathetic joy and dedication toward enlightenment. This mind of sympathetic joy and dedication generated by these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is free from the inversion of perception, free from the inversion of mind, and free from the inversion of view.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding all the merits of the Buddhas and their assemblies of disciples whom they bring to mind, gives rise to the notion that these are the merits of Buddhas and disciples;
regarding the roots of goodness planted by humans, devas, and others, gives rise to the notion that these are the humans, devas, and others who planted those roots of goodness;
