and regarding the mind of sympathetic joy and dedication toward great enlightenment that they have generated, gives rise to the notion that this is the mind of sympathetic joy and dedication toward enlightenment—then the mind of sympathetic joy and dedication generated by this bodhisattva mahāsattva is characterized by a perversion of perception, a perversion of mind, and a perversion of view.
"Furthermore, Great Being!

If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, with such a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), recollects the roots of virtue and merits of all Buddhas and their assemblies of disciples, he correctly understands that this mind is subject to exhaustion, cessation, detachment, and transformation, and thus is not capable of sympathetic joy; he correctly understands that those dharmas are likewise by nature, and thus are not the objects of sympathetic joy; furthermore, he correctly realizes that the dharma-nature of the mind that performs the dedication is also thus, and thus is not capable of dedication; and he correctly realizes that the dharma-nature of the dharmas to which the dedication is made is also thus, and thus are not the objects of dedication."

If there are those who can rely upon this aforementioned method of sympathetic joy and dedication, it is correct and not erroneous; all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice such sympathetic joy and dedication.
"Furthermore, Great Being!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva universally [offers] to all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present—
from their first generation of the mind of awakening until they attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and even unto the [extinction of their] Dharma..."
Regarding cessation, as well as all the merits therein— including the roots of goodness arising from that Buddha-dharma by the disciples of the Buddha and the pratyekabuddhas,
the roots of goodness planted by ordinary beings upon hearing his teaching of the Dharma,
and those of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, and garuḍas— [all these are dedicated].
...the kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others who have planted roots of goodness by hearing his teaching of the Dharma;

those of the great kṣatriya clans, the great brāhmaṇa clans, the great householder clans, and the great lay clans who have planted roots of goodness by hearing his teaching of the Dharma; and those of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings...
Even up to those in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven who hear that teaching and plant roots of goodness, or those sons and daughters of good family who,
hearing that teaching, resolve their minds upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and diligently cultivate the various practices of a bodhisattva.

Having thus gathered all these together and weighed them before oneself, one gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy that surpasses other roots of goodness—being the most excellent, the most superior, the most noble, the highest, the most sublime, the most refined, the supreme, the unsurpassed, the peerless, and equal to the unequaled. Furthermore, with such roots of goodness born of sympathetic joy, one shares them equally with all sentient beings and dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

At such a time, if one correctly understands that all phenomena associated with sympathetic joy and dedication are subject to cessation, separation, and transformation, and that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena associated with sympathetic joy and dedication is empty, then even while knowing this, one is able to perform sympathetic joy and dedication toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, at that time, if one correctly understands that there is no dharma whatsoever that can be rejoiced in or dedicated toward any dharma.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is empty; within emptiness, there is absolutely no dharma that can rejoice or dedicate, nor any object of such rejoicing or dedication.
Although they know this, they are able to rejoice in and dedicate [the merit] toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can thus rejoice in and dedicate [the merit], then in their practice of the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity, they will be free from the inversion of perception, the inversion of mind, and the inversion of view.

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not give rise to attachment toward the mind of sympathetic joy, nor does he attach to the roots of merit and virtue that are the object of that joy; he does not give rise to attachment toward the mind of dedication, nor does he attach to the unsurpassed enlightenment toward which he dedicates them. By being without attachment, he does not fall into error.
In this way, the mind of sympathetic joy and dedication generated by a bodhisattva is called supreme and free from all conceptualization and discrimination.

*The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Fascicle 432, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Second Division, Chapter on Sympathetic Joy and Dedication, Part 37-II. "Furthermore, O Great Being!..."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding the various meritorious deeds they cultivate and perform, understands them as they truly are—being detached from the aggregates, sense bases, and elements; detached from the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity; detached from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature; and detached from the four foundations of mindfulness, as extensively explained, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.

Having understood, as they truly are, all the meritorious deeds he has cultivated and performed, this bodhisattva mahāsattva rejoices with a profound mind and dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Great Being! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva understands,

as it truly is, that the various meritorious deeds accompanied by sympathetic joy are devoid of the intrinsic nature of those meritorious deeds accompanied by sympathetic joy, and understands, as it truly is, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones..."
The Venerable One, having distanced himself from the intrinsic nature of these Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, understands their qualities and roots of goodness as they truly are;
having distanced himself from the intrinsic nature of such qualities and roots of goodness, he understands the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and ordinary beings as they truly are,
having distanced himself from the intrinsic nature of such śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and ordinary beings.
One understands as it truly is that the mind of great enlightenment which rejoices and dedicates is devoid of such a nature of rejoicing and dedicating for the sake of great enlightenment;
one understands as it truly is that the bodhisattva mahāsattva is devoid of such a nature of a bodhisattva mahāsattva;
and one understands as it truly is that the perfection of wisdom is devoid [of intrinsic nature].

The intrinsic nature of the *prajñāpāramitā* is the remoteness from the intrinsic nature of the *prajñāpāramitā*, up to and including the remoteness of the *dānapāramitā* from the intrinsic nature of the *dānapāramitā*;

one knows as it truly is that internal emptiness is remote from the intrinsic nature of internal emptiness, up to and including the remoteness of the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature from the intrinsic nature of the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature.

He understands, as they truly are, that the four foundations of mindfulness are devoid of the intrinsic nature of the four foundations of mindfulness; and so on, in detail, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha being devoid of the intrinsic nature of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

He understands, as they truly are, that the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice is devoid of the intrinsic nature of the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice; and he understands, as they truly are, that the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is devoid of the intrinsic nature of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way, remaining detached from the intrinsic nature of all phenomena through the profound perfection of wisdom, they are able to correctly rejoice in and dedicate [merit] toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
"Furthermore, Great Being!

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas wish to generate a mind of sympathetic joy and dedicate toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment the roots of virtue and merit of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their disciples who have already entered parinirvāṇa, they should perform such dedication with sympathetic joy by forming this thought:

'Just as all those Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their disciples have already entered parinirvāṇa and their intrinsic nature does not exist, so too are their roots of virtue and merit. The mind I have generated for sympathetic joy and dedication toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, and the unexcelled enlightenment toward which it is dedicated, are likewise of that same nature.'"

Having understood this, they give rise to sympathetic joy regarding all roots of goodness and dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, free from inversion of perception, inversion of mind, and inversion of view.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom by means of grasping at signs, and takes signs when rejoicing in and dedicating toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment the roots of virtue and merit of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas who have already entered parinirvāṇa, as well as their disciples, this is not a skillful rejoicing and dedication.

Because the merit and roots of goodness of the past Buddhas and their assemblies of disciples are not objects to be grasped through signs or signlessness, yet this bodhisattva mahāsattva initiates rejoicing and dedication toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment by grasping at signs; therefore, it is not a skillful rejoicing or dedication. Due to these causes and conditions, there is perversion of perception, perversion of mind, and perversion of view.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension of signs, and rejoices in all the roots of goodness and merit of those Buddhas and their disciples while dedicating them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through the departure from signs, this is called "skillful rejoicing and dedication. By virtue of these causes and conditions, this bodhisattva mahāsattva’s rejoicing and dedication is free from the inversion of conceptualization, the inversion of mind, and the inversion of views.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya asked the Venerable Subhūti: "Venerable One, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva,

without apprehending any signs regarding the meritorious roots and the bases of meritorious action associated with rejoicing in the qualities of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their disciples, is nevertheless able to rejoice and dedicate [that merit] toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
Subhūti replied: "Great Being!

You should know that the Prajñāpāramitā in which Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train possesses such skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) that, although they do not grasp at signs, their activities are accomplished. It is not apart from the Prajñāpāramitā that one can correctly initiate meritorious deeds accompanied by sympathetic joy (*anumodanā-sahagata*) and dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Therefore, the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to accomplish what is to be done should study the perfection of wisdom.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva Maitreya said: "Venerable Subhūti!"
Do not speak thus. Why is this?

Because within the *prajñāpāramitā*, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and their disciples, along with the roots of merit and wholesome qualities they have accomplished, are all non-existent and unapprehendable; because the various meritorious deeds performed with sympathetic joy are also non-existent and unapprehendable; and because the arousal of the mind dedicated toward unsurpassed enlightenment is likewise non-existent and unapprehendable.
In this regard, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they should contemplate in this way:

"The nature of the merits and roots of goodness of the past Buddhas and their assemblies of disciples has already ceased; the nature of the meritorious deeds performed with sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) and the resolve for dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) toward unsurpassed enlightenment is entirely quiescent. If I were to grasp at signs and engage in conceptual discrimination regarding the merits and roots of goodness of all those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas and their disciples, or if I were to grasp at signs and engage in conceptual discrimination regarding the meritorious deeds accompanied by sympathetic joy and the resolve for dedication toward unsurpassed enlightenment, then by employing such skillful means of grasping at signs and conceptualizing, to initiate sympathetic joy and dedication toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—this is not permitted by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, nor do they grant their sympathetic joy to it."

Why is this? To take up signs and engage in conceptual discrimination regarding the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, and their disciples who have already entered parinirvāṇa, and then to rejoice and dedicate [the merit] toward unsurpassed bodhi—this is called "great attainment of something."

Therefore, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to correctly generate sympathetic joy toward the roots of virtue and merit of all Buddhas and their assemblies of disciples, and dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, they should not, within that process, generate sympathetic joy or dedication through the conceptualization of signs or the apprehension of anything as attainable. If one were to generate sympathetic joy or dedication within that process through the conceptualization of signs or the apprehension of anything as attainable, the Buddha would not say that such a person possesses great benefit or profit.
Why is this? Because such a mind of sympathetic joy and dedication is a false conceptualization, termed "mixed with poison.

It is like food that, though endowed with exquisite color, fragrance, and flavor, has been mixed with a poisonous drug. A foolish person of shallow understanding greedily takes it up and eats it; although it initially satisfies the senses with joy and pleasure, later, when the food is digested, one undergoes manifold sufferings, or even meets death, or nearly loses one's life.

"In this way, a certain class of individuals, having poorly grasped and poorly examined the words and meanings of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and having poorly recited it and poorly mastered its profound significance, says to those of the Mahāyāna lineage: 'Come!'"
"Noble son! Regarding all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present— from their first generation of the mind of awakening until they attained unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete enlightenment, and turned the sublime wheel of Dharma to deliver immeasurable multitudes— you [should likewise do so]."
From the time they enter the realm of nirvana without remainder until the extinction of the Dharma, whatever roots of virtue they have accumulated, will accumulate,
or are currently accumulating through the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity; and whatever [roots of virtue] they have accumulated, will accumulate,
or are currently accumulating while abiding in inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature— [all these they dedicate].

Roots of goodness: whether they are roots of goodness already accumulated, to be accumulated, or currently being accumulated through the cultivation of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;

or whether they are roots of goodness already accumulated, to be accumulated, or currently being accumulated through the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path; and so on, even up to the cultivation of the ten powers of a Buddha...
The roots of virtue already accumulated, to be accumulated, and currently being accumulated regarding the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
the roots of virtue already accumulated, to be accumulated, and currently being accumulated for the purification of buddha-fields and the maturation of sentient beings;
and all the aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, and wisdom belonging to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas—

The aggregate of liberation and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; whether it be all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);
whether it be the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣadharma*) or the state of constant equanimity (*upekṣā*); as well as other countless, immeasurable, and boundless sublime qualities;
and whatever roots of virtue, whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*), belong to the disciples of the Buddha.

If the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have already, are currently, or will in the future bestow predictions regarding all the merits of the Pratyekabuddha enlightenment for gods, humans, and others; and if there are gods,
nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and...
Regarding the roots of goodness already accumulated, yet to be accumulated, and currently being accumulated by non-humans and others—
if a son or daughter of good family should give rise to sympathetic joy toward all such merits and dedicate those roots of goodness,
then by thus gathering, weighing, and manifesting all these acts of sympathetic joy, they share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them to [unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment].
"to supreme perfect enlightenment.

Such a dedication of merit through sympathetic joy, which employs the means of conceptualizing with the grasping of signs and the notion of something to be attained, is like food mixed with poison—it benefits at first but harms later; therefore, this is not a wholesome dedication of merit through sympathetic joy.

Why is this? Because if one gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy and dedication that involves apprehension, grasping at signs, and conceptual discrimination, there will be causes, conditions, mental engagements, conceptual proliferations, obstructions, and faults; such a mind is not in accordance with the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Because it is mixed with poison, it constitutes a slander against the Buddha; it does not follow the Buddha’s teaching, it is not a discourse in accordance with the Dharma, and it is an unreasonable exposition. A person belonging to the bodhisattva lineage should not study according to what such a person says.
Therefore, O Venerable One!

You should explain how sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva Vehicle should rejoice in and dedicate the roots of virtue and merit of all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as well as their disciples, of the past, future, and present.

That is to say, from the time those Buddhas first resolved their minds toward enlightenment until they attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening; from their turning the sublime wheel of Dharma and delivering immeasurable multitudes, through their entry into the realm of nirvana without remainder and even until the extinction of the Dharma—in the interval between these events, whatever roots of goodness they cultivated, ranging from the perfection of wisdom down to the perfection of generosity; and further, up to the point where sons and daughters of good family give rise to sympathetic joy regarding those merits and dedicate those roots of goodness—how should sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle give rise to sympathetic joy regarding those merits and roots of goodness and dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening?
The Venerable Subhūti said: "O Great Being!

When sons and daughters of good family who abide in the vehicle of the bodhisattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, and if they wish to give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy and dedication without slandering the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, they should form this thought:"

"Just as the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, through their unsurpassed Buddha-wisdom, have fully realized and thoroughly known that these roots of goodness of merit possess such a nature, such characteristics, and such qualities that they may be rejoiced in, so too should I now rejoice in them."

Just as the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, with their unsurpassed Buddha-wisdom, have fully realized and thoroughly understood how these various meritorious deeds should be dedicated toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, so too shall I now dedicate them in this same way.

“Sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle should perform such rejoicing and dedication toward the roots of virtue and merits of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their disciples. If they perform such rejoicing and dedication, they do not slander the Buddha; they act according to the Buddha’s instructions, speak in accordance with the Dharma, and speak in accordance with reason.”
The mind of this bodhisattva-mahāsattva that thus rejoices and dedicates is not mixed with poisonous drugs; it will ultimately reach the ambrosia of great parinirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, Great Being!

Noble sons and noble daughters who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle and practice the perfection of wisdom should, regarding the roots of virtue and merits of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their disciples, perform such rejoicing and dedication.

Just as form, up to and including consciousness, does not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—if it does not fall within the three realms, then it is neither past, future, nor present;

the sense base of the eye, up to and including the sense base of the mind, does not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—if it does not fall within the three realms, then it is neither past, future, nor present;

the sense base of form, up to and including the sense base of mental phenomena, does not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—if it does not fall within the three realms, then it is neither past, future, nor present.

The eye-element, up to and including the mind-element, does not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; if they do not fall within the three realms, then they are neither past, future, nor present.

The form-element, up to and including the phenomena-element, does not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; if they do not fall within the three realms, then they are neither past, future, nor present.

The eye-consciousness-element, up to and including the mind-consciousness-element, does not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; if they do not fall within the three realms, then they are neither past, future, nor present.

Eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact, does not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; if they do not fall within the three realms, then they are neither past, future, nor present.

The various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; if they do not fall within the three realms, then they are neither past, future, nor present.

The perfection of wisdom, up to and including the perfection of generosity, does not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; if they do not fall within the three realms, then they are neither past, future, nor present.

From internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the nature of non-existence, these do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; if they do not fall within the three realms, then they are not of the past, future, or present.

The four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; if they do not fall within the three realms, then they are neither past, future, nor present.

Likewise, even the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; if they do not fall within the three realms, then they are neither past, future, nor present.

Suchness, the dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, the limit of reality, the fixed nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, and the inconceivable realm do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; if they do not fall within the three realms, then they are neither past, future, nor present.

The aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of meditative concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; if they do not fall within the three realms, then they are neither past, future, nor present.

Omniscience, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; if they do not fall within the three realms, then they are neither past, future, nor present.

The quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; if they do not fall within the three realms, then they are neither past, future, nor present.
“Rejoicing and dedication should also be understood in this way.

Why is that? Because those dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*), they do not fall within the three realms and are not subsumed by the three periods of time; rejoicing and dedication are likewise so.”
This means that because the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are empty of intrinsic nature, they do not fall within the three realms and are not subsumed by the three periods of time;
because the merits of the Buddhas are empty of intrinsic nature, they do not fall within the three realms and are not subsumed by the three periods of time;
and because Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, humans, devas, and so forth are empty of intrinsic nature, they do not fall within the three realms and are not subsumed by the three periods of time.
Because those roots of goodness are empty of intrinsic nature, they do not fall into the three realms and are not subsumed within the three periods of time;
because that sympathetic joy is empty of intrinsic nature, it does not fall into the three realms and is not subsumed within the three periods of time;
because the phenomena to which they are dedicated are empty of intrinsic nature, they do not fall into the three realms and are not subsumed within the three periods of time.
Because that which can dedicate [merit] is empty of intrinsic nature, it does not fall into the three realms and is not subsumed within the three times.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know form through to consciousness as they truly are; thus, they do not fall into the three realms and are not subsumed within the three times.

If one does not fall into the three realms and is not subsumed by the three periods of time, then one cannot employ the sign of existence as a means, nor employ the notion of something to be attained as a means, to generate sympathetic joy and dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Why is this? Because dharmas such as form are unarisen by their very nature; if a dharma is unarisen, it is non-existent, and one cannot rejoice in or dedicate that non-existent dharma toward a non-existent [result].
“Knowing the eye-base as it truly is, and so on up to the mind-base, likewise; knowing the form-base as it truly is, and so on up to the mental-object-base, likewise;
knowing the eye-element as it truly is, and so on up to the mind-element, likewise;
knowing the form-element as it truly is, and so on up to the mental-object-element, likewise; knowing the eye-consciousness-element as it truly is...”
It is the same for the realm of mental consciousness; one knows, as it truly is, eye-contact through to mind-contact, and likewise knows, as it truly is,
all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition through to all feelings produced with mind-contact as condition,
and likewise knows the perfection of wisdom through to the perfection of generosity.
The *pāramitā* is also like this; one knows inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the nature of non-existence as it truly is,
and likewise knows the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path as they truly are,
and likewise knows the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as they truly are.
Knowing suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the limit of reality, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, and the inconceivable realm is likewise;

knowing the aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation as they truly are is likewise; and knowing all-knowledge and the path as they truly are is likewise.

The knowledge of marks and the knowledge of all marks are likewise; they know, as it truly is, the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity, do not fall into the three realms, and are not subsumed within the three periods of time.

If one does not fall into the three realms and is not comprised within the three periods of time, then one cannot employ the sign of existence as a means, nor employ the attainment of something as a means, to generate sympathetic joy and dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Why is this? Because the nature of the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant abiding in equanimity are non-arising; if a dharma does not arise, it is non-existent. Since one cannot rejoice in a non-existent dharma and dedicate it toward a non-existent state, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva thus rejoices and dedicates toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, it is untainted by poison and ultimately leads to the ambrosia of great parinirvāṇa.

"If sons of good family or daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle should, by means of signs or by means of apprehension, give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy and dedication toward the roots of goodness and merits of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their disciples, you should know that this is a false sympathetic joy and dedication."
This mind of wrong sympathetic joy and dedication is not praised by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

Because such a mind of sympathetic joy and dedication is not praised by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, one cannot fulfill the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; nor can one fulfill inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature. Likewise, one cannot fulfill the four applications of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; and so on, up to and including the inability to fulfill the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. Furthermore, one cannot fulfill all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), nor can one fulfill the quality of never-forgetting and the state of constant equanimity.
Because their various merits are not perfected, they are unable to purify buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity.
Because they cannot purify buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity, they are unable to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Why is this? Because the rejoicing and dedication generated by them are characterized by signs, involve attainment, and are mixed with the poison of conceptualization.
"Furthermore, O Great Being!..."
When all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should form this thought:

"Just as all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas in the realms of the ten directions have realized the roots of virtue and meritorious qualities through their suchness, and there exists a dharma by which one may generate unerring sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) and dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), so too should I now, relying upon such a dharma, generate sympathetic joy and dedicate [the merit] toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. This is the correct arising of sympathetic joy and dedication; by means of this, one will certainly realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Venerable Subhūti, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"

"Subhūti! You have now performed for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that which is the work of a Buddha; that is to say, you have skillfully and unerringly taught the dedication of merit through sympathetic joy for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Such a teaching on the dedication of merit through sympathetic joy employs as its means the signless, the non-apprehendable, the unborn and undying, the unstained and unpurified, the absence of intrinsic nature and self-nature, emptiness of specific characteristics, emptiness of intrinsic nature, the dharma-realm, suchness, the nature of phenomena, the non-illusory nature, the limit of reality, and the inconceivable realm."

"Subhūti! Suppose all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were to achieve the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers. What do you think?"
"Would the merit of these sentient beings be great? Subhūti replied,
"It would be very great!"
“World-Honored One!
It is very much so! Sugata!”
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family give rise to unattached sympathetic joy and dedicate the roots of goodness of the merits of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as well as their disciples, the merit they obtain will be far greater than the former, beyond measure or calculation.”

Subhūti! This rejoicing and dedication generated by these sons and daughters of good family is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the most sublime, the most wondrous, the most exquisite, the highest, and the unsurpassed; it is peerless and equal to the unequaled.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were to attain the fruit of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha. If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to provide these individuals—from those at the stage of stream-entry up to those at the stage of pratyekabuddha—with as many kinds of clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other requisites as they could possibly require for the rest of their lives, and were to honor, revere, respect, and praise them—what do you think?"
"By this cause and condition, would these sons and daughters of good family acquire much merit? Subhūti replied, "Very much!"
"World-Honored One!
It is very much so! Sugata!"
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

If sons and daughters of good family give rise to unattached rejoicing and dedication toward the roots of goodness and merits of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their disciples, the merit they obtain is far greater than the former.”

"Subhūti! This rejoicing and dedication generated by these sons and daughters of good family is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the most sublime, the most wondrous, the most exquisite, the highest, and the unsurpassed—equal to the unequaled."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were to set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and suppose further that every single sentient being in as many worlds in the ten directions as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River were each to set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in those respective realms, and were each to present to every one of those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas immeasurable kinds of clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other superior and exquisite necessities of life, making offerings, honoring, respecting, and praising them for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges—what do you think?"
"Would these sentient beings, by reason of this cause and condition,
acquire much merit? Subhūti replied, "Very much!"
"O Bhagavān!
It is very much so! O Sugata!"
Such a mass of merit is incalculable, immeasurable, boundless, and limitless; it is difficult to fathom through calculation or analogy.
World-Honored One!
If this mass of merit possessed form and color, the worlds of the ten directions—each as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—would not be sufficient to contain it.
The Buddha said,
“Excellent, Subhūti! Well said!”
Excellent! The measure of that merit is just as you have described, Subhūti!

If good sons or good daughters, regarding the roots of virtue and merit of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their disciples, give rise to unattached sympathetic joy and dedicate them, the mass of merit they obtain will be far greater than the former.

"Subhūti! This rejoicing and dedication generated by these sons and daughters of good family is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the most sublime, the most wondrous, the most exquisite, the highest, and the unsurpassed—peerless and equal to the unequaled—compared to all other roots of virtue."

“Subhūti! If one were to compare that previous merit with this mass of merit, the former would not equal even a hundredth part of it; it would not equal even a thousandth part, nor even a *upaniṣad* part.”
Why is this? Subhūti!

It is because those sentient beings [practice] the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers, all by means of signs and the perception of something to be attained.

Those sons and daughters of good family who, with immeasurable kinds of clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other requisites, offer gifts to stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas, and who provide for them with worship, respect, honor, and praise for as long as their lives last—the mass of merit they obtain is all due to employing the means of having signs and the notion of apprehension.

Suppose those sentient beings were to offer various kinds of clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and all manner of necessities and supreme articles of pleasure to the bodhisattvas who have set out for unsurpassed enlightenment, doing so for as many great eons as there are sands in the Ganges River, making offerings, showing reverence, honoring, and praising them—all while employing the skillful means of conceptual signs and the notion of apprehending an object. The mass of merit obtained from such acts [is surpassed by that of one who practices the perfection of wisdom].
At that time, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, each with their retinue of twenty thousand devaputras, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and, with palms joined, addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are indeed able to initiate such vast sympathetic rejoicing and dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). That is to say, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, through skillful means—employing the means of signlessness (*animitta*), the means of non-apprehensibility (*anupalambha*), the means of non-attachment (*asaṅga*), and the means of non-conditioned activity (*anabhisaṃskāra*)—initiate genuine sympathetic rejoicing toward the roots of virtue and merit of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their disciples, dedicating them toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). Such sympathetic rejoicing and dedication that they initiate do not fall into either dualistic or non-dualistic dharmas; they are untainted and unattached.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devaputras, each holding various celestial and exquisite flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses, robes, necklaces, precious banners, pennants, canopies, and all manner of rare and wonderful treasures, played celestial music as an offering to the Buddha. Prostrating at his feet and joining their palms, they addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!

Those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are indeed able to initiate such vast sympathetic joy and dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). That is to say, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, through their skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), employing the means of signlessness (*animitta*), the means of non-apprehensibility (*anupalambha*), the means of non-attachment (*asaṅga*), and the means of non-conditioning (*anabhisaṃskāra*), generate correct sympathetic joy toward the roots of virtue and merit of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their disciples, and dedicate them toward unexcelled perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). This sympathetic joy and dedication thus initiated does not fall into either dualistic dharmas or non-dualistic dharmas; it is without defilement and without attachment.

At that time, the devaputra Suyāma, the devaputra Santuṣita, the devaputra Sunirmita, and the devaputra Vaśavartin, each accompanied by a retinue of a thousand devaputras, all bearing various celestial and exquisite flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses, robes, necklaces, jeweled banners, pennants, parasols, and other wonderful and rare treasures, played celestial music as an offering to the Buddha. They prostrated at his feet, joined their palms, and said:
“World-Honored One!

Those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are indeed able to initiate such vast sympathetic joy and dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). That is to say, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, through skillful means—employing the means of signlessness, the means of non-apprehension, the means of non-attachment, and the means of non-conditioning—initiate right sympathetic joy toward the roots of virtue and merit of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their disciples, dedicating them toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Such sympathetic joy and dedication as they initiate do not fall into either dualistic or non-dualistic dharmas; they are without defilement and without attachment.

At that time, the Great Brahmā King, together with an immeasurable multitude of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Brahmā deities, approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, joined their palms in reverence, and spoke with one voice:
"How rare! How extraordinary!"

"Bhagavān! Because those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are sustained and protected by the skillful means of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they surpass the roots of goodness cultivated by those sons and daughters of good family who lack skillful means, who dwell on signs, and who grasp at attainments."

At that time, the gods from the Ābhāsvara Heaven up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven each came before the Buddha with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of their own respective celestial hosts. They prostrated at his feet, joined their palms in reverence, and together cried out:
“How marvelous! How rare!”

"Bhagavān! Because those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are sustained by the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they surpass the roots of goodness cultivated by those sons and daughters of good family who previously lacked skillful means, who possessed signs (*nimitta*), and who engaged in apprehension (*upalambha*)."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the gods of the Four Great Kings up to those of the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, saying:
"Suppose all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were to each give rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and universally [venerate] all Tathāgatas,
Arhats, [and Samyaksaṃbuddhas] of the past, future, and present throughout the worlds of the ten directions."
From the initial generation of the mind of awakening until the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
from turning the sublime wheel of Dharma and delivering immeasurable multitudes, through entering the realm of nirvana without remainder until the extinction of the Dharma—
in the interval between these, all the roots of virtue associated with the perfections from generosity up to wisdom that were cultivated;
If they dwell in roots of goodness associated with inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;
if they cultivate roots of goodness associated with the four foundations of mindfulness, as extensively explained up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
if they cultivate roots of goodness associated with the immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas; or if they possess any roots of goodness belonging to the disciples, or any...

The aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation belonging to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, as well as all other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas; and whatever true Dharma has been taught by the Tathāgatas;
and whatever practice of the nature of generosity, the nature of ethical discipline, and the nature of cultivation is undertaken in reliance upon those dharmas.
Regarding the three bases of meritorious action: if one diligently practices and trains in those dharmas, one attains the fruit of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship;
one attains the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, or enters the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth.
Furthermore, if all sentient beings cultivate generosity, pure ethical discipline, patience, and diligence—
Having gathered and weighed together all such roots of goodness induced by meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and so forth,
one manifests sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) by means of signs, by means of apprehension, by means of attachment,
by means of volitional effort, and by means of duality and non-duality. Once [this has been done]...
Having rejoiced, they dedicate [the merit] toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
"There are sons of good family and daughters of good family who have set out for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
universally, toward all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present throughout the worlds of the ten directions..."
From the initial generation of the mind of awakening until the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
from turning the sublime wheel of Dharma and delivering immeasurable multitudes into the realm of nirvana without remainder, up until the extinction of the Dharma— in the interval between these,
all the roots of virtue associated with the perfections from generosity up to wisdom, as explained at length...
If all sentient beings cultivate the roots of goodness induced by generosity, pure ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—
if one were to collect and weigh all such things together, using the signless as a means,
non-apprehension as a means, non-attachment as a means, and non-conceptualization as a means—
Using skillful means and with the non-duality of duality as the means, they manifest sympathetic joy;
having thus rejoiced, they dedicate [the merit] toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

The rejoicing and dedication performed by these sons and daughters of good family is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the highest, the most wondrous, the most subtle, the foremost, the unsurpassed, the peerless, and the equal to the unequaled among all other roots of goodness; it is a hundred times superior, a thousand times superior, a hundred-thousand times superior, and even up to an *upaniṣad*-fold superior to the previous rejoicing and dedication of sentient beings.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

As the Buddha has taught, the rejoicing and dedication performed by these sons and daughters of good family is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the most sublime, the most wondrous, the most exquisite, the highest, and the unsurpassed—equal to the unequaled and peerless among all other roots of goodness.”

"Blessed One, to what extent is this rejoicing and dedication said to be the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the most exalted, the most sublime, the most exquisite, the highest, the unsurpassed, the peerless, and the equal to the unequaled among all other roots of goodness?"
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

These sons and daughters of good family universally regard all the roots of goodness of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and all other sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions—past, future, and present—neither grasping nor rejecting them, neither being conceited nor disparaging them; they do not perceive them as having anything attained, nor as having nothing attained. They realize that all phenomena are without arising and without ceasing, without defilement and without purity, without increase and without decrease, without going and without coming, without accumulation and without dispersal, and without entering and without exiting. They form this thought:”

"Just as the suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-illusory nature, the fixedness of dharmas, and the stability of dharmas of all those phenomena of the past, future, and present are, so too do I, by means of the skillful method of non-apprehension, give rise to right sympathetic joy toward all wholesome dharmas. Having given rise to sympathetic joy, I take these roots of goodness and, sharing them equally with all sentient beings, dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."

"Subhūti! To the extent that this bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to rejoicing and dedication, I declare that it is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the highest, the most sublime, the most exquisite, the superior, the unsurpassed, the peerless, and the equal to the unequaled, compared to all other roots of virtue."

"Subhūti! Such rejoicing and dedication surpasses other forms of rejoicing and dedication by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and even up to an *upaniṣad*-fold. Therefore, I say that this rejoicing and dedication thus generated is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the highest, the most sublime, the most subtle, the superior, the unsurpassed, the unequaled, and the equal to the unequaled, compared to all other roots of virtue."
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Those sons of good family and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle and wish [to know] all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past,
future, and present throughout the worlds of the ten directions, from their first generation of the mind..."
From the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, through turning the sublime wheel of Dharma and delivering immeasurable multitudes of beings,
until entering the realm of nirvana without remainder and even until the extinction of the Dharma— in this interval,
all the roots of virtue associated with the perfections from generosity up to wisdom, as well as the immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas, [are dedicated].
If one were to gather together, weigh, and bring before oneself all the roots of virtue and merit of the śrāvakas,
pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, as well as all the three types of meritorious actions— those consisting of giving, morality, and cultivation—
and all other roots of virtue belonging to other sentient beings, and were to then generate a mind of unerring sympathetic joy and dedication, one should...
He forms this thought:
"Form, up to consciousness, is equal to liberation; the eye-base, up to the mind-base, is equal to liberation;
the form-base, up to the phenomena-base, is equal to liberation; the eye-element, up to the mind-element, is equal to liberation."
Liberation and so forth: the form realm up to the dharma-realm are equal to liberation;
the eye-consciousness realm up to the mind-consciousness realm are equal to liberation; eye-contact up to mind-contact are equal to liberation;
and all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition up to all feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition are equal to liberation.
The perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom are equal to liberation;
internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature are equal to liberation;
the four applications of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path are equal to liberation; and so on, up to the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen [unique qualities].

The Buddha’s unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) are equal to liberation; the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīla-skandha*) up to the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana-skandha*) are equal to liberation;
the resolute confidence (*adhimukti*) arising toward all phenomena is equal to liberation;
and the Buddhas of the past, future, and present are equal to liberation, as are the phenomena of the past, future, and present, which are equal to liberation.
...all rejoicings are equal to liberation; all dedications are equal to liberation;
the ripening of the faculties of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and their disciples is equal to liberation;
the nirvāṇa attained by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and their disciples is equal to liberation; and the faculties of all pratyekabuddhas are [equal to liberation].
The transformation through ripening is equal to liberation; the nirvāṇa attained by all pratyekabuddhas is equal to liberation;
the dharma-nature of all dharmas belonging to the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas is equal to liberation;
and all sentient beings, as well as all dharmas and their dharma-nature, are equal to liberation.

Just as the nature of all phenomena is neither bound nor liberated, neither defiled nor pure, neither arising nor ceasing, neither born nor extinguished, and neither grasped nor relinquished, I rejoice in these roots of goodness and merit that are thus present. Holding these roots of goodness, I share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
In this way, rejoicing is not that which rejoices, because there is nothing to rejoice in.
In this way, dedication is not that which dedicates, because there is nothing to dedicate.
"The rejoicing and dedication thus generated neither proceeds nor ceases, because they are without arising or cessation. Subhūti!

This rejoicing and dedication of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is, compared to other rejoicings and dedications that have been generated, the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the most sublime, the most wondrous, the most exquisite, the highest, and the unsurpassed; it is peerless and equal to the unequaled.
"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such rejoicing and dedication, they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"

If good sons or good daughters who have set out upon the Mahāyāna were to, by means of conceptual signs and by means of apprehending objects, for as long as their lives last, constantly provide all kinds of clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other superior and exquisite articles of life to all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, along with their assemblies of disciples, throughout all the worlds in the ten directions—each as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—and honor, revere, respect, and praise them; yet, even so, [this would not equal the merit of another].

After those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, along with their assemblies of disciples, have entered parinirvāṇa, they collect their śarīras and construct high and vast stūpas made of the seven exquisite precious gems. Day and night, they diligently pay homage, prostrate, and circumambulate them to the right; furthermore, they offer worship, respect, reverence, and praise with various kinds of exquisite flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses, robes, necklaces, jeweled banners, pennants, canopies, rare and wonderful treasures, music, and lamps.

Furthermore, by employing the means of having signs and having something to be attained, they diligently cultivate generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, and other roots of virtue.

There are sons and daughters of good family who have set out in the Great Vehicle; they are able to employ the signless and the non-apprehendable as skillful means to cultivate roots of goodness associated with the perfections from generosity up to wisdom. Through skillful means, they correctly rejoice in all other roots of goodness and merit, and taking these roots of goodness, they share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

Because these sons and daughters of good family, by relying on the skillful means of the *prajñāpāramitā* for their sympathetic rejoicing and dedication, surpass the merit performed by the aforementioned sons and daughters of good family who have set out in the Mahāyāna by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and even up to an *upaniṣad*-fold; therefore, it is said that such sympathetic rejoicing and dedication are the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the highest, the most sublime, the most exquisite, the most superior, the unsurpassed, the peerless, and the equal to the unequaled among all other roots of virtue.

Therefore, Subhūti, bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have set out in the Great Vehicle should, by means of the signless and the non-apprehensible as their skillful method, diligently train in the roots of virtue associated with the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; and relying on the skillful means of the perfection of wisdom, they should generate right sympathetic joy toward the roots of virtue and qualities of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their disciples. Having generated sympathetic joy, they should hold these roots of virtue in common with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can, by means of the signless and the non-apprehendable, initiate such rejoicing and dedication, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and turn the sublime wheel of Dharma to benefit and bring happiness to all."

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 433. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Chapter 38: The Great Teacher, Part Two, Chapter Thirty-Eight: The Great Teacher. At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Thus, this perfection of wisdom is able to provide illumination because it is ultimately pure;
thus, this perfection of wisdom should be paid homage to because it is revered by gods and humans alike;
thus, this perfection of wisdom is without attachment because no worldly phenomena can defile it.
In this way, the *prajñāpāramitā* is free from all cataracts of the triple world, for it can eliminate the darkness of afflictions and all [wrong] views;
in this way, the *prajñāpāramitā* is the foremost, for it is most supreme among all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*);
in this way, the *prajñāpāramitā* can provide security, for it eternally severs all terrors, oppressions, and calamitous events.
In this way, the perfection of wisdom is able to bestow illumination, for it gathers in all sentient beings and enables them to attain the five eyes;
in this way, the perfection of wisdom is able to show the Middle Way, for it causes those who have lost their way to depart from the two extremes;
in this way, the perfection of wisdom is well able to give rise to the knowledge of all aspects, for it eternally severs the continuity of all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies.
Thus, this perfection of wisdom is the mother of all bodhisattva mahāsattvas, for all the Buddha-dharmas practiced by bodhisattvas arise from it;
thus, this perfection of wisdom is neither born nor extinguished, because its own-characteristic is empty;
thus, this perfection of wisdom is free from all birth and death, because it is neither permanent nor subject to destruction.
Thus, this Prajñāpāramitā can serve as a refuge, for it bestows the jewel of the True Dharma upon all sentient beings;
thus, this Prajñāpāramitā can bring to perfection the ten powers of a Tathāgata, for it is able to subdue all heterodox arguments;
thus, this Prajñāpāramitā can turn the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma with its three revolutions and twelve aspects, for it realizes that all phenomena are without turning or returning.
Thus, this Prajñāpāramitā can demonstrate the unerring intrinsic nature of all phenomena, because it clearly reveals the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.
World-Honored One,

how should those bodhisattvas who have set out on the bodhisattva vehicle, those śrāvakas who have set out on the śrāvaka vehicle, and those pratyekabuddhas who have set out on the pratyekabuddha vehicle abide in this Prajñāpāramitā?
The Buddha said: “Śāriputra!

These sentient beings dwelling in this Prajñāpāramitā should regard it as the Great Teacher; they should make offerings to and pay homage to this Prajñāpāramitā just as they would make offerings to and pay homage to the Great Teacher.”

Why is this? Śāriputra, the Great Teacher is not different from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and the perfection of wisdom is not different from the Great Teacher. The Great Teacher is itself the perfection of wisdom, and the perfection of wisdom is itself the Great Teacher.
Śāriputra! All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas appear by means of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Śāriputra!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, pratyekabuddhas, arhats, and even stream-enterers all appear by means of the perfection of wisdom.
Śāriputra! All the ten paths of wholesome action in the world appear by means of the perfection of wisdom. Śāriputra!
All four dhyānas, four immeasurables, four formless attainments, and five supernormal powers arise through the perfection of wisdom.
Śāriputra! All perfections, from the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, arise through the perfection of wisdom.

Śāriputra! All forms of emptiness, from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature; the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; and likewise, from the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and even up to all-aspect omniscience—all these appear by means of the perfection of wisdom.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, thought to himself:
"For what reason and by what cause does Śāriputra now ask the Buddha this question?
Having reflected thus, he addressed Śāriputra, saying:
“Venerable sir, what is the cause and condition for you to ask such a question now?
At that time, Śāriputra said to Śakra: “Kauśika!
Because they are sustained by this perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, through their skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*),
are able [to perceive] throughout the worlds of the ten directions— in the past, future, and present— all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas,
from their first generation of the mind of awakening until their attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and their turning of the wheel of Dharma...
From the time the sublime Wheel of Dharma was turned to deliver immeasurable multitudes until their entry into the realm of nirvana without remainder and even until the extinction of the Dharma—
whatever roots of merit and virtue existed during that interval, whether belonging to śrāvakas,
pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or other sentient beings— all such things can be, through [the power of] non-...
Taking signs and non-apprehension as skillful means, one gathers and weighs them, rejoicing in their presence;
having thus rejoiced, one dedicates this together with all sentient beings equally toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
It is for this reason that I ask about this matter.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
The perfection of wisdom studied by bodhisattva mahāsattvas surpasses the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration by immeasurable multiples."

Kauśika! Suppose there were a hundred, a thousand, or even many hundreds of thousands of those born blind, who, lacking one with pure vision to lead them, could not even approach the right path, much less reach a distant city, royal capital, or kingdom that is secure, prosperous, and blissful!

In this way, these groups of those born blind—consisting of the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration—if they lack the guidance of the pure eye of the perfection of wisdom, cannot even set out upon the correct path of a bodhisattva, let alone reach the distant city of omniscience!
"Furthermore, Kauśika! The five pāramitās, beginning with generosity, are designated as 'possessing eyes' because they are necessarily encompassed and guided by the prajñāpāramitā."
"Furthermore, because they are sustained by the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), these five also receive the name 'reaching the other shore' (*pāramitā*).
Then, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed the Venerable Śāriputra:

"Venerable sir, as you have said that the five perfections, such as generosity and the rest, must be sustained by the perfection of wisdom to be called 'reaching the other shore,' should it not rather be said that the other five receive the name 'reaching the other shore' because they are sustained by the perfections from generosity up to meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*)?"
"If that is so, for what reason do you alone praise the Prajñāpāramitā? Śāriputra replied: "It is so!"
It is so! It is as you have said.

Although the six perfections, such as generosity and the rest, mutually support one another to reach the further shore, it is by abiding in the perfection of wisdom that one possesses great power and skillful means, thereby being able to swiftly fulfill the practiced perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration. Abiding in the first five cannot accomplish this task; therefore, among the previous five, the perfection of wisdom is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most noble, the most sublime, the most refined, the highest, the unsurpassed, the peerless, and the equal to the unequaled.
"For this reason and by these causes and conditions, the Perfection of Wisdom alone is praised as surpassing the other five perfections.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How should the bodhisattva mahāsattvas bring forth the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha said, "Śāriputra!"
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should not cultivate the perfection of wisdom for the sake of producing form through to consciousness;
they should not cultivate the perfection of wisdom for the sake of producing the eye-base through to the mind-base;
they should not cultivate the perfection of wisdom for the sake of producing the form-base through to the phenomena-base.
One should not cultivate the perfection of wisdom for the sake of producing the eye element up to the mind element;
one should not cultivate the perfection of wisdom for the sake of producing the form element up to the phenomena element;
one should not cultivate the perfection of wisdom for the sake of producing the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element.
One should not cultivate the perfection of wisdom for the sake of producing eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact;

one should not cultivate the perfection of wisdom for the sake of producing the various feelings born with eye-contact as condition, up to and including the various feelings born with mind-contact as condition;
one should not cultivate the perfection of wisdom for the sake of producing the perfection of generosity, up to and including the perfection of wisdom.
One should not cultivate the perfection of wisdom for the sake of producing the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;
one should not cultivate the perfection of wisdom for the sake of producing the four applications of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
and likewise, one should not cultivate the perfection of wisdom for the sake of producing the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
One should not cultivate the perfection of wisdom for the sake of bringing forth omniscience, the knowledge of the paths, or the knowledge of all aspects;
one should not cultivate the perfection of wisdom for the sake of bringing forth any phenomena.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how should bodhisattva-mahāsattvas bring forth the perfection of wisdom so as not to bring forth form, nor even all dharmas?”
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!

Because form and all phenomena up to the ultimate are without activity, without arising, without attainment, without destruction, and without intrinsic nature, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of producing form and all phenomena up to the ultimate.”
Then, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
With what phenomena do the bodhisattva mahāsattvas thus bring forth the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) in conjunction?”
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas thus bring forth the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do not conjoin it with any phenomena. Because they do not conjoin it, it is named ‘perfection of wisdom.’”
Śāriputra asked: "With what dharmas is this Prajñāpāramitā not conjoined?
The Blessed One replied:
"In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not conjoin with wholesome dharmas, nor does it conjoin with unwholesome dharmas;
it does not conjoin with mundane dharmas, nor does it conjoin with supramundane dharmas;
it does not conjoin with out-flowing dharmas, nor does it conjoin with out-flow-free dharmas."
It does not associate with dharmas that are subject to fault, nor does it associate with dharmas that are free from fault;
it does not associate with conditioned dharmas, nor does it associate with unconditioned dharmas. Why is this?
Śāriputra! Because this prajñāpāramitā finds nothing to be apprehended in any phenomena, it cannot be said to be conjoined with such phenomena.
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Does this Prajñāpāramitā likewise not accord with the knowledge of all aspects?”
The Buddha said:
"Kauśika, it is so! It is thus!"
So it is! It is as you have said.
Likewise, this perfection of wisdom does not conjoin with the knowledge of all aspects, because therein nothing is apprehended.
“World-Honored One!
How is it that the perfection of wisdom neither joins with nor attains the knowledge of all aspects?
“Kauśika! [the Buddha replied.]
"Bhagavān, it is not the case that the perfection of wisdom, in relation to the knowledge of all aspects, has a union or an attainment [with it] as it does with names, signs, or its own activities."
"How can it be said that the perfection of wisdom has both union and attainment with respect to the knowledge of all aspects? Kausika!

Because the perfection of wisdom, with respect to the knowledge of all aspects, is like names and signs—without receiving or grasping, without abiding or ceasing, and without clinging or relinquishing—it is thus united and attained, yet there is no union or attainment."

Kauśika! Thus, this prajñāpāramitā regarding all dharmas is like their names and characteristics: it is without receiving or grasping, without abiding or ceasing, and without clinging or relinquishing; it is thus attained through union, yet there is no attaining through union.
Then, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How extraordinary!
World-Honored One!”

Thus, because all phenomena are without arising or ceasing, without action or accomplishment, without attainment or destruction, and without intrinsic nature, this Prajñāpāramitā manifests before one. Although there is union and attainment, there is no union and no attainment; such a principle is inconceivable.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, gives rise to such a conception as this:”
"If this *prajñāpāramitā* is conjoined with all phenomena,
or not conjoined with all phenomena," then that bodhisattva-mahāsattva has abandoned both the *prajñāpāramitā* and is far removed from the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

There is another cause and condition by which bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abandon and distance themselves from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā): namely, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they give rise to such a conceptualization:”
"Thus, this prajñāpāramitā is non-existent, unreal, insubstantial, and lacks self-mastery.
In this way, that bodhisattva mahāsattva abandons and distances himself from the prajñāpāramitā.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva has faith in the perfection of wisdom, in what dharmas does he lack faith?”
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva has faith in the perfection of wisdom, they do not have faith in form; they do not have faith in feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness.”
They do not believe in the sense-base of the eye; they do not believe in the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
They do not believe in the sense-base of forms; they do not believe in the sense-bases of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena.
They do not believe in the eye-element; they do not believe in the elements of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
They do not believe in the realm of form; they do not believe in the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena.
They do not believe in the realm of eye-consciousness; they do not believe in the realms of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness.
They do not believe in eye-contact; they do not believe in ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact.

They do not have faith in the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition; they do not have faith in the various feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as conditions.
They do not have faith in the perfection of generosity; they do not have faith in the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration.

They do not have faith in internal emptiness; they do not have faith in external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, beginningless-and-endless emptiness, non-dispersal-and-non-dispersion emptiness, essential nature emptiness, the emptiness of self-characteristics and common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.

They lack faith in the four foundations of mindfulness; they lack faith in the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;

and so on, up to lacking faith in the ten powers of a Buddha, lacking faith in the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they lack faith in the fruit of stream-entry, and lack faith in the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship.
They do not believe in the awakening of a solitary buddha;
they do not believe in the practices of any bodhisattva mahāsattvas, nor do they believe in the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening of all buddhas;
they do not believe in omniscience, nor do they believe in the knowledge of the paths or the knowledge of all aspects.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva has faith in the perfection of wisdom, why is it that they do not have faith in form, and so on, up to and including not having faith in the knowledge of all aspects?"
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), because they observe that all form (rūpa) is unapprehendable, although they have faith in the perfection of wisdom, they do not have faith in form; and so on, in detail, until: because they observe that all-knowledge of aspects (sarvākārajñatā) is unapprehendable, although they have faith in the perfection of wisdom, they do not have faith in all-knowledge of aspects.”

Therefore, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas place their faith in the perfection of wisdom, they do not place their faith in form, and so on, up to and including not placing their faith in the knowledge of all aspects.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the Great Pāramitā.”
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
Based on what intention do you speak thus?”
