"In this way, is this perfection of wisdom the great perfection? Subhūti replied,
"World-Honored One!"
By means of this perfection of wisdom, one does not make form, up to consciousness, great or small;
one does not make the eye-base, up to the mind-base, great or small; one does not make the form-base, up to the phenomena-base, great or small;
one does not make the eye-element, up to the mind-element, great or small.
One does not conceive of them as small regarding the realm of form up to the realm of phenomena;
one does not conceive of them as great or small regarding the realm of eye-consciousness up to the realm of mind-consciousness;

one does not conceive of them as great or small regarding eye-contact up to mind-contact; nor regarding the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to those produced with mind-contact.
One does not regard the various feelings born of conditions as great or small; one does not regard the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom as great or small;
one does not regard inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature as great or small;
and one does not regard the four applications of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path...

One does not conceive of the factors of the path as great or small; likewise, one does not conceive of anything up to the ten powers of a Buddha or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as great or small;
one does not conceive of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha as great or small; and one does not conceive of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as great.
"It is not small,
World-Honored One!
It is for this reason that I say the Prajñāpāramitā is the Great Pāramitā."
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

By means of this prajñāpāramitā, one neither accumulates nor disperses form; one neither accumulates nor disperses feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. In this way, up to and including the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, one neither accumulates nor disperses it; regarding all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, one neither accumulates nor disperses them."
“World-Honored One!
It is for this reason that I say the *prajñāpāramitā* is the great *pāramitā*.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!”

By means of this perfection of wisdom, one does not take form as a measure nor as a non-measure; one does not take feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as a measure nor as a non-measure. In this way, it extends even to not taking unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment as a measure nor as a non-measure, and not taking the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as a measure nor as a non-measure.
“World-Honored One!
It is for this reason that I say the *prajñāpāramitā* is the great *pāramitā*.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!”

By means of this perfection of wisdom, one neither expands nor contracts form; one neither expands nor contracts feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. In this way, up to and including unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, one neither expands nor contracts it; and regarding the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, one neither expands nor contracts them.
"Bhagavān! It is for this reason that I say the Prajñāpāramitā is the Great Pāramitā.
Furthermore, Bhagavān!"

By means of this perfection of wisdom, one does not strengthen or weaken form; one does not strengthen or weaken feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. In this way, it extends even to not strengthening or weakening the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha, nor strengthening or weakening the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
"World-Honored One!
It is for this reason that, based on my understanding, I say that the Prajñāpāramitā is the Great Pāramitā.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has newly set out in the Great Vehicle relies upon the perfection of wisdom and so forth, up to the perfection of generosity, and gives rise to this thought:

"This perfection of wisdom does not make form great or small; it does not make feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness great or small; and so on, up to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha, which it does not make great or small; nor does it make the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas great or small."

In this way, the perfection of wisdom neither accumulates nor disperses form; it neither accumulates nor disperses feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; and so on, up to not accumulating or dispersing the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha, nor accumulating or dispersing the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not establish a measure for form, nor does it establish a non-measure; it does not establish a measure for feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does it establish a non-measure. This extends even to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha, for which it establishes neither a measure nor a non-measure, and likewise for all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, for whom it establishes neither a measure nor a non-measure.

In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not make form broad or narrow; it does not make feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness broad or narrow; and so on, up to not making unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment broad or narrow, nor does it make the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas broad or narrow.

In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not strengthen or weaken form; it does not strengthen or weaken feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; and so on, up to not strengthening or weakening the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha, nor does it strengthen or weaken the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
"World-Honored One!
Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a notion, they are not practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has newly set out in the Great Vehicle relies upon the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity, and gives rise to such a thought as this:

"This perfection of wisdom makes form great or small; it also makes feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness great or small; even unto the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha, it makes them great or small; and even unto the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, it makes them great or small."

In this way, the perfection of wisdom performs both aggregation and dispersion regarding form; it likewise performs both aggregation and dispersion regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; and so on, up to performing both aggregation and dispersion regarding the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha, and even performing both aggregation and dispersion regarding all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

In this way, the perfection of wisdom establishes measure and non-measure regarding form; it likewise establishes measure and non-measure regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; and so on, up to establishing measure and non-measure regarding the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha, as well as establishing measure and non-measure regarding all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

In this way, this perfection of wisdom makes form broad or narrow; it also makes feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness broad or narrow; and so on, up to making unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment broad or narrow, and even making the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas broad or narrow.

In this way, the perfection of wisdom renders form strong or weak; it likewise renders feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness strong or weak; and so on, up to rendering the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha strong or weak, and even rendering the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas strong or weak.
"World-Honored One!
Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a notion, they are not practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has newly set out in the Great Vehicle does not rely on the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity, and gives rise to such a thought as this:

"This perfection of wisdom does not make form great or small; it does not make feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness great or small; and so on, up to: it does not make unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment great or small; nor does it make the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas great or small."

In this way, the perfection of wisdom neither accumulates nor disperses form; it neither accumulates nor disperses feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; and so on, up to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha, which it neither accumulates nor disperses; nor does it neither accumulate nor disperse the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not establish a measure for form, nor does it establish a non-measure; it does not establish a measure for feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does it establish a non-measure. This extends even to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha, for which it establishes neither a measure nor a non-measure, and likewise to all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, for whom it establishes neither a measure nor a non-measure.

In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not make form broad nor narrow; it does not make feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness broad nor narrow; and so on, up to not making unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment broad nor narrow, nor making the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas broad nor narrow.

In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not strengthen or weaken form; it does not strengthen or weaken feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; and so on, up to not strengthening or weakening the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha, nor strengthening or weakening the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
"World-Honored One!
Because this bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives rise to such a notion, they are not practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has newly set out in the Great Vehicle does not rely on the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity, but gives rise to such a thought as this:

"This perfection of wisdom makes form great or small; it also makes feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness great or small; even up to making the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha great or small; and it also makes the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas great or small."

In this way, the perfection of wisdom performs both accumulation and dispersal with respect to form; it performs both accumulation and dispersal with respect to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; and so on, up to performing both accumulation and dispersal with respect to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha, and even performing both accumulation and dispersal with respect to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

In this way, the perfection of wisdom acts as a measure and as a non-measure with respect to form; it likewise acts as a measure and as a non-measure with respect to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; and so on, up to acting as a measure and as a non-measure with respect to the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and even with respect to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

In this way, this perfection of wisdom makes form broad or narrow; it also makes feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness broad or narrow; and so on, up to making unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment broad or narrow, and even making the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas broad or narrow.

In this way, the perfection of wisdom renders form strong or weak; it likewise renders feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness strong or weak; even up to rendering the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha strong or weak, and it also renders the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas strong or weak.
"World-Honored One!
Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a conception, he is not practicing the perfection of wisdom. Why is this?"
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought:

‘This prajñāpāramitā makes form large or small, or does not make it large or small; it makes feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness large or small, or does not make them large or small; and so on, up to making the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha large or small, or not making it large or small; and making the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas large or small, or not making them large or small.’”

In this way, the perfection of wisdom, whether it conceives of form as being accumulated or dispersed, or does not conceive of it as being accumulated or dispersed; whether it conceives of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as being accumulated or dispersed, or does not conceive of them as being accumulated or dispersed; even unto whether it conceives of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha as being accumulated or dispersed, or does not conceive of it as being accumulated or dispersed; and whether it conceives of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as being accumulated or dispersed, or does not conceive of them as being accumulated or dispersed.

In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not treat form as a measure or a non-measure, nor does it fail to treat it as a measure or a non-measure; it does not treat feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as a measure or a non-measure, nor does it fail to treat them as a measure or a non-measure; and so on, up to the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, which it does not treat as a measure or a non-measure, nor does it fail to treat it as a measure or a non-measure; and it does not treat the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as measures or non-measures, nor does it fail to treat them as measures or non-measures.

In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not make form broad or narrow, nor does it fail to make it broad or narrow; it does not make feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness broad or narrow, nor does it fail to make them broad or narrow; and so on, up to making the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha broad or narrow, or failing to make it broad or narrow; and making the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas broad or narrow, or failing to make them broad or narrow.

In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not treat form as strong or weak, nor does it treat it as not strong or weak; it does not treat feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as strong or weak, nor does it treat them as not strong or weak; and so on, up to the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha, which it does not treat as strong or weak, nor does it treat it as not strong or weak; and it does not treat the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as strong or weak, nor does it treat them as not strong or weak.
"World-Honored One!
All such things as these are not the outflow fruits of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
World-Honored One!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought as this:

"This prajñāpāramitā makes form large or small, or does not make it large or small; it makes feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness large or small, or does not make them large or small; even unto making the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha large or small, or not making it large or small; and making all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas large or small, or not making them large or small."

In this way, the perfection of wisdom, whether it treats form as a collection or a dispersion, or does not treat it as a collection or a dispersion; whether it treats feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as a collection or a dispersion, or does not treat them as a collection or a dispersion; even unto whether it treats the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha as a collection or a dispersion, or does not treat it as a collection or a dispersion; and whether it treats the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as a collection or a dispersion, or does not treat them as a collection or a dispersion.

In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not treat form as either finite or infinite, nor does it treat it as neither finite nor infinite; it does not treat feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either finite or infinite, nor does it treat them as neither finite nor infinite; and so on, up to not treating the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha as either finite or infinite, nor treating the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as either finite or infinite, nor treating them as neither finite nor infinite.

In this way, the perfection of wisdom neither expands nor contracts with respect to form; it neither expands nor contracts with respect to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; and so on, up to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha, which it neither expands nor contracts; and with respect to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, it neither expands nor contracts.

In this way, the perfection of wisdom, whether it treats form as strong or weak, or does not treat it as strong or weak; whether it treats feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as strong or weak, or does not treat them as strong or weak; even unto whether it treats the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha as strong or weak, or does not treat it as strong or weak; and whether it treats the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as strong or weak, or does not treat them as strong or weak.

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva is said to have 'great attainment' and is not practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Why is this?"
It is because one cannot realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through the notion of something to be attained. Why is this?

Because sentient beings are unarisen, one should contemplate that the perfection of wisdom is also unarisen;
because form is unarisen, one should contemplate that the perfection of wisdom is also unarisen;
because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unarisen, one should contemplate that the perfection of wisdom is also unarisen.

In this way, up to and including the fact that the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is non-arising, one should contemplate that the perfection of wisdom is also non-arising;
because all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are non-arising, one should contemplate that the perfection of wisdom is also non-arising.
“World-Honored One!
Because sentient beings lack intrinsic nature, one should observe that the perfection of wisdom also lacks intrinsic nature;
because form lacks intrinsic nature, one should observe that the perfection of wisdom also lacks intrinsic nature.”
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness lack intrinsic nature, one should contemplate that the perfection of wisdom also lacks intrinsic nature;

likewise, up to and including the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas, because it lacks intrinsic nature, one should contemplate that the perfection of wisdom also lacks intrinsic nature;
and because all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas lack intrinsic nature, one should contemplate that the perfection of wisdom also lacks intrinsic nature.
“Bhagavān, because sentient beings do not exist, one should contemplate that the perfection of wisdom also does not exist;
because form does not exist, one should contemplate that the perfection of wisdom also does not exist.”
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-existent, one should contemplate that the perfection of wisdom is also non-existent;
likewise, up to and including because the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is non-existent, one should contemplate that the perfection of wisdom is also non-existent;
because all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are non-existent, one should contemplate that the perfection of wisdom is also non-existent.
“Bhagavān! Because sentient beings are empty, one should contemplate that the perfection of wisdom is also empty;
because form is empty, one should contemplate that the perfection of wisdom is also empty.”
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, one should contemplate that the perfection of wisdom is also empty;
likewise, up to and including because the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is empty, one should contemplate that the perfection of wisdom is also empty;
because all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are empty, one should contemplate that the perfection of wisdom is also empty.
“Bhagavān! Because sentient beings are detached, one should contemplate that the perfection of wisdom is also detached;
because form is detached, one should contemplate that the perfection of wisdom is also detached.”
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are detached, one should contemplate that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also detached;
likewise, up to and including the fact that the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is detached, one should contemplate that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also detached;
because all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are detached, one should contemplate that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also detached.
“World-Honored One!
Because sentient beings cannot be apprehended, one should contemplate that the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) also cannot be apprehended;
because form (rūpa) cannot be apprehended, one should contemplate that the perfection of wisdom also cannot be apprehended.”
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unapprehendable, one should contemplate that the perfection of wisdom is likewise unapprehendable;
and so on, up to because the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is unapprehendable, one should contemplate that the perfection of wisdom is likewise unapprehendable;
and because all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are unapprehendable, one should contemplate that the perfection of wisdom is likewise unapprehendable.
“World-Honored One!
Because sentient beings are inconceivable, one should regard the perfection of wisdom as also inconceivable;
because form is inconceivable, one should regard the perfection of wisdom as also inconceivable.”
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are inconceivable, one should contemplate that the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is also inconceivable;
likewise, up to and including because the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is inconceivable, one should contemplate that the perfection of wisdom is also inconceivable;
and because all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are inconceivable, one should contemplate that the perfection of wisdom is also inconceivable.
“World-Honored One!
Because sentient beings are without destruction, one should contemplate that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also without destruction;
because form (*rūpa*) is without destruction, one should contemplate that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also without destruction.”
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are indestructible, one should contemplate that the perfection of wisdom is also indestructible;

likewise, up to and including the fact that the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is indestructible, one should contemplate that the perfection of wisdom is also indestructible;
because all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are indestructible, one should contemplate that the perfection of wisdom is also indestructible.
“Bhagavān! Because sentient beings lack sentience, one should contemplate that the prajñāpāramitā also lacks sentience;
because form lacks sentience, one should contemplate that the prajñāpāramitā also lacks sentience.”
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are devoid of cognition, one should contemplate that the *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise devoid of cognition;

and so on, up to the point that because the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is devoid of cognition, one should contemplate that the *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise devoid of cognition;
and because all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are devoid of cognition, one should contemplate that the *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise devoid of cognition.
“Blessed One! Because the power of sentient beings is unestablished, one should contemplate that the perfection of wisdom is also unestablished in power;
because the power of form is unestablished, one should contemplate that the perfection of wisdom is also unestablished in power.”

Because the power of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is not established, one should contemplate that the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is also not established as a power;

likewise, up to and including the power of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) of all Buddhas being not established, one should contemplate that the perfection of wisdom is also not established as a power;
because the power of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas is not established, one should contemplate that the perfection of wisdom is also not established as a power.

It is for this reason that I say the *prajñāpāramitā* of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is the great *pāramitā*.
Chapter 39: Hell (Part 2), Section 1 of Chapter 39: Hell. At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to have faith and resolve in this *prajñāpāramitā*, from where did that bodhisattva mahāsattva pass away to come and be born here?”
How long has it been since you set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
How many Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have you personally served and made offerings to?
And how long has it been since you have practiced the perfections, from generosity up to wisdom?
"How does one believe and resolve upon such profound meaning and intent of this Prajñāpāramitā?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to believe and resolve upon this Prajñāpāramitā, that bodhisattva mahāsattva has passed away from the assemblies of immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions, and has come to be born here."

This bodhisattva mahāsattva has set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, having already passed through immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva has already drawn near to, served, and made offerings to immeasurable, innumerable, boundless, inconceivable, and unfathomable Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

From the first moment they resolve their mind [on enlightenment], these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constantly and diligently practice the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, having already passed through immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas.
Śāriputra! When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas see or hear this Prajñāpāramitā, they form this thought:
"I am seeing the Great Teacher; I am hearing the Great Teacher’s teaching."

"Śāriputra! By means of the skillful means of signlessness, non-duality, and non-apprehension, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to correctly believe in and understand the profound meaning and intent of this Prajñāpāramitā."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
it is as the Buddha has said."
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva sees or hears this Prajñāpāramitā, they form this thought:
"I see the Great Teacher; I hear the Great Teacher's teaching."
“World-Honored One!
Is there anyone who can hear or see this profound Prajñāpāramitā?
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! In the profound perfection of wisdom, there is truly no one who can hear or see it. Why is this?
Subhūti! This profound *prajñāpāramitā* is truly not a dharma that can be heard or seen. Subhūti!

The *prajñāpāramitā* is neither seen nor heard because all phenomena are insentient; even the *dānapāramitā* is neither seen nor heard because all phenomena are insentient. Internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) is neither seen nor heard because all phenomena are insentient;
even the emptiness of non-existence and intrinsic nature (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*) is neither seen nor heard because all phenomena are insentient.

The four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are neither seen nor heard because all phenomena are insentient; even the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) is neither seen nor heard because all phenomena are insentient.

In this way, up to and including the ten powers of the Tathāgata, they are neither seen nor heard because all phenomena are insentient; up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, they are neither seen nor heard because all phenomena are insentient;

the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas is neither seen nor heard because all phenomena are insentient; and all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are neither seen nor heard because all phenomena are insentient.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
for how long have the bodhisattva mahāsattvas already accumulated practice in order to be able to study and cultivate this profound prajñāpāramitā?”
The Buddha said, “Subhūti! Regarding this matter,
one should explain it by means of differentiation.”

"Subhūti! There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, from the very first production of the thought of awakening, are able to practice and train in the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and are likewise able to practice and train in the perfections of meditative concentration (dhyāna), diligence (vīrya), patience (kṣānti), ethical discipline (śīla), and generosity (dāna)."
Subhūti! Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess skillful means, they do not destroy any phenomena, nor do they perceive any phenomena as increasing or decreasing.

They never depart from the correct practice associated with the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, and they never depart from the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and the assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.

Traveling from one buddha-field to another, they are able to provide, according to their wishes, all manner of supreme and exquisite offerings to honor, revere, respect, and praise the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, as well as the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; furthermore, they are able to plant roots of goodness under those Tathāgatas so that they may quickly reach fulfillment.
Wherever this bodhisattva-mahāsattva receives a body, he is not born from within a mother’s womb;
his mind never dwells in association with afflictions, nor does he ever give rise to the mind of the two vehicles.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva is never separated from sublime supernormal powers, traveling from one buddha-field to another to bring sentient beings to maturity and to adorn and purify buddha-fields.
"Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to correctly practice and study the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
[From] the Great *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Fascicle 434, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Second Division, Chapter on the Hells, Part 39-2: 'Subhūti!'"

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, although they have previously seen a hundred, a thousand, or many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, and have extensively practiced generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom under those Buddhas and their disciples, are nevertheless unable to train in the profound perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity because they employ the method of grasping at attainments.
"Subhūti! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva hears such an exposition of the profound perfection of wisdom, they immediately rises from their seat and departs from the assembly."

"Subhūti! Such a bodhisattva mahāsattva who treats this profound perfection of wisdom with contempt also treats the Buddha with contempt; having abandoned this profound perfection of wisdom, they have also abandoned all Buddhas."
"Subhūti! There are also those of such a kind within this assembly who, upon hearing me proclaim the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, do not find it pleasing and depart from the assembly."

Why is this? Because these sons and daughters of good family, having previously heard the teaching of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and yet departed, now hear this *prajñāpāramitā* being taught and, due to the force of their past habituation, depart once again.

“Subhūti! These sons of good family and daughters of good family, being physically, verbally, and mentally discordant with this profound *prajñāpāramitā* as it has been taught, thereby create and increase sinful karma born of ignorance and impaired wisdom.”

Because they have committed and accumulated sinful karma through their delusion and impaired wisdom, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, they immediately slander, obstruct, and abandon it.
Since they thus slander, obstruct, and abandon this *prajñāpāramitā*, they thereby slander, obstruct, and abandon the omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.

By slandering, obstructing, and abandoning the omniscience of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, they thereby create and increase the karma that leads to the deprivation of the true Dharma.

By having performed and accumulated karma that leads to the deprivation of the True Dharma, they fall into the great hells and remain there for many years—whether for many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, many hundreds of thousands of years, many koṭis of years, many hundreds of koṭis of years, many thousands of koṭis of years, many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of years, or even many hundreds of thousands of koṭi-nayutas of years—experiencing within those great hells various agonizing and intense sufferings.

Because their offenses are grave, they shall pass from one great hell to another within this world until the kalpas of fire, water, and wind have yet to arise, undergoing all manner of agonizing and intensely piercing great suffering.

If, when the fire, water, or wind kalpas arise in this world, because their karma of depleting the Dharma is not yet exhausted, they die and are reborn in a similar great hell in another world, where they undergo various agonizing and intense sufferings within that great hell for many years—whether many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, or even many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of years.

Because their offenses are grave, they travel from one great hell to another in other worlds, undergoing various forms of agonizing and intense suffering until the kalpas of fire, water, and wind have not yet arisen.

If the fire, water, or wind kalpas arise in other worlds, because their karma of depriving others of the Dharma is not yet exhausted, they die and are reborn in a similar great hell in another direction, where they undergo various agonizing and intense sufferings for many years—whether many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, or even many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of years—within that great hell.

Because their offenses are so grave, they pass from one great hell to another in other worlds, undergoing various agonizing and intense sufferings until the fires, waters, and winds of the kalpa-ending calamities have not yet arisen.
In this manner, they successively travel through all other worlds throughout the ten directions, undergoing various forms of agonizing and intense great suffering within the great hells.

Even when the fire, water, and wind kalpas arise in those other worlds of the ten directions, because their karma of obstructing the Dharma remains未尽 (unexhausted), after dying there they are reborn again in the great hells of this world. From one great hell to another great hell, until the fire, water, and wind kalpas have arisen, they continue to undergo various forms of agonizing and intense great suffering.

If the fire, water, or wind kalpas arise in this world, because their karma of deprivation of the Dharma is not yet exhausted, they die here and are reborn in other worlds; they pass through the great hells throughout the ten directions, undergoing various agonizing and intense sufferings of bitter torment.

Thus they wander in saṃsāra for immeasurable kalpas; when the force of their karmic offenses of depriving others of the Dharma has somewhat diminished, they emerge from the hells and fall into the animal realm, where for many years—whether many hundreds, many thousands, or even many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of years—they take on animal bodies and undergo various sufferings such as being slaughtered, harmed, and threatened.

Because their offenses are not yet exhausted, they shall pass from one perilous and evil place to another within this world; until the kalpas of fire, water, and wind have arisen, they will undergo all manner of suffering, including being slaughtered and threatened.

If, at the time this world is destroyed by the three calamities, the residual force of their karma of depriving others of the Dharma has not yet been exhausted, after they die they will be reborn in other worlds among the animal realm (tiryagyoni) of a similar kind, where for many years—whether many hundreds, many thousands, or even many hundreds of thousands of koṭi-nayuta years—they undergo the bodies of animals and suffer the pains of being slaughtered, harmed, and terrified.

Because their transgressions are not yet exhausted, they pass from one perilous and evil place to another within other worlds; until the kalpas of fire, water, and wind have arisen, they undergo all manner of suffering, including being mangled and threatened.

If, at the time when the three calamities destroy other worlds, the residual force of their karma of lacking the Dharma has not yet been exhausted, they die and are reborn in other worlds of a similar kind within the animal realm (*tiryagyoni*), where for many years—whether many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, or even many hundreds of thousands of *koṭi-nayuta* years—they undergo the bodies of animals and suffer the torments of being slaughtered, harmed, and terrified.

Because their offenses are not yet exhausted, they wander from one perilous and evil place to another in other worlds; until the fire, water, and wind kalpas have arisen, they undergo all manner of suffering, including being mangled and threatened.

In this manner, they successively travel through all other worlds throughout the ten directions, taking birth in the bodies of animals and undergoing various sufferings such as being slaughtered, harmed, and threatened.

When those other worlds in the ten directions are destroyed by the three calamities, because the residual force of their karma of depriving others of the Dharma has not yet been exhausted, they die and are reborn here in this world within the realm of animals. From one perilous and evil place to another perilous and evil place, until the kalpas of fire, water, and wind have not yet arisen, they undergo all manner of sufferings such as being slaughtered, harmed, and threatened.

If, when this world is destroyed by the three calamities, the residual force of their karma of obstructing the Dharma has not yet been exhausted, they die and are reborn again in other worlds throughout the ten directions among the realms of animals, where they undergo manifold sufferings.

Thus they circulate in this manner for immeasurable eons; eventually, the force of their karmic offenses from the sin of withholding the Dharma gradually thins, and they escape the realm of animals to fall into the realm of hungry ghosts. There they remain for many years—whether several hundred, several thousand, or even several hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* years—suffering all manner of afflictions within the ghost realm, such as hunger, emaciation, and parching thirst.

Because their offenses are not yet exhausted, they shall wander from one realm of hungry ghosts to another within this world; until the kalpas of fire, water, and wind have arisen, they will undergo all manner of sufferings, such as hunger, emaciation, and parching thirst.

If, at the time this world is destroyed by the three calamities, the residual force of their karma of depleting the Dharma has not yet been exhausted, they die and are reborn in another world within the same class of hungry ghosts (*preta*). There, for many years—whether many hundreds, many thousands, or even many hundreds of thousands of *koṭi-nayuta* years—they undergo all manner of sufferings such as hunger, emaciation, and parching thirst within the realm of ghosts.

Because their offenses are not yet exhausted, they travel from one realm of hungry ghosts to another in other worlds; until the kalpas of fire, water, and wind have arisen, they undergo all manner of sufferings such as hunger, emaciation, and parching thirst.

If, at the time when the three calamities destroy another world, the residual force of their karma of deprivation of the Dharma has not yet been exhausted, they die and are reborn in a similar realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*) in another direction, where they undergo for many years—whether many hundreds, many thousands, or even many hundreds of thousands of *koṭi-nayuta* years—the sufferings of hunger, emaciation, parching thirst, and so forth within that ghost realm.

Because their offenses are not yet exhausted, they travel from one realm of hungry ghosts to another in other worlds; until the kalpas of fire, water, and wind have arisen, they undergo all manner of sufferings such as hunger, emaciation, and parching thirst.

In this manner, they travel successively through all other worlds throughout the ten directions, undergoing within the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*) the sufferings of hunger, emaciation, parching thirst, and so forth.

When those other worlds in the ten directions are destroyed by the three calamities, if the residual force of their karma of deprivation from the Dharma has not yet been exhausted, they die and are reborn here in this world within the destiny of hungry ghosts. From one realm of hungry ghosts to another realm of hungry ghosts, until the fire, water, and wind kalpas have arisen, they undergo the sufferings of hunger, emaciation, parching thirst, and so forth.

If, when this world is destroyed by the three calamities, the residual force of their karma of deprivation of the Dharma has not yet been exhausted, they die and are reborn again in other worlds throughout the ten directions, undergoing manifold sufferings extensively within the realm of hungry ghosts.
Thus they wander through immeasurable eons until the residual force of their karma of withholding the Dharma is nearly exhausted.

They emerge from the realm of hungry ghosts and are reborn among humans; though they obtain human form, they dwell in lowly and base conditions—meaning they may be born into families of those blind from birth or deaf, or into families of *caṇḍālas*, or *pukkasas*, or butchers.
Whether from a family of meat-slicers, or a family of fishermen and hunters, or a family of craftsmen, or a family of musicians, or a family of those with wrong views,
or any other base and miscellaneous families of evil discipline; or whether one has received a body that is without eyes,
without ears, without nose, without tongue, without hands, or without feet— being blind, sightless, deaf, or mute.
Those afflicted with abscesses, carbuncles, scabies, leprosy, insanity, epilepsy, lameness, paralysis, hunchbacks, dwarfs, deformities, contractions,
or deficiencies of the sense organs; those who are dark-complexioned, destitute, dull-witted, or ignorant— whomever they may be among such people,
all will mock and deride them, or in the places where they are born, they shall not hear the names of the Buddha or the Dharma.
They may bear the name of a monk, the name of a bodhisattva, or the name of a pratyekabuddha;
or else they may be born in a world of profound darkness where day and night never exist and no light is seen, dwelling in places that are perilous, foul, and infested with poisonous thorns.
Why is this? Subhūti!

Because their karma of depriving others of the Dharma has been created and increased to such an extreme degree of gravity, they undergo such undesirable and complete fruits of suffering, which are so numerous in their varieties that they are difficult to describe in full.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The Tathāgata has often said that among all sins, the most grave are the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*). Now you speak of a sixth—performing and increasing the karma of destroying the True Dharma—is this similar to the five deeds of immediate retribution?”
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!
The karma of destroying the True Dharma is most extremely coarse and heavy; it cannot be compared even to the five actions of immediate retribution.”
That is to say, upon hearing the teaching of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they immediately fail to believe it and instead slander and revile it, saying:

"Such words were not spoken by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; they are not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not the instruction of the Great Teacher. We should not train ourselves in this."
"Such a person who slanders the Dharma slanders the Prajñāpāramitā themselves, and also teaches immeasurable sentient beings to slander it;
they ruin their own bodies and cause others to ruin theirs;
they drink the poisonous medicine themselves and cause others to drink it as well."
They themselves lose the fruit of happiness of rebirth in heaven and liberation, and cause others to lose it as well;
they themselves provide their own bodies as fuel for the fires of hell, and likewise provide the bodies of others as fuel for the fires of hell;
they themselves lack faith and understanding in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and furthermore teach others so that they too lack faith and understanding in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
"I have submerged myself in the ocean of suffering and cause others to submerge as well. Śāriputra!
Regarding such a profound *prajñāpāramitā*, I do not even wish for those who would slander the true Dharma to hear its name, much less teach it to them!"

Śāriputra! As for those who slander the true Dharma, I do not even permit sons or daughters of good family who have set out upon the Bodhisattva vehicle to hear their names, let alone allow them to see them with their own eyes!
How could it be permitted for them to dwell together?
Why is this so, Śāriputra?

Those who slander and disparage the profound *prajñāpāramitā* should be known as destroyers of the true Dharma; they fall into the class of darkness like filthy snails, defiling themselves and others like a mass of putrid excrement.
If there are those who place their trust in the words of one who destroys the Dharma, they too shall undergo the great suffering previously described. Śāriputra!

You should know that all those who destroy the profound Prajñāpāramitā are, in effect, hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts; they will certainly undergo extremely heavy, fierce, and boundless great suffering. Therefore, the wise should not disparage the profound Prajñāpāramitā.
Then, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

For what reason do you speak only of how those who destroy the true Dharma fall into the great hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts to suffer for a long time, yet do not describe their physical appearance or bodily dimensions?”
The Buddha said: "Śāriputra, stop!
One should not speak of the dimensions of the bodies in the evil destinies that those who destroy the true Dharma will receive in the future.
Why is this? Śāriputra!

If I were to describe in full detail the dimensions of the miserable realms to be experienced in the future by those who destroy the True Dharma, they would be so terrified upon hearing it that they would vomit hot blood and die, or suffer the agony of near-death; their minds would be instantly distressed as if pierced by a poisoned arrow, and their bodies would gradually wither away like grass struck by frost.

Fearing that those who hear of the one who destroys the True Dharma will, upon hearing of such a body of great ugliness and suffering, become needlessly terrified and lose their lives, I have compassion for them and therefore do not describe to you the form, appearance, or dimensions of the body resulting from the sin of destroying the True Dharma.

Śāriputra said: "I pray that the Buddha will describe the dimensions of the miserable realms to be experienced in the future by those who destroy the True Dharma; may he clearly warn those of the future so that they may know that slandering the Dharma shall result in great suffering, and thus refrain from committing such a sin."
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!

What I have previously stated is sufficient as a clear warning: that those sons and daughters of good family in future ages who hear my teaching on the karma of destroying the true Dharma—and who commit, increase, and fully perfect such acts—will fall into the great hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts, suffering for a long time within each of these destinies. This alone is sufficient to cause them to maintain self-restraint and refrain from slandering the true Dharma.”
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: “Indeed,
World-Honored One!”
"Yes indeed, Sugata!

When future sons and daughters of good family hear the Buddha’s previous teaching on how the sin of slandering the True Dharma brings about suffering for a long duration as a sufficient warning, they will surely rather sacrifice their own lives than ever slander the Dharma, lest they themselves suffer such misery in the future."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One!

If there are wise sons and daughters of good family who hear the Buddha’s teaching that those who slander the true Dharma will suffer great misery for a long time in future lives, they should well guard their actions of body, speech, and mind. They must not revile or destroy the true Dharma, lest they fall into the three evil realms and suffer for a long duration; nor shall they fail to see a Buddha, hear the true Dharma, or encounter the Saṅgha for a vast period of time; nor shall they be born in a land where a Buddha dwells. Even if they are born in the human realm, they will be lowly, impoverished, ugly, dull-witted, or physically impaired, and whatever they say will not be believed or accepted by others.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Is it not by practicing the karma of malicious speech that one creates and increases the karma that leads to the deprivation of the Dharma?
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, Subhūti! It is so, it is so!”
This is truly because they have habituated themselves to the karma of harsh speech; thus, they have created and increased the karma that results in the deprivation of the Dharma.

Within my True Dharma and Vinaya, there will be certain foolish renunciants who, though they claim me to be their Great Teacher, will slander and destroy the profound *prajñāpāramitā* that I have taught.
Subhūti, you should know that whoever slanders this profound perfection of wisdom slanders the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas.
If one slanders the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas, then one slanders the knowledge of all aspects of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
If one slanders or disparages the knowledge of all aspects of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, then one slanders all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
If one slanders or reviles all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, then one slanders the Jewel of the Buddha, the Jewel of the Dharma, and the Jewel of the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus.
If one slanders the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, then one slanders right view in the world.

If one slanders right view in the world, then one slanders the perfections of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; one also slanders inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature; one also slanders the four applications of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; and likewise, one slanders the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, as well as all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects.
By slandering the knowledge of all aspects, they thereby take upon themselves immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sinful karma.

Because they have taken upon themselves such immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sinful karma, they thereby take upon themselves the immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless great sufferings of all the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the human world.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By how many causes and conditions do those foolish commoners slander and revile such profound *prajñāpāramitā*?"
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!
Due to four causes and conditions, those foolish persons slander and revile this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.”
What are the four?
First, because they have been instigated and deluded by various evil māras, those foolish persons slander and revile this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
Second, because they lack faith and understanding in the profound Dharma, those foolish persons slander and revile such profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

Third, because they do not apply themselves with diligence, are attached to the five aggregates, and are influenced by evil associates, those foolish persons slander and revile such profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

Fourth, because they harbor much ill will, delight in practicing unwholesome dharmas, take pleasure in self-exaltation, and despise others, those foolish persons slander and revile this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

"Subhūti! Because those foolish persons possess these four causes and conditions, they slander and revile this profound *prajñāpāramitā*; consequently, they shall undergo immeasurable suffering in the future."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Worldly fools who do not apply themselves with diligence, who are influenced by evil associates, who have not planted roots of goodness and are possessed of all manner of unwholesome conduct, will truly find it difficult to believe in and understand the profound *prajñāpāramitā* spoken by the Buddha.”
The Buddha said, “So it is, Subhūti!”
"So it is! It is as you have said.
The foolish people of the world do not apply themselves with diligence and are taken hold of by evil associates."
"Those who have not planted roots of goodness and are possessed of all manner of evil conduct will find it truly difficult to believe and understand the profound *prajñāpāramitā* that I have taught.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In what way is this *prajñāpāramitā* so profound, so difficult to believe, and so difficult to understand?"
The Buddha said,
"Subhūti! Form is neither bound nor liberated."
Why is this? Because the nature of form is its non-existence; this is the intrinsic nature of form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated.

Why is this? Because the non-existence of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness constitutes the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. "Subhūti!..."
The sense base of the eye, up to and including the sense base of the mind, is neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?
Because the nature of non-existence of the sense bases from the eye to the mind constitutes the intrinsic nature of the sense bases from the eye to the mind.
The sphere of form up to the sphere of phenomena are neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?
Because the nature of non-existence of the sphere of form up to the sphere of phenomena constitutes the intrinsic nature of the sphere of form up to the sphere of phenomena.
“Subhūti! The eye element, up to and including the mind element, is neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?
Because the eye-element up to the mind-element have the nature of non-existence as their own-being,
the form-element up to the mental-object-element are neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the non-existence of the form realm up to the dharma realm constitutes the intrinsic nature of the form realm up to the dharma realm.
Thus, from the eye-consciousness realm up to the mind-consciousness realm, there is neither bondage nor liberation.

Why is this? Because the non-existence of the visual consciousness element, up to and including the mental consciousness element, constitutes the intrinsic nature of the visual consciousness element, up to and including the mental consciousness element.
Eye-contact, and so forth up to mind-contact, are neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?
Because the nature of non-existence of eye-contact, and so forth up to mind-contact, constitutes the intrinsic nature of eye-contact, and so forth up to mind-contact.
The various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, up to and including those produced with mind-contact as condition, are neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?

Because the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, up to and including those produced with mind-contact as condition, have the nature of non-existence, which constitutes the intrinsic nature of those feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, up to and including those produced with mind-contact as condition.
“Subhūti! From the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, there is neither bondage nor liberation. Why is that?
Because the non-existent nature of the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom constitutes the intrinsic nature of the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom.
“Subhūti! From internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, there is neither bondage nor liberation. Why is this?

Because the non-existence of everything from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-entities constitutes the intrinsic nature of everything from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-entities. "Subhūti!..."
The four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path are neither bound nor liberated. Why?
Because the non-existent nature of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path constitutes their intrinsic nature.
“Subhūti! In this way, even up to the ten powers of a Tathāgata and even up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, there is neither bondage nor liberation. Why is that?

This is because the nature of non-existence of the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha constitutes the intrinsic nature of the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
“Subhūti! All-knowledge is neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?
Because all-knowledge has the nature of non-existence as its own intrinsic nature,
the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects are neither bound nor liberated.

Why is this? Because the non-existence of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects constitutes the intrinsic nature of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Form is neither bound nor liberated at its prior limit. Why is this?
Because the prior limit of form has the nature of non-existence, it is the self-nature of the prior limit of form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated at their prior limit.

Why is this? Because the prior limit of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is the nature of non-existence, which constitutes the intrinsic nature of the prior limit of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
In this way, even up to omniscience, its prior limit is neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?
Because the prior limit of omniscience has the nature of non-existence as its own intrinsic nature.
The knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects are neither bound nor liberated at the prior limit. Why is this?
Because the non-existence of the prior limit constitutes the intrinsic nature of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects.
"Subhūti! The future limit of form is neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?
Because the posterior limit of form has the nature of non-existence as its own intrinsic nature,
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated at their posterior limit.

Why is this? Because the non-existence of the posterior limit of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness constitutes the intrinsic nature of the posterior limit of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
In this way, even up to omniscience, its posterior limit is neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?
Because the non-existent nature of the posterior limit of omniscience constitutes the very self-nature of the posterior limit of omniscience.
The knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects are neither bound nor liberated at their posterior limit. Why is this?
Because the non-existence of a posterior limit constitutes the intrinsic nature of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects.
"Subhūti! Within form, there is neither bondage nor liberation. Why is this?
Because the middle limit of form has the nature of non-existence as its own intrinsic nature,
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated at their middle limit.

Why is this? Because the middle limit of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is the nature of non-existence, which constitutes the intrinsic nature of the middle limit of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
and so it continues up to omniscience, whose middle limit is neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the middle limit of all-knowledge has the nature of non-existence as its intrinsic nature of the middle limit of all-knowledge.
The middle limit of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects is neither bound nor liberated.

Why is this? Because the non-existence of the middle limit within the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects constitutes the intrinsic nature of the middle limit of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

For those individuals who do not apply themselves with diligence, who have not planted roots of goodness, who possess unwholesome roots, who are under the influence of evil friends, whose laziness is predominant, who follow the course of Māra’s power, whose vigor is feeble, and who lack mindfulness and possess poor wisdom, it is truly difficult to believe in and understand the profound *prajñāpāramitā* spoken by the Buddha.”
The Buddha said,
“Excellent, Subhūti! It is so!”
"So it is! It is just as you have said.

Those individuals who do not exert diligent effort, who have not planted roots of virtue, who possess unwholesome roots, who are under the influence of evil friends, whose laziness is predominant, who follow the course of Māra’s power, whose diligence is feeble, and who lack mindfulness and possess poor wisdom, will find it truly difficult to believe in and understand this profound *prajñāpāramitā* that I have taught."
Why is this so? Subhūti!

The purity of form is the purity of the fruit; the purity of the fruit is the purity of form. This purity of form and purity of the fruit are non-dual, without distinction, indivisible, and uninterrupted.

The purity of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is itself the purity of the fruit; the purity of the fruit is itself the purity of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Thus, this purity of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness and the purity of the fruit are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted.

In this way, up to the point that the purity of all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is the purity of the fruit, and the purity of the fruit is the purity of all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; this purity of all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the purity of the fruit are non-dual, undifferentiated, indestructible, and uninterrupted.

The purity of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is the purity of the fruit; the purity of the fruit is the purity of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas. This purity of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas and the purity of the fruit are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

The purity of form is the purity of the perfection of wisdom; the purity of the perfection of wisdom is the purity of form. This purity of form and this purity of the perfection of wisdom are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted."

The purity of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is the purity of the perfection of wisdom; the purity of the perfection of wisdom is the purity of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. This purity of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness and this purity of the perfection of wisdom are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted.

In this way, up to the point that the purity of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is the purity of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), and the purity of the perfection of wisdom is the purity of all-knowledge; this purity of all-knowledge and the purity of the perfection of wisdom are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted.

The purity of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects is the purity of the perfection of wisdom; the purity of the perfection of wisdom is the purity of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects. This purity of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects and this purity of the perfection of wisdom are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

The purity of form is the purity of the knowledge of all modes; the purity of the knowledge of all modes is the purity of form. This purity of form and this purity of the knowledge of all modes are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted."

The purity of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is the purity of the knowledge of all modes; the purity of the knowledge of all modes is the purity of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. This purity of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness and this purity of the knowledge of all modes are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted.

In this way, up to the point that the purity of all-knowledge is the purity of the knowledge of all-knowledge, and the purity of the knowledge of all-knowledge is the purity of all-knowledge; this purity of all-knowledge and the purity of the knowledge of all-knowledge are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted.

The purity of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects is the purity of the knowledge of all modes; the purity of the knowledge of all modes is the purity of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects. This purity of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects and this purity of the knowledge of all modes are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

The purity of non-duality is the purity of form; the purity of form is the purity of non-duality. This purity of non-duality and the purity of form are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted."

The purity of non-duality is the purity of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; the purity of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is the purity of non-duality. This purity of non-duality and the purity of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-dual, undifferentiated, indestructible, and uninterrupted.

In this way, up to the point that the purity of non-duality is the purity of all-knowledge, and the purity of all-knowledge is the purity of non-duality; this purity of non-duality and the purity of all-knowledge are non-dual, undifferentiated, indestructible, and uninterrupted.

The purity of non-duality is the purity of the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects; the purity of the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects is the purity of non-duality. This purity of non-duality and the purity of the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

The purity of the self, of sentient beings, and so forth, up to the knower and the seer, is itself the purity of form; the purity of form is itself the purity of the self, of sentient beings, and so forth, up to the knower and the seer. This purity of the self, of sentient beings, and so forth, up to the knower and the seer, and this purity of form, are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted."

The purity of the self, of sentient beings, and even of the knower and the seer, is the purity of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; the purity of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is the purity of the self, of sentient beings, and even of the knower and the seer. This purity of the self, of sentient beings, and even of the knower and the seer, and this purity of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted.

In this way, up to and including the purity of the self, sentient beings, and even the knower and the seer, is the purity of all-knowledge; the purity of all-knowledge is the purity of the self, sentient beings, and even the knower and the seer. Thus, the purity of the self, sentient beings, and even the knower and the seer, and the purity of all-knowledge, are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted.

The purity of the self, sentient beings, and even the knower and the seer is the purity of the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects; the purity of the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects is the purity of the self, sentient beings, and even the knower and the seer. Thus, this purity of the self, sentient beings, and even the knower and the seer, and the purity of the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects, are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

The purity of greed, hatred, and delusion is the purity of form; the purity of form is the purity of greed, hatred, and delusion. This purity of greed, hatred, and delusion and this purity of form are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted."

The purification of greed, hatred, and delusion is the purification of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; the purification of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is the purification of greed, hatred, and delusion. This purification of greed, hatred, and delusion and this purification of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-dual, without distinction, indivisible, and uninterrupted.

In this way, up to the point that the purification of greed, hatred, and delusion is the purification of all-knowledge, and the purification of all-knowledge is the purification of greed, hatred, and delusion; this purification of greed, hatred, and delusion and the purification of all-knowledge are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted.

The purity of greed, hatred, and delusion is the purity of the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects; the purity of the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects is the purity of greed, hatred, and delusion. This purity of greed, hatred, and delusion and this purity of the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Because form is pure, feeling is pure; because feeling is pure, form is pure. This purity of form and purity of feeling are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted."
In this way, because feeling is pure, perception is pure; because perception is pure, formations are pure; because formations are pure, consciousness is pure;
because consciousness is pure, the sense-base of the eye up to the sense-base of the mind is pure;
because the sense-base of the mind is pure, the sense-base of forms up to the sense-base of phenomena is pure; because the sense-base of phenomena is pure, the eye-element... [is pure].
...up to the purification of the mind-element (*manodhātu*). Because the mind-element is purified, the form-element (*rūpadhātu*) up to the phenomena-element (*dharmadhātu*) are purified.
Because the phenomena-element is purified, the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) up to the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*) are purified.

Because the mind-consciousness-element is purified, eye-contact (*cakṣuḥsaṃsparśa*) up to mind-contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*) are purified. Because mind-contact is purified, that which is conditioned by eye-contact...
The various feelings born of conditions, up to and including the various feelings born with mental contact as condition, are pure;
because the various feelings born with mental contact as condition are pure, ignorance up to and including old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are pure;
because old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are pure, the *prajñāpāramitā* is [pure].

Up to the purity of the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*); because the perfection of generosity is pure, there is purity from inner emptiness (*adhyātmaśūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature (*abhāvasvabhāvaśūnyatā*);

because the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature is pure, there is purity of the four applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*); because the eightfold noble path is pure, [there is] mutual...
...up to the purification of the ten powers of a Buddha, up to the purification of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;

because the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are purified, all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is purified; because all-knowledge is purified, the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) is purified;
because the knowledge of the aspects of the path is purified, the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is purified; [all-aspect-knowledge...]

Because it is pure, the knowledge of the aspects of the path is pure; this purity of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the purity of the knowledge of all aspects are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Because the perfection of wisdom is pure, form is pure; because form is pure, the knowledge of all modes is pure. Whether it be the purity of the perfection of wisdom, the purity of form, or the purity of the knowledge of all modes, these are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted."

To speak at length, up to: because the perfection of wisdom is pure, the knowledge of all aspects is pure; because the knowledge of all aspects is pure, the knowledge of all-knowing is pure. Whether it be the purity of the perfection of wisdom, the purity of the knowledge of all aspects, or the purity of the knowledge of all-knowing, they are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted.

In this way, up to the point that because the perfection of generosity is pure, form is pure; and because form is pure, the knowledge of all modes is pure. Whether it be the purity of the perfection of generosity, the purity of form, or the purity of the knowledge of all modes, these are non-dual, without distinction, indivisible, and uninterrupted.

To speak at length, up to the point that because the perfection of generosity is pure, the knowledge of all aspects is pure; and because the knowledge of all aspects is pure, the knowledge of all-knowing is pure. Whether it be the purity of the perfection of generosity, the purity of the knowledge of all aspects, or the purity of the knowledge of all-knowing, these are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted.

“Subhūti! Because internal emptiness is pure, form is pure; because form is pure, the knowledge of all modes is pure. Whether it be the purity of internal emptiness, the purity of form, or the purity of the knowledge of all modes, these are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted.”
