To speak in detail, up to: because internal emptiness is pure, the knowledge of all aspects is pure; because the knowledge of all aspects is pure, the knowledge of all-knowledge is pure. Whether it be the purity of internal emptiness, the purity of the knowledge of all aspects, or the purity of the knowledge of all-knowledge, they are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted.

In this way, up to the point that because the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence is pure, form is pure; because form is pure, the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) is pure. Whether it be the purity of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, the purity of form, or the purity of the knowledge of all modes—these are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted.

To speak extensively, up to and including: because the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence is pure, the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is pure; because the knowledge of all aspects is pure, the knowledge of all knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*) is pure. Whether it be the purity of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, the purity of the knowledge of all aspects, or the purity of the knowledge of all knowledge, these are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted.

“Subhūti! Because the four applications of mindfulness are pure, form is pure; because form is pure, the knowledge of all modes is pure. Whether it be the purity of the four applications of mindfulness, the purity of form, or the purity of the knowledge of all modes, they are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted.”

To speak at length, up to: because the four foundations of mindfulness are pure, the knowledge of all aspects is pure; because the knowledge of all aspects is pure, the knowledge of all-knowing is pure. Whether it be the purity of the four foundations of mindfulness, the purity of the knowledge of all aspects, or the purity of the knowledge of all-knowing, they are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted.

In this way, up to and including the purity of the eightfold noble path, because of its purity, form is pure; because form is pure, the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) is pure. Whether it be the purity of the eightfold noble path, the purity of form, or the purity of the knowledge of all modes, these are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted.

To speak at length, up to: because the eightfold noble path is pure, the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is pure; because the knowledge of all aspects is pure, the knowledge of all-knowing (*sarvajñajñāna*) is pure. Whether it be the purity of the eightfold noble path, the purity of the knowledge of all aspects, or the purity of the knowledge of all-knowing, these are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted.
“Subhūti! In this way, up to and including:

because the ten powers of the Tathāgata are pure, form is pure; because form is pure, the knowledge of all modes is pure. Whether it be the purity of the Tathāgata’s ten powers, the purity of form, or the purity of the knowledge of all modes, these are non-dual, without distinction, indivisible, and uninterrupted.”

To speak at length, up to: because the ten powers of the Tathāgata are pure, the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is pure; because the knowledge of all aspects is pure, the knowledge of all knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*) is pure. Whether it be the purity of the Tathāgata’s ten powers, the purity of the knowledge of all aspects, or the purity of the knowledge of all knowledge, they are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted.

In this way, up to and including the purification of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), because they are pure, form (*rūpa*) is pure; because form is pure, the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) is pure. Whether it be the purification of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, the purification of form, or the purification of the knowledge of all modes, these are non-dual, without distinction, indivisible, and uninterrupted.

To speak at length, up to: because the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) are pure, the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is pure; because the knowledge of all aspects is pure, the knowledge of all knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*) is pure. Whether it be the purity of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, the purity of the knowledge of all aspects, or the purity of the knowledge of all knowledge, these are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted.

“Subhūti! Because all-knowledge is pure, form is pure; because form is pure, the wisdom of all-knowledge is pure. Whether it be the purity of all-knowledge, the purity of form, or the purity of the wisdom of all-knowledge, they are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted.”

To speak at length, up to: because the purity of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is the purity of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), and because the purity of the knowledge of all aspects is the purity of the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*). Whether it be the purity of all-knowledge, the purity of the knowledge of all aspects, or the purity of the knowledge of all-knowledge, these are non-dual, without distinction, indivisible, and uninterrupted.

In this way, up to the point that because the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is pure, form (*rūpa*) is pure; and because form is pure, the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) is pure. Whether it be the purity of the knowledge of all aspects, the purity of form, or the purity of the knowledge of all modes, these are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted.

To speak at length, up to: because the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is pure, the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) is pure; because the knowledge of the paths is pure, the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*) is pure. Whether it be the purity of the knowledge of all aspects, the purity of the knowledge of the paths, or the purity of the knowledge of all-knowledge, these are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Because the knowledge of all modes is pure, form is pure; because form is pure, the perfection of wisdom is pure. Whether it be the purity of the knowledge of all modes, the purity of form, or the purity of the perfection of wisdom, these are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted."

To speak at length, up to: because the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*) is pure, the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is pure; because the knowledge of all aspects is pure, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is pure. Whether it be the purity of the knowledge of all-knowledge, the purity of the knowledge of all aspects, or the purity of the perfection of wisdom, they are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted.

In this way, up to and including: because the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) is pure, form (*rūpa*) is pure; because form is pure, the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is pure. Whether it be the purity of the knowledge of all modes, the purity of form, or the purity of the knowledge of all aspects, these are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted.

To speak at length, up to: because the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) is pure, the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) is pure; because the knowledge of the paths is pure, the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is pure. Whether it be the purity of the knowledge of all modes, the purity of the knowledge of the paths, or the purity of the knowledge of all aspects, they are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted.
In each and every one of these phrases, all should be explained in detail according to the preceding sequence. "Furthermore, Subhūti!

Because the conditioned is pure, the unconditioned is pure; because the unconditioned is pure, the conditioned is pure. Whether it be the purity of the conditioned or the purity of the unconditioned, they are non-dual, without distinction, indestructible, and uninterrupted."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Because the past is pure, the future is pure; because the future is pure, the past is pure. Whether it be the purity of the past or the purity of the future, they are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted."

Because the past is pure, the present is pure; because the present is pure, the past is pure. Whether it be the purity of the past or the purity of the present, they are non-dual, undifferentiated, indestructible, and uninterrupted.

Because the future is pure, the present is pure; because the present is pure, the future is pure. Whether it be the purity of the future or the purity of the present, they are non-dual, without distinction, indestructible, and uninterrupted.

Because the past is pure, the future and present are pure; because the future and present are pure, the past is pure. Whether it be the purity of the past or the purity of the future and present, they are non-dual, undifferentiated, indivisible, and uninterrupted.

Because the future is pure, the past and present are pure; because the past and present are pure, the future is pure. Whether it be the purity of the future or the purity of the past and present, they are non-dual, undifferentiated, indestructible, and uninterrupted.

Because the present is pure, the past and future are pure; because the past and future are pure, the present is pure. [Thus ends] the four hundred and thirty-fifth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*;
[beginning of] the four hundred and thirty-sixth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Forty: The Chapter on Purity, Part Two. Chapter Forty: The Chapter on Purity. At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"This Dharma is pure and most profound.
The Buddha said, "It is so,
because it is ultimately pure."
Śāriputra asked: “By virtue of what ultimate purity is this purity of dharmas said to be most profound?
The Buddha replied:
“Śāriputra! Because form is ultimately pure, it is said that the purity of this dharma is most profound;
because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are ultimately pure, it is said that the purity of this dharma is most profound.”
Because the sense base of the eye up to the sense base of the mind are ultimately pure, it is said that this purity of dharmas is most profound;
because the sense base of form up to the sense base of phenomena are ultimately pure, it is said that this purity of dharmas is most profound;
because the eye element up to the mind element are ultimately pure, it is said that this purity of dharmas is most profound.
Because the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) up to the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) are ultimately pure, it is said that the purity of these dharmas is most profound;
because the eye-consciousness realm (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) up to the mind-consciousness realm (*manovijñānadhātu*) are ultimately pure, it is said that the purity of these dharmas is most profound;
and because the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) are ultimately pure, it is said that the purity of these dharmas is most profound.
Because internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature is ultimately pure, it is said that the purity of these dharmas is most profound;
because the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path is ultimately pure, it is said that the purity of these dharmas is most profound;
and so on, up to the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha being ultimately pure, it is said that the purity of these dharmas is most profound.
Because the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are ultimately pure, this purity of dharmas is said to be most profound;
because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are ultimately pure, this purity of dharmas is said to be most profound;
because the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of all buddhas is ultimately pure, this purity of dharmas is said to be most profound.
Because all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are ultimately pure, this purity of dharmas is said to be most profound;
because omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is ultimately pure, this purity of dharmas is said to be most profound;
and because the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are ultimately pure, this purity of dharmas is said to be most profound.
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Dharma is pure and exceedingly clear.”
The Buddha said: "It is because it is ultimately pure. Śāriputra said:
“For what reason is it said that because of ultimate purity, this Dharma is pure and exceedingly clear?
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!”

Because the perfection of wisdom is ultimately pure, it is said that the purity of these dharmas is extremely clear; and so on, up to: because the perfection of generosity is ultimately pure, it is said that the purity of these dharmas is extremely clear.

In this way, because all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is ultimately pure, it is said that the purity of these dharmas is extremely clear; because the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are ultimately pure, it is said that the purity of these dharmas is extremely clear.
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Dharma is pure; it neither revolves nor continues.”
The Buddha said: "It is because it is ultimately pure. Śāriputra said:
“For what reason is it said that because of ultimate purity, this Dharma is pure, non-reverting,
and non-continuing? The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!...”

Because form does not transmigrate and does not continue, being ultimately pure, it is said that this dharma is pure, non-transmigrating, and non-continuing; because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not transmigrate and do not continue, being ultimately pure, it is said that these dharmas are pure, non-transmigrating, and non-continuing.

In this way, up to and including the fact that all-knowledge (sarvajñatā) does not turn back and is not continuous because it is ultimately pure, it is said that these dharmas are pure, do not turn back, and are not continuous; because the knowledge of the aspects of the path (mārgākārajñatā) and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) do not turn back and are not continuous because they are ultimately pure, it is said that these dharmas are pure, do not turn back, and are not continuous.
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Dharma is pure and fundamentally free from defilement.”
The Buddha said, “It is because it is ultimately pure. Śāriputra said:
“For what reason is it said that because this Dharma is ultimately pure, it is fundamentally free from defilement?
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!...”

Because form is ultimately pure, it is said that this dharma is pure and fundamentally free from defilement; because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are ultimately pure, it is said that these dharmas are pure and fundamentally free from defilement.

In this way, up to and including the ultimate purity of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), it is said that these dharmas are pure and fundamentally free from defilement; because the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are ultimately pure, it is said that these dharmas are pure and fundamentally free from defilement.
Then, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Dharma is pure, its intrinsic nature being luminous and pristine.”
The Buddha said: "It is because it is ultimately pure. Śāriputra said:
“By virtue of what ultimate purity is this Dharma said to be pure by nature and radiant?
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!

Because form is ultimately pure, it is said that this dharma is pure by nature and luminously radiant; because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are ultimately pure, it is said that these dharmas are pure by nature and luminously radiant.

In this way, up to and including because all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is ultimately pure, it is said that the nature of these dharmas is pure and inherently radiant; because the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are ultimately pure, it is said that the nature of these dharmas is pure and inherently radiant.
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Dharma is pure, without attainment and without realization.”
The Buddha said, “It is because it is ultimately pure. Śāriputra said:
"For what reason is it said that because of ultimate purity, these dharmas are pure, without attainment and without clear realization?
The Buddha said, "Śāriputra!"

Because the intrinsic nature of form is empty and ultimately pure, it is said that these dharmas are pure, without attainment and without direct realization; because the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is empty and ultimately pure, it is said that these dharmas are pure, without attainment and without direct realization.

In this way, up to and including the fact that the intrinsic nature of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is empty and ultimately pure, it is said that these dharmas are pure, without attainment and without realization; because the intrinsic nature of the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is empty and ultimately pure, it is said that these dharmas are pure, without attainment and without realization.
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Dharma is pure, without arising and without manifestation.”
The Buddha said, "It is because it is ultimately pure. Śāriputra said:
“For what reason is it said that because of ultimate purity, this Dharma is pure, unarisen, and non-manifesting? The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!...”

Because form is unborn, unmanifest, and ultimately pure, it is said that this dharma is pure, unborn, and does not appear. Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unborn, unmanifest, and ultimately pure, it is said that these dharmas are pure, unborn, and do not appear.

In this way, up to and including the fact that all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is unborn, unmanifest, and ultimately pure, it is said that these phenomena are pure, unborn, and non-appearing; because the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are unborn, unmanifest, and ultimately pure, it is said that these phenomena are pure, unborn, and non-appearing.
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Dharma is pure; it is not born in the desire realm, it is not born in the form realm, and it is not born in the formless realm.”
The Buddha said, "It is because it is ultimately pure. Śāriputra said:
"How is it that this Dharma is pure and does not arise in the desire realm, does not arise in the form realm, and does not arise in the formless realm?
The Buddha said, "Śāriputra!..."

Because the intrinsic nature of the three realms cannot be apprehended, it is said that this Dharma is pure and does not arise in the desire realm, does not arise in the form realm, and does not arise in the formless realm.
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
This Dharma is pure, for its intrinsic nature is without cognition."
The Buddha said, "It is because it is ultimately pure. Śāriputra said:
“What is meant by ‘this dharma is pure and its intrinsic nature is without cognition’?
The Buddha said: “Śāriputra!...”
"Because all phenomena are by nature dull, these phenomena are pure and by nature devoid of cognition.
Śāriputra asked: "In what sense are they by nature devoid of cognition that you say these phenomena are pure and by nature devoid of cognition?"
The Buddha said: "Śāriputra!

The intrinsic nature of form is without cognition because its own-characteristic is empty; therefore, it is said that this dharma is pure and its intrinsic nature is without cognition. The intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is without cognition because their own-characteristics are empty; therefore, it is said that these dharmas are pure and their intrinsic nature is without cognition."

In this way, up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), its intrinsic nature is non-cognition because its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is empty; therefore, it is said that this dharma is pure by nature and non-cognitive. The knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) have an intrinsic nature of non-cognition because their own-characteristics are empty; therefore, it is said that these dharmas are pure by nature and non-cognitive.
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Because all dharmas are pure by their very nature, these dharmas are pure.”
The Buddha said:
"It is because all phenomena are ultimately pure in this way. Śāriputra said:
“How is it that because all phenomena are pure by their very nature, this purity of phenomena is spoken of? The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!
"Because all phenomena are unattainable, their intrinsic nature is pure; thus, this Dharma is said to be pure.
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, the perfection of wisdom neither benefits nor harms the knowledge of all aspects.
The Buddha said,
"It is because it is ultimately pure."
Śāriputra asked: "In what way does the perfection of wisdom neither benefit nor harm the knowledge of all aspects?
The Buddha said:
“Śāriputra! Because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is eternally abiding, this perfection of wisdom neither benefits nor harms the knowledge of all aspects.
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is pure by its very nature; it does not grasp or cling to any phenomena.
The Buddha said:
"Thus, because all phenomena are ultimately pure. Śāriputra asked:
"In what way is the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom pure, such that it does not grasp or cling to any phenomenon?"
The Buddha said, "Śāriputra!
Because the dharma-realm is serene and immovable, this perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is pure by its very nature and does not grasp or cling to any phenomena."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Because I am pure, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure."
The Buddha said:
"It is so, because it is ultimately pure.
[He asked: "World-Honored One!"
"For what reason is it said that because the self is pure, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure—this being ultimate purity? "Subhūti!"
“Because the self is non-existent, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also non-existent; this is ultimate purity.
“World-Honored One!
Because the self is pure, the eye-base through to the mind-base are pure.”
The Buddha said:
“It is so, because it is ultimately pure.
[He asked: “World-Honored One!”
"For what reason do you say that because the self is pure, the sense base of the eye up to the sense base of the mind are pure—this being ultimate purity?
"Subhūti, because the self does not exist, the sense base of the eye up to the sense base of the mind also do not exist; this is ultimate purity."
“World-Honored One!
Because I am pure, the sphere of form up to the sphere of mental phenomena are pure.
The Buddha said:
“Because it is thus ultimately pure.
“World-Honored One,
for what reason do you say that because the self is pure, the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) up to the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) are pure, which is ultimate purity?”
"Subhūti! Because the self does not exist, the sphere of form up to the sphere of phenomena also do not exist; this is ultimate purity.
"World-Honored One!"
"Because I am pure, the eye-element, and so forth, up to the mind-element, are pure.
The Buddha said:
"It is because they are ultimately pure."
“World-Honored One!
For what reason do you say that because the self is pure, the eye-element up to the mind-element are pure, being ultimately pure? “Subhūti!
"Because the self does not exist, the eye-element up to the mind-element also do not exist; this is ultimate purity.
"World-Honored One!
Because the self is pure, the form-element up to the dharma-element are pure."
The Buddha said, "It is because it is ultimately pure. [The interlocutor asked:
"World-Honored One!"
"For what reason is it said that because the self is pure, the form realm up to the dharma realm are pure—this being ultimate purity?
"Subhūti, because the self does not exist, the form realm up to the dharma realm also do not exist; this is ultimate purity."
“World-Honored One!
Because I am pure, the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element is pure.
The Buddha said:
“Because it is thus ultimately pure.
“World-Honored One,
for what reason do you say that because the self is pure, the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element are pure, which is ultimate purity?”
“Subhūti! Because the self does not exist, the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element also do not exist; this is ultimate purity.
“World-Honored One!”
"Because I am pure, the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom is pure.
The Buddha said, "It is so,
because it is ultimately pure."
“World-Honored One!
For what reason do you say that because the self is pure, the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom is pure—this being ultimate purity?”
“Subhūti! Because ‘I’ do not exist, the perfection of generosity up to and including the perfection of wisdom also do not exist; this is ultimate purity.”
“World-Honored One!
Because I am pure, inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature is pure.
The Buddha said:
“Because it is thus ultimately pure.
“World-Honored One,
for what reason do you say that because the self is pure, internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature is pure, which is ultimate purity?”
“Subhūti! Because ‘I’ do not exist, from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, these too do not exist; this is ultimate purity.
“World-Honored One!”
"Because I am pure, the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path are pure.
The Buddha said, "It is so,
because they are ultimately pure."
“World-Honored One!
For what reason do you say that because the self is pure, the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path are pure, being ultimately pure?”
“Subhūti! Because the self does not exist, the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path also do not exist; this is ultimate purity.
“World-Honored One!”
"Because I am pure, the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are pure.
The Buddha said:
"It is so, because they are ultimately pure."
“World-Honored One!
For what reason do you say that because the self is pure, the ten powers of the Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are pure—this being ultimate purity?”
“Subhūti! Because the self does not exist, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, also do not exist; this is ultimate purity.”
“World-Honored One!
Because I am pure, the fruit of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment are pure.”
The Buddha said,
“It is so, because it is ultimately pure.
[He asked,] “World-Honored One!”

For what reason is it said that because the self is pure, the purity of the fruit of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is ultimate purity?

“Subhūti! Because the self-characteristic is empty, the fruit of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment are also empty of their own characteristics; this is ultimate purity.”
“World-Honored One!
Because I am pure, all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects are pure.
The Buddha said:
“It is because it is ultimately pure. “World-Honored One, for what reason do you say that because the self is pure,
omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are pure, and thus ultimately pure?”

“Subhūti! Because I am without marks, without attainment, without recollection, and without cognition, all-knowledge (sarvajñatā), the knowledge of the paths (mārgajñatā), and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) are likewise without marks, without attainment, without recollection, and without cognition; this is ultimate purity.”
“World-Honored One!
Because of the purity of these two, there is neither attainment nor clear realization.
The Buddha said:
“Because it is thus ultimately pure.
“World-Honored One,
for what reason do you say that because of the two kinds of purity, there is neither attainment nor clear realization, and this is ultimate purity?”
“Subhūti! Because there is no defilement or purification arising from inversion, there is neither attainment nor clear realization; this is ultimate purity.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Because I am boundless, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also boundless.
The Buddha said:
“Because it is thus ultimately pure.
“World-Honored One,
for what reason do you say that because the self is boundless, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also boundless and ultimately pure?”
“Subhūti! Because of ultimate emptiness and boundless emptiness, this is ultimate purity.
“World-Honored One!”
“Because I am boundless, the sense base of the eye, up to and including the sense base of the mind, is also boundless.
The Buddha said:
“It is so, because it is ultimately pure.”
“World-Honored One!
For what reason do you say that because the self is boundless, the sense base of the eye up to the sense base of the mind are also boundless and thus ultimately pure? “Subhūti!
"Because it is ultimately empty and boundlessly empty, it is ultimately pure.
"World-Honored One!
Because the self is boundless, the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) up to the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) is also boundless."
The Buddha said:
"It is because it is ultimately pure. [Subhūti] said:
"World-Honored One!"
"For what reason do you say that because the self is infinite, the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) up to the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) are also infinite and thus ultimately pure?
"Subhūti, it is because of ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*) and boundless emptiness (*anavaraṇa-śūnyatā*) that they are ultimately pure."
“World-Honored One!
Because I am boundless, the eye-element, and so forth, up to the mind-element, are also boundless.
The Buddha said:
“It is because it is ultimately pure.
“World-Honored One,
for what reason do you say that because the self is infinite, the eye-element up to the mind-element are also infinite and thus ultimately pure?”
“Subhūti! Because of ultimate emptiness and boundless emptiness, this is ultimate purity.
“World-Honored One!”

The Buddha said:

"Subhūti! [The Buddha replied:]

The Buddha said:

Because I am infinite, the fruit of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, pratyekabuddha enlightenment, and unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment are also infinite.

“Subhūti! Because of ultimate emptiness and boundless emptiness, this is ultimate purity.

“It is so, because they are ultimately pure (*atyanta-viśuddha*).”
“World-Honored One!

“Subhūti! Because it is the emptiness of ultimate limit and the emptiness of the boundless, it is ultimately pure.
“World-Honored One!”
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can awaken in this way, this is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
The Buddha said:

“Subhūti! It is because by means of this one can accomplish the knowledge of the aspects of the path.
“World-Honored One!”
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom employs skillful means and forms this thought:
"Form does not know form; feeling does not know feeling; perception does not know perception; formations do not know formations; consciousness does not know consciousness;

The sense-base of form does not know the sense-base of form, and so on up to the sense-base of phenomena (dharmāyatana) which does not know the sense-base of phenomena;

"Omniscience does not know omniscience; the knowledge of the paths does not know the knowledge of the paths; and the knowledge of all aspects does not know the knowledge of all aspects.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva has already entered the stage of right determination regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Buddha said, “So it is, Subhūti!”
"So it is! It is just as you have said.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed Subhūti, saying:
"When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, do those who possess skillful means give rise to dualistic conceptions regarding phenomena?"
Subhūti replied, “Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they possess skillful means, they do not form such a thought:”
"I am able to practice giving, and I give in this manner;
I am able to maintain ethical discipline, and I maintain it in this manner;
I am able to cultivate patience, and I cultivate it in this manner."
"I am able to exert diligence; I exert diligence in this manner.
I am able to enter meditative concentration; I enter meditative concentration in this manner.
I am able to cultivate wisdom; I cultivate wisdom in this manner."
I am able to cultivate merit; I cultivate merit in this manner.
I am able to enter the bodhisattva’s state of certainty; I enter the bodhisattva’s state of certainty in this manner.
I am able to adorn and purify buddha-fields; I adorn and purify buddha-fields in this manner.
"I am able to mature sentient beings; I mature sentient beings in this way.
I shall attain all-aspect omniscience; I shall attain all-aspect omniscience in this way."

"Śāriputra! Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom with skillful means, they are free from all such conceptual discriminations. This is because they have thoroughly realized internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, the emptiness of dispersion and non-dispersion, essential nature emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, and the emptiness of self-characteristics."
Śāriputra! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, because they possess skillful means, they have no attachment whatsoever.
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, asked Subhūti: "Venerable One,
how should one understand the attachments that arise when sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle practice the perfection of wisdom?"
Subhūti replied, “Kauśika!
When sons and daughters of good family who abide in the bodhisattva vehicle practice the perfection of wisdom, because they lack skillful means, they give rise to the notion of a self.”
They give rise to the perception of giving and the perception of the perfection of giving;
they give rise to the perception of ethical discipline and the perception of the perfection of ethical discipline;
they give rise to the perception of patience and the perception of the perfection of patience.
They give rise to the perception of diligence and the perception of the perfection of diligence;
they give rise to the perception of meditative concentration and the perception of the perfection of meditative concentration;
they give rise to the perception of wisdom and the perception of the perfection of wisdom.
They give rise to the perception of internal emptiness, and give rise to the perceptions of external emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature;
they give rise to the perception of the four foundations of mindfulness, and give rise to the perceptions of the four right efforts up to the eightfold noble path;
they give rise to the perception of the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and give rise to the perceptions of the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

One should give rise to the perception of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*); give rise to the perception of the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);
give rise to the perception of the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; give rise to the perception of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas;

give rise to the perception of planting roots of goodness under the Buddhas; and give rise to the perception of collecting and weighing these planted roots of goodness, sharing them equally with all sentient beings, and dedicating them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
“Kauśika! By this you should know the attachments that arise when sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle practice the perfection of wisdom.”

Kauśika! Because these sons and daughters of good family are bound by this attachment, they are unable to practice the unattached *prajñāpāramitā* and dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
Why is this? Kausika!
It is not possible to dedicate the intrinsic nature of form; it is not possible to dedicate the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

"Furthermore, Kauśika, it is not possible for the intrinsic nature of even omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) to be dedicated; nor can the intrinsic nature of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) be dedicated. "Moreover, Kauśika!"

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to manifest, exhort, encourage, and gladden other sentient beings regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should contemplate the equal, true nature of all phenomena. Following this mental engagement, they should manifest, exhort, encourage, and gladden those other sentient beings by saying:
"O sons of good family, O daughters of good family, when you practice the perfection of generosity, you should not discriminate, thinking 'I am able to give';
when you practice the perfection of ethical discipline, you should not discriminate, thinking 'I am able to maintain discipline'."
When practicing the perfection of patience, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to practice patience";
when practicing the perfection of diligence, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to be diligent";
and when practicing the perfection of meditative concentration, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to enter meditative absorption."
When practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to cultivate wisdom.
When practicing inner emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*), one should not discriminate, thinking, "I abide in inner emptiness.

When practicing outer emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*), one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to abide in outer emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature."
When practicing the four foundations of mindfulness, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to practice the four foundations of mindfulness";
when practicing the four right endeavors up to the eightfold noble path, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to practice the four right endeavors up to the eightfold noble path";
and when practicing the ten powers of a Tathāgata, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to practice the ten powers of a Tathāgata."

When practicing the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to practice the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
When practicing all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to practice all-knowledge.

When practicing the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), one should not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to practice the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects."
"When practicing for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, one should not discriminate, thinking, 'I am able to practice for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Kausika!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to manifest, exhort, encourage, inspire, and gladden other sentient beings regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, should manifest, exhort, encourage, inspire, and gladden those other sentient beings in this manner."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to thus manifest, exhort, encourage, and gladden other sentient beings regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they neither harm themselves nor harm others, because they manifest, exhort, encourage, and gladden all sentient beings in accordance with what is permitted by the Tathāgatas.

Kauśika! If sons of good family or daughters of good family who abide in the bodhisattva vehicle can thus manifest themselves to instruct, exhort, encourage, and gladden those sentient beings who are approaching the bodhisattva vehicle, they will be able to remain far removed from all attachments.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Subhūti, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"

You have now skillfully explained the characteristics of attachment for the sake of all bodhisattvas, enabling those sons and daughters of good family who are inclined toward the Mahāyāna to abandon the characteristics of attachment and cultivate the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
"Subhūti! Furthermore, there are other subtle attachments which I shall explain to you; you should listen attentively and reflect upon them well!"
Subhūti replied, "Indeed! I pray that you will speak."
"We would rejoice to hear it," they said. The Buddha said,
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

Any sons or daughters of good family abiding in the Bodhisattva vehicle who wish to proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, if they apprehend signs and bring them to mind regarding the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, all such acts are attachments.

If they apprehend signs and bring to mind the unattached merits of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present—from the first generation of the thought of enlightenment until the endurance of the Dharma—and having brought them to mind, rejoice in them with a profound heart; and having rejoiced, share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—all such apprehension of signs and bringing to mind is termed attachment.

If one grasps at signs when recollecting the wholesome dharmas cultivated by the disciples of all Tathāgatas and other sentient beings, and with a deep mind rejoices in them; having thus rejoiced, one then dedicates these together equally with all sentient beings toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—all such acts are likewise termed attachment.
Why is this? Subhūti!

Regarding the merits and roots of goodness of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as well as their disciples and other sentient beings, one should not apprehend signs, nor dwell upon them with recollection or discrimination; for all who apprehend signs are engaged in what is false and illusory.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is most profound."
The Buddha said: “It is so!
Because all dharmas are by their very nature detached.”
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā should be paid homage in this way.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because its merit is vast, yet this Prajñāpāramitā is uncreated, unmade, and there is no one who can realize it.
"World-Honored One!"
"The nature of all phenomena cannot be realized.
The Buddha said, "In this way,
because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is one and the same, neither the subject that realizes nor the object to be realized can be apprehended."
Subhūti, you should know this:
the single nature of all phenomena is itself the absence of nature; the absence of nature in all phenomena is itself their single nature.
Thus, the single nature and the absence of nature of all phenomena is their fundamental, true nature; this fundamental, true nature is uncreated and unconditioned.

"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can know all phenomena as they truly are—having a single nature, being without intrinsic existence, uncreated, and unconditioned—then they will be able to remain far removed from all attachments."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“In this way, the Prajñāpāramitā is difficult to realize.
The Buddha said:

"It is so! Because this *prajñāpāramitā* is devoid of the characteristics of realization, there is no one who can see it, no one who can hear it, no one who can awaken to it, and no one who can know it."
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is thus inconceivable.
The Buddha said:
"In this way, by means of this *prajñāpāramitā*, it cannot be apprehended by the mind, because it is free from the characteristics of the mind;
it cannot be apprehended by form (*rūpa*) up to consciousness (*vijñāna*), because it is free from their characteristics;
it cannot be apprehended by the eye (*cakṣus*) up to the mind (*manas*), because it is free from their characteristics."
One cannot apprehend it by means of form, up to and including mental phenomena (*dharma*), because one is free from those signs;
one cannot apprehend it by means of eye-consciousness, up to and including mind-consciousness, because one is free from those signs;
one cannot apprehend it by means of the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), up to and including the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), because one is free from those signs.
One cannot apprehend it by means of the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, because one is detached from those signs;
one cannot apprehend it by means of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, because one is detached from those signs;
one cannot apprehend it by means of the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, because one is detached from those signs.
One cannot grasp it by means of all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, or the knowledge of all aspects, because one is detached from their characteristics;
one cannot grasp it by means of any phenomena, because one is detached from their characteristics.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
this perfection of wisdom does not arise from form, nor does it arise from anything up to and including all phenomena.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“Thus, this perfection of wisdom is without any deliberate activity.
The Buddha said, “It is so!”
Because no agent can be apprehended. Subhūti!

Because form cannot be apprehended, an agent cannot be apprehended; because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be apprehended, an agent cannot be apprehended; and so on, up to: because all phenomena cannot be apprehended, an agent cannot be apprehended.
“Subhūti! Because an agent and phenomena such as form cannot be apprehended, this perfection of wisdom is without activity.
Chapter 41: On the Absence of Marks, Part Two, Section One. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)?
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), if they do not practice with respect to form (rūpa), this is practicing the perfection of wisdom;
if they do not practice with respect to feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), formations (saṃskāra), or consciousness (vijñāna), this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.”
Even not practicing all-knowledge is practicing the perfection of wisdom;
not practicing the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Not practicing with regard to form as being either permanent or impermanent is practicing the perfection of wisdom;
not practicing with regard to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as being either permanent or impermanent is practicing the perfection of wisdom;
and so on, up to not practicing with regard to all-knowledge as being either permanent or impermanent is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Not practicing the cognition of the characteristics of the path or the cognition of all aspects as either permanent or impermanent is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Not practicing form as either pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom;
not practicing feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either pleasant or painful is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
In this way, up to not practicing whether all-knowledge is pleasant or painful—this is practicing the perfection of wisdom;
not practicing whether the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects is pleasant or painful—this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Not practicing with regard to form as either self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom;
not practicing with regard to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom;
and so on, up to not practicing with regard to all-knowledge as either self or non-self is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

To not practice the cognition of the characteristics of phenomena (*lakṣaṇajñāna*) or the cognition of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) as either self or non-self is to practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
To not practice form (*rūpa*) as either pure or impure is to practice the perfection of wisdom;
to not practice feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*) as either pure or impure is to practice the perfection of wisdom.
In this way, up to and including not practicing whether all-knowledge is pure or impure—this is practicing the perfection of wisdom;
not practicing whether the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects is pure or impure—this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not even perceive form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness; how much less could they perceive form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness as permanent or impermanent, as pleasant or painful, as self or non-self, or as pure or impure!

In this way, they do not even perceive omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), much less perceive omniscience, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, or the knowledge of all aspects as either permanent or impermanent, as either pleasant or painful, as either self or non-self, or as either pure or impure!

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not practice for the fulfillment of form, nor do they practice for the non-fulfillment of form; this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

They do not practice for the fulfillment of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor do they practice for the non-fulfillment of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; this is practicing the perfection of wisdom."
In this way, up to and including not practicing the fulfillment of all-knowledge, nor practicing the non-fulfillment of all-knowledge—this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom;

not practicing the fulfillment of the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects, nor practicing the non-fulfillment of the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects—this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not even perceive or apprehend form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness; how much less could they perceive or apprehend whether form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness are fulfilled or unfulfilled!

In this way, one does not even see or apprehend omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); how much less could one see or apprehend whether omniscience, the knowledge of the paths, or the knowledge of all aspects is fulfilled or unfulfilled!
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How extraordinary!”
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has skillfully proclaimed for the sake of sons and daughters of good family who follow the Mahāyāna the characteristics of attachment and non-attachment.
The Buddha said, “So it is, Subhūti!”
"So it is! It is just as you have said.

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have skillfully proclaimed, for the sake of sons and daughters of good family who practice the Mahāyāna, the characteristics of attachment and non-attachment."

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not practice by way of attachment or non-attachment to form; this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
They do not practice by way of attachment or non-attachment to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Not practicing with regard to the eye up to the mind, whether through attachment or non-attachment, is practicing the perfection of wisdom;
not practicing with regard to form up to mental phenomena, whether through attachment or non-attachment, is practicing the perfection of wisdom;
not practicing with regard to eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness, whether through attachment or non-attachment, is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

To neither practice nor be attached to, or to neither not practice nor not be attached to, the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom—this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom.

To neither practice nor be attached to, or to neither not practice nor not be attached to, inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature—this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom.

To neither practice nor be attached to, or to neither not practice nor not be attached to, the four applications of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path—this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom.

In this way, up to and including not practicing with regard to the Tathāgata’s ten powers or even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—whether through attachment or non-attachment—is the practice of the perfection of wisdom;
not practicing with regard to all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, or the knowledge of all aspects—whether through attachment or non-attachment—is the practice of the perfection of wisdom;

not practicing with regard to the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha—whether through attachment or non-attachment—is the practice of the perfection of wisdom.

To neither practice nor not practice all the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, and to neither grasp at nor not grasp at the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas—this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this way, they understand as it truly is that form is without attachment and without the characteristic of attachment; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise without attachment and without the characteristic of attachment.

In this manner, up to and including all the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, they understand as they truly are that these are without attachment and without the characteristic of attachment; even the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is without attachment and without the characteristic of attachment.”
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The profound nature of phenomena is most rare; whether it is taught or not taught, it neither increases nor decreases.”
The Buddha said,
“So it is, Subhūti! It is just so.”
"So it is! It is just as you have said.
The profound nature of phenomena is exceedingly rare; whether it is explained or not explained, there is neither increase nor decrease."

"Subhūti! Suppose a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha were to remain for the full span of his lifespan praising or disparaging space; yet that space would neither increase nor decrease. The profound nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is likewise: whether it is explained or not explained, it remains without increase or decrease."

"Subhūti! For example, when a conjured being is praised or reviled, there is neither increase nor decrease, nor is there sorrow or joy; the profound nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is likewise: whether it is explained or not explained, it remains no different from its original state."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is a most difficult task for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to practice the perfection of wisdom.”

That is to say, regarding this *prajñāpāramitā*, whether it is cultivated or not cultivated, there is neither increase nor decrease, neither sorrow nor joy, neither inclination nor aversion; yet one diligently cultivates and studies such *prajñāpāramitā* until reaching unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), never regressing.
Why is this? World-Honored One!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they practice it as if practicing emptiness, wherein nothing at all exists.
World-Honored One!
Just as in space there is no form to be discerned, and no feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness to be discerned;
there is no eye-base to be discerned, and no ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-base to be discerned;
There is no sphere of form to be discerned, nor are there spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena to be discerned;
there is no eye-element to be discerned, nor are there ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-elements to be discerned;
there is no form-element to be discerned, nor are there elements of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena to be discerned.
There is no visual consciousness element to be apprehended; there is no auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, or mental consciousness element to be apprehended.
There is no perfection of generosity to be apprehended; there is no perfection of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom to be apprehended.
There is no inner emptiness to be apprehended; there is no outer emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the essential nature of non-entities, to be apprehended.
There is nothing to be apprehended as the four applications of mindfulness; there is nothing to be apprehended as the four right endeavors, up to and including the eight branches of the noble path;

likewise, up to and including, there is nothing to be apprehended as the ten powers of a Tathāgata; there is nothing to be apprehended as the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
there is nothing to be apprehended as all-knowledge; and there is nothing to be apprehended as the knowledge of the paths or the knowledge of all aspects.
There is no fruit of stream-entry to be realized; there is no fruit of once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship, nor is there any enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha to be realized;

there is no conduct of any bodhisattva mahāsattva to be realized, nor is there any unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas to be realized; and the same applies to the perfection of wisdom that is practiced.

That is to say, within this profound Dharma of the perfection of wisdom, form cannot be apprehended; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be apprehended; and so on, up to the point that no bodhisattva-mahāsattva practice can be apprehended, and no unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas can be apprehended.

Although herein no phenomena whatsoever can be apprehended, bodhisattvas are nonetheless able to apply themselves with diligent vigor to the training in the perfection of wisdom, never regressing until they reach unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; for this reason, I say that it is an exceedingly difficult task for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to practice the perfection of wisdom.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 436. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Second Division, Chapter Forty-one, Part Two: On the Absence of Marks. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
All Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are able to don such armor of great merit should be venerated by all sentient beings.
World-Honored One,

if a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva dons the armor of merit and exerts diligent vigor for the sake of all sentient beings, it is as if they were donning the armor of merit and exerting diligent vigor for the sake of empty space.
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dons the armor of merit and exerts diligent effort for the sake of maturing and liberating sentient beings, it is as if they don the armor of merit and exert diligent effort for the sake of maturing and liberating empty space.”
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dons the armor of merit and exerts diligent vigor for the sake of all dharmas, it is as if they don the armor of merit and exert diligent vigor for the sake of empty space.”

"Bhagavān! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dons the armor of merit and exerts diligent vigor in order to uproot sentient beings from the suffering of birth and death, it is as if one were donning the great armor of merit and exerting diligent vigor in order to lift up empty space and place it upon a high and exalted location."

"Bhagavān! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain the power of great diligence and heroic vigor; for the sake of all sentient beings who are like space, they swiftly set out toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to liberate them from birth and death."

"Bhagavān! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain inconceivable and peerless spiritual power; for the sake of the ocean-like nature of all phenomena, which is like space, they don the armor of merit and set out toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

"Bhagavān! These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are most exceedingly courageous; for the sake of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment sought as vast as space, they don the armor of merit and exert diligent vigor."
“World-Honored One!

It is truly rare that the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, for the sake of bringing to maturity and liberation those sentient beings who are like space, diligently practice austerities desiring to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Why is this so? World-Honored One!

Suppose the great trichiliocosm were filled with Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as dense as a forest of bamboo, hemp, reeds, or sugarcane; and suppose they were to preach the sublime Dharma constantly for all sentient beings for an eon or even more than an eon, each delivering immeasurable and boundless sentient beings into parinirvāṇa and ultimate peace and happiness—yet the realm of sentient beings would neither increase nor decrease.
Why is this? Because all sentient beings are devoid of intrinsic nature and are fundamentally remote from it.
World-Honored One!

Suppose that all the worlds of the ten directions were filled with Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, like a forest of bamboo, hemp, reeds, or sugarcane; and suppose that for an eon or more than an eon, they constantly preached the sublime Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, each delivering immeasurable and boundless sentient beings and causing them to enter nirvāṇa in ultimate peace and happiness, yet the realm of sentient beings neither increased nor decreased.
Why is this? Because all sentient beings are devoid of intrinsic nature and are utterly remote from it.
"World-Honored One!..."
For this reason, I say:

it is truly marvelous that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, for the sake of maturing and liberating all sentient beings—who are like space—diligently practice asceticism with the desire to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu within the assembly had this thought to himself:
"I should pay homage to the profound Prajñāpāramitā."

Within this, although there is no arising or ceasing of any phenomena, there is the obtainable designation of the aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; there is also the obtainable designation of the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship, as well as the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; there is also the obtainable designation of the practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, and the obtainable designation of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; there is also the obtainable designation of the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas and the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas; there is also the obtainable designation of the Jewel of the Buddha, the Jewel of the Dharma, and the Jewel of the Saṅgha; and there is also the obtainable designation of the Buddhas turning the sublime wheel of Dharma to bring benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings.
The Buddha, knowing his thought, said to him:
"Bhikṣu, it is so! It is thus!"
So it is! It is just as you have conceived.
This profound Prajñāpāramitā is subtle and difficult to fathom; although it is not a dharma that exists, it is also not non-existent.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked Subhūti: "Venerable One,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to train in the perfection of wisdom, how should they train?"
Subhūti replied, “Kauśika!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to train in the perfection of wisdom, they should apply themselves with diligent effort as if training in space.”
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If good sons and good daughters should wholeheartedly hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently practice, reflect upon according to principle, transcribe, explain, and widely disseminate this *Prajñāpāramitā*, how should I protect them?”
At that time, Subhūti addressed Śakra, saying:
“Kauśika! Do you perceive any dharma that can be guarded or protected?”
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said: "No,
Venerable Sir!"
"I do not see any dharma that ought to be protected. Subhūti replied: "Kauśika!..."
If sons or daughters of good family abide in the perfection of wisdom as taught by the Buddha, they are thereby protected.

If sons or daughters of good family abide in the perfection of wisdom and never depart from it, one should know that no humans or non-humans who seek an opportunity to cause them harm will ever succeed in doing so.

Kauśika! If one wishes to protect and sustain those sons and daughters of good family who dwell securely in the perfection of wisdom, it is no different from someone conceiving the intention to diligently protect empty space.
Kauśika! If you wish to protect those sons and daughters of good family who practice the perfection of wisdom, your labor will be in vain and will yield no benefit whatsoever.
Kauśika! What do you think?
Is it possible to guard or protect an illusion, a dream, an echo, a reflection, a shadow, a mirage, a transformation, or a city of Gandharvas?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said: “No,
Venerable Sir!”
Subhūti replied: "Kauśika!
If one wishes to protect those sons and daughters of good family who practice the perfection of wisdom, it is likewise so; their labor would be in vain and entirely without benefit."
Kauśika! What do you think?
Is there anyone who can protect all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as well as the emanations created by the Buddhas?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said: "No,
Venerable Sir!"
Subhūti replied, “Kauśika!
If one wishes to protect those sons and daughters of good family who practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), it is likewise so; their labor would be in vain and entirely without benefit.”
Kauśika! What do you think?
Is there anyone who can guard the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, suchness, the limit of reality, the inconceivable realm, or the realm of empty space?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said: “No,
Venerable Sir!”
Subhūti replied, "Kauśika!
If one wishes to protect those sons and daughters of good family who practice the perfection of wisdom, it is likewise so; their labor would be in vain and entirely without benefit."
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked Subhūti:

"Venerable One, how is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, although he knows all phenomena to be like an illusion, like a dream, like an echo, like an image, like a reflection, like a mirage, like a magical creation, and like a city of the gandharvas, yet this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not grasp at them as being an illusion, a dream, an echo, an image, a reflection, a mirage, a magical creation, or a city of the gandharvas; nor does he grasp at them as arising from an illusion up to a city of the gandharvas; nor does he grasp at them as belonging to an illusion up to a city of the gandharvas; nor does he grasp at them as depending upon an illusion up to a city of the gandharvas?"
Subhūti replied, “Kauśika!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not grasp at this as form, nor as feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness.”
Nor does one grasp by way of form, nor by way of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
nor does one grasp as belonging to form, nor as belonging to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
nor does one grasp as dependent upon form, nor as dependent upon feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
In this way, up to and including, one does not grasp at omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);
nor does one grasp by means of omniscience, the knowledge of the paths, or the knowledge of all aspects;
nor does one grasp as belonging to omniscience, the knowledge of the paths, or the knowledge of all aspects.
Nor do they cling to the basis of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the basis of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), or the basis of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), although they know that all phenomena are like illusions and even like cities of *gandharvas*, they are able to refrain from clinging to them as being illusions or even as being cities of *gandharvas*. Furthermore, they do not cling to [phenomena] as arising from illusions or even from cities of *gandharvas*; nor do they cling to [phenomena] as belonging to illusions or even to cities of *gandharvas*; nor do they cling to [phenomena] as having their basis in illusions or even in cities of *gandharvas*.

At that time, through the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata, all the gods from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven within this trichiliocosm each scattered celestial flowers and powdered sandalwood and aloeswood from afar upon the Buddha. They approached the Buddha’s presence, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, the devas saw from afar a thousand buddha-worlds in the eastern direction, each containing a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha proclaiming the Prajñāpāramitā; the meaning, chapters, and names were all identical to those here. The bhikṣus who requested the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā were all named Subhūti as their leaders, and the celestial hosts who posed questions regarding the Prajñāpāramitā were all named Śakra as their leaders. It was likewise so in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:

“When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya realizes unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, he too shall proclaim this Prajñāpāramitā in this very place. Furthermore, all the Buddhas who will appear in this Bhadrakalpa shall likewise proclaim this Prajñāpāramitā in this very place.”
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya realizes unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, by what dharmas, modes of activity, characteristics, and signs will he proclaim the Prajñāpāramitā?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya attains unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, he shall proclaim the perfection of wisdom by teaching that form is neither permanent nor impermanent; he shall proclaim the perfection of wisdom by teaching that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither permanent nor impermanent.

In this manner, up to and including, he shall proclaim the perfection of wisdom by teaching that all-knowledge is neither permanent nor impermanent, and he shall proclaim the perfection of wisdom by teaching that the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects are neither permanent nor impermanent.”

One should teach the perfection of wisdom by declaring that form is neither pleasant nor painful; one should teach the perfection of wisdom by declaring that feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are neither pleasant nor painful;

and so on, up to teaching the perfection of wisdom by declaring that all-knowledge is neither pleasant nor painful, and teaching the perfection of wisdom by declaring that the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects are neither pleasant nor painful.

One should teach the perfection of wisdom by declaring that form is neither self nor non-self; one should teach the perfection of wisdom by declaring that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither self nor non-self.

In this manner, up to and including, one should teach the perfection of wisdom by declaring that all-knowledge is neither self nor non-self, and one should teach the perfection of wisdom by declaring that the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects are neither self nor non-self.

One should teach the perfection of wisdom by declaring that form is neither pure nor impure; one should teach the perfection of wisdom by declaring that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither pure nor impure.

In this manner, up to and including, one should teach the perfection of wisdom by declaring that all-knowledge is neither pure nor impure, and one should teach the perfection of wisdom by declaring that the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects are neither pure nor impure.

One should teach the perfection of wisdom by means of form as neither bound nor liberated; one should teach the perfection of wisdom by means of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as neither bound nor liberated;

and so on, up to teaching the perfection of wisdom by means of all-knowledge as neither bound nor liberated, and teaching the perfection of wisdom by means of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects as neither bound nor liberated.

One should proclaim the perfection of wisdom by means of form as being neither past, nor future, nor present; one should proclaim the perfection of wisdom by means of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as being neither past, nor future, nor present.

In this manner, up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), one should proclaim the perfection of wisdom by means of it as being neither past, nor future, nor present; and one should proclaim the perfection of wisdom by means of the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) as being neither past, nor future, nor present.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya attains unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, what dharma will he realize?”
"What dharma should he teach?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya attains unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, he will realize that form is ultimately pure, and he will teach that form is ultimately pure."
Realizing that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are ultimately pure, one speaks of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as being ultimately pure.
In this way, up to realizing that omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is ultimately pure, one speaks of omniscience as being ultimately pure;

realizing that the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are ultimately pure, one speaks of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects as being ultimately pure.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
by what cause is this perfection of wisdom pure?”
