The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Because form is pure, the perfection of wisdom is pure;
because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure, the perfection of wisdom is pure.”
In this way, up to and including the purity of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is pure;
because of the purity of the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), the perfection of wisdom is pure.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In what way is the perfection of wisdom pure because form is pure?
In what way is the perfection of wisdom pure because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure?"
In this way, up to: how is it that because all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is pure, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is pure?
How is it that because the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are pure, the perfection of wisdom is pure?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Form is pure because it is without arising, without cessation, without defilement, and without purification; because form is pure, the perfection of wisdom is pure.

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure because they are without arising, without cessation, without defilement, and without purification; because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure, the perfection of wisdom is pure."

In this way, up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), it is pure because it is without arising and without cessation, and without defilement and without purification; because all-knowledge is pure, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is pure.

The knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are pure because they are without arising and without cessation, and without defilement and without purification; because the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects are pure, the perfection of wisdom is pure.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, because space is pure, the perfection of wisdom is pure.
"World-Honored One! [Subhūti replied.]
“How is it that because space is pure, the perfection of wisdom is pure?
“Subhūti! Because space is pure—being without birth or cessation, and without defilement or purification—the perfection of wisdom is pure because space is pure.”
Furthermore, Subhūti!
Because form is without defilement, the perfection of wisdom is pure;
because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without defilement, the perfection of wisdom is pure.
In this way, up to and including the fact that all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is undefiled, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is pure;
because the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are undefiled, the perfection of wisdom is pure.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
in what way is the perfection of wisdom pure because form is free from defilement?"
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without defilement, is the perfection of wisdom pure?
Likewise, up to: how is it that because all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is without defilement, the perfection of wisdom is pure;
and because the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are without defilement, the perfection of wisdom is pure?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Because form cannot be grasped, it is without defilement; because form is without defilement, the perfection of wisdom is pure.

Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be grasped, they are without defilement; because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without defilement, the perfection of wisdom is pure."

In this way, up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), because it is ungraspable, it is without defilement; because all-knowledge is without defilement, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is pure.

Because the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are ungraspable, they are without defilement; because the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects are without defilement, the perfection of wisdom is pure.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, because space is unstained, the perfection of wisdom is pure. [Subhūti said:
"World-Honored One!"
"How is it that because space is unstained, the perfection of wisdom is pure?
"Subhūti! Because space cannot be grasped, it is unstained; because space is unstained, the perfection of wisdom is pure."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, because space is merely a conventional designation, the perfection of wisdom is pure. [Subhūti said:
"World-Honored One!"
“How is it that because space is merely a conventional designation, the perfection of wisdom is pure? “Subhūti,
just as two echoes arise in dependence upon space and exist only as conventional designations, so too, because it is merely a conventional designation, the perfection of wisdom is pure.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti, because space is ineffable, the perfection of wisdom is pure. [Subhūti said:
"World-Honored One!"
"How is it that because space is ineffable, the perfection of wisdom is pure?
"Subhūti, because space has no thing that can be expressed, it is ineffable; by this, the perfection of wisdom is pure."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, because space cannot be apprehended, the perfection of wisdom is pure. [Subhūti said:
"World-Honored One!"
“How is it that because space is unobtainable, the perfection of wisdom is pure? “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
Because space has no object that can be obtained, it is unobtainable; by virtue of this, the perfection of wisdom is pure.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Because all phenomena are without arising and without cessation, and without defilement and without purity, the perfection of wisdom is pure."
“World-Honored One!
How is it that because all dharmas are without arising and without cessation, and without defilement and without purity, the Prajñāpāramitā is pure?”

“Subhūti! Because all phenomena are ultimately pure, they are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purification; it is by virtue of this that the perfection of wisdom is pure.”
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If sons or daughters of good family wholeheartedly hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently practice, reflect upon according to principle, transcribe, explain, and widely disseminate this Prajñāpāramitā, these sons and daughters of good family shall have no afflictions of the eyes, ears, nose, or tongue; their limbs shall be without deficiency; they shall not suffer from extreme decay or senility, nor shall they die untimely deaths; and they shall always be respectfully surrounded, followed, and protected by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas.”

When these sons and daughters of good family recite and proclaim this Prajñāpāramitā on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of both the waxing and waning moons, at that time, all the gods from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven will assemble at the place where this Dharma-preacher resides to listen to and receive the Prajñāpāramitā.

Because these sons and daughters of good family read, recite, and proclaim the profound *prajñāpāramitā* within immeasurable great assemblies, they shall obtain immeasurable, innumerable, boundless, inconceivable, and unfathomable supreme merits.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“So it is! So it is! It is just as you have said.”

If good sons or good daughters, with sincere hearts, hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently practice, reflect upon according to principle, transcribe, explain, and widely disseminate this Prajñāpāramitā, these good sons and good daughters shall have no afflictions of the eyes, ears, nose, or tongue; their limbs shall be without defect; they shall not suffer from extreme decay or senility, nor shall they meet with untimely death; and they will always be reverently surrounded, followed, and protected by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas.

When these sons and daughters of good family read, recite, and proclaim this Prajñāpāramitā on the six fast days, at that time the gods from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven will all assemble at the place where this Dharma-preacher is, in order to listen to and receive this Prajñāpāramitā.

Because these sons and daughters of good family read, recite, and proclaim the profound *prajñāpāramitā* within immeasurable great assemblies, they shall obtain immeasurable, innumerable, boundless, inconceivable, and unfathomable, preeminent merits.
Why is this? Subhūti!

This perfection of wisdom is a great treasure. Because of this great treasure of the perfection of wisdom, immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings are liberated from the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts; and it causes immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, non-humans, and others to be liberated from the various sufferings and afflictions of poverty.

They are able to bestow upon immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings the wealth, honor, and peace and happiness of great kṣatriya clans, great brahmin clans, great householder clans, and great lay clans;

they are able to bestow upon immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings the wealth, honor, and peace and happiness of the gods of the Four Great Kings up to the gods of the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception;

and they are able to bestow upon immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings the sovereign peace and happiness of the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship, as well as pratyekabuddha awakening and unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
Why is this? Subhūti!

Within this profound sūtra of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature, the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and all-knowledge, knowledge of the aspects of the path, and all-aspect knowledge are extensively explained and revealed.

In this way, immeasurable sentient beings—countless, innumerable, and boundless—cultivate and train within these precious jewels of immeasurable merit, thereby attaining birth in great clans of kṣatriyas, great clans of brahmins, great clans of householders, and great clans of lay merchants;

immeasurable sentient beings—countless, innumerable, and boundless—cultivate and train within them, thereby attaining birth in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception;
and immeasurable sentient beings—countless, innumerable, and boundless—cultivate and train within them, thereby attaining the fruit of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship.
Immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings train therein and attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;

immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings train therein, enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth, and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Subhūti! For this reason, this Prajñāpāramitā is called a great treasury of jewels, because all the precious virtues of both the mundane and supramundane worlds arise from this profound Prajñāpāramitā.

“Subhūti! Within this great jewel-treasury of the perfection of wisdom, it is not taught that there is even the slightest dharma that arises or ceases, that is defiled or purified, or that is grasped or abandoned.”
Why is this? Subhūti!
Because there is not even the slightest dharma that can arise or cease, that can be defiled or purified, or that can be grasped or abandoned.

Subhūti! Within this great jewel-treasury of the perfection of wisdom, it is not said that there exists any phenomenon that is wholesome or unwholesome, determinate or indeterminate, mundane or supramundane, with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned.
Subhūti! For this reason, this Prajñāpāramitā is called the great dharma-treasury of non-apprehension. Subhūti!
In this great jewel-treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, it is not taught that there is even the slightest phenomenon capable of defiling it. Why is this?
Because there is not the slightest phenomenon that can be defiled, nor is there the slightest phenomenon capable of defiling such a profound and great Dharma-jewel treasury as the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Why is this? Because the phenomena that can defile cannot be apprehended, Subhūti!
For these reasons, this Prajñāpāramitā is called the great dharma-treasury free from defilement.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, they have no such conceptions, no such discriminations, no such acquisitions, and no such conceptual proliferations."
“I am able to practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who is thus able to practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* as it truly is, is also able to draw near to, pay homage to, and serve the Buddhas; traveling from one buddha-field to another, they make offerings to, revere, respect, and praise those Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. Wandering through these buddha-fields, they skillfully grasp their characteristics, purify buddha-lands, mature sentient beings, and cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Subhūti! Thus, this perfection of wisdom regarding all phenomena possesses neither mastery nor lack of mastery; it neither grasps nor relinquishes, neither arises nor ceases, neither defiles nor purifies, and neither increases nor decreases.

Subhūti! This perfection of wisdom is neither past, nor future, nor present; it does not proceed toward the desire realm, does not abandon the desire realm, and does not abide in the desire realm; it does not proceed toward the form realm, does not abandon the form realm, and does not abide in the form realm; it does not proceed toward the formless realm, does not abandon the formless realm, and does not abide in the formless realm.
“Subhūti! In this way, the perfection of wisdom neither bestows nor relinquishes the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
it neither bestows nor relinquishes inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature.
Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, they neither give nor relinquish;
regarding the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, they neither give nor relinquish;
regarding the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, they neither give nor relinquish.
Regarding the bodhisattvas' entry into the state of certainty up to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, he neither gives nor withholds;
regarding all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects, he likewise neither gives nor withholds.
Subhūti! Thus, this perfection of wisdom neither bestows nor relinquishes the dharmas of ordinary beings;
it neither bestows nor relinquishes the dharmas of stream-enterers, up to and including the dharmas of arhats.
Regarding the dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas, they neither give nor withhold;
regarding the dharmas of the bodhisattvas, they neither give nor withhold;
regarding the dharmas of the buddhas, they neither give nor withhold.

Subhūti! Thus, this perfection of wisdom does not bestow the dharmas of śrāvakas nor does it abandon the dharmas of ordinary beings; it does not bestow the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas nor does it abandon the dharmas of śrāvakas; it does not bestow the dharmas of the Buddhas nor does it abandon the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas; it does not bestow unconditioned dharmas nor does it abandon conditioned dharmas.
Why is this? Subhūti!

Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear in the world, these dharmas are eternally unchanging, for the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), the fixedness of phenomena (dharmaniyāmatā), and the stability of phenomena (dharmasthititā) are free from error or deviation.

At that time, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devaputras dwelling in the void of space leaped for joy and scattered upon the Buddha all manner of celestial flowers—*utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, *puṇḍarīka*, and *sugandhika*—as well as various powdered incenses. They congratulated one another and, with one voice, proclaimed:
"We now, in Jambudvīpa, behold the Buddha turning the sublime Wheel of Dharma for a second time."

In this regard, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devaputras, upon hearing the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā*, simultaneously realized the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, the Blessed One addressed Subhūti, saying:
"Such a turning of the wheel of Dharma is neither the first turning nor the second."
Why is this? Subhūti!

This perfection of wisdom appears in the world not for the sake of turning toward all phenomena, nor for the sake of returning from them, but solely because of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
by virtue of what dharma is there the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence?”
"In this way, the perfection of wisdom appears in the world neither for the sake of turning toward nor for the sake of returning from all phenomena.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Because the perfection of wisdom is empty of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom, and so on, up to: because the perfection of generosity is empty of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of generosity."
Because internal emptiness is empty of the nature of internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the nature of the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature;
because the four foundations of mindfulness are empty of the nature of the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including the emptiness of the nature of the eight branches of the noble path;
because the ten powers of a Tathāgata are empty of the nature of the ten powers of a Tathāgata, up to and including the emptiness of the nature of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

Because omniscience is empty of the nature of omniscience; because the knowledge of the paths, the knowledge of all aspects, and the nature of the knowledge of all aspects are empty of the nature of the knowledge of all aspects;

because the state of an ordinary person is empty of the nature of the state of an ordinary person; because the fruit of stream-entry is empty of the nature of the fruit of stream-entry, and so on up to the fruit of arhatship being empty of the nature of the fruit of arhatship; because the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha is empty of the nature of the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;

because all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are empty of the nature of all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; and because the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is empty of the nature of the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas.

Subhūti! Because such dharmas as these are empty of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, this Prajñāpāramitā appears in the world neither for the sake of turning toward nor for the sake of returning from all dharmas.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas is a great pāramitā, because it realizes that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty.”

Although they realize that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas nevertheless rely upon this prajñāpāramitā to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, and deliver immeasurable multitudes.
Although they realize enlightenment, there is nothing realized, for neither the phenomenon of realization nor non-realization can be apprehended;
although they turn the wheel of Dharma, there is nothing turned, for neither the phenomenon of turning nor returning can be apprehended;
although they deliver sentient beings, there is nothing delivered, for neither the phenomenon of seeing nor not seeing can be apprehended.

"Bhagavān! Within this Great Prajñāpāramitā, the turning of the wheel of Dharma is entirely unapprehendable, because all dharmas are eternally unarisen, and because that which turns and that which is turned are both unapprehendable."

Why is this? Within the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, there can be no dharma that can turn forward or turn back, because a dharma characterized by turning forward or turning back cannot be apprehended.
"Bhagavān! If one can thus proclaim, reveal, analyze, and clarify this Prajñāpāramitā so as to facilitate easy entry into it, this is called the well-purified proclamation of the Prajñāpāramitā."

Within this, there is absolutely no speaker, no recipient, and no dharma spoken or received. Since there is no speaker, no recipient, and no dharma, those who could realize [it] are likewise unobtainable. Because there is no one who realizes, there is also no one who can attain *nirvāṇa*. Within this well-expounded teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there is also no field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), because the donor, the recipient, and the object given are all empty by nature. Since the field of merit does not exist, merit is also empty by nature; even the designations of names and words are unobtainable. For these reasons, it is called the Great *Pāramitā*.
Chapter 42: The Inapprehensibility. Part Two, Chapter Forty-two: The Inapprehensibility. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"In this way, this perfection of wisdom is the boundless perfection.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
"Just as space is without limit, so too,
World-Honored One,
this perfection of wisdom is the perfection of equality."
The Buddha said: "It is so!
Because the nature of all dharmas is equal."
“World-Honored One!
This prajñāpāramitā is the pāramitā of detachment.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because of ultimate emptiness.
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, this perfection of wisdom is a perfection that is difficult to overcome.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
"Because the nature of all dharmas is unattainable.
"World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the pāramitā that has no further shore."
The Buddha said: “It is so! Because there is no name or essence.”
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the Pāramitā of Space.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because inhalation and exhalation are unapprehendable.
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, this perfection of wisdom is an ineffable perfection. The Buddha said, "So it is!"
"Because within this, applied thought and sustained thought are unapprehendable.
"World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the nameless pāramitā."
The Buddha said: "It is so!
Because feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention are unapprehendable."
“World-Honored One!
This prajñāpāramitā is the pāramitā of non-practice.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because all dharmas have neither coming nor going.
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection that cannot be taken away.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
"Because all dharmas are invincible.
"World-Honored One!
This perfection of wisdom is the inexhaustible perfection."
The Buddha said: "It is so!
Because all dharmas are ultimately exhausted and yet inexhaustible."
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the pāramitā of non-arising and non-ceasing.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because all dharmas are without arising or ceasing.
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection of non-action.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
“Because no agent can be apprehended.
“World-Honored One!
Thus, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection of non-cognition.”
The Buddha said: "It is so!
For the nature of all dharmas is dull."
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the pāramitā that is without transition.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because one who dies and is reborn cannot be apprehended.
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection that is without loss or destruction.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
"Because all phenomena are without destruction.
"World-Honored One!
This perfection of wisdom is the perfection that is like a dream."
The Buddha said: "It is so!
For all dharmas are like things seen in a dream, and thus cannot be apprehended."
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is an echo-like pāramitā.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because neither the subject who hears nor the object that is spoken can be apprehended.
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, this perfection of wisdom is a perfection that is like a reflection. The Buddha said, "So it is!"
“Because all phenomena are like reflections in a bright mirror and are thus unattainable.
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the Pāramitā of the Mirage and the Illusion.”
The Buddha said: "So it is!
For the characteristics of the flux and transformation of all dharmas are unattainable."
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is thus the Pāramitā of illusory transformations.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because all dharmas, like a magical transformation, cannot be apprehended.
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, this perfection of wisdom is like the perfection of a gandharva-city.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
"Because all phenomena are unattainable, being like a city of gandharvas.
"World-Honored One!
This perfection of wisdom is the perfection of neither defilement nor purity."
The Buddha said: "It is so!
Because the causes of all defilement and purity cannot be apprehended."
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the pāramitā of non-apprehension and the pāramitā that cannot be defiled.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because all dharmas upon which one relies are unapprehendable.
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection that is free from conceptual proliferation.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
"Because it destroys all phenomena of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
World-Honored One!
This *prajñāpāramitā* is the *pāramitā* free from pride and attachment."
The Buddha said: "It is so!
Because it destroys all matters of pride and attachment."
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the Pāramitā of Immovability.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because they abide in the dharma-realm.
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection that is free from defilement.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
"Because one realizes that all phenomena are not false.
"World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the pāramitā of non-arising."
The Buddha said: "It is so!
Because there is no discrimination regarding all phenomena."
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the pāramitā of tranquility.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because nothing can be apprehended regarding the characteristics of all phenomena.
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection of non-attachment.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
"Because all matters of sensual desire are unattainable.
"World-Honored One!
Thus, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection of non-ill will."
The Buddha said: "It is so!
Because it destroys all matters of ill-will."
“World-Honored One!
This perfection of wisdom is the perfection of non-delusion.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because it extinguishes all the darkness of ignorance.
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection free from afflictions.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
“Because it is free from conceptual discrimination. “World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the pāramitā that is free from sentient beings.”
The Buddha said: “It is so!
For one penetrates that all sentient beings are non-existent.”
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the pāramitā that is without interruption or destruction.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! For this can give rise to all phenomena.
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection that is free from the two extremes.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
"Because it is free from the two extremes.
"World-Honored One!
Thus, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection that is without confusion or destruction."
The Buddha said, “It is so!
Because one knows that all dharmas are not mutually connected.”
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the pāramitā of non-attachment.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because they transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, this perfection of wisdom is the non-conceptual perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
"Because all conceptual discriminations are unapprehendable.
"World-Honored One!
This perfection of wisdom is the limitless perfection."
The Buddha said: "It is so!
Because the delimitations of all phenomena cannot be apprehended."
“World-Honored One!
This prajñāpāramitā is the prajñāpāramitā that is like space.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because one penetrates all phenomena without obstruction.
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection of impermanence.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
"Because it can eternally extinguish and destroy all phenomena.
"World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the Pāramitā of Suffering."
The Buddha said: “It is so!
Because it can forever expel all dharmas.”
“World-Honored One!
This perfection of wisdom is the perfection of non-self.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because there is no attachment to any phenomena.
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection of emptiness.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
“Because nothing is apprehended in any phenomena.
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the pāramitā of non-momentariness.”
The Buddha said: “It is so!
Because there is no movement or shifting within all phenomena.”
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the Pāramitā of Internal Emptiness.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! For one thoroughly realizes that internal phenomena are unattainable.
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection of external emptiness.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
"Because one thoroughly realizes that external phenomena are unapprehendable.
"World-Honored One!
This perfection of wisdom is the perfection of internal-and-external emptiness."
The Buddha said: "It is so!
Because internal and external phenomena are found to be unobtainable."
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the Pāramitā of Emptiness-of-Emptiness.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because the dharma of the emptiness of emptiness is unattainable.
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, the perfection of wisdom is the perfection of great emptiness.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
"Because all phenomena are realized to be unattainable.
"World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the Pāramitā of Ultimate Emptiness."
The Buddha said:
"It is so! Because quiescent nirvana cannot be apprehended."
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the pāramitā of conditioned emptiness.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are unapprehendable.
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection of the emptiness of the unconditioned.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
“Because all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) are unapprehendable.
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the Pāramitā of ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).”
The Buddha said: "It is so!
Because the dharma of ultimate emptiness cannot be apprehended."
“World-Honored One!
This prajñāpāramitā is the pāramitā of the emptiness of the limitless.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because the dharma of the emptiness of the limitless is unapprehendable.
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection of the emptiness of the non-dispersal of that which is dispersed.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
"Because the dharma of the emptiness of non-dispersal and non-non-dispersal cannot be apprehended.
"World-Honored One!
This perfection of wisdom is the perfection of the emptiness of intrinsic nature."
The Buddha said: "It is so!
Because conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are unapprehendable."
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the pāramitā of the emptiness of both self-characteristics and common characteristics.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! For one who has realized that dharmas are remote from both specific and general characteristics.
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, the perfection of wisdom is the perfection of the emptiness of all phenomena.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
“Because one knows that internal and external phenomena are unapprehendable.
“World-Honored One!
Thus, this Prajñāpāramitā is the Pāramitā of the emptiness of the unapprehendable.”
The Buddha said: “It is so!
Because the nature of all phenomena is unapprehendable.”
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the pāramitā of the emptiness of non-existence.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because dharmas that are empty of intrinsic nature cannot be apprehended.
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection of the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
"Because the dharmas that are empty of intrinsic nature cannot be apprehended.
"World-Honored One!
Thus, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence."
The Buddha said: "It is so!
Because the dharma of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-nature cannot be apprehended."
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the Pāramitā of the Four Foundations of Mindfulness.
The Buddha said:
“So it is! Because body, sensation, mind, and phenomena cannot be apprehended.
“World-Honored One!”
"In this way, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection of the four right endeavors.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
"Because wholesome and unwholesome dharmas cannot be apprehended.
"World-Honored One!
This perfection of wisdom is the perfection of the four bases of psychic power."
The Buddha said: "It is so!
Because the nature of the four bases of psychic power cannot be apprehended."
“World-Honored One!
This prajñāpāramitā is the pāramitā of the five faculties.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because the intrinsic nature of the five faculties cannot be apprehended.
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection of the five powers.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
“Because the intrinsic nature of the five powers cannot be apprehended.
“World-Honored One!
This perfection of wisdom is the perfection of the seven factors of enlightenment.”
The Buddha said: “It is so!
For the nature of the seven factors of enlightenment is unattainable.”
“World-Honored One!
This perfection of wisdom is the perfection of the eightfold noble path.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because the nature of the eight branches of the noble path cannot be apprehended.
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection of the gate of liberation that is emptiness.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
“Because the characteristics of emptiness are unapprehendable due to its being detached from formative activity. “World-Honored One!
Thus, this Prajñāpāramitā is the pāramitā of the signless door of liberation.”
The Buddha said: “It is so!
Because the characteristics of tranquil conduct cannot be apprehended.”
“World-Honored One!
This perfection of wisdom is the perfection of wishlessness.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because the characteristic of wishlessness cannot be apprehended.
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection of the eight liberations.
The Buddha said: "So it is!"
"Because the nature of the eight liberations cannot be apprehended.
"World-Honored One!
This perfection of wisdom is the perfection of the nine successive attainments."
The Buddha said: "It is so!
Because the intrinsic nature of the nine successive concentrations is unapprehendable."
“World-Honored One!
This perfection of wisdom is the perfection of giving.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! For herein, stinginess and greed are unfindable.
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection of ethical discipline.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
"Because within this, the breaking of precepts cannot be apprehended.
"World-Honored One!
This prajñāpāramitā is the kṣāntipāramitā."
The Buddha said: "It is so!
Because within this, malice is unfindable."
“World-Honored One!
This perfection of wisdom is the perfection of diligence.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! For herein, indolence cannot be apprehended.
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection of meditative concentration.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
"Because within this, a distracted mind cannot be apprehended.
"World-Honored One!
Such a prajñāpāramitā is indeed the prajñāpāramitā."
The Buddha said: "It is so!
Because within this, corrupt wisdom cannot be apprehended."
“World-Honored One!
This perfection of wisdom is the perfection of the ten powers of a Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! For all dharmas are difficult to subdue.
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection of the four fearlessnesses.
The Buddha said, "So it is!"
Because it attains the wisdom of the marks of the Path and is without retrogression or decline.
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the Pāramitā of the four kinds of unimpeded analytical knowledge.”
The Buddha said: "It is so!
Because one has attained all-knowledge and the knowledge of all aspects without hindrance."
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the perfection of great loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because one does not abandon any sentient beings.
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. The Buddha said, "So it is!"
"Because it transcends the dharmas of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
"So it is, World-Honored One!"
"The Prajñāpāramitā is the Tathāgata’s pāramitā. The Buddha said, "So it is!"
"Because it can explain all phenomena as they truly are.
"World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the natural pāramitā."
The Buddha said: "It is so!
Because they exercise mastery over all dharmas."
“World-Honored One!
This perfection of wisdom is the perfection of perfect enlightenment.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because one is able to manifest full awakening regarding all phenomena and all modes of appearance. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Fascicle 437.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle Four Hundred and Thirty-Eight.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.
43. Chapter on the Northeast, Part Two, Chapter Forty-three, Part One. At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, had this thought:

"If good sons and good daughters who hear the name of this profound Dharma-gate of the *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtra but once, those good sons and good daughters must have already approached, made offerings to, and made vast vows before immeasurable Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas in the past; they must have planted various roots of goodness and been sustained by many spiritual friends. How much more so for those who can copy it, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, contemplate it according to the principle, explain it to others, or even practice according to the teaching to the best of their ability!"

It should be known that this person must have, in the past, personally approached, served, made offerings to, honored, respected, and praised immeasurable Buddhas; they have planted the roots of manifold virtues, heard the *prajñāpāramitā*, and having heard it, they have upheld, contemplated, recited, and explained it to others, practicing according to the teaching, or were able to question and answer regarding this sutra. By the power of such merit, they have now accomplished this matter.

If sons or daughters of good family have already made offerings to immeasurable Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their merit is pure, then upon hearing this Prajñāpāramitā, their minds will not be startled, terrified, or afraid; having heard it, they will believe and rejoice in it, practicing according to what is taught. It should be known that such persons, because they cultivated the perfections from generosity up to wisdom over many hundreds of thousands of kalpas in the past, are able to accomplish this matter in their present life.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If good sons and good daughters, upon hearing the meaning and purport contained within this profound *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtra, are not startled, not terrified, and do not give rise to doubt; and having heard it, they receive, uphold, contemplate, recite, transcribe, explain, and practice according to the teaching—then one should know that these persons have attained non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
Why is this? World-Honored One!

The meaning and purpose of this *prajñāpāramitā* are so profound and extremely difficult to believe and understand; how could one who has not practiced the *pāramitās* of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom for a long time in previous lives be able to believe and understand it merely upon hearing it for a moment?
“World-Honored One!

If good sons or good daughters hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being spoken and revile or slander it, one should know that these persons, because their minds were shrouded by greed, hatred, and delusion in previous lives, have likewise previously reviled this profound sūtra of the *prajñāpāramitā*.”
Why is this? World-Honored One!

When such deluded people hear the profound meaning and intent of the *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, due to the power of their habitual tendencies, they lack faith and joy, and their minds are not pure.
Why is this? Because such deluded persons, in past lives, have never drawn near to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, or the assembly of disciples, nor have they ever inquired:
"How should one practice the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā) up to the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)?"
How should one dwell in the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature?
How should one cultivate the four applications of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path?
How should one train in the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha?
"Therefore, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught now, they disparage and slander it, neither believing nor delighting in it, because their minds are not pure.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Thus, the meaning and intent of this *prajñāpāramitā* are extremely profound and exceedingly difficult to believe and understand.
If sons or daughters of good family have not for long believed in and delighted in the practice of the *dānapāramitā* up to the *prajñāpāramitā*,

and have not for long believed in and delighted in abiding in the emptiness of the internal (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) up to [the emptiness of the non-existence of all phenomena], [they will find it difficult to believe].
The nature of self-nature is empty; they have not long been devoted to or practiced the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path,
nor have they long been devoted to or practiced the eight liberations, the nine successive attainments, or the five supernormal powers,
nor have they long been devoted to or trained in the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, or the four [factors of intrepidity] of a Tathāgata.
The analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), great sympathetic joy (*mahāmuditā*), great equanimity (*mahopekṣā*),
the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), and other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas—
if good sons and good daughters hear this profound meaning and intent of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, they may be unable to believe and understand it, or they may even give rise to disparagement.
"O World-Honored One, it is not at all rare for one to slander [this teaching].
I now pay homage to the profound Prajñāpāramitā."
“World-Honored One!
If I pay homage to the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, it is as if I were paying homage to all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying:
"So it is! So it is! It is just as you have said."
To pay homage to the Prajñāpāramitā is to pay homage to the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā).
Why is this so, Kauśika?

Because all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas—whether it be their omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), their knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), or their knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)—are all born from the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Kauśika! If sons or daughters of good family wish to abide in the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all aspects, they should abide in the perfection of wisdom;
if they wish to give rise to the Tathāgata’s omniscience, the knowledge of the paths, and other meritorious qualities, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
Those who wish to permanently sever the continuity of all afflictions and their habitual tendencies should study the Prajñāpāramitā;
those who wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, and deliver sentient beings should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

Kauśika! If good sons and good daughters wish to attain the fruit of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
Kauśika! If good sons and good daughters wish to properly establish those sentient beings of the śrāvaka lineage in the Śrāvaka Vehicle, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā;
if they wish to properly establish those sentient beings of the pratyekabuddha lineage in the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

Those who wish to properly establish sentient beings of the Mahāyāna lineage in the Unsurpassed Vehicle, and cause them to swiftly realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek, should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
Kauśika! If sons or daughters of good family wish to attain the most supreme merit within the triple world, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā;
if they wish to subdue all factions of darkness, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
"One who wishes to properly sustain the community of bhikṣus should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, how do they abide in form?
How do they abide in feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?
How does one abide in the eye, up to and including the mind?
How does one abide in forms, up to and including mental phenomena?
How does one abide in eye-consciousness, up to and including mind-consciousness?
How does one abide in the perfection of wisdom, up to and including the perfection of generosity?
How does one abide in internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature?
"How does one abide in the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path?
How does one abide in the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha? O Bhagavān!"
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, how do they cultivate form?
How do they cultivate feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?
"...up to: how does one practice the ten powers of a Buddha, up to practicing the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha?
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, saying: "Kauśika!"
Excellent! Excellent!
It is because you now rely on the Buddha’s spiritual power that you are able to question the Tathāgata regarding such a profound meaning.
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well!
"I shall now analyze and explain this for you.

Kausika! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), if they do not dwell upon or cultivate form (rūpa), this is precisely what it means to dwell upon and cultivate form."
If one does not dwell upon nor cultivate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, this is to dwell upon and cultivate feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
if one does not dwell upon nor cultivate the eye up to the mind, this is to dwell upon and cultivate the eye up to the mind;
if one does not dwell upon nor cultivate forms up to phenomena, this is to dwell upon and cultivate forms up to phenomena.
If one does not dwell upon nor cultivate anything from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness, this is the dwelling upon and cultivation of eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness;

if one does not dwell upon nor cultivate anything from the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity, this is the dwelling upon and cultivation of the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity;

if one does not dwell upon nor cultivate anything from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, this is the dwelling upon and cultivation of internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.

If one does not dwell upon nor practice the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, this is called dwelling upon and practicing the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;

if one does not dwell upon nor practice the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, this is called dwelling upon and practicing the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Why is this? Kauśika!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they find nothing in form (rūpa) that can be dwelt upon or cultivated; they find nothing in feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), formations (saṃskāra), or consciousness (vijñāna) that can be dwelt upon or cultivated; and so on, up to the ten powers of a Buddha (buddhabala), for which they find nothing that can be dwelt upon or cultivated, and even up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇikabuddhadharma), for which they find nothing that can be dwelt upon or cultivated.

"Furthermore, Kauśika, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), if they neither abide nor do not abide in form (rūpa), and neither cultivate nor do not cultivate it, this is called abiding in and cultivating form;

if they neither abide nor do not abide in feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), formations (saṃskāra), and consciousness (vijñāna), and neither cultivate nor do not cultivate them, this is called abiding in and cultivating feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness."
If one neither dwells nor does not dwell, neither practices nor does not practice, with respect to the eye up to the mind, this is called dwelling in the practice of the eye up to the mind;

if one neither dwells nor does not dwell, neither practices nor does not practice, with respect to forms up to mental phenomena (*dharma*), this is called dwelling in the practice of forms up to mental phenomena;

if one neither dwells nor does not dwell, neither practices nor does not practice, with respect to eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness, this is called dwelling in the practice of eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness.

If one neither dwells nor does not dwell, neither practices nor does not practice, in the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity, this is dwelling in and practicing the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity;

if one neither dwells nor does not dwell, neither practices nor does not practice, in inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature, this is dwelling in and practicing inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature;

if one neither dwells nor does not dwell, neither practices nor does not practice, in the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, this is dwelling in and practicing the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path.

If one neither abides nor does not abide in the Buddha’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and neither practices nor does not practice them, this is called abiding in and practicing the Buddha’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Why is this? Kauśika!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they observe that form (rūpa) is unapprehendable in the past, unapprehendable in the future, and unapprehendable in the present; they observe that feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), formations (saṃskāra), and consciousness (vijñāna) are unapprehendable in the past, unapprehendable in the future, and unapprehendable in the present; and so on, up to observing that the ten powers of a Buddha (buddhabala) are unapprehendable in the past, unapprehendable in the future, and unapprehendable in the present; and so on, up to observing that the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇikabuddhadharma) are unapprehendable in the past, unapprehendable in the future, and unapprehendable in the present.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is most profound.”
The Buddha said: “So it is, Śāriputra!
Because the suchness of form is profoundly deep, the perfection of wisdom is most profound.”
Because the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is profoundly deep, the perfection of wisdom is most profound;
likewise, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, because their suchness is profoundly deep, the perfection of wisdom is most profound.
Then, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is difficult to fathom.”
The Buddha said:
"It is so, Śāriputra! Because the suchness of form (rūpa-tathatā) is difficult to measure, the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is difficult to measure."
Because the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is difficult to measure, the perfection of wisdom is difficult to measure;
and so on, up to: because the suchness of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha is difficult to measure, the perfection of wisdom is difficult to measure.
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is thus most immeasurable."
The Buddha said:
“It is so, Śāriputra! Because the suchness of form is immeasurable, the perfection of wisdom is also immeasurable;”
Because the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is immeasurable, the perfection of wisdom is also immeasurable;
and so on, up to: because the suchness of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha is immeasurable, the perfection of wisdom is also immeasurable.

“Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, not practicing the profound nature of form is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing the profound nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is practicing the perfection of wisdom;
not practicing the profound nature of the eye is practicing the perfection of wisdom, and so on, up to not practicing the profound nature of the mind is practicing the perfection of wisdom.”

Not practicing the profound nature of form is practicing the perfection of wisdom; likewise, not practicing the profound nature of phenomena up to the point of not practicing the profound nature of consciousness is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing the profound nature of eye-consciousness is practicing the perfection of wisdom; likewise, not practicing the profound nature of mental-consciousness is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing the profound nature of the perfection of wisdom is practicing the perfection of wisdom; likewise, not practicing the profound nature of the perfection of generosity is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing the profound nature of internal emptiness is practicing the perfection of wisdom; likewise, not practicing the profound nature of the emptiness of non-existence and intrinsic nature is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing the profound nature of the four foundations of mindfulness is practicing the perfection of wisdom; likewise, not practicing the profound nature of the eightfold noble path is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing the profound nature of the ten powers of a Buddha is practicing the perfection of wisdom; likewise, not practicing the profound nature of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Śāriputra, because the profound nature of form is not form;

the profound nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is not feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; and so on, up to the profound nature of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, which is not the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they do not practice by way of the unfathomable nature of form, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they do not practice by way of the unfathomable nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom;

if they do not practice by way of the unfathomable nature of the eye, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom, and so on, up to: if they do not practice by way of the unfathomable nature of the mind, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom."

Not practicing the immeasurability of form is practicing the perfection of wisdom; likewise, not practicing the immeasurability of any phenomenon up to and including mental phenomena is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing the immeasurability of eye-consciousness is practicing the perfection of wisdom; likewise, not practicing the immeasurability of consciousness up to and including mental consciousness is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing the immeasurability of the perfection of wisdom is practicing the perfection of wisdom; likewise, not practicing the immeasurability of the perfection of generosity up to and including the perfection of wisdom is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

To not practice the unfathomable nature of internal emptiness is to practice the perfection of wisdom; even to not practice the unfathomable nature of the emptiness of non-existence and intrinsic nature is to practice the perfection of wisdom;

to not practice the unfathomable nature of the four applications of mindfulness is to practice the perfection of wisdom; even to not practice the unfathomable nature of the eightfold noble path is to practice the perfection of wisdom;

to not practice the unfathomable nature of the ten powers of a Buddha is to practice the perfection of wisdom; even to not practice the unfathomable nature of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha is to practice the perfection of wisdom.

Why is this? Śāriputra, because the nature of form that is difficult to measure is not form; the nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that is difficult to measure is not feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; and so on, up to the nature of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha that is difficult to measure is not the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, not practicing the immeasurability of form is practicing the perfection of wisdom; not practicing the immeasurability of feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness is practicing the perfection of wisdom;
not practicing the immeasurability of the eye is practicing the perfection of wisdom, and so on, up to not practicing the immeasurability of the mind is practicing the perfection of wisdom."
Not practicing the immeasurability of form is practicing the perfection of wisdom; likewise, not practicing the immeasurability of phenomena is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing the immeasurability of eye-consciousness is practicing the perfection of wisdom; likewise, not practicing the immeasurability of mind-consciousness is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing the immeasurability of the perfection of wisdom is practicing the perfection of wisdom; likewise, not practicing the immeasurability of the perfection of generosity is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing the immeasurability of internal emptiness is practicing the perfection of wisdom; up to and including not practicing the immeasurability of the emptiness of non-existence and intrinsic nature is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing the immeasurability of the four foundations of mindfulness is practicing the perfection of wisdom; up to and including not practicing the immeasurability of the eightfold noble path is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not practicing the immeasurability of the ten powers of a Buddha is practicing the perfection of wisdom; up to and including not practicing the immeasurability of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Śāriputra, because the immeasurable nature of form is not form;

the immeasurable nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is not feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; and so on, up to the immeasurable nature of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, which is not the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Since this Prajñāpāramitā is thus most profound, difficult to fathom, immeasurable, and difficult to believe and understand, it should not be taught before those bodhisattvas who have newly set out in the Mahāyāna.”
Do not let them hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, lest their minds become startled, terrified, or hesitant, and they fail to believe or understand it.

Rather, you should speak it only before those bodhisattvas who are in the stage of non-retrogression; when they hear such profound *prajñāpāramitā*, their minds will not be startled, nor will they be afraid, terrified, or hesitant. Having heard it, they will believe and understand it, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, reflect upon it according to the principle, and explain it to others.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked Śāriputra:
"Venerable One, what fault is there in speaking such Prajñāpāramitā before a newly trained bodhisattva mahāsattva?"
Śāriputra said: “Kauśika!

If one were to speak such a *prajñāpāramitā* in the presence of a newly trained bodhisattva mahāsattva, that person would hear it with alarm, terror, and hesitation; they would be unable to believe or understand it, or might even give rise to slander. By this, they would create and increase karma that leads to rebirth in the evil destinies, sinking into the three miserable realms and dwelling long in saṃsāra, making it difficult for them to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Therefore, a wise person should not speak such a *prajñāpāramitā* in the presence of a newly trained bodhisattva mahāsattva.”
Then Śakra, the Lord of Devas, again asked the Venerable Śāriputra: "Venerable One, is there any bodhisattva who,

though not yet having received the prediction of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, upon hearing this profound perfection of wisdom spoken, does not become startled, alarmed, terrified, or hesitant?"
Śāriputra said: "There is, Kauśika!"
This bodhisattva mahāsattva shall before long receive the prediction of great enlightenment. Kausika!

If, upon hearing this profound perfection of wisdom being taught, a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s mind is not startled, terrified, or afraid, and is free from hesitation, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has already received the prediction of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
If they have not yet received it, they will, after no more than one or two Buddhas, certainly receive the prophecy of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi-vyākaraṇa*).
Were it otherwise, their minds would surely become startled, terrified, and hesitant upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is as you have said, Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva has long studied the Mahāyāna, long generated the great vows, long cultivated the six perfections and other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas, long made offerings to, honored, revered, and praised immeasurable and boundless Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and long served immeasurable and boundless spiritual friends."

By virtue of these causes and conditions, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, their minds will not be startled, terrified, or frightened, nor will they fall into hesitation; having heard it, they will believe and understand it, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, contemplate it according to the principle, and explain it to others, or perhaps write it down and practice in accordance with what has been taught.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I now wish to speak a few illustrative analogies concerning the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion, will grant me leave to do so.”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Regarding that which you wish to speak, speak according to your own inclination. Śāriputra said:

“Bhagavān! Suppose there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who abide in the bodhisattva vehicle, and who, even in their dreams, practice the perfections of wisdom, meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity; who abide in inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature; who practice the four applications of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; who practice the ten powers of a buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha; who practice all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects; and who proceed toward the tree of enlightenment until they sit upon the sublime seat of awakening.”

You should know that these sons and daughters of good family are already close to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; how much more so for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, seeking unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, practices the perfections of wisdom, meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity during the waking state; who dwells in the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature; who practices the four applications of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; who practices the ten powers of a buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha; and who practices all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects—how could such a one not swiftly realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek?

World-Honored One, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva will before long proceed beneath the Bodhi tree; before long he will sit upon the sublime seat of enlightenment, realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening, and turn the sublime wheel of Dharma to bring benefit and happiness to all.
"Blessed One!

If sons or daughters of good family hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, diligently practice and study it, and contemplate it according to the principle, one should know that these sons and daughters of good family have long studied the Mahāyāna, their roots of virtue are matured, they have made offerings to the Buddhas, attended upon many spiritual friends, and planted the foundations of all merit; thus are they able to accomplish such a feat."

“Bhagavān! If sons or daughters of good family hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and having heard it, believe and understand it, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, practice it, contemplate it according to the principle, and explain it to others—these sons or daughters of good family have either already received the prediction of great enlightenment, or they are close to receiving the prediction of great enlightenment.”
"Blessed One!

These sons and daughters of good family are like Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas established in the stage of non-retrogression; they will swiftly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Because of this, they are able to hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and can develop deep faith and understanding, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, contemplate it according to principle, practice in accordance with its teachings, and explain it to others."
“World-Honored One!

It is as if there were a person traveling through a vast wilderness, passing through dangerous paths for a hundred *yojana*s, or two, three, four, or five hundred. Seeing the preliminary signs of a city or royal capital—such as herdsmen, groves, fields, and the like—and having seen these signs, he would think:
‘The city or royal capital is not far from here.’”
Having formed this thought, his body and mind became serene; he feared neither wild beasts, nor evil bandits, nor hunger and thirst.
World-Honored One!

It is the same for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: if they hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, contemplate it according to principle, and give rise to deep faith and understanding, you should know that before long they shall receive a prediction of enlightenment, or have already received it, and will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have no fear of falling into the stages of the śrāvaka or the pratyekabuddha.
Why is this? World-Honored One!
It is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva has already seen, heard, paid homage to, and made offerings to the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, which is the precursor sign of unsurpassed enlightenment.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is as you have said.
Sustained by the Buddha's power, you should speak further on this.
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is as if there were a person who, wishing to behold the great ocean, traveled toward it for a long time without seeing any mountains or forests; he would then think:
‘Seeing these signs now, the great ocean is not far away.’”
Why is this? For land near the seashore must gradually slope downward and be devoid of mountains and forests.
At that time, although that person had not yet seen the sea, seeing these proximate signs, he was filled with joy and leaped for gladness.
“‘I shall surely and swiftly behold the great ocean.

World-Honored One, it is just so for the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: if they hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, contemplate it according to principle, and give rise to deep faith and understanding, then although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have not yet received a face-to-face prophecy from a Buddha:”

"In a future age, after such eons—whether it be a hundred eons, a thousand eons, a hundred thousand eons, or even as many as a hundred thousand koṭi-nayuta eons—you shall attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Thus, one should know for oneself that the prediction of enlightenment is not far off. Why is this?
World-Honored One!"

This is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have already obtained the vision and hearing of, paid reverence and made offerings to, upheld, recited, and reflected upon according to reason upon the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, which is the precursor sign of unsurpassed awakening.
“World-Honored One!
It is like the flowering and fruiting trees during the springtime; when their withered leaves have fallen and their branches and twigs are lush and moist, all people who see them say:
‘New flowers, fruits, and leaves will soon emerge.’”
"Why is this? Because these signs have first appeared upon these trees—their new flowers, fruits, and leaves.
Having seen these signs, the men and women, the great and small, of Jambudvīpa were filled with joy and leaped for gladness, all saying these words:
“World-Honored One! Just as we shall soon behold this abundance of flowers and fruit, so too it is with the bodhisattva mahāsattvas:

if they hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, contemplate it according to the principle, give rise to deep faith and understanding, and pay it respectful homage and offerings, one should know that their roots of goodness from past lives have matured, that they have made many offerings to the Buddhas, and have served many spiritual friends; they shall before long receive the prediction of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
"Bhagavān! This bodhisattva mahāsattva should form this thought:

'I must certainly have possessed superior roots of goodness in the past, capable of attracting unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; therefore, I now see, hear, revere, and make offerings to this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and I uphold, recite, develop deep faith and understanding, contemplate it according to principle, and practice it to the best of my ability.'"
“World-Honored One!
Now, within this assembly, there are sons of the gods who have seen past Buddhas preach this Dharma; they all give rise to joy and together deliberate, saying:

‘In the past, when Bodhisattvas heard such profound Prajñāpāramitā being preached, they immediately received their prediction [of enlightenment]. Now that these Bodhisattvas have heard this profound Prajñāpāramitā being preached, it is certain that before long they shall receive the prediction of Bodhi.’”

“World-Honored One! It is like a woman who has been pregnant for some time; her body becomes increasingly heavy and her movements become unstable. Her food, drink, and sleep all diminish; she takes no pleasure in much speech and grows weary of her usual activities. Because she suffers pain, all her affairs suddenly come to a halt.”
World-Honored One, it is just as when a woman with other children sees these signs and immediately knows that this girl will give birth before long.

World-Honored One, it is likewise for the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: having planted roots of goodness in the past, having made many offerings to the Buddhas, and having long served virtuous friends, because their roots of goodness have matured, they now hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, contemplate it according to the principle, develop deep faith and understanding, and practice it according to their capacity.
“World-Honored One,
you should know that by virtue of these causes and conditions, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will, before long, receive the prediction of unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete enlightenment. At that time, the Buddha praised Śāriputra, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!

It is well that you are able to speak thus regarding the parables of bodhisattvas who hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, uphold it, recite it, contemplate it according to the principle, and give rise to deep faith and understanding. You should know that all this is due to the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, which has inspired such eloquence in you.”
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How marvelous!"
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is well able to sustain all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and well able to entrust all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said. Why is this so? Subhūti!

The bodhisattva-mahāsattvas seek to proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of bringing benefit and happiness to many sentient beings, and out of compassion to enrich all devas and humans.

When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas diligently train in the bodhisattva practices, they do so for the sake of benefiting immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings and for the sake of gathering in immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas, thereby embracing them through the four means of attraction.
What are the four? First, giving; second, kind speech.
Third is beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*).
Fourth is cooperation (*samānārthatā*).
These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas themselves correctly abide in the ten paths of wholesome action and also establish others, causing them to diligently train in the ten paths of wholesome action.
From entering the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, they also teach others to enter the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
they personally practice giving and also teach others to practice giving;
they personally observe pure ethical discipline and also teach others to observe pure ethical discipline.
They practice patience themselves and also teach others to practice patience;
they practice diligence themselves and also teach others to practice diligence;
they practice meditative concentration themselves and also teach others to practice meditative concentration.
They practice prajñā themselves and also teach others to practice prajñā.
Relying on the skillful means of the perfection of prajñā, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, although they teach sentient beings to realize the fruit of stream-entry, do not realize it themselves;
although they teach sentient beings to realize the fruit of once-returning, they do not realize it themselves.
Although he teaches sentient beings to realize the fruit of non-returning, he does not realize it himself;
