Any sons or daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle, yet abandon the profound sūtras of the *prajñāpāramitā* to seek and study other sūtras—know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
Why is this? Subhūti!

Because these sons and daughters of good family abandon the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, which is the root of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), and instead grasp at the branches and leaves of other sūtras; they will ultimately be unable to attain great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
what other sūtras are like branches and leaves, unable to bring forth the knowledge of all aspects?"
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

If one speaks of the dharmas associated with the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, as well as all the sūtras concerning the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—if a son or daughter of good family practices and studies therein, they may attain the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, the fruit of arhatship, or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, but they will not attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. These are called ‘other sūtras,’ which are like branches and leaves; they cannot bring forth the knowledge of all aspects.”
The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is certainly able to bring forth all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), possessing great power and function like the roots of a tree.
If these sons and daughters of good family abandon the profound sūtras of the *prajñāpāramitā* to seek and study other sūtras, they will certainly be unable to attain all-aspect omniscience.
Why is this? Subhūti!
It is because this profound sūtra of the perfection of wisdom gives birth to the mundane and supramundane dharmas of merit for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

Therefore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the profound sūtras of the perfection of wisdom, they are training in all the mundane and supramundane virtuous dharmas and merits of the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

It is as if a starving dog, having abandoned the food of its master, instead seeks it out from the servants. In a future age, there will be sons and daughters of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle who likewise abandon the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the very root of all Buddha-dharma, and seek to study the sūtras associated with the two vehicles; you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Suppose there were a person who, desiring to seek a fragrant elephant, having found this elephant, would abandon it to seek its tracks.
What do you think?"
"Would such a person be considered wise?
Subhūti replied, "Such a person would not be considered wise."
The Buddha said, "Subhūti!

In future ages, there will be sons and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who abandon the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the root of all buddha-dharmas, and instead seek to study scriptures associated with the two vehicles; this, likewise, should be known as a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
It is as if there were a person who wished to see the great ocean; having beheld the great ocean, they instead looked at a cow’s footprint and thought to themselves:
'How could the measure of the water in the great ocean—its depth and breadth—possibly compare to this?'"
“What do you think? Is this person wise? Subhūti replied:
“This person is not wise,” the Buddha said. “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
[He is not wise.]”

In future ages, there will be sons and daughters of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle who abandon the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the root of all Buddha-dharmas, and instead seek to study scriptures associated with the two vehicles; this, too, should be known as a demonic deed (*mārakarman*) of a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

It is as if there were a master carpenter or his apprentice who, wishing to construct a great palace equal in measure to the magnificent palace of Śakra, Lord of the Devas, were to see that palace and instead attempt to take the dimensions of the palaces of the sun and moon."
"What do you think?
Could such a craftsman or his disciple build a great hall equal in measure to the sublime palace of Śakra? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! No!"
“Excellent, Sugata!
The Buddha said,
“Excellent, Subhūti!”
"What do you think? Is this person wise? Subhūti replied:
"This person is not wise; he belongs to the class of the deluded.
The Buddha said, "Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

In future ages, there will be sons and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who, desiring to seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, abandon such profound *prajñāpāramitā* and instead seek to study the sūtras associated with the two vehicles; it shall be just so.
"He will certainly not attain the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, it is like a person who seeks to see a universal monarch (cakravartin), but having seen him, is unable to properly grasp his physical characteristics and then goes elsewhere; there he sees an ordinary minor king, grasps his physical characteristics, and forms this thought:"
"How does the physical form, appearance, and majestic power of a Wheel-Turning Sage King differ from this?
What do you think: would such a person be considered wise?"
Subhūti replied, "Such a person is not wise.
The Buddha said:

“Subhūti! In a future age, there will likewise be sons and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who, desiring to seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, abandon this profound *prajñāpāramitā* and instead seek to study sūtras associated with the two vehicles, saying:
‘These sūtras are no different from those; what is the use of those?’”
These sons and daughters of good family will certainly not attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek; you should know that this is an act of Māra for a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Suppose there were a hungry person who, having obtained food of a hundred flavors, cast it aside to seek out and eat a meal of wild grasses and weeds—what do you think of this?"
"Would this person be considered wise?
Subhūti replied, "This person would not be considered wise."
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

In a future age, there will be sons and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who abandon this profound sūtra of the Great Prajñāpāramitā and seek to study sūtras associated with the two vehicles; their desire to seek all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) therein shall be just like that.”

Those sons and daughters of good family will merely expend their efforts in vain and will certainly be unable to attain all-aspect omniscience; you should know that this constitutes a demonic deed for a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Suppose there were a poor man who, having obtained a priceless jewel, cast it away and instead took up a glass trinket. What do you think?"
"Would this person be considered clever?
Subhūti replied, "This person would not be considered clever."
The Buddha said, "Sudhana!

In a future age, there will be sons and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who abandon the profound sūtras of the Great Prajñāpāramitā and seek to study sūtras associated with the two vehicles; their desire to seek all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) therein shall be just like this."

Those sons and daughters of good family will merely exhaust themselves in vain and will certainly be unable to attain all-aspect omniscience; you should know that this constitutes a demonic activity for a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When sons of good family or daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle are transcribing this profound *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, they may suddenly give rise to inferior discursive thoughts (*vitarka-vicāra*). Due to these discursive thoughts, the transcription of this profound *Prajñāpāramitā* will fail to reach its completion."
What are called inferior thoughts and investigations?

They are thoughts and investigations regarding forms, or sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena; or thoughts and investigations regarding generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; or even thoughts and investigations regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—which prevent the profound *prajñāpāramitā* that has been written down from reaching its ultimate conclusion. One should know that these constitute the work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
Why is this? Subhūti!

Because the profound perfection of wisdom is without applied or sustained thought; because it is inconceivable; because it is without deliberation; because it is without arising or ceasing; because it is without defilement or purity; because it is without concentration or distraction; because it is free from names and words; because it is ineffable; and because it is unapprehendable.
Why is this so? Subhūti!
Within the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, all the dharmas previously mentioned are non-existent and entirely unapprehendable.

When sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle write out this profound *prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, such dharmas disturb their minds and prevent them from reaching completion; therefore, these are called the deeds of Māra for bodhisattvas.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
can this profound prajñāpāramitā be written down?"
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
The profound perfection of wisdom cannot be written down.”
Why is this? Subhūti!

The intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom is non-existent and unapprehendable; likewise, the intrinsic natures of the perfections of meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity are also non-existent and unapprehendable.

The intrinsic nature of internal emptiness is non-existent and unapprehendable; likewise, even the intrinsic nature of the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature is non-existent and unapprehendable.

The intrinsic nature of the four applications of mindfulness is non-existent and unapprehendable, and so on in detail until the intrinsic nature of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha is also non-existent and unapprehendable.

The intrinsic nature of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is non-existent and unapprehendable; the intrinsic natures of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are also non-existent and unapprehendable.
"Subhūti! Because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is non-existent and unapprehendable, it is itself the absence of nature; this very absence of nature is the perfection of wisdom."
A phenomenon that lacks intrinsic nature cannot write down that which lacks intrinsic nature; therefore, the *prajñāpāramitā* cannot be written down. Subhūti!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle should conceive the notion of "lack of intrinsic nature" regarding this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
Then, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
if sons of good family or daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle write down such profound *prajñāpāramitā* and form this thought:”
"I have written down this profound Prajñāpāramitā in words.
If one clings to the Prajñāpāramitā by relying on those words, it should be known that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, Subhūti! It is so!"
So it is! It is just as you have said. Why is this?

"Subhūti! In this profound *prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, form (*rūpa*) is without syllables; feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are likewise without syllables.
The eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) is without syllables; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases (*śrotra-, ghrāṇa-, jihvā-, kāya-, mana-āyatana*) are likewise without syllables."
The sense-base of form is without letters; the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are also without letters.
The eye-element is without letters; the elements of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are also without letters.
The form-element is without letters; the elements of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are also without letters.
The eye-consciousness element is without words; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements are likewise without words.
Eye-contact is without words; ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact are likewise without words.

The various sensations produced with eye-contact as a condition are without words; the various sensations produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact as conditions are likewise without words.

The perfection of wisdom is without letters; the perfections of meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity are also without letters. Inner emptiness is without letters;

outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, beginningless-and-endless emptiness, non-dispersal emptiness, essential emptiness, the emptiness of self-characteristics and common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature are also without letters.
The four applications of mindfulness are without letters; and so on, in detail, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, which are also without letters.
All-knowledge is without words; the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects are likewise without words.
Therefore, one should not cling to the notion that there are words capable of writing down the perfection of wisdom.
“Subhūti! If sons or daughters of good family who have set out in the bodhisattva vehicle should form such an attachment as this:
‘In this profound sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā, there are no syllables that are form; there are no syllables that are feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;’”

"In this way, even up to the point that the absence of characters is omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), and the absence of characters is the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
One should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
those sons of good family or daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle and who write down, receive and uphold,
read and recite, cultivate, contemplate, and explain this profound *prajñāpāramitā*..."
After some time, if he gives rise to mental attention toward a country,
or mental attention toward a city, or mental attention toward a royal capital, or mental attention toward a region, or mental attention toward his preceptor or teacher,
or mental attention toward his fellow students or virtuous friends, or mental attention toward his parents or wife and children;
If one gives rise to the mental attention of brothers and sisters; or if one gives rise to the mental attention of relatives and friends;
or if one gives rise to the mental attention of kings and ministers; or if one gives rise to the mental attention of thieves and wicked people;
or if one gives rise to the mental attention of fierce beasts and malevolent spirits; or if one gives rise to the mental attention of crowds gathered for amusement; or if...
To give rise to thoughts of sensual pleasure with courtesans, or thoughts of seeking revenge or repaying kindness,
or any other various kinds of thoughts, or even to give rise to further thoughts regarding those very thoughts—
all these are instigated by Māra the Evil One, acting as obstacles to the boundless and supreme virtues induced by the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Subhūti, you should know that this is a demonic deed of a bodhisattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when sons of good family or daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva Vehicle write down, receive, uphold, read, recite, practice, contemplate, and expound such a profound *prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, they may obtain great fame, respect, and offerings—namely, clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicinal requisites for illness, and other material wealth. If these sons or daughters of good family become attached to these things and thereby fall away from the boundless, supreme roots of virtue induced by the *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a demonic deed of a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When sons or daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle write down, uphold, read, recite, practice, contemplate, and explain this profound *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, there will be various evil Māras who hold various worldly treatises or even sūtras associated with the two vehicles, and falsely appearing as friends, they will offer them to the Bodhisattvas. These works extensively describe worldly superior matters, or else they extensively describe the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), sense bases (*āyatana*), the truths (*satya*), dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*), the three doors of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*), the four meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), and so forth, claiming that 'the meaning and flavor of these sūtras are profound and subtle; you should diligently practice and study them, and abandon the sūtras you have previously practiced.'"

These sons and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle, through their skillful means, should not accept or become attached to worldly books and treatises given by Māra, nor to scriptures associated with the two vehicles.

Why is this so? Because worldly treatises and the scriptures of the two vehicles cannot bring forth the knowledge of all aspects; they are not the unerring means for proceeding toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, but rather become obstacles to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
"Subhūti! In this profound sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā, I have extensively explained the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of the path of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva seeks skillful means within this [teaching] and diligently trains in the various practices of a bodhisattva, they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

"Subhūti! If sons or daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle abandon the skillful means of the path for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as taught in the profound sūtras of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and instead study the worldly treatises of Māra or sūtras associated with the two vehicles, you should know that this constitutes a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
Chapter 45: On Non-Harmony, Part Two, Section One of Chapter Forty-Five.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when those who are able to study the Dharma take delight in hearing, inquiring about, copying, receiving, upholding, reciting, and practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, yet those who are able to uphold the Dharma—being attached to pleasure and indolent—are unwilling to explain it for them and do not wish to bestow the profound *prajñāpāramitā* upon them, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva. Furthermore, Subhūti..."

One who is able to uphold the Dharma does not cling to pleasure nor is they indolent; they delight in preaching and delight in bestowing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and through skillful means, they encourage others to copy, receive and uphold, recite, and cultivate it. If those who are able to study the Dharma are indolent, cling to pleasure, and do not wish to listen or receive it, one should know that this is a work of Māra for the bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If those who are able to study the Dharma take delight in hearing, questioning about, writing down, receiving, upholding, reciting, and practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, yet those who are able to uphold the Dharma wish to go to another region and fail to receive instruction in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When those who uphold the Dharma delight in speaking of and delight in bestowing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, yet through skillful means they merely exhort others to copy, receive, uphold, recite, and cultivate it, while those who wish to study the Dharma are unable to hear or receive this profound *prajñāpāramitā* because they must go elsewhere—know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

One who upholds the Dharma may possess great evil desires, being deeply attached to fame, profit, clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other material requisites, and never feeling satiated by offerings or respect. Conversely, one who studies the Dharma may have few desires and be easily contented, practicing seclusion, with courageous and correct diligence, endowed with mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, and feeling weary of and fearful toward gain, honor, and reputation. When these two do not harmonize, they will fail to obtain instruction in, listen to, transcribe, uphold, recite, or cultivate the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Those who can uphold the Dharma have few desires and are content;

they practice seclusion, possess courageous and correct diligence, and are endowed with mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. They loathe and fear gain, honor, and reputation. Yet those who are able to study the Dharma possess great and wicked desires, craving and valuing fame, profit, clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other material wealth. Their hearts are never satiated by offerings, honor, and respect. Because these two parties do not harmonize, they fail to obtain instruction, listening, copying, upholding, reciting, and practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! Those who are able to uphold the Dharma are endowed with the twelve dhūta-guṇas (ascetic virtues), namely: dwelling in the forest (āraṇyaka), always begging for food (piṇḍapātika), wearing rag-robes (pāṃsukūlika), eating one meal a day (khalupaścādbhaktika), eating in a single sitting (aikāsanika), eating whatever is obtained (yathāsaṃstarika), dwelling among tombs (śmāśānika), dwelling in the open air (ābhyavakāśika), dwelling at the foot of a tree (vṛkṣamūlika), always sitting without lying down (naiṣadyika), using whatever bedding is available (yathāsaṃstarika), and possessing only the three robes (traicīvarika). Those who are able to study the Dharma do not accept these twelve dhūta-guṇas—meaning they do not dwell in the forest, and so forth, up to not possessing only the three robes. When these two [groups] are not in harmony, they fail to receive instruction, listen to it, write it down, uphold it, recite it, or cultivate the profound Prajñāpāramitā. You should know that this constitutes a Māra-activity of a bodhisattva."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! Those who are able to study the Dharma are endowed with the twelve dhūta-guṇas, namely: dwelling in an araṇya, up to and including possessing only three robes. Those who are able to uphold the Dharma do not accept the twelve dhūta-guṇas, namely: not dwelling in an araṇya, up to and including not possessing only three robes. When these two are not in harmony, they fail to obtain instruction, listening, writing, upholding, reciting, and practicing the profound Prajñāpāramitā; you should know that this constitutes a Māra-activity of a bodhisattva."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose there is one who upholds the Dharma and possesses faith and wholesome qualities, desiring to explain the profound *prajñāpāramitā* to others, and exerts skillful means to encourage them to copy, receive, uphold, recite, and cultivate it; yet there is one who studies the Dharma but lacks faith and wholesome qualities, taking no pleasure in hearing or receiving it. Because these two are not in harmony, they fail to obtain instruction, hearing, copying, upholding, reciting, or cultivating the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There may be one who studies the Dharma and possesses faith and wholesome qualities, seeking to hear, inquire about, write down, receive, uphold, recite, and practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*; yet there may be one who upholds the Dharma but lacks faith and wholesome qualities, having no desire to provide instruction. Because these two do not harmonize, they fail to obtain instruction, hearing, receiving, writing, upholding, reciting, or practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

One who is able to uphold the Dharma has a mind free from stinginess and is able to relinquish everything, whereas one who is able to study the Dharma has a mind possessed by stinginess and is unable to give away. Because these two are not in harmony, they do not obtain the instruction, hearing, writing, upholding, reciting, or cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

One who is able to study the Dharma has a mind free from stinginess and is able to relinquish everything; one who is able to uphold the Dharma has a mind possessed of stinginess and is unable to give away. Because these two are not in harmony, they do not obtain the teaching, nor the hearing, writing, upholding, reciting, or cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If one who is able to study the Dharma seeks to provide offerings—such as clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other necessities—to one who is able to uphold the Dharma, yet the upholder of the Dharma does not wish to accept them, and because of this lack of harmony, they fail to obtain the teaching, listening, copying, reciting, and cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If one who is able to uphold the Dharma desires to provide the robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other necessities for one who is able to study the Dharma, yet that one who studies the Dharma does not wish to accept them, and because of this lack of harmony, they fail to receive instruction, listen to, write down, recite, or cultivate the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

One who upholds the Dharma possesses the wisdom of exposition but does not delight in extensive explanation; one who studies the Dharma possesses the wisdom of performance but does not delight in concise summary. When these two do not harmonize, they fail to obtain the teaching, listening, writing, upholding, reciting, and practicing of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

One who is able to study the Dharma achieves the wisdom of opening [the meaning] and delights only in brief exposition; one who is able to uphold the Dharma achieves the wisdom of expounding and delights only in detailed exposition. If these two do not harmonize, they will fail to obtain the teaching, listening, writing, upholding, reciting, and practicing of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a demonic deed of a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

One who is able to uphold the Dharma takes exclusive delight in extensively knowing the sequential meanings of the twelve divisions of the teaching—namely, the sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, gāthās, udānas, nidānas, itivṛttakas, jātakas, vaipulyas, adbhutadharmas, avadānas, and upadeśas. However, one who is able to study the Dharma does not take delight in extensively knowing the sequential meanings of the twelve divisions of the teaching, from the sūtras up to the upadeśas. When these two do not harmonize, they fail to obtain the instruction, hearing, receiving, writing, upholding, reciting, and practicing of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

One who is able to study the Dharma takes exclusive delight in extensively knowing the sequential meanings of the twelvefold teaching—namely, from the Sūtras up to the Upadeśas—whereas one who is able to uphold the Dharma does not take delight in extensively knowing the sequential meanings of the twelvefold teaching—namely, from the Sūtras up to the Upadeśas. When these two do not harmonize, they fail to obtain the instruction, listening, receiving, writing, reciting, and cultivation of the profound Prajñāpāramitā; you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who upholds the Dharma has accomplished the perfections of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, while the one who listens to the Dharma has not accomplished the perfections from giving through wisdom, the two will not be in harmony. They will fail to obtain the teaching, the listening, the writing, the upholding, the recitation, and the cultivation of the profound perfection of wisdom. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If those who can study the Dharma accomplish the perfections from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, while those who can uphold the Dharma do not accomplish the perfections from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, and the two are thus not in harmony, they will fail to obtain the teaching, the listening, the writing, the upholding, the reciting, and the cultivation of the profound perfection of wisdom. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

One who can uphold the Dharma possesses skillful means regarding the six perfections, whereas one who can study the Dharma lacks skillful means regarding the six perfections. When these two do not harmonize, they fail to obtain the instruction, hearing, writing, upholding, reciting, and cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*; you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If one who is able to study the Dharma possesses skillful means regarding the six pāramitās, while one who is able to uphold the Dharma lacks skillful means regarding the six pāramitās, these two will not be in harmony. They shall fail to obtain the teaching, nor shall they hear, write, uphold, recite, or practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this constitutes a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If one who is able to uphold the Dharma has already attained dhāraṇī, while one who is able to study the Dharma has not yet attained dhāraṇī, and the two do not harmonize, they will fail to obtain the teaching, the listening and receiving, the writing and upholding, the reciting and chanting, and the cultivation of the profound Prajñāpāramitā; you should know that this is an act of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If one who is able to study the Dharma has already attained dhāraṇī, while one who is able to uphold the Dharma has not yet attained dhāraṇī, and these two do not harmonize, they will fail to obtain the teaching, listening, writing, upholding, reciting, and practicing of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If those who are able to uphold the Dharma desire to respectfully copy, receive, maintain, recite, and practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, while those who are able to study the Dharma do not wish to respectfully copy, receive, maintain, recite, and practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and the two do not harmonize, such that they fail to obtain instruction, listening, copying, maintaining, reciting, and practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If those who are able to study the Dharma desire to respectfully copy, receive, uphold, recite, and cultivate the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, while those who are able to uphold the Dharma do not wish to respectfully copy, receive, uphold, recite, and cultivate the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and the two are thus not in harmony, such that they fail to obtain instruction, listening, copying, upholding, reciting, and cultivating the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

One who is able to uphold the Dharma has already abandoned the stain of stinginess and has already abandoned the hindrances of sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt. One who is able to study the Dharma has not yet abandoned the stain of stinginess and has not yet abandoned [the hindrances] from sensual desire up to doubt. Because these two are not in harmony, they do not obtain instruction, nor do they receive, write down, recite, or cultivate the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

One who is able to study the Dharma has already abandoned the stain of stinginess and has abandoned everything from sensual desire up to the hindrance of doubt; yet one who is able to uphold the Dharma has not abandoned the stain of stinginess and has not abandoned everything from sensual desire up to the hindrance of doubt. Because these two do not harmonize, they fail to obtain the teaching, the hearing, the writing, the upholding, the reciting, and the cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when sons or daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle are copying, upholding, reading, reciting, practicing, contemplating, and expounding this profound *prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, if someone comes and describes to them the various sufferings of the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts, saying to them:

'You should exert yourself with diligence in this very body to quickly reach the end of suffering and attain parinirvāṇa; why do you linger in the great ocean of birth and death to undergo hundreds of thousands of kinds of unbearable sufferings for the sake of seeking unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?'"

If these sons or daughters of good family, because of those words, fail to reach the ultimate goal regarding the profound *prajñāpāramitā* sūtra—whether in its transcription, reception and retention, recitation, cultivation, contemplation, or exposition—one should know that this is the work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 443. Translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Two, Chapter Forty-five: Non-Harmony, Section Two. "Furthermore, Subhūti! "

When sons and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle write down, receive, uphold, read, recite, practice, contemplate, and expound this profound *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, if someone should come and praise the various superior matters of the human realm, praise the excellent and wondrous matters of the gods from the Realm of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Control over Others' Emanations, praise the excellent and wondrous matters of the gods from the Brahma Assembly up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, and praise the excellent and wondrous matters of the gods from the Sphere of Infinite Space up to the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception, and then say to them:

"Although you experience the pleasures of desire in the desire realm, the various meditative concentrations and immeasurable joys in the form realm, and the sublime bliss of tranquil attainments in the formless realm, all of these are conditioned, impermanent, suffering, empty, non-self, impure, and subject to decay; they are phenomena that end, fade away, depart, and cease. Why do you not apply yourself with diligence to this very body to attain the fruit of a stream-enterer, or the fruit of a once-returner, or the fruit of a non-returner, or the fruit of an arhat, or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, thereby entering parinirvāṇa for ultimate peace and happiness? What is the use of remaining long in the cycle of birth and death, undergoing various hardships and labors for no purpose on behalf of others, merely to seek the pursuit of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"

"Because of what those sons or daughters of good family have said, they shall not reach the ultimate goal regarding this profound Prajñāpāramitā sūtra—its transcription, its upholding, its recitation, its cultivation, its contemplation, and its exposition. You should know that this is an act of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

One who is able to uphold the Dharma has no attachments in this life and devotes himself exclusively to his own practice, not worrying about the affairs of others; while one who is able to study the Dharma delights in leading a retinue and takes pleasure in attending to the affairs of others, not worrying about his own practice. Since these two are not in harmony, they fail to obtain instruction, listening, transcription, recitation, and cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this constitutes a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

One who is able to study the Dharma is unattached to their own person, devoting themselves solely to their own task and not worrying about the affairs of others. One who is able to uphold the Dharma delights in leading a retinue and enjoys engaging in the affairs of others, not worrying about their own task. Since these two do not harmonize, they fail to obtain the teaching, listening, writing, upholding, reciting, and practicing of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this constitutes a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

One who is able to uphold the Dharma does not delight in clamor and confusion, while one who is able to study the Dharma delights in dwelling amidst clamor and confusion. When these two are not in harmony, they fail to obtain the teaching, the listening, the writing and upholding, the recitation, and the cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*; you should know that this constitutes a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

One who is able to study the Dharma does not delight in noisy commotion, while one who is able to uphold the Dharma delights in staying amidst noisy commotion. When these two are not in harmony, they fail to obtain the teaching, listening, writing, upholding, reciting, and practicing of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If those who uphold the Dharma desire that students assist them in all their undertakings, yet those who study the Dharma do not comply with their wishes, and because the two are not in harmony, they fail to obtain the instruction, hearing, writing, upholding, reciting, and cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If those who are able to study the Dharma take pleasure in assisting the holders of the Dharma in all their undertakings, yet the holders of the Dharma do not comply with their wishes, and because the two are thus at odds, they fail to obtain instruction, to listen and receive it, to write it down and uphold it, to read and recite it, or to cultivate the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! Suppose one who upholds the Dharma, for the sake of fame and profit, desires to preach the profound *prajñāpāramitā* to others, and further wishes to have them copy, uphold, recite, and cultivate it; yet the one who would learn the Dharma knows the [preacher's] motives and does not wish to receive it from him. Because these two are not in harmony, they fail to obtain the teaching, the listening, the copying, the upholding, the reciting, and the cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose there is one who wishes to study the Dharma for the sake of fame and profit, desiring to request another to preach the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and further wishing to skillfully copy, receive, uphold, recite, and practice it; yet the one who possesses the Dharma, knowing the requester's motive, does not comply with the request. Because the two do not harmonize, they fail to obtain instruction, listening, copying, upholding, reciting, or practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose one who is able to uphold the Dharma wishes to go to another region where life and limb are in danger, while one who is able to study the Dharma fears for their life and does not wish to go along with them. Because these two are not in harmony, they do not obtain the opportunity to teach, listen to, write down, recite, or practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose one who is able to study the Dharma wishes to travel to another region where life and limb are in peril, while one who is able to uphold the Dharma fears for their life and does not wish to go with them. Because these two do not harmonize, they fail to obtain the teaching, listening, writing, reciting, and cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose one who is able to uphold the Dharma wishes to go to another land that is beset by many bandits, epidemics, hunger, and thirst, while a student of the Dharma, fearing such hardships, is unwilling to go along with them. Because the two are not in harmony, they fail to obtain instruction, listen to, write down, recite, or practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose one who is able to study the Dharma wishes to travel to another land that is filled with many bandits, epidemics, hunger, and thirst, while one who is able to uphold the Dharma, fearing such hardships, is unwilling to go with them. Because the two are not in harmony, they do not obtain the opportunity to teach, listen to, write down, recite, or practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! Suppose a holder of the Dharma wishes to go to another region that is peaceful, prosperous, and free from calamities, and a student of the Dharma wishes to follow him. The holder of the Dharma, employing skillful means, might say:
'Although you wish to follow me for the sake of gain, will you necessarily achieve your heart's desire upon reaching that place? You should reflect carefully so as not to feel regret later.'"
At that time, the student of the Dharma, having heard this, thought to himself:
"This is his sign of not wishing for me to leave; even if I were to follow him persistently, would I necessarily hear the Dharma?"

For this reason, if one does not follow them away, and the two parties do not reach an accord, such that one fails to obtain instruction, listen to, write down, uphold, recite, or practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! Suppose a holder of the Dharma wishes to travel to another region, and the road he must traverse passes through a wilderness that is vast and perilous, filled with many dangers from bandits, as well as fears of caṇḍālas, wild beasts, hunters, and venomous snakes. A student of the Dharma wishes to follow him, so the holder of the Dharma skillfully tests him, saying:

'For what reason do you now follow me without any business of your own, wishing to pass through such places of peril and hardship? You should reflect upon this carefully, lest you later feel regret.'"
When one who is able to study the Dharma hears this, they think:
"He likely does not wish for me to follow him; even if I were to insist on following, why would I necessarily hear the Dharma?

For this reason, they do not go with him. Because the two are not in harmony, they fail to receive instruction, listen to, write down, uphold, recite, or practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this constitutes a demonic deed (*mārakarman*) of a bodhisattva.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, those who uphold the Dharma will often have many donors following them closely. When students come to request that they preach the *prajñāpāramitā*, or request that they copy, receive, uphold, recite, or practice it according to the teaching, the teachers may be hindered by many such conditions and lack the leisure to instruct them. Consequently, the students may give rise to feelings of resentment; even if the teachers later do provide instruction, the students refuse to listen or accept it. Because the two parties are not in harmony, they fail to obtain the instruction, the listening, the copying, the upholding, the reciting, and the cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

there are certain evil Māras who take the form of bhikṣus and approach the bodhisattva with skillful means to destroy [their practice], so that they do not write down, receive and uphold, read and recite, cultivate, contemplate, or explain to others the Prajñāpāramitā."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how does Māra, the Evil One,

manifest in the form of a bhikṣu and approach a bodhisattva with skillful means to destroy them, so that they are unable to write down, receive and uphold, read, recite, cultivate, contemplate, or explain to others this Prajñāpāramitā?”
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

There are certain evil Māras who take the form of bhikṣus and approach the bodhisattva with skillful means to destroy him, causing him to feel revulsion for and abandon the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, so that he does not write it down, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, cultivate and contemplate it, or explain it to others. They say these words:”
"The markless sūtras you have studied and recited are not the true Prajñāpāramitā; the sūtras with marks that I have studied and recited are the true Prajñāpāramitā."

When these words were spoken, there were bodhisattvas who had not yet received their prediction who then gave rise to doubt and confusion regarding the *prajñāpāramitā*. Because of this doubt and confusion, they gave rise to revulsion and rejection toward the *prajñāpāramitā*. Due to this revulsion and rejection, they consequently failed to write it down, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, cultivate and contemplate it, or explain the profound *prajñāpāramitā* to others; one should know that this constitutes a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are certain evil Māras who, assuming the guise of bhikṣus, approach a bodhisattva and say to them:

'If a bodhisattva practices this perfection of wisdom, they will only realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and attain the fruit of a stream-enterer, or the fruit of a once-returner, or the fruit of a non-returner, or the fruit of an arhat, or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; they will never be able to realize unsurpassed buddhahood. For what reason, then, do you exert yourself here in vain?'"

When a bodhisattva, having heard this, does not write it down, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, cultivate it, contemplate it, or explain it in detail to others, one should know that this is an act of Māra for a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When this profound *prajñāpāramitā* sūtra is being written down, received, upheld, read, recited, practiced, contemplated, and expounded, many evil Māras will create obstacles and hindrances to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment sought by Bodhisattvas. All Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should vigilantly discern and distance themselves from them."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What are called the deeds of Māra and obstacles, which cause bodhisattvas to recognize and distance themselves from them?”
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

When sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle write down, uphold, read, recite, cultivate, contemplate, and expound such profound sūtras on the *prajñāpāramitā*, there will be many demonic obstacles and hindrances resembling the *prajñā*, *dhyāna*, *vīrya*, *kṣānti*, *śīla*, and *dāna* pāramitās. Within these, the bodhisattva should carefully discern them and remain far removed from them.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When sons of good family or daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle write down, uphold, read, recite, cultivate, contemplate, and explain this profound *prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, there will be many demonic activities and obstacles concerning what resembles internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, emptiness of dispersion and non-dispersion, essential emptiness, the emptiness of self-characteristics and common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature. Within these, the bodhisattva should clearly discern them and remain far removed from them."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When sons of good family or daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle write down, uphold, read, recite, cultivate, contemplate, and expound this profound *prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, there will be many demonic obstacles and hindrances—resembling true suchness (*tathatā*), the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), the inconceivable realm, and other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas. Amidst these, the bodhisattva should clearly discern them and remain far removed from them."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when sons of good family or daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle are copying, upholding, reading, reciting, practicing, contemplating, and expounding this profound *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtra, there may be those who hold the sūtras associated with the two vehicles and come to where the Bodhisattvas are, saying these words:
'This is what was truly spoken by the Tathāgata; those who study this Dharma will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.'"
"Such as this is also called an obstacle created by Māra; therein, a bodhisattva should carefully examine and remain far removed from it. Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are certain evil Māras who, assuming the form of bhikṣus, approach the Bodhisattva and proclaim the trainings and practices of the two vehicles, such as internal and external emptiness; or the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path; or the three doors of liberation and so forth. Having taught these dharmas, they say to the Bodhisattva:
"Great Being, you should know this!..."

Moreover, if by diligently training in this Dharma one can attain the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship, or even the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha—thereby becoming far removed from all birth, old age, sickness, and death—what need is there for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?

"By reason of this cause and condition, that bodhisattva will be unable to write down, receive and uphold, read and recite, practice, contemplate, or explain to others the profound perfection of wisdom; you should know that this constitutes a work of Māra for the bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are certain evil Māras who take the form of bhikṣus, with dignified deportment and handsome appearance, and approach the bodhisattva. When the bodhisattva sees them, he develops deep attachment; because of this, he regresses from all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) and fails to hear, write down, receive, uphold, recite, cultivate, contemplate, or explain the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are certain evil Māras who manifest in the form of a Buddha, with bodies the color of pure gold, a constant light extending one fathom, and fully adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs. They approach the bodhisattva, and upon seeing them, the bodhisattva develops deep attachment. Because of this, they regress from all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) and fail to hear, write down, receive, uphold, recite, cultivate, contemplate, or explain the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are evil Māras who manifest themselves as Buddhas, surrounded by bhikṣus proclaiming the essential teachings of the Dharma. They come to where the bodhisattva is, and upon seeing them, the bodhisattva conceives a deep attachment and thinks:
'May I, in the future, become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, surrounded by bhikṣus proclaiming the essential teachings of the Dharma, exactly equal and identical to what I see now.'"

Because of this, they regress from the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), and fail to hear, write down, receive, uphold, recite, cultivate, contemplate, or explain the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this constitutes a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! There are evil Māras who manifest as bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—whether numbering a hundred, a thousand, or even incalculable—as well as those endowed with unimpeded eloquence and adorned with the marks and signs. They transform their own bodies into the likeness of Buddhas and proclaim the essential Dharma for the sake of converting assemblies of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, instructing them to cultivate the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom. Appearing in such forms, they come before the bodhisattvas; when the bodhisattvas see them, they develop deep attachment. Because of this, they regress from all-aspect omniscience and fail to hear, write down, receive, uphold, recite, practice, contemplate, or explain the profound perfection of wisdom. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Why is that? Subhūti!

Within this profound Dharma of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), form (*rūpa*) does not exist and cannot be apprehended; feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) likewise do not exist and cannot be apprehended."
The eye-base is non-existent and unapprehendable; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are likewise non-existent and unapprehendable.
The form-base is non-existent and unapprehendable; the sound, odor, taste, tangible, and mental-object bases are likewise non-existent and unapprehendable.
The eye-element is non-existent and unapprehendable; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements are likewise non-existent and unapprehendable.
The realm of form is non-existent and unattainable; the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are likewise non-existent and unattainable.
The realm of eye-consciousness is non-existent and unattainable; the realms of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness are likewise non-existent and unattainable.
Eye-contact is non-existent and unattainable; ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact are likewise non-existent and unattainable.

The various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are non-existent and unapprehendable; the various feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as conditions are likewise non-existent and unapprehendable.
The earth element is non-existent and unapprehendable; the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are likewise non-existent and unapprehendable.

Ignorance is non-existent and unapprehendable; volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair are likewise non-existent and unapprehendable.
In the desire realm, there is nothing whatsoever that can be apprehended; in the form and formless realms as well, there is nothing whatsoever that can be apprehended.

In the past, there is nothing whatsoever that can be apprehended; in the future and the present as well, there is nothing whatsoever that can be apprehended. Among contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*), there is nothing whatsoever that can be apprehended; among uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsravadharma*) as well, there is nothing whatsoever that can be apprehended.

Among conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), there is nothing whatsoever that can be apprehended; among unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) as well, there is nothing whatsoever that can be apprehended.
Worldly dharmas do not exist and cannot be apprehended; supramundane dharmas likewise do not exist and cannot be apprehended.

The perfection of generosity does not exist and cannot be apprehended; the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom likewise do not exist and cannot be apprehended. Internal emptiness does not exist and cannot be apprehended;

external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, endless emptiness, the emptiness of dispersion and non-dispersion, essential emptiness, the emptiness of self-characteristics and common characteristics, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature likewise do not exist and cannot be apprehended.

Suchness is non-existent and unapprehendable; likewise, the dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, the non-illusory nature, the unchanging nature, equality, the nature of freedom from birth, the fixed nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm are also non-existent and unapprehendable.
The noble truth of suffering is non-existent and unapprehendable; the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are also non-existent and unapprehendable.
The four dhyānas are non-existent and unapprehendable; the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments are also non-existent and unapprehendable.

The eight liberations are non-existent and unattainable; the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten universal bases are likewise non-existent and unattainable.

The four foundations of mindfulness are non-existent and unattainable; the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eight branches of the noble path are also non-existent and unattainable.
The gate of liberation of emptiness is non-existent and unapprehendable; the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are likewise non-existent and unapprehendable.

The stage of pure observation is non-existent and unapprehendable; the stage of the lineage, the eighth stage, the stage of seeing, the stage of refinement, the stage of freedom from desire, the stage of completion, the stage of the solitary realizer, the stage of the bodhisattva, and the stage of the Tathāgata are also non-existent and unapprehendable.

The stage of extreme joy is non-existent and unapprehendable; the stage of freedom from stain, the stage of radiant light, the stage of flaming wisdom, the stage of extreme difficulty to conquer, the stage of presence, the stage of far-reaching, the stage of immovability, the stage of excellent wisdom, and the stage of the cloud of dharma are also non-existent and unapprehendable.
The five eyes are non-existent and unobtainable; the six supernormal powers are also non-existent and unobtainable.

The ten powers of a Tathāgata are non-existent and unobtainable; the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are also non-existent and unobtainable.
The thirty-two marks of a Great Being are non-existent and unobtainable; the eighty secondary characteristics are also non-existent and unobtainable.
The quality of non-forgetfulness is non-existent and unapprehendable; the state of constant abiding in equanimity is likewise non-existent and unapprehendable.
Omniscience is non-existent and unapprehendable; the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects are likewise non-existent and unapprehendable.
The maturation of sentient beings is non-existent and unapprehendable; the purification of Buddha-fields is likewise non-existent and unapprehendable.
The great vows of a bodhisattva are non-existent and unapprehendable; the supernormal powers of a bodhisattva are likewise non-existent and unapprehendable.
All doors of dhāraṇī are non-existent and unapprehendable, and all doors of samādhi are likewise non-existent and unapprehendable.

The fruit of stream-entry is non-existent and unapprehendable, and the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, and the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha are likewise non-existent and unapprehendable.

All the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are non-existent and unapprehendable; the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas is likewise non-existent and unapprehendable.

“Subhūti! In that case, where form does not exist and cannot be apprehended, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness likewise do not exist and cannot be apprehended; and so on, up to the point where all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not exist and cannot be apprehended, and even the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas does not exist and cannot be apprehended.

Furthermore, in this very place, all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as well as the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and all classes of ordinary beings, likewise do not exist and cannot be apprehended.
Why is this? Subhūti!
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When sons of good family or daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle write down, uphold, read, recite, cultivate, contemplate, and expound this profound *prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, many obstacles and hindering circumstances will arise, causing those of meager merit to fail in their undertakings."

Just as there are various precious treasures in Jambudvīpa—namely, vaidūrya, conch shells, jade, coral, stone treasuries, maṇi-jewels, pearls, sapphire, emerald, diamond, amber, gold, silver, and other such gems—which are frequently obstructed by thieves and adversaries, so that those of meager merit are unable to obtain them despite their seeking.

The priceless jewel of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise so: when sons and daughters of good family who belong to the bodhisattva vehicle write down, uphold, read, recite, cultivate, contemplate, and expound this profound *prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, those with meager merit will encounter many obstacles, and various evil māras will create hindrances for them.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying: “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
"So it is! Well-gone One!

It is truly as the Noble One has taught: this profound *prajñāpāramitā* is like the various precious gems of Jambudvīpa, such as lapis lazuli, which encounter many obstacles; those of little merit, though they employ skillful means, are unable to obtain them."

When sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle write down, uphold, read, recite, practice, contemplate, and expound this profound *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtra, those with little merit will encounter many obstacles; though they may have the desire and aspiration, they will be unable to achieve success.

Why is this? There are those who are deluded and act under the influence of Māra; when sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle write down, uphold, read, recite, cultivate, contemplate, and expound such a profound sūtra as this Prajñāpāramitā, they create obstacles for them.

Bhagavān! Those foolish ones possess dull and obscured wisdom; they are unable to conceive of the vast Buddha-dharma. They themselves cannot write down, receive, uphold, recite, cultivate, contemplate, or explain to others the profound sūtras of the *prajñāpāramitā*. Furthermore, they delight in obstructing others from writing down, receiving, upholding, reciting, cultivating, contemplating, or explaining the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Buddha said, “So it is, Subhūti!”

It is so! It is as you have said: there are foolish persons who, acting under the influence of Māra, create obstacles when sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle write down, uphold, read, recite, cultivate, contemplate, and expound this profound *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtra.

Subhūti! Those foolish ones possess dull and obscure wisdom; they are unable to conceive of the vast Buddha-dharma. Having not planted roots of goodness, nor having made great vows before the Buddhas, they are influenced by evil associates. Because their merit is meager, they themselves are unable to write down, accept, uphold, read, recite, practice, contemplate, or explain to others these profound sūtras of the Prajñāpāramitā.

Furthermore, when newly ordained sons and daughters of good family who have set out in the Mahāyāna write down, accept, uphold, read, recite, practice, contemplate, or explain such profound sūtras of the Prajñāpāramitā, they create obstacles for them.

"Subhūti! In future ages, there will be sons of good family and daughters of good family whose wisdom is dull and obscured, whose roots of virtue are meager, and who are influenced by evil associates. They will be unable to have faith or delight in the vast merits of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas; they themselves will not write down, receive, uphold, read, recite, practice, contemplate, or explain to others these profound sūtras of the Prajñāpāramitā. Furthermore, they will take pleasure in obstructing other sons of good family and daughters of good family from writing down, receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, practicing, contemplating, or explaining the profound Prajñāpāramitā. You should know that such persons shall incur immeasurable sin."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Those sons of good family and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle, having written down,
upheld, recited, practiced, contemplated, and expounded this Perfection of Wisdom in such a manner..."
Over a long period of time, many demonic obstacles arise to create hindrances, causing the activities of writing down,
receiving and upholding, reading and reciting, practicing, contemplating, and explaining to others this profound *prajñāpāramitā* to fail in their accomplishment,
so that one is unable to bring to perfection *prajñā*, *dhyāna*, and *vīrya*.
The perfections of patience, ethical discipline, and generosity cannot fulfill internal emptiness,
external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness,
unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, beginningless-and-endless emptiness, and the emptiness of non-dispersal and dispersion, nor can they fulfill the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
Emptiness, the emptiness of self-characteristics and common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable,
the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence cannot fulfill suchness,
the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-falsity, immutability, equality, and freedom from birth.

The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the fixedness of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthititā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*),
and the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*) cannot fulfill the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; they cannot fulfill the four meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*),
the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), nor the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*).

The bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the nine successive attainments (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), and the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*) cannot bring to fulfillment the four foundations of mindfulness,
the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;
nor can they bring to fulfillment the doors of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
One can fulfill the ten stages of a bodhisattva, but cannot fulfill the five eyes, the six supernormal powers,
the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness,
great compassion, great joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; one cannot fulfill them.

Although one may be fully endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great being and the eighty secondary characteristics, one cannot fulfill the quality of non-forgetfulness or the state of constant abiding in equanimity; one cannot fulfill the maturation of sentient beings or the purification of Buddha-fields;
and one cannot fulfill all the doors of dhāraṇī or the doors of samādhi. One cannot fulfill...
The fulfillment of all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of all buddhas— being unable to fulfill omniscience (*sarvajñatā*),
the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*),
and being unable to fulfill these merits— all this is due to the obstacles created by Māra, the evil one.

“Subhūti! When sons and daughters of good family who abide in the bodhisattva vehicle write down, receive, uphold, read, recite, cultivate, contemplate, and expound this profound *prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, if no evil Māras create obstacles for them, and they are further able to fulfill the *prajñā*, *dhyāna*, *vīrya*, *kṣānti*, *śīla*, and *dāna* pāramitās, up to and including fulfilling all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), you should know that all such instances are due to the empowerment and protection of the Tathāgata’s spiritual power.”

May all sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle be free from obstacles in the writing, upholding, reading, reciting, practicing, contemplating, and explaining this profound *prajñāpāramitā*; and may they also bring to perfection the *prajñā*, *dhyāna*, *vīrya*, *kṣānti*, *śīla*, and *dāna* pāramitās, up to and including the perfection of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas currently dwelling in peace and maintaining their presence, teaching the sublime Dharma in the immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless worlds of the ten directions, likewise empower through their spiritual might those sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle, so that they may write down, receive, uphold, recite, cultivate, contemplate, and explain this profound Prajñāpāramitā without any hindrance. They also cause them to fulfill the pāramitās of wisdom, meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity, and even to fulfill all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All the bodhisattva mahāsattvas on the stage of non-retrogression currently residing in the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, likewise provide their spiritual power and protection to these good sons and good daughters who abide in the bodhisattva vehicle, so that they may write down, receive and uphold, read and recite, practice, contemplate, and explain this profound *prajñāpāramitā* without any hindrance. They also cause them to fulfill the *prajñā*, *dhyāna*, *vīrya*, *kṣānti*, *śīla*, and *dāna* *pāramitās*, up to and including the fulfillment of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)."
Chapter 46: The Mother of the Buddha, Part Two, Section One.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose there were a woman who had given birth to many sons—perhaps five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or even a hundred or a thousand. If that mother were to fall ill, her sons would each diligently seek out medical treatment, all thinking:
'How may our mother recover from this illness? How may she attain long life and peace, be free from physical suffering, and have her mind liberated from sorrow and anxiety? "

At that time, the sons vied with one another to employ skillful means to seek out articles of comfort and protection for their mother’s body, so that she would not be afflicted by the touch of mosquitoes, gadflies, snakes, scorpions, wind, heat, hunger, or thirst. Furthermore, they honored and reverenced her with various kinds of excellent and sublime articles of pleasure, saying:
"Our mother is compassionate; she gave birth to us and taught us the various worldly affairs. How could we fail to repay our mother's kindness!"
“Subhūti! In the same way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha likewise constantly observes and protects the profound Prajñāpāramitā with his Buddha-eye.”
Why is this? Subhūti!

This profound Prajñāpāramitā can give birth to all our Buddha-dharmas, can bestow upon us all the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā), and can reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world.

The Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas—immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless in number throughout the worlds of the ten directions—who currently dwell in peace and stability and manifest the teaching of the Dharma, likewise constantly observe, protect, and keep in mind this profound Prajñāpāramitā with their Buddha-eyes.
Why is this? Subhūti!

This profound *prajñāpāramitā* can give birth to all the Buddha-dharmas of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas in the infinite, innumerable, and boundless worlds of the ten directions; furthermore, it can bestow upon them the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) and reveal the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena in the world.
For this reason, we Buddhas constantly observe and protect the profound Prajñāpāramitā with our Buddha-eye; to repay its kindness, we should never abandon it for even a moment.
"Why is this so, Subhūti?

Because all the perfections of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas— from the perfection of meditative concentration up to the perfection of generosity— are brought forth by means of this very profound perfection of wisdom."
All forms of emptiness, from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, are manifested through this profound *prajñāpāramitā*;
all realities, from suchness (*tathatā*) up to the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*), are manifested through this profound *prajñāpāramitā*;
and all the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, are manifested through this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
All four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments arise from this very profound perfection of wisdom;
all eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities arise from this very profound perfection of wisdom;
and all the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path arise from this very profound perfection of wisdom.
All the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are produced from this very profound perfection of wisdom;
all the five eyes and six supernormal powers are produced from this very profound perfection of wisdom;
and all the ten powers of a Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are produced from this very profound perfection of wisdom.
All the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks of exquisite physical form arise from this very profound *prajñāpāramitā*;
all the qualities of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity arise from this very profound *prajñāpāramitā*;
and all the gateways of *dhāraṇī* and the gateways of *samādhi* arise from this very profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

All omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) arise from this very profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*);

all the fruits of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), non-returning (*anāgāmin*), and arhatship, as well as the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, arise from this very profound perfection of wisdom;
