and all the practices of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas arise from this very profound perfection of wisdom.

All stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, exist because they have attained this very profound perfection of wisdom.

"Subhūti! All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas—who have attained, are attaining, or will attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—all do so by means of this profound perfection of wisdom."

For this reason, the profound perfection of wisdom possesses great merit and virtue toward all Tathāgatas; therefore, the Buddhas constantly observe and protect the profound perfection of wisdom with their Buddha-eye.

"Subhūti! If sons of good family or daughters of good family who abide in the bodhisattva vehicle can write down, uphold, read, recite, cultivate, contemplate, and explain this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas will constantly observe and protect them with their Buddha-eye, causing their bodies and minds to always attain peace and happiness, and ensuring that no obstacles shall hinder the wholesome deeds they cultivate."

"Subhūti! If sons of good family or daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle are able to write down, receive, uphold, read, recite, practice, contemplate, and expound this profound Prajñāpāramitā, all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the worlds in the ten directions will together protect and mindfully attend to them, causing them never to regress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

As the Buddha has taught, this profound *prajñāpāramitā* can give birth to all the Buddha-dharmas of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; it can bestow upon the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas all-aspect wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*); and it can reveal the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena in the world."

Bhagavān, how is it that this profound perfection of wisdom can give birth to all the Buddha-dharmas of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; how can it bestow upon the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā); and how can it reveal the true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa) of all phenomena in the world?
How is it that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is born from the profound perfection of wisdom?
And how do the Buddhas describe the characteristics of the world?
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

The profound perfection of wisdom gives birth to all the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and so forth, up to and including the knowledge of all aspects.”

Subhūti! Such immeasurable and boundless merits of the Tathāgatas as these all arise and grow from this profound *prajñāpāramitā*; because they have attained such merits of the Buddhas, they are called "Buddhas."

The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is able to give birth to and bestow upon all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas such Buddha-dharmas as the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Therefore, I say that the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can give birth to all the Buddha-dharmas of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and can bestow upon them the knowledge of all aspects; I also say that the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas arise from it.

"Subhūti! That which is able to demonstrate the true reality of all phenomena in the world—the profound *prajñāpāramitā*—is that which demonstrates the true reality of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) in the world; all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas likewise teach the true reality of the five aggregates in the world."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
how does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha teach and reveal the true reality of the five aggregates in this world through the profound Prajñāpāramitā?”
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, in their profound Prajñāpāramitā, never teach that the five aggregates have arising or perishing, birth or cessation, continuity or interruption, defilement or purification, increase or decrease, or entry or exit. They never teach that the five aggregates belong to the past, the future, or the present; nor do they teach that they are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate; nor that they are bound to the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm.”
Why is that? Subhūti!

It is because the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness have no formation or disintegration, no arising or ceasing, no continuity or interruption, no defilement or purification, no increase or decrease, no entering or exiting, no past, future, or present, no wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate, and no connection with the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm.

"Subhūti! Those dharmas that are without arising, without cessation, without creation, without action, and without intrinsic nature do not undergo formation or destruction, birth or death, continuity or interruption, defilement or purification, increase or decrease, entry or exit, nor do they belong to the past, future, or present; nor are they wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate; nor are they bound to the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm."

“Subhūti! All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, through this profound Prajñāpāramitā, thus reveal the true nature of the five aggregates. This characteristic of the five aggregates is itself the world; therefore, the world is without formation or destruction, without arising or ceasing, without continuity or interruption, without defilement or purity, without increase or decrease, without entering or exiting, without past, future, or present, without being wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate, and without being bound to the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm, nor does it possess any other characteristics.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, relying upon this very profound Prajñāpāramitā, are universally able to realize and know the distinctions in the mental activities of immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings."
However, within this profound meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā*, no sentient being exists, nor can any designation of a sentient being be apprehended;

no form exists, nor can any designation of form be apprehended; no feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness exist, nor can any designations of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness be apprehended;

no eye-base exists, nor can any designation of an eye-base be apprehended; and no ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-base exists, nor can any designations of ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-base be apprehended.

The sphere of formlessness is not to be found, nor can the designation "sphere of formlessness" be apprehended; the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibles, and mental phenomena are not to be found, nor can the designations "sphere of sound," "sphere of odor," "sphere of taste," "sphere of tangibles," or "sphere of mental phenomena" be apprehended.

The eye-element is not to be found, nor can the designation "eye-element" be apprehended; the elements of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are not to be found, nor can the designations "element of ear," "element of nose," "element of tongue," "element of body," or "element of mind" be apprehended.

The element of forms is not to be found, nor can the designation "element of forms" be apprehended; the elements of sound, odor, taste, tangibles, and mental phenomena are not to be found, nor can the designations "element of sound," "element of odor," "element of taste," "element of tangibles," or "element of mental phenomena" be apprehended.

There is no eye-consciousness element, nor can any designation of an eye-consciousness element be apprehended; there is no ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness element, nor can any designation of an ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness element be apprehended;

there is no eye-contact, nor can any designation of eye-contact be apprehended; there is no ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact, nor can any designation of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact be apprehended;

there are no feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, nor can any designation of feelings produced with eye-contact as condition be apprehended; there are no feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as condition, nor can any designation of feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as condition be apprehended.

There is no earth element, nor can any designation of an earth element be found; there is no water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness element, nor can any designation of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness element be found;
there is no ignorance, nor can any designation of ignorance be found, up to and including no aging and death, nor can any designation of aging and death be found;

there is no perfection of generosity, nor can any designation of the perfection of generosity be found, up to and including no perfection of wisdom, nor can any designation of the perfection of wisdom be found.

There is no internal emptiness, nor can any designation of internal emptiness be apprehended; likewise, there is no emptiness of the nature of non-existence, nor can any designation of the emptiness of the nature of non-existence be apprehended.

There is no fourfold application of mindfulness, nor can any designation of the fourfold application of mindfulness be apprehended; likewise, there is no eightfold noble path, nor can any designation of the eightfold noble path be apprehended.

In this manner, up to and including the ten powers of a Tathāgata, there is none, nor can any designation of the ten powers of a Tathāgata be apprehended; likewise, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, there is none, nor can any designation of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha be apprehended.

There is no omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), nor can any designation of omniscience be apprehended; there is no knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) or knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), nor can any designation of knowledge of the paths or knowledge of all aspects be apprehended.
"Subhūti! All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas teach the true nature of the world through this profound Prajñāpāramitā."

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 441. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Second Division, Chapter on the Mother of Buddhas, Part Forty-Six, Section Two. "Furthermore, Subhūti!
The profound perfection of wisdom does not manifest form; it does not manifest feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
It does not manifest the sense base of the eye; it does not manifest the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
It does not manifest the sense base of forms; it does not manifest the sense bases of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena.
They do not manifest the eye-element; they do not manifest the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-element.
They do not manifest the form-element; they do not manifest the sound, odor, taste, tangible, or mental-object-element.
They do not manifest the eye-consciousness-element; they do not manifest the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-consciousness-element.
They do not manifest eye-contact; they do not manifest ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact.
They do not manifest the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition; they do not manifest the various feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as condition.
They do not manifest the earth element; they do not manifest the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements.

They do not manifest ignorance; they do not manifest volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death.
They do not manifest the perfection of generosity; they do not manifest the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom.

They do not manifest internal emptiness; they do not manifest external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, beginningless-and-endless emptiness, non-dispersal emptiness, essential emptiness, the emptiness of self-characteristics and common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, or the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.

They do not manifest true suchness; they do not manifest the dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space, or the inconceivable realm.
They do not manifest the noble truth of suffering; they do not manifest the noble truths of the origin, cessation, or the path.
They do not manifest the four meditative concentrations; they do not manifest the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments.
They do not manifest the eight liberations; they do not manifest the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities.

They do not manifest the four foundations of mindfulness; they do not manifest the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path.
They do not manifest the liberation door of emptiness; they do not manifest the liberation doors of signlessness and wishlessness.

They do not manifest the stage of pure observation; they do not manifest the stage of the spiritual lineage, the eighth stage, the stage of possessing vision, the stage of refinement, the stage of freedom from desire, the stage of having completed what was to be done, the stage of the solitary realizer, the stage of the bodhisattva, or the stage of the Tathāgata.

They do not manifest the stage of extreme joy; they do not manifest the stage of freedom from stain, the stage of radiant light, the stage of flaming wisdom, the stage of extreme difficulty to conquer, the stage of presence, the stage of far-reaching, the stage of immovability, the stage of excellent wisdom, or the stage of the cloud of dharma.
They do not manifest the five eyes; they do not manifest the six supernormal powers.

They do not manifest the ten powers of a Tathāgata; they do not manifest the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they do not manifest the thirty-two marks of a Great Being, nor do they manifest the eighty minor marks;
they do not manifest the quality of non-forgetfulness, nor do they manifest the state of constant abiding in equanimity.
They do not manifest the fruit of stream-entry; they do not manifest the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship; nor do they manifest the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
They do not manifest the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, nor do they manifest the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas.
They do not manifest the turning of the sublime wheel of Dharma, nor do they manifest the deliverance of sentient beings.
They do not manifest the purification of buddha-fields, nor do they manifest the maturation of sentient beings;
they do not manifest any of the doors of dhāraṇī, nor do they manifest any of the doors of samādhi;
they do not manifest all-knowledge, nor do they manifest the knowledge of the paths or the knowledge of all aspects.
Why is this? Subhūti!

Within the profound meaning of this *prajñāpāramitā*, even the profound *prajñāpāramitā* itself does not exist and cannot be apprehended; how much less can form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness—and even all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)—be apprehended or manifested!
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Regarding all sentient beings designated and spoken of within the three realms and five destinies—whether they possess form or are formless, whether they have perception, lack perception, or are neither percipient nor non-percipient; whether they are in this world or in other immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless worlds throughout the ten directions—all such sentient beings, whether their minds are contracted or distracted, and whether their states are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate—the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas know them all as they truly are by means of the profound Prajñāpāramitā."

Subhūti! How does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, in reliance upon the profound Prajñāpāramitā, know as they truly are the minds of sentient beings—whether contracted or distracted, virtuous, non-virtuous, or indeterminate?

"Subhūti! By means of the profound perfection of wisdom, all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, through the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), are able to know, as they truly are, whether the minds of sentient beings are contracted or distracted, and whether they are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate."
Then, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha,

by means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and through the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), know, as they truly are, the contracted minds, distracted minds, or minds that are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate of all classes of sentient beings?”
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

By means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas know, in accordance with reality, that within the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), even the nature of phenomena itself does not exist and cannot be apprehended; how much less could there be sentient beings with concentrated minds, distracted minds, or states that are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate which could be apprehended!”

"Subhūti! In this way, by means of the profound perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, through the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), is able to know, as they truly are, the concentrated minds and distracted minds of sentient beings—whether they are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Relying on the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are able to know, as they truly are, whether the minds of sentient beings are contracted or distracted, and whether they are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate."

Subhūti! How is it that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, is able to know, as they truly are, the concentrated minds and distracted minds of sentient beings, whether they are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate?

"Subhūti! By means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas—through its exhaustion, detachment, cessation, abandonment, tranquility, and seclusion—are able to know, as they truly are, the contracted minds, distracted minds, or minds that are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate of all classes of sentient beings."
Then, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how does the Tathāgata,

the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by relying on the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, through its exhaustion, detachment, cessation, abandonment, tranquility, and seclusion, know, as they truly are, the contracted minds and distracted minds of sentient beings— whether they be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate?”
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

By means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas know, as they truly are, that within exhaustion, detachment, cessation, abandonment, tranquility, and seclusion, even the nature of exhaustion and so forth does not exist and cannot be apprehended; how much less could there be sentient beings whose minds are either concentrated or distracted, or who could be apprehended as virtuous, non-virtuous, or indeterminate!”

“Subhūti! Thus, by means of the profound perfection of wisdom, through its exhaustion, freedom from passion, cessation, abandonment, tranquility, and detachment, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is able to know, as they truly are, the contracted minds and distracted minds of sentient beings, whether they are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

By relying on the profound perfection of wisdom, all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are able to know, as they truly are, the minds of sentient beings—whether they possess a mind of desire or are free from desire, whether they possess a mind of hatred or are free from hatred, and whether they possess a mind of delusion or are free from delusion."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how does the Tathāgata,

the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by relying on the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, know as they truly are the minds of sentient beings— those with desire and those free from desire, those with hatred and those free from hatred, and those with delusion and those free from delusion?”
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

Relying on the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are able to know, as it truly is, the suchness of the minds of those sentient beings that possess desire— neither as minds possessing desire, nor as minds free from desire.”

Why is this? Within the nature of reality as it truly is (*yathābhūtatā*), even the mind and mental factors (*citta-caittadharma*) do not exist and cannot be apprehended; how much less could a mind possessed of greed or a mind free from greed be apprehended!
Furthermore, they know those sentient beings as they truly are: that their minds possess the nature of anger, yet they do not possess anger, nor are they apart from anger.

Why is this? Because within the nature of reality (*tathatā*), even the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) do not exist and cannot be apprehended; how much less could a mind possessing anger or a mind apart from anger be apprehended!
Furthermore, one knows as it truly is that those sentient beings possess the true nature of a deluded mind, yet there is neither a deluded mind nor a mind apart from delusion. Why is this?
Because within the true nature, even the mind and its mental factors do not exist and cannot be apprehended; how much less could a deluded mind or a mind apart from delusion be found!

“Subhūti! In this way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, is able to know, as they truly are, that those sentient beings possess minds of desire, possess minds of hatred, and possess minds of delusion.”

“Subhūti! By means of the profound perfection of wisdom, all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are able to know, as it truly is, the true nature of those sentient beings whose minds are free from attachment—knowing them neither as minds free from attachment, nor as minds not free from attachment, nor as minds possessing attachment.”

Why is this? Within the nature of reality as it truly is (*yathābhūtatā*), even the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*) do not exist and cannot be apprehended; how much less could a mind free from greed or a mind possessed of greed be apprehended!
Furthermore, one knows as it truly is that the true nature of those sentient beings is neither a mind free from hatred, nor a mind possessed of hatred. Why is this?
Because within true nature, even the mind and mental factors do not exist and cannot be apprehended; how much less could a mind free from hatred or a mind possessed of hatred be apprehended!

Furthermore, one knows as it truly is that the minds of those sentient beings are free from the nature of delusion, yet they are neither minds free from delusion nor minds possessed of delusion. Why is this?

Because within the true nature of reality (*tathatā*), even mind and mental factors do not exist and cannot be apprehended; how much less could a mind free from delusion or a mind possessed of delusion be apprehended!

“Subhūti! In this way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, is able to know, as they truly are, those sentient beings whose minds are free from greed, free from hatred, and free from delusion.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Relying on the profound perfection of wisdom, all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are able to know, as they truly are, that those sentient beings possess minds with greed, hatred, and delusion; minds not possessing greed, hatred, and delusion; and minds that are neither free from nor possessed of greed, hatred, and delusion."
Why is this? Because these two minds do not harmonize. "Subhūti!..."

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, by relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, are able to know, as it truly is, that the minds of those sentient beings are free from greed, hatred, and delusion; that they are not free from greed, hatred, and delusion; and that they do not possess greed, hatred, and delusion.
Why is this? Because these two minds do not harmonize, Subhūti!

In this way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, is able to know, as they truly are, whether those sentient beings possess minds of desire or are free from desire, possess minds of hatred or are free from hatred, and possess minds of delusion or are free from delusion.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
By relying on the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are able to know, as they truly are, the expansive minds of all classes of sentient beings."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how does the Tathāgata,
the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, know as they truly are the expansive minds of those sentient beings?"
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

By relying on the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are able to know, as they truly are, the vast minds of those sentient beings— minds that are neither vast nor narrow, neither increasing nor decreasing, and neither departing nor arriving.”
Why is this so? Because the intrinsic nature of the mind is ultimately detached; it is neither broad nor narrow, neither increasing nor decreasing, neither departing nor arriving. Why is this?
The intrinsic nature of the mind is entirely non-existent and ultimately unattainable; how could it be broad or narrow?
How could it increase or decrease?
How could it go or come?
"Subhūti! In this way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, is able to know, as they truly are, all the expansive minds of those sentient beings."
"Furthermore, Subhūti! By relying on the profound perfection of wisdom, all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are able to know, as they truly are, all the great minds of sentient beings."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how does the Tathāgata,
the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by relying on the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, know as they truly are all those great minds of sentient beings?"
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

By relying on the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are able to know, as they truly are, the great minds of those sentient beings— minds that are neither great nor small, neither departing nor arriving, neither arising nor ceasing, neither abiding nor changing, and neither defiled nor pure.”

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of the mind is ultimately detached, the Buddha does not perceive it as having magnitude or minuteness, coming or going, arising or ceasing, abiding or changing, or being defiled or pure.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of the mind is entirely non-existent and ultimately unattainable; how could it be large or small?
How could it go or come?
What arises and what ceases?
What abides and what changes?
What is defiled and what is pure?
"Subhūti! In this way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, is able to know, as they truly are, all the great minds of those sentient beings."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
By relying on the profound perfection of wisdom, all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are able to know, as they truly are, all the immeasurable minds of sentient beings."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how does the Tathāgata,
the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, know all the immeasurable minds of those sentient beings as they truly are?”
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

Relying on the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are able to know, as they truly are, all the immeasurable minds of those sentient beings— minds that are neither finite nor infinite, neither abiding nor non-abiding, and neither departing nor non-departing.”
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of the mind is ultimately detached.
The Buddha does not perceive it as having measure or being immeasurable, as abiding or not abiding, or as going or not going.
Why is this? Since the nature of the immeasurable mind has no basis of reliance, how can one speak of it as being measurable or immeasurable, abiding or non-abiding, departing or non-departing?
Since this mind’s intrinsic nature has no basis and nothing exists within it, such that it is ultimately ungraspable, how could there be measure, or how could there be non-measure?
How could there be abiding, or how could there be non-abiding?
What goes away, and what does not go away? Subhūti!
In this way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, is able to know, as they truly are, all the immeasurable minds of those sentient beings.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, by relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, are able to know, as they truly are, all the minds of sentient beings that are invisible and non-obstructive."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how does the Tathāgata,
the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by relying on the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, know as they truly are all those sentient beings' minds that are invisible and non-obstructive?"
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

By relying on the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are able to know, as they truly are, that the minds of those sentient beings— which are invisible and non-obstructive— are entirely devoid of the characteristics of mind.”
Why is this? Because all minds are empty of their own characteristics, Subhūti!

In this way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, is able to know, as they truly are, all those sentient beings' minds that are non-perceptual and non-obstructive.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
By relying on the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are able to know, as they truly are, all the formless and invisible minds of sentient beings."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

How does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by relying on the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, truly know all those sentient beings' formless and invisible minds?"
The Buddha said: “Subhūti!

Relying on the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are able to know, as they truly are, the formless and invisible minds of those sentient beings; these are not seen by even the five eyes of the Buddhas.”
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of all minds is empty. Subhūti!
In this way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, is able to know, as they truly are, all those formless and invisible minds of sentient beings.

Or, based on form, one may cling to the view that after the Tathāgata’s passing he neither exists nor does not exist, asserting: "This alone is the truth and reality; all else is foolish and false.
Or, based on feeling, one may cling to the view that after the Tathāgata’s passing he exists, asserting: "This alone is the truth and reality; all else is foolish and false."
Or, based on their adherence to views, they hold that it is true and real that the Tathāgata does not exist after death, and that all other [views] are foolish and false.
Or, based on their adherence to views, they hold that it is true and real that the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death, and that all other [views] are foolish and false.

Some, relying on feeling (*vedanā*), cling to the view that after the Tathāgata’s passing he neither exists nor does not exist, asserting: "This alone is the truth and reality; all else is foolish delusion.
Others, relying on perception (*saṃjñā*), cling to the view that after the Tathāgata’s passing he exists, asserting: "This alone is the truth and reality; all else is foolish delusion."
Or, based on conceptualization, one may cling to the view that after the Tathāgata’s passing he does not exist, and hold that this alone is the truth while all else is foolish delusion.

Or, based on conceptualization, one may cling to the view that after the Tathāgata’s passing he both exists and does not exist, and hold that this alone is the truth while all else is foolish delusion.

Or, based on conceptualization, one may cling to the view that after the Tathāgata’s passing away, he neither exists nor does not exist, asserting: "This alone is the truth and reality; all else is foolish and false.
Or, based on formations, one may cling to the view that after the Tathāgata’s passing away, he exists, asserting: "This alone is the truth and reality; all else is foolish and false."

Or, based on conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), one may cling to the view that after the Tathāgata’s passing he does not exist, and hold that this alone is the truth while all else is foolish delusion.

Or, based on conditioned formations, one may cling to the view that after the Tathāgata’s passing he both exists and does not exist, and hold that this alone is the truth while all else is foolish delusion.
Some, relying on the *saṃskāras*, maintain that after the Tathāgata’s passing he neither exists nor does not exist, and that this alone is the truth while all else is foolish delusion.
Others, relying on *vijñāna*, maintain that after the Tathāgata’s passing he exists, and that this alone is the truth while all else is foolish delusion.
Or, based on consciousness, one may cling to the view that after the Tathāgata’s death he does not exist, asserting: "This alone is the truth and reality; all else is foolish and false.

Or, based on consciousness, one may cling to the view that after the Tathāgata’s death he both exists and does not exist, asserting: "This alone is the truth and reality; all else is foolish and false."

Or, based on consciousness, they may cling to the view that after the Tathāgata’s passing away, he neither exists nor does not exist, asserting: "This alone is the truth and reality; all else is foolish and false.

Subhūti, in this way, by means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is able to know, as they truly are, the minds and mental factors of those sentient beings—whether they emerge or submerge, whether they contract or expand.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, in the profound Prajñāpāramitā, know form as it truly is, and they likewise know feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as they truly are."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how does the Tathāgata,
the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, know form as it truly is, and likewise know feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as they truly are?”
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, relying on the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, know form (*rūpa*) as it truly is: as suchness (*tathatā*), without change, without discrimination, without characteristics, without activity, without conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and without apprehension. They likewise know feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) as they truly are: as suchness, without change, without discrimination, without characteristics, without activity, without conceptual proliferation, and without apprehension.”

Subhūti! In this way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, knows form as it truly is, and likewise knows feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as they truly are.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! The suchness of the five aggregates is the suchness of sentient beings; the suchness of sentient beings is the suchness of appearing and disappearing, bending and extending;
the suchness of appearing and disappearing, bending and extending is the suchness of the five aggregates; the suchness of the five aggregates is the ten..."
The suchness of the two bases; the suchness of the twelve bases is the suchness of the eighteen elements;
the suchness of the eighteen elements is the suchness of all phenomena; the suchness of all phenomena is the suchness of the six perfections;
and the suchness of the six perfections is the suchness of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
The suchness of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment is the suchness of the eighteen kinds of emptiness;
the suchness of the eighteen kinds of emptiness is the suchness of the eight liberations; the suchness of the eight liberations is the suchness of the eight bases of mastery;
the suchness of the eight bases of mastery is the suchness of the nine successive meditative attainments; the suchness of the nine successive meditative attainments...
That is to say, the suchness of the Tathāgata’s ten powers is the suchness of the four fearlessnesses;
the suchness of the four fearlessnesses is the suchness of the four analytical knowledges;
the suchness of the four analytical knowledges is the suchness of great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity; [the suchness of] great loving-kindness...
The suchness of great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity is the suchness of the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha;
the suchness of the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha is the suchness of all-knowledge;
the suchness of all-knowledge is the suchness of the knowledge of the paths; and the suchness of the knowledge of the paths is the suchness of the knowledge of all aspects.
The suchness of all-aspect omniscience is the suchness of wholesome phenomena; the suchness of wholesome phenomena is the suchness of unwholesome phenomena;
the suchness of unwholesome phenomena is the suchness of indeterminate phenomena;
the suchness of indeterminate phenomena is the suchness of mundane phenomena; and the suchness of mundane phenomena is the suchness of supramundane phenomena.
The suchness of supramundane phenomena is the suchness of contaminated phenomena;
the suchness of contaminated phenomena is the suchness of uncontaminated phenomena; the suchness of uncontaminated phenomena is the suchness of conditioned phenomena;
the suchness of conditioned phenomena is the suchness of unconditioned phenomena; and the suchness of unconditioned phenomena is the suchness of past phenomena.
The suchness of past phenomena is the suchness of future phenomena; the suchness of future phenomena is the suchness of present phenomena;
the suchness of present phenomena is the suchness of the fruit of stream-entry; the suchness of the fruit of stream-entry is the suchness of the fruit of once-returning;
the suchness of the fruit of once-returning is the suchness of the fruit of non-returning.
The suchness of the fruit of non-returning is the suchness of the fruit of arhatship;
the suchness of the fruit of arhatship is the suchness of pratyekabuddha-bodhi; the suchness of pratyekabuddha-bodhi is the suchness of the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
and the suchness of the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is the suchness of the Buddhas.
The suchness of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is the suchness of the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas; the suchness of all Tathāgatas, Arhats,
and Samyaksaṃbuddhas is the suchness of all sentient beings.

"Subhūti! Whether it be the suchness of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; the suchness of all sentient beings; or the suchness of all phenomena—these are non-dual and have no duality; they are a single suchness. Because this suchness is without distinction, it is indestructible, inexhaustible, and cannot be conceptually differentiated."

"Subhūti! All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, relying upon this profound Prajñāpāramitā, realize the ultimate suchness of all phenomena and thereby attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. For this reason, it is said that the profound Prajñāpāramitā gives birth to all Buddhas; she is the mother of all Buddhas and can reveal to all Buddhas the true reality of the world."

"Subhūti! In this way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by means of the profound Prajñāpāramitā, is able to realize, as they truly are, the suchness (tathatā), the non-falsity, and the non-alteration of all phenomena."
"Because he has awakened to the characteristics of suchness as they truly are, he is called the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
The suchness, non-falsity, and non-alteration of all dharmas realized by the profound *prajñāpāramitā* are exceedingly profound, difficult to see, and difficult to awaken to.

"Bhagavān! All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas manifest and distinguish the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas by means of the suchness of all phenomena, their non-falsity, and their immutability."
“World-Honored One!
Who is able to believe and understand the profound suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena?

Only bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have reached the stage of non-retrogression, as well as arhats who have exhausted their outflows and possess right view, can give rise to faith and understanding upon hearing the Buddha speak of this profound suchness. For their sake, the Tathāgata reveals and distinguishes the characteristics of suchness based on what he himself has realized.”
The Buddha said:
"So it is, Subhūti! It is just so."
So it is! It is just as you have said. Why is this?
“Subhūti! Suchness is profound because it is inexhaustible; only the Tathāgata has realized perfect awakening to this inexhaustible suchness.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By means of what does the Buddha realize inexhaustible *tathatā* (suchness)?
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! It is by means of suchness that the Buddha can realize such inexhaustible suchness.
Then, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Whose inexhaustible *tathatā* (suchness) has the Tathāgata realized?
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! One realizes the inexhaustible suchness of all phenomena. Subhūti!”

Because all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have realized the inexhaustible suchness of all phenomena, they have attained unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and, for the sake of all sentient beings, have analytically demonstrated the characteristic of the suchness of all phenomena; for this reason, they are called "those who speak the truth."

Chapter 47: Showing the Signs, Part Two, Section Fourteen, Part One. At that time, all the devas of the desire realm and the form realm throughout the trichiliocosm each scattered various kinds of exquisite celestial flowers and incense from afar upon the World-Honored One as an offering. They approached the Buddha’s presence, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. Together they addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, what are the characteristics of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* that you have spoken of?”
At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of devas, saying:

"The profound *prajñāpāramitā* has emptiness as its characteristic; the profound *prajñāpāramitā* has signlessness as its characteristic; the profound *prajñāpāramitā* has wishlessness as its characteristic."
The mark [of the Dharma] is that the profound *prajñāpāramitā* has non-creation and non-action as its mark;
the profound *prajñāpāramitā* has non-arising and non-ceasing as its mark;
the profound *prajñāpāramitā* has non-defilement and non-purity as its mark; the profound *prajñāpāramitā* has no...
The characteristic of nature is the absence of characteristics; the profound *prajñāpāramitā* has non-reliance and non-abiding as its characteristic;
the profound *prajñāpāramitā* has neither annihilation nor permanence as its characteristic;
the profound *prajñāpāramitā* has neither identity nor difference as its characteristic; the profound *prajñāpāramitā*...
The *maitrī* has non-coming and non-going as its characteristic; the profound *prajñāpāramitā* has space as its characteristic;
the profound *prajñāpāramitā* possesses such immeasurable characteristics as these.
"O devas, you should know!

These various marks are all designated by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas through conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) for the sake of benefiting the world—including gods, humans, asuras, and others—by means of conceptualization and conventional designations; they do not rely on ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)."
O gods, you should know!
These characteristics of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* cannot be destroyed by anyone in the world, whether among devas, humans, or asuras.
Why is this? Because the world—including devas, humans, asuras, and so forth—all possess signs.
O devas, you should know this!

Characteristics cannot destroy characteristics, nor can characteristics fully know characteristics; characteristics cannot destroy the absence of characteristics (*animitta*), nor can characteristics fully know the absence of characteristics; the absence of characteristics cannot destroy characteristics, nor can the absence of characteristics fully know characteristics; the absence of characteristics cannot destroy the absence of characteristics, nor can the absence of characteristics fully know the absence of characteristics.

Why is this? Whether it be with marks, without marks, or both with and without marks, all are non-existent; for neither that which can destroy nor that which can know, nor that which is destroyed or known, nor the destroyer or the knower, can be apprehended.
"O devas, you should know!
These various marks are not produced by form; they are not produced by feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
they are not produced by the sense-base of the eye; nor are they produced by the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind."
It is not produced by the sphere of form, nor produced by the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena;
it is not produced by the eye-element, nor produced by the elements of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind;
it is not produced by the element of form, nor produced by the elements of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena.
It is not produced by the eye-consciousness element; it is not produced by the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-consciousness elements.
It is not produced by eye-contact; it is not produced by ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-contact.
It is not produced by the various feelings arising with eye-contact as condition; it is not produced by the various feelings arising with ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-contact as condition.
It is not produced by the perfection of generosity; it is not produced by the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom.

It is not produced by inner emptiness; nor is it produced by outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, endless emptiness, the emptiness of dispersion and non-dispersion, essential emptiness, the emptiness of self-characteristics and common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, or the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.

It is not produced by suchness; it is not produced by the dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, the non-erroneous nature, the unchanging nature, equality, the nature free from birth, the fixed nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space, or the inconceivable realm;
it is not produced by the noble truth of suffering, nor by the noble truths of origin, cessation, or the path;
it is not produced by the four dhyānas, nor by the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments.
It is not produced by the eight liberations; it is not produced by the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities.

It is not produced by the four foundations of mindfulness; it is not produced by the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path.
It is not produced by the gate of liberation of emptiness; it is not produced by the gates of liberation of signlessness or wishlessness.

It is not produced by the stage of pure observation; it is not produced by the stage of the lineage, the eighth stage, the stage of possessing vision, the stage of refinement, the stage of freedom from desire, the stage of completion, the stage of the solitary realizer, the stage of the bodhisattva, or the stage of the Tathāgata;

it is not produced by the stage of extreme joy, nor by the stage of freedom from stain, the stage of radiant light, the stage of blazing wisdom, the stage of extreme difficulty to conquer, the stage of presence, the stage of far-reaching, the stage of immovability, the stage of excellent wisdom, or the stage of the cloud of dharma;
it is not produced by the five eyes, nor is it produced by the six supernormal powers.

It is not produced by the ten powers of a Tathāgata; it is not produced by the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
it is not produced by the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, nor by the eighty minor marks;
it is not produced by the quality of non-forgetfulness, nor by the nature of constant dwelling in equanimity.
It is not produced by any of the gateways of dhāraṇī; it is not produced by any of the gateways of samādhi;
it is not produced by all-knowledge; nor is it produced by the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects.

“O devas, you should know! Such signs are not made by devas, nor are they made by non-devas; they are not made by humans, nor are they made by non-humans; they do not belong to devas, nor do they belong to non-devas; they do not belong to humans, nor do they belong to non-humans; they are neither with outflows (*sāsrava*) nor without outflows (*anāsrava*); they are neither worldly (*laukika*) nor supramundane (*lokottara*); they are neither conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); they are without any attachment and are ineffable.”
“O devas, you should know!
The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is free from all marks; one should not ask by what marks the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is characterized.”
"What do you gods think?
If someone were to ask, 'What are the characteristics of space?', would such a question be considered a correct question? The gods replied:
"No, World-Honored One! No!"
"Sugata! Why is this?
Because space has no substance, no marks, and is unconditioned; it is not something to which one should pose such a question."
The World-Honored One said:
“The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise; it should not be the object of such inquiry.

Nevertheless, whether a Buddha appears or not, the characteristics of all phenomena remain fixed within the *dharmadhātu*. Because the Buddha awakens to these characteristics as they truly are, he is called the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.”
At that time, the assembly of devas addressed the Buddha together, saying:
"The various marks realized by the Tathāgata are exceedingly profound, difficult to see, and difficult to realize."
Because the Tathāgata has realized such characteristics as these, unimpeded wisdom operates regarding all phenomena.

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas abide in such characteristics, analytically expounding the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, gathering the characteristics of all phenomena for the sake of sentient beings, and skillfully revealing them so that they may attain unimpeded wisdom regarding the *prajñāpāramitā*.
“Rare indeed, World-Honored One!

This profound *prajñāpāramitā* is the constant sphere of activity for all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas. Because all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present have practiced this sphere, they have realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and have analyzed and revealed the characteristics of all phenomena for the sake of all sentient beings.”
That is to say, it analytically reveals the characteristics of form; it analytically reveals the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
it analytically reveals the characteristics of the eye-base; it analytically reveals the characteristics of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases;
it analytically reveals the characteristics of the form-base; and it analytically reveals the characteristics of the sound, odor, taste, tangible, and mental-object bases.
He analytically reveals the characteristics of the eye-element; he analytically reveals the characteristics of the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements.
He analytically reveals the characteristics of the form-element; he analytically reveals the characteristics of the sound-, odor-, taste-, tangible-, and mental-object-elements.
He analytically reveals the characteristics of the eye-consciousness-element; he analytically reveals the characteristics of the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness-elements.
He analytically reveals the characteristics of eye-contact; he analytically reveals the characteristics of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact.

He analytically reveals the characteristics of all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition; he analytically reveals the characteristics of all feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as condition.

He analytically reveals the characteristics of the perfection of generosity; he analytically reveals the characteristics of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

He analytically reveals the characteristic of internal emptiness; he analytically reveals the characteristics of external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, emptiness of dispersion and non-dispersion, essential nature emptiness, the emptiness of self-characteristics and common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.

He analytically reveals the characteristic of suchness; he analytically reveals the characteristics of the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-falsity, non-alteration, equality, the nature of being free from birth, the fixedness of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm.
He analytically reveals the characteristics of the noble truth of suffering; he analytically reveals the characteristics of the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path;
he analytically reveals the characteristics of the four dhyānas; he analytically reveals the characteristics of the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments;

he analytically reveals the characteristics of the eight liberations; and he analytically reveals the characteristics of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities.

He analytically reveals the characteristics of the four foundations of mindfulness; he analytically reveals the characteristics of the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;
he analytically reveals the characteristics of the liberation door of emptiness; he analytically reveals the characteristics of the liberation doors of signlessness and wishlessness;

he analytically reveals the characteristics of the stage of pure observation; and he analytically reveals the characteristics of the stage of lineage, the eighth stage, the stage of possessing vision, the stage of refinement, the stage of freedom from desire, the stage of completion, the stage of the solitary realizer, the stage of the bodhisattva, and the stage of the Tathāgata.

He analytically reveals the characteristics of the Ground of Utmost Joy; he analytically reveals the characteristics of the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiance, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Extreme Difficulty to Conquer, the Ground of Presence, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud;
he analytically reveals the characteristics of the five eyes; he analytically reveals the characteristics of the six supernormal powers;

he analytically reveals the characteristics of the ten powers of a Tathāgata; and he analytically reveals the characteristics of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
He analytically reveals the characteristics of the thirty-two marks of a great man; he analytically reveals the characteristics of the eighty minor marks;
he analytically reveals the characteristics of the quality of non-forgetfulness; he analytically reveals the characteristics of the state of constant abiding in equanimity;
he analytically reveals the characteristics of all doors of dhāraṇī; and he analytically reveals the characteristics of all doors of samādhi.

He analytically reveals the characteristics of the fruit of stream-entry; he analytically reveals the characteristics of the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship, as well as the characteristics of pratyekabuddha enlightenment;

he analytically reveals the characteristics of all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; he analytically reveals the characteristics of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas;
he analytically reveals the characteristics of omniscience; and he analytically reveals the characteristics of the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 442. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Second Division, Chapter Forty-seven on Manifesting Signs, Part Two. At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of devas, saying:
"It is so! It is thus!"
So it is! It is just as you have said.
O devas, you should know this!

The Tathāgata has realized all phenomena as they truly are to be signless (*animitta*). That is to say: that which is characterized by transformation and resistance is the mark of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*);

the Tathāgata has realized it as it truly is to be signless. That which is characterized by experiencing is the mark of feeling (*vedanā-lakṣaṇa*); the Tathāgata has realized it as it truly is to be signless.
That which is characterized by grasping signs is the mark of perception (*saṃjñā-lakṣaṇa*); the Tathāgata has realized it as it truly is to be signless.
The characteristic of formative activity (*saṃskāra*)—the Tathāgata has realized it as being without characteristics (*animitta*) just as it truly is;
the characteristic of discernment (*vijñāna*)—the Tathāgata has realized it as being without characteristics just as it truly is;
the characteristic of the aggregates (*skandha*) as a mass of suffering and affliction—the Tathāgata has realized it as being without characteristics just as it truly is.
The characteristic of the sense-bases (*āyatana*) is that which grows and arises; the Tathāgata has awakened to them as they truly are, as being without characteristics (*animitta*).
The characteristic of the elements (*dhātu*) is that which is full of poison and harm; the Tathāgata has awakened to them as they truly are, as being without characteristics.
The characteristic of the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) is the ability to give with generosity; the Tathāgata has awakened to it as it truly is, as being without characteristics.

Freedom from the affliction of heat is the characteristic of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*); the Tathāgata has awakened to it as being without characteristics (*animitta*) according to reality.
Absence of anger and resentment is the characteristic of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*); the Tathāgata has awakened to it as being without characteristics according to reality.
Inflexibility is the characteristic of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*); the Tathāgata has awakened to it as being without characteristics according to reality.

Non-distraction is the characteristic of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*); the Tathāgata has realized it as being without characteristics (*animitta*) just as it truly is.
Non-attachment is the characteristic of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); the Tathāgata has realized it as being without characteristics just as it truly is.
Non-existence is the characteristic of internal emptiness (*adhyātmaśūnyatā*) and so forth; the Tathāgata has realized it as being without characteristics just as it truly is.
Non-perversion is the characteristic of suchness and so forth; the Tathāgata has awakened to it as being without characteristics according to reality.
Non-falsity is the characteristic of the Four Noble Truths; the Tathāgata has awakened to them as being without characteristics according to reality.
Absence of agitation and affliction is the characteristic of the four dhyānas; the Tathāgata has awakened to them as being without characteristics according to reality.
Boundlessness and non-obstruction are the characteristics of the four immeasurables; the Tathāgata has awakened to them as they truly are as being signless.
Absence of clamor and confusion are the characteristics of the four formless attainments; the Tathāgata has awakened to them as they truly are as being signless.
Absence of bondage is the characteristic of the eight liberations; the Tathāgata has awakened to them as they truly are as being signless.
The Tathāgata awakens to the characteristics of these eight bases of mastery as being signless, awakening to them as they truly are;
he awakens to the characteristics of these nine successive meditative attainments as being signless, awakening to them as they truly are;
and he awakens to the characteristics of these ten totalities as being boundless and signless, awakening to them as they truly are.
The characteristic of these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment that lead to transcendence, the Tathāgata has awakened to as signless according to reality;
the characteristic of this door of liberation of emptiness that leads to detachment, the Tathāgata has awakened to as signless according to reality;
the characteristic of this door of liberation of signlessness which is free from grasping, the Tathāgata has awakened to as signless according to reality.
The absence of seeking is the characteristic of the liberation door of wishlessness; the Tathāgata awakens to it as being without marks according to reality.
The gathering of the pure stages is the characteristic of the ten stages of the three vehicles; the Tathāgata awakens to it as being without marks according to reality.
The progression toward great awakening is the characteristic of the ten stages of the bodhisattva; the Tathāgata awakens to it as being without marks according to reality.
The ability to observe and reflect upon these five eyes is the characteristic of the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata realizes them as they truly are to be signless (*animitta*).
The absence of obstruction is the characteristic of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*); the Tathāgata realizes them as they truly are to be signless.
The invincibility [to being overcome] is the characteristic of the Tathāgata’s ten powers (*daśabala*); the Tathāgata realizes them as they truly are to be signless.
Fearlessness is the characteristic of the four fearlessnesses; the Tathāgata realizes them as being without characteristics according to reality.
Non-interruption is the characteristic of the four analytical knowledges; the Tathāgata realizes them as being without characteristics according to reality.
Bestowing benefit and happiness is the characteristic of great compassion; the Tathāgata realizes it as being without characteristics according to reality.
The uprooting of decay and suffering is the mark of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); the Tathāgata realizes it, as it truly is, to be signless (*animitta*).
Rejoicing in wholesome matters is the mark of great joy (*muditā*); the Tathāgata realizes it, as it truly is, to be signless.
The discarding of impurities is the mark of great equanimity (*upekṣā*); the Tathāgata realizes it, as it truly is, to be signless.
The remaining "incomparable qualities" are the characteristics of the eighteen unique dharmas of a Buddha; the Tathāgata awakens to them as they truly are, as being without marks (*animitta*).
That which is able to adorn is the characteristic of the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*); the Tathāgata awakens to it as it truly is, as being without marks.
That which is able to recollect is the characteristic of the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣa-dharma*); the Tathāgata awakens to it as it truly is, as being without marks.
Non-apprehension is the characteristic of the nature of equanimity in constant abiding; the Tathāgata has awakened to it as being without characteristics.
Universal upholding is the characteristic of all dhāraṇī-doors; the Tathāgata has awakened to it as being without characteristics.
Universal embracing is the characteristic of all samādhi-doors; the Tathāgata has awakened to it as being without characteristics.
Skillfully receiving the teaching is the characteristic of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya; the Tathāgata awakens to it as being without characteristics according to reality.
Self-awakening is the characteristic of pratyekabuddha-bodhi; the Tathāgata awakens to it as being without characteristics according to reality.
Being able to accomplish the great task is the characteristic of all practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; the Tathāgata awakens to it as being without characteristics according to reality.

Possessing great functional efficacy is the characteristic of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas; the Tathāgata awakens to it as being without characteristics (*animitta*) according to reality.
Manifesting perfect awakening is the characteristic of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*); the Tathāgata awakens to it as being without characteristics according to reality.
Thoroughly and skillfully penetrating is the characteristic of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*); the Tathāgata awakens to it as being without characteristics according to reality.

The distinct awakening to the manifest is the characteristic of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); the Tathāgata awakens to it as being without characteristics (*animitta*) according to reality.
"O devas, you should know!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are able to awaken to all such characteristics of phenomena as being without characteristics according to reality. For this reason, I say that the wisdom and vision of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are unimpeded and have no equal."
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:
“Subhūti, you should know this!

The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is the mother of all Buddhas; the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can reveal the true nature of all phenomena in the world. Therefore, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha dwells in reliance upon this Dharma, and he makes offerings, shows respect, honors, praises, upholds, and protects the Dharma upon which he relies and dwells—this Dharma is precisely the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas do not fail to rely upon this profound Prajñāpāramitā; they make offerings to it, revere it, honor it, praise it, and uphold it with protective care.
Why is this? Subhūti!
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have grown and been brought forth precisely because of this profound Prajñāpāramitā.
The profound *prajñāpāramitā* serves as the basis for all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and is able to reveal the true nature of all phenomena in the world.
“Subhūti, you should know that all Tathāgatas,
Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are those who recognize kindness and are able to repay kindness. Subhūti!”
If someone should ask,
"Who is it that knows gratitude and is able to repay it?
one should answer correctly:
"The Buddha is one who knows gratitude and is able to repay it.
Why is this? Because among all those in the world, none surpasses the Buddha in knowing gratitude and repaying it.
Then, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
how does a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha recognize kindness and repay it?”
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have mounted this vehicle and traveled this path to arrive at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Having attained enlightenment, they have at all times made offerings to, honored, revered, praised, embraced, and protected this vehicle and this path without ever ceasing for even a moment; you should know that this vehicle and this path are none other than the profound Prajñāpāramitā.”
"Subhūti! This is called the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha’s knowing of kindness and repaying of kindness.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, without exception, rely upon the profound Prajñāpāramitā to realize that all phenomena are devoid of agency, because there is no agent to be found.

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, without exception, rely upon the profound Prajñāpāramitā to realize that all phenomena are not established as real entities, because no substantial form can be apprehended.

"Subhūti! Because the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, relying upon this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, realize that all phenomena are devoid of activity and lack anything to be accomplished, and because they have at all times made offerings, shown reverence, honored, and praised it, and have continuously upheld and protected it without interruption, they are therefore called those who truly know gratitude and repay kindness."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are no Tathāgatas, Arhats, or Samyaksaṃbuddhas who do not rely upon the profound Prajñāpāramitā to turn the wheel of wisdom regarding all phenomena as being without action, without accomplishment, and without arising; furthermore, they are able to know the causes and conditions for this non-turning."

Therefore, one should know that the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is able to give birth to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and is also able to reveal the characteristics of the world as they truly are.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The Tathāgata has often said that the nature of all dharmas is unarisen, unproduced, unknowable, and invisible. How can it be said that the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can give birth to the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and can reveal the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena in the world?”
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas declare that all phenomena are unarisen, unoriginated, unknowable, and invisible.

According to conventional discourse, it is said that the profound perfection of wisdom can give birth to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and can also reveal the characteristics of the world as they truly are.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
how is it that all dharmas are without birth, without arising, without cognition, and without vision?”
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

Because all phenomena are empty and non-existent, because they are all devoid of self-mastery, deceptive, and not solid, all phenomena are without birth, without arising, without cognition, and without vision.”
Furthermore, Subhūti!

The nature of all phenomena has no basis for reliance and no point of attachment; by virtue of these causes and conditions, they are without birth, without arising, without cognition, and without vision.
Subhūti, you should know this:

although the profound perfection of wisdom gives birth to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and can also manifest the true reality of the world, it neither gives birth to anything nor manifests anything.
“Subhūti, you should know this:
because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* does not perceive form, it is called that which reveals the characteristic of form;
because it does not perceive feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, it is called that which reveals the characteristics of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.”
Because one does not perceive the sense-base of the eye, it is called "indicating the characteristic of the sense-base of the eye";
because one does not perceive the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, it is called "indicating the characteristics of the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind."
Because one does not perceive the sphere of form, it is called "manifesting the characteristic of the sphere of form";

because one does not perceive the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena, it is called "manifesting the characteristics of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena."
Because one does not perceive the eye-element, it is called "showing the characteristic of the eye-element";
because one does not perceive the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-element, it is called "showing the characteristics of the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements."
Because one does not perceive the realm of form, it is called "manifesting the characteristics of the realm of form";

because one does not perceive the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena, it is called "manifesting the characteristics of the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena."
Because one does not perceive the eye-consciousness element, it is called "demonstrating the characteristic of the eye-consciousness element";

because one does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-consciousness elements, it is called "demonstrating the characteristics of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements."
Because one does not perceive eye-contact, it is called "indicating the characteristic of eye-contact";
because one does not perceive ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact, it is called "indicating the characteristics of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact."

Because one does not perceive the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, this is called demonstrating the characteristic of the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition;

because one does not perceive the various feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as conditions, this is called demonstrating the characteristic of the various feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as conditions.
Because one does not perceive the earth element, it is called "showing the characteristics of the earth element";
because one does not perceive the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements, it is called "showing the characteristics of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements."
Because one does not perceive ignorance, it is called "showing the characteristic of ignorance";

because one does not perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, or old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, it is called "showing the characteristics of volitional formations" up to "old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair."
Because one does not perceive the perfection of generosity, it is called the demonstration of the characteristics of the perfection of generosity;

because one does not perceive the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, they are called the demonstrations of the characteristics of the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom.
Because one does not perceive internal emptiness, it is called the demonstration of the characteristic of internal emptiness;
