because one does not perceive external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, the emptiness of dispersion and non-dispersion, the emptiness of essential nature, the emptiness of self- and common-characteristics, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, it is called the demonstration of the characteristics of external emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.
Because one does not perceive *tathatā* (suchness), it is called "manifesting the characteristic of suchness.

Because one does not perceive the *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm), the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature), the non-illusory nature, the unchanging nature, the nature of equality, the nature of freedom from birth, the fixedness of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space, or the inconceivable realm, it is called "manifesting the characteristics of the dharma-realm up to the inconceivable realm."
Because one does not perceive the Noble Truth of Suffering, it is called "indicating the characteristic of the Noble Truth of Suffering";
because one does not perceive the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path, it is called "indicating the characteristics of the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path."
Because they do not perceive the four dhyānas, they are said to demonstrate the characteristics of the four dhyānas;
because they do not perceive the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments, they are said to demonstrate the characteristics of the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments.
Because they do not perceive the eight liberations, they are said to demonstrate the characteristics of the eight liberations;

because they do not perceive the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, or the ten totalities, they are said to demonstrate the characteristics of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities.
Because one does not perceive the four foundations of mindfulness, it is called "indicating the characteristics of the four foundations of mindfulness";

because one does not perceive the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path, it is called "indicating the characteristics of the four right endeavors" up to "the eightfold noble path."
Because one does not perceive the gate of liberation of emptiness, it is called "showing the characteristic of the gate of liberation of emptiness";
because one does not perceive the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness, it is called "showing the characteristics of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness."
Because one does not perceive the three vehicles and the ten stages, it is called "manifesting the characteristics of the three vehicles and the ten stages";
because one does not perceive the ten stages of the bodhisattva, it is called "manifesting the characteristics of the bodhisattva's ten stages."
Because one does not perceive the five eyes, it is called "manifesting the characteristics of the five eyes";
because one does not perceive the six supernormal powers, it is called "manifesting the characteristics of the six supernormal powers.
Because one does not perceive the ten powers of the Tathāgata, it is called "manifesting the characteristics of the ten powers of the Tathāgata."

Because one does not perceive the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, this is called demonstrating the characteristics of the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Because one does not perceive the thirty-two marks of a great man, it is called "indicating the mark of the thirty-two marks of a great man";
because one does not perceive the eighty secondary characteristics, it is called "indicating the mark of the eighty secondary characteristics."
Because one does not perceive the quality of non-forgetfulness, it is called the manifestation of the characteristic of non-forgetfulness;
because one does not perceive the state of constant abiding in equanimity, it is called the manifestation of the characteristic of constant abiding in equanimity.
Because one does not perceive any dharani-gates, it is called "manifesting the characteristics of all dharani-gates";
because one does not perceive any samadhi-gates, it is called "manifesting the characteristics of all samadhi-gates."
Because they do not perceive the fruit of stream-entry, it is called the manifestation of the characteristics of the fruit of stream-entry;

because they do not perceive the fruits of once-returner, non-returner, or arhatship, nor pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, it is called the manifestation of the characteristics of the fruits of once-returner, non-returner, arhatship, and pratyekabuddha-enlightenment.
Because one does not perceive any practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, it is called "manifesting the characteristics of all practices of bodhisattva mahāsattvas";

because one does not perceive the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas, it is called "manifesting the characteristics of the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas."
Because one does not perceive all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), it is called "manifesting the characteristics of all-knowledge";

because one does not perceive the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), it is called "manifesting the characteristics of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects."

Subhūti! By such a principle, the profound perfection of wisdom can reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world; it is named the Mother of the Tathāgata, for she is able to give birth to the Tathāgatas.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
why is it that this profound perfection of wisdom, by not seeing form, is said to demonstrate the characteristics of form?”
Because one does not see feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, is this called demonstrating the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?
Likewise, up to: because one does not see all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), is this called demonstrating the characteristic of all-knowledge;

because one does not see the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), is this called demonstrating the characteristics of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"The profound *prajñāpāramitā* does not give rise to consciousness by taking form (*rūpa*) as its object; because it does not perceive form, it is called the 'manifestation of the characteristics of form.

It does not give rise to consciousness by taking feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*) as its objects; because it does not perceive feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, it is called the 'manifestation of the characteristics of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.'"

In this way, up to and including the arising of consciousness by not taking omniscience as an object: because one does not perceive omniscience, it is called the manifestation of the characteristic of omniscience;

the arising of consciousness by not taking the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects as objects: because one does not perceive the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects, it is called the manifestation of the characteristics of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects.

Subhūti! By this principle, the profound perfection of wisdom can reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world; it is called the Mother of the Tathāgatas, for she gives birth to the Tathāgatas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

this profound perfection of wisdom is called the Mother of the Tathāgatas because it reveals the emptiness of the world to the Tathāgatas, and it demonstrates the true nature of the world to the Tathāgatas."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
how does this profound perfection of wisdom manifest the emptiness of the world for the Tathāgata?"
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

The profound perfection of wisdom can manifest for the Tathāgata the emptiness of the world of form, and manifest the emptiness of the worlds of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.”
It reveals that the world is empty of the eye-base; it reveals that the world is empty of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases.
It reveals that the world is empty of the form-base; it reveals that the world is empty of the sound, odor, taste, tangible, and mental-object bases.
It reveals that the world is empty of the eye-element; it reveals that the world is empty of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements.
It reveals that the world of the visible-form element is empty; it reveals that the worlds of the sound, odor, taste, tangible-object, and mental-phenomena elements are empty.
It reveals that the world of the eye-consciousness element is empty; it reveals that the worlds of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements are empty.
It reveals that the world of eye-contact is empty; it reveals that the worlds of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact are empty.

It reveals that the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are empty of the world; it reveals that the various feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact as conditions are empty of the world.
It reveals that the earth element is empty of the world; it reveals that the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are empty of the world.
It reveals that the twelve links of dependent origination are empty of the world.
It reveals that the sixty-two views, rooted in the view of a self, are empty of the world;
it reveals that the ten paths of wholesome action are empty of the world;
it reveals that the four dhyānas are empty of the world; and it reveals that the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments are empty of the world.
It reveals that the world is empty of the perfection of generosity, up to and including the revelation that the world is empty of the perfection of wisdom;
it reveals that the world is empty of internal emptiness, up to and including the revelation that the world is empty of the emptiness of the essential nature of non-entities;
it reveals that the world is empty of the noble truth of suffering, and reveals that the world is empty of the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path.
It reveals that the eight liberations are empty of the world; it reveals that the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities are empty of the world;
it reveals that the four foundations of mindfulness are empty of the world, up to and including the revelation that the eight branches of the noble path are empty of the world;
it reveals that the gate of liberation of emptiness is empty of the world, and it reveals that the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are empty of the world.
It reveals that the world of the ten stages of the three vehicles is empty; it reveals that the world of the ten stages of the bodhisattvas is empty;
it reveals that the world of the five eyes is empty; it reveals that the world of the six supernormal powers is empty;
it reveals that the world of the ten powers of a buddha is empty, and so on, up to revealing that the world of the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha is empty.
It reveals that the world is empty of the thirty-two marks of a great man; it reveals that the world is empty of the eighty minor marks;
it reveals that the world is empty of the quality of non-forgetfulness; it reveals that the world is empty of the nature of constant equanimity;
it reveals that the world is empty of all doors of dhāraṇī; and it reveals that the world is empty of all doors of samādhi.
It reveals that the fruit of stream-entry is empty of the world, and so on, up to revealing that the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha is empty of the world;
it reveals that all the practices of bodhisattva mahāsattvas are empty of the world, and reveals that the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas is empty of the world;
it reveals that omniscience is empty of the world, and reveals that the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects are empty of the world.

Subhūti! By this principle, the profound perfection of wisdom can reveal the true reality of the world to the Tathāgata; it is named the Mother of the Tathāgatas, for she gives birth to the Tathāgatas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, by relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, are able to reveal for the world that the world of form is empty, reveal that the worlds of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, and so on, up to revealing that the world of all-knowledge is empty, and revealing that the worlds of the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects are empty; they cause all worlds to experience the emptiness of the world of feeling, the emptiness of the world of perception, the emptiness of the world of volition, and the emptiness of the world of cognition."

Subhūti! By such a principle, the profound perfection of wisdom can reveal to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the true reality of the world; it is called the Mother of the Tathāgatas, for she is able to give birth to the Tathāgatas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, this profound perfection of wisdom enables the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha to perceive that the world is empty."
What does one see as empty regarding the world?

One sees the world of form as empty; one sees the worlds of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as empty. In this manner, up to seeing the world of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) as empty, and seeing the world of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) as empty.

Subhūti! By this principle, the profound perfection of wisdom can reveal the true reality of the world to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; it is called the Mother of the Tathāgatas, for she is able to give birth to the Tathāgatas.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, this profound prajñāpāramitā can demonstrate to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the inconceivable characteristic of the world; it is called the Mother of the Tathāgatas, for she can demonstrate the true characteristic of the world to the Tathāgata."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
how does this profound Prajñāpāramitā demonstrate to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the inconceivable characteristic of the world?”
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

The profound *prajñāpāramitā* can demonstrate to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the inconceivable characteristic of the world of form; the inconceivable characteristic of the worlds of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; and likewise, up to the inconceivable characteristic of the world of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the inconceivable characteristic of the world of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the inconceivable characteristic of the world of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).”

Subhūti! By such a principle, this profound perfection of wisdom can reveal to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the true reality of the world; it is called the Mother of the Tathāgatas, for she is able to give birth to the Tathāgatas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

This profound *prajñāpāramitā* can demonstrate to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the characteristic of the world’s detachment; it is called the Mother of the Tathāgatas, for it can demonstrate to the Tathāgata the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of the world."
Then, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
how does this profound perfection of wisdom demonstrate to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the characteristic of the world’s detachment?”
The Buddha said, “Suvīkṣaṇa!

The profound *prajñāpāramitā* can demonstrate to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the world’s characteristic of remoteness regarding form (*rūpa*), the world’s characteristic of remoteness regarding feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*); and so on, up to the world’s characteristic of remoteness regarding all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the world’s characteristic of remoteness regarding the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the world’s characteristic of remoteness regarding the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).”

Subhūti! By such a principle, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can reveal the true reality of the world to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; it is called the Mother of the Tathāgatas, for she gives birth to the Tathāgatas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

This profound perfection of wisdom can demonstrate to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the characteristic of the world’s tranquility; it is called the Mother of the Tathāgatas, for it can demonstrate the true reality of the world to the Tathāgata."
Then, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One,
how does this profound *prajñāpāramitā* demonstrate to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the characteristic of the world’s tranquility?"
The Buddha said: “Subhūti!

The profound perfection of wisdom can demonstrate the mark of tranquility of the world of form for the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; the mark of tranquility of the worlds of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; and likewise, up to the mark of tranquility of the world of all-knowledge (sarvajñatā), the mark of tranquility of the world of the knowledge of the paths (mārgajñatā), and the mark of tranquility of the world of the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā).”

Subhūti! By this principle, the profound perfection of wisdom can reveal to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the true reality of the world; it is called the Mother of the Tathāgatas, for she gives birth to the Tathāgatas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

This profound perfection of wisdom can demonstrate to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the ultimate mark of emptiness of the world; it is called the Mother of the Tathāgatas, for it can demonstrate to the Tathāgata the true reality of the world."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
how does this profound perfection of wisdom demonstrate to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the ultimate mark of emptiness of the world?”
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

This profound *prajñāpāramitā* can demonstrate that the world of form (*rūpa*) of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is ultimately empty; that the worlds of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are ultimately empty; and likewise, up to the world of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) being ultimately empty, and the worlds of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) being ultimately empty.”

Subhūti! By this principle, the profound perfection of wisdom can reveal the true reality of the world to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; it is called the Mother of the Tathāgatas, for she gives birth to the Tathāgatas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

This profound perfection of wisdom can reveal to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the mark of the emptiness of the non-existence of the world; it is called the Mother of the Tathāgatas, for it can reveal the true reality of the world to the Tathāgata."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
how does this profound *prajñāpāramitā* demonstrate to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the mark of the emptiness of the non-existence of the world?”
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

The profound *prajñāpāramitā* can demonstrate the mark of the emptiness of the lack of intrinsic nature of the world of form (*rūpa*) of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; the mark of the emptiness of the lack of intrinsic nature of the worlds of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*); and so on, up to the mark of the emptiness of the lack of intrinsic nature of the world of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), and the marks of the emptiness of the lack of intrinsic nature of the world of the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).”

Subhūti! By such a principle, the profound perfection of wisdom can reveal the true reality of the world to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; it is called the Mother of the Tathāgatas, for she gives birth to the Tathāgatas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

This profound *prajñāpāramitā* can reveal to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the world’s characteristic of self-nature emptiness; it is called the Mother of the Tathāgatas, for it can reveal to the Tathāgata the true reality of the world."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
how does this profound perfection of wisdom demonstrate to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, that the intrinsic nature of the world is empty?”
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

The profound *prajñāpāramitā* can demonstrate that the world of form (*rūpa*) has the characteristic of the emptiness of its own-being (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), as do the worlds of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). In this way, it extends even to the world of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), and the worlds of the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), which have the characteristic of the emptiness of their own-being.”

"Subhūti! By such a principle, the profound perfection of wisdom can reveal the true reality of the world to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; it is called the Mother of the Tathāgatas, for she gives birth to the Tathāgatas."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

This profound perfection of wisdom can reveal to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas the mark of the emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence in the world; it is called the Mother of the Tathāgatas, for it can reveal the true reality of the world to the Tathāgatas."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
how does this profound *prajñāpāramitā* demonstrate to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the characteristic of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of the non-existence of the world?”
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

The profound perfection of wisdom can demonstrate to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the mark of the emptiness of the lack of intrinsic nature and the intrinsic nature of the world of form; the mark of the emptiness of the lack of intrinsic nature and the intrinsic nature of the worlds of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness; and likewise, up to the mark of the emptiness of the lack of intrinsic nature and the intrinsic nature of the world of all-knowledge, the mark of the emptiness of the lack of intrinsic nature and the intrinsic nature of the world of the knowledge of the paths, and the world of all-aspect knowledge.”

Subhūti! By this principle, the profound perfection of wisdom can reveal to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the true reality of the world; it is called the Mother of the Tathāgatas, for she gives birth to the Tathāgatas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

This profound perfection of wisdom can demonstrate to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha the world’s characteristic of being purely empty; it is called the Mother of the Tathāgatas, for it can demonstrate to the Tathāgata the true reality of the world."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
how does this profound perfection of wisdom demonstrate to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, that the world has the characteristic of being purely empty?”
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

The profound perfection of wisdom can demonstrate to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, that the world of form is purely empty in its characteristic; that the worlds of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are purely empty in their characteristics; and likewise, up to the world of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) being purely empty in its characteristic, and the worlds of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) being purely empty in their characteristics.”

Subhūti! By such a principle, the profound perfection of wisdom can reveal the true reality of the world to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; it is called the Mother of the Tathāgatas, for she is able to give birth to the Tathāgatas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

This profound *prajñāpāramitā* can demonstrate to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the mark of selflessness in the world; it is called the Mother of the Tathāgatas, for it can demonstrate the true reality of the world to the Tathāgata."
Then, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One,
how does this profound Prajñāpāramitā demonstrate to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the characteristic of selflessness in the world?"
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

The profound *prajñāpāramitā* can demonstrate that the world of form (*rūpa*) in the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is without the mark of self; that the worlds of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are without the mark of self; and likewise, up to the world of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) being without the mark of self, and the worlds of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) being without the mark of self.”

Subhūti! By this principle, the profound perfection of wisdom can reveal the true reality of the world to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; it is called the Mother of the Tathāgatas, for she gives birth to the Tathāgatas.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, the profound perfection of wisdom is able to demonstrate the characteristics of the world to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; that is to say, it causes them not to give rise to the notion of 'this world,' nor does it cause them to give rise to the notion of 'another world.'"
Why is this so? Because all phenomena are non-existent and truly unattainable; there is nothing upon which one can rely to give rise to the notion of "this world" or "the other world."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One!

This profound *prajñāpāramitā* appears in the world for a great purpose; it appears in the world for an inconceivable purpose; it appears in the world for an immeasurable purpose; it appears in the world for an incalculable purpose; it appears in the world for a purpose equal to the unequaled.”
The Buddha said,
“So it is, Subhūti! So it is!”
"So it is! It is just as you have said.

This profound *prajñāpāramitā* appears in the world for the sake of a great matter; it appears in the world for the sake of an inconceivable matter; it appears in the world for the sake of an immeasurable matter; it appears in the world for the sake of an incalculable matter; it appears in the world for the sake of a matter that is unequaled."
“Subhūti! In what way does this profound perfection of wisdom appear in the world for the sake of a great task? Subhūti!”

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas take as their primary task the perpetual rescue and liberation of all sentient beings without ever abandoning them for even a moment; it is for this great purpose that the profound Prajñāpāramitā appears in the world.
“Subhūti! How is it that this profound perfection of wisdom appears in the world for the sake of inconceivable matters? Subhūti!”

The state of perfect enlightenment, the nature of a Tathāgata, the nature of self-awakening, and the nature of omniscience belonging to all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are all inconceivable; it is for this inconceivable purpose that the profound Prajñāpāramitā appears in the world.
“Subhūti! How is it that this profound perfection of wisdom appears in the world for the sake of an immeasurable purpose? Subhūti!”

The state of perfect enlightenment, the nature of a Tathāgata, the nature of self-awakening, and the nature of omniscience possessed by all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas cannot be measured by any sentient being, nor by those included within the category of sentient beings, nor by those comprised within the three realms, the five destinies, or the four modes of birth. It is for this immeasurable purpose that the profound Prajñāpāramitā appears in the world.
“Subhūti! How is it that this profound perfection of wisdom appears in the world for the sake of immeasurable matters? Subhūti!”

The state of perfect enlightenment, the Tathāgata-nature, the nature of self-awakened buddhahood, and the nature of omniscience possessed by all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas—certainly no sentient being, nor any being included within the category of sentient beings, nor any being subsumed within the three realms, the five destinies, or the four modes of birth, can know their quantity; it is for this reason that the profound Prajñāpāramitā appears in the world as a matter of immeasurable significance.
“Subhūti! How is it that this profound perfection of wisdom appears in the world for the sake of the peerless task? Subhūti!”

Of all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, their state of perfect enlightenment, their Tathāgata-nature, their self-awakened nature, and their nature of omniscience—among all sentient beings and phenomena in the world, there is not even an equal, let alone anyone who could surpass them!
"The profound perfection of wisdom has appeared in the world for this peerless purpose.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

Is it only the state of perfectly complete awakening, the Tathāgata-nature, the nature of self-awakening, and the nature of omniscience belonging to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas that is inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled, or are there other dharmas as well?
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

It is not only the nature of perfect enlightenment, the nature of a Tathāgata, the nature of self-awakening, and the nature of omniscience belonging to a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha that are inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled; there are also other dharmas that are inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled.”

"Subhūti! Form, too, is inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, too, are inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled."

In this way, even all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled; the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are likewise inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled.
"Subhūti! All dharmas are likewise inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled. Subhūti!"

Within the true *dharmatā* of all phenomena, both mind and mental factors are unapprehendable. Furthermore, Subhūti, form cannot be designated as being inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, or equal-to-the-unequaled;

feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness likewise cannot be designated as being inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, or equal-to-the-unequaled. In this way, even up to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), it cannot be designated as being inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, or equal-to-the-unequaled; the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) also cannot be designated as being inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, or equal-to-the-unequaled.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One,
for what reason is form (rūpa) not to be designated as inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled?"
Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness also incapable of being designated as inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and equal to the unequaled?

In this way, up to and including omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), which is inexpressible, inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled—is the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) likewise inexpressible, inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled?
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

Because form cannot be designated as having the nature of being conceivable, measurable, quantifiable, equal, or unequal; and because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness likewise cannot be designated as having the nature of being conceivable, measurable, quantifiable, equal, or unequal; and so on, up to the fact that even all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) cannot be designated as having the nature of being conceivable, measurable, quantifiable, equal, or unequal; and because the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) likewise cannot be designated as having the nature of being conceivable, measurable, quantifiable, equal, or unequal.”
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, for what reason is form (rūpa) incapable of being designated as having the nature of being conceivable, measurable, quantifiable, equal, or unequal? Why are feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), formations (saṃskāra), and consciousness (vijñāna) also incapable of being designated as having the nature of being conceivable, measurable, quantifiable, equal, or unequal? And so on, up to why omniscience (sarvajñatā) is incapable of being designated as having the nature of being conceivable, measurable, quantifiable, equal, or unequal; and why the knowledge of the aspects of the path (mārgākārajñatā) and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) are also incapable of being designated as having the nature of being conceivable, measurable, quantifiable, equal, or unequal?”
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

Because the intrinsic nature of form is inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, unequaled, and without intrinsic nature, form cannot be designated as being conceivable, measurable, calculable, or characterized by equality or inequality.

Because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is likewise inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, unequaled, and without intrinsic nature, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be designated as being conceivable, measurable, calculable, or as having the qualities of equality or inequality.

In this way, up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), because its intrinsic nature is inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, unequaled, and without self-nature, all-knowledge cannot be designated as having the nature of being conceivable, measurable, calculable, equal, or unequal.

Because the intrinsic nature of the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is likewise inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, unequaled, and without self-nature, the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects also cannot be designated as having the nature of being conceivable, measurable, calculable, equal, or unequal.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Because form (*rūpa*) cannot be apprehended, it is inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled; because feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) also cannot be apprehended, they too are inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled. In this way, up to and including omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), because it cannot be apprehended, it is inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled; and because the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) also cannot be apprehended, they too are inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

For what reason is form unobtainable, and thus inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled; and why are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness likewise unobtainable, and thus inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled? And so on, up to why is all-knowledge (sarvajñatā) unobtainable, and thus inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled; and why are the knowledge of the aspects of the path (mārgākārajñatā) and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) likewise unobtainable, and thus inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled?”
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!
Because form is limitless, it cannot be apprehended; because it cannot be apprehended, it is inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled.”

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise ungraspable because they are without limit; because they are ungraspable, they are inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled.

In this way, up to and including omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), because it is limitless, it cannot be apprehended; because it cannot be apprehended, it is inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled.

The knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are likewise, because they are limitless, cannot be apprehended; because they cannot be apprehended, they are inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, by what causes and conditions is form unattainable because it is limitless; why are feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness also unattainable because they are limitless; and likewise, up to why is all-knowledge (sarvajñā) unattainable because it is limitless, and why are the knowledge of the aspects of the path (mārgākārajñatā) and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) also unattainable because they are limitless?”
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

The characteristic of form is immeasurable because it is inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled; the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise immeasurable because they are inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled. In this way, even up to the characteristic of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), it is immeasurable because it is inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled; the characteristics of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are also immeasurable because they are inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti, what do you think?
Within form that is inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled— can form be apprehended?"

Within feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—which are inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled—can feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness be apprehended?
In this way, even within omniscience—which is inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled—can omniscience be apprehended?

Within the inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled nature of the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects, can the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects be apprehended?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
"No, Sugata! The Buddha said:
“Excellent, Subhūti! It is so, it is so!”
For this reason, Subhūti, all phenomena are inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled.

Because all phenomena are inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled, so too are all the dharmas of perfect enlightenment, the dharmas of a Tathāgata, the dharmas of self-awakened realization, and the dharmas of omniscience belonging to all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas—inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled.

"Subhūti! All the dharmas of perfect enlightenment, the dharmas of a Tathāgata, the dharmas of self-awakening, and the dharmas of omniscience belonging to all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are inconceivable, because conceptualization has ceased;
they are immeasurable, because measurement has ceased."
It is immeasurable, because all measure has ceased;
it is unequaled, because all equality has ceased. Subhūti!
For this reason, all phenomena are likewise inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled. "Subhūti!

All the dharmas of perfect enlightenment, the dharmas of the Tathāgata, the dharmas of self-awakening, and the dharmas of omniscience belonging to all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are inconceivable, for they transcend conception;
they are immeasurable, for they transcend measurement;
they are innumerable, for they transcend number.
"Unequaled, because it transcends all that is equal. Subhūti!
For this reason, all dharmas are likewise inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled."

“Subhūti! That which is inconceivable is merely a designation for the inconceivable; that which is incomparable is merely a designation for the incomparable; that which is immeasurable is merely a designation for the immeasurable; and that which is unequaled is merely a designation for the unequaled.”

Subhūti! For this reason, all the dharmas of perfect enlightenment, the dharmas of a Tathāgata, the dharmas of self-awakened realization, and the dharmas of omniscience belonging to all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are inconceivable and immeasurable;
they are incalculable because, like space, they are incalculable.
"Unequaled," because it is like space, which is unequaled. Subhūti!

For this reason, all the dharmas of perfect enlightenment, the dharmas of a Tathāgata, the dharmas of self-awakened realization, and the dharmas of omniscience belonging to all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled.

“Subhūti! All the dharmas of perfect enlightenment, the dharmas of a Tathāgata, the dharmas of self-awakening, and the dharmas of omniscience belonging to all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas—these cannot be conceived, measured, calculated, or equated by Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or any worldly beings, including devas, humans, and asuras.”

"Subhūti! For this reason, all the dharmas of perfect enlightenment, the dharmas of a Tathāgata, the dharmas of self-awakened realization, and the dharmas of omniscience belonging to all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled."

When the Buddha had spoken this chapter on the inconceivable, the immeasurable, the incalculable, and the unequaled, five hundred bhikṣus among the assembly attained liberation of mind through the destruction of the outflows.
Furthermore, there were two hundred bhikṣuṇīs, all of whom, being free from outflows, attained liberation of mind.
Additionally, six hundred upāsakas, regarding all phenomena, became free from dust and defilement, and the pure Dharma-eye arose within them.
Furthermore, three hundred upāsikās also attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena, becoming free from dust and defilement.

Additionally, two thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) and shall receive their prediction of Buddhahood within this Bhadrakalpa.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 443; The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra,
Fascicle 444.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter 48: Accomplishment, Part Two. Chapter Forty-Eight: Accomplishment. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

The profound perfection of wisdom appears in the world for a great purpose; it appears in the world for an inconceivable purpose; it appears in the world for an immeasurable purpose; it appears in the world for an incalculable purpose; it appears in the world for a purpose that is unequaled.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said:
the profound *prajñāpāramitā* appears in the world for a great purpose, even appearing in the world for the sake of the unequaled.
Why is this? Subhūti!

The profound perfection of wisdom is able to accomplish the perfection of generosity, and it is also able to accomplish the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

They are able to accomplish internal emptiness, and they are also able to accomplish external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, the emptiness of dispersion and non-dispersion, essential nature emptiness, the emptiness of self-characteristics and common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;

they are able to accomplish suchness, and they are also able to accomplish the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-falsity, non-alteration, equality, the nature of being free from birth, the fixedness of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm.
They are able to accomplish the noble truth of suffering, and they are also able to accomplish the noble truths of its origin, cessation, and the path;
they are able to accomplish the four dhyānas, and they are also able to accomplish the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments;
they are able to accomplish the eight liberations, and they are also able to accomplish the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative absorptions, and the ten totalities.

They are able to accomplish the four foundations of mindfulness, and they are also able to accomplish the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path;
they are able to accomplish the gate of liberation of emptiness, and they are also able to accomplish the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness;
they are able to accomplish the ten stages of the three vehicles, and they are also able to accomplish the ten stages of the bodhisattva.
They are able to accomplish the five eyes and also able to accomplish the six supernormal powers;

they are able to accomplish the ten powers of a Tathāgata, as well as the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they are able to accomplish the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and also able to accomplish the eighty minor marks.
They are able to accomplish the quality of non-forgetfulness, and they are also able to accomplish the state of constant equanimity;
they are able to accomplish all doors of dhāraṇī, and they are also able to accomplish all doors of samādhi;
they are able to accomplish the fruit of stream-entry, and they are also able to accomplish the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, and the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
It can accomplish all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and it can also accomplish the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas;
it can accomplish all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), and it can also accomplish the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

“Subhūti! It is like a Kṣatriya great king who has been consecrated by coronation; possessing majestic power and sovereignty, he subdues all, entrusts the affairs of state to his ministers, and remains seated with folded hands in non-action, dwelling in peace and happiness.”

The Tathāgata is likewise; as the Great Dharma King, possessing sovereign majesty and power, he subdues all beings. Whether it be the teachings of the śrāvakas, the teachings of the pratyekabuddhas, the teachings of the bodhisattvas, or the teachings of the buddhas, he entrusts them all to the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. It is by means of this *prajñāpāramitā* that all tasks and activities are accomplished.
Therefore, Subhūti, it is for a great purpose that this profound perfection of wisdom appears in the world, even unto its appearing in the world for the sake of the unequaled.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is without grasping and without attachment toward form (*rūpa*), it appears in the world and is able to accomplish its tasks;

because it is without grasping and without attachment toward feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), it appears in the world and is able to accomplish its tasks."
Because there is no grasping and no clinging toward the sense base of the eye, one manifests in the world to accomplish beneficial tasks;
because there is no grasping and no clinging toward the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, one manifests in the world to accomplish beneficial tasks.
Because they are without grasping or attachment toward the sense base of form, they manifest in the world to accomplish purposeful deeds;
because they are without grasping or attachment toward the sense bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena, they manifest in the world to accomplish purposeful deeds.
Because there is no grasping and no attachment toward the eye-element, one manifests in the world to accomplish purposeful deeds;
because there is no grasping and no attachment toward the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements, one manifests in the world to accomplish purposeful deeds.
Because they are without grasping or attachment toward the realm of form, they appear in the world and are able to accomplish their tasks;
because they are without grasping or attachment toward the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena, they appear in the world and are able to accomplish their tasks.
Because they are without grasping or attachment toward the eye-consciousness element, they appear in the world and are able to accomplish their tasks;
because they are without grasping or attachment toward the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements, they appear in the world and are able to accomplish their tasks.
Because they are without grasping or attachment toward eye-contact, they manifest in the world as those who accomplish their tasks;
because they are without grasping or attachment toward ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact, they manifest in the world as those who accomplish their tasks.
Because they are without grasping and without attachment toward the various feelings arising conditioned by eye-contact, they appear in the world as those who can accomplish their tasks;

because they are without grasping and without attachment toward the various feelings arising conditioned by ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact, they appear in the world as those who can accomplish their tasks.
Because they are without grasping or attachment toward the earth element, they appear in the world and accomplish their tasks;
because they are without grasping or attachment toward the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements, they appear in the world and accomplish their tasks.
Because there is no ignorance, no grasping, and no clinging, one appears in the world to accomplish purposeful deeds;

because there is no grasping and no clinging to volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age and death, one appears in the world to accomplish purposeful deeds.
Because they are without grasping or attachment toward the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), they appear in the world to accomplish purposeful deeds;
and so on, up to because they are without grasping or attachment toward the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they appear in the world to accomplish purposeful deeds.
Because there is no grasping and no clinging toward internal emptiness, one appears in the world to accomplish beneficial tasks;
and so on, up to because there is no grasping and no clinging toward the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, one appears in the world to accomplish beneficial tasks.
Because they are without grasping or attachment toward suchness, they appear in the world to accomplish beneficial tasks;
and so on, up to because they are without grasping or attachment toward the inconceivable realm, they appear in the world to accomplish beneficial tasks.
Because they are without grasping or attachment toward the Noble Truth of Suffering, they appear in the world and are able to accomplish their tasks;
because they are without grasping or attachment toward the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path, they appear in the world and are able to accomplish their tasks.
Because they are without grasping or attachment toward the four dhyānas, they manifest in the world to accomplish beneficial tasks;
because they are without grasping or attachment toward the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions, they manifest in the world to accomplish beneficial tasks.
Because they are without grasping or attachment toward the eight liberations, they appear in the world and are able to accomplish their tasks;

because they are without grasping or attachment toward the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities, they appear in the world and are able to accomplish their tasks.
Because they are without grasping or attachment toward the four foundations of mindfulness, they appear in the world to accomplish beneficial tasks;
and so on, up to because they are without grasping or attachment toward the eightfold noble path, they appear in the world to accomplish beneficial tasks.
Because they are without grasping or attachment toward the liberation door of emptiness, they appear in the world and are able to accomplish their tasks;
because they are without grasping or attachment toward the liberation doors of signlessness and wishlessness, they appear in the world and are able to accomplish their tasks.
Because they are without grasping or attachment toward the ten stages of the three vehicles, they manifest in the world and are able to accomplish their tasks;
because they are without grasping or attachment toward the ten stages of the bodhisattvas, they manifest in the world and are able to accomplish their tasks.
Because they are without grasping or attachment toward the five eyes, they appear in the world and are able to accomplish their tasks;
because they are without grasping or attachment toward the six supernormal powers, they appear in the world and are able to accomplish their tasks.
Because they are without grasping or attachment toward the ten powers of the Tathāgata, they appear in the world and are able to accomplish their tasks;
likewise, because they are without grasping or attachment toward the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, they appear in the world and are able to accomplish their tasks.
Because they are without grasping or attachment toward the thirty-two marks of a great man, they appear in the world and are able to accomplish their tasks;
because they are without grasping or attachment toward the eighty secondary signs, they appear in the world and are able to accomplish their tasks.
Because they are without grasping or attachment toward the quality of non-forgetfulness, they appear in the world to accomplish beneficial tasks;
because they are without grasping or attachment toward the state of constant equanimity, they appear in the world to accomplish beneficial tasks.
Because they are without grasping or attachment toward all dharani-doors, they appear in the world and are able to accomplish their tasks;
because they are without grasping or attachment toward all samadhi-doors, they appear in the world and are able to accomplish their tasks.
Because they are without grasping or attachment toward the fruit of stream-entry, they appear in the world and are able to accomplish their tasks;
and so on, up to because they are without grasping or attachment toward the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, they appear in the world and are able to accomplish their tasks.
Because they are without grasping or attachment toward all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, they appear in the world and are able to accomplish their tasks;
because they are without grasping or attachment toward the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas, they appear in the world and are able to accomplish their tasks.
Because they are without grasping or attachment toward all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), they appear in the world and are able to accomplish their tasks;

because they are without grasping or attachment toward the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), they appear in the world and are able to accomplish their tasks.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, how does this profound *prajñāpāramitā* appear in the world and accomplish its tasks, given that it neither grasps nor clings to form (*rūpa*), nor does it grasp or cling to feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*)—and so on, up to not grasping or clinging to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), nor grasping or clinging to the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)? How is it that, by means of such non-grasping and non-clinging, it appears in the world and brings about the fulfillment of its purpose?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Do you perceive any form that can be grasped or clung to?"
Is there anything seen among feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness that can be grasped or clung to?
Is there anything seen, even up to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), that can be grasped or clung to?
Is there anything seen in the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) that can be grasped or clung to?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
"No, Sugata! The Buddha said:
“Excellent, Excellent, Excellent, Subhūti!”
"So it is! So it is! It is just as you have said."

"Subhūti! I do not perceive form as something to be grasped or clung to; I do not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as something to be grasped or clung to; and so on, up to not perceiving all-knowledge as something to be grasped or clung to, nor perceiving the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects as something to be grasped or clung to. Because I do not perceive them, I do not grasp them; because I do not grasp them, I do not cling to them."

For this reason, in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, there is no grasping and no attachment to form; there is no grasping and no attachment to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; and so on, up to no grasping and no attachment to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), nor is there any grasping or attachment to the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

“Subhūti! I also do not perceive any dharma of perfect enlightenment, any Tathāgata-dharma, any self-awakened dharma, or any all-knowing dharma belonging to all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas that can be grasped or clung to. Because I do not perceive them, I do not grasp them; because I do not grasp them, I do not cling to them.”

The profound perfection of wisdom is likewise: one does not perceive any dharma of perfect enlightenment, any dharma of a Tathāgata, any dharma of self-awakening, or any dharma of omniscience belonging to all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas that can be grasped or clung to; for this reason, there is no grasping and no clinging.

Therefore, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should neither grasp nor cling to form; they should neither grasp nor cling to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. In this way, they should not grasp or cling even to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*); they should not grasp or cling to the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Furthermore, they should not grasp or cling to any of the qualities of perfect enlightenment, the qualities of a Tathāgata, the qualities of self-awakening, or the qualities of all-knowledge belonging to all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
At that time, the hosts of devas from the realms of desire and form all addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One! This Prajñāpāramitā is most profound; it is difficult to see and difficult to realize. It is beyond the reach of discursive thought, transcending the sphere of conceptualization. It is tranquil, subtle, precise, and deep-seated; only those of supreme intelligence can fully comprehend it.”

If there are sentient beings who are able to have deep faith and understanding in this Prajñāpāramitā, it should be known that they have made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas of the past, have made great vows in the presence of those Buddhas, have planted various roots of goodness, have served many virtuous friends, and have been sustained by immeasurable virtuous friends; only then can they believe and understand such Prajñāpāramitā.

If there are those who, upon hearing this Prajñāpāramitā, give rise to profound faith and understanding, you should know that such individuals are indeed bodhisattvas and will certainly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"Bhagavan! Suppose all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were to become those who follow by faith, those who follow by dharma, eighth-stage practitioners, stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas; the wisdom and abandonment they have achieved would not equal that of a person who, for a single day, endures with joy, contemplates, weighs, and examines this profound *prajñāpāramitā*."
The patience achieved by this person regarding this profound *prajñāpāramitā* surpasses that wisdom and abandonment [of others] by an immeasurable and boundless degree. Why is this?

Whatever wisdom or abandonment belongs to those who follow by faith, up to whatever wisdom or abandonment belongs to the pratyekabuddhas, all are but a small fraction of the forbearance of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have already attained the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of devas, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
It is as you have said.

All the knowledge and abandonments of those who follow by faith, those who follow by dharma, the eighth-rank practitioners, stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas, are but a small portion of the forbearance possessed by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have already attained the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
"O celestial hosts, you should know this!

If good sons and good daughters briefly hear such profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and having heard it, believe and understand it, copy it, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, practice it, contemplate it, and explain it to others—then these good sons and good daughters will swiftly transcend birth and death and realize *nirvāṇa*, attaining the wisdom of the Tathāgata’s perfect enlightenment. They surpass those good sons and good daughters who seek the two vehicles and remain far removed from the *prajñāpāramitā*, even if they study other sūtras for an entire kalpa or more than a kalpa."

Why is this so? Because within this profound *prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, all subtle and supreme dharmas are extensively taught; those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*), the eighth-rank practitioners (*aṣṭamaka*), stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*), once-returners (*sakṛdāgāmin*), non-returners (*anāgāmin*), arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should all diligently train in this. According to their respective aspirations, they shall all swiftly bring their undertakings to completion. All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have relied upon this training to realize, are currently realizing, and will realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
At that time, the assembly of devas spoke with one voice, saying:
"This Prajñāpāramitā is the great pāramitā; it is the inconceivable pāramitā, the immeasurable pāramitā, the incalculable pāramitā, and the unequaled pāramitā."

"Bhagavān! Those who follow by faith, those who follow by Dharma, the eighth-rank practitioners, stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas—all of them, through diligent cultivation and study of this profound perfection of wisdom, swiftly transcend birth and death and realize the realm of nirvana without remainder."

All the assembly of Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas diligently study this profound Prajñāpāramitā, swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and enter the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder.

"Bhagavān! Although all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas rely upon this profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) and, through diligent cultivation and study, each attains the ultimate fulfillment of their respective tasks, yet this perfection of wisdom neither increases nor decreases."

At that time, having spoken these words, the assembly of devas from the desire realm and the form realm rejoiced and leaped for joy; they conceived deep faith and delight in this Prajñāpāramitā, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, took their leave of the Buddha, and returned to their palaces. Not long after they had departed from the assembly, they all vanished simultaneously.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, gives rise to deep faith and understanding, and copies it, receives and maintains it, reads and recites it, practices and cultivates it, contemplates it, explains it to others, and makes offerings to it with reverence, respect, honor, and praise—where did such a bodhisattva mahāsattva pass away before coming to be born in this realm?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, develops deep faith and understanding, and copies it, upholds it, reads it, recites it, practices it, reflects on it according to the principle, makes offerings to it, reveres it, honors it, and praises it; and if they constantly follow the Dharma teacher to inquire about its meaning and intent—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—never abandoning it for even a moment, just as a newborn calf does not leave its mother; and until they have attained a thorough mastery of all the meanings and intents of this profound *prajñāpāramitā* and are able to explain them to others, they shall never abandon such profound *prajñāpāramitā* sūtras or the Dharma teacher who preaches them."
"Subhūti, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has passed away from among humans and come to be born here. Why is this?"

"Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva, in previous lives, had already heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā*. Having heard it, he upheld, recited, practiced, and reflected upon it according to the truth. Furthermore, he was able to transcribe it, adorning it with various jewels, and offered worship, respect, reverence, and praise to it with all kinds of exquisite flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses, robes, necklaces, precious banners, pennants, canopies, music, and lamps."

By virtue of these roots of goodness, they will be free from the eight unfavorable conditions; passing away from the human realm, they will be reborn among humans, where they will hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, develop deep faith and understanding, and copy, receive, uphold, read, recite, cultivate, contemplate, and explain it, as well as making offerings to, honoring, respecting, and praising it.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, could there be a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, having accomplished such sublime merit as this, serves and makes offerings to a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha in another direction, and upon passing away from that place, comes to be born here, hears this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, and gives rise to deep faith and understanding, copying it, receiving and upholding it, reading and reciting it, practicing it, contemplating it, and explaining it; and does he honor, revere, respect, and praise it without weariness?”
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, having accomplished such sublime qualities, have made offerings to and served the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas of other directions; passing away from those places, they are born here in this world. Upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, they give rise to deep faith and understanding, and they copy it, uphold it, read it, recite it, cultivate it, contemplate it, and explain it; they honor, revere, respect, and praise it with minds free from weariness or indolence.

Why is this so? It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have previously, in the presence of immeasurable Buddhas in other directions, heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught; they have developed deep faith and understanding, and have transcribed, received, upheld, recited, practiced, contemplated, and explained it. They have made offerings, honored, revered, and praised it with a mind free from weariness. By the power of such roots of goodness, they pass away from those places and are reborn here.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, passing away from the class of beings in Tuṣita Heaven, are reborn among humans; they too have accomplished such meritorious qualities."

Why is this so? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, in previous lives, had already inquired regarding the profound meaning and intent of the *prajñāpāramitā* from the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya in the Tuṣita Heaven. By the power of such roots of goodness, they passed away from that place and were reborn among human beings; upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, they give rise to deep faith and understanding, and they copy it down, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, practice and contemplate it, explain and expound it, and offer it worship, respect, honor, and praise, without a mind of weariness.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are sons and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who, although they heard the *prajñāpāramitā* up to the *dānapāramitā* in previous lives, did not inquire about its profound meaning and intent. Now, having been born among humans and hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, their minds become bewildered and distressed, hesitant and timid, or they develop erroneous interpretations, making them difficult to enlighten."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

there are sons and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who, although they heard in previous lives about internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature, did not inquire about its profound meaning;
and although they heard in previous lives about suchness up to the inconceivable realm, they did not inquire about its profound meaning."
Although they may have heard the Noble Truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path in previous lives, they did not inquire into their profound meaning and intent.

Now, having been born among humans and hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, their minds become confused, hesitant, and timid; they may even develop erroneous interpretations, making them difficult to enlighten.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are sons and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who, although they heard of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments in previous lives, did not inquire about their profound meaning;

and although they heard of the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative concentrations, and the ten totalities in previous lives, they did not inquire about their profound meaning."
Although in previous lives they had heard of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, they did not inquire about their profound meaning;
although in previous lives they had heard of the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—they did not inquire about their profound meaning;
and although in previous lives they had heard of the three vehicles and the ten stages of the bodhisattva, they did not inquire about their profound meaning.

Having now been born among humans, if they hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, their minds may become bewildered and distressed, hesitant, or timid; or they may develop erroneous interpretations, making them difficult to enlighten.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are sons and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who, although they heard of the five eyes and the six supernormal powers in previous lives, did not inquire about their profound meaning;
and although they heard of the ten powers of a buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha in previous lives, they did not inquire about their profound meaning."
Although in previous lives they heard of the thirty-two marks of a great being and the eighty secondary signs, they did not inquire about their profound meaning;
although in previous lives they heard of the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity, they did not inquire about their profound meaning;
although in previous lives they heard of the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi, they did not inquire about their profound meaning.

Although they heard of the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas in previous lives, they did not inquire about their profound meaning;

although they heard of all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) in previous lives, they did not inquire about their profound meaning. Consequently, when they hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā* preached now in the human realm, their minds become confused, hesitant, and weak, or they develop misconceptions, making them difficult to enlighten.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are sons and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who, although they heard the perfection of wisdom in previous lives and also inquired about its profound meaning and intent for one day, two days, three days, four days, or five days, do not practice with diligence according to the teaching."

Having now been born among humans and having heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, even if they should pass one day, two days, three days, four days, or five days with a mind so firm that none can destroy it, yet if they become separated from the profound *prajñāpāramitā* they have heard, they will immediately fall back and their minds will give rise to doubt.
Why is this so? Subhūti!

Because these sons and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle, although they heard the *prajñāpāramitā* in previous lives and even inquired about its profound meaning and intent, did not practice with diligence according to what was taught; therefore, in this present life, if they encounter virtuous friends who earnestly exhort them, they will delight in hearing and receiving this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, but if they do not encounter such virtuous friends who earnestly exhort them, they will not delight in hearing and receiving this sūtra.

Regarding the Prajñāpāramitā, at times they delight in hearing it and at times do not; at times they are steadfast and at times they regress. Their minds are fickle and unstable in their advance and retreat, like light feathers tossed about by the wind.

It should be known that such sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva Vehicle have not long since set out upon the Mahāyāna; they have not yet extensively approached true spiritual friends, nor have they extensively made offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; and they have never yet upheld, recited, copied, contemplated, or expounded the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
“Subhūti, you should know that these sons and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle have not yet studied the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity,
and have not yet studied inner emptiness up to the absence of intrinsic nature.”
