Intrinsic emptiness; not yet having studied true thusness up to the inconceivable realm; not yet having studied the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
not yet having studied the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments;
and not yet having studied the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities.
They have not yet studied the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; they have not yet studied the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
they have not yet studied the three vehicles or the ten stages of a bodhisattva; they have not yet studied the five eyes or the six supernormal powers;
they have not yet studied the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; they have not yet...
One studies the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs, yet has not yet studied the quality of non-forgetfulness or the nature of constant equanimity;
one has not yet studied all the doors of dhāraṇī or the doors of samādhi;
one has not yet studied all the practices of bodhisattvas mahāsattvas or the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas. Not yet...
They study all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Subhūti, you should know that these sons and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who have newly set out in the Great Vehicle possess only a small degree of faith, respect, and affection for the Great Vehicle; they have not yet been able to write down, receive, uphold, read, recite, practice, contemplate, or explain to others this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If those sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle do not write down, receive, uphold, read, recite, cultivate, contemplate, or explain to others this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and if they do not embrace sentient beings by means of the *prajñāpāramitā* up to the *dānapāramitā*, and even if they do not embrace sentient beings by means of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), then these sons and daughters of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle will not be protected by the *prajñāpāramitā* up to the *dānapāramitā*, nor will they be protected by all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects.

These sons and daughters of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle, being unable to practice in accordance with the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity, and even being unable to practice in accordance with all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects, fall by reason of these causes and conditions into the level of the Śrāvakas or the level of the Pratyekabuddhas.

Why is this? Because these sons and daughters of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle are unable to write down, uphold, read, recite, cultivate, contemplate, or explain to others this profound *prajñāpāramitā*. Furthermore, they are unable to use this profound *prajñāpāramitā*—extending even to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)—to gather in sentient beings; they cannot practice in accordance with the *prajñāpāramitā*, extending even to the knowledge of all aspects; and they are not protected by the *prajñāpāramitā*, nor even protected by the knowledge of all aspects. Due to these causes and conditions, they fall to the level of a Śrāvaka or the level of a Pratyekabuddha.
Chapter 49: The Simile of the Ship, Part Two, Section One. The Buddha said to Subhūti:

“Suppose a ship carrying people across the ocean were to break apart; if those on board do not take hold of wood, utensils, life-preservers, planks, or even a corpse to cling to for support, it is certain they will drown and fail to reach the other shore.”

If one can take hold of wood, utensils, a life-preserving float, a plank, or a corpse as something to rely upon, it should be known that such a person will ultimately not perish, but shall reach the safe shore on the other side of the great ocean, remaining unhurt and unharmed while experiencing all manner of happiness.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

If sons or daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle, though they have achieved even a small measure of faith, respect, and affection for the Great Vehicle, do not write down, receive, uphold, read, recite, contemplate, cultivate, or explain to others this profound *prajñāpāramitā* as their point of reliance, you should know that these sons and daughters of good family dwelling in the bodhisattva vehicle will perish midway; they will fail to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and will instead fall back into the stage of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.

If sons or daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle possess perfect faith, reverence, and joyful devotion toward the Mahāyāna, and if they rely upon this profound *prajñāpāramitā* by writing it down, receiving and upholding it, reading and reciting it, reflecting upon it, practicing it, and explaining it to others—then you should know that such sons and daughters of good family dwelling in the bodhisattva vehicle will never fall away midway into the stage of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, but will certainly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

It is as if a person wishing to cross a perilous and desolate wilderness were unable to reach a land of peace and happiness without gathering provisions and equipment; they would encounter suffering and lose their lives along the way."
Thus it is, Subhūti!

If sons or daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle possess faith, patience, a pure mind, a superior intention, desire, resolve, renunciation, and diligence toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, yet do not embrace the profound perfection of wisdom and other meritorious qualities, you should know that such sons or daughters of good family dwelling in the bodhisattva vehicle will fail midway and not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, but will instead fall back into the stage of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.
"Subhūti, you should know this!

Just as a person who wishes to cross a perilous and desolate wilderness will surely reach a land of peace and happiness if they can gather the necessary provisions and equipment, and will never perish midway from suffering."
Thus it is, Subhūti!

If sons or daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle have faith, patience, a pure mind, superior intention, aspiration, resolve, equanimity, and diligence, and are further able to embrace the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and other meritorious qualities, you should know that these sons and daughters of good family dwelling in the bodhisattva vehicle will never suffer loss or retrogression along the way; they will transcend the stages of the śrāvaka and the pratyekabuddha, bring sentient beings to maturity, purify buddha-fields, and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
It is as if a man or a woman were to take an unbaked clay jar and go to a river, or a pond, or a well, or a spring, or a canal to fetch water; you should know that this jar will soon rot and break."
Why is this? Because this jar, being unrefined, is incapable of holding water and will ultimately return to the earth.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
If there are sons or daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who possess faith in,
patience toward, a pure mind for, a superior intention toward, a desire and resolve for,
and equanimity and diligence toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, yet do not embrace this profound perfection of wisdom;
Lacking skillful means, one then becomes distant from the perfections of wisdom, meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline,
and generosity; and likewise, one becomes distant from internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness,
the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, and unconditioned emptiness.
It is also far removed from emptiness, ultimate emptiness, boundless emptiness, emptiness of the non-dispersal of what has been dispersed, essential emptiness,
the emptiness of self-characteristics and common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unobtainable,
the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, as well as from suchness, the dharma-realm, and the dharma-nature.
The nature of phenomena, non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of dharmas,
the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm; furthermore,
it is far removed from the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, and is likewise far removed from the four dhyānas.
The four immeasurables and the four formless attainments are likewise far removed from the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery,
the nine successive meditative concentrations, and the ten totalities; they are likewise far removed from the four foundations of mindfulness,
the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path.
Furthermore, it is far removed from the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
it is also far removed from the ten stages of a bodhisattva; it is also far removed from the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
it is also far removed from the Tathāgata’s ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, and great...

Compassion, great joy, and great equanimity; the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, as well as the quality of being free from forgetfulness and the state of constant abiding in equanimity; furthermore, the doors of dhāraṇī and the doors of samādhi;
furthermore, the maturing of sentient beings and the purification of buddha-fields—these too are far removed.
They are devoid of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

It should be understood that such sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle will decline midway and fail to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, instead falling back into the level of a Śrāvaka or a Pratyekabuddha.
“Subhūti, you should know this!
For example, suppose a man or a woman were to take a well-fired jar and go to a river, a pond, a well, a spring, or a canal to fetch water; you should know that this jar will never break or decay.”
Why is this? Because this jar is well-fired and capable of holding water, being extremely firm and durable.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

There are sons and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who possess faith in, patience toward, a pure mind for, a superior intention for, a desire for, and resolute conviction in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and who, possessing diligence and equanimity, are further able to embrace the skillful means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. Such individuals do not remain distant from the *prajñā*, *dhyāna*, *vīrya*, *kṣānti*, *śīla*, and *dāna* *pāramitās*, and likewise do not remain distant from all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). By virtue of these causes and conditions, they are always embraced and protected by the Buddhas and the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas.

It should be known that such sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle will never suffer decline or defeat midway; they will transcend the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, bring sentient beings to maturity, purify Buddha-fields, and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

It is as if a merchant, lacking skillful means and wisdom, were to place his goods upon a ship at the seashore before it had been properly prepared or repaired, and then pull it into the water and set sail immediately."

You should know that this ship will be wrecked and sink midway; the people, the ship, and the goods will each be scattered to different places. Thus, these merchants, lacking skillful means and wisdom, will lose their lives and their great wealth and treasures.
In this way, Subhūti,
there are sons of good family and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who possess faith in unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete enlightenment, possess patience, possess a pure mind, possess a superior intention, and possess aspiration.
If one possesses resolute conviction and the diligence of equanimity, yet does not embrace the skillful means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*,
then one will be estranged from the *prajñā*, *dhyāna*, *vīrya*, *kṣānti*, *śīla*,
and *dāna* *pāramitās*, and likewise estranged from everything up to and including *sarvajñatā*.

The knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects—one should know that among these sons and daughters of good family who have set out in the Bodhisattva vehicle, such are those who decline midway; they lose their lives and great wealth.
Losing one's life means falling into the level of a Śrāvaka or a Pratyekabuddha; losing wealth means losing [the perfections].
"Unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti, you should know this:

it is like a merchant who possesses skillful wisdom; having first prepared a ship at the seashore, he then draws it into the water to ensure there are no leaks. Only after that does he load his goods upon it and depart. You should know that this ship will certainly not be wrecked or sink, and both the people and their cargo will reach their destination in safety."
Thus it is, Subhūti!

Those sons and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who possess faith in unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; who possess patience, a pure mind, a superior intention, aspiration, and resolute conviction; and who possess equanimity and diligence; and who further are able to embrace the profound perfection of wisdom through skillful means—they do not depart from the perfections of wisdom, meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity, nor do they depart from all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects. By virtue of these causes and conditions, they are always sustained and protected by the Buddhas and the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas.

It should be known that such sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle will never suffer decline or regression midway; they will transcend the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, bring sentient beings to maturity, purify Buddha-fields, and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! Suppose there were a person one hundred and twenty years old, aged, decrepit, and worn out, further afflicted by various illnesses—namely, wind disorders, bile disorders, phlegm disorders, or a combination of these three. What do you think?"
"Can this old, sick man rise up from his bed by himself? Subhūti replied, "No!"
"No, World-Honored One! No, Sugata!"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Even if someone were to support this person and help them stand up, they would still lack the strength to walk even one krośa, two krośas, or three krośas."
Why is that? Because their old age and illness are so severe.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

If there are sons or daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who possess faith in, patience toward, a pure mind for, a superior intention toward, a desire for, and a resolute conviction in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and who also possess equanimity and diligence; yet, if they do not embrace the skillful means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they will then be far removed from the *prajñā*, *dhyāna*, *vīrya*, *kṣānti*, *śīla*, and *dāna* *pāramitās*, and likewise far removed from everything up to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

It should be known that among those sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle in such a manner, they will decline midway; failing to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they will regress and enter the stage of a Śrāvaka or a Pratyekabuddha.

Why is this? Because, by not embracing the skillful means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they are devoid of all meritorious qualities and are thus not protected and sustained by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
“Subhūti, you should know this:

Suppose there were a person, one hundred and twenty years old, decrepit and frail, further afflicted by various ailments—namely, disorders of wind, heat, or phlegm, or a combination of these three. This aged and sick person wishes to rise from his bed and go elsewhere, yet he is unable to do so himself. Then two strong men each support one of his armpits, gently assisting him to stand up and say to him:
‘Do not be distressed; go wherever you wish. We two shall never abandon you; we will surely reach your destination safely and without harm.’”

"In this way, Subhūti, those sons of good family or daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who possess faith in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; who possess patience, a pure mind, superior intention, aspiration, and resolute conviction; and who possess equanimity and diligence; and who further are able to embrace the skillful means of the profound perfection of wisdom—such persons do not remain far removed from the perfections of wisdom, meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity. In this manner, they do not remain far removed from anything up to all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)."

It should be known that such sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle will never suffer decline or regression midway; they will transcend the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, bring sentient beings to maturity, purify Buddha-fields, and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Why is this? Because they are able to embrace the profound *prajñāpāramitā* through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), are endowed with all merits, and are protected and remembered by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One,

how is it that sons and daughters of good family who belong to the bodhisattva vehicle, by not embracing the profound perfection of wisdom through skillful means, become separated from all merits and fall back into the stages of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, rather than realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
The Buddha told Subhūti: “Excellent! Excellent!”

Since you, for the sake of the benefit and happiness of those sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle, have asked such a question, listen attentively now; I shall explain it to you.

Subhūti, you should know that there are sons and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, practice giving up to the perfection of wisdom while grasping at a self and what belongs to a self. When these sons and daughters of good family practice giving, they form this thought:
"I am able to practice giving; I give this object; he receives my gift."
When practicing pure ethical discipline, one forms this thought:
"I am able to uphold the precepts; I uphold these precepts; I am endowed with these precepts.
When practicing patience, one forms this thought:
"I am able to cultivate patience; I am patient toward that [object]; I possess this patience.
When cultivating diligence, one forms such a thought:
"I am able to be diligent; I am diligent for this purpose; I possess this diligence."
When practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one forms such thoughts as:
"I am able to practice concentration; I am practicing concentration for this purpose; I possess this concentration.
When practicing wisdom (*prajñā*), one forms such thoughts:
"I am able to cultivate wisdom; I cultivate this wisdom for this purpose; I possess this wisdom.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when these sons and daughters of good family practice generosity, they grasp at this generosity as being real, they grasp at it as originating from this [self], and they grasp at generosity as belonging to "me."

When practicing pure ethical discipline, one clings to the existence of this pure ethical discipline, clings to it as being derived from this pure ethical discipline, and clings to pure ethical discipline as "mine";
when practicing patience, one clings to the existence of this patience, clings to it as being derived from this patience, and clings to patience as "mine";
when practicing diligence, one clings to the existence of this diligence, clings to it as being derived from this diligence, and clings to diligence as "mine."
When practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one clings to the existence of this concentration, clings to it as being derived from this concentration, and clings to concentration as "mine.
When practicing wisdom (*prajñā*), one clings to the existence of this wisdom, clings to it as being derived from this wisdom, and clings to wisdom as "mine."

Because these sons and daughters of good family are constantly pursued by the grasping at "I" and "mine," their practice of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom increases the cycle of birth and death, and they are unable to liberate themselves from the manifold sufferings of birth and so forth.

Why is this? Because within the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), no such conceptual discrimination can arise to give rise to this attachment; and so it is even up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), wherein likewise no such conceptual discrimination can arise to give rise to this attachment.

Why is this? Because being far removed from this shore and the other shore is the characteristic of the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), and so on, up to the characteristic of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

“Subhūti, you should know that because these sons and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle do not understand the characteristics of this shore and the other shore, they are unable to embrace the perfection of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and so forth, up to being unable to embrace all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects. Due to these causes and conditions, these sons and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle fall into the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha, and do not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 444. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Second Division, Chapter Forty-nine on the Simile of the Ship, Part Two. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

How is it that sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle, by practicing the six perfections without skillful means, fall into the level of a Śrāvaka or a Pratyekabuddha, rather than realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“There are sons and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who, from the time they first resolve their minds, because they lack skillful means, when practicing generosity, form such thoughts as:
‘I am able to practice giving; I give this object; that person receives my gift.’”
When practicing pure ethical discipline, one forms this thought:
"I am able to maintain the precepts; I maintain these precepts; I have perfected these precepts.
When practicing patience, one forms this thought:
"I am able to practice patience; I am patient toward that [object]; I have accomplished this patience.
When practicing diligence, one forms such a thought:
"I am able to be diligent; I am diligent for this purpose; I have accomplished this diligence."
When practicing meditative concentration (dhyāna), one forms this thought:
"I am able to practice concentration; I practice concentration for this purpose; I have accomplished this concentration.
When practicing wisdom (prajñā), one forms this thought:
“I am able to cultivate wisdom; I cultivate this wisdom for this purpose; I have accomplished this wisdom.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when these sons and daughters of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle practice generosity, they grasp at the existence of this generosity, grasp at the means by which this generosity is performed, and grasp at generosity as "mine," thereby giving rise to arrogance.

When practicing pure ethical discipline, one clings to the existence of this pure ethical discipline, clings to it as being derived from this pure ethical discipline, and clings to pure ethical discipline as "mine," thereby giving rise to conceit;
when practicing patience, one clings to the existence of this patience, clings to it as being derived from this patience, and clings to patience as "mine," thereby giving rise to conceit;
when practicing diligence, one clings to the existence of this diligence, clings to it as being derived from this diligence, and clings to diligence as "mine," thereby giving rise to conceit.

When practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one clings to the existence of this concentration, clings to it as being derived from this concentration, and clings to concentration as "mine," thereby giving rise to conceit;
when practicing wisdom (*prajñā*), one clings to the existence of this wisdom, clings to it as being derived from this wisdom, and clings to wisdom as "mine," thereby giving rise to conceit.

Because these sons and daughters of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle are constantly pursued by the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self, the practice of their generosity up to the perfection of wisdom increases the cycle of birth and death, and they are unable to be liberated from the manifold sufferings of birth and so forth.
Why is this? Within the perfection of generosity, there is no such conceptual differentiation, nor does it exist in the manner that it is conceptually differentiated. Why is this so?

It is not that there is a "this shore" or a "far shore" that constitutes the characteristic of the perfection of generosity; likewise, up to and including the perfection of wisdom, there is no such conceptual differentiation, nor does it exist in the manner that it is conceptually differentiated.
Why is this? Because reaching the further shore is not the characteristic of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
"Sudhana, you should know this!"

These sons and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle, because they do not understand the characteristics of this shore and the other shore, are unable to embrace the perfection of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; and thus, they are unable to embrace everything up to all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

For this reason, those sons and daughters of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle may fall into the level of a Śrāvaka or the level of a Pratyekabuddha, and fail to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"Subhūti! Those sons of good family or daughters of good family who abide in the vehicle of the bodhisattvas, yet practice the six perfections without such skillful means, will fall to the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, and will not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,

how do those sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle, by being able to embrace the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and possessing all merits through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), avoid falling into the stages of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha, and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

“There are sons and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, practice generosity up to the perfection of wisdom while remaining detached from the grasping at ‘I’ and ‘mine. When these sons and daughters of good family practice generosity, they do not form such thoughts as:
‘I am able to give; I am giving this thing; that person receives my gift.’”
When practicing pure ethical discipline, one does not form such thoughts as:
"I am able to uphold the precepts," "I am upholding these precepts," or "I am endowed with these precepts.
When practicing patience, one does not form such thoughts:
"One thinks: 'I am able to cultivate patience; I am patient toward that [object]; I am endowed with this patience.
When cultivating diligence, one does not form such thoughts:
'I am able to be diligent; I am practicing this diligence; I am endowed with this diligence.'"
When practicing meditative concentration, one does not form such thoughts as:
"I am able to practice concentration," "I practice concentration for this purpose," or "I possess this concentration.
When practicing wisdom, one does not form such thoughts:
"I am able to cultivate wisdom; I cultivate this wisdom for its own sake; I am endowed with this wisdom.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when these sons and daughters of good family practice generosity, they do not grasp at the existence of generosity, they do not grasp at that by which they give, nor do they grasp at generosity as "mine."

When practicing pure ethical discipline, one does not grasp at the existence of pure ethical discipline, does not grasp at it as being derived from pure ethical discipline, and does not grasp at pure ethical discipline as "mine.
When practicing patience, one does not grasp at the existence of patience, does not grasp at it as being derived from patience, and does not grasp at patience as "mine.
When practicing diligence, one does not grasp at the existence of diligence, does not grasp at it as being derived from diligence, and does not grasp at diligence as "mine."

When practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one does not grasp at the existence of meditative concentration, does not grasp at being [defined] by this meditative concentration, and does not grasp at meditative concentration as "mine.
When practicing wisdom (*prajñā*), one does not grasp at the existence of wisdom, does not grasp at being [defined] by this wisdom, and does not grasp at wisdom as "mine."

Because these sons and daughters of good family are not pursued by the grasping of "I" and "mine," their practice of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom diminishes saṃsāra and enables them to swiftly liberate themselves from the manifold sufferings of birth and so forth.

Why is this? Because within the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), no such conceptual discrimination exists that could give rise to this attachment; and so on, up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), no such conceptual discrimination exists that could give rise to this attachment.

Why is this? Because being free from both this shore and the other shore is the characteristic of the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), and so on, up to the characteristic of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

“Subhūti, you should know that these sons and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle, because they well understand the characteristics of this shore and the other shore, are able to embrace the perfection of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; and in this way, they are even able to embrace all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects.”

By virtue of these causes and conditions, these sons and daughters of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle do not fall into the stages of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,

how do those sons and daughters of good family who abide in the vehicle of the bodhisattvas possess skillful means so that, while practicing the six pāramitās, they do not fall into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"There are sons and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who, from the moment they first resolve upon awakening, possess skillful means; therefore, when practicing generosity, they do not form such thoughts as:
'I am able to practice giving; I give this object; that person receives my gift.'"
When practicing pure ethical discipline, one does not form such thoughts as:
"I am able to maintain the precepts," "I maintain these precepts," or "I have perfected these precepts.
When practicing patience, one does not form such thoughts:
When practicing patience, one does not think: "I am able to practice patience; I am patient toward that; I have accomplished this patience.
When practicing diligence, one does not form such thoughts:
"I am able to be diligent; I am diligent for this purpose; I have accomplished this diligence."
When practicing dhyāna, one does not form such thoughts as:
"I am able to practice concentration; I am practicing this concentration for this purpose; I have accomplished this concentration.
When practicing prajñā, one does not form such thoughts:
"I am able to cultivate wisdom; I cultivate this wisdom for this purpose; I have perfected this wisdom.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when these sons and daughters of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle practice generosity, they do not grasp at the existence of generosity, they do not grasp at that which arises from this generosity, they do not grasp at generosity as "mine," nor do they become conceited.

When practicing pure ethical discipline, one does not grasp at the existence of pure ethical discipline, does not grasp at it as being "by means of" this pure ethical discipline, does not grasp at pure ethical discipline as "mine," and is not conceited;
when practicing patience, one does not grasp at the existence of patience, does not grasp at it as being "by means of" this patience, does not grasp at patience as "mine," and is not conceited;
when practicing diligence, one does not grasp at the existence of diligence, does not grasp at it as being "by means of" this diligence, does not grasp at diligence as "mine," and is not conceited.

When practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one does not grasp at the existence of meditative concentration, does not grasp at it as being "by means of" this meditative concentration, does not grasp at meditative concentration as "mine," and is likewise free from arrogance.

When practicing wisdom (*prajñā*), one does not grasp at the existence of wisdom, does not grasp at it as being "by means of" this wisdom, does not grasp at wisdom as "mine," and is likewise free from arrogance.

Because these sons and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle are not pursued by the grasping at a self or what belongs to a self, their cultivation of the perfections from generosity up to wisdom swiftly brings about liberation from the various sufferings of birth and so forth within saṃsāra.
Why is this so? Within the characteristic of the perfection of generosity, there is no such conceptual differentiation, nor is it as it is conceptually differentiated. Why is this?

It is not that there is a reaching of this shore or the other shore, because such is the characteristic of the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), and so on up to the characteristic of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); within these characteristics, there is no such conceptual differentiation, nor is it as it is conceptually differentiated.
Why is this? Because neither reaching this shore nor reaching the other shore is the characteristic of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
"Subhūti, you should know this!"

Because these sons and daughters of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle well understand the characteristics of this shore and the other shore, they are able to embrace the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and even up to embracing all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). By virtue of these causes and conditions, these sons and daughters of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle do not fall into the levels of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

"Subhūti! Those sons of good family and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle and thus practice the six pāramitās with such skillful means do not fall into the levels of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Chapter 50: The Chapter on Initial Practice, Part One. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is a beginner train in the perfections of wisdom, meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"A beginner bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to practice and train in the perfection of wisdom, meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity should first approach, serve, and make offerings to a true and pure spiritual friend who is skilled in explaining the perfections of wisdom, meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity. That is to say, when such a friend explains the profound sūtras of the perfection of wisdom, they instruct and admonish the beginner bodhisattva mahāsattva, saying: 'Come!'"
"Noble son! You should diligently cultivate the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom."
When you practice diligently, you should take non-apprehension as your skillful means and dedicate [the merit] equally in common with all sentient beings toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

Do not apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of form; nor do you apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

Do not apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the sense base of the eye; nor should you apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.

Do not apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the sense base of form; nor do you apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the sense bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena.

Do not grasp unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the eye-element; nor do you grasp unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-element.

Do not apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the form realm; nor should you apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena.

Do not grasp unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the eye-consciousness element; nor do you grasp unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-consciousness elements.

Do not apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through eye-contact; nor do you apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact.

Do not grasp at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition; nor do you grasp at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the various feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as condition.

Do not take hold of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the perfection of generosity; nor should you take hold of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom.

Do not apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of internal emptiness; nor do you apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the limitless, the emptiness of dispersion and non-dispersion, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of self-characteristics and common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, or the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.

Do not grasp at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of suchness; nor do you grasp at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the reality limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), or the inconceivable realm.

Do not take unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the noble truth of suffering; nor do you take unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the noble truths of origin, cessation, or the path.

Do not take up unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the four dhyānas; nor do you take up unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments.

Do not take hold of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the eight liberations; nor do you take hold of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, or the ten totalities.

Do not grasp at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the four foundations of mindfulness; nor do you grasp at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, or the eightfold noble path.

Do not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the liberation door of emptiness; nor do you realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the liberation doors of signlessness or wishlessness.

Do not grasp at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the five eyes; nor do you grasp at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the six supernormal powers.

Do not grasp at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the ten powers of a Buddha; nor do you grasp at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

Do not apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the thirty-two marks of a great man, nor do you apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the eighty secondary signs.
Do not grasp at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the quality of non-forgetfulness, nor do you grasp at it by means of the state of constant equanimity.

Do not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the gateways of dhāraṇī; nor do you realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the gateways of samādhi.

Do not take hold of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of all-knowledge; nor do you take hold of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects.

Why is this? Because if one does not grasp at form, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; if one does not grasp at feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. In this way, up to and including: if one does not grasp at all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; if one does not grasp at the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
“O son of good family!
When you practice the profound perfection of wisdom, do not give rise to craving for form; do not give rise to craving for feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.”
Why is this? Because form, up to and including consciousness, are not objects of craving.
For what reason?

Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, do not give rise to craving for the sense base of the eye; do not give rise to craving for the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
Why is this so? Because the sense base of the eye, up to and including the sense base of the mind, is not an object of craving.
For what reason?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, do not give rise to craving for the sphere of form; do not give rise to craving for the spheres of sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena.
Why is this? Because the sense base of form, up to and including the sense base of mental phenomena, is not an object of craving.
For what reason?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, do not give rise to craving for the eye-element; do not give rise to craving for the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-element.
Why is this? Because the eye-element, up to and including the mind-element, are not objects of craving.
For what reason?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, do not give rise to craving for the realm of form; do not give rise to craving for the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena.
Why is this? Because the realm of form, up to and including the realm of phenomena, is not something to be craved or attached to.
For what reason?

Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, do not give rise to craving for the sphere of visual consciousness; do not give rise to craving for the spheres of auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, or mental consciousness.
Why is this? Because the visual consciousness element, up to and including the mental consciousness element, are not objects of craving. Why is that?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, do not give rise to craving for eye-contact; do not give rise to craving for ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact.
Why is this so? Because visual contact, and so forth up to mental contact, are not objects of craving.
For what reason?

Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, do not give rise to craving for any feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition; do not give rise to craving for any feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as conditions.

Why is this so? Because the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, are not objects of craving. Why is that?

Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, do not give rise to craving or attachment toward the perfection of generosity; do not give rise to craving or attachment toward the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom.
Why is this? Because the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom are not objects of craving. Why is that?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, do not give rise to craving for internal emptiness;

do not give rise to craving for external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the limitless, the emptiness of dispersion and non-dispersion, the emptiness of essential nature, the emptiness of self-characteristics and common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, or the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.
Why is this? Because inner emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the nature of non-existence, is not something to be craved.
For what reason?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, do not give rise to craving for suchness;

do not give rise to craving for the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-erroneous nature, the unchanging nature, equality, the nature free from birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, or the inconceivable realm.
Why is this so? Because from suchness up to the inconceivable realm, these are not objects of craving. Why is that?

Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, do not give rise to craving for the Noble Truth of Suffering; do not give rise to craving for the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, or the Path.
Why is this? Because the Noble Truth of Suffering, up to and including the Noble Truth of the Path, are not objects of craving.
For what reason?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, do not give rise to craving for the four dhyānas; do not give rise to craving for the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments.
Why is this? The four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments are not objects of craving. Why is that?

Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, do not give rise to craving for the eight liberations; do not give rise to craving for the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities.
Why is this so? Because the eight liberations up to the ten totalities are not objects of craving.
For what reason?

Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, do not give rise to craving for the four foundations of mindfulness; do not give rise to craving for the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path.
Why is this? The four foundations of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path are not objects of craving. Why is that?

Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, do not give rise to craving for the gate of liberation of emptiness; do not give rise to craving for the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.
Why is this? The gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are not objects of craving. Why is that?
Because all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature,
do not give rise to craving for the five eyes, and do not give rise to craving for the six supernormal powers. Why is this?
The five eyes and the six supernormal powers are not objects of craving.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty.

Do not give rise to craving or attachment toward the ten powers of a Buddha; do not give rise to craving or attachment toward the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Why is this? The ten powers of a Buddha, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are not objects of craving. Why is that?
Because all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature,
do not give rise to craving or attachment toward the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, and do not give rise to craving or attachment toward the eighty secondary signs.
Why is this so? The thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs are not objects of craving. Why is that?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature,
do not give rise to craving for the quality of non-forgetfulness, and do not give rise to craving for the state of constant abiding in equanimity. Why is this?
The quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant abiding in equanimity are not objects of craving. Why is this?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature.
Do not give rise to craving for the gates of dhāraṇī; do not give rise to craving for the gates of samādhi.
Why is this? Because the gates of dhāraṇī and the gates of samādhi are not objects of craving.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature.
Do not give rise to craving for omniscience; do not give rise to craving for the knowledge of the paths or the knowledge of all aspects.

Why is this? Because omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are not objects of craving. Why is that?

Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, do not give rise to craving for the fruit of stream-entry; do not give rise to craving for the fruits of once-returner, non-returner, or arhatship, nor for the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
Why is this? The fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha is not something to be craved. Why is that?
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature,
do not give rise to craving for any of the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, and do not give rise to craving for the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas.
Why is this? Because the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas are not objects of craving. Why is that?
"Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

These bodhisattva mahāsattvas are able to perform what is difficult: within the emptiness of intrinsic nature of all phenomena, they aspire for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, desiring to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.

These bodhisattva mahāsattvas perform what is difficult to do; while all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, they aspire to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, desiring to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"Subhūti! Although all bodhisattva mahāsattvas have realized that all phenomena are like illusions, like dreams, like echoes, like reflections, like shadows, like mirages, like magical transformations, and like cities of the gandharvas—being empty of intrinsic nature—they nevertheless set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of attaining benefit for the world;
they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of bringing prosperity to the world."
They set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to bring peace and happiness to the world;
they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment out of a desire to rescue and deliver all the worlds;
they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to serve as a refuge for the world.
They set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to act as a dwelling place for the world;
they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment because they wish to show the ultimate path to the world;
they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to act as an island for the world.
They set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to act as the sun and moon for the world;
they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to act as lamps and torches for the world;
they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to act as guides for the world.
They set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to act as generals for the world;
they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to serve as the destination for the world;
and they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment out of compassion for the suffering of birth and death in the world.
“Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening for the sake of securing the welfare and benefit of all the world? Subhūti!”

Because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, desiring to liberate all sentient beings from the afflictions of suffering, practice the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom through skillful means, they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening for the sake of securing the welfare and benefit of all the world. Subhūti!"
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to bring benefit to the world? Subhūti!

It is because bodhisattva mahāsattvas desire to abide themselves in the six perfections, and through skillful means exhort and inspire all sentient beings so that they too may be established in the six perfections, that they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to bring benefit to the world. Subhūti!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to the world? Subhūti!

It is because bodhisattva mahāsattvas desire to abide themselves in the ten paths of wholesome action, and through skillful means encourage and inspire all sentient beings to likewise abide in the ten paths of wholesome action, that they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
"Subhūti! It is for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to the world that bodhisattva mahāsattvas set out toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Subhūti!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening out of a desire to rescue and deliver all the world? Subhūti!

Bodhisattva mahāsattvas see sentient beings fallen into the three evil destinies; desiring to rescue and deliver them so that they may cultivate wholesome karma and attain a state of security and ultimate coolness, they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
"Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, desiring to rescue and deliver all the world, sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Subhūti!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to serve as a refuge for the world? Subhūti!

Bodhisattva mahāsattvas desire to teach sentient beings the doctrine of non-reliance—that is, that form is non-reliant, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-reliant; and so on, up to omniscience being non-reliant, and the knowledge of paths and the knowledge of all aspects being non-reliant. Having caused sentient beings to hear this, they liberate them from all birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. By means of these causes and conditions, they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
"Subhūti! It is for the sake of providing a refuge for the world that bodhisattva mahāsattvas set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Subhūti!"
How do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to act as a dwelling place for the world? Subhūti!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening because they wish to serve as a place of reliance for sentient beings and to lead them to attain the palace of great nirvāṇa, which is free from fear and dread.
"Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to act as a dwelling place for the world. Subhūti!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to demonstrate the ultimate path to the world? Subhūti,

when bodhisattva mahāsattvas see sentient beings who do not skillfully discern the characteristics of the path and the non-path, and who wander upon the paths of desire, they intend to employ skillful means to proclaim the essential Dharma, so that those beings may understand the characteristics of the ultimate path and set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
What essential Dharma do you wish to preach for sentient beings?

It is this: to preach that form (*rūpa*) is ultimately eternal and free from fear; to preach that feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are ultimately eternal and free from fear; and so on, up to preaching that omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is ultimately eternal and free from fear, and preaching that the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are ultimately eternal and free from fear.

To speak of the ultimate limit of form is to say that it is not form; to speak of the ultimate limit of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is to say that they are not feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. In this way, up to speaking of the ultimate limit of all-knowledge is to say that it is not all-knowledge; to speak of the ultimate limit of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects is to say that they are not the knowledge of the aspects of the path nor the knowledge of all aspects.
"Subhūti! Just as this is the ultimate characteristic of these dharmas, so too is the characteristic of all dharmas.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed [the Buddha], saying:
“World-Honored One!
If the characteristics of all dharmas are identical to their ultimate characteristic, how should a bodhisattva-mahāsattva manifest equal enlightenment regarding all dharmas?”
Why is this so? World-Honored One!
Within the Ultimate of Form (Akaniṣṭha), there is no such discrimination as to say, "This is form."

Nor is there such a conceptual differentiation within the ultimate limit of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as to say, "This is feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
This applies likewise up to the point that there is no such conceptual differentiation within the ultimate limit of all-knowledge as to say, "This is all-knowledge";

nor is there such a conceptual differentiation within the ultimate limit of the knowledge of the paths or the knowledge of all aspects as to say, "This is the knowledge of the paths or the knowledge of all aspects."
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.
Within the ultimate limit of form, there is no such discrimination as "this is form";

likewise, within the ultimate limits of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, there is also no such discrimination as "this is feeling," "this is perception," "these are mental formations," or "this is consciousness."
In this way, up to the ultimate limit of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), there is no such conceptual discrimination as "this is all-knowledge";

nor is there such conceptual discrimination within the ultimate limits of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) as "this is the knowledge of the paths" or "this is the knowledge of all aspects," because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty.

"Subhūti! This is the most extremely difficult task for a bodhisattva mahāsattva: namely, that although they contemplate all phenomena as having the mark of total quiescence—profound and subtle—their mind does not sink into despondency, and they form this thought:

'Having attained manifest and equal awakening to these phenomena, I shall realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and proclaim and reveal such profound and subtle dharmas of quiescence to all sentient beings.'"
"Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, desiring to demonstrate the ultimate path to the world, sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Subhūti!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to act as an island for the world?
Subhūti, it is like this:
for example, in great oceans, rivers, and ponds, a high ground that can be inhabited, surrounded by water on all sides, is called an island.
Thus it is, Subhūti! Form is severed at its prior and posterior limits;

feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are severed at their prior and posterior limits. In this way, even up to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is severed at its prior and posterior limits, and the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are severed at their prior and posterior limits. Because the prior and posterior limits are thus severed, all phenomena (*dharmas*) are severed.

"Subhūti! All these phenomena are severed at their prior and posterior limits; they are quiescence, they are subtle and wondrous, and they are suchness. This refers to emptiness, non-apprehension, the path, the severance of craving, its exhaustion without remainder, the eternal cessation of all affliction, and ultimate nirvāṇa."

"Subhūti! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who seek to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening desire to proclaim and reveal to sentient beings such a profound, subtle, and true Dharma of cessation."
"Subhūti! It is for this reason that a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to act as an island for the world. Subhūti!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to act as the sun, the moon, the lamp, and the torch for the world? Subhūti!

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to proclaim for the sake of sentient beings the six pāramitās, as well as the true meaning and intent of the sūtras associated with the four reliances and the means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), and who, through skillful means and instruction, cause them to apply themselves diligently to study so as to shatter the darkness of all kinds of ignorance and set out toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti! It is for this reason that bodhisattva mahāsattvas set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to act as the sun, the moon, the lamp, and the torch for the world.
“Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to act as a guide and a general for the world?”

"Subhūti! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to cause sentient beings who have entered onto wrong paths to abandon the four improper courses of conduct; to teach them the single path so they may return to the right way; to enable those who are defiled to attain purification; to enable those who are sorrowful and afflicted to attain joy; to enable those who are distressed and suffering to attain happiness; to enable sentient beings who act unreasonably to realize the Dharma that accords with reason; and to enable sentient beings caught in the cycle of existence to attain parinirvāṇa."

“Subhūti! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment desire to proclaim and reveal to sentient beings that form is without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purification; that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purification;
and that the sense-base of the eye is without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purification, as are the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.”

The sphere of form is without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity; the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity.

The eye-element is without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity; the elements of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity.

The element of form is without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity; the elements of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity.

The eye-consciousness element is without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purification; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purification.

Eye-contact is without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purification; ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purification.

All sensations produced with eye-contact as a condition are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purification; all sensations produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact as conditions are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purification.

The perfection of generosity is without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity; the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity. Internal emptiness is without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity;

external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the limitless, the emptiness of dispersion and non-dispersion, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of self-characteristics and common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity.

Suchness is without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity; the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-illusory nature, the unchanging nature, the nature of equality, the nature of transcendence from birth, the fixedness of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity;

the noble truth of suffering is without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity; the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity;

the four dhyānas are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity; the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity.

The eight liberations are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity; the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive absorptions, and the ten totalities are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity;

the four foundations of mindfulness are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity; the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eight branches of the noble path are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity;

the gate of liberation of emptiness is without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity; the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity.

The Stage of Pure Observation is without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity; the Stage of the Spiritual Lineage, the Eighth Stage, the Stage of Possessing Vision, the Stage of Thinness, the Stage of Freedom from Desire, the Stage of Completion, the Stage of the Pratyekabuddha, the Stage of the Bodhisattva, and the Stage of the Tathāgata are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity.

The Stage of Extreme Joy is without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity; the Stage of Freedom from Defilement, the Radiant Stage, the Stage of Blazing Wisdom, the Stage of Supreme Difficulty to Conquer, the Stage of Presence, the Far-Reaching Stage, the Immovable Stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence, and the Cloud of Dharma Stage are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity.

The five eyes are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity; the six supernormal powers are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity.

The fruit of stream-entry is without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity; the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship, as well as the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity.

The ten powers of a Tathāgata are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity; the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity.

The thirty-two marks of a great man are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity; the eighty minor marks are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity.

The quality of non-forgetfulness is without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purification; it abides eternally in the nature of equanimity, being without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purification.

All doors of dhāraṇī are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purification; all doors of samādhi are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purification.

All-knowledge is without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purification; the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purification.
Subhūti! It is for this reason that bodhisattva mahāsattvas set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to act as guides and generals for the world.
“Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to serve as a destination for the world? Subhūti!”

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, seeking unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, desiring to gather all sentient beings through the four means of attraction—namely, giving, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation.

He wishes to proclaim and reveal for the sake of sentient beings that form has space as its destination; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness likewise have space as their destination. In this way, up to and including omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), it has space as its destination; the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) also have space as their destination.

I wish to proclaim and reveal for the sake of sentient beings that the future course of form is empty and thus has no place from which it comes; the past course of form is empty and thus has no place to which it goes; and the present course of form is empty and thus has no place wherein it abides.

Likewise, the future courses of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty and thus have no place from which they come; the past courses of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty and thus have no place to which they go; and the present courses of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty and thus have no place wherein they abide.

In this way, because all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) of the future tends toward emptiness, it comes from nowhere; because all-knowledge of the past tends toward emptiness, it goes nowhere; and because all-knowledge of the present tends toward emptiness, it likewise abides nowhere.
