Because the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) of the future tend toward emptiness, they come from nowhere; because the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects of the past tend toward emptiness, they go nowhere; and because the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects of the present tend toward emptiness, they likewise abide nowhere.
I wish to proclaim and reveal for the sake of sentient beings that form is neither a destination nor a non-destination. Why is this?
Because the nature of form is empty, and within emptiness there is neither destination nor non-destination.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither going nor not going.
Why is this? Because the nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is empty; within emptiness, there is neither going nor not going.
In this way, even omniscience is neither a destination nor a non-destination. Why is this?
Because the nature of omniscience is empty; within emptiness, there is neither a destination nor a non-destination.
The knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects are neither going nor not going. Why is this?
Because the nature of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects is empty; within emptiness, there is neither going nor not going.
"Subhūti! It is for this reason that Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to serve as a destination for the world.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 445, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Second Division, Chapter on Initial Practice, Part Fifty-Two. 'Why is this so?'"
"Subhūti! All dharmas have emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness as their destination; bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination."
Why is this? Because within emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, neither going nor not-going can be apprehended. "Subhūti!..."
All phenomena have non-arising and non-action as their ultimate destination; the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination. Why is this?
Because within non-arising and non-activity, neither going nor not-going can be apprehended.
"Subhūti! All phenomena have non-arising and non-ceasing as their destination; Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination."
Why is this? Because within that which is neither arising nor ceasing, neither going nor not-going can be apprehended. "Subhūti!..."
All phenomena have neither defilement nor purity as their ultimate destination, and the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend this destination. Why is this?
Within that which is neither defiled nor pure, neither going nor not-going is to be found.
"Subhūti! All phenomena have non-existence as their destination; bodhisattva mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination."
Why is this? Because within that which is non-existent, neither going nor not-going can be apprehended. "Subhūti!

All phenomena have illusion, dreams, echoes, reflections, shadows, mirages, transformations, and the city of the gandharvas as their ultimate nature; the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a nature.
Why is this? Because within illusions, dreams, echoes, images, reflections, mirages, transformations, and cities of Gandharvas, neither going nor not-going can be apprehended.
“Subhūti! All phenomena have the immeasurable and boundless as their destination; bodhisattva mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.”
Why is this? Because within the immeasurable and boundless, neither going nor not-going can be apprehended.
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin!..."
All phenomena have non-giving and non-taking as their ultimate course, and the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend this course. Why is that?
Within non-giving and non-taking, neither going nor not-going can be apprehended.
"Subhūti! All dharmas have non-elevating and non-depressing as their destination; Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination."
Why is this? Because within that which is neither rising nor falling, going and not-going cannot be apprehended. "Subhūti!..."
All phenomena have non-going and non-coming as their destination; the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination. Why is this?
Within that which is neither going nor coming, neither a destination nor a non-destination can be apprehended. "Subhūti!
All phenomena have non-increase and non-decrease as their destination; Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination."
Why is this? Because within that which is neither increasing nor decreasing, neither going nor not going can be apprehended. "Subhūti!..."
All dharmas have non-entering and non-exiting as their ultimate course, and the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend this course. Why is this?
Because within that which neither enters nor exits, neither a "going" nor a "non-going" can be apprehended. "Subhūti!
All phenomena have non-accumulation and non-dispersion as their destination; Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination."
Why is this? Because within that which is neither accumulated nor dispersed, neither going nor not-going can be apprehended.
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
All phenomena have non-union and non-separation as their ultimate nature; the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend this nature. Why is this?
Because within that which is neither conjoined nor disjoined, going and not-going cannot be apprehended. "Subhūti!

All dharmas take as their destination the self, the sentient being, the life-principle, the creature, the nourisher, the person, the individual, the mind-born, the youth, the agent, the instigator of action, the originator, the prompter of origin, the experiencer, the prompter of experience, the knower, and the seer; bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination."
Why is this? Because from "self" up to "perceiver," these do not ultimately exist and cannot be apprehended; how much less could there be any going or non-going to be apprehended! "Subhūti!..."

All phenomena have as their destination the absence of a self, the absence of a sentient being, the absence of a life-principle, the absence of a living soul, the absence of a nourisher, the absence of a person, the absence of a pudgala, the absence of a mind-born being, the absence of a human, the absence of an agent, the absence of one who causes to act, the absence of an originator, the absence of one who causes to originate, the absence of an experiencer, the absence of one who causes to experience, the absence of a knower, and the absence of a seer; bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.

Why is this? Because from selflessness up to the absence of a seer, these are ultimately non-existent and unobtainable; how much less could there be any going or not-going to be obtained! "Subhūti!..."
All phenomena have permanence, bliss, self, and purity as their ultimate destination; the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.

Why is this? Since even permanence, bliss, self, and purity are ultimately non-existent and unobtainable, how much less could there be any attainment of a destination or a non-destination! "Subhūti!..."
All phenomena have impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity as their ultimate destination; the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.
Why is this? Since impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity are ultimately non-existent and unobtainable, how much less could there be any attainment of a state of going or not going!
“Subhūti! All phenomena have greed, hatred, and delusion as their objective; bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such an objective.”

Why is this? Since even the phenomena of greed, hatred, and delusion ultimately do not exist and cannot be apprehended, how much less could there be any going or non-going to be apprehended! "Subhūti!..."
All phenomena have various views as their objective domain; Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a domain. Why is this?
Since even the various views and tendencies (*dṛṣṭigati*) ultimately do not exist and cannot be apprehended, how much less could there be any going or non-going to be apprehended!

"Subhūti, all phenomena take True Suchness (*tathatā*), the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena (*dharmasthititā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), and the inconceivable realm as their destination. Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination."
Why is this? Since even suchness up to the inconceivable realm ultimately does not exist and cannot be apprehended, how much less could there be any attainment of going or not going!
“Subhūti! All phenomena have immovability as their destination; bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.”
Why is this? Since even the nature of immovability ultimately does not exist and cannot be apprehended, how much less could there be any going or non-going to be apprehended! "Subhūti!..."
All phenomena have form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as their destination; the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.

Why is this? Because from form (*rūpa*) up to consciousness (*vijñāna*), these do not ultimately exist and cannot be apprehended; how much less could there be any going or not-going to be apprehended! "Subhūti!..."
All phenomena have the sense bases of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as their destination; the bodhisattva mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.

Why is this? Because even the sense-base of the eye up to the sense-base of the mind are ultimately non-existent and unobtainable; how much less could there be any going or not-going to be found! "Subhūti!..."
All phenomena have the spheres of form, sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental objects as their destination; the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.

Why is this? Because from the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) up to the sense-base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), these are ultimately non-existent and unobtainable; how much less could there be any attainment of a "going" or a "not-going"! "Subhūti!..."
All phenomena have the realms of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as their destination; the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.

Why is this? Because from the eye-element up to the mind-element, they are ultimately non-existent and unapprehendable; how much less could there be any going or not-going to be apprehended! "Subhūti!
All dharmas take the realms of form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental objects as their destination; the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.

Why is this? Because from the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) up to the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), there is ultimately nothing that exists and nothing that can be apprehended; how much less could there be any going or not-going to be apprehended! "Subhūti!..."
All phenomena have the realms of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mental consciousness as their destination; the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.

Why is this? Since even the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element are ultimately non-existent and unobtainable, how much less could there be any attainment of going or not going!
“Subhūti! All phenomena have eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact as their destination; bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.”

Why is this? Because from eye-contact through to mind-contact, these do not ultimately exist and cannot be apprehended; how much less could there be any going or non-going to be apprehended! "Subhūti!

All phenomena have as their destination the various feelings produced with contact of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as their condition; Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.

Why is this? Because even the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including those produced with mind-contact as a condition, are ultimately non-existent and unobtainable; how much less could there be any going or not-going to be found!

"Subhūti! All dharmas have the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of diligence, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom as their destination; Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination."

Why is this? Since even the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom ultimately do not exist and cannot be apprehended, how much less could there be any attainment of a destination or a non-destination!

“Subhūti! All dharmas have as their destination the emptiness of the internal, the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of both internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the limitless, the emptiness of dispersion and non-dispersion, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of self-characteristics and common characteristics, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence. Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.”

Why is this? Because even internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the nature of non-existence, ultimately does not exist and cannot be apprehended; how much less could there be any attainment of a "going" or a "not-going"?

“Subhūti! All dharmas have the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path as their destination; bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.”

Why is this? Since even the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path do not ultimately exist and cannot be apprehended, how much less could there be any going or non-going to be apprehended!
“Subhūti! All dharmas have the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path as their destination; bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.”

Why is this? Since even the Noble Truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path are ultimately non-existent and unattainable, how much less could there be any attainment of a "going" or a "not-going"?
“Subhūti! All dharmas have the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments as their destination; bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.”

Why is this? Since the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments are ultimately non-existent and unobtainable, how much less could there be any attainment of a state of going or not going!

“Subhūti! All dharmas have the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten spheres of totality as their destination; bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.”

Why is this? Since even the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality are ultimately non-existent and unobtainable, how much less could there be any attainment of a realm of existence or a realm of non-existence!
“Subhūti! All dharmas take the gateways of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness as their destination; bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.”

Why is this? Since even the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are ultimately non-existent and unattainable, how much less could there be any attainment of going or not going!
“Subhūti! All phenomena have the ten stages of the bodhisattvas of the three vehicles as their destination; bodhisattva mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.”

Why is this? Because even the ten stages of the bodhisattvas of the three vehicles are ultimately non-existent and unobtainable; how much less could there be any going or not-going to be obtained! "Subhūti!..."
All dharmas take the five eyes and the six supernormal powers as their destination; the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination. Why is this?
Since even the five eyes and the six supernormal powers ultimately do not exist and cannot be apprehended, how much less can there be any attainment of a "going" or a "not-going"?
"Subhūti! All dharmas take the doors of dhāraṇī and the doors of samādhi as their destination; bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination."

Why is this? Since even the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi ultimately do not exist and cannot be apprehended, how much less could there be any attainment of a "going" or a "not going"!

“Subhūti! All dharmas have as their destination the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.”

Why is this? Since even the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are ultimately non-existent and unattainable, how much less could there be any attainment of a state of going or not going!
“Subhūti! All dharmas have the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs as their destination; bodhisattva mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.”

Why is this? Since even the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs are ultimately non-existent and unobtainable, how much less could there be any attainment of a realm of existence or non-existence!
“Subhūti! All dharmas have the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity as their ultimate destination; Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.”

Why is this? Since even the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant abiding in equanimity are ultimately non-existent and unattainable, how much less could there be any attainment of a destination or a non-destination!

“Subhūti! All phenomena have all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) as their destination; bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.”

Why is this? Since even all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects are ultimately non-existent and unattainable, how much less could there be any attainment of a state of going or not going!

“Subhūti! All dharmas have the fruit of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, and the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha as their destination; bodhisattva mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.”

Why is this? Since even the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha ultimately does not exist and cannot be apprehended, how much less could there be any attainment of a "going" or a "not-going"?

“Subhūti! All phenomena have all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas as their destination; bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.”

Why is this? Since all practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas are ultimately non-existent and unobtainable, how much less could there be any attainment of a "going" or a "not-going"?

“Subhūti! All dharmas have as their destination the stream-enterer, the once-returner, the non-returner, the arhat, the pratyekabuddha, the bodhisattva, and the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; bodhisattva mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.”

Why is this? Because from the stream-enterer up to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, there is ultimately nothing that exists or can be apprehended; how much less could there be any attainment of a "going" or a "not-going"?
Thus it is, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to serve as a destination for the world. Subhūti!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment out of compassion for the suffering of birth and death in the world? Subhūti!

Bodhisattva mahāsattvas set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to attain unimpeded and sovereign supernormal powers, so as to uproot the great suffering of birth and death for all sentient beings.
"Subhūti! It is for the sake of having compassion for the suffering of birth and death in the world that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Chapter 51: Subduing Greed and Other Defilements, Part Two, Subduing Greed and Other Defilements, Number Fifty-One. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Who is able to give rise to pure faith and superior resolve toward such profound *prajñāpāramitā*?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva has long since set their mind upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, diligently practicing the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; if they have already made offerings to hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of buddhas and have long cultivated the holy life in the presence of those buddhas; if their roots of virtue have matured through the arousal of great vows and they have been sustained and protected by immeasurable spiritual friends—only then will they be able to give rise to pure faith and superior resolve toward such profound prajñāpāramitā."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva can give rise to pure faith and superior resolve toward such profound prajñāpāramitā, what is the nature of that bodhisattva mahāsattva’s mind?”
What are its characteristics? What are its signs?
What is its appearance?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can give rise to pure faith and superior resolve toward such profound prajñāpāramitā,
their mind will have the nature, characteristics, marks, and appearance of being tamed regarding greed, hatred, and delusion, and of being free from greed, hatred, and delusion."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva’s mind has as its nature, characteristic, mark, and appearance the subduing of greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion; it is the distancing from greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion."

"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with such a nature, characteristics, attributes, and appearance, their mind will then be able to give rise to pure faith and superior resolve toward this profound prajñāpāramitā."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can give rise to pure faith and superior resolve toward such profound prajñāpāramitā, where will this bodhisattva mahāsattva be headed?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“This bodhisattva mahāsattva shall proceed toward the knowledge of all modes.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva proceeds toward omniscience, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to serve as a refuge for all sentient beings.”
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can give rise to pure faith and superior resolve toward such profound prajñāpāramitā, that bodhisattva mahāsattva will then be able to advance toward all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna).
"If one can proceed toward the knowledge of all modes, that person will be able to serve as a refuge for all sentient beings.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
This bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to perform what is difficult to do, namely, donning such firm armor as this:

"I shall deliver all sentient beings and cause them all to realize ultimate nirvāṇa; yet, although I perform such deeds for sentient beings, I do not perceive the conceptual designation of 'sentient beings' at all."
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
"It is as you have said.
Furthermore, Subhūti,
the armor donned by this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not belong to form, nor does it belong to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness."

Why is this? Because from form (*rūpa*) up to consciousness (*vijñāna*), all are ultimately non-existent; they are neither the bodhisattva nor the armor. Therefore, it is said that this armor does not belong to form, nor does it belong to feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*).

The armor donned by this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not even belong to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), nor does it belong to the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Why is this? Because omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are ultimately non-existent, being neither the bodhisattva nor the armor; therefore, it is said that this armor does not belong to omniscience, nor does it belong to the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects.
The armor donned by this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not belong to any phenomena. Why is this?
Because all phenomena are ultimately non-existent; since they are neither the bodhisattva nor the armor, it is said that this armor does not belong to any phenomena.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices such profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they are able to don such armor of merit, namely: ‘I shall deliver all sentient beings and cause them all to realize ultimate *nirvāṇa*.’”
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can don such firm armor as this—namely, ‘I shall deliver all sentient beings and cause them all to realize parinirvāṇa’—he will not fall into the stages of the śrāvaka or the pratyekabuddha.”
Why is this? World-Honored One!
This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not establish limits regarding sentient beings when donning such firm armor.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Subhūti, based on what meaning do you speak these words:
'If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can don such firm armor, they will not fall into the levels of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas'?"
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

It is not for the sake of liberating only a small portion of sentient beings that this bodhisattva mahāsattva dons such firm armor; nor is it for the sake of seeking only a small portion of wisdom that he dons such firm armor.”

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas don such firm armor for the sake of universally rescuing all sentient beings and leading them to parinirvāṇa; they don such firm armor solely for the purpose of seeking to attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). By virtue of these causes and conditions, they do not fall into the levels of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
"It is as you have said.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Thus, this perfection of wisdom is most profound; there is no one who can practice it, no dharma to be practiced, no place for practice, nor is there anything by means of which it can be cultivated.
Why is this? World-Honored One!

Within this profound meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there is not even the slightest portion of a real dharma that can be called a "practitioner," nor a "dharma to be practiced," nor a "place of practice," nor that "by which one practices."
“World-Honored One!
If one cultivates space, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
if one cultivates all dharmas, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.”
If one cultivates unreal dharmas, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
if one cultivates non-existence, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
if one cultivates non-appropriation, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
"If one cultivates the removal [of phenomena], this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"By removing what phenomena does one cultivate the perfection of wisdom?"
The Venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One,
the cultivation of the elimination of form is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;”
To cultivate the removal of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the removal of the six internal sense bases is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the removal of the six external sense bases is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the elimination of the six internal elements is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the elimination of the six external elements is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the elimination of the six consciousness elements is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the elimination of the self is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;

to cultivate the elimination of a sentient being, a life-principle, a creature, a nourisher, a person, an individual, a mind-born, a youth, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, and a viewer is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the elimination of the perfection of generosity is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the removal of [clinging to] the perfection of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;

To cultivate the relinquishment of the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the relinquishment of the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the relinquishment of the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the elimination of the Ground of Utmost Joy up to the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;

to cultivate the elimination of the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the elimination of the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary characteristics is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the elimination of the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the elimination of the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Subhūti, one should observe non-regressive bodhisattva mahāsattvas by relying upon this very profound perfection of wisdom; if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom yet remains without attachment, you should know that he is a non-regressive bodhisattva mahāsattva."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfections of dhyāna, vīrya, kṣānti, śīla, and dāna without attachment, one should know that this is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature without attachment, one should know that this is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices from suchness up to the inconceivable realm yet remains without attachment, one should know that this is an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, yet remains without attachment, one should know that this is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the four foundations of mindfulness, and so forth, up to all-aspect omniscience, yet remains without attachment, one should know that this is an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When non-regressive bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not regard the words or instructions of others as the essential truth; they do not act merely out of faith in others. Their minds are not defiled by the dharmas of greed, hatred, delusion, or pride, nor are they led astray by them."
When any non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not depart from the perfection of generosity up to and including the perfection of wisdom.

When any non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, upon hearing this teaching of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, their minds are not startled, not terrified, not afraid, do not sink, and do not become despondent; nor do they ever abandon or retreat from the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek. Regarding the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they joyfully delight in hearing it, receiving and upholding it, reading and reciting it, mastering it thoroughly, and contemplating it with focused mindfulness, practicing exactly as taught without ever becoming weary.

It should be known that such non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, in previous lives, have already heard the meaning and intent of this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, having received, upheld, recited, and contemplated it according to principle, practicing with diligence and without weariness of mind.

Why is this? Because when these non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas hear such profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, their minds are not startled, not terrified, not afraid, do not sink, and do not become despondent; nor do they ever abandon or retreat from the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) they seek. Regarding this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they joyfully delight in hearing it, receiving and upholding it, reading and reciting it, mastering it thoroughly, and reflecting upon it according to the principle; they practice with diligence, their minds never wearying.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing such a profound teaching on the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), their mind is not startled, not terrified, not frightened, does not sink, and does not despair; and if they do not retreat or abandon the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) they seek, but instead joyfully delights in hearing this profound perfection of wisdom, receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, thoroughly mastering, and contemplating it with focused mindfulness, practicing with diligence and without weariness—how should such a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice this profound perfection of wisdom?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, whose mental continuum conforms to, inclines toward, and enters into the knowledge of all modes, should practice the profound perfection of wisdom in this manner."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
how does this bodhisattva mahāsattva continuously accord with, incline toward, and enter into the knowledge of all modes, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva continuously accords with, inclines toward, and enters into emptiness,
signlessness, wishlessness, space, non-existence, non-arising, non-cessation, non-defilement, and..."
Purity, suchness, the dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, non-illusoriness, immutability, equality,
the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space,
the inconceivable realm, being uncreated and unconditioned, like an illusion, like a dream, like an echo.
Like a reflection, like a shadow, like a mirage, like a magical creation, like a city of Gandharvas—

practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way constitutes a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s continuous conformity toward and entry into the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
Then, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, as the Buddha has said:

‘If a bodhisattva mahāsattva continuously accords with, inclines toward, and enters into emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and even the city of the gandharvas, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom—this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva who continuously accords with, inclines toward, and enters into the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), practicing the profound perfection of wisdom.’”
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, does he practice with respect to form?
Does he practice with respect to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness?
"In this way, does one practice for the sake of all-knowledge?
Does one practice for the sake of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not practice with respect to form, nor do they practice with respect to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; and so on, up to not practicing with respect to all-knowledge, nor practicing with respect to the knowledge of the aspects of the path, nor practicing with respect to the knowledge of all aspects."

Why is this? Because for this bodhisattva mahāsattva, that which accords with, tends toward, and enters into the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) has no agent, no destroyer; it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; it abides nowhere, has no direction or region, is innumerable and immeasurable, and neither departs nor arrives. Since neither number nor measure nor coming and going can be apprehended therein, there is likewise nothing that can realize it.

“Subhūti! This omniscience (sarvajñajñāna) cannot be realized through form; it cannot be realized through feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Likewise, it cannot be realized even through omniscience, nor can it be realized through the knowledge of the paths (mārgākārajñatā) or the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā).”

Why is this? Form is the nature of the knowledge of all modes; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the nature of the knowledge of all modes. In this way, up to omniscience itself is the nature of the knowledge of all modes; the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects are the nature of the knowledge of all modes.
Why is this? Whether it be the suchness of form, the suchness of the knowledge of all modes, or the suchness of all phenomena, they are all one single suchness, without duality or distinction.

Whether it be the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, the suchness of the knowledge of all modes, or the suchness of all phenomena, they are all one single suchness, without duality or distinction.

In this way, up to the point that whether it be the suchness of all-knowledge, the suchness of the knowledge of all-knowledge, or the suchness of all phenomena, they are all one single suchness, without duality or distinction;

whether it be the suchness of the knowledge of the paths, the suchness of the knowledge of all aspects, the suchness of the knowledge of all-knowledge, or the suchness of all phenomena, they are all one single suchness, without duality or distinction.

Therefore, the knowledge of all modes cannot be realized through form; it cannot be realized through feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. In this way, it cannot be realized even through the knowledge of all modes, nor can it be realized through the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects.

52. Chapter on Suchness (Tathatā), Part Two, Chapter Fifty-Two, Section One: At that time, the devas of the desire realm and the form realm each took celestial powdered sandalwood incense, *tagara* incense, and *tamāla* incense; they further took celestial *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *pundarīka* flowers, scattering them from afar upon the Buddha. They approached the Buddha’s presence, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

Thus, this Prajñāpāramitā is most profound, difficult to see and difficult to realize; it is beyond discursive thought and transcends the sphere of conceptualization. Subtle, wondrous, and tranquil, it can be known by those who are wise and discerning, yet it is not something that all people in the world can believe and accept—it is the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddha.
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have declared in this profound Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom:
"Form is itself the knowledge of all modes; the knowledge of all modes is itself form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are themselves the knowledge of all modes; the knowledge of all modes is itself feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."
In this way, even up to the point that all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is itself the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), and the knowledge of all-knowledge is itself all-knowledge;

the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are themselves the knowledge of all-knowledge, and the knowledge of all-knowledge is itself the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects.

Why is this? Whether it be the suchness of form, the suchness of the knowledge of all modes, or the suchness of all phenomena, they are all a single suchness, without duality or distinction, and are likewise inexhaustible.

Whether it be the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, the suchness of the knowledge of all modes, or the suchness of all phenomena, they are all a single suchness, without duality or distinction, and are likewise inexhaustible.

In this way, even up to the suchness of all-knowledge, the suchness of the knowledge of all-knowledge, and the suchness of all phenomena—all are a single suchness, without duality or distinction, and are likewise inexhaustible.

Whether it be the suchness of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects, the suchness of the knowledge of all modes, or the suchness of all phenomena, they are all a single suchness, without duality or distinction, and are likewise inexhaustible.
The Buddha addressed the devas of the desire realm and the form realm, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is as you have said.
O devas, you should know!
As I contemplate this matter, my mind constantly inclines toward tranquility and does not delight in preaching the Dharma."

Why is this so? Because this Dharma is extremely profound, difficult to see, and difficult to realize; it is beyond ratiocination and transcends the sphere of thought. It is subtle, wondrous, and profoundly tranquil, to be known only by those who are wise and sagacious. It is not something that all people in the world can believe and accept—namely, that this very profound *prajñāpāramitā* is the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment realized by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"O devas, you should know!
Such unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment cannot be realized; it is not that which is realized; there is no place for its realization, nor is there a time for its realization."
"O devas, you should know!
This Dharma is profound and subtle, its non-dual practice cannot be fathomed or compared by those in the world.
O devas, you should know!"
Because space is profound, this Dharma is profound; because suchness is profound, this Dharma is profound;

because the dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixedness of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable are profound, this Dharma is profound.
Because the realms are profound, this Dharma is profound; because they are immeasurable and boundless, this Dharma is profound;
because there is no coming and no going, this Dharma is profound; because there is no arising and no ceasing, this Dharma is profound;
because there is no defilement and no purity, this Dharma is profound; because there is no knowledge and no...
Because its attainment is profound, this Dharma is profound; because it is without creation or action, this Dharma is profound;

because the self is profound, this Dharma is profound; [and because] sentient beings, life-principles, living beings, nourishers, persons, individuals, mind-born ones, youths, agents, and experiencers are profound, this Dharma is profound.
Because the knower, the cognizer, and the seer are profound, this Dharma is profound; because form is profound, this Dharma is profound;
because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are profound, this Dharma is profound;
and so on, up to: because all-knowledge is profound, this Dharma is profound; [and] because the knowledge of the aspects of the path and all-...
“Because the wisdom of marks is profoundly deep, this Dharma is profoundly deep; because all Buddha-dharmas are profoundly deep, this Dharma is profoundly deep.
At that time, the assembly of devas addressed [the Buddha], saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Dharma that has been taught is extremely profound and subtle; it is not something that the world can readily believe and accept. Why is this so?
This profound and subtle Dharma is not taught for the sake of grasping at form, nor is it taught for the sake of abandoning form;

it is not taught for the sake of grasping at feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor is it taught for the sake of abandoning feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Thus, it is not for the sake of grasping all-knowledge that this is taught, nor is it for the sake of abandoning all-knowledge;

it is not for the sake of grasping the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects that this is taught, nor is it for the sake of abandoning the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects;
it is not for the sake of grasping all Buddha-dharmas that this is taught, nor is it for the sake of abandoning all Buddha-dharmas that this is taught.
“World-Honored One!

Sentient beings in the world mostly practice the grasping of ‘I’ and ‘mine,’ saying: ‘Form is I, it is mine; feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are I, they are mine. In this way, even up to ‘omniscience is I, it is mine; the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects are I, they are mine.’”
At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of devas, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.
This profound and subtle Dharma is not taught for the sake of grasping at form, nor is it taught for the sake of abandoning form;

it is not taught for the sake of grasping at feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor is it taught for the sake of abandoning feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
In this way, it is taught not for the sake of grasping all-knowledge, nor for the sake of abandoning all-knowledge;
it is taught not for the sake of grasping the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects, nor for the sake of abandoning the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects;
it is taught not for the sake of grasping all Buddha-dharmas, nor for the sake of abandoning all Buddha-dharmas.

Sentient beings in the world mostly engage in grasping at "I" and "mine," thinking: "Form is I, form is mine; feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are I, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are mine. In this way, it extends even to: "Omniscience is I, omniscience is mine; the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects are I, the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects are mine."
“O devas, you should know!
If there is a bodhisattva who practices for the sake of grasping at form, or practices for the sake of abandoning form;
who practices for the sake of grasping at feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, or practices for the sake of abandoning feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness—”
In this way, they practice even unto the point of grasping at all-knowledge, or practicing for the sake of abandoning all-knowledge;

they practice for the sake of grasping at the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects, or practicing for the sake of abandoning the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects.

Such a bodhisattva is unable to cultivate the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), nor can they cultivate the perfections of meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity; likewise, they are unable to cultivate anything up to and including omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), nor can they cultivate the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This profound Dharma is able to accord with all dharmas.”
"Bhagavān! To what kind of all dharmas does this profound dharma accord? Bhagavān!"
This profound Dharma accords with the perfection of wisdom, and it also accords with the perfections of meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity.
This profound Dharma accords with internal emptiness, and it also accords with external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.
This profound Dharma accords with suchness, and it also accords with the dharma-realm, up to and including the inconceivable realm.

This profound Dharma accords with the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; this profound Dharma accords with the four foundations of mindfulness, and likewise accords with the four right endeavors up to the eight branches of the noble path.
This profound Dharma is able to accord with the four dhyānas, and it is also able to accord with the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments.

This profound Dharma is able to accord with the eight liberations, and it is also able to accord with the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative concentrations, and the ten totalities.
This profound Dharma accords with the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
This profound Dharma accords with the Stage of Pure Observation, and it also accords with the Stage of the Spiritual Lineage, up to and including the Stage of the Tathāgata.
This profound Dharma accords with the Ground of Extreme Joy, and it also accords with the Ground Free from Defilement up to the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma.
This profound Dharma accords with the five eyes, and it also accords with the six supernormal powers.
This profound Dharma accords with the ten powers of the Tathāgata, and it also accords with the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
This profound Dharma accords with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, and it also accords with the eighty secondary signs.
This profound Dharma accords with the quality of non-forgetfulness and also accords with the nature of constant equanimity.
This profound Dharma accords with the gateways of dhāraṇī and also accords with the gateways of samādhi.
This profound Dharma is conducive to the fruit of stream-entry, and it is also conducive to the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, and the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
This profound Dharma accords with all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and it also accords with the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas.
This profound Dharma accords with all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), and it also accords with the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
“World-Honored One!
This profound Dharma is entirely without obstruction.
World-Honored One!”
"In what, O Bhagavān, is this profound Dharma unimpeded?

This profound Dharma is unimpeded with respect to form; it is unimpeded with respect to feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness; and so on, up to being unimpeded with respect to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), and unimpeded with respect to the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)."
“World-Honored One!
This profound Dharma has non-obstruction as its characteristic. Why is this so?

World-Honored One! It is because of the equality of space; because of the equality of suchness; because of the equality of the dharma-realm up to the inconceivable realm; because of the equality of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; because of the equality of non-creation and non-action; and because of the equality of non-defilement and non-purity.
“World-Honored One!
This profound Dharma is without arising and without cessation. Why is this?
World-Honored One!

Form is without arising and without cessation because it is unapprehendable; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without arising and without cessation because they are unapprehendable; and so on, up to omniscience being without arising and without cessation because it is unapprehendable, and the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects being without arising and without cessation because they are unapprehendable.
“World-Honored One!
This profound Dharma is entirely without tracks. Why is this? Because...”
World-Honored One!

Because the footprint of form cannot be apprehended, and because the footprints of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness likewise cannot be apprehended; and so on, up to the point that the footprint of all-knowledge cannot be apprehended, and the footprints of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects likewise cannot be apprehended.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll 446. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Two, Chapter Fifty-two, "On Suchness" (Tathatā), Section Two. At that time, the assembly of devas from the desire and form realms again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
The Venerable Subhūti is a true disciple of the Buddha who has been born after the Tathāgata. Why is this?
Because, Venerable Subhūti, all the teachings you proclaim are entirely in accord with emptiness.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the hosts of devas of the desire and form realms, saying:
"O hosts of devas, you say of me, Subhūti, that I am a true disciple of the Buddha born after the Tathāgata; in what way, Subhūti, am I born after the Tathāgata?"
This is because he is born in accordance with the *tathatā* (suchness) of the Tathāgata. Why is this so?

Because the *tathatā* of the Tathāgata neither comes nor goes, and the *tathatā* of Subhūti likewise neither comes nor goes; therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born in accordance with the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata’s suchness is the suchness of all phenomena; the suchness of all phenomena is the Tathāgata’s suchness. Such suchness has no nature of suchness, nor does it have a nature of non-suchness. Subhūti’s suchness is also like this; therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born in accordance with the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata has the characteristic of being eternally abiding in suchness; Subhūti’s suchness is likewise. Therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born in accordance with the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata’s suchness is without change and without discrimination, pervading and functioning throughout all phenomena; Subhūti’s suchness is likewise. Therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born in accordance with the Tathāgata.

The *tathatā* of the Tathāgata is without obstruction, and the *tathatā* of all phenomena is likewise without obstruction. Whether it be the *tathatā* of the Tathāgata or the *tathatā* of all phenomena, they are a single *tathatā*, non-dual and undifferentiated, without creation or fabrication. Such *tathatā* is the constant characteristic of *tathatā*; there is no time when it is not the characteristic of *tathatā*. Because this constant characteristic of *tathatā* is at no time other than the characteristic of *tathatā*, it is non-dual and undifferentiated. Subhūti’s *tathatā* is also like this; therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born in accordance with the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata’s suchness is without recollection and without conceptualization in all places; Subhūti’s suchness is likewise. Therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born in accordance with the Tathāgata.
The *tathatā* (suchness) of the Tathāgata is undifferentiated and unapprehendable; the *tathatā* of Subhūti is likewise. Therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born in accordance with the Tathāgata.

The *tathatā* of the Tathāgata is not separate from the *tathatā* of all phenomena, and the *tathatā* of all phenomena is not separate from the *tathatā* of the Tathāgata. Such *tathatā* is the constant characteristic of *tathatā*; there is no time when it is not the characteristic of *tathatā*. The *tathatā* of Subhūti is likewise. Therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born in accordance with the Tathāgata.
Although it is said that he is born in accordance with [the Tathāgata], there is nothing with which he is born in accordance, because Subhūti’s suchness is not different from the Buddha’s.

The suchness of the Tathāgata is neither past, nor future, nor present; the suchness of all dharmas is likewise neither past, nor future, nor present; and the suchness of Subhūti is also thus. Therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born in accordance with the Tathāgata.
"The suchness of the past is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the past.
The suchness of the future is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the future.
The suchness of the present is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the present."

Whether it be the suchness of the past, the suchness of the future, the suchness of the present, or the suchness of the Tathāgata, they are all one and the same suchness, without duality or distinction.

“The suchness of form is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of form. The suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.”

Whether it be the suchness of form, or the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, or the suchness of the Tathāgata—they are all one single suchness, without duality and without distinction.

“The suchness of the eye-base is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the eye-base. The suchness of the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-bases is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-bases.”

Whether it be the suchness of the eye-base, or the suchness of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases, or the suchness of the Tathāgata, they are all one single suchness, without duality and without distinction.

“The suchness of the sphere of form is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the sphere of form. The suchness of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena.”

Whether it be the suchness of the sphere of form, or the suchness of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena, or the suchness of the Tathāgata, they are a single suchness, non-dual and without distinction.

“The suchness of the eye-element is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the eye-element. The suchness of the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements.”

Whether it be the suchness of the eye-element, or the suchness of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements, or the suchness of the Tathāgata—they are all one and the same suchness, without duality and without distinction.

"The suchness of the form realm is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the form realm. The suchness of the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena."

Whether it be the suchness of the form realm, or the suchness of the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena, or the suchness of the Tathāgata—it is all one single suchness, without duality and without distinction.

“The suchness of the visual consciousness element is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the visual consciousness element. The suchness of the auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousness elements is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousness elements.”

Whether it be the suchness of the eye-consciousness element, or the suchness of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-consciousness elements, or the suchness of the Tathāgata—it is all one single suchness, without duality and without distinction.

“The suchness of eye-contact is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of eye-contact. The suchness of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact.”

Whether it be the suchness of eye-contact, or the suchness of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact, or the suchness of the Tathāgata, they are all one and the same suchness, non-dual and without distinction.

“The suchness of all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition. The suchness of all feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as conditions is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of all feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as conditions.”

Whether it be the suchness of all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, or the suchness of all feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-contact as a condition, or the suchness of the Tathāgata—it is one single suchness, without duality and without distinction.

“My own suchness is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is my own suchness. The suchness of sentient beings, life-force, birth, nourishment, person, individual, mind-born, youth, agent, experiencer, knower, and seer is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of sentient beings, up to and including the seer.”

Whether it be the suchness of myself, the suchness of sentient beings up to that of the seer, or the suchness of the Tathāgata, they are all one and the same suchness, non-dual and without distinction.

“The suchness of the perfection of generosity is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the perfection of generosity. The suchness of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom.”

Whether it be the suchness of the perfection of generosity, the suchness of the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom, or the suchness of the Tathāgata, they are all one and the same suchness, non-dual and without distinction.

“The suchness of internal emptiness is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of internal emptiness. The suchness of external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, limitless emptiness, emptiness of dispersion and non-dispersion, essential emptiness, emptiness of self and common characteristics, emptiness of all phenomena, emptiness of the unapprehendable, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of intrinsic nature, and emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.”

Whether it be the suchness of internal emptiness, or the suchness of external emptiness up to the suchness of the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature, or the suchness of the Tathāgata—they are all one and the same suchness, without duality or distinction.

“The suchness of suchness is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of suchness. The suchness of the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-illusory nature, the unchanging nature, the equality, the state beyond birth, the fixedness of dharma, the stability of dharma, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the dharma-realm up to the inconceivable realm.”

Whether it be the suchness of suchness, the suchness of the dharma-realm up to the inconceivable realm, or the suchness of the Tathāgata, they are all one and the same suchness, without duality or distinction.

“The suchness of the noble truth of suffering is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the noble truth of suffering. The suchness of the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path.”

Whether it be the suchness of the noble truth of suffering, the suchness of the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path, or the suchness of the Tathāgata—they are all one and the same suchness, without duality and without distinction.

“The suchness of the four foundations of mindfulness is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the four foundations of mindfulness. The suchness of the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the four right endeavors up to the eightfold noble path.”

Whether it be the suchness of the four foundations of mindfulness, the suchness of the four right efforts up to the eightfold noble path, or the suchness of the Tathāgata, they are all one single suchness, non-dual and without distinction.

“The suchness of the four dhyānas is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the four dhyānas. The suchness of the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments.”

Whether it be the suchness of the four dhyānas, the suchness of the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments, or the suchness of the Tathāgata, they are all one single suchness, non-dual and without distinction.

“The suchness of the eight liberations is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the eight liberations. The suchness of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities.”

Whether it be the suchness of the eight liberations, the suchness of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, or the ten pervasive bases, or the suchness of the Tathāgata—it is all one single suchness, without duality and without distinction.

The suchness of the gate of liberation of emptiness is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the gate of liberation of emptiness. The suchness of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.

Whether it be the suchness of the gate of liberation of emptiness, the suchness of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness, or the suchness of the Tathāgata, they are all one single suchness, non-dual and without distinction.

“The *tathatā* of the ten stages of the three vehicles is the *tathatā* of the Tathāgata; the *tathatā* of the Tathāgata is the *tathatā* of the ten stages of the three vehicles. The *tathatā* of the ten stages of the bodhisattvas is the *tathatā* of the Tathāgata; the *tathatā* of the Tathāgata is the *tathatā* of the ten stages of the bodhisattvas.”

Whether it be the suchness of the ten stages of the three vehicles, the suchness of the ten stages of the bodhisattvas, or the suchness of the Tathāgata, they are one and the same suchness, without duality or distinction.

“The suchness of the five eyes is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the five eyes. The suchness of the six supernormal powers is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the six supernormal powers.”
Whether it be the suchness of the five eyes, the suchness of the six supernormal powers, or the suchness of the Tathāgata, they are one and the same suchness, without duality or distinction.

The suchness of the Buddha’s ten powers is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the Buddha’s ten powers. The suchness of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

Whether it be the suchness of the Buddha’s ten powers, the suchness of the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or the suchness of the Tathāgata, they are all one and the same suchness, non-dual and without distinction.

“The suchness of the thirty-two marks of a great man is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the thirty-two marks of a great man. The suchness of the eighty secondary signs is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the eighty secondary signs.”

Whether it be the suchness of the thirty-two marks of a great man, the suchness of the eighty minor marks, or the suchness of the Tathāgata, they are all one single suchness, without duality and without distinction.

“The *tathatā* of the quality of non-forgetfulness is the *tathatā* of the Tathāgata; the *tathatā* of the Tathāgata is the *tathatā* of the quality of non-forgetfulness. The *tathatā* of the state of constant equanimity is the *tathatā* of the Tathāgata; the *tathatā* of the Tathāgata is the *tathatā* of the state of constant equanimity.”

Whether it be the suchness of the quality of non-forgetfulness, the suchness of the state of constant equanimity, or the suchness of the Tathāgata, they are a single suchness, without duality and without distinction.

“The suchness of the gateways of dhāraṇī is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the gateways of dhāraṇī. The suchness of the gateways of samādhi is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the gateways of samādhi.”

Whether it be the suchness of the gateways of dhāraṇī, the suchness of the gateways of samādhi, or the suchness of the Tathāgata, they are all one and the same suchness, non-dual and without distinction.

"The suchness of the fruit of stream-entry is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the fruit of stream-entry. The suchness of the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, and pratyekabuddha-enlightenment is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the fruit of once-returning up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha."

Whether it be the suchness of the fruit of stream-entry, the suchness of the fruit of once-returning up to the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, or the suchness of a Tathāgata, they are all one single suchness, without duality and without distinction.

“The suchness of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas’ practices is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas’ practices. The suchness of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas.”

Whether it be the suchness of the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the suchness of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas, or the suchness of the Tathāgata, they are a single suchness, non-dual and without distinction.

“The suchness of all-knowledge is the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of all-knowledge. The suchness of the knowledge of the paths and the suchness of all-aspect knowledge are the suchness of the Tathāgata; the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the knowledge of the paths and the suchness of all-aspect knowledge.”

Whether it be the suchness of all-knowledge, the suchness of the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects, or the suchness of the Tathāgata, they are a single suchness, non-dual and without distinction.
“O celestial hosts, you should know!

Because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have directly realized the suchness (tathatā) of all these phenomena, they are called Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas. Since I have deep faith and understanding in the suchness of these phenomena, I say that Subhūti is born from the Tathāgata.”
While these characteristics of suchness were being thus proclaimed, the mountains and the great earth of this trichiliocosm shook in six ways:

it surged in the east and subsided in the west; it surged in the west and subsided in the east; it surged in the south and subsided in the north; it surged in the north and subsided in the south; it surged in the center and subsided at the periphery; and it surged at the periphery and subsided in the center.

At that time, the hosts of devas from the desire realm and the form realm again took powdered celestial candana sandalwood, tagara, and tamāla, as well as celestial utpala, padma, kumuda, and puṇḍarīka flowers, and scattered them over the Tathāgata and Subhūti, addressing the Buddha:
“How marvelous!
“Tathāgata! This is unprecedented!
The Venerable Subhūti is born after the Tathāgata by virtue of suchness.”
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the assembly of devas, saying:
"O devas, you should know this!

I, Subhūti, do not follow the Tathāgata’s birth by means of form; I do not follow the Tathāgata’s birth by means of the suchness of form; I do not follow the Tathāgata’s birth apart from form; nor do I follow the Tathāgata’s birth apart from the suchness of form."

One does not follow the Tathāgata’s birth by virtue of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; one does not follow the Tathāgata’s birth by virtue of the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; one follows the Tathāgata’s birth without being separate from feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; and one follows the Tathāgata’s birth without being separate from the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

In this manner, up to: they do not follow the Tathāgata’s birth by virtue of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), nor do they follow the Tathāgata’s birth by virtue of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all-knowledge; they do not follow the Tathāgata’s birth by being separate from all-knowledge, nor do they follow the Tathāgata’s birth by being separate from the suchness of all-knowledge.

They do not follow the Tathāgata’s birth by virtue of the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), nor do they follow the Tathāgata’s birth by virtue of the suchness of the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects; they do not follow the Tathāgata’s birth by being separate from the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects, nor do they follow the Tathāgata’s birth by being separate from the suchness of the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects.

One does not follow the Tathāgata’s birth by virtue of the conditioned, nor by virtue of the true suchness of the conditioned; one follows the Tathāgata’s birth because one does not depart from the conditioned, nor because one does not depart from the true suchness of the conditioned.
