One does not follow the Tathāgata’s birth by virtue of the unconditioned, nor by virtue of the true suchness of the unconditioned; one follows the Tathāgata’s birth because one does not depart from the unconditioned, nor because one does not depart from the true suchness of the unconditioned.
Why is this? O assembly of devas!

All these phenomena are entirely non-existent; the one who follows along in birth, that which is followed in birth, that by which one follows in birth, and the time and place of such following in birth—all of these are unobtainable.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The suchness of all phenomena, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-falsity, the non-alteration, the equality, the nature of freedom from birth, the fixedness of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm are all most profound.”
This means that herein form is unapprehendable, and the suchness of form is likewise unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because herein even form itself is unapprehendable; how much less could the suchness of form be apprehended!

Within this, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be apprehended, nor can the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness be apprehended. Why is that?

In this context, since feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness cannot even be apprehended, how much less can the suchness of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness be apprehended!
Likewise, up to and including this context, since omniscience cannot be apprehended, the suchness of omniscience also cannot be apprehended.
Why is this? Because within this, even omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) cannot be apprehended, much less the suchness (*tathatā*) of omniscience!

Within this, the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) cannot be apprehended, nor can the suchness of the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects be apprehended.

Why is this? Within this, even the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects cannot be apprehended; how much less can the suchness of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects be apprehended!
The Buddha said,
“Śāriputra, it is so! It is thus!”
"So it is! It is as you have said.

The true suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena, up to the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*), is most profound; that is to say, herein form (*rūpa*) cannot be apprehended, and the true suchness of form likewise cannot be apprehended."
Why is this? Because herein even form (*rūpa*) cannot be apprehended, much less the suchness (*tathatā*) of form!
Thus, up to and including, herein all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) cannot be apprehended, and the suchness of all-aspect omniscience likewise cannot be apprehended.
"Why is this? Because herein even all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) cannot be apprehended, much less can the suchness (*tathatā*) of all-aspect omniscience be apprehended!
When this characteristic of suchness was thus spoken, two hundred bhikṣus had their outflows (*āsrava*) forever exhausted; their minds attained liberation, and they became arhats.

Furthermore, there was an assembly of five hundred bhikṣuṇīs who, having distanced themselves from dust and left behind defilement, attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena; five thousand bodhisattvas were born among gods and humans and attained the patience of non-arising (anutpāda-kṣānti); and six thousand bodhisattvas, with all outflows forever exhausted, attained liberation of mind and became arhats.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:

"In this assembly, there are six thousand bodhisattvas who have already in the past approached and made offerings to five hundred buddhas. At the site of each and every buddha, they gave rise to great vows and left the household life with right faith; yet, although they cultivated generosity, pure ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration, they did not embrace the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Being far removed from skillful means (upāyakauśalya), they gave rise to notions of differentiation and engaged in differentiated practices."
When practicing generosity, one forms this thought:
"This is the act of giving; this is the gift; this is the recipient; I am the one who can practice giving."
When practicing pure ethical discipline, one forms this thought:
"This is pure ethical discipline; this is sinful karma; this is the object to be guarded; I am able to maintain the precepts."
When practicing patience, one forms this thought:
"This is patience; this is an obstacle to patience; this is the object of patience; I am capable of being patient."
When practicing diligence, one forms this thought:
"This is diligence; this is laziness; this is what is to be done; I am capable of being diligent."
When practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one forms this thought:
"This is meditative concentration; this is distraction; this is that which is to be accomplished; I am able to cultivate samādhi."

Not upholding the perfection of wisdom and being devoid of skillful means, they practice the distinct practices of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration based on the notion of differentiation.
Because of their distinct perceptions and distinct practices, they fail to attain the bodhisattva’s non-distinct perception and lose the bodhisattva’s non-distinct practice.

Due to these causes and conditions, they cannot enter the bodhisattva’s stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*). Because they cannot enter the bodhisattva’s stage of right determination, they instead attain the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) and gradually proceed through the stages up to the fruit of arhatship.

Therefore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses the path to awakening as well as the gates of liberation— emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness— but does not embrace the perfection of wisdom and remains far removed from skillful means, they will realize the limit of reality and fall to the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One,

for what cause and condition do individuals belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle or the Pratyekabuddha vehicle cultivate the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, yet fail to embrace the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), remain distant from skillful means (upāyakauśalya), and thereby realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and fall into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha?”

Are there individuals belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who, by cultivating the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and by embracing the perfection of wisdom, rely upon skillful means so that although they realize the limit of reality, they proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!

Those individuals belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle or the Pratyekabuddha vehicle who distance themselves from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), do not embrace the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), and lack skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), yet practice the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, will realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and fall into the level of a Śrāvaka or a Pratyekabuddha.”

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, not departing from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), embrace the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), rely upon skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), and take great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) as their foremost guide, cultivating the dharmas of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*). Although they realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), they are able to enter the bodhisattva’s stage of right determination (*samyaktvaniyāma*) and attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment (*anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi*).
“Śāriputra! It is as if there were a bird whose body was one hundred yojanas long, or perhaps two hundred, or even three hundred yojanas in measure, yet it had no wings.
Suppose this bird were to cast itself down from the Heaven of the Thirty-three, heading toward Jambudvīpa; while on its way, it should again think:
"I wish to return up to the Heaven of the Thirty-three."
"Śāriputra, what do you think? Would this bird be able to return to the Heaven of the Thirty-three?"
Śāriputra said: “No, World-Honored One!”
"No, Sugata! The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"Suppose this bird, while on its way, makes this aspiration:
'When I reach Jambudvīpa, may my body be without injury or affliction. Śāriputra!..."
"What do you think? Can this bird’s wish be fulfilled? Śāriputra replied:
"No, World-Honored One! No!"
"Sugata! When this bird reaches Jambudvīpa, its body will certainly suffer injury and affliction; it will either meet its end or experience suffering bordering on death."
"Why is this? Because this bird's body is large, it falls from a great distance, and it has no wings.
The Buddha said:
“Śāriputra! So it is! So it is!”
"It is as you have said, Śāriputra!

It is likewise with a person belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who, although they have spent immeasurable and incalculable great eons diligently practicing generosity, pure ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration, and have also cultivated wisdom in their quest for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, yet fails to embrace the perfection of wisdom and remains far removed from skillful means; by cultivating the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, they then realize the limit of reality and fall into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha."

Why is this? Śāriputra, because these individuals belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle have distanced themselves from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), even though they spend immeasurable and innumerable great eons diligently practicing generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration, and also practice wisdom (*prajñā*), they do not embrace the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Being devoid of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), they consequently fall into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.

“Śāriputra! Although these individuals belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle recollect all the aggregates of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present, and though they honor, make offerings to, and practice in accordance with them, because they grasp at signs therein, they are unable to correctly understand the perfect merits of the aggregates of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.”

Because these bodhisattvas cannot correctly understand the qualities of the Buddha, although they hear the sounds of the path of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, as well as the teachings on emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, they grasp at the signs based on those sounds; having grasped at these signs, they dedicate [their merit] toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

If this person belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle dedicates [merit] in such a manner, they will not attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, but will instead fall to the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.
Why is this? Śāriputra,

because these individuals belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle do not embrace the perfection of wisdom and are devoid of skillful means, they fall to the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, even though they dedicate their various cultivated roots of virtue toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, there is a person belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who, from the first generation of the mind of awakening, never departs from the mind of omniscience;
with great compassion as their foremost guide, they diligently cultivate generosity, ethical discipline, and patience."
They cultivate diligence and meditative concentration, and by practicing sublime wisdom, they embrace the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā);

they never depart from skillful means (upāyakauśalya), and although they recollect all the aggregates of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation belonging to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present.
Yet they do not grasp at signs; although they cultivate the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—they do not grasp at signs;

and although they recollect the various merits of themselves and others, dedicating them equally and in common with all sentient beings toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they likewise do not grasp at signs.

“Śāriputra, you should know that a person who abides in this way on the bodhisattva vehicle proceeds directly toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and does not fall into the levels of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.”

Why is this? Śāriputra, because these individuals belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle, from their first generation of the mind until their ultimate attainment, never depart from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*). At all times, they take great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) as their foremost guide; although they cultivate generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration, they also cultivate wisdom without grasping at signs. Although they recollect the aggregates of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation belonging to all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the past, future, and present, they do not grasp at signs. Although they cultivate the path of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, they do not grasp at signs.

“Śāriputra! Because these individuals belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle possess skillful means, they practice generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom with a mind free from signs. In this way, they even practice all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and all-aspect knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) with a mind free from signs; through this, they will certainly realize the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment until the ultimate end, embraces the perfection of wisdom and is never separated from skillful means, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is close to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

Why is this? Because from the first production of the thought of enlightenment until its ultimate consummation, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not perceive even the slightest dharma that can be apprehended—whether it be that which realizes, that which is realized, the place of realization, the time of realization, or that by means of which one realizes; none of these can be apprehended at all.

That is to say, whether it be form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness—and likewise, up to and including all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, or the knowledge of all aspects—all these are ultimately unapprehendable.

"Furthermore, Blessed One, there are sons and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who do not embrace the perfection of wisdom and are far removed from skillful means, yet seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. It should be known that regarding the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek, they will be beset by doubt and hesitation as to whether they shall attain it or not."

Why is this? Because these sons and daughters of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva Vehicle do not embrace the perfection of wisdom and are devoid of skillful means; thus, they grasp at signs in the practice of the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and so on, even grasping at signs in the practice of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Due to these causes and conditions, these sons and daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle will harbor doubts and hesitations regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, wondering whether they will attain it or not.
"Therefore, World-Honored One,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they must certainly not be separated from the skillful means of the perfection of wisdom."

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom through skillful means, employing the method of non-apprehension as that skillful means, should cultivate the perfection of generosity with a mind accompanied by the signless; he should likewise cultivate the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom. In this manner, up to and including, with a mind accompanied by the signless, he should cultivate all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in the perfection of wisdom through skillful means, employing the method of non-apprehension as that skillful means, and practices all such buddha-dharmas with a mind conjoined with the signless, they will certainly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, the hosts of devas from the desire realm and the form realm addressed the Buddha together, saying:
“The unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening of all Buddhas is extremely difficult to believe and understand, and exceedingly difficult to realize.”

Why is this? Because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas must realize and know both the specific characteristics and the general characteristics of all phenomena (*dharma*) in order to attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek; yet, for these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the characteristics of the phenomena they know do not exist at all, and are entirely unobtainable.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of devas, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.
The unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is extremely difficult to believe and understand, and exceedingly difficult to realize.
O devas, you should know this!

I too have directly awakened to the characteristics of all phenomena and realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; yet, in the ultimate sense, I have not apprehended any characteristic of phenomena that could be said to be "this is the means of realization," "this is the object realized," "this is the place of realization," "this is the time of realization," or "by means of this one realizes."

Why is this? Because all phenomena are ultimately pure and both conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are ultimately empty; therefore, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is extremely difficult to believe and understand, and exceedingly difficult to realize.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

Regarding what the Buddha has said—that the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is extremely difficult to believe and understand, and exceedingly difficult to realize—according to my contemplation of the meaning of the Buddha’s words, the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is extremely easy to believe and understand, and exceedingly easy to realize."

Why is this? If one can have faith and understanding that there is no phenomenon that can realize, no phenomenon to be realized, no place of realization, no time of realization, and furthermore, nothing by which realization occurs, then one can have faith and understanding in the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas.

If one realizes that there is no dharma that can realize, no dharma that is realized, no place of realization, no time of realization, and nothing by means of which realization occurs, then one will be able to realize the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Why is this? Because all phenomena are ultimately empty; within ultimate emptiness, there is no phenomenon that can be called the "realizer," no phenomenon that can be called the "object realized," no phenomenon that can be called the "place of realization," no phenomenon that can be called the "time of realization," and no phenomenon by which anything is realized.
Why is this? Because the nature and characteristics of all phenomena (*dharma*) are empty; whether increasing or decreasing, they are entirely non-existent and cannot be apprehended.

For this reason, the perfections (*pāramitā*) of giving, pure ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, which Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas constantly practice, are entirely non-existent and cannot be apprehended. This extends even to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), which are entirely non-existent and cannot be apprehended.

Regarding all phenomena contemplated by the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—whether they have form or are formless, whether they are visible or invisible, whether they are resistant or non-resistant, whether they are with outflows or without outflows, and whether they are conditioned or unconditioned—all of them are utterly non-existent and cannot be apprehended.

For this reason, as I contemplate the meaning and intent of what the Buddha has taught, the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is extremely easy to believe and understand, and very easy to realize; therefore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should not consider it difficult to believe and understand, or difficult to realize.
Why is this so? Form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form;

feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. In this way, it extends even to all-knowledge, which is empty of the intrinsic nature of all-knowledge; the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects are empty of the intrinsic nature of the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can develop deep faith and understanding regarding this meaning of the emptiness of intrinsic nature and realize it without error, they will attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"For this reason, the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is extremely difficult to believe and understand, and exceedingly difficult to realize."
Why is this? Because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas contemplate all phenomena as being entirely devoid of intrinsic nature and identical to empty space.
For example, empty space does not form such a thought:
"I shall believe and understand, and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Likewise, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should also not form this thought:
"I shall believe and understand, and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Why is this? All phenomena are empty and equal to space; it is only when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas can believe and understand that all phenomena are empty and equal to space, and realize them without error, that they attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva were to easily give rise to faith and understanding, and easily realize, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment simply by believing that all phenomena are equal to space, then there would not be as many bodhisattva mahāsattvas as the sands of the Ganges who don the great armor of merit and set out for unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, nor would there be any who might fall back or become discouraged in the interim.
"Therefore, know that unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is extremely difficult to believe and understand, and exceedingly difficult to realize.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti said to Śāriputra: "Śāriputra!"
"What do you think?
Does form have any retreat or discouragement regarding the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied:
"No, Śāradvatīputra! Subhūti! "Śāradvatīputra!"
"What do you think?
Do feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness ever retreat or shrink back from the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied:
"No, Śāradvatīputra! Subhūti! "Śāradvatīputra!"
"What do you think?
Could even omniscience ever regress or falter from the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied:
"No, Śāradvatīputra! Subhūti! "Śāradvatīputra!"
"What do you think?
Do the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects ever regress from the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied:
"No, Śāradvatīputra! Subhūti! "Śāradvatīputra!"
"What do you think?
Does the suchness of form ever regress or falter from the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied:
"No, Śāradvatīputra! Subhūti! "Śāradvatīputra!"
"What do you think?
Does the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness ever regress from the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied:
"No, Śāradvatīputra! Subhūti! "Śāradvatīputra!"
"What do you think?
Does the suchness of even omniscience ever retreat or falter from the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied:
"No, Śāradvatīputra! Subhūti! "Śāradvatīputra!"
"What do you think?
Does the suchness of the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects ever regress from the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied:
“No, Śāradvatīputra! Subhūti! “Śāradvatīputra!”
"What do you think?
Is there any phenomenon apart from form that could experience retreat or discouragement regarding the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied:
"No, Śāradvatīputra! Subhūti! "Śāradvatīputra!"
"What do you think?

Apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, is there any dharma that could experience retreat or discouragement regarding the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied:
"No, Śāradvatīputra! Subhūti! "Śāradvatīputra!"
"What do you think?
Is there any phenomenon apart from omniscience that could experience retreat or discouragement regarding the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied:
"No, Śāradvatīputra! Subhūti! "Śāradvatīputra!"
"What do you think?

Apart from the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects, is there any dharma that could cause a Buddha to regress or be discouraged from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied:
"No, Śāradvatīputra! Subhūti! "Śāradvatīputra!"
"What do you think?
Is there any phenomenon apart from the *tathatā* of form that could ever regress or be discouraged from the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied:
"No, Śāradvatīputra! Subhūti! "Śāradvatīputra!"
What do you think?

Apart from the *tathatā* (suchness) of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, is there any dharma that could experience retreat or despondency regarding the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti!”
“Śāriputra, what do you think? Is there any phenomenon,
even up to the *tathatā* (suchness) of all-knowledge, that could ever regress from the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti!”
“Śāriputra, what do you think?

Is there any dharma apart from the suchness of the knowledge of all aspects and the knowledge of all modes that could undergo regression from the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti!”
“Śāriputra, what do you think?
Does the true suchness (tathatā) of all phenomena ever experience retreat or despondency regarding the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti!”
“Śāriputra, what do you think? Regarding the dharmadhātu, the dharmatā, the non-falsity,

the immutability, the sameness, the nature free from birth, the fixedness of dharma, the stability of dharma, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm— do these ever retreat or falter before the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti!”
“Śāriputra, what do you think? Apart from the true thusness (tathatā) of all phenomena,
is there any dharma that could experience retreat or despondency regarding the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti!”
“Śāriputra, what do you think? Apart from the dharmadhātu, the dharmatā, the non-illusory nature,

the unchanging nature, the state of equality, the nature free from arising, the fixedness of dharma, the stability of dharma, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm— does there exist any dharma that could experience retreat or despondency regarding the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”
Śāriputra said: "No, Subhūti!"
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
"If all phenomena are entirely non-existent and cannot be apprehended, what phenomenon could be said to regress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
Then, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:

"According to what you have said, within the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), there is no phenomenon whatsoever, nor is there any bodhisattva who could be said to experience retreat from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. If that is so, for what reason did the Buddha speak of three types of persons who abide in the vehicle of the bodhisattvas, rather than speaking of only one?"
"Furthermore, as you have said, there should be no distinction between the three vehicles of bodhisattvas; there should be only one vehicle of perfectly complete awakening.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"You should question the Venerable Subhūti:"
Do you admit that there is a single Bodhisattvayāna?
Only then can it be challenged:
there should be no establishment of distinctions between three vehicles, but rather only a single vehicle of Perfect Enlightenment (samyaksaṃbuddhayāna).
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti,
"Is it admitted that there is such a thing as the bodhisattva vehicle?
Then, the Venerable Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
“Śāriputra, what do you think? Within the suchness of all phenomena,
are there three distinct characteristics of individuals abiding in the bodhisattva vehicle?”
"Is it that there are those who regress and abide in the Śrāvaka vehicle, or those who regress and abide in the Pratyekabuddha vehicle,
or those who realize the Unsurpassed Vehicle? Śāriputra replied, "No!"
"Subhūti! Śāriputra! What do you think?"
"Within the suchness of all phenomena, are there any distinctions among the bodhisattvas of the three vehicles?
Śāriputra replied, "No!"
"Subhūti! Śāriputra! What do you think?"
"Within the suchness of all phenomena, is there truly any fixed bodhisattva vehicle that does not regress? Śāriputra replied, "No!"
"Subhūti! Śāriputra! What do you think?"
"Within the suchness of all phenomena, does there truly exist a vehicle of the perfectly awakened ones for bodhisattvas?
Śāriputra replied, "No!"
"Subhūti! Śāriputra! What do you think?"
"Does the suchness of all phenomena have one aspect, two aspects,
or three aspects? Śāriputra replied, "No!"
"Subhūti! Śāriputra! What do you think?"
"Within the suchness of all phenomena, can any single phenomenon or any single bodhisattva be apprehended?
Śāriputra replied, "No!"
"Subhūti! At that time, the Venerable Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
"If all dharmas are utterly non-existent and entirely unapprehendable, how could you, Śāriputra, entertain such a thought as to say:..."

In this way, is it certain that such a bodhisattva will regress from the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; or is it certain that such a bodhisattva will not regress from the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; or is it said to be indeterminate whether such a bodhisattva will [regress] from the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; or is such a bodhisattva of the śrāvaka vehicle; or is such a bodhisattva of the pratyekabuddha vehicle; or is such a bodhisattva of the vehicle of perfect enlightenment? Are there thus three, or are there thus one?

“Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva finds nothing at all to be apprehended in any phenomena, and is likewise able to have correct faith and understanding that even the suchness of all phenomena is entirely unapprehendable, and finds nothing to be apprehended in the bodhisattvas, and finds nothing to be apprehended in the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha—know that this one is a true bodhisattva mahāsattva.”

Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing it said that the suchness of all these phenomena has the characteristic of being unapprehendable, their mind is not startled, not terrified, not afraid, does not doubt, does not regret, does not retreat, and does not sink; this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, and in the interim, they will certainly never experience despondency or withdrawal.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 447. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Two, Chapter Fifty-two on Suchness (Tathatā), Section Three. At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Venerable Subhūti, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"

Excellent! You are now able to skillfully expound the essential teachings for the sake of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; everything you have spoken is due to the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata, not your own independent ability.

"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to deep faith and understanding regarding the signless unobtainability of the *tathatā* (suchness) of phenomena, and knows that all phenomena are without differentiated signs; and upon hearing such a teaching on the signless unobtainability of the *tathatā* of all phenomena, their mind is not startled, not terrified, not afraid, does not doubt, does not regret, does not retreat, and does not sink—this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly accomplish the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening they seek."
The Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes this dharma, will they be able to swiftly realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening that they seek?”
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is as you have said.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes these dharmas, they will swiftly be able to realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to swiftly accomplish the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek, in what should they dwell?
How should they dwell?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to swiftly accomplish the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek, they should abide in a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings and should not abide in a mind of partiality;
they should give rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings and should not give rise to a mind of partiality."
One should address all sentient beings with an impartial mind and not with a partial mind.
One should give rise to a mind of great loving-kindness toward all sentient beings and not give rise to a mind of malice;
one should address all sentient beings with a mind of great loving-kindness and not with a mind of malice.
One should give rise to great compassion toward all sentient beings and should not give rise to a mind of malice or harm;
one should address all sentient beings with a mind of great compassion and should not address them with a mind of malice or harm.
One should give rise to a mind of great joy toward all sentient beings and should not give rise to a mind of envy;
one should address all sentient beings with a mind of great joy and should not address them with a mind of envy.
One should give rise to a mind of great equanimity toward all sentient beings and should not give rise to a partisan mind;
one should address all sentient beings with a mind of great equanimity and should not address them with a partisan mind.
One should give rise to a humble mind toward all sentient beings and should not give rise to a conceited mind;
one should address all sentient beings with a humble mind and should not address them with a conceited mind.
One should give rise to a mind of straightforwardness toward all sentient beings and should not give rise to a mind of flattery and deceit;
one should address all sentient beings with a mind of straightforwardness and should not address them with a mind of flattery and deceit.
One should give rise to a mind of gentleness toward all sentient beings and should not give rise to a harsh mind;
one should address all sentient beings with a gentle mind and should not address them with a harsh mind.
One should give rise to a mind of benefit toward all sentient beings and should not give rise to a mind of non-benefit;
one should address all sentient beings with a mind of benefit and should not address them with a mind of non-benefit.
One should give rise to a mind of peace and happiness toward all sentient beings, and not give rise to a mind of suffering;
one should address all sentient beings with words born of a mind of peace and happiness, and not with words born of a mind of suffering.
One should give rise to a mind free from obstruction toward all sentient beings, and not give rise to a mind with obstruction;
one should address all sentient beings with a mind free from obstruction, and not address them with a mind with obstruction.
"One should regard all sentient beings with a mind as if they were one's parents, brothers, sisters, sons, daughters, or kinsmen; furthermore, one should address them with such a mind."
One should give rise to the mind of a friend toward all sentient beings, and one should speak to them with that very same mind.
One should give rise to the mind of a preceptor, a teacher, a disciple, or a fellow student toward all sentient beings, and one should speak to them with that very same mind.

One should give rise toward all sentient beings a mind such as that of a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, an arhat, a pratyekabuddha, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, or a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; and with this very mind, one should address them.
One should give rise to a mind of offering, reverence, respect, and praise toward all sentient beings, and one should also speak to them with that same mind.
One should give rise to a mind of rescue, compassion, and protection toward all sentient beings, and one should also speak to them with that same mind.
One should give rise to a mind that perceives all sentient beings as ultimately empty, non-existent, and ungraspable, and with this very mind, one should speak to them.
One should give rise to a mind of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness toward all sentient beings, and with this very mind, one should speak to them.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to swiftly accomplish the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek, they should personally abstain from taking life, encourage others to abstain from taking life, constantly and correctly praise the practice of abstaining from taking life, and joyfully extol those who abstain from taking life; this should extend even to personally abstaining from wrong views, encouraging others to abstain from wrong views, constantly and correctly praising the practice of abstaining from wrong views, and joyfully extolling those who abstain from wrong views."

One should personally cultivate the four dhyānas, encourage others to cultivate the four dhyānas, constantly and correctly praise the practice of the four dhyānas, and joyfully extol those who cultivate the four dhyānas.

One should personally cultivate the four immeasurables, encourage others to cultivate the four immeasurables, constantly and correctly extol the practice of the four immeasurable dharmas, and joyfully praise those who cultivate the four immeasurables.

One should personally cultivate the four formless absorptions, encourage others to cultivate the four formless absorptions, constantly and correctly extol the practice of the four formless absorptions, and joyfully praise those who cultivate the four formless absorptions.

One should personally fulfill the six perfections, encourage others to fulfill the six perfections, constantly and correctly praise the dharma of fulfilling the six perfections, and joyfully extol those who have fulfilled the six perfections.

One should personally abide in the eighteen kinds of emptiness, encourage others to abide in the eighteen kinds of emptiness, constantly and correctly extol the dharma of abiding in the eighteen kinds of emptiness, and joyfully praise those who abide in the eighteen kinds of emptiness.

One should personally abide in suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm; one should also exhort others to abide in suchness up to the inconceivable realm, constantly and correctly extol the practice of abiding in suchness up to the inconceivable realm, and joyfully praise those who abide in suchness up to the inconceivable realm.

One should abide oneself in the Four Noble Truths, and also encourage others to abide in the Four Noble Truths; one should constantly and correctly extol the dharma of abiding in the Four Noble Truths, and joyfully praise those who abide in the Four Noble Truths.

One should personally cultivate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, encourage others to cultivate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, constantly and correctly praise the practice of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and joyfully extol those who cultivate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.

One should personally cultivate the three gates of liberation, encourage others to cultivate the three gates of liberation, constantly and correctly extol the practice of the three gates of liberation, and joyfully praise those who cultivate the three gates of liberation.

One should personally cultivate the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities; one should also encourage others to cultivate the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities; one should constantly and correctly praise the cultivation of the dharmas of the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities; and one should joyfully extol those who cultivate the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities.

One should personally fulfill the ten stages of a bodhisattva, likewise encourage others to fulfill the ten stages of a bodhisattva, constantly and correctly praise the dharma of fulfilling the ten stages of a bodhisattva, and joyfully extol those who have fulfilled the ten stages of a bodhisattva.

One should personally fulfill the five eyes and six supernormal powers, encourage others to fulfill the five eyes and six supernormal powers, constantly and correctly praise the dharma of fulfilling the five eyes and six supernormal powers, and joyfully extol those who have fulfilled the five eyes and six supernormal powers.

One should personally fulfill the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi, and likewise encourage others to fulfill the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi; one should constantly and correctly praise the teachings on fulfilling the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi, and joyfully extol those who fulfill the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi.

One should personally fulfill the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and likewise encourage others to fulfill the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; one should constantly and correctly praise the dharma of fulfilling the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and joyfully extol those who have fulfilled the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

One should personally fulfill the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs, and likewise encourage others to fulfill the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs; one should constantly and correctly praise the dharma of fulfilling the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs, and joyfully extol those who have fulfilled the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs.

One should personally fulfill the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity; likewise, one should encourage others to fulfill the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity; one should always correctly praise the dharmas of fulfilling the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity; and one should joyfully extol those who have fulfilled the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity.

One should personally contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination in both forward and reverse order, encourage others to likewise contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination in both forward and reverse order, constantly and correctly praise the method of contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination in both forward and reverse order, and joyfully extol those who so contemplate them.

One should personally know suffering, abandon its origin, realize its cessation, and cultivate the path; likewise, one should encourage others to know suffering, abandon its origin, realize its cessation, and cultivate the path; one should constantly and correctly praise the Dharma of knowing suffering, abandoning its origin, realizing its cessation, and cultivating the path; and one should joyfully extol those who know suffering, abandon its origin, realize its cessation, and cultivate the path.

One should personally give rise to the wisdom that realizes the fruit of stream-entry without realizing the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) in order to attain the fruit of stream-entry; one should likewise encourage others to give rise to the wisdom that realizes the fruit of stream-entry and to realize the limit of reality in order to attain the fruit of stream-entry; one should constantly and correctly praise the dharma of giving rise to the wisdom that realizes the fruit of stream-entry and realizing the limit of reality to attain the fruit of stream-entry; and one should joyfully extol those who have given rise to the wisdom that realizes the fruit of stream-entry and realized the limit of reality to attain the fruit of stream-entry.
One should personally give rise to the realization of the fruit of once-returner, non-returner, arhatship, and pratyekabuddha-enlightenment,
yet without realizing the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), one attains the fruit of once-returner, non-returner, arhatship, and pratyekabuddha-enlightenment; furthermore,
one should also encourage others to give rise to the realization of the fruit of once-returner, non-returner, arhatship, and pratyekabuddha-enlightenment.
The wisdom of awakening and the realization of the limit of reality that attains the fruit of a once-returner, a non-returner, an arhat,

or pratyekabuddha-awakening; he constantly and correctly extols and gives rise to the wisdom of awakening and the realization of the limit of reality that attains the fruit of a once-returner, a non-returner, an arhat, or pratyekabuddha-awakening.
They praise and rejoice in the fruits, the dharmas of pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, the wisdom that realizes the fruit of once-returner,
non-returner, arhatship, and pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, as well as the realization of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) which attains the fruit of once-returner,
non-returner, arhatship, and pratyekabuddha-enlightenment.

One should personally enter the bodhisattva stage of the certainty of correctness (*samyaktvaniyāma*), and likewise encourage others to enter the bodhisattva stage of the certainty of correctness; one should constantly and correctly praise the dharma of entering the bodhisattva stage of the certainty of correctness, and joyfully extol those who have entered the bodhisattva stage of the certainty of correctness.

One should personally purify Buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity; one should also exhort others to purify Buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity; one should constantly and correctly praise the methods for purifying Buddha-fields and bringing sentient beings to maturity; and one should joyfully extol those who purify Buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity.

One should personally give rise to the supernatural powers of a bodhisattva, encourage others to give rise to the supernatural powers of a bodhisattva, constantly and correctly praise the method of giving rise to the supernatural powers of a bodhisattva, and joyfully extol those who give rise to the supernatural powers of a bodhisattva.

One should personally give rise to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); one should also exhort others to give rise to all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects; one should constantly and correctly praise the dharmas that give rise to all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects; and one should joyfully extol those who give rise to all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects.

One should personally sever the continuity of all habitual tendencies of the afflictions, and likewise exhort others to sever the continuity of all habitual tendencies of the afflictions; one should constantly and correctly praise the dharma of severing the continuity of all habitual tendencies of the afflictions, and joyfully extol those who have severed the continuity of all habitual tendencies of the afflictions.

One should personally undertake the full attainment of longevity, encourage others to undertake the full attainment of longevity, constantly and correctly praise the teaching on the full attainment of longevity, and joyfully extol those who have undertaken the full attainment of longevity.

One should personally turn the wheel of Dharma, encourage others to turn the wheel of Dharma, constantly and correctly extol the method of turning the wheel of Dharma, and joyfully praise those who turn the wheel of Dharma.

One should personally uphold and protect the True Dharma so that it endures, and likewise exhort others to uphold and protect the True Dharma so that it endures; one should constantly and correctly praise the practice of upholding and protecting the True Dharma so that it endures, and joyfully extol those who uphold and protect the True Dharma so that it endures.
“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to swiftly accomplish the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek, they should abide in these dharmas by means of non-apprehension.”

"Subhūti! All bodhisattva mahāsattvas should train in this way in the skillful means of the profound perfection of wisdom; by training in this way, they are able to abide securely in the dharmas in which they ought to abide."

If one trains in this way and abides in this way, then one will attain non-obstruction regarding form; one will attain non-obstruction regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; and so on, up to attaining non-obstruction regarding the turning of the wheel of Dharma and attaining non-obstruction regarding the endurance of the True Dharma.
Why is that? Subhūti!

From the beginningless past, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have not grasped at form, nor have they grasped at feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; and so on, up to not grasping at the turning of the wheel of Dharma, and not grasping at the endurance of the True Dharma.
Why is this? Subhūti!
Because form cannot be grasped; if form cannot be grasped, then it is not form.

Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be grasped; if feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be grasped, they are not feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
This extends up to the turning of the wheel of Dharma, which cannot be grasped; if the turning of the wheel of Dharma cannot be grasped, it is not the turning of the wheel of Dharma.
Because the abiding of the True Dharma cannot be grasped; if the abiding of the True Dharma cannot be grasped, it is not the abiding of the True Dharma.

When this teaching on the dharmas in which bodhisattvas dwell was being spoken, two thousand bodhisattvas attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Chapter 53: Non-Retrogression, Part Two, Chapter Fifty-Three: Non-Retrogression. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“By what conduct, characteristics, and signs shall we recognize this as a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can know, as they truly are, the stage of ordinary beings, the stage of śrāvakas, the stage of pratyekabuddhas, the stage of bodhisattvas, and the stage of tathāgatas—though these stages are said to be distinct, within the principle of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena, they are without change, without differentiation, and are entirely non-dual and indivisible.”

Although this bodhisattva mahāsattva truly awakens to and enters the suchness of all phenomena, they do not engage in any conceptual discrimination regarding that suchness, because they employ the method of non-apprehension.

Since this bodhisattva mahāsattva has truly realized and entered into the suchness of all phenomena, although they hear that suchness and all phenomena are non-dual and undifferentiated, they encounter no obstruction.
Why is this? Because True Suchness and phenomena cannot be said to be identical, nor can they be said to be different, nor can they be said to be both or neither.
This is likewise true for the Dharma-realm up to the inconceivable realm.
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva never utters speech impulsively; whatever he says is drawn from what is meaningful and beneficial, and if it is not meaningful or beneficial, he never speaks at all.
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva never observes the likes or dislikes, the strengths or weaknesses of others, but preaches the Dharma out of impartial compassion.
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not observe whether the Dharma-preacher’s lineage is noble or base, seeking only the subtle and wondrous meaning of the Dharma being taught.

"Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who is non-retrogressive possesses such practices, tokens, and signs; one should recognize a bodhisattva mahāsattva as non-retrogressive by means of these very practices, tokens, and signs."
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What are called the 'modes,' 'signs,' and 'characteristics' of all conditioned phenomena?
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! That all dharmas are without activity, without characteristics, and without marks—this should be known as their very activity, characteristic, and mark.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If all phenomena are without activity, characteristics, or marks, by what means does this bodhisattva mahāsattva proceed so that he is called 'non-regressive'?
The Buddha said, "Subhūti!..."

This bodhisattva mahāsattva is called "non-retrogressive" because they turn away from form; they are called "non-retrogressive" because they turn away from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

They are called "non-retrogressive" because they turn away from the sense base of the eye; they are called "non-retrogressive" because they turn away from the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

They are called "non-retrogressive" because they turn away from the sense base of forms; they are called "non-retrogressive" because they turn away from the sense bases of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena.
One is called "non-retrogressive" because of the revolution of the eye-element; one is called "non-retrogressive" because of the revolution of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements.

One is called "non-retrogressive" because of the revolution of the form-element; one is called "non-retrogressive" because of the revolution of the sound, odor, taste, tangible, and mental-object elements.

One is called "non-retrogressive" because of the revolution of the eye-consciousness-element; one is called "non-retrogressive" because of the revolution of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements.
One is called "irreversible" because one turns away from eye-contact; one is called irreversible because one turns away from ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact.

One is called irreversible because one turns away from all feelings produced with eye-contact as their condition; one is called irreversible because one turns away from all feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact as their conditions.

One is called irreversible because one turns away from the perfection of generosity; one is called irreversible because one turns away from the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

They are called "non-retrogressive" because they turn toward internal emptiness; they are called "non-retrogressive" because they turn toward external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence;
they are called "non-retrogressive" because they turn toward suchness; they are called "non-retrogressive" because they turn toward the dharma-realm, up to and including the inconceivable realm;

they are called "non-retrogressive" because they turn toward the noble truth of suffering; and they are called "non-retrogressive" because they turn toward the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path.
They are called "non-retrogressive" because they proceed upon the four foundations of mindfulness, and so on, up to proceeding upon the eight branches of the noble path;
they are called "non-retrogressive" because they proceed upon the four dhyānas, and because they proceed upon the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments;
they are called "non-retrogressive" because they proceed upon the eight liberations, and because they proceed upon the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities.

They are called "non-retrogressive" because they proceed within the liberation door of emptiness; they are called "non-retrogressive" because they proceed within the liberation doors of signlessness and wishlessness;

they are called "non-retrogressive" because they proceed within the ten stages of the three vehicles; they are called "non-retrogressive" because they proceed within the ten stages of the bodhisattva;
they are called "non-retrogressive" because they proceed within the doors of dhāraṇī; and they are called "non-retrogressive" because they proceed within the doors of samādhi.
They are called "non-regressive" because they turn toward the five eyes; they are called "non-regressive" because they turn toward the six supernormal powers;
they are called "non-regressive" because they turn toward the ten powers of a Buddha, and so on, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they are called "non-regressive" because they turn toward the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, and they are called "non-regressive" because they turn toward the eighty minor marks.

They are called "non-retrogressive" because they proceed toward the quality of non-forgetfulness; they are called "non-retrogressive" because they proceed toward the state of constant abiding in equanimity;

they are called "non-retrogressive" because they proceed toward all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*); they are called "non-retrogressive" because they proceed toward the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);

they are called "non-retrogressive" because they proceed toward the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjanabhūmi*); and they are called "non-retrogressive" because they proceed toward the stage of śrāvakas, the stage of pratyekabuddhas, the stage of bodhisattvas, and the stage of Tathāgatas.

They are called "non-retrogressive" because they proceed toward all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; they are called "non-retrogressive" because they proceed toward the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas.
Why is this? "Subhūti! The intrinsic nature of form does not exist;

the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness does not exist. In this way, even up to the intrinsic nature of all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas does not exist, and the intrinsic nature of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas does not exist."

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not dwell therein, he is called "one who turns"; because he does not turn back, he is said to be a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva. If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can understand in this way, he is named a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

No non-regressing bodhisattva mahāsattva ever takes pleasure in observing the physical forms or the discourses of outsiders, such as śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; it is impossible that those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas truly know or truly see the dharmas that ought to be known, or that they could establish a gateway to the Dharma of right view."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not give rise to doubt or confusion regarding the Buddha’s well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya. They harbor no grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) concerning worldly matters, nor do they fall into evil views. They do not cling to various worldly auspicious rites as being pure, and they never prostrate to other celestial deities as those worldly non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) do. They certainly do not use various flower garlands, scented ointments, incense, clothing, necklaces, precious banners, flags, canopies, music, or lamps to make offerings to celestial deities or to non-Buddhists."
"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, one should know that he is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are non-retrogressive do not fall into the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, or among the asuras; nor are they born into lowly castes, such as the caṇḍālas or the pukkasas. Furthermore, they never receive the body of a śaṇḍha, a paṇḍaka, one who is sexless, or one with dual sexual organs, nor that of a woman. Nor do they receive bodies characterized by blindness, deafness, muteness, lameness, paralysis, epilepsy, or deformity; nor are they ever born in states where there is no opportunity [to encounter the Dharma]."
"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, one should know that he is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! All non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas always delight in practicing the ten paths of wholesome action. They themselves abstain from taking life and also encourage others to abstain from taking life; they constantly and correctly praise the dharma of abstaining from taking life and joyfully extol those who abstain from taking life. This extends even to their own abstention from wrong views, as well as encouraging others to abstain from wrong views; they constantly and correctly praise the dharma of abstaining from wrong views and joyfully extol those who abstain from wrong views."
This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not manifest the ten paths of unwholesome action even in dreams, much less while awake! Subhūti,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, marks, and characteristics, one should know that this is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are non-retrogressive universally act for the benefit of all sentient beings; by means of non-apprehension as their expedient, they constantly cultivate the perfections from generosity up to wisdom, always without interruption."
"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, know that they are a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"

All non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cause all the sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, gāthās, udānas, nidānas, avadānas, jātakas, vaipulyas, adbhutadharmas, upadeśas, and upadeśas that they receive, uphold, contemplate, and recite to be thoroughly mastered and fully proficient. With such dharmas, they constantly and joyfully practice giving to all sentient beings, always forming this thought:
"How may I cause all classes of sentient beings who seek the true Dharma to have their aspirations fulfilled?"

Using non-apprehension as a skillful means, they further take these roots of goodness from such Dharma-giving and, sharing them equally with all sentient beings, dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, one should know that they are a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
All bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are non-retrogressive never give rise to doubt or hesitation regarding the profound Dharma-gates spoken by the Buddha."
Why is this? Subhūti!
This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive any dharma—whether form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness—in which he might harbor doubt or hesitation.

In this way, one does not perceive any dharma—whether it be the practice of any bodhisattva mahāsattva or the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas—in which one might harbor doubt or hesitation.
"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, one should know that he is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! All non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have accomplished the pliancy of their physical, verbal, and mental actions; their minds are free from obstruction toward all sentient beings; they constantly accomplish loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, giving rise to corresponding physical, verbal, and mental actions; they certainly do not dwell together with the five hindrances—namely, sensual desire, ill-will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt; they have already subdued all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and all fetters, bonds, secondary afflictions, and entanglements never arise again."

In entering and exiting, coming and going, his mind was never confused or mistaken; he constantly dwelt in right mindfulness and right situational awareness. Whether advancing or halting, whether standing, walking, sitting, or lying down—even when lifting or lowering his feet—he acted in this same manner. Wherever he traveled, he invariably observed the ground before him; he walked with composed gravity, maintaining focused attention and gazing straight ahead, and his movements and speech were never abrupt or violent.
"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, one should know him to be a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All bedding, clothing, and articles of use enjoyed by non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are always fragrant and clean, free from any foul odors or impurities; they are also free from filth, grease, lice, nits, and other such insects. Their minds delight in purity and refinement, and their bodies are free from disease."
"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, know that he is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

The body and mind of all non-retrogressive Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are pure; they are not like the bodies of ordinary people, which are constantly being consumed by eighty thousand families of worms."

Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas possess roots of goodness that are superior and transcend the world, and because the bodies they receive are pure both internally and externally, no insects or creatures can infest or devour their bodies.
As their roots of goodness gradually increase, so too do their bodies and minds become increasingly pure.

By virtue of this cause and condition, the bodies and minds of these bodhisattvas become more solid than adamant, such that they cannot be afflicted by adverse conditions—namely, cold and heat, hunger and thirst, mosquitoes and gadflies, wind and sun, venomous insects, swords and staves, and the like—nor can the various fetters afflict them.
Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, one should know that he is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does such a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly attain purity of body, speech, and mind?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"To the extent that the roots of goodness of this bodhisattva mahāsattva gradually increase, to that same extent the crookedness of body, speech, and mind is eliminated by the power of those roots of goodness; thus, they never arise again until the end of the future, and by this means, he constantly attains purity of body, speech, and mind."
Furthermore, Subhūti!

Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constantly manifest the three types of sublime conduct of body, the four of speech, and the three of mind, their body, speech, and mind are pure at all times. By virtue of this purity, they transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; having entered the bodhisattva’s state of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*), they do not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). They always delight in maturing all sentient beings and purifying buddha-fields; through this, they constantly attain purity of body, speech, and mind, abiding firmly and immovably in the rank of a bodhisattva.
"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, one should know that he is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not value gain or offerings, nor do they crave reputation. They have no greedy attachment to food, drink, clothing, bedding, dwellings, or material wealth. Although they practice the twelve dhūta qualities, they rely on none of them at all. Ultimately, they never give rise to a mind associated with stinginess, greed, breaking the precepts, anger, laziness, distraction, delusion, or any other various entanglements of affliction."
"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, one should know that he is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! All non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess firm and fierce awakening-wisdom (*bodhi-jñāna*) that enables them to penetrate deeply; they hear the true Dharma with reverence and faith, and contemplate its ultimate principles with focused mindfulness. Regarding all mundane and supramundane dharmas they have heard, they are able through skillful means (*upāya*) to bring them into accord with the profound principle of the *prajñāpāramitā*. Whatever worldly activities they undertake, they likewise rely on the *prajñāpāramitā* to bring them into accord with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), seeing not a single thing that transcends this nature of phenomena. Even if there should be something that does not correspond to the nature of phenomena, they are still able through skillful means to bring it into accord with the profound principle of the *prajñāpāramitā*, whereby they do not see anything that transcends the nature of phenomena."
"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, one should know him to be a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! Suppose an evil Māra were to manifest before all non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and conjure up eight great hells. Furthermore, within each of these great hells, he would conjure up immeasurable and boundless bodhisattvas, all of whom are being scorched by intersecting fierce flames and each undergoing bitter, agonizing, and poisonous great suffering. Having performed this conjuration, he says to those non-retrogressive bodhisattvas:

'These bodhisattvas have all received the prediction of non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; therefore, they have fallen into such great hells and constantly undergo these various kinds of intense suffering.'"
"Since you Bodhisattvas have received the prediction of non-retrogression from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, you too shall fall into this great hell and undergo various intense sufferings."

"The Buddha has granted you the prophecy that you shall undergo extreme suffering within the great hells; he has not granted you the prophecy of non-retrogression toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Therefore, you should quickly abandon the mind set on great enlightenment (bodhicitta), so that you may escape the sufferings of the great hells and be reborn among the gods or among humans to enjoy various riches and pleasures."
At that time, the irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, seeing and hearing this matter, remains unmoved and neither startled nor doubtful; he simply thinks:
"It is impossible for a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who has received the prediction of irreversibility to fall into the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, or among the asuras."

Why is this? Because a Bodhisattva in the stage of non-retrogression is definitively free from unwholesome karma, nor does he possess wholesome karma that would bring about bitter fruits; because all Buddhas are definitively free from false speech; and because everything spoken by the Tathāgata is for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, flowing forth from a heart of great compassion—therefore, whatever is seen or heard [by such a person] must certainly be the work and speech of an evil Māra.
"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, one should know him to be a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Suppose a Māra, having assumed the form of a śramaṇa, should come to an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva and say these words:

'What you have previously heard—that you should practice the perfection of giving so that it may be swiftly fulfilled; that you should practice the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom so that they may be swiftly fulfilled; and even up to: that you should realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—all such things you have heard are false teachings. You should quickly abandon them and not consider them to be true.'"

Furthermore, what you previously heard—that one should, regarding all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their disciples of the past, future, and present, from their initial generation of the mind of awakening until the endurance of the Dharma, rejoice in all their merits and roots of goodness therein, and having gathered them all together, share them equally with all sentient beings to seek supreme, perfect awakening—this too is a false teaching; you should quickly abandon it and not consider it to be true.

If you abandon those false teachings you have espoused, I shall instruct you in the true Dharma of the Buddha, enabling you to practice and swiftly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"What you have previously heard is not the true word of the Buddha; it is a false compilation composed by a poet. What I have spoken is the true word of the Buddha, which shall cause you to swiftly realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment that you seek."

"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing such words, experiences agitation, fear, or doubt in their mind, you should know that they have not yet received the prediction of non-retrogression; they are not yet certain regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and are not yet called a 'non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva.'"

“Subhūti!
