If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing such words, remains unmoved and neither startled nor doubtful, but dwells in accordance with the nature of phenomena that are unconditioned, signless, and unborn—then this bodhisattva mahāsattva, in all that he undertakes, does not rely on the words of others; he practices the perfection of generosity without following the instructions of others, and he practices the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom without following the instructions of others, even unto proceeding toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without following the instructions of others. It should be known that such a bodhisattva mahāsattva has attained non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

“Subhūti! Just as an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted acts in all matters without relying on the words of others, directly realizing the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) without confusion or doubt, and cannot be shaken by any Māras; likewise, the minds of non-regressing Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas cannot be destroyed or subdued by any Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, followers of external paths, or Māras, nor can they be made to feel despondent regarding their enlightenment.”

“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva has definitely already dwelled on the stage of non-retrogression; all his undertakings are performed after careful reflection, rather than being initiated merely out of faith in others. He does not even lightly accept and practice the teachings of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as they are spoken, let alone act upon the words of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, non-Buddhists, or evil Māras!”
It is impossible that these bodhisattvas would ever act solely out of faith in the practices of others.
Why is this? Subhūti!
This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive any dharma that can be trusted or practiced.
Why is this so? Subhūti!

These bodhisattvas do not perceive any form that can be taken as an object of trustful practice; they do not perceive any feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness that can be taken as an object of trustful practice. Nor do they perceive any suchness of form that can be taken as an object of trustful practice, nor do they perceive any suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness that can be taken as an object of trustful practice. In this manner, they do not perceive even the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas as an object of trustful practice, nor do they perceive any suchness of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas as an object of trustful practice.
"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with such practices, characteristics, and signs, one should know him to be a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Suppose an evil Māra, appearing in the guise of a bhikṣu, should come to a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva and say these words:
'The practices you engage in are the dharmas of saṃsāra; they are not the conduct of a bodhisattva, nor can one attain the knowledge of all modes through them.'"
"You all should now cultivate the path that exhausts suffering, so as to swiftly end all miseries and realize parinirvāṇa.

At that time, Māra the Evil One immediately taught the Bodhisattva a counterfeit path that leads to saṃsāra—namely, the perception of bones, or the perception of bluish discoloration, or the perception of festering pus, or the perception of bloating, or the perception of being eaten by worms, or the perception of a bloody corpse; or else [the meditations on] loving-kindness, compassion, joy, or equanimity; or the four dhyānas, or the four formless attainments—and addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"This is the true path and the true practice. By means of this path and this practice, you shall attain the fruit of a stream-enterer, and even go on to attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha."
"By means of this path and through this practice, you shall swiftly exhaust all birth, old age, sickness, and death; why endure the suffering of birth and death for so long?
You should even now weary of and abandon this present body of suffering, let alone seek to receive another body of suffering in the future!"
"You should examine yourself and abandon what you previously believed. "Subhūti!
When that bodhisattva mahāsattva hears those words, his mind remains unmoved and he is neither startled nor doubtful; he merely thinks this:"

"This bhikṣu has benefited me no small amount, for he has been able to explain to me a counterfeit path. He has enabled me to recognize that this path cannot lead to the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, nor even to the realization of pratyekabuddha enlightenment; how much less could it lead to the realization of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment that I seek!"
Having formed this thought, that bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives rise to profound joy and further reflects:

"This bhikṣu has been of great benefit to me; he has skillfully taught me the dharmas that obstruct the path. Now that I have come to recognize these obstructing dharmas, I shall train with mastery in the paths of the three vehicles."
"Subhūti! At that time, that evil Māra, knowing that this bodhisattva’s heart was filled with deep joy, spoke these words again: 'Alas!'"
"O man! Do you now wish to see those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have long practiced unbeneficial deeds?

That is to say, for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, these assemblies of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have—with immeasurable varieties of exquisite clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, wealth, flowers, incense, and other such things—made offerings to, honored, revered, and praised Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."

Furthermore, they practice the perfection of generosity in the presence of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; they practice the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom. Thus, even in the presence of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they cultivate all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas also drew near to and served Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, and in the presence of those Buddhas, they inquired about the path to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, saying:
"How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva abide in the path to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfections from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom?
How do they abide in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature; abide in suchness up to the inconceivable realm;
abide in the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; and cultivate the four applications of mindfulness?
Up to the eight branches of the noble path; cultivating the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
cultivating the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality; cultivating the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
cultivating the stages from the Ground of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma; and cultivating the five eyes and the six supernormal powers.
They cultivate the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; they cultivate the thirty-two marks of a Great Being and the eighty minor signs;
they cultivate the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity; they cultivate the doors of dhāraṇī and the doors of samādhi;
they cultivate the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination in both forward and reverse order, thereby purifying the buddha-fields.
How does one mature sentient beings, cultivate the various sublime supernormal powers of a bodhisattva, cultivate a perfect lifespan, train in turning the great wheel of Dharma,
protect and uphold the true Dharma so that it may endure for a long time, and cultivate all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*),
and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)?

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have explained this in successive order according to your inquiries. Although these multitudes of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide and train according to the Buddha’s instructions, even after practicing with fervent diligence for immeasurable kalpas, they are still unable to realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek; how much less so can you, who have now merely begun your practice and training, realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment!

“Subhūti! Although this bodhisattva mahāsattva hears these words, his mind remains unchanged; he is neither startled nor terrified, and he is without doubt or confusion. He becomes even more joyful and thinks to himself:

‘This bhikṣu has been of great benefit to me by skillfully explaining to me the dharmas that obstruct the path. Now I know that these dharmas which obstruct the path will certainly prevent me from realizing the fruit of a stream-enterer, up to and including the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; how much less could I realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment that I seek!’”

"Subhūti! At that time, Māra the Evil One, knowing that this bodhisattva’s mind was not retreating or cowed, and was free from confusion and doubt, immediately manifested there the forms of immeasurable bhikṣus and said to the bodhisattva:

'All these bhikṣus diligently sought unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in the past; they practiced various difficult and painful austerities for immeasurable kalpas, yet they were unable to attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they sought. Now they have all regressed and realized the fruit of arhatship; their outflows are exhausted and they have reached the end of suffering. How can you possibly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?'"
“Subhūti! Having seen and heard this, that bodhisattva mahāsattva immediately thinks: ‘This must be an evil Māra who has conjured such an image of a bhikṣu to disturb my mind.

By teaching a counterfeit dharma that resembles the path but constitutes an obstacle, he intends to ensure that there will certainly be no bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, having practiced the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) to the stage of fulfillment, realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, but instead fall back into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.’”
At that time, the Bodhisattva again had this thought:

"If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom until reaching the stage of fulfillment, it is impossible that they would not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;

likewise, up to practicing all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) until reaching the stage of fulfillment, it is impossible that they would not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, one should know that he is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
All non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattvas constantly reflect in this way:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva diligently practices and trains according to the teachings of all Buddhas, never being separated from the mental engagement associated with the sublime conduct encompassed by the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; never being separated from the mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes; and always using skillful means to exhort all sentient beings to diligently practice and train in the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—then this bodhisattva mahāsattva will certainly not regress from the six perfections, up to and including certainly not regressing from the knowledge of all aspects, and will surely realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, one should know that he is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti! All bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are non-retrogressive constantly reflect thus: 'If a bodhisattva mahāsattva recognizes the works of Māra and does not follow those works;

recognizes evil associates and does not follow the words of evil associates; recognizes sensory objects and does not turn according to sensory objects—then this bodhisattva mahāsattva is certain not to regress from the six pāramitās, and even certain not to regress from the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā), and will surely realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.'"
"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, one should know him to be a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, upon hearing the essential teachings of the Dharma spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, experience profound joy in their hearts and receive them with reverence and faith. They skillfully understand their meaning and intent; their minds are as firm and solid as diamond, incapable of being shaken or led astray. They constantly and diligently cultivate the six pāramitās without weariness of heart, and they likewise exhort others to study the six pāramitās without weariness of heart."
"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, one should know him to be a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva."

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 448. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Chapter 54: Turning and Not Turning. Part Two, Chapter Fifty-Four: Turning and Not Turning. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One!"
"Is such a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva called 'non-retrogressive' only by name, or is he also called 'retrogressive'?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Such a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva is both called 'non-retrogressive' and also called 'retrogressive'."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
by what causes and conditions is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is thus non-retrogressive called 'non-retrogressive'?"
“Furthermore, by what causes and conditions is it also called ‘regression’?
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

In this way, an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is certain never again to fall back into the stages of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; they will inevitably attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and for this reason they are called "irreversible. However, because they still possess a conceptualization of phenomena (*dharmasaṃjñā*), they are also said to be "reversible."
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By having a notion of what dharma does this bodhisattva mahāsattva undergo regression, such that he is also called 'regressed'?"
The Buddha said: “Subhūti!
Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva regresses from the perception of form, they are also said to regress; [the same applies] regarding feeling...”
...because there is a turning back from the perception of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, it is also called "turning back";

because there is a turning back from the perception of the six internal bases, it is also called "turning back"; because there is a turning back from the perception of the six external bases, it is also called "turning back";
because there is a turning back from the perception of the six internal elements, it is also called "turning back"; [and] regarding the external...

It is called "reversal" because there is reversal regarding the perception of the six elements; it is also called "reversal" because there is reversal regarding the perception of the six consciousness-elements;
it is also called "reversal" because there is reversal regarding the perception of the six contacts;

it is also called "reversal" because there is reversal regarding the perceptions of the various feelings produced with the six contacts as conditions; [it is also called reversal] regarding craving...
...because there is regression in the perception of hatred and delusion, it is also called "regression";
because there is regression in the perception of various views, it is also called "regression"; because there is regression in the perception of the six perfections, it is also called "regression";
because there is regression in the perception of all emptiness, it is also called "regression"; regarding the truth...
Because there is regression from the perception of equality, it is also called "regression"; because there is regression from the perception of the four noble truths, it is also called "regression";
because there is regression from the perceptions of the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth, it is also called "regression";
because there is regression from the perceptions of the four dhyānas and so forth, it is also called "regression"; [and likewise] regarding the eight liberations...

Because there is regression regarding the perception of equality, it is also called "regression"; because there is regression regarding the perception of the three gates of liberation, it is also called "regression";
because there is regression regarding the perception of the ten stages, it is also called "regression";
because there is regression regarding the perception of the five eyes and six supernormal powers, it is also called "regression"; [and] regarding the dhāraṇīs...
Because one has the notion that there is regression regarding the doors of liberation and the doors of samādhi, it is also called "regression";
because one has the notion that there is regression regarding the ten powers of a Buddha and so forth, it is also called "regression";

because one has the notion that there is regression regarding the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty secondary characteristics, it is also called "regression"; [and] regarding the quality of non-forgetfulness, the constant...
Because there is regression from the perception of the nature of equanimity, it is also called "regression";
because there is regression from the perceptions of the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a solitary buddha, it is also called "regression";

and because there is regression from the perceptions of the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha, it is also called "regression. Regarding...

Because there is a turning back from the conceptualization of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), it is also called "turning back";
because there is a turning back from the conceptualization of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas,
it is also called "turning back."

Why is this? Because such non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas contemplate all phenomena as empty of their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnya*). Having entered the bodhisattva’s stage of right nature and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*), they do not perceive even the slightest phenomenon that can be apprehended; because it cannot be apprehended, there is no volitional activity (*abhisaṃskāra*); because there is no volitional activity, there is ultimately no arising; because there is ultimately no arising, it is called the "patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). By attaining such patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena, they are therefore called non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, one should know that he is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! There are evil Māras who come to where these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell, wishing to cause them to become weary of and turn away from unsurpassed enlightenment. They say to the bodhisattvas: 'The knowledge of all modes is equal to space;

its own-characteristic is fundamentally empty, and its nature is the absence of nature. All phenomena are likewise: their own-characteristic is fundamentally empty, and their nature is the absence of nature, equal to space.'"

All these things are equal to space; within the emptiness of their intrinsic nature and characteristics, there is not a single dharma that can be called the "realizer," nor is there a single dharma that can be called the "object realized. The locus of realization, the time of realization, and that by which one realizes are likewise unobtainable.

Since the nature and characteristics of all dharmas are entirely empty and equal to space, why do you undergo such toil and hardship in vain, seeking to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
"All those bodhisattvas you previously heard of who should seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—this was all the teaching of Māra and not the true word of the Buddha.

You should abandon your vow for great enlightenment; do not, throughout the long night, extensively bring about the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings while undergoing hardship and suffering for yourselves. Even if you practice various difficult and painful asceticisms, you will ultimately never be able to attain enlightenment."
"Why do you all labor in vain? Subhūti!
When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas hear such words of admonition and reproof, they are able to examine them with discernment:
"This is the work of Māra, who seeks to cause me to regress and destroy my great bodhicitta; I must not now believe or accept his words.

Although all phenomena are equal to space and both their nature and characteristics are empty, sentient beings remain in the long night of birth and death, ignorant and sightless, falling into perversity and negligence, and thus undergoing various sufferings and afflictions."

I shall don the armor of merit, whose nature and characteristics are all empty like the great void, and swiftly proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; for the sake of all sentient beings, I shall preach the Dharma as is appropriate, causing them to be liberated from the great suffering of birth and death, so that they may attain the fruit of a stream-enterer, or the fruit of a once-returner, or the fruit of a non-returner, or the fruit of an arhat, or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, or realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"Subhūti! From the moment they first resolve their minds [on awakening], these bodhisattva mahāsattvas have heard this Dharma; their minds are firm, unshakable, and irreversible. Relying upon this firm, unshakable, and irreversible mind, they constantly and correctly practice the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom. Through these six perfections, they become fulfilled according to their respective degrees and have entered the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth."

Furthermore, by correctly practicing the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, they thereby abide on the stage of non-retrogression; thus, although evil Māras employ various means to cause their downfall and destruction, they are unable to turn back the bodhisattvas' resolve for great enlightenment.

"Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva transcends the stages of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; because no demonic activities can cause him to regress from his sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, he is called 'non-regressive. Furthermore, because he is far removed from all dharmas grasped through false conceptualization and from the stages of the two vehicles, he is also called 'regressive. Thus, this bodhisattva receives these two names, unlike those in other stages who are named only 'regressive.'"
"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, one should know that he is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti! All non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to enter the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna can enter them at will;
those who wish to enter the immeasurable state of loving-kindness up to the immeasurable state of equanimity can likewise enter them at will."
He is able to enter them: if he wishes to enter the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he can enter it at will;
if he wishes to enter the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, he can enter them at will;
if he wishes to enter the first liberation up to the liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling, he can enter them at will.
If he wishes to enter the first sphere of mastery up to the eighth sphere of mastery, he is able to enter them at will;
if he wishes to enter the first dhyāna up to the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, he is able to enter them at will;

if he wishes to enter the first universal base up to the tenth universal base, he is able to enter them at will; if he wishes to enter the three doors of liberation, he is able to [enter them] at will.
The mind is able to enter [these states]; if one wishes to evoke the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), one can evoke them at will. Subhūti!

Although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter the four dhyānas and even evoke the five supernormal powers, they do not experience their fruits. For this reason, they are not reborn by the power of the dhyānas, the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), up to the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), nor by the power of other merits. Furthermore, they do not realize the fruit of a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, an arhat, or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha. Rather, for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, they assume whatever bodies they ought to assume according to their wish; indeed, they are able to assume them exactly as they have vowed.
"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, one should know that he is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are non-retrogressive have accomplished the mental engagement of unsurpassed awakening;
they are never separated from the mind of great awakening, and they do not prize form, nor do they prize feeling, perception, [volitional formations, or consciousness]."

Regarding volitional formations and consciousness, they do not hold the sense base of the eye in high regard, nor even the sense base of the mind; they do not hold the sense base of forms in high regard, nor even the sense base of mental phenomena;
they do not hold the eye element in high regard, nor even the mind element; they do not hold the form element in high regard, nor even the mental-phenomena element;
they do not hold the eye-consciousness element in high regard, nor even the mind-consciousness element; they do not hold the eye... in high regard.
From contact up to mental contact, they do not value the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition,
nor those produced with mental-contact as a condition; they do not value signs, they do not value the basis,
they do not value companions, and they do not value the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom.
O Pāramitā, you do not prize the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments;
you do not prize the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
you do not prize the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities; you do not prize emptiness or signlessness.
...the door of liberation through wishlessness; they do not value the Four Noble Truths, do not value the eighteen kinds of emptiness,
do not value true thusness up to the inconceivable realm, do not value the ten stages,
do not value the five eyes and the six supernormal powers, and do not value the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
They do not value the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣa-dharma*), or the state of constant equanimity (*upekṣā-vihāra*);

they do not value the gateways of dhāraṇī or the gateways of samādhi; they do not value all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);
and they do not value the stage of the śrāvaka, the stage of the pratyekabuddha, or the stage of the bodhisattva.
In the stage of the Tathāgata, one does not prize the maturing of sentient beings or the purification of Buddha-fields;
one does not prize all the practices of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas or the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas;
one does not prize frequently beholding the Buddhas, nor does one prize the planting of various roots of goodness.
Why is this? Subhūti!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva realizes that the nature and characteristics of all dharmas are empty and, like space, are entirely unapprehendable. He does not perceive any dharma that can be regarded as precious; the producer, the produced, the time of production, the place of production, and that by which it is produced—all these are unapprehendable.
Why is this so? Subhūti!
All these phenomena are equal to space; their own characteristics are fundamentally empty, and they have non-existence as their very nature.

"Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes the mental attention of unsurpassed enlightenment and is never separated from the mind of great enlightenment. Whether in the four postures of the body—walking, coming and going, entering and exiting, lifting the feet or setting them down—their mind is never distracted. In walking, standing, sitting, lying down, advancing, or halting, in all their movements and every task they undertake, they abide in right mindfulness."
"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, one should know that he is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! All non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, manifest dwelling in the household life. Through skillful means, although they appear to accept the five objects of sensual pleasure, they do not give rise to attachment toward them. This is solely for the purpose of providing for all sentient beings: that is to say, to those who need food they give food; to those who need drink they give drink; to those who need clothing they give clothing; to those who need vehicles they give vehicles; and so on, up to giving whatever things are required, thereby fulfilling their wishes."

Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva personally practices the perfection of giving and also encourages others to practice the perfection of giving; he constantly and correctly extols the dharma of practicing the perfection of giving and joyfully praises those who practice the perfection of giving.

This continues up to his personally practicing the perfection of wisdom, encouraging others to practice the perfection of wisdom, constantly and correctly extolling the dharma of practicing the perfection of wisdom, and joyfully praising those who practice the perfection of wisdom.

Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva, while dwelling in the household life, employs the power of supernormal knowledges or the power of great vows to gather various requisites of the seven precious jewels, filling Jambudvīpa and even the trichiliocosm, which they then offer to the Triple Gem—the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha—and bestow upon all impoverished sentient beings.

"Subhūti! Although this bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in a household, he constantly cultivates the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and never enjoys the objects of the various exquisite desires. Although he appears to acquire various kinds of precious wealth, he does not give rise to stained attachment toward them. Furthermore, when acquiring the requisites for sensual pleasures and precious wealth, he never oppresses sentient beings, causing them to experience sorrow or suffering."
"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, one should know that he is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! All bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are non-retrogressive are constantly followed on their left and right by vajra-wielding yakṣas who secretly provide protection. They always think: 'This bodhisattva mahāsattva shall before long realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment he seeks;

may I always follow him and secretly protect him until that unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is attained. Such bodhisattvas will always have five classes of vajra-wielding deities following and protecting them, never abandoning them for even a moment. Neither humans nor non-humans can cause them harm, nor can any among the devas, Māras, Brahmās, or other worldly beings, by means of any dharma, destroy the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete mind of enlightenment they have generated."
"By virtue of these causes and conditions, until they reach unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, their body and mind will remain peaceful and secure, always free from disturbance. Subhūti!

These bodhisattva mahāsattvas will never lack the five worldly faculties—namely, the faculties of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body—and they will likewise never lack the five supramundane faculties, namely, the faculties of faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom."

Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva’s physical form is perfected and adorned with the primary and secondary marks, and his mental qualities increase moment by moment until the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, one should know that he is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are non-retrogressive always act as superior beings and never act as inferior beings.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed [the Buddha], saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that this bodhisattva-mahāsattva is called one who always acts as a superior person and not as an inferior person?
The Buddha said:

“Subhūti! For this bodhisattva mahāsattva, all afflictions no longer manifest; from moment to moment his merits increase until he reaches unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. At all times his mind is undistracted; therefore, I say that he always acts as a superior person and never as an inferior one.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
This bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes the mental attention of unsurpassed awakening, never being separated from the mind of great awakening,
and constantly cultivates pure livelihood, refraining from practicing incantations, medicine, divination, or any such arts."

Regarding matters of wrong livelihood: one does not, for the sake of fame or profit, recite spells over spirits and deities to cause them to possess men or women so as to inquire about their fortune or misfortune;
nor does one perform incantations or prohibitions over men, women, the young or old, animals, or spirits to manifest rare or miraculous phenomena;
nor does one practice physiognomy or divination regarding the length of one's lifespan, wealth and status, or various good and evil matters concerning sons and daughters.
Furthermore, one does not prophesy cold or heat, abundance or scarcity, good or bad fortune, or pleasant and unpleasant things that delude sentient beings;
nor does one practice incantations or prohibitions, compound decoctions and medicines, employ heterodox methods to treat illness, or cultivate friendships with the noble.
Nor does one act as a messenger for others, manifesting the appearance of a friend to pursue profit or seek fame—yet even such things do not defile them.
When observing with the mind men and women laughing and conversing, how much more so when there are other matters!
Furthermore, they do not respectfully make offerings to spirits or deities; for this reason, I say that one should always act as a superior person and not as an inferior person.
Why is this? Subhūti!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that the nature and characteristics of all phenomena are empty. Within the emptiness of nature and characteristics, they perceive no signs; because they perceive no signs, they remain far removed from various wrong livelihoods, incantations, medical arts, and divination. They seek only unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, constantly bringing benefit to all sentient beings.
"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, one should know that he is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
All non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, although they have attained skillfulness in all worldly literature and arts, do not become attached to them."
Why is this so? Subhūti!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva realizes that the nature and characteristics of all phenomena are empty. Within the emptiness of nature and characteristics, all worldly literature and arts are unobtainable; furthermore, all worldly literature and arts are subsumed under frivolous speech and wrong livelihood. Therefore, the bodhisattva knows them but does not engage in them.
"Subhūti! Although this bodhisattva mahāsattva is well-versed in the secular treatises and scriptures of non-Buddhists, he does not take delight in them nor become attached to them. Why is that?

"Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva realizes that all phenomena are ultimately empty. Within ultimate emptiness, no books or treatises can be apprehended. Furthermore, the principles and matters taught in the secular and non-Buddhist books and treatises often involve increase or decrease; they do not accord with the path of a bodhisattva. They are all categorized as frivolous proliferation and impure speech; therefore, bodhisattvas know them and take no pleasure in them."
"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, one should know that he is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
There are yet other practices, tokens, and signs by which one knows that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is non-retrogressive."
"I shall analyze and explain this for you; you should listen attentively and reflect upon it very thoroughly! Subhūti replied, "So be it!"
"Please speak!
We, this great assembly, focus our minds with joy upon hearing it.
The Buddha said:

“Subhūti! All non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom penetrate the fact that all phenomena are non-existent; they never depart from the mental attention directed toward awakening, and they take no pleasure in examining or discoursing upon the aggregates, the sense bases, or the elements.”

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have already well reflected upon and thoroughly mastered the principle that the nature and characteristics of the aggregates, bases, and elements are empty.
“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not delight in observing or discussing various worldly matters. Why is that?
This is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva has already well reflected upon and thoroughly mastered the fact that the intrinsic natures and characteristics of all phenomena are empty.
"Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not delight in observing or discussing matters concerning kings."

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), and does not perceive even the slightest phenomenon as having the characteristics of being superior or inferior, noble or base. "Subhūti!..."
This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not delight in observing or discussing matters concerning thieves.

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the emptiness of self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), and thus does not perceive even the slightest phenomenon as having the characteristics of gain or loss, or of giving or taking away.
“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not delight in observing or discussing military matters. Why is that?

This bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), because they do not perceive any signs of increase or decrease, or of gathering and dispersal, in any phenomena.
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not delight in observing or discoursing upon matters of war."

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are well-established in the suchness of the emptiness of all phenomena, and they do not perceive even the slightest phenomenon as having the characteristics of strength or weakness, or of attachment and aversion.
“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not delight in observing or discussing matters concerning cities and towns. Why is that?

This bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the emptiness of the realm of space; because they do not perceive even the slightest phenomenon as having the characteristics of being grasped or not grasped, or as being good or evil.
"Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not delight in observing or discussing matters concerning villages."

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell in the emptiness of all phenomena, and do not perceive even the slightest phenomenon as having the characteristics of increase or decrease, or of conjunction or separation.
“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not delight in observing or discussing matters concerning realms. Why is that?

This bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), for he does not perceive any phenomena as having the characteristics of belonging or not belonging to this or that. "Subhūti!
This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not delight in examining or discoursing upon matters concerning a self, a sentient being, and so forth, up to a knower or a viewer."
Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in ultimate emptiness and do not perceive any distinction between the existence or non-existence of anything from a self up to a knower.
“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not delight in observing or discussing signs of auspicious things. Why is that?
This bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells well in the signless, because they do not perceive the differentiated marks of phenomena as being either beautiful or ugly. "Subhūti!
This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not delight in examining or discussing such worldly matters; rather, they delight only in examining and discussing the perfection of wisdom."
Why is that? Because the profound perfection of wisdom is far removed from all signs, and is thus able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. "Subhūti!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva is never separated from the mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes; they practice the perfection of generosity while remaining free from stinginess and greed, they practice the perfection of ethical discipline while remaining free from immoral conduct, they practice the perfection of patience while remaining free from anger and resentment, they practice the perfection of diligence while remaining free from laziness, they practice the perfection of meditative concentration while remaining free from distraction and agitation, and they practice the perfection of wisdom while remaining free from faulty discernment.

“Subhūti! Although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the emptiness of all phenomena, they cherish the true Dharma and do not cherish what is not the Dharma, constantly aspiring to benefit all sentient beings.”

“Subhūti! Although this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the emptiness of non-apprehension, he constantly extols the merits of the Three Jewels and brings benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings.”

“Subhūti! Although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the single-flavored characteristic of the suchness and dharma-realm of all phenomena, they delight in praising the various merits of that suchness and dharma-realm.”
“Subhūti! Although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas know that all phenomena are ultimately empty, they cherish virtuous friends and do not delight in evil friends.

Those called ‘virtuous friends’ refer to Buddhas and bodhisattvas; furthermore, those belonging to the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who are able to skillfully teach and establish sentient beings, leading them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, are also called virtuous friends.”

“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva always delights in personally attending upon all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas. If he hears that a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha is currently teaching the sublime Dharma in another world-system, he immediately takes rebirth in that realm through the power of his vows, in order to make offerings, pay homage, respect, and praise [the Buddha], and to listen to and receive the sublime Dharma.”

“Subhūti! Whether by day or by night, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is never separated from the mental attention of mindfulness of the Buddha, nor is he ever separated from the mental attention of listening to the Dharma. By virtue of these causes and conditions, whenever there is a Buddha, a World-Honored One, currently preaching the True Dharma in any land, he immediately travels there to take birth through the power of his vows, or travels there by means of supernormal powers to listen to the Dharma.”

By reason of these causes and conditions, these bodhisattvas, in every place where they are born, are never separated from the Buddha and constantly hear the true Dharma without interruption or cessation.
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly acts for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, although he is able to manifest the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he skillfully employs expedient means to give rise to a mind of the desire realm to teach sentient beings the ten paths of wholesome action. Furthermore, by the power of his vows, he manifests birth in a buddha-field within the desire realm to make offerings, pay respect, honor, and praise the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, listening to the true Dharma and cultivating sublime practices.
"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, tokens, and signs, one should know that he is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti! All non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattvas constantly cultivate the perfections from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
they constantly practice the emptinesses from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence; and they constantly practice suchness..."
Reaching the inconceivable realm, they constantly practice the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
they constantly cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;

and they constantly cultivate the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, and the nine successive meditative absorptions.
The ten spheres of totality; constantly cultivating the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
constantly cultivating the five eyes and the six supernormal powers; constantly cultivating all doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of samādhi;
constantly cultivating the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and constantly cultivating the quality of non-forgetfulness.
...abiding constantly in equanimity, always cultivating all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);
always practicing all the deeds of a bodhisattva mahāsattva; and always seeking unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva always remains free from doubt regarding his own stage, never entertaining such thoughts as:
‘I am irreversible,’ or ‘I am not irreversible.’”

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive even the slightest dharma that could be said to regress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, nor one that could be said not to regress.
“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva has no confusion and no doubt regarding the dharmas of his own stage. Why is this?
This is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva has already thoroughly understood and fully mastered the dharmas of their own stage.

"Subhūti, it is just as a stream-enterer dwelling in the fruit of stream-entry has no confusion or doubt regarding the dharmas of their own fruit; likewise, a once-returner, a non-returner, an arhat, a pratyekabuddha, and all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, each dwelling in their respective fruits, also have no confusion or doubt regarding the dharmas of their own fruits."
In the same way, this bodhisattva mahāsattva also directly knows and directly sees all the dharmas subsumed within the stage of non-retrogression in which he dwells, being without confusion or doubt.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in this stage, they bring sentient beings to maturity, purify buddha-fields, and cultivate all manner of meritorious qualities. Should demonic activities arise, they are immediately able to recognize them; they do not yield to the power of such demonic activities but are well able to subdue various demonic deeds so that they do not obstruct the meritorious qualities being cultivated.”

“Subhūti! Just as when one has committed an act of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karman*), that immediate state of mind constantly follows them, such that even until the end of life they cannot abandon it.”
Why is this? Subhūti!

Because the power of the obsession that gives rise to the immediate karmic actions (ānantarya-karma) constantly persists with superior force; it cannot be subdued even until the end of life, nor can any other state of mind obstruct it.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva is likewise: dwelling securely in their own stage, their mind is unshakable and free from conceptual discrimination; thus, neither the gods, humans, nor asuras of the world can cause them to waver.
Why is this? Subhūti!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva is firm of mind, transcending all those in the world—gods, humans, māras, brahmās, and asuras—and has already entered the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth, abiding in the stage of non-retrogression. Having attained the bodhisattva’s sublime supernormal powers, they bring sentient beings to maturity and purify buddha-fields. Traveling from one buddha-field to another, they make offerings, show reverence, honor, and praise the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and the disciples of the Buddhas. They listen to the true Dharma in the presence of those Buddhas, plant various roots of goodness, and inquire about the meaning of the dharmas studied by bodhisattvas.

“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in his own stage, practices the perfection of wisdom and other wholesome dharmas; when demonic activities arise, he is immediately able to recognize them and never complies with such demonic activities. Rather, through skillful means, he gathers these demonic activities and places them within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), using skillful means to eliminate them, remaining without confusion or doubt regarding the dharmas of his own stage.”

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows that all phenomena enter into the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); they have realized that the limit of reality is neither one nor many, and within the limit of reality there is no conceptual differentiation. Since they are without delusion or doubt regarding the limit of reality, they likewise have no hesitation concerning the dharmas of their own stage.

“Subhūti! Even if this bodhisattva mahāsattva were to undergo further rebirths, they would never again regress from the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), nor would they ever give rise to a mind directed toward the levels of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.”

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas realize that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty; within this emptiness, they do not perceive any phenomenon as arising or ceasing, nor as defiled or pure.
“Subhūti! Even when this bodhisattva mahāsattva undergoes a transformation of existence, he does not doubt whether he will or will not attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva realizes that all phenomena are empty of their own intrinsic characteristics, which is itself unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. "Subhūti!..."
This bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in his own stage and does not follow other conditions; regarding the dharmas of his own stage, no one is able to destroy them.
Why is this? Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva has accomplished unshakable and non-retrogressive wisdom, such that no adverse conditions can cause him to waver.
“Subhūti! Suppose an evil Māra were to come to this bodhisattva mahāsattva in the form of a Buddha and say to him:
‘You should now seek the fruit of arhatship, exhaust all outflows forever, and realize parinirvāṇa.’”

"You are not yet fit to receive the prediction of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), nor have you yet realized the forbearance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). You do not yet possess the practices, characteristics, and signs of the stage of non-retrogression; therefore, the Tathāgata should not grant you the prediction of unsurpassed great enlightenment. Only when one is fully endowed with the practices, characteristics, and signs of the stage of non-retrogression may one receive from the Buddha the prediction of unsurpassed great enlightenment."

“Subhūti! When that bodhisattva mahāsattva hears those words, his mind remains unshaken; he is not startled, not terrified, does not retreat, and does not sink into despondency. This bodhisattva mahāsattva should know for himself:
‘In the presence of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the past, I must have already received the prediction of great enlightenment.’”
Why is this? Because a bodhisattva who has accomplished such supreme dharmas will certainly receive the prediction of enlightenment from a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Since I have already accomplished such supreme dharmas, why would a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha not grant me that prediction?
"Therefore, in the past, in the presence of various Buddhas, I have certainly already received the prediction of great enlightenment. "Subhūti!

Suppose an evil Māra, or a messenger of Māra, were to assume the form of a Buddha and come to grant a bodhisattva-mahāsattva a prediction regarding the stage of a śrāvaka, or grant a prediction regarding the stage of a pratyekabuddha, saying to that bodhisattva:"
“Good son, what use is unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment to you? You have long endured great suffering within the cycle of birth and death;
it would be better for you to swiftly realize nirvana without remainder for yourself, forever departing from birth and death to attain ultimate peace and happiness!”
"Subhūti! Having heard those words, that bodhisattva mahāsattva will think to himself:

'This is surely a wicked Māra, or a messenger of Māra, who has falsely manifested the form of a Buddha to disturb my mind and grant me a prediction of the stage of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, causing me to retreat from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.'"

Why is this? It is because it is certainly not the case that the Buddhas ever teach bodhisattvas to incline toward the level of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, or to abandon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
"Subhūti! Suppose there is an evil Māra, or a messenger of Māra, who falsely manifests the form of a Buddha and says to the bodhisattva mahāsattva:

'The Mahāyāna sūtras that you have received, upheld, and recited were not spoken by the Buddha, nor were they spoken by the disciples of the Tathāgata; these were spoken by various evil Māras or non-Buddhist heretics in order to deceive and delude you. You should no longer receive, uphold, read, or recite them.'"
Having heard those words, that bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:

"This must be a wicked Māra or a member of Māra’s retinue, who, in order to cause me to become weary of and abandon the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment I seek, declares that these profound Mahāyāna sūtras were not spoken by the Buddha, nor were they spoken by the disciples of the Tathāgata."
Why is that? Because it is absolutely impossible to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment apart from this sūtra. "Subhūti!..."

It should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva already dwells on the stage of non-retrogression; the Buddhas of the past have long ago bestowed upon him the prophecy of great enlightenment. Why is this?

This bodhisattva mahāsattva is fully endowed with the practices, tokens, and signs of the stage of non-retrogression. If any bodhisattvas achieve such practices, tokens, and signs, it should be known that they have already received the prediction of great enlightenment and have certainly established themselves in the stage of non-retrogression.
Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, one should know that he is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When all non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they embrace the true Dharma and protect and uphold the true Dharma, not sparing even their own bodies or lives, let alone other possessions or wealth."
This bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly reflects:
"I would rather abandon my relatives and friends, my precious wealth, and even my own life, than ever forsake the true Dharma of the Buddhas."

Why is this? Friends, wealth, and even one’s own life are always easily obtained throughout every birth; however, the true Dharma of the Buddhas is encountered only once in hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of eons. Having encountered it, one attains great benefit and happiness for a long night. Therefore, I must certainly protect it with diligent effort.
"Subhūti! When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas protect the true Dharma, they should form this thought:

'I do not protect the true Dharma of one Buddha, two Buddhas, or even hundreds of thousands of Buddhas; rather, I universally protect and uphold the true Dharma of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, so that it shall not be diminished or lost.'"
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is called the true Dharma of all Buddhas?”
"How does this bodhisattva mahāsattva protect and uphold [the Dharma] without begrudging body or life?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"All dharmas realized and taught by all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are empty; this is what is called the true Dharma of the Buddhas."

There are those of a deluded nature who slander and revile it, saying: "This is not the Dharma, nor is it the Vinaya; it is not the holy teaching spoken by the Teacher of Gods and Humans. By practicing this dharma, one cannot attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, nor can one realize the ultimate peace and happiness of Nirvana."
"Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva upholds this Dharma without begrudging body or life, constantly reflecting: 'All dharmas spoken by the Buddhas are empty;

this is the place of refuge for all sentient beings. By practicing and studying this, a bodhisattva swiftly realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, uproots the birth, aging, sickness, and death of all sentient beings, and enables them to attain ultimate peace and bliss in nirvāṇa. Therefore, one should uphold it without begrudging body or life.'"
Furthermore, he reflects:

"I too am included among the number of future Buddhas; the Buddha has already bestowed upon me the prophecy of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*). For this reason, the true Dharma of all Buddhas is my own Dharma. I should protect and uphold it without sparing even my body or life, so that when I attain Buddhahood in a future age, I too shall preach these dharmas of emptiness for the sake of sentient beings."

"Subhūti! Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives these benefits, they uphold the true Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata, not begrudging even their own body or life, and remain ever without indolence or abandonment until unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, one should know that he is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are non-retrogressive hear the true Dharma taught by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas without confusion or doubt; having heard it, they receive and uphold it, never forgetting it until they reach unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have already skillfully realized dhāraṇī.
At that time, Subhūti addressed [the Buddha], saying:

“Bhagavān! By having obtained what kind of dhāraṇī has this bodhisattva mahāsattva become free from confusion and doubt upon hearing the true Dharma spoken by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and having heard it, how does he receive and uphold it so that he never forgets it?”
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have already attained the *akṣayakośa-dhāraṇī*, the *sāgaramudrā-dhāraṇī*, the *padmagaṇakośa-dhāraṇī*, and others, that upon hearing the sublime Dharma spoken by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, they are without confusion or doubt; having heard it, they receive and uphold it, never forgetting it.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Does this bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon merely hearing the sublime Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, become free from confusion and doubt; and having heard it, receive and uphold it, never forgetting it? Furthermore, upon hearing the sublime Dharma spoken by bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, śrāvakas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and so forth, is he likewise able to be free from confusion and doubt regarding them; and having heard it, receive and uphold it, never forgetting it?”
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva universally hears the sounds, words, and meanings of all sentient beings; he is able to understand them all completely, without confusion or doubt, and shall never forget them until the end of the future.”
Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have already attained the *akṣayakośa-dhāraṇī* and other such spells, which sustain what they have spoken so that it may not be forgotten.
"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, one should know that he is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva."
Chapter 55: The Chapter on the Profound Meaning, Part Two, Section One. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
In this way, an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva accomplishes vast, immeasurable, incalculable, boundless, and inconceivable, supreme merits.
The Buddha said, “So it is, Subhūti!”
"So it is! It is as you have said.
In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is non-retrogressive accomplishes vast, immeasurable, incalculable, boundless, and inconceivable, supreme merits."
Why is that? Subhūti!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva has already attained the sublime, immeasurable, and boundless wisdom that is not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; abiding in this wisdom, this bodhisattva mahāsattva brings forth the sublime four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).

By virtue of these four supreme analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), no one among the world’s devas, humans, or asuras is able to pose a challenge that could exhaust the wisdom and eloquence of this bodhisattva.
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

One could proclaim for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges the various practices, characteristics, and signs of non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; by means of these practices, characteristics, and signs spoken by the Buddha, one displays how non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have accomplished boundless and supreme merits.”

I only pray that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha will further expound the profound meaning for the sake of the assembly of Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas, so that these Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas may abide therein,
be able to cultivate the perfections from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom until they are swiftly fulfilled, and be able to abide in internal emptiness up to...
They cause the emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence to be swiftly perfected; they cause the abiding in suchness up to the inconceivable realm to be swiftly perfected;
they cause the abiding in the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path to be swiftly perfected;

they cause the cultivation of the four applications of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path to be swiftly perfected; they cause the cultivation of the four... [to be swiftly perfected].
They cause the dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments to be swiftly perfected;
they are able to cultivate the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities so that these are swiftly perfected;
they are able to cultivate the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—so that these are swiftly perfected; they are able to cultivate the dhāraṇīs...

They cause the doors of liberation and the doors of samādhi to be swiftly perfected; they are able to cultivate the stages from the Ground of Extreme Joy up to the Ground of Dharma Cloud so that they are swiftly perfected;
they are able to cultivate the five eyes and the six supernormal powers so that they are swiftly perfected;
they are able to cultivate the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha so that they are swiftly perfected; they are able to cultivate...
They cause the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks to be swiftly perfected;

they are able to cultivate the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity, causing them to be swiftly perfected; and they are able to cultivate all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), causing them to be swiftly perfected.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “Excellent! Excellent!”

It is well that you are now able to question the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding this profound locus of meaning for the sake of the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, so that the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may dwell therein, cultivating and abiding in its merits until they are swiftly perfected.

"Subhūti, you should know that the locus of the profound meaning refers to emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-action, non-arising, non-cessation, quiescence, nirvāṇa, suchness, the dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, and the limit of reality; these and others like them are called the locus of the profound meaning."
“Subhūti, you should know that these various designations for the profound state of meaning thus described all reveal nirvāṇa as the profound meaning.
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Is it only nirvāṇa that is called 'profound meaning,' or are all other dharmas also called 'profound'?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"All other dharmas are also called 'profound.'"
Why is this? Subhūti!
Form is also called profound; feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are also called profound; the eye base...
Even the sense base of mind (*manāyatana*) is called profound; the sense bases from form (*rūpāyatana*) up to mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) are also called profound.
The eye element (*cakṣurdhātu*) up to the mind element (*manodhātu*) is also called profound; the elements from form (*rūpadhātu*) up to mental phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) are also called profound.

The eye-consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) up to the mind-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*) is also called profound; [the same applies to] eye-contact (*cakṣuḥsaṃsparśa*) up to mind-...

Contact is also called profound; the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, are also called profound;
the earth element up to and including the consciousness element are also called profound;
ignorance up to and including old age and death are also called profound; and the perfection of generosity up to and including [the perfection of wisdom]...
If the *pāramitās* are also called profound, the Noble Truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path are also called profound;
the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path are also called profound;
the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments are also called profound; the eight liberations...
The bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the nine successive attainments (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), and the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*) are also called profound;
the doors of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are also called profound; the doors of dhāraṇī and the doors of samādhi are also called profound;
the ten stages (*bhūmi*) practiced by the bodhisattvas of the three vehicles are also called profound; and the five eyes...
The six supernormal powers are also called profound; the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are also called profound;
the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks are also called profound;
the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity are also called profound; the fruit of stream-entry...

Even the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha is called profound; omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are also called profound;
the entire conduct of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas are also called profound.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 449. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Second Division, Chapter on the Profound Meaning, Part Fifty-five, Section Two. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Why is form also called "profound"?
Why are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness also called "profound"?
And so on, up to: why are all the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas also called "profound"?
"Why is the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas also called 'profound'?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Because the suchness of form (*rūpa-tathatā*) is profound, form is also called profound; because the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna-tathatā*) is profound, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also called profound. In this way, up to and including the suchness of all the practices of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas being profound, all the practices of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are also called profound; because the suchness of the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is profound, the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is also called profound."
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In what way is the suchness of form profound?
In what way are the suchnesses of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness profound?"
In this way, up to: why is the suchness of all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas so profound?
Why is the suchness of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas so profound?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“The suchness of form is neither identical to form nor separate from form; therefore, it is profound.

The suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is neither identical to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness nor separate from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; therefore, it is profound.”

In this way, even up to the suchness of all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is neither identical to all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas nor separate from all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; therefore, it is profound.

The suchness of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas is neither identical to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas nor separate from the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas; therefore, it is profound.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Tathāgata possesses most marvelous and subtle skillful means;

for the sake of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas on the stage of non-retrogression, he eliminates all forms and reveals nirvāṇa, and eliminates feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness to reveal it.”
Nirvāṇa— likewise, even to the extent of negating all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to reveal nirvāṇa,
and negating the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas to reveal nirvāṇa—
the World-Honored One possesses most marvelous and subtle skillful means, for the sake of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas on the stage of non-retrogression, negating everything.
Whether they be material or immaterial, visible or invisible, resistant or non-resistant,
mundane or supramundane, common or uncommon, with outflows or without outflows,
conditioned or unconditioned phenomena, they manifest nirvāṇa.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.

The Tathāgata possesses most marvelous and subtle skillful means; for the sake of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas on the stage of non-retrogression, he sets aside all forms (*rūpa*) to reveal nirvāṇa, and sets aside feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) to reveal nirvāṇa. Even unto this, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses most marvelous and subtle skillful means; for the sake of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas on the stage of non-retrogression, he sets aside everything—whether form or formless, visible or invisible, resistant or non-resistant, mundane or supramundane, common or uncommon, with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows, conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas—to reveal nirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Regarding these profound points, bodhisattva mahāsattvas should, relying on the principle corresponding to the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), reflect with careful discernment, weigh, and examine them, thinking thus:
'I should now abide as taught by the profound perfection of wisdom; I should now train as taught by the profound perfection of wisdom.'"

"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able, regarding these profound points, to rely on the principles corresponding to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), to reflect upon them with precision, to weigh and examine them, to abide as taught in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and to train as explained in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*—then by such diligent cultivation and training, through giving rise to even a single thought-moment based on the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, that bodhisattva mahāsattva can still gather countless, immeasurable, and boundless roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), transcend the flow of birth and death for immeasurable eons, and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). How much more so if they can constantly cultivate the *prajñāpāramitā* without interruption and always abide in the mental attention (*manasikāra*) associated with enlightenment!"

"Subhūti! It is like a man of great desire who, having become mutually infatuated with a beautiful woman, makes an appointment with her; yet because she is hindered by some obstacle, she is unable to go to the rendezvous, and this man’s lustful mind continues to flow intensely."
"Subhūti! What do you think?
In what respect does that person’s thought of desire arise?"
“World-Honored One!
This person’s thoughts turn toward women, thinking:
‘When will she come so that we may meet here and enjoy ourselves in pleasure and sport?’”
"Subhūti! What do you think? How many thoughts of desire would arise in that person during a day and night?"
“World-Honored One!
This person has many thoughts of desire day and night.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, relying on the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, gives rise to even a single thought-moment and trains according to what is taught in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the number of kalpas of cyclic existence they transcend is equal to the number of lustful thoughts produced by a person of great desire over the course of a single day and night."

"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates and trains according to the meaning and intent of what is taught in this perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they are able to liberate themselves from all faults and transgressions that obstruct unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi). Therefore, by relying on the profound perfection of wisdom and training with diligent effort, the bodhisattva swiftly realizes unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Subhūti!
