If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in accordance with what is taught in this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the merit obtained by them in a single day and night—if that merit were to have a physical form or measure—could not be contained even within as many trichiliocosm buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.

Even if all other merits were to fill as many trichiliocosm buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, they would not equal even one hundredth part of this merit; they would not equal one thousandth part, nor one hundred-thousandth part, nor even a *upaniṣad* fraction thereof.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva were to remain far removed from the perfection of wisdom, even if they were to practice giving as an offering to the Triple Gem—the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha—for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, Subhūti!"
"What do you think?
By reason of this, would that bodhisattva mahāsattva acquire much merit? Subhūti replied:
“Very much so,
World-Honored One!
That merit would be incalculable, immeasurable, and boundless.”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, relying on the profound perfection of wisdom, studies as taught for even a single day and night, the merit he obtains is far greater than that."
Why is this so? Subhūti!

This profound perfection of wisdom is the path upon which the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas rides; because bodhisattva mahāsattvas ride upon this path, they swiftly reach unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, being far removed from the perfection of wisdom, were for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River to practice giving and make offerings to stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas—Subhūti!"
"What do you think?
By reason of this, would that bodhisattva mahāsattva acquire much merit? Subhūti replied:
“Very much so,
World-Honored One!
That merit would be incalculable, immeasurable, and boundless.”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, relying on the profound perfection of wisdom, practices as taught for even a single day and night, the merit he obtains is far greater than that."
Why is this so? Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, swiftly enter the bodhisattva’s state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), and further gradually cultivate all bodhisattva practices, swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva were to remain far removed from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), even if they were to diligently practice generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River."
"Subhūti! What do you think?
By reason of this, would that bodhisattva mahāsattva acquire much merit?"
Subhūti replied, “Very many,
World-Honored One!”
“Their merit will be incalculable, immeasurable, and boundless.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in accordance with what is taught in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and for even a single day and night diligently practices generosity, pure ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, the merit they obtain will be far greater than that.”
Why is that? Subhūti!
This profound perfection of wisdom is the mother of all bodhisattva mahāsattvas.

Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* gives birth to the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and it is by relying on the profound *prajñāpāramitā* that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to swiftly fulfill all the buddha-dharmas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva were to remain far removed from the perfection of wisdom and, for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, were to give the gift of Dharma to all sentient beings."
"Subhūti! What do you think?
By reason of this cause and condition, would that bodhisattva mahāsattva acquire much merit?"
Subhūti replied, “Very many,
World-Honored One!”
“His merit would be incalculable, immeasurable, and boundless.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in accordance with what is taught in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and for even a single day and night bestows the gift of Dharma upon all sentient beings, the merit he obtains will far exceed that [of the former].”
Why is that? Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is far removed from the perfection of wisdom, then they are far removed from the knowledge of all modes.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not depart from the perfection of wisdom, then they do not depart from the knowledge of all modes. Therefore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should always remain inseparable from the profound perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva were to remain far removed from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā),
even if they were to practice the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā) up to the perfection of wisdom for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges,

and were to abide in the emptiness of the internal (adhyātmaśūnyatā) up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature (abhāvasvabhāvaśūnyatā), and were to abide in suchness (tathatā) up to [the limit of reality]...
Within the inconceivable realm, they dwell securely in the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
they practice the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; they practice the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
and they practice the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities.
Abiding therein, they practice the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
they practice from the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma Stage; they practice all the gates of dhāraṇī and the gates of samādhi;
they practice the five eyes and the six supernormal powers; and they practice the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Regarding the shared dharmas, they practice the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity;
they practice all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and all-aspect knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
“Subhūti! What do you think?
By reason of this cause and condition, would that bodhisattva mahāsattva acquire much merit?”
Subhūti replied, “It is very much so,
World-Honored One!”
"His merit will be incalculable, immeasurable, and boundless.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in accordance with what is taught in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and practices the *dānapāramitā* up to the practice of the *sarvākārajñatā* for even a single day and night, the merit he obtains will be far greater than that."
Why is that? Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not remain apart from the perfection of wisdom, it is impossible for them to regress from omniscience.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva were to distance themselves from the perfection of wisdom, it is possible that they would regress from omniscience. Therefore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should always remain inseparable from the profound perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva were to distance themselves from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), even if they were to practice various kinds of material giving and the giving of Dharma for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, dwelling in secluded places with focused mindfulness and reflection, and dedicate the previously cultivated merit equally to all sentient beings toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment—[this would not equal the merit of one who dwells in the perfection of wisdom].
"Subhūti! What do you think?
By reason of this, would that bodhisattva mahāsattva acquire much merit?"
Subhūti replied, “Very many,
World-Honored One!”
“His merit will be incalculable, immeasurable, and boundless.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in accordance with what is taught in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and for even a single day and night practices various kinds of material giving and the giving of the Dharma, dwelling in a secluded place with focused mindfulness and reflection, and dedicates the previously cultivated merit equally to all sentient beings toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, the merit he obtains is far greater than that [of the former].”
Why is this so? Subhūti!

You should know that the dedication arising from reliance on the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is the most supreme dedication; you should know that the dedication arising apart from the *prajñāpāramitā* is an inferior dedication.
Why is this? Subhūti!
Because the profound perfection of wisdom serves as the leader for all factors conducive to enlightenment.

Therefore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should at all times remain inseparable from the profound perfection of wisdom, and should dedicate the various merits of their practice in common with all sentient beings toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, being far removed from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), were for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River to universally take as their object all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present, along with their disciples, and having combined and rejoiced in their roots of virtue and merit, were to dedicate this together with all sentient beings equally toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment—Subhūti!"
"What do you think?
By reason of this, would that bodhisattva mahāsattva acquire much merit? Subhūti replied:
“Very much so,
World-Honored One!
That merit would be incalculable, immeasurable, and boundless.”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in accordance with what is taught in this profound perfection of wisdom, and for even a single day and night universally takes as their object all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present, along with the roots of virtue and merit of their disciples, rejoicing in them by unifying them and sharing them equally with all sentient beings, dedicating them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—the merit obtained will be far greater than that."
Why is this so? Subhūti!
All roots of merit consisting of rejoicing and dedication have the profound perfection of wisdom as their foremost guide.

Therefore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should always remain inseparable from the profound perfection of wisdom, and should rejoice in all roots of virtue and dedicate them toward the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are produced by conceptualization; they arise from false imagination and are entirely without real existence.”
By what cause and condition do these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by practicing the giving of material wealth and so forth, obtain merit that is incalculable, immeasurable, and boundless?

World-Honored One, the merit produced by the analytical practice of giving material wealth and so forth should not be able to give rise to true right view, nor enable entry into the state of correctness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*), nor allow one to attain the fruit of a stream-enterer, or the fruit of a once-returner, or the fruit of a non-returner, or the fruit of an arhat, or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; nor could it lead to the attainment of the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.

All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are produced by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); arising from false imagination (*parikalpa*), they do not exist at all as realities. Merit derived from conceptual constructions such as the giving of material wealth cannot give rise to true right view; it cannot lead one to enter the state of correctness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*), nor can it result in the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), up to and including the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Subhūti! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they know that all things produced by conceptualization—such as the dharma of material giving—are empty and non-existent, false and unreal.
Why is that? Subhūti!

I have taught that all phenomena produced by conceptual construction—such as the gift of material wealth and so forth—are without exception empty in their nature and characteristics; they do not exist, being false and lacking solidity.
Why is this? Subhūti!

It is because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have well studied the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of the nature of non-existence, and have thereby attained thorough penetration in accordance with what the Buddha has taught.

"Subhūti! Once this bodhisattva mahāsattva is established in emptiness, as they observe and analyze how the meritorious deeds of material giving and so forth are empty, non-existent, false, and unreal, to that same degree they are able not to be separated from the profound perfection of wisdom."

To the extent that one does not depart from this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, to that same extent one obtains incalculable, immeasurable, and boundless merit; by virtue of these causes and conditions, one gives rise to true right view, is able to enter the state of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*), and even realizes the sought-after unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is the distinction between what you have called 'innumerable,' 'immeasurable,' and 'boundless'?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"To say 'incalculable' means that calculation cannot be found; it cannot be calculated within the realm of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-dhātu*), nor can it be calculated within the realm of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-dhātu*).

To say 'immeasurable' means that measurement cannot be found; it cannot be measured among past phenomena (*atīta-dharma*), it cannot be measured among future phenomena (*anāgata-dharma*), and it cannot be measured among present phenomena (*pratyutpanna-dharma*)."
"Regarding 'boundless,' it means that no limit can be found, for its boundaries cannot be measured.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"

Is there any cause or condition by which form is also said to be innumerable, immeasurable, and boundless, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise said to be innumerable, immeasurable, and boundless?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“By reason of certain causes and conditions, form is also said to be innumerable, immeasurable, and boundless; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also said to be innumerable, immeasurable, and boundless.”
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"For what reason and by what conditions is form also said to be innumerable, immeasurable, and boundless; and why are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness also said to be innumerable, immeasurable, and boundless?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Because the intrinsic nature of form is empty, it is also said to be incalculable, immeasurable, and boundless; because the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is empty, they too are said to be incalculable, immeasurable, and boundless."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha again, saying:

"Is it only that the intrinsic nature of form is empty, and the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is empty, or are all phenomena likewise empty of intrinsic nature?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Did I not previously say that all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature? Subhūti replied:

"Although the Buddha has constantly taught that all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, I too have already understood this; yet because sentient beings do not know, see, or realize it, I now ask this question once more."
"Bhagavān! The emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is itself inexhaustible, and it is also incalculable, immeasurable, and boundless. Bhagavān!"

Within the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, exhaustion cannot be found, number cannot be found, measure cannot be found, and limits cannot be found; for these reasons, they are inexhaustible, innumerable, immeasurable, and boundless, such that there is no distinction whatsoever between their meaning and their phrasing.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said:
inexhaustible, innumerable, immeasurable, and boundless; whether in meaning or in phrasing, there is no distinction whatsoever, for they all together reveal the emptiness of all phenomena.

"Subhūti! All phenomena are empty and all are ineffable; yet the Tathāgata, through his skillful means, speaks of them as inexhaustible, or as innumerable, or as immeasurable, or as boundless, or as empty, or as signless, or as wishless, or as unconditioned, or as unborn, or as unceasing, or as free from defilement, or as quiescence, or as nirvāṇa, or as suchness, or as the limit of reality. Such meanings as these are all the skillful teachings expounded by the Tathāgata."
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How extraordinary is this skillful means! The true reality of all phenomena (*dharmāṇāṃ bhūtalakṣaṇam*) is ineffable, yet for the sake of sentient beings, it is expediently revealed.”
“World-Honored One!
As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, the nature of all dharmas is ultimately ineffable.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"So it is! So it is! The nature of all phenomena is entirely ineffable."
"Why is this? Because the nature of all phenomena is ultimately empty, and there is nothing that can be proclaimed as 'ultimately empty.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Is there any increase or decrease in the ineffable meaning?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"The ineffable meaning neither increases nor decreases."
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If the ineffable meaning neither increases nor decreases, then the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom should likewise neither increase nor decrease;
and the four applications of mindfulness up to the eight [applications of mindfulness]...”

The branches of the noble path should likewise be neither increased nor decreased; the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments should likewise be neither increased nor decreased;
the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities should likewise be neither increased nor decreased;
and the [three] gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—should likewise be neither increased nor decreased.
The gates of liberation should likewise be without increase or decrease; from the Ground of Supreme Joy up to the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma, they should likewise be without increase or decrease;
the gates of dhāraṇī and the gates of samādhi should likewise be without increase or decrease;
the five eyes and the six supernormal powers should likewise be without increase or decrease; and the ten powers of the Tathāgata, up to the [ten]...

The eight unique qualities of a Buddha should likewise be without increase or decrease; the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity should likewise be without increase or decrease;
and all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects should likewise be without increase or decrease.

"Bhagavān! If the six pāramitās neither increase nor decrease, and even up to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) likewise neither increase nor decrease, then it follows that the six pāramitās would be non-existent, and even up to all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects would also be non-existent."

If the six perfections do not exist, and even up to all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) also do not exist, how can a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the six perfections up to all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects, and thereby realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”

The ineffable meaning neither increases nor decreases; the six perfections likewise neither increase nor decrease, and even all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects neither increase nor decrease.

The ineffable meaning does not exist; the six perfections also do not exist; and even up to all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects, these also do not exist.
"Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom and abide in the perfection of wisdom, they employ skillful means and do not form such thoughts as:
'I am increasing or decreasing the perfection of wisdom, up to and including the perfection of generosity.'"
"But one should simply form this thought:
'There are only names and concepts which are called the perfection of wisdom, up to and including the perfection of generosity. Subhūti!"

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of generosity, they take up the mental engagement that accompanies this perfection of generosity; together with the mind and roots of virtue arising therefrom, they dedicate them in common with all sentient beings toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, dedicating them in a manner as subtle, profound, and wondrous as the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddha.

In this way, up until the time of practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, one maintains the mental attention (*manasikāra*) that accompanies this *prajñāpāramitā*, and together with the mind and roots of goodness arising from it, dedicates them for the common possession of all sentient beings toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. One performs this dedication in a manner as subtle, profound, and sublime as the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of the Buddha; through the power of such skillful means of dedication, one realizes unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One,
what is meant by unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“The suchness of all phenomena is what is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What is meant by the suchness of all phenomena, and why is it said that the suchness of all phenomena is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“The suchness of form, and the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—this is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
Equal enlightenment: the suchness of the sense-base of the eye up to the suchness of the sense-base of the mind is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
the suchness of the sense-base of form up to the suchness of the sense-base of phenomena is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
the suchness of the eye-element up to the suchness of the mind-element is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The suchness of the form realm up to the suchness of the dharma realm is called unsurpassed perfect enlightenment;
the suchness of the visual consciousness element up to the suchness of the mental consciousness element is called unsurpassed perfect enlightenment;
the suchness of eye-contact up to the suchness of mind-contact is called unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.

The suchness of all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, up to the suchness of all feelings produced with mind-contact as condition—this is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

The suchness of the earth element, up to the suchness of the consciousness element—this is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. The suchness of ignorance, up to the suchness of old age and death.

This is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; the suchness of the perfection of generosity up to the suchness of the perfection of wisdom is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;

the suchness of inner emptiness up to the suchness of the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; [the suchness of] the noble truth of suffering...
The suchness of the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
the suchness of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the suchness of the eight branches of the noble path is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
and the suchness of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments [is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment].

This is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; the suchness of the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities—this is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
the suchness of the door of liberation of emptiness, and the suchness of the doors of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness—this is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

The suchness of equal enlightenment, from the suchness of the stage of pure observation up to the suchness of the stage of the Tathāgata—this is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
the suchness of the stage of extreme joy up to the suchness of the stage of the cloud of dharma—this is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
the suchness of the doors of dhāraṇī and the suchness of the doors of samādhi—[are likewise unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment].

That which is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is the suchness of the five eyes; the suchness of the six supernormal powers is what is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

The suchness of the ten powers of a Buddha, up to and including the suchness of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, is what is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. The suchness of the quality of non-forgetfulness and the suchness of constant abiding...
The suchness of the nature of relinquishment is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
the suchness of the fruit of stream-entry up to the suchness of the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
and the suchness of all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The suchness of birth and death and the suchness of nirvāṇa are what is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. "Subhūti!
Because all suchness is without increase and without decrease, the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is also without increase and without decrease."

"Subhūti! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not depart from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), but always joyfully abide in the suchness (tathatā) of all phenomena, never perceiving any phenomenon as increasing or decreasing."

For this reason, the ineffable meaning neither increases nor decreases; the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) also neither increases nor decreases, and the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom likewise neither increase nor decrease. Even up to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), there is neither increase nor decrease, and the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) also neither increase nor decrease.

The ineffable meaning does not exist; the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) also do not exist; and even up to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), these also do not exist.

"Subhūti! By relying on non-increase and non-decrease, and taking non-existence as their skillful means, bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom; through this gateway, they accumulate all merits and thereby realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, relying upon non-increase and non-decrease as the means of practice, cultivates the perfection of wisdom and, through this gateway, accumulates all merits and thereby realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—does that bodhisattva mahāsattva realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the initial thought-moment arising, or does he realize it by means of the final thought-moment arising?”

"Bhagavān! If this bodhisattva mahāsattva were able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment at the moment the initial thought arises, then at the time the initial thought arises, the subsequent thoughts have not yet arisen; thus, there would be no sense of conjunction."
If the subsequent mind arises and is able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, then at the time the subsequent mind arises, the preceding mind has already ceased;

thus, there is no sense of conjunction. When one thus examines the preceding and succeeding moments of mind and mental factors from every perspective, there is no sense of conjunction. How, then, can roots of virtue be accumulated?

If the roots of goodness cannot be accumulated, then the supreme wisdoms have no means of arising; if the supreme wisdoms do not arise, how can a bodhisattva realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"I shall provide you with a brief analogy, so that those of wisdom may easily understand the meaning of what is being taught. Subhūti!"
What do you think?
When a lamp is lit, is it the initial flame that burns the wick,
or is it the final flame that burns the wick?
Subhūti replied, “As I understand it,
it is not by the first flame that the wick is burned, nor is it apart from the first flame that the wick is burned;
it is not by the last flame that the wick is burned, nor is it apart from the last flame that the wick is burned.”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? When a lamp is lit, does the wick burn?"
Subhūti replied, “In the world,
it is clearly seen that the wick is indeed scorched.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"So too it is for the bodhisattva mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of wisdom and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

It is not by the arising of the first thought that one realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, nor is it apart from the arising of the first thought that one realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

It is not by the arising of the final thought that one realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, nor is it apart from the arising of the final thought that one realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Rather, as the bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, their roots of goodness gradually increase until they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All bodhisattva mahāsattvas, from the first generation of the mind of awakening, practice the perfection of wisdom, fulfill the ten stages, and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By perfecting which ten stages (*bhūmi*) do bodhisattva mahāsattvas train in and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the stages from the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma, bringing them to fulfillment so as to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; they also study the stages from the Stage of Pure Observation up to the Tathāgata stage, bringing them to fulfillment so as to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

"Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas have diligently practiced and attained perfection in these ten stages, they do not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the initial thought-moment, nor do they realize it apart from the initial thought-moment;

they do not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the final thought-moment, nor do they realize it apart from the final thought-moment. Nevertheless, through diligently practicing and perfecting the ten stages, bodhisattva mahāsattvas realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, the principle of dependent origination taught by the Tathāgata is exceedingly profound; namely, that bodhisattva mahāsattvas do not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through the initial arising of the thought of enlightenment, nor do they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment apart from the initial arising of the thought of enlightenment.”

It is not by means of the final thought-moment that one realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, nor is it apart from the final thought-moment that one realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; rather, as Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, their roots of virtue gradually increase, they fulfill the ten stages, and they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
If a mind has already ceased, can it arise again?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“What do you think? Is a mind that has already arisen subject to the nature of cessation?”
Subhūti replied, “So it is, World-Honored One!”
"If a mind has already arisen, it necessarily possesses the nature of cessation.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?"
“Is there not a mind subject to cessation that is not currently ceasing? Subhūti replied, “No!”
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Subhūti, “What do you think?”
“Does the mind abide as the suchness of the mind? Subhūti replied, “It is so!”
“World-Honored One!
Just as the suchness of the mind is, so does the mind abide.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“What do you think? If the mind abides as suchness, is that mind permanent, like suchness? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“What do you think? Is the suchness of all phenomena profound? Subhūti replied:
"So it is, World-Honored One!
The suchness of all phenomena is exceedingly profound."
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Is that very suchness the mind?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Apart from suchness, is there a mind?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Is the mind itself suchness?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“What do you think? Is there suchness apart from the mind?”
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Is it possible for suchness to see suchness?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice in this way, is he practicing the profound perfection of wisdom?"
Subhūti replied, "So it is, World-Honored One!"
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice in this way, they are practicing the profound perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “What do you think?”
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice in this way, where does he practice? Subhūti replied,
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice in this way, there is no place at all where he practices.”
Why is this so? World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), there is no mind that functions, nor is there any locus for such functioning.
Why is this? World-Honored One!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they abide within *tathatā* (suchness), for therein there is absolutely no manifestation, no locus of manifestation, and no manifestor.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, what is it that he practices?"

Subhūti replied: "When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they practice the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). Within this, both the active manifestation and the locus of manifestation are non-existent, because neither the grasper nor the grasped can be apprehended."
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, although they do not apprehend signs while practicing within ultimate truth, do they nevertheless practice signs?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, does he practice within the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) in order to eliminate signs?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, does he, while practicing within the ultimate truth, eliminate the perception of signs?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, how does he neither dispel signs nor dispel the perception of signs?"
Subhūti replied: "When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, he does not form the thought:
'I shall eliminate signs and eliminate the perception of signs.'"
Nor does he form the thought:
"I shall eliminate the signless and eliminate the perception of the signless," because he is without discrimination in every respect.
World-Honored One!

Although this bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, is thus able to remain free from all conceptual discrimination, because his immeasurable and boundless, preeminent qualities—such as the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered understandings, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—are not yet perfected, he has not yet realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"Bhagavān! This bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes subtle and wondrous skillful means; by virtue of these subtle and wondrous skillful means, they neither establish nor destroy, neither grasp nor reject any phenomena."
Why is this? World-Honored One!
It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have realized that all dharmas are empty of their own intrinsic characteristics.

"Bhagavān! This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the emptiness of the intrinsic characteristics of all phenomena, enters the three samādhis in order to deliver all sentient beings; because he is impelled by the power of his great compassion and vows, he brings sentient beings to maturity by relying on these three concentrations."
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
"It is as you have said.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How does this bodhisattva mahāsattva enter these three samādhis to bring sentient beings to maturity?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the *śūnyatā-samādhi*, sees that many sentient beings are attached to a self and what belongs to a self; by means of skillful power, he teaches and instructs them so that they may dwell securely in the *śūnyatā-samādhi*.”

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the signless samādhi, perceives that sentient beings mostly practice with respect to the signs of phenomena; through the power of skillful means, they instruct and lead them to dwell securely in the signless samādhi.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the samādhi of wishlessness, perceives that sentient beings have many desires and inclinations; through the power of skillful means, he teaches and instructs them so that they may dwell securely in the samādhi of wishlessness.

Subhūti! When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they enter these three samādhis and, according to what is appropriate, bring all sentient beings to maturity through skillful means.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 453. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Chapter 56: Practice in Dreams. Part Two, Chapter Fifty-Six: Practice in Dreams. At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices these three samādhis while in a dream, is there any increase in their profound prajñāpāramitā?"

Subhūti replied, “If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices these three samādhis during the day and thereby gains progress in the profound perfection of wisdom, he will likewise gain progress while practicing them in a dream.”
Why is this? Śāriputra,
because there is no difference between the daytime and the dream state.

Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom during the day, it is called the cultivation of the profound perfection of wisdom; likewise, when that bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in a dream, it is also called the cultivation of the three samādhis of the profound perfection of wisdom, and one should understand that they likewise bring about an increase in the profound perfection of wisdom.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"Do the karmic actions performed by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in a dream result in either increase or decrease?"
The Buddha has taught that conditioned phenomena are illusory and unreal, like things created in a dream; how then can those karmas undergo increase or decrease? Why is this so?

The various karmas created within a dream cannot undergo increase or decrease; it is only when one reaches the waking state and engages in conceptualization and discrimination regarding what was done in the dream that there is either augmentation or diminution.

Subhūti replied: "Suppose there is someone who, having taken the life of another during the day, recalls and conceptualizes that act in a dream at night, feeling deep self-congratulation and joy; or suppose there is another person who, having taken the life of another in a dream, claims it occurred while awake and gives rise to great rejoicing. Regarding these two types of karma, what do you think?"
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

"If neither volition nor karma can arise without an object of perception, and volition and karma only arise when there is an object of perception, then upon what object do the volition and karma in a dream arise?"
Subhūti replied: "Whether in a dream or while awake, mental karma does not arise without an object of perception; it is only when there is an object of perception that mental karma arises."

Why is this? Śāriputra, it is because it is only with respect to phenomena that are seen, heard, sensed, and known that cognitive wisdom functions; from this, either defilement or purification arises.
If there were no seeing, hearing, sensing, or cognizing, then among all phenomena there would be no activity of discerning wisdom, nor would there be defilement or purification.

From this it is known that whether in a dream or while awake, mental volition and karma arise only when there is an object of perception; where there is no object of perception, mental volition and karma do not arise.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"The Buddha has taught that all volitional actions are devoid of intrinsic nature; how, then, can it be said that they arise with an object of perception?"

Subhūti replied: "Although all volitional actions (*cetanā-karman*) and their objective referents (*ālambana-vastu*) are empty of intrinsic nature, because one's own mind grasps signs and engages in conceptual differentiation, it is said that volitional action arises with an objective referent; if there were no objective referent, volitional action would not arise."
Then, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom while dreaming, and dedicates these roots of virtue to all sentient beings in common for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—does that bodhisattva mahāsattva truly dedicate toward the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening?"

Subhūti replied: “The Bodhisattva Maitreya has long ago received the prophecy of non-retrogression regarding unsurpassed bodhi; he is separated from buddhahood by only one birth and is certain to become a Buddha. He is fully capable of answering all difficult questions; it is appropriate for him to be questioned here in this assembly, for the Compassionate Honored One, the Successor to the Throne, will surely provide the answers.”
Then, Śāriputra, as Subhūti had said,
respectfully questioned Maitreya Bodhisattva.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva spoke to Śāriputra, saying:
"What do you mean by 'Maitreya' being able to answer?
Is it form (rūpa)?
Or is it feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), mental formations (saṃskāra), or consciousness (vijñāna)?"
Is it form that is empty?
Is it feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness that is empty?

Furthermore, form cannot answer; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness also cannot answer. The emptiness of form cannot answer; the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness also cannot answer.

Why is this? Śāriputra! I do not perceive any dharma that can answer; I do not perceive any dharma that is answered. I do not perceive the place of answering, the time of answering, nor that by which one answers. I do not perceive any dharma that can predict; I do not perceive any dharma that is predicted. I do not perceive the place of prediction, the time of prediction, nor that by which one predicts.

Why is this so? Because the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is empty; they are utterly non-existent, non-dual, and without distinction, for when thoroughly investigated and analyzed, they cannot be apprehended.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra again addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, saying:
"Virtuous One, is the Dharma you have realized exactly as you have described it?"
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya said:
"The Dharma realized by me is not as it has been described. Why is this?"
"Śāriputra! This Dharma realized by me is ineffable.
At that time, Śāriputra had this thought:

“Maitreya Bodhisattva’s wisdom is profound and vast; having long practiced and perfected all forms of the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, he is able to answer such difficult questions by employing the skillful means of non-apprehension.”
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"What do you think? By means of this dharma, you have realized the fruit of arhatship; do you perceive this dharmic nature as something that can be expressed in words?"
Śāriputra said: “No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"The nature of phenomena realized by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the profound perfection of wisdom is likewise thus; it cannot be expressed in words."
Śāriputra! This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not form this thought:
"By means of this dharma, I have already received the prediction regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
He does not form this thought:
"By means of this dharma, I shall realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Śāriputra!
This bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, does not give rise to doubt, wondering:
"Shall I attain or not attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
They simply form this thought:
"I shall certainly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Śāriputra!

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom and hears this most profound Dharma, their mind is not startled, not terrified, not afraid, does not sink, does not despair, and feels no regret; they know with certainty:
"I shall realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment that I seek, bringing benefit and happiness to sentient beings until the end of the future."
Chapter 57: The Chapter on Vows and Practices, Part Two, Chapter Fifty-Seven. At that time, the Buddha addressed the venerable Subhūti:

"There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) and see sentient beings oppressed by hunger and thirst, their clothing tattered and worn, lacking bedding and requisites, and with all their desired wealth and resources failing to meet their expectations."
Having seen this, he reflects:
"How shall I rescue these classes of sentient beings and cause them to be free from stinginess and greed, so that they lack nothing?"
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:

"I shall practice the perfection of generosity with diligent effort and without regard for anything else; I shall mature sentient beings and purify Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill [the requirements] and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, such that within my Buddha-field there shall be no sentient beings who lack the necessities of life."

Just as the gods from the Realm of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Control over Others' Emanations enjoy various kinds of sublime articles of pleasure, so too shall all sentient beings within my buddha-field enjoy various kinds of sublime articles of pleasure.
"Subhūti! By means of this perfection of giving, these bodhisattva mahāsattvas will swiftly bring it to fulfillment and rapidly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of ethical discipline who see sentient beings whose afflictions are raging, who kill one another, and so forth, even holding wrong views. Due to these causes and conditions, they have short lifespans, many illnesses, haggard countenances, and lack majesty; they are destitute of wealth, born into low-born families, with deficient limbs and bodies, and are base and filthy in their conduct."
Having seen this, he reflects:
"How shall I rescue these classes of sentient beings and cause them to remain far removed from the fruits of their various evil karmas?"
Having reflected thus, he made this vow:

"I shall practice with diligent effort and without regard for anything else, cultivating the perfection of pure ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), maturing sentient beings, and purifying Buddha-fields. May I swiftly fulfill these and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). In my Buddha-field, may there be no sentient beings who experience such fruits of evil karma; may all sentient beings practice the ten virtuous actions and receive superior retributions such as long life."
"Subhūti! By means of this perfection of ethical discipline, these bodhisattva mahāsattvas will swiftly bring it to fulfillment and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of patience who see sentient beings mutually enraged, uttering verbal darts of abuse, insults, and humiliation; they harm one another with swords, staves, and the like, even to the point of taking life, yet do not relinquish their evil intentions.
Having seen this, he reflects:
"How shall I rescue these classes of sentient beings and cause them to remain far removed from such evils?"
Having reflected thus, he made this vow:

"I shall practice with diligent effort and without regard for anything else, cultivating the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), maturing sentient beings, and purifying the Buddha-field, so that I may swiftly fulfill [the requirements] and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, there shall be no such sentient beings characterized by afflictions or evil karma; all sentient beings shall look upon one another as fathers, mothers, brothers, sisters, wives, children, or kinsmen, never being at odds."
"Subhūti! By means of this perfection of patience, these bodhisattva mahāsattvas will swiftly fulfill it and rapidly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of diligence who see sentient beings who are indolent and lazy, lacking diligent effort, having abandoned the three vehicles, and being unable to cultivate the wholesome karmas of humans and devas.
Having seen this, he reflects:
"How shall I rescue these classes of sentient beings and cause them to remain far removed from indolence and laziness?"
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:

"I shall practice with diligent effort and without regard for anything else, cultivating the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*), maturing sentient beings and purifying the Buddha-field, so that I may swiftly fulfill [the requirements] and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, there shall be no such sentient beings who are indolent or lazy; all sentient beings shall be courageous and vigorous, diligently cultivating the causes for the happy realms and the three vehicles, and being born among humans or devas, they shall swiftly realize liberation."
"Subhūti! By means of this perfection of diligence, these bodhisattva mahāsattvas will swiftly bring it to fulfillment and rapidly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā) and see that sentient beings are shrouded by the five hindrances (pañcanīvaraṇa), thereby losing all meditative concentrations, the immeasurables (apramāṇa), and the formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti)."
Having seen this, he reflects: "How shall I rescue these classes of sentient beings and cause them to remain far removed from the hindrances and mental distractions?"
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:

"I shall practice with diligent effort and without regard for anything else, cultivating the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), maturing sentient beings and purifying the Buddha-field, so that I may swiftly fulfill all requirements and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, there shall be no such sentient beings who possess the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) or mental distraction; rather, all sentient beings shall enter and emerge at will into the various subtle and supreme concentrations, such as the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*)."
“Subhūti! By means of this perfection of meditative concentration, these bodhisattva mahāsattvas will swiftly fulfill it and rapidly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom who see that sentient beings are deluded and possess evil wisdom; they have lost both mundane and supramundane right views, deny the existence of good and evil karma as well as the fruits of such karma, and cling to various false dharmas such as nihilism, eternalism, oneness, difference, or both and neither."
Having seen this, he reflects:
"How shall I rescue these classes of sentient beings and cause them to remain far removed from evil views and perverse attachments?"
Having reflected thus, he made this vow:

"I shall practice the *prajñāpāramitā* with diligent effort and without regard for anything else, so as to mature sentient beings and purify Buddha-fields, thereby swiftly fulfilling all requirements and rapidly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, may there be no such sentient beings characterized by evil wisdom or false attachments; may all sentient beings achieve right view and be fully adorned with various kinds of sublime wisdom."
"Subhūti! By means of this perfection of wisdom, these bodhisattva mahāsattvas will swiftly fulfill [the perfections] and rapidly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who,
while fully practicing the six perfections, perceive the distinctions among the three categories of sentient beings."
Having seen this, he reflects:
"By what skillful means shall I rescue and deliver all classes of sentient beings, causing them to leave behind the realms of wrong determination and indeterminate destiny?"
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:

"I shall practice the six perfections with diligent effort, free from all attachment or longing, in order to mature sentient beings and purify the Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill [the requirements] and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, even the names 'wrongly fixed' and 'unfixed' shall not exist; all sentient beings shall abide in right concentration."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes."
“Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see sentient beings fallen into the three evil destinies, undergoing various intense sufferings.
Having seen this, he reflected:
"By what skillful means shall I rescue and deliver them, so that they may forever be free from the suffering of the three evil realms?
Having thus reflected, he made this aspiration:

"I shall apply myself with diligent effort, free from all attachment, to practice the six perfections, ripen sentient beings, and purify the Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill these and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; in my Buddha-field, even the names of the three evil destinies shall not exist, and all sentient beings shall be comprised within the good destinies."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and rapidly realize the knowledge of all aspects."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see that all sentient beings, due to the obstructions of their evil karma, dwell upon a great earth that is uneven with high and low ground, mounds and ravines, foul grasses, stumps, poisonous thorns, and brambles, and is filled with impurities."
Having seen this, he reflected:

"By what skillful means shall I rescue and deliver all classes of sentient beings, causing them to forever eliminate their various karmic obstructions, so that the ground where they dwell is as level as the palm of a hand, free from all foul weeds, stumps, and the like?"
Having reflected thus, he made this vow:

"I shall practice with diligent effort, free from all attachment, the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), maturing sentient beings and purifying Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill [the requirements] and quickly realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, may there be no such various defiled karmas; may the great earth it produces be level and magnificent, abundant in flowers and fruits, and exceedingly delightful."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see that because sentient beings have little merit, the great earth they inhabit lacks all precious gems and consists only of various kinds of soil, stones, tiles, and rubble."
Having seen this, he reflects:
"How may I rescue and deliver these sentient beings who have committed many sins and possess little merit, so that the places where they dwell shall abound in precious treasures?"
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:

"I shall practice the six perfections with diligent effort and without regard for anything else; I shall mature sentient beings and purify Buddha-fields, so that they may quickly reach fulfillment and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, there shall be no such sentient beings who have little merit and much sin; the ground shall be strewn with gold and sand, and everywhere there shall be various wondrous and rare jewels such as lapis lazuli, which sentient beings may enjoy without giving rise to attachment."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and rapidly realize the knowledge of all modes."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see that sentient beings, regarding whatever they have grasped, give rise to much attachment and initiate various kinds of evil and unwholesome karma."
Having seen this, he reflects:
"How shall I rescue and deliver these many sentient beings whom I have gathered, so that they may forever be free from attachment and evil karma?"
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:

"I shall practice the six perfections with diligent effort and without regard for anything else; I shall mature sentient beings and purify Buddha-fields, so that they may swiftly reach fulfillment and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, there shall be no such sentient beings who possess many objects of attachment; all sentient beings therein shall have no objects of attachment regarding forms, sounds, and so forth, and shall not give rise to craving or clinging."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and perceive that sentient beings are distinguished into four classes of high and low status, namely: kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, and so forth."
Having seen this, he reflected:
"By what skillful means shall I rescue and deliver all classes of sentient beings, so that there may be no such distinctions between noble and base?"
Having reflected thus, he made this vow:

"I shall practice the six perfections with diligent effort, free from all attachment, in order to ripen sentient beings and purify Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill these and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, there shall be no such fourfold distinctions of high and low based on physical appearance; all sentient beings shall be of one uniform appearance, and all shall be noble, comprised within the human realm."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and perceive that sentient beings have distinctions of inferior, middling, and superior families.
Having seen this, he reflects:
"By what skillful means shall I rescue and deliver all classes of sentient beings, so that there may be no such distinctions among families—whether inferior, middling, or superior?"
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:

"I shall practice the six perfections with diligent effort and without regard for anything else; I shall bring sentient beings to maturity and purify Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill all requirements and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, there shall be no such distinctions of inferior, middling, or superior families; all sentient beings shall be equally of the highest quality."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and perceive the distinctions in the physical forms and appearances of sentient beings, whether they are handsome or ugly.
Having seen this, he reflected:
"By what skillful means shall I rescue and deliver all classes of sentient beings, so that there may be no such distinctions of physical form between the handsome and the ugly?"
Having reflected thus, he made this vow:

"I shall practice the six perfections with diligent effort and without regard for anything else; I shall mature sentient beings and purify buddha-fields so that I may swiftly fulfill [the requirements] and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. In my buddha-field, there shall be no such distinctions among sentient beings regarding their physical appearance as handsome or ugly; all sentient beings shall be of a true golden color, dignified and exquisite, pleasing to all who behold them, and endowed with the foremost, most perfect, and pure form."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see that sentient beings are bound to a sovereign master, such that they lack autonomy in all their actions."
Having seen this, he reflected:
"By what skillful means shall I rescue and deliver all classes of sentient beings so that they may attain mastery?
Having thus reflected, he made this vow:

"I shall apply myself with diligence and without attachment, practicing the six perfections, maturing sentient beings, and purifying the Buddha-field, so that I may swiftly fulfill all requirements and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, all classes of sentient beings shall be without a sovereign; in all their activities, they shall attain mastery, such that they do not even perceive the form of a sovereign, nor hear the name of a sovereign, except for the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who governs by means of the Dharma and is thus called the Dharma King."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and perceive that sentient beings have various distinctions among the realms of existence, such as the hells and so forth."
Having seen this, he reflects:
"How shall I rescue and deliver these classes of sentient beings, so that there may be no distinctions between the various realms of existence, whether good or evil?"
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:
"I shall practice the six perfections with diligent effort and without regard for anything else;
I shall bring sentient beings to maturity and purify Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill [the requirements] and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
“Ānanda, within my buddha-field there are no distinctions between the various realms of good and evil destinies;
indeed, even the names ‘hell,’ ‘animal realm,’ ‘preta realm,’ ‘asura,’ ‘human,’ and ‘deva’ do not exist.
All sentient beings therein are of one single type and collectively cultivate a single karma, namely, they all harmoniously practice generosity.”
Reaching the perfection of wisdom, they dwell in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature;
they dwell in suchness up to the inconceivable realm; they dwell in the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
they practice the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; and they practice the four dhyānas.

...the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments; practicing the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative concentrations, and the ten totalities; practicing the gateways of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
practicing the gateways of dhāraṇī and samādhi; practicing the five eyes and the six [supernormal powers]...
They cultivate the supernormal powers; they cultivate the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;

they cultivate the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity; they cultivate all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);
they cultivate the conduct of a bodhisattva mahāsattva and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha.
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and perceive the four types of birth among sentient beings, namely: birth from a womb, birth from an egg, birth from moisture, and miraculous birth."
Having seen this, he reflected:
"By what skillful means shall I rescue and deliver them so that there are no longer such distinctions among the four modes of birth?
Having thus reflected, he made this vow:

"I shall apply myself with diligence and without regard for anything else, practicing the six perfections to ripen sentient beings and purify buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill all requirements and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; in my buddha-field, there shall be no such distinctions between the four modes of birth, and all classes of sentient beings shall be born exclusively by transformation."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see that sentient beings lack the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), such that they lack mastery over whatever actions they undertake."
Having seen this, he reflected:
"By what skillful means shall I rescue and deliver them all, so that they may all attain the wisdom of the five supernormal powers?
Having thus reflected, he made this vow:

"I shall apply myself with diligent effort, free from all attachment, practicing the six perfections to ripen sentient beings and purify the Buddha-field, so that I may swiftly fulfill these and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and within my Buddha-field, all classes of sentient beings shall attain mastery over the five supernormal powers and wisdom."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see that sentient beings consume solid food, and that their bodies produce various forms of excrement and urine— pus, blood, and foul impurities so loathsome as to be utterly repulsive."
Having seen this, he reflected:
"How might I rescue and deliver these sentient beings who subsist on morsel food, so that there may be no excrement or filth within their bodies?"
Having reflected thus, he made this vow:

"I shall practice the six perfections with diligent effort and without regard for anything else; I shall bring sentient beings to maturity and purify Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill all requirements and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, all classes of sentient beings shall exclusively partake of the sublime food of the joy of the Dharma; they shall all resemble the gods of the Ābhāsvara Heaven, their internal and external bodies free from all impurities."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see that sentient beings lack physical radiance, such that they must seek external illumination for all their activities.
Having seen this, he reflects:
"By what skillful means shall I rescue and deliver all classes of sentient beings, so that they may be freed from such a body devoid of light?"
Having reflected thus, he made this vow:

"I shall apply myself with diligence and without regard for anything else, practicing the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) to ripen sentient beings and purify Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill them and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and in my Buddha-field, all classes of sentient beings shall possess bodily radiance, needing no external illumination."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and perceive that the lands where sentient beings dwell have days and nights, months and half-months, and that the changes of seasons and years are not constant."
Having seen this, he reflects:
"How shall I rescue and deliver these classes of sentient beings, so that the places where they dwell are free from the transformations of the seasons, such as day and night?"
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:

"I shall practice the six perfections with diligent effort and without regard for anything else, maturing sentient beings and purifying Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill all requirements and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and in my Buddha-field, even the names of 'day,' 'night,' 'month,' 'fortnight,' and other such divisions of time shall not exist."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see that the lifespan of sentient beings is short."
Having seen this, he reflects:
"By what skillful means shall I rescue and deliver all classes of sentient beings, so that they may be freed from such a short lifespan?"
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:

"I shall practice the six perfections with diligent effort and without regard for anything else; I shall bring sentient beings to maturity and purify Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill all requirements and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, the lifespan of all sentient beings shall be so long that its duration in kalpas will be difficult to know."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see that sentient beings lack the primary and secondary marks of physical excellence."
Having seen this, he reflected:
"By what skillful means shall I rescue and deliver all classes of sentient beings so that they may attain the primary and secondary marks?
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:

"I shall apply myself with diligent effort, free from all attachment, practicing the six perfections to mature sentient beings and purify buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill them and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and within my buddha-field, all classes of sentient beings shall have their bodies fully adorned with the primary and secondary marks, such that when sentient beings see them, they give rise to pure and sublime joy."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and quickly realize the knowledge of all aspects."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see that classes of sentient beings are devoid of all roots of virtue."
Having seen this, he reflected:
"How shall I rescue and deliver these classes of sentient beings so that they may be endowed with roots of goodness?
Having thus reflected, he made this vow:

"I shall apply myself with diligence and without regard for anything else, practicing the six perfections to ripen sentient beings and purify Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill them and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
