In my Buddha-field, all classes of sentient beings shall achieve supreme and wondrous roots of goodness; by virtue of these roots of goodness, they will be able to prepare various sublime offerings to honor the Buddhas, and through the power of this merit, wherever they are born, they will further be able to make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones."
“Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see that sentient beings are afflicted by diseases of both body and mind.
There are four types of physical illnesses, namely: wind, heat, phlegm, and various miscellaneous ailments.
There are likewise four types of mental illnesses, namely: greed, hatred, delusion, and the illness of pride, etc.
Having seen this, he reflected:
"How shall I rescue and deliver these sentient beings who suffer from such physical and mental ailments?
Having thus reflected, he made this aspiration:

"I shall apply myself with diligence and without regard for anything else, practicing the six perfections to ripen sentient beings and purify Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill all requirements and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and within my Buddha-field, all classes of sentient beings shall have pure bodies and minds, free from all physical and mental suffering, to the point that even the names 'physical illness' and 'mental illness' do not exist."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and quickly realize the knowledge of all aspects."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and perceive the various inclinations and the distinctions between the three vehicles among sentient beings."
Having seen this, he reflects:

"By what skillful means shall I rescue and deliver all classes of sentient beings, causing them to abandon the inclinations of the two vehicles and lead them exclusively toward the unsurpassed Mahāyāna?"
Having reflected thus, he made this vow:

"I shall practice the six perfections with diligent effort and without attachment, maturing sentient beings and purifying the Buddha-field, so that I may swiftly fulfill [the requirements] and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, all classes of sentient beings shall seek only unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; they shall take no pleasure in the fruits of the vehicles of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, to the point that even the names of the two vehicles do not exist."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see sentient beings giving rise to overweening pride— claiming to have attained what they have not attained, and claiming to have realized what they have not realized."
Having seen this, he reflects:
"How shall I rescue and deliver these classes of sentient beings, causing them to abandon the fetter of overweening pride?"
Having reflected thus, he made this vow:

"I shall practice the six perfections with diligent effort and without regard for anything else; I shall bring sentient beings to maturity and purify Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill all requirements and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, there shall be no such persons of overweening pride, and all sentient beings shall be free from overweening pride."
“Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and perceive that the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have limitations in their radiance, lifespan, and the number of their disciples."
Having seen this, he reflected:
"How may I attain an immeasurable lifespan and a number of disciples that are likewise without limit?
Having thus reflected, he made this aspiration:

"I shall apply myself with diligent effort, free from all attachment, to practice the six perfections, ripen sentient beings, and purify Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill them and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and at that time, may my radiance, lifespan, and the number of my disciples be all without limit."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and perceive the lands where Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas dwell as being finite in circumference."
Having seen this, he reflected:
"How shall I obtain a dwelling land that is immeasurable in its circumference?
Having thus reflected, he made this vow:

"I shall apply myself with diligence and without attachment, practicing the six perfections, maturing sentient beings, and purifying buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill [these requirements] and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. May the great trichiliocosm worlds in each of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, merge into a single field; therein I shall dwell and teach the Dharma, transforming and guiding immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and quickly be able to realize the knowledge of all aspects."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and perceive that the cycle of birth and death for sentient beings is long and far-reaching, and that the realm of sentient beings is infinite in number."
Having seen this, he reflected:

"The limits of birth and death are like space, and the realm of sentient beings is also like space. Although there are no truly existent sentient beings who transmigrate through birth and death or attain liberation, sentient beings falsely cling to them as existing, thus wandering in saṃsāra and undergoing boundless suffering. By what skillful means should I rescue and deliver them?"
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:

"I shall practice the six perfections with diligent effort and without regard for anything else; I shall mature sentient beings and purify buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill [the requirements] and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. For the sake of all sentient beings, I shall preach the unsurpassed Dharma, causing them all to be liberated from the great suffering of birth and death, and leading them to realize and know that both birth and death and liberation are ultimately non-existent and entirely empty."
"Subhūti! By means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes."

Chapter 58: The Gaṅgā Devī. Second Division, Chapter Fifty-eight: The Gaṅgā Devī. At that time, there was a goddess among the assembly named Gaṅgā Devī. She rose from her seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, bared her right shoulder while covering her left, knelt with her right knee on the ground, joined her palms in reverence, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

I shall fully cultivate the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; I shall bring sentient beings to maturity and purify a buddha-field, so that all the characteristics of that purified field are as perfectly complete as those described by the World-Honored One for the great assembly in this profound *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtra.

When the goddess Gaṅgā had spoken these words, she immediately took various golden flowers, silver flowers, and blossoms born of both water and land, along with her own ornaments, and holding a pair of golden celestial robes, she reverently and with a sincere heart scattered them over the Buddha. By the Buddha’s supernatural power, they leaped up into the air and circled to the right; above the Buddha’s crown, they transformed into a precious pavilion with four pillars and four corners, exquisitely adorned and most delightful. Thereupon, the goddess took this root of goodness and, sharing it equally with all sentient beings, dedicated it toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the aspirations of that goddess were profound and vast, immediately smiled. It is the natural law of all Buddhas that when they smile, various colored rays of light issue from their faces; now the Buddha was likewise, emitting various lights—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, purple, azure, and green—from his face, which illuminated the infinite and boundless worlds of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions. These lights returned to this land to manifest great spiritual transformations, circled the Buddha three times, and entered the crown of his head.

At that time, having seen and heard this, Ānanda rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"For what cause and for what reason do you manifest this smile?
The manifestation of a smile by the Buddhas is never without cause or condition.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, saying:
"In the future, this goddess shall become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; the eon shall be named Star-like (Tārakopama), and the Buddha’s name shall be Golden Flower (Suvarṇapuṣpa)."

Ānanda, you should know that this goddess has now received her final female body; once she has cast off this body, she will receive a male body and shall never again be female for as long as the future endures.

After passing away from here, she will be reborn in the most delightful buddha-field of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Akṣobhya in the eastern direction; there, in the presence of that Buddha, she will diligently cultivate the holy life. In that realm, this woman shall be known as Suvarṇapuṣpā, and she will practice the various deeds of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Ānanda, you should know this!

After the Bodhisattva Suvarṇapuṣpa has passed away from the world-system of Akṣobhya Buddha, he will be reborn in other directions, traveling from one buddha-field to another, making offerings, paying homage, showing respect, and praising the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. In every place of birth, he shall never be separated from a Buddha, just as a wheel-turning monarch travels from one terrace-pavilion to another, enjoying pleasures and delights, until the end of his life, his feet never touching the ground.

The Bodhisattva Golden Flower is likewise: from one buddha-field to another, until reaching unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, he shall constantly behold all Buddhas in every birth, perpetually hear the true Dharma, and cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva.
At that time, Ānanda had this thought to himself:

"When the Bodhisattva Golden Flower attains Buddhahood, he too shall proclaim the profound Prajñāpāramitā; the number of the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in that gathering shall be equal to that of the present Buddha’s assembly of Bodhisattvas."
The Buddha, knowing his thought, addressed Ānanda, saying: “So it is! So it is!”

Just as you have conceived, when the Bodhisattva Golden Flower (Kanakavatsa) attains Buddhahood, he too shall proclaim this profound Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of the assembly; the number of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in that assembly shall be equal to the number of the Bodhisattva assembly now present before the Buddha.

Ānanda, you should know that when the Bodhisattva Suvarṇapuṣpa attains Buddhahood, his ordained disciples will be so numerous as to be beyond calculation; they cannot be numbered by hundreds, thousands, or hundreds of thousands, but can only be described collectively as an immeasurable, boundless multitude of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas.
Ānanda, you should know that when the Bodhisattva Suvarṇapuṣpa attains Buddhahood, his land will be free from all such various faults and afflictions as those described in this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
At that time, Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"In what previous Buddha did this goddess first resolve her mind upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, plant various roots of goodness, and dedicate them through aspiration, so that she has now encountered the Buddha, made offerings and paid him respect, and received the prediction of non-retrogression?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"This goddess has already resolved her mind toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment under Dīpaṃkara Buddha; having planted various roots of goodness and dedicated them through making vows, she now encounters me, makes offerings and pays respect, and thus receives the prediction of non-retrogression."
Ānanda, you should know!

In the past, at the feet of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, I scattered five stalks of flowers as an offering and dedicated this toward the aspiration for enlightenment. The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara, knowing that my faculties were mature, bestowed upon me this prophecy:
"In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood; your name shall be Śākyamuni, your realm shall be named Sahā, and your kalpa shall be called Bhadraka."

"When the goddess heard the Buddha bestow upon me the prediction of great bodhi, she leaped for joy and immediately scattered golden flowers over the Buddha. She then gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, planting various roots of goodness and dedicating them toward her vows, saying: 'In a future life, when I shall become a Buddha here as a bodhisattva, may I receive the prediction of great bodhi from that Buddha just as this Buddha has now bestowed it upon me before my very eyes. For this reason, I now bestow the prediction upon her."
At that time, Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had said, was filled with joy and exultation, and again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"This goddess has long planted the roots of all virtues for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; now that they have reached maturity, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has granted her this prediction."
The Buddha told Ānanda: “So it is! So it is!”
"It is as you have said.

This goddess Gaṅgā has long planted the roots of merit for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; now that they have reached maturity, I bestow upon her the prophecy of non-retrogression regarding her quest for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 451. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Chapter Fifty-nine: Cultivating Intimacy. Part Two. Chapter Fifty-nine: Cultivating Intimacy. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One!”
For those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice such profound *prajñāpāramitā*, how do they cultivate and approach emptiness?
How do they enter the *samādhi* of emptiness?
How does one cultivate and approach the signless?
How does one enter the signless samādhi?
How does one cultivate and approach the wishless?
How does one enter the samādhi of wishlessness?
How does one cultivate and draw near to the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path?
How does one practice the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path?
How does one cultivate and associate with the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha?
How does one practice the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice such profound prajñāpāramitā should contemplate that form is empty; they should contemplate that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty.
They should contemplate that the eye-base through to the mind-base is empty, and they should contemplate that the form-base through to the phenomena-base is empty.”
One should contemplate that the eye element up to the mind element is empty; one should contemplate that the form element up to the phenomena element is empty;
one should contemplate that the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element is empty; one should contemplate that eye-contact up to mind-contact is empty;
and one should contemplate the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition up to those produced with mind-contact as condition.
All feelings are empty; one should contemplate the emptiness of the earth element up to the consciousness element;
one should contemplate the emptiness of ignorance up to old age and death; one should contemplate the emptiness of the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
one should contemplate the emptiness of internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature; one should contemplate true suchness...
Up to the emptiness of the inconceivable realm, one should contemplate the emptiness of the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
one should contemplate the emptiness of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
one should contemplate the emptiness of the eight liberations up to the ten totalities; and one should contemplate the emptiness of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path.
One should contemplate the emptiness of the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
one should contemplate the emptiness of the three vehicles and the ten stages of the bodhisattva; one should contemplate the emptiness of the gates of dhāraṇī and the gates of samādhi;

one should contemplate the emptiness of the five eyes and the six supernormal powers; and one should contemplate the emptiness of the ten powers of a Buddha, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
One should contemplate that the emptiness of shared dharmas entails the emptiness of the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs;
one should contemplate the emptiness of the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity;

one should contemplate the emptiness of all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects; and one should contemplate the emptiness of the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
One should contemplate that all practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are empty; one should contemplate that the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas is empty;
one should contemplate that contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena are empty; one should contemplate that mundane and supramundane phenomena are empty;
one should contemplate that conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are empty; and one should contemplate the past...
One should contemplate that phenomena of the future and present are empty; one should contemplate that wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena are empty;
and one should contemplate that phenomena of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm are empty.
"Subhūti! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva performs this contemplation, he does not allow the mind to become distracted.
If the mind is not distracted, he does not perceive dharmas; if he does not perceive dharmas, he does not realize them."
Why is this so? Subhūti!

Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have well studied that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty; since there is no phenomenon to increase and no phenomenon to decrease, they neither perceive nor realize any phenomena.
Why is this so? Subhūti!

Within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) of all phenomena, the one who realizes, that which is realized, the place of realization, the time of realization, and that by which it is realized—whether taken together or separately—cannot be apprehended and cannot be seen.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena without realizing it. World-Honored One!"
"How should bodhisattva-mahāsattvas contemplate the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā) without realizing it?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas contemplate the emptiness of phenomena, they first form this thought:"
"I should contemplate that all characteristics of phenomena are empty, yet I should not realize this as a final attainment.
I contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena for the sake of training, not for the sake of realization; now is the time for training, not the time for realization."

"Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva, while not yet having entered the state of meditative equipoise, binds the mind to the object of focus; once he has entered meditative equipoise, he does not bind the mind to the objective sphere."

“Subhūti! At such a time, this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not regress from the perfection of generosity nor does he realize the exhaustion of outflows; likewise, he does not regress from the perfection of wisdom nor does he realize the exhaustion of outflows.

He does not regress from internal emptiness nor does he realize the exhaustion of outflows; likewise, he does not regress from the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence nor does he realize the exhaustion of outflows.”

They do not regress from true thusness, yet they do not realize the exhaustion of outflows; even so, they do not regress from the inconceivable realm, yet they do not realize the exhaustion of outflows.

They do not regress from the noble truth of suffering, yet they do not realize the exhaustion of outflows; they do not regress from the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path, yet they do not realize the exhaustion of outflows.

They do not regress from the four dhyānas, yet they do not realize the exhaustion of outflows; they do not regress from the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments, yet they do not realize the exhaustion of outflows.

They do not regress from the eight liberations, yet they do not realize the exhaustion of outflows; they do not regress from the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, or the ten totalities, yet they do not realize the exhaustion of outflows;

they do not regress from the four foundations of mindfulness, yet they do not realize the exhaustion of outflows, and so on up to not regressing from the eight branches of the noble path, yet not realizing the exhaustion of outflows;

they do not regress from the liberation door of emptiness, yet they do not realize the exhaustion of outflows; they do not regress from the liberation doors of signlessness and wishlessness, yet they do not realize the exhaustion of outflows.
They do not regress from the three vehicles, yet they do not realize the exhaustion of outflows while on the ten stages of a bodhisattva;
they do not regress from the gates of dhāraṇī or the gates of samādhi, yet they do not realize the exhaustion of outflows;
they do not regress from the five eyes or the six supernormal powers, yet they do not realize the exhaustion of outflows.

They do not realize the exhaustion of outflows while remaining non-regressive in the ten powers of a Buddha, nor do they realize the exhaustion of outflows while remaining non-regressive in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they do not realize the exhaustion of outflows while remaining non-regressive in the marks and signs of physical perfection;
they do not realize the exhaustion of outflows while remaining non-regressive in the quality of non-forgetfulness or the nature of constant equanimity.

They do not regress from omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), yet they do not realize the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
They do not regress from the conduct of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, yet they do not realize the exhaustion of outflows.
They do not regress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), yet they do not realize the exhaustion of outflows.
"Why is this? Subhūti!

Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have accomplished such subtle and wondrous great wisdom, abiding well in the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā) and all aspects of the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma), they constantly maintain this thought:"
"At this time, one should train, but not realize [the fruit]. Subhūti!
This bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, constantly reflects in this way:
"Regarding the perfections from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, at this time I should train in them, but I should not realize them.
Regarding the emptinesses from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, at this time I should train in them, but I should not realize them."
Regarding true thusness up to the inconceivable realm, at this time I should train in them but not realize them.
Regarding the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, at this time I should train in them but not realize them.
Regarding the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments, at this time I should train in them but not realize them.
Regarding the eight liberations up to the ten totalities, at this time I should train in them but not realize them.
Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, at this time I should train in them but not realize them.
Regarding the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—at this time I should train in them but not realize them.
Regarding the three vehicles and the ten stages of the bodhisattva, at this time I should study them but not realize them.
Regarding the doors of dhāraṇī and the doors of samādhi, at this time I should study them but not realize them.
Regarding the five eyes and the six supernormal powers, at this time I should train in them but should not realize them.
Regarding the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, at this time I should train in them but should not realize them.
Regarding the primary and secondary marks, at this time I should train in them but not realize them.
Regarding the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity, at this time I should train in them but not realize them.
Regarding all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), I should now train in them but not realize them.
Regarding all the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, I should now train in them but not realize them.
Regarding the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas, I should now train in it rather than realize it.
For the sake of training in the knowledge of all modes, I should train in the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, becoming skillful in them all without realizing them.

“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, should cultivate familiarity with emptiness, should abide in emptiness, and should practice the samādhi of emptiness, yet he should not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).”
One should associate with the signless, abide in the signless, and practice the signless samādhi, yet one should not realize the limit of reality.
One should cultivate and associate with wishlessness, abide in wishlessness, and practice the samādhi of wishlessness, yet one should not realize the limit of reality.

One should cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness, abide in the four foundations of mindfulness, and practice the four foundations of mindfulness, yet one should not realize the limit of reality.

One should cultivate and associate with the four right efforts up to the eight branches of the noble path; one should abide in the four right efforts up to the eight branches of the noble path; one should practice the four right efforts up to the eight branches of the noble path, yet one should not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).

In this way, up to and including the ten powers of a Buddha, one should cultivate them, one should set out toward them, and one should practice them; yet, one should not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).

One should associate with the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha; one should set out toward the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha; one should cultivate the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, yet one should not realize the limit of reality.

“Subhūti! Although this bodhisattva mahāsattva associates with emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and likewise abides in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and also practices the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, he does not realize the fruit of a stream-enterer, nor does he realize up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.”

Although they cultivate and draw near to the four applications of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path, and although they abide in the four applications of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path, and although they practice the four applications of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path, they do not realize the fruit of stream-entry, nor do they realize the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, one does not fall into the levels of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but swiftly realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"Subhūti! It is like a mighty man, handsome in appearance, majestic, fierce, and courageous, whom all who see him rejoice in; he possesses a superior, perfect, and pure retinue, has mastered the arts of war to their ultimate limit, is skilled in wielding weapons, and remains firm and unshakable. He is adept in all sixty-four skills and eighteen branches of knowledge, and is proficient in every craft and technique. All people admire and revere him, bowing in respect before him; because his undertakings are skillful, he achieves great results with little effort."

Because these people constantly provided him with offerings, respect, honor, and praise without ceasing for even a moment, he at that time felt redoubled joy and exultation, and he congratulated himself before his retinue.

Due to certain causes and conditions, he set out for another region with his parents, wife, children, and retinue; on the way, they passed through a perilous wilderness where there were many fearsome occurrences, such as predatory beasts, bandits, and enemies lying in ambush, so that none among the members of the retinue, whether young or old, failed to be struck with alarm.

Relying on his many skills, his formidable and heroic physique, and his own confident mind, he comforted his parents and kinsmen, saying, "Do not have any anxiety or fear; I shall ensure that you suffer no distress."
By means of his skillful arts, that man led his retinue to a place of safety; having escaped the peril, they enjoyed themselves in joy and happiness.
Yet, throughout the wilderness, the wild beasts and hostile bandits harbored no intention to harm them.
Why is this? Because they rely on their own majesty and prowess, possessing all technical skills and being without fear.
"Subhūti, you should know this!

The bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are likewise in this regard: out of compassion for all classes of sentient beings suffering in saṃsāra, they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; they universally take sentient beings as their object and give rise to the four immeasurables, abiding in a mind conjoined with these four immeasurables, and they courageously cultivate the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, causing them to be swiftly fulfilled.

While these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have not yet perfected these six perfections, they do not realize the exhaustion of outflows in their desire to train for the sake of the knowledge of all aspects; although they abide in the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—they do not turn according to their influence, nor are they led away or deprived by them, and they do not realize those gates of liberation.

Because they do not realize [these stages], they do not fall into the levels of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but will certainly proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Subhūti!

It is like a bird with strong wings that soars through the void, flying freely for a long time without falling; though it sports within the void, it does not rely upon the void, nor is it obstructed by the void.

“Subhūti, you should know that it is likewise for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: although they repeatedly approach, abide in, and cultivate the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—they are able not to realize them therein. Because they do not realize them, they do not fall into the levels of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.”

If they have not yet perfected the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, the quality of non-forgetfulness, the nature of constant dwelling in equanimity, the gateways of dhāraṇī, the gateways of samādhi, all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects, as well as other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas, they will never, by relying on the three samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, realize the exhaustion of outflows.

"Subhūti! It is like a strong man well-versed in the art of archery who, wishing to display his skill, shoots an arrow upward into the air. To prevent the arrow from falling to the ground, he then shoots a subsequent arrow into the notch of the preceding one; in this manner, continuing for a long time, each arrow supports the next so that none of them fall."
If one wishes to cause it to fall, one simply stops the subsequent arrow; at that moment, all the arrows will suddenly drop to the ground.

"Subhūti, you should know that it is the same for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: because they are sustained by skillful means while practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, until their roots of goodness from practicing the path have fully matured, they will never prematurely realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) midway on the journey, even unto unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

When all the roots of goodness cultivated through the practices for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment have fully matured, it is then that the bodhisattva realizes the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and attains unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

Therefore, Subhūti, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the profound perfection of wisdom should examine and contemplate with such thorough discernment the true nature of all phenomena as previously described.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One!

It is truly rare and a most difficult feat that these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to accomplish: although they study the suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, and the reality-limit of all phenomena; although they study that all phenomena are ultimately empty, even down to being empty of their own characteristics; although they study the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; although they study the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; and although they study the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—they do not fall into the stages of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas midway, nor do they ever retreat from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas vow not to abandon sentient beings, they make this aspiration:
'If there are sentient beings who have not yet attained liberation, I shall never relinquish the application of effort I have initiated.'"
"Subhūti! The power of the vows of bodhisattva mahāsattvas is preeminent; they constantly maintain this thought:
'As long as all sentient beings have not yet attained liberation, I shall never abandon them.'"
Because they have given rise to such a vast and great mind, they will certainly not fall back midway.
Subhūti! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constantly maintain this thought:

"I must not abandon any sentient beings, but must certainly bring them to liberation; yet, since these sentient beings practice what is not the Right Dharma, I should repeatedly induce the gates of liberation—serenity, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—in order to deliver them. Although I repeatedly induce them, I shall not realize them as a final attainment."

"Subhūti! Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have accomplished the power of skillful means, although they repeatedly manifest the three doors of liberation, they do not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) in the interim. Until they have attained the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), they must first attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment before they finally realize it."
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas always delight in observing the profound depths.

That is to say, they delight in observing internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, emptiness of dispersion and non-dispersion, essential emptiness, the emptiness of self-characteristics and common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence. They also delight in observing that the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, as well as the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are all empty of their own characteristics."
"Subhūti! Having made this observation, that bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to this thought:

'By the power of evil friends, all classes of sentient beings, throughout the long night, give rise to the grasping at the notion of a self, the grasping at the notion of a sentient being, and so on, up to the grasping at the notions of a knower and a viewer.'"
Due to this grasping at conceptualization, one engages in the pursuit of acquisitions and wanders through birth and death, undergoing various sufferings.

To sever such grasping at conceptualization in sentient beings, one should aspire to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and preach the profound and wondrous Dharma for all sentient beings, so that they may sever their grasping at conceptualization and be freed from the suffering of birth and death.
“Subhūti! At that time, although this bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the gate of liberation of emptiness, he does not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) by relying upon it.
Although he trains in the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness, he does not realize the limit of reality by relying upon them.”

Because they do not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), they do not fall into the fruit of a stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, or arhat; nor do they fall into the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
Subhūti! Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom with such mindfulness, they accomplish roots of goodness without realizing the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
Although they have not yet realized the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), they do not fall away from the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments;

nor do they fall away from the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path. Furthermore, they do not...
They do not fall away from the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities;
nor do they fall away from the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
nor do they fall away from inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature; nor do they fall away from suchness up to the inconceivable realm.
Furthermore, they do not fall away from the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
nor do they fall away from the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
nor do they fall away from the gateways of dhāraṇī or the gateways of samādhi; nor do they fall away from the five eyes or the six supernormal powers.
They do not fall away from the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
nor do they fall away from the quality of non-forgetfulness or the state of constant equanimity;

nor do they fall away from all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); nor do they fall away from any other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas.

"Subhūti! At that time, this bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes all factors conducive to enlightenment, and until he realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, his various merits never decline."

"Subhūti! Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom and is sustained by skillful means, the white dharmas increase in every moment of thought, and his faculties become so sharp and keen that they surpass those of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
"Furthermore, Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly reflects:
'Beings of all kinds, throughout the long night, because they have been taken hold of by evil friends, their minds constantly engage in the three or four inversions.'"

That is to say: the perversion of perception, the perversion of mind, and the perversion of view regarding permanence; the perversion of perception, the perversion of mind, and the perversion of view regarding pleasure; the perversion of perception, the perversion of mind, and the perversion of view regarding self; and the perversion of perception, the perversion of mind, and the perversion of view regarding purity.

"For the sake of such sentient beings as these, I should proceed toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva; when I have realized unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, I shall preach the non-erroneous Dharma for all sentient beings—namely, that birth and death are impermanent, without bliss, without self, and without purity, whereas only nirvāṇa is subtle, tranquil, and endowed with the various true merits of permanence, bliss, self, and purity."

"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes this mindfulness and practices the profound perfection of wisdom, being sustained by skillful means, they will never realize the supreme meditative absorption of a Tathāgata as long as the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas have not yet been perfected."

"Subhūti! Although at that time this bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in and masters the entry into and emergence from the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—he does not immediately realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi). This is because, until his unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, his cultivation of merit through practice has not yet reached full perfection; thus he does not realize the limit of reality or other such merits. Only when he attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment can he then realize this limit of reality and so forth."

"Subhūti! At that time, although this bodhisattva mahāsattva has not yet perfected the cultivation of other virtues, he has already perfected the cultivation of the door of the samādhi of wishlessness."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly reflects thus:
'All classes of sentient beings, throughout the long night, have been influenced by evil associates and thus engage in existence (bhava)..."
What is acquired refers to the grasping at a self or a sentient being, up to the grasping at a knower or a viewer;
or the grasping at form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; or the grasping at the sense-base of the eye, up to the sense-base of the mind;
or the grasping at the sense-field of form, up to the sense-field of phenomena; or the grasping at the eye-element, up to—
Regarding the mind-element (*manodhātu*), one may either cling to the existence of the form-element (*rūpadhātu*) up to the phenomena-element (*dharmadhātu*),

or cling to the existence of the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) up to the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*), or cling to the existence of eye-contact (*cakṣuḥsaṃsparśa*) up to mind-contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*),
or cling to the existence of all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition up to all feelings produced with mind-contact as condition, or cling...
There is the earth element up to the consciousness element; or one may cling to the existence of ignorance up to old age and death;
or one may cling to the existence of the ten paths of wholesome action; or one may cling to the existence of the four dhyānas; or one may cling to the existence of the four immeasurables;
or one may cling to the existence of the four formless attainments; or one may cling to the existence of the four means of attraction.

"For the sake of such sentient beings as these, I should proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, and upon realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, cause all sentient beings to forever sever this grasping at objective existence."

"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes this mindfulness and practices the profound perfection of wisdom, being sustained by skillful means, they will never realize the supreme concentration of a Tathāgata until their ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four unhindered understandings, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas have been fully perfected."

"Subhūti! At that time, although this bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—and enters and emerges from them with mastery, he does not yet realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)."

Until one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, the merit of causal practice has not yet been fully perfected; thus, one does not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) or other virtues. Only when one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening can one then realize this limit of reality and so forth.
Subhūti! At that time, although this bodhisattva mahāsattva has not yet perfected the cultivation of other virtues, he has indeed perfected the cultivation of the gate of the samādhi of emptiness.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly reflects thus:
'Beings, throughout the long night, because they have been taken hold of by evil associates, constantly practice upon signs.'"

That is to say, there are those who grasp at the mark of male, or grasp at the mark of female, or grasp at the mark of form, or grasp at the mark of sound, or grasp at the mark of fragrance, or grasp at the mark of taste, or grasp at the mark of touch, or grasp at the mark of phenomena, or further grasp at various other marks therein. For the sake of such sentient beings, I shall proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, and when I realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, cause all sentient beings to forever sever such attachments to marks.
"Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes this thought:

'Because they are embraced by skillful means while practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, [they will attain] the ten powers of a buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, and other immeasurable and boundless buddha-dharmas.'"
"If these are not yet perfected, one will ultimately never realize the supreme meditative absorption of a Tathāgata. Subhūti!

Although at that time this bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—and enters and emerges from them with mastery, they do not immediately realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Until the causal practices and merits for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment are fully perfected, they do not realize the limit of reality or those other merits.
Only when one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment can one realize this limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and so forth. Subhūti!
At that time, although the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s cultivation of other merits may not yet be perfected, their cultivation of the gate of signless samādhi (*animitta-samādhi*) is already perfected.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva has already well cultivated and studied the perfection of giving up to the perfection of wisdom,
and has already well established themselves in inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature, and..."
They are well-established in suchness up to the inconceivable realm; they are well-established in the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
they have well-practiced and studied the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
they have well-practiced and studied the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; they have well-practiced and studied the four...
They have well practiced and mastered the dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
they have well practiced and mastered the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities;
they have well practiced and mastered the ten stages of practice, the doors of dhāraṇī, and the doors of samādhi. They have well practiced and mastered...
The five eyes and the six supernormal powers; having already well practiced and studied the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
having already well practiced and studied the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity;
having already well practiced and studied all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects; having already well practiced and studied the one...
Subhūti, it is impossible that a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has already well-cultivated and studied all the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva and the unsurpassed,

perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas— having accomplished such merit and wisdom— should conceive a notion of pleasure toward saṃsāra, or speak of there being pleasure, or dwell with attachment within the triple world. It can never be so.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva has already well practiced the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) and the dharmas of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas, they should be questioned as follows:

'If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, how should they train in the factors of enlightenment so as not to realize emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, non-cessation, non-action, the unconditioned, the absence of intrinsic nature, and the reality limit (bhūtakoṭi)? Because they do not realize these, they do not attain the fruit of a stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, or arhat, nor the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; yet they diligently train in the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), always remaining without attachment?'"
“Subhūti! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva is asked such a question, if he should answer:

‘Bodhisattva mahāsattvas who wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should only contemplate emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, non-cessation, non-action, the unconditioned, the absence of intrinsic nature, the reality limit, and all other factors conducive to enlightenment; they should not practice or study [anything else].’”

"Subhūti, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has not yet received from the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the prophecy of non-retrogression regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Why is that? Subhūti!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva has not yet been able to demonstrate, predict, or clarify the characteristics of the dharmas practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva who dwells in the stage of non-retrogression.
"Subhūti! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva receives such a question, if he should answer thus:

'Bodhisattvas mahāsattvas who wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening should correctly contemplate emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, non-cessation, non-activity, the unconditioned, the absence of intrinsic nature, and the limit of reality, as well as all other factors conducive to awakening; furthermore, they should skillfully train in them through the aforementioned expedient means, yet not realize [these states prematurely].'"

"Subhūti, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has already received from the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the prediction of non-retrogression regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Why is this? Subhūti!
This bodhisattva mahāsattva has already been able to reveal, predict, and clarify the characteristics of the dharmas practiced by bodhisattva mahāsattvas who abide in the stage of non-retrogression.

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva has not yet been able to explain, prophesy, or clarify the characteristics of the dharmas practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling on the stage of non-retrogression, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has not yet well cultivated the six pāramitās and all other factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma), has not yet entered the Stage of Thinness (tanubhūmi), and has not yet explained, prophesied, or clarified the characteristics of abiding in non-retrogression as do other bodhisattva mahāsattvas dwelling on the stage of non-retrogression.”

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to reveal, predict, and clarify the characteristics of the dharmas practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva who dwells on the stage of non-retrogression, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has already well cultivated the six perfections and all other factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), has already entered the Stage of Thinness (*tanubhūmi*), and has already revealed, predicted, and clarified the signs of dwelling in non-retrogression just like other bodhisattva mahāsattvas who dwell on the stage of non-retrogression.”
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
is it possible for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has not yet attained the stage of non-retrogression to provide such a true and accurate answer?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, although they have not yet attained the stage of non-retrogression, are nevertheless able to provide such a response as this.
Subhūti!...”

Although this bodhisattva mahāsattva has not yet attained the stage of non-retrogression, they are able to cultivate and train in the six pāramitās and all other factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma). Having attained maturity, their awakening wisdom is sharp and keen; whether they hear it or not, they are able to answer in accordance with reality just like a bodhisattva mahāsattva on the stage of non-retrogression.
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"There are many bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, but few are able to answer correctly as one who abides having already well-cultivated the stage of a non-regressive bodhisattva-mahāsattva, or the stage not yet well-cultivated."
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said. Why is this so? Subhūti!

Few bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have received such a prediction of the subtle wisdom of the stage of non-retrogression; those who have received such a prediction are all able to provide a response to this in accordance with reality.

"Subhūti! If one can answer thus according to reality, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva’s roots of goodness are bright and sharp, and his wisdom is profound and vast; neither gods, humans, nor asuras of the world can lead him astray or deprive him of it."
Chapter 60: On Overweening Pride, Part Two, Chapter Sixty-One of the Second Division. At that time, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, even in a dream, does not take delight in praising the stages of the śrāvaka or the pratyekabuddha, nor gives rise to a mind that delights in praising the phenomena of the triple world; and if they constantly contemplate all phenomena as being like a dream, an echo, an image, a magical illusion, a mirage, a reflection, a transformation, or a city of gandharvas—yet despite observing them in this way, do not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)—you should know that such a bodhisattva possesses the marks of non-retrogression."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, in a dream, sees a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of assemblies in inconceivable number, respectfully attending him as he preaches the Dharma."

Having heard the Dharma, they skillfully understand its meaning and intent; having understood its meaning and intent, they practice with diligence, practicing in accordance with the Dharma, practicing with harmony and respect, and practicing in conformity with the Dharma. One should know that these are the signs of a bodhisattva who is non-retrogressive.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, in a dream, sees a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and fully adorned with the eighty secondary signs, with a constant light extending one fathom radiating all around, leaping up into the air with an immeasurable multitude, manifesting great supernormal powers and preaching the essentials of the True Dharma, and creating emanations who go to other boundless Buddha-fields to perform the work of Buddhas—one should know that this bodhisattva possesses the marks of non-retrogression."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees in a dream mad bandits destroying villages and cities; or sees a fire breaking out and burning down a settlement; or sees lions, tigers, wolves, fierce beasts, venomous snakes, or evil scorpions about to come and harm his body; or sees an enemy wishing to cut off his head; or sees his father, mother, brother, sister, wife, children, or kinsmen on the verge of death; or sees himself afflicted by cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and other such painful conditions.
Seeing such terrifying things as these, they are neither startled nor afraid, nor do they feel distress; having awakened from the dream, they are immediately able to reflect:

"The three realms are not real; they are all like what was seen in a dream. When I realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I shall preach the Dharma of the three realms for the sake of sentient beings, explaining that everything is false and illusory, just like a dream, so that all sentient beings will not give rise to attachment."
"You should know that this bodhisattva possesses the marks of non-retrogression. Furthermore, Subhūti,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, even in a dream, sees sentient beings in the realms of hell, animals, or the hungry ghosts, they then form this thought:"

"I shall diligently cultivate the bodhisattva practices and swiftly proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, such that in my buddha-field there shall not even be the names of the evil destinies of hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts."
Upon waking from the dream, he also thinks thus: "Subhūti,
you should know that when this bodhisattva mahāsattva attains buddhahood, there will certainly be no evil destinies within his buddha-field."

Why is this? Because whether in a dream or while awake, all phenomena are non-dual and cannot be divided into two parts; one should know that this is the mark of a bodhisattva who is non-retrogressive.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while in a dream, sees beings in the hells and other realms being consumed by fire, or sees cities, towns, and villages burning, he then makes this vow:

'If I have already received the prediction of non-retrogression and shall attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may these great fires be instantly extinguished and transformed into coolness.'"
"If this bodhisattva, having made such a vow, sees fire in a dream that is immediately and suddenly extinguished, one should know that he has already received the prediction of non-retrogression.
If this bodhisattva, having made such a vow, sees fire in a dream that is not immediately and suddenly extinguished, one should know that he has not yet received the prediction of non-retrogression."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while awake, sees a great fire suddenly break out, burning various cities or villages, he then forms this thought:

'Whether in a dream or in the waking state, I have previously seen signs of my own non-retrogression, though I have not yet verified their reality. If what I have seen is truly real, may this great fire be immediately and completely extinguished and transformed into coolness. "

If this bodhisattva makes such a vow and utters these words of truthful sincerity, at that moment the great fire will be instantly extinguished; one should know that he has already received the prediction of non-retrogression.
If this bodhisattva makes such a vow and utters these words of truth, yet the fire does not suddenly go out, you should know that they have not yet received the prediction of non-retrogression.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while awake, sees fire burning various cities or villages, he then forms this thought:
"Whether in a dream or in the waking state, I have previously seen the signs of my own non-retrogression."
If what I have perceived is truly real and I shall certainly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may this great fire be instantly extinguished and turn into coolness.

After this bodhisattva-mahāsattva has uttered these words of truthful resolve, the great fire does not immediately go out; rather, it burns one house and then skips over another, burning yet another house or a single lane, skipping over one lane and then burning another lane. As it proceeds in this manner, the fire finally goes out. At that time, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva should know for himself that he has certainly attained the prediction of non-retrogression.

However, as for those who are burned, it is because those sentient beings have created and accumulated karma that destroys the True Dharma; by virtue of this karma, they first fell into the evil destinies and underwent the full fruit of suffering for immeasurable eons. Now, having been born in the human realm, they undergo the remaining retribution of that karma; or else, by virtue of this karma, they are destined to fall into the evil destinies and undergo the full fruit of suffering for immeasurable eons, yet now, while in the human realm, a small portion of that retribution manifests first.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Based on the various causes and conditions previously explained, one knows an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Moreover, there are other practices, tokens, and signs by which an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva may be known; I shall analyze and explain them for you, so listen attentively!"
"Excellent is this profound reflection! Subhūti replied,
"I pray that you will explain it for me."
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees a man or a woman who has been possessed by a non-human spirit and is undergoing various sufferings, unable to escape them, he then forms this thought:”

"If the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas know that I have attained pure intention and have conferred upon me the prediction of non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;

if I have long since generated pure mental attention seeking to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, remaining far removed from the mental attention of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and not seeking to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through the mental attention of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas;

and if I shall certainly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in the future, benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings until the end of the future—[then may these roots of virtue be dedicated to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all sentient beings]."

If there truly exist in the worlds of the ten directions immeasurable Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings—those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who see nothing unseen, know nothing unknown, understand nothing uncomprehended, and realize nothing unrealized; who now directly know, see, and awaken to the differences in the inclinations of all sentient beings—I pray that you will look upon my thoughts and my sincere words.

If I am truly able to cultivate the bodhisattva practices and shall certainly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment to rescue and deliver sentient beings from the suffering of birth and death, may this man or this woman not be troubled or harassed by non-human spirits; at my word, they shall immediately depart.
When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva speaks these words, if that non-human being does not depart, one should know that they have not yet received the prediction of non-retrogression.
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva speaks these words, if that non-human being departs immediately, you should know that they have already received the prediction of non-retrogression.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have not yet skillfully practiced the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
who have not yet skillfully dwelled in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence;
who have not yet skillfully dwelled in suchness up to the inconceivable realm; and who have not yet skillfully dwelled in suffering and its origin...
Regarding the noble truths of cessation and the path, they have not yet well cultivated the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
they have not yet well cultivated the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
they have not yet well cultivated the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities. They have not yet well...
They have practiced the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—but have not yet skillfully mastered the gates of dhāraṇī or the gates of samādhi;
they have not yet entered the bodhisattva’s state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), nor have they fully cultivated all the Buddha-dharmas;
they remain far removed from the bodhisattva’s skillful means and have not yet escaped the influence of evil Māras.
Agitated and distracted, they fail to recognize the various works of Māra;
not measuring for themselves the extent of their own roots of goodness, they merely imitate the bodhisattvas by uttering words of solemn truth, and thus they are deceived and deluded by evil Māras.

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva sees a man or a woman who has been possessed by a non-human spirit and is suffering various afflictions, unable to escape them, they immediately utter a word of solemn truth with ease:

"If I have already received from the Buddhas of the past the prediction of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment as one who is irreversible, then let this man or this woman not be troubled by the non-human spirit; let it depart quickly according to my words."
After this bodhisattva-mahāsattva had spoken these words, at that time the evil Māra, for the sake of deception and delusion, immediately drove away and coerced the non-human beings to depart.
Why is this? Because the power of Māra is superior to that of those non-humans; therefore, at Māra’s command, the non-humans immediately depart.
When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva sees this, he leaps for joy and thinks to himself:
"The non-human has now departed because of my spiritual power! Why is this?
It is because the non-human released this man or woman in accordance with the vow I have made, and for no other reason."

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva is unable to perceive that these are the deeds of Māra; instead, he falsely gives rise to joy, thinking it to be his own power. Relying on this, he treats other bodhisattvas with contempt, saying:

"I have already received from the Buddhas of the past the prediction of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment and shall not fall back; the vows I have made shall not be in vain. You, however, have not yet received the prediction from the Buddhas, so you should not emulate me in making such words of solemn truth; even if you were to set a time limit, it would surely be empty and without fruit."

Because this bodhisattva-mahāsattva has treated other bodhisattvas with contempt and derision, falsely relying on their meager abilities and giving rise to many forms of overweening pride regarding their merits, they distance themselves from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and are unable to realize the knowledge of all modes.

Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas lack the power of skillful means, because they have developed many forms of overweening pride, and because they despise and disparage other bodhisattvas, they fall to the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha despite their diligent application of effort.
Because this bodhisattva-mahāsattva possesses meager merit, all the wholesome deeds he performs and the truthful words he utters give rise to the works of Māra.

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva is unable to draw near to, make offerings to, revere, respect, and praise spiritual friends; he is unable to inquire about and receive instruction on the signs of non-retrogression possessed by bodhisattvas; and he is unable to consult regarding the activities of the various evil māra armies. Due to these causes, his bonds of Māra become increasingly firm and solid.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have not long practiced the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and because they lack skillful means, they are deceived and deluded by Māra, the evil one.

Therefore, Subhūti, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should skillfully recognize the various deeds of Māra; they should not give rise to the pride of overestimation, lest they fall away from the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood that they seek.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 452. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Two, Chapter Sixty on Overweening Pride (Adhimāna), Section Two. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

How should Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have not long practiced the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—up to and including those who are far removed from skillful means—be well-aware when they are deceived and deluded by evil Māras? How should they recognize this?

That is to say, there may be an evil Māra who, for the sake of deception and delusion, employs skillful means to manifest various forms and approaches the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, speaking these words: "Alas!..."
"O son of noble family!
Do you know this for yourself?
The Buddhas of the past have already bestowed upon you the prophecy of great enlightenment; you shall certainly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, never again to regress."
I fully know the names and distinctions of your parents, brothers, sisters, friends, and kinsmen, even down to seven generations.

You were born in such-and-such a direction, such-and-such a country, such-and-such a city, such-and-such a town, and such-and-such a village; you were born under such-and-such a year, such-and-such a month, such-and-such a day, such-and-such a time, and such-and-such a lunar mansion, as a son of a king.
If an evil Māra sees that a bodhisattva is by nature gentle and compliant, with dull faculties, he will falsely declare:
"In your previous lives, the nature of your faculties was already like this."
If he sees that a bodhisattva is by nature firm and strong, with faculties that are clear and sharp, he then falsely predicts:
"In your previous lives, the faculties you were endowed with were also like this."
"If one sees a bodhisattva dwelling in an araṇya, or constantly begging for food, or eating at a single reception,
or eating while seated once, or eating from a single bowl, or dwelling among graves, or dwelling in the open air,
or dwelling beneath a tree, or wearing rag-robes, or possessing only the three robes, or always sitting without lying down."
Or [he may be] like one who uses old bedding; or one who has few desires; or one who is content;

or one who delights in seclusion; or one who possesses right mindfulness; or one who delights in tranquil concentration; or one who possesses sublime wisdom; or one who does not value gain and offerings;
or one who does not prize reputation; or one who prefers frugality and does not anoint his feet; or one who sleeps little.
Or they may be free from agitation, or delight in gentle speech, or prefer few words;
when the evil Māra sees such varied conduct in this bodhisattva, he falsely predicts:
"In previous lives as well, you were just like this."

Why is this so? Because you have now accomplished such and such distinguished merits, which are witnessed by all in the world; it must be that you also possessed these various kinds of merits in previous lives. You should feel profound joy and consolation, and never disparage yourself.

"When that bodhisattva-mahāsattva hears that evil Māra describe his past and future merits, as well as the specific names of his current friends and himself, and further praises his various excellent roots of goodness, he becomes overjoyed and leaps for joy, giving rise to overweening pride; he then treats other bodhisattvas with contempt, slights them, and reviles them."
At that time, Māra, knowing that he was dull-witted and had given rise to overweening pride to despise others, spoke to him again, saying:
"You have certainly accomplished supreme merit; the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past have already bestowed upon you a prophecy."
"You shall certainly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and shall never again fall back; such auspicious signs have already appeared before you.

At that time, an evil Māra, in order to disturb him, may falsely manifest in the form of a bhikṣu, or falsely manifest in the form of a householder, or falsely manifest in the form of a parent, a friend, a relative, a human, or a non-human, and appear before him, shouting aloud: "Excellent!

Great Being, you are indeed able to accomplish such merit; the Buddhas of the past have long ago bestowed upon you the prophecy of great enlightenment, and you are already non-retrogressive regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
Why is this? You possess all the marks of the supreme merit of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas of the stage of non-retrogression; you should hold yourself in high esteem and not give rise to doubt.
When that bodhisattva heard those words, his mind of overweening pride became even more firmly established. “Subhūti!
As I have explained, the practices, tokens, and signs by which a truly non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva is characterized do not exist at all for that bodhisattva mahāsattva.”
"Subhūti, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is possessed by Māra and is tormented by Māra,
such that they lack self-mastery. Why is this so?"

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva has not yet truly attained any of the practices, characteristics, or signs of a non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattva; yet, having merely heard an evil Māra falsely proclaiming such virtues, names, and so forth, they give rise to overweening pride and treat other bodhisattvas with contempt, derision, and abuse.

Therefore, Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should skillfully recognize the deeds of Māra, so as not to be deceived by them and give rise to a mind of arrogance.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are possessed by Māra and harassed by Māra; they give rise to arrogance based merely on their empty reputation.
Why is this? Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva has not yet previously cultivated and studied the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
nor has he previously dwelt in the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature. First...
