Before being established in suchness up to the inconceivable realm; before being established in the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
before having previously practiced the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
before having previously practiced the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; before having previously practiced...
One studies the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality, yet has not previously studied the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
one has not previously studied the stages from the Ground of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma;
one has not previously studied the gates of dhāraṇī or the gates of samādhi; and one has not previously studied the five eyes or the six...
Regarding the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*): first, they have not yet cultivated and studied the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
first, they have not yet cultivated and studied the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣadharma*) or the nature of constant equanimity (*upekṣāsatatvasaṃniviṣṭa*);

first, they have not yet cultivated and studied all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); first, they have not yet cultivated and studied any of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas...
Because of these causes and conditions, Māra gains an opportunity.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva is unable to fully comprehend the characteristics of the four māras; by virtue of this cause and condition, Māra gains an opportunity.
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not fully comprehend form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness;
does not fully comprehend the sense base of the eye up to the sense base of the mind; does not fully comprehend the sense base of forms up to the sense base of phenomena;
does not fully comprehend the eye element up to the mind element; and does not fully comprehend the form element up to the phenomena element."
Not understanding the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element; not understanding eye-contact up to mind-contact;
not understanding the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition;
not understanding the earth element up to the consciousness element; not understanding ignorance...
Until their death, they do not understand the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
they do not understand inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature;
they do not understand suchness up to the inconceivable realm; and they do not understand the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
They do not comprehend the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
they do not comprehend the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; they do not comprehend the eight liberations up to the ten totalities;
they do not comprehend the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; and they do not comprehend the stage of extreme joy.
From the first bhūmi up to the Dharma-cloud bhūmi, they do not fully comprehend the gateways of dhāraṇī or the gateways of samādhi;
they do not fully comprehend the five eyes or the six supernormal powers; they do not fully comprehend the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
and they do not fully comprehend the quality of non-forgetfulness or the nature of constant equanimity.
They understand the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, yet they do not understand omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*),
or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); nor do they understand the true reality of the names of sentient beings and all phenomena,
which is called "signlessness" (*animitta*).
By means of these causes and conditions, Māra gains an opportunity and employs skillful means to manifest various forms, saying to this bodhisattva mahāsattva:

"The practices and vows you have cultivated are now fulfilled; you shall realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. When you attain Buddhahood, you shall obtain such supreme merits and a noble title!"
That is to say, that evil Māra knows this bodhisattva’s long-standing thoughts and aspirations:
"When I attain Buddhahood, I shall obtain such meritorious qualities and a name!
He then prophesies for him according to those thoughts and aspirations.
At that time, because this bodhisattva was far removed from the perfection of wisdom and lacked skillful means, upon hearing the Mara’s prophecy, he thought to himself:
"How marvelous!"
"This person has prophesied for me that I shall attain Buddhahood, including my future meritorious name and title; this accords with the long-standing aspirations I have cherished through the night.

By virtue of this, I know that the Buddhas of the past must have already bestowed upon me the prophecy of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), and that I am certain to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) without ever falling back."
"When I attain Buddhahood, I shall certainly obtain such meritorious and venerable names.

When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva is thus prophesied by an evil Māra, or a member of Māra’s retinue, or a śramaṇa sent by Māra regarding his future name upon attaining Buddhahood, his arrogance increases all the more:
"In the future, I shall certainly become a Buddha and obtain such meritorious names; no other bodhisattvas are my equal."
“Subhūti, you should know this:

regarding the practices, signs, and characteristics of non-regressive bodhisattva mahāsattvas as I have described them, this bodhisattva mahāsattva has not yet accomplished any of them. Yet, having merely heard the empty fame of attaining buddhahood spoken by Māra, he immediately gives rise to arrogance and treats other bodhisattva mahāsattvas with contempt, mockery, and derision.”

Subhūti, you should know that because this bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to pride and treats other bodhisattva mahāsattvas with contempt, derision, and disdain, he distances himself from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"Subhūti, you should know that because this bodhisattva mahāsattva is far removed from the perfection of wisdom, lacks skillful means, abandons virtuous friends, and is constantly influenced by evil associates, he will fall to the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha."

"Subhūti, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva may regain right mindfulness regarding this body, sincerely repent, abandon the mind of arrogance, and repeatedly draw near to true, supreme, and virtuous friends."

Although they may wander through birth and death for a long time, they will later rely once more upon the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) to train progressively, and shall realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

"Subhūti, you should know that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses such a body yet fails to attain right mindfulness, is unable to repent their transgressions, does not relinquish a mind of pride, and does not delight in associating with true, supreme, and virtuous friends, they will certainly wander through saṃsāra for a long time. Even if they later apply themselves with diligence to cultivate various wholesome deeds, they will fall to the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha."

For example, just as a bhikṣu seeking the state of a śrāvaka who commits even one of the four grave offenses (pārājika) is no longer a śramaṇa nor a son of the Śākya; he is certainly unable to attain the four fruits of śramaṇaship in the present life.

It is the same with those who falsely cling to the empty title of "Bodhisattva": merely hearing the demonic discourse regarding the hollow name of "attaining Buddhahood," they give rise to arrogance and treat other Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas with contempt and derision. You should know that this transgression is infinitely many times greater than the four grave offenses (pārājika) committed by that bhikṣu; setting aside the four grave offenses of that bhikṣu, this bodhisattva’s transgression is also infinitely many times greater than the five deeds of immediate retribution (ānantarya).

Why is this? It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have not actually accomplished any superior merit; yet, upon hearing the evil Māra proclaim their empty reputation for attaining Buddhahood, they become conceited and look down upon other bodhisattvas. Therefore, this transgression exceeds even the five ānantarya crimes.

From this it should be understood that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should skillfully recognize such subtle demonic activities as the recording of false names and titles, and diligently seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the conduct of seclusion; that is to say, they dwell in mountain forests, empty marshes, or vast wildernesses, residing in *āraṇyakas* to sit in meditation and engage in contemplation."
At that time, an evil Māra came to where he was, paid him respectful homage and praise, and spoke these words: "Excellent,
O Great Being!"
One is able to cultivate such a practice of true seclusion.

This practice of seclusion is praised by all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; it is protected, honored, and revered by Śakra, Lord of Devas, and all other celestial beings and ṛṣis. You should dwell constantly here and not go elsewhere.
"Subhūti, you should know this:
I do not praise those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who dwell in forest hermitages, wildernesses, or mountain groves, sitting in meditation and contemplating while practicing the conduct of seclusion."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,

what other practices of seclusion should bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate, such that the Buddha does not praise dwelling in araṇyas, wildernesses, or mountain forests, nor the merit of abandoning superior bedding and seats for the sake of meditative reflection and solitary seclusion?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Whether Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell in mountain forests, empty marshes, wilderness *āraṇya* hermitages, or reside in the clamorous places of cities, villages, and royal capitals, as long as they can remain far removed from afflictions, evil karma, and the mental orientations of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and diligently cultivate the *prajñāpāramitā* along with other sublime virtues, this is called the true practice of seclusion for a Bodhisattva."

This practice of seclusion is praised by all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and is authorized by all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. It is that which the assembly of Bodhisattvas should constantly study and train in; whether by day or by night, they should correctly contemplate and diligently practice this dharma of seclusion. This is called a Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the practice of seclusion.

This practice of seclusion is unmixed with the mental orientations of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and is unmixed with any afflictions or unwholesome karma; free from all clamor and distraction, it is ultimately pure, causing bodhisattvas to swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and bringing benefit and happiness to sentient beings without ever ceasing.

To praise, as the Māra does, dwelling in seclusion within mountain forests, empty marshes, vast wildernesses, or *āraṇya* hermitages, abandoning superior bedding and seats to practice meditative contemplation—this is not the true practice of detachment for Bodhisattvas.

Why is this? Because even that practice of seclusion may still involve distraction; that is to say, it may be mixed with evil karma and afflictions, or mixed with the mental orientations of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Consequently, one cannot diligently believe in, accept, and train in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and thus cannot fulfill the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*).

“Subhūti, you should know that there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, though they delight in practicing the dharmas of seclusion praised by Māra, give rise to a conceited and impure mind, and thus despise and revile other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.”

This refers to those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, although residing in cities, villages, or royal capitals, maintain a pure mind unmixed with various afflictions, evil karmas, or the mental orientations of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
they diligently practice and study the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom. They...
They diligently abide in inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence;
they diligently abide in suchness up to the inconceivable realm; they diligently abide in the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
they diligently train in the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; and they diligently train in the four dhyānas.
They diligently cultivate and study worldly virtues such as the [four] applications of mindfulness, the four immeasurables, the four formless absorptions, and the five supernormal powers;
they diligently cultivate and study the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
they diligently cultivate and study the ten stages of a bodhisattva; and they diligently cultivate and study the gates of dhāraṇī and the gates of samādhi.
They diligently train in the five eyes and the six supernormal powers; they diligently train in the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality;
they diligently train in the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they diligently train in the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity; and they diligently train in all-knowledge.
The knowledge of the paths, the knowledge of all aspects, the purification of Buddha-fields, and the maturation of sentient beings;
though dwelling amidst the clamor of the world, their minds remain tranquil, and they constantly and diligently cultivate the practice of true seclusion.

"Subhūti, you should know that toward such a community of truly pure bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, his mind is constantly arrogant; he treats them with contempt and derision, slandering and insulting them."

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva is far removed from the perfection of wisdom and lacks skillful means, even though they dwell in a wilderness extending for a hundred yojanas that is utterly devoid of all predatory beasts, snakes, scorpions, and bandits, there are only spirits, rākṣasas, and the like who roam and dwell therein.

Dwelling in such a forest hermitage, even if they spend one year, or five, or ten, or even up to hundreds of thousands of koṭis of years practicing the conduct of seclusion, if they exceed this number yet do not understand true seclusion, [they have not attained it].

This refers to those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, although dwelling amidst the clamor and bustle of the world, maintain mental tranquility; they remain far removed from various afflictions, evil karma, and the mental orientations of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and instead set out toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"Subhūti, you should know that although these bodhisattvas dwell in the wilderness for a long time, they harbor the mental orientations of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; they develop a deep attachment to those two stages, cultivate practices of seclusion based on the dharmas of those two stages, and furthermore, they become deeply immersed in and addicted to such practices."
"Subhūti, you should know that although they practice such conduct of seclusion, it does not accord with the minds of the Tathāgatas.
Subhūti, you should know this!"

The true practice of seclusion that I praise for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is one that these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not accomplish at all; furthermore, within that truly supreme practice of seclusion, they do not perceive even a semblance of such conduct.

Why is this? It is because they do not give rise to love or joy for the true practice of seclusion of a bodhisattva, but instead take pleasure only in diligently cultivating the empty practices of seclusion of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
"Subhūti, you should know that when these bodhisattvas practice the supreme conduct of detachment that is not genuine, Māra will come through the air, joyfully praising them and saying:
'O Great Being!'"
Excellent! Excellent!
You are able to diligently cultivate the practice of true seclusion; this practice of seclusion is praised by all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
"If you apply yourself with diligence to this practice, you will swiftly realize the knowledge of all-knowledge.

Subhūti, you should know that these bodhisattvas, being attached to such practices of seclusion cultivated by those of the two vehicles, treat with contempt and derision those bhikṣus who abide in the vehicle of the bodhisattva, remaining in the midst of bustle yet possessing a tranquil mind. They say of them: "They cannot cultivate the practice of seclusion; though their bodies dwell in bustle, their minds are not tranquil, and they lack the qualities of discipline."

“Subhūti, you should know that these bodhisattvas despise and revile those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who dwell in genuine seclusion as praised by the Buddha, saying: ‘They dwell in clamor and their minds are not tranquil; they are unable to diligently cultivate the practice of genuine seclusion.

Yet they honor and praise those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas whom the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas do not commend for dwelling in genuine clamor, saying: ‘They are not distracted; their minds are tranquil, and they are able to correctly practice the conduct of genuine seclusion.’”

Subhūti, you should know that these bodhisattvas do not approach, revere, or make offerings to those who should be approached, revered, and made offerings to— just as one does to the Buddhas— but instead treat them with contempt and disparagement; conversely, they do approach, revere,
and make offerings to those who should be shunned and not approached or venerated— such as evil associates— treating them as if they were serving the Buddhas themselves.

"Subhūti, you should know that because these bodhisattvas are far removed from the perfection of wisdom and lack skillful means, they falsely give rise to various kinds of conceptualization and attachment."
Why is this? He thinks to himself:
"The practice I am cultivating is true seclusion; therefore, non-human beings praise and protect me."
"Those who dwell in cities and towns have their bodies and minds disturbed; who would protect, mindfully regard, revere, or praise them?

Due to these causes and conditions, the minds of these bodhisattvas become largely arrogant; they look down upon, despise, and disparage the other assemblies of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and their afflictions and evil karma increase day and night.
"Subhūti, you should know that these bodhisattvas act as outcasts (*caṇḍāla*) toward the assembly of other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and defile the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."

Although they appear to possess the marks of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, they are great thieves among gods and humans, deceiving and deluding gods, humans, asuras, and others; for while their bodies wear the dharma robes of a śramaṇa, their minds constantly harbor the intentions of a thief.
Those who have set out upon the bodhisattva vehicle should not associate with, pay homage to, make offerings to, honor, or praise such evil persons. Why is this?
You should know that such a person harbors overweening pride; outwardly appearing to be a bodhisattva, they are inwardly full of afflictions.

Therefore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva truly does not abandon the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), does not abandon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), and with a profound mind desires to seek the knowledge of all modes and realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, they should not associate with, pay homage to, make offerings to, revere, or praise such an evil person.

“Subhūti, you should know that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should constantly and diligently cultivate their own task: to remain far removed from birth and death, not to be attached to the triple world, and to constantly give rise to loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity toward those wicked, murderous outcastes. They should form this thought:

‘I must not give rise to the faults that those evil persons give rise to; even if I should momentarily lose mindfulness and such thoughts arise as they do, I shall immediately recognize them and swiftly eliminate them.’”

Therefore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should skillfully recognize the deeds of Māra; they should apply themselves with diligent vigor to distance themselves from and eliminate such faults as those arising in those bodhisattvas, and should zealously seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with superior mental attention, desires to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should constantly draw near to, revere, make offerings to, honor, and praise true spiritual friends."
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Who are those who are called the true spiritual friends of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are the true spiritual friends of bodhisattvas; all the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are likewise the true spiritual friends of bodhisattvas."

Furthermore, any śrāvakas or other virtuous persons who are able to proclaim, reveal, analyze, and clarify for the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas the meanings and principles associated with the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, making them easy to understand, are also the true spiritual friends of a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
The perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom are the true spiritual friends of bodhisattvas;
the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path are also the true spiritual friends of bodhisattvas."
The four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments are also the bodhisattva’s true spiritual friends;
the eight liberations up to the ten totalities are also the bodhisattva’s true spiritual friends;
the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are also the bodhisattva’s true spiritual friends; and the stage of extreme joy...
The stages from the Ground (Bhūmi) up to the Cloud of Dharma (Dharmameghā) are also the true spiritual friends of a bodhisattva;

the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi are also the true spiritual friends of a bodhisattva; the five eyes and the six supernormal powers are also the true spiritual friends of a bodhisattva;
and the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are also [the true spiritual friends of a bodhisattva].
Furthermore, the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣadharma*) and the state of constant abiding in equanimity (*upekṣā*) are also the true spiritual friends of a bodhisattva;
omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are also the true spiritual friends of a bodhisattva;
and all the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva (*bodhisattvacaryā*) are also the [true spiritual friends] of a bodhisattva.
True spiritual friends: the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is also a true spiritual friend for a bodhisattva;
the permanent severance of the continuity of all habitual tendencies is also a true spiritual friend for a bodhisattva.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! The noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path are the true spiritual friends of bodhisattvas; the causal nature of all phenomena is also a true spiritual friend of bodhisattvas; the members of dependent origination are also true spiritual friends of bodhisattvas; the emptiness of the internal, up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, are also true spiritual friends of bodhisattvas; and suchness, up to the inconceivable realm, are also true spiritual friends of bodhisattvas."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

The perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom serve as teachers and guides for the bodhisattva mahāsattvas; they serve as illumination and torches, as lamps and lights, as understanding and awakening, as knowledge and wisdom, as rescuers and protectors, as shelters and dwellings, as islands and continents, as refuges and destinations, and as fathers and mothers."

The four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path likewise serve as teachers and guides for the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas; they serve as illumination and torches, as lamps and lights, as liberation and awakening, as knowledge and wisdom, as rescue and protection, as a house and a dwelling, as an island and a shore, as a refuge and a destination, and as fathers and mothers.

The four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments likewise serve as teachers and guides for the bodhisattva mahāsattvas; they serve as illumination and torches, as lamps and lights, as understanding and awakening, as knowledge and wisdom, as rescuers and protectors, as shelters and dwellings, as islands and peninsulas, as refuges and destinations, and as fathers and mothers.

The eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality also serve as teachers and guides for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; they serve as illumination, as torches, as lamps, and as lights; they serve as liberation, as awakening, as knowledge, and as wisdom; they serve as rescue and protection, as a shelter and a dwelling, as an island and a promontory, as a refuge and a destination, and as father and mother.

“The gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—also serve as teachers and guides for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; they are a light, a torch, a lamp, and an illumination; they are a release, an awakening, knowledge, and wisdom; they are a rescue, a protection, a shelter, and a dwelling; they are an island, a peninsula, a refuge, and a destination; they are a father and a mother.”

From the Stage of Utmost Joy up to the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma, they likewise serve as teachers and guides for the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; they serve as illumination and torches, as lamps and lights, as understanding and awakening, as knowledge and wisdom, as saviors and protectors, as shelters and dwellings, as islands and peninsulas, as refuges and destinations, and as fathers and mothers.

The gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi likewise serve as teachers and guides for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; they are the illumination and the torch, the lamp and the light, the liberation and the awakening, the knowledge and the wisdom, the rescue and the protection, the shelter and the dwelling, the island and the promontory, the refuge and the destination, and the father and the mother.

The five eyes and six supernormal powers likewise serve as teachers and guides for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; they serve as illumination and torches, as lamps and lights, as liberation and awakening, as knowledge and wisdom, as rescue and protection, as a shelter and a home, as an island and a peninsula, as a refuge and a destination, and as fathers and mothers.

The Tathāgata’s ten powers, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, likewise serve as teachers and guides for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; they are the light, the torch, the lamp, and the illumination; they are the liberation, the awakening, the knowledge, and the wisdom; they are the rescue, the protection, the shelter, and the dwelling; they are the island, the peninsula, the refuge, and the destination; they are the father and the mother.

The quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity likewise serve as teachers and guides for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; they serve as illumination and torches, as lamps and lights, as understanding and awakening, as knowledge and wisdom, as rescuers and protectors, as shelters and dwellings, as islands and peninsulas, as refuges and destinations, and as fathers and mothers.

All-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) likewise serve as teachers and guides for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; they are the illumination, the torch, the lamp, and the light; they are the liberation, the awakening, the wisdom, and the insight; they are the rescue, the protection, the shelter, and the dwelling; they are the island, the peninsula, the refuge, and the destination; they are the father and the mother.

All the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas likewise serve as teachers and guides for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; they serve as illumination and torches, as lamps and lights, as understanding and awakening, as knowledge and wisdom, as rescuers and protectors, as shelters and dwellings, as islands and peninsulas, as refuges and destinations, and as fathers and mothers.

The unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas likewise serves as the teacher and guide for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; it is their illumination and torch, their lamp and light, their liberation and awakening, their knowledge and wisdom, their rescue and protection, their shelter and home, their island and promontory, their refuge and destination, and their father and mother.

Having forever severed all continuities of habitual tendencies, he also serves as the teacher and guide for the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; he is their illumination and torch, their lamp and light, their liberation and awakening, their wisdom and insight, their savior and protector, their shelter and dwelling, their island and promontory, their refuge and destination, and their father and mother.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

The noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path also serve as teachers and guides for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; they serve as illumination and torches, as lamps and lights, as understanding and awakening, as knowledge and wisdom, as rescuers and protectors, as shelters and dwellings, as islands and peninsulas, as refuges and destinations, and as fathers and mothers."

The nature of conditions of all phenomena and the factors of dependent origination also serve as teachers and guides for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; they serve as illumination and torches, as lamps and lights, as understanding and awakening, as knowledge and wisdom, as rescuers and protectors, as shelters and dwellings, as islands and peninsulas, as refuges and destinations, and as fathers and mothers.

From internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the nature of non-existence, these also serve as teachers and guides for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; they serve as illumination, as torches, as lamps, and as lights; as liberation, as awakening, as knowledge, and as wisdom; as rescuers and protectors; as houses and dwellings; as islands and continents; as refuges and destinations; and as fathers and mothers.

From suchness up to the inconceivable realm, they likewise serve as teachers and guides for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; they serve as illumination and torches, as lamps and lights, as understanding and awakening, as knowledge and wisdom, as rescuers and protectors, as shelters and dwellings, as islands and peninsulas, as refuges and destinations, and as fathers and mothers.

Why is this? Because all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present, have all taken the perfection of giving—and so forth, up to the inconceivable realm—as their teacher and guide, as their illumination and torch, as their lamp and light, as their liberation and awakening, as their wisdom and insight, as their savior and protector, as their house and dwelling, as their island and continent, as their refuge and destination, and as their father and mother.
Why is this? Subhūti!
Because all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present, are born from the perfection of giving, and so on, up to the inconceivable realm.
"Therefore, Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva,
with a resolute intention (*adhyāśaya-manasikāra*), desires to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
to bring sentient beings to maturity, and to purify the Buddha-field, they should train in the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) up to [the perfection of wisdom]."
If one is a *pāramitā*, one should study the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
one should study the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; one should study the eight liberations up to the ten totalities;
one should study the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; and one should study the ultimate...
From the Ground of Joy up to the Ground of Dharma Clouds, one should study the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi;
one should study the five eyes and the six supernormal powers; one should study the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
one should study the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity; one should study all [of these].
One should study the knowledge of paths, the knowledge of all aspects, and all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
one should study the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas; one should study the permanent severance of the continuity of all habitual tendencies;
one should study the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; and one should study all phenomena.
Regarding the nature of conditions and the factors of dependent origination, one should study inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence;
one should study suchness up to the inconceivable realm.

“Subhūti! Having trained in the perfection of giving, and so forth, up to the inconceivable realm, this bodhisattva mahāsattva should further gather all sentient beings by means of the four articles of attraction.”
What are the four? First, generosity;
second, pleasant speech.
Third is beneficial conduct;
fourth is cooperation. Subhūti!

It is with reference to this meaning that I have made this statement: all the perfections of giving, and so forth up to the inconceivable realm, serve as teachers and guides for the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and so forth up to serving as fathers and mothers.

Therefore, Subhūti, bodhisattva mahāsattvas who wish not to act according to the words of others, who wish not to abide by the words of others, who wish to sever the doubts of all sentient beings, who wish to fulfill the aspirations of all sentient beings, who wish to purify buddha-fields, and who wish to bring sentient beings to maturity, should study the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Subhūti!

Within this profound *prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, the dharmas that the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should study are extensively explained; all members of the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should diligently practice and study therein.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what are the characteristics of the profound Prajñāpāramitā?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"The profound perfection of wisdom has space as its characteristic, non-attachment as its characteristic, and signlessness as its characteristic."
Why is this so? Subhūti!
Within this profound characteristic of the perfection of wisdom, all phenomena and all characteristics are non-existent and cannot be apprehended.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Is there any basis for saying that the sublime characteristics possessed by the Prajñāpāramitā are also the characteristics possessed by all phenomena?”
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.
Because there are causes and conditions, one may speak of the sublime characteristics possessed by the *prajñāpāramitā*; all phenomena likewise possess such sublime characteristics.
Why is this? Subhūti!
The profound perfection of wisdom has detachment as its characteristic, and all phenomena likewise have detachment as their characteristic.

The profound *prajñāpāramitā* has the characteristic of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), and all phenomena likewise have the characteristic of the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
For this reason, it can be said:
whatever sublime characteristics the profound *prajñāpāramitā* possesses, all phenomena likewise possess such sublime characteristics.
"Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature and devoid of all marks.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature and far removed from all marks, then all phenomena are empty of all phenomena, and all phenomena are devoid of all phenomena; how then are sentient beings designated as defiled or pure?"
It is not that phenomena which are empty of intrinsic nature have defilement or purification, nor is it that there is defilement or purification apart from phenomena;

it is not that phenomena which are empty of intrinsic nature can realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, nor can anything apart from phenomena realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
it is not that a phenomenon can be apprehended within emptiness of intrinsic nature, nor can a phenomenon be apprehended apart from it.

It is not within the emptiness of intrinsic nature that a bodhisattva mahāsattva realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; nor is it apart from [intrinsic nature] that a bodhisattva mahāsattva realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
“World-Honored One!
How may I understand the profound meaning and intent of what the Buddha has spoken?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“What do you think? For a long night, have sentient beings harbored the notions of ‘I’ and ‘mine,’ and have they been mentally attached to ‘I’ and ‘mine’? Subhūti replied:
"So it is, World-Honored One! For a long night,
sentient beings have held to the notions of 'I' and 'mine,' and their minds have been attached to 'I' and 'mine.'"
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “What do you think?
Are the ‘self’ and ‘what belongs to the self’ grasped by sentient beings empty and detached?”
Subhūti replied, “So it is, World-Honored One!”
“The self and what belongs to the self, as clung to by sentient beings, are all empty and remote.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “What do you think?”
"Is it not the case that sentient beings wander through birth and death due to their grasping at 'I' and 'mine'? Subhūti replied, "It is so!"
“World-Honored One!
All classes of sentient beings wander through birth and death due to their grasping at a self and what belongs to a self.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"In this way, sentient beings rush through birth and death due to affliction; therefore, one designates sentient beings as having affliction.
If sentient beings were without mental attachment to 'I' and 'mine,' there would be no affliction. If there were no affliction, they could not rush through birth and death."

Since the rushing flow of birth and death cannot be apprehended, one should know that sentient beings are far removed from defilement; it is by virtue of the absence of defilement that "sentient beings" are conventionally designated. Therefore, Subhūti!
"One should know that although sentient beings are empty of intrinsic nature and devoid of all marks, they can nevertheless be designated as being defiled or purified.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to practice this profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and the emptiness and signless nature of all phenomena, then that bodhisattva mahāsattva does not practice with respect to form (*rūpa*), nor does he practice with respect to feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*);
he does not practice with respect to the sense-base of the eye (*cakṣur-āyatana*), nor does he practice with respect to the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind;

he does not practice with respect to the sense-base of forms (*rūpa-āyatana*), nor does he practice with respect to the sense-bases of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects (*dharma-āyatana*).
They do not engage with the eye element, nor do they engage with the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind elements;
they do not engage with the form element, nor do they engage with the sound, odor, taste, tangible, or mental-object elements;
they do not engage with the eye-consciousness element, nor do they engage with the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-consciousness elements.
One does not engage in eye-contact, nor does one engage in ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact;

one does not engage in the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, nor does one engage in the various feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as condition;
one does not engage in the earth element, nor does one engage in the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements.

They do not engage with the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), nor do they engage with the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), or the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*);

they do not engage with ignorance (*avidyā*), nor do they engage with volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), becoming (*bhava*), birth (*jāti*), or aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*);

they do not engage with the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*), nor do they engage with the perfections of ethical discipline (*śīla*), patience (*kṣānti*), diligence (*vīrya*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), or wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).

They do not practice inner emptiness, nor do they practice outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, the emptiness of dispersion and non-dispersion, essential emptiness, the emptiness of self-characteristics and common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, or the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence;

they do not practice suchness, nor do they practice the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-falsity, non-alteration, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, or the inconceivable realm;
they do not practice the noble truth of suffering, nor do they practice the noble truths of origin, cessation, or the path.

They do not practice the four foundations of mindfulness, nor do they practice the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path;
they do not practice the four dhyānas, nor do they practice the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments;
they do not practice the eight liberations, nor do they practice the eight spheres of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities.
They do not practice the gate of liberation of emptiness, nor do they practice the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness;

they do not practice the stage of pure observation, nor do they practice the stage of the spiritual lineage, the eighth stage, the stage of having seen, the stage of refinement, the stage of freedom from desire, the stage of completion, the stage of the solitary realizer, the stage of the bodhisattva, or the stage of the Tathāgata;

they do not practice the stage of extreme joy, nor do they practice the stage of freedom from stain, the stage of radiant light, the stage of blazing wisdom, the stage of extreme difficulty to conquer, the stage of presence, the stage of far-reaching, the stage of immovability, the stage of excellent intelligence, or the stage of the cloud of dharma.
They do not practice any of the gateways of dhāraṇī, nor do they practice any of the gateways of samādhi;
they do not practice the five eyes, nor do they practice the six supernormal powers;

they do not practice the ten powers of a Buddha, nor do they practice the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
One does not practice the quality of non-forgetfulness, nor does one practice the state of constant equanimity;
one does not practice the fruit of stream-entry, nor does one practice the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, or pratyekabuddha-enlightenment;
one does not practice all-knowledge, nor does one practice the knowledge of the paths or the knowledge of all aspects.
Why is this? Because these dharmas—the one who practices, that which is practiced, that by means of which one practices, the time of practice, and the place of practice—are all unapprehendable.
"World-Honored One! [he said.]
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice in this way, they cannot be overcome by any in the world—whether devas, humans, or asuras—but rather they are able to overcome them.
"Bhagavān! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice in this way, they will not be overcome by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but will rather be able to overcome them."
Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have already attained abiding in the state that cannot be overcome—namely, the bodhisattva’s stage of separation from birth.
World-Honored One!
This bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly dwells in the mental engagement of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) and cannot be overcome.
World-Honored One!
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way, they draw near to the knowledge of all modes and will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Buddha said, “So it is, Subhūti!”
It is so! It is as you have said.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice this profound perfection of wisdom and the emptiness and signless detachment of all dharmas, that bodhisattva mahāsattva does not practice form, nor does he practice feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
This extends even to not practicing all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), nor practicing the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Thus, the one who practices, that which is practiced, that by which one practices, the time of practice, and the locus of practice—all these phenomena are unapprehendable.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice in this way, they will not be overcome by any in the world—whether devas, humans, or asuras—nor will they be overcome by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; rather, they will be able to overcome them.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva has already attained abiding in the invincible stage—namely, the bodhisattva’s stage of separation from birth—which means they constantly abide in the mental engagement of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) and cannot be overcome; thus, they are close to the knowledge of all modes and will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 453. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Two, Chapter Sixty on Overweening Pride (Abhimāna), Section Three. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
What do you think?

Suppose all sentient beings in this Jambudvīpa were to obtain human bodies; having obtained human bodies, they were to resolve their minds upon and practice the various bodhisattva deeds, and all were to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, for the duration of their entire lives, provide all manner of supreme and exquisite worldly articles of pleasure to these Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas—honoring, revering, respecting, and praising them—and furthermore, take these accumulated roots of virtue and, sharing them equally with all sentient beings, dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; [this merit is far greater].
"By this cause and condition, would these sons and daughters of good family acquire much merit? Subhūti replied, "Very much!"
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If good sons and good daughters, among the great assembly, proclaim this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, establishing, defining, analyzing, and elucidating it so that it may be easily understood, and abide in the mental attention associated with this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.”
By reason of these causes and conditions, the merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family is far more vast than the former, immeasurable and incalculable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
What do you think?

Suppose that all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm were to obtain human bodies, and having obtained human bodies, they were to resolve their minds upon practicing the various bodhisattva deeds and all realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Suppose there are sons or daughters of good family who, for the duration of their entire lives, honor, revere, respect, and praise these Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas with all the most excellent and sublime worldly articles of enjoyment; furthermore, they take these accumulated roots of virtue and, sharing them equally with all sentient beings, dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Would these sons and daughters of good family, by reason of this cause and condition,
acquire much merit? Subhūti replied, "Very much!"
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If good sons and good daughters, among a great assembly, proclaim this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, establishing, defining, analyzing, and elucidating it so that it may be easily understood, and if they abide in the mental attention associated with this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, then the merit obtained by these good sons and good daughters through these causes and conditions will be far greater than the former—immeasurable and incalculable.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti, what do you think?
Suppose all the sentient beings in this Jambudvīpa were to simultaneously obtain human bodies, neither before nor after one another."

There may be sons or daughters of good family who, through skillful means, instruct and guide others so that they all come to dwell securely in the ten paths of wholesome action; or in the four dhyānas, or the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments, or the five supernormal powers; or in the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship; or in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, or even in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Furthermore, they take these roots of goodness from such instruction and, sharing them equally with all sentient beings, dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Would these sons and daughters of good family, by reason of this cause and condition,
acquire much merit? Subhūti replied, "Very much!"
"World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If good sons and good daughters, amidst the great assembly, proclaim this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, establishing, defining, analyzing, and elucidating it so that it may be easily understood, and correctly abide in the mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*)."
By these causes and conditions, the merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family is far greater than the former, immeasurable and incalculable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
What do you think?
Suppose that all sentient beings within this trichiliocosm were to simultaneously attain human bodies, neither before nor after one another.

There are sons and daughters of good family who, through skillful means, instruct and guide others so that they all dwell securely in the ten paths of wholesome action; or in the four dhyānas, or the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments, or the five superknowledges; or in the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship; or in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, or even in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Furthermore, they take these roots of goodness from such instruction and, sharing them equally with all sentient beings, dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"By this cause and condition, would these sons and daughters of good family acquire much merit? Subhūti replied, "Very much!"
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If sons or daughters of good family, amidst a great assembly, proclaim this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, establishing, formulating, analyzing, and elucidating it so that it may be easily understood, and correctly abide in the mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñatājñāna*);”
"Subhūti, the merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family through these causes and conditions is far greater than the former,
immeasurable and incalculable."
It should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva, by virtue of the superior power of this diligence, reaches the further shore of the field of merit for all sentient beings. Why is this so?
This bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses such superior power through diligence in the Dharma that no sentient being can equal him, except for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Why is this? Subhūti!

When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they perceive that sentient beings lack benefit and happiness, and thus give rise to a mind of great compassion, which is not something attained by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Seeing sentient beings undergoing decline and suffering, they give rise to great compassion, which is not attained by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas;
seeing sentient beings obtaining benefit and happiness, they give rise to great sympathetic joy, which is not attained by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas;
seeing that all sentient beings are devoid of intrinsic nature and devoid of characteristics, they give rise to great equanimity, which is not attained by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.

Subhūti! Although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas impartially give rise to great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity toward sentient beings, they remain unattached to anything whatsoever; they do not, like ordinary persons, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas, give rise to a mind of attachment based on any arising phenomenon.

"Subhūti! Although this bodhisattva mahāsattva impartially arouses loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity toward sentient beings, he does not dwell constantly in a state of equanimity, because he never for a moment abandons his efforts to benefit those beings whom he transforms."
Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, attains great illumination. That is to say, because he attains the great illumination of the perfection of generosity;

because he also attains the great illumination of the perfection of ethical discipline; because he also attains the great illumination of the perfection of patience; because he also attains the great illumination of the perfection of diligence; because he also attains the great illumination of the perfection of meditative concentration; and because he also attains the great illumination of the perfection of wisdom.

“Subhūti! Although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have not yet realized the knowledge of all modes, because they have attained non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they have reached the further shore of being a field of merit for sentient beings and are worthy of receiving all requisites for life, such as clothing, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicines.”

Subhūti! Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly dwells in mental attention associated with the perfection of wisdom, he is able to ultimately repay the kindness of his donors and is also able to draw near to the knowledge of all modes.

Therefore, Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes not to receive in vain the faithful offerings of kings, ministers, and other sentient beings; wishes to show sentient beings the true and pure path; wishes to act as a great illumination for sentient beings; wishes to liberate sentient beings from the prison of the three realms; wishes to bestow upon sentient beings the pure eye of Dharma; wishes to pull sentient beings out from the ocean of birth and death; wishes to serve as a great island for sentient beings; and wishes to grant sentient beings ultimate peace and happiness, they should always abide in a mental engagement associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can always abide in the mental engagement associated with the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and whatever they speak is all the Dharma associated with the perfection of wisdom; and having spoken the Dharma associated with the perfection of wisdom, they are further able to reflect upon the Dharma associated with the perfection of wisdom in accordance with reality.”
"Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly dwells in mental attention associated with the perfection of wisdom; there is no room for any other mental attentions to arise within that interval."
"Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva practices with diligence day and night, dwelling in mental attention associated with the perfection of wisdom, never for a moment relinquishing it."

It is like a person who previously never possessed a mani jewel, but later by chance obtains one; he rejoices and congratulates himself, yet failing to store it securely, he loses it again due to circumstances. He gives rise to great sorrow and constantly harbors regret, never ceasing to dwell upon the thought of what plan he might employ to recover this jewel.
Because that person attends to it with such corresponding mental engagement (*manasikāra*), they do not part from this precious jewel, which remains at the crown of their head.
In the same way, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas also constantly abide in mental engagement corresponding to the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
If one is separated from the mental engagement associated with the perfection of wisdom, then one loses the mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes. Therefore, Subhūti!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should constantly abide in the mental engagement associated with the profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

If they constantly abide in the mental engagement associated with the profound perfection of wisdom, they will not lose the mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
The intrinsic nature of all mental engagements is empty; the intrinsic nature of all mental engagements is detached; and it is likewise with all phenomena."

Since all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature and devoid of intrinsic nature, and since therein neither the bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor the perfection of wisdom, nor the knowledge of all aspects, nor any mental engagements can be apprehended, how does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha exhort the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas not to be separated from mental engagement associated with the perfection of wisdom, nor to be separated from mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all aspects?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that all phenomena and all mental engagements are empty of intrinsic nature and are devoid of intrinsic nature."
Thus, this emptiness and detachment are not made by śrāvakas, nor made by pratyekabuddhas, nor made by bodhisattvas, nor made by tathāgatas, nor made by anyone else.

However, all phenomena (dharmas) are eternally abiding by their very nature as the fixedness of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the nature of phenomena, the realm of phenomena, non-falsity, non-alteration, equality, the state beyond birth, the realm of space, suchness, the limit of reality, and the inconceivable realm; they are thus established by the very nature of things.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva is thus never apart from the mental engagement associated with the profound perfection of wisdom, nor is he ever apart from the mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes.

Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*), and all mental attentions (*manasikāra*) are all empty of intrinsic nature and all devoid of intrinsic nature.
"In this way, emptiness and detachment are without increase or decrease; to be able to correctly penetrate them is called 'not being detached.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also empty of intrinsic nature and detached from intrinsic nature, how is it that the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having cultivated and realized the equality of the *prajñāpāramitā*, attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When bodhisattva mahāsattvas cultivate and realize the equality of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), there is neither increase nor decrease in the qualities of a buddha (buddhadharma). Nor is there increase or decrease in the fixed nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the stability of phenomena (dharmaniyāmatā), the nature of phenomena (dharmadhātu), the non-falsity of phenomena (avitathatā), the unalterability of phenomena (ananyathābhāvatā), equality, the state beyond birth (anupapatti), the realm of space (ākāśadhātu), suchness (tathatā), the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), or the inconceivable realm (acintyadhātu).”
Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is not one, not two, not three, not four, nor is it many. Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing this teaching of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, their mind is not startled, not terrified, not frightened, does not sink, does not become despondent, and does not give rise to doubt, then that bodhisattva mahāsattva has already attained the ultimate in practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*; they abide securely on the stage of the non-retrogressive bodhisattva and will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, universally bringing great benefit to all sentient beings.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One,
is it this very profound perfection of wisdom— which is empty, non-existent, lacking self-mastery, and lacking solidity— that is able to practice the profound perfection of wisdom?"
"No, World-Honored One! Subhūti, it is not so. "World-Honored One! [Subhūti replied.]

Apart from this profound *prajñāpāramitā*—which is empty, non-existent, lacking self-mastery, and lacking substantiality—is there any dharma that can be apprehended which is able to practice this profound *prajñāpāramitā*?
"No, World-Honored One! Subhūti, it is not so. "World-Honored One! [Subhūti replied.]
"Is it that which is the profound perfection of wisdom itself that is able to practice the profound perfection of wisdom?
"No, Subhūti!"
“World-Honored One!
Is there any dharma that can be apprehended apart from the profound *prajñāpāramitā* that is able to practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*?”
"No, World-Honored One! Subhūti, [it is not so]. "World-Honored One! [Subhūti replied.]
"Is it that the very nature of emptiness can practice emptiness?
"No, Subhūti!"
“World-Honored One!
Is there any dharma that can be apprehended apart from emptiness which is able to practice emptiness? “It is not so.”
"Excellent, Subhūti!
"World-Honored One,
is it that form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness themselves can practice the profound perfection of wisdom?"
"No, World-Honored One! Subhūti, it is not so. "World-Honored One! [Subhūti replied.]
"Is it possible to find a dharma apart from form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that can practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*? "No, it is not."
“Excellent, Subhūti!
“World-Honored One!
Is it the very eye-base, up to and including the mind-base, that can practice the profound perfection of wisdom?”
"No, World-Honored One! Subhūti, it is not so. "World-Honored One! [Subhūti replied.]
"Can one who perceives any dharma apart from the sense bases, from the eye base up to the mind base, practice the profound perfection of wisdom?

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva accomplishes such acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas, the Buddhas will bestow upon them the prediction of non-retrogression regarding unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding the Buddha’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha—these immeasurable and boundless, preeminent virtues—is called one who is capable of diligent practice according to reality.
If one can practice with such diligence, it is impossible that they should not attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, the knowledge of all aspects, great wisdom, and sublime wisdom.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having already realized the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), shall never again suffer any decline or regression in the dharmas they have attained, up until their attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Why is this so? Subhūti! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice such profound prajñāpāramitā, they are free from all such conceptual discriminations.
Why is this? Subhūti!
Because the profound perfection of wisdom is entirely free from all conceptual discrimination.
"If one gives rise to such various conceptual discriminations, one is not practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Chapter Sixty-one: Fellow Students, Part One. At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

Thus, this perfection of wisdom is exceedingly profound, difficult to see, and difficult to realize; it is beyond the sphere of discursive thought and transcends the realm of investigation, being realized by those who are subtle, secret, wise, and sagacious, for it is ultimately free from all conceptual characteristics and discrimination.

"Bhagavān! If good sons and good daughters, regarding this profound sūtra of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, constantly delight in hearing it, receiving and upholding it, reading and reciting it, mastering it thoroughly, reflecting upon it according to the principle, practicing in accordance with the teaching, and correctly explaining it to others—never mingling their minds or mental factors with anything else until they reach unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—then these good sons and good daughters have not accomplished merely a small portion of roots of goodness to be able to perform such a deed."
At that time, the Buddha said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas: "So it is! So it is!"

"It is as you have said, Kauśika! If sons of good family or daughters of good family constantly delight in hearing, receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, thoroughly mastering, reflecting upon according to the principle, practicing in accordance with the teaching, and correctly explaining for others this profound sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā, until they reach unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment— without being distracted by other minds or mental factors— then these sons and daughters of good family will certainly achieve vast roots of goodness and shall be able to accomplish such a task therein."

Kauśika! If good sons and good daughters were able to exhort all sentient beings in this Jambudvīpa, even up to those in the trichiliocosm, to cause them all to receive and practice the ten paths of wholesome action, or the four dhyānas, or the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments, or the five supernormal powers—such immeasurable merits as these.

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, regarding this profound sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā, constantly delight in hearing it, receiving and upholding it, reading and reciting it, mastering it thoroughly, reflecting upon it according to the truth, practicing in accordance with the teaching, and correctly explaining it to others—the merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family surpasses the previous mass of merit by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and even up to an *upaniṣad*-fold.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu in the assembly said to Śakra, the Lord of Devas: “Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters, with their minds collected and undistracted, constantly delight in hearing, receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, thoroughly mastering, reflecting upon according to the principle, practicing in accordance with the teaching, and correctly explaining for others this profound sūtra of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, until they reach unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, without mixing it with other states of mind or mental factors;”

The merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family surpasses the immeasurable merit of all sentient beings throughout Jambudvīpa and even the trichiliocosm who collectively practice the ten paths of wholesome action, or the four dhyānas, or the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments, or the five supernormal powers.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:

“The merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family at the very first moment they give rise to a thought associated with the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) already surpasses, by many hundreds of thousands of times, the immeasurable merit of all sentient beings throughout Jambudvīpa and even the entire trichiliocosm who collectively practice the ten paths of wholesome action, or the four dhyānas, or the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments, or the five supernormal powers.”

How much more so, then, for one who is able, regarding this profound *prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, to collect the mind and remain undistracted, constantly delighting in hearing, receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, mastering it thoroughly, reflecting upon it according to the principle, practicing in accordance with the teaching, and correctly explaining it to others—until reaching unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment—without being mixed with other minds or mental factors; the merit obtained by such a person is beyond all calculation.
“Bhikṣus, you should know!

The merit and wisdom of these sons and daughters of good family not only surpass that of all sentient beings throughout Jambudvīpa, up to and including the entire trichiliocosm, who together practice the ten paths of wholesome action and the immeasurable merits of the four dhyānas and so forth; they also surpass all the merits possessed by the gods, humans, asuras, and others in the world.”
Why is this? Because these sons and daughters of good family will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, thereby benefiting sentient beings without limit.
“Bhikṣus, you should know!

The merit and wisdom of these sons and daughters of good family not only surpass all the merit possessed by the world’s devas, humans, and asuras, but they also surpass the merit of all stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas.”
Why is this? Because these sons and daughters of good family will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, thereby benefiting sentient beings without limit.
“Bhikṣus, you should know!
The merit and wisdom of these sons and daughters of good family not only surpass all the merit of those who are stream-enterers,
once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas, but [far exceed it].”

Furthermore, they surpass all bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, while lacking the skillful means of the perfection of wisdom, practice the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration;
who dwell in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-entities; and who dwell in suchness.
Up to the inconceivable realm, they dwell securely in the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
they practice the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;

they practice the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative concentrations, and the ten totalities; they practice the four foundations of mindfulness, and so forth...
The eight branches of the noble path; the cultivation of the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
the cultivation of the stages from the Ground of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma; the cultivation of all doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of samādhi;
the cultivation of the five eyes and the six supernormal powers; and the cultivation of the ten powers of a Tathāgata, up to...
The eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*): practicing the quality of non-forgetfulness, abiding constantly in equanimity;

practicing all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); practicing the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination in both forward and reverse order;
purifying buddha-fields and maturing sentient beings; and cultivating the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
The practice of the perfections (*pāramitā-caryā*) and all the merits of those who cultivate unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Why is this?
Because these sons and daughters of good family will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete bodhi, thereby benefiting sentient beings without limit.
“Bhikṣus, you should know!
The merit and wisdom of these sons and daughters of good family also surpass all the merit of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, being far removed from skillful means, practice the perfection of wisdom.”
Why is this? Because these sons and daughters of good family will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, thereby bringing benefit to sentient beings without limit.

“Bhikṣus, you should know that these sons and daughters of good family are indeed bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* as it has been taught, they cannot be overcome by any in the world—whether devas, humans, or asuras—nor by other bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, or śrāvakas. They are able to perpetuate the lineage of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*) so that it remains unbroken; they are never separated from the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, their truly excellent and virtuous spiritual friends. Before long, they shall sit upon the sublime seat of awakening (*bodhimanda*), subdue the entire host of Māras, realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), and uproot birth, old age, sickness, and death for all sentient beings, leading them to ultimate peace and happiness.”
“Bhikṣus, you should know!

Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) as it has been taught, they constantly train in the dharmas that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ought to learn, and do not train in the dharmas that śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas ought to learn.”
“Bhikṣus, you should know!

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices such profound *prajñāpāramitā* and constantly trains in that which all bodhisattva mahāsattvas ought to train in, the Four World-Protecting Kings, leading their own celestial hosts, come to his presence to offer worship, respect, honor, and praise, saying: ‘Excellent!’”
"O Mahāsattva!

You should swiftly apply yourself with diligence to study the dharmas that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ought to study; do not study the dharmas that śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas ought to study. If you study in this manner, you will soon sit securely upon the sublime seat of awakening and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Just as the former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas accepted the four bowls offered by the Four Heavenly Kings, you too shall accept them; just as the Four Great Heavenly Kings, the Protectors of the World, formerly presented these four bowls, I too shall now present them.
“Bhikṣus, you should know!

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices such profound *prajñāpāramitā* and constantly trains in that which all bodhisattva mahāsattvas ought to train in, we—the Lord of Devas and our retinue of devas—come to his presence to make offerings, pay homage, show respect, and offer praise, saying: ‘Excellent!’”
"O Great Being!

You should swiftly apply yourself with diligence to the dharmas that all Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas ought to study; do not study the dharmas that Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas ought to study. If you train in this manner, you will quickly sit upon the sublime seat of Bodhi, realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and turn the sublime wheel of Dharma to deliver the multitudes of sentient beings."
“Bhikṣus, you should know!

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices such profound prajñāpāramitā and constantly trains in that which all bodhisattva mahāsattvas ought to train in, the Devaputra Subhakāla, leading a host of Subhakāla devas, came to his place to make offerings, pay homage, show respect, and offer praise, saying: ‘Excellent!’”
"O Mahāsattva!
