Who will realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
Who will turn the wheel of Dharma, preach what Dharma, and deliver which assembly?
"In this regard, nothing at all exists; if it were truly existent, such a thing could never be.
It is merely established by way of conventional designation.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

This Prajñāpāramitā is most extremely profound, difficult to believe, and difficult to understand. Although Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the profound Prajñāpāramitā know that all phenomena are unobtainable, they still seek unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; to wish to proclaim the true Dharma for the sake of sentient beings is truly a most difficult task!”
Why is this? World-Honored One!

It is certainly impossible for one who dwells in *tathatā* (suchness) while practicing the bodhisattva path to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and then preach the true Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings. Yet, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they observe that all phenomena are utterly non-existent; regarding this profound nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), their minds are not startled, not terrified, not afraid, have no doubt, no obstruction, do not sink, do not despair, and are not bewildered. Such matters are truly rare!
At that time, Subhūti said to Śakra: “Kauśika, it is as you have said.”

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they contemplate that all phenomena are utterly non-existent; regarding this profound nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), their minds are not startled, not terrified, not afraid, have no doubt, no obstruction, do not sink, do not become submerged, and are not bewildered. Such matters as these are exceedingly rare.

Kauśika! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they contemplate that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty; within this emptiness there is nothing at all—what, then, could cause alarm, fear, or even confusion?

Therefore, it is not considered extraordinary that when a bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, their mind is not startled, not terrified, not frightened, has no doubt, no obstruction, does not sink, does not drown, is not deluded, and is not distressed regarding the profound nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed Subhūti, saying:
"Virtuous One, all that you have spoken relies upon emptiness; therefore, your words are always free from obstruction."
It is like shooting an arrow upward into the void; whether it travels far or near, it meets no obstruction. What the Venerable One has spoken is likewise so—whosoever would dare to oppose it?
Chapter 65: On Truthful Speech, Part Two, Chapter Sixty-Five, Section One. At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

"Is it correct for me to speak thus, praise thus, and declare thus, in accordance with the World-Honored One’s words of truth and his Dharma, as a true declaration regarding the Dharma and what accords with the Dharma?"
Then the Buddha said to him:
“Kauśika, that you speak thus,

praise thus, and declare thus— in accordance with the true words and the Dharma-words of the Blessed One— truly constitutes a correct declaration regarding the Dharma and what accords with the Dharma.”
Then, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How extraordinary!
World-Honored One!”
Venerable Subhūti, everything you have said is based entirely upon emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
it is also based upon the four applications of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, as well as the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables,
and the four formless attainments, and it is also based upon the eight liberations up to the ten totalities.
The noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path likewise rely upon the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
they likewise rely upon inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature;
they likewise rely upon suchness up to the inconceivable realm; and they likewise rely upon the stages of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Relying upon all the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi; likewise relying upon the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
likewise relying upon the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
likewise relying upon the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity; likewise relying upon all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the [knowledge of all aspects]...
"The wisdom of all aspects also relies upon all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and it also relies upon the unexcelled,
perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of Devas, saying:

“Kauśika! The Venerable Subhūti dwells in the emptiness of all phenomena; he does not apprehend even the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, let alone anyone who practices the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom!”

When one contemplates that even the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path cannot be apprehended, how much less can there be anyone who cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path who can be apprehended!

Since even the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments cannot be apprehended, how much less can there be anyone who cultivates the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments who can be apprehended!

If even the eight liberations up to the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*) cannot be apprehended through contemplation, how much less can there be anyone who cultivates the eight liberations up to the ten totalities who can be apprehended!

If even the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path cannot be apprehended through contemplation, how much less can there be anyone who abides in the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path who can be apprehended!

If even inner emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the nature of non-existence, cannot be apprehended, how much less can one who dwells in inner emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the nature of non-existence, be apprehended!
If even true thusness up to the inconceivable realm cannot be apprehended, how much less can one who dwells in true thusness up to the inconceivable realm be apprehended!

If even the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—cannot be apprehended, how much less can one who cultivates the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—be apprehended!

When even the Joyous Ground up to the Cloud of Dharma Ground cannot be apprehended through contemplation, how much less can there be anyone who cultivates the Joyous Ground up to the Cloud of Dharma Ground who can be apprehended!

When even all the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi cannot be apprehended through contemplation, how much less can there be anyone who cultivates all the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi who can be apprehended!
If one observes that even the five eyes and six supernormal powers are ultimately unattainable, how much more so could there be anyone who brings them forth and attains them!

If one observes that even the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are ultimately unattainable, how much more so could there be anyone who brings them forth and attains them!

Since even the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity cannot be apprehended, how much less can one who brings forth non-forgetfulness and constant equanimity be apprehended!

Since even omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) cannot be apprehended, how much less can there be anyone who brings them forth!

When one contemplates that even the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot be apprehended, how much less can there be anyone who is able to practice the conduct of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who could be apprehended!

When one contemplates that even the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas cannot be apprehended, how much less can there be anyone who can realize that unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas!
When one contemplates omniscient wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*), it is already unattainable; how much more so could there be anyone who attains such omniscient wisdom!
When one contemplates the true wheel of Dharma (*saddharmacakra*), it is already unattainable; how much more so could there be anyone who turns such a true wheel of Dharma!

If even the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs cannot be apprehended upon examination, how much less can there be anyone who possesses a body adorned with such marks and signs!

When even the dharmas that are neither arising nor ceasing cannot be apprehended through contemplation, how much less can there be one who can realize those dharmas that are neither arising nor ceasing!
Why is this? "Kauśika!..."

The Venerable Subhūti dwells in the dwelling of detachment regarding all phenomena; he dwells in the dwelling of tranquility, the dwelling of non-existence, the dwelling of non-apprehension, the dwelling of emptiness, the dwelling of signlessness, and the dwelling of wishlessness.
Kauśika! The Venerable Subhūti dwells in such immeasurable and supreme abodes regarding all phenomena. Kauśika!

The immeasurable, supreme abodes in which Subhūti dwells do not equal even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor even a *upaniṣad*-part of the profound practice and abode of the perfection of wisdom in which the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas dwells.

Why is this so, Kauśika? With the exception of the dwelling of the Tathāgata, this profound practice and dwelling of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) in which these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most venerable, the most sublime, the most wondrous, the most exquisite, the highest, and the unsurpassed— unequaled and equal to the unequaled— compared to the dwellings of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
For this reason, Kauśika,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to abide above all sentient beings, they should abide in the profound practice of the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Kauśika!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in this dwelling, they transcend the stages of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, enter the bodhisattva’s state of correct nature free from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*), and are able to swiftly fulfill all Buddha-dharmas. They permanently sever the continuity of the habitual tendencies of afflictions, are able to quickly realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), receive the name of Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and are able to constantly bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.

At that time, there were immeasurable and innumerable gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven within the assembly who, hearing what the Buddha had said, leaped for joy and rejoiced. Each took exquisite celestial fragrant flowers and scattered them as offerings over the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus.

At that time, six hundred bhikṣus from within the assembly rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, bared their left shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and, bowing with reverence, joined their palms toward the Buddha, gazing up at his venerable countenance without for a moment averting their eyes.

By the spiritual power of the Buddha, exquisite fragrant flowers spontaneously filled the palms of each [monk]; this assembly of bhikṣus was filled with joy and leaped for gladness at such an unprecedented occurrence, and each took these flowers and scattered them over the Buddha and the various bodhisattvas.
Having scattered the flowers, they all made this vow:

"By the power of these supreme roots of goodness, may we always dwell securely in the subtle and profound practice and abiding of the *prajñāpāramitā*, which cannot be dwelled in by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; may we swiftly proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and transcend the stages of all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas."

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the assembly of bhikṣus possessed superior resolve and were intent upon Great Bodhi, being fixed in non-retrogression, smiled in accordance with the constant dharma of Buddhas. From his face, he emitted various rays of light—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, purple, azure, green, gold, silver, and crystal—which illuminated the entire trichiliocosm. These rays gradually withdrew and circled the Buddha’s body three times before entering through the crown of his head.
At that time, Ānanda, having beheld this auspicious omen, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness. He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated before the Buddha, joined his palms, and said:
"World-Honored One, by what cause and by what condition do you manifest this smile?"
"The Buddhas do not manifest a smile without cause or condition; I only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately explain it for us.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"This assembly of bhikṣus shall, in a future age known as the Star-like Kalpa, attain Buddhahood, all bearing the same name: Saṃpuṣpita (Flower-Sprinkler) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Worthy, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān. The lifespan of those Buddhas, the lands in which they dwell, and their bhikṣu disciples shall all be identical."

These Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, from their initial birth and renunciation until after they have attained Buddhahood, constantly rain down subtle and wondrous five-colored flowers of sound, day and night, wherever they may be.
For this reason, Ānanda, I smile. Therefore, Ānanda,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to dwell in the most excellent dwelling, they should practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to dwell securely in the dwelling of a Tathāgata, they should practice the perfection of wisdom.
Ānanda, you should know this!”

If good sons or good daughters diligently cultivate and study the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, these good sons and good daughters have, in previous lives, either passed away from among humans and been reborn here, or passed away from the Tuṣita heaven and come to be born among humans. Because in those previous lives they were either in the human realm or dwelling in the heavens and had extensively heard the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they are now able to diligently cultivate and study the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this present life.
Ānanda, you should know this:

if a son of good family or a daughter of good family is able to diligently study and practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, being without regard for their body, life, or wealth, they are certainly a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 457. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Two, Chapter Sixty-Five (Part Two): The Chapter on True Speech. "Ānanda, you should know this!

If sons or daughters of good family who delight in hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā* as it has been taught, and having heard it, uphold, read, recite, master, diligently practice, and reflect upon it according to the truth, and further explain, reveal, instruct, and advise it for other sons or daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle—then one should know that such persons have, in the past, personally heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught by the Buddhas; having heard it, they too upheld, read, recited, mastered, diligently practiced, and reflected upon it according to the truth, and likewise explained, revealed, instructed, and advised it for others.

“Ānanda, you should know that these sons and daughters of good family have planted various roots of goodness in the presence of immeasurable Buddhas in the past; therefore, they are able to accomplish this matter in their present life.”
These sons and daughters of good family should form this thought:

"I have not previously heard such a profound *prajñāpāramitā* from śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; I have certainly heard such a profound *prajñāpāramitā* from the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
Previously, I did not plant roots of goodness under the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; rather, I certainly planted roots of goodness under the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

By virtue of these causes and conditions, I am now able to hear this profound Prajñāpāramitā, and with love and joy, I accept, uphold, read, recite, master, diligently practice, contemplate according to the principle, and extensively explain it to others, without ever becoming weary.
“Ānanda, you should know this:

if sons or daughters of good family delight in hearing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and having heard it, they uphold, recite, master, diligently practice, and reflect upon it according to the truth—penetrating its meaning, its phrasing, its dharma, its intent, and its discipline (*vinaya*)—then these sons and daughters of good family are, for that reason, directly beholding all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.”
“Ānanda, you should know this:

if sons or daughters of good family, upon hearing the profound meaning and intent of the *prajñāpāramitā*, give rise to pure faith and understanding, and neither disparage nor slander it, remaining unshakable, then these sons and daughters of good family have already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas; they have formed great vows in the presence of those Buddhas; they have planted many roots of merit; and they have also been taken into the care of immeasurable true spiritual friends.”
"Ānanda, you should know that if sons or daughters of good family are able to plant various roots of goodness in the presence of the Tathāgata, the Arhat,
the Samyaksaṃbuddha— the supreme field of merit— they will certainly attain either the fruit of a Śrāvaka or [the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha]..."
To realize the fruit of awakening, or the fruit of the Tathāgata, and to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
one must thoroughly master and be unimpeded regarding the profound meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā*, while practicing the *dānapāramitā* up to the *prajñāpāramitā*,
and abiding in the emptiness of the internal (*adhyātmaśūnyatā*) up to the absence of intrinsic nature (*abhāvasvabhāva*).
[They] dwell in the emptiness of intrinsic nature, from the abiding in *tathatā* (suchness) up to the inconceivable realm;
they abide in the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; they practice the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
they practice the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; and they practice the eight liberations up to...
The ten spheres of totality; the cultivation of the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
the cultivation of the stages from the Ground of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma; the cultivation of all doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of samādhi;
the cultivation of the five eyes and the six supernormal powers; and the cultivation of the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the [ten powers]...
The eight unique qualities of a Buddha: they cultivate the quality of non-forgetfulness and abide constantly in equanimity;
they cultivate all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), bringing them to full perfection.
“Ānanda, you should know this:

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to thoroughly penetrate and remain unimpeded in the profound meaning and intent of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and practices the *dāna-pāramitā*, *śīla-pāramitā*, *kṣānti-pāramitā*, *vīrya-pāramitā*, *dhyāna-pāramitā*, and *prajñā-pāramitā* until they are brought to perfection; and likewise practices up to and including *sarvajñatā*, *mārgākārajñatā*, and *sarvākārajñatā* until they are brought to perfection—if such a bodhisattva mahāsattva should dwell in the stage of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha without realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, that is impossible.”

Therefore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening should attain unimpeded mastery of the profound meaning and intent of the *prajñāpāramitā*. They should practice the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom so that they may be swiftly brought to fulfillment; and likewise, they should practice all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) so that these may be swiftly brought to fulfillment.
Therefore, Ānanda, I entrust this Prajñāpāramitā to you; you should correctly receive, uphold, recite, and master it, ensuring that it is never lost or forgotten.
“Ānanda, you should know this:

if one were to receive and uphold other teachings spoken by me, setting aside this profound sūtra of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, even if one were to forget them, the transgression would still be light. However, if one does not properly receive and uphold this profound sūtra of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and forgets even a single verse, that transgression is extremely grave.”
Ānanda, you should know that if one can properly receive and uphold even a single verse from this profound sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā without forgetting it, the merit obtained will be immeasurable.
If one does not properly uphold this profound sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā, and even forgets a single verse, the amount of grave sin incurred will be equal to the aforementioned merit.

Therefore, Ānanda, I entrust this profound sūtra of the *prajñāpāramitā* to you with earnest care; you should correctly receive, uphold, read, recite, master, and contemplate it according to the principle. You should explain it extensively to others, analyzing and elucidating it so that those who hear and receive it may thoroughly understand the words, the meanings, and the underlying intent, and further be able to expound them to others according to the principle.
“Ānanda, you should know this:

if sons or daughters of good family receive, uphold, read, recite, master thoroughly, contemplate according to the principle, and extensively explain to others this profound sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā, they will thereby receive, uphold, and encompass the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment realized by all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present.”
“Ānanda, you should know that if sons or daughters of good family give rise to a sincere and pure mind,
and in my presence offer various kinds of exquisite flower garlands, powdered and incense scents, robes, necklaces, and jeweled banners;”
Those who, with banners, canopies, music, and lamps, offer worship, reverence, respect,
and praise without weariness, should with a sincere heart listen to,
receive and uphold, read and recite, master thoroughly, reflect upon according to principle, and extensively [expound] this profound sūtra of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
He said: "Furthermore, one should transcribe [this scripture] adorned with various jewels,

and constantly offer worship, respect, reverence, and praise with all kinds of exquisite flower garlands, powdered and incense perfumes, robes, necklaces, precious banners, flags, canopies, music, and lamps, never becoming indolent."
“Ānanda, you should know this!

If sons or daughters of good family offer worship, honor, respect, and praise to the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they thereby offer worship, honor, respect, and praise to me; they also offer worship, honor, respect, and praise to all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas currently teaching the Dharma throughout the worlds of the ten directions, as well as to all Buddhas of the past and the future.”
“Ānanda, you should know this:

if sons or daughters of good family, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, give rise to pure faith, reverence, and joyful affection, they thereby give rise to pure faith, reverence, and joyful affection toward the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment realized by all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present.”

"Ānanda! If you revere, love, and delight in me, and do not abandon me, then you should likewise be courageous and diligent, redoubling your reverence, love, and delight for this profound Prajñāpāramitā, and not allow even a single phrase to be forgotten."

“Ānanda! Although the causes and conditions for my entrusting this profound *prajñāpāramitā* are immeasurable, to state the essentials: just as I am your teacher, you should know that this profound *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise your teacher. Just as you, gods and humans, revere me, you should likewise revere the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.”

Therefore, Ānanda! By means of immeasurable skillful methods, I entrust to you this profound sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā. You should receive and uphold it, never allowing it to be forgotten or lost. Now, in the presence of this great assembly of devas, humans, asuras, and others, I entrust this profound Prajñāpāramitā to you.
"Ānanda! I now speak these sincere words to you:

those who possess pure faith and wish not to abandon the Buddha, wish not to abandon the Dharma, and wish not to abandon the Saṅgha; and furthermore, those who wish not to abandon the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment realized by all Buddhas of the past, future, and present—these must certainly not abandon the profound Prajñāpāramitā. This is what is called our teaching and instruction for all disciples."
“Ānanda, you should know this:

if sons or daughters of good family delight in hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and if they receive, uphold, read, recite, master it thoroughly, reflect upon it according to the principle, and extensively explain it to others through immeasurable gateways—analyzing, revealing, establishing, and instituting it so that others may understand and diligently practice it—then these sons and daughters of good family will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and will be able to draw near to the fulfillment of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).”
Why is this? Ānanda!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have attained their unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by relying upon this very profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Thus it is that they come into being.
"Ānanda, you should know that all Buddhas of the past,
future, and present give birth to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by relying upon this very profound perfection of wisdom."

Therefore, Ānanda! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they should diligently apply themselves with vigor to study this profound perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Ānanda!
This profound Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, for it gives birth to all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

“Ānanda, you should know that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva diligently practices and trains in the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
Therefore, Ānanda, I entrust these six pāramitās to you once more; you should receive and uphold them correctly so that they are not lost or forgotten. Why is this?
These six perfections are the inexhaustible treasury of the Dharma of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, for all the Buddha-dharmas arise from them.
"Ānanda, you should know that the essential teachings spoken by all Buddhas of the present, past, and future are all issued forth from this inexhaustible Dharma-treasury of the six perfections."

Ānanda, you should know that all Buddhas of the present, past, and future have diligently practiced and studied the inexhaustible Dharma-treasury of the six perfections, thereby realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Ānanda, you should know that all Buddhas,

śrāvakas, and saṅghas of the present, past, and future diligently train in the inexhaustible Dharma-treasury of the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) and thereby attain parinirvāṇa in the realm of the wondrous nirvana without remainder (anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu).
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

Suppose you were to teach the Dharma of the śrāvakas to individuals belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas, and by means of that Dharma, every sentient being in the trichiliocosm were to realize the fruit of arhatship; even so, you would not have performed what is required of me as a disciple of the Buddha."

If you can expound even a single verse of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* associated with the Bodhisattva vehicle for a person belonging to that vehicle, you will have performed for me the duty that a disciple of the Buddha ought to perform; I shall rejoice deeply in this deed more than if you were to teach all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm and cause them to realize the fruit of Arhatship.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

Suppose all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm, through the power of another's instruction, were simultaneously to obtain human bodies and at once realize the fruit of arhatship. Whatever meritorious action consisting of giving, meritorious action consisting of ethical discipline, and meritorious action consisting of cultivation belongs to all those arhats—"
"What do you think?
Would that meritorious deed not be great? Ānanda replied:
“Very much, World-Honored One!
That meritorious deed is immeasurable and incalculable.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If there were a śrāvaka disciple who could expound for a bodhisattva mahāsattva the teachings associated with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) for even a single day and night, the mass of merit obtained would be far greater than that."

Ānanda, you should know this! Setting aside one day and night, let it be for just one day; setting aside one day, let it be for just half a day; setting aside half a day, let it be for just one watch (muhūrta); setting aside one watch, let it be for just the time of a meal; setting aside the time of a meal, let it be for just a brief moment (kṣaṇa); setting aside a brief moment, let it be for just an instant (lava); setting aside an instant, let it be for just a flash (tatkṣaṇa). A śrāvaka who can proclaim to the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas the Dharma associated with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) for such a duration as these will acquire a mass of merit far greater than the former.
Why is this? Because the mass of merit obtained by these śrāvakas surpasses all the virtues of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva were to proclaim various Śrāvaka-yāna teachings for individuals belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle, and if, by means of these teachings, every sentient being in the entire trichiliocosm were to realize the fruit of arhatship and be endowed with all manner of sublime qualities—what do you think?
"Would the mass of merit obtained by this bodhisattva mahāsattva through these causes and conditions be great?
Ānanda replied, "It would be very great!"
“World-Honored One!
The mass of merit obtained by this bodhisattva mahāsattva is immeasurable and boundless.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva were to proclaim for a single day and night the Dharma associated with the perfection of wisdom to sons and daughters of good family belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas, or the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, or the unsurpassed vehicle, the mass of merit they would obtain would be far greater than the former.”

Ānanda, you should know this! Setting aside one day and night, let us consider just one day; setting aside one day, let us consider just half a day; setting aside half a day, let us consider just one watch (muhūrta); setting aside one watch, let us consider just the time it takes to eat a meal; setting aside the time of a meal, let us consider just a brief moment; setting aside a brief moment, let us consider just a fleeting instant; and setting aside a fleeting instant, let us consider just the blink of an eye. If a bodhisattva mahāsattva were to proclaim for the sake of sons and daughters of good family belonging to the three vehicles the Dharma associated with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) during even that duration, the mass of merit they would obtain would be immeasurably and incalculably greater than the former.

Why is this? Because the gift of Dharma associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā* surpasses all gifts of Dharma associated with the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, as well as all the merits of those two vehicles.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas seek unexcelled, perfect enlightenment for themselves, and they also demonstrate, instruct, encourage, and gladden other sentient beings with dharmas corresponding to the Great Vehicle, causing them to attain non-retrogression from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

“Ānanda, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva personally cultivates the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, and also teaches others to cultivate the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
he personally cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, and also teaches others to cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path.”

They themselves abide in the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, and they also teach others to abide in the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;
they themselves abide in suchness up to the inconceivable realm, and they also teach others to abide in suchness up to the inconceivable realm;
they themselves abide in the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, and they also teach others to abide in the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.

They personally cultivate the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments, and also teach others to cultivate the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
they personally cultivate the eight liberations up to the ten totalities, and also teach others to cultivate the eight liberations up to the ten totalities;

they personally cultivate the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and also teach others to cultivate the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
They personally cultivate the bodhisattva stages and also teach others to cultivate the bodhisattva stages;
they personally cultivate all doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of samādhi and also teach others to cultivate all doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of samādhi;
they personally cultivate the five eyes and the six supernormal powers and also teach others to cultivate the five eyes and the six supernormal powers.

They personally cultivate the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and also teach others to cultivate the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they personally cultivate the thirty-two marks of a Great Being and the eighty minor signs, and also teach others to cultivate the thirty-two marks of a Great Being and the eighty minor signs;

they personally cultivate the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity, and also teach others to cultivate the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity.

They personally cultivate all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), and they also teach others to cultivate all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects;
they personally cultivate all the practices of bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, and they also teach others to cultivate all the practices of bodhisattvas mahāsattvas;

they personally cultivate the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas, and they also teach others to cultivate the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas.
One cultivates the knowledge of all modes oneself and also teaches others to cultivate the knowledge of all modes.
Through these causes and conditions, one's roots of virtue increase; it is impossible that one would ever regress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

At that time, the Tathāgata, surrounded by the fourfold assembly, praised and expounded the *Prajñāpāramitā* and, having entrusted it to Ānanda, commanded him to uphold it. Subsequently, before a great assembly of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and even humans and non-humans, he manifested supernatural powers so that the multitude all beheld the Tathāgata Acala, surrounded by śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, proclaiming the sublime Dharma to an ocean-like gathering, as well as the magnificent and pure features of that buddha-field.

The assembly of his śrāvakas were all arhats; their outflows were exhausted and they were free from further afflictions. They had attained true mastery, with minds well-liberated and wisdom well-liberated. Like well-trained thoroughbred horses or great dragons, they had done what was to be done and accomplished what was to be accomplished. Having cast off the heavy burdens and attained their own welfare, they had exhausted the fetters of existence and were liberated through right knowledge, reaching the state of supreme perfection and sovereign mastery of mind.
That assembly of bodhisattvas was entirely composed of those renowned to all; they had attained dhāraṇīs and acquired unimpeded eloquence, with merit and wisdom as vast as the great ocean.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One withdrew his supernormal powers, causing this assembly of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and so forth, up to humans and non-humans, no longer to see that Tathāgata Acala, nor the śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and the rest of the great assembly, nor the marks of the pure adornments of that buddha-field.
The assembly of that Buddha and his adorned pure land are all beyond the range of the visual faculty of this land.
Why is this? Because when the Buddha withdraws his supernatural power, there is no causal condition for seeing those distant realms.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Do you see further the land and the assembly of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Akṣobhya?"
Ānanda replied, “I no longer see it,
for that matter is not within the range of these eyes.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"Just as that assembly and land of the Tathāgata are not within the range of the eyes of this land, you should know that all dharmas are likewise: they are not within the range of the eye-faculty and the other faculties; a dharma does not traverse a dharma, a dharma does not see a dharma, a dharma does not know a dharma, and a dharma does not realize a dharma."

"Ānanda, you should know that regarding the nature of all phenomena, there is no one who can practice them, no one who can see them, no one who can know them, and no one who can realize them; they are without movement and without action."
Why is this so? Because all phenomena are like space, devoid of functional activity, and far removed from the nature of grasper and grasped.
Because all phenomena are inconceivable, they are far removed from the nature of that which conceives and that which is conceived.
Because all phenomena are like illusions and so forth, existing only as mere semblances through the conjunction of various conditions;
and because all phenomena lack an agent or recipient, appearing falsely as if they existed while lacking any solid reality.

Ānanda, you should know that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice in this way, see in this way, know in this way, and realize in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and yet they do not cling to the characteristics of these phenomena.
Ānanda, you should know that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, they are training in the perfection of wisdom.
Ānanda, you should know!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to swiftly bring all the pāramitās to full completion, they should study the prajñāpāramitā. Why is this?

One who trains in this manner is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the most exalted, the most sublime, the most subtle, the highest, the unsurpassed, the peerless, and the equal to the unequaled among all trainings. Such a person brings benefit and happiness to all sentient beings; for those without a protector, they act as a protector; for those without a refuge, they act as a refuge; for those without a place of resort, they act as a resort; for those without a dwelling, they act as a dwelling; and for those without a savior, they act as a savior. This is the training in the perfection of wisdom, which has been permitted and praised by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
"Ānanda, you should know this!

If the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas abide in this training, they could take up the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system with their right hand or the tip of their right toe, cast it to another direction, or return it to its original place; yet the sentient beings therein would not know or perceive it, nor would they suffer any harm or fear."
Why is this? Because the merit and power of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* are inconceivable.
"Ānanda, you should know this!"

The Buddhas of the past, future, and present, as well as the assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, having studied this Prajñāpāramitā, have all attained unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding all unconditioned phenomena and the dharmas of the three periods of time.
Therefore, Ānanda, I say that among all trainings,

training in this profound perfection of wisdom is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the most exalted, the most sublime, the most exquisite, the highest, the unsurpassed, the peerless, and the equal to the unequaled.
“Ānanda, you should know this:
those who wish to grasp the measure or the limit of the profound perfection of wisdom are like foolish people who wish to grasp the measure and the limit of space.”
Why is this? Because the merit of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is immeasurable and boundless.
"Ānanda, you should know this!"
I do not say that the merit and benefits of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* are limited by or have a boundary equal to those of the collection of names and so forth. Why is this?

All collections of names (*nāmakāya*), phrases (*padakāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*) are finite phenomena (*parimāṇadharma*). The merit and benefits of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* are not finite phenomena. It is not the case that the various collections of names, phrases, and phonemes can measure the merit and benefits of the *prajñāpāramitā*, nor is it the case that the merit and benefits of the *prajñāpāramitā* are the objects measured by them.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
for what reason and by what causal conditions is the profound *prajñāpāramitā* described as immeasurable?"

The Buddha told Ānanda: “Because the nature of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is inexhaustible, it is said to be immeasurable; because its nature is detached, it is said to be immeasurable; because its nature is quiescent, it is said to be immeasurable; because it is like the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), it is said to be immeasurable; and because it is like space, it is said to be immeasurable.”

Ānanda, you should know that all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present, have studied the *prajñāpāramitā*, attained the ultimate perfection of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and proclaimed and revealed it for the sake of all sentient beings; yet this *prajñāpāramitā* is eternally inexhaustible.
Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is, like space, inexhaustible.
Should anyone wish to exhaust the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they would thereby wish to exhaust the limits of space.
“Ānanda, you should know that the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, up to and including the *dānapāramitā*, has not been exhausted, is not being exhausted, and will not be exhausted; likewise,
from internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*), they have not been exhausted.”

...neither has been exhausted, nor is being exhausted, nor will it be exhausted; true suchness, up to and including the inconceivable realm, neither has been exhausted, nor is being exhausted, nor will it be exhausted;
the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path neither have been exhausted, nor are being exhausted, nor will they be exhausted;
the four applications of mindfulness, up to and including the eightfold noble path, [neither have been exhausted...]

They have not been exhausted, are not being exhausted now, and will not be exhausted in the future; the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments have not been exhausted, are not being exhausted now, and will not be exhausted in the future;
the eight liberations up to the ten totalities have not been exhausted, are not being exhausted now, and will not be exhausted in the future; emptiness, signlessness, and...
The door of liberation of wishlessness has not been exhausted, is not being exhausted, and will not be exhausted;
from the Ground of Extreme Joy up to the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma, they have not been exhausted, are not being exhausted, and will not be exhausted;
all doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of samādhi have not been exhausted, are not being exhausted, and will not be exhausted.
The five eyes and the six supernormal powers have not been exhausted, are not being exhausted now, and will not be exhausted in the future;
likewise, the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha have not been exhausted, are not being exhausted now, and will not be exhausted in the future;
the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks have not been exhausted, are not being exhausted now, [and will not be exhausted in the future].

The quality of non-forgetfulness is not exhausted, has not been exhausted, and will not be exhausted; the state of constant abiding in equanimity is not exhausted, has not been exhausted, and will not be exhausted;

omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are not exhausted, have not been exhausted, and will not be exhausted; the entire bodhisattva-mahāsattva practice is not exhausted...

Exhaustion is not exhausted now, nor will it be exhausted; the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is not already exhausted, not being exhausted now, and not to be exhausted;
and the knowledge of all modes is not already exhausted, not being exhausted now, and not to be exhausted.
"Why is this? Because such dharmas as these are without arising, without cessation, and without abiding or change; how could they be conceived as having an end?
At that time, the World-Honored One extended his broad and long tongue from his mouth, covering his entire face; having displayed this mark of the tongue, he withdrew it back into his mouth.
He addressed Ānanda, saying: "What do you think?
If one possessed such a tongue-mark as this, would there be any falsehood in the speech they uttered?"
Ānanda replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"From this day forward, you should extensively expound such profound *prajñāpāramitā* for the fourfold assembly; analyze and reveal it, establish and ordain it, so that it may be easily understood."

Ānanda, you should know that within this profound *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) and the characteristics of all phenomena are extensively explained. Therefore, all individuals seeking the vehicle of the śrāvaka, those seeking the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha, and those seeking the unsurpassed vehicle should rely upon these dharma-gates taught in this profound *Prajñāpāramitā*, constantly and diligently practicing them without ever becoming weary.
If one can thus constantly and diligently practice and study, one shall swiftly realize the state sought by oneself. "Furthermore, Ānanda!

This profound *prajñāpāramitā* is that which enables the realization of the characteristics of all phenomena; it is that which enables the realization of all syllables; it is that which enables the realization of the gates of *dhāraṇī*. All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should constantly and diligently practice and study such gates of *dhāraṇī*."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva upholds such a dharanī gateway, they will swiftly be able to realize all forms of eloquence and the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
Ānanda, you should know this!
This profound sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom is the inexhaustible Dharma-treasury of all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present.

Therefore, I now clearly tell you: if there are those who uphold, recite, master, and thoroughly penetrate this profound Prajñāpāramitā, and contemplate it according to the principle, they are upholding the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Ānanda, you should know!

This profound *prajñāpāramitā* that I have taught is the firm footing for those who travel the path to enlightenment, and it is also the great *dhāraṇī* of all unsurpassed Buddha-dharmas. If you are able to receive and uphold this profound *prajñāpāramitā* *dhāraṇī*, you will then maintain all Buddha-dharmas in their entirety so as not to forget them, and you will bring great benefit to all sentient beings until the end of the future.
Chapter 66: The Inexhaustible. Second Division: The Inexhaustible Chapter, Number Sixty-Six. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti had this thought:
"This perfection of wisdom is most profound, and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is also most profound; I shall ask the Buddha about these two profound meanings."
Having formed this thought, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of the Buddhas; the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of the Buddhas is the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. Since both this *prajñāpāramitā* and the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of the Buddhas are equally most profound and inexhaustible, for what reason are these two said to be 'inexhaustible'?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha are both like space and cannot be exhausted, they are said to be inexhaustible."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva bring forth the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that form is inexhaustible;
they should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are inexhaustible.”
One should arouse the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that the sense base of the eye, up to the sense base of the mind, are all inexhaustible;
one should arouse the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that the sense base of form, up to the sense base of phenomena, are all inexhaustible;
one should arouse the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that the element of the eye, up to the element of the mind, are all inexhaustible.
One should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that the realm of form up to the realm of phenomena are all inexhaustible;
one should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that the realm of eye-consciousness up to the realm of mind-consciousness are all inexhaustible;
one should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that eye-contact up to mind-contact are all inexhaustible.

One should contemplate that the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including those produced with mind-contact as a condition, are all inexhaustible, and thereby bring forth the perfection of wisdom;
one should contemplate that the earth element, up to and including the consciousness element, are all inexhaustible, and thereby bring forth the perfection of wisdom;
one should contemplate that the causal condition, up to and including the sovereign condition, are all inexhaustible, and thereby bring forth the perfection of wisdom.
One should contemplate that everything from ignorance up to old age and death is inexhaustible, and thereby bring forth the perfection of wisdom;
one should contemplate that everything from the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom is inexhaustible, and thereby bring forth the perfection of wisdom;
one should contemplate that everything from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature is inexhaustible, and thereby bring forth the perfection of wisdom.
One should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that everything from true thusness up to the inconceivable realm is inexhaustible;
one should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path are all inexhaustible;
and one should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that everything from the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path is inexhaustible.
One should give rise to the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments are all inexhaustible;
one should give rise to the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that the eight liberations up to the ten totalities are all inexhaustible;
one should give rise to the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are all inexhaustible.
One should give rise to the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that the stage of pure vision up to the stage of the Tathāgata are all inexhaustible;
one should give rise to the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that the stage of extreme joy up to the stage of the cloud of dharma are all inexhaustible;
one should give rise to the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that all doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of samādhi are all inexhaustible.
One should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that the five eyes and the six supernormal powers are all inexhaustible;
one should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that the ten powers of a Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are all inexhaustible;
one should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that the thirty-two marks of a Great Being and the eighty minor marks are all inexhaustible.
One should contemplate that the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity are both inexhaustible, and thereby bring forth the perfection of wisdom;
one should contemplate that all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects are all inexhaustible, and thereby bring forth the perfection of wisdom;
one should contemplate that the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha are all inexhaustible, and thereby bring forth the perfection of wisdom.
One should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that all practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are inexhaustible;
one should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas is inexhaustible;
and one should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that even the knowledge of all modes is inexhaustible.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that form is inexhaustible like space;
they should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are inexhaustible like space."
In this way, up to and including the observation that the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) is like space and inexhaustible, one brings forth the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should, observing that formations conditioned by ignorance are as inexhaustible as space, bring forth the perfection of wisdom;
they should, observing that consciousness conditioned by formations is as inexhaustible as space, bring forth the perfection of wisdom;
they should, observing that name-and-form conditioned by consciousness is as inexhaustible as space, bring forth the perfection of wisdom.
One should contemplate that name-and-form conditions the six sense bases as being inexhaustible like space, thereby bringing forth the perfection of wisdom;
one should contemplate that the six sense bases condition contact as being inexhaustible like space, thereby bringing forth the perfection of wisdom;
one should contemplate that contact conditions feeling as being inexhaustible like space, thereby bringing forth the perfection of wisdom.
One should contemplate that feeling conditions craving as being as inexhaustible as space, thereby giving rise to the perfection of wisdom;
one should contemplate that craving conditions grasping as being as inexhaustible as space, thereby giving rise to the perfection of wisdom;
one should contemplate that grasping conditions becoming as being as inexhaustible as space, thereby giving rise to the perfection of wisdom.
One should contemplate that birth conditioned by existence is as inexhaustible as space, and thereby bring forth the perfection of wisdom;
one should contemplate that old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair conditioned by birth are as inexhaustible as space, and thereby bring forth the perfection of wisdom.
“Subhūti! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should thus bring forth the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti!”

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas observe the twelve links of dependent origination in this manner, they remain far removed from the two extremes; this is the sublime contemplation unique to the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

"Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas sit beneath the bodhi tree upon the vajra-seat and contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination as they truly are—just as space is inexhaustible—they are able to realize the knowledge of all modes."

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of a practice as inexhaustible as space, brings forth the perfection of wisdom and contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination as they truly are, they will not fall into the levels of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

“Subhūti! Any individuals belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who regress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment have all failed to rely upon the skillful mental engagement that brings forth the perfection of wisdom.”

Because they do not understand this, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) bring forth the perfection of wisdom by abiding in a practice as inexhaustible as space, and observe the twelve links of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) as they truly are?

Subhūti! If any sons of good family or daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle should regress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, it is entirely because they have distanced themselves from the skillful means that give rise to the perfection of wisdom.

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to attain non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, it is entirely due to their reliance on the skillful means that induce the perfection of wisdom.

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom by relying on such skillful means, they evoke the perfection of wisdom through a mode of abiding that is as inexhaustible as space; they observe the twelve links of dependent origination as they truly are. By virtue of these causes and conditions, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to swiftly fulfill the profound perfection of wisdom.

"Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas contemplate the dharma of dependent origination in this way, they do not perceive any phenomenon arising without a cause, nor do they perceive any phenomenon ceasing without a cause. They do not perceive any phenomenon whose nature and characteristics are eternally abiding, neither arising nor ceasing. They do not perceive any phenomenon that possesses a self, a sentient being—and so on, as extensively explained—up to a knower or a seer. They do not perceive any phenomenon as either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or non-tranquil, or secluded or non-secluded."
"Subhūti! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should observe dependent origination in this manner and practice the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti!"
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom by observing the dharma-gate of dependent origination as it truly is,
at that time the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive form as either permanent or impermanent,
as either pleasant or painful, as either self or non-self, as either pure or impure, or as tranquil.
Whether they are non-quiescent or distant or not distant, one likewise does not perceive feeling, perception, formations,
or consciousness as permanent or impermanent, as pleasant or painful,
as self or non-self, as pure or impure, as quiescent or non-quiescent, or as distant or not distant.
Free from [such views], they likewise do not perceive omniscience as either permanent or impermanent,
as pleasure or suffering, as self or non-self, as pure or impure,
as tranquil or untranquil, or as secluded or non-secluded.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner, at that time, although the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, they do not perceive any *prajñāpāramitā* being practiced; nor do they perceive any dharma that can perceive the *prajñāpāramitā* being practiced; nor do they perceive such non-perception.”

Although they practice the perfections of meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity, they do not perceive any such practice of the perfections from meditative concentration to generosity; nor do they perceive any dharma that can perceive the practice of the perfections from meditative concentration to generosity; nor do they perceive even such non-perception.

In this way, even when cultivating the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), one does not perceive any such cultivation of the knowledge of all modes; nor does one perceive any dharma that can perceive the cultivation of the knowledge of all modes; nor does one perceive such non-perception itself; nor does one perceive any dharma capable of severing the continuity of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of all afflictions.
Subhūti! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by means of non-apprehension regarding all phenomena, should practice the perfection of wisdom.

"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension regarding all phenomena, at that time Māra the Evil One gives rise to great sorrow and suffering; he is tormented by resentment and bitterness as if an arrow had pierced his heart."
"It is, for example, like a person whose parents have suddenly passed away; their body and mind are tormented by grief, and the Evil Māra is just the same.
Thereupon, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One!"

Is it because a certain evil Māra, seeing the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension regarding all phenomena, gives rise to great sorrow and suffering, feeling as vexed and tormented as if an arrow had entered his heart?
"Is it the case that all the evil Māras throughout the entire trichiliocosm are likewise so?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"All the evil Māras filling the entire trichiliocosm are likewise so; each is unable to remain at ease upon their own seat."

"Subhūti! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should constantly abide in the subtle practice and dwelling of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva can abide in this manner, the gods, humans, asuras, and others of the world will never be able to find any fault in them, nor will they be able to disturb, harass, or obstruct them."

Therefore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they should diligently abide in the subtle practice and dwelling of the profound perfection of wisdom.

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can correctly abide in the subtle practice and dwelling of the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they will be able to cultivate and fulfill the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom. If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can correctly practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they will be able to fully cultivate and fulfill all the perfections.”
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,

how can a bodhisattva mahāsattva correctly practice the profound perfection of wisdom, and thereby fulfill the perfections of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom without error, they practice giving with a mind associated with the knowledge of all modes; furthermore, they take these merits of giving and, together with all sentient beings, dedicate them toward the knowledge of all modes.”
"Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom correctly, fulfills the perfection of generosity."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom without error, they practice ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom with a mind associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*); furthermore, they take these merits of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom and dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward the knowledge of all modes.

Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to correctly practice the profound perfection of wisdom, thereby fulfilling the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas are able to practice the profound perfection of wisdom correctly, they are then able to cultivate and fulfill the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 458. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Chapter Sixty-seven: Mutual Inclusion. Part Two, Chapter Sixty-seven: Mutual Inclusion. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of generosity, encompass the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving with a mind free from attachment and free from stinginess, and dedicates this giving together with all sentient beings toward omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), dwelling in acts of body, speech, and mind characterized by loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, remaining free from all transgressions.”
"Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of generosity, takes up the perfection of ethical discipline. Subhūti!"

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving with a mind free from attachment and free from stinginess, and dedicates this giving together with all sentient beings toward omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), should there be recipients who are other wicked sentient beings who unreasonably revile, resent, harm, or insult them, the bodhisattva does not give rise toward them to any altered state of mind such as anger, resentment, or malice, nor does he retaliate through body or speech; rather, he gives rise only to a mind of pity and compassion, responding with kind and affectionate words, shame, and humble apology.
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of generosity, takes up the perfection of patience.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin!”

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving with a mind free from attachment and free from stinginess, and dedicates this giving together with all sentient beings toward the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), even if there should be other wicked sentient beings who receive it and treat them unreasonably by reviling, harming, or insulting them, the bodhisattva at that time forms this thought:

"All those who perform such kinds of actions will in turn experience such kinds of results for themselves; I should not now take account of their deeds and neglect the cultivation of my own practice."
He further thought: "I should cause my mind of equanimity and my mind of generosity toward him and other sentient beings to increase even more, without any sense of regret or attachment."
Having formed this thought, he arouses superior physical and mental diligence and constantly practices giving and relinquishment. Subhūti!
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of generosity, encompasses the perfection of diligence.

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving with a mind free from attachment and free from stinginess, and dedicates this giving together with all sentient beings toward omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), maintaining a mind undistracted regarding the recipients and other objects, seeking neither sensual desires nor the three realms nor the two vehicles, but seeking only the fruit of Buddhahood.
“Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of generosity, takes up the perfection of meditative concentration. Subhūti!”

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices giving with a mind free from attachment and free from stinginess, and dedicates this giving together with all sentient beings toward the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), observing that the recipients, the giver, and the gift are all like illusory phenomena, seeing no benefit or harm to sentient beings through this giving, because they have realized that all phenomena are empty in the ultimate sense (paramārtha-śūnyatā).
"Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of giving, embraces the perfection of wisdom.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again, saying:

“Bhagavān! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of ethical discipline, encompass the perfections of generosity, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of ethical discipline and performs the three kinds of meritorious actions of body, speech, and mind, through these meritorious actions they abstain from taking life up to and including wrong views; they do not seek the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but seek only unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

At that time, the bodhisattva dwells securely in pure ethical discipline and extensively practices generosity, bestowing upon sentient beings whatever things they require until all needs are met. Furthermore, taking these roots of goodness from such generosity, he dedicates them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), seeking neither the fruits of the śrāvaka nor the pratyekabuddha.
"Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of ethical discipline, embraces the perfection of generosity. Subhūti!"

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), and various sentient beings should come vying with one another to sever the limbs and members of that bodhisattva, each taking them away, the bodhisattva does not give rise to even a single thought of anger or resentment toward them, but instead reflects:
"I have now obtained a vast and sublime benefit; namely, by relinquishing this foul-smelling, fragile body, I shall attain the pure, vajra-like body of a Buddha."
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of ethical discipline, fully embraces the perfection of patience.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin!”
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of ethical discipline, with physical and mental diligence constant and uninterrupted, dons the armor of great compassion, and makes this vast vow:

"All sentient beings are submerged in the terrifying, violent, and difficult-to-cross ocean of suffering of birth and death; I shall pull them out and establish them within the realm of the deathless."
"Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of ethical discipline, takes up the perfection of diligence. Subhūti!"

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), although they enter the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), or the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), they do not fall into the levels of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor do they realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Instead, acting according to the power of their original vows, they form this thought:

"All sentient beings are submerged in the terrifying, violent, and difficult-to-cross ocean of suffering of birth and death; since I now abide in pure morality (*śīla*), I shall employ skillful means to induce pure meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and shall certainly uproot them and place them within the realm of non-death."
"Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of ethical discipline, fully embraces the perfection of meditative concentration. Subhūti!"

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), they do not perceive any phenomenon—whether wholesome or unwholesome, defined or undefined, with outflows or without outflows, mundane or supramundane, conditioned or unconditioned, falling within the realm of the numerable or the innumerable, or falling within the realm of the characterized or the uncharacterized—but observes only that all phenomena are not separate from suchness (*tathatā*), extending broadly even to the inconceivable realm (*acintya-dhātu*). Furthermore, even these [states] such as suchness cannot be apprehended. By means of this skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*), they do not fall into the levels of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but seek only unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
“Subhūti! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of ethical discipline, embraces the perfection of wisdom.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of patience, encompass the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), from the first generation of the mind of awakening until sitting upon the seat of supreme enlightenment, should there be various kinds of sentient beings who, through improper means, revile, despise, harm, or insult them, even going so far as to sever their limbs and carry them away, the bodhisattva at that time feels no malice or resentment whatsoever.

They think only this: 'These sentient beings are deeply pitiable; afflicted by the demonic disease of the afflictions (kleśa), their bodies and minds are disturbed and they lack self-mastery. Having no refuge and no protector, they are oppressed by poverty and suffering. I shall give them whatever they require—food and drink, clothing, and various other kinds of wealth and requisites—so that they may have no lack. "

Furthermore, taking these roots of goodness from such giving, with non-apprehension as the skillful means, one dedicates them together with all sentient beings toward the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). At the time of dedication, no dualistic mind arises, such as: "Who is it that dedicates?"
"To what is it dedicated? Subhūti!
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of patience, takes up the perfection of generosity."

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of patience, from the first generation of the mind of awakening until sitting upon the seat of sublime enlightenment, during that interval, even for the sake of saving his own life, he shall never harm any sentient being, nor shall he give rise to any evil or false views.”

When a bodhisattva thus cultivates pure ethical discipline, they do not seek the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha. Furthermore, taking these roots of virtue from such pure ethical discipline as their means through the realization of non-apprehension, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*). At the time of this dedication, no dualistic mind arises, such as asking: "Who is it that dedicates?"
"To what is it dedicated? Subhūti!
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of patience, takes up the perfection of ethical discipline."
“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of patience and exerts courageous and superior diligence, they should constantly reflect:
‘If even a single sentient being were at a distance of one yojana, or ten, or a hundred, or even up to [innumerable]—’”
Beyond the measure of *yojanas*, whether outside a single world-system, or beyond ten, a hundred,
