or even an infinite number of world-systems, I shall certainly go to those who are capable of being saved, employing skillful means to instruct and transform them,
so that they may receive and uphold either the eight precepts, the five, the ten, or the complete set of training rules.
Whether it be to establish them in pure observation, the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), the eighth stage, the fruit of stream-entry,
once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, or solitary enlightenment; or to establish them in the various bodhisattva stages,
up to and including unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment— even for these they do not decline the labor, let alone for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings.
‘May I never grow weary while causing immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to obtain benefit and happiness!

Furthermore, taking such roots of virtue from diligence as a means through non-apprehension, one should together with all sentient beings dedicate them toward omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*). At the time of dedication, no dualistic mind arises, thinking: ‘Who is it that dedicates?’”
"To what is it dedicated? Subhūti!
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of patience, fully embraces the perfection of diligence."

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of patience, with mind collected and undistracted, free from desire, evil, and unwholesome states, accompanied by applied and sustained thought, born of seclusion, joy and happiness, enters the first dhyāna—and so on, as extensively described, up to entering the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling—then whatever minds, mental factors, and roots of goodness arise within these various meditative absorptions, he collects them all together and, by means of non-apprehension, dedicates them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*). At the time of dedication, no dualistic mind arises, such that one wonders: ‘Who is it that dedicates?’”
"To what is it dedicated? Subhūti!
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of patience, encompasses the perfection of meditative concentration."

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) and dwells in the contemplation of dharmas (*dharmānupaśyanā*) among all phenomena—whether observing all phenomena through the aspect of detachment, the aspect of tranquility, the aspect of inexhaustibility, or the aspect of ultimate cessation—he does not realize that tranquility prematurely; rather, he proceeds until he sits upon the sublime seat of awakening (*bodhimanda*), realizes unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), and from that seat rises to turn the sublime wheel of Dharma for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings.”

Furthermore, taking these roots of goodness of such sublime wisdom and employing the method of non-apprehension, one dedicates them together with all sentient beings toward the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). At the time of dedication, no dualistic mind arises, such as: "Who is it that dedicates?"
"To what is it dedicated? Subhūti!
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of patience, takes up the perfection of wisdom."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha,

saying: “World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of diligence, encompass the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, meditative concentration, and wisdom?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence, his body and mind are diligent without ever ceasing, and he seeks all wholesome dharmas without weariness, constantly thinking:
'I must certainly attain the knowledge of all modes; it is not possible that I shall not attain it.'"
This bodhisattva mahāsattva, desiring to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, constantly makes this vow:
"If even a single sentient being is beyond one *yojana*, or ten, or a hundred, or even immeasurable *yojanas*;

or if they are beyond a single world-system, or ten, or a hundred, or even immeasurable world-systems—whosoever is capable of being delivered, I shall certainly go to them and skillfully teach and transform them, causing them to abide in the vehicle of the śrāvakas, or the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, or the unsurpassed vehicle, or causing them to undertake and practice the ten paths of wholesome action."
"In this way, they satisfy them all with the gift of Dharma and the gift of material wealth, skillfully guiding and gathering them in.

Furthermore, taking these roots of goodness from such giving, they use the method of non-apprehension to dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*). At the time of dedication, no dualistic mind arises, asking: 'Who is it that dedicates?'"
"To what is it dedicated? Subhūti!
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of diligence, fully embraces the perfection of generosity."

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence, from the first generation of the mind until sitting upon the seat of sublime enlightenment, they personally abstain from taking life and also encourage others to abstain from taking life; they correctly praise the dharma of abstaining from taking life and joyfully extol those who abstain from taking life.

In this manner, up to and including, they personally abstain from wrong views and also encourage others to abstain from wrong views; they correctly praise the dharma of abstaining from wrong views and joyfully extol those who abstain from wrong views.”

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, upholding this perfection of pure ethical discipline, does not seek the fruits of the three realms or the two vehicles; rather, employing the skillful means of non-apprehension, they dedicate it together with all sentient beings toward omniscience (*sarvajñājñāna*). At the time of dedication, no dualistic mind arises, such as: "Who is it that dedicates?"
"To what is it dedicated? Subhūti!
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of diligence, takes up the perfection of ethical discipline."

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence, from the first generation of the mind of awakening until sitting upon the seat of sublime enlightenment, should humans or non-humans come during that interval to harass and provoke him, or even to hack, pierce, and sever his limbs and joints, taking them away as they please, the bodhisattva at that time does not form this thought:
‘Who is hacking and piercing me?’”
"Who is cutting me?
Who is carrying me away?
He should think only this:

"I have now attained a vast and sublime benefit; for the sake of benefiting me, those sentient beings have come to cut and sever my body into its various limbs and members. Yet, I originally received this body for the sake of all sentient beings; thus, they have come to take what is their own and thereby accomplished my purpose."

"In this way, the bodhisattva reflects with thorough discernment upon the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmas*) while practicing patience (*kṣānti*). Sustaining this perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), they do not seek the levels of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha; rather, employing the skillful means of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), they dedicate it together with all sentient beings toward omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*). At the time of dedication, no dualistic mind arises, such as: 'Who is dedicating?'"
"To what is it dedicated? Subhūti!
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of diligence, takes up the perfection of patience."

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence and diligently cultivates the various meditative concentrations—namely, being free from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained thought, born of seclusion, joy and happiness, entering the first dhyāna; and so on, as extensively described, up to entering the fourth dhyāna;

and giving rise to the perception of bestowing happiness toward all sentient beings, applying mental attention to enter the immeasurable state of loving-kindness (maitrī), and so on, as extensively described, up to entering the immeasurable state of equanimity (upekṣā);”

Regarding all forms, they give rise to the perception of revulsion toward coarseness and, through mental attention, enter the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space; this is explained at length up to their entry into the meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling.

Although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate such dhyānas, immeasurables, formless attainments, and the absorption of cessation, they do not grasp the ripening fruit thereof; rather, in accordance with the beings who are ready to be transformed, they take birth within those realms as places to bring about benefit and happiness.

Once they have been born there, he gathers them in through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) and, by skillful means, establishes them so that they diligently practice and train in everything from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

Relying on these meditative concentrations, this bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to superior supernormal powers, traveling from one buddha-field to another to attend upon and make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, inquiring about the profound nature and characteristics of all phenomena, and diligently cultivating and bringing forth sublime roots of goodness.

Taking these roots of goodness as the means through non-apprehension, one dedicates them together with all sentient beings toward the knowledge of all modes; at the time of dedication, no dualistic mind arises, such as: "Who is it that dedicates?"
"To what is it dedicated?
Subhūti, this is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of diligence, takes up the perfection of meditative concentration."
“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence, they do not perceive the perfection of generosity,
up to and including the perfection of wisdom, whether as a name, as a thing, or as an intrinsic nature.”
If, regarding characteristics, one does not perceive the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path—whether by name, entity, nature, or characteristic;
if one does not perceive internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of self-nature—whether by name, entity, nature, or characteristic;
and if one does not perceive suchness up to the inconceivable realm—whether...
Whether as name, entity, nature, or characteristic, they do not perceive the Noble Truths of suffering,
origin, cessation, or the path— whether as name, entity, nature, or characteristic; nor do they perceive the four dhyānas,
the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments— whether as name, entity, nature, or characteristic.
One does not perceive the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality, whether by name, entity, nature, or characteristic;
one does not perceive the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata, whether by name, entity, nature, or characteristic;
one does not perceive the stage of extreme joy up to the stage of the Dharma-cloud, whether by name or entity.
Whether as essence or characteristic, one does not perceive the names, things, essences, or characteristics of any of the *dhāraṇī* gates or *samādhi* gates;
nor does one perceive the names, things, essences, or characteristics of the five eyes or the six supernormal powers;
nor does one perceive the Tathāgata’s ten powers, up to and including the [ten]...
Regarding the eight unique qualities of a Buddha—whether by name, entity, nature, or characteristic—he does not perceive them;
nor does he perceive the thirty-two marks of a great man or the eighty secondary signs—whether by name, entity, nature, or characteristic;
nor does he perceive the quality of non-forgetfulness or the nature of constant equanimity—whether by name, entity, or [characteristic].

Whether by way of nature, or characteristic, one does not perceive omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)—neither their name, nor their substance, nor their nature, nor their characteristic;

one does not perceive the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha—neither their name, nor their substance, nor their nature, nor their characteristic; and one does not perceive any bodhisattva.
Whether by name, substance, nature, or characteristic, the Mahāsattva does not perceive the unsurpassed, perfect,
and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as a name, a substance, a nature, or a characteristic;
nor does he perceive the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) as a name, a substance, a nature, or a characteristic— and so on, up to...
Not perceiving any phenomena— whether by name, substance, nature, or characteristic— one does not give rise to conceptualizations regarding these phenomena,
remaining without attachment, as described in the teaching on "the ability to act."

Furthermore, by means of these accumulated roots of virtue, employing the method of non-apprehension, one dedicates them together with all sentient beings toward the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñājñāna). At the time of dedication, no dualistic mind arises, such as: "Who is it that dedicates?"
"To what is it dedicated? Subhūti!
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of diligence, takes up the perfection of wisdom."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration, encompass the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and wisdom?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā), they abide in the giving of material wealth and the Dharma to all sentient beings; that is to say, free from desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained examination, born of seclusion, joyful and blissful, they enter the first dhyāna, and so on in detail up to entering the fourth dhyāna;

toward all sentient beings, they give rise to the perception of happiness, apply their attention, and enter the immeasurable state of loving-kindness (maitrī-apramāṇa), and so on in detail up to entering the immeasurable state of equanimity (upekṣā-apramāṇa)."

Regarding all forms, he gives rise to the perception of their coarseness and, through mental attention, enters the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space; this is explained in detail up to his entry into the meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), with an undistracted mind, proclaims the sublime Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, practicing both the gift of material goods and the gift of Dharma.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly practices the giving of material goods and the Dharma themselves, and also constantly encourages others to practice the giving of material goods and the Dharma; they always correctly praise the practice of giving material goods and the Dharma, and always joyfully laud those who practice the giving of material goods and the Dharma.

Taking these roots of goodness, they do not seek the levels of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; rather, using non-apprehension as their skillful means, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience (*sarvajñājñāna*). At the time of dedication, no dualistic mind arises, such that one wonders: "Who is it that dedicates?"
"To what is it dedicated? Subhūti!
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of meditative concentration, takes up the perfection of generosity."

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of meditative concentration and upholds pure ethical discipline, they never give rise to a mind accompanied by greed, a mind accompanied by hatred, a mind accompanied by delusion, a mind accompanied by harmfulness, a mind accompanied by stinginess, a mind accompanied by envy, or a mind accompanied by the violation of pure ethical discipline; rather, they always give rise to mental attention accompanied by the knowledge of all modes.”

Furthermore, taking these roots of goodness from such pure ethical discipline, one does not seek the levels of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; rather, employing the skillful means of non-apprehension, one dedicates them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*). At the time of this dedication, no dualistic mind arises, asking: "Who is it that dedicates?"
"To what is it dedicated? Subhūti!
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of meditative concentration, fully embraces the perfection of ethical discipline."

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of meditative concentration and practices patience, they contemplate form as being like a mass of foam, feeling as being like a bubble on the water, perception as being like a mirage, mental formations as being like a plantain tree, and consciousness as being like a magical illusion.”
While performing this contemplation, the perception that the five aggregates of clinging are not solid or substantial constantly manifests before him. He further reflects:
"All phenomena are empty; they are neither self nor belonging to a self. Who is there to cut or dismember?"
Who undergoes being cut?
Who is able to revile?
Who undergoes being reviled?
Who, moreover, would give rise to anger and resentment therein?
Whose form is it? Whose feeling is it?
Whose perception is this perception?
Whose volitional formations are these volitional formations?
Whose consciousness is this consciousness?

"In this way, when a bodhisattva dwells securely in the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*) and is able to maintain patience while scrutinizing phenomena, they further take these accumulated roots of virtue and, using the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*). At the time of dedication, no dualistic mind arises—namely, the thought: 'Who is it that dedicates?'"
"To what is it dedicated? Subhūti!
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of meditative concentration, takes up the perfection of patience."

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of meditative concentration, exerts diligent effort and, free from sensual desires and unwholesome states, accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, enters and dwells in the first dhyāna;

and with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, with internal clarity and mental unification, free from applied and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of concentration, enters and dwells in the second dhyāna;”

Detached from joy, he dwells in equanimity, possessed of mindfulness and clear comprehension; he experiences happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones say, "He who has equanimity and is mindful dwells happily," and thus enters and abides in the third dhyāna.

Having abandoned pleasure and abandoned pain, and with the prior disappearance of joy and sorrow, he enters and abides in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is characterized by purity of equanimity and mindfulness.

In this way, the bodhisattva cultivates all types of meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, and attainments (*samāpatti*); therein, being able to refrain from grasping at their signs, they give rise to various supernormal powers of the knowledge of miraculous feats (*ṛddhividhi-jñānābhijñā*) and can perform boundless great miraculous transformations.

Alternatively, they may further develop the supernormal power of the divine ear, a clear and pure hearing that transcends that of humans and devas, enabling them to hear, as it truly is, the various sounds of sentient and insentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions.

Alternatively, they may develop the supernormal power of knowledge of others' minds, whereby they can know, as it truly is, the minds and mental factors of other sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions.

Or, they may develop the supernormal power of knowledge of past lives, whereby they recollect and know, as it truly is, the various past-life events of immeasurable sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions.

Alternatively, they may further give rise to the supernormal power of the divine eye, which is clear, pure, and surpasses that of human or celestial eyes; they are able to see, as it truly is, the various forms and images of sentient and insentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions, and even know their karmic fruits exactly as they are.

Abiding in these five extraordinary supernormal powers, this bodhisattva mahāsattva proceeds from one buddha-field to another, attending upon and making offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; he inquires about the profound meaning of the Tathāgata’s Dharma, extensively plants immeasurable and subtle roots of goodness, matures sentient beings, purifies buddha-fields, and diligently cultivates the various supreme practices of a bodhisattva.

Taking these roots of goodness, they do not seek the levels of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; rather, using non-apprehension as their skillful means, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*). At the time of dedication, no dualistic mind arises, such as: "Who is dedicating?"
"To what is it dedicated? Subhūti!
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of meditative concentration, takes up the perfection of diligence."
“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of meditative concentration, they perceive that form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are unapprehendable;
they perceive that the sense base of the eye up to the sense base of the mind are unapprehendable.”

One contemplates that the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) up to the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) is unapprehendable; one contemplates that the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) up to the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is unapprehendable;

one contemplates that the form-element (*rūpadhātu*) up to the phenomena-element (*dharmadhātu*) is unapprehendable; one contemplates that the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) up to the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*) is unapprehendable;
one contemplates that eye-contact (*cakṣuḥsaṃsparśa*) up to mind-contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*) is unapprehendable; one contemplates eye-contact...
The various feelings produced with conditions as their basis, up to and including those produced with mental contact as their basis, are unapprehendable;

one contemplates that the earth element, up to and including the consciousness element, is unapprehendable; one contemplates that the causal condition, up to and including the sovereign condition, is unapprehendable;
one contemplates that ignorance, up to and including old age and death, is unapprehendable; and one contemplates the perfection of giving.

From the many up to the *prajñāpāramitā*, they are unapprehendable; from the contemplation of internal emptiness up to the contemplation of the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature, they are unapprehendable;
from the contemplation of suchness up to the contemplation of the inconceivable realm, they are unapprehendable;
from the contemplation of the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, they are unapprehendable; from the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness up to...
The eight branches of the noble path are unattainable; one contemplates that the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments are unattainable;
one contemplates that the eight liberations up to the ten universal bases are unattainable;

one contemplates that the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are unattainable; one contemplates [the stages] from the stage of pure observation up to the stage of suchness...
The ground of coming cannot be apprehended; one cannot apprehend the observation of the Ground of Extreme Joy up to the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma;
one cannot apprehend the observation of all doors of dhāraṇī and doors of samādhi; one cannot apprehend the observation of the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
and one cannot apprehend the observation of the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
One can apprehend them, yet one cannot apprehend the thirty-two marks of a great man or the eighty secondary signs;
one cannot apprehend the quality of non-forgetfulness or the nature of constant equanimity; one cannot apprehend all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, or the knowledge of all aspects;
nor can one apprehend the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
They are unapprehendable; one contemplates that the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are unapprehendable,
one contemplates that the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas is unapprehendable, one contemplates that the knowledge of all modes is unapprehendable,
one contemplates that the realm of the conditioned is unapprehendable, and one contemplates that the realm of the unconditioned is unapprehendable.

"In this way, because the Bodhisattva perceives that all phenomena are unobtainable, they are without action; because they are without action, they are without creation; because they are without creation, they are without arising; because they are without arising, they are without cessation; because they are without cessation, they are without grasping; and because they are without grasping, they are ultimately pure, eternally abiding, and immutable."

Why is this? Because all phenomena—whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear—abide in the nature of reality (dharmatā), the realm of reality (dharmadhātu), and the stability of reality (dharmaniyāmatā); they are without arising or ceasing, eternally unchanging.

The mind of this bodhisattva mahāsattva is always undisturbed; at all times, they dwell securely in mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes, observing that the nature of all phenomena is entirely non-existent as it truly is.

Furthermore, taking these accumulated roots of goodness as the basis, by means of the method of non-apprehension, one should together with all sentient beings dedicate them toward omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*). At the time of dedication, no dualistic mind arises, such as: "Who is it that dedicates?"
"To what is it dedicated? Subhūti!
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of meditative concentration, takes up the perfection of wisdom."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha again,

saying: “World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of wisdom, encompass the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of wisdom, they contemplate all phenomena as empty and non-existent."
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwell in the perfection of wisdom and contemplate all phenomena as empty and non-existent?”
“Subhūti! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom, contemplate internal emptiness and find that the nature of internal emptiness cannot be apprehended;

they contemplate external emptiness and find that the nature of external emptiness cannot be apprehended; they contemplate internal-and-external emptiness and find that the nature of internal-and-external emptiness [cannot be apprehended].”

The nature of intrinsic nature is unapprehendable; the emptiness of emptiness, the emptiness of the emptiness of emptiness, and the nature of the emptiness of emptiness are unapprehendable. The emptiness of the great, the emptiness of the great emptiness, and the nature of the emptiness of the great are unapprehendable.

The emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of the ultimate emptiness, and the nature of the emptiness of the ultimate are unapprehendable. The emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the conditioned emptiness, and the nature of the emptiness of the conditioned are unapprehendable.
The emptiness of the unconditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned emptiness, and the nature of the emptiness of the unconditioned are unapprehendable. The emptiness of the absolute...
Ultimate emptiness is unapprehendable; the emptiness of the limitless is unapprehendable in its nature as the emptiness of the limitless;

the emptiness of dispersion and non-dispersion is unapprehendable in its nature as the emptiness of dispersion and non-dispersion; the emptiness of intrinsic nature is unapprehendable in its nature as the emptiness of intrinsic nature;

the emptiness of self-characteristics and common characteristics is unapprehendable in its nature as the emptiness of self-characteristics and common characteristics; the emptiness of all phenomena is one...
The emptiness of all phenomena is unapprehendable.
Abiding thus in these fourteen kinds of emptiness, the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend form as either empty or non-empty;
they do not apprehend feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either empty or non-empty.

One does not apprehend the sense base of the eye, up to the sense base of the mind, as either empty or not empty; one does not apprehend the sense base of form, up to the sense base of mental phenomena, as either empty or not empty;
one does not apprehend the eye element, up to the mind element, as either empty or not empty;
one does not apprehend the form element, up to the mental-phenomena element, as either empty or not empty; and one does not apprehend the eye-consciousness element.
...up to the element of mental consciousness, whether it be empty or not empty; one does not apprehend eye-contact up to mind-contact, whether they be empty or not empty;
one does not apprehend the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition, whether they be empty or not empty;
one does not apprehend the earth element up to the consciousness element...
If emptiness were not empty, one could not apprehend anything from conditions up to the dominant condition as being either empty or not empty;
one could not apprehend anything from ignorance up to old age and death as being either empty or not empty;
one could not apprehend anything from the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom as being either empty or not empty; and one could not apprehend internal emptiness.
...up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature; whether it be empty or not empty, one does not apprehend suchness up to the inconceivable realm;
whether it be empty or not empty, one does not apprehend the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
whether it be empty or not empty, one does not apprehend the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path.
Amogha, one does not apprehend the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments as either empty or non-empty;
one does not apprehend the eight liberations up to the ten totalities as either empty or non-empty;
one does not apprehend the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—as either empty or non-empty; nor does one apprehend purity.
One does not apprehend the stages from the Stage of the Earth up to the Stage of the Tathāgata as either empty or non-empty;
one does not apprehend the Stages from the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma as either empty or non-empty;

one does not apprehend any of the doors of dhāraṇī or the doors of samādhi as either empty or non-empty; nor does one apprehend the five eyes or the six supernormal powers as either empty or non-empty.
In emptiness, one cannot apprehend the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, whether as empty or non-empty;
one cannot apprehend the thirty-two marks of a great man or the eighty secondary signs, whether as empty or non-empty;
one cannot apprehend the quality of non-forgetfulness or the nature of constant equanimity, whether as empty or non-empty; one cannot apprehend them.
Whether omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is empty or not empty;
whether the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha is empty or not empty; whether the entire conduct of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is empty or not empty;
or whether the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is empty or not empty—none of these can be apprehended.
Whether form is empty or not empty, one does not apprehend the knowledge of all modes as either empty or not empty;

whether the realm of the conditioned is empty or not empty, one does not apprehend it as either empty or not empty; whether the realm of the unconditioned is empty or not empty, one does not apprehend it as either empty or not empty.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom, contemplates all the gifts given by sentient beings—whether food, drink, or other requisites—as empty.
Whether it be the one who gives, that which is given, the merit of giving, or the fruit of giving—all such things are likewise contemplated as empty.
At that time, because the bodhisattva abides in the contemplation of emptiness, there is no room for greed or stinginess to arise.

Why is this? Because when these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), from the first generation of the mind of awakening until sitting upon the seat of sublime enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), such conceptual discriminations do not arise at all.

Just as the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas never for a moment give rise to a mind of attachment or a mind of stinginess, so too it is with this bodhisattva mahāsattva: while practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, minds of attachment and stinginess never arise at all.

One should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is the teacher of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; it enables the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to give rise to no conceptualizations or discriminations, so that all their acts of giving are free from attachment.

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva takes these roots of goodness and, employing the method of non-apprehension, dedicates them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*). At the time of dedication, no dualistic mind arises, such as: "Who is it that dedicates?"
"To what is it dedicated? Subhūti!
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of wisdom, embraces the perfection of generosity."

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of wisdom and maintains pure ethical discipline, there is no possibility for the minds of any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or the like to arise.”

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are all unapprehendable; the mind that dedicates [merit] toward them is also unapprehendable; and even the physical and verbal discipline for dedicating toward those stages is unapprehendable.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom, from the first generation of the mind of awakening until sitting upon the seat of sublime enlightenment, in the interval between these two points, personally abstains from taking life and also encourages others to abstain from taking life; they correctly praise the dharma of abstaining from taking life and joyfully extol those who abstain from taking life.

In this manner, up to and including the point of personally abstaining from wrong views, they also encourage others to abstain from wrong views, correctly praise the dharma of abstaining from wrong views, and joyfully extol those who abstain from wrong views.

When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva takes up these roots of goodness born of maintaining pure ethical discipline, they do not seek the three realms or the teachings of the two vehicles; rather, employing the skillful means of non-apprehension, they dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience (*sarvajñā-jñāna*). At the time of dedication, no dualistic mind arises, such as: "Who is it that dedicates?"
"To what is it dedicated? Subhūti!
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of wisdom, takes up the perfection of ethical discipline."
“Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of wisdom and gives rise to the patience that accords with reality, having attained this patience, they constantly reflect:

‘Among all phenomena, there is not a single phenomenon that arises or ceases, is born or ages, is sick or dies; nor is there one who reviles or is reviled, one who slanders or is slandered, or one who cuts, hacks, pierces, binds, afflicts, or harms, nor anything that is cut, hacked, pierced, bound, afflicted, or harmed. All such natures and characteristics are empty; one should not engage in false conceptualization or discrimination regarding them.’”

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva has attained this patience, from the first generation of the mind of awakening until sitting upon the sublime seat of enlightenment, even if all classes of sentient beings were to come during that interval to revile, slander, and humiliate them, or to harm, strike, throw, cut, hack, and pierce them with various swords, staves, tiles, stones, clods of earth, and so forth, even to the point of dismembering their limbs and joints.
At that time, the Bodhisattva’s mind remained unchanging, and he thought only this: "How truly strange!

Within the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), there is absolutely no such thing as reviling, slandering, insulting, or inflicting harm; yet sentient beings, through their deluded conceptualization and discrimination, grasp at these as being real, thereby giving rise to various afflictions and evil karmas, and undergoing intense suffering in the present and the future."

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva, taking these roots of goodness as a skillful means through non-apprehension, dedicates them together with all sentient beings toward the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). At the time of dedication, no dualistic mind arises, such as: "Who is it that dedicates?"
"To what is it dedicated? Subhūti!
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of wisdom, fully embraces the perfection of patience."

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom and proclaims the true Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, causing them to dwell in the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom; or causing them to dwell in the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; or causing them to attain the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship; or causing them to attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; or causing them to attain the knowledge of all modes.”

Although this bodhisattva-mahāsattva performs these deeds, they do not dwell in the realm of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtadhātu*), nor do they dwell in the realm of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*). Furthermore, taking that which has been accumulated as roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) and employing the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), they dedicate it together with all sentient beings toward omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*). At the time of dedication, no dualistic mind arises, such as: "Who is it that dedicates?"
"To what is it dedicated? Subhūti!
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of wisdom, fully embraces the perfection of diligence."

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom, with the exception of the meditative absorptions (samādhi) of a Buddha, they are able to enter and emerge at will and with mastery in all other meditative absorptions of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas.”
This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the bodhisattva samādhi of mastery, is able to enter into and emerge from the eight liberations with mastery, both in direct and reverse order.
What are these eight?
First, the liberation of one possessing form who perceives external forms;
second, the liberation of one who, being internally without the perception of form, perceives external forms;
third, the liberation of one who realizes for oneself the body of pure resolve.

Fourth, transcending all perceptions of form and extinguishing perceptions of resistance, no longer attending to perceptions of diversity, one enters the sphere of infinite space; this is the liberation of the sphere of infinite space.
Fifth, transcending the sphere of infinite space, one enters the sphere of infinite consciousness; this is the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Sixth, transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, one enters the sphere of nothingness; this is the liberation of the sphere of nothingness.
Seventh, transcending the sphere of nothingness, one enters the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Eighth, transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, which is the liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling.
Furthermore, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to enter and emerge from the nine successive attainments (navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti) with mastery, whether in direct or reverse order.

What are these nine? They are the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti), and the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (nirodhasamāpatti); these are called the nine.

When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva has thoroughly matured their mastery of entering and emerging from the eight liberations and the nine successive attainments in both forward and reverse order, they are able to enter the samādhi of the lion’s sport.
What is the samādhi called "Lion’s Sport"?

Subhūti, it is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, detached from desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and evaluation, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, enters the first dhyāna; proceeding in sequence up to transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling. Then, arising from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, he re-enters the concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, proceeding in sequence back down to the first dhyāna. This is the samādhi of the Lion’s Sport.
“Subhūti! Once this bodhisattva mahāsattva has become well-ripened in this ‘Lion’s Sport’ samādhi, he further enters the bodhisattva ‘Leaping Over’ samādhi.”
What is the bodhisattva’s meditative concentration of transcendence?

Subhūti, it is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, detached from desires and unwholesome states, possessing applied and sustained thought, and experiencing the joy and happiness born of seclusion, enters the first dhyāna; then, arising from the first dhyāna, proceeds in succession until entering the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling; then, arising from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, enters the first dhyāna; and arising from the first dhyāna, enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.

Emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, he enters the second dhyāna; emerging from the second dhyāna, he enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.

Emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, he enters the third dhyāna; emerging from the third dhyāna, he enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.

Emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, he enters the fourth dhyāna; emerging from the fourth dhyāna, he enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.

Emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, he enters the attainment of the sphere of infinite space; emerging from the attainment of the sphere of infinite space, he enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.

Emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, he enters the attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness; emerging from the attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness, he enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.

Emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, he enters the attainment of the sphere of nothingness; emerging from the attainment of the sphere of nothingness, he enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.

Emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, he enters the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; emerging from the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.

Emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, he again enters the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; emerging from the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he falls into an unconcentrated state of mind.

From that unconcentrated state of mind, he returns to the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling; emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, he abides in an unconcentrated state of mind.

From an unsettled mind, he enters the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; arising from the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he abides in an unsettled mind.
From an unsettled mind, he enters the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness; arising from the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness, he abides in an unsettled mind.

From an unsettled mind, he enters the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite consciousness; arising from the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite consciousness, he abides in an unsettled mind.

From an indeterminate state of mind, he enters the concentration of the sphere of infinite space; arising from the concentration of the sphere of infinite space, he abides in an indeterminate state of mind.
From an indeterminate state of mind, he enters the fourth dhyāna; arising from the fourth dhyāna, he abides in an indeterminate state of mind.
From an indeterminate state of mind, he enters the third dhyāna; arising from the third dhyāna, he abides in an indeterminate state of mind.
From the indeterminate mind, one enters the second dhyāna; arising from the second dhyāna, one abides in the indeterminate mind.
From the indeterminate mind, one enters the first dhyāna; arising from the first dhyāna, one abides in the indeterminate mind.
This is the bodhisattva’s leap-over samādhi (*vyutkrāntakasamādhi*).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in this leap-over samādhi, they attain the equal true nature of all phenomena. Furthermore, taking these accumulated roots of goodness as their basis, they employ the method of non-apprehension to dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*). At the time of dedication, no dualistic mind arises, such that one wonders: "Who is it that dedicates?"
"To what is it dedicated? Subhūti!
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of wisdom, takes up the perfection of meditative concentration."

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll 459. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Chapter 68: Skillful Means (Upāyakauśalya), Part Two, Section One. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva has accomplished such power of skillful means, how long has it been since they first resolved upon awakening?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“That bodhisattva mahāsattva has already resolved upon awakening for countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such power of skillful means, how many Buddhas has he already approached, served, and made offerings to?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva has already drawn near to, served, and made offerings to as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such power of skillful means, what kind of superior roots of goodness has he already planted?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Since this bodhisattva mahāsattva first resolved his mind [on awakening], there has been no root of virtue induced by the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom that he has not fully perfected through diligent cultivation; by reason of these causes and conditions, he has accomplished such power of skillful means."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such power of skillful means, they are truly rare!”
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva is truly most rare.
Subhūti, you should know this!

Just as the orbs of the sun and moon revolve around and illuminate the four great continents, performing various activities, so too do all things therein—whether sentient or insentient—turn according to the power of that light and each accomplish its own task.

In this way, the *prajñāpāramitā* extensively illuminates and touches upon the other five *pāramitās*, performing all their various activities; the five *pāramitās*, such as generosity (*dāna*), proceed in accordance with the power of the *prajñāpāramitā*, each accomplishing its own task.
“Subhūti, you should know this:
just as a wheel-turning monarch is not called a wheel-turning monarch if he lacks the seven treasures, but is only called a wheel-turning monarch when he possesses the seven treasures;

so too it is with the five perfections such as generosity—if they are separated from the perfection of wisdom, they cannot be called ‘perfections,’ but when they are not separated from the perfection of wisdom, they can be called ‘perfections.’”
“Subhūti, you should know this:

suppose there is a woman who is beautiful and very wealthy; if she is not protected by a powerful husband, she will easily be insulted and oppressed by wicked people, but if she is protected by a powerful husband, she will not be insulted or oppressed by wicked people.”

The same applies to the five perfections, such as generosity and the rest: if they are not sustained by the power of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they are easily thwarted and destroyed by the celestial Māras and their retinues; however, if they are sustained by the power of the perfection of wisdom, no celestial Māras or their retinues can thwart or destroy them.
“Subhūti, you should know this:
just as a valiant general, well-versed in the art of war and fully equipped with various kinds of sturdy armor and weapons, cannot be harmed by the enemy forces of a neighboring kingdom.”

The five pāramitās, beginning with generosity, are likewise thus: when not separated from the prajñāpāramitā, they cannot be destroyed by the hosts of Māra, by those of overweening pride, nor even by bodhisattvas who are like caṇḍālas.
“Subhūti, you should know this!
Just as the various minor kings of Jambudvīpa attend upon the wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin) at all times, and by relying on that wheel-turning king, they reach superior states.”

The same applies to the five perfections, such as generosity and the rest; by assisting the perfection of wisdom and being guided by its power, they are able to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes.
"Subhūti, you should know this!
Just as all the waters in the eastern regions of Jambudvīpa flow toward the great river Gaṅgā, following the course of the Gaṅgā to enter the great ocean."

The same applies to the five perfections, such as generosity and the rest; none of them fail to be encompassed and drawn forth by the profound perfection of wisdom, whereby one is able to realize the knowledge of all modes.
“Subhūti, you should know that just as a person’s right hand is capable of performing all manner of tasks, so too does the perfection of wisdom draw forth all supreme wholesome dharmas.”
“Subhūti, you should know that just as a person’s left hand is not dexterous for performing tasks, so too the first five pāramitās cannot induce the arising of all supreme wholesome dharmas.”
“Subhūti, you should know this!
Just as all streams, great or small, once they enter the great ocean,
are all given the single name ‘salty,’ so too these first five perfections must enter the perfection of wisdom before they can be called ‘perfections that reach the other shore.’”
“Subhūti, you should know this:

when a wheel-turning monarch wishes to go somewhere, his fourfold army follows him with the wheel-treasure leading the way. When the king and the fourfold army desire to eat and drink, the wheel immediately comes to a halt; once they have eaten and drunk, when the king desires to proceed, the wheel moves on ahead. Whether the wheel halts or proceeds, it follows the king’s intention, and only upon reaching its destination does it no longer move forward.”

In this way, the first five perfections and all wholesome dharmas, when seeking to proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, must take the perfection of wisdom as their guide; they follow it in both advancing and halting, never being separated from it, until they reach unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, after which they no longer proceed further.
“Subhūti, you should know this:

when a wheel-turning monarch wishes to go somewhere, his fourfold army and seven precious jewels escort him from front to back; at that time, although the wheel-treasure is foremost, it does not differentiate between the characteristics of front and back.”

In this way, when the first five perfections and all wholesome dharmas seek to proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they must necessarily have the perfection of wisdom as their precursor; yet, this perfection of wisdom does not form the thought:
"I am the foremost precursor among the first five perfections, and they follow after me."
The five perfections, such as generosity and the rest, do not form this thought:
"The profound perfection of wisdom precedes us; we shall follow after her."

Why is this so? Because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these six perfections (*pāramitā*) and all phenomena (*dharma*) is insentient; they are incapable of agency, devoid of a sovereign controller, false and unreal, empty and non-existent, and characterized by a lack of self-mastery. They are like a mirage, a reflection, the moon in water, a magical illusion, or a dream; within them, there is absolutely no real essence of conceptual differentiation or functional activity.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature and lack any real characteristic or function, how do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfections of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, seeking to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas correctly practice these six perfections, they constantly reflect: 'Sentient beings in the world have minds that are perpetually inverted;
submerged in birth and death, they cannot liberate themselves. If I do not cultivate skillful and superior practices, I will be unable to rescue them from the suffering of birth and death.'"

I shall diligently cultivate the skillful and supreme practices, from the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, for the sake of those sentient beings, in order to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and liberate all sentient beings from the great suffering of birth and death.
Having formed this thought, that bodhisattva mahāsattva relinquishes all internal and external possessions for the sake of all sentient beings.
Having made this relinquishment, he further reflects:
"I have relinquished nothing at all, internally or externally."
Why is this? Because these internal and external things are empty and lack intrinsic nature, they cannot be relinquished as gifts; they do not belong to me alone.
By means of this contemplation, the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of generosity until it is swiftly fulfilled, and quickly realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of liberating sentient beings from the suffering of birth and death, never violates the precepts. Why is this?
Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly maintains this thought:"

"For the sake of liberating all sentient beings from the suffering of birth and death, I seek to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; I must certainly not take the life of any living being, nor even hold wrong views. Furthermore, I must certainly not seek the objects of exquisite desire, nor seek celestial wealth and pleasure, nor seek to become Śakra, Māra, or Brahmā. Nor must I certainly seek the stage of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha for the sake of mere personal liberation."

By means of this contemplation, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of ethical discipline until it is swiftly fulfilled, and they quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

“Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva seeks to liberate sentient beings from the suffering of birth and death, he never gives rise to thoughts of anger or resentment; even if he were constantly subjected to slander, humiliation, pain, and reproach that pierce to the very marrow of his bones, he would never give rise to a single thought of malice.”

Even if they were constantly subjected to blows from swords, staves, tiles, stones, clubs, or clods of earth, or were cut, sliced, pierced, and mangled limb by limb, they would not give rise to a single thought of malice.

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva-mahāsattva observes all sounds as being like echoes and all forms as being like masses of foam; he should not, within these, falsely give rise to anger or resentment that would destroy his various wholesome qualities.
By means of this contemplation, this bodhisattva mahāsattva swiftly fulfills the perfection of patience through practice and rapidly realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of liberating sentient beings from the suffering of birth and death, diligently seeks all sublime and virtuous dharmas; until they reach unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they remain ever free from indolence throughout that interval."
Why is this? It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constantly maintain this thought:

"If I am indolent, I shall be unable to rescue and deliver all sentient beings, enabling them to distance themselves from the great suffering of birth and death, nor shall I be able to attain the knowledge of all modes."

By means of this observation, that bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of diligence until it is swiftly brought to fulfillment, and quickly realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"For the sake of liberating sentient beings from the suffering of birth and death, this bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates all supreme concentrations up to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, never giving rise to a distracted mind associated with greed, hatred, or delusion."
Why is this? It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constantly maintain this thought:

"If I give rise to a distracted mind associated with greed, hatred, or delusion, I will be unable to accomplish the welfare and happiness of others, nor will I be able to realize the sought-after fruit of Buddhahood."

"By means of this contemplation, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas swiftly bring the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā) to fulfillment and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

"In order to liberate sentient beings from the suffering of birth and death, this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not depart from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and until reaching unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, constantly and diligently cultivates the subtle and supreme mundane and supramundane wisdom."
Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constantly maintain this thought:
"If one is separated from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), one cannot bring sentient beings to maturity, nor can one attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna)."

"By means of this contemplation, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) until it is swiftly brought to fulfillment, and they quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

"Subhūti! For this reason, although all phenomena lack any real characteristic or function and their intrinsic nature is entirely empty, the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas diligently cultivates the six perfections, never wearying, in order to seek the realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If the nature of all the perfections (*pāramitā*) is without distinction—because they are all embraced by the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), and because they are all brought to fulfillment through the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom—they ought to be consolidated into a single perfection, namely, the perfection of wisdom. How, then, can it be said that the perfection of wisdom is the foremost, the most excellent, the most venerable, the highest, the sublime, the most subtle, the superior, the unsurpassed, the peerless, and the equal to the unequaled among the five perfections?”
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.

These six kinds of *pāramitās* are undifferentiated in nature because they are all sustained by the *prajñāpāramitā*. Without the *prajñāpāramitā*, the five [perfections] such as giving (*dāna*) cannot be called *pāramitās*; it is only by depending upon the *prajñāpāramitā* that the five, such as giving, are designated as *pāramitās*.

Therefore, the first five perfections are subsumed within the perfection of wisdom; because of this single perfection—namely, the perfection of wisdom—the nature of all perfections is without distinction.

"Subhūti, you should know that although there are various distinctions among the physical bodies of sentient beings, if they draw near to Sumeru, the King of Mountains, they all become one and the same color."

Thus, although these first five pāramitās possess various distinctions of category, because they are embraced by the prajñāpāramitā and because they are all brought to completion through the cultivation of the prajñāpāramitā, they all enter into the prajñāpāramitā; it is impossible to designate them as having distinct names or natures.

Furthermore, it is by relying upon the perfection of wisdom that the perfections such as generosity can enter into the knowledge of all modes; only then are they called "those who have reached the other shore. Therefore, the six perfections are of a single flavor, their nature being without distinction, such that one cannot designate them as "this is the perfection of generosity" up to "this is the perfection of wisdom."

Why is this so? Because these six kinds of *pāramitās* all equally enter into the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*) and are able to reach the further shore; their nature is without distinction. For this reason, it cannot be established that the six, such as generosity and the rest, possess different natures.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If, according to their ultimate meaning, the perfections and all phenomena are devoid of any distinction of 'this' or 'that,' superiority or inferiority, for what reason is it said that the perfection of wisdom is the foremost, the most excellent, the most honorable, the highest, the sublime, the most subtle, the superior, the unsurpassed, the unequaled, and the equal to the unequaled among the five perfections?"
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.

If one follows the ultimate meaning, the pāramitās and all phenomena are entirely devoid of such distinctions as "this" and "that," or superiority and inferiority; it is only by relying on conventional designations and functional activity that one speaks of such distinctions as "this" and "that," or superiority and inferiority.

The establishment of the perfections, from the perfection of giving up to the perfection of wisdom, is for the purpose of liberating all sentient beings from the worldly functions of birth, old age, sickness, and death; yet, these births, old ages, sicknesses, and deaths of sentient beings are not truly existent, but are merely conventional designations.

Why is this so? Because sentient beings do not exist, one should know that all phenomena likewise do not exist. The profound *prajñāpāramitā* realizes that all phenomena are entirely non-existent, yet it can extract sentient beings from the worldly functions of birth, old age, sickness, and death. For this reason, it is said that among the five *pāramitās*, the *prajñāpāramitā* is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the most exalted, the most sublime, the most exquisite, the highest, the unsurpassed, the unequaled, and the equal to the unequaled.
Subhūti, you should know this:

just as the woman-jewel possessed by a universal monarch is the most excellent, the most superior, the most noble, the most eminent, the most sublime, the most exquisite, the highest, the unsurpassed, the peerless, and the equal to the unequaled among all women of the human realm, so too is this perfection of wisdom the most excellent, the most superior, the most noble, the most eminent, the most sublime, the most exquisite, the highest, the unsurpassed, the peerless, and the equal to the unequaled among the perfections such as generosity.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One,

for what reason do you repeatedly praise and speak of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* as being the foremost, the most excellent, the most honored, the highest, the sublime, the most subtle, the superior, the unsurpassed, the peerless, and the equal to the unequaled, compared to the other *pāramitās* such as giving?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Because this prajñāpāramitā, by means of non-apprehension as its expedient, is able to universally encompass all wholesome dharmas, harmonizing and entering into the knowledge of all modes, and abiding therein immovably, I repeatedly praise and speak of the prajñāpāramitā."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Does this profound prajñāpāramitā involve the grasping or the abandoning of any wholesome dharmas?
The Buddha said:
"No, indeed! The profound *prajñāpāramitā* neither grasps nor abandons any dharma whatsoever. Why is this?
"Because all dharmas are neither to be grasped nor to be relinquished.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In what dharmas does this profound perfection of wisdom neither grasp nor relinquish?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"The profound *prajñāpāramitā* neither grasps nor abandons form; it neither grasps nor abandons feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
it neither grasps nor abandons the sense base of the eye, up to and including the sense base of the mind."
Equanimity: there is neither grasping nor relinquishing with respect to the sense-field of form up to the sense-field of mental phenomena;

there is neither grasping nor relinquishing with respect to the eye-element up to the mind-element; there is neither grasping nor relinquishing with respect to the form-element up to the mental-phenomena-element;

there is neither grasping nor relinquishing with respect to the eye-consciousness-element up to the mind-consciousness-element; and there is neither grasping nor relinquishing with respect to eye-contact up to mind-contact.

There is neither grasping nor relinquishing; regarding all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, up to those produced with mind-contact as condition, there is neither grasping nor relinquishing;
regarding the earth element up to the consciousness element, there is neither grasping nor relinquishing;

regarding the causal condition up to the sovereign condition, there is neither grasping nor relinquishing; and regarding ignorance up to old age and death, there is neither grasping nor relinquishing.
Without grasping or rejecting, one neither grasps nor rejects anything from the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
one neither grasps nor rejects anything from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature;
one neither grasps nor rejects anything from suchness up to the inconceivable realm; [and one neither grasps nor rejects] suffering, its origin, and its cessation...

The Noble Truth of the Path is without grasping and without relinquishing; regarding the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, it is without grasping and without relinquishing;
regarding the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments, it is without grasping and without relinquishing;
regarding the eight liberations up to the ten totalities, it is without grasping and without relinquishing; regarding emptiness, non-...
The gate of liberation of signlessness and the gate of liberation of wishlessness are without grasping and without relinquishing;

from the stage of pure observation up to the stage of a Tathāgata, they are without grasping and without relinquishing; from the stage of extreme joy up to the stage of the cloud of dharma, they are without grasping and without relinquishing;
regarding all doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of samādhi, they are without grasping and without relinquishing; regarding the five eyes...
...the six supernormal powers are without grasping or abandoning; regarding the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, they are without grasping or abandoning;
regarding the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty secondary signs, they are without grasping or abandoning;
regarding the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity, they are without grasping or abandoning. Regarding—
All-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects are without grasping and without relinquishing;

regarding the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, they are without grasping and without relinquishing; regarding all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, they are without grasping and without relinquishing;
and regarding the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas, they are without grasping and without relinquishing.
"In the knowledge of all modes, there is neither grasping nor relinquishing.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is it that the profound perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor relinquishes form, and so on, up to the knowledge of all modes?"

The Buddha told Subhūti: "The profound *prajñāpāramitā* does not conceptualize form; therefore, regarding form, there is neither grasping nor relinquishing. This extends even to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*); it does not conceptualize the knowledge of all modes; therefore, regarding the knowledge of all modes, there is neither grasping nor relinquishing."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is it that the perfection of wisdom does not contemplate form, nor even contemplate the knowledge of all aspects?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Because this prajñāpāramitā does not contemplate any marks regarding form, nor does it contemplate any objects of perception; therefore, it does not contemplate form. This extends even to the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñājñāna), where it does not contemplate any marks, nor does it contemplate any objects of perception; therefore, it does not contemplate the knowledge of all modes."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not contemplate form, nor even contemplate the knowledge of all aspects, how do the roots of virtue they have planted increase?"
If one does not increase the roots of virtue that have been planted, how can one fulfill the perfections?
If one does not fulfill the perfections, how can one realize the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not contemplate form, nor even contemplate the knowledge of all aspects, at that time the bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to increase the roots of virtue they have planted."
Because the roots of virtue they have planted increase, they are able to bring the pāramitās to perfection.
Because the pāramitās are brought to perfection, they are able to realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek.
Why is this? Subhūti!

It is because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas must not conceptualize form, nor even conceptualize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), only then can they fully cultivate the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"For what reason must a bodhisattva mahāsattva not conceptualize form, and so on, up to not conceptualizing the knowledge of all aspects, before they are able to fully cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas contemplate form, and so on, up to contemplating the knowledge of all modes, they will have something apprehended. Because they have something apprehended, they become attached to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm. If they are attached to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm, they cannot fully cultivate the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, nor can they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not contemplate form, and so on, up to not contemplating the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), then there is nothing to be apprehended; because there is nothing to be apprehended, they do not cling to the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm. If they do not cling to the desire, form, or formless realms, they are then able to fully cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Therefore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to fully cultivate all the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, and wishes to swiftly realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek, they should diligently study the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and should not engage in conceptualization or attachment toward any phenomena.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva diligently practices and studies this profound perfection of wisdom, in what should they abide?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva diligently practices and studies the profound perfection of wisdom, they should not dwell on form, nor should they dwell on anything up to and including the knowledge of all aspects.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“For what reason should a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while diligently training in the profound perfection of wisdom, not abide in form, nor even abide in the knowledge of all aspects?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva diligently practices and studies the profound perfection of wisdom, because they have no attachment to any phenomena, they should not dwell in form, nor should they dwell in anything up to and including the knowledge of all aspects."
Why is this? Subhūti!
This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive any dharma within which he might give rise to attachment or upon which he might dwell.
"Subhūti! In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of non-attachment and non-abiding as their skillful means, diligently practices and studies the profound perfection of wisdom."
"Furthermore, Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva forms this thought:

'If one can thus practice the profound perfection of wisdom with non-attachment and no fixed abiding, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom.'"
I am able to practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, free from all attachment;
I am able to proceed in the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, free from all attachment—this is the practice of *prajñāpāramitā*.
“Subhūti! Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva apprehends signs and clings to them through such recollections, he distances himself from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If he distances himself from the perfection of wisdom, then he distances himself from the perfections of concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity; he also distances himself from inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.”
It is also detached from suchness up to the inconceivable realm; it is also detached from the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
it is also detached from the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
it is also detached from the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the eight liberations.
