...up to the ten spheres of totality (*daśa-kṛtsnāyatana*), they are also far removed from the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
they are also far removed from the stages from the Ground of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma;
they are also far removed from all doors of dhāraṇī and doors of samādhi; they are also far removed from the five eyes and the six supernormal powers; they are also far removed.
The ten powers of the Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are also remote from the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity;
they are also remote from all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);
they are also remote from all the practices of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, and also remote from the [qualities] of the Buddhas.
Even unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment is likewise remote from the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). Why is this?
Because the profound perfection of wisdom has no attachment toward any phenomena; the profound perfection of wisdom possesses neither an agent of attachment nor the nature of attachment.
Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* has no intrinsic nature whatsoever that could be grasped or attached to among all phenomena. Therefore, Subhūti!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they give rise to such a thought:
"This is the perfection of wisdom; I am practicing the perfection of wisdom."
Thus, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they have no attachment whatsoever toward any phenomena or toward the profound perfection of wisdom itself.
Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they give rise to this thought:
"This is the perfection of wisdom; I am practicing the perfection of wisdom, which is the universal traversal of the true reality of all phenomena."

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought, they retreat from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); if they retreat from the perfection of wisdom, they then retreat from all sublime, pure dharmas (śukladharma).
Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is the root of all pure dharmas (*śukladharma*); if one regresses from the *prajñāpāramitā*, one thereby falls away from all pure dharmas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva forms this thought:

'The profound perfection of wisdom encompasses the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration, up to and including the encompassing of the knowledge of all aspects.'"

This bodhisattva mahāsattva falls away from the perfection of wisdom; if they fall away from the perfection of wisdom, they will be unable to embrace the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration, and so on, up to being unable to embrace the knowledge of all aspects.
Why is this? Subhūti!
It is not apart from the perfection of wisdom that one can fully embrace the factors conducive to enlightenment, nor can one realize the knowledge of all aspects.
Furthermore, Subhūti,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva forms this thought:
"By abiding in the perfection of wisdom, I shall certainly receive the prediction of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Such a bodhisattva mahāsattva then falls away from the perfection of wisdom; if they fall away from the perfection of wisdom, they will not receive the prediction of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Why is that? Subhūti,
it is because one cannot receive the prediction of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment apart from the perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva forms this thought:

'By abiding in the perfection of wisdom, one can bring forth the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of meditative concentration; and in this way, up to, one can bring forth great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity.'"

Such a bodhisattva mahāsattva then falls away from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). If they fall away from the perfection of wisdom, they will be unable to bring forth the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā) up to the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā); likewise, they will be unable to bring forth great loving-kindness (maitrī), great compassion (karuṇā), great sympathetic joy (muditā), and great equanimity (upekṣā).
Why is this? Subhūti!
It is not apart from the perfection of wisdom that one can bring forth and abide in the sublime Dharma.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva forms this thought:
"The Buddha, knowing that all phenomena have the characteristic of being without grasping, has personally realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Once he has attained awakening, he will proclaim and reveal the true nature of all phenomena for the sake of all sentient beings"—
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva thinks thus, he is then falling away from the profound perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Subhūti!
The Tathāgata has no knowledge, no realization, no speech, and no demonstration regarding phenomena.
Why is this? Because the true nature of all phenomena (dharmas) cannot be cognized or conceptualized; how, then, could there be one who cognizes and teaches and points out all phenomena?
"If it were said that there truly exists a cognition that can demonstrate all phenomena, such a thing is impossible.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“How should bodhisattva mahāsattvas, when practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), come to be free from such various faults?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, forms this thought:”

"All dharmas are non-existent and ungraspable; if dharmas are non-existent and ungraspable, then there is no one who can realize perfect enlightenment, nor is there anyone who can proclaim or reveal them."
If one practices in this manner, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) free from all faults.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes attached to dharmas that are non-existent and ungraspable, then they depart from the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Subhūti!

The profound *prajñāpāramitā* has no attachment to and no grasping of any phenomena (*dharma*). If one were to have attachment to or grasp at any phenomena, then one would be far removed from the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
is the perfection of wisdom distant from the perfection of wisdom, or is it not distant?”
Up to and including: Is the perfection of generosity distant from the perfection of generosity, or is it not distant?
Likewise, up to and including: Is the knowledge of all modes distant from the knowledge of all modes, or is it not distant?

"Bhagavān! If the perfection of wisdom is either distant from or not distant from the perfection of wisdom, how can a bodhisattva mahāsattva, free from attachment, bring forth the perfection of wisdom?"

Furthermore, if the perfection of generosity is either distant from or not distant from the perfection of generosity, how can a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of generosity without attachment?

In this way, even up to the case where the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) is either distant from or not distant from the knowledge of all modes—how can a bodhisattva mahāsattva, being without attachment, bring forth the knowledge of all modes?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"The perfection of wisdom is neither separate from nor not separate from the perfection of wisdom; likewise, even up to the knowledge of all aspects is neither separate from nor not separate from the knowledge of all aspects."
For this reason, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to bring forth the perfection of wisdom without attachment, and even bring forth the knowledge of all modes. Why is this?
"Subhūti! It is neither identical to intrinsic nature, nor is it apart from intrinsic nature, yet it is able to abide in and bring forth intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"
When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they do not cling to form, thinking, "This is form," or "This form belongs to that.

Nor do they cling to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, thinking, "This is feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness," or "This feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness belongs to that.
In this manner, they do not cling even to the knowledge of all modes, thinking, "This is the knowledge of all modes," or "This knowledge of all modes belongs to that."

Subhūti! Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva has no attachment to any of these dharmas, he is able to bring forth the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity, and even bring forth the knowledge of all modes.
Why is this? Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom has any attachment toward phenomena—thinking "this is a phenomenon" or "this phenomenon belongs to that"—then they will be unable to spontaneously manifest and abide in supreme and wondrous merits at will.
Furthermore, Subhūti,
when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they do not contemplate form as either permanent or impermanent,
as either pleasant or painful, as either self or non-self, or as either pure or impure.
Whether it be tranquil or untranquil, detached or undetached, one likewise does not contemplate feeling,
perception, formations, or consciousness as permanent or impermanent,
as pleasant or painful, as self or non-self, as pure or impure, as tranquil or untranquil, or as detached.
If they do not distance themselves from, nor fail to distance themselves from, even up to the point of not contemplating omniscience—
whether as permanent or impermanent, as pleasure or suffering, as self or non-self, as pure or impure,
as tranquil or untranquil, or as distant or not distant— then that bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding...

Because all these phenomena are not observed, one is able to bring forth the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity; likewise, one is able to bring forth even the knowledge of all modes.
Why is this? Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom observes among all phenomena anything as permanent or impermanent, as blissful or suffering, as self or non-self, as pure or impure, as tranquil or non-tranquil, or as secluded or non-secluded, then they will be unable to give rise to and abide in supreme and wondrous merit at will.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom,
they are practicing the perfections of meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity."
To dwell in inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence;
to likewise dwell in suchness up to the inconceivable realm; to likewise dwell in the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
to likewise practice the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; and to likewise practice the four dhyānas.
...the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments; also for the practice of the eight liberations up to the ten totalities;
also for the practice of the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
also for the practice of the ten stages of a bodhisattva; and also for the practice of all dharani-gates and samādhis.
The gateway of the stages is also for the practice of the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
it is also for the practice of the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;

it is also for the practice of the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity; and it is also for the practice of all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects.
Wisdom is also for the sake of practicing all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, for the sake of practicing the unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas, and for the sake of practicing the knowledge of all modes of knowing.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Wherever the profound *prajñāpāramitā* proceeds, all the *pāramitās* and all other factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) proceed along with it;
wherever the profound *prajñāpāramitā* arrives, all the *pāramitās* and all other factors of enlightenment arrive along with it."
"Subhūti! Just as wherever a wheel-turning monarch travels, his fourfold army follows him; and just as wherever the wheel-turning monarch arrives, his fourfold army arrives with him."

The profound perfection of wisdom is likewise: wherever it proceeds and whithersoever it goes, all the other perfections and all the remaining factors conducive to enlightenment follow it, until they ultimately reach the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
"Subhūti! It is like a skilled charioteer who, driving a four-horse chariot, avoids dangerous paths and travels upon the right road, reaching his destination according to his original intention."

The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise: it skillfully guides all the *pāramitās* and all other factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), causing them to avoid the perilous paths of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, to proceed upon the right path of self-benefit and benefit for others, and to reach the omniscience (*sarvajñājñāna*) that was originally sought.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what constitutes the path for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?”
"What is the non-path?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"The path of ordinary beings, the path of śrāvakas, or the path of pratyekabuddhas is not the path of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, because by means of these one cannot proceed to the knowledge of all aspects."

The six perfections induced by the profound *prajñāpāramitā* constitute the path of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, for by relying upon them, they are certainly able to proceed to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*).
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"The profound perfection of wisdom appears in the world to accomplish a great task; that is to say, it demonstrates the characteristics of the path and the non-path for all bodhisattva mahāsattvas, enabling the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas to know what is the path and what is not the path, so that they may swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes."
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.

This profound perfection of wisdom appears in the world to accomplish a great task; that is to say, it demonstrates the characteristics of the path and the non-path for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, enabling the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to know what is the path and what is not the path, so that they may swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

Furthermore, Subhūti, the appearance of the profound perfection of wisdom in the world is able to accomplish a great task; that is to say, it brings immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings across [to liberation], enabling them to attain supreme benefit and peace and happiness.
"Subhūti, you should know that although the profound perfection of wisdom performs boundless deeds for the benefit and happiness of others, it remains without attachment to these deeds."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Although the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can manifest the functions of form, it does not grasp or cling to these functions;
although it can manifest the functions of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, it does not grasp or cling to these functions."
In this way, even though they are able to manifest all the activities of the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), they have no attachment to these activities;
even though they are able to manifest the activities of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, they have no attachment to these activities.

Subhūti! Although the profound perfection of wisdom can guide the assembly of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, causing them to remain far removed from the levels of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, it neither gives rise to nor extinguishes any phenomena, because the stability of dharmas (*dharmasthititā*) serves as its definitive standard.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If the profound perfection of wisdom is such that all phenomena are neither produced nor extinguished, how is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they should practice giving for the sake of sentient beings, maintain pure ethical discipline, arouse patience, exert diligence, abide in meditative concentration, and cultivate wisdom?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they take all-knowledge as their object and, for the sake of all sentient beings, should practice giving, should maintain pure ethical discipline, should arouse patience, should exert diligence, should abide in meditative concentration, and should cultivate wisdom.”

"Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva takes these roots of goodness and, together with all sentient beings, dedicates them toward omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*). By dedicating them in this manner toward omniscience, they swiftly bring the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) to full completion; they also swiftly bring the bodhisattva’s loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity to full completion. Thus, until they sit upon the sublime seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*), they never depart from these six perfections."
If one does not distance oneself from these six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), then one does not distance oneself from the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Therefore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes, they should diligently apply themselves to training in the six perfections and diligently practice the six perfections. If a bodhisattva mahāsattva diligently applies themselves to training in and practicing these six perfections, all roots of virtue will quickly reach fulfillment, and they will be able to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes.
Therefore, Subhūti, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should always remain in conjunction with the six perfections and never be separated from them.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva can always remain in conjunction with the six pāramitās, never being separated from them?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates form as it truly is—neither associated nor dissociated—and contemplates feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as they truly are—neither associated nor dissociated—and likewise contemplates even the knowledge of all modes as it truly is—neither associated nor dissociated—then this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to remain constantly and inseparably associated with the six perfections.”
Furthermore, Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly reflects thus: "I should not dwell in form, nor should I dwell in that which is not form;

I should not dwell in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor should I dwell in that which is not feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; and so on, up to: I should not dwell in the knowledge of all modes, nor should I dwell in that which is not the knowledge of all modes."

Why is this? Because form is neither that which abides nor that in which it abides; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise neither that which abides nor that in which they abide. Thus, even up to the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), it is neither that which abides nor that in which it abides.
"Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to remain constantly associated with the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), never being separated from them. Subhūti!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice the six perfections by means of such non-abiding skillful methods, that bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes.

“Subhūti! It is as if there were a person who, wishing to eat *āmra* fruits or *panasa* fruits, first takes their seeds and plants them in fertile, excellent soil; he irrigates them at the proper times, guards and tends them, and as they gradually grow with sprouts, stems, branches, and leaves, when the seasons converge, flowers and fruits appear. Once the fruits have ripened, he takes them and eats them.”
Thus it is, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they must first train in the six perfections and then gather in sentient beings through generosity, or through kind words, or through beneficial conduct, or through cooperation.

Having thus gathered them in, he instructs them to abide in the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; once they have so abided, they are liberated from all birth, aging, sickness, and death, and realize the state of eternal, ultimate bliss.
In this way, a bodhisattva shall attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, turn the sublime wheel of Dharma,
and deliver immeasurable multitudes. Therefore, Subhūti,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to realize and understand all phenomena through their own insight without relying on others, and wishes—
One who is able to bring all sentient beings to maturity; who desires to skillfully adorn and purify Buddha-fields;

who desires to swiftly sit upon the sublime seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); who desires to subdue all armies of Māra; who desires to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*);
who desires to turn the wheel of Dharma and liberate sentient beings from old age, sickness, death, and suffering; and who desires to realize—
Abiding eternally in ultimate peace and bliss, one should train in the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) and,
through the skillful means of the four means of attraction (catvāri saṃgrahavastūni), gather all sentient beings; having gathered them,
one should cause them to dwell securely in the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
"When a bodhisattva thus diligently practices and trains, they should constantly and diligently practice and train in the *prajñāpāramitā*.

[From] the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Fascicle 463, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree, Second Division, Chapter Sixty-Eight, Part Two: "Skillful Means. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
has the Buddha taught that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should constantly and diligently train in the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"So it is! So it is! I say that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should constantly and diligently train in the perfection of wisdom."
"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain great mastery over all dharmas, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Why is that?"
The profound perfection of wisdom possesses great power, for it enables the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas to attain mastery over all phenomena.
"Subhūti, you should know that this profound prajñāpāramitā is the gateway through which all wholesome dharmas proceed, just as the great ocean is the gateway through which all waters proceed."

Therefore, Subhūti, whether they be persons belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas, persons belonging to the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, or persons belonging to the vehicle of the bodhisattvas, all should constantly and diligently train in this profound perfection of wisdom.
“Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas diligently train in this perfection of wisdom,
they should also constantly train in the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of meditative concentration.”
One should always abide in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;
one should always abide in suchness up to the inconceivable realm; one should always abide in the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
and one should always abide in the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path.
In training, one should also constantly train in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
one should constantly train in the eight liberations up to the ten totalities;
one should constantly train in the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; and one should [constantly train] in the bodhisattva mahāsattva...
One should also constantly practice and study the stages of a bodhisattva; one should also constantly practice and study all the doors of dhāraṇī and the doors of samādhi;
one should also constantly practice and study the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;

one should also constantly practice and study the ten powers of a Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; one should [also constantly practice and study] the unconditioned...
One should also constantly practice and study the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity;
one should also constantly practice and study all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);

one should also constantly practice and study all the practices of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas; and one should also constantly practice and study the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas.
In training, one should also constantly practice for the sake of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). "Subhūti!
It is like a skilled archer whose armor is firm and whose bow and arrows are at will; such a person has no fear of enemies."

In the same way, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who embrace the skillful means of the perfection of wisdom and are endowed with all meritorious qualities cannot be defeated by any of the demonic armies or the heterodox arguments of outsiders.
Therefore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes, they should diligently practice and study the profound perfection of wisdom.

"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to constantly and diligently train in the perfection of wisdom, they will be constantly protected and remembered by all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in the immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless worlds of the ten directions."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,

how is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly and diligently practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they are constantly protected and remembered by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, throughout the immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless worlds of the ten directions?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to constantly and diligently train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they will then be able to practice the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā), up to and including the practice of the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā). Because of this, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, throughout the immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless worlds of the ten directions, will always protect and mindfully attend to them."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“How does this bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of generosity, up to and including practicing the knowledge of all aspects, such that he is constantly protected and remembered by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in the immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless worlds of the ten directions?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of generosity, they observe that the perfection of generosity is unapprehendable; up to and including when they practice the knowledge of all aspects, they observe that the knowledge of all aspects is unapprehendable. Because of this, they are constantly protected and remembered by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in the immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless worlds of the ten directions."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Thus, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in the immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless worlds of the ten directions, constantly protect and mind this bodhisattva mahāsattva because form is unapprehendable; they constantly protect and mind this bodhisattva mahāsattva because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unapprehendable; and so on, up to the point that they constantly protect and mind this bodhisattva mahāsattva because even the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) is unapprehendable."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Thus, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in the immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless worlds of the ten directions, do not constantly protect and mind this bodhisattva mahāsattva by way of form; they do not constantly protect and mind this bodhisattva mahāsattva by way of feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness; and so on, up to: they do not constantly protect and mind this bodhisattva mahāsattva by way of the knowledge of all modes."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Although bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train in many places, they have nothing in which to train.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"So it is! So it is! Although bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train in many places, they have nothing in which to train."
"Why is this? Because, in reality, there is no dharma whatsoever that can cause the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to train and study within it.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!

For the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, please teach the dharmas associated with the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), whether in brief or in detail. If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), they should, regarding these teachings on the dharmas associated with the six perfections—whether concise or extensive—listen to them, receive and uphold them, read and recite them, and master them thoroughly. Having mastered them, they should reflect upon them according to reason; having reflected, they should examine them with precise correctness; and having examined them correctly, they should cause the mind and its mental factors to no longer turn toward the characteristics of objects.”
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is as you have said.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas diligently train in the teachings corresponding to the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One—whether in brief or in detail—they should understand, in accordance with reality, the characteristics of both the concise and the detailed aspects of all phenomena."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva correctly understand, in accordance with reality, the concise and detailed characteristics of all phenomena?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva understands, as they truly are, the suchness-characteristic of form, the suchness-characteristic of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness;
and understands, as they truly are, the suchness-characteristic of the sense-base of the eye, up to the sense-base of the mind...”

Regarding the characteristic of the suchness of the sense-bases (*āyatana*), he understands as they truly are the characteristic of the suchness of the form-base (*rūpāyatana*) up to the characteristic of the suchness of the mental-object-base (*dharmāyatana*);
he understands as they truly are the characteristic of the suchness of the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) up to the characteristic of the suchness of the mind-element (*manodhātu*);

he understands as they truly are the characteristic of the suchness of the form-element (*rūpadhātu*) up to the characteristic of the suchness of the mental-object-element (*dharmadhātu*). He understands them as they truly are.
One understands, as they truly are, the suchness-characteristics of the visual consciousness element up to the mental consciousness element;
one understands, as they truly are, the suchness-characteristics of visual contact up to mental contact;
and one understands, as they truly are, the suchness-characteristics of all feelings produced with visual contact as condition up to all feelings produced with mental contact as condition.
They understand, as they truly are, the *tathatā* (suchness) characteristic of the earth element up to the *tathatā* characteristic of the consciousness element;
they understand, as they truly are, the *tathatā* characteristic of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) up to the *tathatā* characteristic of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*);

they understand, as they truly are, the *tathatā* characteristic of ignorance (*avidyā*) up to the *tathatā* characteristic of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*); they understand, as they truly are, the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*)...
He understands, as they truly are, the suchness-characteristics of the perfection of generosity up to the suchness-characteristics of the perfection of wisdom;
he understands, as they truly are, the suchness-characteristics of internal emptiness up to the suchness-characteristics of the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature;
and he understands, as they truly are, the suchness-characteristics of the noble truth of suffering, and the suchness-characteristics of the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path.
One knows, as they truly are, the suchness-characteristics of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the suchness-characteristics of the eightfold noble path;
one knows, as they truly are, the suchness-characteristics of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
and one knows, as they truly are, the suchness-characteristics of the eight liberations up to the suchness-characteristics of the ten totalities.
He understands, as they truly are, the marks of the suchness of the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, and the gate of liberation of wishlessness;
he understands, as they truly are, the marks of the suchness of the stage of pure observation up to the marks of the suchness of the stage of the Tathāgata;
and he understands, as they truly are, the marks of the suchness of the stage of extreme joy up to the stage of the cloud of dharma.
The characteristic of suchness: one understands as they truly are the characteristic of suchness of all *dhāraṇī* gates and the characteristic of suchness of all *samādhi* gates;
one understands as they truly are the characteristic of suchness of the five eyes and the characteristic of suchness of the six supernormal powers;
one understands as they truly are the characteristic of suchness of the Tathāgata’s ten powers, up to and including the eighteen [unshared dharmas].
The Tathāgata’s unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) have the characteristic of suchness;
he understands, as they truly are, the suchness-characteristic of the thirty-two marks of a great man and the suchness-characteristic of the eighty minor marks;

he understands, as they truly are, the suchness-characteristic of the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣa-dharma*) and the suchness-characteristic of the nature of constant equanimity (*upekṣā*); and he understands, as they truly are, the suchness-characteristic of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
He understands, as they truly are, the suchness-characteristic of the knowledge of the paths, the knowledge of all aspects,
and the suchness-characteristic of the fruit of stream-entry up to the suchness-characteristic of pratyekabuddha enlightenment; he understands, as they truly are,
the suchness-characteristic of all bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices and the suchness-characteristic of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas.
To know, as they truly are, the marks of the suchness of all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna), this is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s knowing,
as they truly are, the concise and detailed marks of all phenomena (dharma).
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, what is the characteristic of the suchness of form; what is the characteristic of the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; and so on, up to: what is the characteristic of the suchness of the knowledge of all modes? How do bodhisattva mahāsattvas understand these as they truly are and train therein, and how do they understand the concise and detailed characteristics of all phenomena as they truly are?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“The suchness of form is without arising and without cessation, and it cannot be designated as having duration or change; this is called the characteristic of the suchness of form.

The suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is without arising and without cessation, and it cannot be designated as having duration or change; this is called the characteristic of the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.”

Even up to the suchness of the knowledge of all modes, which is without arising and without cessation, and cannot be designated as having abiding or change—this is called the characteristic of the suchness of the knowledge of all modes.
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should understand things as they truly are and train therein; they should understand, as they truly are, the concise and extensive characteristics of all phenomena.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva understands, as they truly are, the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) of form, the reality-limit of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and even understands, as they truly are, the reality-limit of the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), then this bodhisattva mahāsattva understands, as they truly are, the concise and detailed characteristics of all phenomena.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, what is the mark of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of form? What is the mark of the limit of reality of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness? And so on, up to: what is the mark of the limit of reality of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*)? How do the bodhisattva mahāsattvas understand these as they truly are and train therein; and how do they understand, as they truly are, the concise and detailed marks of all phenomena?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“The limit of formlessness is called the mark of the reality-limit of form; the limits of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are called the marks of the reality-limit of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness; and so on, up to the limit of the knowledge of all modes, which is called the mark of the reality-limit of the knowledge of all modes.”
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should understand things as they truly are and train therein; they should understand, as they truly are, the concise and detailed characteristics of all phenomena.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva truly understands the characteristic of the dharma-realm of form, the characteristic of the dharma-realm of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and even truly understands the characteristic of the dharma-realm of the knowledge of all modes, then this bodhisattva mahāsattva truly understands the concise and detailed characteristics of all phenomena.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One! What is the dharma-realm characteristic of form? What are the dharma-realm characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness? And so on, up to: what is the dharma-realm characteristic of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*)? How do the bodhisattva mahāsattvas understand these as they truly are and train therein; and how do they understand, as they truly are, the concise and extensive characteristics of all dharmas?”
The Buddha told Subhūti: "Form is like space;

it is without obstruction or hindrance, without arising or ceasing, and without interruption or continuity, such that it can be designated. This is called the characteristic of the dharma-realm of form.

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are like space; they are without obstruction or hindrance, without arising or ceasing, and without interruption or continuity, such that they can be designated. This is called the characteristic of the dharma-realm of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."

Even up to the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), it is like space: unobstructed and unhindered, without arising and without ceasing, without interruption and without continuity, such that it can be designated; this is called the characteristic of the dharma-realm of the knowledge of all modes.
"All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should understand things as they truly are and train therein; they should understand, as they truly are, the concise and detailed characteristics of all phenomena.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How further should Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas understand the concise and detailed characteristics of all phenomena?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva understands, in accordance with reality, that all phenomena are neither conjoined nor dispersed, then this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should thus know the concise and detailed characteristics of all phenomena."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what are all those dharmas that are neither conjoined nor dispersed?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Form is neither conjoined nor disjoined; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither conjoined nor disjoined.
The sense base of the eye up to the sense base of the mind are neither conjoined nor disjoined; the sense base of form up to the sense base of phenomena are neither conjoined nor disjoined.”
The eye-element up to the mind-element are neither conjoined nor dispersed; the form-element up to the phenomena-element are neither conjoined nor dispersed;
the eye-consciousness-element up to the mind-consciousness-element are neither conjoined nor dispersed; eye-contact up to mind-contact are neither conjoined nor dispersed;
and the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to those produced with mind-contact as a condition...
The various feelings born of conditions are neither conjoined nor disjoined; the earth element up to the consciousness element are neither conjoined nor disjoined;
the causal condition up to the dominant condition are neither conjoined nor disjoined; ignorance up to old age and death are neither conjoined nor disjoined;
greed, hatred, and delusion are neither conjoined nor disjoined; the desire realm...
The realm of form and the formless realm are neither conjoined nor dispersed; the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom are neither conjoined nor dispersed;
internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature are neither conjoined nor dispersed;
suchness up to the inconceivable realm are neither conjoined nor dispersed; suffering and its origin...
The noble truths of suffering, origination, cessation, and the path are neither conjoined nor dispersed;

the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path are neither conjoined nor dispersed; the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments are neither conjoined nor dispersed;
the eight liberations up to the ten totalities are neither conjoined nor dispersed; emptiness, signlessness, and...
The door of liberation of wishlessness is neither conjoined nor dispersed; from the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata, they are neither conjoined nor dispersed;
from the stage of extreme joy up to the stage of the Dharma-cloud, they are neither conjoined nor dispersed;
all doors of dhāraṇī and doors of samādhi are neither conjoined nor dispersed; the five eyes and the six supernormal powers are not conjoined... [with anything].
They are not dispersed; the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are neither conjoined nor dispersed;
the thirty-two marks of a Great Being and the eighty minor marks are neither conjoined nor dispersed;
the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity are neither conjoined nor dispersed; omniscience, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and all...
The marks of wisdom are neither conjoined nor dispersed; the fruit of stream-entry up to the awakening of a pratyekabuddha are neither conjoined nor dispersed;
all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are neither conjoined nor dispersed; the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening of all buddhas is neither conjoined nor dispersed;
the knowledge of all modes is neither conjoined nor dispersed; the realm of the conditioned is neither...
Neither conjoined nor disjoined; the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛta-dhātu*) is neither conjoined nor disjoined.

Why is this? Because all such phenomena (*dharma*) lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); if they lack intrinsic nature, they do not exist; and if they do not exist, one cannot speak of their conjunction or disjunction. When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas understand all phenomena in this way, they are able to understand the characteristics of both the concise and the detailed.
The Venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, this is called the concise summary of all the pāramitās; if bodhisattva mahāsattvas train therein, they will be able to accomplish much."

"Bhagavān! These perfections, thus briefly summarized, should be constantly practiced and studied by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are beginners in their practice, and they should likewise be constantly practiced and studied by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwelling in even the tenth stage."
"Bhagavān! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva studies this concise summary of the pāramitās, they will be able to know the concise and extensive characteristics of all phenomena as they truly are."
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
"It is as you have said.

Subhūti, you should know that this Dharma-door of the perfections, thus briefly summarized, can be entered by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of sharp faculties, but not by those of dull faculties; it can be entered by those with faculties in meditative equipoise, but not by those whose faculties are not in equipoise; it can be entered by those who exert diligent effort, but not by those who do not exert diligent effort; it can be entered by those who possess right mindfulness, but not by those who lack right mindfulness; and it can be entered by those who possess sublime wisdom, but not by those who possess corrupt wisdom."
"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to abide in the stage of non-retrogression, they should diligently apply skillful means to enter this Dharma-gate;
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes even to abide in the tenth stage, they should diligently apply skillful means to enter this Dharma-gate."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain even the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), they should diligently apply skillful means to enter this dharma-gate.
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in accordance with what is taught in this perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), this is..."
The bodhisattva mahāsattva is thus able to train accordingly in the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
they are also able to train accordingly in inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature;
they are also able to train accordingly in suchness up to the inconceivable realm; and they are also able to train accordingly in suffering, its origin, and its cessation.
...the Noble Truth of the Path; they can also train accordingly in the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the Noble Path;
they can also train accordingly in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
they can also train accordingly in the eight liberations up to the ten totalities; and they can also train accordingly in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
They are also able to follow and study the gates of liberation; they are also able to follow and study all the gates of dhāraṇī and the gates of samādhi;
they are also able to follow and study the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
they are also able to follow and study the ten powers of a Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and they are also able to follow...
They train in the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant abiding in equanimity;

they are also able to train accordingly in all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); they are also able to train accordingly in all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
they are also able to train accordingly in the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas; and they are also able to train accordingly in everything.
The Knowledge of Knowledges. "Subhūti!

To the extent that a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains by relying upon what is taught in this profound perfection of wisdom, to that same extent that bodhisattva mahāsattva draws closer to the omniscient knowledge they seek."

"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in accordance with what is taught in this perfection of wisdom, all their karmic obstructions and demonic activities will be extinguished as soon as they arise."

Therefore, Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to swiftly eliminate all karmic obstructions and demonic activities, and wishes to correctly embrace the power of skillful means, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices this perfection of wisdom, cultivates this perfection of wisdom, and trains in this perfection of wisdom, at that time the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, currently teaching the Dharma in immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless worlds throughout the ten directions, will constantly protect and mindfully attend to that bodhisattva mahāsattva."
Why is that? Subhūti!
Because all Buddhas of the past, future, and present have appeared without exception from this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
Therefore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to practice the perfection of wisdom, they should form this thought:
"The dharmas realized by all Buddhas of the past, future, and present— those I too shall likewise attain."

"Subhūti! All bodhisattva mahāsattvas should diligently train in the profound perfection of wisdom; if they diligently train in the profound perfection of wisdom, they will swiftly be able to realize the knowledge of all modes."
Therefore, Subhūti, bodhisattva mahāsattvas should always practice the perfection of wisdom without abandoning the mental engagement associated with the profound perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices this perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) according to reality for even as long as a finger-snap, the mass of merit (puṇyaskandha) obtained will be exceedingly great."

Suppose there were someone who taught all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm, causing them all to abide in generosity, pure ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; or causing them to abide in liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation; or causing them to abide in the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha. Although such a person would acquire an immeasurable mass of merit, it would still not equal the mass of merit obtained by practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* sūtra for even the duration of a finger-snap in accordance with reality.
Why is this? Subhūti!

This perfection of wisdom can give rise to all perfections of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; it can give rise to all liberations and the knowledge and vision of liberation; and it can give rise to all fruits from the stage of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.

All the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, currently residing in the infinite, countless, and boundless worlds of the ten directions, have all appeared by means of this profound *prajñāpāramitā*; the same is true for the Buddhas of the past and the future.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to remain without being separated from the mental engagement associated with the profound perfection of wisdom while practicing the perfection of wisdom, even for a brief moment or half a [moment]..."
Whether for a day, or half a month, or a month, or a season, or a year, or a hundred years,
or even longer than that, the mass of merit obtained by this bodhisattva mahāsattva is exceedingly vast;
it surpasses [the merit of] teaching in each of the ten directions as many times as there are sands in the Ganges.

May all sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges be established in generosity, pure ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; or be established in liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation;
or be established in the merits obtained from the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.

Why is this so? Because it is from this perfection of wisdom that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present are born; and because they, for the sake of all sentient beings, truly establish the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; truly establish liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation; truly establish the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; and truly establish the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas—therefore, this mass of merit surpasses that [other merit].
"Furthermore, Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in accordance with what is taught in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*,
you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is no longer subject to regression and is constantly protected and remembered by all Buddhas."
Having accomplished the most excellent skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*), having already approached and made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Buddhas,
having already planted immeasurable subtle and wondrous roots of goodness in the presence of those Buddhas,
having already been taken into the care of immeasurable true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), and having long practiced the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*)...

From the *pāramitās* up to the *prajñāpāramitā*, they have long dwelt securely in the emptiness of the internal (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of the nature of non-existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*);
they have long dwelt securely in suchness (*tathatā*) up to the inconceivable realm (*acintya-dhātu*);
they have long dwelt securely in the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; and they have long practiced the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Up to and including the eight branches of the noble path; having long practiced the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions;
having long practiced the eight liberations up to the ten totalities;
having long practiced the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; and having long practiced all the bodhisattva stages.
For a long time they have practiced all the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi;

for a long time they have practiced the five eyes and the six supernormal knowledges; for a long time they have practiced the ten powers of a Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
and for a long time they have practiced all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects.

Jñāna has long practiced all the conducts of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; he has long practiced the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas; and he has long practiced the knowledge of all modes of knowledge.

It should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells on the stage of the youthful (kumārabhūmi), such that all his aspirations are fulfilled without exception; he constantly beholds the Buddhas without ever abandoning them for even a moment; he never departs from the roots of goodness; he is always able to bring the sentient beings to be converted to maturity; he is always able to adorn and purify the Buddha-fields where he dwells; proceeding from one Buddha-field to another Buddha-field, he makes offerings, pays homage, respects, and praises the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, listening to and practicing the Dharma of the Unsurpassed Vehicle.

It should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has already attained uninterrupted and inexhaustible eloquence; has already attained the accomplishment of the subtle dhāraṇī-dharma and a most supreme and subtle form-body; has already received from all Buddhas the prophecy of perfection; and has already attained mastery in assuming various bodies of existence as he pleases for the sake of liberating sentient beings.

"You should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has skillfully entered into the objects of focus, skillfully entered into the modes of activity, skillfully entered into the phenomena of syllables and skillfully entered into the phenomena beyond syllables; skillfully entered into speech and skillfully entered into non-speech;
skillfully entered into single words, skillfully entered into dual words, and skillfully entered into manifold words; and skillfully entered into feminine speech."
He skillfully enters into the speech of men; he skillfully enters into the speech of those who are neither women nor men;
he skillfully enters into the speech of the past, the speech of the future, and the speech of the present;
he skillfully enters into all meanings and all phrasing; he skillfully enters into form, sensation, perception, and mental formations.

He skillfully enters into consciousness; he skillfully enters into the aggregates, the sense bases, and the elements; he skillfully enters into dependent origination and the factors of dependent origination;
he skillfully enters into the mundane world and into nirvāṇa; he skillfully enters into the characteristics of phenomena;
he skillfully enters into the characteristics of the conditioned and the characteristics of the unconditioned; and he skillfully enters into both the conditioned and the unconditioned.
Regarding characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*): he skillfully enters into the characteristic of practice and the characteristic of non-practice;
he skillfully enters into the characteristic of characteristics and the characteristic of non-characteristics; he skillfully enters into existence and non-existence;
he skillfully enters into intrinsic nature and extrinsic nature; he skillfully enters into conjunction, separation, and both conjunction and separation. He skillfully enters into...
He skillfully enters into association; he skillfully enters into non-association; he skillfully enters into both association and non-association.

He skillfully enters into suchness, skillfully enters into non-falsity, skillfully enters into immutability, skillfully enters into the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), skillfully enters into the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), skillfully enters into the fixed nature of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), skillfully enters into the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthititā*), and skillfully enters into the nature of conditions (*pratyayatā*).
He skillfully enters the nature of non-conditioning; he skillfully enters the noble truths;

he skillfully enters the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*); he skillfully enters the six perfections (*pāramitā*);

he skillfully enters the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*); and he skillfully enters the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*) up to the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
Abiding therein, they skillfully enter the gates of dhāraṇī, skillfully enter the gates of samādhi, skillfully enter the three gates of liberation,
skillfully enter all modes of emptiness, skillfully enter the five eyes, skillfully enter the six supernormal powers,
skillfully enter the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and skillfully enter non-forgetfulness.

They have lost their dharmas; they have skillfully entered the state of constant abiding in equanimity, skillfully entered all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), skillfully entered the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and skillfully entered the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);
they have skillfully entered the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛtadhātu*) and skillfully entered the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*);
they have skillfully entered the elements (*dhātu*) and skillfully entered that which is not an element (*adhātu*).

“Skillfully entering the mental attention toward form, up to the mental attention toward consciousness; skillfully entering the mental attention toward the sense base of the eye, up to the mental attention toward the sense base of the mind;
skillfully entering the mental attention toward the sense base of form, up to the mental attention toward the sense base of phenomena;

skillfully entering the mental attention toward the element of the eye, up to the mental attention toward the element of the mind; skillfully entering the mental attention toward the element of form, up to the [element of] phenomena.”
He skillfully enters the mental attention to the elements; he skillfully enters the mental attention to the eye-consciousness element up to the mental consciousness element;
he skillfully enters the mental attention to eye-contact up to mind-contact;
he skillfully enters the mental attention to all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition up to all feelings produced with mind-contact as condition; he skillfully enters the earth [element].
He skillfully enters into the mental engagement with the element of earth up to the mental engagement with the element of consciousness;

he skillfully enters into the mental engagement with the causal condition up to the mental engagement with the dominant condition; he skillfully enters into the mental engagement with ignorance up to the mental engagement with old age and death;
he skillfully enters into the mental engagement with the perfection of generosity up to the mental engagement with the perfection of wisdom.
The mental engagement with internal emptiness up to the mental engagement with the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;

the mental engagement with the skillful entry into suchness up to the mental engagement with the inconceivable realm; the mental engagement with the skillful entry into the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
and the mental engagement with the skillful entry into the four applications of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path.
They apply their attention to entering the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;

they skillfully enter the application of attention to the eight liberations up to the ten totalities; they skillfully enter the application of attention to the doors of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
and they skillfully enter the application of attention to the stage of pure observation up to the stage of a Tathāgata.
He skillfully enters the mental engagements of the Stage of Utmost Joy up to the mental engagements of the Cloud of Dharma;
he skillfully enters the mental engagements of all doors of dhāraṇī and doors of samādhi; he skillfully enters the mental engagements of the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
he skillfully enters the mental engagements of the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
He is skilled in the mental engagement with the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks;
he is skilled in the mental engagement with the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity;

he is skilled in the mental engagement with all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects; and he is skilled in the mental engagement with the fruit of stream-entry up to that of the pratyekabuddha.
The mental engagement of bodhi, which skillfully enters into the mental engagement of all practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, skillfully enters into the mental engagement of the unexcelled,
perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas, and skillfully enters into the mental engagement of the knowledge of all modes.
“Skillfully entering into the emptiness of the characteristics of form; skillfully entering into the emptiness of the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
and thus, up to, skillfully entering into the emptiness of the characteristics of the knowledge of all modes and the knowledge of all modes itself;
skillfully entering into the path of pliancy and the path of non-pliancy; skillfully entering into arising...”
...skillfully entering cessation; skillfully entering the difference between abiding and entering; skillfully entering right view and skillfully entering wrong view;
skillfully entering views and skillfully entering non-views; skillfully entering greed, hatred, and delusion, and skillfully entering non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion;
skillfully entering all views, obsessions, latent tendencies, fetters, and bonds, and skillfully entering all views...

Having severed the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), fetters (*saṃyojana*), and bonds (*bandhana*), he skillfully enters into name (*nāman*), skillfully enters into form (*rūpa*), and skillfully enters into name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

He skillfully enters into the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), skillfully enters into the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), skillfully enters into the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), and skillfully enters into the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). He skillfully enters into formations (*saṃskāra*), skillfully enters into characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), skillfully enters into causes (*hetu*), and skillfully enters into fruits (*phala*).
He skillfully enters into suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;

he skillfully enters into the hells and the way to the hells, skillfully enters into the animal realm and the way to the animal realm, skillfully enters into the realm of hungry ghosts and the way to the realm of hungry ghosts, skillfully enters into humans and the way to the human realm, skillfully enters into devas and the way to the deva realm; and he skillfully enters into the stream-enterer and the fruit of stream-entry.
They skillfully enter the path of the stream-enterer, the fruit of the stream-enterer, and the path to the fruit of the stream-enterer;
they skillfully enter the non-returner, the fruit of the non-returner, and the path to the fruit of the non-returner;
they skillfully enter the arhat, the fruit of the arhat, and the path to the fruit of the arhat; and they skillfully enter the pratyekabuddha and the awakening of a pratyekabuddha.
The path of pratyekabuddha-enlightenment thoroughly enters into all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and all bodhisattva practices;
it thoroughly enters into all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas;
it thoroughly enters into all-knowledge and the path to all-knowledge; and it thoroughly enters into the characteristics of the path.
He skillfully enters into knowledge and the path of the knowledge of paths; he skillfully enters into the knowledge of all aspects and the path of the knowledge of all aspects;
he skillfully enters into the faculties, skillfully enters into the perfection of the faculties, and skillfully enters into the superiority and inferiority of the faculties;
he skillfully enters into wisdom, skillfully enters into swift wisdom, skillfully enters into sharp wisdom, skillfully enters into rapid wisdom, and skillfully enters into powerful wisdom.
Skillfully entering and attaining wisdom; skillfully entering vast wisdom; skillfully entering profound wisdom; skillfully entering great wisdom;
skillfully entering peerless wisdom; skillfully entering true wisdom; skillfully entering jewel-like wisdom;
skillfully entering the past world, skillfully entering the future world, skillfully entering the present world, and skillfully entering skillful means.
He skillfully enters into the consideration of sentient beings, skillfully enters into their intentions, and skillfully enters into their superior intentions;
he skillfully enters into the characteristics of words and meanings, skillfully enters into all the noble dharmas, and skillfully enters into the expedient means for establishing the three vehicles.

"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, draws forth the profound perfection of wisdom, and cultivates the profound perfection of wisdom, they will attain such various benefits as these."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom?”
"How does one draw forth the profound perfection of wisdom?
How does one cultivate the profound perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* by contemplating that form (*rūpa*) up to consciousness (*vijñāna*) are subject to decay, destruction, dispersal, lack of autonomy, lack of solidity, and are by nature deceptive.”
"Subhūti! Regarding your question, 'How do bodhisattva mahāsattvas bring forth the profound perfection of wisdom?',
bodhisattva mahāsattvas should bring forth the profound perfection of wisdom just as they would bring forth the emptiness of emptiness."
"Subhūti! Regarding your question, 'How do bodhisattva mahāsattvas cultivate profound prajñāpāramitā?',
bodhisattva mahāsattvas should cultivate profound prajñāpāramitā by dismantling all phenomena."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
for how long should bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, elicit the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and cultivate the profound *prajñāpāramitā*?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

“All bodhisattva mahāsattvas, from their first generation of the mind of awakening until they sit upon the sublime seat of enlightenment, should practice the profound perfection of wisdom, draw forth the profound perfection of wisdom, and cultivate the profound perfection of wisdom.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,

in what kind of mind should bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide so that they may practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* uninterruptedly, draw forth the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and cultivate the profound *prajñāpāramitā*?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"All bodhisattva mahāsattvas, from their first generation of the mind until they sit upon the seat of sublime awakening, must not allow any other mental engagements to arise indiscriminately; rather, they should always abide in mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, drawing forth the profound perfection of wisdom, and cultivating the profound perfection of wisdom."

Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is even able to prevent the mind and mental factors from turning toward objects, they may be said to be practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, drawing forth the profound perfection of wisdom, and cultivating the profound perfection of wisdom.
“World-Honored One!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, draw forth the profound perfection of wisdom, and cultivate the profound perfection of wisdom, will they attain the knowledge of all modes?”
"No, World-Honored One! Subhūti, it is not so. "World-Honored One! [Subhūti replied.]

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not practice the profound perfection of wisdom, do not bring forth the profound perfection of wisdom, and do not cultivate the profound perfection of wisdom, will they attain the knowledge of all modes?
"No, World-Honored One! Subhūti, it is not so. "World-Honored One! [Subhūti replied.]

Do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain the knowledge of all aspects by neither practicing nor not practicing, neither inducing nor not inducing, and neither cultivating nor not cultivating this profound perfection of wisdom?
"No, World-Honored One! Subhūti, it is not so. "World-Honored One! [Subhūti replied.]
“If that is so, how shall the bodhisattva mahāsattvas attain the knowledge of all modes? “Subhūti,
the bodhisattva mahāsattvas shall attain the knowledge of all modes in the manner of suchness.”
“World-Honored One!
What is suchness? “Suvikrāntavikrāmin! [Listen.]”
"It is like the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi). “World-Honored One!
What is the limit of reality?”
“Subhūti! It is like the dharma-realm.
“World-Honored One!”
"What is the dharma-realm? "Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

It is like the realm of the self, the realm of sentient beings, the realm of the life-principle, the realm of the born, the realm of the nourisher, the realm of the person, and the realm of the individual."
“World-Honored One!
What are the self-element up to the person-element? “Sudhana!
[The Buddha replied: “Sudhana!”
What do you think?
Can a self, or a sentient being, or a life-force, or a living being, or a nourisher, or a person, or a pudgala be apprehended?
“No, World-Honored One! “Excellent, Subhūti!
If the self, up to and including the person, cannot be apprehended, how could I possibly designate a "self-element" or even a "person-element"?
Thus it is, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not designate the perfection of wisdom, nor does he designate the knowledge of all modes, nor does he designate any phenomena, that bodhisattva mahāsattva will certainly realize the knowledge of all modes.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Is it only the perfection of wisdom that cannot be designated, or are the perfection of meditative concentration and even the perfection of generosity likewise incapable of being designated?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Not only is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) ineffable, but the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā) up to the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā) are also ineffable; whether they be the dharmas of śrāvakas, the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of bodhisattvas, or the dharmas of tathāgatas, these too are ineffable.”
“Subhūti! To put it briefly, all phenomena—whether conditioned or unconditioned—are inexpressible.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again, saying:

"If all phenomena are ultimately ineffable, how can one designate them as 'hell-being,' 'animal,' 'hungry ghost,' 'human,' or 'deva'; or as 'stream-enterer,' 'once-returner,' 'non-returner,' 'arhat,' 'pratyekabuddha,' 'bodhisattva,' 'tathāgata,' or 'all phenomena'?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Can the designation of sentient beings and the designation of phenomena be truly apprehended?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If the designation of sentient beings and the designation of phenomena cannot be found in reality, how could I designate: 'this is hell,' 'this is the animal realm,' 'this is the realm of hungry ghosts,' 'this is a human,' 'this is a deva,' 'this is a stream-enterer,' 'this is a once-returner,' 'this is a non-returner,' 'this is an arhat,' 'this is a pratyekabuddha,' 'this is a bodhisattva,' 'this is a Tathāgata,' or 'these are all phenomena'?"
Thus it is, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should train in all phenomena as being unestablishable, thereby proceeding toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, should they not train in form?"
"Should one not train in feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness?
Likewise, should one not train even in the knowledge of all aspects?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

“When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should train in form without increasing or decreasing it; they should train in feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness without increasing or decreasing them; and so on, up to training in the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) without increasing or decreasing it.”
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, how should they train in form so that it neither increases nor decreases?”
How should one train in feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness so as to neither increase nor decrease them?
And likewise, how should one train in the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) so as to neither increase nor decrease it?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should train in form by way of its non-arising and non-cessation; they should train in feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness by way of their non-arising and non-cessation; and so on, up to training in the knowledge of all aspects by way of its non-arising and non-cessation."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, how should they train in form by way of its non-arising and non-ceasing?”
One should ask: how should one train in feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness by means of non-arising and non-ceasing?
And so on, up to: how should one train in the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) by means of non-arising and non-ceasing?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
