"When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they should train by neither giving rise to nor performing any formations regarding form—whether by way of cultivation or by way of rejection; they should train by neither giving rise to nor performing any formations regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness—whether by way of cultivation or by way of rejection; and so on, up to training by neither giving rise to nor performing any formations regarding the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvajñatā*)—whether by way of cultivation or by way of rejection."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,

when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, how should they train so as not to give rise to or perform any formations regarding form— whether by way of cultivation or by way of relinquishment?”
How should one train so as not to give rise to or perform any formations regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness—whether by way of cultivation or abandonment?

Likewise, how should one train so as not to give rise to or perform any formations regarding everything up to and including the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna)—whether by way of cultivation or abandonment?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should train by contemplating that the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena are empty, and thus neither arising nor producing any formations regarding form—whether cultivating them or abandoning them;

they should train by contemplating that the specific characteristics of all phenomena are empty, and thus neither arising nor producing any formations regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness—whether cultivating them or abandoning them."

In this way, up to and including the point where one should train by observing that the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena are empty, and by neither initiating nor performing any conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*) regarding omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), whether through cultivation or through elimination.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 461. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Second Division, Chapter Sixty-Eight on Skillful Means (3). At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, contemplate that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty?
The Buddha said,
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin!"

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should contemplate that form is empty of form; they should contemplate that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
They should contemplate that the eye-base is empty of the eye-base; they should contemplate that the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are empty of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases.

They should contemplate that the form-base is empty of the form-base; they should contemplate that the sound, odor, taste, tangible, and phenomena-bases are empty of the sound, odor, taste, tangible, and phenomena-bases.

One should contemplate that the eye-element is empty by virtue of the eye-element; one should contemplate that the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements are empty by virtue of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements.

One should contemplate that the form-element is empty by virtue of the form-element; one should contemplate that the sound, odor, taste, tangible, and mental-object elements are empty by virtue of the sound, odor, taste, tangible, and mental-object elements.

One should contemplate that the eye-consciousness-element is empty by virtue of the eye-consciousness-element; one should contemplate that the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness-elements are empty by virtue of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness-elements.
One should contemplate that eye-contact is empty of eye-contact; one should contemplate that ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact are empty of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact.

One should contemplate that all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition are empty of those feelings produced with eye-contact as condition; one should contemplate that all feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as conditions are empty of those feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as conditions.

One should contemplate that the earth element is empty of the earth element; one should contemplate that the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are empty of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements.

One should contemplate that causes and conditions are empty of causes and conditions; one should contemplate that the immediately preceding condition, the object condition, and the dominant condition are empty of the immediately preceding condition, the object condition, and the dominant condition.

One should contemplate that ignorance is empty of ignorance; one should contemplate that volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, existence, birth, and old age and death are empty of volitional formations up to old age and death.

One should contemplate that the perfection of generosity is empty of the perfection of generosity; one should contemplate that the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are empty of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

One should contemplate inner emptiness as being empty by means of inner emptiness; one should contemplate outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, the emptiness of the non-dispersal of dispersion, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of self and common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, by means of outer emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.

One should contemplate that suchness is empty of suchness; one should contemplate that the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), non-erroneousness, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena (*dharmasthiti*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), and the inconceivable realm are empty of the dharma-realm up to the inconceivable realm.

One should contemplate that the noble truth of suffering is empty of the noble truth of suffering; one should contemplate that the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are empty of the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path.

One should contemplate that the four foundations of mindfulness are empty of the four foundations of mindfulness; one should contemplate that the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path are empty of the four right efforts up to the eightfold noble path.

One should contemplate that the four dhyānas are empty of the four dhyānas; one should contemplate that the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments are empty of the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments;

one should contemplate that the eight liberations are empty of the eight liberations; one should contemplate that the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative concentrations, and the ten totalities are empty of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative concentrations, and the ten totalities;

one should contemplate that the door of liberation of emptiness is empty of the door of liberation of emptiness; and one should contemplate that the doors of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are empty of the doors of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.

One should contemplate that the Stage of Pure Vision is empty of the Stage of Pure Vision; one should contemplate that the Stage of Lineage, the Eighth Stage, the Stage of Vision, the Stage of Refinement, the Stage of Freedom from Desire, the Stage of Completion, the Stage of the Pratyekabuddha, the Stage of the Bodhisattva, and the Stage of the Tathāgata are empty of the Stage of Lineage up to the Stage of the Tathāgata;

one should contemplate that the Stage of Extreme Joy is empty of the Stage of Extreme Joy; and one should contemplate that the Stage of Freedom from Defilement, the Radiant Stage, the Blazing Wisdom Stage, the Extremely Difficult to Conquer Stage, the Manifesting Stage, the Far-Reaching Stage, the Immovable Stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence, and the Cloud of Dharma Stage are empty of the Stage of Freedom from Defilement up to the Cloud of Dharma Stage.
One should contemplate that all dharani-doors are empty by virtue of all dharani-doors; one should contemplate that all samadhi-doors are empty by virtue of all samadhi-doors;
one should contemplate that the five eyes are empty by virtue of the five eyes; one should contemplate that the six supernormal powers are empty by virtue of the six supernormal powers;

one should contemplate that the ten powers of a Tathagata are empty by virtue of the ten powers of a Tathagata; and one should contemplate that the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are empty by virtue of the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

One should contemplate that the thirty-two marks of a great man are empty of the thirty-two marks of a great man; one should contemplate that the eighty minor marks are empty of the eighty minor marks;

one should contemplate that the quality of non-forgetfulness is empty of the quality of non-forgetfulness; one should contemplate that the nature of constant equanimity is empty of the nature of constant equanimity;

one should contemplate that all-knowledge is empty of all-knowledge; and one should contemplate that the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects are empty of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects.

One should contemplate that the fruit of stream-entry is empty of the fruit of stream-entry; one should contemplate that the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, and pratyekabuddha-enlightenment are empty of the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, and pratyekabuddha-enlightenment;

one should contemplate that all bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices are empty of all bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices; one should contemplate that the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas is empty of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas; and one should contemplate that the knowledge of all modes is empty of the knowledge of all modes.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should contemplate that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If form is empty of form, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and so on up to the knowledge of all modes being empty of the knowledge of all modes, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the profound perfection of wisdom?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva has no practice at all, this is the practice of the profound perfection of wisdom.
The venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
for what reason does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the profound perfection of wisdom while not practicing anything at all?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* cannot be apprehended, the bodhisattva mahāsattva also cannot be apprehended; neither can the practice be apprehended. Whether it be the one who practices, that by which one practices, the time of practicing, or the locus of practice—all these cannot be apprehended.”

Therefore, Subhūti, when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have no [object of] activity at all, they are practicing the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), because within it, all conceptual proliferations (prapañca) are unapprehendable.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom by not practicing anything at all, how then does a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is a beginner in their practice cultivate the profound perfection of wisdom?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should constantly train in the non-apprehension of all phenomena.
Having trained in this way, they should practice generosity by employing non-apprehension as their skillful means."
From the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, one should abide in inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;
one should abide in suchness up to the inconceivable realm; one should abide in the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
and one should cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path.
One should cultivate the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions;
one should cultivate the eight liberations up to the ten totalities; one should cultivate the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
one should cultivate the stages of a bodhisattva mahāsattva; and one should cultivate all dhāraṇī-doors and samādhis.
Regarding the gateway of the stages, one should cultivate the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
one should cultivate the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; one should cultivate the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity;
one should cultivate all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects; and one should cultivate all bodhisattvas.
"A Mahāsattva should cultivate the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas; he should cultivate the knowledge of all modes.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed [the Buddha], saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is called ‘having something to be attained,’ and what is called ‘having nothing to be attained’?”
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!
All that is dual is called ‘having something to be apprehended’; all that is non-dual is called ‘having nothing to be apprehended.’”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In what way is duality called 'attainment,' and in what way is non-duality called 'non-attainment'?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“The eye and forms are two; even so, the mind and mental phenomena are two. ‘Form’ and ‘formlessness’ are two;
‘visible’ and ‘invisible’ are two; ‘resistant’ and ‘non-resistant’ are two.”
Outflows and outflow-free states constitute a duality; conditioned and unconditioned phenomena constitute a duality;
mundane and supramundane states constitute a duality; saṃsāra and nirvāṇa constitute a duality; the dharmas of ordinary beings and ordinary beings themselves constitute a duality;
the dharmas of stream-enterers and stream-enterers themselves constitute a duality; and so on, up to the enlightenment of pratyekabuddhas and pratyekabuddhas themselves.
Second, "Bodhisattva-mahāsattva" and "the practice of a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva" are two; "Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment of a Buddha" and "the Buddha" are two.
In this way, all such things involving conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) are called "two.
All that is dual involves apprehension (*upalambha*).

"Subhūti! It is not that the eye and forms are non-dual; even up to it is not that the mind and phenomena are non-dual. Likewise, up to it is not that the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and the Buddha are non-dual. All such things that are free from conceptual proliferation are called 'non-dual,' and all that is non-dual is unapprehendable."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
is it because there is something to be attained that there is no attainment?”
"Is it because there is nothing to be attained that there is no attainment?
The Buddha said,
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin!"

It is not because there is something obtained that there is non-attainment; nor is it because there is nothing obtained that there is non-attainment. Rather, the equality of obtaining and non-obtaining is called non-attainment.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should diligently train in the equality of that which is apprehended and that which is non-apprehended. Subhūti!
"When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train in this manner, they are said to be training in the perfection of wisdom as those who do not apprehend anything.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), does not cling to anything that can be apprehended and does not cling to anything that cannot be apprehended, how does this bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the profound perfection of wisdom so as to gradually fulfill it, proceeding from one stage (bhūmi) to the next?
“If there is no gradual fulfillment from one stage to the next, how can one attain the knowledge of all modes?
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they do not abide in the practice of apprehending something as they practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* while gradually perfecting the attainment of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*) from one stage to the next; nor do they abide in the practice of non-apprehension as they practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* while gradually perfecting the attainment of the knowledge of all modes from one stage to the next.
Why is this so? Subhūti!

The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is non-apprehensible; omniscience (*sarvajñājñāna*) is also non-apprehensible; the one who practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also non-apprehensible; and even this non-apprehensibility is itself non-apprehensible.
"Subhūti! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice the profound perfection of wisdom in this manner.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again, saying:

“If the profound *prajñāpāramitā* cannot be apprehended, omniscience (*sarvajñājñāna*) also cannot be apprehended, and even the one who can practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* cannot be apprehended, how then does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, always delight in the discernment of all phenomena?”
That is to say: "This is form; this is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
This is the eye-base up to the mind-base. This is the form-base up to the phenomena-base. This is the eye-element up to the mind-element.
This is the form-element up to the phenomena-element. This is the eye-consciousness-element up to the mind-consciousness-element."

The elements: these are eye-contact through to mind-contact; these are the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition through to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition; these are the earth element through to the consciousness element;
these are the causal condition through to the sovereign condition; these are ignorance through to old age and death.
This is the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
this is inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature; this is suchness up to the inconceivable realm;
this is the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; this is the four applications of mindfulness up to...
These are the eight branches of the noble path; these are the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
these are the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality; these are the gateways to liberation through emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
these are the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata; these are the stage of extreme joy.
Up to the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), these are all the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi;
these are the five eyes and the six supernormal powers; these are the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
these are the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty minor marks; these are...
The quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity; this is omniscience, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects;
this is the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of the pratyekabuddhas;
this is the entire conduct of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas; this is the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas; this...
“What is this omniscient wisdom?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, although they always delight in discerning all phenomena, they do not apprehend form, nor do they apprehend feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness; and so on, up to and including the non-apprehension of omniscient wisdom.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), if they do not apprehend form (rūpa), nor apprehend feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), formations (saṃskāra), or consciousness (vijñāna), and so on up to not apprehending even the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā), how can they fulfill the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā) up to the perfection of wisdom?"
If one cannot fulfill the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, how can one enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth?
If one cannot enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth, how can one bring sentient beings to maturity?
If one cannot bring sentient beings to maturity, how can one purify a buddha-field?
If one cannot purify the Buddha-fields, how can one attain the knowledge of all modes?
If one cannot attain the knowledge of all modes, how can one turn the wheel of the true Dharma and perform the deeds of a Buddha?

If one cannot turn the wheel of the sublime Dharma and perform the deeds of a Buddha, how could one liberate immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of sentient beings from old age, sickness, death, and suffering, and cause them to attain ultimate peace and bliss in nirvāṇa?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not practice the profound perfection of wisdom for the sake of form; nor do they practice the profound perfection of wisdom for the sake of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; and so on, up to and including not practicing the profound perfection of wisdom for the sake of the knowledge of all modes."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, for what purpose do they practice this profound perfection of wisdom?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they practice the profound perfection of wisdom because there is nothing for which they act."
Why is this? Subhūti!

All dharmas are unconditioned and uncreated; the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also unconditioned and uncreated; the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*) is also unconditioned and uncreated; and the bodhisattva mahāsattvas are likewise unconditioned and uncreated.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice the profound perfection of wisdom by means of the unconditioned and the uncreated as their skillful method.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If all phenomena are unconditioned and uncreated, one should not designate distinctions among the three vehicles—namely, the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, or the Unsurpassed Vehicle."
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"The designation of the unconditioned and the uncreated cannot be apprehended; it is only the designation of the conditioned and the created that can be apprehended. Why is this so?"
"Subhūti! There are foolish, unlearned ordinary beings who cling to form, cling to feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, and even cling to the knowledge of all modes."

Due to attachment, by recollecting form one obtains form; by recollecting feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, one obtains feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness; and so on, up to recollecting the knowledge of all modes, one obtains the knowledge of all modes.
By virtue of attaining mindfulness, he reflects thus:
"I shall certainly attain the knowledge of all modes; I shall liberate all sentient beings from birth, old age, sickness, and death, and cause them to attain ultimate peace and happiness in nirvāṇa."
"Subhūti! These foolish, unlearned worldlings, through their perverted views, engage in such reflections and thereby slander the Buddha. Why is this so?

"Subhūti! With the five eyes, the Buddha seeks form and does not find it; he seeks feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness and does not find them. Even seeking the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñājñāna) he does not find it, and seeking sentient beings he likewise does not find them."

Those foolish, unlearned ordinary beings, blind and lacking the eye of wisdom, who cling to all phenomena—it is impossible that they could ever realize the knowledge of all modes, liberate all sentient beings from birth, old age, sickness, and death, and cause them to attain ultimate peace and bliss in nirvāṇa!
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying: "If all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, seeking with their five purified eyes, cannot find form;

cannot find feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; and so on, up to not finding the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvajñajñāna*), nor finding sentient beings—then there should be no realization of the knowledge of all aspects, nor the liberation of sentient beings from birth, old age, sickness, and death, nor the attainment of ultimate peace and bliss in *nirvāṇa*. How then, Blessed One, can you yourself realize the knowledge of all aspects and establish the distinctions among the three categories of sentient beings: those fixed in the right nature, those fixed in the wrong nature, and those who are indeterminate?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Having realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I have observed with my purified five eyes according to reality and determined that there is truly no sentient being who can realize the knowledge of all modes; thus, I establish the distinctions among the three groups of sentient beings."

However, because sentient beings are deluded and inverted, they give rise to the notion of real dharmas regarding what are not real dharmas, and the notion of real sentient beings regarding what are not real sentient beings. To eliminate their false attachments, I speak in accordance with conventional truth, not ultimate truth.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Does the Tathāgata abide in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) when he realizes the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*)?
The Buddha said:
"Not so," [the Buddha replied]. Subhūti asked again:
"Does the Tathāgata dwell in perversion when he realizes all-knowledge?"
The Buddha said:
"It is not so. Subhūti asked again:

“If the Tathāgata does not abide in the ultimate truth to realize all-knowledge, nor does he abide in perversion to realize all-knowledge, would it not be the case that the Tathāgata is unable to realize all-knowledge?”
The Buddha said:
"It is not so! Good Manifestation, you should know this!"
Although I have realized the knowledge of all modes, I abide nowhere; that is to say, I do not abide in the realm of the conditioned, nor do I abide in the realm of the unconditioned. Subhūti!

For example, a transformation being created by a Tathāgata does not abide in the realm of the conditioned, nor does it abide in the realm of the unconditioned; yet, it still possesses coming and going, walking, standing, sitting, and reclining.
Subhūti! If that which is emanated practices the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
or dwells in inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature; or dwells in suchness...
Upon reaching the inconceivable realm, whether one abides in the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
or cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path; or cultivates the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions;
or cultivates the eight liberations up to the ten totalities; or cultivates emptiness—
The gateways of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness; whether cultivating from the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma;
whether cultivating all the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi; whether cultivating the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
whether cultivating the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; or whether cultivating...

The quality of non-forgetfulness, the state of constant equanimity, the cultivation of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);
the cultivation of all the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva; the cultivation of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas;
the realization of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatājñāna*); and the turning of the wheel of Dharma to perform [all beneficial deeds].
This is the Buddha-work.
Those who have been emanated further transform themselves into immeasurable sentient beings, within whom he establishes the distinctions of the three categories. Subhūti!
What do you think?
Do these emanations produced by the Tathāgatas truly have coming and going, walking, standing, sitting, and lying down?
And even so, do they truly establish the distinctions among the three groups of sentient beings?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin! It is the same for the Tathāgata:

he knows that all phenomena are like magical transformations, and he teaches that all phenomena are also like magical transformations. Although he performs deeds, they lack true reality; although he delivers sentient beings, there are no beings delivered—just as a magically transformed being delivers other magically transformed beings.”
Thus it is, Subhūti!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should be like those emanated by the Tathāgata; though they perform actions, they remain without attachment.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If all phenomena are like magical transformations, and the Tathāgata is likewise so, then what difference is there between the Tathāgata and a magical transformation?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“The Tathāgata and that which is emanated by him, as well as all dharmas, are in reality without distinction. Why is this?

"Subhūti! All the deeds performed by the Tathāgata, and even those things emanated by him, are able to perform the very same functions that the Tathāgata himself performs. Therefore, there is no distinction between the Tathāgata, his emanations, and all phenomena."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If there were no one transformed by the Buddha, could the Tathāgata alone perform the deeds to be done?
And if there were no Tathāgata, would that which was transformed be able to perform those deeds alone?"
The Buddha said, "One can. Subhūti asked:
"What is this matter? The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Suppose there were a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śāntamati. Having already delivered all those who were to be delivered by him, and at a time when there was no bodhisattva capable of receiving the Buddha’s prediction, he then manifested a transformation Buddha to remain in the world, while he himself entered the realm of great nirvāṇa without remainder."

At that time, those emanated Buddhas performed various Buddha-activities for half an eon; once the half-eon had passed, they bestowed the prediction of great enlightenment upon a bodhisattva and manifested entry into nirvana.
At that time, the devas, humans, asuras, and others all thought that the Buddha had now entered nirvana; yet the body of the transformation Buddha truly has neither arising nor ceasing.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should believe and know that all phenomena are like magical transformations.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If the body of the Tathāgata and that which he has emanated are equal and without distinction, how is it that [the Tathāgata] can serve as a truly pure field of merit for the world’s donors?"

If sentient beings, for the sake of nirvāṇa, offer worship and respect to the Tathāgata, their merit is inexhaustible until they finally enter the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder; likewise, if there are those who, for the sake of nirvāṇa, offer worship and respect to a transformation body of the Buddha, the mass of merit they obtain shall also be inexhaustible until they finally enter the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"Just as the body of a Tathāgata, by virtue of its dharmatā, is able to serve as a pure field of merit for devas, humans, and asuras, so too is that which is emanated by the Buddha; by virtue of its dharmatā, it is likewise able to serve as a pure field of merit for devas, humans, and asuras."

Just as the Tathāgata’s body receives the offerings and respect of various donors, causing the merit of those donors to be inexhaustible until the end of saṃsāra, so too it is with the emanations of the Buddha; they receive the offerings and respect of various donors, likewise causing the merit of those donors to be inexhaustible until the end of saṃsāra.
"Subhūti, you should know this!

Setting aside for a moment the merit obtained by making offerings to and honoring the Tathāgata and his emanations, if a son or daughter of good family gives rise to thoughts of loving-kindness and reverence toward the Tathāgata and mindfully recollects him, the roots of goodness of those sons and daughters of good family will be inexhaustible, until they finally reach the end of suffering."
Subhūti, you should know this!

Let alone the merit obtained by conceiving thoughts of loving-kindness and respect toward the Buddha and recollecting him; if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha, were to scatter even a single flower into the air, the roots of virtue of such sons and daughters of good family would be inexhaustible, until they finally reach the end of suffering.
"Subhūti, you should know this!

Setting aside for a moment the merit obtained by scattering even a single flower into the air for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, at the very least, utters the name 'Namo Buddhāya, the Great Tamer,' the roots of goodness of those sons and daughters of good family will be inexhaustible, until they finally reach the end of suffering."
Thus it is, Subhūti!
By making offerings and showing reverence to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas—the great fields of merit—one obtains such great benefits of merit that their measure is difficult to fathom.
Therefore, Subhūti, you should know this:
the Tathāgata and the emanated Buddha are both donors, and as true, pure fields of merit, they are equal and without distinction, for they take the nature of all phenomena as their standard measure.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All bodhisattva mahāsattvas should take the dharma-nature of these dharmas as their standard measure and practice the profound perfection of wisdom. Having entered the dharma-nature of all dharmas through skillful means, they do not destroy the dharma-nature of those dharmas; that is to say, they do not discriminate:
'This is the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity,' nor do they discriminate: 'This is the dharma-nature of the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity.'"

This is the emptiness of the internal, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature; this is the dharma-nature of the emptiness of the internal, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.
This is suchness, up to and including the inconceivable realm; this is the dharma-nature of suchness, up to and including the inconceivable realm.
This is the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; this is the dharma-nature of the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
These are the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path; this is the dharma-nature of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path.
These are the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; this is the dharma-nature of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments.
These are the eight liberations up to the ten totalities; this is the dharma-nature of the eight liberations up to the ten totalities.
This is the gate of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; this is the dharma-nature of the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
This is the Ground of Utmost Joy up to the Ground of Dharma Clouds; this is the dharma-nature of the Ground of Utmost Joy up to the Ground of Dharma Clouds.
This is all the gates of dhāraṇī and all the gates of samādhi; this is the dharma-nature of all the gates of dhāraṇī and all the gates of samādhi.
These are the five eyes and the six supernormal powers; this is the dharma-nature of the five eyes and the six supernormal powers.
These are the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; this is the dharma-nature of the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
These are the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks; this is the dharma-nature of the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks.
This is the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity; this is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity.

This is all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); this is the true nature of all-knowledge, knowledge of the paths, and knowledge of all aspects.
This is the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; this is the true nature of the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
This is the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; this is the dharma-nature of the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
This is the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas;
this is the dharma-nature of the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas. This is the knowledge of all modes; this is the dharma-nature of the knowledge of all modes.

"Subhūti! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should not differentiate the specific characteristics of the dharma-nature among all phenomena in such a way as to destroy that dharma-nature."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the profound perfection of wisdom should not differentiate among the dharmas by destroying their dharma-nature, why does the World-Honored One himself speak of the distinctions among the dharma-natures of all dharmas, thereby destroying that dharma-nature?”

That is to say, the Blessed One has taught: "This is form; this is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; these are the sense-base of the eye up to the sense-base of the mind; these are the sense-base of forms up to the sense-base of phenomena; these are the element of the eye up to the element of the mind; these are the element of forms up to the element of phenomena; these are the element of eye-consciousness up to the element of mind-consciousness; these are eye-contact up to mind-contact; these are all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, up to all feelings produced with mind-contact as condition; these are the earth element up to the consciousness element; these are the causal condition up to the dominant condition;
these are ignorance up to old age and death; these are internal phenomena; these are external phenomena; these are wholesome phenomena; these are unwholesome phenomena."
"This is a determinate dharma; this is an indeterminate dharma;
this is a contaminated dharma; this is an uncontaminated dharma;
this is a mundane dharma; this is a supramundane dharma."
"This is a shared dharma; this is an unshared dharma.
This is a dharma subject to contention; this is a dharma free from contention.
This is a conditioned dharma; this is an unconditioned dharma."
“World-Honored One!
Since you have thus explained the various distinctions among these dharmas, will you not, World-Honored One, yourself destroy the nature of dharmas?
The Buddha said:

“Subhūti! I do not destroy the dharmatā of phenomena; rather, by means of provisional designations through names and signs, I cause sentient beings to awaken to and enter the equality of the dharmatā of all phenomena, so that they may transcend birth and death and realize nirvāṇa.”
Therefore, Subhūti, although all Tathāgatas,
Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas speak of the various names and characteristics of all phenomena, they are able not to destroy the true nature of those phenomena.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If the Buddha merely uses names and signs as provisional designations for the dharmic nature of all phenomena, so that sentient beings may skillfully awaken to and enter into the equality of the dharmic nature, thereby departing from birth and death and realizing nirvāṇa—how is it that the Buddha speaks of these nameless and signless phenomena using names and signs, yet says they are not destroyed?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"I follow worldly convention in provisionally establishing names and signs for all phenomena; I skillfully teach them for the sake of sentient beings without attachment, and therefore there is nothing that can be destroyed."
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

Just as foolish commoners, upon hearing the teaching of suffering and so forth, cling to names and signs and fail to understand that these are merely provisional designations, so it is not with the Tathāgatas and their disciples who hear the teaching of suffering and so forth. They do not cling to names and signs; rather, they know them as they truly are as conventional expressions, understanding that there are no real names or signs for any phenomena.”

"Subhūti! If noble ones were to cling to names as names, and cling to signs as signs, then they would likewise have to cling to emptiness as emptiness, cling to signlessness as signlessness, cling to wishlessness as wishlessness, cling to suchness as suchness, cling to the dharma-realm as the dharma-realm, cling to the limit of reality as the limit of reality, and cling to the unconditioned as the unconditioned."

"Subhūti! All these phenomena possess only provisional names and only provisional characteristics, lacking any reality; even the noble ones do not cling to them as being merely provisional names and characteristics."
Thus it is, Subhūti!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, abiding in all phenomena, practice the profound perfection of wisdom through mere conventional designations and signs, yet they remain without any attachment therein.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If all phenomena consist merely of names and signs, for what purpose do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas generate the mind of enlightenment and undergo various hardships to practice the bodhisattva path— that is, to personally and diligently practice with austerity?"
From the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
abiding in inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature; abiding in suchness up to the inconceivable realm;
abiding in the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; and practicing the four applications of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path.
Vimalakīrti, he practices the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
he practices the eight liberations up to the ten universal bases; he practices the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
he practices the stages from the Ground of Extreme Joy up to the Ground of the Dharma Cloud; and he practices all the doors of dhāraṇī.
...the doors of samādhi; practicing the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
practicing the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; practicing the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity;
practicing all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects; practicing the one...
All the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the cultivation of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas,
and the cultivation of the knowledge of all modes of knowing are all brought to full perfection.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Because all phenomena possess only names and signs, and such names and signs are merely conventional designations, the nature of names and signs is empty. Yet sentient beings, through their inverted attachments, sink and wallow in birth and death, failing to realize nirvāṇa."

Therefore, out of compassion for them, the assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas resolves upon Bodhicitta and undergoes various hardships while practicing the Bodhisattva path. Gradually, they realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). Having personally realized this knowledge of all modes, they turn the wheel of the true Dharma and, through the skillful means of the three vehicles, deliver beings, causing them to emerge from birth and death and enter the realm of *nirvāṇa* without remainder. Yet, regarding all names and characteristics, there is neither arising nor ceasing, nor can any establishment of duration or change be found.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
does the Buddha speak of ‘all-knowledge wisdom’ as being ‘all-knowledge wisdom’?”
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
I speak of omniscient wisdom as omniscient wisdom.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“The Tathāgata has previously taught that the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) is briefly of three kinds, namely: the knowledge of all things (sarvajñatā), the knowledge of the paths (mārgākārajñatā), and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā).”
“What are the characteristics of these three types of knowledge,
and what are their distinctions?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Knowledge of all things refers to the wisdom shared by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Knowledge of the aspects of the path refers to the wisdom shared by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Knowledge of all aspects refers to the sublime, unshared wisdom of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“For what reason is all-knowledge (sarvajñatā) the wisdom common to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Omniscience (sarvajñatā) refers to the various dharma-gates such as the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements. Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are also able to understand these distinctions among dharma-gates; however, because they cannot know all aspects of the paths, all phenomena, and all modes of appearance, omniscience is a wisdom shared with śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“For what reason is the knowledge of the aspects of the path the wisdom common to bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should study to fully know the characteristics of all paths—namely, the characteristics of the path of the śrāvakas, the characteristics of the path of the pratyekabuddhas, the characteristics of the path of the bodhisattvas, and the characteristics of the path of the Tathāgatas. Regarding these various paths, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should constantly practice and study them so that they may be swiftly perfected.”

Although this path causes that which is to be done to be performed, it does not cause one to realize and abide in the limit of reality; therefore, the knowledge of the aspects of the path is the wisdom common to bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Once Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have cultivated the path of the Tathāgata to full completion, do they not likewise realize and abide in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have not yet perfected their maturation of sentient beings, their purification of Buddha-fields, and their cultivation of great vows, they should not yet realize and abide in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi). Once these are perfected, they may then realize and abide in the limit of reality."
The Venerable Subhūti again asked the Blessed One:
“Do bodhisattva mahāsattvas abide in the path and realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) while so abiding?
The Buddha said:
"No, it is not so. Subhūti asked again:
"Do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell in what is not the path in order to realize and abide in the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*)?"
The Buddha said,
“It is not so. Subhūti asked again:
"Do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell in the realization of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) by abiding in what is both the path and the non-path? The Buddha said: "No!"
Subhūti asked again:
"Do bodhisattva mahāsattvas dwell in the realization of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) by abiding in that which is neither a path nor a non-path?
The Buddha said:
"Not so! The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"If that is so, in what do the bodhisattva mahāsattvas abide when they realize and dwell in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)?
The Buddha said,
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin!"
"What do you think?
Do you abide in the Path and thereby attain the liberation of mind through the exhaustion of all outflows? "No, sir."
“World-Honored One!
“‘Subhūti! Do you abide in what is not the Path and thereby attain the exhaustion of all outflows and the liberation of mind?”’”
"No, World-Honored One! " "Excellent, Subhūti!"
“Do you attain the liberation of mind through the exhaustion of all taints by abiding in what is the path or what is not the path? “No,
World-Honored One!”
“Subhūti! Do you abide in that which is neither a path nor a non-path to attain the liberation of mind through the exhaustion of all outflows?
“No, [World-Honored One].”
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, “Sudhana!”
"In what state do you abide such that you have exhausted all outflows and your mind is eternally liberated?

Subhūti replied, "It is not by abiding anywhere that I have exhausted all outflows and my mind is eternally liberated; rather, having exhausted the outflows and attained liberation, my mind abides nowhere at all."
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"It is the same for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, they abide nowhere at all when realizing the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what reason is 'all-aspect omniscience' called 'all-aspect omniscience'?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"To know that all phenomena are of one single characteristic—that is, the characteristic of quiescence—is therefore called the knowledge of all aspects.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"

"All conditioned phenomena, their modes, and their characteristics can represent all dharmas; the Tathāgata has realized them through thorough and actual awakening, and for this reason it is called 'the knowledge of all aspects' (*sarvākārajñatā*).
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Regarding these three knowledges—the knowledge of all (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects—are there any differences in the abandonment of the afflictions?"
“Is there a distinction between abandonment with remainder and abandonment without remainder?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“There is no difference in the abandonment of the afflictions themselves; however, all Tathāgatas have forever severed the continuity of the latencies (*vāsanā*) of all afflictions, whereas Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have not yet forever severed the continuity of their latencies.”
Subhūti asked again:
"Is the abandonment of all afflictions the attainment of the unconditioned?
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Subhūti then asked again:
"Do Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas not attain the unconditioned, yet sever their afflictions?"
The Buddha said:
"It is not so. Subhūti asked again:
“Is there any distinction among unconditioned phenomena? The Buddha said, “No!”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If unconditioned phenomena have no distinctions, for what reason does the Buddha say that all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have forever severed the continuity of habitual tendencies, whereas Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have not yet forever severed the continuity of habitual tendencies?"
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

The continuity of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-saṃtati*) is truly not an affliction (*kleśa*). Nevertheless, although the afflictions of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have been severed, they still possess slight manifestations of what resembles greed, hatred, and delusion that stir the body and speech; it is precisely this that is called the continuity of habitual tendencies.”

This [habitual tendency] can induce what is meaningless within the mental continuums of foolish ordinary beings, but it cannot induce what is meaningless within the mental continuums of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; such habitual tendencies in their continuums are ultimately non-existent for all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Since both the path and nirvāṇa are devoid of intrinsic nature, for what reason does the Buddha say, ‘This is a stream-enterer; this is a once-returner; this is a non-returner; this is an arhat; this is a pratyekabuddha; this is a bodhisattva; this is a tathāgata’?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Whether it be a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, an arhat, a pratyekabuddha, a bodhisattva, or a tathāgata—all of these are manifested by the unconditioned."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Within unconditioned phenomena, is there truly any distinction in meaning between the stream-enterer and so forth, up to the Tathāgata?
The Buddha said:
"Not so! Subhūti asked again:
"If that is so, for what reason did the Buddha say that everything from the stream-enterer up to the Tathāgata is all manifested through the unconditioned?"
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

It is by relying on conventional discourse that I manifest the distinctions indicated by those such as the stream-enterer; it is not by relying on the ultimate truth, for nothing can be manifested within the ultimate truth.”

Why is this? Because within the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), there is no path of speech, nor any analytical wisdom, nor even these two; nevertheless, because various phenomena are ceased through various conventional expressions, one designates the "subsequent limit" (*paścimakoṭi*) of those various conventionally expressed phenomena.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If all phenomena are empty of their own characteristics, such that even a prior limit does not exist, how much less could there be a subsequent limit? How, then, can a subsequent limit be designated?"
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said:
all phenomena are empty of their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnya*); since even a prior limit (*pūrvānta*) does not exist, how much less could there be a subsequent limit (*aparānta*)!

That a subsequent limit truly exists is absolutely impossible. Nevertheless, because sentient beings are unable to comprehend that all phenomena are empty of their own characteristics, for their benefit, one employs skillful means and speaks by way of conventional designation:
"This is the prior limit; this is the subsequent limit.
However, within the emptiness of intrinsic nature of all phenomena, neither a prior limit nor a subsequent limit can be apprehended.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
Having realized that all phenomena are empty of their own intrinsic characteristics, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice the perfection of wisdom.

Subhūti, you should know that all bodhisattva mahāsattvas realize that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty; they practice the perfection of wisdom and remain without attachment to any phenomena. That is to say, they do not cling to the distinctions between phenomena—whether internal or external, wholesome or unwholesome, determinate or indeterminate, mundane or supramundane, with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned—and they likewise do not cling to the dharmas of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or tathāgatas. These are merely established through conventional designations based on worldly discourse, and not based on the ultimate truth.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 462. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Second Division, Chapter Sixty-Eight on Skillful Means (Fourth Part). At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
The Tathāgata constantly speaks of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*; for what reason is this profound *prajñāpāramitā* called *prajñāpāramitā*?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* reaches the ultimate further shore of all phenomena, it is named *prajñāpāramitā*."
Furthermore, Subhūti!

Because śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas are able to reach the other shore by means of this profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), it is named the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Subhūti,

because the profound perfection of wisdom analyzes all phenomena down to a degree subtler than the most minute atom, and ultimately finds not even the slightest reality to be apprehended, it is called the perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
This profound perfection of wisdom encompasses suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, and so forth, up to the inconceivable realm; therefore, it is called the 'perfection of wisdom.'"

Furthermore, Subhūti, in this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, there is not the slightest dharma that is either joined or dispersed, whether it be with form or formless, visible or invisible, resistant or non-resistant; therefore, it is called *prajñāpāramitā*.

Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is neither joined nor dispersed; it is formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possesses a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*).
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can give birth to all subtle and excellent dharmas, can bring forth all wisdom and eloquence, can lead to all mundane and supramundane happiness, and can penetrate all profound meanings of the Dharma, it is called *prajñāpāramitā*."

Furthermore, Subhūti, the principle of the profound perfection of wisdom is firm and solid, and cannot be shaken or destroyed. If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices this profound perfection of wisdom, no evil Māras, nor their retinues, nor śrāvakas, nor pratyekabuddhas, nor outsiders, nor brahmins, nor evil friends, nor enemies can destroy them.

Why is this so? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* teaches that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty, and thus all evil Māras and the like are unfindable; for this reason, it is named *prajñāpāramitā*.

"Subhūti! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice the profound meaning of this perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) in accordance with reality; that is to say, the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty, and no adverse conditions can disturb or destroy them."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to practice the profound meaning and intent of the *prajñāpāramitā* should practice the meaning of impermanence, the meaning of suffering, the meaning of emptiness, the meaning of selflessness, the meaning of tranquility, and the meaning of detachment. They should practice the meaning of the wisdom of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; they should practice the meaning of the knowledge of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; they should practice the meaning of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*); they should practice the meaning of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) and ultimate knowledge (*paramārtha-jñāna*); they should practice the meaning of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*); and they should practice the meaning of the knowledge of all that exists (*yāvadbhāvikatā-jñāna*) and the knowledge of things as they are (*yathāvadbhāvikatā-jñāna*)."
"Subhūti! In order to practice the profound meaning and intent of the perfection of wisdom, bodhisattva mahāsattvas should practice the perfection of wisdom."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Within this profound and subtle principle of the *prajñāpāramitā*, neither ‘meaning’ (*artha*) nor ‘non-meaning’ (*anartha*) can be apprehended. How, then, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of practicing the profound significance of the *prajñāpāramitā*, practice the *prajñāpāramitā*?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, practicing the profound meaning and purpose of the *prajñāpāramitā*, should form this thought:

'I should not practice the meaning or non-meaning of greed; I should not practice the meaning or non-meaning of hatred; I should not practice the meaning or non-meaning of delusion; I should not practice the meaning or non-meaning of wrong view; I should not practice the meaning or non-meaning of wrong concentration; and I should not practice the meaning or non-meaning of any view whatsoever.'"

Why is this so? Because greed, hatred, delusion, wrong views, and wrong concentration—even all modes of view—whether they be suchness or the limit of reality, do not constitute either benefit or harm to any phenomena.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
For the sake of practicing the profound meaning and intent of the perfection of wisdom, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should form this thought:
'I should not practice regarding the meaning or non-meaning of form; I should not practice regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, [or consciousness].'"
Discerning what is meaningful and what is meaningless, I should not engage with the meaning or meaninglessness of the sense-base of the eye up to the sense-base of the mind;
I should not engage with the meaning or meaninglessness of the sense-base of forms up to the sense-base of mental phenomena;

I should not engage with the meaning or meaninglessness of the eye-element up to the mind-element; and I should not engage with the meaning or meaninglessness of the form-element up to the mental-phenomena-element.
I should not practice with regard to the meaning or non-meaning of the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element;
I should not practice with regard to the meaning or non-meaning of eye-contact up to mind-contact;

I should not practice with regard to the meaning or non-meaning of the various feelings produced conditioned by eye-contact up to the various feelings produced conditioned by mind-contact; I should not...
I should not practice the meaning or non-meaning of the element of earth up to the element of consciousness;
I should not practice the meaning or non-meaning of the causal condition up to the sovereign condition; I should not practice the meaning or non-meaning of ignorance up to old age and death;
I should not practice the meaning or non-meaning of the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom.
Regarding meaning, I should not practice the meaning or non-meaning of inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence;
I should not practice the meaning or non-meaning of suchness up to the inconceivable realm;
I should not practice the meaning or non-meaning of the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; I should not practice the four foundations of mindfulness... [and so forth].

Regarding the meaning or lack of meaning of the eight branches of the noble path, I should not practice them; regarding the meaning or lack of meaning of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments, I should not practice them;
regarding the meaning or lack of meaning of the eight liberations up to the ten totalities, I should not practice them;
and regarding the meaning of the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—I should not practice them.
Non-meaning; I should not practice the meaning or non-meaning of the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata;
I should not practice the meaning or non-meaning of the Joyful Stage up to the Cloud of Dharma Stage;
I should not practice the meaning or non-meaning of all dhāraṇī-doors and samādhi-doors; I should not practice the five eyes.

I should not engage with the meaning or non-meaning of the six supernormal powers; I should not engage with the meaning or non-meaning of the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
I should not engage with the meaning or non-meaning of the thirty-two marks of a great man or the eighty secondary signs;
I should not engage with the meaning or non-meaning of the quality of non-forgetfulness or the nature of constant equanimity.

Regarding what is meaningful and what is meaningless, I should not practice the meaning or the meaninglessness of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);
I should not practice the meaning or the meaninglessness of the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
I should not practice the meaning or the meaninglessness of any of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices; I should not...
‘I should not practice for the sake of, nor against, the meaning or non-meaning of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas;
I should not practice for the sake of, nor against, the meaning or non-meaning of the knowledge of all modes. Why is this?
“Subhūti! When the Tathāgata attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, he could not find any meaning or non-meaning in any phenomena whatsoever.
Subhūti, you should know this!”

Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear in the world, the dharma-nature of all phenomena, their stability, their fixedness, and their suchness remain eternally present; no phenomenon can be either beneficial or non-beneficial to another phenomenon.

"Subhūti! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should abandon all attachment to what is meaningful and what is meaningless, and should constantly practice the profound significance of the perfection of wisdom."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“For what reason does the perfection of wisdom not constitute either a benefit or a disadvantage for all phenomena?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* seeks to realize and enter into unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), it does not function as either a benefit or a detriment toward any phenomena.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“Is it not the case that all noble ones (*ārya*) take the unconditioned as their ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.
Among all noble and holy ones, there are none who do not take the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as the ultimate truth; yet, the unconditioned dharma neither benefits nor harms any phenomena.

Subhūti! For example, just as space, suchness, and the dharma-realm neither benefit nor harm any phenomena, so too is the profound prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas; it neither benefits nor harms any phenomena. Therefore, the prajñāpāramitā does not constitute either benefit or harm for any phenomena.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Do not all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas necessarily train in the unconditioned *prajñāpāramitā* before they are able to realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*)?"
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.

Only by training in the profound, unconditioned *prajñāpāramitā* can bodhisattva-mahāsattvas realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), employing the non-dual dharma as their skillful means.
Subhūti asked again:
"Is it by means of non-dual dharmas that one attains the non-dual dharma?
The Buddha said:
"No, it is not so. Subhūti asked again,
"Is it by means of dual dharmas that one attains the non-dual dharma?"
The Buddha said, "It is not so. Subhūti replied:
"If neither duality nor non-duality can be attained by means of duality or non-duality, how then shall the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain the knowledge of all modes?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Both duality and non-duality are unattainable. Therefore, the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) that is attained is not attained by means of dualistic dharmas or non-dualistic dharmas; rather, it is through the dharma of non-attainment that one attains non-attainment."
Why is this? Because both the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*) are both unapprehendable.
Chapter Sixty-nine: The Parable of the Tree, Part Two. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

This perfection of wisdom is most profound. It is a difficult feat that these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to perform, in that they do not apprehend any sentient beings, nor do they apprehend the designations for sentient beings, yet they swiftly seek to realize the knowledge of all modes.”
“World-Honored One!
It is as if, for example, there were someone who wished to plant a tree in space—which is formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and without support—that would be extremely difficult.”

It is likewise for the bodhisattva mahāsattvas: not finding sentient beings nor the designations for them, yet seeking to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) for the sake of sentient beings, is an extremely difficult task.
The Buddha said,
“So it is, Subhūti! It is just so.”
"So it is! It is as you have said.

This Prajñāpāramitā is most profound; Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas perform what is difficult to do, for while they find no sentient beings nor even the designation of 'sentient being,' they yet swiftly seek to realize the knowledge of all modes for the sake of sentient beings."

"Subhūti, you should know that although bodhisattva mahāsattvas do not perceive any real sentient beings, nor do they perceive the designations for them, sentient beings—due to their ignorance and perversion—cling to them as being truly existent. Sunk in saṃsāra, they undergo endless suffering. To pull them out, the bodhisattvas swiftly seek to realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) and deliver them through skillful means."

It is like a person who plants a tree in a fertile field; although this person does not recognize the roots, trunk, branches, leaves, flowers, or fruits of that tree, once it has been planted, they irrigate it at the proper times and diligently protect it. Later, as the tree gradually grows, its roots, trunk, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits become lush and abundant, so that all people enjoy them, their illnesses are cured, and they attain peace.

It is just so with the bodhisattva mahāsattvas: although they do not perceive the existence of sentient beings as recipients of karmic retribution, they swiftly seek to realize the knowledge of all modes for the sake of sentient beings. They practice in successive stages the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as other immeasurable factors conducive to enlightenment. Once these are fully perfected, they are able to realize the knowledge of all modes, enabling all sentient beings to enjoy the fruits of their actions, so that branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits each receive their benefit.
“Subhūti, you should know this!
The benefit of the branches and leaves is that all sentient beings rely upon this bodhisattva to be liberated from the evil destinies.

The benefit of the flowers is that all sentient beings rely upon this bodhisattva to be born into a great kṣatriya clan, or a great brāhmaṇa clan, or a great householder clan, or a great merchant clan; or to be born among the gods of the Four Great Kings, up to and including the gods of the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception.”

The benefit of the fruit refers to this bodhisattva’s own realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, thereby causing all sentient beings to abide in the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship, or to abide in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, or to abide in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; as these sentient beings diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas and gradually realize the nirvana of the three vehicles by means of the path of the three vehicles—this is called the benefit of the ripened fruit.

"Subhūti! Although bodhisattva mahāsattvas perform such great deeds of benefit, they ultimately do not perceive any real sentient beings who attain nirvāṇa; they see only the cessation of the manifold sufferings of conceptual construction."
Thus it is, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not apprehend sentient beings nor their designations. For the sake of eliminating the inversion of grasping at self and mine, and for the sake of swiftly seeking to realize the knowledge of all modes, this is, by such causes and conditions, an exceedingly difficult task.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
You should know that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are like the Buddha."

Why is this? Because by relying upon the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, one is able to forever sever all the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts, and is also able to forever sever all the manifold sufferings of the three realms—including those of the states of no leisure, poverty, and low birth.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should know that they are like Buddhas.

If there were no assembly of bodhisattvas in the world, there would be no Tathāgatas of the three times, nor would there be any assembly of pratyekabuddhas or śrāvakas; furthermore, there would never be a time when all suffering in the three realms—namely, the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, and other states of lack of leisure, poverty, and low birth—is forever severed.
Therefore, Subhūti!
What you have said—that the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is like the Buddha—is indeed as you have stated.
Furthermore, Subhūti, you should know this!
The assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is itself the Tathāgata. Why is this so? Subhūti!
If it is by means of this suchness that a Tathāgata is designated, it is by means of this same suchness that a Pratyekabuddha is designated;
it is also by means of this same suchness that a Śrāvaka is designated; it is also by means of this same suchness that all noble ones (ārya) are designated;
and it is also by means of this same suchness that form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are designated.
It is by means of this suchness that the sense-base of the eye is designated, up to and including the sense-base of the mind;

it is also by means of this suchness that the sense-base of form is designated, up to and including the sense-base of mental phenomena; it is also by means of this suchness that the element of the eye is designated, up to and including the element of the mind;
it is also by means of this suchness that the element of form is designated, up to and including the element of mental phenomena; and it is also by means of this suchness...
The designation of the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element is also based on this suchness;

the designation of eye-contact up to mind-contact is also based on this suchness; the designation of all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition up to all feelings produced with mind-contact as condition is also based on this suchness; and the designation of the earth element is also based on this suchness.

Even up to the element of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*), it is by means of this *tathatā* that the conditions from the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) up to the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) are designated;
even up to ignorance (*avidyā*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), they are designated by means of this *tathatā*;
even up to the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they are designated by means of this [tathatā].
