Just as the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature is designated, so too are the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path designated by means of this very suchness;
likewise, the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path are designated by means of this very suchness;
and likewise, the four dhyānas, the four [immeasurables]... [are designated by means of this very suchness].

The [four] immeasurables and the four formless absorptions are also designated by means of this suchness; the eight liberations up to the ten universal bases are also designated by means of this suchness;
the doors of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are also designated by means of this suchness;
and the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata are also designated by means of this suchness. Furthermore, by means of this...
The designation of the stages from the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma is established by means of this very suchness;

likewise, the designation of all doors of dhāraṇī and doors of samādhi is established by means of this very suchness; likewise, the designation of the five eyes and the six supernormal powers is established by means of this very suchness;
and likewise, the designation of the ten powers of a Tathāgata, up to the [ten]... is established by means of this very suchness.
The eight unique qualities of a Buddha are also designated by virtue of this suchness; the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks are also designated by virtue of this suchness;
the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity are also designated by virtue of this suchness;
and omniscience, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects are also designated by virtue of this suchness.
Wisdom, too, is designated by means of this very suchness as all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
it is also by means of this very suchness that the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas is designated;

it is also by means of this very suchness that the knowledge of all modes is designated; and it is also by means of this very suchness that the conditioned realm is designated. Furthermore, by means of this...
It is by means of this suchness that the unconditioned realm is designated; it is also by means of this suchness that all phenomena are designated;
it is also by means of this suchness that all sentient beings are designated; and it is also by means of this suchness that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are designated.
"In this way, Subhūti!

Whether it be the suchness of a Tathāgata, the suchness of a Pratyekabuddha, the suchness of a Śrāvaka, the suchness of all noble ones, the suchness of all phenomena such as form, the suchness of all sentient beings, or the suchness of all Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas—such suchnesses are in reality entirely without difference. Because they are without difference, they are called 'suchness.'"

When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas bring their cultivation and study of this suchness to perfection, they are able to realize the knowledge of all modes; having realized the knowledge of all modes, they are therefore called Tathāgatas.

For this reason, one should know that the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is itself the Tathāgata, because all phenomena and all sentient beings take true suchness (*tathatā*) as their definitive standard.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should train in the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
If they train in the profound perfection of wisdom, they will be able to train in the suchness (tathatā) of all phenomena; if they train in all...
If one attains mastery over the suchness of all phenomena, then one attains the knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties of all sentient beings;

if one attains the knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties of all sentient beings, then one is able to fully know the differences in the inclinations of all sentient beings; if one is able...
To fully know the differences in the inclinations of all sentient beings is to know that all sentient beings experience the fruits of their own karma;
if one knows that all sentient beings experience the fruits of their own karma, then the wisdom of aspiration becomes perfected;

if the wisdom of aspiration is perfected, then one is able to purify and cultivate the sublime wisdom of the three times; and if one is able to purify and cultivate the sublime wisdom of the three times, then...
One can fulfill the knowledge of all modes; if one fulfills the knowledge of all modes, then one can practice the bodhisattva conduct without error;
if one practices the bodhisattva conduct without error, then one can constantly benefit sentient beings through the giving of material wealth and the giving of the Dharma;
if one can constantly benefit sentient beings through the giving of material wealth and the giving of the Dharma...
Thus one can mature sentient beings according to reality; if one can mature sentient beings according to reality, then one can purify Buddha-fields according to reality;
if one can purify Buddha-fields according to reality, then one can realize the knowledge of all modes;
if one can realize the knowledge of all modes, then one can truly turn the sublime wheel of Dharma.
If one can thus turn the sublime wheel of Dharma as it truly is, one can establish sentient beings upon the paths of the three vehicles;
if one can establish sentient beings upon the paths of the three vehicles, one can cause them to enter the realm of nirvana without remainder.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas see such immeasurable merits of both self-benefit and benefiting others, they should, desiring to make the great mind of awakening they have generated firm and non-regressive, diligently apply themselves with vigor to the practice of the perfection of wisdom through skillful means.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to resolve upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and practices the profound perfection of wisdom as it has been taught, all those in the world—gods, humans, and asuras—should pay him homage.”
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can resolve upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening and practice the profound perfection of wisdom as it has been taught, then all the worldlings—including devas, humans, and asuras—should pay them homage.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of universally benefiting all sentient beings, first generates the mind set on unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, how much merit does he obtain?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Suppose all sentient beings filling a small thousandfold world system were to set out for the stage of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha; what do you think?"
"Would these sentient beings have much merit? Subhūti replied, "Very much!"
“World-Honored One!
The merit obtained by that person would be immeasurable and boundless.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"The mass of merit acquired by all those sentient beings does not equal even a hundredth part of the mass of merit acquired by a single bodhisattva mahāsattva who has first resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening for the sake of universally benefiting all sentient beings; it does not equal a thousandth part, nor even a hundred-thousand-koṭi-nayuta-th part."

Why is this? It is because Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas all exist in dependence upon Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; it is not that Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas exist in dependence upon Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

Setting aside the mass of merit obtained by all sentient beings throughout a small thousand-world system, or a medium thousand-world system, were they all to enter the stage of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.
Suppose that all sentient beings filling the entire trichiliocosm were to attain the stage of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha; what do you think?
Would the merit of those sentient beings be great?
Subhūti replied, “Very many,
World-Honored One!”
"The merit obtained by them would be immeasurable and boundless.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"The mass of merit obtained by all those sentient beings does not equal even a hundredth part of the mass of merit obtained by a single bodhisattva mahāsattva who has first resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening for the sake of universally benefiting all sentient beings; it does not equal a thousandth part, nor even a hundred-thousand-koṭi-nayuta-th part."

Why is this? It is because śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas all exist in dependence upon bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; it is not that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas exist in dependence upon śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
Setting aside the mass of merit obtained by all sentient beings filling a trichiliocosm who have all entered the stage of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.
Suppose that all sentient beings throughout the three thousandfold world system were to abide on the stage of pure observation; what do you think?
Would the merit of these sentient beings be great?
Subhūti replied, “It is very much so,
World-Honored One!”
"The merit they obtain will be immeasurable and boundless.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"The mass of merit obtained by all those sentient beings does not equal even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor even a hundred-thousand-koṭi-nayuta-th part of the mass of merit obtained by a single bodhisattva mahāsattva who has first resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment for the sake of universally benefiting all sentient beings, as you have asked."

Why is this? It is because śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas all exist in dependence upon bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; it is not that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas exist in dependence upon śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
Setting aside the mass of merit obtained by all sentient beings filling a trichiliocosm who abide on the stage of pure observation;

suppose there were all sentient beings filling a trichiliocosm who abide on the stage of the spiritual lineage, or the eighth stage, or the stage of those who have seen the truths, or the stage of refinement, or the stage of freedom from desire, or the stage of those who have completed their task—the mass of merit they would obtain [is likewise set aside].
Suppose that all sentient beings filling the entire trichiliocosm were to abide on the level of a pratyekabuddha; what do you think?
Would the merit of these sentient beings be great?
Subhūti replied, “Very many,
World-Honored One!”
“The merit obtained by them will be immeasurable and boundless.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“The mass of merit obtained by all those sentient beings does not equal even a hundredth part of the mass of merit obtained by a single bodhisattva mahāsattva who has first resolved upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening for the sake of universally benefiting all sentient beings—as you have asked; it does not equal a thousandth part, nor even a hundred-thousand-koṭi-nayuta-th part.”
Why is this? Because śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas all exist in dependence upon bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; it is not that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas exist in dependence upon śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose all sentient beings throughout a trichiliocosm were each to universally benefit all sentient beings by first generating the mind set on unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. The mass of merit obtained by all those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas would not equal even a hundredth part of the mass of merit obtained by a single bodhisattva-mahāsattva who has entered the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth; it would not equal a thousandth part, nor even a hundred-thousand-koṭi-nayuta-th part."
Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose all sentient beings filling a trichiliocosm were to enter the bodhisattva’s state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*). The mass of merit obtained by this assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas would not equal even one hundredth of the mass of merit obtained by a single bodhisattva-mahāsattva who is practicing for enlightenment; it would not equal one thousandth, nor even one part in a hundred-thousand-koṭi-nayuta fraction.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose all sentient beings throughout a trichiliocosm were to practice toward awakening; the mass of merit acquired by that assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas would not equal even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor even a hundred-thousand-koṭi-nayuta-th part of the mass of merit possessed by a single Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
what do those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have first resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment contemplate?”
The Buddha said,
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
This bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly and correctly contemplates the knowledge of all modes."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is the nature of the knowledge of all modes?
What is its object of focus?"
What is its predominance?
What is its mode of activity?
What is its characteristic?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"The knowledge of all modes has non-existence as its nature, because it is signless, causeless, without anything to be awakened to, and because it manifests through non-arising."
Furthermore, as to your question: "What is the object of focus (*ālambana*) of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*),
what is its dominant influence (*adhipati*),
and what are its aspects (*ākāra*)?"
"What is its characteristic?

Subhūti, it takes the non-existence of all-knowledge as its object, has right mindfulness as its dominant influence, has tranquility as its mode of activity, and takes the dharma-realm as its characteristic.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Is it only the knowledge of all modes that has non-existence as its nature?
Or do form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness also have non-existence as their nature?"
Is it that the sense-base of the eye, up to and including the sense-base of the mind, has "the absence of intrinsic nature" as its intrinsic nature?
Is it that the sense-base of form, up to and including the sense-base of phenomena, has "the absence of intrinsic nature" as its intrinsic nature?
Is it that the element of the eye, up to and including the element of the mind, has "the absence of intrinsic nature" as its intrinsic nature?
Is it that the form realm up to the dharma realm also has non-existence as its nature?
Is it that the eye-consciousness realm up to the mind-consciousness realm also has non-existence as its nature?
Is it that eye-contact up to mind-contact also has non-existence as its nature?
Are all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, up to and including those produced with mind-contact as condition, also of the nature of being without intrinsic nature?
Are the earth element, up to and including the consciousness element, also of the nature of being without intrinsic nature?
Are the causal conditions, up to and including the dominant condition, also characterized by the absence of intrinsic nature?
Are ignorance, up to and including old age and death, also characterized by the absence of intrinsic nature?
Are the perfection of generosity, up to and including the perfection of wisdom, also characterized by the absence of intrinsic nature?
Is it that from inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, they also have non-existence as their nature?
Is it that from suchness up to the inconceivable realm, they also have non-existence as their nature?
Are the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path also characterized by the absence of intrinsic nature?
Are the four applications of mindfulness, up to and including the eight branches of the noble path, also characterized by the absence of intrinsic nature?
Are the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments also characterized by the absence of intrinsic nature?
Are the eight liberations, up to and including the ten totalities, also characterized by the absence of intrinsic nature?
Are the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—also characterized by the absence of intrinsic nature as their nature?
Are the stages from the Ground of Pure Contemplation up to the Tathāgata Ground also characterized by the absence of intrinsic nature as their nature?
Is it that the stages from the Ground of Utmost Joy up to the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma also have non-existence as their nature?
Is it that all doors of dhāraṇī and doors of samādhi also have non-existence as their nature?
Is it that the five eyes and the six supernormal powers also have non-existence as their intrinsic nature?
Is it that the Tathāgata’s ten powers, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, also have non-existence as their intrinsic nature?
Are the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks also characterized by the nature of being without intrinsic nature?
Are the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity also characterized by the nature of being without intrinsic nature?
Are omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) also characterized by the absence of intrinsic nature?
Are even the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*) up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha (*pratyekabodhi*) characterized by the absence of intrinsic nature?
Is the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas also characterized by the nature of being without intrinsic nature?
Is the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas also characterized by the nature of being without intrinsic nature?
"Is the conditioned realm also characterized by the absence of intrinsic nature as its nature?
Is the unconditioned realm also characterized by the absence of intrinsic nature as its nature?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Not only is the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) characterized by the absence of intrinsic nature, but form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also characterized by the absence of intrinsic nature; likewise, even the conditioned realm (saṃskṛtadhātu) and the unconditioned realm (asaṃskṛtadhātu) are characterized by the absence of intrinsic nature."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“For what reason is the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) of the nature of non-existence?
And why are form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness also of the nature of non-existence?”
"In this way, even up to the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛtadhātu*) and the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*), do they also have 'the absence of intrinsic nature' as their intrinsic nature?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Because the intrinsic nature of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) does not exist, if a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, that phenomenon has 'the absence of intrinsic nature' as its nature. Because form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness also lack intrinsic nature, if a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, that phenomenon has 'the absence of intrinsic nature' as its nature."

In this way, even up to the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛta-dhātu*) and the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛta-dhātu*), they likewise lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). If a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, then that phenomenon has "the absence of nature" as its nature.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what reason is the intrinsic nature of the knowledge of all modes non-existent?
Why is it that form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are also without intrinsic nature?"
"In this way, even the conditioned realm and the unconditioned realm are without intrinsic nature?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Because the knowledge of all modes lacks an inherent nature of synthesis, if a dharma lacks an inherent nature of synthesis, that dharma takes non-existence as its nature."

Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness likewise lack an inherent nature of synthesis; if a phenomenon lacks an inherent nature of synthesis, that phenomenon has non-existence as its very nature.

In this way, even the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛta-dhātu*) and the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛta-dhātu*) likewise lack an inherent nature of combination; if a phenomenon lacks an inherent nature of combination, then that phenomenon has non-existence as its very nature.
Subhūti! For this reason, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should know that all phenomena have the absence of intrinsic nature as their nature.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
All phenomena have emptiness as their intrinsic nature, signlessness as their intrinsic nature, and wishlessness as their intrinsic nature. Subhūti!
For this reason, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should know that all phenomena have the absence of intrinsic nature as their nature.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
All phenomena have true suchness as their intrinsic nature, the limit of reality as their intrinsic nature, and the dharma-realm as their intrinsic nature. Subhūti!
"For this reason, Subhūti, you should know that all dharmas have 'the absence of intrinsic nature' as their intrinsic nature.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If all dharmas are devoid of intrinsic nature, by what kind of skillful means do those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have first resolved upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening become accomplished, so that they are able to practice the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, ripening sentient beings and purifying buddha-fields?"

What kind of skillful means must one accomplish to be able to dwell in the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, while maturing sentient beings and purifying buddha-fields?

What kind of skillful means must one accomplish to be able to abide in true thusness (*tathatā*) up to the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*), thereby maturing sentient beings and purifying buddha-fields?
What kind of skillful means must one accomplish to abide in the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, while maturing sentient beings and purifying buddha-fields?

What kind of skillful means must one accomplish to be able to practice the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, thereby maturing sentient beings and purifying Buddha-fields?

What kind of skillful means must one accomplish to be able to practice the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions, thereby maturing sentient beings and purifying buddha-fields?
What kind of skillful means must one accomplish to be able to practice the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality, thereby maturing sentient beings and purifying Buddha-fields?

What kind of skillful means must be accomplished to be able to practice the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—and thereby mature sentient beings and adorn and purify Buddha-fields?
What kind of skillful means must they accomplish to be able to practice the stages of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, maturing sentient beings and purifying buddha-fields?
What kind of skillful means must they accomplish to be able to practice all the doors of dhāraṇī and the doors of samādhi, maturing sentient beings and purifying buddha-fields?
By accomplishing what kind of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) can one practice the five eyes and the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), maturing sentient beings and purifying Buddha-fields?

By accomplishing what kind of skillful means can one practice the Tathāgata’s ten powers (*daśabala*) up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*), maturing sentient beings and purifying Buddha-fields?

What kind of skillful means must one accomplish to be able to practice the quality of non-forgetfulness and abide constantly in equanimity, thereby maturing sentient beings and purifying Buddha-fields?

By accomplishing what kind of skillful means is one able to practice all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), thereby maturing sentient beings and purifying Buddha-fields?
What kind of skillful means must one accomplish to be able to carry out all the practices of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, ripening sentient beings and purifying buddha-fields?
By accomplishing what kind of skillful means is one able to practice the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas, maturing sentient beings and purifying Buddha-fields?
"What kind of skillful means does he accomplish that enables him to practice the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), to mature sentient beings, and to purify Buddha-fields?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes the most supreme skillful means; although he knows that all phenomena have 'absence of intrinsic nature' as their nature, he constantly exerts himself with diligence to mature sentient beings and purify Buddha-fields."

Although they constantly and diligently bring sentient beings to maturity and adorn and purify Buddha-fields, they always penetrate the fact that all sentient beings and all Buddha-fields have no-nature as their very nature.

"Subhūti! Although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom while training in the path to enlightenment, they know that from the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, as well as the path to enlightenment, all are characterized by the nature of non-existence (*abhāva-svabhāva*). Likewise, even though they practice the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvajñatā*) while training in the path to enlightenment, they know that from the knowledge of all aspects up to the path to enlightenment, all are characterized by the nature of non-existence."

Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva thus practices the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom while training in the path to enlightenment—and as has been explained at length, up to when they thus practice the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) while training in the path to enlightenment—if they have not yet perfected the Tathāgata’s ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, the quality of non-forgetfulness, the state of constant abiding in equanimity, the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), and the other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-qualities, they are said to be training in the path to enlightenment but not yet having attained its fulfillment.
If one has already perfected the training in this path, through the wisdom associated with a single moment, one is able to realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

At that time, because the continuity of all subtle habitual tendencies of affliction never arises again, it is called "abandonment without remainder," and one is named a Buddha. Furthermore, with the unobstructed and pure Buddha-eye, one surveys the phenomena of the ten directions and the three periods of time; since even non-existence cannot be apprehended, how much less could existence be found!
"In this way, Subhūti, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice the perfection of wisdom, with conviction and understanding that all phenomena have non-existence as their nature."

"Subhūti! This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s accomplishment of the most excellent skillful means: namely, when practicing the perfection of wisdom and contemplating all phenomena, they do not even apprehend non-existence, let alone existence!"

"Subhūti! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of generosity, he does not even perceive the non-existence of this generosity—the giver, the recipient, the gift, the fruit of giving, and the mind of enlightenment—much less would he perceive their existence!"

In this way, up until the time one realizes the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), regarding that knowledge of all modes—whether it be the one who realizes it, that which is realized, that by means of which it is realized, or the time and place of its realization—one does not even perceive non-existence, much less perceive existence!
Why is that? Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly forms this thought:

"All phenomena have non-existence as their nature. This non-existence is not made by Buddhas, nor by Bodhisattvas, nor by Pratyekabuddhas, nor by Śrāvakas, nor by anyone else; for all phenomena are without an agent, because they are devoid of an agent."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Are not all phenomena devoid of the intrinsic nature of phenomena?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"It is indeed so!
All phenomena are devoid of the intrinsic nature of phenomena. Subhūti asked again:
“If all phenomena are separated from the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), how could that which is separated from phenomena know whether that which is separated from phenomena exists or does not exist?
World-Honored One!

An existent phenomenon should not be able to know a non-existent phenomenon; a non-existent phenomenon should not be able to know an existent phenomenon; an existent phenomenon should not be able to know an existent phenomenon; and a non-existent phenomenon should not be able to know a non-existent phenomenon.”
“World-Honored One!
Since all these dharmas have non-cognition as their nature, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*,
manifest various distinctions among these dharmas, such as form (*rūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), and so forth?”
Whether feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness exist or do not exist; whether the eye-base up to the mind-base exists or does not exist;
whether the form-base up to the mental-object-base exists or does not exist; whether the eye-element up to the mind-element exists or does not exist;
whether the form-element up to the mental-object-element exists or does not exist; and whether the eye-consciousness-element up to... [the mental-consciousness-element] exists or does not exist.
Whether the consciousness element exists or does not exist; whether eye-contact up to mind-contact exists or does not exist;
whether the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition exist or do not exist;
whether the earth element up to the consciousness element exists or does not exist; and [whether] the causal condition up to the sovereign condition [exist or do not exist].
Whether existence or non-existence, whether ignorance up to old age and death exists or does not exist;
whether the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom exists or does not exist;
whether inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the nature of non-nature exists or does not exist; whether suchness up to the inconceivable realm exists or does not exist...
Whether the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path exist or do not exist;

whether the four applications of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path exist or do not exist; whether the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions exist or do not exist;
and whether the eight liberations up to the ten totalities exist or do not exist.
Whether the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—exist or do not exist;
whether the stage of pure observation up to the stage of a Tathāgata exists or does not exist; whether the stage of extreme joy up to the stage of the Dharma-cloud exists or does not exist;
whether all the doors of dhāraṇī and the doors of samādhi exist or do not exist; the five eyes...
Whether the six supernormal powers exist or do not exist; whether the ten powers of a Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, exist or do not exist;
whether the thirty-two marks of a Great Being and the eighty secondary signs exist or do not exist;
whether the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity exist or do not exist; [whether] omniscience and the path...
Whether the knowledge of characteristics and the knowledge of all aspects exist or do not exist;
whether the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha exists or does not exist; whether the entire conduct of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas exists or does not exist;
whether the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas exists or does not exist; and whether the knowledge of all modes exists or does not exist.
"Does the conditioned realm and the unconditioned realm exist or not?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they manifest whether phenomena exist or do not exist in accordance with worldly convention, but not in accordance with the ultimate truth."
Subhūti asked again:
"Are the conventional and the ultimate truth different?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"The ultimate truth does not exist separately from the conventional. Why is this so?

The suchness of the conventional is itself the ultimate truth. Yet, because sentient beings hold perverted and false attachments, they neither know nor see this suchness. Therefore, for their benefit, the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas manifest the existence or non-existence of all phenomena according to conventional characteristics, rather than according to the ultimate truth."

Furthermore, Subhūti, immeasurable sentient beings give rise to the notion that the aggregates and other phenomena are truly existent, or they give rise to the notion that they are truly non-existent; they do not realize that all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent. For the benefit of these beings, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas manifest whether the aggregates and so forth are existent or non-existent, so that sentient beings may, by means of this, understand that the aggregates and all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent—not because they wish them to cling to the characteristics of true existence or non-existence.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should apply themselves with diligent vigor, free from the grasping at existence and non-existence, and practice the profound perfection of wisdom.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 463. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Chapter 70: The Practice of the Bodhisattva. Part Two: The Practice of the Bodhisattva, Chapter Seventy. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One!”
Regarding what was said about "practicing the bodhisattva practice," what dharma is called the bodhisattva practice?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"As for practicing the bodhisattva practice, it is called the bodhisattva practice because one practices within saṃsāra for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
in what place should bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the bodhisattva path?"
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice the awakening within the emptiness of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.”
In the practice of awakening, one should practice the bodhisattva conduct by dwelling in the emptiness of the sense bases from the eye base up to the mind base;

one should practice the bodhisattva conduct by dwelling in the emptiness of the sense fields from the form field up to the phenomena field; one should practice the bodhisattva conduct by dwelling in the emptiness of the elements from the eye element up to the mind element;
one should practice the bodhisattva conduct by dwelling in the emptiness of the objects from the form element up to the phenomena element. One should...
One should practice the bodhisattva conduct within the emptiness of the visual consciousness element up to the mental consciousness element;
one should practice the bodhisattva conduct within the emptiness of visual contact up to mental contact;

one should practice the bodhisattva conduct within the emptiness of all feelings produced with visual contact as a condition up to all feelings produced with mental contact as a condition; and one should [practice] within the earth element...

One should practice the bodhisattva conduct by means of the emptiness of the realm of consciousness; one should practice the bodhisattva conduct by means of the emptiness of the causal conditions up to the dominant conditions;
one should practice the bodhisattva conduct by means of the emptiness of ignorance up to old age and death;
and one should practice the bodhisattva conduct by relying on the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom.
One should practice the bodhisattva path by relying on inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature;

one should practice the bodhisattva path by relying on suchness up to the inconceivable realm; one should practice the bodhisattva path by relying on the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
and one should practice the bodhisattva path by relying on the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path.
In practice, one should practice the bodhisattva path by relying on the four dhyānas; one should practice the bodhisattva path by relying on the four immeasurables;
one should practice the bodhisattva path by relying on the four formless attainments; one should practice the bodhisattva path by relying on the eight liberations;
one should practice the bodhisattva path by relying on the eight bases of mastery; and one should practice the bodhisattva path by relying on the nine successive meditative concentrations.
A bodhisattva’s practice should be carried out by relying on the ten universal bases; a bodhisattva’s practice should be carried out by relying on the three doors of liberation;
a bodhisattva’s practice should be carried out by relying on the ten stages;
a bodhisattva’s practice should be carried out by relying on all doors of dhāraṇī; and a bodhisattva’s practice should be carried out by relying on all doors of samādhi.
One should practice the bodhisattva path by relying on the five eyes; one should practice the bodhisattva path by relying on the six supernormal powers;
one should practice the bodhisattva path by relying on the ten powers of a Tathāgata; one should practice the bodhisattva path by relying on the four fearlessnesses;
one should practice the bodhisattva path by relying on great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity. One should...
One should practice the bodhisattva conduct by relying on the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;

one should practice the bodhisattva conduct by relying on the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity; one should practice the bodhisattva conduct by relying on all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects;
one should practice the bodhisattva conduct by relying on the purification of the buddha-fields; one should rely on...
To mature sentient beings while practicing the bodhisattva path, one should practice the bodhisattva path by relying on the dhāraṇī that brings forth syllables;

one should practice the bodhisattva path by relying on the dhāraṇī that penetrates syllables; one should practice the bodhisattva path by relying on the dhāraṇī that penetrates the absence of syllables;
and one should practice the bodhisattva path by relying on the bringing forth of unimpeded eloquence.

When practicing the bodhisattva conduct, one should practice the bodhisattva conduct by relying on the realm of the conditioned; one should practice the bodhisattva conduct by relying on the realm of the unconditioned. "Subhūti!

When all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the bodhisattva path in this manner, they do not conceive of dualistic characteristics regarding any phenomena, just as the Buddha does not conceive of dualistic characteristics regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this manner, it is called practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
“Subhūti! If bodhisattva mahāsattvas can cultivate the bodhisattva practice in this way, they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Regarding the Buddha spoken of by the Blessed One, for what reason is he called ‘Buddha’?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Because of the meaning of awakening, the meaning of reality, and the meaning of Bhagavān, he is called ‘Buddha.’”
"Furthermore, Subhūti! One is called a Buddha because of having attained manifest, perfect enlightenment regarding all true dharmas. Furthermore, Subhūti!"
Because he has thoroughly realized the true nature of phenomena,
he is called a Buddha. "Furthermore, Subhūti,
because he possesses non-erroneous awakening regarding the suchness and the exhaustiveness of all phenomena, he is called a Buddha."
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Because unobstructed knowledge functions regarding all phenomena of the three times as well as unconditioned phenomena, he is called a Buddha.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"
"Because he awakens all sentient beings to reality as it is, causing them to be free from perversion, he is called a Buddha.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, regarding what you have called 'bodhi,' for what reason is it named 'bodhi'?"

The Buddha told Subhūti: "Awakening is the meaning of emptiness; it is the meaning of suchness; it is the meaning of the limit of reality; it is the meaning of the nature of phenomena; it is the meaning of the realm of phenomena."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Because it is able to truly awaken to that which is most supreme, excellent, and sublime through the provisional establishment of names, signs, and conventional designations, it is called 'bodhi' (enlightenment)."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
The meaning of being indestructible is the meaning of bodhi; the meaning of non-conceptuality is the meaning of bodhi.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"
It is true, it is real, not false, and not subject to change; therefore, it is called bodhi.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Only conventional designations exist, and no substantial reality can be found; therefore, it is called bodhi."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
That which all Buddhas possess as true, pure, and universal awakening is therefore called bodhi.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"
"Because all Buddhas, by means of this, realize perfectly complete enlightenment regarding all phenomena in all their aspects and characteristics, it is therefore called bodhi.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, for the sake of awakening, practice the six pāramitās up to the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), in what dharma do they find benefit or harm, increase or decrease, arising or cessation, or defilement or purification?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, for the sake of awakening, practice the six pāramitās up to the knowledge of all aspects, they neither benefit nor harm, neither increase nor decrease, neither produce nor extinguish, and neither defile nor purify any phenomena.”

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, for the sake of awakening, practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* by means of having no objective referent whatsoever regarding any phenomena; they do not bring about benefit or harm, increase or decrease, arising or ceasing, nor defilement or purity.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of awakening, practices the six pāramitās up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvajñājñāna*), employing as a skillful means the state of having no objective referent whatsoever regarding any phenomena—such that neither benefit nor harm, neither increase nor decrease, neither arising nor ceasing, nor defilement nor purity appear before them—then while this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices profound prajñāpāramitā, how does he embrace the dānapāramitā up to the prajñāpāramitā?”
How does one encompass internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature?
How does one encompass suchness up to the inconceivable realm?
How does one encompass the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path?
How does one embrace the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path?
How does one embrace the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions?
How does one encompass the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality?
How does one encompass the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness?
How does one encompass the various bodhisattva stages?
How does one embrace the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi?
How does one embrace the five eyes and the six supernormal powers?
How does one embrace the ten powers of a Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha?
How does one embrace the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity?
How does one embrace all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)?
How does one transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, enter the bodhisattva’s state of right determination free from outflows, and gradually realize the knowledge of all modes?
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not, by means of duality, take up and practice the six perfections, nor do they, by means of duality, gradually realize the knowledge of all aspects.”
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha again:

“If, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not grasp at the practice of the six perfections by means of duality, and so on, up to not gradually realizing all-knowledge by means of duality, then how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly increase all wholesome dharmas from the first production of the thought of enlightenment until the final thought?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices by means of duality, then all wholesome dharmas will not increase. Why is that?"
Because foolish ordinary beings all rely on duality, the wholesome dharmas they produce do not increase.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices by way of non-duality, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment until the final thought, they constantly increase all wholesome dharmas.

Therefore, Subhūti, the roots of goodness of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas are firm and solid; the world with its gods, humans, and asuras cannot destroy them or cause them to fall to the levels of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

The various evil and unwholesome dharmas of the world cannot be subdued, such that when practicing the six pāramitās up to the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), all wholesome dharmas fail to increase.
"In this way, Subhūti,
all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice the profound perfection of wisdom that is non-dual.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed [the Buddha], saying:
“World-Honored One,
do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of their roots of goodness?
The Buddha said:

"No, it is not so! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not practice the profound perfection of wisdom for the sake of roots of virtue, nor do they practice the profound perfection of wisdom for the sake of unwholesome roots."

Why is this? It is because it is the natural law for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that as long as they have not drawn near to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; as long as their roots of goodness are not fully perfected; and as long as they have not been extensively sustained by true spiritual friends, they can never attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva attend upon the Buddhas, fulfill the roots of goodness, and be extensively sustained by true spiritual friends, so as to be able to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes?”
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, bodhisattva mahāsattvas draw near to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas to hear the teaching of the true Dharma—namely, from the sūtras up to the upadeśas. Having heard them, they receive and uphold them, repeatedly rehearsing them until they have mastered them thoroughly. Once they have mastered them thoroughly, they contemplate and examine them; having examined them, they deeply perceive their underlying intent. Having perceived the intent, they further achieve thorough penetration. Having achieved thorough penetration, they attain dhāraṇī and give rise to unimpeded eloquence, even unto the realization of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). In whatever place they are born, they never forget or lose the teachings and meanings of the true Dharma that they have heard and upheld.”

Having extensively planted roots of virtue in the presence of all Buddhas, they are sustained by the power of those roots of virtue and thus do not fall into the miserable realms or the states of lack of leisure.

Furthermore, being sustained by those roots of virtue, their intentions become pure; and being upheld by the power of that pure intention, they are always able to correctly bring sentient beings to maturity and adorn and purify Buddha-fields.

Furthermore, because they are sustained by these roots of goodness, they never remain apart from true, pure, and virtuous friends—namely, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as well as the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and others who can praise the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.

"So it is, Subhūti! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who attend upon the Buddhas, perfect their roots of goodness, and are extensively sustained by true spiritual friends, will swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes."
Therefore, Subhūti!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the profound perfection of wisdom and wish to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) should apply themselves with diligent vigor, draw near to the Buddhas, fully embrace the roots of virtue they have planted, and serve spiritual friends without ever becoming weary.
Chapter 71: Cultivating Intimacy, Part Two, Chapter Seventy-one on Cultivating Intimacy. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not draw near to the Buddhas, does not fulfill the roots of goodness, and does not serve spiritual friends, could such a bodhisattva mahāsattva possibly attain the knowledge of all modes?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If one cannot draw near to the Buddhas, fulfill the roots of goodness, and serve virtuous friends, they are not yet called a bodhisattva mahāsattva; how much less could they realize the knowledge of all modes!"

Why is this? For there are some bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, despite having drawn near to the Buddhas, planted various roots of goodness, and attended upon spiritual friends, are still unable to attain the knowledge of all modes; how much less could one who has failed to draw near to the Buddhas, fulfill their roots of goodness, and attend upon spiritual friends ever realize the knowledge of all modes!
If they were to attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), such a thing would be impossible.

Therefore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to be truly called a bodhisattva mahāsattva and wishes to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes, they should constantly draw near to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; they should bring their roots of virtue to fulfillment and serve spiritual friends without ever becoming weary.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"By what causes and conditions do some bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, though they have drawn near to the Buddhas, planted various roots of goodness, and served virtuous friends, yet are unable to attain the knowledge of all modes?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Because those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are far removed from the power of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), although they draw near to the Buddhas, plant various roots of goodness, and serve virtuous friends, they are unable to attain the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvajñajñāna*)."

This means that although those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have approached the Buddhas, planted various roots of goodness, and served spiritual friends, they do not hear from the Buddhas or their spiritual friends the teaching on the sublime skillful means; consequently, they are unable to attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha again, saying:

"What is called 'skillful means' (upāyakauśalya), such that when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish such skillful means, they are certain to realize all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna) in whatever they undertake?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first generation of the mind of awakening, practices the perfection of generosity while maintaining mental orientations associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), whether giving to the Buddhas, or to bodhisattvas, or to pratyekabuddhas, or to śrāvakas, or to other śramaṇas and brahmins, or to non-Buddhist practitioners of the holy life, or to the poor, travelers, ascetics, and beggars, or to all humans and non-humans—this bodhisattva mahāsattva, having accomplished such mental orientations associated with the knowledge of all modes, practices generosity yet has no perception of a gift, no perception of a recipient, and no perception of a self or what belongs to a self."

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas contemplate that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty—without reality, without accomplishment, without transition, and without cessation—and they enter into the characteristics of all phenomena, knowing that all phenomena are without action and without agency, thereby entering into the characteristics of all conditioned formations.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, having accomplished such skillful means, constantly increases the roots of goodness conducive to awakening; because these roots of goodness are perpetually increasing, they are able to practice the perfection of generosity, ripening sentient beings and purifying buddha-fields.

Although they practice generosity, they do not seek the fruits obtained from giving; that is, they do not dedicate [the merit] toward desirable objects or superior states of rebirth, but rather practice the perfection of generosity solely for the sake of protecting those who are unprotected and desiring to liberate those who are not yet liberated.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline from the first generation of the mind of awakening, they maintain pure ethical discipline through mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes. Their minds never give rise to the latent tendencies or fetters of greed, hatred, or delusion, nor do they give rise to other unwholesome dharmas that obstruct awakening—namely, stinginess, immoral conduct, anger, laziness, inferiority of mind, distractedness of mind, faulty wisdom, pride, excessive pride, pride beyond pride, the pride of 'I,' overweening pride, condescension, false pride, or mental engagements associated with śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."

Why is this so? Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty—without reality, without formation, without transition, and without cessation—and thus enters into the characteristics of all phenomena. He knows that all phenomena are without action and without agency, and thus enters into the characteristics of all conditioned formations.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, having accomplished such skillful means, constantly increases the roots of goodness of the factors of enlightenment; because these roots of goodness are perpetually increasing, they are able to practice the perfection of ethical discipline, maturing sentient beings and purifying buddha-fields.

Although they practice pure ethical discipline, they do not seek the fruits obtained from that discipline—meaning they do not dedicate it toward desirable objects or superior states of rebirth—but rather practice the perfection of pure ethical discipline solely for the sake of protecting those who lack protection and desiring to liberate those who are not yet liberated.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of patience from the first generation of the mind of awakening, training in patience with mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes, that bodhisattva mahāsattva will not, even for the sake of protecting his own life, give rise to a single thought of anger, harsh speech, or a retaliatory intent of resentment."

Even if someone were to come wishing to take his life, plunder his wealth, violate his wife, slander and insult him, obstruct or belittle him, or strike, pierce, cut, or maim him, and inflict various other harmful acts upon him, he would harbor no resentment whatsoever toward that sentient being, seeking only their benefit and happiness.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas contemplate that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty—without reality, without accomplishment, without transition, and without cessation—and they enter into the characteristics of all phenomena, knowing that all phenomena are without action and without agency, thereby entering into the characteristics of all conditioned formations.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, having accomplished such skillful means, constantly increases the roots of goodness that are the factors of enlightenment; because these roots of goodness increase perpetually, they are able to practice the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) to mature sentient beings and purify buddha-fields.

Although they practice patience, they do not seek the fruits obtained through patience—meaning they do not dedicate it toward desirable objects or superior states of rebirth—but practice the perfection of patience solely for the sake of protecting those who lack protection and desiring to liberate those who are not yet liberated.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of diligence from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, they do so with mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes. They initiate right effort that is courageous and fearless, remaining far removed from indolence and inferiority of mind. Seeking awakening, they do not shrink from any suffering, cultivating all wholesome dharmas constantly without negligence or desistance."

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty—lacking reality, lacking formation, lacking transformation, and lacking cessation—and thus enters into the characteristics of all phenomena, knowing that all phenomena are without action and without agency, and enters into the characteristics of all conditioned formations.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such skillful means and constantly increases the roots of virtue conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣa*). Because these roots of virtue are perpetually increasing, he is able to practice the perfection of diligence (*vīryapāramitā*) to ripen sentient beings and adorn and purify buddha-fields.

Although they practice diligence, they do not seek the fruits obtained through such effort; that is, they do not dedicate it toward desirable objects or superior states of rebirth, but practice the perfection of diligence solely for the sake of protecting those without protection and desiring to liberate those who are not yet liberated.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first production of the thought of awakening, practices the perfection of meditative concentration, they train in various samādhis with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes."

When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva sees forms with the eye, hears sounds with the ear, smells odors with the nose, tastes flavors with the tongue, feels tangibles with the body, and cognizes phenomena with the mind, they do not grasp at their signs nor grasp at their secondary characteristics. They immediately guard the sense faculties in those instances, dwelling in heedfulness so as not to give rise to worldly greed and sorrow, evil and unwholesome states, or the outflows of the afflictions; they single-mindedly cultivate mindfulness and concentration to protect the sense faculties.

Whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, speaking, or remaining silent, this bodhisattva-mahāsattva is never separated from sublime śamatha; they remain far removed from all manner of defiled dharmas. With body and mind tranquil, their deportment and conduct are uniform and consistent; there is nothing in their actions that is not disciplined and excellent, and their mind is constantly settled and free from conceptual discrimination.

Why is this? It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas contemplate that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty—lacking reality, lacking formation, lacking transformation, and lacking cessation—and thus they enter into the characteristics of all phenomena. Knowing that all phenomena are without action and without agency, they enter into the characteristics of all conditioned formations.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such skillful means and constantly increases the roots of goodness of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*). Because these roots of goodness increase perpetually, they are able to practice the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*) to mature sentient beings and purify buddha-fields.

Although they practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they do not seek the fruits obtained from that concentration—meaning they do not dedicate it toward desirable objects or superior states of rebirth—but rather practice the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*) solely for the sake of protecting those who lack protection and desiring to liberate those who are not yet liberated.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva first generates the mind of awakening and practices the perfection of wisdom, they cultivate sublime insight by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes."

This bodhisattva mahāsattva is free from all wrong wisdom; others cannot lead his mind astray, nor does he give rise to the grasping of "I" or "mine. He remains far removed from all views of a self, views of a sentient being, and so forth, up to views of a knower, views of a seer, views of existence and non-existence, and all evil tendencies of view. Free from pride and without conceptual discrimination, he brings forth various kinds of sublime roots of goodness.

Why is this? It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas contemplate that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty—without reality, without formation, without transition, and without cessation—and they enter into the characteristics of all phenomena, knowing that all phenomena are without action and without agency, thereby entering into the characteristics of all conditioned formations.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such skillful means and constantly increases the roots of goodness pertaining to the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*). Because these roots of goodness increase perpetually, they are able to practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) to mature sentient beings and purify buddha-fields.

Although they practice *prajñā*, they do not seek the fruits obtained through wisdom; that is, they do not dedicate [their merit] toward desirable objects or superior states of rebirth, but rather practice the *prajñāpāramitā* solely for the sake of protecting those who lack protection and desiring to liberate those who are not yet liberated.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom from the first production of the thought of awakening, they enter the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes."
Although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter and emerge with mastery from the dhyānas, the immeasurables, and the formless attainments, they do not appropriate the ripening of their fruits.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have accomplished the most supreme skillful means (upāya-kauśalya) and contemplate that the specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) of all dhyānas, immeasurables (apramāṇa), and formless attainments (ārūpya) are all empty—devoid of reality, devoid of formation, devoid of transformation, and devoid of cessation—and thus enter into the characteristic of all dharmas. They know that all dharmas are without action and without agency, and they enter into the characteristic of all conditioned formations (saṃskāra).

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, having accomplished such skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), constantly increases the roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*) pertaining to the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).

Because these roots of goodness increase perpetually, they are able to practice the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*); by practicing the meditative concentrations, the immeasurables, and the formless attainments, they are then able to spontaneously mature sentient beings and purify Buddha-fields.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva first resolves upon awakening and practices the perfection of wisdom, they train in all the factors conducive to awakening (bodhipakṣadharma) with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā). Having accomplished such skillful means, although they practice the path that abandons through seeing and cultivation, they do not grasp at the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, or the awakening of a pratyekabuddha."

Why is this? It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas contemplate that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty—lacking reality, lacking formation, lacking transformation, and lacking cessation—and thus they enter into the characteristics of all phenomena, knowing that all phenomena are without action and without agency, and they enter into the characteristics of all conditioned formations.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes the most excellent skillful means and constantly increases the roots of goodness conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣika-kuśalamūla*). Because these roots of goodness increase perpetually, they are able to practice all factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*), transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and enter the bodhisattva’s state of certainty (*samyaktvaniyāma*); this is called the bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*).
By virtue of this patience, one is always able to freely mature sentient beings and purify Buddha-fields.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, although they attain mastery in entering and emerging from the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative concentrations, the ten totalities, and so forth—by means of mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes—they are nevertheless able to accomplish skillful means and do not grasp at the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha."

Why is this? It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas contemplate that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty—without reality, without accomplishment, without transition, and without cessation—and thus they enter into the characteristics of all phenomena, knowing that all phenomena are without action and without agency, and they enter into the characteristics of all conditioned formations.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes the most supreme skillful means and constantly increases the roots of goodness pertaining to the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*). Because these roots of goodness are perpetually increasing, they are able to freely bring sentient beings to maturity and adorn and purify buddha-fields; they enter the bodhisattva stage of non-retrogression and receive the patient acceptance of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa-kṣānti*).
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes, they diligently cultivate the Tathāgata’s ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and other such immeasurable and boundless buddha-qualities; yet, until they have fully matured sentient beings and purified a buddha-field, they do not yet realize the knowledge of all modes."

Why is this? It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas contemplate that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty—lacking reality, lacking formation, lacking transformation, and lacking cessation—and they enter into the characteristics of all phenomena, knowing that all phenomena are without action and without agency, thereby entering into the characteristics of all conditioned formations.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes the most supreme skillful means and constantly increases the roots of goodness pertaining to the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*). Because these roots of goodness increase perpetually, he is able to bring sentient beings to full maturity and purify buddha-fields, gradually attaining the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

“Subhūti! This is called skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*). If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such skillful means, whatever they undertake will certainly enable them to realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).”
Such supreme skillful means as these are all accomplished through the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Therefore, Subhūti,
bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should diligently train in the profound perfection of wisdom, and in whatever they do, they should not hope for a karmic reward.
"If one can thus diligently practice and study this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one will swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Chapter 72: Universal Training, Part Two, Universal Training, Section 72-1. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having accomplished such supreme awakening wisdom, are able to receive and practice the pure and profound Dharma, yet they do not grasp at superior karmic rewards.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have accomplished such supreme awakening-wisdom are able to receive and practice the pure, profound Dharma, yet they do not grasp at superior karmic rewards.
"Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are immovable regarding the intrinsic nature of phenomena.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed [the Buddha], saying:
“World-Honored One!
In what phenomena is the nature of this bodhisattva-mahāsattva immovable?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“This bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to remain unmoved within the self-nature of non-existence.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“In what [regarding] the self-nature of non-existence is this bodhisattva mahāsattva unmoved?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“This bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to remain unmoved within the intrinsic nature of form; able to remain unmoved within the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
and able to remain unmoved within the intrinsic nature of the sense base of the eye, up to and including the sense base of the mind.”
Movement: being able to remain unmoved in the intrinsic nature of the sense-base of form up to the sense-base of mental phenomena;

being able to remain unmoved in the intrinsic nature of the eye-element up to the mind-element; being able to remain unmoved in the intrinsic nature of the form-element up to the mental-phenomena-element;
being able to remain unmoved in the intrinsic nature of the eye-consciousness-element up to the mind-consciousness-element; and being able to remain unmoved in eye-contact...

...up to the fact that the intrinsic nature of mental contact is immovable; being able to remain immovable within the intrinsic nature of all feelings produced with visual contact as a condition, up to all feelings produced with mental contact as a condition;
being able to remain immovable within the intrinsic nature of the perfection of generosity, up to the perfection of wisdom; and being able to remain immovable within the four dhyānas...
The four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the nature of the [four] foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path are immovable in their intrinsic nature;

they are immovable in their intrinsic nature regarding the three doors of liberation, the eight liberations, and the nine successive attainments; they are immovable in their intrinsic nature regarding the Tathāgata...
The ten powers, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are by nature immovable; likewise, up to and including omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*),
they are by nature immovable, and they are by nature immovable within the entire realm of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtadhātu*) and the realm of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*).

Why is this so? Because these dharmas are themselves without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas do not waver from this self-nature of being without intrinsic nature; yet, that which is without intrinsic nature cannot realize that which is without intrinsic nature through direct realization.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
can a dharma that possesses intrinsic nature realize through direct perception a dharma that possesses intrinsic nature?”
The Buddha said,
“It is not so. [He replied,] “World-Honored One!”
“Can a dharma that lacks intrinsic nature be directly realized as having intrinsic nature? The Buddha said, “No!”
“World-Honored One!
Can a dharma that possesses intrinsic nature realize the absence of intrinsic nature?
The Buddha said:
"Not so! "World-Honored One, can a dharma that lacks intrinsic nature realize the absence of intrinsic nature?"
The Buddha said,
"It is not so. [He replied,] "World-Honored One!"

If that were so, there would also have to be cases where existence cannot realize existence, non-existence cannot realize existence, existence cannot realize non-existence, and non-existence cannot realize non-existence; would this not mean that the Blessed One has neither attainment nor realization?
The Buddha said:
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
Although there is attainment and there is clear realization, they are nonetheless free from the four extremes.”
“World-Honored One!
How can there be attainment and clear realization apart from the four propositions? “Subhūti!

Whether it be attainment or clear realization, they are neither existent nor non-existent, transcending all conceptual proliferation; therefore, I speak of there being attainment and clear realization, yet they are free from the four extremes.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas engage in conceptual proliferation?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas regard form, up to and including consciousness, as either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or untranquil, and detached or undetached; these are conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*).”

"To contemplate the sense base of the eye, and so on up to the sense base of the mind, as either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or untranquil, detached or undetached—this is conceptual proliferation."

"To contemplate the sense base of form, up to the sense base of mental phenomena, as either permanent or impermanent, as pleasure or suffering, as self or non-self, as pure or impure, as tranquil or not tranquil, as detached or not detached—this is conceptual proliferation."

"To contemplate the eye-element up to the mind-element as either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or untranquil, detached or undetached—this is conceptual proliferation."

"To contemplate the realm of form up to the realm of phenomena—whether as permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or non-tranquil, detached or non-detached—is conceptual proliferation."

"To contemplate the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element—whether as permanent or impermanent, as pleasure or suffering, as self or non-self, as pure or impure, as tranquil or untranquil, as detached or undetached—is conceptual proliferation."

"To contemplate eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact—whether as permanent or impermanent, as pleasure or suffering, as self or non-self, as pure or impure, as tranquil or untranquil, or as secluded or unsecluded—is conceptual proliferation."

"To contemplate the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition—whether as permanent or impermanent, as pleasure or pain, as self or non-self, as pure or impure, as tranquil or untranquil, as detached or undetached—is conceptual proliferation."
