"To contemplate the earth element up to the consciousness element as either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or not tranquil, detached or not detached—this is conceptual proliferation."

"To contemplate the causal conditions up to the dominant conditions as either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or untranquil, detached or undetached—this is conceptual proliferation."

"To contemplate ignorance up to old age and death as either permanent or impermanent, as pleasure or suffering, as self or non-self, as pure or impure, as tranquil or not tranquil, or as secluded or not secluded—this is conceptual proliferation."

"To contemplate the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom as either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or untranquil, or secluded or non-secluded—this is conceptual proliferation."

"To contemplate inner emptiness, up to the emptiness of the non-existence of self-nature, as either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or non-tranquil, or detached or non-detached—this is conceptual proliferation."

"To contemplate true thusness up to the inconceivable realm as either permanent or impermanent, as pleasure or suffering, as self or non-self, as pure or impure, as tranquil or non-tranquil, or as detached or non-detached—this is conceptual proliferation."

"To contemplate the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—whether as permanent or impermanent, as pleasure or pain, as self or non-self, as pure or impure, as tranquil or untranquil, or as secluded or non-secluded—is conceptual proliferation."

"To contemplate the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path as either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or not tranquil, secluded or not secluded—this is conceptual proliferation."

"To contemplate the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments as either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or untranquil, or detached or undetached—this is conceptual proliferation."

"To contemplate the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality as either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or not tranquil, detached or not detached—this is conceptual proliferation."

"To contemplate the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—as being either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or not tranquil, detached or not detached, is conceptual proliferation."

"To regard the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata as either permanent or impermanent, as either pleasant or painful, as either self or non-self, as either pure or impure, as either tranquil or not tranquil, or as either secluded or not secluded—this is conceptual proliferation."

"To contemplate the stages from the Ground of Utmost Joy up to the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma as either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or non-tranquil, or detached or non-detached—this is conceptual proliferation."

"To observe any dharani-gate or samadhi-gate as permanent or impermanent, as pleasant or painful, as self or non-self, as pure or impure, as tranquil or not tranquil, or as detached or not detached—this is conceptual proliferation."

"To regard the five eyes and the six supernormal powers as either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or not tranquil, or detached or not detached—this is conceptual proliferation."

"To regard the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or not tranquil, or detached or not detached—this is conceptual proliferation."

"To contemplate the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs as either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or not tranquil, detached or not detached—this is conceptual proliferation."

"To contemplate the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity as either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or not tranquil, or detached or not detached—this is conceptual proliferation."

"To contemplate all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) as either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or not tranquil, or detached or not detached—this is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*)."

"To regard the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha as either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or untranquil, or detached or undetached—this is conceptual proliferation."

"To contemplate the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or untranquil, detached or undetached—this is conceptual proliferation."

"To contemplate the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas as either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or non-tranquil, or detached or non-detached—this is conceptual proliferation."

"To contemplate omniscience as either permanent or impermanent, as pleasure or suffering, as self or non-self, as pure or impure, as tranquil or untranquil, or as detached or undetached—this is conceptual proliferation."
"Furthermore, Subhūti! If bodhisattva mahāsattvas should form this thought:

'The noble truth of suffering should be fully known; the noble truth of the origin should be permanently abandoned; the noble truth of cessation should be realized; the noble truth of the path should be cultivated. "
"This is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). If one should think:
'One ought to cultivate the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments.'"
This is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
If one should think: "One ought to cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path," [this too is conceptual proliferation].
This is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). If one should think:
"One ought to cultivate the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness," [this too is conceptual proliferation].
This is conceptual proliferation.
If one should think:
"One ought to cultivate the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities."
This is frivolous conceptualization (*prapañca*). If one should think:
"I ought to transcend the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a solitary buddha (*pratyekabuddha*)."
This is conceptual proliferation.
If one should form such a thought as:
"One ought to practice the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom," [this is also conceptual proliferation].
This is frivolous conceptualization (*prapañca*).
If one forms this thought:
"One should abide in internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence," [this is also frivolous conceptualization].
This is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
If one forms the thought:
"I should abide in suchness (*tathatā*) up to the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*)," [this too is conceptual proliferation].
"This is conceptual proliferation.
If one should think:
'I ought to enter the bodhisattva's state of right determination and departure from birth.'"
This is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). If one should think:
"I should fulfill the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of a bodhisattva," [this too is conceptual proliferation].
This is frivolous conceptualization (*prapañca*).
If one forms this thought:
"One should give rise to all doors of dhāraṇī and doors of samādhi."
This is frivolous conceptualization (*prapañca*).
If one should form this thought:
"One ought to bring forth the five eyes and the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*)."
This is frivolous conceptualization (*prapañca*). If one should think:
"One should bring forth the ten powers of a Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha," [this too is frivolous conceptualization].
This is frivolous conceptualization (*prapañca*).
If one should form this thought:
"I should fulfill the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty secondary characteristics."
This is frivolous conceptualization (*prapañca*).
If one forms this thought:
"One should bring forth the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity."
This is conceptual proliferation.
If one should form this thought:
"One should bring forth all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects."
This is conceptual proliferation.
If one forms this thought:
"I should practice all the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva," [this too is conceptual proliferation].
This is conceptual proliferation.
If one forms this thought:
"I should realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas."
This is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). If one should think:
"I shall adorn and purify the Buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity," [this too is conceptual proliferation].
This is frivolous conceptualization (*prapañca*). If one should think:
"I shall realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*)," [this too is frivolous conceptualization].
This is frivolous conceptualization.
If one should think:
"I shall forever sever the continuity of all afflictions and their habitual tendencies," [this too is frivolous conceptualization].
"This is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Subhūti!
It is through such various kinds of discrimination that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas engage in conceptual proliferation."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should contemplate form, up to and including consciousness, as either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or non-tranquil, detached or non-detached; because all these are beyond conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), they should not be conceptually proliferated.

In this same way, up to and including the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), whether it is something to be realized or not to be realized, both are beyond conceptual proliferation and thus should not be conceptually proliferated."

One should contemplate the continuity of all afflictive habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*)—whether they should be permanently severed or should not be permanently severed—as being equally beyond conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and thus one should not engage in such proliferation.

“Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should contemplate all such dharmas and sentient beings as being beyond conceptual proliferation; therefore, they should not engage in conceptual proliferation regarding them.”

Why is this? Because regarding all phenomena and all sentient beings, that which possesses existence cannot conceptualize existence; that which possesses existence cannot conceptualize non-existence; that which lacks existence cannot conceptualize non-existence; and that which lacks existence cannot conceptualize existence. Apart from existence and non-existence, neither the one who conceptualizes, nor the object of conceptualization, nor the locus of conceptualization, nor the time of conceptualization can be apprehended.
Therefore, Subhūti! Form is without conceptual proliferation;

feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also without conceptual proliferation. In this way, up to and including the knowledge of all modes, there is no conceptual proliferation; even the permanent severance of the continuity of the habitual tendencies of afflictions is without conceptual proliferation.
"In this way, Subhūti,
all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice the profound perfection of wisdom that is free from conceptual proliferation.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed [the Buddha], saying:
“World-Honored One!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, how do they contemplate form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, up to and including the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvajñājñāna*), so as to forever sever the continuity of the habitual tendencies of afflictions (*kleśavāsanā*)? Since all these are beyond conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), why should one not engage in conceptual proliferation?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should contemplate that form has no intrinsic nature, and that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness likewise have no intrinsic nature. In this way, they should even contemplate that the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) has no intrinsic nature, and that the perpetual severance of the continuity of the habitual tendencies of afflictions also has no intrinsic nature. If a phenomenon has no intrinsic nature, it cannot be the object of conceptual proliferation.”

Therefore, Subhūti, because form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are beyond conceptual proliferation, bodhisattva mahāsattvas should not engage in conceptual proliferation; likewise, up to and including the knowledge of all modes and the permanent severance of the continuity of the habitual tendencies of afflictions, because these are beyond conceptual proliferation, bodhisattva mahāsattvas should not engage in conceptual proliferation.

"Subhūti! If bodhisattva mahāsattvas can thus remain free from all conceptual proliferation regarding all phenomena, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom with skillful means, they will enter the bodhisattva’s state of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*). Having entered it, they will swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*)."

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 464. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Second Division, Chapter on Universal Training, Number Seventy-Two, Part Two. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

If all dharmas are devoid of intrinsic nature, free from all conceptual proliferation, and unapprehendable, by what path do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth?
Is it the path of the śrāvaka?
Is it the path of the pratyekabuddha?
Or is it the path of the Tathāgata?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not enter the bodhisattva’s state of certainty (samyaktva-niyāma) by way of the path of the śrāvakas, nor by way of the path of the pratyekabuddhas, nor by way of the path of the Tathāgatas; rather, having fully studied and perfected all paths, they enter the bodhisattva’s state of certainty by way of the bodhisattva path.”

For example, it is like the eighth person who first trains in various paths and subsequently enters the state of correct determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) of his own vehicle by means of his own path; yet, until he has generated the path of the complete fruit, he is unable to realize the ultimate fruit of his own vehicle.

It is the same for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: having first fully trained in and perfected all paths, they subsequently enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth by means of their own path; yet, until they have aroused the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi), they are still unable to attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
"If one enters this meditative absorption, one can realize the knowledge of all modes through the wisdom associated with a single moment.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva first trains fully in all paths and subsequently enters the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth by means of their own path..."

Is it not the case that the paths of the eighth person, the stream-enterer, the once-returner, the non-returner, the arhat, the pratyekabuddha, and the Tathāgata—each directed toward their respective fruits—are distinct from one another?

"Bhagavān! If these various paths are each distinct, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having first fully studied and mastered all these paths, subsequently enters the bodhisattva’s state of certainty (samyaktva-niyāma) by means of his own path?"

That is to say, if Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas were to give rise to the eighth path, they would become those of the eighth stage; if they were to give rise to the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), they would become stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*); if they were to give rise to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), they would become once-returners (*sakṛdāgāmin*) or non-returners (*anāgāmin*); if they were to give rise to the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), they would become arhats; and if they were to give rise to the path of the solitary realizer (*pratyekabuddhamārga*), they would become solitary realizers.
“World-Honored One!
It is impossible for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has become an eighth-rank practitioner to enter the bodhisattva’s state of certainty (samyaktva-niyāma).
It is also impossible, without entering the bodhisattva’s state of certainty, to realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).”

"Bhagavān! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva has already become a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, an arhat, or a pratyekabuddha, it is impossible that they could then enter the bodhisattva’s state of certainty (samyaktvaniyāma)."
It is impossible that one could realize the knowledge of all aspects without entering the bodhisattva’s state of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
World-Honored One,

how am I to truly understand, in accordance with reality, that bodhisattva mahāsattvas must first fully train in and perfect all paths before entering the bodhisattva’s state of certainty, without contradicting the principle?
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having become an eighth-rank [śrāvaka], and so forth up to having become a pratyekabuddha, were able to enter the bodhisattva’s state of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*), such a thing is impossible; nor is it possible that, without entering the bodhisattva’s state of certainty, one could realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One,

if that is so, how is it that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having first fully trained in and perfected all paths, subsequently enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth by means of their own path?"

“Having entered the bodhisattva’s state of correct determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), they gradually realize the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) and forever sever the continuity of all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“From their first production of the thought of awakening, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the six perfections with courageous diligence; by means of superior wisdom and vision, they transcend the eight stages, namely, from the Stage of Pure Observation (*śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi*) up to the stage of the Pratyekabuddhas.”

Although they thoroughly train in all eight stages thus described, they are able to transcend them through superior wisdom and vision; by means of the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), they enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktvaniyāma*).

Having already entered the bodhisattva’s state of certainty beyond regression, they gradually further realize the omniscience of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), thereby attaining the perfect knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) and forever severing the continuity of all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
"Subhūti, you should know this!

The wisdom of the eighth stage is itself the patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva; furthermore, whatever wisdom or abandonment belongs to stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas is also the patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva."
In this way, Subhūti, after bodhisattva mahāsattvas have fully trained in and perfected all paths, they subsequently enter the bodhisattva’s state of certainty through their own path.
Having entered the bodhisattva’s state of certainty (*samyaktva-nyāma*), they gradually realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Once they have realized the knowledge of all modes, they benefit all sentient beings through that fruition.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

As it has been said that the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should train in the thorough knowledge of all the characteristics of the paths—whether the path of śrāvakas, the path of pratyekabuddhas, the path of bodhisattvas, or the path of tathāgatas—and that the knowledge of all the aspects of these paths is called the ‘knowledge of the characteristics of the paths’ (mārgajñatā)—how should bodhisattva-mahāsattvas give rise to this knowledge of the characteristics of the paths?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

“Those marks, signs, and characteristics that can correctly manifest the knowledge of the aspects of the path are such that all bodhisattva mahāsattvas universally and perfectly awaken to them. Having perfectly awakened to them, they explain, reveal, designate, and establish them for others as they truly are, so that sentient beings may attain unerring understanding and proceed toward the benefit and happiness they seek according to their needs.”

This bodhisattva mahāsattva should attain the gate of dhāraṇī that is skillful in all sounds and languages; by means of this skillful gate of dhāraṇī, they produce various sounds and languages to proclaim the sublime Dharma for all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm, causing them to know that what they hear is like an echo—though there is comprehension, there is no attachment.
“Subhūti! For this reason, bodhisattva mahāsattvas should train to perfect the knowledge of the aspects of all paths (*sarvamārgākārajñatā*).

Having trained to perfect the knowledge of the aspects of all paths, they should know, as they truly are, the various distinctions among the inclinations (*āśaya*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of all sentient beings, and accordingly act for their benefit and happiness. That is to say, they should know, as they truly are, the inclinations and latent tendencies of sentient beings in the hells, as well as their causes and effects; having known them, they employ skillful means to block those paths.”

Likewise, they know, as it truly is, the inclinations, latent tendencies, and the causes and effects of sentient beings in the animal realm; having known these, they employ skillful means to obstruct those paths.

They likewise know, as it truly is, the inclinations, latent tendencies, and the causes and effects of sentient beings in the preta realm; having known these, they employ skillful means to obstruct those paths.

They likewise know, as it truly is, the inclinations, latent tendencies, and the causes and effects of nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and so forth; having known these, they employ skillful means to obstruct those paths.

He also knows, as they truly are, the inclinations, latent tendencies, and the causes and effects of human beings and the gods of the desire realm; having known them, he employs skillful means to obstruct their path.

He also knows, as they truly are, the inclinations, latent tendencies, and the causes and effects of the gods of the Brahma assembly up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven of the form realm; having known them, he employs skillful means to obstruct their path.

He also knows, as they truly are, the inclinations, latent tendencies, and the causes and effects of the gods of the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; having known them, he employs skillful means to obstruct their path.
He also knows, as they truly are, the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eight factors of the noble path, as well as their causes and results;

he also knows, as they truly are, the three doors of liberation and their causes and results; he also knows, as they truly are, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and their causes and results; and he also knows, as they truly are, the eight liberations.
He also knows as they truly are the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities, along with their causes and results;
he also knows as they truly are the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, along with their causes and results;
and he also knows as they truly are the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, along with their causes and results.
They truly know the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, as well as their causes and effects;
they also truly know suchness up to the inconceivable realm, as well as their causes and effects;

they also truly know the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata, as well as their causes and effects; and they also truly know the stage of extreme joy up to the stage of the Dharma...
He knows the stages of the clouds and their causes and conditions as they truly are; he also knows all dharani-doors and all samadhi-doors, along with their causes and conditions, as they truly are;
he also knows the five eyes and the six supernormal powers, along with their causes and conditions, as they truly are;
and he also knows the ten powers of a Tathagata, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, as they truly are.

He also knows, as they truly are, the cause and effect of that; he also knows, as they truly are, the quality of non-forgetfulness, the state of constant equanimity, and their respective causes and effects;

and he also knows, as they truly are, all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), along with their respective causes and effects.

"Subhūti! Once bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have truly understood the paths of the śrāvakas and others, along with their causes and effects, they establish sentient beings in the paths of the three vehicles as appropriate, causing them to practice diligently so that each attains the ultimate goal."

“Subhūti! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should give rise to this knowledge of the characteristics of all paths (*sarvamārgākārajñatā*). If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva can train in this knowledge of the characteristics of all paths, they will be able to penetrate the various elements, dispositions, and latent tendencies of all sentient beings.”
Having thus attained realization, he preaches the True Dharma according to what is appropriate for each, causing all to obtain the supreme fruits they seek, never in vain. Why is this so?

This bodhisattva mahāsattva has skillfully mastered the superior and inferior faculties of sentient beings and understands, as they truly are, the distinctions among the mental states of all sentient beings regarding their coming and going, death and birth; therefore, the Dharma he teaches is never in vain.
Subhūti! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) in this manner regarding all these paths. Why is that?

All the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), which constitute the path to be studied by all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, are entirely subsumed within this profound *prajñāpāramitā*; it is through training in this that all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas attain their ultimate consummation.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), up to and including enlightenment itself, are in every respect neither joined nor dispersed, formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and of a single characteristic—namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics (*animitta*)—how can such factors conducive to enlightenment apprehend enlightenment?”
"World-Honored One!

All things are neither joined nor dispersed; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic—namely, the characteristic of signlessness (animitta-dharma). Within these, there is no grasping or rejecting of other dharmas."

For example, just as space neither grasps nor abandons any phenomena because its intrinsic nature is empty, so too are all phenomena: their intrinsic natures are all empty, and there is no grasping or abandoning of other phenomena. How, then, can it be said that the factors of enlightenment, such as the four foundations of mindfulness, can grasp enlightenment?
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.

Because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, there is neither grasping nor abandoning; yet, sentient beings are unable to comprehend the meaning of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena. For their benefit, one employs skillful means to proclaim the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*), which enable the attainment of awakening.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Whatever form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness there may be; whatever sense-base of the eye up to the sense-base of the mind;
whatever sense-object of form up to the sense-object of mental phenomena; whatever element of the eye up to the element of the mind; or whatever element of form..."
Up to the dharma-element; whether it be the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element; whether it be eye-contact up to mind-contact;
whether it be the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition;
whether it be the earth element up to the consciousness element; or whether it be the causal condition up to the sovereign condition.
Whether it be from ignorance up to old age and death; or from the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
or from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature; or from suchness up to the inconceivable realm;
or the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; or the four applications of mindfulness.
Up to and including the eight branches of the noble path; whether they be the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments;
or the three gates of liberation; or the eight liberations up to the ten totalities;
or the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata; or the stage of extreme joy up to the stage of the cloud of dharma; or all [of these].
The gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi; whether it be the five eyes or the six supernormal powers;
whether it be the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;

whether it be the thirty-two marks of a great man or the eighty secondary characteristics; whether it be the quality of non-forgetfulness or the state of constant equanimity; or whether it be all-knowledge.
the knowledge of the paths, the knowledge of all aspects; whether it be the fruit of a stream-enterer up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
whether it be the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; whether it be the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas;
whether it be the severance of the continuity of the habitual tendencies of afflictions; or whether it be the knowledge of all modes—such as these are one.
All phenomena, within the noble Dharma and Vinaya, are neither conjoined nor dispersed;
they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic—namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.

The Tathāgata, for the benefit of all sentient beings, so that they may give rise to correct understanding and enter into the true reality of phenomena, speaks according to worldly convention and not according to the ultimate truth.
Subhūti, you should know that bodhisattva mahāsattvas should train in knowledge and vision regarding all these phenomena.
"Having studied and gained insight, one should, according to reality, thoroughly penetrate that such dharmas are fit for enjoyment, while such dharmas are not fit for enjoyment.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In regard to which dharmas do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having studied and gained insight, thoroughly penetrate according to reality that they are not fit for enjoyment?"
"In what dharmas, having trained in knowledge and vision, should one realize them as they truly are so that they may be utilized?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have trained in knowledge and vision regarding the dharmas of the levels of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, having realized them as they truly are, they should not utilize them."

Having studied the knowledge and vision regarding all phenomena associated with the knowledge of all modes, one penetrates them as they truly are, such that they may be utilized in accordance with all their aspects. Subhūti!
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should train in this profound perfection of wisdom within this noble Dharma and Vinaya.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
Regarding the "noble Dharma and Vinaya" that has been taught: what is meant by the "noble Dharma and Vinaya"?
The Buddha told Subhūti: "Whether they be śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or tathāgatas..."
It is neither conjoined with nor dissociated from greed, hatred, and delusion; it is neither conjoined with nor dissociated from the five fetters conducive to the lower realms;

it is neither conjoined with nor dissociated from the five fetters conducive to the higher realms; it is neither conjoined with nor dissociated from the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
and it is neither conjoined with nor dissociated from the four applications of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path.
The factors of the path are neither conjoined nor dispersed; they are neither conjoined nor dispersed with the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
they are neither conjoined nor dispersed with the three gates of liberation; they are neither conjoined nor dispersed with the eight liberations up to the ten universal bases;
and they are neither conjoined nor dispersed with the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata.
It is neither conjoined with nor separate from the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
it is neither conjoined with nor separate from the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;

it is neither conjoined with nor separate from inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature; and it is neither conjoined with nor separate from suchness up to the inconceivable realm.
It is neither conjoined nor dissociated from the Stage of Utmost Joy up to the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma;

it is neither conjoined nor dissociated from all doors of dhāraṇī and doors of samādhi; it is neither conjoined nor dissociated from the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
[it is neither conjoined nor dissociated] from the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty...
The secondary marks are neither conjoined with nor separated from the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity;
they are neither conjoined with nor separated from omniscience, the knowledge of paths, and the knowledge of all aspects;
they are neither conjoined with nor separated from the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; and they are neither conjoined with nor separated from all bodhisattvas.
The practice of a mahāsattva is neither conjoined with nor dissociated from the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas;

it is neither conjoined with nor dissociated from the permanent severance of the continuity of all afflictions and habitual tendencies; it is neither conjoined with nor dissociated from the knowledge of all modes;
it is neither conjoined with nor dissociated from the realm of the conditioned; it is neither conjoined with nor dissociated from the unconditioned...
"It is a realm that is neither joined nor dispersed. Subhūti!
That is called 'noble,' and this is their noble Dharma-Vinaya; therefore, it is named the Noble Dharma-Vinaya."

Why is this so? Because all these phenomena are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic—namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics—and it is these very phenomena that the noble ones perceive as they truly are.

Subhūti, you should know this: formless phenomena and formless phenomena are neither conjoined nor dispersed; invisible phenomena and invisible phenomena are neither conjoined nor dispersed; non-obstructive phenomena and non-obstructive phenomena are neither conjoined nor dispersed; phenomena of a single characteristic and phenomena of a single characteristic are neither conjoined nor dispersed; and signless phenomena and signless phenomena are neither conjoined nor dispersed.

"Subhūti! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should constantly train in this profound perfection of wisdom—which is formless, invisible, non-obstructive, of a single characteristic, and signless—and having so trained, they do not grasp at the characteristics of any phenomena."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
should Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas not train in the marks of form, up to and including the marks of consciousness?”
Should one not train in the characteristics of the sense-base of the eye up to the sense-base of the mind?
Should one not train in the characteristics of the sense-field of form up to the sense-field of mental phenomena?
Should one not train in the characteristics of the eye-element up to the mind-element?
Should one not train in the characteristics of the form realm up to the characteristics of the dharma realm?
Should one not train in the characteristics of the eye-consciousness realm up to the characteristics of the mind-consciousness realm?
Should one not train in the characteristics of eye-contact, up to and including the characteristics of mind-contact?
Should one not train in the characteristics of all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, up to and including the characteristics of all feelings produced with mind-contact as condition?
Should one not train in the characteristics of the earth element up to the characteristics of the consciousness element?
Should one not train in the characteristics of the causal condition up to the characteristics of the sovereign condition?
Should one not train in the characteristics of ignorance up to the characteristics of old age and death?
Should one not train in the characteristics of the perfection of generosity up to the characteristics of the perfection of wisdom?
Should one not train in the characteristics of inner emptiness up to the characteristics of the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature?
Should one not train in the characteristics of suchness, up to the characteristics of the inconceivable realm?
Should one not train in the characteristics of the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path?
Should one not train in the characteristics of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments?
Should one not train in the characteristics of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path?
Should one not train in the characteristics of the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality?
Should one not train in the characteristics of the gates of liberation: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness?
Should one not train in the characteristics of the stage of pure observation up to the characteristics of the stage of the Tathāgata?
Should one not train in the characteristics of the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the characteristics of the Cloud of Dharma stage?
Should one not train in the characteristics of all dhāraṇī-doors and samādhi-doors?
Should one not train in the characteristics of the five eyes and the six supernormal powers?
Should one not train in the characteristics of the Tathāgata’s ten powers, up to and including the characteristics of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha?
Should one not train in the characteristics of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty minor marks?
Should one not train in the characteristics of the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity?
Should one not train in the characteristics of all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects?
Should one not train in the characteristics of the fruit of stream-entry, up to the characteristics of the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha?
Should one not train in the characteristics of all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas?
Should one not train in the characteristics of the permanent severance of the continuity of the habitual tendencies of afflictions and in the characteristic of the knowledge of all modes?
Should one not train in the characteristics of knowing suffering, abandoning its origin, realizing its cessation, and cultivating the path?
Should one not study the characteristics of the dependent origination of favorable and unfavorable conditions?
Should one not study the characteristics of the noble qualities of all noble ones?
Should one not study the characteristics of the conditioned realm and the unconditioned realm?
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not train in the characteristics of these dharmas, they likewise should not train in the characteristics of conditioned formations.
World-Honored One!”

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is unable to train in the characteristics of all phenomena and the characteristics of all conditioned formations, how can they transcend the stages of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?
If one cannot transcend the stages of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, how can one enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth?
If one cannot enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth, how can one attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna)?
If one cannot attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), how can one turn the sublime wheel of Dharma?

If one cannot turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, how can one establish sentient beings in the true Dharma of the three vehicles and cause them to emerge from the boundless ocean of birth-and-death suffering?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If all dharmas possessed a real mark, then bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should train therein.
Because all dharmas do not possess a real mark, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not train in marks, nor do they train in the dharma of marklessness."

Why is this? Whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, the dharma-realm remains eternally constant; all phenomena possess a single characteristic, which is the so-called "markless. Since such marklessness is neither a positive mark nor an absence of mark, it cannot be learned.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are neither characterized by marks nor devoid of marks, how can a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the perfection of wisdom?”
"Bhagavān! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva cannot cultivate the perfection of wisdom, they should be unable to transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and the stage of the pratyekabuddhas."
If one cannot transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and the stage of the pratyekabuddhas, one should be unable to enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth.
If one cannot enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth, one should be unable to give rise to the bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas.

If one cannot give rise to the bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one should be unable to manifest the bodhisattva’s sublime and wondrous supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
If one cannot manifest the bodhisattva’s sublime and wondrous supernormal powers, one should be unable to purify buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity.
If one cannot purify buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity, one should be unable to realize the knowledge of all modes.
If one cannot realize the knowledge of all modes, one should be unable to turn the sublime wheel of Dharma.

If one cannot turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, then one would be unable to establish sentient beings so that they abide in the fruit of a stream-enterer, or the fruit of a once-returner, or the fruit of a non-returner, or the fruit of an arhat, or in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, or even in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, one would likewise be unable to establish sentient beings so that they might abide in meritorious actions consisting of generosity, or meritorious actions consisting of ethical discipline, or meritorious actions consisting of cultivation, thereby attaining the wealth, happiness, and sovereignty of humans and devas.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.

All phenomena are neither characterized by marks nor devoid of marks. If a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that all phenomena—whether they possess marks or are markless—are of one single mark, namely, marklessness, then cultivating this marklessness is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates this signlessness, he is cultivating the perfection of wisdom?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the relinquishment of all phenomena, this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the relinquishment of all phenomena; how is this the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates the relinquishment of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.”
To cultivate the removal of the sense base of the eye up to the sense base of the mind is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the removal of the sense base of form up to the sense base of phenomena is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the removal of the eye constituent up to the mental constituent is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the removal of the sphere of form up to the sphere of phenomena is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the removal of the eye-consciousness sphere up to the mind-consciousness sphere is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the removal of eye-contact up to mind-contact is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.

To cultivate the removal of all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including all feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the removal of the earth element, up to and including the consciousness element, is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the removal of the causal condition, up to and including the dominant condition, is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the elimination of ignorance up to old age and death is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the elimination of the meditation on impurity is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the elimination of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.

To cultivate the mental elimination of the recollection of the Buddha, the recollection of the Dharma, the recollection of the Saṅgha, the recollection of ethical discipline, the recollection of relinquishment, the recollection of the devas, the recollection of tranquility, and the recollection of mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;

to cultivate the mental elimination of the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering, the perception of non-self, the perception of emptiness, the perception of origination, the perception of cause, the perception of production, the perception of condition, the perception of cessation, the perception of peace, the perception of excellence, the perception of renunciation, the perception of the path, the perception of suchness, the perception of proceeding, and the perception of emergence is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;

to cultivate the mental elimination of the perception of a self, the perception of a sentient being, up to the perception of a knower and the perception of a viewer is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the elimination of the notion of permanence, the notion of pleasure, the notion of self, and the notion of purity is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the elimination of the notion of dependent origination is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the elimination of the notion of the noble truths is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the elimination of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the elimination of the three gates of liberation is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the elimination of the eight liberations up to the ten totalities is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.

To cultivate the elimination of the samādhi with applied thought and sustained thought, the samādhi without applied thought and with only sustained thought, and the samādhi without applied thought and without sustained thought, is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the elimination of the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;

to cultivate the elimination of the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, the knowledge of cessation, the knowledge of the path, the knowledge of phenomena, the subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, and the knowledge as it is, is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the removal of [the conceptualization of] the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the removal of inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the removal of suchness up to the inconceivable realm is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the elimination of the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the elimination of the stage of extreme joy up to the stage of the cloud of dharma is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the elimination of all doors of dhāraṇī and doors of samādhi is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the elimination of the five eyes and the six supernormal powers is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the elimination of the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the elimination of the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor characteristics is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the removal of the dharma of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the removal of all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the removal of the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the elimination of all bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the elimination of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the elimination of the knowledge of all modes is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
"To cultivate the elimination and severance of the continuity of all habitual tendencies of the afflictions is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates the elimination of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness; how is this the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom?"

“In this way, up to the point of cultivating the elimination and the permanent severance of the continuity of all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the afflictions—is this the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, if they conceive of form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, they are not eliminating form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness; they are not cultivating the perfection of wisdom.”

In this way, up to and including: if one conceives of the permanent severance of the continuity of all habitual tendencies of the afflictions as being the act of severing them, rather than the non-conceptual removal of that continuity, one is not practicing the perfection of wisdom.

However, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not conceive of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; this relinquishing of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

In this way, up to and including not even conceiving the thought that there is a permanent severance of the continuity of all habitual tendencies of affliction—this very removal of the notion of a permanent severance of the continuity of all habitual tendencies of affliction is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Why is this? It is because one who possesses conceptual perception is unable to cultivate the perfection of wisdom. Therefore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the elimination of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); likewise, up to and including the practice of eliminating the continuous succession of all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Those who dwell with the perception of existence are unable to cultivate the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
they are also unable to cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, nor are they able to..."
They cannot abide in inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;
nor can they abide in suchness up to the inconceivable realm; nor can they abide in the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
nor can they cultivate the liberations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; nor can they cultivate the four supreme [bases of psychic power].
They are likewise unable to cultivate the dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments;
they are unable to cultivate the eight liberations up to the ten totalities; they are unable to cultivate the stages from the Ground of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma;
they are unable to cultivate any of the doors of dhāraṇī or the doors of samādhi; and they are unable to cultivate the five eyes.
...the six supernormal powers, nor can they cultivate the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
nor can they cultivate the quality of non-forgetfulness or the nature of constant equanimity;
nor can they cultivate all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, or the knowledge of all aspects; nor can they cultivate any of the bodhi-qualities.
They cannot practice the conduct of a bodhisattva mahāsattva; they cannot cultivate the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas;
they cannot cultivate the knowledge of all modes; nor can they cultivate the permanent severance of the continuity of all afflictions and habitual tendencies.

Why is this? Those who dwell in the perception of existence will inevitably grasp at a self and what belongs to a self (*ātman* and *ātmīya*). Due to this grasping, they become attached to the two extremes; because they are attached to the two extremes, they are certainly unable to be liberated from birth and death. For them, there is no path and no nirvāṇa. How, then, could they cultivate the six *pāramitās* as they truly are, up to and including the permanent severance of the continuity of all afflictions and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*)?
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What is existence? What is non-existence?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Duality is existence; non-duality is non-existence.
Subhūti asked again:
“What are these two? What is non-duality?
The World-Honored One replied:

"The perception of form up to the perception of consciousness constitutes duality; the emptiness of the perception of form up to the emptiness of the perception of consciousness constitutes non-duality.

The perception of the eye-base up to the perception of the mind-base constitutes duality; the emptiness of the perception of the eye-base up to the emptiness of the perception of the mind-base constitutes non-duality.

The perception of the form-base up to the perception of the phenomena-base constitutes duality; the emptiness of the perception of the form-base up to the emptiness of the perception of the phenomena-base constitutes non-duality."

The perception of the eye-element up to the perception of the mind-element constitutes duality; the emptiness of the perception of the eye-element up to the emptiness of the perception of the mind-element constitutes non-duality.

The perception of the form-element up to the perception of the phenomena-element constitutes duality; the emptiness of the perception of the form-element up to the emptiness of the perception of the phenomena-element constitutes non-duality.

The perception of the eye-consciousness-element up to the perception of the mind-consciousness-element constitutes duality; the emptiness of the perception of the eye-consciousness-element up to the emptiness of the perception of the mind-consciousness-element constitutes non-duality.

The perception of eye-contact up to the perception of mind-contact constitutes duality; the emptiness of the perception of eye-contact up to the emptiness of the perception of mind-contact constitutes non-duality.

The perceptions of all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition up to the perceptions of all feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition constitute duality; the emptiness of the perceptions of all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition up to the emptiness of the perceptions of all feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition constitutes non-duality.

The perception of the earth element up to the perception of the consciousness element constitutes duality; the emptiness of the perception of the earth element up to the emptiness of the perception of the consciousness element constitutes non-duality.

The perception of causes and conditions up to the perception of the dominant condition constitutes duality; the emptiness of the perception of causes and conditions up to the emptiness of the perception of the dominant condition constitutes non-duality.

The perception of ignorance up to the perception of old age and death constitutes duality; the emptiness of the perception of ignorance up to the emptiness of the perception of old age and death constitutes non-duality.

The perception of the perfection of generosity up to the perception of the perfection of wisdom constitutes duality; the emptiness of the perception of the perfection of generosity up to the emptiness of the perception of the perfection of wisdom constitutes non-duality.

The perception of internal emptiness up to the perception of the emptiness of the nature of non-existence constitute duality; the emptiness of the perception of internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the perception of the nature of non-existence constitutes non-duality.

The perception of suchness up to the perception of the inconceivable realm constitute duality; the emptiness of the perception of suchness up to the emptiness of the perception of the inconceivable realm constitutes non-duality.

The perception of the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path constitute duality; the emptiness of the perception of the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path constitutes non-duality.

The perception of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the perception of the eightfold noble path constitutes duality; the emptiness of the perception of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the emptiness of the perception of the eightfold noble path constitutes non-duality.

The perception of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments constitutes duality; the emptiness of the perception of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments constitutes non-duality.

The perception of the eight liberations up to the perception of the ten totalities constitutes duality; the emptiness of the perception of the eight liberations up to the emptiness of the perception of the ten totalities constitutes non-duality.

The perception of the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—is duality; the emptiness of the perception of the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—is non-duality.

The perception of the stage of pure observation up to the perception of the stage of a Tathāgata is duality; the emptiness of the perception of the stage of pure observation up to the emptiness of the perception of the stage of a Tathāgata is non-duality.

The perception of the stage of extreme joy up to the perception of the stage of the cloud of dharma is duality; the emptiness of the perception of the stage of extreme joy up to the emptiness of the perception of the stage of the cloud of dharma is non-duality.

To conceive of the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi as two is dualistic; to conceive of the emptiness of the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi as non-dual is non-dualistic.
To conceive of the five eyes and the six supernormal powers as two is dualistic; to conceive of the emptiness of the five eyes and the six supernormal powers as non-dual is non-dualistic.

To conceive of the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as two is dualistic; to conceive of the emptiness of the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the emptiness of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as non-dual is non-dualistic.

The perception of the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks as two is duality; the emptiness of the perception of the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks is non-duality.

The perception of the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity as two is duality; the emptiness of the perception of the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity is non-duality.

The perception of all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) as two is duality; the emptiness of the perception of all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects is non-duality.

The notion of the fruit of stream-entry up to the notion of pratyekabuddha-enlightenment constitutes duality; the emptiness of the notion of the fruit of stream-entry up to the emptiness of the notion of pratyekabuddha-enlightenment is non-duality.

The notion of all bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices and the notion of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas constitute duality; the emptiness of the notion of all bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices and the emptiness of the notion of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is non-duality.

The notion of the conditioned realm and the notion of the unconditioned realm constitute duality; the emptiness of the notion of the conditioned realm and the emptiness of the notion of the unconditioned realm is non-duality.

"Subhūti! To the extent that all perceptions are dualistic, to the extent that all duality is existence, and to the extent that all existence involves birth and death—those who possess birth and death cannot be liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair."

"Subhūti! Those for whom all perceptions are empty are non-dual; those who are non-dual are not-existent; those who are not-existent have no birth-and-death; and those who have no birth-and-death are able to be liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair."

"Subhūti! By this cause and condition, you should know that for all those who possess the perception of duality, there is certainly no perfection of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom; they have neither attainment nor clear realization, and even the 'patience in accordance with truth' does not exist for them, let alone the ability to fully know form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness!"
In this way, how much less could they possibly know all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna)!

They are not even able to cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; how much less could they attain the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha!
"How much less could they attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), or forever sever the continuity of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of all afflictions!
Chapter 73: Gradual Progression, Part Two, Section One. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."

For one who dwells in the state of having perceptions, if there is no patient acceptance (kṣānti), there can likewise be no realization through the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) to attain the fruit; how then could one who dwells in the state of non-perception possess patient acceptance? Whether on the stage of pure observation (śuddhādhyāśaya-bhūmi) or even up to the stage of a Tathāgata, if one cultivates the noble path, is it by virtue of cultivating that noble path that one abandons all afflictions?

Because they are obscured and hindered by these afflictions, they are unable to even realize the stages associated with the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, let alone enter the Bodhisattva’s state of right determination and transcendence of birth!
If one cannot enter the bodhisattva’s state of correct determination and transcendence of birth, how could one possibly realize the knowledge of all modes?
If one cannot realize the knowledge of all modes, how could one ever permanently sever the continuity of the habitual tendencies of all afflictions?

"Bhagavān! If all dharmas are entirely non-existent, neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure—if such dharmas are fundamentally unarisen, how can one realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna)?"
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.

Those who dwell in non-conceptualization (asaṃjñin) likewise lack the patient acceptance that accords with truth (anulomikī kṣānti), and so forth, up to lacking the permanent severance of the continuity of the habitual tendencies of afflictions (kleśavāsanā).

If all phenomena are entirely non-existent—neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure—then since such phenomena do not arise at all, how could one possibly realize the wisdom of all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna)?
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, do they have the perception of existence, or do they have the perception of non-existence?”
Do you have the notion of form, or the notions of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?
Likewise, do you have the notion of the knowledge of all-knowledge?
Do you have the notion of the permanent severance of the continuity of the habitual tendencies of all afflictions?
Is there the perception of form, and is there the perception of the abandonment of form?
Is there the perception of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, and is there the perception of the abandonment of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness?
Is there the perception of the sense-base of the eye, up to the sense-base of the mind; and is there the perception of the cessation of the sense-base of the eye, up to the sense-base of the mind?

Is there the perception of the sense-base of form, up to the sense-base of mental phenomena; and is there the perception of the cessation of the sense-base of form, up to the sense-base of mental phenomena?
Is there the perception of the eye-element up to the mind-element, and is there the perception of the cessation of the eye-element up to the mind-element?
Is there the perception of the form-element up to the mental-object-element, and is there the perception of the cessation of the form-element up to the mental-object-element?
Is there the notion of the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element? Is there the notion of the cessation of the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element?
Is there the notion of eye-contact up to mind-contact? Is there the notion of the cessation of eye-contact up to mind-contact?

Regarding the perceptions arising from feelings conditioned by eye-contact, up to and including the perceptions arising from feelings conditioned by mind-contact: is there a perception of the cessation of those feelings arising from eye-contact, up to and including those feelings arising from mind-contact?
Is there the perception of the earth element up to the consciousness element? Is there the perception of the cessation of the earth element up to the consciousness element?
Is there the perception of the causal condition up to the dominant condition? Is there the perception of the cessation of the causal condition up to the dominant condition?
Is there a perception of greed, hatred, and delusion? Is there a perception of the abandonment of greed, hatred, and delusion?

Is there a perception of ignorance up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair? Is there a perception of the abandonment of ignorance up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair?
Is there the perception of the noble truth of suffering, and is there the perception of the abandonment of the noble truth of suffering?
Is there the perception of the noble truth of the origin of suffering, and is there the perception of the abandonment of the noble truth of the origin of suffering?
When there is the perception of the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, is there also the perception of the abandonment of the noble truth of the cessation of suffering?

When there is the perception of the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering, is there also the perception of the realization of the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering?
In this way, up to the point: is there even the notion of "the wisdom of all-knowledge," or the notion of "realizing the wisdom of all-knowledge"?

Is there the notion of "the continuity of the habitual tendencies of all afflictions that are to be abandoned," or the notion of "permanently severing the continuity of the habitual tendencies of all afflictions"?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they have neither any perception of all phenomena nor any non-perception.”

If there is neither perception nor non-perception, one should know that this is precisely the bodhisattva’s conformative patience (*ānulomikī kṣānti*), as well as the cultivation of the path, the attainment of the fruit, and clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas take non-existence as the noble path and take non-existence as clear realization, penetrating that all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature."
"For this reason and by these causes and conditions, you should know that all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, how is it that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, having attained perfect awakening to the fact that all phenomena have non-existence as their nature, is called a 'Buddha,' and has attained sovereign mastery over all phenomena and all objective spheres?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
All phenomena have the absence of intrinsic nature as their own nature.

When I was originally training in the bodhisattva path, I practiced the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom without error. By means of this, I became detached from desires and unwholesome states; with directed thought and evaluation, born of seclusion, joy and happiness, I entered and dwelt in the first dhyāna. In this manner, up to the point where pleasure and pain were abandoned, and previous joy and sorrow had vanished, I entered and dwelt in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant, characterized by equanimity and pure mindfulness.

At that time, although I skillfully grasped the signs of the various dhyānas and their factors, I harbored no attachment; I did not give rise to craving for the various dhyānas and their factors, nor did I apprehend any [intrinsic reality] within the various dhyānas and their factors.
At that time, regarding the four dhyānas, my mental engagement was pure and free from conceptual differentiation.

Although at that time I was thoroughly proficient in the various dhyānas and their factors (*dhyānāṅga*), I did not experience the karmic fruition derived from them. Rather, relying upon dhyāna, I brought forth the supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) of psychic power, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, and the divine eye. Although I skillfully grasped the signs of these five supernormal powers, I was without attachment or relish for them; regarding the objects of these powers, I perceived nothing at all, and dwelling as if in emptiness, I made no conceptual distinctions.

At that time, I contemplated all phenomena as being perfectly equal, having non-existence as their very nature. Through the wisdom (prajñā) associated with a single moment, I realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; that is to say, I knew, in accordance with reality, that this is the Noble Truth of Suffering, this is the Noble Truth of the Origin, this is the Noble Truth of Cessation, and this is the Noble Truth of the Path—all of which share one and the same characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (animitta), and such signlessness is itself nothing at all.

By means of this, he accomplishes the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity, as well as the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha and other immeasurable, innumerable, inconceivable, and subtle merits. With the sublime wisdom of a Buddha, he establishes sentient beings into the distinctions of the three categories—namely, the category of those fixed in the right nature, the category of those fixed in the wrong nature, and the category of the undetermined—and having thus established these three categories, he skillfully guides them according to their needs, causing them to obtain supreme benefit and peace.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"How does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, within the naturelessness of all phenomena, give rise to the four dhyānas and develop the five supernormal powers, realize great bodhi, possess all meritorious qualities, and establish the three groups of sentient beings in benefit and happiness?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If those various desires, evil, and unwholesome dharmas possessed even the slightest intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) or if they had another nature as their intrinsic nature, then when I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, I would not have attained the realization that all desires, evils, and unwholesome dharmas take non-nature as their intrinsic nature, and thereby departed from desire and evil to enter the first dhyāna, up to being able to enter and fully abide in the fourth dhyāna. Because all desires, evils, and unwholesome dharmas lack both intrinsic nature and other-nature, and take only non-nature as their intrinsic nature, when I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, I realized that desires, evils, and unwholesome dharmas all take non-nature as their intrinsic nature; having done so, I departed from desire and evil to enter the first dhyāna, up to being able to enter the fourth dhyāna."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the five supernormal powers possessed even the slightest intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) or extrinsic nature (*parabhāva*) as their essence, then when I was formerly practicing the bodhisattva path, I would not have attained the realization that all supernormal powers have non-existence as their essence, nor would I have manifested various sovereign supernormal powers with unimpeded and wondrous application across all spheres of experience."
