Because all supernatural powers (abhijñā) are entirely devoid of self-nature and other-nature, having non-nature as their very nature; when I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, having realized that all supernatural powers have non-nature as their nature, I gave rise to various sovereign supernatural powers, which function with wondrous and unimpeded efficacy within all realms of experience.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of a Buddha possessed even the slightest intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) or extrinsic nature as its essence, then when I was formerly practicing the bodhisattva path, I would not have attained unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and all its qualities after realizing that the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas and all those merits have non-existence as their essence. Yet, having realized this, I did attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, complete with all its qualities."

Because the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and all its merits lack both intrinsic nature and extrinsic nature, and because their very nature is the absence of nature, when I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, I thoroughly realized that unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment has the absence of nature as its nature; having thus attained unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, I am endowed with all merits.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If sentient beings possessed even a slight intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), or if they possessed another nature as their intrinsic nature, then after I had attained Buddhahood, I would not have realized that all sentient beings take the absence of nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) as their intrinsic nature, nor would I have established the distinctions among the three groups of sentient beings (*triniṣṭha-pudgala*) and guided them through appropriate skillful means to enable them to obtain supreme benefit and happiness."

Because all sentient beings lack both intrinsic nature and extrinsic nature, and because they have the absence of nature as their very nature, once I have attained Buddhahood and realized that all sentient beings have the absence of nature as their nature, I shall establish the distinctions among the three groups of sentient beings and guide them through appropriate skillful means, causing them to obtain supreme benefit and peace.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 465. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Two: The Chapter on Gradual Progression, Number Seventy-three, Part Two. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, within the naturelessness of all phenomena, gives rise to the four dhyānas and develops the five supernormal powers, realizes unexcelled perfect enlightenment, possesses all merits, establishes sentient beings in the three categories of their differentiation, and causes them to obtain beneficial and blissful matters—how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has first resolved on enlightenment perform gradual karma, practice gradual training, and carry out gradual conduct within the naturelessness of all phenomena, so as to realize unexcelled perfect enlightenment and perform deeds for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas first produce the thought of enlightenment, they hear it either from a Buddha, or from a multitude of holy ones—Buddhas, bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, arhats, non-returners, once-returners, and stream-enterers—who say: 'One who has realized that all phenomena have non-existence as their nature (abhāva-svabhāva) to the ultimate degree of perfection is called a Buddha; one who gradually realizes that all phenomena have non-existence as their nature is called a bodhisattva; even down to a stream-enterer who deeply believes that all phenomena have non-existence as their nature is called a virtuous person (satpuruṣa). Therefore, among all phenomena and all sentient beings, there is not one that does not have non-existence as its nature. Neither phenomena nor sentient beings possess a self-nature (svabhāva) that can be apprehended, even as small as the tip of a hair.'"
“Having heard this, that bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects:

‘If all phenomena and all sentient beings have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, it is because of realizing this that one is called a Buddha; and even those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry are called noble persons because they have deep faith in this.’”

Whether I shall realize unsurpassed perfect enlightenment or not, since all phenomena and sentient beings always have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, I must certainly set out for unsurpassed perfect enlightenment; and having realized enlightenment, if there are sentient beings who act with conceptualization, I shall through skillful means establish them so that they abide in non-conceptualization.

Having formed this thought, that bodhisattva mahāsattva seeks to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of leading all sentient beings to nirvāṇa; thus, they perform gradual deeds, cultivate gradual training, and practice gradual conduct.

Just as the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of past ages, seeking to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, first studied the gradual stages of karma, training, and practice, thereby realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva is also like this: first, they should practice and study the perfection of generosity; next, they should practice and study the perfection of ethical discipline; next, they should practice and study the perfection of patience; next, they should practice and study the perfection of diligence; next, they should practice and study the perfection of meditative concentration; and finally, they should practice and study the perfection of wisdom.

“Subhūti, you should know that when these bodhisattva mahāsattvas first resolve their minds on awakening and practice the perfection of generosity, they should personally practice giving, encourage others to practice giving, correctly proclaim the merits of giving, and joyfully praise those who practice giving.”

By virtue of these causes and conditions, they attain great wealth and status, and constantly practice generosity, free from the mind of stinginess. They bestow upon sentient beings, according to their needs, all manner of requisites: food and drink, clothing, bedding, necklaces, incense and flowers, wealth and jewels, lamps, vehicles, dwellings, and other articles of utility.
By means of giving, this bodhisattva mahāsattva upholds the aggregate of ethical discipline and is born among gods and humans, attaining great nobility;
by means of giving and ethical discipline, he further attains the aggregate of concentration;
and by means of giving, ethical discipline, and concentration, he further attains the aggregate of wisdom.
By means of generosity, ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom, one further attains the aggregate of liberation;
by means of generosity, ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, and liberation, one further attains the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation.

Through the perfection of these—from generosity up to the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation—one transcends the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and enters the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth.
Having entered the Bodhisattva’s state of correct determination free from birth, they bring sentient beings to maturity and purify Buddha-fields.

Having performed these deeds, they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and turn the sublime wheel of Dharma; by means of the three vehicles, they establish and deliver all classes of sentient beings, causing them to transcend birth and death and realize nirvana.

"Subhūti! Because of this giving, although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are thus able to perform gradual deeds, cultivate gradual training, and practice gradual conduct, they do not apprehend anything at all in any of these."
Why is this? Because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature. Furthermore, Subhūti!

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline from the first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment, they should personally practice pure ethical discipline, encourage others to practice pure ethical discipline, correctly proclaim the merits of pure ethical discipline, and joyfully praise those who practice pure ethical discipline.

By means of these causes and conditions, their aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*) becomes purified; they are born among gods and humans and attain great nobility, bestowing upon the poor whatever wealth and necessities they require.

Having practiced such giving, they abide securely in the aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of concentration (*samādhiskandha*), the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñāskandha*), the aggregate of liberation (*vimuktiskandha*), and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśanaskandha*).

By virtue of the purification of the aggregates of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, they transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and freedom from birth.
Having entered the Bodhisattva’s state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), they bring sentient beings to maturity and purify Buddha-fields.

Having performed these deeds, they realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and turn the sublime wheel of Dharma; by means of the three vehicles, they establish and deliver all classes of sentient beings, causing them to transcend birth and death and realize nirvāṇa.

"Subhūti! Because of their pure ethical discipline, although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to perform gradual deeds in this way, cultivate gradual training, and practice gradual conduct, they do not apprehend anything at all."
Why is this? Because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature. Furthermore, Subhūti!

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of patience from the first generation of the mind of awakening, they should personally practice patience, encourage others to practice patience, correctly proclaim the merits of patience, and joyfully praise those who practice patience.
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices patience, he is able to give material requisites to all sentient beings so that they are fully satisfied.

Having practiced giving, he abides securely in the aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation.

By virtue of the purification of the aggregates of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, they transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and freedom from birth.
Having entered the Bodhisattva’s state of right determination free from birth, they bring sentient beings to maturity and purify Buddha-fields.

Having performed these deeds, they realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment and turn the sublime wheel of Dharma; by means of the three vehicles, they establish and deliver all classes of sentient beings, causing them to transcend birth and death and realize nirvana.

"Subhūti! Because of their patience, although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to perform gradual deeds in this way, cultivate gradual training, and practice gradual conduct, they do not apprehend anything at all in any of these."
Why is this? Because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature. Furthermore, Subhūti!

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of diligence from the first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment, they should personally exert diligent effort toward all wholesome dharmas, encourage others to exert diligent effort toward all wholesome dharmas, correctly proclaim the merits of diligence, and joyfully praise those who practice diligence.
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices diligence, he is able to provide material requisites to all sentient beings so that they are fully satisfied.

Having practiced giving, he dwells securely in the aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation.

By virtue of the purification of the aggregates of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, they transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth.
Having entered the Bodhisattva’s state of right determination and freedom from birth, they bring sentient beings to maturity and purify Buddha-fields.

Having performed these deeds, they realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment and turn the sublime wheel of Dharma. By means of the three vehicles, they establish and deliver all classes of sentient beings, causing them to transcend birth and death and realize nirvāṇa.

"Subhūti! Because of their diligence, although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are thus able to perform gradual deeds, cultivate gradual training, and practice gradual conduct, they do not apprehend anything at all in any of these."
Why is this? Because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature. Furthermore, Subhūti!

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of meditative concentration from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, they should personally enter the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; they should also encourage others to enter the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; they should unerringly proclaim the merits of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; and they should joyfully praise those who enter the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments.
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he is able to provide material requisites to all sentient beings so that they are fully satisfied.

Having practiced giving, he abides in the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*), the aggregate of concentration (*samādhiskandha*), the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñāskandha*), the aggregate of liberation (*vimuktiskandha*), and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśanaskandha*).

By virtue of the purification of the aggregates of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, they transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and freedom from birth.
Having entered the Bodhisattva’s state of right determination and freedom from birth, they bring sentient beings to maturity and purify Buddha-fields.

Having performed these deeds, they realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment and turn the sublime wheel of Dharma. By means of the three vehicles, they establish and deliver all classes of sentient beings, causing them to transcend birth and death and realize nirvana.

"Subhūti! Because of their meditative concentration, although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to perform gradual deeds in this way, cultivate gradual training, and practice gradual conduct, they do not apprehend anything at all."
Why is this? Because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature. Furthermore, Subhūti!

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva first resolves on awakening and practices the perfection of wisdom, they should, by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method, personally practice the six perfections, encourage others to practice the six perfections, correctly proclaim the merits of the six perfections, and joyfully praise those who practice the six perfections.

By means of skillful means regarding the six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva transcends the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and enters the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and freedom from birth.
Having entered the Bodhisattva’s state of right determination and freedom from birth, they bring sentient beings to maturity and purify Buddha-fields.

Having performed these deeds, they realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment and turn the sublime wheel of Dharma; by means of the three vehicles, they establish and deliver all classes of sentient beings, causing them to transcend birth and death and realize nirvana.

"Subhūti! Because of their prajñā, although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to perform gradual deeds in this way, cultivate gradual training, and practice gradual conduct, they do not apprehend anything at all."
Why is this? Because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature. "Subhūti!..."

This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has first resolved upon awakening, relying on the training in the six perfections, performs gradual deeds, cultivates gradual training, and practices gradual conduct, thereby bringing about the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas perform gradual karma, cultivate gradual training, and practice gradual conduct, they should, from the first production of the thought of awakening, employ mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*). They should first train in the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*), next train in the recollection of the Dharma (*dharmānusmṛti*), next train in the recollection of the Saṅgha (*saṅghānusmṛti*), next train in the recollection of ethical discipline (*śīlānusmṛti*), next train in the recollection of relinquishment (*tyāgānusmṛti*), and finally train in the recollection of the devas (*devatānusmṛti*). They should understand that all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature."
“Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the recollection of the Buddha?

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the recollection of the Buddha, they should not contemplate the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha by means of form; nor should they contemplate the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha by means of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.”

Why is this? Because from form (*rūpa*) up to consciousness (*vijñāna*), all lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). If a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, it cannot be recollected nor can it be conceptualized. Why is that?
If there is no recollection and no mental engagement, this is the recollection of the Buddha.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice and study the recollection of the Buddha, they should not engage in mental engagement with the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by means of the thirty-two marks of a great man; nor should they engage in mental engagement with the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by means of his body of golden hue, his constant fathom-wide radiance, or his eighty secondary signs."

Why is this? Such marks and embellishments, as well as the golden-hued body, are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature; if a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, it cannot be recollected nor can it be contemplated.
Why is this? If there is no recollection and no mental engagement, this is the recollection of the Buddha. Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the recollection of the Buddha, they should not contemplate the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha by means of the aggregate of ethical discipline; nor should they contemplate the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha by means of the aggregates of concentration, wisdom, liberation, or the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Why is this? Because these aggregates are all devoid of intrinsic nature; if a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, it cannot be recollected and cannot be contemplated. Why is that?
If there is no recollection and no mental engagement, this is the recollection of the Buddha.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the training in the recollection of the Buddha, they should not engage in mental engagement with the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha by means of the five eyes or the six supernormal powers; nor should they engage in mental engagement with the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha by means of the ten powers of a Buddha, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha."
Why is this? Because all such phenomena lack intrinsic nature; if a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, it cannot be recollected and cannot be contemplated. Why is that?
If there is no recollection and no mental engagement, this is the recollection of the Buddha.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the training in the recollection of the Buddha, they should not contemplate the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha by means of the quality of non-forgetfulness or the nature of constant equanimity; nor should they contemplate the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha by means of all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, the knowledge of all aspects, or any other immeasurable and boundless buddha-dharmas."
Why is this? Because all such phenomena lack intrinsic nature; if a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, it cannot be recollected nor can it be contemplated. Why is that?
If there is no recollection and no mental engagement, this is the recollection of the Buddha.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice and train in the recollection of the Buddha, they should not contemplate the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha by means of dharmas that have causal conditions; they should not contemplate the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha by means of dharmas that arise through dependent origination.

Why is this? Because both conditions (*pratyaya*) and dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). If a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, it cannot be recollected and cannot be conceptualized. Why is that?
If there is no recollection and no mental engagement, this is the recollection of the Buddha. "Subhūti!
When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should train in the recollection of the Buddha in this manner."
If one trains in this way in the recollection of the Buddha, this constitutes performing gradual karma, practicing gradual training, and engaging in gradual conduct.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to perform gradual karma, practice gradual training, and engage in gradual conduct in this manner, they will then be able to fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path. Furthermore, it...
They are able to fulfill the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
they are also able to fulfill the eight liberations up to the ten totalities; they are also able to fulfill the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
and they are also able to fulfill inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature.
Emptiness can also fulfill everything from suchness up to the inconceivable realm;
it can also fulfill the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; it can also fulfill the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
it can also fulfill all the bodhisattva stages, and it can also fulfill all dhāraṇīs.
They can also fulfill the dhāraṇī-doors and the samādhi-doors; they can also fulfill the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
they can also fulfill the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they can also fulfill the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity; and they can also fulfill all-knowledge and the path.
The knowledge of characteristics and the knowledge of all characteristics—by means of these, one realizes the knowledge of all-knowledge. Subhūti!

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva employs the skillful means of taking the absence of intrinsic nature as the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, they awaken to the fact that all phenomena are devoid of self-nature; therein, there is neither perception nor non-perception.

"Subhūti! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should train in the recollection of the Buddha in this way: within the nature of the non-nature of all phenomena, even a Buddha cannot be apprehended, much less the recollection of the Buddha!"

“Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the recollection of the Dharma? When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the recollection of the Dharma, they should not contemplate wholesome dharmas or unwholesome dharmas;

they should not contemplate determinate dharmas or indeterminate dharmas; they should not contemplate mundane dharmas or supramundane dharmas; they should not contemplate dharmas with relishable flavor or dharmas without relishable flavor; they should not contemplate dharmas involving contention or dharmas free from contention; they should not contemplate noble dharmas or non-noble dharmas; they should not contemplate contaminated dharmas or uncontaminated dharmas; they should not contemplate dharmas that fall within the three realms or dharmas that do not fall within the three realms; and they should not contemplate dharmas of the conditioned realm or dharmas of the unconditioned realm.”
Why is this? Because all such phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); if a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, it cannot be recollected nor can it be contemplated. Why is that?
If there is no recollection and no mental engagement, this is the recollection of the Dharma. Subhūti!
When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should train in the recollection of the Dharma in this way.
If one trains in this way by recollecting the Dharma, this constitutes performing gradual deeds, practicing gradual training, and engaging in gradual conduct.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to perform gradual deeds, practice gradual training, and engage in gradual conduct in this manner, they will be able to fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness, and so on extensively up to all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), thereby realizing the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).

"Subhūti! By means of the power of skillful means—taking the absence of intrinsic nature in all phenomena as their very nature—this bodhisattva mahāsattva realizes that all phenomena are devoid of self-nature; therein, there is neither perception nor even non-perception."

"Subhūti! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should train in the recollection of phenomena (dharmānusmṛti) in this way: within the nature of the non-nature of all phenomena, even phenomena themselves cannot be apprehended, let alone the recollection of phenomena!"
“Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the recollection of the Saṃgha?
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the recollection of the Saṃgha, they should form this thought:”

“The community of the Buddha’s disciples is endowed with the aggregate of pure ethical discipline, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation. These four pairs and eight types of individuals (*pudgala*) are all manifested by the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and take the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) as their own-being; for this reason, they should not be conceptualized.”
Why is this? Such virtuous persons are all devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); if a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, it cannot be recollected nor can it be contemplated. Why is that?
"If there is no recollection and no mental engagement, this is the recollection of the Saṅgha. Subhūti!
When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should train in the recollection of the Saṅgha in this manner.
If one trains in this manner in the recollection of the Saṃgha, this constitutes performing gradual karma, practicing gradual training, and engaging in gradual conduct.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to perform gradual karma, practice gradual training, and engage in gradual conduct in this way, they will then be able to fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness, and so on extensively up to the knowledge of all aspects, thereby realizing the knowledge of all modes.

"Subhūti! By the power of skillful means, through which all phenomena have non-existence as their very nature, this bodhisattva mahāsattva realizes that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature; therein, there is neither conceptualization nor even the absence of conceptualization."

"Subhūti! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should train in the recollection of the Saṃgha in this way: within the nature of the non-nature of all phenomena, even the Saṃgha cannot be apprehended, let alone the recollection of the Saṃgha!"
“Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the recollection of ethical discipline (*śīlānusmṛti*)?

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the recollection of ethical discipline, from the first generation of the mind of awakening, they should recollect the noble ethical discipline as being without deficiency, without flaw, without blemish, without impurity, and without attachment; as being worthy of offerings, praised by the wise, excellently undertaken, excellently perfected, and conforming to supreme meditative concentration. They should contemplate that this ethical discipline has non-substantiality as its nature; for this reason, it should not be conceptually constructed.”
Why is this? Such noble precepts have no intrinsic nature at all; if a dharma lacks intrinsic nature, it cannot be recollected nor can it be contemplated. Why is that?
If there is no recollection and no mental engagement, this is the recollection of ethical discipline (*śīlānusmṛti*). Subhūti!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they should train in the recollection of ethical discipline in this way.
If one practices and trains in this way by recollecting the precepts, this constitutes performing gradual karma, cultivating gradual training, and practicing gradual conduct.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to perform gradual karma, cultivate gradual training, and practice gradual conduct in this manner, they will then be able to fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness, and so on, up to the knowledge of all aspects; through this, they realize the wisdom of all modes of knowing.

"Subhūti! By means of the skillful power that takes the absence of intrinsic nature as the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, this bodhisattva mahāsattva awakens to the fact that all phenomena are devoid of self-nature; therein, there is neither perception nor even non-perception."

"Subhūti! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should train in the recollection of ethical discipline (*śīlānusmṛti*) in this way: within the nature of the lack of intrinsic nature of all phenomena, even ethical discipline cannot be apprehended, let alone the recollection of ethical discipline!"
“Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the recollection of relinquishment?

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the recollection of relinquishment, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment they should constantly recollect relinquishment—whether recollecting their own relinquishment, the relinquishment of others, the relinquishing of material wealth, or the relinquishing of the Dharma—and throughout the state of giving, they never give rise to such thoughts as:”
"I am able to give or not to give.
Even when giving away all his limbs and members, he does not give rise to the thought:
"I am able to give or not to give."
Nor does he contemplate the merit of giving or the fruit of giving—whether that which is relinquished or that which is bestowed. Why is this?
Because all such phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); if a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, it cannot be recollected and cannot be contemplated.
Why is this? If there is no mindfulness and no mental engagement, this constitutes the recollection of relinquishment. Subhūti!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should train in this way in the recollection of equanimity (*upekṣā-anusmṛti*).
If they train in this way in the recollection of equanimity, this constitutes performing gradual karma, cultivating gradual training, and practicing gradual conduct.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to perform gradual karma, cultivate gradual training, and practice gradual conduct in this manner, they can then fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness, and so on, up to the knowledge of all aspects; by means of this, they are able to realize the knowledge of all modes.

"Subhūti! By means of the skillful power that takes the absence of intrinsic nature as the very nature of all phenomena, this bodhisattva mahāsattva realizes that all phenomena are devoid of self-nature; therein, there is neither perception nor even non-perception."

"Subhūti! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should train in the recollection of relinquishment (*tyāgānusmṛti*) in this way: within the nature of the non-nature of all phenomena, even relinquishment cannot be apprehended, let alone the recollection of relinquishment!"
“Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the recollection of the devas?
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the recollection of the devas, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, they should form this thought:”

"From the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations, because they possess pure faith, ethical discipline, learning, renunciation, and wisdom, they pass away from here and are reborn in those celestial realms."
"I too now possess such pure faith, ethical discipline, learning, relinquishment, and wisdom, which are similar in merit to those of these devas.
He further reflects:

"That stream-enterers and others are born in the six heavens of the desire realm, and that non-returners and others are born in the two higher realms—all such things are unattainable and should not be conceptualized."
Why is this? Because all these devas lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); if a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, it cannot be recollected nor can it be contemplated. Why is that?
"If there is no recollection and no mental engagement, this is the recollection of the devas. Subhūti!
When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should train in the recollection of the devas in this manner.
If one trains in this way by recollecting the devas, this constitutes performing gradual karma, practicing gradual training, and engaging in gradual conduct.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to perform gradual karma, practice gradual training, and engage in gradual conduct in this manner, they will then be able to fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness, and so on, up to and including all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), thereby realizing the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).

"Subhūti! Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses the skillful power of taking the absence of intrinsic nature as the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, he realizes that all phenomena are devoid of self-nature; therein, there is neither perception nor even non-perception."

"Subhūti! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should train in the recollection of the devas in this way: within the nature of the absence of intrinsic nature of all phenomena, even a 'deva' cannot be apprehended, much less the recollection of the devas!"
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, if they wish to fulfill gradual karma,
cultivate gradual training, and perform gradual practices, [they should do so] by means of the non-existence of all phenomena."
By the power of skillful means regarding the nature of things, one should study inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;
one should study true suchness up to the inconceivable realm; one should study the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
one should study the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; and one should study the four dhyānas.
One should study the four immeasurables, the four formless absorptions, the eight liberations up to the ten totalities;
one should study the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
one should study the perfections from the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom; and one should study the stages of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
One should study all the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi; one should study the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
one should study the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
one should study the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity; and one should study all-knowledge and the knowledge of the aspects of the path.

“O Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way on the path to enlightenment, they realize that all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature; therein, not even the slightest thought can be apprehended, much less a thought of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness!”
How much less could there be mindfulness of the sense base of the eye, up to the sense base of the mind!
How much less could there be mindfulness of the sense base of forms, up to the sense base of mental phenomena!
How much less could there be mindfulness of the eye constituent, up to the mind constituent!
How much less could there be mindfulness of the form realm up to the dharma realm!
How much less could there be mindfulness of the eye-consciousness realm up to the mind-consciousness realm!
How much less could there be mindfulness of eye-contact up to mind-contact!
How much less could there be mindfulness of the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, up to and including the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition!
How much less could there be mindfulness of the earth element, up to and including the consciousness element!
How much less could there be mindfulness of conditions from the causal condition up to the dominant condition!
How much less could there be mindfulness of ignorance up to old age and death!
How much less could there be mindfulness of the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom!
How much less could there be mindfulness of inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature!
How much less could there be mindfulness of suchness up to the inconceivable realm!
How much less could there be mindfulness of the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path!
How much more so for mindfulness of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path!
How much more so for mindfulness of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments!
How much more so for mindfulness of the eight liberations up to the ten totalities!
How much more so for mindfulness of the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness!
How much more so for mindfulness of the stages from the Pure Observation Ground up to the Tathāgata Ground!
How much more so for mindfulness of the stages from the Extremely Joyful Ground up to the Dharma Cloud Ground!
How much more so for the recollection of all dharani-doors and samadhi-doors!
How much more so for the recollection of the five eyes and the six supernormal powers!
How much more so for the recollection of the Tathagata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha!
How much more so for those who maintain mindfulness of the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs!
How much more so for those who maintain mindfulness of the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity!
How much more so for those who maintain mindfulness of all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects!
How much less could there be mindfulness of the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha!
How much less could there be mindfulness of all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas!
How much less could there be mindfulness of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas!
How much more so for one who maintains mindfulness of the knowledge of all-knowledge! Subhūti,
it is impossible that these various forms of mindfulness and the dharmas that are their objects should have even the slightest degree of real existence.

"In this way, Subhūti, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, although they perform gradual deeds, cultivate gradual training, and engage in gradual practices, their minds do not waver therein, because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One!

If all dharmas are devoid of intrinsic nature, then there should be no form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, and so on, up to no ‘knowledge of all aspects. In that case, there would be no Buddha, Dharma, or Saṅgha Jewel; no defilement or purification regarding the fruits of the path; and neither attainment nor clear realization. Thus, all dharmas should be non-existent!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Within the nature of the absence of nature in all phenomena, can existence or non-existence be apprehended?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"If, within the nature of the absence of nature of all phenomena, both existence and non-existence are unapprehendable, how can you now say:

'If all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, then there should be no form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, and so on, up to there should be no attainment or clear realization; thus, all phenomena should be non-existent'?"

Subhūti replied, "I have no doubt regarding this meaning myself; however, it is for the sake of future bhikṣus who may seek the state of a śrāvaka, or seek the state of a pratyekabuddha, or seek the fruit of Buddhahood, and who might think:
'If all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, who is it that is defiled?'"
Who is purified?
Who is bound?
Who is liberated?

Because they do not understand the meaning of defilement and purification, or bondage and liberation, they violate their precepts, their views, their conduct, and their pure livelihood; consequently, they shall fall into the three evil destinies and undergo various intense sufferings from which it is difficult to attain release.
"I observe that such terrifying events will occur in the future; therefore, I have made this statement. However, regarding this matter, I truly have no doubt.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "Excellent!"

Excellent! That you are now able to ask such a question for the sake of the bhikṣus of future ages is truly commendable. However, within the naturelessness of all phenomena, neither existence nor non-existence can be apprehended.
Chapter 74: The Chapter on Signlessness (Animitta), Part Two, Section One. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

If all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, for what purpose do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas perceive any meaning such that they seek to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment out of a desire to benefit and bring peace and happiness to sentient beings?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Because all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, bodhisattva mahāsattvas act for the sake of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to sentient beings."

Why is this? Because all classes of sentient beings are possessed of the views of annihilationism and eternalism; dwelling in the apprehension of objective existence, they are difficult to subdue, and being deluded and inverted, they are difficult to liberate.

Subhūti, you should know that for one who dwells in the apprehension of something, because of the perception of apprehending something, there is no attainment, no clear realization, and no unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha again:

"If for one who has something to attain there is no attainment, no clear realization, and no unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, then for one who has nothing to attain, is there attainment, is there clear realization, and is there unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If there is no attainment, that itself is attainment, that itself is clear realization, and that itself is unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Why is this so?
Because that dharma-realm is indestructible.
Subhūti, you should know this:

if anyone, within this state of non-apprehension, desires to apprehend something, desires to attain clear realization, or desires to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, you should know that they desire to destroy the dharma-realm.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If that which is attained is non-attainment, and there is neither realization nor unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment; and if non-attainment itself is attainment, is realization, and is unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment—such that within non-attainment there is no attainment, no realization, and no unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment—then how can bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain the first stage through to the tenth stage?"

How can there be the attainment of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)? How can there be the attainment of supernormal powers as a result of maturation (*vipākaja-abhijñā*)?
How can there be the attainment of the perfections of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*) up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) as a result of maturation?

How can it be that one who abides in such dharmas born of maturation (*vipākaja*) for the sake of ripening sentient beings and purifying Buddha-fields, and who has acquired roots of goodness by making respectful offerings of supreme and exquisite requisites to the Buddhas—how can these roots of goodness remain inexhaustible until the fruit of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, and even continue through successive stages until after his final *parinirvāṇa*, such that his own *śarīra* relics and his disciples still receive various forms of respect and offerings, only when the power of those roots of goodness is finally exhausted?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Because all dharmas are unattainable, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain the first bhūmi through to the tenth bhūmi; it is by virtue of this that they attain the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti); it is by virtue of this that they attain the supernormal powers of maturation (vipākaja-abhijñā); and it is by virtue of this that they attain the maturation of the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramitā) through to the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā)."

Precisely because of this, one is able to abide in the maturation of dharmas born of ripening (*vipākaja*) to mature sentient beings and purify Buddha-fields; and the roots of goodness obtained through reverently making offerings of supreme and exquisite requisites to the Buddhas remain inexhaustible until unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, yielding their fruit continuously even after one’s parinirvāṇa, such that one’s own *śarīra* relics and disciples still receive various forms of reverence and offerings until the power of those roots of goodness finally comes to an end.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If all phenomena are non-apprehendable, what difference is there between the perfections of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as the various supernormal powers?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"For those who have nothing to apprehend, the six perfections beginning with giving and the various supernormal powers are all without distinction. However, in order to lead those who do apprehend something to abandon all defiled attachments, he employs skillful means to proclaim that the six perfections beginning with giving and the various supernormal powers possess distinct characteristics."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what cause and condition are the six perfections, such as giving, and the various supernormal powers said to be without distinction for one who has nothing to be attained?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not apprehend giving, they do not apprehend the giver,
they do not apprehend the recipient, they do not apprehend that which is given, and they do not apprehend the act of giving."
While practicing generosity, they do not grasp at pure ethical discipline yet maintain it; while practicing patience, they do not grasp at it yet cultivate it;
while exerting diligence, they do not grasp at it yet apply themselves with vigor; while entering meditative concentration, they do not grasp at it yet enter it;
while giving rise to wisdom, they do not grasp at it yet give rise to it; and while manifesting supernormal powers, they do not grasp at them yet bring them forth.
Without apprehending the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, one cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
without apprehending the three doors of liberation, one cultivates the three doors of liberation;
without apprehending the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments, one cultivates the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments.
While not attaining the four formless absorptions, they cultivate the eight liberations up to the ten totalities;
while not attaining the bodhisattva stages, they cultivate the bodhisattva stages;
while not attaining the doors of dhāraṇī and the doors of samādhi, they cultivate the doors of dhāraṇī and the doors of samādhi.
One does not attain the five eyes or the six supernormal powers while cultivating the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
one does not attain the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha while cultivating the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
one does not attain the quality of non-forgetfulness or the state of constant equanimity while cultivating non-forgetfulness...

They lose the dharmas and abide constantly in equanimity; they do not attain omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), yet they cultivate omniscience, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects;
they do not apprehend sentient beings, yet they bring sentient beings to maturity; they do not apprehend buddha-fields, yet they adorn and purify buddha-fields; they do not apprehend...
They realize all Buddha-dharmas and attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Thus, Subhūti, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice the profound perfection of wisdom that is non-apprehensible; if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva can practice this profound perfection of wisdom that is non-apprehensible, no evil Māras or their retinues will be able to destroy them.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, manifest with a single mind?”

When they arise, they are able to encompass the six pāramitās; they are also able to encompass the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; they are also able to encompass the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;
they are also able to encompass the three gates of liberation; and they are also able to encompass the eight liberations up to the ten totalities.
Furthermore, it can also encompass all dhāraṇī-doors and samādhi-doors; it can also encompass the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
it can also encompass the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
and it can also encompass the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity.
Can it also encompass all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*),
and can it also encompass the thirty-two marks of a great man (*dvātriṃśanmahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*) and the eighty secondary signs (*aśītyanuvyañjana*)?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, the cultivation of the perfections from generosity up to wisdom is only brought to fulfillment when it is embraced by the perfection of wisdom.”

In this way, even up to the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor signs that are produced, all are brought to full completion only when they are embraced by the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Thus it is, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, when they bring it forth with a single-minded focus, they are able to encompass the six perfections; in this way, they are even able to encompass the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, how is it that because all their actions are embraced by the perfection of wisdom, a single thought-moment can embrace the six perfections, and even the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, all their cultivation of the perfections from generosity up to wisdom is embraced by the *prajñāpāramitā*; therefore, they remain free from dualistic conceptions. This extends even to the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor characteristics that they bring forth, which likewise, being embraced by the *prajñāpāramitā*, are free from dualistic conceptions."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, although they practice from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, they have no dualistic perception; and likewise, even when they manifest the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks, they have no dualistic perception?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, for the sake of fulfilling the *dānapāramitā*, they practice giving by encompassing all the *pāramitās* up to the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks within that very *dānapāramitā*; through this causal condition, they maintain no dualistic conception."

In this manner, up to and including the desire to fulfill the eighty minor marks (*anuvyañjana*), one gathers within those very eighty minor marks all the *pāramitās* through to the thirty-two marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*) and the eighty minor marks, thereby drawing forth the eighty minor marks; by virtue of these causes and conditions, there is no dualistic conception.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, when they practice the perfection of giving, they abide in an untainted mind while practicing the perfection of giving."

When practicing the perfection of ethical discipline up to the perfection of wisdom, one dwells in an untainted mind while practicing the perfection of ethical discipline up to the perfection of wisdom.
Therefore, although they practice from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, they maintain no dualistic conception.
Likewise, when manifesting the thirty-two marks of a Great Being, they do so while abiding in an untainted mind;
when manifesting the eighty secondary signs, they do so while abiding in an untainted mind.
"Therefore, although one may cite the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs, there is no dualistic conception.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, when practicing the perfection of giving, abide in an untainted mind while practicing the perfection of giving; and likewise, up to when citing the eighty secondary signs, abide in an untainted mind while citing the eighty secondary signs?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they practice the perfection of giving with a mind free from signs, not perceiving any signs—namely, not perceiving who is able to give."
What is the object given?
Who receives this gift?
How is the gift bestowed?

Abiding in this untainted mind that is free from signs, one practices the perfection of giving while being free from craving and stinginess; at that time, one does not perceive the act of giving, nor does one perceive this untainted mind, nor even perceive any of the Buddha-dharmas. In this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the untainted mind and practices the perfection of giving.

In this way, even when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they do so with a mind free from signs (*animitta*), not perceiving any signs as they bring forth the eighty secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*). That is to say, they do not perceive who it is that can bring forth these eighty secondary marks.
With respect to whom are the eighty minor marks induced?
For what purpose are the eighty minor marks induced?
In what manner are the eighty minor marks induced?

Abiding in this untainted mind that is free from signs, without defilement or attachment, one brings forth the eighty minor marks; yet at that time, one does not perceive the eighty minor marks being brought forth, nor does one perceive this untainted mind, nor even perceive any of the Buddha-dharmas. In this way, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva abides in the untainted mind and brings forth the eighty minor marks.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, and all phenomena are without marks and without volitional activity, how can they fulfill the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom?”
"In this way, up until: how can they fulfill the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they are able to practice giving with a mind free from signs and untainted (*anāsrava*). They bestow all necessary provisions upon sentient beings according to their needs; if there are those who require internal gifts such as head, eyes, marrow, brain, skin, flesh, limbs, joints, sinews, bones, or even life itself, they bestow these as well."
If there are those who require foreign cities, wives and children, beloved relatives, or various kinds of ornaments, he likewise bestows them all as gifts.
When giving in this manner, even if someone were to come before him and revile him, saying:
"Alas! [What a pity!]"
"O Great Being!
Why do you practice this unbeneficial giving? Such giving brings much suffering and affliction in both this life and future lives!
Although the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva hears these words because he practices the profound Prajñāpāramitā, he does not retreat or yield, but instead thinks:

"Although that person comes to revile and disparage me, I should not give rise to sorrow or regret in my mind; rather, I shall courageously bestow upon all sentient beings whatever they require, without weariness of body or mind."
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva takes this act of giving and, sharing it equally with all sentient beings, dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
When practicing such giving and dedicating the merit, one does not perceive their characteristics; that is to say, one does not perceive who is able to give,
what object is being given,
or who is receiving this gift.
How does one practice giving?
Furthermore, one does not perceive anyone who can dedicate [the merit],
nor anything toward which it is dedicated.
What is dedication? Where is it dedicated?
One does not perceive any such things whatsoever.

Why is this? It is because all these phenomena are empty, none excepted, by virtue of internal emptiness, and so on, up to being empty by virtue of the emptiness of their own specific characteristics.
Having contemplated that there are no phenomena that are not empty, this bodhisattva mahāsattva further reflects:
"Who is it that dedicates? What is it that is dedicated? How is it dedicated?"
"To what place is it dedicated?
Such phenomena as these are all unattainable.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices dedication through such contemplation and such mindfulness, that dedication is called "skillful dedication."

By means of this, one is further able to bring sentient beings to maturity and to purify Buddha-fields; one is also able to fulfill the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, and likewise, even to fulfill the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks.
“Although this bodhisattva mahāsattva is thus able to fulfill the perfection of generosity, they do not appropriate the karmic maturation of that generosity.
Although they do not appropriate the karmic maturation of generosity, because the perfection of generosity is thoroughly purified, they are able to provide all necessary requisites at will.”

Just as for the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*), everything they require appears at will, so it is with this bodhisattva mahāsattva: whatever he requires can be accomplished at will. He is able to offer various sublime articles of worship to honor, revere, respect, and praise the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; he is also able to satisfy the needs of the world’s devas, humans, asuras, and others with all necessary provisions. By means of this perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), he gathers in all sentient beings and, through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), establishes them in the three vehicles (*tri-yāna*), causing each to obtain benefit and happiness according to what is appropriate for them.

"So it is, Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, by means of the power of their untainted mind which is free from all signs, they are able to fulfill the perfection of generosity within the signless and unconditioned state, and they are likewise able to fulfill all other meritorious qualities."

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 466. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Second Division, Chapter on Signlessness (Animittaparivarta), Number Seventy-Four, Part Two. "Furthermore, Subhūti!..."

When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they are able to uphold the pure precepts with a mind free from signs and untainted (*anāsrava*). This refers to the naturally attained, virtuous, and perfectly pure precepts subsumed within the noble, untainted factors of the path. Such pure precepts are without deficiency or flaw, without blemish or impurity, and without attachment; they are worthy of offerings and praised by the wise.

By means of this pure ethical discipline, one has no grasping or attachment toward any phenomena; that is to say, one does not grasp or attach to form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness;
one does not grasp or attach to the sense base of the eye up to the sense base of the mind; one does not grasp or attach to the sense base of forms up to the sense base of phenomena;
one does not grasp or attach to the eye constituent up to the mind constituent; one does not grasp or attach to...

They do not grasp at or become attached to the realm of form, up to and including the realm of phenomena; they do not grasp at or become attached to the realm of eye-consciousness, up to and including the realm of mind-consciousness;
they do not grasp at or become attached to the thirty-two marks of a great man or the eighty secondary signs;
they do not grasp at or become attached to the great clans of kṣatriyas, the great clans of brahmins, the great clans of householders, or the great clans of lay merchants. They do not...
They do not grasp at the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Control over Others' Emanations;
they do not grasp at the Heaven of Brahma’s Retinue up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven; they do not grasp at the Sphere of Infinite Space up to the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception;
they do not grasp at the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha. They do not...
One might grasp at the position of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), or other positions such as those of minor kings, ministers, or officials;

yet, one dedicates the very precepts thus undertaken and observed to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) in common with all sentient beings. At the time of this dedication, one employs the skillful means of signlessness (*animitta*), non-apprehensibility (*anupalambha*), and non-duality (*advaya*), rather than the skillful means of having signs, apprehensibility, or duality; this is done by way of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), not by way of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
By virtue of these causes and conditions, all Buddha-dharmas are fully perfected.

Through this skillful means of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), this bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to the stages of further progress within the four dhyānas; because they employ non-attachment as their skillful means, they bring forth the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

By means of the pure divine eye born of maturation, this bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly beholds the Buddhas of the present in the boundless worlds of the ten directions, dwelling in peace and stability, proclaiming the sublime Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, until they attain the knowledge of all modes; furthermore, he is never forgetful of what he has seen.

By means of the pure divine ear that transcends that of humans, this bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly hears the Dharma being preached by all Buddhas throughout the boundless worlds of the ten directions; until they realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), they are able to never forget what they have heard, and according to the teachings they have heard, they are able to perform deeds for the benefit and happiness of themselves and others without ever failing.

By means of the knowledge of others' minds, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to know the minds and mental factors of the Buddhas and sentient beings in the ten directions; having known them, they are able to initiate all manner of beneficial and blissful activities for all sentient beings.

By means of the knowledge of past lives, this bodhisattva mahāsattva knows the karma previously created by sentient beings; because that created karma is never lost or destroyed, they are born in various places to experience all manner of suffering and pleasure. Having known this, he explains the causal conditions of their original karma to them, causing them to remember and recognize it so as to perform acts of benefit for them.

By means of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas establish sentient beings, causing some to abide in the fruit of stream-entry, some to abide in the fruit of once-returning, some to abide in the fruit of non-returning, some to abide in the fruit of arhatship, some to abide in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, some to abide in the supreme state of a bodhisattva, or some to abide in the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

In brief, wherever this bodhisattva mahāsattva is born, he employs skillful means to establish sentient beings within superior categories of virtue, according to their respective capacities and differences.

"In this way, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, by means of the power of their untainted mind which is free from all signs, they are able to fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline within the signless and unconditioned state, and they are also able to fulfill all other meritorious qualities."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they cultivate patience with a mind that is free from signs and untainted."

"From the first generation of the mind of awakening until sitting upon the seat of sublime enlightenment, even if all sentient beings were to come together, each wielding various swords, staves, tiles, and stones to inflict harm, this bodhisattva mahāsattva would not give rise to a single thought of anger or resentment."
At that time, a bodhisattva should cultivate two kinds of patience. What are these two?
First, one should endure all verbal abuse, insults, and physical harm from sentient beings without giving rise to anger or resentment; this is the patience of subduing ill-will.
Second, they should give rise to the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
"If this bodhisattva-mahāsattva encounters various insults and verbal abuse, or is harmed by various weapons and staves, they should carefully reflect and examine:
'Who is it that can insult and abuse? "
Who can inflict harm?
Who receives abuse? Who undergoes injury?
"Who gives rise to anger and resentment?
Who should endure it?

Furthermore, one should carefully examine that the nature of all phenomena is ultimately empty; since even phenomena themselves cannot be apprehended, how much less could there be a "nature of phenomena"!
Since even the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) does not exist, how much less could there be sentient beings!

When observing in this way, that which insults, that which is insulted, that which inflicts harm, and that which is harmed are all non-existent. Even when one’s body and limbs are severed piece by piece, the mind remains patient and free from any discursive thought. By thus observing the nature of all phenomena as it truly is, one is further able to realize the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
What is called the "patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)?

It refers to causing all afflictions not to arise, maintaining a subtle and wondrous wisdom that is constantly uninterrupted, and observing that all phenomena are ultimately unarisen; for these reasons, it is called the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena.
“Abiding in these two kinds of patience, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to swiftly cultivate and fulfill the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
swiftly cultivate and fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; and swiftly cultivate and fulfill the four dhyānas and the four immeasurables.”
...the four formless absorptions; they can swiftly cultivate and fulfill the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality;
they can swiftly cultivate and fulfill the gateways of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
they can swiftly cultivate and fulfill all the bodhisattva stages; and they can swiftly cultivate and fulfill all the gateways of dhāraṇī and samādhi. Swiftly...

They are able to fully cultivate and perfect the five eyes and the six supernormal powers; they can swiftly cultivate and perfect the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they can swiftly cultivate and perfect the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity;
they can swiftly cultivate and perfect all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); they can swiftly...
They cultivate and fulfill the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks.

Having established themselves in these qualities of a Buddha, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain perfection in all the noble, untainted, supramundane, and unique superknowledges (abhijñā) of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Having established themselves in such supreme supernormal powers, they constantly behold with their pure divine eye the Buddhas of the present dwelling in peace and stability throughout the infinite worlds of the ten directions, as they proclaim the True Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings; until they attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), they give rise to the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti) without interruption.

With their pure divine ear, they constantly hear the Buddhas of the ten directions preaching the Dharma; having heard it, they receive and uphold it without ever forgetting, and they proclaim it to all sentient beings exactly as it is.

By means of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), he is able to correctly measure the minds and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*) of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; he is also able to correctly know the minds and mental factors of Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas; and he is also able to correctly know the minds and mental factors of other classes of sentient beings, preaching the True Dharma to them as appropriate so that they may give rise to resolute faith (*adhimukti*).

By means of the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), he knows the various differences in the roots of goodness planted by sentient beings in the past; having known these, he employs skillful means to manifest, exhort, encourage, and gladden them, causing them to obtain supreme benefit and peace.

By means of the knowledge of the destruction of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*), he establishes sentient beings in the Three Vehicles as appropriate, enabling them to attain liberation from birth, old age, sickness, and death.

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom and accomplishing sublime skillful means, purifies buddha-fields and matures sentient beings; they will swiftly fulfill all-aspect omniscience, realize unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, and turn the wondrous wheel of Dharma to deliver the multitudes of sentient beings."

"In this way, Subhūti, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, by means of the power of their untainted mind that is free from all signs, they are able to fulfill the perfection of patience within the signless and unconditioned state, and they are also able to fulfill all other meritorious qualities."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they cultivate diligence with a mind that is free from signs and untainted."

This bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes courageous physical and mental diligence; by means of this, they are able to enter and dwell fully in the first dhyāna, up to entering and dwelling fully in the fourth dhyāna. Relying on these four dhyānas, they manifest immeasurable kinds of supernatural powers and transformations, even to the point of touching and stroking the sun and moon with their hands and turning them at will without finding it difficult.

Because they have accomplished the physical diligence of valor, by means of their supernormal powers, they are able to reach Buddha-worlds in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in a mere instant. Furthermore, with various kinds of food, drink, clothing, bedding, medicine, and other requisites, they reverently make offerings to, respect, and praise the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, who are currently preaching the True Dharma; through the inexhaustible fruit and retribution of these roots of goodness, they shall eventually realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

Having attained Buddhahood through the predominant power of these roots of goodness, he will further be reverently honored, supported, respected, and praised by immeasurable multitudes of worldly devas, humans, and asuras, who will offer him countless varieties of food and drink, clothing, bedding, medicine, and other requisites.

By the superior power of these roots of goodness, even after his parinirvāṇa, his physical relics and his disciples shall still be venerated, honored, respected, and praised by immeasurable worlds of devas, humans, asuras, and others.

"Furthermore, by means of their supernormal powers, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to reach Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions. There, in the presence of those Buddhas, they listen to the sublime Dharma; having heard it, they receive and uphold it, never forgetting it until they attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Furthermore, by means of their supernormal powers, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to reach Buddha-worlds in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, where they bring sentient beings to maturity and adorn and purify buddha-fields. Diligently training in the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), once they have attained perfection, they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, and deliver the multitudes of sentient beings.

“In this way, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, because they achieve courageous physical diligence, they are able to swiftly bring the perfection of diligence to fulfillment.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, because they have accomplished a courageous mind and diligence, they are able to swiftly fulfill the noble, untainted path and the perfection of diligence subsumed within its branches; by means of this, they ensure that no unwholesome actions of body, speech, or mind can arise."
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, among all phenomena, never grasps or adheres to them as either permanent or impermanent,
pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or non-tranquil, or secluded or non-secluded."
Whether it be the conditioned realm or the unconditioned realm; whether the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm;
whether the tainted realm or the untainted realm; or the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments;
or the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power;
