The five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eight branches of the noble path;
the doors of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; and suchness up to...
The inconceivable realm: whether it be the Noble Truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
or the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten universal bases;
or the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata; or the stage of extreme joy up to the stage of the Dharma-cloud; or all dhāraṇīs.
the gateways, all the gateways of samādhi; whether it be the five eyes or the six supernormal powers;
whether it be the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; whether it be the thirty-two marks of a great man or the eighty minor marks;
whether it be the quality of non-forgetfulness or the nature of constant equanimity; or whether it be omniscience—
The knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects; whether they be impermanence, suffering, emptiness, or non-self;
or the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, the fruit of arhatship, or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
or the entire conduct of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, or the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas.

Subhūti, this bodhisattva mahāsattva likewise does not grasp at or adhere to the notion that "this is a stream-enterer," "this is a once-returner," "this is a non-returner," "this is an arhat," "this is a pratyekabuddha," "this is a bodhisattva," or "this is a Tathāgata. Furthermore, he does not grasp at or adhere to such sentient beings as they are manifested through inferior qualities, as they are manifested through middling qualities, as they are manifested through superior qualities; nor as they are manifested through lower portions, nor as they are manifested through middle portions; nor as they are manifested through the Śrāvaka vehicle, nor as they are manifested through the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, nor as they are manifested through the Unsurpassed Vehicle. This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not grasp at or adhere to any such phenomena or sentient beings whatsoever.
Why is this? It is because both the phenomena to which one becomes attached and all sentient beings lack any intrinsic nature that could serve as an object of attachment.

"Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva has accomplished a courageous mind of diligence, although he constantly performs all manner of deeds for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings, he perceives no sentient beings whatsoever."
Although they constantly fulfill the perfection of diligence, they do not apprehend the perfection of diligence at all;
although they constantly fulfill all Buddha-dharmas, they do not apprehend any Buddha-dharma at all;
although they constantly adorn and purify all Buddha-fields, they do not apprehend any Buddha-field at all.

“Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva has accomplished such physical and mental diligence, although they are able to remain far removed from all unwholesome dharmas, they are also able to embrace all wholesome dharmas without any grasping or attachment.”

Because they are free from grasping and attachment, they travel from one buddha-field to another and from one world-system to another; for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, they are able to freely and unimpededly manifest whatever supernatural powers they wish to display.

That is to say, he may manifest the raining down of various exquisite flowers, the scattering of various famous incenses, and the playing of various musical instruments; he may manifest the sound of clouds and thunder that shakes the great earth.

Or again, he may manifest worlds adorned with various wonderful seven-jeweled treasures; his body emits light that illuminates all blindness and darkness, and from his body issues a sublime fragrance that causes all who are foul and impure to become fragrant and clean.

Alternatively, they may manifest the performance of great sacrificial rites, yet within them do not afflict any sentient beings; by means of this, they transform and guide immeasurable sentient beings, causing them to enter the right path and abandon taking life, up to and including wrong views.

By means of generosity up to and including wisdom, they gather in all sentient beings; desiring to benefit them, they may relinquish wealth and treasures, or relinquish wife and children, or relinquish their royal throne, or relinquish their limbs and members, or relinquish their very body and life. According to whatever skillful means are appropriate for each sentient being to obtain benefit, they benefit them by employing those very same skillful means.

"So it is, Subhūti! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, by means of the power of their untainted mind that is free from all signs, they are able to fulfill the perfection of diligence within the signless and unconditioned dharmas, and they are also able to fulfill all other meritorious qualities."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they cultivate meditative concentration with a mind that is free from signs and untainted."
This bodhisattva mahāsattva, with the exception of the concentrations of the Buddhas, is able to bring all other concentrations to full perfection.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, detached from desires and unwholesome states, possessing applied and sustained thought, and experiencing the joy and happiness born of seclusion, enters and dwells in the first dhyāna; and so on, until: having abandoned pleasure and abandoned pain, and with the prior disappearance of joy and sorrow, entering into a state that is neither painful nor pleasant, with equanimity and mindfulness purified, he enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells pervading one direction, and so on up to all ten directions of the entire world, with a mind imbued with loving-kindness; likewise, he dwells pervading one direction, and so on up to all ten directions of the entire world, with a mind imbued with equanimity.

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva transcends all perceptions of form, extinguishes perceptions of sensory resistance, and does not attend to perceptions of diversity; he enters the sphere of infinite space and dwells fully endowed with it. In this manner, up until he transcends the sphere of nothingness in every respect, he enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and dwells fully endowed with it."

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā), is able to enter, in both forward and reverse order, the eight liberations (aṣṭavimokṣa), the eight spheres of mastery (aṣṭābhibhvāyatana), the nine successive attainments (navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti), and the ten spheres of totality (daśakṛtsnāyatana), remaining fully established therein.

“This bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to dwell fully endowed with the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—and is able to dwell fully endowed with the samādhi of uninterruptedness, the samādhi like lightning, the noble and correct samādhi, and the diamond-like samādhi.”

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration, cultivates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the knowledge of the aspects of the path, bringing them all to full completion.

Having embraced all samādhis by means of the knowledge of the aspects of the path, one gradually cultivates the stages from the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the pratyekabuddha, thereby entering the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth. Once having entered the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth, one cultivates the practices of the various stages until the perfection of the Buddha-stage.

Although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas gradually cultivate and leap through the various stages, they do not realize the fruits of attainment therein until they have attained the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration, proceeds from one buddha-field to another, reverently making offerings to, honoring, and praising the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. Under those Buddhas, they plant various roots of goodness, ripen sentient beings, and purify buddha-fields; proceeding from one world-system to another, they benefit sentient beings with bodies and minds free from weariness."

They gather sentient beings through generosity, or through ethical discipline, or through patience, or through diligence, or through meditative concentration, or through the perfection of wisdom; or they gather sentient beings through the aggregate of ethical discipline, or the aggregate of concentration, or the aggregate of wisdom, or the aggregate of liberation, or the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; or they instruct sentient beings to abide in the fruit of a stream-enterer, or in the fruit of a once-returner, or in the fruit of a non-returner, or in the fruit of arhatship; or they cause them to abide in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, or in the stage of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, or in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. According to the power of the roots of virtue of those sentient beings and the growth of their wholesome qualities, they cause them to abide securely through various skillful means.

“This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), is able to bring forth all doors of dhāraṇī and doors of samādhi, and is able to attain the four supreme analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) as a result of karmic maturation.”

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, having accomplished the extraordinary supernormal powers of karmic maturation, will certainly never again enter a mother's womb, nor experience sensual pleasures, nor undergo birth, nor be defiled by the faults associated with birth."
Why is this? It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas clearly perceive and thoroughly understand that the nature of all phenomena is entirely like an illusion or a magical transformation.
Although they know that all conditioned activities are like illusions and transformations, they benefit sentient beings by riding upon their compassionate vows.
Although one benefits sentient beings by riding upon compassionate vows, one realizes that both sentient beings and their designations are unattainable.

Although one realizes that both sentient beings and their designations are unattainable, one is nevertheless able to establish all sentient beings, causing them to abide in the dharma of non-attainability; this is based on the conventional, not the ultimate truth.

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration, practices all dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, and attainments, until they fulfill their sought-after unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; throughout this time, they never abandon the perfection of meditative concentration they have cultivated."

“This bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the knowledge of the aspects of the path and, through skillful means, brings forth the knowledge of all aspects; abiding therein, they forever sever the continuity of all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). They are able to correctly benefit themselves and correctly benefit others, and they serve as a pure field of merit for all the world—including devas, humans, and asuras—being worthy of receiving the world’s offerings and respect.”

"In this way, Subhūti, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, by means of the power of their untainted mind that is free from all signs, they are able to fulfill the perfection of meditative concentration within the signless and unconditioned dharmas, and they are also able to fulfill all other meritorious qualities."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they are able to cultivate wisdom with a mind that is free from signs and untainted."

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive even the slightest dharma as truly existent or established; that is to say, he does not perceive form as truly existent or established, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as truly existent or established.
He does not perceive the arising of form, nor the arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
He does not perceive the cessation of form, nor the cessation of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness."
Not seeing form is a gate of superimposition; not seeing feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness is a gate of superimposition.
Not seeing form is a gate of denial; not seeing feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness is a gate of denial.
Not seeing form as having accumulation; not seeing feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness as having accumulation.
He does not perceive the disintegration of form, nor does he perceive the disintegration of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

In this way, up to and including, he does not perceive that any contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) truly exist as established, nor does he perceive that any uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) truly exist as established;
he does not perceive the arising of any contaminated phenomena, nor does he perceive the arising of any uncontaminated phenomena.
They do not perceive the cessation of any contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena, nor do they perceive the cessation of any uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena;
they do not perceive any contaminated phenomena as a gate of increase, nor do they perceive any uncontaminated phenomena as a gate of increase;
they do not perceive any contaminated phenomena as a gate of decrease, nor do they perceive any uncontaminated phenomena as a gate of decrease.
One does not perceive any accumulation of all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), nor does one perceive any accumulation of all uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*);
one does not perceive any dispersal of all contaminated phenomena, nor does one perceive any dispersal of all uncontaminated phenomena.

One contemplates form as it truly is: as false, unsubstantial, and lacking self-mastery; one contemplates feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as they truly are: as false, unsubstantial, and lacking self-mastery.

In this way, one contemplates all contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) as they truly are: as false, unsubstantial, and lacking self-mastery; and one contemplates all uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsravadharma*) as they truly are: as false, unsubstantial, and lacking self-mastery.

"When this bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates in this manner, he does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of form; he does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. In this way, he does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of any contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), nor does he apprehend the intrinsic nature of any uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*)."

"When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom and contemplates in this manner, they develop deep faith and understanding toward all phenomena, [realizing] that their very nature consists in the absence of intrinsic nature."
Having given rise to faith and understanding regarding such matters, one is able to practice inner emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.
When practicing in this way, one has no attachment to any phenomena;
that is, one does not attach to form, nor to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor to the sense base of the eye, up to and including the sense base of the mind.
One does not cling to the sphere of forms up to the sphere of mental phenomena; one does not cling to the eye-element up to the mind-element;
one does not cling to the form-element up to the mental-phenomena-element; one does not cling to the eye-consciousness-element up to the mind-consciousness-element;
one does not cling to eye-contact up to mind-contact; nor does one cling to that which is conditioned by eye-contact.
Regarding all feelings produced, up to those produced with mental contact as a condition, one does not cling to the earth element up to the consciousness element;
one does not cling to the causal conditions up to the dominant conditions; one does not cling to ignorance up to old age and death;
and one does not cling to the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom.
Pāramitā, one does not cling to internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature;
one does not cling to suchness up to the inconceivable realm; one does not cling to the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
one does not cling to the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; one does not cling to the four dhyānas...
They do not cling to the applications of mindfulness, the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments; they do not cling to the eight liberations up to the ten totalities;
they do not cling to the doors of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
they do not cling to the stage of pure observation up to the stage of a Tathāgata; and they do not cling to the stage of extreme joy up to the stage of the cloud of dharma.
They do not cling to any of the *dhāraṇī* gates or *samādhi* gates; they do not cling to the five eyes or the six supernormal powers;
they do not cling to the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they do not cling to the thirty-two marks of a Great Man or the eighty minor marks; they do not cling.

The quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity; non-attachment to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);
non-attachment to the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
non-attachment to all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; and non-attachment to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas.
Bodhi. "When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* of non-existence, he is able to fulfill the bodhisattva path;
that is to say, he is able to fulfill the six *pāramitās*, and he is also able to..."
They fulfill the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;
they also fulfill true suchness up to the inconceivable realm; they also fulfill the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
they also fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; and they also fulfill the four dhyānas.
...the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments; they can also fulfill the eight liberations up to the ten totalities;
they can also fulfill the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
they can also fulfill all the bodhisattva stages, as well as all the dharani-gates and samādhis.
The gateway of the stages can also bring to perfection the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
it can also bring to perfection the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;

it can also bring to perfection the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity; and it can also bring to perfection all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects.
Wisdom can also bring to perfection the thirty-two marks of a great being and the eighty minor signs.

Once this bodhisattva mahāsattva has perfected such a bodhisattva path, they are further able to perfect the Buddha-path free from darkness, which means they can perfect the six pāramitās and all other immeasurable and boundless buddha-dharmas.

“Abiding in this path to buddhahood free from darkness, this bodhisattva mahāsattva brings forth the extraordinary supernormal powers of karmic maturation. Accordingly, for those sentient beings who should be gathered through generosity up to wisdom, he gathers them by means of generosity up to wisdom;

for those who should be gathered by the aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, or the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation, he gathers them by means of the aggregate of ethical discipline up to the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation.”

Regarding those who should be established in the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship, or in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, or in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—one employs skillful means to establish them in the fruit of stream-entry up to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to perform various supernatural transformations and manifestations; if he wishes to go to worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he can go there at will.
If he wishes to manifest various kinds of rare jewels within those worlds he visits, he can manifest them at will.
If he wishes to cause the sentient beings in those worlds to enjoy various rare jewels, he causes them all to be fully satisfied according to their inclinations."

"This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva travels from one world-system to another, benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings. Beholding the various exquisite signs of adornment in these worlds, he is able to personally appropriate and manifest Buddha-lands adorned according to his own wishes. Just as the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations have all manner of exquisite objects of pleasure appear before them according to their minds, so too does this Bodhisattva, according to his will, appropriate and manifest various adornments of immeasurable Buddha-lands. Within these appropriated Buddha-lands, which are subtle, pure, and free from all defiled phenomena, everything he desires is able to be manifested."

"Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom born of maturation (*vipākaja*), possesses the various sublime supernormal powers born of maturation, and possesses the bodhisattva path born of maturation, they practice the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*); and through the maturation attained by means of the knowledge of the aspects of the path, they are further able to realize the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)."

By attaining this wisdom, one does not grasp at any phenomena; that is, one does not grasp at form, nor does one grasp at feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. In this way, one does not grasp at anything from wholesome or unwholesome phenomena, defined or undefined phenomena, mundane or supramundane phenomena, contaminated or uncontaminated phenomena, or conditioned or unconditioned phenomena. One does not grasp at the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening that is realized, nor does one grasp at any objects of enjoyment in any buddha-field; therein, sentient beings likewise do not grasp at any phenomena.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have not previously grasped any phenomena, because they do not apprehend anything among all phenomena, and because they correctly proclaim to all sentient beings that the nature of all phenomena is without grasping.

"So it is, Subhūti! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, by means of the power of their untainted mind which is free from all signs, they are able to fulfill the perfection of wisdom within the signless and unconditioned state, and they are also able to fulfill all other meritorious qualities."
75. Chapter on Non-Confusion, Second Part, Chapter on Non-Confusion 75-1. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
How can one fulfill the six pāramitās within all phenomena that are unmixed, signless, and empty of intrinsic nature?
How can one establish distinctions within all phenomena that are without distinction?
How does one thoroughly understand the distinct characteristics of all such phenomena?
How is it that within the *prajñāpāramitā* one can encompass all six *pāramitās*, and likewise encompass all mundane and supramundane phenomena?

How is it that within all phenomena of diverse characteristics one establishes a single characteristic—namely, the characteristic of signlessness—and within phenomena of a single characteristic or no characteristic, one establishes all the various characteristics of differentiated phenomena?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they abide within the five aggregates of clinging—which are like a dream, like an echo, like a reflection, like a shadow, like a mirage, like an illusion, and like a magical creation—and for the sake of all sentient beings, they practice giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and train in wisdom. They understand, in accordance with reality, that these five aggregates, from those like a dream up to those like a magical creation, all share one single characteristic: namely, the characteristic of signlessness.”

Why is this so? Because from dreams up to transformations, all are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). If a dharma lacks intrinsic nature, that dharma is without marks (*animitta*); if a dharma is without marks, that dharma has but a single mark, namely, the markless.
By this causal condition, one should know that the giver, the recipient, the gift, the nature of giving, the fruit of giving, and the conditions for giving are all equally without marks.

“If one practices giving while knowing in this way, then one will be able to fulfill the perfection of giving that is practiced; if one can fulfill the perfection of giving that is practiced, then one does not depart from the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.”
Abiding in these six pāramitās, one is able to bring to perfection the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
one is also able to bring to perfection the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path,
as well as the three doors of liberation, and from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence itself.
The emptiness of intrinsic nature can also fulfill true suchness up to the inconceivable realm;
it can also fulfill the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; it can also fulfill the eight liberations up to the ten totalities;
it can also fulfill the bodhisattva stages; and it can also fulfill the five hundred dhāraṇīs.

The gateways of the bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*) and the five hundred gateways of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), as well as the ability to fulfill the five eyes and the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*),
the ability to fulfill the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*),
the ability to fulfill the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣadharma*) and the nature of constant equanimity (*upekṣā*), and the ability to fulfill all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
The knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects.

"Abiding within such matured, noble, and untainted dharmas, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to travel to Buddha-worlds in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and with immeasurable kinds of supreme and exquisite offerings, he reverently makes offerings to, honors, and praises the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. He brings about the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings; those who should be gathered through the perfections from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, he gathers them by means of those very perfections from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
those who should be gathered by other various wholesome dharmas, he gathers them by means of those other various wholesome dharmas."

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva has accomplished all supreme roots of goodness and has attained mastery over all phenomena; although they undergo birth and death, they are not defiled by the faults of birth and death."

For the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, one accepts the sovereignty of wealth and honor among gods and humans; by the power of this sovereignty of wealth and honor, one is able to perform various beneficial deeds for sentient beings and gather them in through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that all phenomena are signless, although they know the fruit of stream-entry, they do not abide in the fruit of stream-entry; and so on, up to: although they know the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, they do not abide in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having understood all phenomena as they truly are, desire to realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), which is not shared with any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
"In this way, Subhūti!

Because Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas know that all phenomena are signless, they understand in accordance with reality that the six perfections, such as giving, and all other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas are likewise identical in being signless."
By means of these causes and conditions, one is able to universally fulfill all Buddha-dharmas and can thereby realize the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they abide within the five aggregates of clinging—which are like a dream, an echo, a reflection, a shadow, a mirage, an illusion, and a transformation—and thereby fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline.

When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva understands, as they truly are, the five aggregates as being like a dream and even like a magical illusion, he is then able to fulfill the perfection of pure ethical discipline that is signless.

Such pure ethical discipline is without deficiency or flaw, without blemish or impurity; it is free from attachment, worthy of offerings, praised by the wise, excellently undertaken, and excellently brought to completion. It is noble, untainted, and subsumed within the factors of the supramundane path.

Abiding securely in this precept, one is able to properly receive and uphold the precepts of designation, the precepts acquired through the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the precepts of restraint (*saṃvara*), manifest precepts, non-manifest precepts, active precepts, non-active precepts, precepts of dignified conduct (*airyāpathika*), and precepts of non-dignified conduct.
"Although this bodhisattva-mahāsattva is fully accomplished in such precepts, he has no grasping or attachment toward any phenomena, nor does he form the thought:

'By means of these precepts, I shall be born into a great kṣatriya clan, or a great brāhmaṇa clan, or a great householder clan, or a great merchant clan, possessing wealth, nobility, and sovereign power.'"
One does not form this thought:
"By means of these precepts, I shall become a minor king, or a great king, or a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), or a minister, or attain wealth, nobility, and sovereign power."
He does not form this thought:
"By means of these precepts, I shall be reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings, up to the gods who Control the Creations of Others, possessing wealth, nobility, and sovereignty."
They do not form such thoughts as:

"By means of this precept, I shall attain the fruit of a stream-enterer, or the fruit of a once-returner, or the fruit of a non-returner, or the fruit of an arhat; or I shall enter the bodhisattva’s state of right determination, or attain the bodhisattva’s forbearance toward the non-arising of phenomena, or attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Why is this so? Because all such dharmas share one and the same characteristic, namely: being without characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*), non-abiding, and unattainable.

A dharma without characteristics cannot attain being without characteristics; a dharma with characteristics cannot attain having characteristics; a dharma without characteristics cannot attain having characteristics; and a dharma with characteristics cannot attain being without characteristics. For these reasons, there is ultimately nothing to be attained.
"So it is, Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they are swiftly able to fulfill the signless perfection of pure ethical discipline;
having fulfilled the signless perfection of pure ethical discipline, they swiftly enter the bodhisattva’s state of certainty and departure from birth."

Having entered the bodhisattva’s state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), they further attain the bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);

having attained the bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena, they practice the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and, proceeding toward the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), they obtain the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) as a result of maturation (*vipāka*).

Furthermore, they attain five hundred dharanī-gates and also five hundred samādhi-gates; abiding therein, they further realize the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid), traveling from one buddha-field to another to attend upon and make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, bringing sentient beings to maturity and adorning and purifying the buddha-fields.
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of transforming sentient beings, although manifests the transmigration through the various realms of birth and death, is not defiled by their faults."
Just as a person created by magical illusion may manifest the acts of walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, yet lacks any real activity such as coming or going;
and although they may manifest various ways of benefiting sentient beings, there is absolutely nothing to be apprehended regarding those sentient beings or their designations.

Suppose there were a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śāntaviśuddha, who had realized unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, turned the sublime wheel of Dharma, and delivered immeasurable multitudes, causing them to transcend birth and death and realize nirvāṇa; yet, there was no sentient being capable of receiving a prediction of attaining unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.

At that time, that Tathāgata manifested a transformation Buddha (nirmāṇa-buddha) to remain in the world for a long duration, while he himself relinquished the life-faculty (jīvita-saṃskāra) and entered the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder (anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu).

After that transformation body of the Buddha had remained for one kalpa and bestowed the prophecy of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) upon a bodhisattva, it then entered nirvāṇa.

Although that Buddha’s emanation performs various deeds to benefit sentient beings, he has no attainment; that is to say, he does not attain form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does he attain anything up to all contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena, as well as sentient beings.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva is also like this: although there is that which is performed, there is nothing attained. "It is thus, Subhūti!

When all bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline. Because they fulfill this perfection of ethical discipline, they are able to encompass all buddha-dharmas, and by means of this, they realize the knowledge of all modes."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they abide within the five aggregates of clinging—which are like a dream, like an echo, like a reflection, like a shadow, like a mirage, like a magical illusion, and like a transformation—and thereby fulfill the perfection of patience."

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva understands, as they truly are, the five aggregates as being like a dream and even like a magical illusion, he is then able to fulfill the perfection of signless patience.

“Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, truly understand the five aggregates as being like a dream and even like a magical creation, and thereby fulfill the signless perfection of patience?”

Subhūti! Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva understands, as they truly are, that these five aggregates of clinging lack any real characteristic, he cultivates two kinds of patience and is thus able to bring to perfection the perfection of patience characterized by signlessness.
What are these two? They are the patience of acceptance and the patience of discernment. Regarding the patience of acceptance:

it refers to when Bodhisattvas, from their first generation of the mind of awakening until they sit upon the sublime seat of enlightenment, should encounter all classes of sentient beings who come in competition to revile and disparage them, using coarse and evil words to scold and insult them, and further inflicting harm with tiles, stones, swords, and staves.

At that time, in order to fulfill the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), the Bodhisattva does not give rise to even a single thought of anger or resentment, nor does he conceive the intention to retaliate; rather, he thinks:

"Those sentient beings are deeply pitiable; their minds are agitated by the intensity of their afflictions (*kleśa*) such that they lack self-mastery, and thus they have initiated such evil karma against me. I should not harbor anger or hatred toward them."
He further reflects:
"Because I have grasped at these aggregates that are like enemies, those sentient beings have caused me to give rise to such evil karma; I should only reproach myself and not feel anger toward them."
When the Bodhisattva observes in this manner, he gives rise to profound compassion for those sentient beings; such categories as these are called "endurance through acceptance" (*kṣānti*).
Regarding "endurance through observation," it means that all Bodhisattvas reflect as follows:

"All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are like illusions, false and unreal, and lack autonomy. They are also like space, devoid of self (*anātman*). Sentient beings, life-principles, living beings, nourishers, persons, individuals, mind-born ones, youths, agents, experiencers, knowers, and seers are all unfindable; they arise solely from false conceptualization, and everything is a transformation of one’s own mind."
Who reviles me? Who abuses me? Who insults me?
Who is it that inflicts various injuries upon me with tiles, stones, swords, or staves?
And who is it that undergoes such insults and harm?

All this is merely the false conceptualization of one's own mind; I should not now give rise to groundless attachment. For all such phenomena are entirely non-existent, being empty of intrinsic nature and empty of ultimate reality.

"When a Bodhisattva observes in this manner, they understand all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as empty and quiescent in accordance with reality, and do not give rise to divergent conceptions regarding any phenomena; such categories are termed 'patience through observation' (*vipaśyanākṣānti*)."

"Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates these two kinds of patience, they are able to fulfill the perfection of patience that is signless (*animitta-kṣānti-pāramitā*). By fulfilling the perfection of patience that is signless, they immediately attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by the ‘patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas’?”
"What is this that is abandoned?
Furthermore, what is this wisdom?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"By the power of this, even the slightest portion of evil and unwholesome dharmas cannot arise; therefore, it is called the 'patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas' (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

This causes all afflictions such as pride regarding 'self' and 'mine' to never arise again, and allows one to truly endure and accept that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are like dreams, and even like magical illusions."
"This patience is called wisdom; because one attains this wisdom, it is said that one has 'attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas' (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is the distinction between the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas of the śrāvakas, the pratyekabuddhas, and the bodhisattvas?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Whatever wisdom or abandonment belongs to those who have entered the stream, up to whatever wisdom or abandonment belongs to the pratyekabuddhas, is also called the patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.”
Furthermore, there is the patience of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, which is the patience that all phenomena are ultimately non-arising; this constitutes the distinction.
"Subhūti, you should know that because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have accomplished such extraordinary patience, they surpass all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in this maturation-patience (*vipāka-kṣānti*) while practicing the bodhisattva path, they are able to fulfill the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*).

Because they have accomplished such knowledge of the aspects of the path, they are never separated from the four applications of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, nor are they separated from the three doors of liberation, nor are they separated from the supernormal powers of maturation.

By not being separated from the supernormal powers that ripen [their karma], they proceed from one buddha-field to another buddha-field, attending upon and making offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, maturing sentient beings, and purifying buddha-fields.
Having performed these deeds, by means of the wisdom associated with a single kṣaṇa, he realizes unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
"Thus it is, Subhūti!"
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they are able to swiftly fulfill the signless perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā).
Because this perfection of patience is fulfilled, they are able to fulfill all Buddha-dharmas, and thereby realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñājñāna).

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 467. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Two, Chapter on Non-confusion, Number Seventy-five, Part Two. "Furthermore, Subhūti!..."

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they dwell within the five aggregates of grasping—which are like a dream, an echo, an image, a reflection, a mirage, an illusion, and a transformation—and having realized as they truly are that these five aggregates, from being like a dream up to being like a transformation, lack any real characteristic, they arouse courageous physical and mental diligence.

“Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva has initiated courageous physical diligence, they have brought forth superior and swift supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). They are able to travel to Buddha-worlds in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, to approach the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and to offer, revere, honor, respect, and praise them with immeasurable kinds of sublime and excellent offerings. In the presence of those Buddhas, they plant various roots of goodness, benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings, and are also able to adorn and purify various Buddha-fields.”

By means of physical diligence, this bodhisattva mahāsattva brings sentient beings to maturity, establishing them each in the ultimate goal through the skillful means of the three vehicles according to what is appropriate for them.
"In this way, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they are able to swiftly fulfill the signless perfection of vigor through physical vigor."
Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva has aroused a courageous mind and diligence, they bring forth the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*)—
the perfect holy path comprised of the various noble, untainted path-factors (*ārya-anaśrava-mārgāṅga*). Within this, they are fully capable of encompassing all wholesome dharmas,
namely the four applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), as well as emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and non-existence (*abhāva*).
the signless and wishless doors of liberation; whether they be the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments;
whether they be the eight liberations up to the ten totalities; whether they be the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
or whether they be the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom; or...
From the Ground of Utmost Joy up to the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma; whether it be all the doors of dhāraṇī or the doors of samādhi;
whether it be inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence; whether it be suchness up to the inconceivable realm;
whether it be the five eyes or the six supernormal powers; or whether it be the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen [unique qualities].

The unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) consist of: the quality of being without forgetfulness, the state of constant abiding in equanimity, as well as all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
By means of mental diligence, this bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the perfection of all primary marks and secondary signs, and emits great radiance that illuminates boundless realms.

Because mental diligence is utterly perfected, he is able to forever sever the continuity of all afflictions and habitual tendencies, realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, and turn the wondrous wheel of Dharma endowed with the thirty-two marks, causing the three-thousandfold world system to shake in six ways.

The sentient beings therein, touched by the light, beholding these transformations, and hearing the sound of the True Dharma, attain non-retrogression in the path of the Three Vehicles according to their respective capacities, each reaching ultimate realization.

"So it is, Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they fulfill the perfection of diligence. By means of this perfection of diligence, they perform many deeds; these bodhisattva mahāsattvas, abiding in the perfection of diligence, are able to swiftly fulfill all Buddha-dharmas and rapidly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they abide within the five aggregates of clinging— which are like a dream, like an echo, like a reflection, like a shadow, like a mirage, like a magical illusion, and like a transformation— and thereby fulfill the perfection of meditative concentration."

Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, abide within the five aggregates of clinging—which are like a dream and even like a magical creation—and fulfill the perfection of meditative concentration?

This refers to when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, understands as they truly are that the five aggregates—from those like a dream up to those like a magical creation—are without real characteristics. Having done so, they enter the first *dhyāna* through to the fourth *dhyāna*; they enter the immeasurables of loving-kindness through to equanimity; they enter the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space through to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; they cultivate the three samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; they cultivate the lightning-like samādhi; they cultivate the diamond-like samādhi; they cultivate the noble and correct samādhi; and they abide within the diamond-like samādhi.

With the exception of the Tathāgata’s own meditative concentration, he is able to enter and fully abide in all other superior concentrations—whether shared with the two vehicles or otherwise—yet he does not give rise to attachment toward such dhyānas, immeasurables, or formless attainments, nor does he crave the fruits derived from them.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas understand, as it truly is, that the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), and all phenomena are identical in having no marks (*animitta*) and having non-existence as their nature; they should not relish the markless through the markless, nor should they relish non-existence through non-existence.

Because they are free from attachment to flavors, they never follow the power of the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), or the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) to be born in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) or the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Why is this so?

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva finds nothing at all to be apprehended within any realm; they find nothing to be apprehended regarding the one who enters meditative absorption, the absorption entered, the means by which one enters absorption, or the purpose for which one enters absorption.

"Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend any phenomena, he is able to swiftly fulfill the perfection of signless meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*); by means of this perfection of meditative concentration, he transcends the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
how does this bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfill the perfection of signless meditative concentration and transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva has well studied the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, he is able to fulfill the perfection of signless meditative concentration and transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
This bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells within all these emptinesses; regarding all phenomena, they find nothing at all to be apprehended, nor do they see any phenomenon that is apart from emptiness.

Abiding therein, this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not attain the fruit of a stream-enterer, up to and including the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, nor do they attain the practices of a bodhisattva or the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha, because these various forms of emptiness are themselves empty.
By dwelling in this emptiness, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas born?
By what are they separated from birth?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas take all that is apprehended as birth, and take all that is non-apprehended as freedom from birth."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
by what do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constitute ‘having something to be apprehended’?”
“What constitutes non-apprehension?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“For all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all dharmas constitute apprehension; that is to say, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas...”

The Bodhisattva takes form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as being objects of attainment; he takes the sense base of the eye up to the sense base of the mind as being objects of attainment;
he takes the sense base of form up to the sense base of phenomena as being objects of attainment;
he takes the element of the eye up to the element of the mind as being objects of attainment; and he takes the element of form up to the element of phenomena as being objects of attainment.
To have something to apprehend: to have something to apprehend in the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element;

to have something to apprehend in eye-contact up to mind-contact; to have something to apprehend in all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition up to all feelings produced with mind-contact as condition; and to have something to apprehend in the earth element up to...
The element of consciousness is apprehended; the causal conditions, up to and including the dominant condition, are apprehended;
ignorance, up to and including old age and death, are apprehended; the perfection of generosity, up to and including the perfection of wisdom, are apprehended;
and internal emptiness, up to and including the absence of intrinsic nature, are apprehended.
To regard the emptiness of intrinsic nature as an object of attainment; to regard true thusness, up to and including the inconceivable realm, as objects of attainment;

to regard the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path as objects of attainment; to regard the four applications of mindfulness, up to and including the eightfold noble path, as objects of attainment;
and to regard the liberations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness as objects of attainment.
To regard the doors of liberation as something to be attained; to regard the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments as something to be attained;
to regard the eight liberations up to the ten totalities as something to be attained;
to regard the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata as something to be attained; and to regard the stage of extreme joy up to the [Dharma]...
To regard the stage of clouds as something to be attained; to regard all the doors of dhāraṇī and the doors of samādhi as something to be attained;
to regard the five eyes and the six supernormal powers as something to be attained;
to regard the ten powers of a Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, as something to be attained; and to regard the thirty-two marks of a Great Man...

regarding the [major] marks and the eighty secondary signs as being objects of apprehension; regarding the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity as being objects of apprehension;
regarding all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects as being objects of apprehension;
and regarding the fruit of stream-entry up to the awakening of a pratyekabuddha as being objects of apprehension—by means of...

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas act as if there were something to be attained; they regard the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas as something to be attained, and they regard the knowledge of all modes as something to be attained.
"Subhūti! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas take such various dharma-gates as having something to be apprehended, that very apprehension of something is what is called 'arising'."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas take the fact that all dharmas are without activity, without attainment, without explanation, and without demonstration as being non-apprehendable."

It means that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas regard form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as non-attainable by virtue of their being without activity, without acquisition, without explanation, and without demonstration.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of form, up to and including the intrinsic nature of consciousness, cannot be practiced, attained, explained, or demonstrated.
Thus, for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the non-practice, non-attainment, non-explanation, and non-demonstration of the sense bases from the eye base up to the mind base constitute non-apprehension.

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of the sense-base of the eye, up to and including the intrinsic nature of the sense-base of the mind, cannot be practiced, attained, explained, or demonstrated.

Thus, for the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the absence of practice, attainment, explanation, and demonstration regarding the sense-bases of form, up to and including mental phenomena (*dharma*), constitutes non-apprehension.

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) up to the intrinsic nature of the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) are all unpracticable, unattainable, unspeakable, and undemonstrable.

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas take the absence of practice, attainment, speech, and demonstration regarding the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) up to the mind-element (*manodhātu*) as non-apprehension (*anupalambha*).
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) up to the intrinsic nature of the mind-element (*manodhātu*) cannot be practiced, attained, spoken of, or demonstrated.

Thus, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas take the absence of practice, attainment, speech, and demonstration regarding the form-element (*rūpadhātu*) up to the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) as non-apprehension (*anupalambha*).

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), up to and including the intrinsic nature of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), cannot be practiced, attained, explained, or demonstrated.

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas regard the non-practice, non-attainment, non-explanation, and non-demonstration of the eye-consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) up to and including the mental-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*) as "non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*).

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of the eye-consciousness element, up to and including the intrinsic nature of the mind-consciousness element, cannot be practiced, attained, spoken of, or demonstrated.
Thus, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas take the absence of practice, attainment, speech, and demonstration regarding eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact, as non-apprehension.
Why is this so? Because the intrinsic nature of visual contact, up to and including the intrinsic nature of mental contact, cannot be practiced, attained, explained, or demonstrated.

For Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the various feelings produced with visual contact as a condition, up to and including the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition, constitute non-apprehension because they are without practice, without attainment, without explanation, and without demonstration.

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including the intrinsic nature of all feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, cannot be practiced, attained, explained, or demonstrated.

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas regard the non-activity, non-attainment, non-explanation, and non-demonstration of the element of earth up to the element of consciousness as non-apprehension. Why is this so?
Because the intrinsic nature of the earth element, up to and including the intrinsic nature of the consciousness element, cannot be practiced, attained, explained, or demonstrated.

Thus, for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, the absence of practice, attainment, explanation, or demonstration regarding causal conditions, up to and including dominant conditions, constitutes non-apprehension.

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) up to the intrinsic nature of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) cannot be practiced, attained, spoken of, or demonstrated.

For all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the absence of practice, attainment, speech, or demonstration regarding everything from ignorance (*avidyā*) to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) constitutes non-apprehension (*anupalambha*).
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of ignorance, up to and including the intrinsic nature of old age and death, cannot be practiced, attained, explained, or demonstrated.

Thus, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas take the non-practice, non-attainment, non-explanation, and non-demonstration of the perfection of generosity, up to and including the perfection of wisdom, as "non-apprehension."

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of the perfection of generosity, up to and including the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom, cannot be practiced, attained, explained, or demonstrated.

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas regard the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature as being without practice, without attainment, without explanation, and without demonstration, such that they are non-apprehendable.

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of internal emptiness, up to and including the intrinsic nature of the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, cannot be practiced, attained, described, or demonstrated.
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas regard the non-practice, non-attainment, non-exposition, and non-demonstration of true thusness (tathatā) up to the inconceivable realm as non-apprehension.

Why is this? Because the self-nature of true thusness (*tathatā*), up to and including the self-nature of the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*), cannot be practiced, attained, spoken of, or demonstrated.

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas regard the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path as non-practice, non-attainment, non-exposition, and non-demonstration, thereby realizing non-apprehension.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path cannot be practiced, attained, explained, or demonstrated.

Thus, for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the absence of practice, attainment, explanation, or demonstration regarding the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path constitutes non-apprehension.

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including the intrinsic nature of the eightfold noble path, cannot be practiced, attained, explained, or demonstrated.

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas take the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—as being without practice, without attainment, without explanation, and without demonstration, thereby regarding them as non-apprehensible.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—is such that they cannot be practiced, attained, explained, or demonstrated.

Thus, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas regard the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments as non-practice, non-attainment, non-explanation, and non-demonstration, which constitutes their non-apprehension.
Why is this so? Because the intrinsic nature of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions cannot be practiced, attained, explained, or demonstrated.

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas regard the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality as non-practice, non-attainment, non-explanation, and non-demonstration, thereby taking them as non-apprehendable.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of the eight liberations up to the intrinsic nature of the ten totalities cannot be practiced, attained, explained, or demonstrated.

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas regard the stages from the Stage of Pure Observation up to the Tathāgata Stage as non-practice, non-attainment, non-explanation, and non-demonstration, which constitutes their "non-apprehension."

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of the stage of pure observation (*śuddhadarśana-bhūmi*) up to the intrinsic nature of the stage of the Tathāgata are all unpracticable, unattainable, unspeakable, and undemonstrable.

Thus, for the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the fact that the stages from the Stage of Extreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) up to the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*) are without practice, without attainment, without speech, and without demonstration constitutes their non-apprehension.

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of the Stage of Extreme Joy, up to and including the intrinsic nature of the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma, cannot be practiced, attained, explained, or demonstrated.

Thus, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas regard the fact that all dhāraṇī-doors and samādhi-doors are without practice, without attainment, without explanation, and without demonstration as "non-apprehension."
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of all dharani-doors and samadhi-doors cannot be practiced, attained, explained, or demonstrated.

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas regard the five eyes and six supernormal powers as non-attainment through their lack of activity, lack of acquisition, lack of verbalization, and lack of demonstration. Why is this so?
Because the intrinsic nature of the five eyes and the six supernormal powers cannot be practiced, attained, explained, or demonstrated;

likewise, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas take the non-practice, non-attainment, non-explanation, and non-demonstration of the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as "non-apprehension."
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of the Tathāgata’s ten powers, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, cannot be practiced, attained, explained, or demonstrated.

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas regard the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs as non-activity, non-attainment, non-explanation, and non-demonstration, thereby taking them as non-apprehension.
Why is this? Because the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs are, by their very nature, all unapproachable, unattainable, unspeakable, and unindicatable.

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas regard the dharma of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant abiding in equanimity as being without activity, without attainment, without explanation, and without demonstration, such that they are non-apprehendable.
Why is this? Because the nature of the qualities of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant abiding in equanimity is such that they cannot be practiced, attained, explained, or demonstrated.

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by means of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), take the absence of practice, the absence of attainment, the absence of explanation, and the absence of demonstration as non-apprehension.

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) cannot be practiced, attained, explained, or demonstrated.

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas regard the fruit of a stream-enterer up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha as non-attainment, because they are without activity, without acquisition, without explanation, and without demonstration.

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of the fruit of stream-entry, up to and including the intrinsic nature of the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, cannot be practiced, attained, described, or demonstrated.
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas take the non-practice, non-attainment, non-exposition, and non-demonstration of all bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices as non-apprehension.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of all practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is such that it cannot be practiced, attained, explained, or demonstrated.

Thus, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas regard the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as non-attainment because it is without practice, without attainment, without explanation, and without demonstration.
Why is this? Because the nature of the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas is such that it cannot be practiced, attained, explained, or demonstrated.
Thus, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by means of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), regard non-practice, non-attainment, non-explanation, and non-demonstration as non-apprehension.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of the knowledge of all modes is entirely beyond practice, attainment, expression, or demonstration. "Subhūti!..."

When all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, through such various dharma-gates, regard non-practice, non-attainment, non-exposition, and non-demonstration as non-apprehension, this very non-apprehension is termed "departure from birth."

Once the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have entered the stage of the certainty of correctness (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and perfected all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, and attainments (*samāpatti*), they do not even arise under the influence of those meditative states, much less under the influence of afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion!
It is impossible that they would arise through the power of secondary afflictions!
It is also impossible that this bodhisattva mahāsattva, while dwelling therein, would perform various karmas and, by the power of those karmas, transmigrate through the various realms of existence!

Although this bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells amidst the mass of conditioned phenomena that are like an illusion, he brings about the true benefit of all sentient beings, yet he does not apprehend either the illusion or those sentient beings.
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva finds nothing to be apprehended in such matters, they never grow weary or negligent in maturing sentient beings and purifying buddha-fields.
"It is thus, Subhūti!"
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they are swiftly able to fulfill the *dhyānapāramitā* of signlessness (*animitta*).

Because this *dhyānapāramitā* is swiftly fulfilled, they rapidly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), turn the wondrous wheel of Dharma, and deliver the multitudes of sentient beings; such a wheel of Dharma is called "non-apprehension" (*anupalambha*).

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they abide within the five aggregates of clinging— which are like a dream, like an echo, like a reflection, like a shadow, like a mirage, like a magical illusion, and like a transformation— and thereby fulfill the perfection of wisdom."

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva understands, as they truly are, that the nature and characteristics of all phenomena are entirely like a dream and even like a magical creation, he is then able to fulfill the signless prajñāpāramitā.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One,

how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, truly understand that the nature and characteristics of all phenomena are entirely like a dream, and even like a magical creation?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive dreams, nor do they perceive one who sees a dream;
they do not hear echoes, nor do they perceive one who hears an echo."
One does not see the image, nor does one see the one who sees the image;
one does not see the reflection, nor does one see the one who sees the reflection;
one does not see the mirage, nor does one see the one who sees the mirage.
One does not see the illusion, nor does one see the one who sees the illusion;
one does not see the transformation, nor does one see the one who sees the transformation. Why is this so?

Dreams, and so forth up to emanations, are all that which foolish ordinary beings cling to through their inversions; yet the Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, the assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, and the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, do not perceive dreams, nor do they perceive those who see dreams;
and so on, up to not perceiving emanations, nor perceiving those who see emanations.

Why is this? Because all dharmas have non-existence as their nature; they are neither produced nor real, being signless and unconditioned. They do not possess a truly existent nature and are equal to nirvāṇa.

If all phenomena have non-existence as their nature, and so on, up to being equal to nirvāṇa, how is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they give rise to the notion of existence, the notion of formation, the notion of reality, the notion of marks, the notion of the conditioned, and the notion of a real nature regarding all phenomena?
If one were to give rise to such a thought, it would be impossible. Why is this?

If all phenomena possessed even the slightest intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), if they were established or real, if they possessed characteristics or were conditioned, or if a real nature could be apprehended therein, then the practice of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* would not be *prajñāpāramitā*.
"In this way, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not cling to form up to consciousness;
they do not cling to the eye base up to the mind base; they do not cling to the form base up to the mental phenomena base."
He does not cling to the eye-element up to the mind-element; he does not cling to the form-element up to the phenomena-element;
he does not cling to the eye-consciousness-element up to the mind-consciousness-element; he does not cling to eye-contact up to mind-contact;
and he does not cling to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition.
They do not cling to the element of earth, up to and including the element of consciousness; they do not cling to the causal condition, up to and including the dominant condition;
they do not cling to the various phenomena produced from conditions; they do not cling to ignorance, up to and including old age and death;
they do not cling to the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; they do not cling to any of the meditative concentrations, liberations, or...
They do not cling to the dhāraṇīs or meditative attainments; they do not cling to the four applications of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path;
they do not cling to the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; they do not cling to the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
they do not cling to the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path. They do not...
They do not cling to inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature; they do not cling to suchness up to the inconceivable realm;
they do not cling to the stage of pure observation up to the stage of a Tathāgata; they do not cling to the stage of extreme joy up to the stage of the Dharma-cloud;
they do not cling to any of the doors of dhāraṇī or the doors of samādhi; they do not cling...
They do not cling to the five eyes or the six supernormal powers; they do not cling to the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they do not cling to the thirty-two marks of a great man or the eighty secondary signs;
they do not cling to the quality of non-forgetfulness or the nature of constant equanimity; they do not cling to all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, or all-aspect knowledge.
The wisdom of signs does not cling to the fruit of stream-entry up to and including the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;

it does not cling to any of the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva; it does not cling to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas; and it does not cling to the knowledge of all modes.

"When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, because they do not cling to any such dharma-gates, they are able to fulfill the first through the tenth bodhisattva grounds, yet they do not give rise to craving or attachment toward them."

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not apprehend the perfection of the first through the tenth stages, nor the subject and object of that perfection; how then could they give rise to attachment toward them?

Although this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not apprehend the profound perfection of wisdom; because they do not apprehend the profound perfection of wisdom, they likewise do not apprehend any phenomena.
Although this bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates that the perfection of wisdom encompasses all phenomena, they do not apprehend any phenomenon whatsoever. Why is this?
All phenomena and this perfection of wisdom are non-dual and without distinction. Why is this?
Because the nature of all phenomena cannot be conceptually differentiated as suchness, nor as the dharma-realm, nor as the limit of reality; for all phenomena are unmixed and without differentiation.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If all dharmas are by nature unmixed and without distinction, how can one speak of such differentiated categories of dharmas as being wholesome or unwholesome, determinate or indeterminate, with outflows or without outflows, mundane or supramundane, conditioned or unconditioned, and so forth?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “What do you think?

Within the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), is there any phenomenon that can be described as wholesome or unwholesome, determinate or indeterminate, with outflows or without outflows, mundane or supramundane, conditioned or unconditioned, the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, the fruit of arhatship, the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, the practice of any bodhisattva mahāsattva, or the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas?”
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"By this cause and condition, you should know that all dharmas are unmixed, without distinction, without marks, without arising, without cessation, without obstruction, without speech, and without demonstration."
"Subhūti, you should know that when I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, I attained nothing at all regarding the intrinsic nature of phenomena;
