that is to say, I did not attain form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, nor did I attain the sense bases from the eye base up to the mind base."
One does not apprehend the sphere of forms, up to and including the sphere of phenomena; one does not apprehend the eye element, up to and including the mind element;
one does not apprehend the form element, up to and including the phenomenon element; one does not apprehend the eye-consciousness element, up to and including the mind-consciousness element;

one does not apprehend eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact; and one does not apprehend the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, up to and including [feelings produced with] mind-contact.
The various feelings produced with contact as a condition cannot be apprehended; from the earth element up to the consciousness element, they cannot be apprehended.
From the causal condition up to the dominant condition, they cannot be apprehended. The various phenomena produced from conditions cannot be apprehended.
From ignorance up to old age and death, they cannot be apprehended. The desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm cannot be apprehended. The wholesome cannot be apprehended.
...it is not wholesome; it cannot be designated as either determinate or indeterminate; it cannot be designated as either outflow-tainted or outflow-free;
it cannot be designated as either mundane or supramundane; it cannot be designated as either conditioned or unconditioned;
it cannot be designated as the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path; it cannot be designated as the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the four...
One does not attain the formless absorptions, nor the eight liberations up to the ten totalities;
one does not attain the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; one does not attain the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
one does not attain the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom; one does not attain the internal...
From emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, one does not apprehend suchness up to the inconceivable realm;
one does not apprehend the stage of pure observation up to the stage of a Tathāgata; one does not apprehend the stage of extreme joy up to the stage of the cloud of dharma;
one does not apprehend any doors of dhāraṇī or doors of samādhi; and one does not apprehend the five eyes.
...the six supernormal powers; they do not attain the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they do not attain the thirty-two marks of a great man or the eighty minor marks; they do not attain the quality of non-forgetfulness or the nature of constant equanimity;
they do not attain all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, or the knowledge of all aspects.
One cannot attain the fruit of stream-entry up to and including the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; one cannot attain any of the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva;
and one cannot attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas.

"In this way, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, from their first generation of the mind until they sit upon the seat of sublime awakening, they should always train well in the intrinsic nature of all phenomena."

If one can skillfully study the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, then one will be able to thoroughly purify the path to great enlightenment, fulfill all bodhisattva practices, ripen sentient beings, and adorn and purify buddha-fields. One will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, turn the wondrous wheel of Dharma, and through the skillful means of the three vehicles, tame the multitudes of sentient beings, causing them no longer to transmigrate within the three realms of existence and leading them to realize the ultimate peace and happiness of nirvana.
"In this way, Subhūti, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should train in the perfection of wisdom by employing the method of signlessness."
Chapter 76: The Chapter on the Marks of Multitudinous Virtues, Part One. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
If all phenomena are without exception like a dream, an echo, a reflection, a shadow, a mirage, an illusion,
and a magical creation— lacking any substantial reality, having non-existence as their nature, and being empty of intrinsic characteristics—
how can one establish that something is wholesome or unwholesome, or determinate or indeterminate?
These are with outflows (*sāsrava*), these are without outflows (*anāsrava*); these are mundane (*laukika*), these are supramundane (*lokottara*);

these are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), these are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Thus, even up to: these are the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*), these are the dharmas capable of realizing the fruit of stream-entry;
these are the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*), these are the dharmas capable of realizing the fruit of once-returning; these are the fruit of... [non-returning].
The fruit of the non-returner, which is the dharma capable of realizing the fruit of the non-returner; the fruit of the arhat, which is the dharma capable of realizing the fruit of the arhat;
the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, which is the dharma capable of realizing the awakening of a pratyekabuddha;
and the stages of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, which are the dharmas capable of realizing the [stages] of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Are these the dharmas of the stages of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, and are they the dharmas by which the unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas is realized?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Worldly fools, unlearned ordinary beings, perceive dreams and perceive those who see dreams; likewise, they even perceive emanations and perceive those who see emanations."

In this way, foolish worldlings who have not heard the Dharma, having encountered dreams up to and including emanations and so forth, grasp at them with perversion; they may perform unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind, or they may perform wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind, or they may perform indeterminate actions of body, speech, and mind; they may perform non-meritorious actions of body, speech, and mind, or they may perform meritorious actions of body, speech, and mind, or they may perform immovable actions of body, speech, and mind. By means of these volitional formations, they come and go within birth and death, revolving without end.
"When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they observe all phenomena through two kinds of emptiness.
What are these two kinds of emptiness?"

"At that time, the Bodhisattva, possessing skillful means and great supernormal power, employs expedient means to rescue and deliver those sentient beings who possess stinginess and greed, causing them to be free from such states. Once these sentient beings have become free from stinginess and greed, he instructs them to cultivate the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). By virtue of this giving, these sentient beings attain great wealth, status, prosperity, and mastery."

Furthermore, from this state, he skillfully delivers them and instructs them to cultivate the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*); by means of this ethical discipline, these sentient beings attain birth in the higher realms with honor, nobility, and sovereignty.

Furthermore, from this state, he employs skillful means to rescue and deliver them, instructing them to cultivate the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*); by means of this patience, these sentient beings are able to swiftly attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Furthermore, from this state, they employ skillful means to rescue and deliver them, instructing them to cultivate the perfection of diligence; by means of this diligence, these sentient beings shall never again regress from any wholesome dharmas until they reach unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, from this state, they skillfully deliver them and, according to what is appropriate for each, cause them to abide in one of the three vehicles;
or cause them to abide in the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; or cause them to abide in the three doors of liberation;
or cause them to abide in the eight liberations up to the ten totalities; or cause them to abide in the four noble truths; or cause them...
They cause them to abide in the six *pāramitās*, or cause them to abide in inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;
or cause them to abide in suchness up to the inconceivable realm; or cause them to abide in the stage of Extreme Joy up to the stage of Dharma Cloud;
or cause them to abide in the gates of *dhāraṇī* and the gates of *samādhi*; or cause them to abide...
They cause them to abide in the five eyes and the six supernormal powers; or they cause them to abide in the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
or they cause them to abide in the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity;
or they cause them to abide in all-knowledge, the knowledge of paths, and the knowledge of all aspects.

“By means of skillful means, this bodhisattva mahāsattva, seeing that sentient beings are attached to the karmic fruits obtained from conditioned generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, and other wholesome dharmas, comforts and delivers them through various expedients, causing them to abide in the realm of nirvana without remainder.”

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom through skillful means, achieves the truly untainted dharmas that are formless, invisible, and non-obstructive, and dwells therein. If there are sentient beings who should attain the fruit of a stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, arhat, or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, or even unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, he manifests himself before them, exhorts, encourages, inspires, and gladdens them, employing skillful means to rescue and deliver them, causing them to attain the fruit of a stream-enterer, and so on, up to causing them to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"So it is, Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they contemplate the two kinds of emptiness. Although they know that all phenomena are like dreams and even like magical illusions—none of which are real, all of which have non-existence as their nature, and whose specific characteristics are entirely empty—they are nevertheless able to establish wholesome and unwholesome phenomena. As explained at length, up to and including the realization of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas, all of this is without confusion."

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 468. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Second Division, Chapter on the Characteristics of All Virtues, Number Seventy-Six, Part Two. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

The bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are truly rare and marvelous; practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and contemplating the two kinds of emptiness, they know that all phenomena are like dreams, echoes, reflections, shadows, mirages, illusions, and transformations—all of which are not substantially existent, having non-existence as their nature, and being empty of intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). Yet, they are able to establish the distinctions between phenomena such as the wholesome and the unwholesome, all without any confusion.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.

These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are truly rare; practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they contemplate the two kinds of emptiness. Although they know that all phenomena are like dreams and so forth, being entirely without real existence, having non-existence as their very nature, and being empty of intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), they are nevertheless able to establish the distinctions between phenomena such as the wholesome and the unwholesome, without confusing them.

If you were to know all the most marvelous and extraordinary qualities possessed by bodhisattva mahāsattvas when they practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*—qualities which neither śrāvakas nor pratyekabuddhas have accomplished and cannot fathom—then all of you śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas would not even be able to match the eloquence of these bodhisattva mahāsattvas, let alone be able to provide a response!
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“What are those most marvelous and extraordinary qualities of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas that arise when they practice the profound perfection of wisdom—qualities which śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not possess and cannot fathom?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!"
Reflect upon this well; I shall now analyze and explain for you all the most marvelous and extraordinary dharmas that arise when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound Prajñāpāramitā.

“Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they abide in the maturation of the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom; or in the five supernormal powers; or in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; or in dhāraṇīs; or in samādhis; or in the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; or in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; or in the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative concentrations, and the ten totalities; or in other immeasurable and boundless buddha-dharmas.”
Going to the worlds of the ten directions, if there are sentient beings who should be gathered through generosity up to wisdom, he gathers them through generosity up to wisdom;

if they should be gathered through the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he gathers them through the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
if they should be gathered through loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity, he gathers them through loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity.
Those who should be sustained by the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, one sustains them with the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
those who should be sustained by the three samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, one sustains them with the three samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
and those who should be sustained by other various wholesome dharmas, one sustains them with those other various wholesome dharmas.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, abide in the perfections of maturation, the five supernormal powers, and other immeasurable merits, and thereby gather in all sentient beings through giving and the other perfections?"

The Buddha told Subhūti: "When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they give to sentient beings whatever things they require: if they require food and drink, they give them food and drink; if they require clothing, they give them clothing; if they require vehicles, they give them vehicles; if they require flowers and incense, they give them flowers and incense; if they require bedding and seats, they give them bedding and seats; if they require houses and dwellings, they give them houses and dwellings; if they require lamps and light, they give them lamps and light; if they require medicine, they give them medicine; and if they require any other various kinds of requisites, they give them all so that there is no lack."

Or they may give to śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, dwellings, requisites, various exquisite flowers and incense, precious banners, pennants, canopies, music, lamps, ghee and oil, and all other such articles of offering.

When giving in this manner, one practices generosity with a mind of equanimity, free from discriminatory thoughts; as one gives to those who observe the precepts, so too does one give to those who violate them;
as one gives to those of the human realm, so too does one give to non-humans;
as one gives to those of the inner path, so too does one give to those of the outer paths.
Just as one gives to the noble ones, so too does one give to ordinary beings;
just as one gives to those of high status, so too does one give to those of low station.
From the Buddhas above down to the animals below, [the mind] is perfectly equal and without discrimination, not observing any difference in the superiority or inferiority of the field of merit.

Why is this? Because all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas thoroughly understand that all self-characteristics are empty; since within emptiness there is no distinction of high or low, they practice giving without conceptual differentiation or discrimination.

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving without conceptual differentiation and without discursive thought, they shall attain the non-differentiated and non-conceptual Dharma—namely, the attainment of the complete knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) and other immeasurable qualities of the Buddhas.
“Subhūti, you should know that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees one among the animals or others who comes to beg, they should give rise to this thought:
‘Since this person who has come to beg is either a Tathāgata, an Arhat, or a Samyaksaṃbuddha— the true field of merit— I ought to give to them.’”
"If it were not for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, these beings such as animals would not be fields of merit; therefore, one should not give them the requisites they require.
For a bodhisattva mahāsattva to give rise to such a thought is to transgress the bodhisattva dharma.
Why is this? Because for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the field of merit must first be purified by purifying one's own mind.
Upon seeing a beggar, they should not think:
"If one thinks, 'To such a sentient being who comes begging, I should give;

to such a sentient being who comes begging, I should not give,' one violates the original great bodhicitta that was generated. This refers to when Bodhisattvas generate the mind of enlightenment, thinking:
'I shall act as a refuge, an island, a dwelling, and a place of protection for all sentient beings.'"
Upon seeing one who comes to beg, he should give rise to this thought:
"Now this sentient being is poor, destitute, and exposed; I shall embrace them through giving.

By reason of this, they will not steal the property of others, will have few desires and be content, and will be able to give to others in turn. Through these causes and conditions, they will abstain from taking life—and so on, as extensively described, up to abstaining from frivolous speech—and will also be able to subdue greed, malice, and wrong views. At the dissolution of the body after death, by virtue of their prior meritorious karma, they will be reborn into a great kṣatriya clan, or a great brāhmaṇa clan, or a great householder clan, or a great merchant clan, or some other wealthy family, possessing abundant wealth and jewels, and practicing various wholesome deeds."

Or, through the causal conditions of gathering others by means of giving, they gradually rely upon the three vehicles to proceed toward parinirvāṇa; that is to say, they cause them to attain the realm of parinirvāṇa of the Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, and Anuttarayāna vehicles.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! If there should be enemies or other sentient beings who come to where a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells for the purpose of causing harm, or if they are destitute and beg for his limbs or various material possessions."
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva should never give rise to a discriminatory mind, thinking:
"This should be given; this should not be given.
Rather, they should generate a mind of equanimity and bestow upon those who seek it all parts of their body as well as all material wealth.

Why is this? It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas seek to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of universally benefiting all sentient beings, and not for the sake of their own personal benefit, happiness, or life.
If one were to give rise to a discriminating and dualistic mind, thinking: "This should be given;

this should not be given," one would be censured by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as well as by the Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and the assembly of noble ones among the world's devas, humans, and asuras.

"Who requested that you give rise to the bodhicitta, vowing to universally benefit and bring happiness to all classes of sentient beings—acting as a refuge for those without refuge, a dwelling for those without a dwelling, an island for those without an island, and a protector for those without protection; and bringing peace and happiness to those who lack it? Yet now, why do you discriminate between those to whom you give and those from whom you withhold?"

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, if a human or a non-human being comes to him and begs for various kinds of marrow, brain, or limbs and joints."
This bodhisattva mahāsattva should not give rise to the dualistic discrimination of "giving" or "not giving," but should instead form this thought:
"I shall certainly grant whatever they request."
Why is this? It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constantly maintain this thought:

"I have received this body for the sake of bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings; whenever anyone comes to me seeking anything, I must certainly give it to them, and I should not fail to give."
Therefore, upon seeing a beggar, he immediately gives rise to this thought:

"This body of mine was originally received for the sake of others; since I should have delivered it to them even if they had not come to take it, how much more so when they come to beg—how could I fail to give!"
Having formed this thought, he was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; he dislocated his own limbs and gave them to him, further congratulating himself, saying:
"I have now attained a great benefit, in that I have cast off impurity to obtain a body of pure essence."
“Subhūti! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the profound perfection of wisdom should train in this way.
Furthermore, Subhūti!”
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon seeing a beggar, gives rise to this thought:
"Now, within this context, who is the giver?
Who is the receiver?"
What is the object given?
By what means is it given?
For what purpose is it given?
How does one practice giving?
The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is entirely unattainable. Why is this so?
"In this way, all these phenomena are ultimately empty; within the emptiness of phenomena, there is no giving or taking, no bestowing or receiving. Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should train in the emptiness of all phenomena in this manner—namely, that they are empty by virtue of internal emptiness, and so on, up to being empty by virtue of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in this emptiness while practicing generosity, constantly and without interruption fulfilling the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*). Because this perfection of generosity has been fulfilled, when others cut, maim, or plunder all internal and external things from him, his mind is entirely free of conceptualization or resentment; he thinks only this:
"Sentient beings and all phenomena are entirely empty. Who is it that cuts me?"
Who robs me? Who receives it? Who makes such an observation?

"Furthermore, Subhūti! With my Buddha-eye, I behold throughout the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, desiring to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, intentionally enter the great hells by means of their vows. Seeing sentient beings undergoing various intense sufferings, and having seen them, they give rise to the three kinds of demonstrations."
What are the three?
First, the demonstration through miraculous powers;
second, the demonstration through mind-reading prophecy.
Third is the guidance through instruction.

By means of the guidance of miraculous powers (*ṛddhiprātihārya*), this bodhisattva mahāsattva eliminates the various instruments of suffering in the hells, such as boiling water, fire, and blades; by means of the guidance of telepathic declaration (*ādeśanāprātihārya*), he declares the thoughts in the minds of those sentient beings and preaches the Dharma for them; and by means of the guidance of instruction (*anuśāsanīprātihārya*), he gives rise to loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity toward them and preaches the Dharma for them.

May all sentient beings in those hells give rise to pure faith toward the Bodhisattva; by this cause and condition, may they emerge from hell and be reborn in the heavens or among humans, gradually relying upon the Three Vehicles to reach the ultimate limit of suffering and realize the state of Nirvana, which is supreme peace and bliss.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

With my Buddha-eye, I survey throughout the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and see bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who serve and make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones."

When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva serves and makes offerings to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, he does so with a profound mind of joy, delight, and reverence; it is not that he lacks joy, delight, and reverence.

Regarding the sublime Dharma taught by all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, they listen with reverence, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, and never forget it until reaching unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; according to the teachings they have heard, they are able to proclaim them unerringly to sentient beings, causing them to obtain supreme benefit and peace.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

With my Buddha-eye, I survey throughout the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and see bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, desiring to benefit sentient beings within the realm of animals, sacrifice their own bodies and lives."

When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva sees various animals oppressed by the fires of hunger and about to harm one another, he gives rise to a heart of compassion and pity; he severs his own body and cuts off his limbs and joints, scattering them throughout the ten directions to let them eat as they please.

When any among the various classes of animals eat the flesh of this bodhisattva’s body, they all develop a profound sense of love, respect, shame, and remorse toward the bodhisattva. By virtue of these causes and conditions, they are liberated from the animal realm and are reborn in the heavens or among human beings. There, they encounter a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, hear the teaching of the True Dharma, and practice according to reality. Gradually relying upon the three vehicles, they proceed toward parinirvāṇa—meaning they successively realize and enter the unsurpassed Mahāyāna, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, or the Śrāvaka vehicle of parinirvāṇa.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to perform for the world deeds that are difficult to perform and bring great benefit; that is to say, for the sake of the welfare, happiness, and liberation of all sentient beings, they themselves generate the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and cause others to generate it as well, and they themselves practice various kinds of authentic and correct conduct and cause others to practice them as well.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! With my Buddha-eye,
I behold throughout the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who,
out of a deliberate intention and vow, desire to benefit the sentient beings within the realm of hungry ghosts."
Entering that realm, he employs skillful means to pacify and eliminate sufferings such as hunger and thirst;
once the manifold sufferings of the hungry ghosts have been stilled, they develop a heart of deep affection, reverence, and a sense of shame toward this bodhisattva.

He then further proclaims for them the essential teachings on transcending stinginess, so that upon hearing them, they give rise to the mind of generous giving and, by virtue of these roots of goodness, are liberated from the realm of hungry ghosts.
Those in the realm of hungry ghosts may be reborn in the heavens or among human beings, where they encounter a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha;
having made offerings and shown reverence, they hear the sound of the true Dharma and gradually practice the correct conduct of the three vehicles,
eventually realizing and entering the parinirvāṇa realm of the unsurpassed Mahāyāna, the Pratyekabuddhas, or the Śrāvakas.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in great compassion toward sentient beings, giving rise to boundless skillful means to lead them, according to their capacities, to realize entry into the nirvāṇa of the three vehicles.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

With my Buddha-eye, I survey throughout the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, where there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, through their skillful means, proclaim the true Dharma for the gods of the Four Great Kings, and so on, up to proclaiming the true Dharma for the gods of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven."

Having heard the True Dharma from the Bodhisattva, these hosts of devas gradually rely upon the three vehicles to diligently cultivate correct practice, and accordingly realize entry into the realm of parinirvāṇa.

Subhūti, you should know that among those hosts of devas, there are sons of gods who are deeply attached to the five kinds of exquisite sensual pleasures of the heavens and to the various jeweled palaces where they dwell. To cause them to give rise to weariness and fear, this bodhisattva mahāsattva manifests a fire that burns their palaces, and then preaches the Dharma for their sake, saying:
"Sons of gods!..."

"One should carefully observe that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, and cannot be relied upon with confidence; what wise person would take delight in or become attached to them?

At that time, having heard this sound of the Dharma, the sons of the gods conceived a profound sense of weariness and fear toward the five kinds of exquisite sensual desires. They observed their own bodies and lives as false and impermanent, like plantain trees, flashes of lightning, or mirages, and they viewed the various palaces as if they were prisons.

Having made this contemplation, they gradually rely upon the three vehicles to diligently cultivate correct practice and proceed toward parinirvāṇa; that is to say, they gradually realize entry into the nirvāṇa of the three vehicles.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

With my Buddha-eye, I survey throughout the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and see bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, seeing that the various Brahmā devas are attached to various views and inclinations, employ skillful means to transform and guide them, causing them to grow weary of and abandon those attachments, and say to them:
"O celestial seers!..."
Why do you give rise to such evil views regarding these conditioned aggregates, which are empty, signless, illusory, and unreal?
You should quickly abandon them, accept the true Dharma with faith, and thereby bring about your own benefit and happiness for a long night!
"In this way, Subhūti, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
abiding in great compassion, proclaim the essentials of the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings. Subhūti!"
This is the most marvelous and extraordinary quality possessed by bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
Furthermore, Subhūti, with my unobstructed and pure Buddha-eye,

I survey throughout the ten directions all worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, seeing bodhisattva mahāsattvas who gather in sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
What are the four? First, giving; second, kind speech.
Third is beneficial conduct;
fourth is cooperation. "Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva gather sentient beings through the practice of giving? Subhūti!
Bodhisattva mahāsattvas gather sentient beings through two kinds of giving.
What are the two? First, the gift of material wealth;
second, the gift of the Dharma.
“Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva gather in sentient beings through the gift of material wealth? Subhūti!”
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they are able to give various kinds of food and drink,
clothing, dwellings, bedding, vehicles, lamps, music, incense and flowers,
precious banners, pennants, canopies, and necklaces to all sentient beings; or else, with...
He gives gold, silver, vaidūrya gems, sphatika gems, conch shells, jade, indranīla, mahānīla,
maṇi-jewels, pearls, stone treasuries, mace-treasuries, red lotuses, and other such jewels to sentient beings;
or he gives his wives and concubines, sons and daughters, male and female servants, and attendants.
One gives to sentient beings such things as lands, elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, and medicine;
or one gives to sentient beings various kinds of wealth, treasures, treasuries, cities, villages, and royal thrones;
or one gives to sentient beings parts of one's own body, such as hands, feet, limbs, joints, head, eyes, marrow, and brain.
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva places various kinds of objects at the crossroads and ascends a high platform, proclaiming these words:

"All sentient beings who have any need, come and take as you please; do not harbor doubt or hesitation. Take them as if they were your own property and do not entertain thoughts of them as belonging to another. Even my own body, hands, feet, limbs, head, eyes, marrow, and brain—take them as you wish; I have no stinginess toward you."
"Having given to sentient beings whatever things they require, this bodhisattva mahāsattva further exhorts them to take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha;
or exhorts them to receive and uphold the five precepts of a lay follower (upāsaka); or exhorts them to receive and uphold the eight precepts of the one-day fast (upavāsa);
or exhorts them to receive and uphold the ten paths of wholesome action; or exhorts them to practice and study the first [dhyāna]..."
They encourage the cultivation of the dhyānas up to the fourth dhyāna; or they encourage the cultivation of the immeasurables from loving-kindness (*maitrī*) up to equanimity (*upekṣā*);
or they encourage the cultivation of the meditative attainments from the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;

or they encourage the cultivation of the recollections from the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*) up to the recollection of the deities (*devatānusmṛti*); or they encourage the cultivation of the meditation on impurity (*aśubha*).
They may encourage the practice of contemplation and mindfulness of breathing; or encourage the cultivation of the perception of impermanence up to the perception of cessation;
or encourage the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
or encourage the cultivation of the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; or encourage the cultivation of the eight liberations up to the ten universal bases.
Some are exhorted to practice and study the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
some are exhorted to abide in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the nature of non-existence;
some are exhorted to abide in suchness up to the inconceivable realm; and some are exhorted to abide in the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
Some are exhorted to cultivate and study all *dhāraṇī* gates and *samādhi* gates;

some are exhorted to cultivate and study from the Stage of Pure Observation up to the Tathāgata Stage; some are exhorted to cultivate and study from the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Dharma-Cloud Stage;
some are exhorted to cultivate and study the five eyes and the six supernormal powers; and some are exhorted to cultivate and study the ten [powers] of a Tathāgata.
From the [ten] powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, they may encourage the cultivation and study of the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks;
or they may encourage the cultivation and study of the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity;

or they may encourage the cultivation and study of all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); or they may encourage the cultivation...
They cause others to train for the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; or they exhort them to train in all the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva;
or they exhort them to train in the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas.

“In this way, Subhūti, bodhisattva mahāsattvas practicing the profound perfection of wisdom with skillful means, having first bestowed material gifts upon sentient beings, further skillfully establish those classes of sentient beings, causing them to abide in the unsurpassed dharma of peace and security, even unto the attainment of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).”
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
This is the most marvelous and extraordinary quality possessed by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom.
Suvikrāntavikrāmin!”
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, gather in all sentient beings through the gift of Dharma?
Subhūti, there are two kinds of the gift of Dharma; what are these two?
First is the gift of Dharma pertaining to the mundane world;
second is the gift of Dharma pertaining to the supramundane.
What is called the gift of Dharma pertaining to the mundane world?

This refers to when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, while practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, proclaim, reveal, analyze, and clarify the sublime worldly dharmas for the sake of all sentient beings—namely, the contemplation of impurity, mindfulness of breathing, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the five supernormal powers, or other worldly dharmas shared with ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). This is called the gift of worldly dharmas.
"Subhūti! For what reason is this dharma called 'mundane'?
It is because those who study this dharma have not yet been able to ultimately transcend the world; therefore, it is called mundane."

“Subhūti! Having performed this sublime gift of Dharma for the world, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas transform and guide sentient beings through various skillful means, causing them to distance themselves from all worldly dharmas; they transform and guide sentient beings through various skillful means, causing them to abide in the noble dharmas and the fruits of the noble dharmas.”
"Subhūti! What are the noble dharmas and the fruit of the noble dharmas? Subhūti!"
The "noble dharmas" refers to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the three gates of liberation, and so forth;
the "fruits of the noble dharmas" refers to the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
“Subhūti! Why is this dharma called ‘transcending the world’?
It is because by training in this dharma, one is able to bring about ultimate departure from the world; therefore, it is called transcending the world.”

"Furthermore, Subhūti! The noble dharmas of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas consist of the six pāramitās; the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten bases of totality; the doors of dhāraṇī and the doors of samādhi; the bodhisattva stages; the five eyes and the six superknowledges; the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity; the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; the quality of non-forgetfulness, the nature of constant abiding in equanimity, all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects—these and other such untainted dharmas."
The fruit of the noble dharmas refers to the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of a Buddha and the realm of great parinirvāṇa. "Furthermore, Subhūti,
the noble dharmas of bodhisattva mahāsattvas refer to the knowledge of the fruit of stream-entry and the knowledge of the fruit of once-returning."

the knowledge of the fruit of non-returning, the knowledge of the fruit of arhatship, the knowledge of pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, and the knowledge of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas; the knowledge of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
the knowledge of the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four...
The knowledge of the formless attainments; the knowledge of the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative concentrations, and the ten totalities;
the knowledge of the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
the knowledge of all dhāraṇī-doors and samādhi-doors; and the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
The wisdom of the [four] truths; the wisdom of inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;
the wisdom of suchness up to the inconceivable realm; the wisdom of the Joyful Ground up to the Cloud of Dharma Ground; the wisdom of the five eyes and six supernormal powers;
the wisdom of the Stage of Pure Contemplation up to the Tathāgata Ground; and the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen [unshared dharmas].

The knowledge of the Buddha’s unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*); the knowledge of the thirty-two marks of a great man (*dvātriṃśan-mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*) and the eighty secondary signs (*aśīty-anuvyañjana*);

the knowledge of the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣa-dharma*) and the nature of constant equanimity (*upekṣā-sthiti*); the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all-aspect-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*);

the knowledge of wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*) and unwholesome phenomena (*akuśala-dharma*); and the knowledge of determinate phenomena (*vyākṛta-dharma*) and indeterminate phenomena (*avyākṛta-dharma*).
Knowledge of contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena, knowledge of mundane and supramundane phenomena,
and knowledge of conditioned and unconditioned phenomena— these are called the noble dharmas.
"The fruit of the noble Dharma refers to the permanent severance of the continuity of all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies; this is called the fruit of the noble Dharma.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“Can all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas also attain the knowledge of all aspects?
The Buddha told Subhūti: “It is so!”
"It is so! These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are also called those who are able to attain all-aspect omniscience.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is also said to be able to attain all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), what difference is there between them and the Buddha, the World-Honored One?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Bodhisattva mahāsattvas are said to be ‘those who are attaining all-aspect omniscience,’ whereas the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are said to be ‘those who have already attained all-aspect omniscience.’”

Why is this? It is because Bodhisattvas are not categorically different from the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. That is to say, both Bodhisattvas and Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, abide together in the non-differentiated nature of all phenomena (*dharmāṇām aviśeṣatā*). One who seeks perfect and complete enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) regarding the characteristics of all phenomena is called a Bodhisattva; when that state reaches its ultimate consummation, one is called a Buddha, the World-Honored One.

However, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, clearly perceives all phenomena—both their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)—without any obscuration; being pure and fully perfected, he is called a bodhisattva while in the causal stage, and a Buddha, the World-Honored One, upon reaching the resultant stage.

This is what is meant by saying that although both the bodhisattva and the Buddha, the World-Honored One, are said to have attained the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), there is still a distinction between them. "Subhūti!

This is called the mundane gift of Dharma of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. By relying upon and taking as a cause this mundane gift of Dharma, bodhisattva mahāsattvas are further able to practice the supramundane gift of Dharma; that is to say, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, through their skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), they first bestow upon sentient beings the wholesome dharmas of the mundane world, and subsequently cause them to become weary of and detached from those mundane wholesome dharmas, establishing them in the supramundane, untainted (*anāsrava*) noble dharmas, until they cause them to attain the knowledge of all aspects."

"Subhūti! What are called the supramundane noble dharmas that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas proclaim, reveal, analyze, and elucidate for the sake of sentient beings, which they designate as the gift of Dharma?"
Subhūti! All the wholesome dharmas not shared with ordinary beings, which, when correctly cultivated and studied, cause all sentient beings to transcend the world and abide in peace and security—
namely, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the three gates of liberation.
The eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, the knowledge of the four noble truths, the perfections,
the knowledge of all the emptinesses and so forth, the ten stages of the bodhisattva, the five eyes, the six supernormal powers,
the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and great compassion.
Great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity; the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor characteristics;
all doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of samādhi—all such untainted wholesome dharmas as these are collectively termed supramundane noble dharmas.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva proclaims, reveals, analyzes, and elucidates such dharmas for the sake of all sentient beings, this is called the bodhisattva’s supramundane gift of Dharma.
“Subhūti! In this context, what are called the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment? They are:
the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path.”
"Subhūti! These are called the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. Subhūti!"

Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness: it means that a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells observing the body in the internal body, the external body, and both the internal and external body; endowed with right effort, right knowledge, and right mindfulness, they eliminate worldly greed and sorrow. They dwell observing the arising of the body and dwell observing the cessation of the body. Because they dwell observing the body, observing its arising, and observing its cessation, they are without dependence and without grasping toward any world;
this is the first. It is the same for feelings, the mind, and phenomena.
These are called the four foundations of mindfulness. "Subhūti! As for the four right endeavors:

they refer to when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, in order that unarisen evil and unwholesome dharmas may never arise; in order that arisen evil and unwholesome dharmas may be permanently abandoned and extinguished; in order that unarisen wholesome dharmas may arise; and in order that arisen wholesome dharmas may remain firm, not be forgotten, and be cultivated to fulfillment, increase, expand, and be realized through wisdom—generates the desire, exerts diligent effort, rouses the mind, and sustains the mind. These are called the four right endeavors."

“Subhūti! The four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are: the basis of psychic power consisting in the cultivation of concentration of desire accompanied by the formation of abandonment; the basis of psychic power consisting in the cultivation of concentration of energy accompanied by the formation of abandonment; the basis of psychic power consisting in the cultivation of concentration of mind accompanied by the formation of abandonment; and the basis of psychic power consisting in the cultivation of concentration of investigation accompanied by the formation of abandonment. These rely on disenchantment, rely on detachment, rely on cessation, and are directed toward relinquishment. These are called the four bases of psychic power.”

“Subhūti! The five faculties refer to the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s faculty of faith, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom; these are called the five faculties.”

“Subhūti! As for the five powers, they are the bodhisattva mahāsattvas’ power of faith, power of diligence, power of mindfulness, power of concentration, and power of wisdom; these are called the five powers.”

“Subhūti! The seven factors of enlightenment are as follows: for a bodhisattva mahāsattva, they are the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena, the factor of enlightenment of diligence, the factor of enlightenment of joy, the factor of enlightenment of pliancy, the factor of enlightenment of concentration, and the factor of enlightenment of equanimity. These are called the seven factors of enlightenment.”

“Subhūti! The eight branches of the noble path refer to the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration; these are called the eight branches of the noble path.”
“Subhūti! The three gates of liberation refer to the bodhisattva mahāsattvas’ gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
What is the gate of liberation of emptiness?
It refers to the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva gathering the mind into a single point through the mental aspects of emptiness and signlessness; this is called the gate of liberation of emptiness.
What is the gate of liberation of signlessness?

It refers to the bodhisattva-mahāsattva gathering the mind into a single point through the modes of cessation and tranquility; this is called the signless door of liberation (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*).
What is the wishless door of liberation (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*)?

It means that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva collects the mind into a single focus through the mental aspects of suffering and impermanence, this is called the door of liberation of wishlessness. "Subhūti!..."
Regarding the eight liberations: for a bodhisattva mahāsattva, to perceive external forms while possessing internal form-perception is the first liberation.
To perceive external forms while having no internal perception of form is the second liberation.
The third liberation is the realization through direct experience of the body of pure resolve.

The fourth liberation is the attainment of the sphere of infinite space, wherein one transcends all perceptions of form, ceases perceptions of sensory resistance, does not attend to perceptions of diversity, and dwells fully established in the meditative concentration of the sphere of infinite space.
Transcending the sphere of infinite space, one enters and dwells, having fully attained the concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness; this is the fifth liberation.
Transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, one enters and dwells, having fully attained the concentration of the sphere of nothingness; this is the sixth liberation.
Transcending the sphere of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is the seventh liberation.
Transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters and dwells in the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling; this is the eighth liberation.

“Subhūti! As for the nine successive attainments, they are as follows: a bodhisattva mahāsattva, detached from desires and unwholesome states, possessing applied and sustained thought, and experiencing the joy and happiness born of seclusion, dwells having fully attained the first dhyāna; this is the first successive attainment.

With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, through internal serenity and one-pointedness of mind, being without applied or sustained thought, one dwells having attained the second dhyāna, which is born of concentration and characterized by joy and bliss; this is the second successive attainment.

Detached from joy, one dwells in equanimity, with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension; experiencing happiness with the body, which the Noble Ones describe as "dwelling in happiness through equanimity and mindfulness," one enters and dwells in the third dhyāna, complete with its factors; this is the third successive concentration.

With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the prior disappearance of joy and sorrow, one dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is characterized by purity of equanimity and mindfulness; this is the fourth successive concentration.

Transcending all perceptions of form, with the cessation of perceptions of sensory resistance, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, one enters and dwells, having fully attained the concentration of the sphere of infinite space; this is the fifth successive attainment.

In this way, proceeding until one transcends the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, dwelling therein in its full perfection—this is the ninth successive concentration.

“Subhūti! As for the knowledge of the four noble truths, it refers to the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin, knowledge of cessation, and knowledge of the path; these are called the knowledge of the four noble truths.”

“Subhūti! The pāramitās refer to the bodhisattva mahāsattvas’ pāramitā of generosity, the pāramitā of ethical discipline, the pāramitā of patience, the pāramitā of diligence, the pāramitā of meditative concentration, the pāramitā of wisdom, the pāramitā of skillful means, the pāramitā of sublime aspiration, the pāramitā of power, and the pāramitā of knowledge; these are called the pāramitās.”

“Subhūti! The wisdoms of the various emptinesses and so forth refer to the wisdom of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva regarding internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, as well as the wisdom regarding suchness up to the inconceivable realm; these are called the wisdoms of the various emptinesses and so forth.”

“Subhūti! The ten stages of a bodhisattva refer to the bodhisattva mahāsattvas’ Stage of Utmost Joy, the Stage of Purity, the Stage of Radiant Light, the Stage of Blazing Wisdom, the Stage of Extreme Difficulty to Conquer, the Stage of Manifestation, the Stage of Far-Going, the Immovable Stage, the Stage of Excellent Wisdom, and the Stage of the Dharma Cloud; these are called the ten stages of a bodhisattva.”

“Subhūti! As for the five eyes, they refer to the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the noble wisdom eye, the dharma eye, and the buddha eye, which are sought by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; these are called the five eyes.”

“Subhūti! The six supernormal powers refer to what the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas study: the supernormal power of the realization of knowledge of the miraculous domain, the supernormal power of the realization of knowledge of the divine eye, the supernormal power of the realization of knowledge of the divine ear, the supernormal power of the realization of knowledge of the minds of others, the supernormal power of the realization of knowledge of recollecting past lives, and the supernormal power of the realization of knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows. These are called the six supernormal powers.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Regarding the ten powers of a Tathāgata:
when the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas know, as it truly is, what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible, this is the first power."

If the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas know, as they truly are, the past, future, and present karmas of sentient beings, as well as the locations, causes, and maturations of their various experiences of phenomena, this is the second power.
If the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas know, as they truly are, the various distinctions among the many diverse elements within all worlds, this is the third power.

If the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas truly know, as they really are, the various differences in the diverse and manifold inclinations and discursive thoughts within all worlds, this is the fourth power.
If the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas truly know, as they really are, the superior and inferior faculties of all sentient beings and individuals, this is the fifth power.
If the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas know, as they truly are, all paths leading everywhere, this is the sixth power.

If the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas know, as they truly are, all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), meditative stabilizations (*samādhi*), and attainments (*samāpatti*), as well as their defilement, purification, and various distinctions of establishment, this is the seventh power.

If the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, with the pure divine eye that transcends that of humans, see sentient beings at the time of death and birth, and their various wholesome and unwholesome deeds—such as how these sentient beings, due to threefold misconduct of body, speech, and mind, due to wrong views, and due to slandering the noble ones, fall into the evil destinies; and how these sentient beings, due to threefold sublime conduct of body, speech, and mind, due to right views, and due to praising the noble ones, are born into the good destinies;

and furthermore, with the pure divine eye that transcends that of humans, they see the beautiful and ugly complexions of sentient beings at the time of death and birth, and their subsequent rebirth in good or evil destinies—knowing, according to reality, how all sentient beings are born into good or evil destinies through the power of their karma—this is the eighth power.

If the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, regarding the infinite past lives of sentient beings—whether one birth, ten births, a hundred births, a thousand births, or immeasurable births; or one eon, ten eons, a hundred eons, a thousand eons, or immeasurable eons—truly know all their conduct, speech, and characteristics as they really are, this is the ninth power.

If the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas truly know, as it is, the liberation of mind through the exhaustion of all outflows and the liberation by wisdom through the exhaustion of all outflows; and if, regarding their own true liberation through the exhaustion of outflows, they dwell having personally realized and attained supernormal knowledge, and truly experience and realize:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence"—this is the tenth power.
These are called the ten powers of the Tathāgata. "Subhūti!
As for the four fearlessnesses:

if a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha declares of himself, 'I am a perfectly awakened one,' and if there should be any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world who, relying on the Dharma, raises an objection or attempts to cause him to be reminded [of a flaw]:
"Regarding this Dharma, the Buddha is not perfectly enlightened"—as for this challenge, I see no ground for it.

Because I see no ground for this challenge, I abide in peace, free from fear and dread; I declare myself to occupy the exalted position of the Great Sage, and amidst the great assembly, I roar the true lion’s roar and turn the Great Brahma Wheel. Among all śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, Māras, Brahmas, or anyone else in the world, there is certainly none who can turn it in accordance with the Dharma. This is the first fearlessness.

If any Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha declares, "I have eternally exhausted all outflows," and if there should be any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world who, relying on the Dharma, raises an objection or calls it to mind, saying:
"The Buddha has not yet eternally exhausted these outflows."

"Regarding that challenge, I correctly perceive it to be without basis; because I correctly perceive that challenge to be without basis, I abide in peace, free from fear and dread. I declare myself to occupy the exalted position of a Great Sage, and amidst the great assembly, I roar the true lion’s roar and turn the Great Brahma Wheel. Among all śramaṇas, brahmins, gods, Māras, Brahmas, or anyone else in the world, there is certainly none who can turn it according to the Dharma. This is the second fearlessness.

If the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, having declared for their assembly of disciples that "these are obstructive dharmas which will certainly act as obstructions," there should be any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world who, relying on the Dharma, raises an objection or causes [the Buddha] to be reminded:
"There are such dharmas which, though defiling, cannot act as obstructions."

"Regarding that challenge, I correctly perceive the absence of a cause; because I correctly perceive the absence of a cause in that challenge, I dwell in peace, free from fear and dread. I declare myself to occupy the exalted position of a Great Sage, and amidst the great assembly, I roar the true lion’s roar and turn the Great Brahma Wheel. Among all śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, Māras, Brahmas, or anyone else in the world, there is certainly no one who can turn it in accordance with the Dharma. This is the third fearlessness.

If the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas themselves declare, "I have proclaimed to my assembly of disciples the path of deliverance, which the noble ones cultivate to achieve certain deliverance, certain penetration, the complete exhaustion of all suffering, and the making of an end to suffering," and if there should be any śramaṇa, brahmin, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world who, relying on the Dharma, raises an objection or brings it to mind, saying:
"This path that has been cultivated is not the correct deliverance, not the correct penetration, not the correct exhaustion of suffering, nor the making of an end to suffering."

"Regarding that challenge, I correctly perceive it to be without basis. Because I correctly perceive that challenge to be without basis, I dwell in peace, free from fear and intimidation. I declare myself to occupy the exalted position of a Great Sage; amidst the great assembly, I roar the true lion’s roar and turn the Great Brahma Wheel. Among all śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, Māras, Brahmas, or anyone else in the world, there is certainly none who can turn this wheel in accordance with the Dharma. This is the fourth fearlessness.
These are called the four fearlessnesses. "Subhūti! As for the four analytical knowledges, they are:

the analytical knowledge of meaning, the analytical knowledge of phenomena, the analytical knowledge of language, and the analytical knowledge of eloquence. These are called the four analytical knowledges."
Subhūti! What is the analytical knowledge of meaning?
It refers to the unimpeded wisdom that takes meaning as its object.
What is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid)? It is the unimpeded knowledge that takes phenomena as its object.
What is the analytical knowledge of language (nirukti-pratisaṃvid)?
That is to say, it is the unimpeded knowledge based on words.
What is the analytical knowledge of eloquence?
It is the unimpeded knowledge based on eloquence.
“Subhūti! As for the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, they are as follows: all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are always free from error;
they have no harsh or abrupt speech; they have no loss of mindfulness; they have no unconcentrated mind; they have no...”
Regarding various perceptions, there is nothing that is not relinquished through discernment;

his aspiration does not regress, his diligence does not regress, his mindfulness does not regress, his wisdom (*prajñā*) does not regress, his liberation (*vimukti*) does not regress, and his knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*) do not regress.
Whether it be knowledge or vision, regarding the past, they are unattached and unimpeded; whether it be knowledge or vision, regarding the present...
In the present life, he is unattached and unimpeded; his knowledge and vision are likewise unattached and unimpeded regarding future lives.
All his bodily actions are preceded by wisdom and proceed in accordance with wisdom; all his verbal actions are preceded by wisdom and proceed in accordance with wisdom;
all his mental actions are preceded by wisdom and proceed in accordance with wisdom. This is...
These are called the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, as for the thirty-two marks of a Great Man:

it is said that the Tathāgata has the mark of level and full soles on his feet, which rest excellently and well like the bottom of a casket; though the ground be uneven, wherever his feet tread, it becomes entirely level and touches it without any inequality—this is the first."
The Tathāgata’s soles bear the mark of a thousand-spoked wheel, with its rim and hub all perfectly complete; this is the second.
The Tathāgata’s hands and feet are entirely soft and supple, like *tūla* cotton, surpassing all others; this is the third.

Between each of the Tathāgata’s fingers and toes, there are webbed membranes like those of a king of geese; they are golden, interlaced, and their patterns are like exquisite embroidery—this is the fourth [mark].
The Tathāgata’s fingers and toes are all perfectly rounded, slender, and long, being exceedingly lovely; this is the fifth.
The Tathāgata’s heels are broad, long, and well-rounded, being in perfect proportion to the insteps and surpassing those of other sentient beings; this is the sixth.
The Tathāgata’s insteps are long, high, and full, soft, exquisite, and well-proportioned to his heels; this is the seventh.
The Tathāgata’s two calves are gradually tapered and rounded, like those of the king of antelopes, the eneya; this is the eighth.
The Tathāgata’s two arms are long, straight, and well-rounded; standing upright, they reach his knees like the trunk of an elephant king—this is the ninth.
The Tathāgata’s male organ is concealed within a sheath, just like that of a dragon-horse or an elephant king—this is the tenth.
Each pore of the Tathāgata grows a single hair, which is soft, supple, deep blue-black, and curls to the right; this is the eleventh.
The tips of the Tathāgata’s hair all point upward, curling to the right, being soft, supple, and deep blue-black, adorning his golden body in a most lovely and delightful manner; this is the twelfth.
The skin of the Tathāgata’s body is fine, thin, and smooth, such that dust, grime, water, and the like do not adhere to it; this is the thirteenth [mark].

The skin of the Tathāgata’s body is entirely the color of pure gold, radiant and brilliant like a magnificent golden pedestal, adorned with various jewels and pleasing for all to behold; this is the fourteenth [mark].
The Tathāgata’s two feet, the palms of his two hands, his neck, and both shoulders—these seven places are full; this is the fifteenth.
The Tathāgata’s shoulders and neck are perfectly rounded and exquisite; this is the sixteenth.
The Tathāgata’s shoulders and armpits are both fully filled; this is the seventeenth.
The Tathāgata’s countenance and deportment are grand, full, upright, and straight; this is the eighteenth.
The Tathāgata’s bodily marks are well-proportioned, expansive, and dignified; this is the nineteenth.
The Tathāgata’s physical form is equal in height and breadth, perfectly rounded like a nyagrodha tree; this is the twentieth.
The Tathāgata’s jaw, chest, and upper body possess a majestic presence as vast as that of a lion king; this is the twenty-first.
The Tathāgata’s constant radiance extends one fathom in every direction; this is the twenty-second.
The Tathāgata’s forty teeth are even and level, pure and closely set with deep roots, and whiter than white jade or snow; this is the twenty-third.
The Tathāgata’s four canine teeth are brilliant white and sharp; this is the twenty-fourth.
The Tathāgata always obtains the supreme flavor among all flavors; this is the twenty-fifth.
The Tathāgata’s tongue is thin, pure, broad, and long, capable of covering the face up to the ears and the hairline; this is the twenty-sixth.

The Tathāgata’s Brahma-voice is grand and elegant in its diction and rhythm; whether the assembly is large or small, all hear it equally. His voice resounds powerfully like a celestial drum, and his speech is refined and graceful like the song of the kalaviṅka bird. This is the twenty-seventh.
The Tathāgata’s eyelashes are like those of a bull king, deep blue, even, and not disordered; this is the twenty-eighth.
The Tathāgata’s eyes are deep blue with a bright white sclera, adorned with a crimson rim that is pure and clearly defined; this is the twenty-ninth.
The Tathāgata’s facial orb is like the full moon, and his eyebrows are bright and pure like the bow of Śakra; this is the thirtieth.

Between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows is the white tuft mark (*ūrṇā-kośa*), which curls to the right and is as soft as *tūla* cotton; its brilliant white radiance surpasses that of jade or snow; this is the thirty-first.
The *uṣṇīṣa* upon the Tathāgata’s crown is lofty, prominent, and perfectly circular, like a celestial canopy; this is the thirty-second.
These are called the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*).

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Four Hundred and Sixty-nine. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Second Division, Chapter on the Characteristics of All Virtues, Number Seventy-six, Part Three. "Furthermore, Subhūti!

Regarding the eighty secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*): the Tathāgata’s fingernails and toenails are narrow, long, thin, and supple; they are lustrous, pure, and bright like red copper—this is the first.
The Tathāgata’s fingers and toes are rounded, slender, and long; they are supple and straight with the joints and bones not visible—this is the second.
The Tathāgata’s hands and feet are each equal and without disparity, and the spaces between all the fingers and toes are completely filled and closely set—this is the third.
The Tathāgata’s hands and feet are perfectly rounded and as he wishes, soft, pure, and lustrous like the color of a lotus; this is the fourth.
The Tathāgata’s sinews are coiled and firm, deeply hidden and not visible; this is the fifth.
The Tathāgata’s two ankles are both concealed and not visible; this is the sixth.
The Tathāgata’s gait is straight, steady, and deliberate, like that of a dragon-elephant king; this is the seventh.
The Tathāgata’s gait and majestic bearing are as dignified and solemn as those of a lion king; this is the eighth.
The Tathāgata’s gait is steady, level, and composed, neither overstepping nor falling short, like that of a bull king; this is the ninth.
The Tathāgata’s gait, whether advancing or halting, is dignified and graceful like that of a king of geese; this is the tenth.
When the Tathāgata looks back, he always turns his body to the right, as a king of nāgas or elephants turns his entire body along with him; this is the eleventh.
The Tathāgata’s limbs and joints are gradually rounded and well-proportioned, beautifully and harmoniously arranged; this is the twelfth.
The Tathāgata’s bones and joints are interlocked without any gaps, like the coils of a dragon; this is the thirteenth.
The Tathāgata’s kneecaps are beautifully positioned, firm, and perfectly rounded; this is the fourteenth.
The Tathāgata’s private parts are well-formed with exquisite patterns, endowed with majesty, perfect, and pure; this is the fifteenth.
The limbs of the Tathāgata’s body are moist, supple, radiant, fresh, and pure, such that dust and grime do not adhere to them; this is the sixteenth.
The Tathāgata’s physical bearing is dignified and majestic, fearless, and never timid; this is the seventeenth.
The limbs and members of the Tathāgata’s body are firm, dense, and well-proportioned; this is the eighteenth.
The limbs and members of the Tathāgata’s body are stable, heavy, and never flickering, being perfectly complete and indestructible; this is the nineteenth.
The physical form of the Tathāgata is like that of a royal seer, majestic and dignified on all sides, radiant and pure, free from any obscuration; this is the twentieth.
The body of the Tathāgata is surrounded by a halo of light that constantly illuminates him during walking and other activities; this is the twenty-first.
The Tathāgata’s abdomen is square and well-proportioned, without deficiency; it is supple and adorned with various marks—this is the twenty-second.
The Tathāgata’s navel is deep, spiraling to the right, perfectly round, exquisite, pure, and lustrous—this is the twenty-third.
The Tathāgata’s navel is thick, neither sunken nor protruding, and is exquisitely beautiful all around; this is the twenty-fourth.
The Tathāgata’s skin is free from scabies and eczema, and likewise lacks any defects such as dark spots or warts; this is the twenty-fifth.
The palms of the Tathāgata’s hands are full and soft, and the soles of his feet are level; this is the twenty-sixth.
The lines on the Tathāgata’s hands are deep, long, clear, straight, glossy, and unbroken; this is the twenty-seventh.
The Tathāgata’s lips are glossy and radiant with a crimson glow, resembling the *bimba* fruit and being perfectly proportioned above and below; this is the twenty-eighth.
The Tathāgata’s face is neither too long nor too short, neither too large nor too small, but is well-proportioned and majestic; this is the twenty-ninth.
The Tathāgata’s tongue is soft, thin, broad, and long, with the color of red copper; this is the thirtieth.
The sound the Tathāgata utters is majestic, far-reaching, and profound, like the roar of a king of elephants, brilliant and clear; this is the thirty-first.
The Tathāgata’s vocal resonance is exquisite and complete, like an echo from a deep valley; this is the thirty-second.
The Tathāgata’s nose is high, long, and straight, with the nostrils not visible; this is the thirty-third.
The Tathāgata’s teeth are even, regular, and brilliant white; this is the thirty-fourth.
The Tathāgata’s canines are round, white, pure, and gradually tapering to sharp points; this is the thirty-fifth.
The Tathāgata’s eyes are pure, with the blue and white clearly distinguished; this is the thirty-sixth.
The Tathāgata’s eye-mark is long and wide, like the petals of a blue lotus, most lovely and delightful; this is the thirty-seventh.
The Tathāgata’s eyelashes are even above and below, thick and dense, and not white; this is the thirty-eighth.
The Tathāgata’s eyebrows are long, not white, closely set, fine, and soft; this is the thirty-ninth.
The Tathāgata’s eyebrows are elegantly arched, following one another in sequence, and are the color of deep blue lapis lazuli;
this is the fortieth. The Tathāgata’s eyebrows are prominent, radiant, and lustrous, shaped like the crescent moon; this is the forty-first.
The Tathāgata’s ears are thick, broad, long, and fully developed with well-formed lobes; this is the forty-second.
The Tathāgata’s two ears are beautiful, symmetrical, and free from all defects; this is the forty-third.
The Tathāgata’s dignified demeanor causes those who see him to be free from harm and defilement, and to give rise to love and respect; this is the forty-fourth.
The Tathāgata’s forehead is broad, full, level, and upright, with a most exquisite form; this is the forty-fifth.
The Tathāgata’s body is perfectly proportioned from top to bottom, possessing a majestic dignity like that of a lion king such that none can rival it;
this is the forty-sixth. The Tathāgata’s hair is long, deep blue-black, thick, and free of gray; this is the forty-seventh.
The Tathāgata’s hair is fragrant, clean, fine and soft, lustrous, and curls to the right; this is the forty-eighth.
The Tathāgata’s hair is even and orderly, neither disheveled nor intermingled; this is the forty-ninth.
The Tathāgata’s hair is firm and unbreakable, never falling out; this is the fiftieth.
The Tathāgata’s hair is smooth and exquisite, with no dust or grime adhering to it; this is the fifty-first.
The Tathāgata’s limbs are firm and full, surpassing those of Nārāyaṇa; this is the fifty-second.
The Tathāgata’s body is tall, large, and straight; this is the fifty-third.
The Tathāgata’s bodily orifices are pure, perfect, and well-formed; this is the fifty-fourth.
The Tathāgata’s physical limbs possess a preeminent power that none can equal; this is the fifty-fifth.
The physical marks of the Tathāgata are such that all who behold them find delight and never tire of gazing upon them; this is the fifty-sixth.
The circle of the Tathāgata’s face is well-proportioned in its length and breadth, pure and radiant like the full moon in autumn; this is the fifty-seventh.
The Tathāgata’s countenance is relaxed and dignified, radiant and manifest; he smiles and speaks first, facing others rather than turning away from them—this is the fifty-eighth.
The Tathāgata’s face is lustrous and serene, free from the faults of frowning or discoloration such as blueness or redness—this is the fifty-ninth.
