The Tathāgata’s limbs and members are pure, stainless, and forever free from foul odors; this is the sixtieth.
From all the pores of the Tathāgata’s body, there constantly issues a subtle and wondrous fragrance that fulfills all wishes; this is the sixty-first.
The Tathāgata’s face constantly emits the most supreme and excellent fragrance; this is the sixty-second.
The Tathāgata’s cranial protuberance is perfectly round, exquisite, and beautiful, like a madana tree or a celestial canopy; this is the sixty-third.
The Tathāgata’s body hairs are deep blue-black, radiant and pure, like the red luster on a peacock’s neck, exquisitely adorned and the color of refined copper; this is the sixty-fourth.
The Tathāgata’s Dharma voice accords with the capacity of the assembly, neither increasing nor decreasing, responding to principle without error; this is the sixty-fifth.
The Tathāgata’s cranial protuberance (uṣṇīṣa) cannot be seen by anyone; this is the sixty-sixth.
The joints of the Tathāgata’s fingers and toes are distinct and clearly defined, adorned with exquisite beauty like the color of red copper; this is the sixty-seventh.
Sixty-eighth: When the Tathāgata walks, his feet remain four finger-widths above the ground, yet they leave imprints. Sixty-ninth:
The Tathāgata maintains himself independently without relying on others for protection; his body is without swaying or staggering.
The Tathāgata’s majestic virtue resounds afar, such that those with malicious hearts see joy and those who are terrified find peace; this is the seventieth.
The Tathāgata’s voice is neither too high nor too low; he speaks in harmony and with pleasant cheer according to the inclinations of sentient beings; this is the seventy-first.
Seventy-second: The Tathāgata is able to preach the Dharma according to the speech, sounds, and mental dispositions of various classes of sentient beings. Seventy-third:
When the Tathāgata expounds the sublime Dharma with a single voice, each class of sentient beings understands it according to their own capacity.
The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma always follows a sequential order; his words are invariably based on causes and conditions and none are unwholesome—this is seventy-fourth.
The Tathāgata regards all classes of sentient beings with impartiality, praising the good and censuring the evil without affection or aversion—this is seventy-fifth.
The Tathāgata acts only after first observing, his conduct being perfectly complete so that beings may recognize him as pure and virtuous; this is seventy-sixth.
The marks and signs of the Tathāgata cannot be fully perceived by any sentient being; this is seventy-seventh.
The cranial bone of the Tathāgata is firm, solid, and perfectly rounded; this is the seventy-eighth.
The countenance of the Tathāgata is eternally youthful and ageless, and he delights in visiting former places; this is the seventy-ninth.

The Tathāgata’s hands, feet, and the area before his chest are all marked with the auspicious *śrīvatsa* sign; its patterns are like exquisite paintings and its color resembles vermilion. This is the eightieth [mark].
These are called the eighty minor marks (*anuvyañjana*). "Subhūti!

Because the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has accomplished such primary and secondary marks, the radiance of his body spontaneously illuminates the trichiliocosm, pervading it entirely without exception. If he so intends, he can illuminate immeasurable, boundless, and innumerable worlds; yet, out of compassion for all sentient beings, he withdraws that light and constantly illuminates an area of one fathom around each person. If he were to let forth the full radiance of his body, the light of the sun, moon, and other luminaries would all cease to appear, and sentient beings would be unable to distinguish day from night, the half-month, the month, the season, or the year, and their various undertakings would fail to be accomplished."

The Buddha’s voice spontaneously pervades the trichiliocosm; when he directs his attention, it can fill immeasurable, boundless, and innumerable worlds. Nevertheless, for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, the sound conforms to the capacity of the assembly, neither diminishing nor increasing.
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

Such meritorious benefits and excellences were already accomplished by me while I was practicing the perfection of wisdom in my previous stage as a bodhisattva; therefore, I am now adorned with the perfection of the primary and secondary marks, and all sentient beings who see me rejoice and obtain supreme benefit and peace.”

"In this way, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they are able to gather in all sentient beings through the two kinds of giving—material wealth and the Dharma. This is a most marvelous and rare quality."
“Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva gather sentient beings through the practice of kind speech? Subhūti!”

When the bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they use gentle voices to first teach the perfection of generosity to sentient beings, next the perfection of ethical discipline, next the perfection of patience, next the perfection of diligence, next the perfection of meditative concentration, and finally the perfection of wisdom, skillfully gathering them through these means.
Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they extensively teach these six perfections in gentle tones in order to gather in classes of sentient beings.
Why is this? Because these six perfections are able to universally encompass all wholesome dharmas.
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin!..."
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva gather sentient beings through the practice of beneficial conduct? Subhūti!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, throughout the long night they employ various skillful means to exhort all sentient beings to diligently cultivate and study the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as other various sublime and virtuous dharmas, never flagging or abandoning them.
“Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva gather sentient beings through the practice of sameness of purpose? Subhūti!”

When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, by means of their superior supernormal powers and the force of their great vows, they manifest within the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and gods; there, through shared activities and skillful means, they gather them in and cause them to obtain supreme benefit and peace.

“Subhūti! That bodhisattva mahāsattvas are able to gather in all sentient beings through such [means] as giving, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation—this is a most marvelous and rare quality.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

With my Buddha-eye, I behold throughout the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, while practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, instruct and exhort other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, saying: 'Come!'"

"Good son! You should skillfully study the dhāraṇī gateways for eliciting all syllables; that is to say, you should skillfully study one syllable, two syllables, and so on up to ten syllables, and likewise up to twenty, thirty, even a hundred, a thousand, or ten thousand, and even to the incalculable, until you attain mastery in their elicitation."

Furthermore, one should skillfully train so that all languages enter into a single syllable, or enter into two syllables, up to ten; likewise, they may enter into twenty, thirty, or even a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, or even an infinite number, thereby inducing mastery.
Furthermore, one should skillfully train in how a single syllable encompasses all syllables and how all syllables encompass a single syllable, thereby inducing mastery.
Moreover, one should skillfully train in how a single syllable can encompass the forty-two root-syllables, and how those forty-two root-syllables can encompass a single syllable.

"Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva should thus skillfully train so that the forty-two letters enter into a single letter, and a single letter likewise enters into the forty-two letters. Having trained in this way, they will induce skillfulness regarding all letters; having attained skillfulness in inducing the letters, they will further induce skillfulness regarding the absence of letters."

Just as all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are skillful in phenomena and skillful in syllables, and because they are skillful in phenomena and syllables, they also attain skillfulness in the absence of syllables; by virtue of this skillfulness, they are able to teach beings the dharma with syllables and the dharma without syllables, and to teach the dharma without syllables through the dharma with syllables.

Why is this so? Because there is no difference between the absence of letters and the absence of words regarding the Buddha-dharma; that which transcends all letters and names is the true Buddha-dharma. Why is this so?
"Because all phenomena and all sentient beings are ultimately empty and boundlessly empty.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

If all phenomena and all sentient beings are ultimately empty and boundlessly empty, and thus transcend all syllables, then the intrinsic nature of all phenomena and all sentient beings is ultimately unapprehendable; how then do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom?
How does one practice the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments?
How does one practice the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path?
How does one practice the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness?
How does one abide in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature?
How does one abide in suchness up to the inconceivable realm?
How does one dwell securely in the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path?
How does one practice the eight liberations up to the ten universal bases?
How does one practice the stages from the Ground of Extreme Joy up to the Ground of the Dharma Cloud?
How does one practice all the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi?
How does one practice the five eyes and the six supernormal powers?
How does one practice the ten powers of a Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha?
How does one practice the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity?
How does one practice all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)?
How does one cultivate the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs?
How does one abide in the six perfections of maturation and the six supernormal powers, and proclaim the sublime Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings?
“World-Honored One!
All sentient beings are unapprehendable, and even the designation of ‘sentient being’ is unapprehendable.
Because all sentient beings are unapprehendable, everything from form (*rūpa*) up to consciousness (*vijñāna*) is also unapprehendable, as is the sense-base of the eye (*cakṣur-āyatana*).”
Even the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*) is unapprehendable; the sense-bases of form (*rūpāyatana*) up to the sense-base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) are also unapprehendable;
the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) up to the mind-element (*manodhātu*) are also unapprehendable; the form-element (*rūpadhātu*) up to the phenomena-element (*dharmadhātu*) are also unapprehendable;
the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) up to the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*) are also unapprehendable; [and] eye-contact (*cakṣuḥsaṃsparśa*) up to mind-...
Contact is also unapprehendable; the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including those produced with mind-contact as a condition, are also unapprehendable.
The earth element, up to and including the consciousness element, is also unapprehendable.
The causal conditions, up to and including the dominant condition, are also unapprehendable; and the various phenomena produced from conditions are likewise unapprehendable.
They cannot be apprehended; from ignorance up to old age and death, they also cannot be apprehended;

from the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, they also cannot be apprehended; the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments also cannot be apprehended;
and from the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, they also [cannot be apprehended].
They are unattainable; the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are also unattainable;
everything from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the nature of non-nature is also unattainable;
everything from suchness up to the inconceivable realm is also unattainable; and the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path are also unattainable.
The eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality are also unapprehendable; the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata is also unapprehendable;
the stage of extreme joy up to the stage of the cloud of dharma is also unapprehendable;
all doors of dhāraṇī and doors of samādhi are also unapprehendable; the five eyes and the six supernormal powers...
The superknowledges (*abhijñā*) are also unapprehendable; the ten powers (*bala*) of a Tathāgata, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), are also unapprehendable;
the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣadharma*) and the nature of constant equanimity (*upekṣā*) are also unapprehendable;

omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are also unapprehendable; and the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*), up to that of the solitary realizer...
Awakening to bodhi is also unattainable; all the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas, and even the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs are likewise unattainable.

“Bhagavān! Within that which is unapprehendable, there are no sentient beings, nor is there any designation for them; there is no form, up to and including consciousness, nor is there any designation for them;
there is no eye-base, up to and including the mind-base, nor is there any designation for them; there is no form-base...”
Even the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) lacks that designation; the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) up to the mind-element (*manodhātu*) also lack that designation;

the form-element (*rūpadhātu*) up to the phenomena-element (*dharmadhātu*) also lack that designation; the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) up to the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*) also lack that designation;
and the eye-contact (*cakṣuḥsaṃsparśa*) up to the mind-contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*) also lack it.
There is no designation for those [feelings] born with eye-contact as condition, nor even for those feelings born with mind-contact as condition;
there is no designation for the earth element, nor even for the consciousness element;
there is no designation for the causal condition, nor even for the sovereign condition; there is no [designation] arising from conditions...
The arising of all phenomena is also without that designation; from ignorance up to old age and death, there is also no designation for them;
from the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, there is also no designation for them;
and from the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments, there is likewise no designation for them.
Furthermore, there is no establishment of the four applications of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path, nor is there any designation for them;
there is no establishment of the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—nor is there any designation for them;

there is no establishment of inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-entities, nor is there any designation for them; and there is no establishment of suchness up to the inconceivable realm.
Furthermore, there is no designation for those; there are no Noble Truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, nor is there any designation for them;
there are no eight liberations up to the ten totalities, nor is there any designation for them;
there is no stage of pure observation up to the stage of a Tathāgata, nor is there any designation for them; and there is no stage of extreme joy up to the cloud of dharma.
There is no designation for "grounds," nor is there any designation for any of the *dhāraṇī* doors or *samādhi* doors;
there is no designation for the five eyes or the six supernormal powers;
there is no designation for the ten powers of a Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and there is no designation for non-forgetfulness.
There is no designation for the loss of dharmas, nor is there any designation for the state of constant equanimity;
there is no designation for omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);
there is no designation for the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; and there is no designation for any of the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas or for the Buddhas.
Unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is also without that designation; the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary characteristics are likewise without that designation.
“World-Honored One!

Since all phenomena and designations pertaining to sentient beings are unobtainable and utterly non-existent, what dharma do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas teach to sentient beings when they practice the profound perfection of wisdom?”

"Bhagavān! May it not be that the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas themselves abides in unrighteousness, teaches unrighteousness to sentient beings, exhorts sentient beings to abide in unrighteousness, and establishes sentient beings in perverted dharmas."
Why is this? Because when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound Prajñāpāramitā, they do not even apprehend awakening, much less the factors conducive to awakening!
"One does not even apprehend a bodhisattva mahāsattva, much less the dharmas of a bodhisattva mahāsattva!
The Buddha told Subhūti: "It is so! It is so!"
So it is! It is just as you have said.
All sentient beings are unapprehendable; even the designation of all sentient beings is unapprehendable. All phenomena are unapprehendable; even the designation of all phenomena is unapprehendable.
Because they are unapprehendable and entirely non-existent, and because they are non-existent, one should know that there is internal emptiness,
external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena,
the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the beginningless and endless, the emptiness of dispersion and non-dispersion, and the emptiness of intrinsic nature.

One should know that emptiness, the emptiness of self-characteristics and common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of the unapprehendable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāva-śūnyatā*), as well as the emptiness of suchness (*tathatā*), the emptiness of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*),
the emptiness of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), the emptiness of non-falsity (*avitathatā*), the emptiness of non-alteration (*ananyathātā*), and the emptiness of equality (*samatā*).

Emptiness, the emptiness of the nature of arising, the emptiness of the fixed nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the emptiness of the stability of phenomena, the emptiness of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*),
the emptiness of the realm of space, and the emptiness of the inconceivable realm— one should know that the Noble Truth of Suffering is empty,
the Noble Truth of Origination is empty, the Noble Truth of Cessation is empty, and the Noble Truth of the Path is empty; one should know the aggregate of form up to the aggregate of consciousness.
Emptiness: one should know that the sense-base of the eye up to the sense-base of the mind is empty; one should know that the sense-base of forms up to the sense-base of phenomena is empty;
one should know that the element of the eye up to the element of the mind is empty; one should know that the element of forms up to the element of phenomena is empty;
one should know that the element of eye-consciousness up to the element of mind-consciousness is empty; one should know that eye-contact up to...
Mind-contact is empty; one should know that all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including those produced with mind-contact as a condition, are empty.
One should know that the earth element, up to and including the consciousness element, is empty.

One should know that the causal condition, up to and including the dominant condition, is empty. One should know that all phenomena produced from conditions are empty. One should know non-existence...
One should know that from ignorance up to old age and death are empty; one should know that the self, sentient beings, and so forth, up to the knower and the seer, are empty;
one should know that the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom are empty;
one should know that the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions are empty; one should know the four applications of mindfulness...
One should know that the dwellings up to the eight factors of the noble path are empty; one should know that the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are empty;
one should know that the eight liberations up to the ten universal bases are empty; one should know that the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata is empty;
one should know that the stage of extreme joy up to the stage of the cloud of dharma is empty.
One should know that all doors of dhāraṇī and doors of samādhi are empty; one should know that the five eyes and the six supernormal powers are empty;
one should know that the ten powers of a Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are empty;
one should know that the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity are empty; and one should know that all-knowledge and the path [are empty].
The knowledge of signs and the knowledge of all aspects are empty; one should know that the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha is empty;
one should know that the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s entry into the state of certainty is empty;
one should know that the ripening of sentient beings and the purification of buddha-fields are empty; and one should know that all the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva are empty.

"You should know that the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is empty; you should know that the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs are empty. Subhūti!"

When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, having seen that all phenomena are entirely empty, they proclaim the Dharma to all sentient beings so that they may be freed from perversion.

Although they proclaim all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings, they do not apprehend any sentient beings at all, nor do they apprehend any dharmas; regarding the characteristics of emptiness, they neither increase nor decrease them, neither grasping nor abandoning them.
For this reason, although all phenomena are spoken of, there is nothing that is spoken of. "Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates all phenomena in this manner, they attain unobstructed wisdom. By means of this wisdom, they do not destroy the non-dual discrimination of all phenomena, and they proclaim them as they truly are for the sake of all sentient beings. This causes them to abandon the deluded attachments of false imagination, so that they may, according to their respective capacities, proceed toward the fruits of the three vehicles and realize ultimate, eternal bliss in nirvāṇa."
Suppose a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha were to manifest a single Buddha, and that Buddha were further able to manifest immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of assemblies.
At that time, the emanated Buddha caused the assembly of emanated beings to practice the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
or caused them to practice the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
or caused them to practice the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path.
Or they cause them to practice the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
or they cause them to abide in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence; or they cause them to abide in suchness up to the inconceivable realm;
or they cause them to abide in the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; or they cause them to practice.
They cause [beings] to practice the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality; or they cause them to practice the stage of pure observation up to the stage of a Tathāgata;
or they cause them to practice the stage of extreme joy up to the stage of the cloud of dharma;
or they cause them to practice all doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of samādhi; or they cause them to practice the five eyes and the six supernormal powers.
They cause them to practice the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
or they cause them to practice the thirty-two marks of a Great Being and the eighty minor marks;
or they cause them to practice the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity; or they cause them to practice all-knowledge and the knowledge of the paths.
...or the knowledge of all aspects; or they cause them to abide in the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
or they cause them to abide in the sublime state of a bodhisattva; or they cause them to abide in unsurpassed enlightenment.
"Subhūti, what do you think? At that time,
did the emanated Buddha and the emanated assembly have any conceptual discrimination or any destruction regarding any phenomena?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
"Because all transformations are without discrimination regarding all phenomena.
The Buddha said, "Subhūti!"

By this causal connection, one should know that the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas likewise practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way: they preach the Dharma to all sentient beings as is appropriate, yet without discriminating or destroying the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), they are able to establish sentient beings in accordance with reality, causing them to dwell securely in the stage to which they should abide;

although they apprehend neither sentient beings nor any phenomena whatsoever, they cause sentient beings to be liberated from false imaginings, inverted attachments, and clinging, by means of the skillful method of being neither bound nor liberated.
Why is that? "Subhūti!
The intrinsic nature of form, up to and including the intrinsic nature of consciousness, is neither bound nor liberated."
If the intrinsic nature of phenomena is neither bound nor liberated, then these phenomena are not form, and so on, up to and including not consciousness.
Why is this? Because form, and so on, up to and including consciousness, are ultimately pure.
“Subhūti! The intrinsic nature of the sense base of the eye, up to the intrinsic nature of the sense base of the mind, is neither bound nor liberated.
If a phenomenon’s intrinsic nature is neither bound nor liberated, that phenomenon is not the sense base of the eye, up to and including not the sense base of the mind.”
Why is this? Because the sense base of the eye, up to and including the sense base of the mind, is ultimately pure. "Subhūti!
The intrinsic nature of the sphere of form, up to the intrinsic nature of the sphere of mental phenomena, is neither bound nor liberated.
If the intrinsic nature of a phenomenon is neither bound nor liberated, that phenomenon is not the sphere of form, nor is it any phenomenon up to the sphere of mental phenomena.
Why is this? Because the sense base of form, up to and including the sense base of mental phenomena, is ultimately pure. "Subhūti!..."
The intrinsic nature of the eye-element, up to and including the intrinsic nature of the mind-element, is neither bound nor liberated.
If a dharma’s intrinsic nature is neither bound nor liberated, that dharma is not the eye-element, up to and including not the mind-element.
Why is this? Because the eye-element, up to and including the mind-element, is ultimately pure. "Subhūti!
The intrinsic nature of the realm of form, up to the intrinsic nature of the realm of phenomena, is neither bound nor liberated.
If the intrinsic nature of a phenomenon is neither bound nor liberated, then that phenomenon is not the realm of form, nor is it the realm of phenomena.
Why is this? Because the realm of form, up to and including the realm of phenomena, is ultimately pure. "Subhūti!
The intrinsic nature of the eye-consciousness element, up to and including the intrinsic nature of the mind-consciousness element, is neither bound nor liberated.
If a phenomenon’s intrinsic nature is neither bound nor liberated, that phenomenon is not the eye-consciousness element, nor is it anything up to and including the mind-consciousness element.
Why is this? Because the eye-consciousness element, up to and including the mind-consciousness element, are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!
The intrinsic nature of eye-contact, up to and including the intrinsic nature of mind-contact, is neither bound nor liberated.
If a phenomenon’s intrinsic nature is neither bound nor liberated, that phenomenon is not eye-contact, nor is it mind-contact.
Why is this? Because visual contact, up to and including mental contact, is ultimately pure. "Subhūti!..."
The intrinsic nature of all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, up to the intrinsic nature of all feelings produced with mind-contact as condition, is neither bound nor liberated.

If a phenomenon’s intrinsic nature is neither bound nor liberated, that phenomenon is not a feeling produced with eye-contact as condition, nor is it a feeling produced with mind-contact as condition.

Why is this? Because the various sensations produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including the various sensations produced with mind-contact as a condition, are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!..."
The intrinsic nature of the earth element, up to and including the intrinsic nature of the consciousness element, is neither bound nor liberated.
If the intrinsic nature of a phenomenon is neither bound nor liberated, that phenomenon is not the earth element, nor is it any element up to and including the consciousness element.
Why is this? Because the element of earth, up to and including the element of consciousness, is ultimately pure. "Subhūti!..."
The intrinsic nature of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) up to the sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is neither bound nor liberated.
If the intrinsic nature of a phenomenon is neither bound nor liberated, then that phenomenon is not a causal condition, nor is it any condition up to the sovereign condition.
Why is this? Because the causal conditions, up to and including the dominant condition, are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!..."
The intrinsic nature of all phenomena produced from conditions is neither bound nor liberated.
If a phenomenon’s intrinsic nature is neither bound nor liberated, that phenomenon is not among those phenomena produced from conditions.
Why is this? Because all phenomena produced from conditions are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!..."
The intrinsic nature of ignorance, up to and including the intrinsic nature of old age and death, is neither bound nor liberated.
If a phenomenon’s intrinsic nature is neither bound nor liberated, that phenomenon is not ignorance, nor is it anything up to and including old age and death.
Why is this? Because ignorance up to old age and death are ultimately pure. "Sudhana!..."
The intrinsic nature of the perfection of generosity, up to and including the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom, is neither bound nor liberated.
If a phenomenon’s intrinsic nature is neither bound nor liberated, that phenomenon is not the perfection of generosity, up to and including not the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Because the perfection of generosity, up to and including the perfection of wisdom, is ultimately pure.
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin! [It is so]."
The intrinsic nature of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments is neither bound nor liberated.
If a phenomenon’s intrinsic nature is neither bound nor liberated, that phenomenon is not the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments.
Why is this? Because the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!
The intrinsic nature of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the intrinsic nature of the eightfold noble path is neither bound nor liberated.
If a phenomenon’s intrinsic nature is neither bound nor liberated, that phenomenon is not the four foundations of mindfulness, nor is it anything up to the eightfold noble path.
Why is this? Because the four applications of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!
The intrinsic nature of the gate of liberation of emptiness, and the intrinsic nature of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness, are neither bound nor liberated.
If a dharma’s intrinsic nature is neither bound nor liberated, that dharma is not the gate of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness.
Why is this? Because the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!..."
The intrinsic nature of inner emptiness, up to and including the intrinsic nature of the emptiness of non-existence of self-nature, is neither bound nor liberated.
If a dharma’s intrinsic nature is neither bound nor liberated, then that dharma is not inner emptiness, nor is it the emptiness of non-existence of self-nature.
Why is this? Because internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, is ultimately pure. "Subhūti!..."
The nature of suchness, up to and including the nature of the inconceivable realm, is neither bound nor liberated.
If the nature of a phenomenon is neither bound nor liberated, that phenomenon is not suchness, up to and including not the inconceivable realm.
Why is this? Because from suchness up to the inconceivable realm, they are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!
The noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path are by nature neither bound nor liberated.
If a phenomenon is by nature neither bound nor liberated, that phenomenon is not the noble truth of suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path.
Why is this? Because the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!
The intrinsic nature of the eight liberations up to the intrinsic nature of the ten totalities are neither bound nor liberated.
If the intrinsic nature of a phenomenon is neither bound nor liberated, that phenomenon is not the eight liberations, nor is it the ten totalities.
Why is this? Because the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!
The intrinsic nature of the stage of pure observation (*śuddhadarśana-bhūmi*) up to the intrinsic nature of the stage of the Tathāgata is neither bound nor liberated.
If the intrinsic nature of a dharma is neither bound nor liberated, that dharma is not the stage of pure observation, nor is it any stage up to the stage of the Tathāgata.
Why is this? Because the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata is ultimately pure. "Subhūti!..."
The intrinsic nature of the stage of Utmost Joy is neither bound nor liberated, up to and including the intrinsic nature of the stage of Dharma Cloud.
If the intrinsic nature of a phenomenon is neither bound nor liberated, that phenomenon is not the stage of Utmost Joy, nor is it anything up to and including the stage of Dharma Cloud.
Why is this? Because from the Stage of Utmost Joy up to the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma, they are ultimately pure. “Subhūti!
The intrinsic nature of the dharani-gates and the intrinsic nature of the samadhi-gates are neither bound nor liberated.
If the intrinsic nature of a phenomenon is neither bound nor liberated, that phenomenon is not a dharani-gate nor a samadhi-gate.
Why is this? Because the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!..."
The intrinsic nature of the five eyes and the intrinsic nature of the six supernormal powers are neither bound nor liberated.
If the intrinsic nature of a phenomenon is neither bound nor liberated, that phenomenon is not the five eyes or the six supernormal powers.
Why is this? Because the five eyes and the six supernormal powers are ultimately pure.
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin! [It is so]."
The intrinsic nature of the Tathāgata’s ten powers, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, is neither bound nor liberated.
If the intrinsic nature of a phenomenon is neither bound nor liberated, then that phenomenon is not the Tathāgata’s ten powers, nor is it the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Why is this? Because the ten powers of the Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!
The intrinsic nature of the thirty-two marks of a great man and the intrinsic nature of the eighty secondary characteristics are neither bound nor liberated.
If the intrinsic nature of a phenomenon is neither bound nor liberated, that phenomenon is not the thirty-two marks of a great man nor the eighty secondary characteristics.
Why is this? Because the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!
The intrinsic nature of the quality of non-forgetfulness and the intrinsic nature of the state of constant equanimity are neither bound nor liberated.
If a dharma’s intrinsic nature is neither bound nor liberated, that dharma is not the quality of non-forgetfulness nor the state of constant equanimity.
Why is this? Because the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant abiding in equanimity are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!..."
The intrinsic nature of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is neither bound nor liberated.
If a phenomenon’s intrinsic nature is neither bound nor liberated, that phenomenon is not all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, or the knowledge of all aspects.
Why is this? Because all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!..."
The intrinsic nature of the fruit of stream-entry, up to and including the intrinsic nature of pratyekabuddha enlightenment, is neither bound nor liberated.
If the intrinsic nature of a phenomenon is neither bound nor liberated, that phenomenon is not the fruit of stream-entry, up to and including not being pratyekabuddha enlightenment.
Why is this? Because the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha is ultimately pure. "Subhūti!..."
The intrinsic nature of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas’ practices and the intrinsic nature of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas are neither bound nor liberated.

If a dharma’s intrinsic nature is neither bound nor liberated, that dharma is not the practice of any bodhisattva-mahāsattva, nor is it the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of any buddha.
Why is this? Because all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!..."
Wholesome dharmas and unwholesome dharmas are by nature neither bound nor liberated.
If a dharma is by nature neither bound nor liberated, that dharma is neither wholesome nor unwholesome.
Why is this? Because wholesome dharmas and unwholesome dharmas are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!
Dharmas that are determinate and dharmas that are indeterminate are, by their very nature, neither bound nor liberated.
If a dharma is by its very nature neither bound nor liberated, that dharma is neither a determinate dharma nor an indeterminate dharma.
Why is this? Because dharmas that are determinate and dharmas that are indeterminate are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!..."
The nature of contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) and uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) is neither bound nor liberated.
If a phenomenon is by nature neither bound nor liberated, that phenomenon is neither a contaminated phenomenon nor an uncontaminated phenomenon.
Why is this? Because contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) and uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!..."
The nature of mundane phenomena and supramundane phenomena is neither bound nor liberated.
If a phenomenon is by nature neither bound nor liberated, that phenomenon is neither a mundane phenomenon nor a supramundane phenomenon.
Why is this? Because worldly phenomena and supramundane phenomena are ultimately pure. "Subhūti!..."
Conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena are by nature neither bound nor liberated.
If a phenomenon is by nature neither bound nor liberated, that phenomenon is neither a conditioned phenomenon nor an unconditioned phenomenon.
Why is this? Because conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena are ultimately pure. "Thus it is, Subhūti!"
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom,
although they proclaim all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings, they do not apprehend either sentient beings or the intrinsic nature of dharmas at all.
Why is this? Because sentient beings and all phenomena are unapprehendable. "Furthermore, Subhūti!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they employ the skillful means of non-apprehension and abide within the non-apprehension of all phenomena.
That is to say, by employing the method of non-apprehension, one dwells in the emptiness of form up to the emptiness of consciousness;
by employing the method of non-apprehension, one dwells in the emptiness of the eye-base up to the emptiness of the mind-base;
by employing the method of non-apprehension, one dwells in the emptiness of the form-base up to the emptiness of the phenomena-base.
By means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, they abide in the emptiness of the eye-element up to the emptiness of the mind-element;
by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, they abide in the emptiness of the form-element up to the emptiness of the phenomena-element;
by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, they abide in the emptiness of the eye-consciousness-element up to the emptiness of the mind-consciousness-element.
Taking non-apprehension as the means, he dwells in the emptiness of eye-contact up to the emptiness of mind-contact;
taking non-apprehension as the means, he dwells in the emptiness of all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition up to the emptiness of all feelings produced with mind-contact as condition;
taking non-apprehension as the means, he dwells in the emptiness of the earth element up to the emptiness of the consciousness element.
Using non-apprehension as a skillful means, they abide in the emptiness of causes and conditions up to the emptiness of dominant conditions;
using non-apprehension as a skillful means, they abide in the emptiness of all phenomena produced from conditions;
using non-apprehension as a skillful means, they abide in the emptiness of ignorance up to the emptiness of old age and death.
By means of non-apprehension as a skillful means, they abide in the emptiness of the perfection of giving up to the emptiness of the perfection of wisdom;
by means of non-apprehension as a skillful means, they abide in the emptiness of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
by means of non-apprehension as a skillful means, they abide in the emptiness of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the emptiness of the eight branches of the noble path.
Using non-apprehension as the skillful means, they abide in the emptiness of the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
using non-apprehension as the skillful means, they abide in the emptiness of internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence;
using non-apprehension as the skillful means, they abide in the emptiness of suchness up to the emptiness of the inconceivable realm.
Using non-apprehension as the skillful means, they abide in the emptiness of the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
using non-apprehension as the skillful means, they abide in the emptiness of the eight liberations up to the emptiness of the ten totalities;
using non-apprehension as the skillful means, they abide in the emptiness of the stage of pure observation up to the emptiness of the stage of the Tathāgata.
By means of non-apprehension as a skillful method, they abide in the emptiness of the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the emptiness of the Cloud of Dharma Stage;
by means of non-apprehension as a skillful method, they abide in the emptiness of all dharani-doors and samadhi-doors;
by means of non-apprehension as a skillful method, they abide in the emptiness of the five eyes and the six supernormal powers.
Using non-apprehension as a skillful means, they dwell in the emptiness of the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
using non-apprehension as a skillful means, they dwell in the emptiness of the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary characteristics;
using non-apprehension as a skillful means, they dwell in the emptiness of the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity.

Using non-apprehension as the skillful means, they dwell in the emptiness of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);

using non-apprehension as the skillful means, they dwell in the emptiness of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*) up to the emptiness of the enlightenment of a solitary buddha (*pratyekabuddhabodhi*);

using non-apprehension as the skillful means, they dwell in the emptiness of all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*).
Using non-apprehension as a skillful means, they abide in the emptiness of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas;
using non-apprehension as a skillful means, they abide in the emptiness of determinate and indeterminate dharmas;
using non-apprehension as a skillful means, they abide in the emptiness of outflowing and non-outflowing dharmas.
Using non-apprehension as a skillful means, they abide in the emptiness of mundane phenomena and supramundane phenomena;
using non-apprehension as a skillful means, they abide in the emptiness of conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena.

“Subhūti! You should know that from form (*rūpa*) up to consciousness (*vijñāna*) there is no place of abiding; and from the emptiness of form up to the emptiness of consciousness, there is likewise no place of abiding. Why is this?

Form up to consciousness lack intrinsic nature and cannot be apprehended; the emptiness of form up to the emptiness of consciousness likewise lacks intrinsic nature and cannot be apprehended, because that which lacks intrinsic nature and cannot be apprehended has no place in which to abide.

In this way, up to and including all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas, there is nothing that abides; even the emptiness of all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas has no abiding.

Why is this? Because all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas lack intrinsic nature and cannot be apprehended; and because the emptiness of all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas also lacks intrinsic nature and cannot be apprehended. This is because a dharma that lacks intrinsic nature and cannot be apprehended has no place in which to abide.
Wholesome dharmas and unwholesome dharmas have no place of abiding; the emptiness of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas likewise has no place of abiding.

Why is this? Because wholesome and unwholesome dharmas lack intrinsic nature and cannot be apprehended; the emptiness of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas also lacks intrinsic nature and cannot be apprehended. This is because that which lacks intrinsic nature and cannot be apprehended has no place of abiding.
Dharmas that are determinate and dharmas that are indeterminate do not abide anywhere; the emptiness of determinate and indeterminate dharmas likewise does not abide anywhere. Why is this?

Because determinate and indeterminate dharmas lack intrinsic nature and cannot be apprehended, and the emptiness of determinate and indeterminate dharmas likewise lacks intrinsic nature and cannot be apprehended; for there is no abiding in a dharma that lacks intrinsic nature and cannot be apprehended.

Contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) and uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) do not abide anywhere; the emptiness of contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena likewise does not abide anywhere. Why is this?

Because contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and are unapprehendable; the emptiness of contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena also lacks intrinsic nature and is unapprehendable. For that which is unapprehendable due to the absence of intrinsic nature cannot have any place of abiding.
Worldly dharmas and supramundane dharmas have no place of abiding; the emptiness of worldly and supramundane dharmas likewise has no place of abiding. Why is this?

Worldly phenomena and supramundane phenomena lack intrinsic nature and cannot be apprehended; the emptiness of worldly and supramundane phenomena also lacks intrinsic nature and cannot be apprehended, for there is no phenomenon lacking intrinsic nature that can abide.

Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) have no place of abiding; the emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of conditioned and unconditioned phenomena likewise has no place of abiding. Why is this?

Because conditioned and unconditioned phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and are unapprehendable; the emptiness of conditioned and unconditioned phenomena also lacks intrinsic nature and is unapprehendable. This is because that which lacks intrinsic nature and is unapprehendable cannot have a place of abiding.

“Subhūti, you should know this: a dharma that lacks intrinsic nature does not abide in a dharma that lacks intrinsic nature; a dharma that possesses intrinsic nature does not abide in a dharma that possesses intrinsic nature; a dharma that lacks intrinsic nature does not abide in a dharma that possesses intrinsic nature; and a dharma that possesses intrinsic nature does not abide in a dharma that lacks intrinsic nature.

A dharma that is self-nature does not abide in a dharma that is self-nature; a dharma that is other-nature does not abide in a dharma that is other-nature; a dharma that is self-nature does not abide in a dharma that is other-nature; and a dharma that is other-nature does not abide in a dharma that is self-nature.”
Why is this? Because all these dharmas are unapprehendable; how could that which is unapprehendable have any place of abiding?
"It is thus, Subhūti!"

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they eliminate all phenomena by means of these various emptinesses, and are also able to teach and reveal them to sentient beings in accordance with reality.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice the profound perfection of wisdom in this manner, they will be without fault before all the noble ones—the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, and śrāvakas.

Why is this so? Because all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and all noble ones (ārya) are able to realize this dharma-nature; having realized it, they proclaim it without error for the sake of all sentient beings.
Although one proclaims all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings, one neither shifts nor transcends the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Why is this?

The true nature of all dharmas is the true *dharmadhātu*, *tathatā*, and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); such a *dharmadhātu*, *tathatā*, and *bhūtakoṭi* cannot be shifted nor can they be transcended.

Why is this? Because such things as the dharma-realm, true thusness, and the limit of reality all lack intrinsic nature and are entirely unapprehendable; for there is no dharma that is unapprehendable which can be transcended or surpassed.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll 473, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree. Second Division, Chapter on the Characteristics of Various Virtues, Part 76-4. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

If the true dharma-realm, suchness, and the limit of reality do not undergo transformation nor transcendence, then are form through consciousness different from the true dharma-realm, suchness, and the limit of reality?

It is established that white karma has a white maturation, namely, that which brings about rebirth as a human or a deva.

It is established that black-and-white karma has a black-and-white maturation, namely, that which brings about a portion of the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, and a portion of the human realm.

The Buddha told Subhūti:

Why is this so? Because within the principle of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the nature and characteristics of all phenomena (*dharma*) are beyond conceptual differentiation, ineffable, and unindicatable; how, then, could there be any distinction between cause and effect?

The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If the distinctions between the stages of cause and effect are established based on worldly convention and not based on the ultimate truth, then all foolish ordinary beings would also possess the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship, as well as pratyekabuddha awakening and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening of a Buddha."
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Do foolish ordinary beings realize the principles of the two truths—the conventional and the ultimate—according to reality?"

If one were to realize the principle of the two truths as they truly are, then there would likewise be the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship, as well as the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a buddha.

However, because foolish ordinary beings do not realize the conventional and the ultimate as they truly are, they lack the noble path and the cultivation of the noble path; thus, it is impossible to establish the various distinctions of the stages of the fruits of sainthood.

Because only the noble ones (ārya) can realize the conventional and the ultimate as they truly are, there exists the noble path and the cultivation of the noble path; it is through this that the distinctions among the fruits of the noble ones (āryaphala) come to exist.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If one cultivates the noble path, does one attain the noble fruit?
The Buddha said:
"No, World-Honored One!
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By not cultivating the Noble Path, can one attain the fruits of the noble ones?"
The Buddha said:
"No, Subhūti! You should know this!"

One cannot attain the fruit of the noble ones by practicing the noble path, nor can one attain the fruit of the noble ones without practicing the noble path; one cannot attain the fruit of the noble ones apart from the noble path, nor can one attain the fruit of the noble ones while dwelling within the noble path.
Why is this? Because, in the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), neither the path nor its fruit, nor cultivation or non-cultivation, can be apprehended.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, although they establish various distinctions among the noble fruits for the sake of sentient beings, they do not conceptually differentiate between establishing these distinctions of the stages of the noble fruits within the realm of the conditioned or the realm of the unconditioned.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

World-Honored One!

The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva is themselves without attachment to any phenomena, and is also able to teach others to be without attachment to any phenomena;
that is to say, they are without attachment to the perfection of giving up to the perfection of wisdom,

They have no attachment to the four formless absorptions; they also have no attachment to the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
they also have no attachment to the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
they also have no attachment to inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature; and they also have no attachment to...
They have no attachment to anything from suchness up to the inconceivable realm; they have no attachment to the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
they have no attachment to anything from the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality;
and they have no attachment to anything from the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma Stage. Furthermore, they have no attachment...
They are without attachment to any of the dharani-doors or samadhi-doors; they are without attachment to the five eyes or the six supernormal powers;
they are without attachment to the ten powers of a Tathagata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
and they are likewise without attachment to the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity.

They are without attachment; they are also without attachment to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);

they are also without attachment to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas; and they are also without attachment to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).
They are without attachment.
Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are without attachment, they attain non-obstruction in all places.

Just as those who are emanated by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, although they practice the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, do not accept or dwell in the fruits thereof, but act solely for the sake of the parinirvāṇa of sentient beings; likewise, even though they practice the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvajñajñāna*), they do not accept or dwell in its fruit, but act solely for the sake of the parinirvāṇa of sentient beings.

It is the same for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, they have no attachment and no obstruction toward any phenomena—whether wholesome or unwholesome, determinate or indeterminate, with outflows or without outflows, mundane or supramundane, conditioned or unconditioned.
Why is this? Because they have skillfully realized the true nature (*yathābhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena.
Chapter 77: Skillful Realization, Part Two, Section One. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, how do they skillfully penetrate the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they are like a magical emanation;
they do not engage in any fetters of greed, hatred, or delusion; they do not engage with the aggregate of form, up to the aggregate of consciousness;

One does not practice with respect to the eye-element up to the mind-element; one does not practice with respect to the form-element up to the phenomena-element;

they do not practice the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;

One does not practice the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; one does not practice any of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices;
one does not practice the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas; one does not practice the knowledge of all modes;
one does not practice internal or external phenomena; one does not practice latent tendencies or active fetters; one does not practice the wholesome.
They do not practice dharmas that are non-dharmas, nor dharmas that are wholesome or unwholesome; they do not practice dharmas that are determinate or indeterminate;
they do not practice dharmas that are with outflows or without outflows; they do not practice worldly dharmas or supramundane dharmas;

When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, it is likewise thus: they do not engage with any phenomena at all; this is what is meant by being well-versed in the true reality of all phenomena.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?

That which is emanated by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas possesses not the slightest substantial reality; nor does defilement or purification depend upon such things, nor is there any transmigration through the various realms of birth and death.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they likewise thoroughly penetrate the true reality of all phenomena; they realize that all phenomena are entirely devoid of any substantial entity."

The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
“Form and all other phenomena are none other than like a magical transformation.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If all phenomena are like magical transformations, then all that is transformed lacks real form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including lacking real conditioned and unconditioned phenomena. Because of this, there is neither affliction nor purification, nor is there the cycle of birth and death through the various realms of existence, nor is there the meaning of liberation from them. How then can a bodhisattva mahāsattva exercise the superior activity of a great being toward sentient beings?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas were originally practicing the bodhisattva path, did they perceive any sentient beings who could be liberated from the realms of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, or devas?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas originally practiced the bodhisattva path, they did not perceive any sentient beings who could be liberated from the three realms. Why is this?

Because when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they thoroughly penetrate and know that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations, and are in no way truly existent.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva realizes and perceives that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations, being entirely without substantial reality, for what purpose do bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the six pāramitās?"
