One should take up the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, but one should not take up the thirty-two marks of a great man or the eighty secondary signs;
one should not take up the quality of non-forgetfulness or the nature of constant equanimity;
one should not take up omniscience, the knowledge of the paths, or the knowledge of all aspects; nor should one take up the fruit of a stream-enterer.
...up to and including the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; do not grasp at any bodhisattva-mahāsattva practice,
do not grasp at the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas, do not grasp at wholesome or unwholesome phenomena, do not grasp at defined or undefined phenomena,
do not grasp at contaminated or uncontaminated phenomena, do not grasp at mundane [phenomena], and so forth.
Regarding supramundane dharmas, do not grasp at conditioned or unconditioned dharmas.

Why is this? All giving is empty of the nature of giving; all givers are empty of the nature of a giver; all recipients are empty of the nature of a recipient; and all fruits of giving are empty of the nature of the fruit of giving. Within emptiness, giving, the giver, the recipient, and the fruits of giving are all unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because the distinct intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of all such phenomena are ultimately empty; within ultimate emptiness, such phenomena cannot be apprehended.
"Because these phenomena are unattainable, other objects of apprehension are likewise unattainable.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they accomplish such skillful means; by the power of this skillful means, they establish sentient beings and cause them to abide in pure ethical discipline."
Having established them thus, he further spoke these words:
"You should now cultivate deep compassion for all sentient beings; abstain from taking life, and so forth, up to abstaining from wrong views and practicing right view."
Why is this so? Because all such phenomena are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature; you should not engage in conceptual differentiation or cling to them.
Furthermore, you should observe according to reality: what phenomenon is called "the arising of desire" that one would seek to sever its life?
Furthermore, by what cause is that life severed?
To speak at length, up to: what dharma is called the object of wrong view from which wrong view arises?
And by what cause does wrong view arise?
"In this way, all intrinsic natures are empty. "Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they achieve such skillful means that they are able to bring sentient beings to full maturity. Through immeasurable approaches, they teach them that both the fruit of generosity and the fruit of pure ethical discipline are unapprehendable, causing them to know that the intrinsic nature of the fruits of generosity and pure ethical discipline is entirely empty."

Having realized that the nature of the fruits of the practiced generosity and pure ethical discipline is empty, they are able to give rise to no attachment toward them. Because their minds are free from attachment, they are undistracted; being undistracted, they are able to produce sublime wisdom. Through this sublime wisdom, having forever severed the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the active fetters (*paryavasthāna*), they enter the realm of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
"Subhūti! Thus it is spoken according to worldly convention and not according to the ultimate truth. Why is that?

In space, not even the slightest dharma can be found—whether it be that which has already entered parinirvāṇa, that which will enter parinirvāṇa, that which is currently entering parinirvāṇa, the one who enters parinirvāṇa, or that by means of which one attains parinirvāṇa. All such things are entirely non-existent; they are all ultimately empty. This ultimate emptiness is itself nirvāṇa, and apart from this nirvāṇa, there is no other dharma.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they achieve such skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). By the power of these skillful means, seeing that the minds of sentient beings are largely filled with anger and resentment, they give rise to deep compassion and provide instruction through skillful means, saying:
'You all should now cultivate patience (*kṣānti*), delight in the dharma of patience, subdue your minds, and undertake the practice of patience.'"
The intrinsic nature of the phenomena toward which you feel anger is entirely empty; how, then, can you give rise to anger and resentment within them?
You should further observe in accordance with reality: by means of what phenomenon does this anger and resentment arise?
Who can be angry? At whom can one be angry?
All such phenomena are empty by their very nature; that which is empty by nature has never not been empty.

Thus, this emptiness was not made by a Buddha, nor by a Bodhisattva, nor by a Pratyekabuddha, nor by a Śrāvaka; it was also not made by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, or non-humans; nor was it made by the gods from the Realm of the Four Great Kings up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods; nor was it made by the gods from the Brahmakāyika heaven up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven; nor was it made by the gods from the Ākāśānantyāyatana heaven up to the Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana heaven.
You should further observe according to reality: from what does such anger and resentment arise?
To whom does it belong?
And toward whom does it arise?
What fruit shall one obtain?
What benefit shall one gain in this present life?
All these phenomena are empty by their very nature; within emptiness, there is no room for anger or resentment. Therefore, one should practice patience to bring benefit to oneself.

"In this way, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they achieve supreme skillful means and establish sentient beings in the principle of intrinsic emptiness and the causes and effects of intrinsic emptiness. They gradually manifest, exhort, encourage, and gladden them with unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, causing them to dwell securely therein and swiftly attain its realization."
"Subhūti! Thus it is spoken according to worldly convention, not according to the ultimate truth. Why is that?
Within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, that which attains, that which is attained, the locus of attainment, and the time of attainment— all these do not exist. Subhūti,
you should know that this is called the principle of the emptiness of intrinsic nature regarding the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

In order to benefit all sentient beings, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom by relying on this principle of the emptiness of the fundamental nature of the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi), yet they do not apprehend sentient beings nor their designations.
Why is this? Subhūti!

Because all phenomena are devoid of sentient beings, and because sentient beings are devoid [of intrinsic nature], phenomena cannot be apprehended; for both phenomena and sentient beings are established through mutual dependence.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they achieve such skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). By the power of these skillful means, seeing that sentient beings are physically and mentally indolent and have fallen away from diligence, they skillfully exhort and guide them to arouse physical and mental diligence to cultivate all wholesome dharmas, saying:
'O sons of good family!'"

One should have deep faith and acceptance that within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, there is no phenomenon of indolence, no indolent person, no place of indolence, no time of indolence, and no phenomenon from which indolence arises; all such things are empty by intrinsic nature and do not transcend the principle of emptiness.

You all should arouse physical and mental diligence, abandon all laziness, and diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas—namely, the cultivation of the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
or the cultivation of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; or the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path.
Kātyāyanīputra, if one cultivates the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
or dwells in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature; or dwells in suchness up to the inconceivable realm;
or dwells in the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; or cultivates the eight liberations up to the ten totalities.
Whether one cultivates the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata;
or cultivates the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma stage; or cultivates all the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi;
or cultivates the five eyes and the six supernormal powers; or cultivates the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
If one cultivates the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs; if one cultivates the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity;
if one cultivates all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);
if one cultivates the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; or if one cultivates all the stages of a bodhisattva.
In the practice of a Mahāsattva, whether cultivating the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas or cultivating any other immeasurable Buddha-dharmas,
one should apply oneself with diligent vigor and not give rise to indolence; for if indolence arises, one will suffer without end.
"O sons of good family!

All these phenomena are by their very nature empty and free from all obstructions. You should contemplate that within the principle of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, which is without obstruction, there is no phenomenon of indolence, nor is there anyone who is indolent; neither this place, nor time, nor conditions can be apprehended therein."

"In this way, Subhūti, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they achieve sublime skillful means and establish sentient beings so that they abide in the principle of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena; yet, while establishing them therein, they harbor no notion of duality."

Why is this? Because the principle of the emptiness of intrinsic nature is non-dual and without distinction; it is not that there is no duality such that one could form dualistic conceptions regarding it.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, instructs and exhorts all classes of sentient beings based on the teaching of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, causing them to practice diligently, saying:
"O sons of good family!..."

You should apply yourself with diligent vigor toward wholesome dharmas. When practicing the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, you should not conceptualize these dharmas in terms of duality or non-duality;
when practicing the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments, you should not conceptualize these dharmas in terms of duality or non-duality;
and when practicing the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, you should not conceptualize these dharmas in terms of duality or non-duality.
When practicing the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—one should not contemplate these phenomena in terms of dualistic or non-dualistic characteristics;
when abiding in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, one should not contemplate these phenomena in terms of dualistic or non-dualistic characteristics;
and when abiding in suchness up to the inconceivable realm, one should not contemplate these phenomena in terms of dualistic or non-dualistic characteristics.
When abiding in the noble truths of suffering, origination, cessation, and the path, one should not contemplate these phenomena in terms of dualistic or non-dualistic characteristics;
when cultivating the eight liberations up to the ten totalities, one should not contemplate these phenomena in terms of dualistic or non-dualistic characteristics;
and when cultivating the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata, one should not contemplate them in terms of dualistic or non-dualistic characteristics.
When cultivating from the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma Stage, one should not contemplate these dharmas in terms of dual or non-dual characteristics;
when cultivating all dharani-doors and samadhi-doors, one should not contemplate these dharmas in terms of dual or non-dual characteristics;
when cultivating the five eyes and the six supernormal powers, one should not contemplate these dharmas in terms of dual or non-dual characteristics.
When cultivating the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, one should not contemplate these dharmas in terms of dualistic or non-dualistic characteristics;
when cultivating the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty minor marks, one should not contemplate these dharmas in terms of dualistic or non-dualistic characteristics;
when cultivating the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity, one should not contemplate these dharmas in terms of dualistic or non-dualistic characteristics.

When cultivating all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), one should not contemplate these phenomena in terms of dualistic or non-dualistic characteristics;
when cultivating the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, one should not contemplate these phenomena in terms of dualistic or non-dualistic characteristics;

and when cultivating all the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas, one should not contemplate these phenomena in terms of dualistic or non-dualistic characteristics.
When practicing any other immeasurable Buddha-dharmas, one should not contemplate these dharmas in terms of dualistic or non-dualistic characteristics. Why is this?
O son of good family!
"In this way, all these phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature; because the principle of emptiness of intrinsic nature should not be conceptualized as dual or non-dual. "Thus it is, Subhūti!"

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they achieve sublime skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) and carry out the bodhisattva conduct to mature sentient beings. Once these sentient beings have been matured, they establish them gradually according to what is appropriate for each: some they cause to abide in the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), some in the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), some in the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*), or some in the fruit of arhatship (*arhat*); some they cause to abide in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, some in the superior state of a bodhisattva, or some in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they achieve such skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). By the power of these skillful means, they see sentient beings whose minds are largely distracted, who do not restrain their sense faculties regarding the objects of desire, and who initiate various kinds of non-quiescent actions. Having seen them, they employ skillful means to cause them to enter superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*), saying: 'Come!'"
"Good son! You should cultivate the supreme samādhi, and do not give rise to thoughts of distraction or even the notion of 'supreme concentration. Why is this?
All these phenomena are empty by their very nature; within this emptiness of intrinsic nature, no phenomenon can be found that may be called "distracted" or "one-pointed.

If you are able to abide in this sublime concentration, all the wholesome deeds you perform will be swiftly fulfilled, and you shall likewise abide in the emptiness of intrinsic nature according to your wish.
What is called "wholesome deeds performed"?
It refers to the arousal of superior and pure actions of body, speech, and mind;
whether it be the cultivation of the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, or the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path.
If one cultivates the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
if one dwells in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature; if one dwells in suchness up to the inconceivable realm;
if one dwells in the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; or if one cultivates the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four...
Regarding the meditative concentrations on form: whether one cultivates the eight liberations up to the ten totalities;
or cultivates the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata; or enters the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth;
or cultivates the stages from the Ground of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma; or cultivates all doors of dhāraṇī and doors of samādhi; or...
If one cultivates the five eyes and the six supernormal powers; if one cultivates the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
if one cultivates the thirty-two marks of a Great Being and the eighty minor marks;
if one cultivates the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity; if one cultivates all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the [knowledge of all aspects]...
The wisdom of all aspects: whether one cultivates the path of the śrāvaka, the path of the pratyekabuddha, the path of the bodhisattva, or the path of the Tathāgata;
whether one cultivates the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;

whether one cultivates the conduct of a bodhisattva mahāsattva and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha; or whether one brings sentient beings to maturity and purifies the buddha-fields.

"Earth. In this way, all these supreme, pure, and virtuous dharmas are swiftly accomplished through the power of meditative concentration, and one abides in the emptiness of intrinsic nature according to one's aspiration. "Thus it is, Subhūti!"

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), from their first production of the thought of enlightenment until its ultimate consummation, seek to accomplish virtuous benefits without ever ceasing. For the sake of bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, they travel from one buddha-field to another, attending upon and making offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. In the presence of these Buddhas, they listen to and receive the True Dharma; even as they relinquish one body and take up another throughout immeasurable eons, until they reach unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they never forget or lose it during that interval.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva has attained dhāraṇīs and his faculties are undiminished.
Why is this? Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly and fully cultivates the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), and is able to engage in all activities with skillful reflection.

By virtue of possessing well-cultivated omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), they are able to skillfully contemplate all that they do and can fully cultivate all paths—namely, the path of the śrāvakas, the path of the pratyekabuddhas, the path of the bodhisattvas, the path of the buddhas, the superior path of devas, the superior path of humans, and the superior supernormal powers of the bodhisattvas.

Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in the superior power of the superknowledges, they constantly perform deeds for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings; although they pass through the cycles of birth and death in the various realms of existence, their superior superknowledges never diminish.
By means of the superknowledges of maturation, which are never subject to decline, they constantly perform supreme deeds for the benefit of both themselves and others.

Thus, Subhūti, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, dwelling in the skillful means of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, they are able to effectively bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they achieve such skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). By the power of these skillful means, they abide in the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) and perceive that sentient beings possess meager wisdom, and that through delusion and inversion they perform various evil deeds. They then employ skillful means to lead them into the profound perfection of wisdom, speaking thus: 'Come!'"

"Noble sons! You should cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) and contemplate that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty and quiescent. If you can cultivate this perfection of wisdom and contemplate that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty and quiescent, then all the physical, verbal, and mental actions you practice will lead toward the deathless (amṛta) and attain the fruit of the deathless; they will certainly have the deathless as their final limit."
"O sons of good family!

All these phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature. Within this emptiness of intrinsic nature, although sentient beings and phenomena cannot be apprehended, that which is practiced is likewise never lost."
Why is this? Son of good family!
The principle of the emptiness of intrinsic nature neither increases nor decreases; within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, there is likewise no phenomenon that increases or decreases.

Why is this so? Because the principle of original nature-emptiness takes non-existence as its very nature; it is free from all conceptual discrimination and transcends all frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*). Therefore, within this, there is no phenomenon to be increased or diminished, and by virtue of this, there is also no loss or retrogression in what has been accomplished.
"Therefore, you all should cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) and, contemplating essential emptiness (prakṛti-śūnyatā), perform what is to be done. Thus, Subhūti,

when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they skillfully employ means (upāya-kauśalya) to instruct and admonish sentient beings, causing them to enter the perfection of wisdom, abide in essential emptiness, and cultivate all wholesome deeds.

“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva thus instructs and exhorts sentient beings without ever becoming weary or negligent; that is to say, he himself constantly practices the ten paths of wholesome action and also encourages others to constantly practice the ten paths of wholesome action;
he himself constantly upholds the five precepts of a lay follower (*upāsaka*) and also encourages others to constantly uphold the five precepts of a lay follower.”
They themselves constantly observe the eight precepts of the upavāsa, and they also encourage others to constantly observe the eight precepts of the upavāsa;
they themselves constantly observe the monastic precepts, and they also encourage others to constantly observe the monastic precepts;

they themselves constantly practice the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments, and they also encourage others to constantly practice the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments.

They themselves constantly practice the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, and they also exhort others to constantly practice the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;

they themselves constantly practice the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and they also exhort others to constantly practice the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;

they themselves constantly practice the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, and they also exhort others to constantly practice the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom.

They themselves constantly abide in inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature, and they also exhort others to constantly abide in inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature;
they themselves constantly abide in suchness up to the inconceivable realm, and they also exhort others to constantly abide in suchness up to the inconceivable realm;

they themselves constantly abide in the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, and they also exhort others to constantly abide in the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.

They themselves constantly practice the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality, and they also encourage others to constantly practice the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality;
they themselves constantly practice all the bodhisattva stages, and they also encourage others to constantly practice all the bodhisattva stages;
they themselves constantly practice all the doors of dhāraṇī and the doors of samādhi, and they also encourage others to constantly practice all the doors of dhāraṇī and the doors of samādhi.

They themselves constantly cultivate and study the five eyes and the six supernormal powers, and they also encourage others to constantly cultivate and study the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;

they themselves constantly cultivate and study the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and they also encourage others to constantly cultivate and study the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;

they themselves constantly cultivate and study the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks, and they also encourage others to constantly cultivate and study the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks.

They themselves constantly cultivate and study the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of equanimity, and they also encourage others to constantly cultivate and study the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of equanimity;

they themselves constantly cultivate and study all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), and they also encourage others to constantly cultivate and study all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects;

they themselves constantly initiate the wisdom of the fruit of stream-entry up to the wisdom of pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, yet they do not dwell in the fruit of stream-entry up to pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, and they also encourage others to constantly initiate the wisdom of the fruit of stream-entry up to the wisdom of pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, or cause them to dwell in the fruit of stream-entry up to pratyekabuddha-enlightenment.
They themselves constantly initiate the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and also exhort others to constantly initiate the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;

they themselves constantly initiate the path to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas and also exhort others to constantly initiate the path to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas.

"In this way, Subhūti, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they cultivate wholesome deeds themselves through skillful means, never becoming weary or negligent, and they instruct and guide all sentient beings to cultivate wholesome deeds, never becoming weary or negligent."
“Subhūti! This is called the skillful means of bodhisattva mahāsattvas when they practice the profound perfection of wisdom.
By the power of this skillful means, they establish sentient beings within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), yet they are able not to destroy the characteristics of the limit of reality.”
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If all dharmas are empty by their very nature, and within this emptiness of intrinsic nature neither sentient beings nor dharmas can be apprehended—and since there is likewise no ‘non-dharma’ therein—how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva seeks to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of sentient beings, desiring to constantly provide benefit throughout the future?”
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said:

all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature. Within this emptiness of intrinsic nature, neither sentient beings nor phenomena can be apprehended; therefore, within it, there is also no such thing as non-phenomena.
Subhūti, you should know this:

if all phenomena were not empty by their very nature, then when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they would not abide in the principle of emptiness of intrinsic nature to seek the realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, nor would they preach the Dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature for the benefit of sentient beings.

Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they abide in the principle that all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature; seeking to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they teach the dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature for the benefit of sentient beings.

“Subhūti! What are those dharmas whose intrinsic nature is entirely empty, such that when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, having realized intrinsic emptiness as it truly is, they abide in intrinsic emptiness and teach the Dharma to others?”

"Subhūti! From form (*rūpa*) up to consciousness (*vijñāna*), their intrinsic nature is entirely empty; from the sense-base of the eye (*cakṣur-āyatana*) up to the sense-base of the mind (*mano-āyatana*), their intrinsic nature is entirely empty;

from the sense-base of forms (*rūpa-āyatana*) up to the sense-base of phenomena (*dharma-āyatana*), their intrinsic nature is entirely empty; and from the element of the eye (*cakṣurdhātu*) up to the element of the mind (*manodhātu*), their intrinsic nature is entirely empty."
Emptiness: the intrinsic nature of the form realm up to the dharma-realm is entirely empty;
the intrinsic nature of the eye-consciousness realm up to the mind-consciousness realm is entirely empty; the intrinsic nature of eye-contact up to mind-contact is entirely empty;
and the intrinsic nature of all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition up to all feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition is entirely empty.
The element of earth up to the element of consciousness are all empty of intrinsic nature; the causal condition up to the dominant condition are all empty of intrinsic nature;
all phenomena produced from conditions are empty of intrinsic nature; ignorance up to old age and death are all empty of intrinsic nature;
and the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom [are all empty of intrinsic nature].
Their nature is entirely empty; the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments are all empty by nature.
The four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path are all empty by nature. The gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are all empty by nature.
From internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, they are all empty by nature.
Their nature is entirely empty; from suchness up to the inconceivable realm, their intrinsic nature is entirely empty;
the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, their intrinsic nature is entirely empty; the eight liberations up to the ten totalities, their intrinsic nature is entirely empty;
the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata, their intrinsic nature is entirely empty; and the stage of extreme joy...
Up to and including the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), their intrinsic nature is empty;
all doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of samādhi are empty by intrinsic nature; the five eyes and the six supernormal powers are empty by intrinsic nature;
the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are empty by intrinsic nature; and the thirty-two marks of a Great Being are [empty].
The eighty minor marks are empty of intrinsic nature; the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity are empty of intrinsic nature;
all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects are empty of intrinsic nature;
the fruit of stream-entry up to the awakening of a pratyekabuddha are empty of intrinsic nature; all bodhisattvas...
The nature of the bodhisattva’s practice is entirely empty; the nature of the Buddhas’ unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is entirely empty;
and the nature of the perpetual severance of the continuity of all afflictions and habitual tendencies is entirely empty.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they understand as it truly is that the aggregates, such as form (*rūpa*), up to and including the continuity of all habitual tendencies of the afflictions (*kleśavāsanā*), are by nature empty. Having thus abided in this emptiness of intrinsic nature, they proclaim for the sake of all sentient beings this Dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the emptiness of the internal were not empty by its very nature, or if the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned, the absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the beginningless and endless, the emptiness of dispersion and non-dispersion, the emptiness of essential nature, the emptiness of self- and common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence were also not empty by their very nature, then when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should not teach sentient beings that all phenomena are empty by their very nature; to do so would be to destroy the emptiness of essential nature."
However, the principle of the emptiness of intrinsic nature is indestructible; it is neither eternal nor annihilated. Why is this so?
Because the principle of the emptiness of intrinsic nature has no direction and no location; it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.

This principle of emptiness is also called the "abiding nature of phenomena" (*dharmasthititā*). Within it, there is no phenomenon, no aggregation and no dispersal, no decrease and no increase, no arising and no ceasing, and no purity and no impurity; this is the fundamental nature in which all phenomena abide.

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell therein, seeking to proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; yet they do not perceive any dharma that is being sought or proceeded toward, nor do they perceive any dharma that is not being sought or proceeded toward. Because all dharmas are entirely without a place of abiding, it is called the "abiding of dharmas" (*dharmasthiti*).

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas abide in this practice and cultivate the profound perfection of wisdom, having seen that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, they will certainly attain non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not perceive any dharma capable of acting as an obstacle; since they see all dharmas as being without obstruction, they give rise to no doubt or hesitation regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and thus they do not regress.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
dwelling in the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, contemplate that within this emptiness of intrinsic nature nothing at all can be apprehended—
namely, a self, a sentient being, a life-principle, a soul, a nourisher, or a person."
Indeed, the person (pudgala), the mind-born (manomaya), the youth (māṇava), the agent, the experiencer, the knower, and the seer are all unapprehendable;
from form (rūpa) up to consciousness (vijñāna), they are also unapprehendable; from the eye-base (cakṣur-āyatana) up to the mind-base (mano-āyatana), they are also unapprehendable;
and from the form-base (rūpa-āyatana) up to the phenomena-base (dharma-āyatana), they are also unapprehendable.
The eye-element up to the mind-element is also unapprehendable; the form-element up to the phenomena-element is also unapprehendable;
the eye-consciousness-element up to the mind-consciousness-element is also unapprehendable; the eye-contact up to the mind-contact is also unapprehendable;
and the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to those produced with mind-contact as a condition...
The various feelings that arise are also unapprehendable; the earth element up to the consciousness element are also unapprehendable;
the causal conditions up to the dominant condition are also unapprehendable; the phenomena produced from conditions are also unapprehendable;
ignorance up to old age and death are also unapprehendable; and the perfection of generosity [is likewise unapprehendable].

Even the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is unapprehendable; from internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*), they too are unapprehendable;
from suchness (*tathatā*) up to the inconceivable realm (*acintya-dhātu*), they too are unapprehendable;

the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path (*duḥkha-samudaya-nirodha-mārga-āryasatya*) are also unapprehendable; and from the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the eight [path factors]...
The branches of the noble path are also unattainable; the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions are also unattainable;
the eight liberations up to the ten totalities are also unattainable; the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are also unattainable;
and [the stages] from the stage of pure observation up to the Tathāgata are also unattainable.
The stages (*bhūmi*) are also unapprehendable; from the Stage of Extreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) up to the Cloud of Dharma Stage (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), they are also unapprehendable.

All doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of samādhi are also unapprehendable. The five eyes and the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are also unapprehendable, and the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) are also unapprehendable.
The quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣadharma*) and the state of constant equanimity (*upekṣā*) are unobtainable;
omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are also unobtainable;

the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*) up to the awakening of a solitary buddha (*pratyekabuddhabodhi*) are unobtainable; and all the practices of bodhisattva mahāsattvas (*bodhisattvamahāsattvacaryā*) are also unobtainable.
The unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is also unattainable; wholesome dharmas and unwholesome dharmas are also unattainable;
dharmas with definite maturation and dharmas without definite maturation are also unattainable;
contaminated dharmas and uncontaminated dharmas are also unattainable; mundane dharmas and supramundane dharmas are also unattainable.

They cannot be apprehended; conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena likewise cannot be apprehended, and the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks likewise cannot be apprehended.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 473. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Two, Chapter Seventy-Eight on the Reality Limit (Bhūtakoṭi), Section Two. "Subhūti, you should know this!"

Suppose a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha were to manifest four assemblies—namely, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—and that manifested Buddha were to preach the sublime Dharma to those four assemblies for an eon, or even more than an eon. What do you think?

Among those thus transformed, is there anyone who has attained the fruit of a stream-enterer, or the fruit of a once-returner, or the fruit of a non-returner, or the fruit of arhatship; or who has attained the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; or who has received the prediction of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
"Why is this? Because these transformed beings have no substantial reality; it is not possible for those who lack the reality of dharmas to attain fruition or receive a prediction of enlightenment.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"All dharmas are likewise; they are all empty of intrinsic nature and entirely devoid of substantial reality. Within this, what bodhisattva mahāsattva could teach what dharma to what sentient beings so that they might realize the fruit of a stream-enterer, or the fruit of a once-returner, or the fruit of a non-returner, or the fruit of arhatship, or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, or receive the prediction of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
“Subhūti, you should know this:

although bodhisattva mahāsattvas proclaim the dharma of emptiness for the sake of sentient beings, those sentient beings are in fact unapprehendable. Out of compassion for those who have fallen into inverted dharmas, they deliver them and cause them to abide in non-inverted dharmas.”

Non-inversion means the absence of conceptual construction; because there is no inversion where there is no conceptual construction, whereas if there is conceptual construction, there is inversion, as it is the outflow thereof.
“Subhūti, you should know that perversion is itself the dharma of non-perversion. Within non-perversion there is no self and no sentient being;
as explained at length, there is none who knows and none who sees, nor is there form, feeling, perception, [volition, or consciousness].”
Formations and consciousness likewise lack the sense base of the eye up to the sense base of the mind; they lack the sense base of form up to the sense base of mental phenomena;
they lack the element of the eye up to the element of the mind; they lack the element of form up to the element of mental phenomena;
they lack the element of eye-consciousness up to the element of mind-consciousness; and they lack eye-contact up to mind-contact.
Furthermore, there are no feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition;
there are no earth element, up to and including the consciousness element; there are no causal conditions, up to and including predominant conditions;
there are no phenomena produced from conditions; there is no ignorance, up to and including old age and death; nor is there anything else.

The perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom; likewise, the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-entities; likewise, true suchness up to the inconceivable realm;
likewise, the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; and likewise, the four applications of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path—none of these exist.
Furthermore, there are no four dhyānas, four immeasurables, or four formless attainments;
nor are there the eight liberations up to the ten totalities; nor are there the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
nor are there the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata; nor are there the stage of extreme joy up to the [Dharma]...
In the stage of Clouds, there are likewise no dhāraṇī-doors or samādhi-doors; there are no five eyes or six supernormal powers;
there are no Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
there are no thirty-two marks of a great man or eighty minor characteristics; and there is no non-forgetfulness.
In the Dharma, there is neither the nature of constant equanimity, nor omniscience, the knowledge of the paths, or the knowledge of all aspects;
nor is there the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
nor is there any practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas.

“Subhūti! This ‘non-existence’ is itself the emptiness of intrinsic nature. When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they abide within this and perceive that sentient beings have fallen into perverted conceptions; [thereupon,] by means of skillful methods...”
He skillfully brings about liberation, meaning he causes them to be liberated from the notion of a self where there is no self, and the notion of a sentient being where there is no sentient being;
as explained at length, this extends even to the notion of a knower where there is no knower, and the notion of a seer where there is no seer;
and he also causes them to be liberated from the notion of permanence where there is no permanence, the notion of pleasure where there is no pleasure, and the notion of a self where there is no self.
The perception of purity in the impure also brings about liberation from the notions of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness;
it also brings about liberation from the notions of the eye-base through to the mind-base;
and it also brings about liberation from the notions of the form-element through to the mental-object-element.

The perception of the sense-field of form up to the sense-field of mental phenomena is also made to be liberated; the perception of the eye-element up to the mind-element is also made to be liberated;
the perception of the eye-element up to the mind-element is also made to be liberated; the perception of the form-element up to the mental-phenomena-element is also made to be liberated;
and the perception of the eye-consciousness-element up to the mind-consciousness-element is also made to be liberated.
The perception of the element of consciousness up to the element of mental consciousness is also made to be liberated; the perception of eye-contact up to mind-contact is also made to be liberated;

and the perceptions of the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition, and the feeling produced with eye-contact as condition... [are also made to be liberated].

He also causes the various feelings and perceptions arising with mental contact as a condition to be liberated from the element of earth up to the element of consciousness, and from the perception of the element of earth up to the perception of the element of consciousness;

he also causes them to be liberated from the absence of causal conditions up to the absence of predominant conditions, and from the perception of causal conditions up to the perception of predominant conditions; he also causes them to be liberated from that which arises from conditions.
One causes liberation from the conceptualization of all phenomena as being produced from conditions;
one also causes liberation from ignorance up to old age and death, and from the conceptualization of ignorance up to old age and death;
one also causes liberation from the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, and from the conceptualization of the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom.
It also brings liberation from the notion of "many flavors," and it brings liberation from the notions of "inner emptiness" up to "emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence";
it also brings liberation from the notions of "suchness" up to "the inconceivable realm"; and it also brings liberation from the notions of "suffering" and "origination."
...the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; he also brings about liberation from the notion of the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.

He also brings about liberation from the absence of the four applications of mindfulness up to the eight factors of the noble path, as well as from the notions of the four applications of mindfulness up to the eight factors of the noble path.
He also brings about liberation from the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments.
He brings about liberation from the perceptions of the dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
he also brings about liberation from the perceptions of the eight liberations up to the ten totalities;
and he brings about liberation from the doors of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—from emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness itself.
The perception of the gates also causes liberation from the perception of the Stage of Pure Contemplation up to the Stage of the Tathāgata;
it also causes liberation from the perception of the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Stage of the Dharma Cloud; it also causes liberation from the perception of all dhāraṇī-gates.
...the gateways of samādhi and all the gateways of dhāraṇī; he causes them to be liberated even from the conceptualization of the gateways of samādhi.
He causes them to be liberated even from the absence of the five eyes and six supernormal powers, as well as the conceptualization of the five eyes and six supernormal powers.

He causes them to be liberated even from the absence of the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, as well as [the conceptualization of] the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
They cause liberation from the notion of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;

they also cause liberation from the notion that there are no thirty-two marks of a great man and eighty secondary signs, as well as from the notion of the thirty-two marks of a great man and eighty secondary signs;

they also cause liberation from the absence of the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity, as well as from the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity.
He also causes them to be liberated from the notion of "all-knowledge," "knowledge of the paths," and "knowledge of all aspects";
he also causes them to be liberated from the absence of the notion of "all-knowledge," "knowledge of the paths," and "knowledge of all aspects";

he also causes them to be liberated from the fruits of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, as well as from the notions of the fruits of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; he also causes them to be liberated...
They liberate them from all conceptions of the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and from all practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;

they also cause them to be liberated from all conceptions of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas and from the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas;
they also cause them to be liberated from the five aggregates of clinging and all other contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*). They also cause them to be liberated...
They would have to be liberated from the various untainted dharmas, such as the four foundations of mindfulness. Why is this?

Because the various untainted dharmas, such as the four foundations of mindfulness, are not like the ultimate truth—which is without arising or cessation, without marks, unconditioned, free from conceptual proliferation, and non-discriminative—and therefore they too would have to be liberated.

That dharma which is the true ultimate meaning is the emptiness of intrinsic nature; this emptiness of intrinsic nature is precisely the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment realized by all Buddhas.
"Subhūti, you should know this!"
In this, there is no self up to and including a "seer" to be found; nor is there form up to and including consciousness to be found;
nor is there the eye-base up to and including the mind-base to be found; nor is there the form-base up to and including the phenomena-base to be found;
nor is there the eye-element up to and including the mind-element to be found; nor is there the form-element up to and including the phenomena-element [to be found].
The element of the eye can be apprehended, yet the element of visual consciousness up to the element of mental consciousness cannot be apprehended;

the contact of the eye up to the contact of the mind cannot be apprehended; the various feelings produced with the contact of the eye as condition up to the various feelings produced with the contact of the mind as condition cannot be apprehended; and the earth element up to the consciousness element cannot be apprehended.
One cannot find causes and conditions, nor even dominant conditions; one cannot find any phenomena produced from conditions;
one cannot find ignorance, nor even old age and death; one cannot find the perfection of generosity, nor even the perfection of wisdom; nor can one find internal emptiness...
One cannot find the emptiness of the nature of non-nature; nor can one find anything from suchness up to the inconceivable realm;
nor can one find the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
nor can one find the four applications of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; nor can one find the four dhyānas or the four immeasurables.
The four formless absorptions cannot be apprehended; nor can the eight liberations up to the ten totalities be apprehended;
nor can the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—be apprehended;
nor can the stage of pure observation up to the stage of a Tathāgata be apprehended; nor can the stages from the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma be apprehended.
Furthermore, there are no dhāraṇī-doors or samādhi-doors to be found; there are no five eyes or six supernormal powers to be found;
there are no Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha to be found;
and there are no thirty-two marks of a Great Man or eighty minor characteristics to be found.
Furthermore, there is no dharma of non-forgetfulness nor the state of constant equanimity to be found;
there is no all-knowledge, no knowledge of the paths, and no knowledge of all aspects to be found;
there is no fruit of the stream-enterer up to and including the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha to be found; and there is no conduct of any bodhisattva mahāsattva to be found.
There is no unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas that can be attained.
"Subhūti, you should know this!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not seek to proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of a path to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; rather, they seek to proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment solely for the sake of the fact that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty."
This intrinsic nature is empty of the past, future, and middle limits; it is eternally intrinsically empty and has never not been empty.

Abiding in the perfection of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the knowledge of the aspects of the path for the sake of liberating all sentient beings from their grasping at the notion of a "sentient being" and the notion of "dharmas."

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the knowledge of the aspects of the path, they immediately attain all paths—namely, the path of the śrāvakas, the path of the pratyekabuddhas, the path of the bodhisattvas, and the path of the buddhas.

“Subhūti, you should know that once these bodhisattva mahāsattvas have attained perfection in all paths, they are able to bring the sentient beings to be converted to maturity, and they are also able to purify the buddha-fields they seek to adorn; they then maintain their life-force and proceed toward the realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
Having realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, one is able to ensure that the Buddha-eye is forever uninterrupted and indestructible.
What is meant by the Buddha-eye? It refers to the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).

All Buddhas of the past, future, and present, dwelling in the worlds of the ten directions, proclaim the sublime Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings; there are none who do not take this emptiness of intrinsic nature as their Buddha-eye.
“Subhūti, you should know this:

there are certainly no Buddhas who appear in the world apart from the emptiness of intrinsic nature. Of those Buddhas who appear in the world, there are none who do not all teach the meaning of the emptiness of intrinsic nature. The sentient beings to be converted must hear the Buddhas teach the principle of the emptiness of intrinsic nature before they can enter the noble path and attain the fruits of the noble path; apart from the emptiness of intrinsic nature, there is no other expedient means.”

"Therefore, Subhūti, bodhisattva mahāsattvas who wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should correctly abide in the principle of the emptiness of intrinsic nature and practice the six perfections as well as the other practices of bodhisattva mahāsattvas."

If one correctly abides in the principle of the emptiness of intrinsic nature and practices the six perfections as well as other bodhisattva-mahāsattva deeds, one will never fall away from the knowledge of all modes, and will always be able to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is truly rare for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to practice all dharmas while knowing that they are all empty by their very nature.”

Yet, within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, there is never any loss or destruction; that is to say, one does not grasp at form up to consciousness as being different from the emptiness of intrinsic nature,
nor does one grasp at the sense base of the eye up to the sense base of the mind as being different from the emptiness of intrinsic nature,

nor does one grasp at the sense base of forms up to the sense base of phenomena as being different from the emptiness of intrinsic nature, nor does one grasp at the element of the eye up to the element of the mind.
One does not grasp at the emptiness of distinct intrinsic nature regarding the form realm up to the dharma realm;
nor does one grasp at the emptiness of distinct intrinsic nature regarding the eye-consciousness realm up to the mind-consciousness realm;
nor does one grasp at the emptiness of distinct intrinsic nature regarding eye-contact up to mind-contact; nor does one grasp at the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition.
Even up to the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition, they are not different from the emptiness of their own nature;

nor do they grasp the earth element up to the consciousness element as being different from the emptiness of their own nature; nor do they grasp the causal conditions up to the dominant conditions as being different from the emptiness of their own nature;
nor do they grasp the phenomena produced from conditions as being different from the emptiness of their own nature; nor...
One does not grasp that ignorance up to old age and death are distinct from the emptiness of intrinsic nature;
nor does one grasp that the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom are distinct from the emptiness of intrinsic nature;

nor does one grasp that inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature are distinct from the emptiness of intrinsic nature; nor does one grasp that suchness up to the inconceivable...

One does not conceive of the sphere of phenomena as being distinct from emptiness of intrinsic nature; nor does one conceive of the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path as being distinct from emptiness of intrinsic nature;
nor does one conceive of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path as being distinct from emptiness of intrinsic nature;
nor does one conceive of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments as being distinct from emptiness of intrinsic nature.
Nor does one grasp the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality as being other than the emptiness of intrinsic nature;
nor does one grasp the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—as being other than the emptiness of intrinsic nature;

nor does one grasp the stage of pure observation up to the stage of a Tathāgata as being other than the emptiness of intrinsic nature; nor does one grasp the stage of extreme joy up to the [Dharma-]...

One does not conceive of the earth element as being distinct from emptiness of intrinsic nature; nor does one conceive of all the doors of dhāraṇī and the doors of samādhi as being distinct from emptiness of intrinsic nature;
nor does one conceive of the five eyes and the six supernormal powers as being distinct from emptiness of intrinsic nature;
nor does one conceive of the ten powers of a Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, as being distinct from emptiness of intrinsic nature.
Nor does one grasp the thirty-two marks of a great man or the eighty secondary signs as being other than the emptiness of their own nature;
nor does one grasp the qualities of non-forgetfulness or the state of constant equanimity as being other than the emptiness of their own nature;
nor does one grasp all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, or the knowledge of all aspects as being other than the emptiness of their own nature; nor does one grasp the stage of stream-entry...
The fruits of the stream-enterer up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha do not differ from intrinsic emptiness;

nor does one grasp at the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as being different from intrinsic emptiness; nor does one grasp at the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as being different from intrinsic emptiness.

“World-Honored One! Form is itself the emptiness of intrinsic nature; the emptiness of intrinsic nature is itself form. Thus it continues up to: the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is itself the emptiness of intrinsic nature; the emptiness of intrinsic nature is itself the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas.”
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.
These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are truly rare; although they practice all dharmas, which are all empty of intrinsic nature, they never lose or destroy that emptiness of intrinsic nature.

“Subhūti, you should know this: form is not different from the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of intrinsic nature is not different from form; form itself is the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of intrinsic nature itself is form. This continues in the same way up to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas: it is not different from the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of intrinsic nature is not different from the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas; the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas is itself the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of intrinsic nature is itself the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas.”
“Subhūti, you should know this:

if form were different from the emptiness of its own nature, or if the emptiness of its own nature were different from form; if form were not the emptiness of its own nature, or if the emptiness of its own nature were not form—and likewise, up to and including, if the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas were different from the emptiness of its own nature, or if the emptiness of its own nature were different from the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas; if the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas were not the emptiness of its own nature, or if the emptiness of its own nature were not the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas—then when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they would not contemplate all phenomena as being empty by their very nature, nor would they be able to realize the knowledge of all aspects.”

Because form is not different from the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of intrinsic nature is not different from form; form itself is the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of intrinsic nature is itself form—and so on, up to the point that the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas is not different from the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of intrinsic nature is not different from the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas; the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas is itself the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of intrinsic nature is itself the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas—therefore, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they contemplate all phenomena as being empty of intrinsic nature, and are thus able to realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*).

Why is this? Apart from the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), there is not a single dharma that is real, permanent, destructible, or subject to cessation. Within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, likewise, there is not a single dharma that is real, permanent, destructible, or subject to cessation. It is only because foolish worldlings are deluded, mistaken, and inverted that they give rise to notions of differentiation, claiming that form (*rūpa*) is distinct from the emptiness of intrinsic nature; or that feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are distinct from the emptiness of intrinsic nature; and so on, up to claiming that all the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva are distinct from the emptiness of intrinsic nature, or that the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) of all buddhas is distinct from the emptiness of intrinsic nature.

Because these foolish people discriminate between phenomena and their intrinsic emptiness as being distinct, they do not know form as it truly is, nor do they know feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as they truly are.
Due to ignorance, one becomes attached to form, and becomes attached to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Due to this attachment, one conceives of form as "I" or "mine," and conceives of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as "I" or "mine."

Due to false conceptualization, one clings to internal and external things, thereby undergoing the aggregates of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness in future lives. Consequently, one is unable to attain liberation from birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and affliction within the various realms of existence, wandering endlessly through the cycle of the three realms of being.

"For this reason, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in the perfection of the emptiness of intrinsic nature and practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not grasp at form, nor do they negate form as being either empty or non-empty;
they do not grasp at feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor do they negate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as being either empty or non-empty."
In this way, up to and including, they do not grasp at any bodhisattva-mahāsattva practice, nor do they disrupt any bodhisattva-mahāsattva practice as being either empty or non-empty;

they do not grasp at the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas, nor do they disrupt the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas as being either empty or non-empty.
Why is this? Form does not destroy emptiness, nor does emptiness destroy form; one does not say, "This is form" and "This is emptiness.

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not destroy emptiness, nor does emptiness destroy feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; one does not say, "This is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness," and "This is emptiness."

In this way, up to and including all the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the emptiness does not destroy them, nor do they destroy the emptiness; that is to say, "this is all the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas" and "this is emptiness.

The unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas does not destroy emptiness, nor does emptiness destroy the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas; that is to say, "this is the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas" and "this is emptiness."
For example, space does not destroy space; the internal realm of space does not destroy the external realm of space, nor does the external realm of space destroy the internal realm of space.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
Form does not destroy emptiness, and emptiness does not destroy form;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not destroy emptiness, and emptiness does not destroy feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Why is this? Because all such phenomena are equally devoid of intrinsic nature and cannot be differentiated by saying, "this is empty" or "this is not empty.

In this way, even up to the point that the non-deteriorating emptiness of all bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices does not destroy emptiness, and emptiness does not destroy all bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices.
The unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas does not destroy emptiness, nor does emptiness destroy the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas. Why is this?
Because all such phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature and cannot be differentiated, such that one could say, "this is empty" and "this is not empty."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are by their very nature empty and entirely without distinction, in what state do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide when they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”

The unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas has no dualistic aspect; one cannot realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through dualistic aspects. We only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion, will explain this for us!
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said:

the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas has no dualistic aspect; it is not by means of a dualistic aspect that one can realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Why is this? Because awakening is non-dual and without discrimination; if one practices with respect to awakening by means of dualistic marks or through discrimination, one will certainly be unable to realize the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

“Subhūti, you should know that bodhisattva mahāsattvas do not practice toward awakening by means of dualistic marks, nor do they engage in conceptual discrimination; remaining entirely without abiding, they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.”

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not engage in dualistic characteristics regarding all phenomena, nor do they engage in conceptual discrimination, and remain entirely without engagement, they are then able to realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment that they seek.
“Subhūti, you should know that the unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete enlightenment sought by bodhisattva mahāsattvas cannot be realized by practicing with dualistic characteristics.”

The bodhi of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas does not engage with anything whatsoever; that is to say, it does not engage with form, nor does it engage with feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. In this way, it does not engage even with any of the practices of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, nor does it engage with the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening of the Buddhas.

Why is this? Because the enlightenment of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas does not take name and fame as a condition for grasping at a self or what belongs to a self; that is to say, they do not form such thoughts as:
"I am practicing with regard to form," or "I am practicing with regard to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."
In this way, he does not even form such thoughts as:
"I am practicing all the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva; I am practicing for the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas."
"Furthermore, Subhūti! The bodhi of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is not practiced for the sake of grasping, nor is it practiced for the sake of relinquishing.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed [the Buddha], saying:
“World-Honored One!
If the bodhi of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is not practiced by way of grasping and not practiced by way of abandoning, then where should the bodhi of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas be practiced?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Where would the bodhi of a transformation body of the Tathāgata function?"
"Is it for the sake of grasping that one practices,
or is it for the sake of relinquishing that one practices? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
Since the transformation body of the Tathāgata is truly non-existent, how could one speak of there being any bodhi or any sphere of activity to be either grasped or abandoned?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Where would the bodhi of all arhats go while they are in a dream?"
"Is it for the sake of grasping that one practices,
or is it for the sake of relinquishing that one practices? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One!

For all Arhats, the outflows are forever exhausted; the hindrances of sloth and torpor have been extinguished along with their entanglements, and they are ultimately without dreams. How could there be any place for the practice of awakening within a dream, whether involving grasping or relinquishing?"
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.

All Arhats are ultimately without dreams, because their conceptualizations of torpor and sleep have been exhausted. The awakening of all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise: they do not practice by way of grasping, nor do they practice by way of abandoning; there is no place of practice at all, for they have realized that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If the bodhi of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the profound perfection of wisdom is practiced neither through grasping nor through relinquishing,
and is entirely without a locus of practice— meaning one does not practice with regard to form— "
Furthermore, if one does not practice with respect to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness—
and likewise does not practice even unto all the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor practice with respect to the unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas— would it not be the case that the bodhisattva mahāsattva acts for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings?
They practice the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
they do not practice inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the nature of non-nature; they do not practice suchness up to the inconceivable realm;
they do not practice the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; they do not practice the four applications of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path.
The factors of the path do not practice the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments;
they do not practice the eight liberations up to the ten totalities; they do not practice the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
they do not practice the stages from the Ground of Extreme Joy up to the Ground of Dharma Clouds; and they do not practice any dhāraṇīs.
They do not engage with the doors of liberation or the doors of samādhi; they do not engage with the five eyes or the six supernormal powers;

they do not engage with the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; they do not engage with the thirty-two marks of a great man or the eighty secondary characteristics;
they do not engage with the quality of non-forgetfulness or the nature of constant equanimity; they do not engage with the one...

By means of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), how does a bodhisattva— without abiding [in those states]—
utilize their superior supernormal powers to mature sentient beings and purify buddha-fields, thereby attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Although the bodhi of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas has no place of practice, yet for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas must practice the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom; likewise, they must practice all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); they must abide in the sublime supernormal powers of a bodhisattva to mature sentient beings and purify buddha-fields, and only then attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening."
