The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If all the bodhi of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas has no sphere of activity, will it not be that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, do not abide in the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, but long cultivate them until they are fulfilled; and likewise, do not abide in all-knowledge, the knowledge of paths, and the knowledge of all aspects, but long cultivate them until they are fulfilled; and do not abide in the sublime supernormal powers of a bodhisattva to mature sentient beings and purify buddha-fields, but long cultivate them until they are fulfilled, yet still attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Although the bodhi of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas has no place of practice, yet for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas must abide in the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, practicing them for a long time until they are fulfilled. Likewise, they must abide in all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñā*), practicing them for a long time until they are fulfilled; and they must abide in the sublime supernormal powers of a bodhisattva to mature sentient beings and purify buddha-fields, practicing them for a long time until they are fulfilled, before they attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening."

Subhūti, you should know that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva has not yet fully perfected all the roots of goodness, they will ultimately be unable to attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek.
"Subhūti, you should know this!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should abide in the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of form;
they should abide in the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; and so on, up to..."
Abiding in the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices, one should abide in the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of the unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas; one should abide in the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena,
and one should abide in the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all sentient beings, while practicing the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom.
Having brought the *prajñāpāramitā* to fulfillment, and likewise having brought to fulfillment the cultivation of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*),
the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*),

and having perfected the maturation of sentient beings and the purification of Buddha-fields through the cultivation of the bodhisattva’s sublime supernormal powers, one then attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

“Subhūti, you should know that the principle of the intrinsic emptiness of all these phenomena, as well as the principle of the intrinsic emptiness of all sentient beings, is utterly quiescent; there is not the slightest phenomenon capable of increasing or decreasing, arising or ceasing, being annihilated or eternal, being defiled or purified, or attaining a fruit or realizing clear observation.”

"Subhūti, you should know that it is by relying on worldly convention that bodhisattva mahāsattvas are said to cultivate the perfection of wisdom; having realized the emptiness of intrinsic nature as it truly is, they attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—not by relying on the ultimate truth."

Why is this so? Because within true ultimate reality, form cannot be apprehended, nor can feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness be apprehended; likewise, up to and including all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, they cannot be apprehended, nor can the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas be apprehended.

There is no one who practices all the practices of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who can be apprehended, nor is there anyone who practices the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas who can be apprehended.
"Subhūti! Thus all these dharmas are established by means of conventional designations; they do not depend on the ultimate truth. Subhūti!"

When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, although from their first generation of the mind they engage in the conduct of awakening for the sake of all sentient beings with extreme vigor, they do not apprehend this mind at all; they do not apprehend sentient beings, nor do they apprehend great awakening, nor do they apprehend Buddhas or Bodhisattvas, because all phenomena and all sentient beings are unapprehendable.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are entirely non-existent and all are unobtainable, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the conduct of enlightenment?”
How can one attain the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
Who practices the conduct of enlightenment?
And who, moreover, is able to realize it?
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?

At that former time, when you relied upon the realm of abandonment to sever all afflictions and obtain the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), and while abiding in the concentration of immediate succession (*ānantarya-samādhi*) attained the fruit of stream-entry, then the fruit of once-returning, then the fruit of non-returning, and finally the fruit of arhatship—did you at that time perceive any sentient being, or mind, or path, or fruit of the paths, as something that could be apprehended?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If at that time you, relying on the realm of abandonment, had abandoned all afflictions and attained the untainted faculties, yet found nothing whatsoever to be apprehended in the minds of sentient beings, nor in the path or the fruit of the path, how could you say that you attained the fruit of arhatship?”
Subhūti replied, “It is according to conventional discourse, not according to the ultimate truth.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"So it is! So it is! It is just as you have said."

So too it is with the bodhisattva mahāsattvas: they practice the path to enlightenment and attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening by relying on conventional discourse, not by relying on the ultimate truth.

“Subhūti, you should know that it is based on worldly convention (*saṃvṛti*) that one speaks metaphorically of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness; likewise, up to and including, it is based on worldly convention that one speaks metaphorically of all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas; and it is based on worldly convention that one speaks metaphorically of sentient beings, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas—it is not based on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).”

“Subhūti, you should know that bodhisattva mahāsattvas do not perceive any dharma that can increase or decrease, or benefit or harm, in regard to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, because the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is empty.”

"Subhūti, you should know that for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, even the intrinsic emptiness of all phenomena cannot be apprehended; how much less can an initial resolve to attain awakening be apprehended!"

Since even the initial arousal of the mind of enlightenment cannot be apprehended, how much less can there be anything apprehended in the cultivation of the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom!
How much less could there be anything to be apprehended by one who dwells in inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature!
How much less could there be anything to be apprehended by one who dwells in suchness up to the inconceivable realm!
How much less could there be anything to be attained while abiding in the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path!
How much less could there be anything to be attained while cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path!
How much less could there be anything to be attained through the cultivation of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments!
How much less could there be anything to be attained through the cultivation of the eight liberations up to the ten totalities!
How much less could there be anything to be attained by practicing the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness!
How much less could there be anything to be attained by practicing the stages from the Ground of Extreme Joy up to the Ground of the Dharma Cloud!
How much less could there be anything to be attained through the cultivation of all the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi!
How much less could there be anything to be attained through the cultivation of the five eyes and the six supernormal powers!
How much less could there be anything to be attained by cultivating the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha!
How much less could there be anything to be attained by cultivating the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs!
How much less could there be anything to be apprehended in the cultivation of the quality of non-forgetfulness or the state of constant equanimity!
How much less could there be anything to be apprehended in the cultivation of all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, or the knowledge of all aspects!
How much less could there be anything to be attained in practicing all the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva!
How much less could there be anything to be attained in practicing the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas!
"Subhūti! It is impossible that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, while dwelling in the cultivation of any of the Buddha-dharmas, should have any apprehension of them.
Thus it is, Subhūti!"

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) cultivate the conduct of great awakening through skillful means (upāya), realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings without interruption.
Chapter 79: On Being Without Deficiency, Part One. Second Division, Chapter 79: On Being Without Deficiency, Part One. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, although diligently applying effort in the practice of the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom,
abides in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature,
abides in suchness up to the inconceivable realm, and abides in the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path—
He practices the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path;
he practices the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; he practices the eight liberations up to the ten totalities;
he practices the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; and he practices from the Stage of Extreme Joy up to...
On the Dharma-Cloud Stage (*dharmameghā bhūmi*), one practices all *dhāraṇī* gates and *samādhi* gates;
one practices the five eyes and the six supernormal powers; one practices the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
one practices the thirty-two marks of a Great Being and the eighty minor marks; and one practices non-forgetfulness.
If one loses the dharma and the state of constant equanimity (*upekṣā*), or if one practices all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*),
and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), practices all the conducts of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, and practices the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas,
yet the cultivation of the path to enlightenment remains incomplete, one will be unable to realize what is sought.
Unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the path to enlightenment so that it becomes fully perfected, enabling them to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, is endowed with superior skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), then by the power of these skillful means, when practicing the *dānapāramitā*, they do not apprehend the gift, they do not apprehend the giver, and they do not apprehend the recipient; yet they do not practice the *dānapāramitā* while remaining distant from such dharmas. When this bodhisattva mahāsattva gives in this manner, they are able to fully illuminate the path to *sambodhi*, and they will swiftly accomplish the cultivation of that path."
Thus it is, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they cultivate the path to enlightenment through skillful means until it is brought to fulfillment, and are thus able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they possess sublime skillful means; by the power of these skillful means, they practice the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and so forth, up to practicing all the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas—all of which should be explained extensively as appropriate.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, cultivate the path to enlightenment with courageous and correct diligence?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom with skillful means, they do not conjoin form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, nor do they disperse form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness;
they do not conjoin the eye-base up to the mind-base, nor do they disperse the eye-base up to the mind-base."
The sphere of form up to the sphere of mental phenomena are neither conjoined nor dispersed;
the eye-element up to the mind-element are neither conjoined nor dispersed;
the form-element up to the mental-phenomena-element are neither conjoined nor dispersed.
They do not conjoin with the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element, nor do they disperse from the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element;
they do not conjoin with eye-contact up to mind-contact, nor do they disperse from eye-contact up to mind-contact;

they do not conjoin with the various feelings produced conditioned by eye-contact up to the various feelings produced conditioned by mind-contact, nor do they disperse from the various feelings produced conditioned by eye-contact up to the various feelings produced conditioned by mind-contact.
The earth element is neither conjoined with nor dissociated from the consciousness element;
the causal conditions are neither conjoined with nor dissociated from the dominant conditions;
and all phenomena arising from conditions are neither conjoined with nor dissociated from those very conditions.
Ignorance up to old age and death are neither conjoined nor dispersed.
Why is this? Because all such phenomena lack any intrinsic nature that could be conjoined or dispersed.

“Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, through skillful means, they do not conjoin the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, nor do they disperse the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
they do not conjoin inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature, nor do they disperse inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature.”
The suchness of non-conjunction up to the inconceivable realm, and the suchness of non-dispersion up to the inconceivable realm;
the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path as non-conjoined, and the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path as non-dispersed;
the four applications of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path as non-conjoined, and the four applications of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path as non-dispersed.

They do not combine with the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments, nor do they disperse from the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments;
they do not combine with the eight liberations up to the ten totalities, nor do they disperse from the eight liberations up to the ten totalities;
they do not combine with the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—nor do they disperse from the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
They do not conjoin with the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata, nor are they dissociated from the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata;
they do not conjoin with the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma Stage, nor are they dissociated from the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma Stage;
they do not conjoin with all the gateways of dhāraṇī and all the gateways of samādhi, nor are they dissociated from all the gateways of dhāraṇī and all the gateways of samādhi.
They do not conjoin with the five eyes and the six supernormal powers, nor do they disperse the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
they do not conjoin with the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, nor do they disperse the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they do not conjoin with the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs, nor do they disperse the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs.
They do not conjoin with the quality of non-forgetfulness or the state of constant equanimity, nor do they disperse from the quality of non-forgetfulness or the state of constant equanimity;

they do not conjoin with omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), nor do they disperse from omniscience, the knowledge of the paths, or the knowledge of all aspects;
they do not conjoin with the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, nor do they disperse from the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
They do not combine with all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, nor are they separated from all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
they do not combine with the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas, nor are they separated from the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas.
Why is this? Because all such phenomena lack any intrinsic nature that could be joined or separated. "Thus it is, Śāriputra!"
"When the bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they cultivate the path to enlightenment with courageous and correct diligence.
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If all phenomena are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature such that there is nothing to be joined or separated, how do bodhisattva mahāsattvas bring forth the *prajñāpāramitā* and train within it?"
"Bhagavan! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not train in the perfection of wisdom, they will ultimately be unable to attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek."
The Buddha told Śāriputra: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said:
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not train in the perfection of wisdom, they will ultimately be unable to attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment that they seek.
Śāriputra! Only by training in the perfection of wisdom can bodhisattva mahāsattvas realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek.
Śāriputra! The unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment sought by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas can only be realized through skillful means; it cannot be realized without skillful means.

“Śāriputra! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, if they were to perceive any dharma with an intrinsic nature that could be apprehended, then they would have something to grasp; but since they do not perceive any dharma with an intrinsic nature that can be apprehended, what is there to be grasped?”
That is to say, not grasping at the thought: "This is the perfection of wisdom" up to "this is the perfection of generosity";
"this is form" up to "this is consciousness"; "this is the sense base of the eye" up to "this is the sense base of the mind";
"this is the sense base of form" up to "this is the sense base of phenomena"; "this is the element of the eye" up to "this is the element of the mind"; "this is the element of form" up to...
Up to the dharma-element: this is the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element; this is eye-contact up to mind-contact;
this is the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition;
this is the earth element up to the consciousness element; this is the causal condition up to...
The dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*): these are all phenomena produced from conditions; these are ignorance up to old age and death;
these are inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature; these are suchness up to the inconceivable realm;
these are the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; these are the four...

These are the foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; these are the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; these are the eight liberations up to the ten totalities;
these are the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; these are the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata. These...
These are the stages from the Ground of Utmost Joy up to the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma;
these are all the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi; these are the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
these are the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; these are the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty secondary characteristics.
Excellent! This is the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity;

this is all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); this is the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
this is the entire conduct of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; and this is the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas.
"Bodhi—this is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), this is a śrāvaka, this is a pratyekabuddha, this is a bodhisattva, and this is a Tathāgata.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 474. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Second Division, Chapter on Non-Deficiency, Number 79-2. "Śāriputra!..."
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they understand, as it truly is,
that the nature of all phenomena is entirely ungraspable; that is to say, from the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity,
all are ungraspable, and from form (rūpa) up to consciousness (vijñāna), these too are ungraspable, as is the sense base of the eye (cakṣur-āyatana).
Even the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*) is ungraspable; the sense-base of forms (*rūpāyatana*) up to the sense-base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) are also ungraspable.
The eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) up to the mind-element (*manodhātu*) are also ungraspable; the form-element (*rūpadhātu*) up to the phenomena-element (*dharmadhātu*) are also ungraspable.
The eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) up to the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*) are also ungraspable; the eye-contact (*cakṣuḥsaṃsparśa*) up to the mind-...
Contact is also ungraspable; the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including those produced with mind-contact as a condition, are also ungraspable.
The earth element, up to and including the consciousness element, is also ungraspable.
The causal conditions, up to and including the dominant condition, are also ungraspable, and the dharmas produced from conditions are likewise [ungraspable].
It cannot be grasped; from ignorance up to old age and death, they also cannot be grasped.
From internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature, they also cannot be grasped. From suchness up to the inconceivable realm, they also cannot be grasped.
The noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path also cannot be grasped. From the four foundations of mindfulness up to...
The eight branches of the noble path are also not to be grasped; the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments are also not to be grasped;
the eight liberations up to the ten totalities are also not to be grasped;
the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are also not to be grasped; [and] from the stage of pure observation up to the stage of a Tathāgata...
The stage of coming forth (*āgama-bhūmi*) is also ungraspable; from the Stage of Extreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) up to the Cloud of Dharma Stage (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), they too are ungraspable;
all doors of dhāraṇī and doors of samādhi are also ungraspable; the five eyes and the six supernormal powers are also ungraspable;
and the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) are also [ungraspable].
They cannot be grasped; the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs cannot be grasped;
the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity cannot be grasped;
omniscience, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects cannot be grasped; nor can the fruit of stream-entry up to the awakening of a pratyekabuddha.
Furthermore, it cannot be grasped; the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot be grasped,
the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas cannot be grasped,
and all ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas cannot be grasped.

“Śāriputra! Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the profound perfection of wisdom understand, as it truly is, that the nature of all phenomena cannot be grasped, they attain non-obstruction regarding all phenomena.”

Śāriputra! This perfection that cannot be grasped is itself the unobstructed perfection; this unobstructed perfection is itself the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), in which all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should train.

Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can train in this, they do not apprehend anything at all among all phenomena; since they do not even apprehend training, how much less could they apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening!
How much more so for attaining the Prajñāpāramitā!
How much more so for attaining the dharmas of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas! Why is this?
Śāriputra! There is not even the slightest dharma that possesses a real intrinsic nature. Within all dharmas that lack intrinsic nature, what is the dharma of an ordinary person?
What is the dharma of a stream-enterer?
What is the dharma of the once-returner?
What is the dharma of the non-returner?
What is the dharma of the arhat?
What are the dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas?
What are the dharmas of the bodhisattvas?
What are the dharmas of the Tathāgatas?
Śāriputra! Since these dharmas are thus unattainable, by means of what dharma can a *pudgala* (person) be conventionally designated?

Since a *pudgala* is unattainable, how can it be said that "this is an ordinary person," "this is a stream-enterer," "this is a once-returner," "this is a non-returner," "this is an arhat," "this is a pratyekabuddha," "this is a bodhisattva," or "this is a Tathāgata"?
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If all dharmas are entirely without intrinsic nature and none are truly existent, by virtue of what basis can one discern that ‘this is an ordinary person’ or ‘these are the dharmas of an ordinary person’?”
"Extending this detailed explanation even to: 'This is the Tathāgata;
this is the Dharma of the Tathāgata'? The Buddha said to Śāriputra: "What do you think?"
Is there truly a form that has existed or will exist in the way that foolish ordinary worldlings cling to it?
Is there truly feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness that has existed or will exist in the way that foolish ordinary worldlings cling to them?
Is it thus that there exists, as a reality, any practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva—whether past or future—as is grasped by foolish ordinary beings?
Is it thus that there exists, as a reality, the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment of the Buddhas—whether past or future—as is grasped by foolish ordinary beings?

Do ordinary beings, stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or tathāgatas—whether they have been so in the past or will be so in the future—truly exist as those foolish ordinary beings grasp them to be?
Śāriputra said: “No, World-Honored One!”
"It is only because of their inverted views that foolish, ordinary worldlings harbor such attachments.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the profound perfection of wisdom with skillful means, although they observe that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature and are not truly existent, nevertheless seek unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment by relying on worldly convention. For the sake of all sentient beings, they employ skillful means to teach them, enabling them to attain correct understanding and become free from all inversions."
Then, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), although they observe that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and are not truly existent, they nevertheless seek to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) by relying on worldly convention (*saṃvṛti*), and skillfully proclaim it for the sake of all sentient beings, causing them to attain correct understanding and be free from all perversions?"
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they accomplish such skillful means that they do not perceive even the slightest real dharma in which they might abide. Because they would abide therein, there would be obstruction; because of obstruction, there would be regression; because of regression, the mind becomes weak; and because the mind is weak, laziness arises.”
“Śāriputra! Because all phenomena are entirely devoid of substantial reality, are free from ‘I’ and ‘mine,’ and take non-existence as their intrinsic nature—
being by nature empty and quiescent, and by their own characteristics empty and quiescent— there exists only the deluded common person.”
Ordinary worldlings are deluded and inverted; they cling to the aggregate of form up to the aggregate of consciousness;
they cling to the sense base of the eye up to the sense base of the mind; they cling to the sense base of forms up to the sense base of mental phenomena;

they cling to the element of the eye up to the element of the mind; they cling to the element of forms up to the element of mental phenomena; and they cling to the element of eye-consciousness up to the element of mind-consciousness.
They cling to the element of consciousness; they cling to eye-contact through to mind-contact;

they cling to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition through to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition; they cling to the earth element through to the consciousness element;
they cling to the causal condition through to the dominant condition; and they cling to all phenomena produced from conditions.
Attachment to ignorance up to old age and death; attachment to the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
attachment to inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;
attachment to suchness up to the inconceivable realm; and attachment to the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
They are attached to the [four] truths; they are attached to the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
they are attached to the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; they are attached to the eight liberations up to the ten totalities;
they are attached to the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; and they are attached to the stage of pure observation up to...
Attachment to the stage of the Tathāgata; attachment to the stages from the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma;
attachment to all doors of dhāraṇī and doors of samādhi; attachment to the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
attachment to the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and attachment to the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
[They] are attached to the [major] marks and the eighty secondary characteristics; they are attached to the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity;
they are attached to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and all-aspect knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*);
they are attached to the fruit of stream-entry up to the awakening of a pratyekabuddha; they are attached to all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; they are attached to all...
The Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is attached to ordinary beings, stream-enterers, once-returners,
non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas.

"For this reason, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas observe that all phenomena are entirely devoid of substantial reality; they are free from 'self' and 'what belongs to self,' and take non-existence as their very nature. Being by nature empty and quiescent, and by their own characteristics empty and quiescent, they practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and, acting like magicians themselves, preach the Dharma to sentient beings: to those who are stingy and greedy, they preach generosity; to those who violate the precepts, they preach pure morality; to those who are angry and resentful, they preach patience; to those who are indolent, they preach diligence; to those who are distracted, they preach meditative concentration; and to those who are ignorant, they preach wisdom."

Having established sentient beings so that they dwell in the perfections from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, this bodhisattva mahāsattva further proclaims for them the sublime, noble dharmas capable of bringing about transcendence from birth and death. Relying upon these, sentient beings practice and train, whereby some attain the fruit of stream-entry, some the fruit of once-returning, some the fruit of non-returning, or some the fruit of arhatship; some attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, some enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from corruption, some abide on the stages of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, or some realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, why are they not called those who have something to be attained?"

That is to say, although sentient beings do not truly exist, he causes them to abide in the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom; furthermore, he proclaims for them the sublime noble dharmas capable of bringing about transcendence from birth and death, or causes them to attain the fruit of stream-entry, up to and including causing them to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not apprehend any sentient beings as having real existence.”

Why is this? Śāriputra, when these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive even the slightest substantial reality of sentient beings; there are only sentient beings as conventional designations.
Śāriputra! When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they abide in the two truths and proclaim the true Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.
What are the two truths?
First, the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
Second, the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).

Śāriputra! Although neither the two truths nor the designation of sentient beings can be apprehended, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they employ skillful means to proclaim the true Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings. Having heard the true Dharma, these sentient beings do not even apprehend a self in the present life, let alone apprehend the fruit to be attained or the one who attains it!

In this way, Śāriputra, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they skillfully employ means to proclaim the true Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, causing them to cultivate correct practice and attain the fruits of realization; yet their minds apprehend nothing at all regarding those beings, because they have realized that all phenomena are unapprehendable.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not apprehend a single nature in all phenomena, nor a diverse nature, nor a collective nature, nor a distinct nature, they nevertheless don such great armor of merit.”

By being armored in such great merit, they do not appear in the desire realm, do not appear in the form realm, do not appear in the formless realm, do not appear in the conditioned realm, and do not appear in the unconditioned realm.
Although one transforms sentient beings to cause them to transcend the three realms, one apprehends no sentient being whatsoever, nor does one apprehend the designation "sentient being.

Because the designation "sentient being" cannot be apprehended, there is neither bondage nor liberation; because there is neither bondage nor liberation, there is neither defilement nor purity; because there is neither defilement nor purity, the distinctions between the various realms of existence (*gati*) cannot be discerned; because the distinctions between the various realms of existence cannot be discerned, there is neither karma nor affliction; and because there is neither karma nor affliction, there is also no ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*). Since there is no ripening fruit, how could there be a self or a sentient being that transmigrates through the various realms and manifests the manifold distinctions of the three realms?
The Buddha told Śāriputra: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said, Śāriputra!

If sentient beings existed previously and later ceased to exist, then Bodhisattvas and Buddhas would be at fault; if the cycle of birth and death within the various realms of existence existed previously and later ceased to exist, then Bodhisattvas and Buddhas would likewise be at fault.
The principle that what did not previously exist comes into being later is likewise untenable.

Therefore, Śāriputra, whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, the characteristics of phenomena (dharmatā) abide eternally; suchness, the dharma-realm, and the nature of non-falsity never undergo change or transformation.

Because the dharma-nature, dharma-realm, dharma-abiding, dharma-stability, suchness, the limit of reality, non-falsity, and non-alteration of all dharmas are like space, even within this there is no self or anything else to be found, much less any dharmas such as form that could be found!
Since no phenomena such as form and so forth can be apprehended, how could there be the cycle of birth and death within the various realms of existence?
Since the cycle of birth and death within the various realms cannot be apprehended, how could there be the maturing of sentient beings to bring them to liberation?
They exist only as conventional designations.

"Śāriputra! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have heard from the Buddhas of the past that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty; yet sentient beings, due to their inverted attachments, hear this and contemplate it with mindfulness exactly as it is."
In order to liberate sentient beings from their inverted attachments, they seek to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; yet while seeking it, they do not form such thoughts as:
"I have already attained or shall attain this Dharma, and I have already delivered or shall deliver those sentient beings from the manifold sufferings of birth and death to which they are attached."

“Śāriputra! These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, in order to liberate sentient beings from their inverted attachments, don the armor of merit and the great vow as their adornment. With courageous and right diligence, they have no lingering attachments; they do not retreat from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and they never harbor doubt regarding enlightenment, wondering:
‘Shall I realize it, or shall I not?’”
One should simply maintain right mindfulness, thinking:

"I shall certainly realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment that I seek, and bring true benefit to all sentient beings; that is to say, I shall cause them to be liberated from the suffering of birth and death through wandering among the various realms of existence due to delusion, error, and perversion."

"Śāriputra! Although bodhisattva-mahāsattvas liberate sentient beings from the delusions, errors, and inversions of the various realms of birth and death, they do so without apprehending anything; it is only in accordance with worldly convention that such a thing is said to exist."

"Śāriputra! It is as if a master illusionist or his disciple, relying on the art of Indra’s Net, were to conjure up immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of sentient beings, and further create various kinds of exquisite food and drink to bestow upon those conjured beings so that they are all fully satisfied. Having performed this deed, he joyfully proclaims:
'I have already obtained a vast accumulation of merit. "
"What do you think?
Does that master illusionist or his disciple actually cause sentient beings to become satiated?
Śāriputra replied:
"No, World-Honored One! The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“In the same way, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, practice the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
they abide in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; they abide in suchness up to...”
The inconceivable realm consists of abiding securely in the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
practicing the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; practicing the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
practicing the eight liberations up to the ten totalities; and practicing emptiness and...
The gate of liberation of signlessness and the gate of liberation of wishlessness; practicing the stages from the Ground of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma Ground;
practicing all dharani-gates and samadhi-gates; practicing the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
practicing the ten powers of a Tathagata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and practicing the three [wheels of dharma]...
The thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary characteristics; practicing the quality of non-forgetfulness and abiding constantly in equanimity;
practicing all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);
perfecting the great path of bodhi of a bodhisattva; maturing sentient beings and purifying buddha-fields.
“Śāriputra! Although bodhisattva-mahāsattvas perform these deeds, they apprehend neither sentient beings nor any phenomena whatsoever. They do not form such thoughts as:

‘By means of this dharma, I shall subdue such classes of sentient beings, causing them to distance themselves from inverted attachments and no longer transmigrate through the various realms of birth and death.’”
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is called the bodhisattva’s path to great enlightenment?”

How do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, practicing this path, through skillful means bring sentient beings to maturity and purify buddha-fields, so as to swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"From their first production of the thought of enlightenment, all bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
they practice inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature."
The suchness of their practice up to the inconceivable realm; the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path as practiced by them;
the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path as practiced by them;
the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments as practiced by them; and the eight liberations up to the ten totalities as practiced by them.
The spheres of activity: the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
the spheres of activity from the Ground of Extreme Joy up to the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma; the spheres of activity of all *dhāraṇī* gates and *samādhi* gates;
the spheres of activity of the five eyes and the six superknowledges; and the spheres of activity of the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
The unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), the quality of non-forgetfulness in practice, the state of constant equanimity,

the practice of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), as well as other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-qualities—
all these constitute the Great Path to Bodhi for a bodhisattva.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice this path, they skillfully employ expedient means to mature sentient beings and purify Buddha-fields, swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, yet without any conceptualization of "sentient beings," "Buddha-fields," or the like.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of generosity, skillfully mature sentient beings through expedient means?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"There is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, when practicing the perfection of generosity, employs skillful means; he practices generosity himself and also encourages others to practice generosity, earnestly instructing and exhorting them, saying:
'O sons of good family!'"
Do not be attached to giving; if you are attached to giving, you will undergo further rebirths, and through these successive rebirths, you will undergo immeasurable, fierce, and intense suffering.
"O sons of noble family!

Within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), there is no giving, nor is there a giver, a recipient, the object given, or the fruits of giving. All such phenomena are empty by their very nature (*prakṛti-śūnya*). Within this emptiness of intrinsic nature, there is no phenomenon that can be grasped, and even the emptiness of phenomena cannot be grasped."

"In this way, Subhūti, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of generosity, although they personally practice giving to sentient beings and also exhort others to give, they apprehend nothing at all regarding the act of giving, the giver, the recipient, the gift, or the fruit of giving. Such a perfection of generosity is called the 'perfection of non-apprehension.'"

"Subhūti! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva finds nothing to be apprehended among these dharmas, through skillful means he is able to transform sentient beings, causing them to abide in the fruit of a stream-enterer, or the fruit of a once-returner, or the fruit of a non-returner, or the fruit of arhatship, or in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, or to proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Thus it is, Subhūti!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of generosity, they bring sentient beings to maturity, causing them to attain supreme benefit.

“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva personally practices giving, encourages others to practice giving, correctly extols the dharma of practicing giving, and joyfully praises those who practice giving.”

“Subhūti! Having given such gifts, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas will be born into great kṣatriya clans, or great brahmin clans, or great householder clans; or they will be born into wealthy and prosperous layman clans with abundant treasures; or they will become minor kings, possessing wealth and sovereignty over small territories; or they will become great kings, possessing wealth and sovereignty over large territories; or they will become universal monarchs (cakravartin), possessing wealth and sovereignty over the four continents.”

“Having been born in such noble and honorable places, this bodhisattva mahāsattva gathers sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*). First, he teaches sentient beings to abide in generosity; by the causes and conditions of giving, their minds become disciplined and well-tamed, and he gradually leads them to abide in ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom. Furthermore, he leads them to abide in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments. He further leads them to abide in the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, and finally leads them to abide in the gateways to liberation: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.”

Having established all sentient beings in such wholesome dharmas as these, this bodhisattva mahāsattva causes them either to enter the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) and attain the fruit of a stream-enterer up to the fruit of an arhat;
or causes them to enter the state of rightness and departure from birth and gradually realize the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
or causes them to enter the state of rightness and departure from birth and gradually train in the stages of a bodhisattva, swiftly proceeding toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
He further addressed them, saying:
"O sons of noble family!
You should conceive the great vow to swiftly proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and perform supreme deeds for the benefit of all sentient beings."

All phenomena grasped through the false conceptualizations of sentient beings are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature; they exist only because of inverted and deluded attachments. Therefore, you should always apply yourselves with diligence to eliminate your own inversions and encourage others to sever theirs; liberate yourselves from birth and death and cause others to be liberated as well; attain great benefit for yourselves and enable others to attain it too.

“Subhūti! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should constantly practice the perfection of generosity in this manner. By means of this perfection of generosity, from the first generation of the mind of awakening until the ultimate end, they do not fall into the evil destinies or among the poor, lowly, or outcaste. For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, they are frequently reborn in the human realm as universal monarchs (cakravartin kings), possessing wealth, sovereignty, and great power to benefit many.”
Why is this so? Because one obtains such fruits according to the power of one's karma.
That is to say, when that bodhisattva was a wheel-turning monarch, upon seeing a beggar approach, he would think:

"For what purpose have I transmigrated through birth and death to become a Wheel-Turning King? Is it not so that I dwell within saṃsāra for the benefit of sentient beings, accepting this supreme fruit and nothing else?"
Having formed this thought, he said to the beggar:
"I shall give you whatever you require; when you take these things, do so as if taking your own property, without harboring any other thoughts."

Why is this? It is for the sake of bringing you benefit that I have taken on this body and accumulated these wealth and goods; therefore, these goods belong to you. Take them as you please—whether for your own use or to bestow upon others—and do not harbor any doubt or hesitation.
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva thus feels compassion for all sentient beings, his objectless great compassion (anālambana-mahākaruṇā) is swiftly brought to fulfillment.

Because this great compassion is swiftly fulfilled, although he constantly benefits immeasurable sentient beings, he apprehends no sentient beings at all, nor does he apprehend any superior fruit obtained; he is able to know it as it truly is:
"It is merely by means of conventional designations and verbal expressions that the various activities of benefiting sentient beings are established."
Furthermore, one knows things as they truly are:
"All phenomena that are conceptually designated are like echoes; although they appear to exist, they lack true reality.
By means of this, one grasps nothing at all regarding phenomena.

“Subhūti! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should always practice the perfection of generosity in this way: they should have no regard whatsoever for sentient beings, even to the point of being able to give away their own flesh and bones, let alone external possessions which they can easily relinquish!”
"This means that all requisite provisions gather in and sustain sentient beings, causing them to swiftly attain liberation from birth, old age, sickness,
and death. The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying, "World-Honored One!"
“What are the requisites that sustain sentient beings and cause them to swiftly attain liberation from birth, old age, sickness, and death?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“They are the requisites ranging from the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramitā) up to the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā).”
Whether it be the requisites of inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature;
whether it be the requisites of suchness up to the inconceivable realm; whether it be the requisites of the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
whether it be the requisites of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; or whether it be the four dhyānas and the four immeasurables...
The requisites for the four formless absorptions; the requisites for the eight liberations up to the ten totalities;
the requisites for the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; the requisites for the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata;
the requisites for the stage of extreme joy up to the stage of the cloud of dharma; and all...
the requisites for the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi; the requisites for the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
the requisites for the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
the requisites for the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity; and the requisites for all-knowledge and the knowledge of the aspects of the path.
The requisites for the knowledge of all aspects; the requisites for the fruit of a stream-enterer up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
the requisites for all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; and the requisites for the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas.

"Subhūti! Such virtuous dharmas as these serve as requisites for gathering in sentient beings, enabling them to swiftly attain liberation from birth, old age, sickness, and death. Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constantly gather in sentient beings with such various requisites, enabling them to swiftly attain liberation from birth, old age, sickness, and death."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in the perfection of generosity, they practice giving themselves and encourage all sentient beings to practice giving. If they see sentient beings who have violated the pure precepts, they give rise to deep compassion and say to them:
'You should now receive and uphold the pure precepts; I shall provide you with various requisites so that you lack for nothing.'"
"Because you lack the necessities of life, you have violated the pure precepts and committed various evil deeds; I shall provide you with all the requisites that you lack."

Once you have established yourselves in the discipline of the precepts, you will gradually be able to bring an end to suffering; by relying on the Dharma of the Three Vehicles as appropriate for each, you shall transcend birth and death and attain ultimate bliss.

"Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of generosity, personally upholds pure ethical discipline, encourages others to uphold pure ethical discipline, correctly extols the dharma of upholding pure ethical discipline, and joyfully praises those who uphold pure ethical discipline."
Thus it is, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of generosity, they exhort all sentient beings to abide in pure ethical discipline, so that they may be liberated from all birth, old age, sickness, and death, and realize ultimate benefit and happiness.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When bodhisattva mahāsattvas abide in the perfection of generosity, if they see sentient beings who are mutually angry and resentful, they give rise to deep compassion and say to them:
'For what reason do you all become mutually angry and resentful?'"

If you should suffer from any lack and, in mutual dependence, give rise to various evils, you should ask me for what you need; I shall provide for you. Whatever various requisites you require, I will bestow them all upon you so that you may have no lack.
"You should not harbor mutual anger or resentment; you should cultivate patience and together give rise to a mind of loving-kindness. Subhūti!
Having established those sentient beings in the perfection of generosity and exhorted them to practice patience, that bodhisattva mahāsattva, wishing to make it firm, further says to them:
"The causes and conditions for anger and resentment have no fixed reality at all; they all arise from false conceptualization, because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty.
For what reason do you give rise to anger and resentment toward things that lack reality, and further harm one another?"

Do not, based on false conceptualization, harbor mutual anger and resentment to create various evil karmas; you shall otherwise fall into the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, or other evil states to undergo intense sufferings. Those agonies will be harsh, fierce, and sharp, pressing upon both body and mind in a manner most utterly difficult to endure.

"You all must not cling to what is not a real entity, nor harbor false anger and resentment to commit such evil karma. Because of this evil karma, it is difficult even to obtain the body of an inferior human being, let alone attain birth in heaven, or encounter a Buddha to hear the True Dharma and practice according to its teachings!"
"You should all know that a human body is difficult to obtain, an encounter with a Buddha is difficult to meet, and the arising of faith is likewise difficult.

Now that you possess these conditions, do not lose this favorable opportunity through anger; if this moment is lost, it cannot be recovered. Therefore, you should not give rise to anger toward sentient beings, but should instead cultivate patience."

"Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of generosity, personally practices patience, encourages others to practice patience, correctly extols the dharma of practicing patience, and joyfully praises those who practice patience."
Thus it is, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas abide in the perfection of generosity, they exhort all sentient beings to practice patience; through this, those sentient beings gradually rely upon the three vehicles and attain liberation.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When bodhisattva mahāsattvas abide in the perfection of generosity, they see sentient beings who are physically and mentally indolent; they give rise to deep compassion and address them, saying:
'For what reason do you not diligently apply yourselves with vigor to cultivate the various wholesome dharmas, but instead give way to indolence?'"
He said this: "I lack the necessary provisions and am unable to diligently cultivate various virtuous deeds.
The Bodhisattva told him:
"I can provide you with whatever provisions you lack; you should diligently cultivate the dharmas of generosity, pure ethical discipline, and patience.

At that time, those sentient beings, having obtained the provisions bestowed by this bodhisattva so as to lack nothing, were able to arouse physical and mental diligence to cultivate all wholesome dharmas and swiftly attain their fulfillment.

Because all wholesome dharmas are brought to fulfillment, they gradually induce the arising of all untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas. By means of these untainted dharmas, one attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*), or the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), or the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*), or the fruit of arhatship; or one enters the stages (*bhūmi*) of the bodhisattvas and gradually attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of generosity, personally practices diligence, encourages others to practice diligence, correctly extols the dharma of practicing diligence, and joyfully praises those who practice diligence.”
Thus it is, Subhūti!

By abiding in the perfection of generosity, bodhisattva mahāsattvas cause sentient beings to distance themselves from indolence, diligently cultivate all virtues, swiftly realize liberation, and further bring benefit and happiness to all classes of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in the perfection of generosity, they see sentient beings whose faculties are distracted and who have lost right mindfulness; they give rise to deep compassion and say to them:
'For what reason do you not cultivate meditative concentration? Why are you distracted, lose mindfulness, and sink into birth and death, suffering without end? "
He spoke thus: "Because I lack the necessary requisites, I am unable to apply myself diligently to meditative concentration.
The Bodhisattva said to him:

“I can provide you with whatever requisites you lack; from this day forward, you should no longer give rise to false discursive thoughts, nor allow yourselves to be disturbed by grasping at internal or external objects.”

At that time, those sentient beings, having obtained the requisites bestowed by this Bodhisattva, were free from all lack; they were thus able to subdue and sever false discursive thoughts (*vitarka-vicāra*) and enter the first *dhyāna*. Gradually, they further entered the second, third, and fourth *dhyānas*. Relying upon these *dhyānas*, they were further able to induce the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*): loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. With the *dhyānas* and immeasurables as their support, they were further able to induce the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*). Once the mind had been made supple through the cultivation of the *dhyānas*, immeasurables, and formless states, they practiced the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), progressing step by step up to the eight branches of the noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*). By means of this, they were further able to induce superior wholesome dharmas such as emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), thereby attaining the fruits of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) as appropriate.

“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of generosity, personally cultivates meditative concentration, encourages others to cultivate meditative concentration, correctly extols the practice of meditative concentration, and joyfully praises those who cultivate it.”
Thus it is, Subhūti!

All bodhisattva mahāsattvas, dwelling securely in the perfection of generosity, exhort all sentient beings to distance themselves from distraction, so that they may cultivate the various meditative concentrations and attain great benefit and happiness.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in the perfection of generosity, they see sentient beings who are deluded and inverted; they give rise to deep compassion and address them, saying:
'For what reason do you not cultivate sublime wisdom, such that through delusion and inversion you suffer without end?'"
He replied, "Because I lack the necessary provisions, I am unable to apply myself diligently to sublime wisdom.
The Bodhisattva said to him:
"I can provide you with whatever requisites you lack; you may accept them.

Once you have brought to perfection the practices of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration, you should carefully investigate the true nature of all phenomena and practice the perfection of wisdom."
That is to say, at that time, one should carefully examine whether there is even the slightest dharma that can be apprehended—
namely, whether a self, a sentient being, and so forth, up to a knower or a seer, can be apprehended.
Can form, up to and including consciousness, be apprehended?
Can the eye-base, up to and including the mind-base, be apprehended?
Can the form-base, up to and including the mental-object-base, be apprehended?
Can the eye-element up to the mind-element be apprehended?
Can the form-element up to the phenomena-element be apprehended?
Can the eye-consciousness-element up to the mind-consciousness-element be apprehended?
Can eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact, be apprehended?
Can the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, up to and including the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition, be apprehended?
Can the earth element up to the consciousness element be apprehended?
Can the causal condition up to the dominant condition be apprehended?
Can the various phenomena produced from conditions be apprehended?
Can ignorance up to old age and death be apprehended?
Can the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm be apprehended?
Can the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom be apprehended?
Can inner emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the nature of non-existence, be apprehended?
Can suchness, up to and including the inconceivable realm, be apprehended?
Can the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path be apprehended?
Can the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path be attained?
Can the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments be attained?
Can the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality be attained?
Can the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—be attained?
Can the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata be attained?
Can the stages from the Ground of Utmost Joy up to the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma be apprehended?
Can all the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi be apprehended?
Can the five eyes and the six supernormal powers be apprehended?
Can the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha be apprehended?
Can the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty minor marks be apprehended?
Can the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant abiding in equanimity be attained?
Can omniscience, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects be attained?
Can the fruit of stream-entry, up to and including the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, be apprehended?
Can the conduct of all bodhisattva mahāsattvas be apprehended?
Can the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas be apprehended?

“Once those sentient beings have obtained all necessary provisions without deficiency, they rely on the Bodhisattva’s words to first cultivate generosity, pure ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration; having brought these to perfection, they further examine the true nature of all phenomena and practice the perfection of wisdom.”

When examining them closely, as previously stated, the true nature of all phenomena is found to be unapprehendable; because it is unapprehendable, there is no attachment; and because there is no attachment, one does not perceive even the slightest phenomenon as arising or ceasing, or as being defiled or purified.

When they do not apprehend any phenomena, they give rise to no conceptual discrimination regarding anything whatsoever; that is to say, they do not discriminate, "This is hell, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the asuras, or humans, or devas"; nor do they discriminate, "This is one who upholds the precepts, this is one who violates the precepts"; nor do they discriminate, "This is an ordinary person, this is a noble one, this is a stream-enterer, this is a once-returner, this is a non-returner, this is an arhat, this is a pratyekabuddha, this is a bodhisattva, this is a buddha, this is conditioned, or this is unconditioned."

Because they are thus free from conceptual discrimination, they shall, according to their respective capacities, gradually realize the ultimate peace and happiness of nirvāṇa through the three vehicles. “Subhūti!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of generosity, personally cultivates wisdom, encourages others to cultivate wisdom, unerringly extols the practice of the dharma of wisdom, and joyfully praises those who cultivate wisdom.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
All bodhisattva mahāsattvas, dwelling securely in the perfection of generosity, exhort all sentient beings to diligently cultivate wisdom, causing them to attain ultimate benefit and peace.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, abiding in the perfection of generosity, personally practice the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, and having also exhorted others to practice the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, they further see sentient beings circling through the various realms of existence, undergoing immeasurable suffering and failing to attain liberation. Desiring to liberate them from the suffering of birth and death, they first benefit them with various material requisites, and subsequently sustain them with the supramundane, untainted dharmas through skillful means."
Once those sentient beings have obtained the necessary provisions and lack nothing, their bodies and minds become courageous and resolute;
they are able to abide in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, and they are also able to abide in suchness up to the inconceivable realm,
and they are also able to abide in the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, and they are also able to cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness.
Up to and including the eight branches of the noble path, they are also able to cultivate the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
they are also able to cultivate the eight liberations up to the ten totalities;

they are also able to cultivate the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; and they are also able to cultivate the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata.
They are also able to cultivate the stages from the Ground of Extreme Joy up to the Ground of Dharma Clouds;
they are also able to cultivate all doors of dhāraṇī and doors of samādhi; they are also able to cultivate the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
they are also able to cultivate the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and they are also able to cultivate non-forgetfulness.
The Dharma, the state of constant equanimity, can also cultivate all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*),
and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), as well as cultivate all other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas.
Because those sentient beings are sustained by untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*), they are liberated from birth and death and realize the ultimate peace and happiness of nirvāṇa. "Subhūti!..."

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of generosity, personally practices various sublime, untainted dharmas, encourages others to practice various sublime, untainted dharmas, correctly extols the practice of various sublime, untainted dharmas, and joyfully praises those who practice various sublime, untainted dharmas.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, dwelling securely in the perfection of generosity, gather in sentient beings through untainted dharmas, causing them to be liberated from the manifold sufferings of birth and death, to realize the ultimate and eternal bliss of nirvāṇa, and also enabling them to bring great benefit to others.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas abide in the perfection of generosity, they see sentient beings who are without a refuge, beset by many sufferings and lacking in the necessities of life; they give rise to deep compassion and comfort them, saying:
'I can act as a refuge for you and cause you to be liberated from the suffering you endure.'"

"Whatever you require—food and drink, clothing, bedding, vehicles, dwellings, incense and flowers, music, lamps, wealth and treasures, servants, or any other various necessities for your livelihood—you may ask for them all according to your wishes; do not hesitate or have any doubt. I shall grant you whatever you request, so that you may enjoy benefit and peace for a long night."
When you receive the gifts I bestow, accept them as if they were your own property and do not harbor thoughts of them being another's. Why is this?
Throughout the long night, I have accumulated wealth and goods solely for the sake of securing your benefit and happiness.
Now, with minds free from hesitation, you should accept these riches as you please.
Having accepted them, you should first properly enjoy them yourselves to cultivate various virtuous deeds;

subsequently, you should give these things to all sentient beings so that they too may cultivate virtue—namely, leading them to practice the pāramitās from the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom.
...the Perfection [of Wisdom], and also cause them to abide in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence;
and also cause them to abide in suchness up to the inconceivable realm; and also cause them to abide in the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
and also cause them to practice the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; and also cause them...
They cause them to practice the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
they also cause them to practice the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality; they also cause them to practice the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
they also cause them to practice from the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata; they also cause them to practice...
From the Stage of Utmost Joy up to the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma, they also cause them to practice all doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of samādhi;
they also cause them to practice the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
they also cause them to practice the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and they also cause them to practice non-forgetfulness.
The Dharma, the state of constant dwelling in equanimity, also causes one to practice all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*),
and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), and likewise causes one to practice all other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas.
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

After this bodhisattva mahāsattva has thus instructed all sentient beings, he further causes them, according to their respective capacities, to practice the various untainted dharmas (anāsrava-dharma), so that they may abide in the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala), or the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmi-phala), or the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmi-phala), or the fruit of arhatship (arhat-phala), or in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, or even in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).”

"In this way, Subhūti, bodhisattva mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of generosity use skillful means to bring sentient beings to maturity, causing them to be liberated from the miserable realms and the cycle of birth and death, so that they may, as appropriate, realize the nirvāṇa of the three vehicles, thereby benefiting themselves and others with ultimate peace and happiness."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), as well as the other paths to great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*) for bodhisattvas, and through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) bring sentient beings to maturity?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, while practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) see sentient beings lacking material resources and with afflictions (*kleśa*) raging so intensely that they are unable to cultivate virtue. Out of compassion, they say to them:
