‘If you are unable to cultivate virtue because you lack the necessary conditions and resources, I shall provide you with various kinds of such resources. You must not give rise to afflictions or evil karma; you should correctly practice virtues such as generosity (*dāna*).’”

"Thus, this bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), appropriately gathers in all classes of sentient beings: those who are stingy and greedy, he causes to practice generosity, having no regard for body, life, or wealth;

those who violate ethical discipline, he causes to practice pure discipline, enabling them to correctly undertake and carry out the ten paths of wholesome action, abiding in the vows of restraint without breaking or piercing them, being unstained, unmixed, and free from grasping;
and those who are prone to anger and resentment, he causes to practice patience."
They cause those who are indolent to cultivate diligence;
those who are distracted to cultivate meditative concentration;
and those who are deluded to cultivate sublime wisdom.
Those who cling to phenomena are made to cultivate the emptiness of phenomena;
those who lack various supreme merits are made to fully cultivate and study them.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, dwelling securely in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), employ skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) to bring sentient beings to maturity, causing them to be liberated from the miserable realms and the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), so that they may, as appropriate, realize the nirvāṇa of the three vehicles and achieve ultimate peace and happiness for both themselves and others.

“Subhūti, you should know that when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the other four perfections and the other paths to great enlightenment, each one is able to employ skillful means to bring all beings to maturity through every form of goodness, causing them to be liberated from the miserable destinies and the cycle of birth and death, so that they may, as appropriate, realize the nirvāṇa of the three vehicles and benefit themselves and others with ultimate peace and happiness. Each of these should be explained in detail as previously described for the perfection of giving.”

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Four Hundred and Seventy-five. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Chapter Eighty: The Path and the Soil. Part Two, Chapter Eighty: The Path and the Soil. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti had this thought:
"What is called the path of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?"
"How do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, dwelling securely in this path, don the armor of various supreme merits and truly benefit all sentient beings?
The World-Honored One, knowing what was in his mind, addressed him, saying:
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin, you should know!
The perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom is the path of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas;
the four applications of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path is the path of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas;
internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature is the path of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas; the truth...
From the inconceivable realm up to these are the paths of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas;
the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path are the paths of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas;
the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions are the paths of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas; the eight liberations, and so forth...
The ten spheres of totality are the path of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are the path of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
the stages from the Ground of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma are the path of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
and all doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of samādhi are [the path of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas].
The path of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas consists of the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
the path of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas consists of the ten powers of the Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
and the path of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas consists of the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity.
The Path—namely, all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)—is the path of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas;
furthermore, all other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas are the path of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
All dharmas in their entirety constitute the path of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti!
What do you think? Is there any dharma that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should not study?
Without studying such a dharma, could a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”

There is certainly no dharma that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not study; if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not study this dharma, they will certainly be unable to attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek.
"Why is that? If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not train in all dharmas, they will certainly be unable to attain the knowledge of all aspects.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva train, and in what?

If there is something to be trained in, would it not be that the Blessed One is engaging in conceptual proliferation where there is no proliferation—claiming that certain dharmas are 'this' or 'that,' 'due to this' or 'for this';
that 'this is the mundane' and 'this is the supramundane'?"
"What is this that is with outflows and what is this that is without outflows?
What is this that is conditioned and what is this that is unconditioned?

What is this that is the dharma of ordinary beings, what is this that is the dharma of stream-enterers, what is this that is the dharma of once-returners, what is this that is the dharma of non-returners, what is this that is the dharma of arhats, what is this that is the dharma of pratyekabuddhas, what is this that is the dharma of bodhisattvas, and what is this that is the dharma of Tathāgatas?"
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said:
all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature.
If all phenomena were not empty of intrinsic nature, then the bodhisattva mahāsattva would not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti, as you have asked: "If all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, in what does the bodhisattva mahāsattva train, and where?"

If there were anything to be learned, would it not be that the World-Honored One is engaging in conceptual proliferation regarding that which is free from proliferation—namely, by asserting that there are dharmas which are "this" or "that," "thereby" or "for this purpose," and so forth, up to saying they are the "Dharma of the Tathāgata"?

"Subhūti, if all sentient beings were to know that all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, then bodhisattva mahāsattvas would not need to train in all phenomena, realize the knowledge of all aspects, and establish and proclaim them for the sake of sentient beings."

Because sentient beings do not know that all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas must certainly train in all phenomena, realize the knowledge of all modes, and establish and proclaim them for the sake of all sentient beings.
"Subhūti, you should know that when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas first begin to train in the bodhisattva path, they should carefully examine:
'The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is entirely unapprehendable; there is only that which is produced by the conjunction of attachments.'"
One should examine that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is ultimately empty and should not have any attachment toward them;
that is to say, one should not be attached to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
one should not be attached to the sense base of the eye up to the sense base of the mind; one should not be attached to the sense base of forms up to the sense base of phenomena; one should not...
One should not cling to the eye-element up to the mind-element; one should not cling to the form-element up to the phenomena-element;
one should not cling to the eye-consciousness-element up to the mind-consciousness-element; one should not cling to eye-contact up to mind-contact;
nor should one cling to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to those produced with mind-contact.
Regarding the various feelings produced by conditions, one should not cling to the earth element up to the consciousness element;
one should not cling to the causal condition up to the dominant condition; one should not cling to the phenomena produced from conditions;
one should not cling to ignorance up to old age and death; and one should not cling to the perfection of giving.

From the *Prajñāpāramitā* up to the *Prajñāpāramitā*, one should not cling to anything from internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*);
one should not cling to anything from suchness (*tathatā*) up to the inconceivable realm (*acintya-dhātu*);
one should not cling to the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; one should not cling to the four applications of mindfulness...
Up to the eightfold noble path, one should not be attached to the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments;
one should not be attached to the eight liberations up to the ten totalities;
one should not be attached to the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; and one should not be attached to the stage of pure observation, up to...
One should not be attached to the stage of a Tathāgata, nor should one be attached to the stages from the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma;
one should not be attached to any of the doors of dhāraṇī or the doors of samādhi; one should not be attached to the five eyes or the six supernormal powers;
and one should not be attached to the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
One should not be attached to the thirty-two marks of a great man or the eighty minor marks;

one should not be attached to the quality of non-forgetfulness or the nature of constant equanimity; one should not be attached to all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, or the knowledge of all aspects;
and one should not be attached to the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
Subhūti, one should not be attached to any of the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, nor should one be attached to the unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas. Why is this?

Since all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, one should not cling to emptiness as being emptiness; for within emptiness, even emptiness itself cannot be apprehended, let alone an emptiness that could cling to emptiness!
"Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas observe all phenomena in this manner, although they have no attachment to the nature of phenomena, they study all phenomena without weariness."

Abiding in this training, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas observe the distinctions in the mental activities of sentient beings, specifically examining where the mental activities of these sentient beings are directed.
Having observed this, he understands that mind as it truly is: it merely functions through the grasping of what is false.
At that time, the bodhisattva thinks:
"Since that mind functions through the grasping of what is false, it will not be difficult for me to bring about its liberation."
Having formed this thought, that bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in the perfection of wisdom and, through skillful means, instructs and exhorts all sentient beings, saying:
"You all should now distance yourselves from false attachments and enter the true Dharma to cultivate all virtuous practices."
He further spoke these words:
"You should now practice generosity; you shall thereby obtain all necessary provisions without lack, yet do not rely on this to give rise to arrogance or negligence."
Why is this so? Because herein there is absolutely no core of substantiality.

You should now practice pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), patience (*kṣānti*), diligence (*vīrya*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). You shall thereby attain the fullness of various merits; however, do not rely upon these to give rise to arrogance or negligence.
Why is this? Because herein there is absolutely no solid or substantial reality.
You all should now practice the emptiness of the internal, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, and you should practice suchness.
Up to and including the inconceivable realm, one should practice the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
one should practice the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; one should practice the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
one should practice the eight liberations up to the ten totalities; and one should practice emptiness.
...the gateways of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness; one should practice the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata;
one should practice the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma stage; one should practice all the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi;
one should practice the five eyes and the six supernormal powers; one should practice the ten [powers] of the Tathāgata...
From the powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, one should practice the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity;
one should practice all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects;
one should practice the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; and one should practice all the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
One should practice the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas, and one should practice all other immeasurable Buddha-dharmas;
however, do not rely upon these to give rise to arrogance or negligence. Why is this so?
"Because therein there is no core of substantial reality whatsoever. "Subhūti!
When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in the perfection of wisdom and, through skillful means, instruct and admonish sentient beings, they practice the bodhisattva path without any attachment."

Why is this? One should not cling to the nature of all phenomena; for whether it be that which clings, that which is clung to, the time of clinging, or the place of clinging, none possess intrinsic nature, because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty.

"In this way, Subhūti! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the bodhisattva path in such a manner, they do not abide in any phenomena at all. Taking non-abiding as their skillful means, although they practice the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, they do not abide in them at all;
although they practice inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, they do not abide in them at all."
Although they practice true thusness up to the inconceivable realm, they abide nowhere within them;
although they practice the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, they abide nowhere within them;
although they practice the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, they abide nowhere within them.
Although they practice the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments, they abide in none of them;
although they practice the eight liberations up to the ten totalities, they abide in none of them;
although they practice the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, they abide in none of them.
Although they practice from the Stage of Pure Observation up to the Stage of the Tathāgata, they abide nowhere within them;
although they practice from the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma Stage, they abide nowhere within them;
although they practice all the gates of dhāraṇī and the gates of samādhi, they abide nowhere within them.
Although they practice the five eyes and the six supernormal powers, they abide nowhere within them;
although they practice the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, they abide nowhere within them;
although they practice the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity, they abide nowhere within them.
Although they practice all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects, they do not abide in any of them;
although they practice the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, they do not abide in any of them;
although they practice all the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, they do not abide in any of them.
Although they practice the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas, they abide nowhere therein;
although they practice all other immeasurable Buddha-dharmas, they abide nowhere therein.
Why is this? Because such intrinsic nature, the practitioner, and the characteristics of practice are all empty; therein, there is absolutely no place to abide.
"Subhūti, you should know this!"
Although the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to attain the fruit of a stream-enterer up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, they do not wish to realize or abide therein. Why is this?
There are two reasons. What are these two?
First, that fruit is entirely devoid of intrinsic nature; thus, both the abider and the place of abiding are unobtainable.
Second, they do not give rise to contentment with those [attainments], and therefore they do not wish to realize and abide therein.
That is to say, Bodhisattvas constantly maintain this thought:
"I must certainly attain the fruit of a Stream-enterer up to the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha; it is not that I shall not attain them, yet I should not realize and abide within them."

Why is this? Since I first resolved upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, at all times I have had no other thought, seeking nothing but unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Nevertheless, I shall certainly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; how could I dwell in any other fruit in the interim? "Subhūti!

From the first production of the thought of awakening until entering the bodhisattva’s correct nature free from outflows, that bodhisattva mahāsattva never entertains any other thought, seeking only unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

"Subhūti! From the time this bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the first bhūmi, continuing through to the attainment of the tenth bhūmi, they never harbor any divergent thoughts, but seek only unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

"Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva single-mindedly seeks unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; at all times his mind is undistracted, and whatever physical, verbal, or mental actions he initiates, none are not accompanied by the bodhicitta."
“Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the mind of awakening and gives rise to the path of awakening, without allowing his mind to be disturbed by other matters.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed [the Buddha], saying:
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are ultimately unarisen, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva give rise to the path to enlightenment?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"So it is! So it is! As you have said, 'All dharmas are unarisen. Furthermore, how is it that they are all without activity and without destination?"
This is because one knows that all phenomena are fundamentally non-arising.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Is it not the case that whether Buddhas appear in the world or do not appear in the world, the dharma-realm of all phenomena remains eternally as it is?”
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"

However, sentient beings are unable to understand that the dharma-realm of all phenomena is by its very nature eternally abiding; thus they transmigrate through birth and death, undergoing various sufferings and afflictions.

For their benefit, the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas give rise to the path to enlightenment (*bodhimārga*); by means of this path to enlightenment, they cause all sentient beings to ultimately be liberated from the manifold sufferings of birth and death and to realize the eternal, blissful, and cool state of *nirvāṇa*.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain awakening by means of a path that has arisen?
The Buddha said:
"No, World-Honored One! Is bodhi attained by means of a path that does not arise?"
The Buddha said,
“No. [He replied,] “World-Honored One!”
"Is enlightenment attained by means of a path that arises,
or by one that does not arise? The Buddha said, "No!"
“World-Honored One!
Is bodhi attained by means of a path that neither arises nor does not arise?
The Buddha said:
"No, it is not so! The Venerable Subhūti further addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If that is so, by what means is bodhi attained?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Awakening is not attained by means of the path, nor is it attained apart from the path. Why is this so?
“Awakening is itself the path, and the path is itself awakening; therefore, it is not attained by means of the path or by what is not the path.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If awakening is itself the path and the path is itself awakening, then would it not be the case that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having already attained the path to awakening, should have already attained awakening?”

If that is so, for what reason does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha further teach the bodhisattvas the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, the thirty-two marks, the eighty minor characteristics, and other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas, so that they may cultivate and realize them?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Do you perhaps believe that the Buddha has attained bodhi?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
Why is this? Because the Buddha is itself awakening (bodhi), and awakening is itself the Buddha; therefore, one should not say that the Buddha attains awakening.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"So it is! So it is! However, as for what you have asked: 'Since a bodhisattva mahāsattva has already attained the path to awakening, should they not have already attained awakening?'"
"Subhūti, since the bodhisattva mahāsattvas have not yet perfected their cultivation of the path to awakening, how can it be said that they have already attained awakening?"
“Subhūti, you should know that if bodhisattva mahāsattvas have already perfected the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
if they have already perfected inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature; if...
Having fully perfected true thusness up to the inconceivable realm; having fully perfected the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
having fully perfected the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
having fully perfected the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; having fully perfected...
They have fulfilled the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality; they have fulfilled the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
they have fulfilled the stages from the Ground of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma;
they have fulfilled all doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of samādhi; and they have fulfilled the five eyes.
...the six supernormal powers; if they have already perfected the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
if they have already perfected the thirty-two marks of a Great Being and the eighty minor marks;
if they have already perfected the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity; if they have already perfected all-knowledge;...
Having perfected the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects, as well as all other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas,
immediately thereafter, by means of the sublime wisdom associated with the vajra-like concentration in a single moment,
one forever severs the continuity of the coarse habitual tendencies of the two obscurations and realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
He is thus named Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; having attained great mastery over all phenomena, he benefits sentient beings until the end of the future.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva purify a buddha-field?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, from their first production of the thought of enlightenment until their final existence, constantly purify the three types of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*) of their own body, speech, and mind, and also purify those three types of coarse heaviness in others, they are able to adorn and purify the buddha-fields where they dwell."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What are called the three types of heavy burdens of body, speech, and mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If one takes life, takes what is not given, or engages in sexual misconduct, these are the coarseness of body;
if one speaks falsely, speaks divisively, speaks harshly, or engages in idle chatter, these are the coarseness of speech;
if one harbors covetousness, malice, or wrong views, these are the coarseness of mind."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s aggregate of ethical discipline, aggregate of concentration, aggregate of wisdom, aggregate of liberation, and aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation are all impure, these are also called *dausthulya* (coarse heaviness)."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses a mind of stinginess and greed, a mind of violating the precepts, a mind of anger and resentment, a mind of laziness, a mind of distraction, or a mind of corrupted wisdom, these are also called 'coarse heaviness' (dauṣṭhulya)."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva distances his mind from the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, this is also called a heavy burden (dauṣṭhulya)."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva distances himself from the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, this too is called a heavy burden (dauṣṭhulya)."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s mind is distant from true thusness (tathatā) up to the inconceivable realm (acintyadhātu), this is also called a heavy burden of affliction (dausthulya)."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is separated from the mind [oriented toward] the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, this too is called a heavy burden (dauṣṭhulya)."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva distances his mind from the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments, this is also called a heavy burden (dauṣṭhulya).
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva distances their mind from the eight liberations up to the ten totalities, this is also called a heavy burden (dauṣṭhulya)."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva distances himself from the mind of the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—this is also called a heavy burden (dauṣṭhulya)."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva distances themselves from the mind of the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma, this is also called a heavy burden (dauṣṭhulya)."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva distances their mind from all dhāraṇī-doors and samādhi-doors, this is also called a heavy burden (dauṣṭhulya).
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva distances their mind from the five eyes and the six supernormal powers, this is also called a heavy burden (dauṣṭhulya). Furthermore, Subhūti!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva distances their mind from the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, this is also called a heavy burden (*dausthulya*).
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva distances themselves from the mind of the quality of non-forgetfulness and constant abiding in equanimity, this is also called a heavy burden (*dausthulya*).
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva distances themselves from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), this is also called a "heavy burden" (*dausthulya*). "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva distances themselves from the mind of all bodhisattva mahāsattva practices, this is also called a heavy burden (*dauṣṭhulya*). Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva distances themselves from the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, this is also called a heavy burden (*dausthulya*).
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is greedily attached to the fruit of a stream-enterer up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, this is also called a heavy burden (*dauṣṭhulya*).
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives rise to the notion of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, this is also called a heavy burden;
if they give rise to the notion of the sense-base of the eye up to the sense-base of the mind, this is also called a heavy burden;
if they give rise to the notion of the sense-field of form up to the sense-field of mental phenomena, this is also called a heavy burden.
To give rise to the perception of the eye-element up to the mind-element is also called *dausthulya*;
to give rise to the perception of the form-element up to the phenomena-element is also called *dausthulya*;
to give rise to the perception of the eye-consciousness-element up to the mind-consciousness-element is also called *dausthulya*.
The arising of the perception of eye-contact up to mind-contact is also called *dausthulya* (coarseness);
the arising of the perceptions of all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition up to all feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition is also called *dausthulya*;
the arising of the perception of the earth element up to the consciousness element is also called *dausthulya*.
To give rise to the perception of conditions from the causal condition up to the dominant condition is also called *dausthulya* (coarseness);
to give rise to the perception of all phenomena produced from conditions is also called *dausthulya*;
and to give rise to the perception of ignorance up to old age and death is also called *dausthulya*.
To give rise to the thought of the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom is also called a heavy burden;
to give rise to the thought of internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the nature of non-nature is also called a heavy burden;
to give rise to the thought of suchness up to the inconceivable realm is also called a heavy burden.
To give rise to the perception of the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path is also called a heavy burden;
to give rise to the perception of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path is also called a heavy burden;
to give rise to the perception of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments is also called a heavy burden.
To give rise to the perception of the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality is also called "coarseness";

to give rise to the perception of the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—is also called "coarseness"; to give rise to the perception of the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata is also called "coarseness";
to give rise to the perception of the stage of extreme joy up to the stage of the Dharma-cloud is also called "coarseness."
To give rise to the perception of all dharanī-gates and samādhi-gates is also called a coarse heaviness;
to give rise to the perception of the five eyes and six supernormal powers is also called a coarse heaviness;
to give rise to the perception of the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha is also called a coarse heaviness.
To give rise to the perception of the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks is also called a heavy burden;
to give rise to the perception of the qualities of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity is also called a heavy burden;
to give rise to the perception of all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects is also called a heavy burden.
To give rise to the notion of the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha is also called a heavy burden;
to give rise to the notion of all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is also called a heavy burden;
to give rise to the notion of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas is also called a heavy burden.

To give rise to the notion of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), the notion of a śrāvaka, the notion of a pratyekabuddha, the notion of a bodhisattva, or the notion of a Tathāgata is also called *dausthulya*.

To give rise to the notion of hell-beings, the notion of animals, the notion of hungry ghosts, the notion of humans, the notion of devas, the notion of male, or the notion of female is also called *dausthulya*.
To give rise to the notion of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the notion of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), or the notion of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is also called *dausthulya*.
To give rise to the perception of wholesome dharmas or the perception of unwholesome dharmas is also called *dausthulya*;
to give rise to the perception of dharmas with a definite moral quality (*vyākṛta*) or the perception of indeterminate dharmas (*avyākṛta*) is also called *dausthulya*;
to give rise to the perception of contaminated dharmas (*sāsrava*) or the perception of uncontaminated dharmas (*anāsrava*) is also called *dausthulya*.
To give rise to the notion of mundane phenomena and the notion of supramundane phenomena is also called *dausthulya*;
to give rise to the notion of conditioned phenomena and the notion of unconditioned phenomena is also called *dausthulya*.

"Subhūti! All such immeasurable and boundless attachments to phenomena and sentient beings, as well as their false conceptualizations, along with the physical, verbal, and mental actions they give rise to, and the corresponding lack of pliancy (akarmaṇyatā) of those types—all these are called 'gross heaviness' (dauṣṭhulya), which all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should completely abandon."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they remain far removed from such heavy burdens as have been described; they personally practice the perfection of giving and also teach others to practice the perfection of giving."

If there are sentient beings who require food, he gives them food; those who require drink, he gives them drink; those who require vehicles, he gives them vehicles; those who require clothing, he gives them clothing; and whatever other various requisites they may require, he gives them all at the appropriate time and place. Just as he practices this himself, he likewise instructs others to do so.

Having given in this manner, he takes these roots of virtue and shares them equally with all sentient beings, dedicating them toward the adornment and purification of his future buddha-field, so that it may be swiftly perfected for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva personally practices the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and also teaches others to practice ethical discipline up to and including the perfection of wisdom.

Having performed these deeds, they take these roots of goodness and, sharing them equally with all sentient beings, dedicate them toward the adornment and purification of the Buddha-fields where they dwell, so that those fields may be swiftly perfected for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
By the power of their supernormal vows, bodhisattva mahāsattvas fill the trichiliocosm with the most excellent seven treasures and offer them to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha."
Having given the gift, he joyfully makes this great vow:

"By means of these roots of goodness I have planted, I share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward the adornment of a pure Buddha-field. May my land be adorned with the seven treasures, and may all sentient beings enjoy various exquisite jewels according to their wishes, without any attachment."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! By the power of their supernormal vows, bodhisattva mahāsattvas strike and play immeasurable exquisite musical instruments among the devas and humans, making offerings to the Three Jewels and the stūpas of the Buddhas."
Having made these offerings, they joyfully made this great vow:

"By means of these roots of goodness I have planted, may I share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward the attainment of a pure and adorned buddha-field; may such sublime music always be played in my land, so that any sentient being who hears it will experience joy in body and mind without falling into attachment."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! By the power of their supernormal vows, bodhisattva mahāsattvas fill the three-thousandfold world system with all manner of exquisite incense and flowers from among humans and devas, making offerings to the Three Jewels and the stūpas of the Buddhas."
Having made the offering, he joyfully gave rise to this great vow:

"By means of these roots of goodness I have planted, I shall share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward the adornment of a pure Buddha-field. May my land always possess such exquisite fragrant flowers, so that sentient beings, upon using them, may experience delight in body and mind without any attachment."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! By the power of their supernormal vows, bodhisattva mahāsattvas prepare exquisite foods of a hundred flavors to make offerings to the Buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, śrāvakas, and the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas."
Having made the offering, he joyfully made this great vow:

"By means of these roots of goodness I have planted, I shall share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward the attainment of a pure and adorned Buddha-field. When I attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may all the sentient beings within my land partake of such food of a hundred flavors, which nourishes and gladdens their bodies and minds without giving rise to attachment."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! By the power of their supernormal vows, bodhisattva mahāsattvas prepare various kinds of exquisite unguents and fine, soft garments from among humans and devas, and offer them to the Buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, śrāvakas, and the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas; or they may offer them to the Dharma and to the stūpas of the Buddhas."
Having given the gift, he joyfully makes this great vow:

"By means of these roots of virtue I have planted, I share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward the attainment of a pure and adorned Buddha-field. When I attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may all the sentient beings within my land always obtain such clothing and ointments, enjoying them as they wish without any attachment."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! By the power of their supernormal vows, bodhisattva mahāsattvas provide all kinds of the five exquisite objects of desire—arising according to their wishes among humans and devas—to make offerings to the Buddhas, the shrines of the Buddhas (caityas), pratyekabuddhas, śrāvakas, and the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and they bestow them upon other sentient beings."
Having given the gift, he joyfully makes this great vow:

"By means of these roots of virtue that I have planted, I share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward the attainment of a pure and adorned Buddha-field. When I attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, may all sentient beings within my land experience, according to their inclinations, sublime objects of form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch, arising at the mere thought of them; and may they enjoy them with joy, free from any attachment."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they exert courageous and correct diligence to give rise to great vows; they themselves abide in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, and they also teach others to abide in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence."
Having performed these deeds, he further made this aspiration:

"When I attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field never be separated from inner emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they exert courageous and correct diligence and give rise to great vows; they themselves abide in suchness up to the inconceivable realm, and they also teach others to abide in suchness up to the inconceivable realm."
Having performed these deeds, he further made this vow:
"When I attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field never be separated from suchness, up to and including the inconceivable realm."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they exert courageous and correct diligence and give rise to great vows; they themselves abide in the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, and they also teach others to abide in the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path."
Having performed this deed, he further made this vow:

"When I attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field never be separated from the Noble Truths of Suffering, Origination, Cessation, and the Path."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they exert themselves with courageous diligence and give rise to great vows; they personally cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, and they also teach others to cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path."
Having performed this deed, he further made this aspiration:

"When I attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field never be separated from the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they exert themselves with courageous diligence and give rise to great vows; they personally cultivate the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments, and they also teach others to cultivate the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments."
Having performed this deed, he further made this vow:
"When I attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field never be separated from the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they exert themselves with courageous diligence and give rise to great vows; they cultivate for themselves the eight liberations up to the ten totalities, and they also teach others to cultivate the eight liberations up to the ten totalities."
Having performed these deeds, he further made this vow:
"When I attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field never be separated from the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they exert themselves with courageous diligence and give rise to great vows; they cultivate for themselves the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—and they also teach others to cultivate the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness."
Having performed this deed, he further made this vow:

"When I attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field never be separated from the gates of liberation: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they exert courageous and correct diligence to give rise to great vows; they personally cultivate the stages from the Ground of Extreme Joy up to the Ground of the Dharma Cloud, and they also teach others to cultivate the stages from the Ground of Extreme Joy up to the Ground of the Dharma Cloud."
Having performed these deeds, he further made this vow:

"When I attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field never be separated from the stages, beginning with the Stage of Utmost Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they exert courageous and correct diligence to give rise to great vows; they cultivate for themselves all doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of samādhi, and they also teach others to cultivate all doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of samādhi."
Having performed this deed, he further made this vow:
"When I attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field never be separated from any of the dhāraṇī-doors or samādhi-doors."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they exert themselves with courageous diligence and give rise to great vows; they cultivate for themselves the five eyes and the six supernormal powers, and they also teach others to cultivate the five eyes and the six supernormal powers."
Having performed these deeds, he further made this vow:
"When I attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field never be separated from the five eyes and the six supernormal powers."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they exert themselves with courageous diligence and give rise to great vows; they personally cultivate the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and they also teach others to cultivate the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha."
Having performed this deed, he further made this vow:

"When I attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field never be separated from the Tathāgata’s ten powers, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they apply themselves with courageous and correct diligence, giving rise to great vows; they personally cultivate the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs, and they also teach others to cultivate the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs."
Having performed this deed, he further made this vow:

"When I attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field never be separated from the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor signs."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they exert themselves with courageous and correct diligence, giving rise to great vows; they personally cultivate the quality of non-forgetfulness and abide constantly in equanimity, and they also teach others to cultivate the quality of non-forgetfulness and to abide constantly in equanimity."
Having performed this deed, he further made this aspiration:

"When I attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field never be separated from the quality of non-forgetfulness and may they always abide in equanimity."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they exert themselves with courageous diligence and give rise to great vows; they cultivate for themselves all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), and they also teach others to cultivate all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects."
Having performed this deed, he further made this vow:

"When I attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field never be separated from omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they exert courageous and correct diligence to give rise to great vows; they personally cultivate all the practices of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva and also instruct others to cultivate all the practices of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva."
Having performed this deed, he further made this vow:
"When I attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field never be separated from the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they exert courageous and correct diligence and give rise to great vows; they cultivate for themselves the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of all buddhas, and they also teach others to cultivate the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of all buddhas."
Having performed this deed, he further made this vow:
"When I attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field never be separated from the unexcelled, perfect, and complete bodhi of the Buddhas."

"Thus it is, Subhūti! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, by means of such vows and practices they are able to adorn and purify the buddha-fields in which they dwell."

“Subhūti, you should know that for as long as these bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the path to awakening, they shall fulfill the aspirations and practices they have undertaken; for that same duration, they shall diligently train themselves.”

By means of these causes and conditions, one is able to accomplish all wholesome dharmas for oneself and can also cause others to gradually accomplish all wholesome dharmas; one is able to cultivate and attain a body adorned with the most excellent marks and signs for oneself, and can also cause others to gradually cultivate and attain a body adorned with the most excellent marks and signs, because of being sustained by vast merit.

“Subhūti, you should know that when these bodhisattva mahāsattvas have brought their cultivated vows and practices to fulfillment, and each attains unexcelled, perfect enlightenment within their respective adorned and purified buddha-fields, the sentient beings they transform will also be born in those lands to together enjoy the great Dharma-joy of the pure lands.”
“Subhūti, you should know this!”

These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should cultivate such purification of buddha-fields as follows: that within those lands, one never hears of the three evil destinies; nor does one hear of various wrong views; nor does one hear of the poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion; nor does one hear of the physical forms of men or women; nor does one hear of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; nor does one hear of disagreeable matters such as suffering or impermanence; nor does one hear of the acquisition of material requisites; nor does one hear of the grasping at "I" and "mine," underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), fetters (*paryavasthāna*), or inverted attachments; nor does one hear of the establishment of distinctions among the fruit-attainments of sentient beings; rather, one hears only the sounds of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), non-arising (*anutpāda*), non-ceasing (*anirodha*), and the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).

This means that according to the various inclinations of sentient beings, within external and internal objects such as groves of trees, subtle winds constantly strike one another, giving rise to all manner of exquisite sounds. Within those sounds it is said: "All phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature;

because they lack intrinsic nature, they are empty; because they are empty, they are signless; because they are signless, they are wishless; because they are wishless, they are unarisen; and because they are unarisen, they are unceasing."

Therefore, all phenomena are originally quiescent and by nature in *nirvāṇa*; whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, the *dharmadhātu* of all phenomena remains eternally as it is—namely, that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature, empty, and so forth.
"In that Buddha-field, all sentient beings—whether by day or night, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—constantly hear such sounds of the sublime Dharma."

“Subhūti, you should know that when these bodhisattva mahāsattvas, each dwelling in their own adorned and purified buddha-field, realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the ten directions will all together proclaim the names of those respective Buddhas. If any sentient beings hear such names of these Buddhas, they will certainly attain non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

“Subhūti, you should know that when these bodhisattva mahāsattvas, each dwelling in their own adorned and purified buddha-field, realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they will proclaim the true Dharma for the sake of sentient beings; having heard it, those beings will certainly not give rise to doubt as to whether it is the Dharma or not the Dharma.”

Why is this? Because those sentient beings realize that all phenomena are precisely suchness (*tathatā*), the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); everything is the Dharma, and there is nothing that is not the Dharma.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
All these bodhisattva mahāsattvas are able to adorn and purify such buddha-fields.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have beings among those to be converted who possess unwholesome roots; they have not planted roots of goodness under the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, or śrāvakas; because they are influenced by evil friends and separated from virtuous friends, they do not hear the true Dharma; they are constantly gripped and stored within by various views of a self and sentient beings, as well as various speculative tenets, and they fall into the biased attachments of the two extremes of nihilism and eternalism.

These sentient beings give rise to false attachments on their own and constantly teach others to do the same; they perceive what is not the Triple Gem as the Triple Gem, and regard that which is the Triple Gem as not being the Triple Gem. They slander the True Dharma and praise false teachings. Due to these causes and conditions, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into the various evil realms and undergo intense suffering.

Once these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have each attained unexcelled, perfect enlightenment while dwelling in their own lands, they see those sentient beings sinking in saṃsāra and undergoing immeasurable suffering; through the power of their supernormal knowledges and skillful means, they teach and transform them, causing them to abandon wrong views and abide in right view, and to emerge from the evil destinies to be born in the human realm.

Having been born into the human realm, he further employs various supernatural powers and skillful means to teach and transform others, causing them to abide within the assembly of those destined for right determination; by virtue of this, they ultimately never fall into the evil realms.

Furthermore, they cause them to diligently cultivate sublime vows and practices, so that at the end of life they may be reborn in a pure and adorned buddha-field and enjoy the Mahāyāna Dharma-bliss of that pure land.
"Thus it is, Subhūti!"
All these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to adorn and purify buddha-fields in this manner.

Because the lands they inhabit are utterly pure, the sentient beings born there do not give rise to doubt or confusion regarding any phenomena, such as thinking, "This is a worldly phenomenon; this is a supramundane phenomenon";
or "This is a contaminated phenomenon; this is an uncontaminated phenomenon."
"This is a conditioned phenomenon; this is an unconditioned phenomenon.
Such doubts and conceptual discriminations do not arise at all; by virtue of these causes and conditions, those sentient beings will certainly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
“Subhūti! This is the mark of the merit of a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s purification of a buddha-field.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 476, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Chapter 81: On Right Concentration (Samyaksamādhi), Part Two, Chapter Eighty-one. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Do these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in the fixed category of rightness, or do they abide in the indefinite category?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas all abide in the fixed category of rightness (samyaktva-niyāma), not in the indeterminate category.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In what kind of fixed category of rightness do these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide?"
Is it the Śrāvaka vehicle?
The Pratyekabuddha vehicle?
Or the Bodhisattva vehicle?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“All these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in the fixed destiny of the bodhisattva’s right nature; they do not abide in the fixed destiny of the two vehicles’ right nature.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"At what time do these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in the fixed determination of the right nature (samyaktva-niyāma)—
at the initial generation of the mind?"
"Is it the stage of non-retrogression?
Or is it the final existence?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Whether these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have first resolved their minds, or have reached the stage of non-retrogression, or are in their final existence, they all abide in the bodhisattva’s fixed determination for the right state."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Do Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who abide in the fixed determination of the right nature fall into the evil destinies?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who abides in the fixed determination of the right nature will certainly not fall into the various evil destinies.
He then addressed Subhūti again: “What do you think?”
"Eighth, do stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, or pratyekabuddhas fall into the miserable destinies?
Subhūti replied, "No, they do not."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“It is likewise for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; from their first production of the thought of enlightenment, they practice the perfection of giving up to the perfection of wisdom, as well as other immeasurable and boundless buddha-dharmas, thereby severing all unwholesome dharmas.”

For this reason, it is impossible that they would fall into the various evil realms, nor is it possible that they would be reborn in the long-lived heavens—meaning that in those places, the various supreme wholesome dharmas could not be manifested.

It is impossible for this bodhisattva mahāsattva to be born in a remote borderland, or among the Da-xu or Mlecchas; that is to say, it is impossible for him to be in a place where he cannot practice sublime wholesome dharmas, where many hold wrong views and do not believe in cause and effect, where they constantly delight in practicing various defiled and evil deeds, and where they do not hear the names of the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha, nor where there are the fourfold assembly—namely, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.

It is impossible for a bodhisattva-mahāsattva to be born into a family of wrong views—that is, to be born into such a family where they cling to various evil perspectives, deny the existence of virtuous conduct, non-virtuous conduct, and their results, fail to cultivate wholesome qualities, and delight in committing evil deeds; therefore, bodhisattvas are not born into such families.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
It is impossible for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who have first resolved upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment to practice the ten paths of unwholesome action with a superior intention.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first production of the thought of awakening, accomplishes such meritorious roots of goodness that they are not born in evil realms, for what reason does the Tathāgata frequently speak to the assembly of his own past lives in their many hundreds of thousands of varieties, some of which include births in various evil realms? At those times, where were those roots of goodness?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not receive bodies in the miserable realms due to defiled karma; rather, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, they intentionally take on such bodies through their vows. Therefore, one should not cite this as a difficulty.”
Again, he addressed Subhūti: "What do you think?

Are there any pratyekabuddhas or arhats who possess such skillful means as the bodhisattvas, having accomplished such superior skillful means that they take the bodies of animals such as white elephants; and when they see enemies or robbers coming with the intent to cause them harm, they immediately give rise to unsurpassed patience and compassion, and for the sake of bringing benefit and happiness to those people, sacrifice their own lives rather than harming them?"
Subhūti replied, “The Pratyekabuddhas do not possess such things.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"By this causal condition, it should be known that because a bodhisattva desires to benefit all sentient beings and to swiftly fulfill great compassion, although they manifest in various bodies of animals, they are not defiled by the faults of animal existence."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In which roots of goodness do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide that, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, they take on the bodies of animals?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"What roots of goodness are there that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should not bring to fulfillment?

Indeed, for the sake of seeking unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should bring every root of goodness to fulfillment; that is to say, from the first generation of the mind of awakening until sitting upon the seat of sublime enlightenment, there is no root of goodness that should not be brought to fulfillment."

One must fully perfect all wholesome dharmas before attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; it is impossible to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment if even a single wholesome dharma has not been perfected.

Therefore, from the first generation of the mind of awakening until sitting upon the sublime seat of enlightenment, a bodhisattva constantly trains to perfect all wholesome dharmas; having so trained, they shall attain the knowledge of all aspects, forever sever the continuity of all habitual tendencies, and thereby realize the wisdom of all-knowledge.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having accomplished the white dharmas and true noble wisdom, is born in the evil destinies and receives the body of an animal?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Has the Tathāgata accomplished all pure dharmas through true noble wisdom?"
Subhūti replied, “The Tathāgata has accomplished all pure dharmas and true noble wisdom.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Would the Tathāgata, having manifested a body belonging to the animal realm, perform the work of a Buddha for the benefit of sentient beings? Subhūti replied:
“The Tathāgata manifests the body of an animal to benefit sentient beings and perform the work of a Buddha.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “What do you think?”
"When the Tathāgata manifests in the form of an animal, is he actually an animal that experiences that suffering? Subhūti replied,
"When the Tathāgata manifests in the form of an animal, he is not actually an animal and does not experience that suffering."
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"It is the same for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; although they have accomplished the white dharmas and true noble wisdom, for the sake of bringing sentient beings to maturity, they employ skillful means to assume the bodies of animals, maturing various classes of sentient beings as appropriate."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, what do you think?

Is there an Arhat whose outflows are forever exhausted who can manifest a transformation body to perform various activities, and by means of those activities, cause others to give rise to a heart of joy?"

Subhūti replied, “There are Arhats whose outflows are forever exhausted who can manifest emanated bodies to perform various activities; by means of those activities, they are able to cause other beings to give rise to great joy.”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"It is likewise for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Although they have accomplished the pure dharmas (*śukla-dharma*) and true noble wisdom (*ārya-jñāna*), for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, they employ skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) to take birth in the bodies of the evil destinies, maturing various classes of sentient beings as appropriate.
Although they take such bodies, they do not undergo the various sufferings and afflictions like those [beings], nor are they defiled by the faults of those realms."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, what do you think?

Suppose there were a master illusionist or his apprentice who conjured various things such as elephants and horses by means of illusion, causing a great multitude to see them and rejoice with leaping joy. Would those elephants, horses, and so forth exist as realities?"
Subhūti replied, “In that regard,
there are no real elephants, horses, or such things.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"So too it is with the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: although they have perfected the pure dharmas (*śukla-dharma*) and true noble wisdom (*ārya-jñāna*), for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, they manifest by assuming various bodies such as those of animals. Although they assume those bodies, they are in reality not those [beings], nor are they defiled by their faults."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess such vast skillful means that, although they have accomplished pure dharmas and true noble wisdom, they assume various bodies for the sake of sentient beings, manifesting whatever benefit is appropriate for them.”

"Bhagavān! Abiding in what dharmas are the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas able to exercise such skillful means that, although they undergo various physical forms within the various realms of existence, they are not defiled by their faults?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwelling in profound *prajñāpāramitā* are able to exercise such skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*). By the power of these skillful means, although they travel to Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions and manifest various bodies to benefit and bring peace and happiness to those sentient beings, they do not give rise to any defiled attachment therein."

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva finds nothing at all in any phenomena; that is to say, they find nothing whatsoever that can defile, nothing that is defiled, and no causes or conditions for defilement.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, Subhūti!
One should know that emptiness cannot defile emptiness, emptiness cannot defile other phenomena, and no other phenomenon can defile emptiness. Why is this so?
Even emptiness itself cannot be apprehended within emptiness, let alone any other phenomena that could be apprehended!

This is called the emptiness of the unapprehendable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*). Abiding therein, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas are able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, constantly bringing benefit to all sentient beings.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Do Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas perform such skillful means by dwelling solely in the profound perfection of wisdom, or do they also dwell in other dharmas?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Is there any other dharma not encompassed by the profound perfection of wisdom, such that you now give rise to such a doubt?"
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Since the profound perfection of wisdom is empty of intrinsic nature, how can it be said that the profound perfection of wisdom encompasses all phenomena?”
"It cannot be said that within emptiness there are phenomena that are either included or not included.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Are not all phenomena empty of the intrinsic nature of phenomena?"
Subhūti replied, “So it is! So it is!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"If all phenomena are empty of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, would it not be the case that within emptiness all phenomena are subsumed? Subhūti replied:
"So it is! So it is! the Buddha told Subhūti.

"For this reason, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* encompasses all phenomena; one should know that a bodhisattva dwelling in the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is able to exercise such skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*)."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, abide in the emptiness of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) of all phenomena, and thereby evoke the *abhijñāpāramitā*; and how, abiding in the *abhijñāpāramitā*, can they travel to Buddha-worlds in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to honor and revere the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, listen to and receive the True Dharma from those Buddhas, and plant immeasurable, supreme roots of goodness?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they universally observe that the nature of all Buddha-worlds in the ten directions—as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—as well as the assemblies of Buddhas and the teachings they proclaim, is entirely empty. There are only conventional, provisional designations and names spoken of as 'worlds,' 'Buddha-assemblies,' and 'teachings'; yet these conventional, provisional designations and names are themselves empty of intrinsic nature."
“Subhūti, you should know this!

If the worlds of the ten directions, the assemblies of Buddhas, and the teachings they proclaim were not empty of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) in their conventional designations, then the emptiness that has been taught would be merely partial. Since the emptiness taught is not partial, the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is entirely empty; this principle is all-encompassing, non-dual, and without distinction.”

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), by means of skillful means that universally contemplate emptiness, they bring forth the perfection of supernormal powers (abhijñāpāramitā). Abiding in the perfection of supernormal powers, they are then able to bring forth the subtle and wondrous superknowledges (abhijñā) of the divine eye, the divine ear, the power of psychic travel, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, and the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya-jñāna).
“Subhūti, you should know this:

it is not apart from the perfection of supernormal powers that bodhisattva mahāsattvas are able to freely mature sentient beings, purify buddha-fields, and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

Therefore, the perfection of supernormal powers is the path to enlightenment; all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas rely upon this path to seek and proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. While seeking and proceeding, they are able to personally fulfill all wholesome dharmas and can also teach others to cultivate various wholesome dharmas; yet, although they perform these deeds, they have no attachment whatsoever to those wholesome dharmas.

Why is this? It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas know that all wholesome dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*). There is no attachment to that which is empty of intrinsic nature; if there were attachment, there would be craving for its flavor (*āsvāda*). Because there is no attachment, there is no craving for its flavor. Since there is no craving for its flavor within the emptiness of intrinsic nature—the taster, the tasted, and the causal conditions for tasting cannot be apprehended within the dharma of emptiness.

“Subhūti, you should know that when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they abide in the perfection of supernormal powers and manifest a purified divine eye that transcends that of humans; with this divine eye, they observe that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty.”

Because they see that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, they do not engage in the fabrication of various karmas based on the characteristics of phenomena; although they teach such a Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, they likewise do not apprehend the characteristics of sentient beings nor their conventional designations.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of non-apprehension as a skillful method, brings forth the sublime supernormal powers of a bodhisattva, and employs these supernormal powers to perform all activities that ought to be performed.
“With the extremely pure divine eye that transcends that of humans, this bodhisattva mahāsattva surveys the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions,

as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Having seen them, he manifests the supernormal power of the knowledge of miraculous feats (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna-abhijñā*) and goes there to benefit sentient beings,
whether by means of the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*) up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).”
They bring benefit by means of the *pāramitās*; or they bring benefit by means of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
or they bring benefit by means of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
or they bring benefit by means of the eight liberations up to the ten totalities; or...
They bring benefit by means of the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
or they bring benefit by means of other various excellent wholesome dharmas; or they bring benefit by means of the dharmas of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and all buddhas.

“If this bodhisattva mahāsattva, within the worlds of the ten directions, sees sentient beings who are full of stinginess and greed, he gives rise to deep compassion and teaches them the Dharma in this way:

‘You sentient beings should practice generosity. Those who are stingy and greedy suffer the pain of poverty; because of poverty, they lack majesty and virtue, such that they cannot even benefit themselves, let alone others!’”

Therefore, you all should diligently practice giving; by doing so, you will bring peace and happiness to yourselves as well as to others. Do not, out of poverty, devour one another, for in this way you will both fail to be liberated from the sufferings of the evil realms.
"If he sees sentient beings who have violated their pure precepts, he gives rise to deep compassion and teaches them this Dharma:

'You sentient beings should maintain pure precepts! Those who break the precepts undergo the suffering of the evil realms; those who violate the precepts possess no majestic virtue and cannot benefit themselves, much less others!'"

Due to the causes and conditions of breaking the precepts, one falls into the three evil realms, where the ripening of suffering is so agonizing and unbearable that one cannot even save oneself, let alone save others!
Therefore, you all should maintain pure precepts; you must not allow a thought of breaking the precepts to remain for even a single kṣaṇa, much less for a long period of time!
"Do not give rein to your own minds, lest you later feel sorrow and regret.
If he sees sentient beings who are further incited by mutual anger, harboring resentment toward one another, and harming each other, he gives rise to deep compassion and speaks this Dharma:

"You sentient beings should cultivate patience; do not harbor mutual anger, resentment, or harm one another. All hearts of anger and resentment are contrary to wholesome dharmas; they increase unwholesome dharmas and invite present decline and loss."

Because of this mind of anger and resentment, when your bodies perish and your lives end, you shall fall into the evil realms and undergo various extreme sufferings from which there will be no prospect of escape for a long time.
