Therefore, you should not allow the mind of anger and resentment to remain for even a single moment, much less let it continue in succession for a long duration!
"You all should now take one another as objects of mutual concern, giving rise to a heart of loving-kindness and performing deeds that bring benefit.
"If he sees sentient beings who are indolent and lax, he gives rise to deep compassion and teaches them this Dharma:

'You sentient beings should be diligent and energetic; do not be indolent or lax regarding wholesome dharmas. Those who are lax will be unable to accomplish any wholesome dharmas or any sublime matters.'"

Because of this, you have fallen into the various evil destinies and experienced immeasurable suffering; therefore, you should not allow even a single moment of a lazy mind to take hold, much less permit it to continue for a long duration!
"If he sees sentient beings who have lost mindfulness, whose minds are distracted, and whose hearts are not at peace, he gives rise to deep compassion and teaches them this Dharma:

'You sentient beings should cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Do not give rise to thoughts of lost mindfulness or distraction; such states of mind do not accord with wholesome dharmas, but increase unwholesome dharmas and bring about present ruin.'"

Because of this, when your bodies perish and your lives end, you will fall into the evil realms and undergo immeasurable suffering; therefore, you should not allow a mind associated with forgetfulness and distraction to persist for even a single moment, let alone for a long duration.
"If he sees sentient beings who are foolish and possess evil wisdom, he gives rise to deep compassion and teaches them this Dharma:

'You sentient beings should cultivate superior wisdom and not give rise to evil wisdom; those who give rise to evil wisdom cannot even proceed to the various happy realms, much less attain liberation!'"

Because of this cause and condition of unwholesome wisdom, you have fallen into the various evil destinies and undergone immeasurable suffering; therefore, you should not allow a mind associated with such foolish and unwholesome wisdom to remain for even a single moment, much less permit it to continue in succession for a long time!
"If he sees sentient beings who have much greed and desire, he gives rise to deep compassion and employs skillful means to lead them to practice the contemplation of impurity;
if he sees sentient beings who have much anger and hatred, he gives rise to deep compassion and employs skillful means to lead them to practice the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion."

If he sees sentient beings who are largely ignorant, he gives rise to deep compassion and employs skillful means to lead them to practice the contemplation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

If he sees sentient beings who are largely arrogant, he gives rise to deep compassion and employs skillful means to lead them to practice the contemplation of the analysis of the elements (*dhātuprabheda*).

If he sees sentient beings who have many discursive thoughts and investigations, he gives rise to deep compassion and employs skillful means to lead them to practice mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).

If he sees sentient beings who have lost the right path, he gives rise to deep compassion and employs skillful means to instruct and lead them into the right path—whether the path of the Śrāvaka, the path of the Pratyekabuddha, or the path of the Tathāgata—and employs skillful means to teach them this Dharma:

"All that you grasp at is empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*). Within the dharma of emptiness, there can be nothing to grasp, for the characteristic of emptiness consists in the absence of grasping."

"Thus it is, Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they must abide in the perfection of supernormal powers (*abhijñāpāramitā*) before they can freely proclaim the true Dharma to benefit, bring peace, and bring happiness to all sentient beings."

"Subhūti, you should know that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva is far removed from the perfection of supernormal powers (abhijñā-pāramitā), they will be unable to freely proclaim the true Dharma and perform beneficial deeds for all sentient beings."

"Subhūti, you should know that just as a bird without wings cannot fly freely through the air to travel far distances, so too it is with bodhisattva mahāsattvas: if they lack the perfection of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-pāramitā*), they cannot freely proclaim the true Dharma or perform beneficial deeds for all sentient beings."

Therefore, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should bring forth the perfection of supernormal powers. If they bring forth the perfection of supernormal powers, they will be able to freely proclaim the true Dharma, benefiting and gladdening all sentient beings according to their wishes.
“Subhūti, you should know that bodhisattva mahāsattvas, with their extremely pure divine eye that transcends that of humans,
survey all the Buddha-worlds in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and observe the sentient beings born therein; having seen them, they [draw them forth]...”
Having manifested the supernormal power of the knowledge of miraculous feats, he traveled to that realm in an instant; then, with the knowledge of others' minds,
he understood as they truly are the minds and mental factors of those sentient beings, and according to what was appropriate for them,
he taught the essentials of the Dharma— namely, the teachings on the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom— or...
He taught the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
or he taught the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; or he taught the eight liberations up to the ten totalities;
or he taught the gateways of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; or he taught all the gateways of dhāraṇī and the three...

The gateways of meditative concentration (*samādhi*): sometimes they are explained as inner emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of the nature of non-existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*);
sometimes they are explained as suchness (*tathatā*) up to the inconceivable realm (*acintya-dhātu*); sometimes they are explained as the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;

sometimes they are explained as the causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) up to the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*); or sometimes they are explained as all phenomena produced from conditions. Or they are explained as...
From ignorance up to old age and death, he may teach by way of the various aggregates, bases, and elements;
or he may teach the path of the śrāvakas, the path of the pratyekabuddhas, or the path of the bodhisattvas;
or he may teach awakening, or teach nirvāṇa. Having heard these teachings, those sentient beings all attain extraordinary benefits.
"Furthermore, they bring peace and happiness.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of an extremely pure divine ear that transcends those of humans and gods, is able to hear the voices of all humans and non-humans.

By means of this divine ear, they hear everywhere throughout the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions—as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—all the true Dharma spoken by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas. Having heard it, they receive, uphold, and contemplate its meaning and intent; according to the Dharma they have heard, they are able to proclaim it to sentient beings as it truly is—whether teaching the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, or explaining extensively up to awakening, or even nirvāṇa—so that once those sentient beings have heard this Dharma, they all obtain supreme benefit and peace."

"By means of the extremely pure supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds, this bodhisattva mahāsattva understands, as they truly are, the minds and mental factors of all sentient beings. According to what is appropriate for them, he teaches the essentials of the Dharma—namely, the perfection of giving up to the perfection of wisdom—and explains at length everything up to either awakening or nirvāṇa. Having heard this Dharma, those sentient beings all obtain supreme benefit and peace."
“By means of the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives with purified clarity, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to remember the various events of his own and others’ previous births.

Through this supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives, he truly remembers and knows the names and other distinctions of the Buddhas of the past and their assemblies of disciples. If there are sentient beings who would benefit from hearing accounts of past lives, he then proclaims those accounts of past lives for them. By means of this skillful method, he teaches the true Dharma—namely, teaching the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, and so on extensively until perhaps teaching awakening or nirvāṇa—so that once those sentient beings have heard this Dharma, they all obtain supreme benefit and peace.”

“By means of the extremely swift supernormal power of the knowledge of the movement of the mind, this bodhisattva mahāsattva travels to the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, to attend upon and make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. Having planted roots of goodness in the presence of those Buddhas, he returns to his own land to speak of the matters of the various Buddha-fields for the sake of sentient beings. Through these skillful means, he preaches the True Dharma—namely, preaching the perfection of giving up to the perfection of wisdom, and so on extensively until he speaks of either enlightenment or nirvāṇa—so that after sentient beings have heard this Dharma, they all obtain supreme benefit and peace.”

“By means of the supernormal power of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows as it has been attained, this bodhisattva mahāsattva knows, in accordance with reality, which classes of sentient beings have exhausted their outflows and which have not; he also knows, in accordance with reality, the expedient means for the exhaustion of outflows. For those who have not yet exhausted them, he proclaims the essential points of the Dharma—namely, the teaching on the perfection of giving up to the perfection of wisdom, and so forth at length, even to the point of teaching either bodhi or nirvāṇa—so that once these sentient beings have heard this Dharma, they all obtain supreme benefit and peace.”
"In this way, Subhūti, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should bring forth the perfection of supernormal powers."

Because this bodhisattva-mahāsattva has cultivated the perfection of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-pāramitā*) to full completion, they assume various bodies according to their wishes, yet are not defiled by the faults of suffering or pleasure; just as a Buddha’s emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), though able to perform various activities, is not contaminated by those faults of suffering or pleasure.

"So it is, Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should sport in the perfection of supernormal powers (*abhijñāpāramitā*). If they sport in the perfection of supernormal powers, they will be able to bring sentient beings to maturity and purify buddha-fields, swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

"Subhūti, you should know that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not bring sentient beings to maturity and purify buddha-fields, they will ultimately be unable to attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek."

Why is this? Because if bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have not yet perfected the provisions for awakening, they will certainly be unable to realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening they seek.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, what are called the provisions for enlightenment of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas? By fulfilling these provisions for enlightenment, how do bodhisattva mahāsattvas then realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"All wholesome dharmas are the provisions for a bodhisattva’s enlightenment.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What are called all wholesome dharmas?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, from their first production of the thought of awakening, practice the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, they have no conceptualization or attachment therein, such that they form this thought:”
"There is this giving, up to and including wisdom; it is for this reason and for this purpose that one practices giving, up to and including wisdom.
Such threefold conceptualization and attachment are entirely absent, because one knows that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty.

Because these six perfections, such as generosity and the rest, when cultivated, are able to benefit oneself and also benefit all sentient beings by causing them to transcend birth and death and realize nirvāṇa, they are called wholesome dharmas; they are also termed the bodhisattva’s provisions for enlightenment, and are also termed the path of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Because the assemblies of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the past, future, and present practice this path, they have already attained, will attain, and are now attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; furthermore, they have already, will, and are now causing sentient beings to cross the great ocean of birth and death and obtain the bliss of nirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the four applications of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
they abide in inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature; they abide in suchness up to..."
In this inconceivable realm, they dwell securely in the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
they practice the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; they practice the eight liberations up to the ten totalities;
they practice the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; and they practice as bodhisattvas.
The stage of the Mahāsattva consists of practicing all the gateways of dhāraṇī and samādhi;
practicing the ten powers of the Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
practicing the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity; and practicing all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects.
Within this, they have no conceptual discrimination or attachment, thinking:

"This is the four applications of mindfulness up to the knowledge of all aspects; for this reason and for this purpose, I cultivate the four applications of mindfulness up to the knowledge of all aspects."
In this state, all three types of conceptualization and attachment are entirely absent, because one knows that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is empty.

By means of this, the four applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) that are cultivated can benefit oneself and also benefit all sentient beings, causing them to transcend birth and death and attain *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, these are called "wholesome dharmas" (*kuśaladharma*), are also termed the "requisites for a bodhisattva’s enlightenment" (*bodhisambhāra*), and are also termed the "path of a bodhisattva mahāsattva."

Because the assemblies of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the past, future, and present practice this path, they have already attained, will attain, and are now attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; furthermore, they have caused, will cause, and are now causing sentient beings to cross the great ocean of birth and death and attain the bliss of nirvāṇa.

“Subhūti, you should know that there are further immeasurable collections of merit cultivated by the multitude of bodhisattvas, all of which are called wholesome dharmas, are also called the provisions for the enlightenment of a bodhisattva, and are also called the path of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.”

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas must cultivate such supreme wholesome dharmas until they are perfectly fulfilled before they can realize the knowledge of all modes; only after having realized the knowledge of all modes are they able to turn the wheel of the sublime Dharma without error, bringing ultimate peace and happiness to all sentient beings.
Chapter 82: On the Buddha-Dharma, Part Two, Chapter Eighty-Two. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“If these various wholesome dharmas are the dharmas of a bodhisattva, what then are the dharmas of a Buddha?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“The very dharmas of a bodhisattva are also the dharmas of a Buddha; that is to say, because all bodhisattvas awaken to all aspects regarding all dharmas, they shall thereby attain the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) and forever sever the continuity of all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).”

When the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have attained manifest and complete enlightenment regarding all phenomena through the sublime wisdom associated with a single moment, they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

"Subhūti! This is called the distinction between the two dharmas of the bodhisattva and the Buddha. Just as two noble ones, though both are noble, have the distinction of being on the path of practice versus abiding in the fruit, so too the dharmas they have accomplished are not without difference."
Thus it is, Subhūti!

When one practices among all phenomena within the path of uninterrupted continuity (*ānantarya-mārga*), yet has not yet abandoned the obscuration of darkness, has not yet reached the further shore, has not yet attained mastery, and has not yet realized the fruit—at that time, one is called a bodhisattva.

When one practices among all phenomena within the path of liberation, having already departed from the obscuration of darkness, having reached the further shore, having attained mastery, and having realized the fruit—at that time, one is called a Buddha.

"This constitutes the difference between a bodhisattva and a Buddha; while there is no lack of distinction due to the difference in their stages, one cannot say that there is a difference in the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If all phenomena are empty of intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), how can there be various distinctions within this emptiness of intrinsic characteristics? That is to say: 'This is a hell-being,' 'this is an animal,' 'this is a hungry ghost,' 'this is a human,' 'this is a deva,' 'this is one of the lineage-ground (*gotrabhūmi*),' 'this is the eighth ground,' 'this is a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*),' 'this is a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*),' 'this is a non-returner (*anāgāmin*),' 'this is an arhat,' 'this is a pratyekabuddha,' 'this is a bodhisattva,' and 'this is a Tathāgata'?"
World-Honored One!

Since such a person (pudgala) as has been described cannot be found, the karma they have created also cannot be found; and since that karma which has been created cannot be found, its ripened fruit (vipāka-phala) also cannot be found.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said:

all phenomena are empty of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). Within this emptiness of specific characteristics, since the person (*pudgala*) does not exist, the maturation of the fruit of karma (*karmavipāka*) likewise does not exist; and within that which does not exist, there are no distinct characteristics.

However, all sentient beings do not know, as it truly is, the principle that all phenomena are empty of intrinsic characteristics; they thus perform various actions, whether wholesome or unwholesome. Due to the performance and accumulation of wholesome karma, they are born among humans or devas; due to the performance and accumulation of unwholesome karma, they fall into the three evil destinies; and within wholesome karma, due to the performance and accumulation of determinate karma, they are born in the form realm or the formless realm.
By these causes and conditions, bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
they abide in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;
they abide in suchness up to the inconceivable realm; and they abide in suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
The Noble Truths; practicing the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path;
practicing the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; practicing the eight liberations up to the ten totalities;
practicing the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; and practicing the stage of extreme joy...
Upon reaching the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), one practices all *dhāraṇī* gates and *samādhi* gates;
one practices the five eyes and the six supernormal powers; one practices the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
one practices the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity; and one practices all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects. "Subhūti!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas cultivate these factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) continuously and without interruption until they are perfected, having thus perfected them, they are able to induce the diamond-like concentration (vajropamasamādhi) that closely assists awakening. They then realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, bringing great benefit to all sentient beings, always remaining indestructible. Because they are indestructible, they cause all sentient beings to be liberated from the various sufferings and afflictions of birth and death."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"After the Buddha has attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, have you attained the dharmas of birth and death within the various realms of existence?
The Buddha said:
"No, indeed! The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"After the Buddha has attained unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, does he thereby attain black karma, white karma, black-and-white karma, or neither-black-nor-white karma?"
The Buddha said, “No.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If the Buddha did not perceive the various realms of birth and death, nor the distinctions among karmas, how could he designate: 'This is hell; this is the animal realm; this is the realm of hungry ghosts; this is a human; this is a deva; this is the stage of the lineage (gotrabhūmi); this is the eighth stage; this is a stream-enterer; this is a once-returner; this is a non-returner; this is an arhat; this is a pratyekabuddha; this is a bodhisattva; this is a Tathāgata'?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Do sentient beings know for themselves that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"If all sentient beings were to know for themselves that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty, then Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas would have no need to seek realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, nor would they employ skillful means to rescue sentient beings from the miserable realms and the cycle of birth and death."

Because sentient beings do not know that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty, they transmigrate through the various realms of existence and undergo immeasurable suffering. Therefore, having heard from the Buddhas that all phenomena are empty of self-characteristics, the Bodhisattva, desiring to benefit all sentient beings, seeks to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, employing skillful means to extract sentient beings from the evil destinies and the cycle of birth and death.
“Subhūti, you should know that bodhisattva mahāsattvas always maintain this thought:
‘No phenomena possess an intrinsic nature as they are grasped by foolish, ordinary worldlings; however...’”
Due to the power of that distorted discrimination, one gives rise to the perception of real existence toward what is not truly existent;
that is, one gives rise to the perception of a self toward what is non-self, the perception of a sentient being toward what is not a sentient being, and so on,
up to giving rise to the perception of a seer toward what is not a seer, and the perception of form toward what is formless, [the perception of] feeling toward what is not feeling, and so forth.
Within feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, one gives rise to the ideation of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;

even so, within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), through the power of false discrimination and inversion, one regards what is unreal as real and clings to what does not exist as existing.
Consequently, one performs actions of body, speech, and mind, and is unable to be liberated from the evil destinies.
"I shall rescue those in birth and death and cause them to attain liberation.

Having formed this thought, that bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, incorporating all wholesome dharmas therein. He practices the various bodhisattva deeds without error, gradually fulfilling the provisions for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*). Once these provisions for enlightenment are fulfilled, he realizes unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Having attained awakening, he proclaims, reveals, analyzes, and establishes the meaning of the Four Noble Truths for all sentient beings, saying: "This is the noble truth of suffering; this is the noble truth of the origin of suffering; this is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering; this is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering."

Furthermore, all factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) are subsumed within these four noble truths by means of the wisdom of thorough penetration; moreover, based upon all factors conducive to enlightenment, the Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha are established through subtle wisdom.

Because these Three Jewels appear in the world, all sentient beings are liberated from birth and death; yet if sentient beings are unable to take refuge with faith in the Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, they will perform various karmas and transmigrate through the various realms, suffering without end. Therefore, one should take refuge in the Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Is it by means of the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path that sentient beings attain parinirvāṇa?"
"Is it by means of the noble wisdom regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path that sentient beings attain parinirvāṇa?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"It is not by means of the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path that sentient beings attain parinirvāṇa."
Sentient beings do not attain parinirvāṇa by means of the noble wisdom regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path.

Subhūti! I say that the equality of the four noble truths is itself nirvāṇa. Such nirvāṇa is not attained through the truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path, nor is it attained through the wisdom of suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path; rather, it is called the attainment of nirvāṇa when one realizes this equality by means of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What is meant by the equality of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If, in this state, there is no truth of suffering, origin, cessation, or path, and no knowledge of suffering, origin, cessation, or path, it is called the nature of equality of the four noble truths; this very nature of equality is itself the four noble truths."

All suchness, the dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm—whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, their nature and characteristics remain eternally constant, without loss or change. This is what is called the equal nature of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they do so because they wish to realize the equality of these four noble truths. When they are able to realize the equality of these four noble truths, it is called truly realizing all noble truths, and they swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they practice the profound perfection of wisdom for the sake of awakening to the equality of these four noble truths? When one awakens to the equality of these four noble truths, why is this called truly awakening to all noble truths, such that one does not fall into the levels of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but enters the bodhisattva’s state of certainty and transcendence?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, there is not the slightest dharma that they do not see as it truly is. When they see all dharmas as they truly are, they apprehend nothing at all regarding any dharma. When they apprehend nothing regarding any dharma, they then see all dharmas as empty as they truly are; that is to say, they see as they truly are that all dharmas—both those subsumed within and those not subsumed within the Four Noble Truths—are empty."
When one perceives in this manner, one is able to enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Because one is able to enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth, one then abides within the stage of the bodhisattva lineage (*gotra-bhūmi*).

Once one dwells within the stage of the bodhisattva lineage-ground, one is definitively able to avoid falling from the summit; for were one to fall from the summit, one would fall into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely within the stage of the bodhisattva lineage-ground, gives rise to the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments.
Dwelling thus in this stage of śamatha, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is then able to discern the nature of all phenomena and to realize the principles of the Four Noble Truths accordingly.

At that time, although the Bodhisattva fully understands suffering, he does not give rise to a mind that clings to suffering as its object; although he has forever severed the origin [of suffering], he does not give rise to a mind that clings to the origin as its object; although he is able to realize cessation, he does not give rise to a mind that clings to cessation as its object; although he is able to cultivate the path, he does not give rise to a mind that clings to the path as its object. Rather, he gives rise to a mind that accords with, inclines toward, and enters into unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, observing the true reality of all phenomena as they truly are.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How does this bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplate the true reality of all phenomena?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva contemplates all phenomena as being without exception empty; this is what is meant by 'observing the true nature of all phenomena.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How does this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva observe that all phenomena are empty?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“This bodhisattva mahāsattva observes all phenomena as they truly are, seeing that they are all empty of their own characteristics; in this way, he observes that all phenomena are empty.”

By means of such vipaśyanā, this bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives all phenomena as they truly are—namely, that they are all empty—and does not perceive any self-nature of phenomena in which he might abide; rather, by abiding in that very nature, he realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Why is this? Because the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas and all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature;
that is to say, from form (*rūpa*) up to consciousness (*vijñāna*), they all have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, and from the sense base of the eye (*cakṣur-āyatana*)...
The sense base of mind also has non-existence as its intrinsic nature; the sense bases from form up to mental phenomena also have non-existence as their intrinsic nature;
the sense fields from the eye field up to the mind field also have non-existence as their intrinsic nature;
the sense fields from the form field up to the mental phenomena field also have non-existence as their intrinsic nature; and the eye-consciousness field...
Even up to the consciousness element, it has non-existence as its intrinsic nature; from eye-contact up to mind-contact, they also have non-existence as their intrinsic nature;

from all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition up to all feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, they also have non-existence as their intrinsic nature; and even up to the earth element...
The consciousness element also has non-existence as its intrinsic nature; the causal conditions, up to and including the dominant condition, also have non-existence as their intrinsic nature;
all phenomena produced from conditions also have non-existence as their intrinsic nature;
ignorance, up to and including old age and death, also have non-existence as their intrinsic nature; and the perfection of giving...
The *pāramitās*, up to and including the *prajñāpāramitā*, also have non-existence as their intrinsic nature;
internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, also have non-existence as their intrinsic nature;
suchness, up to and including the inconceivable realm, also have non-existence as their intrinsic nature; [and likewise] suffering, its origin, and its cessation...

The Noble Truth of the Path also has non-existence as its intrinsic nature; the four applications of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the Noble Path also have non-existence as their intrinsic nature;
the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments also have non-existence as their intrinsic nature;
and the eight liberations up to the ten totalities likewise have non-existence as their intrinsic nature.

Furthermore, they take the absence of intrinsic nature as their own nature; the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—also take the absence of intrinsic nature as their own nature;
the stages from the Ground of Pure Contemplation up to the Ground of the Tathāgata also take the absence of intrinsic nature as their own nature;
and the stages from the Ground of Utmost Joy up to the Ground of the Dharma Cloud also take the absence of intrinsic nature as their own nature.
Nature: All *dhāraṇī* gates and all *samādhi* gates also have non-nature as their intrinsic nature;
the five eyes and the six supernormal powers also have non-nature as their intrinsic nature;
the ten powers of a Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, also have non-nature as their intrinsic nature. Thirty...
The two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks also have non-existence as their intrinsic nature;
the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity also have non-existence as their intrinsic nature;
omniscience, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects also have non-existence as their intrinsic nature; and the fruit of stream-entry...
Even the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha has non-existence as its intrinsic nature;

all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have non-existence as their intrinsic nature; and even the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas has non-existence as its intrinsic nature.

Thus, this absence of intrinsic nature was not created by the Buddhas, nor by the Pratyekabuddhas, nor by the Bodhisattvas, nor by the Śrāvakas; nor was it created by those who abide in the fruits or those who are practicing toward them. It exists solely because sentient beings do not know and do not see that all phenomena are, in reality, entirely empty.

The assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom through skillful means, expounds it to all sentient beings exactly as they have realized it themselves, causing them to abandon attachment and be liberated from all birth, aging, sickness, and death, so that they may attain parinirvāṇa and ultimate peace and happiness.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll 477, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Chapter 83: On Non-Entity (Avastuka), Part Two, Chapter Eighty-three. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

If all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, and such non-existence was not created by the Buddhas, nor by the Pratyekabuddhas, nor by the Bodhisattvas, nor by the Śrāvakas, nor even by those abiding in the fruits or treading the paths—how can one designate various distinctions among phenomena?

That is to say: "This is hell; this is the animal realm; this is the realm of hungry ghosts; this is the human realm; these are the gods of the Four Great Kings up to the gods of Paranirmita-vaśavartin; these are the gods of Brahmakāyika up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven; these are the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Space up to the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception; this is a stream-enterer; this is a once-returner; this is a non-returner; this is an arhat; this is a pratyekabuddha; this is a bodhisattva; this is a Tathāgata?"

By virtue of this karma, hell is designated; by virtue of this karma, the animal realm is designated; by virtue of this karma, the realm of hungry ghosts is designated; by virtue of this karma, human beings are designated; by virtue of this karma, the gods from the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations are designated; by virtue of this karma, the gods from the Brahma Assembly up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven are designated; by virtue of this karma, the gods from the Sphere of Infinite Space up to the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception are designated; by virtue of these dharmas, the Stream-enterer, Once-returner, and Non-returner are designated; by virtue of these dharmas, the Arhat is designated; by virtue of these dharmas, the Pratyekabuddha is designated; by virtue of these dharmas, the Bodhisattva is designated; and by virtue of these dharmas, the Tathāgata is designated?
“World-Honored One!
Since dharmas that lack intrinsic nature are necessarily devoid of activity, how can it be said that by such karma one is born in hell,
by such karma one is born among animals, or by such karma one is born in the realm of hungry ghosts?”
By such karma one is born among human beings; by such karma one is born in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Control over Others' Emanations;
by such karma one is born in the Heaven of Brahma’s Retinue up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven;
and by such karma one is born in the Sphere of Infinite Space up to the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception.
"O Deva, by means of such dharmas one attains the fruit of stream-entry; by means of such dharmas one attains the fruit of once-returning;
by means of such dharmas one attains the fruit of non-returning; by means of such dharmas one attains the fruit of arhatship;
by means of such dharmas one attains the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; and by means of such dharmas one enters the stage of a bodhisattva and practices the conduct of a bodhisattva."
“By means of such dharmas as these, one attains the knowledge of all aspects and is named a Buddha, a World-Honored One, who causes all sentient beings to be liberated from birth and death?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"So it is! So it is! It is just as you have said."
Within phenomena that lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), it is impossible to designate any differentiation among phenomena; there is no karma, no fruit, and no functional activity.

It is only because foolish worldlings do not understand the Noble Dharma and Vinaya that they do not know, as it truly is, that all phenomena have the absence of intrinsic nature as their very nature. Out of delusion and inversion, they give rise to various actions of body, speech, and mind, and according to the distinctions of those actions, they receive various bodies.

Based on such distinctions in the categories of bodies, there are the designations of the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, humans, gods, and even up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Desiring to rescue and deliver such foolish, deluded, and inverted beings who undergo the suffering of birth and death, one establishes the various stages of the noble Dharma and the Vinaya; based upon these stages, one designates the categories from stream-enterer up to pratyekabuddha, bodhisattva, and tathāgata.

However, all phenomena take the absence of intrinsic nature as their very nature; within the state of the absence of intrinsic nature, there are truly no distinct phenomena, no karma, no fruit, and no activity, because phenomena that lack intrinsic nature are eternally devoid of intrinsic nature.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

As you have said, 'Dharmas that lack intrinsic nature are necessarily devoid of activity; how can it be said that by means of such dharmas one attains the fruit of a stream-enterer, and so on in detail, up to attaining the name of Buddha, the World-Honored One, who possesses all-knowledge, and causes all sentient beings to escape from birth and death?'"
"What do you think? Are all the paths cultivated devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*)?

Are the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, the fruit of arhatship, the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, and the path of a bodhisattva leading to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) devoid of intrinsic nature?"
Subhūti replied: "So it is! So it is!"
"All paths of cultivation, from those explained at length up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), are without intrinsic nature.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?"
“Can a dharma that lacks intrinsic nature be attained by a dharma that lacks intrinsic nature? Subhūti replied, “No!”
“World-Honored One! The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Non-existence and the path—all these dharmas are neither associated nor dissociated; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (*animitta*). Fools and ordinary worldlings, through their ignorance and perversion, give rise to the perception of existent dharmas regarding these signless dharmas. They grasp at the five aggregates, giving rise to the perception of permanence amidst impermanence, the perception of pleasure amidst suffering, the perception of self amidst non-self, and the perception of purity amidst impurity; they cling to the existence of intrinsic nature within dharmas that lack intrinsic nature.”

By means of these skillful means of practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas delivers such sentient beings, causing them to abandon inverted and false conceptualizations; they skillfully establish them within the signless (*animitta*) dharma, enabling them to diligently practice and train for liberation from birth and death, and to realize the ultimate, eternal bliss of *nirvāṇa*.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Is there any object of attachment clung to by foolish ordinary beings that is truly real and not false, such that having clung to it, they perform various karmas, and by reason of these causes and conditions, they sink into the various realms of existence and are unable to be liberated from the suffering of birth and death?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Regarding the objects to which foolish commoners are attached, there is not even as much as the tip of a fine hair that can be said to be real rather than false. Having become attached to these, they perform various karmas; by reason of these causes and conditions, they sink into the various realms of existence and cannot liberate themselves from the manifold sufferings of birth and death, possessing only false, inverted attachments."

I shall now provide you with an extensive analogy to further clarify this meaning so that it may be easily understood; for those who possess wisdom can generate correct understanding of the meaning explained through various analogies.
“Subhūti, what do you think?

When one sees a person in a dream experiencing the pleasures of the five desires, is there even the slightest real thing within that dream by which that person could experience those sensual pleasures?”
Subhūti replied, “If even the person seen in a dream does not truly exist, how much less could there be any real thing by which that person might experience the pleasures of the five senses!
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"What do you think?

Are there any phenomena—whether wholesome or unwholesome, determinate or indeterminate, with outflows or without outflows, mundane or supramundane, conditioned or unconditioned—that are not like things seen in a dream?"
Subhūti replied:

"There is certainly no phenomenon—whether wholesome or unwholesome, defined or undefined, with outflows or without outflows, mundane or supramundane, conditioned or unconditioned—that is not like a thing seen in a dream."
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Within a dream, is there any reality whatsoever regarding the various realms of existence, or the process of coming and going through birth and death within them?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Is there, within a dream, any truly real cultivation of the path, by means of which cultivation one might become free from defilement and attain purification?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”

Why is this so? Because the phenomena seen in a dream have no reality whatsoever; they are neither that which can be designated nor that which is designated. If even the cultivation of the path does not exist, how much less could there be the departure from defilement or the attainment of purity based upon the cultivation of the path!
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?

Do the various images reflected in a bright mirror or similar objects possess any substantial reality upon which one could rely to perform karma, such that by virtue of the karma performed, one would fall into hell, or fall among animals, or fall into the realm of hungry ghosts, or be born among humans, or be born in the heavens to experience suffering or pleasure?"

Subhūti replied: "The various images manifested in a bright mirror and the like have no substantial reality whatsoever; they merely deceive the ignorant child. How could they serve as a basis for performing karmic actions, such that by those performed actions one might fall into the evil destinies, or be born among humans or devas to experience various sufferings and pleasures?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Do these reflected images possess a real path of cultivation, such that by relying on that path of cultivation one might become free from defilement and attain purity?"

Subhūti replied: "The images in a bright mirror and the like have no substantial reality; they are neither that which designates nor that which is designated. Since even the path of cultivation does not exist, how much less could there be freedom from affliction or the attainment of purity based upon the path of cultivation!"
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?

Do the various echoes produced within mountains, valleys, and the like possess any substantial reality upon which one could rely to create karma, such that by virtue of the karma created, one would fall into hell, or fall among animals, or fall into the realm of hungry ghosts, or be born among humans, or be born in the heavens to experience suffering or pleasure?"

Subhūti replied: "The various echoes produced within valleys and the like have no substantial reality whatsoever; they merely deceive the foolish and ignorant. How could one rely upon them to perform karmic actions, such that by those performed actions one might fall into the evil destinies or be born among humans or gods to experience various sufferings and pleasures?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Does an echo possess any real path of cultivation? By means of such a path of cultivation, could one become free from defilement and attain purity?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”

Why is this so? Because echoes in mountain valleys and the like have no substantial reality; they are neither that which can designate nor that which is designated. If even the cultivation of the path does not exist, how much less could there be the departure from defilement or the attainment of purity based upon the cultivation of the path!
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “What do you think?

Regarding those things that appear like water and so forth within a mirage, is there any real entity therein upon which one could rely to perform karma, such that by virtue of the karma performed, one would fall into hell, or fall among animals, or fall into the realm of hungry ghosts, or be born among humans, or be born in the heavens, and experience suffering or pleasure?”

Subhūti replied: "The water and such things manifested within a mirage have no substantial reality whatsoever; they merely deceive foolish children. How could one rely upon them to perform various karmic actions, such that by those performed actions one might fall into the evil destinies, or be born among humans or devas to experience various sufferings and pleasures?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Within those mirages, is there any water or the like that possesses a real path of cultivation? By relying upon such a path of cultivation, could one become free from defilement and attain purity?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”

Why is this? Because a mirage, water, and so forth have no real substance whatsoever; they are neither that which can designate nor that which is designated. If even the cultivation of the path does not exist, how much less could there be the departure from defilement and the attainment of purity based upon the cultivation of the path!
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?

Do the forms and appearances manifested within various reflections and shadows possess any substantial reality that could serve as a basis for performing karma, such that by virtue of the karma performed one would fall into hell, or fall among animals, or fall into the realm of hungry ghosts, or be born among humans, or be born in the heavens to experience suffering or pleasure?"

Subhūti replied: "The forms and appearances manifested within all shadows and reflections have no substantial reality whatsoever; they merely deceive the ignorant and childish. How could one rely upon them to perform various karmas, such that by those performed karmas one might fall into the evil destinies, or be born among humans or devas to experience various sufferings and pleasures?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “What do you think?
Within the various reflections and shadows, is there any truly real cultivation of the path? By relying upon such cultivation of the path, could one become free from defilement and attain purity?”
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”

Why is this so? Because reflections, shadows, colors, and forms possess no substantial reality; they are neither that which can designate nor that which is designated. If even the cultivation of the path does not exist, how much less could there be the departure from defilement or the attainment of purity based upon the cultivation of the path!
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?

Suppose a magician were to conjure by illusion an army of four divisions—elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—or perhaps he were to conjure by illusion oxen, sheep, men, women, and various other most rare wonders. Would these illusory elephants and so forth possess any real substance upon which one could rely to perform karma, such that through the karma performed one would fall into hell, or fall among the animals, or fall into the realm of hungry ghosts, or be born among humans, or be born in the heavens to experience suffering or pleasure?"

Subhūti replied: "Illusions, horses, and the like have no substantial reality; they merely deceive the foolish and ignorant. How could one rely upon them to perform various karmic actions, such that by those performed actions one might fall into the evil destinies, or be born among humans or devas to experience various sufferings and pleasures?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Does an illusory being possess a genuine path of cultivation, such that by relying on that path of cultivation, one could become free from defilement and attain purity?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”

Why is this so? Illusions such as elephants and horses have no real substance whatsoever; they are neither the agents of designation nor the objects of designation. If even the cultivation of the path does not exist, how much less could there be the departure from defilement or the attainment of purity based upon that cultivation of the path!
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?

Does the body emanated by one who possesses the power of transformation have any substantial reality upon which karma can be based, such that through the karma thus created, it would fall into hell, or fall among animals, or fall into the realm of hungry ghosts, or be born among humans, or be born in the heavens, thereby experiencing suffering or pleasure?"

Subhūti replied, "Since all emanated bodies lack any substantial reality, how could they perform any karma? And how could one, by virtue of the karma thus performed, fall into the evil destinies or be born among humans or gods to experience various sufferings and pleasures?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Does an emanation have any real cultivation of the path? By means of that cultivation of the path, is there any departure from defilement and attainment of purity?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”

Why is this? All transformation bodies (nirmāṇakāya) are entirely devoid of substantial reality; they are neither the agent of designation nor the object of designation. Since even the cultivation of the path does not exist, how much less could there be freedom from defilement or the attainment of purity based upon that cultivation of the path!
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “What do you think?

Regarding the various things manifested within the city of Gandhavatī, do they possess any substantial reality upon which one could rely to perform karma, such that by virtue of the karma performed, one would fall into hell, or fall among the animals, or fall into the realm of hungry ghosts, or be born among humans, or be born in the heavens, experiencing suffering or pleasure?”

Subhūti replied: "The various things manifested within the city of Gandhavatī have no substantial reality at all. How could they serve as a basis for performing karmic actions, such that by virtue of those performed actions one might fall into the evil destinies or be born among humans or gods to experience various sufferings and pleasures?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Within the city of Gandhavatī, are there any entities that truly practice the path, such that by relying on that practice of the path, one might become free from defilement and attain purity?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”

Why is this so? Because all the phenomena manifested within the City of Fragrance (Gandhavatī) are devoid of any substantial reality; they are neither that which designates nor that which is designated. If even the cultivation of the path does not exist, how much less could there be the departure from defilement or the attainment of purity based upon the cultivation of the path!
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Within this, is there any real entity that is defiled or purified?"
Subhūti replied, “In this,
there is truly neither one who is defiled nor one who is purified.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Just as those who are defiled and those who are purified do not exist in reality, for this reason, both defilement and purification also do not exist in reality. Why is this so?

Sentient beings who dwell in the false discrimination of "self" and "what belongs to self" claim that there is defilement and purification; for this reason, they speak of defilement and purification. However, those who see reality do not speak of there being defilement or purification.
One who sees things as they truly are knows that there is neither defilement nor purity; likewise, no real entity of defilement or purity can be found, because all phenomena are ultimately empty.
Chapter 84: Exposition of Reality. Second Division, Chapter Eighty-four: Exposition of Reality. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
For those who see reality, there is neither affliction nor purification; for those who do not see reality, there is likewise neither affliction nor purification. Why is this so?
Because all phenomena are non-existent,
World-Honored One,
those who speak of reality have neither defilement nor purification, and those who speak of unreality likewise have neither defilement nor purification.
Why is this? Because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature,
World-Honored One.

Since phenomena lacking intrinsic nature are neither defiled nor purified, and phenomena possessing intrinsic nature are likewise neither defiled nor purified, all phenomena—whether possessing intrinsic nature or lacking it—are neither defiled nor purified.
Why is this? Because all phenomena take the absence of intrinsic nature as their own nature.
World-Honored One!
"For one who sees reality and the real, I declare that the equality of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-samatā*) is the pure dharma.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"What is meant by the equality of all phenomena?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"The suchness of all phenomena, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-illusory nature, the unchanging nature, the state of equality, the nature free from birth, the fixedness of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm—whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, their essential characteristics remain eternally constant. This is called the equality of all phenomena; this equality is called the pure dharma."

This is described as "pure" according to conventional truth; although the city appears to exist, it lacks any substantial reality. How can the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, relying upon these phenomena that lack true existence, resolve their minds toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and make this vow:
"I shall fulfill the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
I shall fulfill the supreme perfection of supernormal powers; I shall fulfill skillful means"?
...the perfections of skillful means, vows, power, and wisdom; I shall fulfill the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
I shall fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
I shall fulfill the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; I shall...
I shall fulfill the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality;
I shall fulfill inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature; I shall fulfill true suchness up to the inconceivable realm;
I shall fulfill the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; I shall fulfill the Stage of Extreme Joy...
Upon reaching the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (Dharmameghā-bhūmi), I shall fulfill all doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of samādhi;

I shall fulfill the five eyes and the six supernormal powers; I shall fulfill the ten powers of a Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and I shall fulfill the quality of non-forgetfulness and constant abiding.
With a nature of relinquishment, I shall fulfill all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects;
I shall fulfill the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks;
and I shall generate immeasurable light that universally illuminates the boundless worlds of the ten directions.

"Shall I not produce a single sublime sound that pervades the infinite worlds of the ten directions, and according to the differences in the inclinations (*adhimukti*) of the minds and mental factors of all sentient beings, preach various subtle and wondrous Dharma-gates for them to obtain benefit and happiness?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Is not all that you have taught like a dream, an image, an echo, a mirage, a shadow, an illusion, a magical creation, or a city of gandharvas?"
Subhūti replied, “So it is! So it is!”

"Bhagavān! If all phenomena are like dreams and even like cities of Gandharvas, such that none possess any substantial reality, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, makes this great vow:
'I shall fulfill all merits and bring benefit, peace, and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings'?"
“World-Honored One!

That which is seen in a dream, and so forth, up to the various things manifested within the City of Fragrance, cannot practice the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), much less bring them to fulfillment!”
All other phenomena should also be understood in this way, for they are equally not real.
World-Honored One!

It is not as with things seen in a dream; [this applies] to the full range of objects appearing even within the city of Gandharvas, let alone those who can practice the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty secondary signs—how much less could they ever be perfected!
All other phenomena should likewise be understood in this way, for they are equally not real.
World-Honored One!

Just as what is seen in a dream—and as has been explained at length down to the objects appearing within the City of Gandharvas—which can accomplish all desired tasks, so too should all other phenomena be understood, for they are equally not real.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
As you have said,
even a non-existent dharma cannot practice the perfection of generosity, up to and including the perfection of wisdom, let alone bring them to fulfillment!
In this way, even non-substantial dharmas cannot manifest the thirty-two marks of a great man or the eighty minor signs, much less perfect them.
Non-substantial dharmas cannot accomplish the deeds intended by one's vows; non-substantial dharmas cannot realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment that is sought.
“Furthermore, Subhūti!

Because the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as other immeasurable and boundless wholesome dharmas, are not truly existent, one cannot realize the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

Subhūti, you should know that all such phenomena are merely conceptual constructions; and whatever is produced through conceptual construction cannot attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Although these dharmas can induce the path to enlightenment, they have no contributory function toward its fruit, because these dharmas are without birth, without arising, and lack any real characteristic."

When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, although from their first production of the thought of enlightenment they give rise to various forms of physical, verbal, and mental goodness—namely, practicing the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and so on, up to practicing all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)—they know that all these are like dreams, images, echoes, mirages, reflections, illusions, magical emanations, and cities of Gandharvas, and that none of them possess real existence.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Although these dharmas do not exist as real entities, if they were not fully perfected, one could certainly not bring sentient beings to maturity, purify a buddha-field, or realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

That is to say, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not bring to perfection the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), they will certainly be unable to mature sentient beings, purify buddha-fields, or realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When these bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they know all the wholesome dharmas in which they dwell and practice as they truly are—like dreams, and so on, up to like a city of gandharvas. That is to say, when they practice the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, they are able to know them as they truly are—like dreams, and so on, up to like a city of gandharvas;

likewise, up to when they practice all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), they are able to know them as they truly are—like dreams, and so on, up to like a city of gandharvas."

If they seek to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by ripening sentient beings and purifying Buddha-fields, they are able to know, as it truly is, that [all things] are like dreams and even like cities of Gandharvas; and they likewise know, as it truly is, the differences in the mental activities of all classes of sentient beings as being like dreams and even like cities of Gandharvas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When these bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not apprehend any phenomena as existent, nor do they apprehend them as non-existent. Even if they were to realize the knowledge of all aspects through such apprehension, they would know those phenomena to be like a dream, up to and including being like a city of gandharvas; they do not apprehend them as existent, nor do they apprehend them as non-existent."

Why is this? Because the perfection of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), are all ungraspable; because wholesome and unwholesome phenomena are ungraspable; because conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are ungraspable; because phenomena that are specified and unspecified are ungraspable; because contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena are ungraspable; and because mundane and supramundane phenomena are ungraspable.
Having realized that all phenomena are ungraspable, this bodhisattva mahāsattva seeks to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are ungraspable and entirely devoid of substantial reality, being like a dream, and so forth, up to being like a city of gandharvas.

A dharma that cannot be grasped cannot realize a dharma that cannot be grasped; yet, because sentient beings do not know and do not see such dharmas, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva seeks to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of benefiting those sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings; it is not for his own sake nor for any other purpose. For the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, he seeks to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; it is not for his own sake nor for any other purpose."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, he sees that all foolish commoners dwell upon the notion of a self where there is no self; they dwell upon the notion of a sentient being where there is no sentient being, and so on, up to dwelling upon the notion of a knower where there is no knower, and dwelling upon the notion of a seer where there is no seer."

Having seen this, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives rise to deep compassion and employs skillful means to teach and transform them, causing them to abandon inverted delusions and attachments, and establishing them within the realm of signlessness (*animitta-amṛta-dhātu*). Abiding in this realm, they no longer manifest the notion of a self (*ātma-saṃjñā*) up to the notion of a knower or a seer (*jñātṛ-draṣṭṛ-saṃjñā*). At that time, all agitation, distraction, conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and discrimination no longer manifest; their minds dwell predominantly in a state of tranquility, detachment, and the realm free from conceptual proliferation.

“Subhūti! By means of this skillful method, this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom; he himself has no attachment to any phenomena, and he is also able to teach others that they should have no attachment to any phenomena.”
"This is based on the conventional truth, not on the ultimate truth, because within the ultimate truth there is no attachment, and the distinction between self and other cannot be found.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

When the Buddha attained unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, was the realization of the Buddha-dharmas attained in reliance upon conventional truth, or was it attained in reliance upon ultimate truth?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“When a Buddha attains unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, the Buddha-dharma realized therein is said to be ‘attained’ only by way of worldly convention, not by way of ultimate truth.”
If one relies on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), both the attainer and that which is attained are unattainable. Why is this so?

If one were to say that this person attains such a dharma, there would then be something attained; and for one who has something attained, there is grasping at duality. One who grasps at duality cannot attain the fruit, nor can they achieve clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If grasping at duality cannot lead to the attainment of the fruit nor to clear realization, then does grasping at non-duality enable the attainment of the fruit and the presence of clear realization?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"One who clings to duality cannot attain the fruit, nor can they realize clear observation; one who clings to non-duality is likewise so, because there is clinging, just as in the case of clinging to duality."
If one does not grasp at duality, nor grasp at non-duality, this is called attaining the fruit and is also called clear realization (*abhisamaya*). Why is this so?

If one grasps that by means of this one can attain the fruit and possess clear realization, or grasps that by means of that one cannot attain the fruit and lacks clear realization—both are conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*). Within the equality of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-samatā*), there are no conceptual proliferations; only when one is free from conceptual proliferation can it be called the equality of phenomena.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, what therein is meant by the equality of phenomena?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If, in a certain place, there is neither existence nor non-existence, and it cannot even be described as the nature of equality—it is only thus that it is called the equality of dharmas."

Subhūti, you should know that the equality of phenomena (dharmasamatā) is neither expressible nor cognizable; apart from this equality, no phenomenon can be apprehended, and apart from all phenomena, there is no equality.
"Subhūti! You should know that the equality of phenomena cannot be traversed by either ordinary beings or noble ones, for it is not within their domain.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“Is the equality of phenomena (*dharmasamatā*) not also beyond the range of the Buddha’s activity?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“The equality of phenomena is such that all noble ones (*ārya*) cannot engage in it nor realize it—namely, whether they be stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*), once-returners (*sakṛdāgāmin*), non-returners (*anāgāmin*), arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or tathāgatas—all of them cannot take the equality of phenomena as an object of their activity, because within this, all conceptual proliferation and discrimination (*prapañca-vikalpa*) do not operate.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Buddha has attained mastery over all phenomena; how can it be said that the equality of phenomena is not even within the range of the Buddhas' activity?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Although the Buddha has attained mastery over all phenomena, if the nature of equality were distinct from the Buddha, one could say it is the objective range traversed by the Buddha; however, since the nature of equality is not distinct from the Buddha, how can it be said that the Buddha traverses that range?"
“Subhūti, you should know this!

Whether it be the equality of the dharmas of ordinary beings, or the equality of the dharmas of stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or Tathāgatas—all such equalities of dharmas have one and the same characteristic, namely, the absence of characteristics (*animitta*). This single equality is non-dual and undifferentiated; therefore, it cannot be said that ‘this is the equality of the dharmas of ordinary beings,’ and so on, up to ‘this is the equality of the dharmas of the Tathāgata.’”

Within this equality of all phenomena, since no forms of equality can be apprehended, neither the distinctions between ordinary beings nor those between stream-enterers and others can be apprehended therein.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If, within the equality of all phenomena, no distinct characteristics whatsoever can be apprehended, then there should be no distinction between ordinary beings, stream-enterers, and so forth, in terms of their dharmas or their sentient nature."
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.
Within the equality of all phenomena, there is no distinction between ordinary beings, noble ones, or even Tathāgatas, nor between their dharmas and sentient beings.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If within the equality of all phenomena there is no distinction between the dharmas of ordinary beings and noble ones, nor between sentient beings, how is it that the Three Jewels appear in the world—namely, the Jewel of the Buddha, the Jewel of the Dharma, and the Jewel of the Saṅgha?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Are the dharmas of the Treasures of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha each distinct from one another in their equality?"

Subhūti replied, “As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is no distinction whatsoever among the dharmas of the Jewels of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha; they are all equal in their nature.”

Why is this so? Because the dharmas of the Jewels—the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha—are equal in nature; all such things are neither associated nor dissociated, formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and of a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.

Nevertheless, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, through his skillful means regarding the signless dharma, establishes various distinctions of names and characteristics for phenomena and sentient beings, such that he designates: "This is an ordinary person and their phenomena," up to "This is a Tathāgata and their phenomena."
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.
The Buddhas possess skillful means regarding the Dharma; they are able to establish the various distinctions of phenomena and the names and characteristics of sentient beings within the signless.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, what do you think?

If the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas had not realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, or even if they had realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, but did not establish the distinctions of names and signs for all phenomena for the sake of sentient beings, would those classes of sentient beings be able to know for themselves: [that they exist]?"
"This is hell; this is the animal realm; this is the realm of hungry ghosts; this is the human world;
this is the deva world—ranging from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception;
this is form up to consciousness; this is the eye-base up to the mind-base; this is the form-base..."
Upon reaching the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), [he discerns]: "This is the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) up to the mind-element (*manodhātu*);
