this is the form-element (*rūpadhātu*) up to the phenomena-element (*dharmadhātu*); this is the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) up to the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*);

this is eye-contact (*cakṣuḥsaṃsparśa*) up to mind-contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*); and this is the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with eye-contact as condition, up to those produced with mind-contact as condition."
All feelings; these are the earth element up to the consciousness element; these are the causal conditions up to the dominant condition;
these are all phenomena produced from conditions; these are ignorance up to old age and death;
these are wholesome and unwholesome phenomena; these are determinate and indeterminate phenomena; these are conditioned...
These are the tainted and untainted dharmas; these are the mundane and supramundane dharmas;
these are the conditioned and unconditioned dharmas; these are the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
these are the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; these are internal emptiness up to...
The emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence; this is suchness, up to and including the inconceivable realm;
this is the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; this is the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
this is the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; this is the eight...
From liberation up to the ten spheres of totality—these are the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata;
these are the stage of extreme joy up to the stage of the cloud of dharma; these are all the doors of dhāraṇī and the doors of samādhi;
these are the five eyes and the six supernormal powers; these are the ten powers of the Tathāgata... [and so forth].
Up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—these are the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks;
these are the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity;
these are all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects; these are the sublime knowledge of aspiration regarding all aspects; these are...
The knowledge of all modes of knowledge—this is the Three Jewels, this is the Three Vehicles.
Are sentient beings able to know for themselves such distinct names and characteristics?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”

If the Buddha did not establish such various distinctions of names and characteristics for sentient beings, these classes of sentient beings would be unable to know for themselves such various distinctions of names and characteristics.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Therefore, the Tathāgata, through skillful means regarding signless phenomena (*animitta-dharma*), establishes various differentiated names and signs for sentient beings, yet remains unshakable within the equality of all phenomena;
though he bestows great benefaction upon sentient beings, he is able to remain without grasping at signs therein."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

Just as the Tathāgata does not stir at all within the equality of all phenomena, do all these ordinary beings, stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas likewise not stir within the equality of all phenomena?"
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
Because all phenomena and all sentient beings do not transcend the nature of equality.

Just as it is with the nature of equality, one should know that it is likewise for true thusness (*tathatā*), and so on, up to the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*); for there is no distinction between ordinary beings and noble ones regarding true thusness and the other such states.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If the nature of equality of all ordinary beings, all noble ones, and all phenomena is without distinction, then since the characteristics of all phenomena and sentient beings are each distinct, their natures should also be distinct; in that case, [how can there be no difference]?"

The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) should likewise be distinct; that is to say, because the characteristics of form (*rūpa*) up to consciousness (*vijñāna*) are distinct, their nature should also be distinct.
Because the characteristics of the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) up to the mind-base (*manas-āyatana*) are distinct, their nature should also be distinct.

Because the characteristics of the form-base (*rūpa-āyatana*) up to the mental-object-base (*dharma-āyatana*) are distinct, their nature should also be distinct. And because the characteristics of the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) up to the mind-element (*manodhātu*) are distinct...

Therefore, their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) should also be different; because the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the form element (*rūpadhātu*) up to the phenomena element (*dharmadhātu*) are each different, their intrinsic nature should also be different.

Because the characteristics of the eye-consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) up to the mind-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*) are each different, their intrinsic nature should also be different.

Because the characteristics of eye-contact (*cakṣuḥsaṃsparśa*) up to mind-contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*) are each different, their intrinsic nature should also be different. [Furthermore,] the various [phenomena] produced with eye-contact as a condition...

Since the characteristics of the feelings arising with conditions ranging from sensation up to those conditioned by mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśa*) are each distinct, their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) must also be distinct.

Since the characteristics of the elements ranging from the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) up to the consciousness element (*vijñāna-dhātu*) are each distinct, their intrinsic natures must also be distinct.

Since the characteristics of the conditions ranging from the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) up to the sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) are each distinct, their intrinsic natures must also be distinct; for the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharma*) produced from conditions are each distinct.

Therefore, their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) must also be distinct; because the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of everything from ignorance (*avidyā*) up to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) are each distinct, their intrinsic natures must also be distinct.

Because the characteristics of greed, hatred, and delusion (*rāga-dveṣa-moha*) are each distinct, their intrinsic natures must also be distinct. Because the characteristics of the various views and inclinations of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are each distinct, their intrinsic natures must also be distinct.
[The same applies to] the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).

Because their characteristics are each distinct, their natures should also be distinct; because the characteristics of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path are each distinct, their natures should also be distinct;
because the characteristics of the doors of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are each distinct, their natures should also be distinct;
and because the characteristics of internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature are each distinct, their natures...
It should also be different; because the characteristics of true thusness (*tathatā*) up to the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*) are each distinct, their natures should also be distinct.
Because the characteristics of the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path are each distinct, their natures should also be distinct.
Because the characteristics of the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) are each distinct, their natures should also be [distinct].
Because the characteristics of the eight liberations up to the ten totalities are each distinct, their natures should also be distinct;
because the characteristics of the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata are each distinct, their natures should also be distinct;
because the characteristics of the stage of extreme joy up to the stage of the cloud of dharma are each distinct, their natures should also be distinct; [and so on for] all doors of dhāraṇī...

Since the characteristics of the samādhi-gates differ, their natures should also differ; since the characteristics of the five eyes and six supernormal powers differ, their natures should also differ;
since the characteristics of the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha differ, their natures should also differ;
[and so too for] the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs.

Because their characteristics are each distinct, their natures should also be distinct; because the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity have distinct characteristics, their natures should also be distinct;
because omniscience, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects have distinct characteristics, their natures should also be distinct;
and because the characteristics of foolish ordinary beings up to those of the Tathāgata are each distinct.
The nature [of phenomena] should also be different; because the characteristics of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas are each distinct, their nature should also be different.

Because the characteristics of determinate and indeterminate dharmas are each distinct, their nature should also be different. Because the characteristics of contaminated and uncontaminated dharmas are each distinct, their nature should also be different.
Because the characteristics of mundane and supramundane dharmas are each distinct, [their nature should also be different].

The intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*) should also be different, because the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena are each distinct; therefore, their intrinsic nature should also be distinct.
"World-Honored One!

If the characteristics of such phenomena as these are each distinct, then their dharma-nature should also be distinct. How can one establish a single characteristic for the dharma-nature within all these phenomena that possess distinct characteristics?"
How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not discriminate between phenomena and sentient beings as having various natures?
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not differentiate between phenomena and sentient beings as having various natures, then they would be unable to practice the profound perfection of wisdom.
If one is unable to practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, then one will be unable to proceed from one bodhisattva stage to another.
If one is certainly unable to proceed from one bodhisattva stage to another, then one will be unable to enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktvaniyāma*).
If one is certainly unable to enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from corruption, then one must be unable to transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
If one is certainly unable to transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, then one must be unable to fulfill the perfection of supernormal powers (abhijñā-pāramitā).

If one cannot fulfill the perfection of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-pāramitā*) through meditative concentration, then one will be unable to exercise mastery and playfulness (*vikrīḍita*) with those supernormal powers.

If one cannot exercise mastery and playfulness with those supernormal powers, then one will be unable to fulfill the perfections from the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*) up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).

If one cannot fully perfect the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom through meditative concentration, then one would be unable to travel from one buddha-field to another to attend upon and make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

If one were unable, through meditative concentration, to travel from one Buddha-field to another to attend upon and make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, then one would be unable to plant roots of goodness in the presence of those Buddhas.
If one were certainly unable to plant various roots of goodness in the presence of the Buddhas, then one would be unable to adorn and purify Buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity.

If one were certainly unable to adorn and purify Buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity, then one would be unable to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, turn the wheel of the true Dharma, and deliver the multitudes of sentient beings, causing them to forever leave behind the evil realms and the cycle of birth and death.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "As you have said:

'If the nature of equality of all ordinary beings, all noble ones, and all phenomena is without distinction, then since the characteristics of all phenomena and sentient beings are each different, their natures should also be different; thus, the dharma-nature would also be distinct for each. How then can one establish the dharma-nature as having a single characteristic amidst these phenomena of diverse characteristics?'"

How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not discriminate between phenomena and sentient beings as having various natures, and so forth, as explained at length?
"Subhūti, what do you think?
Is the dharmatā of all form-phenomena emptiness?"
Is the dharma-nature of all feelings, perceptions, mental formations, and consciousnesses emptiness?
Likewise, is the dharma-nature of all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena emptiness?
Subhūti replied, “So it is! So it is!”
“The nature of all phenomena is emptiness.
The Buddha said to Subhūti, “What do you think?”
Within emptiness, can the distinct characteristics of dharmas be apprehended?
That is to say, can the distinct characteristic of form—and so on, as extensively explained—up to the distinct characteristics of all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena be apprehended?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
"In emptiness, all distinct characteristics are unapprehendable.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"By this you should know that the equality of phenomena is neither identical to all foolish common worldlings, nor is it separate from all foolish common worldlings; likewise, it is neither identical to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, nor is it separate from the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."

The equality of dharmas is not identical to form, nor is it separate from form; it is not identical to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor is it separate from feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. This extends even to the point that it is not identical to conditioned or unconditioned dharmas, nor is it separate from conditioned or unconditioned dharmas.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Is the equality of phenomena conditioned or unconditioned?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“The equality of phenomena is neither conditioned nor unconditioned; yet, apart from conditioned phenomena, unconditioned phenomena cannot be found, and apart from unconditioned phenomena, conditioned phenomena likewise cannot be found.”
Subhūti, you should know this:

whether it be the conditioned realm or the unconditioned realm, these two realms are neither joined nor dispersed; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic—namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics. All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas speak of them based on conventional truth, not based on ultimate truth.

Why is this so? Because within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), bodily activity, verbal activity, and mental activity cannot be apprehended; nor can the ultimate truth be apprehended apart from bodily, verbal, and mental activity.

Subhūti, you should know that the very nature of equality of conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena is called the ultimate truth; it is not that there is an ultimate truth existing separately from all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena.

Therefore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they practice the conduct of a bodhisattva mahāsattva without wavering from the ultimate truth; they bring sentient beings to maturity, purify buddha-fields, realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, turn the sublime wheel of Dharma to deliver the multitudes of sentient beings, and cause them to forever leave behind birth, old age, sickness, and death, realizing the ultimate, eternal bliss of nirvāṇa.
Chapter 85: On Emptiness, Part Two, Chapter Eighty-Five: On Emptiness. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

If all phenomena are equal in their nature of being empty by nature, and this emptiness of nature is neither an agent nor an object among all phenomena, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, benefit sentient beings through the four means of attraction without wavering from the ultimate truth?
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”

The nature of equality of all phenomena is the emptiness of intrinsic nature; this emptiness of intrinsic nature is neither an agent nor an object among all phenomena, yet Bodhisattvas are able to perform beneficial deeds for sentient beings through generosity and other such means.
If all sentient beings were to know for themselves that all phenomena are empty by their very nature,

then the Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas would not manifest supernatural powers or perform rare and wondrous deeds; that is to say, although there is no movement within the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena,
they cause sentient beings to distance themselves from various kinds of conceptual constructions and inversions, thereby causing sentient beings—
They cause them to remain far removed from the notion of a self, the notion of a sentient being, and so forth, up to the notions of a knower and a viewer;

they also cause them to remain far removed from the notions of form up to consciousness, the notions of the eye-base up to the mind-base, the notions of the form-base up to the phenomena-base, and the notions of the eye-element up to the mind-element, and the notions of the form-element up to the phenomena-element. The eye...
The perception of the element of consciousness up to the element of mental consciousness; the perception of eye-contact up to mind-contact;

the perception of all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition up to all feelings produced with mind-contact as condition; the perception of the earth element up to the element of consciousness;
and the perception of ignorance up to old age and death—these also cause one to distance oneself from the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛtadhātu*).
Contemplation:
Abiding in the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛta-dhātu*), one is liberated from all birth, old age, sickness, and death.
This unconditioned realm is the emptiness of all phenomena; it is designated by conventional designation as the "unconditioned realm."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By virtue of what emptiness do you say that all phenomena are empty?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Because perception is empty, all phenomena are said to be empty. Furthermore,
Subhūti, what do you think?"
"If a transformation body further performs transformative acts, does this possess substantial reality and not emptiness?
Subhūti replied, "All that is transformed possesses no substantial reality whatsoever; all is empty."
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"These two dharmas—transformation and emptiness—are neither conjoined nor dispersed. Both are empty because they are empty of emptiness; one should not make the distinction that 'this is emptiness' and 'that is transformation.'"
Why is this? Because within emptiness itself, neither the two things of "emptiness" nor "transformation" can be apprehended, for all phenomena are ultimately empty.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"

The formless is not a transformation; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not transformations. All that is a transformation is entirely empty; other phenomena and sentient beings should be known to be likewise.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If all worldly phenomena such as the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, as well as all sentient beings, are indeed transformations, then how could supramundane phenomena such as the four foundations of mindfulness, as well as sentient beings, also be transformations?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"All things in the world and those transcending the world are equally without exception transformations. Within them, there are transformations of śrāvakas, transformations of pratyekabuddhas, transformations of bodhisattvas, transformations of tathāgatas, transformations of afflictions, and transformations of various karmas. For these reasons, I say that all things are equal and without distinction, just like transformations."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Are all the fruits of abandonment—namely, the fruit of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, pratyekabuddhahood, and the Tathāgata’s permanent severance of the continuity of the habitual tendencies of afflictions—are these also emanations?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"In this way, all these dharmas that are associated with the two characteristics of arising and ceasing are also all transformations.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What phenomena are not transformations?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“If a phenomenon does not conjoin with the characteristics of arising and ceasing, that phenomenon is not a transformation.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Which phenomena do not conjoin with the characteristics of arising and ceasing?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“The dharma of non-deceptiveness is itself nirvāṇa; this dharma does not conjoin with the characteristics of arising and ceasing, and for this reason it is not a transformation.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“As the World-Honored One has taught, the equal nature of dharmas is entirely empty; nothing can move it, no duality can be found, and there is not the slightest dharma that is not empty of its own nature. How, then, can it be said that nirvāṇa is not a transformation?”
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.

There is not even the slightest dharma that is not empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*). This emptiness of intrinsic nature was not made by śrāvakas, nor by pratyekabuddhas, nor by bodhisattvas, nor by tathāgatas, nor was it made by anyone else; whether a buddha appears or does not appear, its nature is eternally empty. This is itself nirvāṇa.
Therefore, I say that nirvāṇa is not a transformation; it is not a truly existent phenomenon that is called nirvāṇa, which can be described as unarisen, unceasing, and non-transformed.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

For the sake of newly initiated bodhisattvas, I have taught that nirvāṇa is not a transformation-body (nirmāṇa), nor is there a separate, truly existent, non-empty nirvāṇa; therefore, one should not hold this as a point of objection.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what skillful means should one instruct and admonish newly ordained bodhisattvas, so that they may understand that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is eternally empty?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"How could it be that all phenomena first exist and later cease to exist, such that they are not eternally empty?
Rather, since all phenomena neither existed previously nor do not exist later, their self-nature is eternally empty; you should not be terrified by this."
"One should employ such skillful means to instruct and guide newly initiated bodhisattvas, causing them to know that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is eternally empty.

When the Bhagavān had finished speaking this sutra, the immeasurable assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, with the Bodhisattva Maitreya as their leader; the venerable Subhūti, Śāriputra, Mahākauṣṭhila, Mahākāśyapa, Ānanda, and other great śrāvakas; and the entire great assembly including devas, nāgas, asuras, and others, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced, and they faithfully accepted and practiced it.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll 478. Part 3: Preface to the Third Assembly of the Great Prajñā Sūtra. Written by the Śramaṇa Xuánzé of Xīmíng Monastery. Now, correct principle is obscured when one follows the whims of emotion, yet emotion is reflected through principle;
wondrous contemplation is estranged when one pursues external traces, yet those traces are unified through contemplation.
Yet, as both the emotional traces and the objective reality are revered, one indulges in practice through provisional names and signs;
thus, when principle and contemplation are both uprooted from delusion, one relies on gradual soaking through extensive learning.
This is why the royal city was repeatedly visited, and why the seat of the Sage has once again been made level here.
Thus, he enters the Samādhi of Play, unfolding the divine traces of his past encounters;
he issues forth subtle and wondrous sounds, gathering the distant realizations of former times.

He spreads the light of the Dharma to moisten all, purifying the source of the mind. Desiring to benefit those who have not yet benefited within the realm of emotions, and to deliver those beings who have not yet been delivered, he employs the six supernormal powers within immediate stillness and flows with the four analytical eloquences beyond the need for words. He shall surely abide in the inconceivable and attain non-discrimination.
Even as when one dreams within a dream, one still suffers the toil of frantic pursuit;
yet upon awakening from that state and subsequently attaining true enlightenment, there arises the joy of dispelling ignorance.
Why is it that every object appears so exceptionally dazzling, while suchness remains so rarely beheld?
That which is "as-it-is" (tathatā) and "thus-as-it-is" (tathatā) is not different from that which is "other-than-as-it-is.

Whether enmeshed in afflictions or emerged from them, its nature is pure; whether a Buddha appears or does not appear, its essence is eternal. To realize this is to return home, and thus one is called a Tathāgata;
to deviate from it is to flow into difference, and thus one is termed an ordinary being (pṛthagjana).
The past limit is empty and thus afflictions are exhausted; the future limit is empty and thus virtues are fulfilled.

In opening the gate of ambrosia and sitting upon the Vajra-seat, one employs provisional names beyond phenomena to adorn that which is formless, and within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) to awaken that which is mindless. Thus, one is able to sever the evil grasping of stagnation in emptiness through emptiness, and open the skillful means (*upāya*) of non-explanation through provisional explanation. To manifest the sublime countenance of wondrous forms and pour forth the perfect voice for each individual’s understanding—all this has none other than Prajñā as its source and relies upon Prajñā to complete its study.
Like the lofty and sublime King of Mountains or the venerable Patriarch of the Valley Kings, its meaning is necessarily profound and deep, and its phrasing is likewise rich and esoteric.
Consisting of fifty-nine fascicles and thirty-one chapters, it has no connection with previous translations and is thus termed a "single translation."
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle Four Hundred and Seventy-nine.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Chapter One: The Dependent Origination, Part Three of the Third Section. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of five hundred million bhikṣus.

All were arhats whose outflows were exhausted and who were free from further afflictions; they had attained true mastery, being well-liberated in mind and well-liberated in wisdom. They were like well-trained thoroughbred horses and like great dragons; they had done what was to be done and accomplished their task; having laid down the heavy burden and attained their own benefit, they had exhausted the fetters of existence and were liberated through right knowledge. Their minds reached the state of sovereign mastery and the supreme consummation, with the sole exception of Ānanda, who remained alone on the stage of training. Śāriputra and others served as the leaders of the assembly.
Furthermore, there was a community of five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, all of whom were arhats, with Yaśodharā as their leader.
Additionally, there were many thousands of upāsakas and upāsikās who had already seen the Dharma.

Furthermore, there was an assembly of immeasurable, innumerable, incalculable, unfathomable, and ineffable great bodhisattvas, unequaled and peerless, all of whom had attained the supreme samādhi of great dhāraṇīs; they dwelt securely in emptiness and practiced within the realm of signlessness;
their vows were non-conceptual, and they had attained the patience regarding the equality of all phenomena;

they possessed unimpeded analytical knowledge, and in all that they expounded, their eloquence regarding the profound and subtle principles was inexhaustible; they sported with the five supernormal powers, never regressing or losing them.
His temperament was harmonious and refined, and all held him in reverent esteem; he was diligent and courageous, free from any indolence;

he abandoned kin, renounced wealth, and disregarded his own life to sacrifice it for others; without resorting to deception or seeking anything through greed, he proclaimed the sublime principles for the sake of all sentient beings;
having realized the profound *dharmakṣānti*, he reached the ultimate state, attaining great fearlessness with a serene body and mind.
They transcend all the activities of Māra, subdue the enemy of afflictions, and bring rest to all karmic obstructions;
they cannot be overcome by any heterodox arguments, and their measure is unfathomable to Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;
they have attained mastery over both phenomena and the mind, and are liberated from all obstacles of karma and affliction.
He is not unskilled in explaining the various conditions; he accords with the inexhaustible principle of profound dependent origination.

Having extinguished views and latent tendencies, and severed all fetters, he has thoroughly realized the wisdom and principles of the various truths. Having made great vows, many eons have already passed.
He smiles before speaking, his countenance is relaxed and serene, his diction is harmonious and beautiful, and his eloquence is inexhaustible.

Amidst the assembly, his majesty was dignified and his countenance solemn; his movements and deportment were elegant and refined, fearless and composed. For nayuta-kalpas, he has preached skillfully and inexhaustibly.

Observing all dharma-doors as being like illusions, mirages, dreams, the moon reflected in water, or echoes; resembling flowers in the sky, reflections in a mirror, or shadows and light; and like transformations or the city of Gandharvas—though their substance is truly non-existent, they appear as if they exist—he speaks of the profound principle without fear, praising with skillful artistry and a mind free from inferiority.
They skillfully know the subtle distinctions in the various inclinations, mental activities, and destinies of sentient beings; they are adept at penetrating the future limit without obstruction;

they have accomplished the supreme patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and have realized the equality of all phenomena (*dharma-samatā*) as it truly is; they embrace boundless great vows and Buddha-fields;
and through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they constantly bring to mind the presence of countless Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions.

All Tathāgatas who appear in the world are able to attend upon them without fail, and they are also able to entreat them to remain long in the world, turning the wheel of the sublime Dharma to deliver immeasurable multitudes;

they are well able to subdue and extinguish all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), various views, afflictions (*kleśa*), and defilements of entanglement (*paryavasthāna*), and they are able to evoke and sport within hundreds of thousands of samādhis, skillfully awakening into and entering all gateways of the Dharma.

This assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas was endowed with such immeasurable merits that they could not be fully extolled even after countless kalpas. Their names were: Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, Bodhisattva Ratnākara, Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇa, Bodhisattva Maitreya, Bodhisattva Nakṣatradatta, Bodhisattva Varuṇadeva, Bodhisattva Indradatta, Bodhisattva Uttaramati, Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, Bodhisattva Vajramati, Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāhasta, Bodhisattva Nityotkṣiptahasta, and Bodhisattva Maitreya. These and countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas served as the leaders.

At that time, the World-Honored One, upon the lion throne, spread out his own *niṣīdana* and sat cross-legged. With body upright and resolve correct, he dwelt in mindfulness directed toward the object before him and entered the sublime samādhi known as the King of Samādhis;
for all other samādhis are subsumed within this samādhi, being its outflow.

At that time, the World-Honored One, with perfect knowledge and mindfulness, arose calmly from the Samādhirāja-samādhi. With his pure divine eye, he surveyed the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; his entire body was filled with joy, and from the thousand-spoked wheel marks on the soles of both feet, he emitted sixty hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* rays of light each.

From his ten toes, both insteps, both heels, both ankles, both shins, both calves, both knees, both thighs, both hips, waist, ribs, abdomen, back, the navel, the heart, the *śrīvatsa* mark on the chest, the marks of a Great Man, both breasts, both armpits, both shoulders, both upper arms, both elbows, both forearms, both wrists, both hands, both palms, ten fingers, the nape of the neck, the chin, the jaw, the cheeks, the forehead, the crown of the head, both eyebrows, both eyes, both ears, both nostrils, the four teeth of the mouth, the forty teeth, and the *ūrṇā-kośa* between the brows—from each and every part of his body, he emitted sixty hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* rays of light.

Each of these individual rays of light illuminates a trichiliocosm; from there, they radiate successively until they pervade the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Any sentient being who comes into contact with this light will certainly attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

At that time, every single pore of the World-Honored One’s body was filled with serene joy, and from each emerged sixty hundred thousand koṭi-nayuta rays of light. Each of these individual rays illuminated a trichiliocosm, and from there they spread successively to illuminate all the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Any sentient being who came into contact with this light would surely attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening.

At that time, the World-Honored One emanated from his body a constant light that illuminated this trichiliocosm; from there, it spread successively until it pervaded the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Any sentient being therein who came into contact with this light was certain to attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One extended his broad and long tongue from his mouth, completely covering the trichiliocosm, and smiled with serene joy.

Furthermore, from this mark of the tongue, he emitted immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of rays of light; these rays were of various colors, and from each of these multicolored rays appeared precious lotus flowers. Each flower had a thousand petals, all of a true golden color and adorned with various jewels.
In this manner, the light and flowers pervaded the trichiliocosm, and from there they spread successively throughout the worlds of the Ganges-sand number of Buddhas in the ten directions.

Within each flower pedestal was a transformation Buddha, seated in the full lotus posture, proclaiming the sublime sound of the Dharma; every single sound of the Dharma expounded teachings corresponding to the six pāramitās, such that any sentient being who heard it would surely attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One, without rising from his seat, again entered the samādhi of the Lion’s Play and manifested supernormal powers, causing this trichiliocosm to shake in six ways:

it surged in the east and subsided in the west; it surged in the west and subsided in the east; it surged in the south and subsided in the north; it surged in the north and subsided in the south; it surged in the center and subsided at the periphery; and it surged at the periphery and subsided in the center.
The ground was pure, radiant, fine, and soft, bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.

At that time, all sentient beings within this trichiliocosm—including those in the realms of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, and other perilous and miserable states of non-leisure—were entirely freed from suffering and hardship. Passing away from those states, they were reborn among humans and the six heavens of the desire realm. Remembering their past lives, they leaped for joy and together proceeded to the Buddha’s dwelling, where with hearts of pure devotion, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
From there, the sixfold earth-movements, through the Buddha’s supernormal power, spread successively throughout the worlds of the Ganges-sand number of Buddhas in the ten directions.

At that time, all sentient beings in the evil realms and other states within those worlds were freed from suffering and hardship; they passed away from those states and were reborn among humans and in the six heavens of the desire realm. All of them remembered their past lives and, leaping for joy, each went from their respective realms to the presence of the Buddha, prostrating at his feet.

At that time, within this trichiliocosm and other worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions, sentient beings were transformed: the blind could see, the deaf could hear, the mute could speak, the insane regained their mindfulness, the distracted attained concentration, the poor became wealthy, the naked obtained clothing, the hungry received food, the thirsty received drink, the sick were healed, the ugly became handsome, those with physical deformities became complete, those with impaired faculties became whole, the bewildered and dazed became awakened, and the exhausted and weary found peace and comfort.

At that time, all sentient beings turned their minds toward one another, regarding each other as fathers and mothers, elder and younger brothers, elder and younger sisters, friends, and kinsmen. They abandoned wrong speech, action, and livelihood, cultivating right speech, action, and livelihood; they abandoned the ten paths of unwholesome action and cultivated the ten paths of wholesome action; they abandoned evil thoughts and cultivated wholesome thoughts; they abandoned non-celibate conduct and cultivated pure celibacy. Delighting in purity and discarding filth, finding joy in stillness and renouncing clamor, their bodies and minds became serene, and suddenly a sublime bliss arose within them, like that of a practitioner who has entered the third dhyāna.
Furthermore, a superior wisdom suddenly manifested before them, and they all thought:

"Generosity, self-restraint, patience, diligence, tranquility, and discernment; being free from negligence, practicing the holy life, and maintaining loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity toward all sentient beings without causing them any harm—how excellent this is!"

At that time, the World-Honored One sat upon the lion throne, his radiance extraordinary and his majestic virtue towering; he eclipsed the trichiliocosm as well as the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Mount Sumeru, the Cakravāḍa mountains, and all other palaces of nāgas, devas, and even those of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, were all rendered invisible.

He was like the full autumn moon outshining the host of stars, like the summer sun’s orb overwhelming all colors with its light, or like the Great King of Mountains composed of the four jewels, who obscures all other peaks and causes them to lose their luster.
By means of his supernormal power, the Buddha manifested his original form-body, causing all sentient beings throughout this trichiliocosm to behold it.
At that time, the immeasurable and innumerable devas of the Pure Abodes within this trichiliocosm,
down to the Cāturmahārājakāyika devas of the desire realm, as well as all others— both humans and non-humans— all saw the Tathāgata.
Approaching the lion throne, their majestic radiance shone brilliantly like a great mountain of gold; filled with joy and leaping for gladness, they marveled at such an unprecedented sight.

Each held various kinds of exquisite flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses, robes, necklaces, precious banners, flags, canopies, music, and all manner of rare treasures, as well as immeasurable varieties [of offerings].
They took celestial blue lotuses, celestial red lotuses, celestial white lotuses, celestial fragrant lotuses,
celestial yellow lotuses, celestial crimson lotuses, celestial *dīnāra* tree flowers, and their fragrant leaves,
along with immeasurable other flowers growing in water and on land, and went to the place where the Buddha was to scatter them over him as an offering.

Through the Buddha’s supernatural power, the various flower garlands and other offerings whirled upward and merged to form a flower pedestal, equal in size to the trichiliocosm; celestial flower canopies, jeweled bells, and pearl banners hung down from it, their exquisite decorations profuse and most delightful.
At that time, this buddha-field was exquisitely adorned, just like the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.

The Buddha’s radiance illuminated the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system, such that all things and the void alike became the color of gold; it was likewise so in each of the ten directions throughout as many buddha-worlds as there are sands in the Ganges River.

At that time, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, all the devas and humans within this trichiliocosm each saw the Buddha sitting directly before them, and everyone thought, "The Tathāgata is preaching the Dharma to me alone."

At that time, the World-Honored One did not rise from his seat; with a joyful smile, he emitted a great radiance from the gate of his face, which illuminated the trichiliocosm Buddha-field as well as the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

At that time, all sentient beings within this trichiliocosm, by means of the Buddha’s radiance, universally beheld all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas in as many Buddha-worlds in the ten directions as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, surrounded by assemblies of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, as well as all other categories of sentient and insentient beings.

At that time, all sentient beings in as many Buddha-worlds in the ten directions as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, following the Buddha’s light, also beheld this land and Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, surrounded by an assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, as well as all other categories of sentient and insentient beings.

At that time, in the eastern direction, throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a final world named Prabhūtaratna. There, a Buddha named Ratnagotra Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, was currently teaching the Great Prajñāpāramitā to an assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

In that world there was a bodhisattva named Samantaprabha. Seeing this great light, the trembling of the great earth, and the marks of the Buddha’s body, his mind was filled with uncertainty, so he went before the Buddha and said:
“World-Honored One!
"For what cause and for what reason has this auspicious omen appeared?
At that time, the Buddha Ratnagotra addressed Samantaprabha, saying:

"From this western direction, passing through as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, there is a final world named Sahā. There, a Buddha named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, is currently teaching the Great Prajñāpāramitā to a multitude of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. It is by the spiritual power of that Buddha that this auspicious omen has been manifested."
Having heard this, Samantaraśmi was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, saying to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
I now request permission to go to the Sahā world to behold, pay homage to, and make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha and the assembly of bodhisattvas; I only pray that you will grant me leave!”
At that time, the Buddha Ratnagotra said to Samantaprabha, "Now is the very time; go as you intend.
He then took a thousand-stalked golden lotus, its petals numbering a thousand and adorned with various jewels, and bestowed it upon Samantaprabha, instructing him thus:
“Take these flowers to the presence of Śākyamuni Buddha and speak these words on my behalf:
‘The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnasaṃbhava inquires after your welfare immeasurably; he sends these lotus flowers to entrust to the World-Honored One as a Buddhist rite.’”
"When you arrive in that realm, you should abide in right mindfulness; do not look upon that Buddha-land and its great assembly with a mind of pride, lest you bring harm upon yourself. Why is this?"

Those bodhisattvas have attained the dhāraṇī-gates of unimpeded understanding, the gates of samādhi, and mastery over supernormal powers; dwelling in their final bodies, they are worthy successors to the Buddha’s position. Their majestic virtue is difficult to equal, and with compassion and vows permeating their hearts, they are born in that realm through great causal conditions.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantaprabha, having received flowers from the Buddha Ratnagotra and been charged with his command, set out together with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as countless hundreds of thousands of boys and girls. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and took their leave. Each carrying immeasurable, most excellent offerings, they proceeded forth; in every Buddha-world they passed through in the eastern direction, they made offerings to each Buddha, honoring, respecting, revering, and praising them, never passing by any without doing so.
Arriving at the place where the Buddha was, they prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, and then withdrew to stand to one side.
The Bodhisattva Samantaprabha came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

From here, extending eastward through worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is a final world named Prabhūtaratna. There dwells a Buddha named Ratnaguṇasaṃcaya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who sends his boundless greetings to the World-Honored One and presents these thousand-stemmed golden lotuses to the World-Honored One as a Buddhist ritual offering.
Then, Śākyamuni Buddha accepted these lotuses and scattered them back toward the eastern buddha-worlds, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

By the Buddha’s spiritual power, these lotuses pervaded all those buddha-fields; within each flower calyx, there appeared a transformation Buddha seated in the full lotus posture, preaching the Dharma associated with the Great Prajñāpāramitā to the bodhisattvas. Any sentient beings who heard it would certainly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

At that time, when Samantaprabha and his retinue witnessed this event, they were filled with joy and leaped for gladness, exclaiming that it was unprecedented. Each, according to their own roots of goodness and the extent of their offerings, made offerings, paid homage, showed respect, and praised the Buddha and the bodhisattvas; having done so, they withdrew and sat to one side.
The same was true for the other realms of the eastern direction.

At that time, in the southern direction, throughout as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, the final world was named Free from All Sorrow; the Buddha there was named Virtue of Freedom from Sorrow, and he had a bodhisattva named Freedom from Sorrow.

In the western direction, throughout as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, the final world was named Near Tranquility; the Buddha there was named Jewel Flame, and he had a bodhisattva named Practice of Wisdom.

To the north, throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is a final world named Most Victorious; the Buddha there is named Victorious Sovereign, and he has a bodhisattva named Victorious Bestower.

To the northeast, throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is a final world named Adorned with Stability; the Buddha there is named Supreme Virtue of the Stable Elephant, and he has a bodhisattva named Dust-Free Valor.

To the southeast, throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is a final world named Adorned with Sublime Awakening, which is most delightful; the Buddha there is named Supreme Virtue of the Lotus, and he has a bodhisattva named Lotus Hand.

To the southwest, throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, the final world is named Free from the Accumulation of Dust; the Buddha there is named Supreme Virtue of the Sun’s Universal Radiance, and there is a bodhisattva there named Light.

To the northwest, throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, the final world is named True Sovereignty; the Buddha there is named Supreme Single Jewel Canopy, and there is a bodhisattva there named Jewel Victorious.

To the nadir, throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, the final world is named Lotus; the Buddha there is named Lotus Virtue, and there is a bodhisattva there named Lotus Victorious.
Above, throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is a final world named Joy; the Buddha there is named Virtue of Joy, and he has a bodhisattva named Bestowing Joy.
In every respect, it was exactly as in the eastern direction.

At that time, this Sahā world-system of three thousandfold worlds was filled with various jewels; exquisite fragrant flowers were strewn across its ground; jeweled banners, pennants, and canopies were arrayed everywhere; and it was completely adorned with trees of flowers, fruits, incense, garlands, jewels, garments, and various ornaments, making it exceedingly delightful—just like the Buddha-land of the Tathāgata Samantakusuma in the world-system Padmāvatī, which is the original dwelling place of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva Susthitamati, and other immeasurable Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas of great majestic virtue.

Chapter Two: Śāriputra, Part Three, Section One. At that time, the Blessed One, knowing that all the worlds—whether gods, Māras, or Brahmās; whether śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas; whether the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have succeeded to the position of the Honored One; or all other humans and non-humans who have a connection with the Dharma—had gathered together, addressed the venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to perfectly awaken to all the characteristics of all phenomena, they should train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, Śāriputra joined his palms in reverence and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to perfectly awaken to all the characteristics of all phenomena train in the perfection of wisdom?”
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:

“All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should, by means of non-abiding as their expedient, dwell in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), because neither that which is dwelt upon nor that which dwells can be apprehended;
they should, by means of non-renunciation as their expedient, fulfill the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), because neither the giver nor the recipient can be apprehended.”
One should fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline by means of non-protection, because the characteristics of transgression and non-transgression cannot be apprehended;
one should fulfill the perfection of patience by means of non-appropriation, because the characteristics of agitation and non-agitation cannot be apprehended;
one should fulfill the perfection of diligence by means of non-exertion, because the characteristics of physical and mental exertion or indolence cannot be apprehended.

One should fulfill the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*) by means of non-conceptualization, because neither the presence of flavor nor the absence of flavor can be apprehended;
one should fulfill the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) by means of non-attachment, because neither the nature of existence nor the nature of non-existence can be apprehended.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, bodhisattva mahāsattvas dwelling in the perfection of wisdom,

by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method, should cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;
they should cultivate the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, and the gate of liberation of wishlessness."
One should cultivate the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
one should cultivate the eight liberations and the nine successive attainments;
one should cultivate the nine perceptions—what are these nine?

These are the perception of bloating, the perception of festering, the perception of bloody disfigurement, the perception of livid discoloration, the perception of being devoured by scavengers, the perception of scattering, the perception of skeletal remains, the perception of burning, and the perception of repulsive decay;
one should also cultivate the ten recollections. What are these ten?

These are: recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dharma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of ethical discipline, recollection of relinquishment, recollection of the devas, recollection of inhalation and exhalation, recollection of disenchantment, recollection of death, and recollection of the body.
One should cultivate ten perceptions; what are these ten?

They are: the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering, the perception of non-self, the perception of impurity, the perception of death, the perception that all worlds are not worth delighting in, the perception of revulsion toward food, the perception of abandonment, the perception of dispassion, and the perception of cessation;
one should cultivate eleven types of knowledge. What are these eleven?

That is to say: the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of the origin, the knowledge of cessation, the knowledge of the path, the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, the knowledge of phenomena, the subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, the knowledge of others' minds, and the knowledge as it is;

one should cultivate the concentration with applied thought and sustained thought, the concentration without applied thought and with only sustained thought, and the concentration without applied thought and without sustained thought;
one should cultivate the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known."
One should cultivate the contemplation of the impure, the contemplation of the spheres of totality, and the knowledge of all modes; one should cultivate śamatha and vipaśyanā;
one should cultivate the three insights, the four analytical knowledges, and the four fearlessnesses.
One should cultivate the five superknowledges that are non-retrogressive;
one should cultivate the six perfections, the seven noble riches, the eight awakenings of the great beings, and the knowledge of the nine abodes of sentient beings;
one should cultivate the ten powers of a Tathāgata and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
One should cultivate great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity;
one should cultivate all the immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable merits of the Buddhas, such as the subtle wisdom regarding all marks.
Because these dharmas are thus unattainable.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), they should train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

One who wishes to swiftly perfect all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of the mental activities of all sentient beings, should study the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
One who wishes to eradicate all afflictions and their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) should study the perfection of wisdom.
One who wishes to enter the bodhisattva’s stage of right determination (*samyaktvaniyāma*) should study the perfection of wisdom.
Those who wish to transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas should study the perfection of wisdom;
those who wish to abide on the stage of the bodhisattva’s non-retrogression should study the perfection of wisdom;
and those who wish to attain the six extraordinary supernormal powers should study the perfection of wisdom.
If one wishes to know the various transformations and distinctions in the mental activities of all sentient beings, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*;
if one wishes to surpass the wisdom and functional efficacy of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*;
if one wishes to attain all dhāraṇī-doors and samādhi-doors, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
If one wishes, with a single thought of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), to surpass all the giving of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*;
if one wishes, with a single thought of sympathetic joy, to surpass all the pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*;

if one wishes, with a single thought of sympathetic joy, to surpass all the concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśana*) of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.

If one wishes, with a single thought of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā-citta*), to surpass all the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as well as other wholesome dharmas, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.

If one wishes, with a single thought of the wholesome dharmas practiced, to surpass all the wholesome dharmas of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.

If one wishes to practice even a small portion of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) to equally dedicate them toward the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), thereby attaining immeasurable and innumerable merits, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to cause the cultivation of the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom to be swiftly brought to fulfillment and remain free from all obstacles, they should study the perfection of wisdom.

If they wish to see the Buddhas in every lifetime, constantly hear the true Dharma, attain the awakening of a Buddha, and receive the Buddhas' mindfulness, instructions, and exhortations, they should study the perfection of wisdom."
If one wishes to attain the body of a Buddha, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man and fully adorned with the eighty secondary characteristics, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.

If one wishes to be born into the family of the Buddhas, enter the stage of the youthful truth (*kumārabhūmi*), and never be separated from the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.

If one wishes, by the power of various supreme roots of goodness, to be able to procure superior and exquisite offerings at will to offer, revere, respect, and praise all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, thereby causing all those roots of goodness to quickly reach fulfillment, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.

One who wishes to fulfill the needs of all sentient beings—providing them with food, drink, clothing, beds, bedding, medicinal requisites for illness, various flowers and perfumes, lamps, vehicles, gardens, dwellings, wealth, grain, precious gems, ornaments, music, and other such various excellent articles of enjoyment used by kings and others, as well as all mundane and supramundane sublime wholesome dharmas—should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to universally establish all sentient beings throughout the entirety of space, the dharma-realm, and all worlds, causing them all to abide in the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as other boundless and preeminent wholesome dharmas, they should study the perfection of wisdom.

If they wish to obtain the merit gained from generating a single thought of goodness such that it remains inexhaustible until they sit upon the sublime seat of enlightenment and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they should study the perfection of wisdom."

If one wishes to be praised, protected, and empowered by all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and the assemblies of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas throughout the worlds of the ten directions, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If one wishes that, with a single arousal of the mind, one may travel everywhere to as many world-systems in each of the ten directions as there are sands in the Ganges, to make offerings to, revere, honor, and praise all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and the assemblies of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, thereby benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If one wishes that, with a single voice, one may pervade as many world-systems in each of the ten directions as there are sands in the Ganges to praise the Buddhas and instruct sentient beings, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

"Those who wish to perpetuate the lineage of the Three Jewels so that it remains unbroken, and who desire to benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings, should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to penetrate inner emptiness, outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, great emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, emptiness of the non-dispersal of dispersion, emptiness of intrinsic nature, emptiness of self-characteristics and common characteristics, emptiness of all phenomena, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, as well as the emptiness of the object of focus, the emptiness of increase, the emptiness of equality and non-equality, and so forth, they should train in the perfection of wisdom.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to penetrate the suchness of all phenomena, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-falsity, the non-alteration, the equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, and the limit of reality, they should study the perfection of wisdom.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to know the number of all the atoms of earth, space, mountains, great oceans, rivers, streams, ponds, ravines, lakes, and the elements of earth, water, fire, and wind throughout the trichiliocosm worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees the kalpa-fire arise, burning throughout the trichiliocosm until heaven and earth are ablaze, and wishes to blow it out all at once with a single breath, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees the wind-kalpa arise, wherein the wind-wheel—the most fundamental support of the trichiliocosm—surges upward with violent impact, about to blow away all things within the trichiliocosm, including Mount Sumeru and the Cakravāḍa mountains, reducing them to pieces like withered leaves; and if that bodhisattva wishes to obstruct the force of that wind with a single finger so that it ceases and does not arise, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to fill the entirety of space within a trichiliocosm while sitting in a single cross-legged posture, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to take all things within the trichiliocosm—the Sumeru mountains, the Cakravāḍa mountains, and so forth—with a single hair and cast them beyond immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless worlds in other directions without harming the sentient beings therein, they should train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to provide offerings, honor, respect, and praise to all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, along with their assemblies of disciples, throughout as many worlds in each of the ten directions as there are grains of sand in the Ganges—using a single meal, a single incense, a single flower, a single garland, a single robe, a single banner, a single parasol, a single lamp, a single pennant, or any such articles of offering, and doing so to the point that they are fully satisfied—they should train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to universally establish all sentient beings in each of the worlds of the ten directions—each as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—in the aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; or wishes to establish them in the fruit of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship, or in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; or even wishes to lead them into the realm of nirvana without remainder for ultimate peace and happiness, they should study the perfection of wisdom.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they are able to know, as it truly is, that practicing generosity yields great fruit and retribution; that is to say, they know as it truly is:

'By such generosity one is born into a great kṣatriya clan; by such generosity one is born into a great brāhmaṇa clan; by such generosity one is born into a great householder clan; by such generosity one is born into a great merchant clan. "

Furthermore, one knows as it truly is that by such giving one is reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings; by such giving one is reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three; by such giving one is reborn in the Yāma Heaven; by such giving one is reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven; by such giving one is reborn in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; and by such giving one is reborn in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
Furthermore, one knows as it truly is that by relying on this giving one attains the first dhyāna, or the second dhyāna, or the third dhyāna, or the fourth dhyāna.

Furthermore, one knows as it truly is that by relying on this giving one attains the concentration of the sphere of infinite space, or the concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness, or the concentration of the sphere of nothingness, or the concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Furthermore, one knows as it truly is that based on this generosity, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment arise; by these causes and conditions, one attains the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship, or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, or the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Being able to know, as it truly is, the practice of pure ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and thereby attaining great fruits and rewards, is likewise so.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are able to know things as they truly are:

In this way, skillful means in giving can fulfill the perfection of generosity; in this way, skillful means in giving can fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline; in this way, skillful means in giving can fulfill the perfection of patience; in this way, skillful means in giving can fulfill the perfection of diligence; in this way, skillful means in giving can fulfill the perfection of meditative concentration; and in this way, skillful means in giving can fulfill the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, one knows as it truly is that such skillful means in ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom each likewise fulfill the six perfections.
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) know, as it truly is, such skillful means (upāyakauśalya) of giving that can fulfill the perfections from giving through to wisdom; and how does he know, as it truly is, such skillful means of ethical discipline through to wisdom that can fulfill the perfections from ethical discipline through to meditative concentration (dhyāna)?"
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:

“By means of taking non-apprehension as the expedient, that is to say, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving, because they thoroughly understand that the characteristics of both the gift and the recipient are unapprehendable, they are able to fulfill the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā);
because the characteristics of transgression and non-transgression are unapprehendable, they are able to fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).”
Because the characteristics of movement and stillness cannot be apprehended, one is able to fulfill the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*);
because physical and mental exertion or indolence cannot be apprehended, one is able to fulfill the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*);
and because distraction and non-distraction cannot be apprehended, one is able to fulfill the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).
Because the intrinsic nature and characteristics of all phenomena are unapprehendable, one is able to fulfill the perfection of wisdom. Śāriputra,
this is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing generosity, employs skillful means to fulfill the six perfections.
In this way, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices pure ethical discipline, and so on up to practicing wisdom, they are each able to fulfill the six pāramitās through skillful means.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain the sublime qualities of all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to reach the ultimate further shore of all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to reach the suchness (tathatā), the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), the dharma-nature (dharmatā), non-arising (anutpāda), and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) of all phenomena of the past, future, and present, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to always serve as the leader for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to serve as the personal attendant to the Buddhas, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to become an inner retinue to the Buddhas, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to possess a great retinue in every birth, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to have bodhisattvas as their constant retinue, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to be a truly pure field of merit for the world, they should study the perfection of wisdom.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to subdue the mind of stinginess and greed, quiet the mind that violates the precepts, eliminate the mind of anger and resentment, abandon the mind of laziness, still the mind of distraction, and depart from the mind of evil wisdom, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to skillfully establish all sentient beings in the meritorious action consisting of giving, the meritorious action consisting of ethical discipline, the meritorious action consisting of cultivation, the meritorious action consisting of service, and the meritorious action consisting of material support, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain the five eyes— what are these five? Namely, the fleshly eye,
the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the dharma eye, and the buddha eye— they should study the perfection of wisdom."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to see, with the divine eye, the bodies of all Buddhas endowed with sublime marks and signs throughout as many worlds in the ten directions as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, they should study the perfection of wisdom.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to hear with the divine ear all the essential teachings of the Dharma expounded by the Buddhas in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions, they should study the perfection of wisdom.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to know, as they truly are, the minds and mental factors of all Tathāgatas in each of the worlds of the ten directions—each as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to hear the Dharma preached by all Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions, and even until their unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, so that it remains forever uninterrupted, they should study the perfection of wisdom.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to see all the buddha-fields of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present throughout the ten directions, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to receive, uphold, and master to the ultimate degree all the sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, gāthās, udānas, nidānas, avadānas, jātakas, vaipulyas, adbhutadharmas, upadeśas, and saṃprakāśanas spoken by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present throughout the ten directions—teachings that the śrāvakas and others have never before heard—they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to personally receive, uphold, master thoroughly, and practice according to the instructions all the dharma-gates taught by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present throughout the ten directions—and furthermore, wishes to explain them extensively and accurately for others, exhorting them to practice accordingly—they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to provide illumination for the dark worlds of the ten directions—equal in number to the sands of the Ganges—or for the intermediate spaces between worlds where the light of the sun and moon does not reach, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to transform and guide the sentient beings within immeasurable worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions—beings who have accomplished false views, who have not heard the names of the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha, and who do not believe in cause and effect—so that they may give rise to right view, hear the names of the Triple Gem, and develop deep faith in cause and effect, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of their own power, desires to cause the sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions such that the blind can see, the deaf can hear, the mute can speak,
the insane regain mindfulness, the distracted attain concentration, the poor obtain wealth, the naked obtain clothing, and the hungry...
The hungry shall obtain food, the thirsty shall obtain drink, the sick shall be healed, the ugly shall become dignified and handsome, those with physical deformities shall attain completeness,
those with impaired faculties shall become perfect, the bewildered and fainting shall regain their clarity, and the exhausted shall find peace;
all sentient beings shall face one another with hearts of loving-kindness, and those fallen into the evil realms [shall be delivered].
Those bound for the lower realms attain birth in the happy realms; those who habitually engage in unwholesome actions all cultivate wholesome karma;

those who have violated the precepts abide in the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*); those who have not attained concentration abide in the aggregate of concentration (*samādhiskandha*);
