"Furthermore, Subhūti! For example, the sense base of the eye is merely a conventional designation; likewise, this conventional dharma is neither born nor extinguished, existing only as a conceptualization, a designation, and a verbal expression.

In the same way, the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are also merely conventional designations; likewise, these conventional dharmas are neither born nor extinguished, existing only as conceptualizations, designations, and verbal expressions."
All these are merely conventional designations; these conventional designations do not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between the two, because they cannot be apprehended.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

Whether it be the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), the bodhisattva mahāsattva, or these two names, all are merely conventional phenomena (prajñapti-dharma). Such conventional phenomena are neither born nor extinguished; they exist only as provisional designations and verbal expressions, neither within, nor without, nor in between, because they are ultimately ungraspable.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! For example, just as the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) is merely a conventional phenomenon (*prajñapti-dharma*), so too this conventional phenomenon is neither born nor extinguished; it exists only as a designation through conceptual thought and verbal expression.

Likewise, the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) are also merely conventional phenomena; such conventional phenomena are neither born nor extinguished, existing only as designations through conceptual thought and verbal expression."
All these are merely conventional designations; these conventional designations do not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between the two, because they are unapprehendable.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

Whether it be the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), the bodhisattva mahāsattva, or these two names, they are all merely conventional dharmas. Such conventional dharmas are neither born nor extinguished; they exist only as provisional designations and verbal expressions, neither within, nor without, nor in between, because they are ultimately unapprehendable.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! For example, the eye-element, the form-element, and the eye-consciousness-element are merely conventional phenomena (*prajñapti-dharma*). Such conventional phenomena are neither born nor extinguished; they exist only as designations, conventions, and verbal expressions.

Likewise, the ear-element, sound-element, and ear-consciousness-element; the nose-element, odor-element, and nose-consciousness-element; the tongue-element, taste-element, and tongue-consciousness-element; the body-element, tangible-object-element, and body-consciousness-element; and the mind-element, mental-phenomena-element, and mind-consciousness-element are merely conventional phenomena. Such conventional phenomena are neither born nor extinguished; they exist only as designations, conventions, and verbal expressions."

All these are merely conventional designations; these conventional designations do not exist internally, nor do they exist externally, nor do they exist in between the two, because they cannot be apprehended.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

Whether it be the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), or the bodhisattva mahāsattva, or these two names—all are merely conventional dharmas (*prajñapti-dharma*). Such conventional dharmas are neither born nor extinguished; they exist only as provisional designations and verbal expressions, neither within, nor without, nor in between, because they are ultimately ungraspable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

For example, all that exists within the body—the head and neck, shoulders and upper arms, abdomen and back, chest and ribs, waist and spine, thighs and knees, calves and shins, feet, and so forth—consists merely of skin, flesh, bone, and marrow, which possess only conventional designations (*prajñapti*). Thus, these names are conventionally designated as neither arising nor ceasing; they exist only as conceptual notions established through verbal expression.
These various conventional designations do not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between the two, because they are ultimately ungraspable."
Thus it is, Subhūti!

Whether it be the perfection of wisdom, or the bodhisattva mahāsattva, or these two names—all are merely conventional dharmas. Such conventional dharmas are neither born nor extinguished; they exist only as provisional designations and verbal expressions. They do not abide within, nor do they abide without, nor do they abide in between, for they cannot be apprehended.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

For example, all external things—such as grasses, trees, roots, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits—exist only as provisional designations (*prajñapti*). Thus, these names are merely provisional; they are neither produced nor extinguished, existing only as conceptual identifications and verbal expressions.
These various provisional designations do not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between the two, because they are unapprehendable."
Thus it is, Subhūti!

Whether it be the perfection of wisdom, or the bodhisattva mahāsattva, or these two names—all are merely conventional dharmas. Such conventional dharmas are neither born nor extinguished; they exist only as provisional designations and verbal expressions. They do not abide within, nor do they abide without, nor do they abide in between the two, for they cannot be apprehended.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

For example, just as the Buddhas of the past and future exist only as provisional names, so too these names are merely conventional designations that are neither born nor extinguished; they are nothing more than conceptual labels established through verbal expression.
These provisional names do not exist internally, nor do they exist externally, nor do they exist in between the two, for they cannot be apprehended."
Thus it is, Subhūti!

Whether it be the perfection of wisdom, or the bodhisattva mahāsattva, or these two names—all are merely conventional dharmas. Such conventional dharmas are neither born nor extinguished; they exist only as provisional designations established by speech. They do not abide within, nor without, nor in between the two, for they are ungraspable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

For example, just as dream-objects, echoes, reflections, illusions, mirages, the moon in water, and transformations exist only as provisional designations (*prajñapti*), so too these names are provisionally designated as neither arising nor ceasing; they are merely conceptual identifications established through verbal expression.
These various provisional designations do not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between the two, because they are unapprehendable."
Thus it is, Subhūti!

Whether it be the perfection of wisdom, or a bodhisattva mahāsattva, or these two names—all are merely provisional dharmas. Such provisional dharmas are neither born nor extinguished; they exist only as provisional designations established by speech, being neither internal, nor external, nor in between, because they cannot be apprehended.

"In this way, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should correctly train in the conventional designation of names for all phenomena and the conventional designation of phenomena themselves."
"In this way, Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should not view form as either permanent or impermanent,
as either pleasant or painful, as either self or non-self, or as either pure or impure."
Whether pure or empty or not empty, with signs or signless, with aspiration or aspirationless,
tranquil or not tranquil, secluded or not secluded,
conditioned or unconditioned, with outflows or without outflows, arising or ceasing, or wholesome...
It is neither wholesome nor unwholesome, whether with fault or without fault, whether with affliction or without affliction,
whether mundane or supramundane, whether defiled or pure, and whether pertaining to saṃsāra or pertaining to nirvāṇa;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom should not contemplate the sense-base of the eye as either permanent or impermanent,
as either pleasure or suffering, as either self or non-self, or as pure or impure."
Impure, or empty or non-empty; with signs or signless; with aspiration or aspirationless;
tranquil or non-tranquil; secluded or non-secluded;
conditioned or unconditioned; with outflows or without outflows; arising or ceasing; or wholesome.
Whether they are wholesome or unwholesome, with fault or without fault, with affliction or without affliction,
mundane or supramundane, defiled or purified, pertaining to saṃsāra or pertaining to nirvāṇa—
the same applies to the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom should not view the sphere of form as either permanent or impermanent,
as either pleasure or suffering, as either self or non-self, or as either pure or [impure]."
Whether impure, or empty or not empty, with signs or signless, with aspiration or aspirationless,
tranquil or not tranquil, secluded or not secluded,
conditioned or unconditioned, with outflows or without outflows, arising or ceasing, or wholesome.
Whether they are wholesome or unwholesome, with fault or without fault, with affliction or without affliction,
mundane or supramundane, defiled or pure, pertaining to saṃsāra or pertaining to nirvāṇa—
the same applies to the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental objects.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom should not contemplate the eye-element as either permanent or impermanent,
as either pleasant or painful, as either self or non-self, or as pure or impure."
Impure, or empty or non-empty; with signs or signless; with aspiration or aspirationless;
tranquil or non-tranquil; secluded or non-secluded;
conditioned or unconditioned; with outflows or without outflows; arising or ceasing; or wholesome.
Whether they are wholesome or unwholesome, with fault or without fault, with affliction or without affliction,
mundane or supramundane, defiled or purified, pertaining to saṃsāra or pertaining to nirvāṇa—
the same applies to the auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental elements.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom should not regard the realm of form as either permanent or impermanent,
as either pleasant or painful, as either self or non-self, or as either pure or impure."
Impure; or empty or not empty; with signs or signless; with aspirations or aspirationless;
tranquil or not tranquil; secluded or not secluded;
conditioned or unconditioned; with outflows or without outflows; arising or ceasing; or wholesome.
Whether they are wholesome or unwholesome, with fault or without fault, with affliction or without affliction,
mundane or supramundane, defiled or pure, pertaining to saṃsāra or pertaining to nirvāṇa—
the same applies to the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom should not contemplate the eye-consciousness element as either permanent or impermanent,
as either pleasant or painful, as either self or non-self, or as pure."
Whether impure or empty or not empty, whether with signs or signless, whether with aspiration or aspirationless,
whether tranquil or not tranquil, whether secluded or not secluded,
whether conditioned or unconditioned, whether with outflows or without outflows, whether arising or ceasing...
Whether it be wholesome or unwholesome, with fault or without fault, with affliction or without affliction,
mundane or supramundane, defiled or purified, pertaining to saṃsāra or pertaining to nirvāṇa—
the same applies to the auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousness elements.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom should not contemplate eye-contact."
Whether permanent or impermanent, whether pleasant or painful, whether self or non-self, whether pure or impure,
whether empty or non-empty, whether with signs or signless, whether with aspirations or aspirationless,
whether tranquil or non-tranquil, whether secluded or non-secluded, or whether...
Whether conditioned or unconditioned, with outflows or without outflows,
arising or ceasing, wholesome or unwholesome, faulty or faultless, afflicted or unafflicted,
mundane or supramundane, defiled or purified, or pertaining to birth and death—
They belong to nirvāṇa; the same is true for the contacts of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, bodhisattva mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom should not contemplate eye-contact."
The various feelings produced by conditions—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant;
whether permanent or impermanent; whether pleasant or painful; whether self or non-self; whether pure or impure;
whether empty or non-empty; whether with signs or signless; whether with aspiration or aspirationless; or...
Whether quiescent or not quiescent, whether secluded or not secluded, whether conditioned or unconditioned,
whether with outflows or without outflows, whether arising or ceasing, whether wholesome or unwholesome,
whether faulty or faultless, whether with afflictions or without afflictions, or whether mundane...
Whether supramundane, whether afflicted or purified, whether pertaining to saṃsāra or pertaining to nirvāṇa,
the same applies to all feelings— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— that arise conditioned by ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact.
"Why is this? Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), whether it be the perfection of wisdom, or the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, or these two names—none of them are perceived as existing within the realm of the conditioned (saṃskṛtadhātu), nor are they perceived as existing within the realm of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛtadhātu). Why is this so?"
Subhūti! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they do not give rise to conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding any of these phenomena.

“Subhūti! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he abides in the non-conceptuality of all phenomena. For the sake of cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness, up to the eightfold noble path, although he practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive the name ‘perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive the bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor does he perceive the name ‘bodhisattva mahāsattva. He does not perceive the Buddhas, nor does he perceive the names of the Buddhas; he seeks only the gnosis of omniscience with correct reflection.”

“Subhūti! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the non-conceptuality of all phenomena. For the sake of practicing the perfection of generosity, up to the perfection of wisdom; for the sake of practicing the ten powers of a buddha, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha—they practice the perfection of wisdom, yet they do not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor do they perceive the name ‘perfection of wisdom. They do not perceive the bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor do they perceive the name ‘bodhisattva mahāsattva. They do not perceive the buddhas, nor do they perceive the names of the buddhas; they simply seek with correct mindfulness the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).”

“Subhūti! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they thoroughly penetrate the true nature of all phenomena; that is to say, they penetrate the fact that within them there is neither defilement nor purity.”
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 482. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Three, Chapter on Subhūti, Section Two: "Thus it is, Subhūti!"
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should, regarding all phenomena, realize them as they truly are: as mere designations and as mere phenomena.

“Subhūti! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva has realized, as they truly are, that all dharmas are merely designations for names and designations for dharmas, he does not grasp at form; he does not grasp at feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness.

He does not grasp at the eye-base and the form-base; he does not grasp at the ear-base and the sound-base; he does not grasp at the nose-base and the odor-base; he does not grasp at the tongue-base and the taste-base; he does not grasp at the body-base and the tangible-base; he does not grasp at the mind-base and the mental-object-base.”

One does not grasp at or cling to the eye-element, the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, and eye-contact, nor to the various feelings—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arise conditioned by eye-contact;

one does not grasp at or cling to the ear-element, the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element, and ear-contact, nor to the various feelings—whether pleasant... [that arise conditioned by ear-contact].
Whether it be painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, one does not cling to the nose element, the odor element, the nose-consciousness element,
nor to nose-contact and the various feelings— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— that arise conditioned by nose-contact; one does not cling to the tongue element,
the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, nor to tongue-contact and [tongue-contact-conditioned feelings].
Regarding the various feelings— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— that arise conditioned by these, one does not grasp at or cling to the body-element,
the contact-element, the body-consciousness-element, or the body-contact and the various feelings—
whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— that arise conditioned by that body-contact; nor does one grasp at or cling to the mind-element, the mental-object-element, or the mind-...
The element of consciousness, as well as mental contact and the various feelings— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant— that arise conditioned by mental contact;
one does not cling to the conditioned realm, nor does one cling to the unconditioned realm.
They do not grasp at or cling to the perfection of generosity; they do not grasp at or cling to the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom;
they do not grasp at names, they do not grasp at signs;
and they do not grasp at the body of a bodhisattva.
They do not cling to the flesh eye; they do not cling to the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the Dharma eye, or the Buddha eye.
They do not cling to the perfection of knowledge (*jñāna-pāramitā*); they do not cling to the perfection of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-pāramitā*).

They do not cling to internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*); they do not cling to external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*), internal-and-external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), great emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*), ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), conditioned emptiness (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), unconditioned emptiness (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), absolute emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), boundless emptiness (*anavara-agra-śūnyatā*), non-dispersal emptiness (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*), essential nature emptiness (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), characteristic emptiness (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*), and the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
They do not cling to suchness; they do not cling to the limit of reality or the dharma-realm;
they do not cling to the maturation of sentient beings; they do not cling to the purification of buddha-fields;
and they do not cling to skillful means.
Why is that? Subhūti!
Because all phenomena—whether that which grasps, that which is grasped, the time of grasping, or the locus of grasping—are all non-existent.

"In this way, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom without grasping or attachment to any phenomena, they increase the perfection of generosity, and they increase the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; they enter the stage of the bodhisattva’s fixed determination, abide on the bodhisattva stage of non-retrogression, and bring to fulfillment the bodhisattva’s sublime supernormal powers."
Having thus attained perfection in these supernormal powers, they travel from one buddha-field to another, making offerings to, honoring, respecting, and praising the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

For the sake of bringing all sentient beings to maturity; for the sake of purifying one’s own buddha-field; and for the sake of beholding the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, they bring forth various kinds of sublime roots of virtue.
Having already aroused these supreme roots of goodness, they are able to hear and receive all the true Dharma of the Buddhas according to their inclinations.

Once they have heard and received it, they shall never forget it until they sit upon the sublime seat of enlightenment; the Dharma gates they have received will likewise remain uninterrupted, and they will attain mastery over all dhāraṇī gates and samādhi gates.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they are able to realize all phenomena as they truly are—namely, as mere designations and mere conventional constructs—and thus remain without grasping or attachment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, what do you think?
Is that which is called 'bodhisattva' the bodhisattva who is form, or even consciousness?"
Are form and so forth, up to consciousness, the bodhisattva?
Is there a bodhisattva within form and so forth, up to consciousness?
Or is there form and so forth, up to consciousness, within the bodhisattva?
"Is there a bodhisattva apart from form,
up to and including consciousness? Subhūti replied, "No!"
“World-Honored One!
Furthermore, Subhūti, what do you think?”
Regarding the term "bodhisattva": is it that the eye-base through to the mind-base is the bodhisattva?
Is it that something other than the eye-base through to the mind-base is the bodhisattva?
Or is there a bodhisattva within the eye-base through to the mind-base?
“Is there the eye-base up to the mind-base within a bodhisattva?
Or is there a bodhisattva apart from the eye-base up to the mind-base? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! "Furthermore, Subhūti!
What do you think?
Is that which is called a "bodhisattva" the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) up to the sense-sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*)?
Or is the bodhisattva something other than the sense-sphere of form up to the sense-sphere of phenomena?
Is there a bodhisattva within the sense-sphere of form up to the sense-sphere of mental phenomena?
Is there the sense-sphere of form up to the sense-sphere of mental phenomena within a bodhisattva?
Is there a bodhisattva apart from the sense-sphere of form up to the sense-sphere of mental phenomena?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
"Furthermore, Subhūti, what do you think?
Is that which is called a 'bodhisattva' the eye-element, and so forth, up to the mind-element?"
Is the bodhisattva something other than the eye-element up to the mind-element?
Is the bodhisattva within the eye-element up to the mind-element?
Or are the eye-element up to the mind-element within the bodhisattva?
"Apart from the eye-element up to the mind-element,
is there a bodhisattva? Subhūti replied, "No!"
“World-Honored One!
“Furthermore, Subhūti, what do you think?”
Regarding the term "bodhisattva": is it that the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) up to the dharma realm (*dharmadhātu*) is the bodhisattva?
Is it that something distinct from the form realm up to the dharma realm is the bodhisattva?
Or is it that there is a bodhisattva within the form realm up to the dharma realm?
“Is there, within the Bodhisattva, the realm of form up to the realm of phenomena?
Or is there a Bodhisattva apart from the realm of form up to the realm of phenomena? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! Furthermore, Subhūti!"
What do you think?
Is that which is called a "bodhisattva" the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element?
Or is the bodhisattva something other than the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element?
Is there a bodhisattva within the visual consciousness element up to the mental consciousness element?
Is there a visual consciousness element up to a mental consciousness element within a bodhisattva?
Is there a bodhisattva apart from the visual consciousness element up to the mental consciousness element?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
"Furthermore, Subhūti, what do you think?
Is that which is called a 'bodhisattva' the earth element, or even the consciousness element, that is the bodhisattva?"
Is the bodhisattva the earth element, up to and including the consciousness element?
Is the bodhisattva within the earth element, up to and including the consciousness element?
Or are the earth element, up to and including the consciousness element, within the bodhisattva?
"Is there a bodhisattva apart from the element of earth,
up to and including the element of consciousness? Subhūti replied, "No!"
“World-Honored One!
Furthermore, Subhūti, what do you think?”
Regarding what is called a "bodhisattva": is it that ignorance through to old age and death is the bodhisattva?
Is the bodhisattva something other than ignorance through to old age and death?
Or does the bodhisattva exist within ignorance through to old age and death?
“Is there ignorance up to and including old age and death within a bodhisattva?
Or is there a bodhisattva apart from ignorance up to and including old age and death? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What meaning do you perceive that leads you to say: 'Form and the other aggregates are not the bodhisattva;

something other than form and the other aggregates is not the bodhisattva; there is no bodhisattva within form and the other aggregates; there are no form and the other aggregates within the bodhisattva; nor is there a bodhisattva apart from form and the other aggregates'?"
Subhūti replied, “World-Honored One! Since awakening,
the bodhisattva, and form and so forth are ultimately non-existent and cannot be apprehended, how much less could there be a bodhisattva!”
Since this [bodhisattva] does not exist [in any of these ways], how can it be said that:

the bodhisattva is identical to form and so forth; the bodhisattva is distinct from form and so forth; the bodhisattva exists within form and so forth; form and so forth exist within the bodhisattva; or that the bodhisattva exists apart from form and so forth?
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “Excellent! Excellent!”
It is as you have said.
Subhūti, you should know that because awakening, the bodhisattva, and form and so forth are unapprehendable, bodhisattvas are likewise unapprehendable.
Because all bodhisattvas are unapprehendable, the *prajñāpāramitā* they practice is likewise unapprehendable. Subhūti!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the *prajñāpāramitā*, they should diligently train in this meaning.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, what do you think? Is the suchness of form,
up to and including consciousness, the bodhisattva?"
Is the suchness of form, up to and including consciousness, the bodhisattva?
Is there a bodhisattva within the suchness of form, up to and including consciousness?
Or is there the suchness of form, up to and including consciousness, within the bodhisattva?
“Is there a bodhisattva in the suchness of form, up to and including the suchness of consciousness? Subhūti replied, “No!”
“World-Honored One!
Furthermore, Subhūti, what do you think?”
Is the suchness of the eye-base, up to and including the mind-base, the bodhisattva?
Is the suchness distinct from the eye-base, up to and including the mind-base, the bodhisattva?
Does the bodhisattva exist within the suchness of the eye-base, up to and including the mind-base?
“Is there suchness within the bodhisattva from the eye-base up to the mind-base?
Or is there a bodhisattva apart from the suchness of the eye-base up to the mind-base? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! Furthermore, Subhūti!"
What do you think? Is the suchness of the sense-base of form, up to and including the sense-base of mental phenomena, the bodhisattva?
Or is the suchness distinct from the sense-base of form, up to and including the sense-base of mental phenomena, the bodhisattva?
Is there a bodhisattva within the suchness of the sense-sphere of form up to the sense-sphere of mental phenomena?
Is there the suchness of the sense-sphere of form up to the sense-sphere of mental phenomena within a bodhisattva?
Is there a bodhisattva apart from the suchness of the sense-sphere of form up to the sense-sphere of mental phenomena?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
"Furthermore, Subhūti, what do you think? Is the suchness of the eye-element,
up to and including the mind-element, the bodhisattva?"
Is the suchness of the visual faculty up to the mental faculty the bodhisattva?
Is there a bodhisattva within the suchness of the visual faculty up to the mental faculty?
Or is there the suchness of the visual faculty up to the mental faculty within the bodhisattva?
"Apart from the true suchness (tathatā) of the eye-element up to the mind-element,
is there a bodhisattva? Subhūti replied, "No!"
“World-Honored One!
Furthermore, Subhūti, what do you think?”
Is the suchness of the form realm up to the dharma realm the bodhisattva?
Is the suchness distinct from the form realm up to the dharma realm the bodhisattva?
Does the bodhisattva exist within the suchness of the form realm up to the dharma realm?
“Within the Bodhisattva, is there the suchness of the form realm up to the dharma realm?
Or, apart from the suchness of the form realm up to the dharma realm, is there a Bodhisattva? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! Furthermore, Subhūti!"
What do you think?
Is the suchness of the eye-consciousness element, up to and including the mind-consciousness element, the bodhisattva?
Or is the bodhisattva something other than the suchness of the eye-consciousness element, up to and including the mind-consciousness element?
Is there a bodhisattva within the suchness of the visual consciousness element up to the mental consciousness element?
Or is there the suchness of the visual consciousness element up to the mental consciousness element within the bodhisattva?
"Is there a bodhisattva within the suchness of the eye-consciousness element,
up to and including the mind-consciousness element? Subhūti replied, "No!"
“World-Honored One!
Furthermore, Subhūti, what do you think?”
Is the suchness of the earth element, up to and including the consciousness element, the bodhisattva?
Is the suchness that is distinct from the earth element, up to and including the consciousness element, the bodhisattva?
Does the bodhisattva exist within the suchness of the earth element, up to and including the consciousness element?
“Is there suchness of the earth element up to the consciousness element within a bodhisattva?
Or, apart from the suchness of the earth element up to the consciousness element, is there a bodhisattva? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! Furthermore, Subhūti!"
What do you think?
Is the suchness of ignorance up to old age and death the bodhisattva?
Or is the bodhisattva something other than the suchness of ignorance up to old age and death?
Is there a bodhisattva within the suchness of ignorance up to old age and death?
Is there the suchness of ignorance up to old age and death within a bodhisattva?
Is there a bodhisattva apart from the suchness of ignorance up to old age and death?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "Subhūti, based on what meaning do you speak these words:

'That which is the suchness of form and so forth is not the bodhisattva; that which is other than the suchness of form and so forth is not the bodhisattva; there is no bodhisattva within the suchness of form and so forth; there is no suchness of form and so forth within the bodhisattva; nor is there a bodhisattva apart from the suchness of form and so forth'?"
Subhūti replied: “World-Honored One!
Since even phenomena such as form ultimately do not exist and cannot be apprehended, how much less could there be a *tathatā* (suchness) of form and so forth!”
Since this suchness is neither existent nor non-existent, how can it be said that the suchness of form and so forth is the bodhisattva,

that the suchness distinct from form and so forth is the bodhisattva, that the bodhisattva exists within the suchness of form and so forth, that the suchness of form and so forth exists within the bodhisattva, or that there is a bodhisattva apart from the suchness of form and so forth?
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “Excellent! Excellent!”
"It is as you have said.

Subhūti, you should know that because dharmas such as form (*rūpa*) are unapprehendable, the suchness (*tathatā*) of form and so forth is also unapprehendable. Because dharmas such as form and their suchness are unapprehendable, bodhisattvas are also unapprehendable; and because bodhisattvas are unapprehendable, the *prajñāpāramitā* they practice is also unapprehendable."
"Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should diligently train in this meaning.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"

Is the designation of the eye-element up to the mind-element, whether afflicted or purified, the bodhisattva?
"Are the eye-element up to the mind-element— whether they belong to saṃsāra or to nirvāṇa—
the designations for a bodhisattva? Subhūti replied, "No!"
“World-Honored One!
“Furthermore, Subhūti, what do you think?”
When one speaks of a "bodhisattva," is it the designation for the realm of form up to the realm of phenomena that is the bodhisattva?
Or is it the designation for the realm of form up to the realm of phenomena as being either permanent or impermanent that is the bodhisattva?
Is the designation of the form realm up to the dharma realm as either pleasure or pain the bodhisattva?

Is the designation "empty" or "not empty" regarding the realm of form up to the realm of phenomena the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation "whether with signs or signless" regarding the realm of form up to the realm of phenomena the Bodhisattva?

Is the designation "whether the realm of form up to the realm of phenomena is tranquil or not tranquil" the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation "whether the realm of form up to the realm of phenomena is detached or not detached" the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation of the form realm up to the dharma realm, whether conditioned or unconditioned, the bodhisattva?
Is the designation of the form realm up to the dharma realm, whether with outflows or without outflows, the bodhisattva?
Is the designation of the arising or the ceasing of the realm of form, up to and including the realm of phenomena, the bodhisattva?
Is the designation of the wholesome or the unwholesome of the realm of form, up to and including the realm of phenomena, the bodhisattva?
Is the designation "whether the realm of form up to the realm of phenomena has faults or is without faults" the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation "whether the realm of form up to the realm of phenomena has afflictions or is without afflictions" the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation of the form realm up to the dharma realm, whether mundane or supramundane, the bodhisattva?
Is the designation of the form realm up to the dharma realm, whether afflicted or purified, the bodhisattva?
"Is the designation 'belonging to saṃsāra' or 'belonging to nirvāṇa' applied to the realm of form,
up to and including the realm of phenomena, a bodhisattva? Subhūti replied, "No!"
“World-Honored One!
“Furthermore, Subhūti, what do you think?”
Regarding the term "bodhisattva," is it the designation for the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element that is the bodhisattva?
Or is it the designation for the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element as being either permanent or impermanent that is the bodhisattva?
Is the designation "pleasure" or "suffering" regarding the visual consciousness element up to the mental consciousness element the bodhisattva?
Is the designation "self" or "non-self" regarding the visual consciousness element up to the mental consciousness element the bodhisattva?
Is the designation "whether pure or impure" applied to the visual consciousness element up to the mental consciousness element the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation "whether empty or non-empty" applied to the visual consciousness element up to the mental consciousness element the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation "having signs" or "being signless" regarding the visual consciousness element up to the mental consciousness element the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation "having aspirations" or "being aspirationless" regarding the visual consciousness element up to the mental consciousness element the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation "pacified" or "not pacified" regarding the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation "detached" or "not detached" regarding the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation "conditioned" or "unconditioned" applied to the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation "with outflows" or "without outflows" applied to the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation "arising" or "ceasing" of the visual consciousness element up to the mental consciousness element the bodhisattva?
Is the designation "wholesome" or "unwholesome" of the visual consciousness element up to the mental consciousness element the bodhisattva?
Is the designation "whether the visual consciousness element up to the mental consciousness element is with fault or without fault" the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation "whether the visual consciousness element up to the mental consciousness element is with affliction or without affliction" the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation of the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element—whether mundane or supramundane—the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation of the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element—whether afflicted or purified—the Bodhisattva?
“Are the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element— whether they pertain to saṃsāra or to nirvāṇa—
the designations for a bodhisattva? Subhūti replied, “No!”
“World-Honored One!
Furthermore, Subhūti, what do you think?”
Regarding what is called a "bodhisattva": is the designation for eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact, the bodhisattva?
Is the designation for whether eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact, is permanent or impermanent, the bodhisattva?
Is the designation of eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact, as either pleasant or painful the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation of eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact, as either self or non-self the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation "whether pure or impure" applied to eye-contact through to mind-contact the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation "whether empty or non-empty" applied to eye-contact through to mind-contact the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation "with signs" or "signless" applied to eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact, the bodhisattva?
Is the designation "with aspiration" or "without aspiration" applied to eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact, the bodhisattva?
Is the designation "whether eye-contact through to mind-contact is tranquil or not tranquil" the bodhisattva?
Is the designation "whether eye-contact through to mind-contact is detached or not detached" the bodhisattva?
Is the designation of eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact, whether conditioned or unconditioned, the bodhisattva?
Is the designation of eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact, whether with outflows or without outflows, the bodhisattva?
Is the designation "arising" or "ceasing" of eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact, the bodhisattva?
Is the designation "wholesome" or "unwholesome" of eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact, the bodhisattva?
Is the designation "whether with fault or without fault" regarding eye-contact up to mind-contact the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation "whether with affliction or without affliction" regarding eye-contact up to mind-contact the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation for eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact—whether mundane or supramundane—the bodhisattva?
Is the designation for eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact—whether afflicted or purified—the bodhisattva?
"Are eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact— whether pertaining to saṃsāra or pertaining to nirvāṇa—
the designation for a bodhisattva? Subhūti replied, "No!"
“World-Honored One!
“Furthermore, Subhūti, what do you think?”

When one speaks of a "bodhisattva," is it a designation for the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition?

Are the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition—whether they be permanent or impermanent—the designations for a bodhisattva?
Is the designation "pleasant" or "painful" for all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including all feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation "self" or "non-self" for all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including all feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, the Bodhisattva?
Are the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including those produced with mind-contact as a condition—whether pure or impure—the designations for a bodhisattva?
Are those feelings born with eye-contact as condition, up to and including those feelings born with mind-contact as condition—whether they are designated as "empty" or "not empty"—the Bodhisattva?

Are those feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including those feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition—whether they possess signs or are signless—the designations for a bodhisattva?

Are those feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including those feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition—whether they are accompanied by aspiration or without aspiration—the designations for them "Bodhisattva"?

Are those feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including those feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition—whether they be tranquil or untranquil—the designations for a bodhisattva?

Are those feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including those feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition—whether they are detached or not detached—the designations for a bodhisattva?

Are the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, up to and including the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition—whether conditioned or unconditioned—the designations for a bodhisattva?

Are all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including all feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition—whether they are with outflows or without outflows—the designation "Bodhisattva"?

Is the designation "arising" or "ceasing" applied to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, the Bodhisattva?

Is the designation "wholesome" or "unwholesome" applied to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, the Bodhisattva?

Are those feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including those feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition—whether they are blameworthy or blameless—the designations for a bodhisattva?

Are those feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including those feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition—whether accompanied by afflictions or free from afflictions—the designations for a bodhisattva?
Are all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, up to and including all feelings produced with mind-contact as condition—whether mundane or supramundane—designations for a bodhisattva?

Are those feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including those feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition—whether defiled or purified—the designations for a bodhisattva?

Are those feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including those feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition—whether they pertain to saṃsāra or pertain to nirvāṇa—the designations for a bodhisattva?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
"Furthermore, Subhūti, what do you think?
Is that which is called 'bodhisattva' a designation for the earth element, up to and including the consciousness element?"
Is the designation "the earth element up to the consciousness element is permanent" or "the earth element up to the consciousness element is impermanent" the bodhisattva?
Is the designation "the earth element up to the consciousness element is pleasant" or "the earth element up to the consciousness element is suffering" the bodhisattva?
Is the designation "self" or "non-self" regarding the earth element up to the consciousness element the bodhisattva?
Is the designation "pure" or "impure" regarding the earth element up to the consciousness element the bodhisattva?
Is the designation "whether the earth element up to the consciousness element is empty or not empty" the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation "whether the earth element up to the consciousness element has signs or is signless" the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation "whether the element of earth, up to the element of consciousness, has a wish or is without a wish" the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation "whether the element of earth, up to the element of consciousness, is tranquil or not tranquil" the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation "whether the earth element up to the consciousness element is detached or not detached" the bodhisattva?
Is the designation "whether the earth element up to the consciousness element is conditioned or unconditioned" the bodhisattva?
Is the designation for the element of earth, up to and including the element of consciousness—whether with outflows or without outflows—the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation for the arising or the cessation of the element of earth, up to and including the element of consciousness, the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation "wholesome" or "unwholesome" applied to the element of earth, up to and including the element of consciousness, the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation "faulty" or "faultless" applied to the element of earth, up to and including the element of consciousness, the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation "whether with afflictions or without afflictions" applied to the element of earth, up to and including the element of consciousness, the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation "whether mundane or supramundane" applied to the element of earth, up to and including the element of consciousness, the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation "defiled" or "purified" regarding the element of earth up to the element of consciousness the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation "belonging to saṃsāra" or "belonging to nirvāṇa" regarding the element of earth up to the element of consciousness the Bodhisattva?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
"Furthermore, Subhūti, what do you think?
Is that which is called 'bodhisattva' a designation for ignorance up to old age and death?"
Is the designation "whether ignorance through old age and death are permanent or impermanent" the bodhisattva?
Is the designation "whether ignorance through old age and death are pleasant or painful" the bodhisattva?
Is the designation "self" or "non-self" regarding ignorance up to old age and death the bodhisattva?
Is the designation "pure" or "impure" regarding ignorance up to old age and death the bodhisattva?
Is the designation "whether ignorance through old age and death are empty or not empty" the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation "whether ignorance through old age and death have signs or are signless" the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation "whether ignorance up to old age and death involve aspiration or lack aspiration" the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation "whether ignorance up to old age and death are peaceful or not peaceful" the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation "whether one is detached from or not detached from ignorance up to old age and death" the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation "whether ignorance up to old age and death are conditioned or unconditioned" the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation of ignorance up to old age and death as either with outflows or without outflows the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation of ignorance up to old age and death as either arising or ceasing the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation "ignorance" up to "old age and death," whether wholesome or unwholesome, the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation "ignorance" up to "old age and death," whether faulty or faultless, the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation "whether there are afflictions or no afflictions" applied to ignorance up to old age and death the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation "whether worldly or supramundane" applied to ignorance up to old age and death the Bodhisattva?
Is the designation for ignorance up to old age and death, whether as defilement or as purification, the bodhisattva?
Is the designation for ignorance up to old age and death, whether as belonging to saṃsāra or as belonging to nirvāṇa, the bodhisattva?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Subhūti, based on what meaning do you speak these words:
'The designations for form and so forth are not the bodhisattva'?"
Furthermore, with what meaning in mind do they speak thus:
regarding the designations of form and other phenomena as either permanent or impermanent, as either pleasure or suffering,
as either self or non-self, as either pure or impure, or as either empty or non-empty?
Speech: whether it be the designation for the characterized or the uncharacterized, the designation for the with-vow or the vowless,
the designation for the tranquil or the non-tranquil, the designation for the secluded or the non-secluded,
the designation for the conditioned or the unconditioned, the designation for the out-flowing or the non-out-flowing, or [the designation for] arising.

Whether it be the designation "cessation," the designation "wholesome" or "unwholesome," the designation "blameworthy" or "blameless," the designation "with affliction" or "without affliction," the designation "worldly" or "transcendent," the designation "defiled" or "purified," or the designation "belonging to saṃsāra" or "belonging to nirvāṇa."
"Is it that the designation is not the Bodhisattva? Subhūti replied,
"World-Honored One!"
Since phenomena such as form ultimately do not exist and cannot be apprehended, how much less could there be a designative expression for form and so forth?
Since this designative expression does not exist, how can it be said that the designative expression "form and so forth" is a bodhisattva?
World-Honored One!

Since even dharmas such as form ultimately do not exist and cannot be apprehended, how much less could there be anything regarding form—whether it be permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, empty or non-empty, with signs or signless, with aspiration or aspirationless, tranquil or non-tranquil, detached or non-detached, conditioned or unconditioned, outflowing or non-outflowing, arising or ceasing, wholesome or unwholesome, faulty or faultless, afflicted or non-afflicted, mundane or supramundane, defiled or purified, or belonging to saṃsāra or belonging to nirvāṇa?

Since this [designation] does not exist, how much less could there be designations such as "permanent" or "impermanent" for phenomena like form, up to and including designations such as "belonging to saṃsāra" or "belonging to nirvāṇa"? Since these designations do not exist,

how can it be said that the designation "permanent or impermanent" for phenomena like form is a bodhisattva, or even that the designation "belonging to saṃsāra or belonging to nirvāṇa" is a bodhisattva?
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “Excellent! Excellent!”
"It is as you have said.

Subhūti, you should know that because phenomena such as form, as well as [the concepts of] permanence and impermanence, are unapprehendable, the designations for phenomena such as form, as well as the designations for permanence and impermanence, are also unapprehendable. Because both phenomena and their designations are unapprehendable, bodhisattvas are also unapprehendable. Because bodhisattvas are unapprehendable, the *prajñāpāramitā* they practice is also unapprehendable."
"Subhūti! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should diligently train in this meaning.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"
As for what you previously said— that "no dharma is seen that can be named a bodhisattva-mahāsattva"— it is so! It is so!
It is as you have said.
Subhūti, you should know this:
phenomena do not perceive the dharma-realm, the dharma-realm does not perceive phenomena, phenomena do not perceive phenomena, and the dharma-realm does not perceive the dharma-realm.
Subhūti, you should know this:
the realm of form does not see the dharma-realm, and the dharma-realm does not see the realm of form;

the realms of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not see the dharma-realm, and the dharma-realm does not see the realms of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Subhūti, you should know this:
the eye-consciousness element does not see the dharma-element, nor does the dharma-element see the eye-consciousness element;
the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements do not see the dharma-element, nor does the dharma-element see the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements.
The realm of form does not see the dharma-realm, and the dharma-realm does not see the realm of form;
the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, and phenomena do not see the dharma-realm, and the dharma-realm does not see the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, and phenomena.
The eye-consciousness element does not see the dharma-element, and the dharma-element does not see the eye-consciousness element;
the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements do not see the dharma-element, and the dharma-element does not see the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements.
Subhūti, you should know this:
the earth element does not perceive the dharma-element, nor does the dharma-element perceive the earth element;
the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements do not perceive the dharma-element, nor does the dharma-element perceive the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements.
"Subhūti, you should know this!
The conditioned realm does not perceive the unconditioned realm, and the unconditioned realm does not perceive the conditioned realm.
Subhūti, you should know this!"
Apart from the conditioned realm, the unconditioned realm cannot be designated; apart from the unconditioned realm, the conditioned realm cannot be designated.
"Thus it is, Subhūti!"

When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive any phenomena at all. Because they perceive nothing, their minds are neither startled, nor terrified, nor afraid; regarding all phenomena, their minds neither sink nor fall into sorrow or regret.
Why is that? Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices this profound perfection of wisdom in such a manner, they do not perceive form, nor do they perceive feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness.
They do not perceive the sense-base of the eye; they do not perceive the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
They do not perceive the sense-base of forms; they do not perceive the sense-bases of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena.
They do not perceive the eye-element; they do not perceive the elements of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
One does not perceive the realm of form; one does not perceive the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena.
One does not perceive the realm of eye-consciousness; one does not perceive the realms of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness.
One does not perceive the earth element; one does not perceive the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness.

One does not perceive ignorance; one does not perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, or aging-and-death.
One does not perceive desire-attachment; one does not perceive hatred or delusion.

One does not perceive a self; one does not perceive a sentient being, a life-principle, a soul, a nourisher, a spirit, a person, an individual, a mind-born, a youth, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, or a seer.
One does not perceive the desire realm, nor does one perceive the form or formless realms;

one does not perceive śrāvakas or the dharmas of śrāvakas, nor pratyekabuddhas or the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, nor bodhisattvas or the dharmas of bodhisattvas, nor Tathāgatas or the dharmas of Tathāgatas;
one does not perceive awakening, nor does one perceive nirvāṇa.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive any phenomena at all. When they do not perceive anything, their minds are neither startled, nor terrified, nor frightened; regarding all phenomena, their minds do not sink into despondency, nor do they feel regret.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), by what causes and conditions does their mind not sink into despondency nor feel regret regarding all phenomena?"
The Buddha said, “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they neither see nor apprehend any mind or mental factors whatsoever. For this reason, their minds do not sink or become despondent regarding any phenomena.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“For what reason and by what causal conditions do the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, have minds that are not startled, not terrified, and not afraid regarding all phenomena?”
The Buddha said,
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they neither see nor apprehend any mental element (*manodhātu*) or mental consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*).”
Thus it is, Subhūti!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, their minds are not startled, not terrified, and not afraid regarding all phenomena.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, seeing nothing and attaining nothing regarding all phenomena, should practice the perfection of wisdom."
That is to say: there is neither seeing nor obtaining of form; there is neither seeing nor obtaining of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
there is neither seeing nor obtaining of the sense-base of the eye; there is neither seeing nor obtaining of the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind;
there is neither seeing nor obtaining of the sense-base of forms; and there is neither seeing nor obtaining of the sense-bases of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena.
In the eye-element there is neither seeing nor attainment; in the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-elements there is neither seeing nor attainment.
In the form-element there is neither seeing nor attainment; in the sound, odor, taste, tangible, and mental-object-elements there is neither seeing nor attainment.
In the eye-consciousness-element there is neither seeing nor attainment; in the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness-elements there is neither seeing nor attainment.
One neither sees nor apprehends visual contact; one neither sees nor apprehends auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, or mental contact.

One neither sees nor apprehends the various feelings produced with visual contact as their condition; one neither sees nor apprehends the various feelings produced with auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, or mental contact as their conditions.
One neither sees nor apprehends the earth element; one neither sees nor apprehends the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements.

One neither perceives nor apprehends ignorance; one neither perceives nor apprehends volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, or old age and death.

One neither perceives nor apprehends the perfection of generosity; one neither perceives nor apprehends the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom. One neither perceives nor apprehends internal emptiness;

one neither perceives nor apprehends external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the limitless, the emptiness of non-dispersal, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-existence, or the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.

One neither sees nor attains true suchness; one neither sees nor attains the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-illusory nature, the unchanging nature, the state of equality, the state free from birth, the fixedness of dharma, the stability of dharma, or the limit of reality.

One neither sees nor attains the four foundations of mindfulness; one neither sees nor attains the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path.
One neither sees nor attains the noble truth of suffering; one neither sees nor attains the noble truths of origination, cessation, or the path.
One neither sees nor attains the four dhyānas; one neither sees nor attains the four immeasurables or the four formless absorptions;
one neither sees nor attains the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive absorptions, or the ten totalities;
one neither sees nor attains the gate of liberation of emptiness, nor the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.

Regarding all *dhāraṇī* gates, there is neither seeing nor attaining; regarding all *samādhi* gates, there is neither seeing nor attaining. Regarding the Ground of Extreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), there is neither seeing nor attaining;

regarding the Ground of Purity (*vimalā-bhūmi*), the Ground of Radiance (*prabhākārī-bhūmi*), the Ground of Blazing Wisdom (*arciṣmatī-bhūmi*), the Ground of Utmost Difficulty to Conquer (*sudurjayā-bhūmi*), the Ground of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), the Ground of Far-Going (*dūraṅgamā-bhūmi*), the Ground of Immovability (*acalā-bhūmi*), the Ground of Good Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*), and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), there is neither seeing nor attaining.
Regarding the five eyes, there is neither seeing nor attaining; regarding the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*), there is neither seeing nor attaining.

Regarding the ten powers of a Buddha, there is neither seeing nor attaining; regarding the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, there is neither seeing nor attaining;
regarding the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, there is neither seeing nor attaining; regarding the eighty minor marks, there is neither seeing nor attaining;
regarding the quality of non-forgetfulness, there is neither seeing nor attaining; regarding the nature of constant abiding in equanimity, there is neither seeing nor attaining.
One neither perceives nor apprehends all-knowledge; one neither perceives nor apprehends the knowledge of the paths or the knowledge of all aspects.
One neither perceives nor apprehends the fruit of stream-entry; one neither perceives nor apprehends the fruits of once-returner, non-returner, or arhatship.

One neither perceives nor apprehends the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; one neither perceives nor apprehends any of the practices of bodhisattva mahāsattvas; one neither perceives nor apprehends the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, seeing nothing and attaining nothing in regard to all phenomena, should practice the perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), at all places and at all times, they do not apprehend the perfection of wisdom, nor do they apprehend the name 'perfection of wisdom';
they do not apprehend the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, nor do they apprehend the name 'bodhisattva-mahāsattva'."
"Subhūti! You should instruct and advise all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in this way, so that they may reach the ultimate consummation in the perfection of wisdom."

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 483. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Three, Chapter on Subhūti, Section Three. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
If bodhisattvas wish to fulfill the perfection of generosity, they should study the perfection of wisdom;
if they wish to fulfill the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If bodhisattvas wish to fully know form, they should study the perfection of wisdom;
if they wish to fully know feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If bodhisattvas wish to fully know the sense base of the eye, they should study the perfection of wisdom;
if they wish to fully know the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If bodhisattvas wish to fully know the sphere of form, they should study the perfection of wisdom;
if they wish to fully know the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If bodhisattvas wish to fully know the eye-element, they should study the perfection of wisdom;
if they wish to fully know the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If bodhisattvas wish to fully know the realm of form, they should study the perfection of wisdom;
if they wish to fully know the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If bodhisattvas wish to fully know the eye-consciousness element, they should study the perfection of wisdom;
if they wish to fully know the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If bodhisattvas wish to fully know eye-contact, they should study the perfection of wisdom;
if they wish to fully know ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If bodhisattvas wish to fully know all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, they should study the perfection of wisdom;
if they wish to fully know all feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as condition, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
“If bodhisattvas wish to fully know the earth element, they should study the perfection of wisdom;
if they wish to fully know the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements, they should study the perfection of wisdom.”
If bodhisattvas wish to fully know ignorance, they should study the perfection of wisdom;

if they wish to fully know volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age and death, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If bodhisattvas wish to permanently sever desire, they should study the perfection of wisdom;
if they wish to permanently sever hatred and delusion, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If bodhisattvas wish to permanently sever the view of a personal identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā);

if they wish to permanently sever clinging to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa), doubt (vicikitsā), sensual desire (kāmarāga), and ill will (vyāpāda), they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If bodhisattvas wish to permanently sever craving for form, they should train in the perfection of wisdom;
if they wish to permanently sever craving for the formless, ignorance, pride, and restlessness, they should train in the perfection of wisdom.
“If bodhisattvas wish to forever sever all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and fetters (*paryavasthāna*), they should train in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
If bodhisattvas wish to forever sever the four kinds of nutriment (*āhāra*), they should train in the perfection of wisdom.”
If bodhisattvas wish to eternally sever the four yokes, the four floods, the four graspings, the four bodily fetters, and the four inversions, they should train in the perfection of wisdom.
If bodhisattvas wish to distance themselves from the ten unwholesome paths of action, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If bodhisattvas wish to undertake and practice the ten wholesome paths of action, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If bodhisattvas wish to fulfill the four dhyānas, they should study the perfection of wisdom;
if they wish to fulfill the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If bodhisattvas wish to fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness, they should study the perfection of wisdom;

if they wish to fulfill the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If bodhisattvas wish to fulfill the ten powers of a Buddha, they should study the perfection of wisdom;

if they wish to fulfill the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If bodhisattvas wish to enter with mastery the meditative concentration on the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-samādhi*), they should train in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

If bodhisattvas wish to enter with mastery the "Lion’s Play" (*siṃhavikrīḍita*) meditative concentration and even the "Lion’s Rush" (*siṃhavijṛmbhita*) meditative concentration, they should train in the perfection of wisdom.
If bodhisattvas wish to attain mastery over all dharani-doors and samadhi-doors, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
“If bodhisattvas wish [to master] the *gamanapratikrama-samādhi*, the *ratnamudrā-samādhi*, the *candraprabha-samādhi*,
the *candraketudhvaja-samādhi*, the *sarvadharmamudrāpraveśa-samādhi*,
the *avalokanamudrā-samādhi*, the *dharmadhātuniyata-samādhi*, the *niyatadhvajaketu-samādhi*, and the *vajropama-samādhi*...”
The Samādhi of Equality, the Samādhi of Entering All Dharma-Gates, the Samādhi of the King of Samādhis,
the Samādhi of the Royal Seal, the Samādhi of the Array of Powers, the Samādhi of the Jewel Casket, the Samādhi of Entering the Certainty of the Terminology of All Dharmas,
the Samādhi of Entering the Wisdom that Accepts All Dharmas, the Samādhi of Observing the Ten Directions, and the One...
The samādhi of the dhāraṇī-door of the seal of all phenomena, the samādhi of not forgetting all phenomena,
the samādhi of the seal of the marks of the practice leading to the equality of all phenomena, the samādhi of abiding in the realm of space, the samādhi of the purity of the three wheels,
the samādhi of non-retrogressive supernormal powers in accordance with [reality], the samādhi of emerging from within a vessel, and the supreme concentration.
One should study the *prajñāpāramitā* in order to attain mastery over the *samādhi* of the banner-sign, the *samādhi* of subduing afflictions,
the *samādhi* of destroying the four armies of Māra, the *samādhi* of accomplishing the ten powers, and all other immeasurable and boundless *samādhis*.
If bodhisattvas wish to fulfill the aspirations of all sentient beings, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If bodhisattvas wish to fulfill all supreme roots of virtue—by means of which, through their fulfillment, they do not fall into the evil destinies, are not born into lowly families, do not fall to the level of śrāvakas, do not fall to the level of pratyekabuddhas, and are certain not to fall from the summit of the bodhisattva path—they should study the perfection of wisdom.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti,
"What is meant by the 'summit-fall' of a bodhisattva? Subhūti replied:

"If bodhisattvas practice the six pāramitās without skillful means, and dwell in the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness without skillful means, they fall back into the stage of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha; they do not attain the bodhisattva's position of right determination, nor do they enter the bodhisattva's state of correct nature beyond birth. This is called the 'fall from the summit' of a bodhisattva."
Then Śāriputra asked Subhūti, "What dharma is called 'arising'? Subhūti replied:
"Birth refers to a bodhisattva’s attachment to the Dharma.
Śāriputra asked, "What is meant by a bodhisattva’s attachment to the Dharma?"

Subhūti replied: "If bodhisattvas, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, dwell upon the emptiness of form and give rise to conceptions and attachments; dwell upon the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness and give rise to conceptions and attachments;

dwell upon the signlessness of form and give rise to conceptions and attachments; dwell upon the signlessness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness and give rise to conceptions and attachments;"

They dwell upon the arising of perceptions regarding the wishlessness of form, and they dwell upon the arising of perceptions regarding the wishlessness of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness;

they dwell upon the arising of perceptions regarding the tranquility of form, and they dwell upon the arising of perceptions regarding the tranquility of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness;

they dwell upon the arising of perceptions regarding the seclusion of form, and they dwell upon the arising of perceptions regarding the seclusion of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.

Abiding in the impermanence of form, they give rise to perceptions and become attached; abiding in the impermanence of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, they give rise to perceptions and become attached.

Abiding in the suffering of form, they give rise to perceptions and become attached; abiding in the suffering of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, they give rise to perceptions and become attached.

Abiding in the selflessness of form, they give rise to perceptions and become attached; abiding in the selflessness of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, they give rise to perceptions and become attached.

Abiding in the impurity of form, they give rise to perceptions and become attached; abiding in the impurity of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, they give rise to perceptions and become attached. Śāriputra!
This is what constitutes a bodhisattva’s attachment to the Dharma in accordance with it;
this very attachment to the Dharma is said to be "birth. Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva should think thus:
"This form should be abandoned; because of this, form should be abandoned.
This feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness should be abandoned; because of this, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness should be abandoned."
"This suffering should be fully understood; for this reason, suffering should be fully understood.
This origin should be permanently abandoned; for this reason, the origin should be permanently abandoned.
This cessation should be realized; for this reason, cessation should be realized."
"This path should be cultivated; for this reason, the path should be cultivated.
This is affliction; this is purification.
This should be approached; this should not be approached."
"This should be practiced; this should not be practiced;
this is the path; this is not the path;
this should be cultivated; this should not be cultivated."
"This should be practiced; this should not be practiced.
This is the perfection of generosity; this is not the perfection of generosity.

This is the perfection of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; this is not the perfection of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom."
"This is the skillful means of a bodhisattva; this is not the skillful means of a bodhisattva.
This is the birth of a bodhisattva; this is the bodhisattva’s departure from birth."

"Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, dwells in these various dharma-gates and gives rise to conceptions or attachments toward them, this constitutes a bodhisattva’s compliance with craving for dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*); this very craving for dharmas is what is called 'birth.
Just as undigested food that has been consumed can become a source of affliction, because one eliminates this [craving], it is called 'leaving behind birth.'"
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"In what way is a bodhisattva mahāsattva said to have entered the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth? Subhūti replied:
