the concentration of gathering all merits, the concentration of abiding in certainty, the concentration of the pure exquisite flower, and the concentration of endowment...
The concentration of the factors of enlightenment, the concentration of boundless eloquence, the concentration of the unequaled, the concentration that transcends all,
the concentration of excellent discernment, the concentration of dispersing the net of doubt, the concentration of non-abiding,
the concentration of the adornment of a single characteristic, the concentration of manifesting the characteristics of practice, and the concentration of a single practice.
The samādhi of equanimity regarding the characteristics of formations; the samādhi of penetrating the transformations at the depths of all existences;
the samādhi of entering into all conventional designations and linguistic expressions; the samādhi of liberation from sounds and letters; the samādhi of possessing majestic power;
the samādhi of the blazing torch; the samādhi of the pure eye; the samādhi of unclouded patience; and the samādhi of entering into all conditioned phenomena.
The samādhi of equality, the samādhi of disliking all [other] samādhis, the samādhi of inexhaustible marks, the samādhi of possessing dhāraṇīs,
the samādhi of subduing all correct and false natures, the samādhi of being free from the favorable and the adverse,
the samādhi of being free from hatred and love, the samādhi of stainless clarity, the samādhi of possessing firmness, and the samādhi of fulfillment.
The samādhi of moon-pure light, the samādhi of lightning-flash eloquence, the samādhi of great adornment, the samādhi that illuminates all worlds,
the samādhi of equanimity of mind in meditative concentration, the samādhi of the principle of equality between the dustless and the dusty,
the samādhi of the principle of equality between the non-contentious and the contentious, and the samādhi of being without a nest.
The samādhi of being without signs, the samādhi of dwelling decisively in suchness, the samādhi of destroying misconduct of body,
speech, and mind, the samādhi that is like space, and the samādhi of non-attachment like space.
“Śāriputra! If bodhisattvas constantly abide in and do not forsake such supreme samādhis as these, they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

“Śāriputra! Furthermore, there are other immeasurable and innumerable gateways of samādhi and gateways of dhāraṇī; if bodhisattvas constantly train in these, they too will swiftly realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek.”
At that time, Subhūti, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, again addressed the Venerable Śāriputra:

“If bodhisattvas abide in such supreme samādhis, you should know that they have already received the prediction of enlightenment from the Buddhas of the past, and they shall also receive the prediction of enlightenment from the Buddhas of the present throughout the ten directions.”
“Śāriputra! Although these bodhisattvas abide in such samādhis, they do not perceive these samādhis, nor do they become attached to the names of these samādhis, nor do they think:
‘I have entered, am entering, or shall enter such samādhis.’”
Nor does he think: "Only I am able to enter these supreme meditative concentrations, and not others.
All such discursive thoughts and conceptualizations do not arise at all due to the power of those meditative concentrations.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"Is it certain that there are distinct bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who abide in such a supreme samādhi and have already received the prediction of enlightenment from the Buddhas of the past and present?"
Subhūti replied, “No, Śāriputra!”
Why is this? Śāriputra!

Whether it be the perfection of wisdom, or meditative concentration, or the bodhisattvas, there is no difference between them. The perfection of wisdom is itself meditative concentration, and meditative concentration is itself the bodhisattvas.
"Why is this? Because the nature of all phenomena is equal.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

"If samādhi is not different from the bodhisattva, and the bodhisattva is not different from samādhi—if samādhi is the bodhisattva and the bodhisattva is samādhi, because all dharmas are equal—then can these bodhisattvas manifest the very samādhi they have personally realized?"
Subhūti replied, “No, Śāriputra!”
Śāriputra asked, “Do these bodhisattvas form conceptualizations regarding samādhi? Subhūti replied:
"These bodhisattvas do not form conceptualizations or interpretations regarding their samādhis. Śāriputra asked:
"How is it that these bodhisattvas do not form conceptualizations or interpretations regarding their own samādhis?"
Subhūti replied, “Because these bodhisattvas are free from conceptual discrimination. Śāriputra said:
"Why is he without conceptual discrimination? Subhūti replied:
"Because these bodhisattvas know that all phenomena and all samādhis are non-existent; and within that which is non-existent, there is no possibility for conceptualization or understanding to arise."
At that time, the Bhagavān praised Subhūti, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
It is as you have said.

Therefore, I declare that among my assembly of śrāvakas, you are the foremost in abiding in the concentration of non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*); for this reason, my statement is consistent with the meaning, as there is no conflict or contention within the state of equality.

"In this way, Subhūti! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to train in the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity should train in this manner; those who wish to train in the applications of mindfulness up to the factors of the path should train in this manner; and those who wish to train in the ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha should train in this manner."
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, is he training correctly in the perfection of wisdom, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha?"
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they are training correctly in the perfection of wisdom up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method.”
Then, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, do they train in the perfection of wisdom up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha by taking non-apprehension as their means?”
The Buddha said:

“Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they do so by taking non-apprehension as the means, training in the perfection of wisdom up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.”
Śāriputra asked: “For one who has nothing to attain, what is it that cannot be attained?
The Buddha said:
“Śāriputra! That which is non-apprehensible means that a self is unapprehensible, up to and including a viewer, because it is ultimately pure;
the aggregates, bases, elements, and dependent origination are unapprehensible, because they are ultimately pure.”
The desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm are unapprehendable because they are ultimately pure;
the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path are unapprehendable because they are ultimately pure;
and the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are unapprehendable because they are ultimately pure.
From generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, these are unapprehendable because they are ultimately pure;
from the stream-enterer up to the pratyekabuddha, these are unapprehendable because they are ultimately pure;
and the bodhisattva, the enlightenment of the Buddhas, and nirvāṇa are unapprehendable because they are ultimately pure.
Śāriputra asked: "What is the meaning of 'ultimate purity'?
The Buddha said:

“Śāriputra! That all phenomena are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity, without emergence and without disappearance, and without attainment and unconditioned—this is called the meaning of ultimate purity.”
Then Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When bodhisattvas train in this manner, in what dharma do they train?
The Buddha said:
“Śāriputra! When bodhisattvas train in this manner, they do not train in anything at all regarding phenomena. Why is that?
"Śāriputra! All phenomena do not exist in the manner that foolish, ordinary worldlings grasp them; one should train within this [understanding]. Śāriputra said:
“If that is so, how do all phenomena exist?
The Buddha said:
“All phenomena exist in the manner of non-existence; if one cannot thoroughly comprehend such phenomena as being non-existent, this is called ignorance.”
Śāriputra asked: "What dharma is non-existent, such that failing to comprehend it is called ignorance?
The Buddha said:

“Śāriputra! Form up to consciousness does not exist; likewise, everything up to the four foundations of mindfulness and up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha does not exist, because of internal emptiness and so forth, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.”
Śāriputra! That foolish common person cannot penetrate such non-existent phenomena; this is called ignorance (*avidyā*).

Driven by the power of ignorance and craving, they conceptually cling to the two extremes of annihilation and permanence, and because of this, they neither know nor see the non-existent nature of all phenomena, but instead conceptualize them.

Due to conceptualization, one becomes attached to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. Because of this attachment, one conceptualizes all phenomena as being of a non-existent nature; consequently, one neither knows nor sees these phenomena.
Śāriputra asked: "Regarding what dharmas are they neither known nor seen?
The Buddha said:

“Śāriputra! Not knowing and not seeing form, up to and including consciousness; likewise, not knowing and not seeing the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.”
"Because they neither know nor see all phenomena, they fall among the ranks of foolish commoners and are unable to transcend them.
Śāriputra asked, "In what respect are they unable to transcend?"
The Buddha said,
“Śāriputra! They are unable to transcend the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm.”

Because one cannot transcend the three realms, one is unable to accomplish the dharmas of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and all Buddhas; even if one were able to transcend the three realms, one would still not be able to transcend the two vehicles, and for this reason, one cannot have faith-understanding in the profound Dharma.
Śāriputra asked: "In what profound dharma are they unable to have faith and understanding?
The Buddha said:

“Śāriputra! They are unable to have faith and understanding in the emptiness of form, up to the emptiness of consciousness; likewise, they are unable to have faith and understanding in the emptiness of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.”
Because they cannot believe in or understand the emptiness of the subject that perceives and the object that is perceived, they are unable to abide in the dharmas in which they ought to train.
Śāriputra asked: “In what training are they unable to abide?”
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!

They are unable to abide in anything from the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, nor can they abide in the stage of non-retrogression or in other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas. For this reason, they are called foolish ordinary beings (*bāla-pṛthagjana*), because they cling to the existence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in all phenomena—namely, clinging to form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness; the sense bases from the eye base up to the mind base; the sense objects from the form base up to the mental-object base; the elements from the eye element up to the mind-consciousness element; greed, hatred, delusion, and various views; and even the foundations of mindfulness up to enlightenment and nirvāṇa—they maintain that all these possess intrinsic nature.”
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,

is it possible that there might be a bodhisattva who trains in such a way, yet does not train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and thus fails to accomplish the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñājñāna)?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“There are bodhisattvas who train in such a manner that they do not train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) and are unable to accomplish the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).”
Śāriputra asked, “In what way does a bodhisattva train in such a manner that they are not training in the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha said:
“Śāriputra! If bodhisattvas lack skillful means and conceptually cling to the perfection of wisdom, up to conceptually clinging to the perfection of generosity;
if they conceptually cling to the four foundations of mindfulness, up to conceptually clinging to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha;”
They conceptually discriminate and cling to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

For this reason, there are bodhisattvas who train in such a manner; they are not training in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and cannot accomplish the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Śāriputra said: "When these bodhisattvas train in this way, are they not certainly training in the perfection of wisdom, and will they not be able to accomplish the knowledge of all aspects?"
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!
When these bodhisattvas train in this manner, they are certainly not training in the perfection of wisdom, and they will be unable to accomplish the knowledge of all modes.”

Śāriputra asked: "How does a bodhisattva practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and by training in this perfection of wisdom, how does one, when so training, become able to accomplish the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna)?"
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!

If bodhisattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor do they perceive anything up to and including all-aspect knowledge (sarvākārajñatā). When bodhisattvas practice the perfection of wisdom in this way, they are training in the perfection of wisdom; training in this manner, they are able to accomplish the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), by means of taking non-apprehension as their skillful method.”
Śāriputra asked: “By means of the non-apprehension of what phenomena do these bodhisattvas employ skillful means?
The Buddha said:

“Śāriputra! When these bodhisattvas practice the perfection of generosity, they do so by means of non-apprehension of the perfection of generosity; likewise, when they practice up to the perfection of wisdom, they do so by means of non-apprehension of the perfection of wisdom; even when seeking awakening, they do so by means of non-apprehension of awakening; and even when seeking the knowledge of all aspects, they do so by means of non-apprehension of the knowledge of all aspects.”
Śāriputra said: "When these bodhisattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, by means of what non-apprehension do they employ skillful means?"
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra,

when these bodhisattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do so by means of the non-apprehension of internal emptiness (adhyātma-śūnyatā), up to and including the non-apprehension of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence (abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā).”
"By means of these causes and conditions, one will swiftly be able to accomplish the knowledge of all modes.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Suppose someone were to come and ask this question:

"If those who are like magical illusions were to train in the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity, and train in the applications of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, would they be able to accomplish the knowledge of all modes?"
“World-Honored One!
When I encounter this question, how should I answer it?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“I ask you further; answer as you see fit. What do you think?
Is there any difference between form up to consciousness and a magical illusion?”
Are the sense bases from the eye base up to the mind base different from a magical illusion?
Are the sense bases from the form base up to the mental phenomena base different from a magical illusion?
Is the eye-element, up to and including the mind-element, different from that which is conjured by illusion?
Is the form-element, up to and including the phenomena-element, different from that which is conjured by illusion?
Is the visual consciousness element, up to and including the mental consciousness element, different from a magical illusion?
Are visual contact, up to and including mental contact, different from a magical illusion?
Are the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including those produced with mind-contact as a condition, different from a magical illusion?
Are the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including the eightfold noble path, different from a magical illusion?
Are the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—different from a magical illusion?
Are the perfection of generosity up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha different from a magical illusion?
“Is the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas different from a magical illusion? Subhūti replied, “No!”
World-Honored One!

Why is this? Form is not different from illusion, and illusion is not different from form; form is itself illusion, and illusion is itself form. This is likewise true even up to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Do those who are like magical illusions have defilement or purification?"
"Is there arising and ceasing? Subhūti replied, "No!"
"World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?"

If dharmas are without defilement or purity, and without arising or ceasing, can such dharmas study the *prajñāpāramitā* up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), and thereby accomplish the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*)?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Within the five aggregates, does one give rise to a perception, a conceptualization, a designation, or a verbal expression, and thereby provisionally name it a 'bodhisattva mahāsattva'?"
Subhūti replied, “So it is, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?

Within the five aggregates, can one find anything that arises and ceases, or anything that is defiled or purified, by means of conceptualization, perception, designation, verbal expression, or conventional establishment?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?

If a dharma is without perception, without equal perception, without designation, without verbal expression, without conventional name, without body or bodily action, without speech or vocal action, without mind or mental action, without arising or ceasing, and without defilement or purification—could such a dharma study the perfection of wisdom and accomplish the knowledge of all modes?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If bodhisattvas, by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method, practice and study this profound perfection of wisdom, they will certainly be able to accomplish the knowledge of all modes."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If bodhisattvas wish to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) like an illusory person."
"Why is that? You should know that the illusory person is none other than the five aggregates.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“What do you think?
Can the five aggregates, which are like an illusion, study the perfection of wisdom and accomplish the knowledge of all aspects? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! Why is this? Because..."
"The five aggregates, which are like an illusion, have non-substantiality as their intrinsic nature, because an intrinsic nature that is non-substantial cannot be apprehended.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?"

Can one who studies the *prajñāpāramitā* and accomplish the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*) by means of the five aggregates that are like a dream, like an echo, like a reflection in light, like a mirage, like a mirror-image, or like a magical transformation?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
Why is this? Because from echoes up to the five aggregates of transformation, they have non-existence as their intrinsic nature; for an intrinsic nature of non-existence cannot be apprehended.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Do the five aggregates, such as the illusory one, each have a distinct nature? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! Why is this? Because..."

Since illusory forms and so forth are identical to dream-like forms up to transformation-like forms, the five aggregates and the six sense faculties likewise possess no distinct nature; thus, all these are unapprehendable in their intrinsic nature because of the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If bodhisattvas who have newly set out in the Great Vehicle hear this teaching of such profound prajñāpāramitā, will their minds not become startled, terrified, or afraid?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If bodhisattvas who have newly set out in the Great Vehicle practice the perfection of wisdom, yet lack skillful means and are not sustained by virtuous friends, their minds will be startled, terrified, and frightened upon hearing this teaching of the profound perfection of wisdom.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"What kind of bodhisattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, possesses skillful means such that, upon hearing this profound perfection of wisdom being taught, their mind is not startled, not terrified, and not afraid?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If bodhisattvas, with a mental orientation corresponding to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), contemplate that from form (*rūpa*) up to consciousness (*vijñāna*)—their impermanence, suffering, selflessness, impurity, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, tranquility, and detachment—are likewise unapprehendable, these bodhisattvas are practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Because they possess skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), when they hear this profound perfection of wisdom being taught, their minds are not startled, not terrified, and not afraid."
"Furthermore, Subhūti! If bodhisattvas, having made this observation, further think:

'I shall, by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, teach all sentient beings that these five aggregates are impermanent, and so on, up to the fact that even their characteristic of being detached is unapprehendable.'"
This is the bodhisattva’s unattached perfection of generosity. Furthermore, Subhūti,

if bodhisattvas do not attend to the mental orientations of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, and contemplate the five aggregates as impermanent, up to their being characterized by detachment, yet find them ultimately unapprehendable— by means of this non-apprehension— it is the bodhisattva’s unattached perfection of ethical discipline.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If bodhisattvas, employing the method of non-apprehension, practice the perfection of wisdom and contemplate that from the earth element up to the consciousness element—all are impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self—they should not harbor resentment but should instead practice patience; this is the bodhisattva’s perfection of unattached patience."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If bodhisattvas, with a mental orientation corresponding to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), observe that from form (*rūpa*) up to consciousness (*vijñāna*)—from their impermanence up to their characteristic of being detached—they are likewise unapprehendable; and though they employ non-apprehension as their means, they never abandon the mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes while diligently cultivating all wholesome dharmas: this is the bodhisattva’s perfection of diligence (*vīryapāramitā*) free from attachment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If bodhisattvas do not intermingle their pure mental attention as bodhisattvas with the mental attention of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor with other unwholesome, distracted states of mind, this is the bodhisattva’s perfection of meditative concentration free from attachment."

“Furthermore, Subhūti! When bodhisattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they observe according to reality that it is not because form is empty that form is said to be empty; rather, form itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is form. It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

It is likewise for the sense bases from the eye base up to the mind base; the objects of the senses from the form base up to the phenomena base; the elements from the eye element up to the mind element; the elements of consciousness from the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element; the contacts from eye-contact up to mind-contact; the feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition up to the feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition; and the four applications of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. This is the bodhisattva’s unattached perfection of wisdom.”

"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this way, because they possess skillful means, their mind is not startled, alarmed, or terrified upon hearing this profound perfection of wisdom being taught."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is it that a bodhisattva, being sustained and protected by virtuous friends, hears this profound perfection of wisdom being taught without his mind being startled, terrified, or afraid?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Those who are the good friends of bodhisattvas are those who, employing the method of non-apprehension, teach that from form through consciousness, the characteristics of impermanence, suffering, selflessness, impurity, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, tranquility, and detachment are also unapprehendable; they teach that from the eye through the mind, the characteristics of impermanence up to detachment are also unapprehendable;
and they teach that from form through mental phenomena (*dharma*), the characteristics of impermanence up to detachment are also unapprehendable."
To say that the characteristics of impermanence up to the characteristic of detachment regarding eye-consciousness up to mental-consciousness are also unapprehendable;

and to say that the characteristics of impermanence up to the characteristic of detachment regarding eye-contact up to mental-contact are also unapprehendable, while encouraging one to diligently cultivate roots of virtue based on this, dedicating them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment rather than toward the levels of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas—one should know such a person to be a virtuous friend of a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Those who are the good friends of bodhisattvas are those who, employing the method of non-apprehension, teach that the cultivation of the four applications of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path is unapprehendable;
they teach that the cultivation of the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—is unapprehendable."
To teach that the cultivation of the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha is unattainable;

to teach that the cultivation of all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is unattainable, yet to exhort one to diligently cultivate roots of virtue based upon these, dedicating them toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment rather than toward the levels of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas—one should know such a person to be a bodhisattva’s spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

“Subhūti! If bodhisattvas are sustained and protected by such virtuous friends, their minds will not be startled, terrified, or frightened upon hearing this teaching of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.”
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“How is it that a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, due to a lack of skillful means, becomes startled, terrified, and afraid upon hearing this teaching of the profound perfection of wisdom?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If bodhisattvas, employing the method of apprehending something as real, depart from the mental attention directed toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā-jñāna*), and practice the perfections from generosity up to wisdom, they will have apprehension and reliance regarding what they practice;

employing the method of apprehending something as real, they depart from the mental attention directed toward omniscience and contemplate form up to consciousness, inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature, and they will have apprehension and reliance regarding their contemplation of these emptinesses."

Taking "attainment" as their means, they contemplate the eye up to the mind; they contemplate forms up to mental phenomena (*dharma*); they contemplate eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness; they contemplate eye-contact up to mind-contact; they contemplate the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition; they contemplate inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature (*abhāvasvabhāvaśūnyatā*). While contemplating these emptinesses, they have attainment and reliance.

Taking "attainment" as their means, they depart from the mental attention directed toward the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), and they practice the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, having attainment and reliance regarding what they practice.

"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this way, because they lack skillful means, their mind becomes startled, terrified, and afraid upon hearing this profound perfection of wisdom being taught."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“How is it that a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, having been led astray by evil associates, feels alarm, fear, and terror upon hearing this teaching of the profound perfection of wisdom?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Those who are evil friends to bodhisattvas are those who teach them to become weary of and detached from the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity, saying: ‘Good son!...’”
"You should not train yourselves in this. Why is that?

These six perfections were not spoken by the Buddha; they are fabrications created by poets out of falsehood. Therefore, you should not listen to them, study them, recite them, uphold them, contemplate them, investigate them, or explain them to others."
"You should know that such a person is an evil friend of a bodhisattva. Furthermore, Subhūti,
those who are evil friends of bodhisattvas are those who do not explain for them the deeds of Māra or the faults of Māra."
That is to say, there may be an evil Māra who assumes the form of a Buddha and comes to instruct a bodhisattva to become weary of and detached from the six perfections, saying:
"O son of good family!..."
"What is the use of practicing these pāramitās?

Furthermore, an evil Māra may manifest in the form of a Buddha and come to the bodhisattva to proclaim and reveal the teachings associated with the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—namely, from the sūtras up to the upadeśas—analyzing and clarifying them so that [the bodhisattva] will focus exclusively on their practice and study.
"Furthermore, an evil Māra may assume the form of a Buddha and come to where the bodhisattva is, saying these words:

'You are not a bodhisattva; you lack the mind of awakening (bodhicitta); you cannot abide in the stage of non-retrogression, nor can you realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening that you seek.'"
"Furthermore, an evil Māra may assume the form of a Buddha and go to where the Bodhisattva is, saying these words:
'O Son of Good Family!'"

Form up to consciousness is empty, without self, and without what belongs to a self; the eye up to the mind is empty, without self, and without what belongs to a self; form up to mental phenomena (*dharma*) is empty, without self, and without what belongs to a self; eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness is empty, without self, and without what belongs to a self; eye-contact up to mind-contact is empty, without self, and without what belongs to a self; the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition are empty, without self, and without what belongs to a self; the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom is empty, without self, and without what belongs to a self; the four applications of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are empty, without self, and without what belongs to a self—what use is there for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
"Furthermore, there may be an evil Māra who assumes the form of a Pratyekabuddha and approaches the Bodhisattva, saying:
'O Son of Good Family!

All Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the assembly of Śrāvakas throughout the worlds of the ten directions are entirely empty. You should have deep faith and acceptance in this matter; do not exert yourself in toil to seek offerings, to hear the True Dharma, or to practice according to its teachings.'"

"Furthermore, there may be an evil Māra who assumes the form of a śrāvaka and approaches the bodhisattva, causing him to develop a deep sense of weary detachment toward the mental engagement associated with omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), and instead inciting him to diligently cultivate and study the mental engagements associated with the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."

Furthermore, there may be an evil Māra who assumes the form of a preceptor or a teacher and approaches the Bodhisattva, causing him to feel deep revulsion for the sublime practices of a Bodhisattva—namely, the six perfections—and causing him to feel revulsion for the knowledge of all modes, namely, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. Instead, he instructs him only to diligently cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth, leading him to quickly realize the enlightenment of the two vehicles and causing him to abandon the sought-after fruit of the Unsurpassed Vehicle.
Furthermore, there may be an evil Māra who assumes the form of one's father or mother and approaches the Bodhisattva, saying:
"Child! Child!"

"You should diligently strive to realize the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship; this is sufficient to bring about eternal liberation from the great suffering of birth and death. What need have you for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"

Those who seek Bodhi must pass through immeasurable and incalculable great kalpas, cycling through birth and death to transform sentient beings; they cast away their bodies and lives and sever their hands and feet—this is merely self-inflicted toil and hardship, so who can bear your kindness?
"The enlightenment sought may or may not be attained.
Furthermore, an evil Māra assumes the form of a bhikṣu and approaches the bodhisattva;
using the notion of "attainment" as a means, he teaches that from form up to consciousness there are the characteristics of impermanence, suffering, and non-self.

The characteristic of signs, the characteristic of impurity, the characteristic of emptiness, the characteristic of signlessness, the characteristic of wishlessness, the characteristic of tranquility, and the characteristic of detachment can be truly apprehended;
it is said that from the eye up to the mind, the characteristics of impermanence up to detachment can be truly apprehended;
and it is said that from form up to mental phenomena (*dharma*), the characteristics of impermanence up to detachment [can be truly apprehended].

The reality of the signless can be apprehended; it is said that from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness, the reality of the characteristics of impermanence up to the characteristic of detachment can be apprehended;
it is said that from eye-contact up to mind-contact, the reality of the characteristics of impermanence up to the characteristic of detachment can be apprehended;
and it is said regarding all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to...
The various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition possess characteristics ranging from impermanence to detachment that can be truly apprehended;

by using such apprehension as a skillful means, he teaches that the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha can be truly apprehended, leading them to practice and train therein.
If one does not explain such matters as these to cause awakening, you should know that this person is a bad friend of the bodhisattva. "Subhūti!

If bodhisattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom are led astray by such bad friends, their minds will be startled, terrified, and afraid when they hear this profound perfection of wisdom being taught."

Therefore, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should carefully examine and skillfully distance themselves from all evil associates; lest by associating with them, they should cause their bodhicitta to regress, abandon the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and fail to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 485. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Three, Chapter on Subhūti, Section Five. At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Regarding what has been called a 'bodhisattva-mahāsattva,' what is the meaning of the term 'bodhisattva'?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“The meaning of ‘bodhisattva’ is the meaning of ‘no-meaning. Why is this?
"Subhūti! Awakening is non-arising and sentient beings do not exist; because no logical basis for a term can be found therein, the meaning of 'no term' is the meaning of the term 'bodhisattva'."
“Subhūti! For example, just as there is truly no trace of a bird in the sky, so too is the meaning of the term ‘bodhisattva’ truly non-existent. Subhūti!”
For example, just as the objects of a dream do not exist in reality, so too the meaning of the term "bodhisattva" does not exist in reality. "Subhūti!
For example, just as a magical illusion does not exist in reality, so too the meaning of the term 'bodhisattva' does not exist in reality."
“Subhūti! For example, a mirage has no real existence; likewise, the referent of the term ‘bodhisattva’ also has no real existence. Subhūti!”
For example, just as light, shadow, echoes, reflections, and transformations have no real existence, so too the meaning of the term "bodhisattva" has no real existence. "Subhūti!..."
For example, just as the referent of the term "suchness" (tathatā) is in reality non-existent, so too is the referent of the term "bodhisattva" in reality non-existent. Subhūti!
For example, just as the referent of the term "dharma-realm" (dharmadhātu) is in reality non-existent, so too is the referent of the term "bodhisattva" in reality non-existent.
“Subhūti! For example, just as the referent of the term ‘dharmatā’ truly does not exist, so too the referent of the term ‘bodhisattva’ truly does not exist. Subhūti!”

For example, just as the nature of non-falsity, the nature of non-alteration, sameness, the nature of being free from birth, the fixed nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), and the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) are in truth non-existent, so too the referent of the term "bodhisattva" is likewise in truth non-existent.

“Subhūti! For example, just as the referential meaning of the term ‘form’ up to the referential meaning of the term ‘consciousness’ does not exist in reality, so too the referential meaning of the term ‘bodhisattva’ does not exist in reality.”

“Subhūti! For example, just as the referential meaning of the sense-base of the eye, up to the referential meaning of the sense-base of the mind, does not exist in reality, so too the referential meaning of a bodhisattva does not exist in reality.”

“Subhūti! For example, just as the referential meaning of the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) up to the referential meaning of the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) truly does not exist for an illusory person, so too the referential meaning of a bodhisattva truly does not exist.”

“Subhūti! For example, just as the referential meaning of the term ‘eye-element’ up to the referential meaning of the term ‘mind-element’ truly does not exist for an illusory person, so too the referential meaning of the term ‘bodhisattva’ truly does not exist.”

“Subhūti! For example, just as the referents of the terms for the realm of form, up to the referents of the terms for the dharma-realm, do not exist in reality, so too the referent of the term ‘bodhisattva’ does not exist in reality.”

"Subhūti! For example, just as the referential meaning of the eye-consciousness element, up to the referential meaning of the mind-consciousness element, does not exist in reality, so too the referential meaning of 'bodhisattva' does not exist in reality."

“Subhūti! For example, just as the referential meaning of eye-contact, up to and including the referential meaning of mind-contact, does not exist in reality for an illusory person, so too the referential meaning of a bodhisattva does not exist in reality.”

“Subhūti! For example, just as the referential meaning of all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to the referential meaning of all feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, does not exist in reality, so too the referential meaning of a bodhisattva does not exist in reality.”

"Subhūti! For example, just as the referential meaning of the term 'earth element' up to the referential meaning of the term 'consciousness element' does not exist in reality, so too the referential meaning of the term 'bodhisattva' does not exist in reality."

“Subhūti! For example, just as the referents of the terms from ignorance up to old age and death do not exist in reality for an illusory person, so too the referent of the term ‘bodhisattva’ does not exist in reality.”

“Subhūti! For example, just as the referents of the phrases from ‘inner emptiness’ up to ‘the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence’ practiced by an illusory person do not exist in reality, so too the referent of the term ‘bodhisattva’ does not exist in reality.”

“Subhūti! For example, the referential meaning of the four foundations of mindfulness, up to the referential meaning of the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, as practiced by an illusory person, truly does not exist; likewise, the referential meaning of a bodhisattva also truly does not exist.”

“Subhūti! For example, just as the referential meaning of the marks of form up to the referential meaning of the marks of consciousness belonging to a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha truly does not exist, so too, when Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas practice the profound Prajñāpāramitā, the referential meaning of ‘Bodhisattva’ likewise truly does not exist.”

“Subhūti! For example, just as the meaning of the characteristics and phrases of the sense-base of the eye, up to the meaning of the characteristics and phrases of the sense-base of the mind, belonging to a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, truly does not exist at all, so too, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, the meaning of the term ‘Bodhisattva’ likewise truly does not exist at all.”

“Subhūti! For example, just as the sign, phrase, and meaning of the form-base (rūpāyatana), up to the sign, phrase, and meaning of the phenomena-base (dharmāyatana), truly do not exist for a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, so too, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), the meaning of the term ‘Bodhisattva’ likewise truly does not exist.”

“Subhūti! For example, just as the characteristics, terms, and meanings of the eye-element, up to and including the mind-element, of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha do not truly exist, so too, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, the term ‘Bodhisattva’ likewise does not truly exist.”

“Subhūti! For example, just as the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has no real existence whatsoever in the sign-terms and meanings of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), up to and including the sign-terms and meanings of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), so too, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the sign-term ‘Bodhisattva’ likewise has no real existence whatsoever.”

"Subhūti! For example, just as the characteristics, phrases, and meanings of the visual consciousness element, up to and including the mental consciousness element, truly do not exist for a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, so too, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound Prajñāpāramitā, the phrase 'Bodhisattva' likewise truly does not exist."

“Subhūti! For example, just as the meaning of the phrase regarding the characteristic of eye-contact, up to the meaning of the phrase regarding the characteristic of mind-contact, truly does not exist for a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, so too, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound Prajñāpāramitā, the meaning of the phrase ‘Bodhisattva’ likewise truly does not exist.”

“Subhūti! For example, just as the characteristics, phrases, and meanings of all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition—and even those produced with mind-contact as a condition—belonging to a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, do not exist in reality; so too, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound Prajñāpāramitā, the meaning of the term ‘Bodhisattva’ likewise does not exist in reality.”

“Subhūti! For example, just as the meaning of the characteristics and terms of the earth element, up to the meaning of the characteristics and terms of the consciousness element, does not exist at all in reality, so too, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, the meaning of the term ‘bodhisattva’ likewise does not exist at all in reality.”

“Subhūti! For example, just as the meaning of the term ‘ignorance’ up to the meaning of the term ‘old age and death’ truly does not exist for a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, so too, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound Prajñāpāramitā, the meaning of the term ‘Bodhisattva’ likewise truly does not exist.”

“Subhūti! For example, just as the referential meaning of the characteristics of the emptiness of internal phenomena, up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, belonging to a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, truly does not exist; so too, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound Prajñāpāramitā, the referential meaning of ‘Bodhisattva’ likewise truly does not exist.”

“Subhūti! For example, just as the meaning of the signs and phrases of the four foundations of mindfulness, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, belonging to a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, truly does not exist, so too, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, the meaning of the term ‘Bodhisattva’ likewise truly does not exist.”

“Subhūti! For example, within the unconditioned realm (asaṃskṛtadhātu), the referential meaning of the term ‘conditioned realm’ (saṃskṛtadhātu) truly does not exist; likewise, within the conditioned realm, the referential meaning of the term ‘unconditioned realm’ also truly does not exist. When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), the referential meaning of the term ‘Bodhisattva’ is likewise truly non-existent.”

"Subhūti! For example, just as the referents of 'non-arising,' 'non-ceasing,' 'unconditioned,' 'uncreated,' 'non-formation,' 'non-destruction,' 'non-attainment,' 'non-relinquishment,' 'non-defilement,' and 'non-purity' are in reality non-existent, so too, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, the referent of 'bodhisattva' is likewise in reality non-existent."
"Why is this so? Subhūti!

For example, just as the meaning of the phrases from 'form' through 'consciousness'—up to the meaning of the phrases 'without arising and without ceasing,' and even 'without defilement and without purification'—is truly non-existent, so too is the meaning of the term 'bodhisattva' for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas when they practice the profound perfection of wisdom; it is likewise truly non-existent."

“Subhūti! For example, just as the meaning of the phrases from ‘the sense-base of the eye’ up to ‘the sense-base of the mind,’ and even the meaning of the phrases from ‘non-arising and non-ceasing’ up to ‘non-defilement and non-purity,’ truly do not exist at all; so too, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, the meaning of the phrase ‘bodhisattva’ likewise truly does not exist at all.”

“Subhūti! For example, just as the meaning of the phrases regarding the non-arising and non-ceasing of the sense-sphere of form up to the sense-sphere of phenomena, and even the meaning of the phrases regarding their being neither defiled nor pure, truly does not exist at all; so too, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, the meaning of the phrase ‘bodhisattva’ likewise truly does not exist at all.”

"Subhūti! For example, just as the meaning of the phrases from 'the eye-element' up to 'the mind-element,' and even the meaning of the phrases from 'non-arising and non-ceasing' up to 'non-defilement and non-purification,' truly do not exist at all; so too, Subhūti, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, the meaning of the phrase 'bodhisattva' likewise truly does not exist at all."

“Subhūti! For example, just as the referents of the phrases from ‘the non-arising and non-ceasing of form up to the dharma-realm’ to ‘the non-defilement and non-purification’ truly do not exist, so too, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, the referent of the phrase ‘bodhisattva’ likewise truly does not exist.”

“Subhūti! For example, just as the meaning of the phrases from ‘the eye-consciousness element’ up to ‘the mind-consciousness element,’ and even the meaning of the phrases from ‘non-arising and non-ceasing’ up to ‘non-defilement and non-purity,’ truly do not exist at all; so too, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the meaning of the phrase ‘bodhisattva’ likewise truly does not exist at all.”

“Subhūti! For example, just as the meaning of the phrases from ‘the non-arising and non-ceasing of eye-contact’ up to ‘the non-defilement and non-purification of mind-contact’ truly does not exist, so too, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, the meaning of the phrase ‘bodhisattva’ likewise truly does not exist.”

“Subhūti! For example, just as the state of being without arising and without cessation, up to the state of being without defilement and without purification, regarding all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to all feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, truly does not exist; so too, Subhūti, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term ‘bodhisattva’ likewise truly does not exist.”

“Subhūti! Just as the elements from the earth element up to the consciousness element have no such thing as a phrase or meaning of non-arising and non-cessation, up to and including the phrase or meaning of non-defilement and non-purity, so too, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, the phrase or meaning of ‘bodhisattva’ likewise has no such thing as a real existence.”

“Subhūti! For example, just as the meaning of the phrases from ‘ignorance’ up to ‘old age and death,’ and even the meaning of the phrases from ‘neither arising nor ceasing’ up to ‘neither defilement nor purification,’ truly do not exist at all; so too, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, the meaning of the phrase ‘bodhisattva’ likewise truly does not exist at all.”

“Subhūti! For example, just as the referents of the terms from ‘emptiness of the internal’ up to ‘emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature,’ and even the referents of the terms from ‘non-arising and non-ceasing’ up to ‘non-defilement and non-purification,’ truly do not exist; so too, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term ‘bodhisattva’ likewise truly does not exist.”

“Subhūti! For example, just as the meaning of the phrases regarding the non-arising and non-ceasing of the four applications of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and even the meaning of the phrases regarding non-defilement and non-purity, truly do not exist at all; so too, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, the meaning of the term ‘bodhisattva’ likewise truly does not exist at all.”

“Subhūti! For example, just as the phrases and meanings of the signs of form up to consciousness—which are ultimately pure—do not exist at all in reality, so too, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, the phrase ‘bodhisattva’ likewise does not exist in reality.”

"Subhūti! For example, just as the ultimate purity of the sense bases from the eye-base up to the mind-base is such that their characteristics, phrases, and meanings truly do not exist, so too, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, the phrase 'bodhisattva' likewise truly does not exist."

“Subhūti! For example, just as the ultimate purity of the spheres of form up to the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana) means that the referents of their characteristics are truly non-existent, so too, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), the referent of the term ‘bodhisattva’ is likewise truly non-existent.”

“Subhūti! For example, just as the eye-element up to the mind-element are ultimately pure and lack any real basis for their designations, so too, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, the designation ‘bodhisattva’ likewise lacks any real basis whatsoever.”

“Subhūti! Just as the phrases and meanings of the signs of the ultimate purity of everything from the form realm up to the dharma-realm do not exist at all in reality, so too, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, the phrase ‘bodhisattva’ likewise does not exist at all in reality.”

“Subhūti! For example, just as the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element—being ultimately pure—are in reality devoid of any marks, phrases, or referents, so too is the referent of the term ‘bodhisattva mahāsattva’ when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom; it is likewise in reality non-existent.”

“Subhūti! For example, just as the referents of the terms for the ultimate purity of everything from eye-contact through to mind-contact do not exist in reality, so too, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term ‘bodhisattva’ likewise does not exist in reality.”

“Subhūti! For example, just as the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including those produced with mind-contact as a condition, are ultimately pure and lack any real basis for the terms and meanings [of ‘feeling’], so too, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, the term and meaning of ‘bodhisattva’ likewise lack any real existence.”

“Subhūti! For example, from the element of earth up to the element of consciousness, because they are ultimately pure, the referents of their characteristics and terms do not exist at all; likewise, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term ‘bodhisattva’ also does not exist at all.”

“Subhūti! For example, just as the essential meaning of the characteristics of everything from ignorance through old age and death is ultimately pure and truly non-existent, so too is the essential meaning of a ‘bodhisattva’ when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom; it is likewise truly non-existent.”

“Subhūti! For example, just as the phrases and meanings of all signs—from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence—are ultimately pure and truly non-existent, so too, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, the phrase ‘bodhisattva’ is likewise truly non-existent.”

“Subhūti! For example, just as the phrases and meanings of the signs of the four applications of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are ultimately pure and truly non-existent, so too, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, the phrase ‘bodhisattva’ is likewise truly non-existent.”

“Subhūti! For example, just as within the ultimate purity of the referents of the terms from ‘I’ up to ‘seer,’ there is truly nothing whatsoever because they do not exist; so too, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term ‘bodhisattva’ likewise truly does not exist.”

“Subhūti! For example, when the sun appears, the referent of the term ‘darkness’ truly does not exist at all; likewise, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, the referent of the term ‘bodhisattva’ also truly does not exist at all.”

“Subhūti! For example, when a great kalpa comes to an end, the referents of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) truly do not exist; likewise, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), the referent of ‘bodhisattva’ also truly does not exist.”

"Subhūti! For example, within the aggregate of pure ethical discipline (śīla-skandha) of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, the referent of the term 'transgression' does not exist at all; within the aggregate of pure concentration (samādhi-skandha), the referent of the term 'distraction' does not exist at all; within the aggregate of pure wisdom (prajñā-skandha), the referent of the term 'delusion' does not exist at all; within the aggregate of liberation (vimukti-skandha), the referent of the term 'bondage' does not exist at all; and within the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimukti-jñāna-darśana-skandha), the referent of the term 'lack of knowledge and vision of liberation' does not exist at all. In the same way, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), the referent of the term 'Bodhisattva' likewise does not exist at all."

“Subhūti! For example, among the various radiances of the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens up to those of the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, the meaning of the term ‘Buddha-light’ does not exist at all in reality; likewise, when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, the meaning of the term ‘Bodhisattva’ also does not exist at all in reality.”
"Why is this so? Subhūti!

Whether it be awakening, or a sentient being, or a bodhisattva, or the referent of the term 'bodhisattva'—all such dharmas are neither associated nor dissociated; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and of a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness."
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should diligently train in and correctly awaken to the fact that they are without attachment or obstruction regarding all phenomena, which lack true existence.”
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What are all phenomena?"

How should the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas diligently train in and correctly awaken to the fact that they are without attachment and without obstruction regarding all phenomena, which lack true existence?

The Buddha told Subhūti: “All phenomena (sarvadharma) refer to wholesome phenomena and unwholesome phenomena; determinate phenomena and indeterminate phenomena; mundane phenomena and supramundane phenomena; tainted phenomena and untainted phenomena; conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena; shared phenomena and unshared phenomena—all such categories as these are called ‘all phenomena.’”

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, regarding all these phenomena as lacking true existence, should diligently train in non-attachment and non-obstruction, and should correctly awaken to them through knowledge.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What are called the worldly wholesome dharmas?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Worldly wholesome dharmas refer to: filial piety toward one's parents; making offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; honoring and serving teachers and elders;
meritorious deeds consisting of the nature of giving; meritorious deeds consisting of the nature of ethical discipline;
meritorious deeds performed together with attending to the sick; and meritorious deeds performed through skillful means."
Whether it be the ten paths of wholesome worldly action, or the perception of bloatedness, the perception of festering, the perception of lividness,
the perception of bloody disfigurement, the perception of mangled dismemberment, the perception of being devoured by scavengers, the perception of scattered fragments,
the perception of bleached bones, or the perception of burning; or whether it be the four worldly meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).
The four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the recollection of the Buddha, the recollection of the Dharma, the recollection of the Saṅgha, the recollection of ethical discipline,
the recollection of relinquishment, the recollection of the devas, the recollection of inhalation and exhalation,
the recollection of peace, the recollection of the body, and the recollection of death— these are called mundane.
“Wholesome dharmas.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What are called unwholesome dharmas?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Non-virtuous dharmas refer to taking life, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, harsh speech, divisive speech, frivolous speech, covetousness, malice, wrong view, anger, harmfulness, envy, and stinginess. Such things as these are called non-virtuous dharmas."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is meant by 'dharmas that are definitively explained'?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"All wholesome dharmas and unwholesome dharmas are called determinate dharmas.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What are called indeterminate dharmas?"

The Buddha told Subhūti: "If there are neutral (avyākṛta) bodily actions, verbal actions, or mental actions; if there are neutral four great elements (mahābhūta); if there are neutral five faculties (indriya); if there are neutral six bases (āyatana); if there are neutral formless aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), or bases (āyatana); or if there is neutral maturation (vipāka)—all such things as these are called neutral phenomena."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What are called worldly dharmas?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"It refers to the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the ten paths of action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the twelve links of dependent origination—all such things as these are called mundane dharmas."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What are called supramundane dharmas?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

That is to say: the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the three doors of liberation; the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known";

the concentration with directed thought and sustained thought, the concentration without directed thought but with sustained thought, and the concentration without directed thought or sustained thought; and the liberation through clear knowledge.
Whether it be mindfulness and clear comprehension, or appropriate mental attention; whether it be the eight liberations, the nine successive attainments;

or internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, and non-dispersal.
Emptiness, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-existence,
and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; as well as the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses,
and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha— these are called supramundane dharmas.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha,
saying, “What are called contaminated phenomena?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Those comprised within the three realms—namely, the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements; or the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments—all such things as these are called contaminated phenomena (sāsrava-dharma)."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying,
"What is meant by 'outflow-free dharmas' (anāsrava-dharma)?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"It refers to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and so forth, up to the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four analytical knowledges, and eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; all such things as these are called untainted phenomena (anāsrava-dharma)."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What are called conditioned phenomena?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If there are dharmas that possess arising, abiding, change, and cessation; whether they are subsumed within the three realms or among the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and so forth, up to the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four analytical knowledges, and eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—all such things as these are called conditioned dharmas."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha,
saying, “What is meant by ‘unconditioned phenomena’?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If there are dharmas that are without arising, abiding, change, or cessation; or if there is the exhaustion of greed, hatred, and delusion; or if there is suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-falsity, immutability, equality, the nature of being free from birth, the fixedness of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, or the limit of reality."
"All such things as these are called unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What are called common phenomena (*sādhāraṇa-dharma*)?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"That which consists of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments of the world—such as these are called common dharmas."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What is meant by ‘unshared dharmas’?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"This refers to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the three gates of liberation, and so forth, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
All such things as these are called the 'unshared dharmas' (āveṇika-dharma)."

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should not cling to such phenomena as these, which are empty of their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇaśūnya*), because all phenomena are without conceptual differentiation (*avikalpa*).
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should, regarding all phenomena, realize them as they truly are by means of non-duality (*advaya*), because all phenomena are immovable (*aniñja*).”

Subhūti, you should know that in all phenomena, non-duality, immovability, non-conceptualization, and non-attachment constitute the meaning of the term "bodhisattva. For this reason, the absence of any fixed meaning is the meaning of the term "bodhisattva."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
for what reason is a bodhisattva called a mahāsattva?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Because these bodhisattvas shall become leaders among the great assembly of sentient beings, they are further named ‘Mahāsattvas.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed [the Buddha], saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by ‘a great assembly of sentient beings,’ among whom a bodhisattva should act as the leader?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

Whether they belong to the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotrabhūmi*), the eighth stage, stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*), once-returners (*sakṛdāgāmin*), non-returners (*anāgāmin*), arhats, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattva-mahāsattvas from their first resolve up to the stage of non-retrogression—all such as these are called the great assembly of sentient beings; because the bodhisattva shall be the leader among them, he is further named a mahāsattva.

This means that because these bodhisattvas have already generated a firm, vajra-like mind that is certain not to regress or be destroyed, they are able to serve as leaders among the great assembly of sentient beings.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by the ‘firm, adamantine-like mind’?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought:
'I shall now don the great armor of merit; within the vast wilderness of boundless birth and death, I shall destroy the enemy of afflictions for the sake of all sentient beings.'"
I shall universally, for the sake of all sentient beings, dry up the boundless great ocean of birth and death.
I shall relinquish all that I possess to bring great benefit to all sentient beings.
I shall impartially benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings, my mind free from partiality.
I shall cause all classes of sentient beings to travel the paths of the three vehicles and proceed toward the city of Nirvāṇa.
Although I shall deliver all sentient beings by means of the three vehicles, I shall never perceive even a single sentient being who attains nirvana.
I shall realize that the nature of all phenomena is neither defiled nor pure, neither arising nor ceasing.
I shall practice the perfections from generosity through to the perfection of wisdom solely with mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes.
I shall diligently train to enter the gateways of the subtle, ultimate, and penetrating wisdom that reaches the furthest limit.
I shall penetrate the single gateway of principle regarding the characteristics of all phenomena;
I shall penetrate the dual gateway of principle regarding the characteristics of all phenomena;
and I shall penetrate the manifold gateways of principle regarding the characteristics of all phenomena without any attachment.
"I shall practice and study various sublime wisdoms to penetrate the nature of all phenomena and bring forth supreme merit. Subhūti!
This is called the bodhisattva’s firm, diamond-like resolve.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, employing the skillful means of non-apprehension, abides in this mind, they will certainly be able to become the foremost among the great assembly of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
All bodhisattva mahāsattvas give rise to this thought:

'Whatever sufferings and afflictions are experienced by all sentient beings within the realms of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and gods, I shall take them upon myself in their stead, so as to bring them peace and happiness.'"
All Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas give rise to this thought:

"For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, I shall undergo various kinds of heavy suffering in the great hells for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas, teaching and transforming them through countless skillful means so that they may attain nirvana without remainder."

In this manner, for the sake of universally benefiting all sentient beings, he shall, for each and every one of them, undergo various heavy sufferings in the great hells for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas; and for each, he shall employ countless skillful means to teach and transform them so that they attain nirvana without remainder.

Having performed these deeds and planted roots of goodness for themselves, they further pass through immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas, fully cultivating and accumulating the provisions for enlightenment, and only thereafter do they realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening they seek.
"Subhūti! Such a vast vow is also called the bodhisattva’s firm resolve, which is like a diamond.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, employing the skillful means of non-apprehension, abides in this mind, they will certainly become a leader among the great assembly of sentient beings."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
All bodhisattva mahāsattvas should constantly give rise to a vast mind; by virtue of this mind, they will certainly be able to serve as the leaders among the great assembly of sentient beings."
In this context, the "vast mind" of a bodhisattva refers to the thought generated by bodhisattvas as follows:

"From the initial generation of the mind of great enlightenment until the realization of the knowledge of all modes, I shall certainly never give rise to thoughts of desire, hatred, delusion, anger, malice, views, or pride; nor shall I ever give rise to thoughts seeking the levels of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."
This is the vast mind of a bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, employing the skillful means of non-apprehension, abides in this mind, they will certainly be able to become the leader among the great assembly of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
All bodhisattva mahāsattvas should constantly give rise to an unshakable mind; by means of this mind, they will certainly be able to become the foremost among the great assembly of sentient beings."
In this context, what is meant by the "unshakable mind"?
It refers to the bodhisattvas generating such a thought:
"I shall always rely upon the mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), cultivating and undertaking all practices and activities without conceit."
This is called the unshakable mind of a bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, employing the skillful means of non-apprehension, abides in this mind, they will certainly be able to become the leader among the great assembly of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas impartially give rise to a mind that seeks the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings; by virtue of this mind, they will certainly become leaders among the great assembly of sentient beings."
In this context, the bodhisattva’s mind of benefit and happiness refers to the thought generated by bodhisattvas:
"I shall, for certain, until the end of the future, bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, acting as their refuge, island, and dwelling, never abandoning them."
This is called the bodhisattva’s mind of benefit and happiness.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, employing the skillful means of non-apprehension, abides in this mind, they will certainly be able to become a leader among the great assembly of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are always diligent and energetic, loving the Dharma, delighting in the Dharma, rejoicing in the Dharma, and finding joy in the Dharma. By virtue of these causes and conditions, they will certainly be able to become leaders among the great multitudes of sentient beings."
In this context, "Dharma" refers to the non-differentiated nature of all phenomena; this is what is called Dharma.
"Loving the Dharma" means to give rise to desire and aspiration for this Dharma.
To speak of "delighting in the Dharma" means to praise the merits of this Dharma.
To speak of "rejoicing in the Dharma" means to receive it with joy and faith.
To speak of "finding pleasure in the Dharma" means to delight in its frequent cultivation.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, employing the skillful means of non-apprehension, is always able to love, delight in, rejoice in, and find joy in the undifferentiated Dharma without attachment, they will certainly become a leader among the great assembly of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, employing the method of non-apprehension, and abides in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will certainly become a leader among the great assembly of sentient beings."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, employing the method of non-apprehension to cultivate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and so on extensively up to the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four analytical knowledges, and eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—this bodhisattva mahāsattva will certainly become a leader among the great assembly of sentient beings."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), employing the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), and abides in the vajra-like samādhi, up to and including abiding in the samādhis that are unattached, unconditioned, undefiled, liberated, and like space—this bodhisattva mahāsattva will certainly be able to become the foremost among the great assembly of sentient beings."

“Subhūti! You should know that when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in these subtle and supreme dharmas and practice the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they will certainly become leaders among the great multitude of sentient beings; for this reason, a bodhisattva is called a mahāsattva.”
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By means of my eloquence, I would like to explain why a bodhisattva is called a ‘mahāsattva’ for these reasons; I only pray that you will grant me leave to do so!”
