The Buddha told Śāriputra: "Speak as you wish. Śāriputra said:
"By means of their skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), bodhisattvas are able to proclaim the essential teachings of the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings,
causing them to sever the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, up to the view of a knower and the view of a perceiver; they cause them to sever the view of permanence,
the view of nihilism, the view of existence, the view of non-existence, the views regarding the aggregates, bases, and elements, and the views regarding the noble truths."
And as for the view of dependent origination, it causes one to sever the views regarding the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—
explained at length up to the views regarding the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha— the views regarding the maturation of sentient beings,
the purification of buddha-fields, the view of a bodhisattva, the view of a Tathāgata, the view of enlightenment, the view of nirvāṇa, and the view of turning the wheel of Dharma.

By means of the skillful means of the bodhisattvas, employing non-apprehension as their expedient, they proclaim for the sake of all sentient beings the teaching on the permanent severance of these views; it is by virtue of this meaning that they are called "Mahāsattvas."
At that time, Subhūti asked the venerable Śāriputra:

"If bodhisattva mahāsattvas are able to teach sentient beings the essential Dharma for severing all views by employing the method of non-apprehension, for what cause and for what reason do some bodhisattvas, employing the method of apprehension, give rise to views regarding the aggregates and so forth?"

Śāriputra said: "If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, lacks skillful means and gives rise to views regarding the aggregates and so forth by way of apprehending something, then because that bodhisattva mahāsattva lacks skillful means, he will certainly be unable, for the sake of sentient beings, to proclaim the essential dharma for the permanent severance of all views by way of non-apprehension."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, possesses skillful means, they are able to teach sentient beings the essential dharma for permanently severing all views by employing the method of non-apprehension; such a bodhisattva mahāsattva will certainly not give rise to views regarding the aggregates and so forth.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
By means of my eloquence, I would like to explain why a bodhisattva is called a 'mahāsattva' on account of this meaning; I only pray that you will grant me leave to do so!"
The Buddha said to Subhūti, “Speak as you wish. Subhūti replied:

"Because these bodhisattvas, desiring to realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), have generated the mind of awakening, the unequaled mind, and the mind not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas—and yet do not even cling to such a mind—it is by virtue of this meaning that they are called 'mahāsattvas'."

Why is this? Because the mind of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna-citta) is truly untainted (anāsrava) and does not fall within the three realms; the seeking of the mind of the knowledge of all modes is likewise truly untainted and does not fall within the three realms. One should not form attachments to such a mind; for this reason, a bodhisattva is called a mahāsattva.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
“In what way does a bodhisattva mahāsattva possess a mind that is unequaled and not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas?”
Subhūti replied:

"From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, bodhisattva mahāsattvas do not perceive even the slightest dharma as having arising or ceasing, increasing or decreasing, going or coming, or being defiled or purified. If they do not perceive any dharma as having arising or ceasing, increasing or decreasing, going or coming, or being defiled or purified, they likewise do not perceive the mind of a śrāvaka, a pratyekabuddha, or a bodhisattva. This is called the 'unequaled mind' of the bodhisattva mahāsattva—the mind that is not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas—and yet bodhisattva mahāsattvas do not cling even to such a mind."
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be attached to such a mind, then they should also not be attached to the minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; nor should they be attached to the minds regarding all aggregates, bases, and elements, as well as the minds regarding the four foundations of mindfulness, and so on, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha."
"Why is that? Because these various minds have no nature of mind. Subhūti replied:
"So it is! So it is! At that time, Śāriputra addressed Subhūti, saying:

"If all minds are without the nature of mind and thus should not be clung to, then the aggregates, bases, and elements—and so forth, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—are likewise without that nature and should not be clung to."
Subhūti replied, “So it is! So it is!”

Śāriputra said: "If the mind of the knowledge of all modes is truly untainted and does not fall within the three realms, then the minds of foolish ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas should also be truly untainted and not fall within the three realms. Why is this?"
"Because all such minds are empty by their very nature. Subhūti replied, "So it is!"
"So be it! Śāriputra said:

"If this mind, because its intrinsic nature is empty, is truly untainted and does not fall within the three realms, then the aggregates, sense bases, elements, and so forth—extensively explained up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—should also be truly untainted and not fall within the three realms. Why is that?"
"Because the aggregates, sense bases, elements, and so forth are all empty of intrinsic nature. Subhūti replied, "So it is!"

"So be it! Śāriputra said: "If phenomena such as mind and form should not be grasped because they lack the intrinsic nature of mind and form, then all phenomena would necessarily be equal and entirely without distinction."
Subhūti replied, “So it is! So it is!”
Śāriputra said: “If all phenomena are equal and without distinction, why does the Tathāgata speak of various differences such as mind and form? Subhūti replied:
"This is the Tathāgata speaking in accordance with worldly convention, not in accordance with the ultimate truth. Śāriputra said:

"If the minds, forms, and other phenomena of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas are all truly untainted and do not fall within the three realms, then there would be no distinction between ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas."
Subhūti replied, “So it is! So it is!”

Śāriputra said: "If there is no distinction between ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas, why has the Buddha taught that there are various differences among the ordinary and the noble, and the great and the small?"
Subhūti replied: “This too is spoken by the Tathāgata in reliance upon conventional truth, not in reliance upon ultimate truth, Śāriputra.”

When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, by means of the expedient of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), they neither rely upon nor cling to the great bodhicitta they have generated—the mind that is unequaled and not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. They neither grasp nor adhere to the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), and so forth, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*). Based on this meaning, they are called "mahāsattvas."
At that time, the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By means of my eloquence, I would like to explain why a bodhisattva is called a ‘mahāsattva’ for these reasons; I only pray that you will grant me your permission!”
The Buddha said to Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, “Speak as you wish.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:

"Because all bodhisattvas universally don the great armor of merit for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, because they set out upon the Great Vehicle, and because they ride the Great Vehicle, they are called Mahāsattvas."
At that time, Śāriputra asked Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva don the great armor of merit for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings?"
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:

“When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of generosity, they do not do so for the benefit and happiness of a few sentient beings, but rather for the universal benefit and happiness of all sentient beings; it is likewise when they practice the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.”
"Śāriputra! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva dons the great armor of merit for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
The bodhisattva-mahāsattvas don the great armor of merit for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to sentient beings without limitation; they do not form such thoughts as:
"I shall rescue this many sentient beings and lead them into the realm of nirvana without remainder, but I shall not lead that many sentient beings there;
I shall rescue this many sentient beings and establish them in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, but I shall not establish that many sentient beings therein."

Nevertheless, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas universally act to deliver all sentient beings by leading them into the realm of nirvana without remainder and establishing them in unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
"Śāriputra! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva dons the great armor of merit for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
The bodhisattva mahāsattvas form this thought:
"I shall personally fulfill the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and I shall also cause all sentient beings to fulfill them."
Again, he forms this thought:

"Relying upon the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), I myself abide in internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*); I myself cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*). I shall also cause sentient beings to rely upon these six perfections, to abide securely in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, and to cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha."
He further reflects:

"Relying upon these six perfections, I shall swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and enter the realm of nirvana without remainder; I shall also cause sentient beings to rely upon these six perfections so that they too may swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and enter the realm of nirvana without remainder."
"Śāriputra! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva dons the great armor of merit for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the perfection of generosity, they do so by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), practicing the perfection of generosity without mixing it with the mental attention of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas. Taking these roots of goodness as their basis, using the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), they share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
When practicing generosity, being entirely without stinginess is the great armor of the perfection of generosity;
when practicing generosity, not giving rise to the mental orientations of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas is the great armor of the perfection of ethical discipline;
when practicing generosity, having faith, patience, aspiration, and delight in cultivating the dharma of generosity is the great armor of the perfection of patience.
When practicing generosity, to apply oneself with diligent vigor and not abandon one's application is the great armor of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).

When practicing generosity, to single-mindedly direct oneself toward omniscience (*sarvajñājñāna*) for the ultimate benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, without being mixed with the mental orientations of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, is the great armor of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).

When practicing generosity, to abide in the realization that it is like an illusion, not apprehending a giver, a recipient, the gift, or the fruit obtained from giving, is the great armor of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of generosity in this manner, they are fully armored with the great armor of merit of the six perfections.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes, practices the perfection of generosity while neither grasping nor apprehending the characteristics of the six perfections, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has donned the great armor of merit.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), they do so with a mental orientation (*manasikāra*) associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*). They practice the perfection of ethical discipline without being mixed with the mental orientations of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas. Taking these roots of virtue as their basis, by means of the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), they share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*)."
When practicing pure ethical discipline, being entirely free from stinginess regarding all things constitutes the great armor of the perfection of generosity;
when practicing pure ethical discipline, one does not even seek the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, much less the stage of ordinary beings!
This is the great armor of merit of the perfection of pure ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).

When practicing pure ethical discipline, having faith, patience, and aspiration for the dharma of pure ethical discipline is the great armor of merit of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). When practicing pure ethical discipline, applying oneself with diligent vigor and not abandoning one's application is the great armor of merit of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).

When practicing pure ethical discipline, taking great compassion as the primary guide, one does not even intermingle the mental engagements of the two vehicles, much less the minds of ordinary beings!
This is the great armor of merit of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).

When practicing pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), one dwells in all phenomena as being like illusions; regarding the practice of pure ethical discipline, one is without reliance and without attainment, realizing the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*). This is the great armor of merit of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline in this manner, they are fully armored with the great armor of the six perfections.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes, practices the perfection of ethical discipline while apprehending neither the characteristics nor the attainment of the six perfections, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has donned the great armor of merit.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), they do so by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). They practice the perfection of patience without mixing it with the mental attention of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Taking these roots of goodness as their basis, and employing the method of non-apprehension (anupalambha), they share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
When practicing patience, having no attachment to one’s body, life, or possessions for the sake of accomplishing patience is the great armor of the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).
When practicing patience, not being mixed with the inferior mental orientations of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is the great armor of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
When practicing patience, having faith, acceptance, and a longing for the dharma of patience is the great armor of the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*).
When practicing patience, to apply oneself with vigorous diligence and not abandon one's application is the great armor of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).

When practicing patience, to collect the mind in a single point so that it is not disturbed even when encountering various sufferings is the great armor of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).

When practicing patience, to abide in the illusion-like nature of reality for the sake of gathering the Buddha-dharmas and maturing sentient beings, observing the emptiness of all phenomena and not clinging to resentment or harm, is the great armor of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of patience in this way, they are fully armored with the great armor of the six perfections.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes, practices the perfection of patience while neither grasping nor apprehending the characteristics of the six perfections, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has donned the great armor of merit.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 486. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Three, Chapter on Subhūti, Section Six. "Furthermore, Śāriputra!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of diligence, they do so by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), practicing the perfection of diligence without being mixed with the mental attention of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Taking these roots of virtue as their basis, they employ the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) to dedicate them equally and in common with all sentient beings toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
When practicing diligence, one is able to diligently train in the practice of difficult-to-perform giving; this is the great armor of the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*).
When practicing diligence, one diligently guards pure ethical discipline without ever violating it; this is the great armor of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).
When practicing diligence, one is able to diligently train in the practice of difficult-to-perform patience; this is the great armor of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
When practicing diligence, being able to diligently train in beneficial ascetic practices constitutes the great armor of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*);

when practicing diligence, being able to diligently train in meditative concentration and attainment (*dhyāna-samāpatti*) constitutes the great armor of the perfection of concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*);
when practicing diligence, being able to diligently train in wisdom free from grasping constitutes the great armor of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of diligence in this manner, they are fully armored with the great armor of the six perfections.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes, practices the perfection of diligence while perceiving neither the signs nor the attainment of the six perfections, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has donned the great armor of merit.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā), they do so by means of mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). They practice the perfection of meditative concentration without being mixed with the mental attention of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Taking these roots of virtue as their basis, they employ the method of non-apprehension (anupalambha) to dedicate them equally in common with all sentient beings toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

When practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one practices giving with a tranquil mind; since a distracted mind and stinginess no longer manifest, this is the great armor of the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).

When practicing meditative concentration, one guards the precepts with a concentrated mind, ensuring that various unwholesome precepts no longer appear; this is the great armor of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).

When practicing meditative concentration, one abides in the samādhi of loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*) and cultivates patience (*kṣānti*) without harming sentient beings; this is the great armor of the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*).

When practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), abiding in pure samādhi and diligently cultivating merit while remaining free from all indolence is the great armor of the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*).

When practicing meditative concentration, relying on such concentrations to induce superior samādhi and remain free from a distracted mind is the great armor of the perfection of concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).

When practicing meditative concentration, relying on such concentrations to induce superior wisdom and remain free from a mind of unwholesome insight is the great armor of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of meditative concentration in this way, they are fully armored with the great armor of the six perfections.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of meditative concentration with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes, neither grasps nor apprehends the characteristics of the six perfections, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is clad in the great armor of merit.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they do so by means of mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*). They practice the perfection of wisdom without being mixed with the mental engagements of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Taking these roots of goodness as their basis, they employ the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) to dedicate them equally and in common with all sentient beings toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

When practicing *prajñā*, although one gives all things, one is able not to perceive the three [aspects] such as the giver; this is the great armor of merit of the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*).

When practicing *prajñā*, although one guards pure precepts, one is able not to perceive the distinction between upholding and violating them; this is the great armor of merit of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).

When practicing *prajñā*, one cultivates patience based on the supreme wisdom of emptiness, not perceiving such things as the one who endures or that which is endured; this is the great armor of merit of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).

When practicing *prajñā*, although one contemplates that all phenomena are ultimately empty, one diligently cultivates wholesome dharmas through great compassion; this is the great armor of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).

When practicing *prajñā*, although one cultivates sublime concentrations (*samādhi*), one contemplates that the objects of concentration are all ultimately empty; this is the great armor of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).

When practicing *prajñā*, one contemplates that all phenomena, all sentient beings, and all conditioned activities are like illusions, dreams, reflections, echoes, images, mirages, transformations, and cities of Gandharvas, while cultivating various forms of wisdom free from grasping; this is the great armor of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this way, they are fully armored with the great armor of the six perfections.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes, does not grasp at nor apprehend the characteristics of the six perfections, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has donned the great armor of merit.
“Śāriputra! This is called the donning of the great armor of merit by all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings. Śāriputra!”

When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in each and every pāramitā, they cultivate all six pāramitās so that they may be brought to perfection; for this reason, they are said to be "donning the armor of great merit."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, although bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter into the meditative concentrations (dhyāna), the immeasurables (apramāṇa), and the formless attainments (ārūpya), they do not relish them, nor are they led away by their power, nor do they take birth in accordance with their power."
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of wisdom, characterized by skillful means, donned by bodhisattva mahāsattvas when they practice the perfection of meditative concentration.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, although bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), they maintain the vision of detachment, the vision of tranquility, and the visions of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; yet they do not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), nor do they fall into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, thereby surpassing all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
Śāriputra! This is the great armor of the perfection of wisdom, characterized by skillful means, donned by bodhisattva mahāsattvas when they practice the perfection of meditative concentration.
“Śāriputra! Because bodhisattvas universally don such great armor of merit for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, they are further called ‘mahāsattvas.’”

“Śāriputra! Thus, the bodhisattva mahāsattva who has donned the great armor of merit for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to sentient beings is joyfully praised by all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas throughout the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, amidst their great assemblies, saying:

‘In such-and-such a direction, in such-and-such a world, there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva named so-and-so, who has donned the great armor of merit for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings; he purifies buddha-fields, matures sentient beings, sports with supernatural powers, and performs what ought to be done.’”
Thus, as the sound spread from one to another throughout the ten directions, humans, devas, and others who heard it were all filled with great joy and spoke these words:
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva will before long realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment he seeks, causing all sentient beings to obtain benefit and happiness."
At that time, Śāriputra asked Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out upon the Great Vehicle for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings?"
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:

“All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, have already donned the great armor of the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā). Furthermore, for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, they—free from desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and evaluation, born of seclusion, joyful and blissful—enter and fully abide in the first dhyāna; and so on, as extensively described, until: having abandoned pleasure and abandoned pain, with the prior disappearance of joy and sorrow, neither painful nor pleasant, with equanimity and mindfulness purified, they enter and fully abide in the fourth dhyāna.”

Furthermore, relying on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he gives rise to a mind accompanied by loving-kindness (*maitrī*), characterized by vastness, non-duality, immeasurability, freedom from enmity, freedom from malice, freedom from resentment, and freedom from affliction; having thoroughly cultivated this resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) so that it is all-pervasive, overflowing throughout the ten directions, exhausting the entirety of space and reaching the limits of the Dharma-realm, he dwells fully endowed with this resolute conviction of a compassionate mind.

He likewise gives rise to minds accompanied by compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), and his resolute convictions regarding these mental aspects are exactly the same.

Relying on this preparatory practice, one further transcends all perceptions of form, extinguishes perceptions of sensory resistance, and does not attend to perceptions of diversity; thus one enters and fully dwells in the sphere of infinite space.
To speak at length, this continues until one transcends the sphere of nothingness and enters and fully dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, taking these meditative concentrations, immeasurables, and formless attainments, uses the method of non-apprehension to share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Śāriputra! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out upon the Great Vehicle for the sake of universally bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings. Furthermore, Śāriputra!

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, first personally abide in such meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), and they skillfully discern and know the modes of entering, abiding in, and emerging from these states, as well as their respective activities, characteristics, and signs.
Having attained mastery, he further reflects:

"I should now, with a mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) and with great compassion as my foremost motive, in order to sever the afflictions of sentient beings, teach the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*). I shall analyze and reveal them so that they may thoroughly understand the gratification, the disadvantage, and the escape regarding these meditative absorptions, as well as the modes, characteristics, and signs of entering, abiding in, and emerging from them."

Taking these roots of goodness as a basis, employing the method of non-apprehension, he dedicates them for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, sharing them equally with all sentient beings.

Śāriputra! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, relying upon the perfection of meditative concentration, practices the perfection of generosity, setting out upon the Great Vehicle for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings.

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes and with great compassion as the foremost, teaches the meditative concentrations, the immeasurables, and the formless attainments, does so without being interrupted by the minds of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or others; taking these roots of goodness, he employs the method of non-apprehension to equally share them with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Śāriputra! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, relying upon the perfection of meditative concentration, practices the perfection of ethical discipline, setting out upon the Great Vehicle for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings.

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes and with great compassion as the foremost, teaches the various dhyānas, immeasurables, and formless attainments, and possesses faith, patience, desire, and delight in such dharmas, he takes these roots of goodness and, by means of non-apprehension as his expedient, dedicates them together with all sentient beings equally toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.”

Śāriputra! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, relying upon the perfection of meditative concentration, practices the perfection of patience, setting out upon the Great Vehicle for the sake of bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes and with great compassion as the foremost, cultivates the various dhyānas, the immeasurables, and the formless attainments, they diligently cultivate these roots of goodness without ceasing. Taking these roots of goodness, by means of the method of non-apprehension, they dedicate them equally and in common with all sentient beings toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening."

Śāriputra! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, relying upon the perfection of meditative concentration, practices the perfection of diligence, setting out upon the Great Vehicle for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings.

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes and with great compassion as the foremost, relies upon the various dhyānas, immeasurables, and formless attainments to induce superior meditative absorptions, concentrations, liberations, bases of mastery, and bases of totality, attaining mastery in entering, abiding in, and emerging from them; and without falling into the levels of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, takes these roots of goodness and, by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, dedicates them equally in common with all sentient beings toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Śāriputra! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, relying upon the perfection of meditative concentration and practicing the perfection of meditative concentration, sets out upon the Great Vehicle for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings.

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes and with great compassion as the foremost, cultivates the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), they correctly observe those meditative concentrations, immeasurables, formless attainments, and their constituent factors through the aspects of impermanence, suffering, and non-self, as well as through the aspects of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. Without abandoning great compassion, they do not fall into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; taking these roots of goodness, they use the method of non-apprehension to share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Śāriputra! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, relying upon the perfection of meditative concentration, practices the perfection of wisdom and sets out upon the Great Vehicle for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva,
with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes and with great compassion as the foremost, cultivates the concentration of loving-kindness, they form this thought:
'I shall rescue and succor all sentient beings, causing them all to attain happiness.'"
When practicing the meditative concentration of compassion, one forms this thought:
"I shall rescue and deliver all sentient beings, causing them all to be free from suffering.
When practicing the meditative concentration of sympathetic joy, one forms this thought:
"I shall encourage and inspire all sentient beings so that they may all attain liberation.
When practicing the meditative concentration of equanimity (*upekṣā-samādhi*), one forms this thought:
"I shall benefit all sentient beings equally so that they may all exhaust their outflows (*āsrava*)."

Taking these roots of goodness as a basis, by means of the expedient of non-apprehension, they share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Śāriputra! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, relying upon the immeasurable, practices the perfection of generosity and sets out upon the Great Vehicle for the sake of universally bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes and with great compassion as the foremost, enters, abides in, and emerges from the four immeasurables, never seeks the level of a śrāvaka or others, but seeks only unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, desiring to benefit and bring happiness to all beings throughout the future.

Śāriputra! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, relying upon the immeasurable, practices the perfection of ethical discipline and sets out upon the Great Vehicle for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings.

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) and taking great compassion as the foremost, enters, dwells in, and emerges from the four immeasurables without mixing in the mental orientations of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but instead possesses faith, patience, desire, and joy for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and taking these roots of virtue, by means of the method of non-apprehension, shares them equally with all sentient beings and dedicates them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Śāriputra! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, relying upon the immeasurable, practices the perfection of patience and sets out upon the Great Vehicle for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings.

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes and with great compassion as the foremost, diligently abandons all evils and diligently cultivates all virtues at the times of entering, abiding in, and emerging from the four immeasurables, seeking to advance toward enlightenment without ever abandoning it for even a moment; and taking these roots of goodness, using the method of non-apprehension, shares them equally with all sentient beings and dedicates them to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Śāriputra! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, relying on the immeasurable, practices the perfection of diligence and sets out upon the Great Vehicle for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings.

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes and with great compassion as the foremost, enters, abides in, and emerges from the four immeasurables, can induce various meditative concentrations and attainments therein, and attains great mastery over them, such that he is not led away or captivated by those states of concentration, nor is he reborn under their influence; and taking these roots of virtue, using the method of non-apprehension, he shares them equally with all sentient beings and dedicates them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Śāriputra! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, relying upon the immeasurable, practices the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā) and sets out upon the Great Vehicle for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings.

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes and with great compassion as the foremost, at the time of entering, abiding in, and emerging from the four immeasurables, observes them as they truly are through the aspects of impermanence, suffering, and non-self, and through the aspects of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; and without abandoning great compassion, without falling into the levels of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, takes these roots of goodness and, by means of the method of non-apprehension, dedicates them equally in common with all sentient beings toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

Śāriputra! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, relying on the immeasurable, practices the perfection of wisdom and sets out upon the Great Vehicle for the sake of bringing universal benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.

“Śāriputra! By relying on such skillful means as these, bodhisattva mahāsattvas cultivate the six perfections and set out upon the Great Vehicle for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings.”

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes and taking great compassion as the foremost, cultivates all aspects of the four foundations of mindfulness, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and the three doors of liberation, up to the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha; and having taken these roots of goodness, through the skillful means of non-apprehension, dedicates them equally in common with all sentient beings toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Śāriputra! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out upon the Great Vehicle for the sake of universally bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings. Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes and with great compassion as the foremost, employs the method of non-apprehension to cultivate the wisdom of internal emptiness and so forth, as well as the wisdom of suchness and so forth, and then takes these roots of goodness and, employing the method of non-apprehension, dedicates them equally in common with all sentient beings toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Śāriputra! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out upon the Great Vehicle for the sake of universally bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes, taking great compassion as the foremost,
and employing the method of non-apprehension, gives rise toward all phenomena to a wisdom that is neither distracted nor concentrated,
neither permanent nor impermanent, neither pleasant nor painful, neither self nor...
The wisdom of non-self; the wisdom that is neither pure nor impure; the wisdom that is neither empty nor non-empty;
the wisdom that is neither with signs nor signless; the wisdom that is neither with aspiration nor aspirationless; the wisdom that is neither tranquil nor non-tranquil;
the wisdom that is neither detached nor non-detached; the wisdom that is neither real nor unreal.
Taking these roots of goodness, with non-apprehension as the means, they share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Śāriputra! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out upon the Great Vehicle for the sake of universally bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, with mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes and with great compassion as the foremost, gives rise to sublime wisdom that does not operate within the past, future, or present, yet is not ignorant of the phenomena of the three periods of time;
does not operate within the desire, form, or formless realms, yet is not ignorant of the phenomena of the three realms;
and does not operate within the wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate, yet is not ignorant of the phenomena of the three natures.
They do not practice with regard to the contaminated or the uncontaminated, yet they are not ignorant of the dharmas that are contaminated or uncontaminated;
they do not practice with regard to the mundane or the supramundane, yet they are not ignorant of the dharmas that are mundane or supramundane;

they do not practice with regard to the conditioned or the unconditioned, yet they are not ignorant of the dharmas that are conditioned or unconditioned. Taking these roots of goodness as their basis, employing the method of non-apprehension, they share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Śāriputra! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out upon the Great Vehicle for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings. Śāriputra!

Because these bodhisattvas, through such skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), act for the universal benefit and happiness of all sentient beings and have set out upon the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*), they are further called "Great Beings" (*mahāsattva*).

“Śāriputra! Thus, for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to sentient beings, all those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have set out in the Great Vehicle are joyfully praised by all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas throughout the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, amidst their great assemblies, who speak these words:

‘In such-and-such a direction, in such-and-such a world, there is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva of such-and-such a name, who has set out in the Great Vehicle for the universal benefit and happiness of all sentient beings; he brings sentient beings to maturity, purifies buddha-fields, sports with supernatural powers, and performs what is to be done.’”
Thus, as the sound spread from one to another until it pervaded the ten directions, humans, devas, and others who heard it were all filled with great joy and said:
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva will before long realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening he seeks, causing all sentient beings to obtain benefit and happiness."
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra asked the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
"In what way does a bodhisattva mahāsattva mount the Great Vehicle for the sake of universally bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings?"
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, with mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñatājñāna*), taking great compassion as the foremost, and employing the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), although they ride upon the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), they do not apprehend the perfection of giving; nor do they apprehend the bodhisattva who receives, the object given, or the phenomena that are excluded.

Although they ride upon the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), they do not apprehend the perfection of ethical discipline; nor do they apprehend the bodhisattva, the one who violates ethical discipline, or the phenomena that are excluded.”
Although they ride upon the perfection of patience, they do not apprehend the perfection of patience, nor do they apprehend the bodhisattva, the objects of patience, or the phenomena to be averted;
although they ride upon the perfection of diligence, they do not apprehend the perfection of diligence, nor do they apprehend the bodhisattva, the indolent, or the phenomena to be averted;

although they ride upon the perfection of meditative concentration, they do not apprehend the perfection of meditative concentration, nor do they apprehend the bodhisattva, the distracted, the state of concentration, or the phenomena to be averted.

Although one rides upon the *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not apprehend the *prajñāpāramitā*, nor does one apprehend the bodhisattva, the foolish person, the sphere of wisdom, or the phenomena that are to be excluded.
Śāriputra! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva mounts the Great Vehicle for the sake of universally bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings. Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes, taking great compassion as the foremost, and employing the method of non-apprehension, practices the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the three doors of liberation, and even the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, for the sake of relinquishing cultivation.
Śāriputra! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva mounts the Great Vehicle for the sake of universally bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings. Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes, taking great compassion as the foremost, employs the method of non-apprehension to observe, in accordance with reality, that bodhisattvas mahāsattvas exist only as mere designations, because both "bodhisattva" and "sattva" are empty of intrinsic nature and unapprehendable;
that from form up to consciousness exist only as mere designations, because they are all empty of intrinsic nature and unapprehendable;
and that from the eye-base up to the mind-base exist only as mere designations, because they are all empty of intrinsic nature and unapprehendable.
The sense base of form up to the sense base of mental phenomena exist as mere designations, for they are all empty of intrinsic nature and unapprehendable;
the eye element up to the mind element exist as mere designations, for they are all empty of intrinsic nature and unapprehendable;
the form element up to the mental-phenomena element exist as mere designations, for they are all empty of intrinsic nature and unapprehendable.
The visual consciousness element up to the mental consciousness element exist only as provisional designations, for they are all empty of intrinsic nature and unapprehendable;
ignorance up to old age and death exist only as provisional designations, for they are all empty of intrinsic nature and unapprehendable;
the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha exist only as provisional designations, for they are all empty of intrinsic nature and unapprehendable.
From internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, there are only provisional designations, for they are all empty of intrinsic nature and unapprehendable;
from suchness up to the limit of reality, there are only provisional designations, for they are all empty of intrinsic nature and unapprehendable;
and from awakening to the Buddha, there are only provisional designations, for both are empty of intrinsic nature and unapprehendable.
Śāriputra! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva mounts the Great Vehicle for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings. Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment until the realization of the knowledge of all modes, employs non-apprehension as the means, constantly cultivates the perfect supernormal powers of a bodhisattva, matures sentient beings, and purifies buddha-fields; traveling from one buddha-field to another, they personally attend upon and make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and in the presence of those Buddhas listen to and receive the true Dharma—namely, the sublime Dharma associated with the Mahāyāna, which is also the essential method of training for bodhisattvas.

Śāriputra! Although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas ride upon the Great Vehicle, traveling from one buddha-field to another to attend upon and make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; and while they bring sentient beings to maturity, purify buddha-fields, and hear and receive the true Dharma in the presence of those Buddhas, their minds harbor no conceptualization whatsoever regarding buddha-fields or the like.

Śāriputra! This bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the stage of non-duality; observing which body among all sentient beings should be used for their deliverance, he immediately manifests and assumes such a body.
Śāriputra! These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, until they realize the knowledge of all modes, shall never be separated from the true Dharma of the Mahāyāna in whatever place they are born.
Śāriputra! This bodhisattva mahāsattva will before long attain the knowledge of all modes; for the sake of gods, humans, and others, he shall turn the wheel of the true Dharma.
Such a wheel of Dharma cannot be turned by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, devas, māras, brahmās, asuras, or any others.

"Śāriputra! Because these bodhisattvas universally seek the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, and because they ride upon the Great Vehicle, they are further called 'Mahāsattvas. Śāriputra!"

Thus, for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to sentient beings, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who have mounted the Great Vehicle are universally praised with joy by all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas within the great assemblies of Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions. They speak these words:

"In such-and-such a direction, in such-and-such a world, there is a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva named so-and-so, who has mounted the Great Vehicle for the universal benefit and happiness of all sentient beings. Before long, he shall attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) and turn the wheel of the true Dharma for gods, humans, and others—a wheel that none of the śrāvakas in the world can turn."
Thus, as the sound spread from one to another throughout the ten directions, humans, devas, and others who heard it were all filled with great joy and spoke these words:
"This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva will before long attain the knowledge of all modes; he shall turn the sublime wheel of Dharma and deliver immeasurable multitudes."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
as the World-Honored One has said:..."
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are clad in the armor of the Great Vehicle.
To what extent, Subhūti, should it be said that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are clad in the armor of the Great Vehicle?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can don the armor of the perfection of generosity up to the armor of the perfection of wisdom, this is what it means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to don the armor of the Great Vehicle."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can don the armor of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the armor of the eight branches of the noble path, this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva donning the armor of the Great Vehicle.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can don the armor of internal emptiness, up to and including the armor of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva donning the armor of the Great Vehicle.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can don the armor of suchness (*tathatā*) up to the armor of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva donning the armor of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can even don the armor of the ten powers (*daśabala*) of a Tathāgata up to the armor of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*), this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva donning the armor of the Great Vehicle.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can don the armor of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva donning the armor of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can transform his own body into the form of a Buddha, emitting great radiance that illuminates the trichiliocosm and even all the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, performing beneficial deeds for all sentient beings—this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva donning the armor of the Mahāyāna.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dons such armor of merit as these, they emit a great radiance that universally illuminates the trichiliocosm and even the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. They also cause those worlds to undergo six kinds of movement, thereby performing great benefit for all sentient beings; that is to say, they extinguish the blazing fires of all hells and cause the manifold sufferings of those sentient beings to cease."

Once the Bodhisattva knows that their various sufferings have ceased, he manifests a vast sound of praise for the Buddha and pays homage to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. Having caused those in the hells to hear the sound of the Buddha, they all attain peace, stability, joy, and bliss in body and mind; they emerge from the hells to be born among gods and humans, where they encounter and serve the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of those realms.

He likewise causes all animals and hungry ghosts to hear the sound of the Buddha, whereby their bodies and minds become peaceful and happy; they pass away from those destinies to be born among gods and humans, where they encounter and serve the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of those realms.
"Subhūti! This is what it means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to don the armor of the Great Vehicle. Subhūti!"

Suppose a skilled illusionist or his apprentice, standing at a crossroads before a great assembly, were to conjure up the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts; and then, by praising the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, cause those beings to experience peace and happiness in body and mind upon hearing it, so that they pass away from those states and are reborn among gods and humans.
"What do you think?
Does such an illusory phenomenon have any reality? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"So too it is with the bodhisattva mahāsattvas: although they cause the sentient beings of countless and boundless worlds to escape the three evil destinies, there are no sentient beings who have attained liberation."
Why is this? Because the nature and characteristics of all phenomena are like illusions. Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can don the great armor of merit of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), universally transforming the trichiliocosm into pure vaidūrya, and personally manifesting as a wheel-turning sage king (*cakravartin*) with a retinue of the seven treasures all perfectly complete, providing food to those who need food, drink to those who need drink, clothing to those who need clothing, vehicles to those who need vehicles, and bestowing all other necessary requisites upon all sentient beings.

Having performed such giving, he further teaches them, as appropriate, the dharmas associated with the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, so that upon hearing them, they shall never abandon the dharmas associated with the perfections until they reach unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Subhūti! This is what it means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to don the armor of the Mahāyāna. Subhūti!"

It is like a skilled illusionist or his apprentice who, standing at a crossroads before a great assembly, conjures various impoverished beings and, according to their needs, magically creates and bestows upon them whatever they require.
"What do you think?
Does such an illusory phenomenon have any reality? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are also like this: they can don the great armor of the merit of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), either transforming worlds into vaidūrya or transforming themselves into the position of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*). They bestow upon sentient beings whatever they require and proclaim for them the teachings corresponding to the perfections; yet, although such bodhisattvas have these activities, they possess no substantial reality.”
Why is this? Because the nature and characteristics of all phenomena are like illusions.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having donned the great armor of the merit of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) for the sake of sentient beings, is born into the family of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), succeeds to the rank of a universal monarch with wealth, nobility, and sovereignty, and establishes immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of beings in the ten paths of wholesome action; or in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, or the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and so forth, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*); and furthermore, proclaims the teachings corresponding to such merits, causing them to abide therein until they reach unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, never being parted from it.
"Subhūti! This is what it means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to don the armor of the Great Vehicle. Subhūti!"

It is like a skilled illusionist or his disciple who, standing at a crossroads before a great assembly, conjures hundreds of thousands of immeasurable sentient beings and causes them to abide in the ten paths of wholesome action, and so on extensively up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
“What do you think?
Is such an illusory phenomenon real? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! The Buddha told Subhūti:

"In the same way, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are born into the royal house of a wheel-turning monarch for the sake of sentient beings; having inherited the position of a wheel-turning monarch with its wealth, nobility, and sovereignty, they establish immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of beings in the ten paths of wholesome action, and so on, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha."
Thus, although a bodhisattva has things to do, they have no reality.
Why is this? Because the nature and characteristics of all phenomena are like illusions.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva personally dons the great armor of the merit of the perfection of patience, and also encourages immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings to don the great armor of the merit of the perfection of patience."

“Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva themselves don the great armor of the merit of the perfection of patience, and also encourage immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings to don the great armor of the merit of the perfection of patience?”
"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first generation of the mind of awakening until the realization of the knowledge of all modes, dons the armor of patience and constantly reflects:

'Even if all classes of sentient beings were to come and inflict harm upon me with instruments of suffering, such as swords and staves, I would never give rise to even a single thought of anger, and I shall encourage all sentient beings to likewise cultivate this patience.'"

"Subhūti! This bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to accomplish everything according to what the mind intends, up until unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening; they never abandon such patience, and they also cause sentient beings to cultivate such patience."
"Subhūti! This is what it means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to don the armor of the Great Vehicle. Subhūti!"

It is like a skilled illusionist or his apprentice who, standing at a crossroads before a great assembly, conjures various kinds of sentient beings; some are shown wielding instruments of suffering and inflicting harm upon one another, while others are seen exhorting one another to practice the dharma of patience.
"What do you think?
Does such an illusory phenomenon have any reality? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are also like this: they themselves don the great armor of the merit of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), and they also encourage immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings to don the great armor of the merit of the perfection of patience. Although such bodhisattvas have these activities, they possess no [inherent] reality.”
Why is this? Because the nature and characteristics of all phenomena are like illusions. Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva personally dons the great armor of the merit of the perfection of diligence, they also encourage immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings to don the great armor of the merit of the perfection of diligence.

Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva personally don the great armor of the merit of the perfection of diligence, and also encourage immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings to don the great armor of the merit of the perfection of diligence?

"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes and with great compassion as the foremost, initiates various forms of physical and mental diligence, and also exhorts immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings to initiate various forms of physical and mental diligence."
"Subhūti! This is what it means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to don the armor of the Great Vehicle. Subhūti!"

Just as a skilled illusionist or his apprentice, standing at a crossroads before a great multitude, manifests various kinds of sentient beings and both personally cultivates diligence and encourages others to do so.
"What do you think?
Is such an illusory phenomenon real? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"So too it is with the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: through mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes, and with great compassion as their foremost priority, they cultivate diligence themselves and also exhort sentient beings to cultivate diligence."
In this way, although a bodhisattva performs actions, they have no reality.
Why is this? Because the nature and characteristics of all phenomena are like illusions.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva personally dons the great armor of the merit of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), and also encourages immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings to don the great armor of the merit of the perfection of meditative concentration."

Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva personally don the great armor of the merit of the dhyāna-pāramitā, and also encourage immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings to don the great armor of the merit of the dhyāna-pāramitā?

"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the equality of all phenomena, they do not perceive any phenomena as being either concentrated or distracted, yet they constantly cultivate this perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*). They also exhort sentient beings to cultivate such equalized meditative concentration, never departing from this equalized meditative concentration until they reach unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Subhūti! This is what it means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to don the armor of the Mahāyāna. Subhūti!"

Just as a skilled illusionist or his apprentice, standing at a crossroads before a great assembly, might conjure various kinds of sentient beings and cause them to cultivate the meditative concentration on the equality of all phenomena, and likewise encourage them to cultivate such concentration.
"What do you think?
Does such an illusory phenomenon have any reality? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"So too it is with the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: dwelling within the state of equality of all phenomena, they likewise exhort sentient beings to cultivate such a samādhi."
Thus, although a bodhisattva has that which they do, there is no reality in it.
Why is this? Because the nature and characteristics of all phenomena are like illusions.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva personally dons the great armor of the merit of the prajñāpāramitā, and also exhorts immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings to don the great armor of the merit of the prajñāpāramitā."

Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva personally don the great armor of the merit of the perfection of wisdom, and also encourage immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings to don the great armor of the merit of the perfection of wisdom?

"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in this profound *prajñāpāramitā* free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), they do not apprehend any distinction between this shore, the other shore, defilement, or purification; furthermore, they encourage immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings to abide in such wisdom free from conceptual proliferation."
"Subhūti! This is what it means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to don the armor of the Great Vehicle. Subhūti!"

Just as a skilled illusionist or his apprentice, standing at a crossroads before a great assembly, might conjure various kinds of sentient beings and cause them to abide in the wisdom free from conceptual proliferation, while also exhorting others to abide in such wisdom.
"What do you think?
Does such an illusory phenomenon have any reality? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"So too it is with the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: they themselves are able to abide in wisdom free from conceptual proliferation, and they also exhort sentient beings to abide in such wisdom."
In this way, although a bodhisattva performs actions, they possess no substantial reality.
Why is this? Because the nature and characteristics of all phenomena are like illusions.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having donned the armor of the aforementioned virtues, contemplates all sentient beings in the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River."

If there are sentient beings who embrace false teachings and engage in various evil deeds, this bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of supernormal powers, transforms his own body so that it pervades all such buddha-worlds. According to the inclinations of those sentient beings, he manifests the practice of the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*) himself and also encourages others to practice the perfection of generosity; likewise, up to and including the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*), he practices it himself and encourages others to practice it. Having performed these deeds, he further speaks to them in their respective languages, teaching the dharmas associated with the six perfections, so that once they have heard them, they shall never abandon such sublime dharmas until they attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
"Subhūti! This is what it means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to don the armor of the Great Vehicle. Subhūti!"

Suppose a skilled illusionist or his apprentice, standing at a crossroads before a great multitude, were to conjure various types of sentient beings and cause them to abide in the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, and likewise encourage others to abide in the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom.
"What do you think?
Does such an illusory phenomenon have any reality? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! The Buddha told Subhūti:

"So too, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas likewise manifest their own bodies throughout the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. They dwell appropriately in the six pāramitās, such as generosity, never abandoning them, and they also exhort others to dwell in the six pāramitās, such as generosity, never abandoning them."
Thus, although a bodhisattva performs actions, they possess no substantial reality.
Why is this? Because the nature and characteristics of all phenomena are like illusions.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is clad in the armor of the aforementioned virtues, attends with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), takes great compassion as the foremost, employs the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), and brings benefit and happiness to all sentient beings without mixing in the mental orientations of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."
This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not form such a thought:
"I shall establish this many sentient beings in the perfection of giving, and I shall not establish that many sentient beings in the perfection of giving."
They should simply form this thought:
"I shall establish immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings in the perfection of giving.
Thus, they do not even form such thoughts as these:

"I shall establish all those sentient beings so that they abide in the perfection of wisdom; yet, there are no such sentient beings who should be established so that they abide in the perfection of wisdom."
He should merely form this thought:
"I shall establish immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings so that they abide in the perfection of wisdom.
He should not form this thought:
"One should not think: 'I shall establish so many sentient beings in the emptiness of the internal, but I shall not establish so many sentient beings in the emptiness of the internal.
Rather, one should simply form this thought:
'I shall establish immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings in the emptiness of the internal.'"
In this way, up to and including not forming this thought:

"I shall establish so many sentient beings in the emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence, and I shall not establish so many sentient beings in the emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence."
He merely forms this thought:
"I shall establish immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings so that they abide in the emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence.
He does not form this [other] thought:

"I shall establish all those sentient beings so that they dwell in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; I shall not establish those [other] sentient beings so that they dwell in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment."
One should simply form this thought:
"I shall establish immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings so that they abide in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
One does not form this thought:

"I shall establish all those sentient beings so that they abide in the three gates of liberation; yet, there are those sentient beings whom I should not establish so that they abide in the three gates of liberation."
He merely forms this thought:
"I shall establish immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings, causing them to abide in the three gates of liberation.
This is explained at length until it says he does not form such thoughts as:

"I shall establish all those sentient beings so that they abide in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; yet, there are no such sentient beings who should be established so that they abide in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha."
One should simply form this thought:
"I shall establish immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings, causing them to abide in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha."
They do not form such thoughts as:

"I shall establish all these sentient beings and cause them to abide in the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, while those other sentient beings I shall not establish and cause to abide in the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha."
They should simply form this thought:
"I shall establish immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings, causing them to abide in the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha."
They do not form such thoughts as:

"I shall establish this many sentient beings in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, but I shall not establish that many sentient beings in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
One should simply form this thought:
"I shall establish immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Subhūti!
This is what it means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to don the armor of the Great Vehicle. "Subhūti!

It is like a skilled illusionist or his apprentice who, standing at a crossroads before a great multitude, conjures up countless and immeasurable sentient beings and causes them to abide in the six perfections, up to and including unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"What do you think?
Does such an illusory phenomenon have any reality? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! The Buddha told Subhūti:
