"So too, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, by means of mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes, with great compassion as their foremost priority, and employing the method of non-apprehension, establish countless and immeasurable sentient beings, causing them to abide in the six perfections up to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Thus, although a bodhisattva has things to do, there is no reality to them.
Why is this? Because the nature and characteristics of all phenomena are like illusions.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 487. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Three, Chapter on Subhūti, Section Seven. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, one should know that when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not don the armor of merit, they are truly donning the armor of the Mahāyāna, because all dharmas are empty of their own characteristics.
Why is that? World-Honored One!

Form is empty of the characteristic of form, and so on, up to consciousness being empty of the characteristic of consciousness; the eye-base is empty of the characteristic of the eye-base, and so on, up to the mind-base...

The sphere of the eye is empty of the characteristic of the sphere of the eye; the sphere of form is empty of the characteristic of the sphere of form, and so on up to the sphere of mental phenomena being empty of the characteristic of the sphere of mental phenomena;
the eye-element is empty of the characteristic of the eye-element, and so on up to the mind-element being empty of the characteristic of the mind-element;

the form-element is empty of the characteristic of the form-element, and so on up to the dharma-element being empty of the characteristic of the dharma-element; the eye-consciousness-element is empty of the characteristic of the eye-consciousness-element, and so on...

The consciousness element is empty of the characteristic of the consciousness element; eye-contact is empty of the characteristic of eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact being empty of the characteristic of mind-contact;

and the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are empty of the characteristic of the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition being empty of the characteristic of the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition.

The characteristic of feeling is empty; the perfection of generosity is empty of the characteristic of the perfection of generosity, up to and including the perfection of wisdom being empty of the characteristic of the perfection of wisdom.

Internal emptiness is empty of the characteristic of internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature being empty of the characteristic of the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature. The four foundations of mindfulness... [four foundations of mindfulness]... are empty.

The foundations of mindfulness are empty of the characteristics of the foundations of mindfulness, up to and including the eight branches of the noble path, which are empty of the characteristics of the eight branches of the noble path;

likewise, up to and including the ten powers of a Tathāgata, which are empty of the characteristics of the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, which are empty of the characteristics of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
the bodhisattva mahāsattva is empty of the characteristics of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Clad in the armor of great merit, clad in the armor of great merit, its characteristic is emptiness.
"World-Honored One!
For this reason, one should know that when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas do not don the armor of merit, they are truly donning the armor of the Great Vehicle."
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said. Why is this?

Because the knowledge of all-knowledge is neither created nor fashioned; all sentient beings are likewise neither created nor fashioned; and those afflictions are also neither created nor fashioned. It is for this reason that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas don the armor of the Great Vehicle.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:

"For what reason is the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) uncreated and unconditioned, and why are all sentient beings likewise uncreated and unconditioned, and those afflictions likewise uncreated and unconditioned, such that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas don the armor of the Great Vehicle for this purpose?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Because no agent can be apprehended, the knowledge of all modes is neither created nor made; all sentient beings are likewise neither created nor made; and those afflictions are also neither created nor made."
Why is that? Subhūti!
From form up to consciousness, they are neither created nor uncreated, neither made nor unmade.
Why is this? Because from form (*rūpa*) up to consciousness (*vijñāna*), these are ultimately unapprehendable.
The sense bases from the eye base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) up to the mind base (*mana-āyatana*) are neither created nor uncreated, neither produced nor unproduced.
Why is this? Because the sense base of the eye, up to and including the sense base of the mind, are ultimately unobtainable.
The sense base of forms, up to and including the sense base of phenomena, are neither created nor uncreated, neither made nor unmade.
Why is this? Because the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) up to the sense-base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) are ultimately unattainable.
The eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) up to the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is neither created nor uncreated, neither made nor unmade.
Why is this? Because the eye-element, up to and including the mind-element, are ultimately unobtainable.
The form-element, up to and including the phenomena-element, are neither created nor uncreated, neither made nor unmade.
Why is this? Because from the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) up to the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), they are ultimately unapprehendable.
From the realm of eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) up to the realm of mind-consciousness (*manovijñānadhātu*), they are neither created nor uncreated, neither produced nor unproduced.
Why is this? Because from the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element, they are ultimately unattainable.
Eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact, is neither created nor not created, neither made nor not made.
Why is this? Because eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact, are ultimately unobtainable.

The various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, are neither created nor uncreated, neither made nor unmade.
Why is this? Because the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, are ultimately unattainable.
From "self" up to "seer," there is neither creating nor not-creating, neither acting nor not-acting.
Why is this? Because from the self up to the "seer," these are ultimately unfindable.
Dreams, illusions, echoes, images, reflections, mirages, transformations, and the city of the gandharvas are neither created nor uncreated, neither made nor unmade.
Why is this? Because from dreams up to the city of Gandharvas, they are ultimately unattainable.
From internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature, they are neither created nor uncreated, neither made nor unmade.
Why is this? Because from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, they are ultimately unapprehendable.
The four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path are neither created nor uncreated, neither made nor unmade.
Why is this? Because the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path are ultimately unapprehendable.
The gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are neither created nor not created, neither made nor not made.
Why is this? Because the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are ultimately unattainable.

To speak at length, even up to the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, these are neither created nor uncreated, neither produced nor unproduced.
Why is this? Because the ten powers of the Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are ultimately unattainable.

Suchness, the dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, non-falsity, immutability, equality, the nature free from birth, the fixedness of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, and the limit of reality are neither created nor uncreated, neither made nor unmade.
Why is this? Because from true thusness (*tathatā*) up to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), these are ultimately unapprehendable.
Thus, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas neither create nor do not create; they neither act nor do not act.
Why is this? Because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are ultimately unapprehendable.
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas neither create nor do not create; they neither act nor do not act.
Why is this? Because all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are ultimately unattainable.

All-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are neither created nor uncreated, neither made nor unmade.

Why is this? Because omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are ultimately unattainable. "Subhūti!..."

For this reason, the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) is without creation or fabrication; all sentient beings are likewise without creation or fabrication; and those afflictions are also without creation or fabrication. It is for the sake of these matters that Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas don the armor of the Great Vehicle.
"Subhūti! By this principle, you should know that when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not don the armor of merit, they are truly donning the armor of the Great Vehicle.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, from form up to consciousness, there is neither bondage nor liberation.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked Subhūti:
“Venerable One, do you say that from form up to consciousness there is neither bondage nor liberation? Subhūti replied, “It is so!”
"So it is! Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:
"In what way are form, and so on, up to consciousness, neither bound nor liberated?"
Subhūti replied: "Just as with a dream, up to and including a city of gandharvas, so too from form up to consciousness there is neither bondage nor liberation. Why is this?
In this way, because all form up to consciousness are non-existent, remote, quiescent, signless, unconditioned, unborn, unceasing, unstained, and unpurified, they are neither bound nor liberated.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

Past form, up to and including consciousness, are neither bound nor liberated; future form, up to and including consciousness, are neither bound nor liberated; present form, up to and including consciousness, are neither bound nor liberated."

Why is this? Because all these things, from form up to consciousness, are non-existent, detached, quiescent, signless, unconditioned, unborn, unceasing, unstained, and unpurified; therefore, they are neither bound nor liberated.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

Wholesome form, up to and including consciousness, are neither bound nor liberated; unwholesome form, up to and including consciousness, are neither bound nor liberated; indeterminate form, up to and including consciousness, are neither bound nor liberated."

Why is this? Because all these things, from form up to consciousness, are non-existent, detached, quiescent, signless, unconditioned, unborn, unceasing, undefiled, and unpurified; therefore, they are neither bound nor liberated.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
There is no bondage and no liberation for tainted form, up to and including consciousness; there is no bondage and no liberation for untainted form, up to and including consciousness."

Why is this? Because all these things, from form up to consciousness, are non-existent, detached, quiescent, signless, unconditioned, unborn, unceasing, unstained, and unpurified; therefore, they are neither bound nor liberated.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
There is no bondage and no liberation for tainted form, up to and including consciousness; there is no bondage and no liberation for untainted form, up to and including consciousness."

Why is this so? Because all these things, from form (*rūpa*) up to consciousness (*vijñāna*), are non-existent, detached, quiescent, signless, unconditioned, unborn, unceasing, unstained, and unpurified; therefore, they are neither bound nor liberated.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Worldly form, up to and including consciousness, is neither bound nor liberated; supramundane form, up to and including consciousness, is neither bound nor liberated."

Why is this? Because all these things, from form up to consciousness, are non-existent, detached, quiescent, signless, unconditioned, unborn, unceasing, unstained, and unpurified; therefore, they are neither bound nor liberated.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
From contaminated form up to consciousness, there is neither bondage nor liberation; from pure form up to consciousness, there is neither bondage nor liberation."

Why is this? Because all these things, from form (*rūpa*) up to consciousness (*vijñāna*), are non-existent, detached, quiescent, signless, unconditioned, unborn, unceasing, unstained, and unpurified; they are neither bound nor liberated.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
All dharmas are neither bound nor liberated. Why is this so?
Because all dharmas are non-existent, detached, quiescent, signless, unconditioned, unborn, unceasing, undefiled, and unpurified, they are neither bound nor liberated.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
From the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, there is neither bondage nor liberation. Why is this so?
Because the perfections such as generosity are non-existent, remote, quiescent, signless, unconditioned, unborn, unceasing, unstained, and unpurified, they are neither bound nor liberated.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
From internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, there is neither bondage nor liberation. Why is this so?

Because inner emptiness and so forth are non-existent, because they are remote, because they are quiescent, because they are signless, because they are unconditioned, because they are unborn, because they are unceasing, because they are neither defiled nor pure, there is neither bondage nor liberation.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
The four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path are neither bound nor liberated. Why is this? "

Because the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth are non-existent, remote, quiescent, signless, unconditioned, unborn, unceasing, undefiled, and unpurified, they are neither bound nor liberated.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
The gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are neither bound nor liberated. Why is this so?
Because the gates of liberation are non-existent, detached, quiescent, signless, unconditioned, unborn, unceasing, unstained, and unpurified, they are neither bound nor liberated.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

In this way, even up to the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four unhindered understandings, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—these are neither bound nor liberated."

Why is this? Because the ten powers and so forth are non-existent, because they are detached, because they are tranquil, because they are signless, because they are unconditioned, because they are unborn, because they are unceasing, because they are unstained, and because they are unpurified, there is neither bondage nor liberation.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
All-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are neither bound nor liberated. Why is this so?
Because these various knowledges are non-existent, remote, quiescent, signless, unconditioned, unborn, unceasing, unstained, and unpurified, they are neither bound nor liberated.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice that which is neither bound nor liberated. Why is this so?

Because the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are non-existent, detached, quiescent, signless, unconditioned, unborn, unceasing, unstained, and unpurified, they are neither bound nor liberated.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
The unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is neither bound nor liberated. Why is this so?

Because the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddha is non-existent, remote, quiescent, signless, unconditioned, unborn, unceasing, unstained, and unpurified, it is neither bound nor liberated.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?
Because the bodhisattva mahāsattva is non-existent, detached, quiescent, signless, unconditioned, unborn, unceasing, unstained, and unpurified, they are neither bound nor liberated.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are neither bound nor liberated. Why is this so?

Because all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are non-existent, detached, quiescent, signless, unconditioned, unborn, unceasing, unstained, and unpurified, they are neither bound nor liberated.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

Suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the nature of non-falsity, the nature of non-alteration, equality, the nature of transcendence from birth, the fixedness of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, and the limit of reality are neither bound nor liberated."

Why is this? Because true thusness (tathatā) and so forth are non-existent, because they are remote, because they are quiescent, because they are signless, because they are unconditioned, because they are unborn, because they are unceasing, because they are neither defiled nor pure, they are neither bound nor liberated.
“Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, regarding this subtle dharma-gate that is neither bound nor liberated, should know it as it truly is by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method.”
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

All bodhisattva mahāsattvas should diligently train in these six perfections, up to and including all-aspect omniscience—which are neither bound nor liberated—by employing the skillful means of non-apprehension.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
All bodhisattva mahāsattvas should correctly abide in these six perfections that are neither bound nor liberated, up to and including all-aspect omniscience.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

By means of non-apprehension as their skillful means, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should bring to maturity sentient beings who are neither bound nor liberated; they should purify buddha-fields that are neither bound nor liberated; they should attend upon and make offerings to Buddhas who are neither bound nor liberated; and they should listen to and receive the dharma-gates that are neither bound nor liberated.

“Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra! This bodhisattva mahāsattva is never separated from the Buddhas who are neither bound nor liberated; he is never separated from the supernormal powers that are neither bound nor liberated; he is never separated from the five eyes that are neither bound nor liberated; he is never separated from the dhāraṇī-doors that are neither bound nor liberated; and he is never separated from the samādhi-doors that are neither bound nor liberated.”
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva will certainly give rise to the knowledge of the aspects of the path that is neither bound nor liberated; he will certainly realize all-knowledge and the knowledge of all aspects that are neither bound nor liberated; he will certainly turn the wheel of Dharma that is neither bound nor liberated; and he will certainly establish all classes of sentient beings—themselves neither bound nor liberated—in the essential teachings of the Three Vehicles that are neither bound nor liberated, causing them to realize ultimate nirvāṇa that is neither bound nor liberated.
“Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās that are neither bound nor liberated, they are able to realize that all dharmas are neither bound nor liberated because they are non-existent, remote, quiescent, signless, unconditioned, unborn, unceasing, unstained, and unpurified. Thus they are neither bound nor liberated.”
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

You should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is called one who has donned the great armor of neither bondage nor liberation. This bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and will be able to bring benefit, welfare, and happiness to all classes of sentient beings throughout the future.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is called the characteristic of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?”
By what means should one know that the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have set out upon the Great Vehicle?
From where does such a Great Vehicle emerge, and to where does it abide?
In what does such a Great Vehicle reside?
"Who, moreover, will mount this Great Vehicle and depart?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Regarding what you previously asked: 'What is called the characteristic of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?'"
"Subhūti, you should know this:
these six perfections are the characteristics of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are the six? "
First, the perfection of generosity;
second, the perfection of ethical discipline;
third, the perfection of patience.
Fourth is the perfection of diligence;
fifth is the perfection of meditative concentration;
sixth is the perfection of wisdom.
"What is the perfection of generosity?

It refers to a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes and with great compassion as the foremost, personally relinquishes all internal and external possessions and also encourages others to relinquish all internal and external things. Taking these roots of virtue and employing the method of non-apprehension, they share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; this is the perfection of generosity."
"What is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*)?

It refers to a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), and taking great compassion as the foremost, personally undertakes the ten paths of wholesome action and also exhorts others to undertake the ten paths of wholesome action. Taking these roots of goodness as a means through non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), they share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; this is the perfection of ethical discipline."
"What is the perfection of patience?

It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes and with great compassion as the foremost, personally possesses superior patience and also encourages others to possess superior patience; taking these roots of goodness and using the method of non-apprehension, they share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—this is the perfection of patience."
"What is the perfection of diligence?

It refers to a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes and with great compassion as the foremost, personally and untiringly practices the five perfections, and likewise encourages others to untiringly practice the five perfections. Taking these roots of virtue and using non-apprehension as the skillful means, they share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; this is the perfection of diligence."
"What is the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*)?

It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, through mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), taking great compassion as the foremost, enters the various meditative concentrations by means of their own skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), yet does not take birth according to the power of those concentrations; and likewise encourages others to enter the various meditative concentrations by means of skillful means, so that they too do not take birth according to the power of those concentrations. Taking these roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*) and, employing the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), dedicating them together with all sentient beings toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment—this is the perfection of meditative concentration."
"What is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)?

It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) and taking great compassion as the foremost, observes the nature of all phenomena (dharmatā) as it truly is; regarding the nature of all phenomena, they neither grasp nor cling to them. Furthermore, they encourage others to observe the nature of all phenomena as it truly is, so that they too neither grasp nor cling to the nature of all phenomena. Taking these roots of virtue, by means of the expedient of non-apprehension, they share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment—this is the perfection of wisdom."
"Subhūti! This is the characteristic of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"

The characteristics of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are as follows: namely, internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, great emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, non-dispersal emptiness, essential nature emptiness, characteristic emptiness, emptiness of all phenomena, emptiness of non-existence, and emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.
"What is internal emptiness?
'Internal' refers to internal phenomena, namely: the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
It should be understood that herein, the eye is empty of the eye; it is neither permanent nor subject to destruction."
Why is this? Because such is its intrinsic nature.
Thus, even up to the mind, the mind is empty of the mind; it is neither permanent nor subject to destruction.
Why is this so? Because such is its intrinsic nature.
This is what is meant by internal emptiness.
"What is external emptiness?
'External' refers to external phenomena, namely form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental objects.
It should be known that herein, form is empty of form; it is neither permanent nor subject to destruction."
Why is this? Because such is their intrinsic nature.
Thus, even up to the point where phenomena are empty of phenomena; they are neither permanent nor subject to destruction.
Why is this? Because such is its intrinsic nature.
This is called external emptiness.
"What is internal and external emptiness?
'Internal and external' refers to internal and external phenomena, namely the six internal bases and the six external bases.
It should be known that herein, internal phenomena are empty of external phenomena; they are neither permanent nor subject to destruction."
Why is this? Because such is their intrinsic nature; that is to say, the six internal bases are empty of the six external bases.
External phenomena are empty of internal phenomena, being neither permanent nor subject to destruction.
Why is this? Because such is its intrinsic nature;
that is to say, the six external bases are empty of the six internal bases.
This is called "internal-and-external emptiness."
"What is the great emptiness?
'Great' refers to the ten directions.
It should be known that herein, the eastern direction is empty of the eastern direction, being neither permanent nor subject to destruction."
Why is this? Because such is their intrinsic nature.
Thus it continues down to the lower direction, which, by virtue of being empty of a lower direction, is neither permanent nor subject to destruction.
Why is this? Because such is its intrinsic nature.
This is called the Great Emptiness.
"What is the emptiness of emptiness?
Herein, 'emptiness' refers to the emptiness of all phenomena.
This emptiness, in turn, is empty by means of the emptiness of emptiness; it is neither permanent nor subject to destruction."
Why is this? Because such is its intrinsic nature.
This is called the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*).
"What is the emptiness of the ultimate?
Herein, the ultimate is nirvāṇa.
One should know that nirvāṇa is empty of nirvāṇa; it is neither permanent nor subject to destruction."
Why is this? Because such is its intrinsic nature.
This is called the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
"What is the emptiness of the conditioned?
Herein, 'the conditioned' refers to the three realms.
One should know that the desire realm is empty of the desire realm; it is neither permanent nor subject to destruction."
Why is this? Because such is their intrinsic nature.
The realm of form and the formless realm are empty of the realm of form and the formless realm; they are neither permanent nor subject to destruction.
Why is this? Because such is its intrinsic nature.
This is called the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*).
"What is the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*)?
The unconditioned refers to phenomena that are without arising, without change, and without cessation.
One should know that the unconditioned is empty of the unconditioned; it is neither permanent nor subject to destruction."
Why is this? Because such is its intrinsic nature.
This is called the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*).
"What is ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*)?
'Ultimate' refers to that which is ultimately unobtainable.
One should know that the ultimate is empty of the ultimate; it is neither permanent nor subject to destruction."
Why is this so? Because such is its intrinsic nature.
This is called ultimate emptiness.
"What is the emptiness of the limitless (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*)?

'Limitless' means that no beginning limit, end limit, or middle limit can be apprehended. If a phenomenon has no beginning, middle, or end limit that can be apprehended, then that phenomenon neither comes nor goes."
One should know that the limitless is empty of the limitless; it is neither eternal nor subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because such is its intrinsic nature.
This is the emptiness of the limitless (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*).
What is the emptiness of non-dispersal (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*)?
Dispersal refers to the fact that phenomena can be released, discarded, or relinquished; if a phenomenon cannot be released, discarded, or relinquished, it is called "non-dispersal."
In this regard, non-dispersal is empty by virtue of non-dispersal; it is neither permanent nor subject to destruction.
Why is this? Because such is its intrinsic nature.
This is the emptiness of the non-dispersed (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*).
What is the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*)?

"Intrinsic nature" refers to the nature of all phenomena, whether conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Such an intrinsic nature is not made by śrāvakas, nor by pratyekabuddhas, nor by bodhisattvas, nor by buddhas, nor was it made by anyone else; its nature is simply so by way of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), and thus it is called "intrinsic nature."
One should know that intrinsic nature is empty of intrinsic nature; it is neither eternal nor subject to destruction.
Why is this? Because such is the nature of intrinsic nature.
This is the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*). What is the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*)?
"Characteristics" refers to the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena.
One should know that herein, characteristics are empty of characteristics; they are neither eternal nor subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because such is their intrinsic nature.
This is the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*). What is the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*)?

"All phenomena" refers to form (*rūpa*) up to consciousness (*vijñāna*); the eye (*cakṣus*) up to the mind (*manas*); forms (*rūpa*) up to mental objects (*dharma*); eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) up to mind-consciousness (*manovijñāna*); eye-contact (*cakṣuḥsaṃsparśa*) up to mind-contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*); and the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with eye-contact as a condition up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition—whether they be conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) or unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*)—these are called "all phenomena."
In this regard, all phenomena are empty of all phenomena; they are neither permanent nor subject to destruction.
Why is this? Because such is their intrinsic nature.
This is the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*). What is the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*)?
"Non-existence" refers to the fact that within this, not even the slightest existence can be found.
One should know that non-existence is empty of non-existence; it is neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because its intrinsic nature is such.
This is the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*).
What is the emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*)?

The "self-nature of non-existence" refers to the fact that among all phenomena there is no nature capable of being compounded, nor is there any self-nature of that which is compounded, because they arise from a multitude of conditions.
One should know that the nature of non-nature is empty of the nature of non-nature; it is neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because its intrinsic nature is such.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Existence is empty of existence;
non-existence is empty of non-existence; intrinsic nature is empty of intrinsic nature; and other-nature is empty of other-nature."
"What is meant by 'existence is empty of existence'?
Existence refers to conditioned phenomena, which are the five aggregates.
Thus, existence is empty of existence because the five aggregates, such as form and so forth, cannot be apprehended and because they are of a nature that is unarisen."
"What is the emptiness of non-existence by means of non-existence?

'Non-existence' refers to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). In this context, unconditioned phenomena are empty of unconditioned phenomena; this is what is meant by the emptiness of non-existence by means of non-existence."
"What is meant by 'intrinsic nature is empty of intrinsic nature'?

It means that all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature; this emptiness is not produced by wisdom, nor produced by views, nor produced by anything else. Therefore, it is called 'intrinsic nature is empty of intrinsic nature.'"
“What is the emptiness of other-nature by way of other-nature?

It refers to all phenomena—whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear—the abiding of phenomena, the fixedness of phenomena, the dharma-realm, suchness, non-falsity, non-alteration, the limit of reality, and the natural state of things, which are empty of other-nature. Therefore, it is called the emptiness of other-nature by way of other-nature.”
“Subhūti! This is the mark of the Great Vehicle of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas when they practice the profound perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Subhūti!”
The characteristics of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are as follows:

namely, the Samādhi of Heroic Progress, the Samādhi of the Jewel Seal, the Samādhi of the Lion’s Play, the Samādhi of the Wondrous Moon, the Samādhi of the Moon Banner Mark, the Samādhi of the Surge of All Dharmas, the Samādhi of Contemplating the Summit, and the Dharma... [text truncated]
The concentration of the determination of the elements, the concentration of the determined banner-sign, the diamond-like concentration,
the concentration of entering the seal of the Dharma, the king of concentrations, the well-established concentration,
the emission of light concentration, the multitude of powers concentration, and the equal surging concentration.
...the samādhi of definitive verbal expression, the samādhi of entering into synonyms, the samādhi of observing the directions,
the samādhi of holding the seal, the samādhi of non-forgetfulness,
the samādhi of the ocean-seal that is the universal course of all dharmas, the samādhi of pervading space, and the samādhi of the vajra-wheel...
The earth [samādhi], the immeasurable light samādhi, the unattached and unobstructed samādhi,
the samādhi that cuts off the turning of all dharmas, the relinquishing-jewel samādhi, the universally illuminating samādhi, the unblinking samādhi,
the dwelling-in-signlessness samādhi, the non-mental-conception samādhi, and the stainless lamp [samādhi].
the samādhi of concentration, the samādhi of boundless light, the samādhi of emitting light, the samādhi of universal illumination,
the samādhi of pure firmness, the samādhi of stainless light, the samādhi of emitting sublime bliss,
the samādhi of the lightning lamp, the samādhi of the inexhaustible, and the samādhi of possessing majestic radiance.
The earth-like samādhi, the samādhi of detachment from exhaustion, the indestructible samādhi,
the opening samādhi, the sun-lamp samādhi, the pure moon samādhi, the pure light samādhi,
the immovable samādhi, the illuminating samādhi, and the samādhi of what should and should not be done.
The samādhi of the mark of the banner of wisdom, the samādhi of the vajra-garland, the samādhi of abiding mind,
the samādhi of universal illumination, the samādhi of excellent abiding, the samādhi of the jewel-accumulation, the samādhi of the seal of the sublime Dharma,
the samādhi of the equality of phenomena, and the samādhi of relinquishing attachment and delight.
The samādhi of the overflowing of the Dharma, the samādhi of scattering, the samādhi of discerning the phrases of the Dharma,
the samādhi of the equality of the characteristics of syllables, the samādhi of being free from the characteristics of syllables,
the samādhi of severing the object of focus, the samādhi of non-alteration, the samādhi of non-categorization, and the entry into names.
The samādhi of signs, the samādhi of signless practice, the samādhi of freedom from cataracts and darkness,
the samādhi of endowed practice, the samādhi of immovability, the samādhi of transcending the sphere of objects,
the samādhi of detachment from the accumulation of all virtues, the samādhi of dwelling in certainty, and the samādhi of pure and wondrous flowers.
The samādhi of the factors of enlightenment, the samādhi of boundless eloquence, the samādhi of the peerless,
the samādhi that universally transcends all, the samādhi that definitively discerns all,
the samādhi that dispels doubt, the samādhi of non-abiding, and the samādhi of the adornment of the single characteristic.
The samādhi of the manifestation of mental formations, the samādhi of a single mental formation, the samādhi of being free from mental formations,
the samādhi of sublime mental formations, the samādhi that penetrates and shatters the depths of all existence,
the samādhi of the adamantine jewel, the samādhi of liberation from sounds and syllables, and the entry into conventional designations.
They are: the samādhi called Samādhi, the samādhi called Blazing Torch, the samādhi called Adorned with Pure Marks, the samādhi called Signless,
the samādhi called Endowed with Exquisite Marks, the samādhi called Indifference Toward All Suffering and Pleasure,
the samādhi called Inexhaustible Aspect, the samādhi called Endowed with Dhāraṇī, and the samādhi called Subduing.
The samādhi of all right and wrong natures, the samādhi of ceasing opposition and compliance, the samādhi of departing from love and hatred,

the samādhi of stainless clarity, the samādhi of possessing firmness, the samādhi of the pure light of the full moon, the samādhi of great adornment, and the samādhi of universally illuminating the world.
The samādhi of the equality of meditative concentration; the samādhi of being free from dust and defilement;
the samādhi of the principle of equality regarding contention and non-contention; the samādhi of being without a nest, without signs, and without attachment;
the samādhi of definitive abiding in suchness; and the samādhi of being free from the impurities of body, speech, and mind.

The Ground Samādhi, the Space-like Samādhi, and the Untainted and Unattached Samādhi—there are hundreds of thousands of such samādhis as these; this is the characteristic of the Great Vehicle of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
“Subhūti! In this context, what is called the ‘Vīryāpāramitā’ (Heroic Stride) samādhi?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is able to universally experience the spheres of practice of all meditative concentrations; therefore, it is named the Vīryāpāramitā samādhi.”
"What is called the 'Jewel-Seal Samādhi'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is able to seal the various characteristics and distinctions of all meditative concentrations; therefore, it is named the Jewel-Seal Samādhi."
"What is called the 'Lion’s Play Samādhi'?
It means that when one abides in this samādhi, one plays with sovereign mastery over all meditative concentrations; therefore, it is called the Lion’s Play Samādhi."
"What is called the 'Exquisite Moon Samādhi'?
It refers to when one dwells in this samādhi, it universally illuminates all meditative concentrations like the pure, full moon; therefore, it is named the Exquisite Moon Samādhi."
"What is called the Moon Banner Sign Samādhi?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is universally able to sustain the banner signs of all meditative concentrations; therefore, it is named the Moon Banner Sign Samādhi."
"What is called the 'Samādhi of the Surge of All Dharmas'?
It means that when one abides in this samādhi, one is able to universally surge forth all supreme concentrations; therefore, it is named the 'Samādhi of the Surge of All Dharmas'."
"What is called the 'Samādhi of Observing the Summit'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is able to universally observe the summits of all supreme concentrations; therefore, it is named the Samādhi of Observing the Summit."
"What is called the 'Samādhi of the Certainty of the Dharma-realm'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is able to definitively illuminate and realize the dharma-realm; therefore, it is named the Samādhi of the Certainty of the Dharma-realm."
"What is called the samādhi of the mark of the banner of certainty?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is able to certainly uphold the marks of the banners of all concentrations; therefore, it is named the samādhi of the mark of the banner of certainty."
"What is called the 'vajra-like samādhi'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, it can destroy all other meditative concentrations and cannot itself be overcome by them; therefore, it is named the vajra-like samādhi."
"What is called the 'Samādhi of Entering the Seal of All Dharmas'?
It means that when one abides in this samādhi, one is able to universally awaken to and enter the seal of all dharmas; therefore, it is named the 'Samādhi of Entering the Seal of All Dharmas'."
"What is called the 'Samādhi King of Concentrations'?
It is that when one dwells in this samādhi, one attains mastery over all meditative absorptions; therefore, it is named the Samādhi King of Concentrations."
"What is called the 'well-established samādhi'?
It refers to when one dwells in this samādhi, one is able to well establish oneself within the king of concentrations; therefore, it is named the 'well-established samādhi'."
"What is called the 'Radiating Light Samādhi'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is able to universally manifest all the lights of meditative concentration; therefore, it is named the Radiating Light Samādhi."
"What is called the 'Multitude of Powers' samādhi?
It refers to when, while abiding in this samādhi, one can generate the manifold powers of all meditative concentrations; therefore, it is named the 'Multitude of Powers' samādhi."
"What is called the Samādhi of Equal Surge?
It refers to when one abides in this samādhi, causing all supreme concentrations to surge forth equally; therefore, it is named the Samādhi of Equal Surge."
"What is called the 'Samādhi of Entering the Certainty of Words'?

It means that when one abides in this samādhi, one is necessarily able to penetrate the definitive terminology of meditative concentration; therefore, it is named the 'Samādhi of Entering the Certainty of Words'."
"What is called the 'samādhi of equal entry into designations' (*adhivacanapraveśa*)?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one enters into the principles of etymological interpretation regarding the names of all meditative concentrations with equanimity; therefore, it is called the 'samādhi of equal entry into designations.'"
"What is called the samādhi of observing the directions?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is able to universally observe and illuminate all the directions of meditative concentration; therefore, it is called the samādhi of observing the directions."
"What is called the 'Seal-holding Samādhi'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is able to universally maintain the sublime seals of all meditative concentrations; therefore, it is named the Seal-holding Samādhi."
"What is called the 'samādhi of non-forgetfulness'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is able not to forget any of the characteristics of meditative concentration; therefore, it is called the 'samādhi of non-forgetfulness'."
"What is called the 'Samādhi of the Ocean Seal to which All Dharmas Equally Converge'?

It means that when one abides in this samādhi, it causes all supreme concentrations to enter into equality, just as the ocean seal receives and gathers all streams; therefore, it is named the 'Samādhi of the Ocean Seal to which All Dharmas Equally Converge'."
"What is called the 'Samādhi that Pervades and Covers Space'?

It refers to when one dwells in this samādhi, being able to pervasively cover and protect all other meditative concentrations (samādhis) without any discrimination, just like the great void of space; therefore, it is named the Samādhi that Pervades and Covers Space."
"What is called the Vajracakra Samādhi?

It refers to when one dwells in this samādhi, being able to universally sustain all supreme concentrations so that they do not disintegrate, like a vajra-wheel; therefore, it is named the Vajracakra Samādhi."
"What is called the 'Infinite Light Samādhi'?

It means that when one abides in this samādhi, one emits infinite light that illuminates sentient beings, causing them to recollect the teachings they have previously received and to perform various great acts of benefit; therefore, it is called the 'Infinite Light Samādhi'."
"What is called the 'unattached and unobstructed samādhi'?
It refers to when one dwells in this samādhi, being free from all defiled attachments and all obstructions; therefore, it is named the 'unattached and unobstructed samādhi'."
"What is called the 'Samādhi that Severs the Turning of All Phenomena'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one realizes the principle of the non-arising of all phenomena, causing the suffering of birth and death to never again continue. Therefore, it is named the 'Samādhi that Severs the Turning of All Phenomena'."
"What is called the 'Samādhi of Discarding Jewels'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is even able to relinquish the characteristics of all meditative concentrations; how much more so would one relinquish the afflictions and the characteristics of other phenomena!"
Therefore, it is called the "Treasure-Relinquishing Samādhi.
What is called the "Pervasive Illumination Samādhi"?
It refers to when one dwells in this samādhi, it universally illuminates all meditative concentrations, making them exceedingly radiant; therefore, it is called the "Pervasive Illumination Samādhi."
“What is called the ‘Unblinking Samādhi’?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, there is no seeking or wishing regarding any phenomena; therefore, it is called the ‘Unblinking Samādhi.’”
"What is called the 'Samādhi of Abiding in the Signless'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one does not perceive even the slightest phenomenon within any meditative concentration in which one could abide; therefore, it is called the 'Samādhi of Abiding in the Signless'."
"What is called the 'non-mentation samādhi'?
It refers to when one abides in this samādhi, all inferior states of mind and mental factors cease to arise; therefore, it is called the non-mentation samādhi."
"What is called the 'Stainless Lamp Samādhi'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, it is like holding a pure lamp that illuminates all meditative concentrations; therefore, it is called the Stainless Lamp Samādhi."
"What is called the 'Infinite Light Samādhi'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one can emit a great light that illuminates infinite boundaries; therefore, it is called the Infinite Light Samādhi."
"What is called the 'Radiant' samādhi?
It means that if one abides in this meditative concentration, one is immediately able to radiate the light of all supreme concentrations; therefore, it is named the Radiant Samādhi."
"What is called the Samādhi of Universal Illumination?

It means that if one attains this meditative concentration (*samādhi*), immediately thereafter one is able to universally illuminate all gateways to the superior concentrations; therefore, it is named the Samādhi of Universal Illumination."
"What is called the 'Pure Firmness Samādhi'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one attains the pure state of equality of all samādhis; therefore, it is named the Pure Firmness Samādhi."
"What is called the 'Stainless Light Samādhi'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is able to universally eliminate all defilements of meditative concentration and also illuminate all samāpattis; therefore, it is named the 'Stainless Light Samādhi'."
"What is called the 'Emanation of Sublime Bliss' samādhi?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is able to universally experience the sublime bliss of all meditative concentrations; therefore, it is named the 'Emanation of Sublime Bliss' samādhi."
"What is called the 'Lightning Lamp' samādhi?
It refers to when one dwells in this samādhi, it illuminates all meditative absorptions like a flash of lightning; therefore, it is called the 'Lightning Lamp' samādhi."
"What is called the 'Inexhaustible Samādhi'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one perceives no exhaustion in any of the meditative concentrations; therefore, it is named the 'Inexhaustible Samādhi'."
"What is called the samādhi of possessing majestic radiance?

It refers to when, while abiding in this samādhi, one’s majestic radiance alone is preeminent among all meditative concentrations; therefore, it is called the samādhi of possessing majestic radiance."
"What is called the 'samādhi free from exhaustion'?

It refers to when, while dwelling in this samādhi, one perceives all meditative absorptions as entirely inexhaustible, yet does not perceive even the slightest mark of a phenomenon; therefore, it is named the 'samādhi free from exhaustion'."
"What is called the 'indestructible samādhi'?
It means that when one abides in this samādhi, all meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) are seen to be without flaw or fissure; therefore, it is called the indestructible samādhi."
"What is called the 'Development' samādhi?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one sees that there is no meditative concentration (samādhi) that is not developed; therefore, it is named the 'Development' samādhi."
"What is called the Sun-Lamp Samādhi?
It means that when one abides in this samādhi, it causes all gateways of concentration to emit light and shine everywhere; therefore, it is named the Sun-Lamp Samādhi."
"What is called the 'Pure Moon Samādhi'?
It refers to when, while abiding in this samādhi, one causes all meditative concentrations (samādhis) to shatter darkness like the moon; therefore, it is named the Pure Moon Samādhi."
"What is called the 'Samādhi of Pure Light'?
It means that when one abides in this samādhi, one attains unimpeded understanding regarding all meditative concentrations; therefore, it is named the Samādhi of Pure Light."
"What is called the 'Unshakable Samādhi'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, it causes all meditative absorptions to be without agitation, pride, or movement, and also free from conceptual proliferation; therefore, it is called the Unshakable Samādhi."
"What is called the 'Illumination-Producing' (*prabhākara*) samādhi?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, it causes all gateways of concentration to produce illumination and shine everywhere; therefore, it is named the 'Illumination-Producing' samādhi."
"What is called the samādhi of what should and should not be done?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, it illuminates all matters of what should and should not be done regarding all meditative concentrations (samādhis), making them clearly manifest; therefore, it is named the samādhi of what should and should not be done."
"What is called the 'Samādhi of the Mark of the Banner of Wisdom'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one perceives the mark of the banner of sublime wisdom within all meditative concentrations; therefore, it is named the Samādhi of the Mark of the Banner of Wisdom."
“What is called the Vajramālā Samādhi?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, although one can penetrate all phenomena, one does not perceive any marks; therefore, it is called the Vajramālā Samādhi.”
"What is called the 'Samādhi of Abiding Mind'?

It refers to when, while abiding in this samādhi, the mind does not waver, does not turn, does not illuminate, and is not diminished; furthermore, one does not even think that there is a mind. Therefore, it is called the Samādhi of Abiding Mind."
"What is called the Samādhi of Universal Radiance?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is able to universally observe and illuminate all concentrations; therefore, it is named the Samādhi of Universal Radiance."
"What is called the 'Samādhi of Excellent Abiding'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is able to abide excellently within all meditative concentrations; therefore, it is named the Samādhi of Excellent Abiding."
"What is called the Jewel-Heap Samādhi?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one contemplates all meditative concentrations as being like a heap of jewels; therefore, it is named the Jewel-Heap Samādhi."
"What is called the Samādhi of the Seal of the Sublime Dharma?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is able to seal all meditative concentrations (samādhis) by means of the seal of 'no-seal'; therefore, it is named the Samādhi of the Seal of the Sublime Dharma."
"What is called the samādhi of the equality of phenomena?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one does not perceive even the slightest phenomenon that is apart from the nature of equality; therefore, it is called the samādhi of the equality of phenomena."
"What is called the 'samādhi of relinquishing attachment and delight'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one relinquishes attachment and delight toward all meditative concentrations and all phenomena; therefore, it is called the 'samādhi of relinquishing attachment and delight.'"
"What is called the 'Samādhi of the Overflowing Fulfillment of Dharmas'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, the characteristics of all dharmas entirely surge forth, and there are no Buddha-dharmas that are not fully perfected; therefore, it is named the 'Samādhi of the Overflowing Fulfillment of Dharmas.'"
"What is called the 'dispersing samādhi'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, it can cause all concentrations to disperse all phenomena; therefore, it is called the dispersing samādhi."
"What is called the *dharmapadavibhajanā* samādhi?
It refers to when, while abiding in this samādhi, one is well able to discern the various dharmapadas of the meditative concentrations; therefore, it is called the *dharmapadavibhajanā* samādhi."
"What is called the samādhi of the mark of equal syllables?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one attains the mark of equal syllables of all samādhis, which is exceedingly delightful; therefore, it is called the samādhi of the mark of equal syllables."
"What is called the 'samādhi of being free from the marks of words'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, not even a single word among all meditative concentrations can be found as an object of attachment or delight; therefore, it is called the 'samādhi of being free from the marks of words'."
"What is called the 'samādhi that severs the object of focus'?

It refers to when, while abiding in this samādhi, one severs all characteristics of the objects of focus of various meditative concentrations; therefore, it is called the 'samādhi that severs the object of focus.'"
"What is called the 'unchanging samādhi'?
It means that when one abides in this samādhi, one does not perceive the characteristics of change in any phenomena; therefore, it is called the unchanging samādhi."
"What is called the 'categoryless samādhi'?
It means that when one abides in this samādhi, one does not apprehend the distinct characteristics of the categories of all phenomena; therefore, it is called the categoryless samādhi."
"What is called the samādhi of entering names and characteristics?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one realizes and enters into the distinctions among the names and characteristics of all phenomena; therefore, it is called the samādhi of entering names and characteristics."
"What is called the 'samādhi of signless practice'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, no signs of any meditative concentrations whatsoever are apprehended; therefore, it is called the 'samādhi of signless practice'."
"What is called the 'Samādhi Free from Obscuration and Darkness'?

It means that when one abides in this samādhi, one is universally able to dispel the obscurations and darkness of all meditative concentrations; therefore, it is named the 'Samādhi Free from Obscuration and Darkness'."
"What is called the 'Samādhi Endowed with Activity'?
It refers to when, while abiding in this samādhi, one perceives the distinct characteristics of the activities of all samādhis; therefore, it is named the Samādhi Endowed with Activity."
"What is called the 'Immovable Samādhi'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one perceives no movement or fluctuation among all meditative absorptions; therefore, it is called the Immovable Samādhi."
"What is called the 'Samādhi that Transcends the Sphere of Objects'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one transcends the characteristics of the objects of focus of all other meditative concentrations; therefore, it is called the 'Samādhi that Transcends the Sphere of Objects'."
"What is called the 'Samādhi of Being Free from the Accumulation of All Virtues'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one does not perceive any characteristic of accumulation regarding any phenomena or any meditative concentrations, because all phenomena cannot be accumulated. Therefore, it is called the 'Samādhi of Being Free from the Accumulation of All Virtues.'"
"What is called the 'Samādhi of Decisive Abiding'?

It means that when one abides in this samādhi, although the mind remains decisively settled within all meditative concentrations, its characteristics are ultimately found to be ungraspable; therefore, it is called the Samādhi of Decisive Abiding."
"What is called the 'Pure and Wondrous Flower' samādhi?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, it causes all meditative concentrations (samādhis) to become pure, adorned and radiant like a wondrous flower; therefore, it is named the 'Pure and Wondrous Flower' samādhi."
"What is called the 'Samādhi Endowed with the Factors of Enlightenment'?

It refers to when, while abiding in this samādhi, one cultivates the seven factors of enlightenment and swiftly attains their perfection; therefore, it is named the 'Samādhi Endowed with the Factors of Enlightenment'."
"What is called the 'Infinite Eloquence Samādhi'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one attains infinite eloquence regarding all phenomena; therefore, it is called the Infinite Eloquence Samādhi."
"What is called the 'Unequaled and Equal' (*asamasama*) samādhi?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one attains the unequaled and equal nature of all meditative concentrations; therefore, it is named the 'Unequaled and Equal' samādhi."

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 488. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Three, Chapter on Subhūti, Section Eight: "What is called the Samādhi that Universally Transcends All?"

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one universally transcends all phenomena pertaining to sentient beings within the three realms; therefore, it is named "The Samādhi of Universal Transcendence."
"What is called the 'Samādhi that Decisively Discerns All'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is universally able to decisively discern all phenomena pertaining to sentient beings; therefore, it is named the 'Samādhi that Decisively Discerns All'."
“What is called the samādhi that disperses hesitation?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, all hesitations regarding all meditative concentrations and all phenomena are dispersed and extinguished; therefore, it is called the samādhi that disperses hesitation.”
"What is called the 'Samādhi of Non-Abiding'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one does not perceive any place where phenomena abide; therefore, it is called the 'Samādhi of Non-Abiding'."
"What is called the 'Samādhi Adorned with a Single Characteristic'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one does not perceive even the slightest characteristic in any phenomena; therefore, it is called the 'Samādhi Adorned with a Single Characteristic'."
"What is called the samādhi of manifesting various aspects?

It refers to when one dwells in this samādhi, although one can manifest various aspects regarding all meditative concentrations and all phenomena, one perceives neither the agent who manifests nor the objects manifested; therefore, it is called the samādhi of manifesting various aspects."
"What is called the 'single-aspect samādhi'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one perceives all meditative concentrations as having no dual aspects; therefore, it is called the single-aspect samādhi."
"What is called the 'samādhi free from the aspect of activity'?

It means that when one abides in this samādhi, one perceives that all meditative absorptions (samādhis) are entirely devoid of the aspect of activity; therefore, it is called the 'samādhi free from the aspect of activity'."
"What is called the 'Samādhi of Subtle Conduct' (*sūkṣmacaryā-lakṣaṇa-samādhi*)?

It means that when one abides in this samādhi, it causes all meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) to have subtle modes of conduct (*caryā-lakṣaṇa*) free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); therefore, it is named the Samādhi of Subtle Conduct."
"What is called the *sarvabhavatalavidhvaṃsana-samādhi*?

It refers to when, while abiding in this samādhi, one attains the wisdom of thorough penetration regarding all meditative concentrations and all phenomena, entering into them as they truly are. Having attained such entry, one thoroughly penetrates and disperses all phenomena of existence so that nothing remains; therefore, it is named the *sarvabhavatalavidhvaṃsana-samādhi*."
"What is called the 'jewel-solidity samādhi'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one perceives that the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha are indestructible, because they are identical with the signless (animitta). For this reason, it is called the jewel-solidity samādhi."
"What is called the 'Liberation from Sound and Syllables' samādhi?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one perceives all meditative absorptions as liberated from all sounds and syllables, with all signs extinguished; therefore, it is called the 'Liberation from Sound and Syllables' samādhi."
"What is called the 'samādhi of entering into designations and linguistic expressions'?

It means that when one abides in this samādhi, one penetrates all dharmas of all meditative concentrations (samādhis), such that there is no attachment or obstruction regarding designations and linguistic expressions; therefore, it is called the 'samādhi of entering into designations and linguistic expressions.'"
"What is called the 'Blazing Torch' samādhi?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, it illuminates all other meditative concentrations with its majestic radiance; therefore, it is named the 'Blazing Torch' samādhi."
"What is called the Samādhi of Adorned and Purified Marks?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one is universally able to adorn and purify all marks of meditative concentration; therefore, it is named the Samādhi of Adorned and Purified Marks."
"What is called the 'signless samādhi'?
It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one perceives no signs within any meditative concentrations; therefore, it is called the signless samādhi."
"What is called the samādhi endowed with excellent marks?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, there are no excellent marks of all meditative concentrations that are not fully possessed; therefore, it is called the samādhi endowed with excellent marks."
"What is called the 'samādhi that does not delight in any suffering or pleasure'?

It refers to when one dwells in this samādhi, one does not take pleasure in observing the characteristics of pleasure or suffering within any meditative absorptions; therefore, it is called the 'samādhi that does not delight in any suffering or pleasure.'"
"What is called the 'samādhi of inexhaustible characteristics'?

It means that when one abides in this samādhi, one does not perceive any exhaustion in the characteristics of the various meditative concentrations; therefore, it is named the 'samādhi of inexhaustible characteristics'."
"What is called the samādhi endowed with dhāraṇī?
It refers to when, while abiding in this samādhi, one is able to universally sustain the supreme qualities of all meditative concentrations; therefore, it is called the samādhi endowed with dhāraṇī."
"What is called the 'Samādhi that Subdues All Righteousness and Unrighteousness'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, regarding the righteousness and unrighteousness of all meditative concentrations, it subdues all views so that they do not arise; therefore, it is named the 'Samādhi that Subdues All Righteousness and Unrighteousness.'"
"What is called the 'Samādhi of Stilling Contrariety and Accordance'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, regarding all meditative absorptions and all phenomena, one perceives no signs whatsoever of contrariety or accordance; therefore, it is named the Samādhi of Stilling Contrariety and Accordance."
"What is called the 'samādhi free from attachment and aversion'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one perceives no signs of attachment or aversion whatsoever regarding any meditative concentrations or all phenomena; therefore, it is called the 'samādhi free from attachment and aversion'."
"What is called the 'Stainless Radiance Samādhi'?
It means that when one abides in this samādhi, one perceives neither the mark of defilement nor the mark of radiance; therefore, it is named the Stainless Radiance Samādhi."
"What is called the samādhi endowed with firmness?
It means that when one abides in this samādhi, it causes all meditative concentrations (samādhis) to become firm; therefore, it is named the samādhi endowed with firmness."
"What is called the 'Full Moon Pure Radiance Samādhi'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, the merits of all meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) are increased, just as the pure full moonlight increases the waters of the ocean; therefore, it is named the Full Moon Pure Radiance Samādhi."
"What is called the 'Great Ornament Samādhi'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, it causes all meditative concentrations (samādhis) to accomplish various subtle, wondrous, and great ornamental feats; therefore, it is named the Great Ornament Samādhi."
"What is called the 'Samādhi that Universally Illuminates the World'?

It refers to when one abides in this samādhi, it illuminates all meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and all phenomena (*dharma*), causing all classes of sentient beings to attain clear understanding; therefore, it is named the 'Samādhi that Universally Illuminates the World'."
"What is called the samādhi of the equality of concentration?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one does not perceive any distinction between meditative equipoise and distraction; therefore, it is called the samādhi of the equality of concentration. What is called the samādhi of being free from dust and stain?"
"What is called the samādhi of the principle of equality regarding the contentious and the non-contentious?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one does not perceive any distinction between the characteristics of the contentious and non-contentious natures of all phenomena and all meditative concentrations; therefore, it is named the samādhi of the principle of equality regarding the contentious and the non-contentious."
"What is called the 'nestless, signless, and desireless samādhi'?

It refers to when one dwells in this samādhi, one destroys all nests, abandons all signs, and cuts off all desires without any grasping; therefore, it is called the nestless, signless, and desireless samādhi."
"What is called the samādhi of definitive abiding in suchness?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, regarding all meditative concentrations and all phenomena, one never abandons the true mark of suchness; therefore, it is called the samādhi of definitive abiding in suchness."
"What is called the 'samādhi that is free from the defilements of body, speech, and mind'?

It refers to when one dwells in this samādhi, there is no apprehension whatsoever of body, speech, or mind; one destroys all evils of body, speech, and mind, and attains unimpeded mastery over all meditative concentrations. For this reason, it is called the 'samādhi that is free from the defilements of body, speech, and mind.'"
"What is called the 'space-like samādhi'?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one contemplates all phenomena as being utterly non-existent, unobstructed and unhindered like the great void of space; therefore, it is called the 'space-like samādhi'."
“What is called the ‘stainless and unattached samādhi’?

It means that when one dwells in this samādhi, one contemplates all phenomena as having a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness; being stainless and unattached, it is therefore called the ‘stainless and unattached samādhi.’”
"Subhūti! This is the mark of the Great Vehicle when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The characteristics of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are the four foundations of mindfulness.
What are the four? First, the foundation of mindfulness of the body.
2. The application of mindfulness to feelings (vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna).
3. The application of mindfulness to the mind (citta-smṛtyupasthāna). 4. The application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharma-smṛtyupasthāna).
"What is the application of mindfulness to the body?

It means that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, by way of non-apprehension as a skillful means, although they abide in the contemplation of the body—whether regarding the internal body, the external body, or both the internal and external body—they are able to give rise to no discursive thoughts associated with the body. They exert fervent diligence, possess correct knowledge and full mindfulness, and eliminate worldly greed and sorrow."
"What is the application of mindfulness to feelings?

It refers to when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, by means of non-apprehension as a skillful method, dwells observing feelings within, or feelings without, or feelings both within and without; yet they are able to give rise to no discursive thoughts associated with feeling, maintaining ardent diligence, correct knowledge, and full mindfulness, thereby removing worldly greed and sorrow."
“What is the application of mindfulness to the mind?

It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, dwells observing the mind internally, or externally, or both internally and externally; yet he is able to give rise to no discursive thoughts associated with the mind, maintaining ardent diligence, clear comprehension, and full mindfulness, thereby removing worldly greed and sorrow.”
"What is the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*)?

It refers to when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, dwells in the contemplation of phenomena (*dharmānupaśyanā*) regarding internal phenomena, external phenomena, or both internal and external phenomena; yet, he is able to give rise to no discursive thoughts associated with phenomena, exerts ardent diligence, possesses correct knowledge and full mindfulness, and eliminates worldly greed and sorrow."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they dwell in the contemplation of the body within the body by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method; they are ardent in vigor, possessed of correct knowledge and mindfulness, and have removed worldly greed and sorrow. This means that when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they use non-apprehension as their skillful method to examine their own bodies: when walking, they know they are walking as it truly is; when standing, they know they are standing as it truly is; when sitting, they know they are sitting as it truly is; and when lying down, they know they are lying down as it truly is. In whatever way their bodily postures differ, they know each exactly as it truly is. Thus, being ardent in vigor, possessed of correct knowledge and mindfulness, they have removed worldly greed and sorrow."

This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, dwells contemplating the body within the body by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, ardent in vigor, clearly comprehending and possessed of mindfulness, having removed worldly covetousness and grief.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they dwell in the contemplation of the body within the body by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method; they are ardent in vigor, possessed of correct knowledge and mindfulness, having removed worldly greed and sorrow. This means that when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they use non-apprehension as their skillful method to closely observe their own bodies: they have correct knowledge of coming and going, correct knowledge of looking ahead and looking back, correct knowledge of bending and stretching, correct knowledge of wearing the saṃghāṭī robe, holding the robes and bowl, eating or drinking, lying down or resting, walking, sitting, rising, receiving guests, waking or sleeping, speaking or remaining silent, and entering or emerging from various meditative concentrations—all while maintaining mindfulness and correct knowledge."

This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, dwells contemplating the body within the body by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, ardent in energy, clearly comprehending and mindful, having removed worldly covetousness and grief.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they dwell in the contemplation of the body within the body by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method; they are ardent in diligence, possessed of correct knowledge and mindfulness, and have removed worldly greed and sorrow. This means that when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they carefully observe their own bodies by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method: when the breath enters, they know the breath entering as it truly is; when the breath exits, they know the breath exiting as it truly is; when the breath is long, they know the breath long as it truly is; and when the breath is short, they know the breath short as it truly is."

Just as a wheelwright or his apprentice, when the momentum of the wheel is long, knows truly that the momentum of the wheel is long, and when the momentum of the wheel is short, knows truly that the momentum of the wheel is short.
In this same way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva also knows, as it truly is, whether the breath enters or exits, and its distinctions of length.
