This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, dwells in contemplation of the body within the internal body by means of non-apprehension; with ardent diligence, correct knowledge, and full mindfulness, they eliminate worldly desire and distress.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! When Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they dwell in the contemplation of the body within the body by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method; they are ardent in diligence, possessed of correct knowledge and mindfulness, and have removed worldly greed and sorrow. This means that when Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they take non-apprehension as their skillful method and, in accordance with reality, understand the various distinctions of the elements (*dhātu*) belonging to their own bodies: they understand, in accordance with reality, that 'this is the earth element' regarding all earth elements; they understand, in accordance with reality, that 'this is the water element' regarding all water elements; they understand, in accordance with reality, that 'this is the fire element' regarding all fire elements; and they understand, in accordance with reality, that 'this is the wind element' regarding all wind elements."

Just as a skilled butcher or his apprentice, having taken the life of an ox, uses a sharp knife to dissect its body into four parts, whether sitting or standing, observes and understands them exactly as they are.

In the same way, when this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they employ the method of non-apprehension to observe the distinctions between the four elements of their own body: earth, water, fire, and wind.

This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, dwells contemplating the body within the body by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, ardent in vigor, clearly comprehending and possessed of mindfulness, having removed worldly greed and sorrow.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom,
they dwell observing the body within the body by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method, with ardent diligence and clear comprehension."
"Endowed with mindfulness, having removed worldly greed and sorrow" means that when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*,

using non-apprehension as a skillful means, they carefully contemplate their own body from the feet to the crown of the head as being filled with various kinds of impurities, externally enveloped by a thin layer of skin.
What is called this body consists only of various kinds of hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, leather, blood, flesh, tendons, veins, bones, marrow,
heart, liver, lungs, kidneys, spleen, gallbladder, bladder, stomach, large intestine, small intestine,
excrement, urine, nasal mucus, saliva, spittle, tears, sweat, phlegm, pus, fat, grease, brain, membranes, and lymph. It is as follows:
This body is filled with impurities.

It is like a farmer or a householder whose granary is filled with various kinds of grain—namely rice, hemp, millet, beans, wheat, and so forth—and a person with clear vision opens the granary and beholds it, being able to know according to reality that there are only various grains within, such as rice, hemp, and millet.

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva is likewise: he carefully contemplates his own body from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head as being filled with impurities, such that it is not to be craved or delighted in.

This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, dwells observing the body within the body by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, ardent in vigor, clearly comprehending and possessed of mindfulness, having removed worldly greed and sorrow.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they dwell in the contemplation of the body within the body by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method; they are ardent in vigor, possessed of correct knowledge and mindfulness, having removed worldly greed and sorrow. This refers to when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, go to a cemetery by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method and observe discarded corpses that have been dead for one day, or two days, up to seven days; their bodies are bloated, their color has turned bluish-purple, they are putrid and rotting with the skin pierced, and pus and blood flow out."

Having seen this, he reflects to himself: "My own body possesses such a nature and is endowed with such qualities; until I attain nirvana, it will ultimately end in this same way. Thus, he develops a profound sense of weary detachment.

This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, dwells contemplating the body within the body by means of non-apprehension as the skillful means, ardent in vigor, clearly comprehending and possessed of mindfulness, having removed worldly covetousness and grief.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they dwell in the contemplation of the body within the body by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method; they are ardent in vigor, possessed of right knowledge and mindfulness, having removed worldly greed and sorrow. This refers to when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, go to a cemetery by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method to observe discarded corpses that have been dead for one day, two days, or even up to seven days, being pecked at or clawed by various birds and beasts such as vultures, eagles, crows, magpies, hawks, owls, tigers, leopards, jackals, wolves, wild dogs, and dogs, with their bones and flesh strewn about as they are torn apart and devoured."

Having seen this, he reflects: "My own body possesses such a nature and is endowed with such qualities; until I attain nirvana, it will ultimately end in this way. Thus, he gives rise to a profound sense of weary detachment.

This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, dwells observing the body within the body by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, ardent in vigor, clearly comprehending and possessed of mindfulness, having removed worldly greed and sorrow.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they dwell in the contemplation of the body within the body by means of non-apprehension as their skillful means; they are ardent in vigor, possessed of correct knowledge and mindfulness, having removed worldly greed and sorrow. This refers to when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* by means of non-apprehension as their skillful means, going to cemeteries to observe discarded corpses that have been devoured by birds and beasts, becoming impure and putrid, with pus and blood flowing out, and from which immeasurable kinds of worms and maggots emerge, foul and filthy beyond even a dead dog."

Having seen this, he reflects to himself: "My own body possesses such a nature and is endowed with such qualities; until I attain nirvana, it will ultimately end in this same way. Thus, he develops a profound sense of weary detachment.

This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, dwells contemplating the body within the body by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, ardent in vigor, clearly comprehending and possessed of mindfulness, having removed worldly greed and sorrow.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they dwell in the contemplation of the body within the body by means of non-apprehension as their skillful means; they are ardent in vigor, clearly comprehending and possessed of mindfulness, having removed worldly greed and sorrow. This refers to when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, go to a cemetery by means of non-apprehension as their skillful means and observe discarded corpses: after they have been eaten by worms and maggots, the flesh has fallen away from the bones which now appear, with the limbs and joints still connected, bound by sinews and smeared with blood, yet with putrid flesh still remaining."

Having seen this, he reflects to himself: "My own body possesses such a nature and is endowed with such qualities; until I attain nirvana, it will ultimately end in this same way. Thus, he develops a profound sense of weary detachment.

This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, dwells observing the body within the body by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, ardent in vigor, clearly comprehending and possessed of mindfulness, having removed worldly covetousness and grief.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they dwell in the contemplation of the body within the body by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method; they are ardent in vigor, possessed of correct knowledge and mindfulness, having removed worldly greed and sorrow. This refers to when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, go to a cemetery by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method and observe discarded corpses that have become skeletons, with the flesh and blood entirely gone and only the remaining sinews still connecting them."

Having seen this, he reflects to himself: "My own body possesses such a nature and is endowed with such qualities; until I attain nirvana, it will ultimately end in this same way. Thus, he gives rise to a profound sense of weary detachment.

This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, dwells observing the body within the body by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, ardent in vigor, clearly comprehending and possessed of mindfulness, having removed worldly covetousness and grief.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they dwell in the contemplation of the body within the body by means of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), ardent in vigor, clearly comprehending and possessed of mindfulness, having removed worldly greed and sorrow. This refers to when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* by means of non-apprehension, go to a cemetery and observe discarded corpses that are nothing but a heap of bones, their color white as snow, conch shells, or cowries, with all tendons rotted away and the joints separated."

Having seen this, he reflects to himself: "My own body possesses such a nature and is endowed with such qualities; until I have attained nirvana, it will ultimately end in this same way. Thus, he gives rise to a profound sense of weary detachment.

This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, dwells observing the body within the body by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, ardent in vigor, clearly comprehending and possessed of mindfulness, having removed worldly greed and sorrow.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they dwell in the contemplation of the body within the body by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method; they are ardent in vigor, possessed of correct knowledge and mindfulness, having removed worldly greed and sorrow. This refers to when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, go to a cemetery and observe discarded corpses that have turned white, with their limbs and joints scattered and fallen apart in various directions."

Having seen this, he reflects to himself: "My own body possesses such a nature and is endowed with such dharmas; until I have attained nirvana, it will ultimately end in this same way. Thus, he gives rise to a profound sense of weary detachment.

This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, dwells observing the body within the body by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, with ardent diligence, clearly comprehending and possessed of mindfulness, having removed worldly greed and sorrow.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom,
they dwell in the contemplation of the body within the body by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method, with ardent diligence and clear comprehension."

"Endowed with mindfulness and having removed worldly greed and sorrow" refers to when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, employing the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), goes to a cemetery and observes discarded corpses:
the various bones are scattered, each in a different place; the foot bones are in one place, the shin bones in another.
As for the locations: the knee bones are in one place, the thigh bones in another, the hip bones in another,
the vertebrae in another, the ribs in another, the breastbone in another, the shoulder blades in another,
the arm bones in another, the hand bones in another, the nape of the neck in another, the jawbones in another, and the cheekbones in another.
The skull bones are also in another place. Having seen this, he reflects:
"My own body possesses such a nature and is endowed with such qualities; until I attain Nirvana, it will ultimately end in this way. Thus, he gives rise to a profound sense of weary detachment.

This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, dwells observing the body within the body by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, ardent in vigor, clearly comprehending and possessed of mindfulness, having removed worldly greed and sorrow.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they dwell in the contemplation of the body within the body by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method; they are ardent in diligence, possessed of right knowledge and mindfulness, having removed worldly greed and sorrow. This refers to when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, go to a cemetery by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method and observe discarded corpses: the bones scattered about, blown by the wind, scorched by the sun, drenched by rain, and encrusted with frost for many years, appearing white like jade or snow."

Having seen this, he reflects to himself: "My own body possesses such a nature and is endowed with such qualities; until I attain nirvana, it will ultimately end in this same way. Thus, he develops a profound sense of weary detachment.

This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, dwells observing the body within the body by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, ardent in vigor, clearly comprehending and possessed of mindfulness, having removed worldly greed and sorrow.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they dwell in the contemplation of the body within the body by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method, ardent in vigor, clearly comprehending and possessed of mindfulness, having removed worldly greed and sorrow. This refers to when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, go to a cemetery and observe discarded corpses: other bones scattered upon the ground for many hundreds or many thousands of years, their appearance turned blue like the color of a pigeon, or some being rotten and reduced to dust-like powder, mixed with the earth so that they can hardly be distinguished."

Having seen this, he reflects: "My own body possesses such a nature and is endowed with such qualities; until I have attained nirvana, it will ultimately end in this same way. Thus, he develops a profound sense of weary detachment.

This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, dwells observing the body within the body by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, ardent in vigor, clearly comprehending and possessed of mindfulness, having removed worldly greed and sorrow.

“Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they employ the method of non-apprehension. Just as they dwell in the contemplation of the body internally with such distinctions—ardently diligent, clearly comprehending, and possessed of mindfulness, having removed worldly greed and sorrow—they likewise dwell in the contemplation of the body externally, and they dwell in the contemplation of the body both internally and externally; being ardently diligent, clearly comprehending, and possessed of mindfulness, they have removed worldly greed and sorrow, and it is the same for all that is appropriate.”

"Subhūti! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they employ the method of non-apprehension regarding internal, external, and both internal and external feelings, mind, and phenomena. They abide in the contemplation of feelings, mind, and phenomena, exerting ardent diligence, possessing correct knowledge and mindfulness, and removing worldly greed and sorrow; all this should be explained in detail according to what is appropriate."

"Subhūti! Thus, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, they abide in the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena—both internally and externally—and while observing the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena, although they perform this observation, there is nothing to be apprehended."
"Subhūti! This is the mark of the Great Vehicle when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The characteristics of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas consist of the four right endeavors (*samyakprahāṇa*). What are these four?
Subhūti, you should know this!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, employing the method of non-apprehension, they generate desire, exert themselves, arouse right effort, and apply themselves with mental vigor and mental sustenance so that unarisen evil and unwholesome states do not arise; this is the first.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, employing the method of non-apprehension, they generate desire, exert effort, arouse right diligence, and apply themselves with mental exertion and mental sustenance for the sake of permanently abandoning all evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen; this is the second [basis of power].

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, employing the method of non-apprehension, they generate desire, exert effort, arouse right diligence, and uplift and sustain the mind so that wholesome dharmas not yet arisen may arise; this is the third [basis of power].

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, employing the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), they generate the desire, exert themselves, arouse right effort, and apply themselves with mental application and maintenance of the mind, so that already arisen wholesome dharmas may remain stable, not be forgotten, and be further increased, expanded, repeatedly cultivated, and brought to fulfillment; this is the fourth [basis of psychic power].
"Subhūti! This is the mark of the Great Vehicle when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The characteristics of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas consist of the four bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*). What are these four?
Subhūti, you should know this!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, employing the method of non-apprehension, they cultivate the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration of desire and the formations of abandonment; relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and culminating in relinquishment—this is the first.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, cultivates the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration through exertion and the accomplishment of the formative forces of abandonment, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and resulting in relinquishment—this is the second.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, they cultivate the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration of mind and the accomplishment of the application of effort; relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and resulting in relinquishment—this is the third.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, cultivates the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration through contemplation and the accomplishment of the formations of abandonment, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and resulting in relinquishment—this is the fourth.
"Subhūti! This is the mark of the Great Vehicle when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"
Subhūti, you should know that the characteristics of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are the five faculties. What are these five?
Subhūti, you should know!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they cultivate the faculty of faith, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
"Subhūti! This is the mark of the Great Vehicle when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The characteristics of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas consist of the five powers.
What are these five? Subhūti, you should know this!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they cultivate the power of faith, the power of diligence, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method.
"Subhūti! This is the mark of the Great Vehicle when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The characteristics of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas consist of the seven factors of enlightenment.
What are these seven?
Subhūti, you should know this!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, they cultivate the awakening factor of mindfulness, the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena, the awakening factor of energy, the awakening factor of joy, the awakening factor of tranquility, the awakening factor of concentration, and the awakening factor of equanimity; these are based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and result in relinquishment.
"Subhūti! This is the mark of the Great Vehicle when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The characteristics of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas consist of the eightfold noble path.
What are these eight?
Subhūti, you should know this!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, they cultivate right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration; these are based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and dedicated to relinquishment.
"Subhūti! This is the mark of the Great Vehicle when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The characteristics of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas consist of the three gates of liberation.
What are these three?
"Subhūti, you should know this!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, they contemplate that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty; their mind abides therein, which is called the gate of liberation of emptiness and is also called the samādhi of emptiness. This is the first [gate]; all bodhisattva mahāsattvas who wish to study the Great Vehicle should train within this.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, they contemplate that all phenomena are signless because their own-characteristics are empty; their mind abides therein, which is called the gate of liberation of signlessness and is also called the samādhi of signlessness. This is the second [gate], in which all bodhisattva mahāsattvas who wish to study the Great Vehicle should train.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, by means of non-apprehension as a skillful means, they contemplate that all phenomena are empty of intrinsic characteristics and thus have no object of aspiration; their mind abides in peace, which is called the gate of liberation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*), and is also called the concentration of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-samādhi*). This is the third [gate]; all bodhisattva mahāsattvas who wish to study the Great Vehicle should train therein.
"Subhūti! This is the mark of the Great Vehicle when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The characteristics of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas consist of eleven types of knowledge.
What are these eleven? They are:

the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of the origin, the knowledge of cessation, the knowledge of the path, the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, the knowledge of phenomena, the subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, the knowledge of others' minds, and the knowledge as it was taught.
"What is the knowledge of suffering?
It is the knowledge that, by means of non-apprehension as its expedient, knows that suffering should not arise; this is the knowledge of suffering.
What is the knowledge of origination?"
That is to say, if wisdom takes non-apprehension as its means and knows that origination should be permanently abandoned, this is the knowledge of origination.
What is the knowledge of cessation?
If wisdom takes non-apprehension as its means and knows that cessation should be realized, this is the knowledge of cessation.
"What is the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)?
It is the knowledge that, employing the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), knows that the path should be cultivated; this is the knowledge of the path.
What is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*)?"
That is to say, if wisdom takes non-apprehension as its means and knows that greed, hatred, and delusion are exhausted, this is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
"What is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*)?
It is said that if wisdom takes non-apprehension as its skillful means and knows that all existents will not arise again, this is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
What is the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)?
It means that if wisdom, employing the method of non-apprehension, knows the individual intrinsic natures of the five aggregates and so forth, this is called "knowledge of phenomena" (dharmajñāna).
What is "subsequent knowledge" (anvayajñāna)?

That is to say, when wisdom takes non-apprehension as its expedient means to know the specific characteristics of the five aggregates and so forth—namely, suffering, impermanence, emptiness, and selflessness—this is called subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
"What is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*)?

It refers to that knowledge which, employing the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), knows the differences in the practices of sentient beings, as well as the distinctions between the names and characteristics (*nāmalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena; this is conventional knowledge."
"What is the knowledge of others' minds?

It refers to that wisdom which, employing non-apprehension as its means, knows the minds and mental factors of other sentient beings and persons without any doubt or obstruction; this is called the knowledge of others' minds."
"What is the knowledge of things as they are described?

It refers to the knowledge that, by taking non-apprehension as its expedient means, knows that the characteristic of all phenomena as they are described is itself the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all aspects; this is the knowledge of things as they are described."
Subhūti, you should know that these eleven knowledges constitute the mark of the Great Vehicle when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the characteristic of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas consists of the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).
What are these three?
First, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown";
second, the faculty of "knowing";
third, the faculty of "one who has fully known."
"What is the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown' (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*)?

It refers to all the faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom possessed by those individuals in training (*śaikṣa-pudgala*) who have not yet realized the noble truths and have not yet attained the fruit of sainthood; these constitute the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown'."
"What is the faculty of one who has already known?

It refers to all the faculties of faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom belonging to those individuals in training (śaikṣa-pudgala) who have already attained clear realization (abhisamaya) regarding the noble truths and have already attained the fruits of the noble ones; these are called the faculty of one who has already known."
"What is the faculty of one who has already known?

It refers to all those individuals beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), whether they be Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas already established in the ten stages, or Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas—their faculties of faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom constitute the faculty of one who has already known."

If these three faculties take non-apprehension as their skillful means, one should know that this is the characteristic of the Great Vehicle when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
the characteristic of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas consists of the three samādhis.
What are these three?
First, the samādhi with directed thought and sustained investigation;
second, the samādhi without directed thought and with only sustained investigation;
third, the samādhi without directed thought and without sustained investigation.
"What is the samādhi with vitarka and vicāra?

It refers to the bodhisattva-mahāsattva who, detached from desires and unwholesome states, possessing vitarka and vicāra, and experiencing the joy and happiness born of seclusion, enters and fully dwells in the first dhyāna; this is called the samādhi with vitarka and vicāra."
"What is the samādhi without vitarka and with vicāra only?
It refers to whatever intermediate concentration between the first dhyāna and the second dhyāna belongs to a bodhisattva mahāsattva; this is called the samādhi without vitarka and with vicāra only."
"What is the concentration without vitarka and vicāra?

It refers to the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s meditative absorptions from the second dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is called the concentration without vitarka and vicāra."

"If these three types [of phenomena] are taken as a skillful means through non-apprehension, one should know that this is the mark of the Great Vehicle when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
the characteristics of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas consist of the ten recollections. What are these ten?
First, mindfulness of the Buddha;
second, mindfulness of the Dharma;
third, mindfulness of the Sangha.
Fourth is the recollection of ethical discipline (*śīlānusmṛti*).
Fifth is the recollection of relinquishment (*tyāgānusmṛti*).
Sixth is the recollection of the devas (*devatānusmṛti*).
Seventh, the recollection of disenchantment;
eighth, the recollection of death;
ninth, the recollection of the body.
Tenth is mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).

If these ten types [of dharmas] are practiced with non-apprehension as the skillful means, one should know that this constitutes the characteristic of the Great Vehicle when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

The characteristics of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas consist of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, the ten totalities, and other such pure and wholesome dharmas; one should know that these, practiced by means of non-apprehension, constitute the characteristics of the Great Vehicle when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
the characteristic of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas consists of the ten powers of a Buddha. What are these ten?

“Subhūti, you should know that the first power is the ability to understand, through the skillful means of non-apprehension, the characteristics of what is possible and what is impossible regarding phenomena such as cause and effect, exactly as they are.”

"If, by means of non-apprehension as a skillful method, one understands as they truly are the various distinct characteristics of the causes and effects of the karmic dharmas and experiences of all classes of sentient beings in the past, future, and present—this is the second power."
"If, by means of non-apprehension as a skillful means, one knows as it truly is that the world consists of various and manifold elements (*dhātu*), this is the third power.
If, by means of non-apprehension as a skillful means, one knows as it truly is the various and manifold inclinations (*adhimukti*) of sentient beings, this is the fourth power."
"If, employing the means of non-apprehension, one knows as they truly are the superior and inferior faculties of all classes of sentient beings, this is the fifth power.
If, employing the means of non-apprehension, one knows as they truly are the pervasive modes of activity, this is the sixth power."

"If one employs skillful means through non-apprehension and, in accordance with reality, thoroughly understands the differences among sentient beings regarding their faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, liberations, meditative absorptions, concentrations, attainments, and their defilement or purification—this is the seventh power."
"If, by means of non-apprehension as a skillful expedient, one knows as they truly are the immeasurable varieties of past lives among classes of sentient beings, this is the eighth power."

"If one takes non-apprehension as the skillful means, by means of the purified divine eye, one knows as they truly are the immeasurable varieties of death and birth among sentient beings; this is the ninth power."

"If one takes non-apprehension as the skillful means, one understands as it truly is the permanent exhaustion of all taints (*āsrava*), attains the untainted liberation of mind (*cittavimukti*) and the untainted liberation by wisdom (*prajñāvimukti*), and dwells having personally realized and fulfilled [this] in the present life, correctly knowing: 'Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence. This is the tenth power."
"You should know that this is the mark of the Great Vehicle when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The characteristics of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas consist of the four fearlessnesses.
What are these four? "Subhūti, you should know this!

If, employing skillful means while having nothing to apprehend, one declares oneself to be a Truly Perfectly Awakened One (samyaksambuddha), then even if there should be a śramaṇa, a brāhmaṇa, a deva, a Māra, a Brahmā, or anyone else in the world who, according to the Dharma, raises an objection or calls for recollection, saying that regarding this Dharma one is not a Truly Perfectly Awakened One—I see no grounds for such an objection.

Because there is no basis for such challenges being seen therein, he dwells in peace, free from fear and dread; he declares himself to occupy the exalted position of a Great Sage, and amidst the great assembly, he truly roars the lion’s roar and turns the sublime Brahma-wheel.
That wheel is pure, correct, true, and unsurpassed; among all śramaṇas, brahmins, and others, there is none who is able to turn it in accordance with the Dharma.
This is the first fearlessness.

"If one employs skillful means through non-apprehension and claims for oneself, 'I have eternally exhausted all outflows,' then even if there should be a śramaṇa, a brāhmaṇa, a deva, a māra, a brahmā, or anyone else in the world who, according to the Dharma, raises an objection or brings it to mind, saying that such outflows have not been eternally exhausted, I see no grounds for responding to that objection."

Because there is no basis for such challenges being seen therein, he dwells in peace, free from fear and dread; he declares himself to occupy the exalted position of a Great Sage, and amidst the great assembly, he truly roars the lion’s roar and turns the sublime Wheel of Brahmā.
This wheel is pure, correct, true, and unsurpassed; among all śramaṇas, brahmins, and others, there is none who is able to turn it in accordance with the Dharma.
This is the second fearlessness.

"If one employs skillful means through non-apprehension, one explains to the disciples the dharmas that obstruct the Path. Should any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world, relying on some doctrine, raise an objection or cause me to be reminded, saying that practicing these dharmas cannot obstruct the Path, I see no grounds for such an objection."

Because there is no basis for such challenges being seen therein, he dwells in peace, free from fear and dread; he declares himself to occupy the exalted position of a Great Sage, and amidst the great assembly, he rightly roars the lion’s roar and turns the sublime Brahma-wheel.
That wheel is pure, correct, true, and unsurpassed; among all śramaṇas, brahmins, and others, there is none who is able to turn it in accordance with the Dharma.
This is the third fearlessness.

"If one employs skillful means based on non-apprehension to teach disciples the path for the exhaustion of suffering, then even if there should be any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world who, relying on the Dharma, raises an objection or attempts to provoke recollection by saying that 'cultivating this path cannot exhaust suffering,' I see no grounds for such an objection."

Because there is no basis for such challenges being seen therein, he dwells in peace, free from fear and intimidation; he declares himself to occupy the exalted position of a Great Sage, and amidst the great assembly, he rightly roars the lion’s roar and turns the sublime Brahma-wheel.
That wheel is pure, correct, true, and unsurpassed; among all śramaṇas, brahmins, and others, there is none who is able to turn it in accordance with the Dharma.
This is the fourth fearlessness.
“You should know that this is the mark of the Great Vehicle when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom.
*The Great Perfection of Wisdom Sūtra*, Fascicle 489, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Three, Subhūti Chapter, Part Nine. “Furthermore, Subhūti!”
The characteristics of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas refer to the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
What are the four? The first is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*).
Second is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid).
Third is the analytical knowledge of expression (nirukti-pratisaṃvid).
Fourth is the analytical knowledge of eloquence (pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid).

Subhūti! These four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), practiced by means of non-apprehension, should be known as the characteristics of the Great Vehicle when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
The characteristic of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas consists of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*).
What are these eighteen?
This refers to all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas:

from the night they first attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment until the night they enter nirvana without remainder, during that interval, they are always without error, without harsh sounds, without loss of mindfulness, without diverse perceptions, and without... [inattention].
With a concentrated mind, there is no equanimity that is not discerning;

his aspiration does not regress, his diligence does not regress, his mindfulness does not regress, his concentration does not regress, his wisdom does not regress, and his knowledge and vision of liberation does not regress.
All bodily actions are preceded by wisdom and follow after wisdom; all verbal actions are preceded by wisdom and follow after wisdom.
Furthermore, all mental actions proceed with wisdom as their precursor and follow after wisdom;
his wisdom and vision regarding the past are unattached and unimpeded, his wisdom and vision regarding the future are unattached and unimpeded,
and his wisdom and vision regarding the present are unattached and unimpeded.

Thus, these eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are all without exception characterized by the expedient means of non-apprehension; one should know that this is the mark of the Great Vehicle when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
The characteristic of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas consists of the dhāraṇī-doors of syllables.
What are the dhāraṇī-doors of syllables?"
This refers to entering the gateways of all syllables through the equality of letters and the equality of speech.
What is meant by entering the gateways of all syllables through the equality of letters and the equality of speech?

“Subhūti, you should know that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, they enter the gateway of the letter *ṅa*, realizing that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen;
they enter the gateway of the letter *la*, realizing that all phenomena are free from dust and defilement.”
One enters the gateway of the letter *pa*, for it awakens one to the realization that all phenomena are the teaching of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*);

one enters the gateway of the letter *ja*, for it awakens one to the realization that all phenomena are far removed from death and birth, employing the skillful means of finding nothing whatsoever in either death or birth;

one enters the gateway of the letter *na*, for it awakens one to the realization that all phenomena are far removed from names and signs (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*), employing the skillful means of finding nothing whatsoever in either name or sign.
One enters the letter-gateway *la*, for one awakens to the fact that all phenomena transcend the world, as the causes and conditions of passionate attachment do not manifest;
one enters the letter-gateway *ḍha*, for one awakens to the fact that all phenomena are tamed, quiescent, true thusness, equal, and non-discriminative;
one enters the letter-gateway *ba*, for one awakens to the fact that all phenomena are free from bondage and liberation.
One enters the gateway of the letter *ṭa*, realizing that all phenomena are free from feverish affliction and corruption, thereby attaining purity;
one enters the gateway of the letter *śa*, realizing that all phenomena are without obstruction;
one enters the gateway of the letter *ba*, realizing that the path of verbal expression for all phenomena is severed.
One enters the gateway of the syllable *ḍha*, because one realizes that all phenomena are the immovable suchness;
one enters the gateway of the syllable *ya*, because one realizes that all phenomena are unborn according to reality;
one enters the gateway of the syllable *ṣṭa*, because one realizes that the characteristics of the subduing and sustaining of all phenomena are unapprehendable.
One enters the gateway of the letter Ka, because one realizes that an agent of all phenomena cannot be apprehended;
one enters the gateway of the letter Sa, because one realizes that the temporal equality of all phenomena cannot be apprehended;
one enters the gateway of the letter Ma, because one realizes that the nature of grasping at "mine" in all phenomena cannot be apprehended.
One enters the gateway of the letter Ga, for one realizes that the nature of movement, activity, and grasping in all phenomena is unapprehendable;
one enters the gateway of the letter Tha, for one realizes that the nature of the locus upon which all phenomena depend is unapprehendable;
one enters the gateway of the letter Ja, for one realizes that the nature of the producer and the produced in all phenomena is unapprehendable.
One enters the gateway of the letter Śva, because one realizes that the nature of tranquility in all phenomena is unattainable;
one enters the gateway of the letter Dha, because one realizes that the nature of the sustaining element in all phenomena is unattainable;
one enters the gateway of the letter Śa, because one realizes that the nature of śamatha in all phenomena is unattainable.
Entering the gateway of the letter Kha, one awakens to the fact that all phenomena are like the great void, for their nature of equality cannot be apprehended;
entering the gateway of the letter Chaṃ, one awakens to the fact that the nature of exhaustion of all phenomena cannot be apprehended;
entering the gateway of the letter Sva, one awakens to the fact that the nature of sustenance of all phenomena cannot be apprehended.
Entering the gateway of the letter Ja, one awakens to the fact that the nature of all phenomena as subject and object cannot be apprehended;
entering the gateway of the letter Tha, one awakens to the fact that the nature of all phenomena as objects of attachment cannot be apprehended;
entering the gateway of the letter Ha, one awakens to the fact that the nature of all phenomena as causes cannot be apprehended.
One enters the gateway of the letter *ba*, realizing that the destructible nature of all phenomena is unattainable;
one enters the gateway of the letter *ca*, realizing that the nature of all phenomena being shrouded by desire and pleasure is unattainable;
one enters the gateway of the letter *smā*, realizing that the nature of all phenomena being subject to recollection is unattainable.
One enters the gateway of the syllable *kha* because one realizes that the nature of all phenomena as being summonable is unattainable;
one enters the gateway of the syllable *ca* because one realizes that all phenomena are devoid of vigor;
one enters the gateway of the syllable *ga* because one realizes that the nature of all phenomena as being thick and equal is unattainable.
Entering the gateway of the letter *ca*, one realizes that the nature of the accumulation of all phenomena is unattainable;
entering the gateway of the letter *ṇa*, one realizes that all phenomena are free from clamor and confusion;
entering the gateway of the letter *pha*, one realizes that all phenomena have no karmic retribution.
Entering the syllable-gateway *saka*, one realizes that all phenomena are devoid of the nature of the aggregates (*skandha*);
entering the syllable-gateway *eṣa*, one realizes that the characteristics of aging and decay in all phenomena are unapprehendable;
entering the syllable-gateway *ca*, one realizes that all phenomena leave no trace.
One enters the gate of the syllable Ṭha, because one realizes that the nature of all phenomena as being driven and pressured is unapprehendable;
one enters the gate of the syllable Dha, because one realizes that the ultimate location of all phenomena is unapprehendable.

“Subhūti, you should know that this gateway of the syllable ‘vicaya’ (discernment) is the means for entering the limit of the emptiness of phenomena; apart from these syllables which express the emptiness of all phenomena, nothing further can be found.”

Why is this? Because the meanings of these syllables cannot be proclaimed, cannot be displayed, cannot be written down or maintained, cannot be grasped, and cannot be observed, for they are free from all signs (nimitta).
Subhūti, you should know this!
Just as space is the destination to which all things return, so too it is with these gateways of syllables:
the meaning of the emptiness of all phenomena must enter these gateways before it can be fully revealed.
“Subhūti, you should know that entering this syllable *gaṃ* and others is called ‘entering the gates of all syllables.

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain skillful wisdom by entering such gates of all syllables, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas will be without obstruction regarding all sounds and expressions that signify or represent; they will fully realize and maintain the equal emptiness of all phenomena, and they will attain skillfulness in all forms of speech and sound.”

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to hear such seal-marks and seal-words that enter the gateways of all syllables, and having heard them, receives, maintains, recites, masters, and explains them to others without attachment—neither seeking fame, nor gain, nor honor—by virtue of these causes and conditions, they shall obtain thirty kinds of meritorious benefits.
What are these thirty? They are: attaining powerful mindfulness; attaining superior shame and remorse; attaining firm strength; attaining the essential purport of the Dharma;
attaining superior awakening; attaining distinguished wisdom; attaining unimpeded eloquence; and attaining the gateways of dhāraṇī.
One attains freedom from doubt; one attains the state where neither love nor hatred arises toward words that are either favorable or unfavorable;

one attains dwelling in equanimity, free from high or low; one attains skillfulness regarding the vocal expressions of sentient beings; one attains skillfulness regarding the aggregates (*skandha*); one attains skillfulness regarding the elements (*dhātu*);

one attains skillfulness regarding the sense bases (*āyatana*); one attains skillfulness regarding the truths (*satya*); one attains skillfulness regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). One attains...
Through skill in causes, one attains skill in conditions, skill in phenomena, skill in the knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties,
skill in the knowledge of others' minds, skill in the knowledge of supernormal powers, skill in the knowledge of the divine ear,
skill in the knowledge of recollecting past lives, and skill in the knowledge of death and rebirth.
Skillfulness in the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows, skillfulness in the knowledge of what is possible and impossible, skillfulness in the knowledge of coming and going,
and skillfulness in the knowledge of the modes of deportment— these constitute thirty meritorious benefits.

“Subhūti, you should know that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), by means of the method of non-apprehension, they attain such dharanī-doors of syllables; you should know that this is the mark of the Great Vehicle (mahāyāna) when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Regarding your subsequent question,
'To what extent should one know that bodhisattva mahāsattvas have set out in the Great Vehicle?',
Subhūti, you should know this:"

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva diligently practices the six perfections and proceeds from one stage to the next, it should be known that by this measure, the bodhisattva mahāsattva has set out upon the Mahāyāna.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, diligently practicing the six perfections, proceed from one stage to the next?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that all phenomena come from nowhere and go nowhere. Why is this so?"
Because all phenomena have neither going nor coming, and no departure or arrival, due to the fact that those phenomena are subject to no transformation or decay.

Thus, the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not recollect or contemplate the ground from which they depart or the ground to which they proceed; although they cultivate the karmic activities for purifying the grounds, they do not perceive those grounds. This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva diligently practices the six perfections to proceed from one ground to the next.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the deeds of the stages?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell in the first stage, they should skillfully cultivate and purify ten kinds of superior activities. What are these ten?

First, by means of non-apprehension as their expedient, they should skillfully cultivate and purify the activity of the pure superior intention (*adhyāśaya*), because the characteristics of beneficial things cannot be apprehended."
Second, by taking non-apprehension as the means, one should skillfully cultivate the mental karma of equanimity toward all sentient beings, because all sentient beings are unapprehendable.

Third, by taking non-apprehension as the skillful means, one should properly cultivate all acts of relinquishment and giving, because the giver, the recipient, and the object given cannot be apprehended.

Fourth, taking non-apprehension as the skillful means, one should skillfully cultivate the practice of attending upon spiritual friends, because of being without attachment toward those spiritual friends.
Fifth, by taking non-apprehension as the skillful means, one should skillfully cultivate and diligently seek the activity of the true Dharma, because all dharmas sought cannot be apprehended.

Sixth, by taking non-apprehension as the skillful means, one should properly cultivate the practice of always delighting in leaving the home life, because the household one abandons cannot be apprehended.

Seventh, by taking non-apprehension as the skillful means, one should skillfully cultivate the practice of loving respect for the Buddha’s body, because the causes for the various marks and signs cannot be apprehended.

Eighth, by taking non-apprehension as the means, one should skillfully cultivate and expound the activity of the Dharma teachings, because the dharmas that are conceptually discriminated cannot be apprehended.
Ninth, by taking non-apprehension as the means, one should skillfully cultivate and purify the karma that destroys pride, for all phenomena of prosperity are unapprehendable.
Tenth, taking non-apprehension as the skillful means, one should skillfully cultivate the karma of speech that is always joyful and truthful, because all speech is unapprehendable.

"Subhūti, you should know that when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell in the first stage, they should skillfully cultivate these ten superior deeds; by means of this, the first stage will be swiftly brought to fulfillment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When bodhisattva mahāsattvas abide in the second bhūmi, they should cultivate and contemplate eight dharmas so that they may be swiftly perfected."
What are the eight?
First, pure ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Second, recognizing kindness and repaying it.
Third, abiding in the power of patience;
fourth, experiencing supreme joy;
fifth, not abandoning sentient beings.
Sixth, to constantly give rise to great compassion.
Seventh, to respectfully and faithfully consult, receive instruction from, and make offerings to one's teachers and elders as if serving the Buddhas.
Eighth, to diligently seek and practice the pāramitās.

Subhūti, you should know that when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell in the second bhūmi, they should correctly contemplate these eight dharmas and diligently practice them so as to bring them quickly to fulfillment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When bodhisattva mahāsattvas dwell in the third stage, they should diligently abide in five dharmas.
What are these five?
First, they diligently seek extensive learning without ever becoming weary or satisfied, yet they do not cling to the literal words of the teachings they have heard.
Second, with an undefiled mind, they constantly practice the gift of Dharma; though they extensively transform and guide others, they remain free from self-exaltation.
Third, for the sake of adorning and purifying the buddha-field, they plant various roots of goodness; though they dedicate these merits, they do not exalt themselves.
Fourth, for the sake of transforming sentient beings, they do not grow weary of the boundless cycle of birth and death, yet they remain free from arrogance and indolence.
Fifth, although they abide in a sense of shame and dread of blame,
they harbor no attachment. Subhūti,
you should know that when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell in the third stage, they should always remain established in these five dharmas and must not abandon them for even a moment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell in the fourth stage, they should uphold and not abandon ten dharmas. What are these ten?
First, to dwell in forest hermitages (āraṇya) and never abandon them;
second, to always delight in having few desires;
third, to always delight in contentment.
Fourth, they never abandon the virtues of the dhūta ascetic practices.
Fifth, they never forsake any of the training rules (*śikṣāpada*).
Sixth, they develop a profound sense of weary detachment toward all sensual pleasures.
Seventh, they always delight in initiating a mind conjoined with nirvāṇa.
Eighth, they always delight in relinquishing all things.
Ninth, at all times their minds do not sink into despondency.
Tenth, they are always without attachment to any phenomena.
Subhūti, you should know that when bodhisattva mahāsattvas dwell in the fourth stage, they should uphold these ten dharmas and not abandon them.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in the fifth stage, they should distance themselves from ten things. What are these ten?
First, one should distance oneself from household life.
Second, one should distance oneself from bhikṣuṇīs.
Third, one should distance oneself from stinginess regarding households.
Fourth, one should distance oneself from quarrels and disputes within assemblies.
Fifth, one should distance oneself from praising oneself and disparaging others.
Sixth, one should distance oneself from the ten paths of unwholesome action.
Seventh, one should distance oneself from overweening pride and arrogance.
Eighth, one should distance oneself from perversions.
Ninth, one should distance oneself from hesitation.
Tenth, one should remain far removed from greed, hatred, and delusion.
Subhūti, you should know that when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell in the fifth stage, they should constantly remain far removed from these ten dharmas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When bodhisattva mahāsattvas dwell in the sixth stage, they should fulfill six dharmas and should distance themselves from six dharmas."
What is meant by "perfecting six dharmas"?
It refers to perfecting the six pāramitās, such as generosity and the rest.
What is meant by "avoiding six dharmas"?
This means that one should distance oneself from six inferior states of mind. What are these six?
First, one should distance oneself from the mind of a śrāvaka.
Second, one should distance oneself from the mind of a pratyekabuddha.
Third, one should distance oneself from a mind of feverish distress.
Fourth, one should distance oneself from a mind that feels displeasure and sorrow when seeing a beggar approach.
Fifth, one should distance oneself from a mind of regret and longing for all things that have been relinquished.
Sixth, one should distance oneself from a mind that employs artifice and evasion toward those who come seeking [one's help].

"Subhūti, you should know that when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell in the sixth stage, they should always fulfill the six dharmas previously mentioned and should remain far removed from the six dharmas subsequently mentioned."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell in the seventh stage, they should always remain far removed from twenty dharmas and should always bring twenty dharmas to full completion."
What are the twenty things that one should always avoid?
First, one should always avoid the grasping at a self, up to and including the grasping at a viewer.
Second, one should always avoid the grasping at nihilism.
Third, one should always remain far removed from the attachment to permanence.
Fourth, one should always remain far removed from the attachment to the perception of signs.
Fifth, one should always remain far removed from the attachment to views.
Sixth, one should always remain far removed from attachment to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Seventh, one should always remain far removed from attachment to the aggregates (*skandha*).
Eighth, one should always remain far removed from attachment to the sense-bases (*āyatana*).
Ninth, one should always remain far removed from attachment to the elements (*dhātu*).
Tenth, one should always remain far removed from attachment to the truths (*satya*).
Eleventh, one should always remain far removed from attachment to dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Twelfth, one should always remain far removed from attachment to the grasping at the three realms.
Thirteenth, one should always remain far removed from grasping at all phenomena (*dharma*).
Fourteenth, one should always remain far removed from grasping at all phenomena as being either conformable or non-conformable to reality.
Fifteenth, one should always remain far removed from attachment to views based on the Buddha.
Sixteenth, one should always remain far removed from attachment to views based on the Dharma.
Seventeenth, one should always remain far removed from attachment to views based on the Sangha.
Eighteenth, one should always remain far removed from attachment to views based on the precepts.
Nineteenth, one should always remain far removed from attachment to views based on emptiness.
Twentieth, one should always remain far removed from aversion to and fear of emptiness.
What are the twenty dharmas that one should always bring to perfection?
First, one should always bring to perfection the thorough realization of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Second, one should always bring to perfection the realization of signlessness (*animitta*).
Third, one should always fulfill the knowledge of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
Fourth, one should always fulfill the purity of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍalapariśuddhi*).
Fifth, one should always fulfill compassion for sentient beings, as well as non-attachment toward sentient beings.
Sixth, one should always fulfill the vision of the equality of all phenomena, as well as remain without attachment therein.
Seventh, one should always fulfill the vision of the equality of all sentient beings, as well as remain without attachment therein.
Eighth, one should always fulfill the ultimate penetration into the true nature of reality, as well as remain without attachment therein.
Ninth, one should always fulfill the wisdom of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Tenth, one should always fulfill the principle of explaining all phenomena as having a single characteristic.
Eleventh, one should always fulfill the elimination of conceptual discrimination.
Twelfth, one should always fulfill the distancing from all mental perceptions.
Thirteenth, one should always fulfill the complete distancing from all views.
Fourteenth, one should always fulfill the complete distancing from afflictions.
Fifteenth, one should always fulfill skillfulness in śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Sixteenth, one should always fulfill the nature of a mind that is thoroughly subdued.
Seventeenth, one should always fulfill the nature of a tranquil mind.
Eighteenth, one should always fulfill the nature of unimpeded wisdom.
Nineteenth, one should always fulfill being free from all attachment and defilement.
Twentieth, one should always fulfill the ability to travel to any buddha-field at will and manifest one's own body within the assemblies of those Buddhas.

"Subhūti, you should know that when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell in the seventh stage, they should always remain far removed from the former twenty dharmas and always bring the latter twenty dharmas to fulfillment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When bodhisattva mahāsattvas dwell in the eighth stage, they should always bring four kinds of dharmas to perfection. What are these four?
First, one should always fulfill the realization of the mental activities of all sentient beings.
Second, one should always fulfill the mastery of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
Third, one should always fulfill the vision of all Buddha-fields, and according to what is seen therein, personally adorn and purify various Buddha-fields.
Fourth, one should always fully accomplish the service and offerings to all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and observe the body of the Tathāgata as it truly is.
Subhūti! You should know that when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dwell in the eighth stage, they should always fully accomplish these four dharmas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell in the ninth stage, they should always bring four kinds of dharmas to perfection. What are these four?
First, one should always fulfill the knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties of sentient beings.
Second, one should always fulfill the purification of Buddha-fields.
Third, one should always fulfill the frequent entry into various meditative absorptions, such as the illusion-like samādhi.

Fourth, they should always fulfill the practice of entering into various states of existence by manifesting through spontaneous birth, in order to bring the roots of virtue of sentient beings to maturity according to their needs.
Subhūti, you should know this!
"When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell in the ninth stage, they should constantly bring these four dharmas to perfection. Furthermore, Subhūti!
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell in the tenth stage, they should constantly bring twelve dharmas to perfection."
What are the twelve?
First, one should always fully accomplish the great vow to encompass infinite locations, so that whatever is vowed may all be realized.

Second, one should always fully perfect the knowledge of the diverse languages of all classes of beings, such as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans.
Third, one should always fulfill unimpeded eloquence in teaching.
Fourth, one should always fulfill the perfection of entering the womb.
Fifth, one should always fulfill the perfection of birth.
Sixth, one should always fulfill the perfection of a complete family lineage.
Seventh, one should always fulfill the perfection of a complete caste.
Eighth, one should always fulfill the perfection of a complete retinue.
Ninth, one should always fulfill the perfection of the excellence of the birth-body.
Tenth, one should always fulfill the perfection of the excellence of renunciation.
Eleventh, one should always fulfill the perfection of the excellence of adorning the Bodhi tree.
Twelfth, one should always fulfill the complete accomplishment and perfection of all merits.
Subhūti, you should know that when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in the tenth stage, they should always fulfill these twelve dharmas.

Subhūti, you should know that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva has dwelled in the tenth stage and has brought to full completion all the superior dharmas cultivated in the preceding stages, they may be said to be no different from the Tathāgatas.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of non-apprehension as a skillful method, properly cultivate and purify the karma of the superior intention?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, through mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes, cultivates and accumulates all supreme roots of goodness, this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s thorough cultivation and purification of the activity of the superior intention by means of non-apprehension."
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of non-apprehension as a skillful method, properly cultivate and purify the karma of a mind of equality toward all sentient beings?”

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, through mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes, evokes the four immeasurable states of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, this is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of non-apprehension as a skillful method, should properly cultivate the karma of a mind of equality toward all sentient beings.”
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of non-apprehension as a skillful expedient, properly cultivate and purify all acts of relinquishment and giving?”

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving toward all sentient beings without making any conceptual distinctions, this is for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to skillfully cultivate all acts of relinquishment and generosity by taking non-apprehension as the means.”
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of non-apprehension as a skillful method, properly cultivate and purify the practice of attending upon spiritual friends?”

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees virtuous friends who exhort and transform sentient beings, causing them to cultivate the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), he immediately draws near to them, honoring, making offerings to, respecting, and praising them; he receives the true Dharma from them and serves them day and night with a mind free from weariness. This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of non-apprehension as the skillful means, should properly cultivate the practice of drawing near to virtuous friends.”
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, by means of non-apprehension as a skillful method, properly cultivate and purify the activity of diligently seeking the true Dharma?”

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes, diligently seeks the unsurpassed true Dharma of the Tathāgata and does not fall into the levels of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of skillfully cultivating and purifying the task of diligently seeking the true Dharma by means of non-apprehension.”
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of non-apprehension as a skillful method, properly cultivate and purify the practice of always delighting in leaving the household life?”

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, in all places of birth, always loathes the clamor and confinement of the household life as if it were a prison, and constantly delights in the pure renunciation of the Buddha-dharma, which is tranquil, unconditioned, and unimpeded like space—this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s thorough cultivation of the practice of always delighting in renunciation, by means of non-apprehension as a skillful method.”
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of non-apprehension as a skillful method, properly cultivate and purify the practice of loving respect for the Buddha’s body?”

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the very first moment they behold the physical form and marks of a Buddha, until they realize the knowledge of all modes, never abandons the mental engagement of mindfulness of the Buddha—this is what is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva skillfully cultivating the practice of loving respect for the Buddha’s body, taking non-apprehension as the means.”
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of non-apprehension as a skillful method, properly cultivate and clarify the activity of expounding the Dharma teachings?”

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, whether while the Buddha is in the world or after his parinirvāṇa, expounds the Dharma teaching for the sake of all sentient beings—teachings that are excellent in the beginning, middle, and end, skillful in both word and meaning, pure, complete, and the pristine holy life; namely, the sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, gāthās, udānas, nidānas, jātakas, itivṛttakas, jātaka-sources, avadānas, vaipulyas, adbhuta-dharmas, and upadeśas—this is what is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, employing the method of non-apprehension, should skillfully cultivate and expound the activity of the Dharma teaching.”
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of non-apprehension as a skillful method, properly cultivate and purify the karma of destroying arrogance?”

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva always maintains humility and respect, subduing the mind of pride, he will not be born into a low caste or inferior lineage by virtue of this. This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, employing the skillful means of non-apprehension, should properly cultivate and purify the karma that destroys pride.”
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of non-apprehension as a skillful method, properly cultivate and purify the karma of always delighting in truthful speech?”

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva speaks in accordance with what they know and their words accord with their deeds, this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s thorough cultivation of the karma of speech that is always joyful and truthful, by means of non-apprehension as the skillful means.”
“Subhūti, you should know that when bodhisattva mahāsattvas dwell in the first stage, they should skillfully cultivate these ten superior deeds so that they may be swiftly perfected.”
“World-Honored One!
How is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s ethical discipline (*śīla*) is pure? “Excellent One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not give rise to the mind of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, nor any other factors that obstruct enlightenment through breaking the precepts, this is called the pure ethical discipline (śīla) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva recognize kindness and repay it?
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin! [The Buddha replied:]”

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the various supreme conducts of a bodhisattva, if they receive even a small kindness from another, they are still able to repay it with great weight; how much more so for abundant favors—how could they fail to requite them!
"This is what constitutes a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s knowing gratitude and repaying kindness.
"World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva abide in the power of patience?"

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, even when all sentient beings should harm them, is able to maintain a mind free from resentment or malice toward them, this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva abiding in the power of patience.”
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva experience supreme joy? “Sudhana!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees sentient beings who have already attained maturity in the practices of the three vehicles and feels deep joy in their hearts, this is what constitutes a bodhisattva mahāsattva receiving supreme joy.
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva not abandon sentient beings?
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly and universally rescues and delivers all sentient beings, causing them to be free from suffering and hardship, this is what is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva not abandoning sentient beings.
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly give rise to great compassion?
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the sublime conduct of all bodhisattvas, they constantly form this thought:

"For the benefit of each and every sentient being, even if I must remain in the great hells for as many immeasurable and incalculable *gaṅgā* sands of eons as there are beings—there undergoing various heavy sufferings, whether being burned, boiled, hacked, or severed; or being impaled, suspended, ground, or pounded—I shall endure such immeasurable hardships until all those sentient beings have mounted the Tathāgata Vehicle and entered parinirvāṇa."
"In this way, even when the entire realm of sentient beings is exhausted, my great compassionate heart shall never grow weary or desist.
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly gives rise to great compassion.
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind of reverence and faith toward all teachers and elders, consult them, receive their instructions, and make offerings to them as if serving the Buddhas?”

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, seeking unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, reverently complies with their teachers and elders without any attachment or longing, this is what it means for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to consult, receive instruction from, and make offerings to all teachers and elders with a mind of reverence and faith, as if serving the Buddhas.”
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva diligently seek and practice the pāramitās?
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin! [The Buddha replied:]”

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva single-mindedly trains in all the pāramitās without regard for other matters, desiring to bring all sentient beings to maturity, this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s diligent pursuit and cultivation of the pāramitās.
“Subhūti, you should know that when bodhisattva mahāsattvas dwell in the second bhūmi, they should contemplate and train in these eight dharmas so as to bring them quickly to fulfillment.”
“World-Honored One!
