Because the individuals from those on the Stage of Utmost Joy up to those on the Stage of the Dharma-Cloud do not possess a real nature, and because they are of a non-existent nature, this Great Vehicle universally transcends all worlds—including gods, humans, and asuras—and is the most honored and supreme.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the dharmas from the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata were of a truly existent nature and not of a non-existent nature, then this Great Vehicle would not be venerable or supreme, and it would not transcend all the worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras."

Because the dharmas from the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata do not possess a real intrinsic nature, and because they are of a non-existent nature, this Great Vehicle universally transcends all worlds—including gods, humans, and asuras—and is thus most honored and most supreme.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the individuals from those on the stage of pure observation up to those on the stage of a Tathāgata were of a truly existent nature and not of a non-existent nature, then this Great Vehicle would not be venerable or supreme, and it would not transcend all the world with its gods, humans, and asuras."

Because the individuals from those on the stage of pure observation up to those on the stage of the Tathāgata do not possess a real nature, and because they lack such a nature, this Great Vehicle universally transcends all worlds, including devas, humans, and asuras, being the most honored and most supreme.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If all those in the world—gods, humans, and asuras—were of a truly existent nature and not of a non-existent nature, then this Great Vehicle would not be venerable or supreme, nor would it transcend all those in the world—gods, humans, and asuras."

Because all those in the world—gods, humans, asuras, and so forth—do not possess a real nature and are of a non-existent nature, this Mahāyāna universally transcends all those in the world—gods, humans, asuras, and so forth—and is thus most honored and most supreme.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the various immeasurable kinds of minds that arise within a bodhisattva mahāsattva from the first generation of the mind until sitting upon the seat of sublime enlightenment were of a truly existent nature and not of a non-existent nature, then this Great Vehicle would not be honored or supreme, and it would not transcend all the worlds of devas, humans, and asuras."

From the first generation of the mind of awakening until sitting upon the sublime seat of enlightenment, the immeasurable varieties of minds that arise therein are not of a truly existent nature; because they are of a non-existent nature, this Great Vehicle universally transcends all worlds, including gods, humans, and asuras, and is thus most honored and supreme.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the diamond-like wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva were an existent nature and not a non-existent nature, then this Great Vehicle would not be supreme or preeminent, and it would not transcend all the world with its gods, humans, and asuras."

Because the diamond-like wisdom of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is not of a truly existent nature, and because it is of a non-existent nature, this Great Vehicle universally transcends all worlds, including gods, humans, and asuras, being the most honored and most supreme.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the continuity of the habitual tendencies of the afflictions severed by the vajra-like wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva were of a truly existent nature rather than a non-existent nature, then this vajra-like wisdom that severs them would be unable to realize their total lack of intrinsic nature. It would not have attained the unsurpassed, subtle, and wondrous knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna); it would be neither venerable nor supreme, and would not transcend all the worlds of devas, humans, and asuras."

The continuity of the habitual tendencies of the afflictions, which are severed by the diamond-like wisdom (*vajropama-jñāna*), does not possess a real nature; because it is non-existent, this diamond-like wisdom that severs them realizes that they are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature. Having thus severed them, one attains the unsurpassed, subtle, and wondrous knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), universally transcending all worlds—including gods, humans, and asuras—as the most honored and supreme.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the bodies of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas—adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs—were of a nature that exists substantially and not of a nature that does not exist, then the majestic radiance and sublime virtues of those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas would not be supreme or preeminent, nor would they transcend all the world, including its gods, humans, and asuras."

Because the bodies of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas—adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs—are not of a truly existent nature, and because they are of a non-existent nature, the majestic radiance and sublime virtues of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas universally transcend all the worlds of devas, humans, and asuras, being most honored and most supreme.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the light emitted by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas were of an existent nature and not of a non-existent nature, then the light emitted by those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas would not be venerable or supreme; it would not be able to universally illuminate worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions, nor would it transcend all the world with its gods, humans, and asuras."

Because the light rays emitted by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are not of a truly existent nature, and because they are non-existent in nature, the light rays emitted by all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are able to universally illuminate worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions, universally surpassing all that exists among gods, humans, and asuras in the world, being most honored and most supreme.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the sixty melodious qualities of the voice possessed by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas were of a nature that exists substantially and not of a nature that does not exist, then those sixty melodious qualities of the voice possessed by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas would not be venerable or supreme; they could not universally address the sentient beings to be converted throughout the immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Gaṅgā-sand-like worlds in the ten directions, nor would they transcend all the world with its gods, humans, asuras, and others."

Because the sixty melodious qualities of the voice possessed by all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are not of a truly existent nature, and because they are of a non-existent nature, these sixty melodious qualities of the voice possessed by all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are able to reach and inform all sentient beings to be converted throughout the immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of worlds, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, in the ten directions; they universally transcend all those in the world, including devas, humans, and asuras, being most honored and most supreme.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the unsurpassed, subtle wheel of Dharma turned by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas were of a nature that exists as a real entity and not of a non-existent nature, then the unsurpassed, subtle wheel of Dharma turned by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas would not be venerable, nor supreme, nor utterly pure; nor would it be that which cannot be turned by any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas in the world, nor would it transcend all the worlds of devas, humans, and asuras."

Because the unsurpassed, subtle wheel of Dharma turned by all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas is not of a nature that truly exists, and because it is of a non-existent nature, the unsurpassed, subtle wheel of Dharma turned by all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas is utterly pure; no śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others in any world are able to turn it according to the Dharma, as it universally transcends all worlds of devas, humans, and asuras, being most honored and most supreme.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the sentient beings emanated by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas were of a truly existent nature rather than of a non-existent nature, then the unsurpassed, subtle Dharma wheel turned by those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas would not be venerable nor supreme; it would not enable those classes of sentient beings to enter the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder, nor would they transcend all worlds, including the devas, humans, and asuras."

Because the sentient beings emanated by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas do not possess a real nature and are of a non-existent nature, the unsurpassed, subtle, and wondrous Wheel of Dharma turned by those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas is able to cause all those classes of sentient beings to enter the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder, universally transcending all that is in the world of devas, humans, and asuras, being most honored and most supreme.
"For these various reasons and conditions, it is said that the Mahāyāna universally transcends all worlds—including devas, humans, and asuras—and is the most honored and supreme."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
As for what you have said, 'This Great Vehicle is equal to space,' it is so! It is thus!"
So it is! It is just as you have said. Why is this so?

For example, just as in space one cannot find any directional divisions—east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, or below—the Great Vehicle is likewise; in east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below, no directional divisions can be found. Therefore, it is said that the Great Vehicle is equal to space.

"Furthermore, just as in space one cannot find any form or color—whether long or short, high or low, square or round, oblique or upright—the Mahāyāna is also like this; one cannot find any form or color—whether long or short, high or low, square or round, oblique or upright—and therefore it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to space."

"Furthermore, just as in space the manifest colors—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, purple, azure, green, and pale—are all unapprehendable, so it is with the Mahāyāna: the manifest colors—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, purple, azure, green, and pale—are all unapprehendable; therefore, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to space."

"Furthermore, just as space is neither past, nor future, nor present, so too is the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) neither past, nor future, nor present; therefore, it is said that the Great Vehicle is equal to space."

"Furthermore, just as space neither increases nor decreases, neither advances nor recedes, so too is the Mahāyāna: it neither increases nor decreases, neither advances nor recedes; therefore, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to space."
"Furthermore, just as space is neither defiled nor pure, so too is the Great Vehicle neither defiled nor pure; therefore, it is said that the Great Vehicle is equal to space."

"Furthermore, just as space is without arising, without cessation, without abiding, and without change, so too is the Great Vehicle without arising, without cessation, without abiding, and without change; therefore, it is said that the Great Vehicle is equal to space."

"Furthermore, just as space is neither wholesome, nor unwholesome, nor indeterminate, so too is the Mahāyāna neither wholesome, nor unwholesome, nor indeterminate; therefore, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to space."

"Furthermore, just as space is without seeing, hearing, sensing, or cognizing, so too is the Mahāyāna without seeing, hearing, sensing, or cognizing; therefore, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to space."

"Furthermore, just as space is neither an object of knowledge nor an object of cognition, so too is the Great Vehicle neither an object of knowledge nor an object of cognition; therefore, it is said that the Great Vehicle is equal to space."

"Furthermore, just as space is not something to be fully known, not something to be permanently abandoned, not something to be realized, and not something to be cultivated, so too is the Great Vehicle: it is not something to be fully known, not something to be permanently abandoned, not something to be realized, and not something to be cultivated; therefore, it is said that the Great Vehicle is equal to space."

"Furthermore, just as space is neither a fruit nor a dharma that is a fruit, neither a maturation nor a dharma that is a maturation, so too is the Great Vehicle: it is neither a fruit nor a dharma that is a fruit, neither a maturation nor a dharma that is a maturation; therefore, it is said that the Great Vehicle is equal to space."

"Furthermore, just as space is neither a phenomenon characterized by desire nor a phenomenon free from desire, neither a phenomenon characterized by hatred nor a phenomenon free from hatred, neither a phenomenon characterized by delusion nor a phenomenon free from delusion, so too is the Great Vehicle: it is neither a phenomenon characterized by desire nor a phenomenon free from desire, neither a phenomenon characterized by hatred nor a phenomenon free from hatred, neither a phenomenon characterized by delusion nor a phenomenon free from delusion. Therefore, it is said that the Great Vehicle is equal to space."

"Furthermore, just as space does not fall within the desire realm, does not fall within the form realm, and does not fall within the formless realm, so too is the Great Vehicle: it does not fall within the desire realm, does not fall within the form realm, and does not fall within the formless realm; therefore, it is said that the Great Vehicle is equal to space."

"Furthermore, just as space has no initial arousal of the mind, nor a second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, or tenth arousal of the mind, so too is the Mahāyāna: it has no initial arousal of the mind, up to and including no tenth arousal of the mind; therefore, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to space."

"Furthermore, just as in space one cannot find the stage of pure observation (*śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi*), the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra-bhūmi*), the eighth stage (*aṣṭamaka-bhūmi*), the stage of having seen [the truths] (*darśana-bhūmi*), the stage of refinement (*tanū-bhūmi*), the stage of freedom from desire (*vītarāga-bhūmi*), the stage of completion (*kṛtāvi-bhūmi*), the stage of the solitary realizer (*pratyekabuddha-bhūmi*), the stage of the bodhisattva (*bodhisattva-bhūmi*), or the stage of the Tathāgata (*tathāgata-bhūmi*), so it is with the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*): one cannot find the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata. Therefore, it is said that the Great Vehicle is equal to space."

"Furthermore, just as in space one cannot find those practicing for the fruit of stream-entry or the fruit of stream-entry itself, nor those practicing for the fruit of once-returning or the fruit of once-returning itself, nor those practicing for the fruit of non-returning or the fruit of non-returning itself, nor those practicing for the fruit of arhatship or the fruit of arhatship itself, nor those practicing for the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood or the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood itself, nor a bodhisattva or a Tathāgata; so too it is with the Great Vehicle—within it one cannot find those practicing for the fruit of stream-entry or the fruit of stream-entry itself, up to and including a bodhisattva or a Tathāgata. Therefore, it is said that the Great Vehicle is equal to space."

"Furthermore, just as in space the stages of the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, the bodhisattva, and the Tathāgata cannot be apprehended, so it is with the Great Vehicle: the stages of the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, the bodhisattva, and the Tathāgata cannot be apprehended; therefore, it is said that the Great Vehicle is equal to space."

"Furthermore, just as space is neither material nor immaterial, neither visible nor invisible, neither resistant nor non-resistant, neither conjoined nor dispersed, so too is the Great Vehicle: it is neither material nor immaterial, neither visible nor invisible, neither resistant nor non-resistant, neither conjoined nor dispersed; therefore, it is said that the Great Vehicle is equal to space."

"Furthermore, just as space is neither permanent nor impermanent, neither pleasant nor painful, neither self nor non-self, neither pure nor impure, so too is the Mahāyāna: it is neither permanent nor impermanent, neither pleasant nor painful, neither self nor non-self, neither pure nor impure; therefore, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to space."

"Furthermore, just as space is neither empty nor non-empty, neither characterized by marks nor markless, and neither characterized by aspiration nor aspirationless, so too is the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna): it is neither empty nor non-empty, neither characterized by marks nor markless, and neither characterized by aspiration nor aspirationless; therefore, it is said that the Great Vehicle is equal to space."

"Furthermore, just as space is neither tranquil nor non-tranquil, neither remote nor non-remote, so too is the Great Vehicle: it is neither tranquil nor non-tranquil, neither remote nor non-remote; therefore, the Great Vehicle is said to be equal to space."
"Furthermore, just as space is neither light nor darkness, so too is the Mahāyāna neither light nor darkness; therefore, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to space.
Furthermore, just as space is neither obtainable nor unobtainable, so too is the Mahāyāna neither obtainable nor unobtainable; therefore, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to space."

"Furthermore, just as space is neither the aggregates, sense-bases, nor elements, nor is it separate from the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements, so too is the Great Vehicle: it is neither the aggregates, sense-bases, nor elements, nor is it separate from the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements; therefore, it is said that the Great Vehicle is equal to space."
"Furthermore, just as space is neither expressible nor inexpressible, so too is the Mahāyāna neither expressible nor inexpressible; therefore, it is said that the Mahāyāna is equal to space."

"Furthermore, just as space is neither characterized by conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) nor devoid of conceptual proliferation, so too is the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*); it is neither characterized by conceptual proliferation nor devoid of conceptual proliferation. Therefore, it is said that the Great Vehicle is equal to space."
For these and various other such reasons, it is said:
"This Mahāyāna is equal to space. Furthermore, Subhūti!
You have made this statement: "Just as space can universally contain immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings;
so too is the Mahāyāna, which can universally contain immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings."
"It is so! It is so! It is just as you have said."
Why is this? Because sentient beings do not exist, one should know that space also does not exist.
Because space does not exist, one should know that the Great Vehicle also does not exist.
For this reason, it is said that the Mahāyāna is like space, for it can universally contain immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings. Why is this so?
Whether it be sentient beings, space, or the Great Vehicle—all such things are non-existent and cannot be apprehended.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Because sentient beings are immeasurable, one should know that space is also immeasurable;
because space is immeasurable, one should know that the Great Vehicle is also immeasurable.
Because sentient beings are innumerable, one should know that space is also innumerable.
Because space is incalculable, one should know that the Mahāyāna is also incalculable.
Because sentient beings are boundless, one should know that space is also boundless;
because space is boundless, one should know that the Mahāyāna is also boundless.
Based on this meaning, it is said that the Mahāyāna is like space, for it can universally accommodate immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings. Why is this?

Whether it be sentient beings, who are immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless; or space, which is immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless; or the Great Vehicle, which is immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless—all such things are non-existent and cannot be apprehended.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Because sentient beings do not exist, you should know that space also does not exist;
because space does not exist, you should know that the Great Vehicle also does not exist."
Because the Mahāyāna is non-existent, one should know that the immeasurable is also non-existent;
because the immeasurable is non-existent, one should know that the innumerable is also non-existent;
because the innumerable is non-existent, one should know that the boundless is also non-existent.
Because it is boundless and non-existent, one should know that all phenomena are likewise non-existent.
By virtue of this principle, it is said that the Mahāyāna is like space, universally able to contain immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings.

Why is this? Whether it be sentient beings, space, the Great Vehicle, the immeasurable, the innumerable, the boundless, or all dharmas—all such things as these are non-existent and cannot be apprehended.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Because the self does not exist, you should know that sentient beings also do not exist.
Because sentient beings do not exist, you should know that the life-principle also does not exist."
Because the "life-principle" (jīva) does not exist, one should know that the "born-being" (jāta) also does not exist.
Because the "born-being" does not exist, one should know that the "nourisher" (poṣa) also does not exist.
Because the nourisher is non-existent, one should know that the person (*puruṣa*) is also non-existent.
Because the person is non-existent, one should know that the individual (*pudgala*) is also non-existent.
Because the *pudgala* does not exist, one should know that the mind-born (*manomaya*) also does not exist.
Because the mind-born does not exist, one should know that the youth (*māṇava*) also does not exist.
Because the "Child of the Sages" (Mañjuśrī) is non-existent, one should know that the agent is also non-existent.
Because the agent is non-existent, one should know that the recipient is also non-existent.
Because the experiencer does not exist, one should know that the knower also does not exist.
Because the knower does not exist, one should know that the seer also does not exist.
Because the seer does not exist, one should know that space also does not exist.
Because space does not exist, one should know that the Great Vehicle also does not exist.
Because the Mahāyāna is non-existent, one should know that the immeasurable (*apramāṇa*) is also non-existent.
Because the immeasurable is non-existent, one should know that the innumerable (*asaṃkhyeya*) is also non-existent.
Because the "innumerable" does not exist, one should know that the "boundless" also does not exist.
Because the "boundless" does not exist, one should know that all phenomena (*dharmas*) also do not exist.
Based on this meaning, it is said that the Mahāyāna is like space, for it can universally accommodate immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings. Why is this so?

Whether it be "I" up to "the seer," or space, or the Great Vehicle, or the immeasurable, or the innumerable, or the boundless, or all dharmas—all such things as these are non-existent and cannot be apprehended.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Because everything from the self up to the knower does not exist, you should know that everything from suchness up to the inconceivable realm likewise does not exist in relation to one another."
Because true thusness, up to and including the inconceivable realm, is non-existent, one should know that space is also non-existent.
Because space is non-existent, one should know that the Great Vehicle is also non-existent.
Because the Mahāyāna is non-existent, one should know that the immeasurable, the innumerable, and the boundless are likewise non-existent in their mutual succession.
Because the immeasurable, the innumerable, and the boundless are non-existent, one should know that all dharmas are also non-existent.
Based on this meaning, it is said that the Mahāyāna is like space, for it can universally contain immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings. Why is this?

Whether it be "I" up to "the seer," or "suchness" up to the "inconceivable realm," or the "immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless," or "all phenomena"—all such things as these are non-existent and unobtainable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Because from 'self' up to 'perceiver' there is nothing whatsoever, you should know that from the realm of cessation up to the unconditioned realm, each is likewise non-existent."
Because the realm of cessation up to the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛta-dhātu*) is non-existent, one should know that space (*ākāśa*) is also non-existent.
Because space is non-existent, one should know that the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*) is also non-existent.
Because the Mahāyāna is non-existent, one should know that the immeasurable, the innumerable, and the boundless, which follow one another, are likewise non-existent.
Because the immeasurable, the innumerable, and the boundless are non-existent, one should know that all dharmas are also non-existent.
Based on this meaning, it is said that the Mahāyāna is like space, for it can universally contain immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings. Why is this so?

Whether it be "I" up to "the seer," or the realm of cessation up to the unconditioned realm, or space, or the Great Vehicle, or the immeasurable, the incalculable, the boundless, or all dharmas—all such things as these are non-existent and cannot be apprehended.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Because from 'self' up to 'perceiver' there is nothing whatsoever, you should know that from the aggregate of form up to the aggregate of consciousness, each is likewise non-existent."

"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Because everything from 'self' up to 'perceiver' does not exist, you should know that the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Tathāgata vehicle likewise do not exist in relation to one another."
Because the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, and the vehicle of the Tathāgatas do not exist, one should know that space also does not exist.
Because space does not exist, one should know that the Great Vehicle also does not exist.
Because the Mahāyāna is non-existent, one should know that the immeasurable, the innumerable, and the boundless are likewise non-existent in their mutual relation.
Because the immeasurable, the innumerable, and the boundless are non-existent, one should know that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are also non-existent.
Based on this meaning, it is said that the Mahāyāna is like space, for it can universally contain immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings. Why is this?

Whether it be "I" up to "the seer," or the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, the Tathāgata vehicle, or space, or the Mahāyāna, or that which is immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless, or all phenomena—since all such things as these are non-existent and unobtainable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Just as the realm of nirvāṇa can universally accommodate immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings, so too does the Great Vehicle universally accommodate immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings."
For this reason, it is said:
just as space can universally contain immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings, so too does the Mahāyāna universally contain immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, you have said: 'Just as space cannot be seen to come, go, or abide,
so too the Great Vehicle cannot be seen to come, go, or abide.'"
"So it is! So it is! It is just as you have said."
Why is this so? Because all phenomena neither come nor go, and furthermore, they do not abide. Why is that?
Because all phenomena— whether moving or stationary— are unapprehendable, for this reason,
the Great Vehicle likewise has no place from which it comes, no place to which it goes, and no place where it abides that can be apprehended.

Why is this so? Because from form (*rūpa*) up to consciousness (*vijñāna*), there is no coming, no going, and likewise no abiding; the intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) of form up to consciousness has no coming, no going, and likewise no abiding; the suchness (*tathatā*) of form up to consciousness has no coming, no going, and likewise no abiding; the self-nature (*svabhāva*) of form up to consciousness has no coming, no going, and likewise no abiding; and the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of form up to consciousness have no coming, no going, and likewise no abiding.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature, suchness, self-nature, and self-characteristic of form, up to and including consciousness, cannot be apprehended whether they are moving or stationary.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"

The sense base of the eye, up to and including the sense base of the mind, has no coming, no going, and likewise does not abide; the intrinsic nature of the sense bases from the eye to the mind has no coming, no going, and likewise does not abide; the suchness of the sense bases from the eye to the mind has no coming, no going, and likewise does not abide; the self-nature of the sense bases from the eye to the mind has no coming, no going, and likewise does not abide; the specific characteristics of the sense bases from the eye to the mind have no coming, no going, and likewise do not abide.

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature, suchness, self-nature, and self-characteristic of the sense-base of the eye, up to and including the sense-base of the mind, cannot be apprehended whether they are moving or stationary.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! The sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) up to the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) neither comes nor goes, nor do they abide. The intrinsic nature of the sphere of form up to the sphere of phenomena neither comes nor goes, nor does it abide. The suchness (*tathatā*) of the sphere of form up to the sphere of phenomena neither comes nor goes, nor does it abide. The self-nature (*svabhāva*) of the sphere of form up to the sphere of phenomena neither comes nor goes, nor does it abide. The specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the sphere of form up to the sphere of phenomena neither come nor go, nor do they abide."

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature, suchness, self-nature, and specific characteristics of the sense-base of form up to the sense-base of mental phenomena—whether moving or abiding—are unfindable.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! The eye constituent (*cakṣur-dhātu*) up to the mind constituent (*mano-dhātu*) neither comes nor goes, nor do they abide; the intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) of the eye constituent up to the mind constituent neither comes nor goes, nor does it abide; the suchness (*tathatā*) of the eye constituent up to the mind constituent neither comes nor goes, nor does it abide; the self-nature (*svabhāva*) of the eye constituent up to the mind constituent neither comes nor goes, nor does it abide; the self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the eye constituent up to the mind constituent neither comes nor goes, nor does it abide."
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature, suchness, self-nature, and specific characteristics of the eye-element up to the mind-element—whether moving or abiding—cannot be apprehended.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! The realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) up to the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) neither comes nor goes, nor do they abide. The intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) of the realm of form up to the realm of phenomena neither comes nor goes, nor does it abide. The suchness (*tathatā*) of the realm of form up to the realm of phenomena neither comes nor goes, nor does it abide. The self-nature (*svabhāva*) of the realm of form up to the realm of phenomena neither comes nor goes, nor does it abide. The specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the realm of form up to the realm of phenomena neither come nor go, nor do they abide."

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature, suchness, self-nature, and self-characteristic of the realm of form, up to and including the realm of phenomena, cannot be apprehended as either moving or abiding.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! The eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element has no coming, no going, and likewise does not abide; the intrinsic nature of the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element has no coming, no going, and likewise does not abide; the suchness of the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element has no coming, no going, and likewise does not abide; the self-nature of the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element has no coming, no going, and likewise does not abide; the specific characteristics of the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element have no coming, no going, and likewise do not abide."

Why is this? Because the nature, suchness, self-nature, and specific characteristics of the visual consciousness element, up to and including the mental consciousness element, cannot be apprehended as either moving or abiding.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! Eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact, neither comes nor goes, nor do they abide. The intrinsic nature of eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact, neither comes nor goes, nor does it abide. The suchness of eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact, neither comes nor goes, nor does it abide. The self-nature of eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact, neither comes nor goes, nor does it abide. The specific characteristics of eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact, neither come nor go, nor do they abide."

Why is this? Because the essential nature, suchness, intrinsic nature, and specific characteristics of visual contact, up to and including mental contact, cannot be apprehended whether they are moving or stationary.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including all feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, neither come nor go, nor do they abide. All feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including all feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, are by nature without coming or going, nor do they abide. All feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including all feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, are in their *tathatā* (suchness) without coming or going, nor do they abide. All feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including all feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, are in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) without coming or going, nor do they abide. All feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including all feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, are in their own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) without coming or going, nor do they abide.

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature, suchness, self-nature, and specific characteristics of all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including all feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, cannot be apprehended whether they are moving or stationary.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! The earth element up to the consciousness element has no coming and no going, nor does it abide; the intrinsic nature of the earth element up to the consciousness element has no coming and no going, nor does it abide; the suchness of the earth element up to the consciousness element has no coming and no going, nor does it abide; the self-nature of the earth element up to the consciousness element has no coming and no going, nor does it abide; the specific characteristics of the earth element up to the consciousness element have no coming and no going, nor do they abide."
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature, suchness, self-nature, and own-characteristic of the earth element up to the consciousness element—whether moving or abiding—cannot be apprehended.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! The causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) up to the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) neither comes nor goes, nor do they abide. The intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) of the causal condition up to the dominant condition neither comes nor goes, nor does it abide. The suchness (*tathatā*) of the causal condition up to the dominant condition neither comes nor goes, nor does it abide. The self-nature (*svabhāva*) of the causal condition up to the dominant condition neither comes nor goes, nor does it abide. The specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the causal condition up to the dominant condition neither comes nor goes, nor does it abide."

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature, suchness, self-nature, and self-characteristic of the causal conditions, up to and including the dominant conditions, cannot be apprehended as either moving or remaining.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! Ignorance up to old age and death have no coming and no going, nor do they abide. The intrinsic nature of ignorance up to old age and death has no coming and no going, nor does it abide. The suchness of ignorance up to old age and death has no coming and no going, nor does it abide. The self-nature of ignorance up to old age and death has no coming and no going, nor does it abide. The specific characteristics of ignorance up to old age and death have no coming and no going, nor do they abide."

Why is this? Because it is impossible to find any movement or stillness in the fundamental nature, suchness, self-nature, or specific characteristics of anything from ignorance up to old age and death.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! From suchness up to the inconceivable realm, there is no coming and no going, nor do they abide. From suchness up to the inconceivable realm, their intrinsic nature has no coming and no going, nor does it abide. From suchness up to the inconceivable realm, the suchness of suchness has no coming and no going, nor does it abide. From suchness up to the inconceivable realm, their self-nature has no coming and no going, nor does it abide. From suchness up to the inconceivable realm, their own-characteristic has no coming and no going, nor does it abide."
Why is this? Because the movement or stillness of the intrinsic nature, true suchness, self-nature, and self-characteristic of true suchness, up to the inconceivable realm, cannot be apprehended.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

The realm of abandonment, the realm of detachment, the realm of cessation, the realm of peace, the realm of tranquility, the realm of non-arising, the realm of non-cessation, the realm of non-defilement, the realm of non-purity, the realm of non-action, and the realm of the unconditioned neither come nor go, nor do they abide. From the realm of abandonment up to the realm of the unconditioned, their intrinsic nature neither comes nor goes, nor does it abide. From the realm of abandonment up to the realm of the unconditioned, their suchness neither comes nor goes, nor does it abide. From the realm of abandonment up to the realm of the unconditioned, their self-nature neither comes nor goes, nor does it abide. From the realm of abandonment up to the realm of the unconditioned, their own-characteristic neither comes nor goes, nor does it abide."
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature, suchness, self-nature, and self-characteristic of the realm of cessation up to the unconditioned realm—whether moving or abiding—cannot be apprehended.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! From internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, there is no coming and no going, nor do they abide. The intrinsic nature of internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature has no coming and no going, nor does it abide. The suchness of internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature has no coming and no going, nor does it abide. The self-nature of internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature has no coming and no going, nor does it abide. The own-characteristic of internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature has no coming and no going, nor does it abide."

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature, suchness, self-nature, and specific characteristics of everything from internal emptiness to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature cannot be apprehended, whether they move or remain still.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! The noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path neither come nor go, nor do they abide. The intrinsic nature of the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path neither comes nor goes, nor does it abide. The suchness of the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path neither comes nor goes, nor does it abide. The self-nature of the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path neither comes nor goes, nor does it abide. The specific characteristics of the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path neither come nor go, nor do they abide."

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature, suchness, self-nature, and specific characteristics of the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path—whether in motion or at rest—cannot be apprehended.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! From the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, there is no coming and no going, nor do they abide. The intrinsic nature of the perfections from generosity up to wisdom has no coming and no going, nor does it abide. The suchness of the perfections from generosity up to wisdom has no coming and no going, nor does it abide. The self-nature of the perfections from generosity up to wisdom has no coming and no going, nor does it abide. The specific characteristics of the perfections from generosity up to wisdom have no coming and no going, nor do they abide."

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature, suchness, self-nature, and specific characteristics of the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom cannot be apprehended, whether in motion or at rest.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! The four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path have no coming and no going, nor do they abide; the intrinsic nature of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path has no coming and no going, nor does it abide; the suchness of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path has no coming and no going, nor does it abide; the self-nature of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path has no coming and no going, nor does it abide; the specific characteristics of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path have no coming and no going, nor do they abide."

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature, suchness, essence, and specific characteristics of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path cannot be apprehended, whether in motion or at rest.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! The four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments have no coming and no going, nor do they abide. The intrinsic nature of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments has no coming and no going, nor does it abide. The suchness of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments has no coming and no going, nor does it abide. The self-nature of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments has no coming and no going, nor does it abide. The specific characteristics of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments have no coming and no going, nor do they abide."

Why is this? Because the nature, suchness, essence, and specific characteristics of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments—whether in motion or at rest—are unfindable.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! The eight liberations and the nine successive attainments have no coming and no going, nor do they abide; the intrinsic nature of the eight liberations and the nine successive attainments has no coming and no going, nor does it abide; the suchness of the eight liberations and the nine successive attainments has no coming and no going, nor does it abide; the self-nature of the eight liberations and the nine successive attainments has no coming and no going, nor does it abide; the specific characteristics of the eight liberations and the nine successive attainments have no coming and no going, nor do they abide."

Why is this? Because the essential nature, suchness, intrinsic nature, and specific characteristics of the eight liberations and the nine successive attainments—whether moving or abiding—cannot be apprehended.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! The gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—have no coming and no going, nor do they abide. The intrinsic nature of the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—has no coming and no going, nor does it abide. The suchness of the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—has no coming and no going, nor does it abide. The self-nature of the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—has no coming and no going, nor does it abide. The specific characteristics of the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—have no coming and no going, nor do they abide."

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature, suchness, self-nature, and specific characteristics of the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—cannot be apprehended as either moving or abiding.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! From the Ground of Extreme Joy up to the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma, there is no coming and no going, nor do they abide. The intrinsic nature of the Grounds from Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma has no coming and no going, nor does it abide. The suchness of the Grounds from Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma has no coming and no going, nor does it abide. The self-nature of the Grounds from Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma has no coming and no going, nor does it abide. The specific characteristics of the Grounds from Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma have no coming and no going, nor do they abide."

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature, suchness, self-nature, and self-characteristic of the stages from the Stage of Utmost Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma cannot be apprehended, whether in motion or at rest.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! From the Stage of Pure Observation up to the Stage of the Tathāgata, there is no coming and no going, nor do they abide. The intrinsic nature of the stages from the Stage of Pure Observation up to the Stage of the Tathāgata has no coming and no going, nor does it abide. The suchness of the stages from the Stage of Pure Observation up to the Stage of the Tathāgata has no coming and no going, nor does it abide. The self-nature of the stages from the Stage of Pure Observation up to the Stage of the Tathāgata has no coming and no going, nor does it abide. The specific characteristics of the stages from the Stage of Pure Observation up to the Stage of the Tathāgata have no coming and no going, nor do they abide."

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature, suchness, self-nature, and self-characteristic of the stages from the Ground of Pure Contemplation up to the Tathāgata Ground cannot be apprehended, whether in motion or at rest.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! The gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi neither come nor go, nor do they abide; the intrinsic nature of the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi neither comes nor goes, nor does it abide; the suchness of the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi neither comes nor goes, nor does it abide; the self-nature of the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi neither comes nor goes, nor does it abide; the specific characteristics of the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi neither come nor go, nor do they abide."
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature, suchness, self-nature, and self-characteristic of the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi—whether in motion or at rest—are unapprehendable.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! The five eyes and six supernormal powers have no coming and no going, nor do they abide; the intrinsic nature of the five eyes and six supernormal powers has no coming and no going, nor does it abide; the suchness of the five eyes and six supernormal powers has no coming and no going, nor does it abide; the self-nature of the five eyes and six supernormal powers has no coming and no going, nor does it abide; the specific characteristics of the five eyes and six supernormal powers have no coming and no going, nor do they abide."
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature, suchness, self-nature, and self-characteristic of the five eyes and six supernormal powers—whether they move or abide—cannot be apprehended.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! The ten powers of the Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, neither come nor go, nor do they abide. The intrinsic nature of the ten powers of the Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, neither comes nor goes, nor does it abide. The suchness of the ten powers of the Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, neither comes nor goes, nor does it abide. The self-nature of the ten powers of the Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, neither comes nor goes, nor does it abide. The specific characteristics of the ten powers of the Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, neither come nor go, nor do they abide."

Why is this? Because it is impossible to find any movement or stillness in the fundamental nature, suchness, self-nature, or self-characteristic of the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! The quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣadharma*) and the state of constant equanimity (*upekṣā-vihāritā*) have no coming and no going, nor do they abide. The intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) of the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity has no coming and no going, nor does it abide. The suchness (*tathatā*) of the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity has no coming and no going, nor does it abide. The self-nature (*svabhāva*) of the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity has no coming and no going, nor does it abide. The specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity has no coming and no going, nor does it abide."

Why is this? Because it is impossible to find any movement or stillness within the nature of the quality of non-forgetfulness, the nature of constant abiding in equanimity, suchness, intrinsic nature, or specific characteristics.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! All-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) neither come nor go, nor do they abide. The intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) of all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects neither comes nor goes, nor does it abide. The suchness (*tathatā*) of all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects neither comes nor goes, nor does it abide. The self-nature (*svabhāva*) of all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects neither comes nor goes, nor does it abide. The specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects neither come nor go, nor do they abide."

Why is this? Because the movement or stillness of the intrinsic nature, suchness, self-nature, and specific characteristics of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) cannot be apprehended.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! A bodhisattva and the qualities of a bodhisattva neither come nor go, nor do they abide; a bodhisattva and the qualities of a bodhisattva are by nature without coming or going, nor do they abide; a bodhisattva and the qualities of a bodhisattva are in their suchness (tathatā) without coming or going, nor do they abide; a bodhisattva and the qualities of a bodhisattva are in their intrinsic nature (svabhāva) without coming or going, nor do they abide; a bodhisattva and the qualities of a bodhisattva are in their specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) without coming or going, nor do they abide."
Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva, the intrinsic nature of the Bodhisattva-dharmas, suchness, self-nature, and self-characteristics—whether in motion or at rest—are all unapprehendable.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! Awakening (bodhi) and the Buddha neither come nor go, nor do they abide; the intrinsic nature (prakṛti) of awakening and the Buddha neither comes nor goes, nor does it abide; the suchness (tathatā) of awakening and the Buddha neither comes nor goes, nor does it abide; the self-nature (svabhāva) of awakening and the Buddha neither comes nor goes, nor does it abide; the specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) of awakening and the Buddha neither come nor go, nor do they abide."
Why is this? Because it is impossible to find any movement or stillness within the nature of bodhi, the essence of a buddha, suchness, self-nature, or self-characteristic.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! Conditioned and unconditioned phenomena have no coming and no going, nor do they abide. The intrinsic nature of conditioned and unconditioned phenomena has no coming and no going, nor does it abide. The suchness of conditioned and unconditioned phenomena has no coming and no going, nor does it abide. The self-nature of conditioned and unconditioned phenomena has no coming and no going, nor does it abide. The specific characteristics of conditioned and unconditioned phenomena have no coming and no going, nor do they abide."
Why is this? Because the conditioned, the unconditioned, fundamental nature, suchness, self-nature, and self-characteristics—whether moving or abiding—are all unapprehendable.
“Subhūti, you should know that for this reason it is said:
furthermore, just as space cannot be seen to come, to go, or to abide;”
The Mahāyāna is likewise: no coming, no going, and no abiding can be perceived.
*The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Fascicle 494, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Third Division, Subhūti Chapter, Part Three, Section Fourteen: "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

You have made this statement: "Just as space cannot be apprehended in its prior, posterior, or middle limits, so too is the Great Vehicle; its prior, posterior, and middle limits are all unapprehendable. Thus, even up to the point that it is equal throughout the three times and transcends the three times, it is therefore called the 'Great Vehicle'."
"So it is! So it is! It is just as you have said."

Why is this? The past world is empty of the past world; the future world is empty of the future world; the present world is empty of the present world. The three periods of time are equal, and the three periods of time are empty of the three periods of time being equal. That which transcends the three periods of time is empty of transcending the three periods of time; the Great Vehicle is empty of the Great Vehicle; the Bodhisattva is empty of the Bodhisattva.
Why is this? Subhūti!

Emptiness possesses none of the characteristics of one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, or ten, and so on, up to a hundred, a thousand, and so forth; therefore, the Great Vehicle is equal throughout the three periods of time and transcends the three periods of time.

“Subhūti, you should know that within this Great Vehicle, neither the characteristic of equality nor the characteristic of inequality can be apprehended; likewise, the characteristics of attachment and non-attachment, hatred and non-hatred, delusion and non-delusion, and pride and non-pride cannot be apprehended.”

In this way, up to and including: the characteristics of the wholesome and the unwholesome; the characteristics of the determinate and the indeterminate; the characteristics of the outflowing and the non-outflowing; the characteristics of the faulty and the faultless; the characteristics of defilement and purification; the characteristics of the mundane and the supramundane; the characteristics of being with attachment and being free from attachment;

and the characteristics of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa—these too are unapprehendable. Furthermore, the characteristics of the permanent and the impermanent; the characteristics of suffering and non-suffering; the characteristics of the self and the selfless; the characteristics of the pure and the impure; the characteristics of tranquility and non-tranquility; and the characteristics of detachment and non-detachment—these too are unapprehendable.
Likewise, the characteristics of transcending the desire realm, transcending the form realm, and transcending the formless realm—such characteristics as these are also unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because within this Mahāyāna, the intrinsic nature of all phenomena cannot be apprehended.
"Subhūti, you should know this!"

The aggregates of form through consciousness of the past, future, and present are all empty of their own intrinsic nature; within emptiness, the aggregates of form through consciousness of the past, future, and present are all unapprehendable.

Why is this? Because the past, future, and present aggregates of form, up to and including the aggregate of consciousness, are all emptiness; emptiness itself is empty. Within emptiness, even emptiness cannot be apprehended—how much less could there be an intrinsic nature of the past, future, and present aggregates of form, up to and including the aggregate of consciousness, to be found within emptiness!

"Subhūti, you should know that the past, future, and present bases of eye, up to and including the base of mind, are all empty of the intrinsic nature of the past, future, and present bases of eye, up to and including the base of mind. Within emptiness, the past, future, and present bases of eye, up to and including the base of mind, are all unapprehendable."

Why is this? The sense bases from the eye-base through to the mind-base, whether past, future, or present, are all empty; emptiness itself is also empty. Within emptiness, even emptiness cannot be apprehended, let alone the self-nature of the sense bases from the eye-base through to the mind-base that could be found within emptiness in the past, future, or present!
"Subhūti, you should know this:

the past, future, and present bases of form (*rūpāyatana*) up to the bases of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*)—the past, future, and present bases of form up to the bases of mental phenomena—are all empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Within emptiness, the past, future, and present bases of form up to the bases of mental phenomena are all unapprehendable."

Why is this? Because the past, future, and present bases of form (*rūpāyatana*) up to the base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) are all emptiness itself; even the nature of emptiness is empty. Within emptiness, even the nature of emptiness cannot be apprehended, let alone the self-nature of the past, future, and present bases of form up to the base of phenomena that could be found within emptiness!
"Subhūti, you should know this:

the眼界 (cakṣurdhātu), up to and including the 意界 (manodhātu) of the past, future, and present—the self-nature of these眼界, up to and including the 意界, of the past, future, and present, is entirely empty. Within emptiness, the眼界, up to and including the 意界, of the past, future, and present, are all unattainable."

Why is this? Because the eye-element of the past, future, and present, up to and including the mind-element, are all themselves empty; even the nature of emptiness is empty. Within emptiness, even the nature of emptiness cannot be apprehended, let alone the self-nature of the eye-element of the past, future, and present, up to and including the mind-element, which could be found within emptiness!

"Subhūti, you should know that the past, future, and present form realm, up to and including the dharma-realm, are all empty of the intrinsic nature of the past, future, and present form realm, up to and including the dharma-realm. Within emptiness, the past, future, and present form realm, up to and including the dharma-realm, are all unapprehendable."

Why is this? Because the past, future, and present form-realm (*rūpadhātu*), up to and including the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), are all themselves empty; the nature of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is also empty. Within emptiness, even the nature of emptiness cannot be apprehended, let alone the self-nature of the past, future, and present form-realm, up to and including the dharma-realm, which could be apprehended within emptiness!

“Subhūti, you should know that the past, future, and present eye-consciousness element, up to and including the past, future, and present mental-consciousness element, are all empty of their own intrinsic nature. Within emptiness, the past, future, and present eye-consciousness element, up to and including the mental-consciousness element, are all unapprehendable.”

Why is this? Because the eye-consciousness element of the past, future, and present, up to and including the mind-consciousness element, are all themselves empty; even emptiness itself is empty. Within emptiness, even emptiness itself cannot be apprehended, let alone the self-nature of the eye-consciousness element of the past, future, and present, up to and including the mind-consciousness element, which could be found within emptiness!

“Subhūti, you should know that the past, future, and present eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact—the self-nature of these past, future, and present eye-contacts, up to and including mind-contacts—is entirely empty. Within emptiness, past, future, and present eye-contacts, up to and including mind-contacts, are all unapprehendable.”

Why is this? Eye-contact, and so forth up to mind-contact, of the past, future, and present, are all themselves empty; even the nature of emptiness is empty. Within emptiness, even the nature of emptiness cannot be apprehended, let alone the self-nature of eye-contact, and so forth up to mind-contact, of the past, future, and present, which could be found within emptiness!
“Subhūti, you should know this:

all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including all feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, in the past, future, and present, are empty of intrinsic nature. Within emptiness, all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including all feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, in the past, future, and present, are non-apprehendable.”

Why is this? All feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including all feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, in the past, future, and present, are themselves empty. Even emptiness is empty; within emptiness, even emptiness itself cannot be apprehended, let alone the intrinsic nature of all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including all feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, that could be found within emptiness in the past, future, or present!

“Subhūti, you should know that the past, future, and present earth element, up to and including the consciousness element, are all empty of the intrinsic nature of the past, future, and present earth element, up to and including the consciousness element. Within emptiness, the past, future, and present earth element, up to and including the consciousness element, are all unapprehendable.”

Why is this? Because the past, future, and present elements of earth, up to the element of consciousness, are all themselves empty; emptiness itself is also empty. Within emptiness, even emptiness itself cannot be apprehended, so how much less could there be any intrinsic nature of the past, future, or present elements of earth, up to the element of consciousness, to be found within emptiness!

“Subhūti, you should know that the past, future, and present causal conditions—even up to the dominant conditions—have a nature that is empty of the past, future, and present causal conditions, even up to the dominant conditions. Within emptiness, the past, future, and present causal conditions—even up to the dominant conditions—are all unapprehendable.”

Why is this so? Because the past, future, and present causal conditions, up to and including the sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), are all themselves empty; emptiness itself is also empty. Within emptiness, even emptiness itself cannot be apprehended, let alone the self-nature of the past, future, and present causal conditions, up to and including the sovereign condition, being apprehendable within emptiness!
“Subhūti, you should know this!

The past, future, and present ignorance, up to and including old age and death, as well as the intrinsic nature of the past, future, and present ignorance, up to and including old age and death, are all empty. Within emptiness, the past, future, and present ignorance, up to and including old age and death, are all unapprehendable.”

Why is this? Because past, future, and present ignorance up to old age and death are all empty; even the nature of emptiness is empty. Within emptiness, even the nature of emptiness cannot be apprehended, let alone the self-nature of past, future, and present ignorance up to old age and death that could be found within emptiness!

"Subhūti, you should know that the past, future, and present perfections of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom are all empty of the intrinsic nature of the past, future, and present perfections of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom. Within emptiness, the past, future, and present perfections of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom are all unapprehendable."

Why is this? Because the past, future, and present perfections of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom are all emptiness itself; emptiness is also empty. Within emptiness, even emptiness itself cannot be apprehended, let alone the self-nature of the past, future, and present perfections of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom that could be found within emptiness!
“Subhūti, you should know this:

the past, future, and present four applications of mindfulness, up to and including the eight branches of the noble path—the self-nature of these past, future, and present four applications of mindfulness, up to and including the eight branches of the noble path, is entirely empty. Within emptiness, the past, future, and present four applications of mindfulness, up to and including the eight branches of the noble path, are all unapprehendable.”

Why is this? Because the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path of the past, future, and present are all emptiness itself; even the nature of emptiness is empty. Within emptiness, even the nature of emptiness cannot be apprehended, let alone the self-nature of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path of the past, future, and present that could be found within emptiness!
“Subhūti, you should know this!

The past, future, and present four dhyānas, four immeasurables, and four formless attainments are all empty of the intrinsic nature of the past, future, and present four dhyānas, four immeasurables, and four formless attainments. Within emptiness, the past, future, and present four dhyānas, four immeasurables, and four formless attainments are all unapprehendable.”

Why is this? Because the past, future, and present four dhyānas, four immeasurables, and four formless attainments are all emptiness; emptiness itself is also empty. Within emptiness, even emptiness itself cannot be apprehended, let alone the self-nature of the past, future, and present four dhyānas, four immeasurables, and four formless attainments that could be found within emptiness!
“Subhūti, you should know this:

the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—of the past, future, and present are empty of the very nature of the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—of the past, future, and present. Within emptiness, the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—of the past, future, and present are all unapprehendable.”

Why is this? The past, future, and present emptinesses, as well as the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness, are all themselves empty; even the nature of emptiness is empty. Within emptiness, even the nature of emptiness cannot be apprehended, let alone the self-nature of the past, future, and present emptinesses, or the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness, which could be found within emptiness!

“Subhūti, you should know that the eight liberations and the nine successive attainments of the past, future, and present are all empty of their own intrinsic nature. Within emptiness, the eight liberations and the nine successive attainments of the past, future, and present are all unapprehendable.”

Why is this? Because the eight liberations and the nine successive attainments of the past, future, and present are all emptiness itself; even the nature of emptiness is empty. Within emptiness, even the nature of emptiness cannot be apprehended, let alone the self-nature of the eight liberations and nine successive attainments of the past, future, and present that could be found within emptiness!

“Subhūti, you should know that the stages from the Stage of Pure Observation up to the Stage of the Tathāgata—past, future, and present—are all empty of their own intrinsic nature. Within emptiness, the stages from the Stage of Pure Observation up to the Stage of the Tathāgata, past, future, and present, are all unapprehendable.”

Why is this? Because the stages from the Ground of Pure Contemplation up to the Tathāgata Ground—whether past, future, or present—are all emptiness itself; emptiness is also empty. Within emptiness, even emptiness itself cannot be apprehended, let alone the intrinsic nature of the stages from the Ground of Pure Contemplation up to the Tathāgata Ground that could be found within emptiness!
“Subhūti, you should know this!

The past, future, and present stages, from the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma, are all empty of their own inherent nature. Within that emptiness, the past, future, and present stages, from the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma, are all unapprehendable.”

Why is this? Because the past, future, and present stages, from the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma stage, are all themselves empty; emptiness itself is also empty. Within emptiness, even emptiness itself cannot be apprehended, let alone the self-nature of the past, future, and present stages, from the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma stage, which could be found within emptiness!

“Subhūti, you should know that the dhāraṇī-doors and samādhi-doors of the past, future, and present are all empty of the intrinsic nature of the dhāraṇī-doors and samādhi-doors of the past, future, and present. Within emptiness, the dhāraṇī-doors and samādhi-doors of the past, future, and present are all unapprehendable.”

Why is this? The gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi of the past, future, and present are all emptiness; emptiness itself is also empty. Within emptiness, even emptiness cannot be apprehended, let alone the self-nature of the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi of the past, future, and present that could be found within emptiness!

“Subhūti, you should know that the five eyes and six superknowledges of the past, future, and present, as well as the intrinsic nature of those five eyes and six superknowledges of the past, future, and present, are all empty. Within emptiness, the five eyes and six superknowledges of the past, future, and present are all unapprehendable.”

Why is this? The five eyes and six supernormal powers of the past, future, and present are all emptiness; even the nature of emptiness is empty. Within emptiness, even the nature of emptiness cannot be apprehended, let alone the self-nature of the five eyes and six supernormal powers of the past, future, and present that could be found within emptiness!
“Subhūti, you should know this!

The ten powers of the Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are all empty of their own intrinsic nature. Within emptiness, the ten powers of the Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are all unapprehendable.”

Why is this? The ten powers of the Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are all emptiness; even the nature of emptiness is empty. Within emptiness, even the nature of emptiness cannot be apprehended, let alone the self-nature of the ten powers of the Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, which could possibly be found within emptiness!

“Subhūti, you should know that the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity of the past, future, and present are all empty of their own intrinsic nature. Within emptiness, the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity of the past, future, and present are all unapprehendable.”

Why is this? The qualities of non-forgetfulness regarding the past, future, and present, as well as the state of constant equanimity, are all empty; emptiness itself is also empty. Within emptiness, even emptiness cannot be apprehended, let alone the possibility of finding an intrinsic nature for the qualities of non-forgetfulness regarding the past, future, and present, or for the state of constant equanimity, within that emptiness!

“Subhūti, you should know that all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) of the past, future, and present are empty of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all-knowledge, knowledge of the paths, and knowledge of all aspects of the past, future, and present. Within emptiness, all-knowledge, knowledge of the paths, and knowledge of all aspects of the past, future, and present are all unapprehendable.”

Why is this? Because all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) of the past, future, and present are themselves empty; emptiness itself is also empty. Within emptiness, even emptiness itself cannot be apprehended, let alone the intrinsic nature of the all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects of the past, future, and present that could be found within emptiness!
“Subhūti, you should know this:

the past, future, and present ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas—indeed, the intrinsic nature of all these from past, future, and present ordinary beings up to the tathāgata—are all empty. Within emptiness, past, future, and present ordinary beings up to the tathāgata are all unapprehendable.”

Why is this? Because ordinary beings of the past, future, and present, up to and including the Tathāgata, are all emptiness itself; emptiness is also empty. Within emptiness, even emptiness itself cannot be apprehended, let alone the self-nature of ordinary beings of the past, future, and present, up to and including the Tathāgata, which could be found within emptiness!
Because a self, a sentient being, and so forth, up to a knower and a seer, cannot be apprehended. "Furthermore, Subhūti!

The aggregate of form, up to the aggregate of consciousness, cannot be apprehended in the past, future, or middle limits; nor can the aggregates from form through consciousness be apprehended within the equality of the three limits."

Why is this so? Because within equality, the intrinsic nature of the aggregate of form—from the past, future, and present limits—up to the intrinsic nature of the aggregate of consciousness, is entirely unapprehendable.
For what reason?

Even the state of equality within equality cannot be apprehended; how much less can the intrinsic nature of the aggregate of form, up to the intrinsic nature of the aggregate of consciousness, be apprehended within that equality at its prior, subsequent, or middle limits!
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

The eye-base, and so on up to the mind-base, are all unapprehendable in the past, future, and middle limits; within the equality of the three limits, the eye-base, and so on up to the mind-base, are likewise unapprehendable."

Why is this? Because within equality, the intrinsic nature of the sense-base of the eye—from the past, future, and present limits—up to the intrinsic nature of the sense-base of the mind, is entirely unapprehendable. Why is that?

Even the state of equality within equality cannot be apprehended; how much less can the intrinsic nature of the sense-base of the eye, up to the intrinsic nature of the sense-base of the mind, be apprehended within that equality—whether in the past, future, or middle limit!
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

The sense base of form, up to the sense base of phenomena, cannot be apprehended in the past, future, or middle limits; within the equality of the three limits, the sense base of form, up to the sense base of phenomena, likewise cannot be apprehended."

Why is this? Because within equality, the intrinsic nature of the sphere of form—from the past, future, and present limits—up to the intrinsic nature of the sphere of mental phenomena, is entirely unapprehendable. Why is this so?

Even the state of equality within equality cannot be apprehended; how much less can the intrinsic nature of the sphere of form—from its beginning, middle, and end—up to the intrinsic nature of the sphere of phenomena be apprehended within that equality!
