“Śāriputra! Just as the names ‘suchness’ up to ‘the inconceivable realm’ are comprised merely of adventitious designations. Why is this so?

Suchness and so forth are not names, and names are not suchness and so forth; within suchness and so forth there are no names, and within names there is no suchness and so forth. They are neither conjoined nor dispersed, but are merely provisional designations.
Why is this? Because both suchness and its names are empty of intrinsic nature; within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, neither suchness nor names exist at all, and are entirely unobtainable.

The names of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are likewise thus, being comprised solely of adventitious designations; for this reason, it is said that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess only provisional names and have no intrinsic nature whatsoever.
“Śāriputra! Just as the realm of cessation up to the unconditioned realm are designated merely as adventitious designations. Why is this so?

The realms of abandonment (*prahāṇadhātu*) and so forth are not names, and names are not the realms of abandonment and so forth. Within the realms of abandonment and so forth there are no names, and within names there are no realms of abandonment and so forth. They are neither conjoined nor dispersed; they are merely conventional designations (*prajñapti*).

Why is this? Because the realm of cessation and so forth, together with their designations, are empty of intrinsic nature; within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, whether it be the realm of cessation and so forth, or the designation, both are non-existent and entirely unapprehendable.

The names of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are likewise thus, being comprised solely of adventitious designations; for this reason, it is said that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess only provisional names and have no intrinsic nature whatsoever.
“Śāriputra! Just as the names of the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path are merely designated by adventitious factors. Why is this so?

The Noble Truth of Suffering and so forth are not names, and names are not the Noble Truth of Suffering and so forth. Within the Noble Truth of Suffering and so forth there are no names, and within names there are no Noble Truths of Suffering and so forth; they are neither conjoined nor dispersed, but are merely provisional designations.

Why is this? Because the Noble Truth of Suffering and so forth, together with their names, are empty of intrinsic nature; within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, neither the Noble Truth of Suffering and so forth nor the name are anything at all and are entirely unobtainable.

The names of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are likewise thus, being comprised solely of adventitious designations; for this reason, it is said that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess only provisional names and have no intrinsic nature whatsoever.
“Śāriputra! Just as the names of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path are merely comprised of adventitious designations. Why is this so?

The four foundations of mindfulness and so forth are not names, and names are not the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth. Within the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth there are no names, and within names there are no four foundations of mindfulness and so forth. They are neither joined nor dispersed, but are merely conventional designations.

Why is this? Because the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth, together with their names, are empty of intrinsic nature; within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, neither the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth nor the name are anything at all and are entirely unobtainable.

The names of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are likewise thus, being comprised solely of adventitious factors; for this reason, it is said that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess only a provisional name and have no intrinsic nature whatsoever.
“Śāriputra! Just as the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions are designated as being comprised of mere adventitious factors. Why is this so?

The four dhyānas and so forth are not names, and names are not the four dhyānas and so forth. Within the four dhyānas and so forth there are no names, and within names there are no four dhyānas and so forth. They are neither conjoined nor dispersed; they are merely conventional designations.

Why is this? Because the four dhyānas and so forth, together with their names, are empty of intrinsic nature; within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, neither the four dhyānas and so forth nor their names exist at all and are entirely unapprehendable.

The names of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are likewise thus, being comprised solely of adventitious factors; for this reason, it is said that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess only provisional names and have no intrinsic nature whatsoever.
“Śāriputra! Just as the eight liberations and the nine successive attainments are designated as being comprised of mere adventitious factors. Why is this so?

The eight liberations and so forth are not names, and names are not the eight liberations and so forth. Within the eight liberations and so forth there are no names, and within names there are no eight liberations and so forth. They are neither conjoined nor dispersed; they are merely conventional designations.

Why is this? Because the eight liberations and so forth, together with their names, are empty of intrinsic nature; within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, both the eight liberations and so forth, and their names, are equally non-existent and utterly unobtainable.

The names of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are likewise thus, being comprised solely of adventitious factors; for this reason, it is said that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess only provisional names and have no intrinsic nature whatsoever.
“Śāriputra! Just as the names of the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are merely comprised of adventitious factors. Why is this so?

The doors of liberation such as emptiness are not names, and names are not the doors of liberation such as emptiness; within the doors of liberation such as emptiness there are no names, and within names there are no doors of liberation such as emptiness. They are neither conjoined nor dispersed, but are merely conventional designations.

Why is this? Because the gateways to liberation such as emptiness, together with their names, are empty of intrinsic nature; within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, both the gateways to liberation such as emptiness and their names are non-existent and entirely unapprehendable.

The names of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are likewise thus, being comprised solely of adventitious designations; for this reason, it is said that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess only provisional names and have no intrinsic nature whatsoever.
“Śāriputra! Just as the stages from the Stage of Pure Observation up to the Stage of the Tathāgata are designated merely as adventitious. Why is this?

The stages such as the Ground of Pure Observation are not names, and names are not the stages such as the Ground of Pure Observation. Within the stages such as the Ground of Pure Observation there are no names, and within names there are no stages such as the Ground of Pure Observation. They are neither conjoined nor dispersed, being merely conventional designations.

Why is this? Because the Stage of Pure Observation and so forth, together with their names, are empty of intrinsic nature; within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, neither the Stage of Pure Observation and so forth nor the name are anything at all, and are utterly unobtainable.

The names of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are likewise thus, being comprised solely of adventitious designations; for this reason, it is said that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess only provisional names and have no intrinsic nature whatsoever.
“Śāriputra! Just as the names of the stages from the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma are comprised merely of adventitious designations. Why is this so?

The names such as "the Stage of Supreme Joy" are not the stages themselves, and the stages such as "the Stage of Supreme Joy" are not the names. Within the stages such as "the Stage of Supreme Joy" there are no names, and within the names there are no stages such as "the Stage of Supreme Joy. They are neither conjoined nor dispersed; they are merely conventional designations.

Why is this? Because the Ground of Supreme Joy and so forth, together with their names, are empty of intrinsic nature; within that emptiness of intrinsic nature, neither the Ground of Supreme Joy and so forth nor the names are anything at all and are entirely unapprehendable.

The names of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are likewise thus, being comprised solely of adventitious designations; for this reason, it is said that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess only conventional names and have no intrinsic nature whatsoever.
“Śāriputra! Just as the names ‘five eyes’ and ‘six supernormal powers’ are merely comprised of adventitious designations. Why is this so?

The five eyes and so forth are not names, and names are not the five eyes and so forth; within the five eyes and so forth there are no names, and within names there are no five eyes and so forth. They are neither conjoined nor dispersed, but are merely provisional designations.

Why is this? Because the five eyes and so forth, together with their names, are empty of intrinsic nature; within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, whether it be the five eyes and so forth or their names, both are non-existent and entirely unapprehendable.

The names of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are likewise thus, being comprised solely of adventitious factors; for this reason, it is said that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess only provisional names and have no intrinsic nature at all.
“Śāriputra! Just as the names of the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are comprised merely of adventitious designations. Why is this so?

The ten powers of the Tathāgata and so forth are not names, and names are not the ten powers of the Tathāgata and so forth. Within the ten powers of the Tathāgata and so forth there are no names, and within names there are no ten powers of the Tathāgata and so forth. They are neither conjoined nor dispersed, but are merely provisional designations.

Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s ten powers and so forth, together with their names, are empty of intrinsic nature; within this emptiness of intrinsic nature, both the Tathāgata’s ten powers and so forth, and their names, are equally non-existent and utterly unapprehendable.

The names of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are likewise thus, being comprised solely of adventitious designations; for this reason, it is said that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess only provisional names and have no intrinsic nature whatsoever.
“Śāriputra! Just as the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant abiding in equanimity are designated as being comprised solely of adventitious factors. Why is this so?

The dharmas such as non-forgetfulness are not the name; the name is not the dharmas such as non-forgetfulness. Within the dharmas such as non-forgetfulness there is no name, and within the name there are no dharmas such as non-forgetfulness. They are neither conjoined nor dispersed, being merely conventional designations.

Why is this? Because the dharmas such as non-forgetfulness and their names are both empty of intrinsic nature; within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, whether it be the dharmas such as non-forgetfulness or their names, both are non-existent and entirely unobtainable.

The names of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are likewise thus, being comprised solely of adventitious designations; for this reason, it is said that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess only conventional names and have no intrinsic nature whatsoever.
“Śāriputra! Just as the names ‘knowledge of all things,’ ‘knowledge of the aspects of the path,’ and ‘knowledge of all aspects’ are comprised of mere adventitious designations. Why is this so?

The omniscience and so forth are not the name, and the name is not the omniscience and so forth; within the omniscience and so forth there is no name, and within the name there is no omniscience and so forth. They are neither conjoined nor dispersed, being merely conventional designations.

Why is this? Because all-knowledge and so forth, together with their names, are empty of intrinsic nature; within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, whether it be all-knowledge and so forth, or the name, both are non-existent and entirely unapprehendable.

The names of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are likewise thus, being comprised solely of adventitious designations; for this reason, it is said that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess only provisional names and have no intrinsic nature whatsoever.
“Śāriputra! Just as the names of the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi are merely designated by adventitious factors. Why is this so?

The dharani-gates and so forth are not names, and names are not the dharani-gates and so forth; within the dharani-gates and so forth there are no names, and within names there are no dharani-gates and so forth. They are neither conjoined nor dispersed, but are merely conventional designations.

Why is this? Because the gateways of dhāraṇī and so forth, together with their names, are empty of intrinsic nature; within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, whether it be the gateways of dhāraṇī and so forth or their names, both are non-existent and entirely unobtainable.

The names of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are likewise thus, being comprised solely of adventitious designations; for this reason, it is said that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess only provisional names and have no intrinsic nature whatsoever.
“Śāriputra! Just as the names ‘Hearer,’ ‘Solitary Realizer,’ and ‘Mahāyāna’ are merely designated by adventitious factors. Why is this so?

The śrāvakas and others are not the name, and the name is not the śrāvakas and others; within the śrāvakas and others there is no name, and within the name there are no śrāvakas and others. They are neither conjoined nor dispersed, being merely conventional designations.

Why is this? Because both the śrāvakas and so forth, along with their names, are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*). Within this emptiness of intrinsic nature, neither the śrāvakas and so forth nor their names exist; they are entirely unapprehendable.

The names of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are likewise thus, being comprised solely of adventitious designations; for this reason, it is said that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess only provisional names and have no intrinsic nature whatsoever.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, regarding what the Venerable One asked:
'For what reason is it said that we are ultimately unarisen, existing only as provisional designations and lacking any intrinsic nature?'"
"O Śāriputra! Since 'I' ultimately does not exist and cannot be apprehended, how could there be birth?
Even up to 'the seer,' since that too ultimately does not exist and cannot be apprehended, how could there be birth?"
Śāriputra! Since form is ultimately non-existent and unapprehendable, how could it have arising?
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also ultimately non-existent and unapprehendable; how could they have arising?
In this way, up to and including the Śrāvakayāna, it is ultimately non-existent and unapprehendable; how, then, could there be its arising?
The Pratyekabuddhayāna and the Mahāyāna are likewise ultimately non-existent and unapprehendable; how, then, could there be their arising?
Śāriputra! For this reason, I say: as it is said that "we" are ultimately unarisen, they exist only as provisional designations and possess no intrinsic nature whatsoever.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra! Regarding what the Venerable One asked:
'For what reason is it said that all phenomena are likewise ultimately unarisen, existing only as provisional designations and entirely lacking intrinsic nature?'"
"Thus it is, Śāriputra! All phenomena (dharmas) are entirely devoid of a self-nature that arises through combination. Why is this?"
"Because phenomena that arise through combination are empty of intrinsic nature. Then, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"What phenomena are entirely devoid of a combined intrinsic nature?"
Subhūti replied, “Śāriputra!

The aggregate of form has no inherent nature of synthesis; the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness likewise have no inherent nature of synthesis. In this way, even up to the vehicle of the śrāvakas, there is no inherent nature of synthesis; the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas and the Great Vehicle also have no inherent nature of synthesis.”
Śāriputra! For this reason, I say: all phenomena are likewise ultimately unarisen;
they possess only provisional names and lack any intrinsic nature whatsoever.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, all phenomena are neither permanent nor subject to dispersion. Why is this?
"If a phenomenon is not permanent, it is because it lacks the nature of inexhaustibility.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"What phenomenon is neither impermanent nor subject to dispersal?"
Subhūti replied, “Śāriputra!

The aggregate of form is neither permanent nor subject to dispersal; the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither permanent nor subject to dispersal. In this way, even up to the vehicle of the śrāvakas, it is neither permanent nor subject to dispersal; the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas and the Great Vehicle are likewise neither permanent nor subject to dispersal.”
Why is this? Śāriputra, if a phenomenon is not permanent, it has no intrinsic nature; and if it has no intrinsic nature, it is inexhaustible.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, all things are not pleasure, nor are they subject to dispersal. Why is this?
"If a phenomenon is not pleasure, it is because it lacks the nature of inexhaustibility.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"What phenomenon is neither pleasure nor subject to dispersal?"

Subhūti replied: “The aggregate of form is neither pleasure nor subject to dispersal; the aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are neither pleasure nor subject to dispersal. In this way, even up to the vehicle of the śrāvakas, it is neither pleasure nor subject to dispersal; the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas and the Great Vehicle are neither pleasure nor subject to dispersal.”
Why is this? Śāriputra, if a phenomenon is not pleasure, it lacks intrinsic nature; and if it lacks intrinsic nature, it is inexhaustible.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, all things are not-self and yet there is no loss. Why is this?
"If a phenomenon is not self, it is because it has the nature of being inexhaustible.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"What phenomenon is neither self nor subject to dispersal?"
Subhūti replied, “Śāriputra!

The aggregate of form is not self, yet it is without dispersal; the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not self, yet they are without dispersal. In this way, even up to the vehicle of the śrāvakas, it is not self, yet it is without dispersal; the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas and the Great Vehicle are not self, yet they are without dispersal.”
Why is this? Śāriputra, if a phenomenon is not self, it lacks intrinsic nature; and if it lacks intrinsic nature, it is inexhaustible.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, all phenomena are quiescent and without dissipation. Why is this?
"If a phenomenon is quiescent, it is because its nature is inexhaustible.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"What phenomenon is both quiescent and without dispersal?"
Subhūti replied, “Śāriputra!

The aggregate of form is quiescent and without loss; the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are quiescent and without loss. Likewise, even up to the vehicle of the śrāvakas being quiescent and without loss, and the vehicles of the pratyekabuddhas and the Great Vehicle being quiescent and without loss.”
Why is this? Śāriputra!
If a phenomenon is quiescent, it has no intrinsic nature; and if it has no intrinsic nature, it is inexhaustible.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, all phenomena are detached and yet there is no loss. Why is this?
"If a phenomenon is detached, it is because its nature is inexhaustible.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"What phenomenon is detached and yet not lost?"
Subhūti replied, “Śāriputra! The aggregate of form is detached and yet there is no loss;

the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are detached and yet there is no loss. In this way, even up to the vehicle of the śrāvakas being detached and yet there is no loss, and the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas and the Great Vehicle being detached and yet there is no loss.”
Why is this? Śāriputra, if a phenomenon is detached, it has no intrinsic nature; and if it has no intrinsic nature, it is inexhaustible.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, all dharmas are empty, signless, wishless, and yet without dispersal. Why is this?"
"If dharmas are empty, signless, and wishless, it is because they have an inexhaustible nature.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"What dharmas are empty, signless, wishless, and also without dispersal?"
Subhūti replied, “Śāriputra!

The aggregate of form is empty, signless, wishless, and without dispersal; the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, signless, wishless, and without dispersal. In this way, up to and including the vehicle of the śrāvakas, it is empty, signless, wishless, and without dispersal; the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas and the Great Vehicle are also empty, signless, wishless, and without dispersal.”
Why is this? Śāriputra, if a dharma is empty, signless, and wishless, it has no intrinsic nature; and if it has no intrinsic nature, it is inexhaustible.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
All phenomena are wholesome, blameless, untainted, undefiled, supramundane, pure, unconditioned, and moreover, without dispersal."
Why is this? Because if a phenomenon is wholesome, blameless, untainted, undefiled, supramundane, pure, unconditioned, it possesses the nature of inexhaustibility.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"What dharma is wholesome, blameless, untainted, free from passion, supramundane, pure, unconditioned, and without loss?"
Subhūti replied: "Śāriputra!

The aggregate of form is wholesome, blameless, untainted, free from passion, supramundane, pure, unconditioned, and without dispersal. The aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are wholesome, blameless, untainted, free from passion, supramundane, pure, unconditioned, and without dispersal. Likewise, even up to the vehicle of the śrāvakas, it is wholesome, blameless, untainted, free from passion, supramundane, pure, unconditioned, and without dispersal; and the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas and the Great Vehicle are wholesome, blameless, untainted, free from passion, supramundane, pure, unconditioned, and without dispersal."

Why is this? Śāriputra, if a dharma is wholesome, blameless, untainted, free from passion, supramundane, pure, and unconditioned, then it has no intrinsic nature; and if it has no intrinsic nature, then it is inexhaustible.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, all phenomena are neither permanent nor subject to destruction.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed Subhūti, saying:
“What phenomena are neither impermanent nor subject to destruction? Subhūti replied: “Śāriputra!...”
The aggregate of form is neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why?
Because such is its intrinsic nature.
The aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why?
Because such is their intrinsic nature.
In this way, even the Śrāvaka vehicle is neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why?
Because such is its intrinsic nature.
The vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas and the Great Vehicle are likewise neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because such is their intrinsic nature.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra! To state it briefly:

whether they be wholesome dharmas or unwholesome dharmas, conditioned dharmas with a definite outcome or neutral dharmas, dharmas with fault or dharmas without fault, dharmas with outflows or dharmas without outflows, defiled dharmas or undefiled dharmas, mundane dharmas or supramundane dharmas, dharmas of affliction or dharmas of purification, dharmas of saṃsāra or dharmas of nirvāṇa, or conditioned dharmas or unconditioned dharmas—all such things as these are neither permanent nor subject to destruction."
Why is this? Because such is their intrinsic nature, Śāriputra!
For this reason, I say: all phenomena are likewise ultimately unarisen;
they exist merely as provisional designations and possess no intrinsic nature whatsoever. Furthermore, Śāriputra:
As for the Venerable’s question: "For what reason do you say that form, and so on up to consciousness, are ultimately non-arising?
And likewise, up to what extent are the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the Great Vehicle ultimately non-arising?"
"Śāriputra, the intrinsic nature of all form, up to and including consciousness,
is non-arising. Why is this?"
Form, and so forth up to consciousness, are all by nature empty, unconditioned, and unarisen. Why is this?
Because within the dharma of emptiness, an agent cannot be found.
In this way, even all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the Mahāyāna are by nature unborn. Why is this?
Because all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the Mahāyāna are by nature empty, unconditioned, and unarisen.
Why is this? Because in the dharma of emptiness, an agent cannot be found. Śāriputra!
For this reason, I say: What is form, up to consciousness, that is ultimately non-arising? And so on, up to:
what are the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the Great Vehicle that are ultimately non-arising?
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, regarding what the Venerable One asked:

'For what reason is it said that if there is ultimate non-arising, then it is not called form, up to and including consciousness; and likewise, up to and including, if there is ultimate non-arising, then it is not called śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, or Mahāyāna? "

"Śāriputra, because the intrinsic nature of form up to consciousness is empty, if a phenomenon is empty of intrinsic nature, it cannot be designated as arising, ceasing, abiding, or changing. For this reason, that which is ultimately unarisen is not called form, nor is it called consciousness."

Why is this? Because emptiness is not form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; and so on, up to the fact that the intrinsic nature of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and the Mahāyāna is empty. If a phenomenon is empty of intrinsic nature, then it cannot be designated as arising, ceasing, abiding, or changing. For this reason, if there is ultimate non-arising, one does not designate it as "Śrāvaka," "Pratyekabuddha," or "Mahāyāna."
Why is this? Because emptiness is not the Śrāvaka, the Pratyekabuddha, or the Mahāyāna. Śāriputra!

For this reason, I say: if there is ultimate non-arising, then it is not called form, up to and including consciousness; and so on, until: if there is ultimate non-arising, then it is not called Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, or Mahāyāna.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, regarding what the Venerable One asked:
'For what reason do you say, "How could I possibly instruct and admonish a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is ultimately unarisen by means of the perfection of wisdom that is ultimately unarisen?"'..."
"Śāriputra, that which is ultimately non-arising is itself the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and the perfection of wisdom is itself ultimate non-arising."
Why is this? Because ultimate non-arising and the perfection of wisdom are non-dual and cannot be divided into two. Śāriputra!
Ultimate non-arising is itself the bodhisattva mahāsattva, and the bodhisattva mahāsattva is himself ultimate non-arising. Why is this?
Because ultimate non-arising and the bodhisattva mahāsattva are neither two nor divisible into two.
Śāriputra! For this reason, I say: How could I instruct or admonish a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is ultimately unarisen by means of a prajñāpāramitā that is ultimately unarisen?
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, regarding what the Venerable One asked:
'For what reason is it said that because there is no ultimate non-arising, there is also no bodhisattva mahāsattva who can practice unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening?'"

"Śāriputra, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do not perceive a profound perfection of wisdom apart from that which is ultimately unarisen, nor do they perceive a bodhisattva mahāsattva apart from that which is ultimately unarisen."
Why is this? Because that which is ultimately unarisen, the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and the bodhisattva mahāsattva are all non-dual and cannot be divided into two.
Śāriputra! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive any form, nor even consciousness, apart from that which is ultimately unarisen.
Why is this? Because whether it be ultimate non-arising, or form up to consciousness, all are without duality and without division.
In this way, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound Prajñāpāramitā, they do not perceive any Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, or Mahāyāna apart from ultimate non-arising.
Why is this? Whether it be ultimate non-arising, or whether it be Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or the Mahāyāna, they are all non-dual and indivisible. Śāriputra!
For this reason, I say: apart from that which is ultimately unarisen, there is no bodhisattva mahāsattva who can practice for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, regarding what the Venerable One asked:

'For what reason is it said that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing such a teaching, does not sink into despondency nor feel regret, and his mind is not startled, terrified, or afraid, one should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)?'"

"Śāriputra, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they do not perceive any phenomena as having cognition or function. They contemplate all phenomena as being like an illusion, like a dream, like an echo, like a reflection, like a shadow, like a mirage, like a magical creation, and like a city of *gandharvas*; though they appear to exist, they lack any reality. Hearing it said that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, they leap for joy and take deep faith and delight."
Śāriputra! For this reason, I say this:

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing such an exposition, does not become despondent nor feel regret, and his mind is neither startled, terrified, nor afraid, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom and contemplates all phenomena, at that time the bodhisattva mahāsattva apprehends nothing at all regarding form, up to and including consciousness; there is no receiving, no grasping, no dwelling, and no attachment, nor does he designate them as the aggregate of form, up to and including the aggregate of consciousness.”

It is likewise for the sense-base of the eye up to the sense-base of the mind; for the sense-base of forms up to the sense-base of phenomena; for the element of the eye up to the element of the mind; for the element of forms up to the element of phenomena; for the element of eye-consciousness up to the element of mind-consciousness; for eye-contact up to mind-contact; for all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition up to all feelings produced with mind-contact as condition; for the earth element up to the consciousness element; for the causal condition up to the sovereign condition; and for ignorance up to old age and death.

At that time, the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend anything at all regarding the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom; there is no receiving, no grasping, no dwelling, and no attachment, nor does he designate them as the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom.
Regarding internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature; regarding the noble truth of suffering up to the noble truth of the path;
regarding the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; regarding the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
regarding the eight liberations and the nine successive meditative concentrations; regarding emptiness and...
The signless and wishless doors of liberation; from the stage of pure observation up to the stage of a Tathāgata;
from the stage of extreme joy up to the stage of the cloud of dharma; the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity.
Regarding all dhāraṇī-doors and samādhi-doors; regarding the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices and the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas;
regarding suchness up to the inconceivable realm; regarding the realm of cessation up to the unconditioned realm;
regarding all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the [knowledge of all modes]...
The wisdom of all characteristics is also like this. Why is this so,
World-Honored One?

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive the aggregate of form up to the aggregate of consciousness; likewise, they do not perceive anything up to all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Why is this? Because the nature of form is empty, being without arising and without cessation; the natures of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, being without arising and without cessation. Thus it continues until: because the nature of all-knowledge is empty, being without arising and without cessation; and the natures of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects are empty, being without arising and without cessation.
“World-Honored One!

That form is without arising and without cessation is not form; that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without arising and without cessation are not feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. In this way, up to and including omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), that which is without arising and without cessation is not omniscience; that the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are without arising and without cessation is not the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects.”

Why is this? Form, up to and including consciousness, is non-dual with and indivisible from non-arising and non-ceasing; likewise, up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), they are non-dual with and indivisible from non-arising and non-ceasing.
Why is this? World-Honored One!
Because the dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing is neither one, nor two, nor many, nor different.

Therefore, that form through to consciousness is without arising and without cessation is itself not form through to consciousness; likewise, up to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), their being without arising and without cessation is itself not omniscience, knowledge of the aspects of the path, or knowledge of all aspects.
“World-Honored One!

Form is non-dual, and that which is non-dual is not form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-dual, and that which is non-dual is not feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.”

In this way, up to and including omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), non-duality is itself not omniscience; the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)—non-duality is itself not the knowledge of the paths nor the knowledge of all aspects.

"Bhagavan! Form enters into the category of non-dual dharmas; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness enter into the category of non-dual dharmas. For this reason they are called 'form' up to 'consciousness. Likewise, up to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), it enters into the category of non-dual dharmas; the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) enter into the category of non-dual dharmas. For this reason they are called 'omniscience,' 'knowledge of the aspects of the path,' and 'knowledge of all aspects.'"
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the venerable Subhūti, saying:
"Venerable sir, as you have said: 'When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom and contemplates all phenomena...'"
Regarding this, what is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
What is meant by the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)?
And how does one observe all phenomena (dharmas)?
Subhūti replied, "Regarding what the Venerable One asked— 'What is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva?'— O Śāriputra!..."

Because he diligently seeks unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, he is called a bodhisattva; and because he possesses authentic awakening and, although he thoroughly understands the characteristics of all phenomena, remains free from attachment, he is further called a mahāsattva.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"How is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, possessing such realization as it truly is, thoroughly understands the characteristics of all phenomena yet remains without any grasping?"
Subhūti replied, “Śāriputra!

Although bodhisattva mahāsattvas know all characteristics of form as they truly are, they have no attachment to them; although they know all characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as they truly are, they have no attachment to them.”

In this way, even though they know all aspects of the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*) as they truly are, they have no attachment; even though they know all aspects of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) and all aspects of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) as they truly are, they have no attachment.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti,
"What is called the characteristic of all phenomena? Subhūti replied:

“If, by means of such modes, characteristics, and signs, one discerns that these phenomena are form, sound, odor, taste, tangible object, or mental phenomenon; internal or external; with outflows or without outflows; conditioned or unconditioned—these are called the characteristics of all phenomena.”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra! Regarding what the Venerable One asked— 'What is meant by Prajñāpāramitā?'— Śāriputra!"
"Because there is a supreme and wondrous wisdom that can realize all phenomena as they truly are and is far removed from [all attachments], it is called Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"From what phenomena is this able to remain far removed?"

Subhūti replied, “Because it is able to remain detached from all phenomena— such as the aggregates, the sense bases, the elements, and dependent origination— it is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).”
Furthermore, Śāriputra, there is a sublime and wondrous wisdom that can realize all phenomena as they truly are and reach far; for this reason, it is called Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"To what dharma is it able to reach far? Subhūti replied:

"This reaches far beyond the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom; likewise, it reaches far beyond everything from all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*) and the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); therefore, it is called the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)."
Śāriputra! For these reasons, it is called the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā). Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Regarding the Venerable’s question, "How does one observe all phenomena? Śāriputra,
when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they observe form as follows:
Up to consciousness, it is neither permanent nor impermanent, neither pleasure nor suffering,
neither self nor non-self, neither pure nor impure, neither empty nor non-empty, neither with signs nor signless,
neither with aspiration nor aspirationless, neither tranquil nor non-tranquil, and neither detached nor non-detached.
Detached; and so on, up to the observation that omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*),
and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are neither permanent nor impermanent, neither pleasure nor suffering, neither self nor non-self, neither pure nor impure,
neither empty nor non-empty, neither with signs nor signless, and neither with vows nor vowless.
It is not wishless, neither quiescent nor non-quiescent, neither detached nor non-detached.
Śāriputra, these are called the contemplation of all phenomena.
“Śāriputra! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should observe all phenomena in this manner.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the venerable Subhūti, saying:

“Virtuous one, for what reason do you say that from form up to consciousness, being without arising and without cessation, they are not form up to consciousness; and likewise, up to all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects, being without arising and without cessation, they are not all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects?”
Subhūti replied: "Śāriputra!

From form up to consciousness, the nature of form up to the nature of consciousness is empty. Within this emptiness of nature, there is neither arising nor ceasing, nor is there form up to consciousness. For this reason, it is said:..."
That form up to consciousness is without arising and without cessation is itself not form up to consciousness.

In this way, up to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), these—namely all-knowledge, knowledge of the paths, and knowledge of all aspects—are empty of intrinsic nature. Within this emptiness of intrinsic nature, there is neither arising nor cessation, nor is there all-knowledge, knowledge of the paths, or knowledge of all aspects. For this reason it is said:
that all-knowledge, knowledge of the paths, and knowledge of all aspects are without arising and without cessation is itself not all-knowledge, knowledge of the paths, or knowledge of all aspects.
At that time, Śāriputra asked the venerable Subhūti:
"Venerable sir, for what reason do you say this:

that form up to consciousness are non-dual and are not form up to consciousness; and likewise, up to omniscience, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects are non-dual and are not omniscience, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects?"
Subhūti replied, “Śāriputra!

Whether it be form or non-duality, up to and including whether it be consciousness or non-duality—and likewise, up to and including whether it be all-knowledge or non-duality, or whether it be the knowledge of the paths or the knowledge of all aspects or non-duality—all such things are neither joined nor dispersed; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, which is to say, the characteristic of signlessness.”
For this reason it is said:

form up to consciousness are non-dual and are not form up to consciousness; likewise, up to all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), they are non-dual and are not all-knowledge, knowledge of the aspects of the path, or knowledge of all aspects.
At that time, Śāriputra asked the venerable Subhūti:
"For what reason, worthy one, do you speak thus:

'From form up to consciousness, they enter into the category of non-dual dharmas; therefore they are called form up to consciousness. And so on, up to: 'The knowledge of all, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects enter into the category of non-dual dharmas; therefore they are called the knowledge of all, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects'?"
Subhūti replied, "Śāriputra!

Form through consciousness is not different from non-arising and non-ceasing; non-arising and non-ceasing are not different from form through consciousness. Form through consciousness is itself non-arising and non-ceasing; non-arising and non-ceasing is itself form through consciousness."

In this way, even up to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), these are not different from non-arising and non-ceasing; non-arising and non-ceasing are not different from omniscience, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects. Omniscience, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects are themselves non-arising and non-ceasing; non-arising and non-ceasing are themselves omniscience, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects.
For this reason it is said:

form through to consciousness enter the category of non-dual dharmas; therefore they are called "form" through to "consciousness. Likewise, up to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), they enter the category of non-dual dharmas; therefore they are called "omniscience," "knowledge of the aspects of the path," and "knowledge of all aspects."

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll 497. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Three, Chapter on Subhūti, Section Seventeen. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and observes the characteristics of all phenomena as they truly are, at that time the bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives the non-arising of the self, up to and including the perceiver, because they are ultimately pure;
he perceives the non-arising of form, up to and including consciousness, because they are ultimately pure;
he perceives the non-arising of the sense base of the eye, up to and including the sense base of the mind, because they are ultimately pure.
He perceives that the sphere of forms up to the sphere of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) are non-arising, because they are ultimately pure;
he perceives that the eye-element up to the mind-element (*manodhātu*) are non-arising, because they are ultimately pure;
he perceives that the form-element up to the mental-phenomena-element (*dharmadhātu*) are non-arising, because they are ultimately pure.
He sees that the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element is non-arising, because it is ultimately pure;
he sees that eye-contact up to mind-contact is non-arising, because it is ultimately pure;
he sees that all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition up to all feelings produced with mind-contact as condition are non-arising, because they are ultimately pure.
They see that the element of earth, up to the element of consciousness, is non-arising because it is ultimately pure;
they see that the causal condition, up to the sovereign condition, is non-arising because it is ultimately pure;
they see that ignorance, up to old age and death, is non-arising because it is ultimately pure.
One sees that from the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom there is no arising, because they are ultimately pure;
one sees that from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature there is no arising, because they are ultimately pure;
one sees that from suchness up to the inconceivable realm there is no arising, because they are ultimately pure.
One sees that the realm of the abandonable and so forth, up to the unconditioned realm, are non-arising, because they are ultimately pure;
one sees that the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path are non-arising, because they are ultimately pure;
one sees that the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth, up to the eightfold noble path, are non-arising, because they are ultimately pure.
They see that the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments are non-arising, because they are ultimately pure;
they see that the eight liberations and the nine successive concentrations are non-arising, because they are ultimately pure;
they see that the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are non-arising, because they are ultimately pure.
One sees that from the Stage of Pure Observation up to the Stage of the Tathāgata there is non-arising, because they are ultimately pure;
one sees that from the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma there is non-arising, because they are ultimately pure;
one sees that the five eyes and the six supernormal powers are non-arising, because they are ultimately pure.
They see that the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are non-arising, because they are ultimately pure;
they see that the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity are non-arising, because they are ultimately pure;
they see that all doors of dhāraṇī and doors of samādhi are non-arising, because they are ultimately pure.
One perceives that all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are unarisen, because they are ultimately pure;
one perceives that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and the dharmas of ordinary beings are unarisen, because they are ultimately pure;
one perceives that stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) and the dharmas of stream-enterers are unarisen, because they are ultimately pure.
He sees the once-returner and the dharmas of the once-returner as non-arising, because they are ultimately pure;
he sees the non-returner and the dharmas of the non-returner as non-arising, because they are ultimately pure;
he sees the arhat and the dharmas of the arhat as non-arising, because they are ultimately pure.
He sees that the Pratyekabuddhas and the dharmas of the Pratyekabuddhas are non-arising, because they are ultimately pure;
he sees that the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas and the dharmas of the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are non-arising, because they are ultimately pure;
he sees that the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas and the dharmas of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas are non-arising, because they are ultimately pure.
At that time, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:

"As I understand the meaning of what you have said, the self and sentient beings are ultimately unarisen; form through consciousness are ultimately unarisen; and even the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, as well as the dharmas of a Tathāgata, are ultimately unarisen."

If this were so, there would be no distinction among ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) in their rebirth within the six destinies; a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) should not attain the fruit of stream-entry, a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) should not attain the fruit of once-returning, a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) should not attain the fruit of non-returning, an arhat should not attain the fruit of arhatship, a pratyekabuddha should not attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas should not, for the sake of attaining all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), diligently train and gradually realize the five kinds of enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If all phenomena are ultimately unarisen, how could a stream-enterer diligently cultivate the true path for the perpetual abandonment of the three fetters in order to attain the fruit of stream-entry?"
How does a once-returner, for the sake of the fruit of once-returning, diligently cultivate the path that eternally abandons greed, hatred, and delusion?

How does a non-returner, for the sake of the fruit of non-returning, diligently cultivate the path that eternally abandons the fetters conducive to the lower realms, thereby establishing five distinct stages of differentiation?
How does an arhat, for the sake of the fruit of arhatship, diligently cultivate the path that leads to the permanent abandonment of the higher fetters?
How does a pratyekabuddha, for the sake of pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, diligently cultivate the path of independently awakening to the principle of dependent origination?

How is it that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, for the sake of delivering immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings, cultivate hundreds of thousands of difficult and painful practices, and undergo immeasurable great sufferings that are hard to endure?
"How does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, having realized unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, turn the sublime wheel of Dharma to deliver sentient beings?
Subhūti replied: "Śāriputra!..."
It is not that I, within that state of non-arising, allow for the distinctions of ordinary beings who, driven by afflictions and karma, travel through the six realms of existence and undergo rebirth;
nor is it that I, within that state of non-arising, allow for those capable of entering the clear realization of the truths;
nor is it that I, within that state of non-arising, allow for stream-enterers who have attained the fruit of stream-entry.
Up to the point where even Pratyekabuddhas attain Pratyekabuddha-enlightenment— within those phenomena of non-arising,
I do not allow for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to diligently train for the sake of attaining all-aspect omniscience and gradually realize the five kinds of enlightenment;
nor, within those phenomena of non-arising, do I allow for [the existence of] Stream-enterers...
The stream-enterer diligently cultivates the true path for the permanent abandonment of the three fetters;
up to the solitary realizer who, for the sake of solitary enlightenment, diligently cultivates the path of realizing dependent origination through personal awakening.

It is not that I do not permit within those dharmas of non-arising the existence of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, for the sake of liberating immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings, [diligently cultivate the path].
They have cultivated hundreds of thousands of difficult practices and ascetic austerities, fully experiencing immeasurable and unbearable great sufferings.

"Nevertheless, although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas perform immeasurable kinds of difficult practices and ascetic austerities for the sake of sentient beings, they harbor no notion of 'ascetic practice' therein."

Why is this? If one dwells upon ascetic practices with the perception of them as mere asceticism, one will ultimately be unable to bring great benefit to immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings.

All the assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, employing the skillful means of non-apprehension, regard all sentient beings as their own parents, brothers, wives, children, and even themselves; for the sake of delivering them, they give rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, thereby able to bring great benefit to those immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings.
“Śāriputra! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should form this thought:

‘Just as my own self-nature cannot be found when sought through all modes, in all places, and at all times among all phenomena, so too it is with internal and external phenomena; they are entirely non-existent and cannot be apprehended.’”

If one abides in this perception, one will not perceive any difficulty in performing arduous and ascetic practices; by means of this, one is able to perform hundreds of thousands of difficult and ascetic practices for the sake of immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings, thereby bringing them great benefit.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas seek all phenomena and all sentient beings in every way, in all places, and at all times, and find them to be unobtainable; therefore, they have no attachment toward them.

“Śāriputra! It is not that within those dharmas of non-arising I permit a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, to turn the wondrous wheel of Dharma, and to deliver sentient beings.”
Why is this? Śāriputra,
because all phenomena and all sentient beings are entirely non-existent and unattainable, there is no realization and no deliverance, nor is there one who realizes or delivers.
At that time, Śāriputra asked the venerable Subhūti: "What do you think?

Do you maintain that one who possesses the nature of arising realizes a dharma that has the nature of arising, or do you maintain that one who possesses the nature of non-arising realizes a dharma that has the nature of non-arising?"
Subhūti replied, "I do not maintain that a produced phenomenon realizes a produced phenomenon, nor do I maintain that an unproduced phenomenon realizes an unproduced phenomenon.
Then, Śāriputra again asked the venerable Subhūti:
"What do you think?

Do you maintain that one who has realized the dharma of non-arising realizes the dharma of arising, or do you maintain that one who has realized the dharma of non-arising realizes the dharma of non-arising? Subhūti replied:
“I do not permit the realization of the unarisen dharma by means of an arisen dharma, nor do I permit the realization of an arisen dharma by means of the unarisen dharma.
Śāriputra said: “If this is so, is there then absolutely no attainment and no clear observation?”
Subhūti replied: "Although there is attainment and there is clear realization, one does not realize by means of these two dharmas.
Rather, attainment and clear realization are merely provisionally established according to worldly convention; they do not exist in the ultimate sense."

It is merely in accordance with worldly convention that one designates the existence of stream-enterers and the fruit of stream-entry, and so on, up to the existence of Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment of a Buddha; these things do not exist in the ultimate sense.

Śāriputra said: "If it is the case that 'attainment,' 'clear realization,' and 'stream-entry' are merely designated according to worldly convention and do not exist in the ultimate sense, then are the distinctions among the six destinies also merely designated according to worldly convention and not existent in the ultimate sense?"
Subhūti replied, “So it is! So it is!”

"Why is that? Because within the ultimate truth (paramārtha), there are no afflictions, karma, or the maturation of its results (vipāka)—neither arising nor ceasing—nor any phenomena of defilement or purification.
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:
"What do you think? Do you assert that an unarisen phenomenon arises, or do you assert that an already arisen phenomenon arises? Subhūti replied:
“I do not allow the arising of unarisen phenomena, nor do I allow the arising of already arisen phenomena.
Śāriputra asked, “What are these unarisen phenomena that you do not allow to arise?”
Subhūti replied: "Form up to consciousness are unborn phenomena; I do not admit that they arise. Why is that? Because..."
Because they are empty of intrinsic nature.
In this way, up to and including the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas, which is an unarisen dharma, I do not allow for its arising. Why is that?
"Because their intrinsic nature is empty. Śāriputra said:
"What kind of already-arisen phenomena do you not allow to arise?"
Subhūti replied: "From form up to consciousness, these are dharmas already arisen; I do not admit that they arise. Why is that? Because..."
Because its intrinsic nature is empty.
In this way, up to and including the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas, which is a dharma already arisen—I do not allow for its arising. Why is that?
"Because its intrinsic nature is empty.
At that time, Śāriputra again asked the venerable Subhūti: "What do you think?"
"Do you assert that arising arises, or do you assert that non-arising arises? Subhūti replied,
"I do not assert that arising arises, nor do I assert that non-arising arises."

Why is this so? Birth and non-birth—these two dharmas are neither joined nor dispersed; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness.
"By this principle, I do not admit that what has already arisen arises, nor do I admit that what has not yet arisen arises.
At that time, Śāriputra asked the venerable Subhūti:
"Venerable sir!"
"Do you take pleasure in discoursing upon the characteristics of non-arising regarding the dharma of non-arising that has been taught? Subhūti replied,
"I do not take pleasure in discoursing upon the characteristics of non-arising regarding the dharma of non-arising that has been taught."

Why is this so? Whether it be non-arising dharmas, the characteristic of non-arising, delight, or discursive explanation—all such things are neither joined nor dispersed; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and of a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (animitta), which cannot be discursively explained.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"When one gives rise to the expression 'non-arising' with respect to non-arisen phenomena, is this expression of 'non-arising' itself also non-arisen?"
Subhūti replied, “So it is! So it is!”
Regarding the dharma of non-arising, one utters the words "non-arising"; both this dharma and these words share the meaning of non-arising.
Why is this so? Because from form (*rūpa*) up to consciousness (*vijñāna*), all are non-arising.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is empty.
From the sense-base of the eye up to the sense-base of the mind, all are without arising.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is empty.
From the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) up to the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), all are without arising.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is empty.
From the eye-element up to the mind-element, all are non-arising.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is empty.
From the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) up to the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), all are non-arising.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is empty.
From the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element, all are without arising.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is empty.
From eye-contact through to mind-contact, all are without arising.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is empty.
All feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including all feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, are entirely non-arising.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is empty.
From the earth element up to the consciousness element, all are without arising.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is empty;
from the causal condition up to the dominant condition, all are non-arising.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is empty.
From ignorance up to old age and death, all are without arising.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is empty;
thus, all activities of body, speech, and mind are unarisen.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is empty.
From the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, all are non-arising.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is empty.
In this way, up to and including all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), all are non-arising.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is empty. "Śāriputra!..."
By this principle, regarding dharmas that are unarisen, one utters the words "unarisen"; both these dharmas and these words share the meaning of being unarisen.
"Śāriputra, whether it be the dharma spoken, the words by which it is spoken, the speaker, or the listener—all have the meaning of being unarisen."
"Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, and within emptiness there is no sense of that which produces or that which is produced.
At that time, Śāriputra praised Subhūti, saying:
"Among those who preach the Dharma, you, O Benevolent One, are foremost; none can equal you except for the World-Honored Buddha. Why is this?
Because regarding whatever various Dharma gates you are questioned or interrogated upon, you are able to provide answers without any obstruction."

Subhūti replied: "Those disciples of the Buddhas who are without dependence or attachment toward any phenomena are, by the very nature of things, able to answer each and every question they are interrogated with, freely and fearlessly."
Why is this? It is because all phenomena have nothing upon which they rely.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
“How is it that all phenomena have no basis whatsoever?

Subhūti replied, “Because the intrinsic nature of form through to consciousness is empty, they do not rely on the internal, they do not rely on the external, and they do not rely on what is between the two. In this way, up to and including the knowledge of all aspects, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all characteristics, because their intrinsic nature is empty, they do not rely on the internal, they do not rely on the external, and they do not rely on what is between the two.”
Śāriputra! For this reason, I say that all phenomena are entirely without dependence. Thus it is, Śāriputra!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the six perfections, they should purify form; they should purify feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; and in this manner, up to and including, they should purify all-knowledge, purify the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and purify the knowledge of all aspects, as well as purify the path to enlightenment.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva purify the path to enlightenment while practicing the six perfections?"
Subhūti replied, “Śāriputra,
each of the perfections— generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom— is of two kinds: namely, mundane and supramundane.”
Śāriputra asked: "What is the mundane perfection of generosity?
What is the supramundane perfection of generosity?"
Subhūti replied, “Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva acts as a great donor, he is able to give clothing, food and drink, and other requisites to all śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the poor, the sick, the destitute, travelers on the road, and beggars.”

Furthermore, if there should come those who beg for a son, he gives a son; those who beg for a daughter, he gives a daughter; those who beg for a wife or concubine, he gives a wife or concubine; those who beg for official rank, he gives official rank; those who beg for a kingdom, he gives a kingdom; those who beg for the throne, he gives the throne; those who beg for his head, he gives his head; those who beg for his eyes, he gives his eyes; those who beg for his hands or feet, he gives his hands or feet; those who beg for his limbs and joints, he gives his limbs and joints; those who beg for his flesh and blood, he gives his flesh and blood; those who beg for his skin and bones, he gives his skin and bones; those who beg for servants, he gives servants; and those who beg for living beings, he gives living beings. In all such cases, according to their requests, he bestows everything, both internal and external.
Although one performs such giving, there is still a basis upon which it rests; that is to say, one forms this thought: "I am the giver and he is the recipient;
I am the donor; I am not stingy or greedy; I am able to relinquish everything in accordance with the Buddha's teaching; I am practicing the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā)."

When he practices giving, he employs the skillful means of perceiving an object of attainment, sharing it equally with all sentient beings, and dedicating it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Again, he forms this thought:
"I dedicate this merit to all sentient beings, so that they may attain peace and happiness in this life and future lives, even unto the realization of nirvana without remainder."
He practices giving while attached to the three spheres:
first, the conception of a self;
second, the conception of another.
Third is the perception of the gift.
Because one practices giving while being attached to these three wheels, it is called the mundane perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).
Why is this generosity termed mundane?
Because it is practiced in common with the world and cannot move beyond worldly phenomena, this is called the mundane perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving, the three spheres are pure:
first, they do not grasp at themselves as the giver.
Second, not grasping at that [recipient] as a recipient;
third, not grasping at the gift or the fruit of giving.
These are the three purities of the wheel when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices generosity.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva takes great compassion as the foremost guide, dedicates the merit of the practice of giving universally to all sentient beings, and perceives no sentient being whatsoever in those beings; although they equally share this with sentient beings and dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they do not perceive even the slightest mark therein."
Because one practices giving without any attachment whatsoever, it is called the supramundane perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).
Why is this generosity termed "supramundane"?
Because one practices not in common with the world and is able to forever transcend worldly dharmas, this is called the supramundane perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
Śāriputra asked: "What is the mundane perfection of ethical discipline up to the mundane perfection of wisdom?
What is the supramundane perfection of ethical discipline up to the supramundane perfection of wisdom?"
Subhūti replied, “Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices from pure ethical discipline up to wisdom, if there is anything upon which they rely, they are attached to the three spheres; therefore, it is called a mundane pāramitā, because it is practiced in common with the world and cannot move beyond worldly phenomena.”

When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice from pure ethical discipline up to wisdom, because they lack any basis due to the purity of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍalapariśuddhi*), it is called a supramundane *pāramitā*; for they do not practice in common with the world and are able to forever transcend mundane phenomena.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, the prajñāpāramitā cultivated by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is both mundane and supramundane. What is called mundane prajñāpāramitā?
What is called the supramundane perfection of wisdom?
"Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices generosity, they practice it by relying on the apprehension of something to be attained, thinking as follows:"
"I am able to subdue the mind of stinginess and practice giving.
Because this bodhisattva-mahāsattva relies on the notions of a self, sentient beings, and giving, although they relinquish all internal and external possessions, it is not called supramundane prajñā.
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing pure ethical discipline, practices it based on the apprehension of something to be attained—meaning they think:
'I am able to abide in the qualities of the dhūtas; I am able to subdue body, speech, and mind; I am able to practice the ten paths of wholesome action. "

If this bodhisattva mahāsattva relies upon the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, and the view of various wholesome dharmas, and although they are able to practice various pure precepts and maintain them by sharing them equally with all sentient beings and dedicating them toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, yet they regard that enlightenment as truly existent, and based on those merits praise themselves and disparage others, this is not called supramundane prajñā.
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing patience, practices it by relying on the apprehension of something real, thinking:
'I am able to endure all the various evil deeds that sentient beings may do toward me.'"

Because this bodhisattva-mahāsattva relies on the view of a self and sentient beings regarding patience, although they are able to endure the evils committed by others and can take these roots of goodness of patience and share them equally with all sentient beings, dedicating them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, because they employ the method of "having something to be attained," it is also not called supramundane prajñā.
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing diligence, practices it based on apprehension, thinking:
'I am able to initiate physical and mental diligence, and diligently cultivate the two kinds of provisions: merit and wisdom.'"

Although this bodhisattva-mahāsattva constantly arouses physical and mental diligence and assiduously cultivates the two kinds of provisions—merit and wisdom—he nevertheless perceives the characteristics of physical and mental merit and wisdom, as well as the characteristic of a self and the characteristics of all sentient beings, and he also perceives the characteristic of the sought-after bodhi. Because he employs "having something to be attained" as his means, he cannot yet be said to possess supramundane prajñā.
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing dhyāna, practices it by relying on apprehension, thinking:

'I am able to practice loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, equanimity, meditative concentration (*samādhi*), meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), dhyāna, and the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), entering and emerging from them with mastery.'"

This bodhisattva mahāsattva develops a deep attachment to the various dhyānas; although they take the roots of goodness obtained from these dhyānas and, together with all sentient beings, dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, because they employ the method of "having something to be attained," this is not yet called supramundane prajñā.
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing *prajñā*, practices it based on apprehension, thinking:

'I am able to observe that all phenomena are empty—namely, that form is empty up to consciousness being empty—and likewise, even the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is entirely empty.'"

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva, employing the method of apprehending something as real, although he contemplates that all things are ultimately empty, still takes these roots of goodness and bestows them upon sentient beings, dedicating them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. He likewise gives rise to a mind of equal rejoicing toward the wholesome dharmas practiced by both himself and others; he is able to repent and eliminate his own misdeeds; he is able to exhort the immeasurable Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the ten directions to turn the wondrous wheel of Dharma to deliver the multitudes of sentient beings; and he is able to make vows and give rise to supreme supernormal powers to bring great benefit to all sentient beings. However, because he employs the method of apprehending something as real, this is not yet called supramundane prajñā.
This is called mundane *prajñāpāramitā*.

"Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing generosity, employs subtle wisdom and takes non-apprehension as the means, such that they apprehend neither self, sentient beings, nor the act of giving itself; and if, for the sake of attaining unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, they practice the perfection of generosity with the three spheres purified to cleanse the path to awakening—this is called supramundane *prajñā*."

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, employing subtle wisdom and taking non-apprehension as the skillful means, finds no apprehension of a self, sentient beings, or pure ethical discipline, and cultivates the perfection of ethical discipline and the path of pure awakening for the sake of the threefold purity in order to proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—this is called supramundane prajñā."

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, employing subtle wisdom and taking non-apprehension as the skillful means, finds no apprehension of a self, sentient beings, or patience itself, and cultivates the perfection of patience as the path to purifying the bodhi-path for the sake of attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through the purity of the three wheels—this is called supramundane prajñā."

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, employing subtle wisdom and taking non-apprehension as the means, finds no attainment whatsoever regarding the physical and mental diligence of self and sentient beings, nor regarding the accumulations of merit and wisdom; and for the sake of proceeding toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment with the three spheres purified, cultivates the perfection of diligence as the path to purifying bodhi—this is called supramundane prajñā."

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, employing subtle wisdom and taking non-apprehension as the means, finds no apprehension of a self, sentient beings, or any dhyānas, samādhis, or samāpattis, and cultivates the perfection of dhyāna as the path to purifying the awakening for the sake of attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through the purity of the three spheres—this is called supramundane prajñā."

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, employing subtle wisdom and taking non-apprehension as the skillful means, finds nothing to be apprehended among all phenomena and all sentient beings, and cultivates the perfection of wisdom—the path to purifying enlightenment—in order to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening through the purity of the three spheres, this is called supramundane prajñā."
