"This bodhisattva mahāsattva takes all such roots of goodness and, sharing them equally with all sentient beings, dedicates them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

One should know that such dedication is the unsurpassed dedication, the non-differentiated dedication, the dedication equal to the unequaled, the inconceivable dedication, the peerless dedication, the immeasurable dedication, and the sublime dedication.
This is called the supramundane *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Śāriputra, for what reason are these six *pāramitās* called mundane?"
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions is it called "transcending the world"? "Śāriputra!
As for 'the world,' it refers to those six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā); because they are worldly, they are called 'the world. "
It is called "the world" because it creates the world;
it is called "the world" because it arises from the world;
it is called "the world" because it acts for the sake of the world.
Because it arises from the world, it is called "the world";
because it belongs to the world, it is called "the world";
because it relies upon the world, it is called "the world."
“Śāriputra! That which transcends the world refers to these six perfections (pāramitās). Because they transcend the world, they are called ‘transcendent’;
because they uproot the world, they are called ‘transcendent.’”
It is called "transcending the world" because it emerges from the world;
it is called "transcending the world" because it causes the world to emerge [from suffering];
it is called "transcending the world" because it departs from the world.
Because it emerges from the world, it is called "supramundane";
because it emerges by relying upon the world, it is called "supramundane. "Śāriputra!
"In this way, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six perfections, they purify the path to enlightenment.
At that time, Śāriputra asked the venerable Subhūti,
"What is called the path to enlightenment for bodhisattva mahāsattvas?"
Subhūti replied, “Śāriputra,
the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom are the bodhisattva mahāsattvas.”
The path to enlightenment: from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to enlightenment;
from suchness up to the inconceivable realm is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to enlightenment;
the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to enlightenment.
The four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path are the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to awakening;
the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments are the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to awakening;
the eight liberations and the nine successive attainments are the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to awakening; emptiness...
The gates of liberation—signlessness, wishlessness, and emptiness—are the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to enlightenment;
the stages from the Ground of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma are the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to enlightenment;
all the doors of dhāraṇī and the doors of samādhi are the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to enlightenment; and the five eyes [are likewise].

The six supernormal powers are the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to enlightenment; the ten powers of a Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to enlightenment;

the quality of non-forgetfulness and the constant abiding in equanimity are the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to enlightenment; and all-knowledge and the knowledge of the paths [are the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to enlightenment].
The knowledge of marks and the knowledge of all marks are the path to enlightenment for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Śāriputra,
all such immeasurable and boundless aggregates of great merit are entirely the path to enlightenment for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
At that time, Śāriputra asked the venerable Subhūti:
"By the power of which perfection (pāramitā) is this aforementioned mass of great merit accomplished?"
Subhūti replied: “This great mass of merit thus described is all accomplished through the power of the perfection of wisdom. Why is this? ”
Śāriputra! Thus, this perfection of wisdom is the mother of all wholesome dharmas, for all the wholesome dharmas of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas arise from it.
In this way, the perfection of wisdom universally encompasses all wholesome dharmas, for all the wholesome dharmas of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas abide by means of it.

Śāriputra! Because the assemblies of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in the past fully perfected their cultivation and study of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they have already attained unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
because the assemblies of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in the future will fully perfect their cultivation and study of the perfection of wisdom, they shall attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

Now, in the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, immeasurable assemblies of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having brought the cultivation and study of the *prajñāpāramitā* to ultimate perfection, have now attained unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā*, has no doubt or confusion in mind and does not become bewildered, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in such a dwelling as never to abandon it; that is to say, taking non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) as the means, they constantly and diligently strive to rescue and deliver all sentient beings."
"You should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has accomplished such a supreme mental engagement (*manasikāra*), namely, the mental engagement associated with great compassion.
At that time, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in such a dwelling and never abandons it, accomplishing the mental engagement associated with great compassion, then all sentient beings should also accomplish the state of a bodhisattva mahāsattva."

Why is this? Because if all sentient beings were likewise never to abandon this dwelling and this mental attention, then there would be no distinction between bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and all sentient beings.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti replied to Śāriputra:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
It is exactly as you have said; you have understood the intent of what I have taught according to reality, and though it appears as if you are challenging me, you have in fact established my meaning.
Why is this? Śāriputra!
Because sentient beings up to the seer do not exist, one should know that such dwelling and mental attention also do not exist;
because sentient beings up to the seer lack reality, one should know that such dwelling and mental attention also lack reality;
because sentient beings up to the seer lack intrinsic nature, one should know that such dwelling and mental attention also lack intrinsic nature.
Because sentient beings, up to and including the seer, are empty, one should know that such dwelling and mental attention are also empty;
because sentient beings, up to and including the seer, are detached, one should know that such dwelling and mental attention are also detached;
because sentient beings, up to and including the seer, are quiescent, one should know that such dwelling and mental attention are also quiescent.
Because sentient beings, up to and including the seer, lack awareness, you should know that this dwelling and mental attention likewise lack awareness.

Śāriputra, because form, up to and including consciousness, does not exist, is unreal, lacks intrinsic nature, is empty, is detached, is quiescent, and lacks awareness, you should know that this dwelling and mental attention likewise do not exist, are unreal, lack intrinsic nature, are empty, are detached, are quiescent, and lack awareness.

In this way, up to and including the fact that śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and unsurpassed enlightenment are non-existent, unreal, without intrinsic nature, empty, detached, quiescent, and devoid of cognition, one should know that such dwelling and mental attention are likewise non-existent, unreal, without intrinsic nature, empty, detached, quiescent, and devoid of cognition.

Śāriputra! By virtue of these causes and conditions, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are never separated from such dwelling and this mental attention, nor do they differ from all sentient beings; for all phenomena and all sentient beings are ultimately empty and without distinction.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Subhūti, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
You are well able to proclaim the *prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; all of this is through the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata.
Should anyone wish to proclaim the *prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, they should do so exactly as you have proclaimed it.
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to study the perfection of wisdom, they should all study it according to what you have said.

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas study the perfection of wisdom according to what you have said, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas will swiftly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings until the end of the future.
When the Venerable Subhūti was proclaiming the profound Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of the assembly, this trichiliocosm shook in six ways:

it rose in the east and sank in the west; it rose in the west and sank in the east; it rose in the south and sank in the north; it rose in the north and sank in the south; it rose in the center and sank at the edges; and it rose at the edges and sank in the center.
At that time, the World-Honored One smiled. The Venerable Subhūti addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One, for what cause and for what reason do you manifest this smile?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Just as I am now, in this trichiliocosm, proclaiming the *prajñāpāramitā* for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, so too, in each of the immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless worlds throughout the ten directions, there are Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas who likewise proclaim the *prajñāpāramitā* for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."

Just as I now, within this trichiliocosm, proclaim the *prajñāpāramitā*, and twelve *koṭis* of devas and other assemblies have attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of all phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);

so too, in each of the immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless worlds throughout the ten directions, there are immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless classes of sentient beings who, hearing those Buddhas proclaim the *prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, develop deep faith and understanding in the dharma of emptiness, and all resolve to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, diligently practicing the conduct of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

Chapter 4: The Chapter on the Lord of Devas (Śakradevendra), Part 3, Section 4-1. At that time, in this trichiliocosm Buddha-world, all the Four Great Kings and the various lords of devas, extending even up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, each arrived at the assembly together with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of followers.

Although the light from the bodies of these devas, produced as the maturation (*vipāka*) of their pure karma, is capable of illuminating, it does not equal even one hundredth part, nor one thousandth part, nor even one *upaniṣad* (infinitesimal) part of the constant light manifested by the Tathāgata.

Why is this so? Because the Buddha’s body possesses a constant radiance of majestic virtue that is most honored and supreme among all lights, most excellent and wondrous, peerless and unequaled, the unsurpassed first; it eclipses the lights of all devas so that they do not appear, just as the full moon in autumn outshines the multitude of stars.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed Subhūti, saying:

"Now all the Four Great Kings and the various lords of the devas throughout this trichiliocosm, extending even up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, have each come together with their retinues, desiring to hear the Venerable One proclaim the Prajñāpāramitā. We pray that the Venerable One will compassionately speak for us."
"Venerable Sir!
What is the profound *prajñāpāramitā* of the bodhisattva mahāsattva?
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva abide in the *prajñāpāramitā*?"
"How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva train in the perfection of wisdom?
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed Śakra, the Lord of Devas, saying: "Kauśika!..."
"All you hosts of devas, listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well!

I shall, by the power of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority and in accordance with the Tathāgata’s intention, proclaim the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, so that Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may abide therein in such a manner and train therein in such a manner."
“Kauśika! You gods who have not yet resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta should all now resolve upon it. Kauśika!”
Those who have already entered the fixed course of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas can no longer give rise to the mind of great enlightenment.
Why is this, Kauśika?
Since they have already established a boundary across the stream of birth and death,
if there are any among them who can give rise to the unsurpassed bodhicitta,
I likewise rejoice in it. Why is this?
All superior persons should seek the supreme Dharma; I shall never obstruct another’s pursuit of superior wholesome qualities. "Kauśika!
You asked, 'What is the profound Prajñāpāramitā of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva?'"
"Listen attentively! Listen attentively!
I shall explain it for you."
“Kauśika! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to the mind directed toward the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), employing the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*),
and contemplates the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) up to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) as either impermanent, or suffering, or [selfless]...”
Whether it be that the self is impure, or empty, or signless, or wishless; or that it is tranquil, or secluded;
or that it is like a disease, or like an abscess, or like an arrow, or like a wound;
or that it is feverish affliction, or oppressive, or disintegrating, or decayed, or subject to change.
Whether it be swiftly extinguished, or fearsome, or loathsome; whether there be calamities, or untimely misfortunes, or epidemics, or pestilences;
whether it be insecure, unreliable, unarisen, unextinguished, unstained, unpurified, unconditioned, and uncreated; [in all these cases, one should remain equanimous].

Contemplating the sense-base of the eye up to the sense-base of the mind; contemplating the sense-base of forms up to the sense-base of phenomena; contemplating the eye-element up to the mind-element; contemplating the form-element up to the phenomenon-element; contemplating the eye-consciousness-element up to the mind-consciousness-element; contemplating eye-contact up to mind-contact; contemplating all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition up to all feelings produced with mind-contact as condition; contemplating the earth-element up to the consciousness-element; and contemplating ignorance up to old age and death—likewise, it is the same for each.
Kauśika! This is called the profound *prajñāpāramitā* of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to the mind directed toward the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), employing the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), they contemplate that ignorance conditions volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); volitional formations condition consciousness (*vijñāna*); consciousness conditions name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); name-and-form conditions the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); the six sense bases condition contact (*sparśa*); contact conditions feeling (*vedanā*); feeling conditions craving (*tṛṣṇā*); craving conditions grasping (*upādāna*); grasping conditions becoming (*bhava*); becoming conditions birth (*jāti*); and birth conditions old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), up until the entire great mass of suffering arises.

Furthermore, by means of non-apprehension as a skillful method, one contemplates that because ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease; because volitional formations cease, consciousness ceases; because consciousness ceases, name-and-form ceases; because name-and-form ceases, the six sense bases cease; because the six sense bases cease, contact ceases; because contact ceases, feeling ceases; because feeling ceases, craving ceases; because craving ceases, clinging ceases; because clinging ceases, existence ceases; because existence ceases, birth ceases; and because birth ceases, old age and death, up to the entire mass of suffering, cease. Thus, these cessations are without self, empty, signless, wishless, tranquil, detached, unarisen, unceasing, unstained, unpurified, unconditioned, and uncreated.
Kauśika! This is called the profound *prajñāpāramitā* of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to the mind that corresponds to the knowledge of all modes, employing the method of non-apprehension, they contemplate inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence as being without self or what belongs to a self, signless, wishless, quiescent, detached, unarisen, unceasing, unstained, unpurified, unconditioned, and uncreated.
Kauśika! This is called the profound perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to the mind directed toward the knowledge of all modes, employing the method of non-apprehension, they contemplate that from suchness up to the inconceivable realm there is no self and nothing belonging to a self; it is signless, wishless, quiescent, secluded, unarisen, unceasing, unstained, unpurified, uncreated, and unconditioned.
Kauśika! This is called the profound *prajñāpāramitā* of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to the mind directed toward the knowledge of all modes, employing the method of non-apprehension, they contemplate the realm of cessation up to the unconditioned realm as being without self or what belongs to a self, signless, wishless, tranquil, secluded, unborn, unceasing, unstained, unpurified, uncreated, and unconditioned.
Kauśika! This is called the profound Prajñāpāramitā of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to the mind directed toward the knowledge of all modes, employing the method of non-apprehension, they contemplate the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
they contemplate the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; and they contemplate the four dhyānas and the four immeasurables.
the four formless absorptions; contemplating the eight liberations and the nine successive attainments;
contemplating the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; contemplating the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata;
contemplating the stages from the Ground of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma; and contemplating the five eyes and the six supernormal powers.
One contemplates the ten powers of the Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
one contemplates the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity; one contemplates all doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of samādhi;
and one contemplates all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects—all of which are non-existent.
It is permanent, selfless, empty, signless, wishless, tranquil, secluded, subject to change,
swiftly perishing, unreliable, unarisen, unceasing, unstained, unpurified,
unconditioned, and uncreated.
Kauśika! This is called the profound *prajñāpāramitā* of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. "Furthermore, Kauśika!"

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to the mind directed toward the knowledge of all modes, employing the method of non-apprehension, they abide in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence; they abide in suchness up to the inconceivable realm; they abide in the realm of cessation up to the unconditioned realm; and they abide in the noble truth of suffering up to the noble truth of the path.
Kauśika! This is called the profound perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to the mind directed toward all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna), employing the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), they practice the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
they practice the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; and they practice the four dhyānas and the four immeasurables.
...the four formless absorptions; practicing the eight liberations and the nine successive attainments;
practicing the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; practicing from the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Stage of Dharma-Cloud;
practicing the five eyes and the six supernormal powers; and practicing the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen [unique qualities].
The unique qualities of a Buddha: practicing the quality of non-forgetfulness, practicing the constant abiding in equanimity,
practicing all doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of samādhi, practicing all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths,
and the knowledge of all aspects, practicing all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and practicing all...
The unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddha. Kausika!
This is called the profound perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 498. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Three, Chapter Four: The Devendra Section, Part Two. "Furthermore, Kauśika!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they contemplate in this way:

"There are only phenomena that mutually condition and assist one another, moistening, increasing, and pervading one another; within them, there is absolutely no self or what belongs to a self, for such things cannot be found when observed according to reality."
Again, they form this contemplation:

"The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas take the sublime roots of goodness they have cultivated and accumulated and, sharing them equally with all sentient beings, dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
The mind that accumulates roots of goodness does not unite with the mind of dedication, nor does the mind of dedication unite with the mind that accumulates roots of goodness;
the mind of dedication does not unite with the bodhicitta, nor does the bodhicitta unite with the mind of dedication.

The mind that accumulates roots of goodness is non-existent and unobtainable within the mind of dedication, and the mind of dedication is likewise non-existent and unobtainable within the mind that accumulates roots of goodness.

The mind of dedication does not exist and cannot be apprehended within the mind of enlightenment; likewise, the mind of enlightenment does not exist and cannot be apprehended within the mind of dedication.
"Although the bodhisattva mahāsattvas contemplate all phenomena as they truly are, they do not perceive anything at all within those phenomena. Kausika!
This is called the profound prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked Subhūti:
"Venerable One,

how is it that the bodhisattva mahāsattvas' mind that accumulates roots of goodness does not unite with the mind of dedication, and the mind of dedication likewise does not unite with the mind that accumulates roots of goodness?"
The mind of dedication does not unite with the mind of bodhicitta, nor does the mind of bodhicitta unite with the mind of dedication;

the mind that accumulates roots of goodness is non-existent and unobtainable within the mind of dedication, and the mind of dedication is likewise non-existent and unobtainable within the mind that accumulates roots of goodness;
the mind of dedication is non-existent and unobtainable within the mind of bodhicitta, and the mind of bodhicitta is likewise non-existent and unobtainable within the mind of dedication.
Subhūti replied, "Kauśika!

The mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva that gathers roots of goodness is not a mind; the mind of dedication and the mind of awakening are also not minds. That which is not a mind cannot gather anything—neither that which dedicates nor that to which it is dedicated."
One should not dedicate a non-mind to a non-mind, nor should a mind dedicate itself to a non-mind;
one should not dedicate a non-mind to a mind, nor should a mind dedicate itself to a mind.
Why is this? Kausika!

That which is non-mind is itself the inconceivable, and that which is the inconceivable is itself non-mind. These two kinds are both non-existent; within that which is non-existent, there is no meaning of dedication.
Kauśika! The mind has no intrinsic nature, and mental factors are likewise;
since both the mind and mental factors lack intrinsic nature, the mind also lacks the sense of "dedicating" the mind.
Kauśika! If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas engage in such contemplation, this is called the profound prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Subhūti, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!”

You are now well able to proclaim the Perfection of Wisdom for the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and you are also able to exhort and encourage the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, causing them to feel deep joy and diligently cultivate the Perfection of Wisdom.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Since I recognize your kindness, how could I fail to repay it?
For what reason?"

The Buddhas of the past and their disciples have, for the sake of the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, proclaimed the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), demonstrating, instructing, exhorting, gladdening, comforting, and establishing them so that they may attain the ultimate goal.

“World-Honored One, at that time you were also training therein; now you have realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and turned the sublime wheel of Dharma to benefit us. Therefore, I should now follow the Buddha’s teaching and proclaim the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) for the assembly of Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas, demonstrating, instructing, exhorting, gladdening, comforting, and establishing them so that they may attain the ultimate, quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, and bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings until the end of the future. This is what is called repaying his debt of gratitude.”
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, saying:
"Kauśika, you asked: 'How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwell in the perfection of wisdom?'"
"Listen attentively! Listen attentively!
I shall explain to you the characteristics of how bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should and should not abide in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*."

“Kauśika! The aggregate of form up to the aggregate of consciousness are empty of the nature of the aggregate of form up to the aggregate of consciousness; the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are empty of the nature of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.”
If the nature of the aggregate of form up to the aggregate of consciousness is empty, and if the nature of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas is empty, then all such things are non-dual and indivisible.
Kauśika! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should abide in the profound perfection of wisdom in this manner. "Kauśika!"
The sense base of the eye up to the sense base of the mind are empty of the nature of the sense base of the eye up to the sense base of the mind;

the sense base of form up to the sense base of phenomena are empty of the nature of the sense base of form up to the sense base of phenomena; the eye element up to the mind element are empty of the nature of the eye element up to the mind element;
the form element up to the phenomena element are empty of the nature of the form element up to the phenomena element.
The visual consciousness element up to the mental consciousness element are empty of the nature of the visual consciousness element up to the mental consciousness element;
eye-contact up to mind-contact are empty of the nature of eye-contact up to mind-contact;

and the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition are [empty of] the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition.
Even the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition are empty of intrinsic nature;
the earth element up to the consciousness element are empty of intrinsic nature; the causal conditions up to the dominant conditions are empty of intrinsic nature;
and ignorance up to old age and death are empty of intrinsic nature.
The cessation of ignorance up to the cessation of old age and death; the emptiness of the nature of the cessation of ignorance up to the cessation of old age and death;
the emptiness of the nature of the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
and the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.
Emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence is empty of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence;
suchness up to the inconceivable realm is empty of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of suchness up to the inconceivable realm;

the realm of cessation up to the unconditioned realm is empty of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of the realm of cessation up to the unconditioned realm; and the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path [are likewise empty]. Suffering, origin...

The noble truth of cessation and the noble truth of the path are empty of intrinsic nature; the four applications of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path are empty of the intrinsic nature of the four applications of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;

the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments are empty of the intrinsic nature of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; the eight liberations...
The nine successive attainments and the eight liberations are empty of the nature of the nine successive attainments and the eight liberations;
the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are empty of the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata is empty of the nature of the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata; [and] the stage of extreme joy...
Up to and including the Dharma-cloud stage (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*) and the Joyous stage (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), their nature is empty;
the five eyes and the six supernormal powers, their nature is empty;
the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, their nature is empty; there is no forgetting.
The loss of dharmas and the nature of constant abiding in equanimity are empty of their own nature;
all doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of samādhi are empty of their own nature;
the vehicles of the śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, and the unsurpassed [yāna]—the śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, and...
The supreme vehicle is empty of its own nature; the stream-enterer up to the Tathāgata is empty of the nature of the stream-enterer up to the Tathāgata;

omniscience, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects are empty of the nature of omniscience, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects;
and the bodhisattva mahāsattvas are empty of the nature of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
Emptiness;
if the nature of the eye base up to the knowledge of all aspects is empty, and if the nature of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas is empty—all such things are non-dual and indivisible.
"Kauśika! All bodhisattva mahāsattvas should abide in the profound perfection of wisdom in this manner.
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, asked Subhūti:
“How is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, should not abide?
Subhūti replied: “Kauśika!...”

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should not dwell upon the aggregate of form, nor should they dwell upon the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Why is this? Because they take that which is attained as their means.

In this way, one should not abide in all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), nor should one abide in the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Why is this? Because they employ the attainment of something as their means. "Furthermore, Kausika!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should not dwell on the thought, "This is the aggregate of form," nor should they dwell on the thought, "These are the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."
Why is this? Because they take that which is apprehended as their means (*upāya*).

Likewise, one should not dwell on the thought that "this is omniscience" (*sarvajñatā*), nor should one dwell on the thought that "this is the knowledge of the aspects of the path" (*mārgākārajñatā*) or "the knowledge of all aspects" (*sarvākārajñatā*). Why is this?
Because they take that which is attained as their means. "Furthermore, Kauśika,

when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should not dwell upon the aggregate of form, up to the aggregate of consciousness, as either permanent or impermanent, as either pleasant or painful, as either self or non-self, as either pure or impure, as either empty or non-empty, as either with signs or signless, as either with aspiration or aspirationless, as either tranquil or non-tranquil, or as either secluded or non-secluded."
Why is this? Because they employ the method of "attainment.

In this way, one should not abide in omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)—whether as permanent or impermanent, as pleasure or suffering, as self or non-self, as pure or impure, as empty or non-empty, as with signs or signless, as with aspirations or aspirationless, as tranquil or non-tranquil, or as secluded or non-secluded.
Why is this? Because they employ the means of "attaining something. Furthermore, Kauśika!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should not dwell upon the fruit of a stream-enterer as being manifested by the unconditioned. Why is this?

Because they take "attainment" as their means, they should not dwell on the fruit of a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat; nor on the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, or the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas, as being manifested by the unconditioned.
Why is this? Because they employ the attainment of something as their means. "Furthermore, Kauśika!
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should not dwell on the notion that a stream-enterer is a field of merit who should receive offerings. Why is this?

Because they employ the means of "attaining something," one should not dwell on the idea that the Once-returner, the Non-returner, the Arhat, the Pratyekabuddha, the Bodhisattva, or the Tathāgata are fields of merit who should receive offerings. Why is this?
Because they take that which is attained as their means. "Furthermore, Kauśika,
when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should not abide in the first stage."
Why is this? Because they employ the attainment of something as a means.
One should not dwell in the second bhūmi, nor even in the tenth bhūmi; why is this?
Because they take that which is attained as their means.

"Furthermore, Kauśika, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should not, upon first generating the mind of enlightenment, dwell in the thought: [that they have already attained it]."

“I shall fulfill the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom; I shall fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path; I shall fulfill the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; I shall fulfill the eight liberations and the nine successive meditative concentrations; I shall fulfill the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Once my cultivation of these preparatory practices is complete, I shall enter the bodhisattva’s state of certainty.”
I have already entered the state of rightness and departure from birth; I shall abide on the stage of non-retrogression of a bodhisattva;
I shall fulfill the five supernormal powers of a bodhisattva;

abiding in the fulfillment of the five supernormal powers of a bodhisattva, I shall travel to immeasurable and incalculable buddha-fields to pay homage to, gaze upon, serve, and make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; in the presence of those Buddhas, I shall hear the true Dharma, contemplate it according to principle, and extensively explain it to others.

I shall purify and adorn a buddha-field like those inhabited by the Buddhas of the ten directions and establish sentient beings therein; I shall manifest transformations into buddha-fields like those inhabited by the Buddhas of the ten directions and establish sentient beings therein;
I shall bring all classes of sentient beings to maturity, causing them to realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, or to attain nirvāṇa, or to dwell in the happy realms;

I shall travel to immeasurable and incalculable buddha-fields to attend upon and serve the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and further offer boundless flowers, incense, necklaces, jeweled banners, pennants, canopies, music, lamps, robes, food, drink, and other requisites to them, honoring, revering, respecting, and praising them.
"I shall establish immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings so that they attain non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Why is this?
Because they take that which is apprehended as their means.
"Furthermore, Kausika, when bodhisattva mahasattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should not dwell upon or form this thought: [that there is anything to be attained]."
"I shall accomplish the five pure eyes, namely: the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the Dharma eye, and the Buddha eye.
One should not dwell upon such thoughts as:

"I shall accomplish the six extraordinary supernormal powers, namely: the extraordinary power of the knowledge of miraculous feats, the power of the knowledge of the divine eye, the power of the knowledge of the divine ear, the power of the knowledge of others' minds, the power of the knowledge of recollecting past lives, and the power of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows."
One should not dwell on the thought:
"I shall accomplish all the most excellent gateways of samādhi, and I shall sport with sovereign mastery within all meditative concentrations according to my will."
One should not dwell upon the thought:
"I shall accomplish all supreme dharanī-doors and attain mastery over all activities performed through these total retentions."
One should not dwell upon the thought:
"I shall accomplish the ten powers of a Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
One should not dwell upon such thoughts.

"I shall accomplish a body adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor signs, so that all sentient beings who see it will rejoice, never weary of gazing upon it, and obtain supreme benefit and happiness."
One should not dwell on the thought:
"I shall accomplish the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity.
One should not dwell on such a thought.
"I shall accomplish all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects, and penetrate all phenomena with non-attachment and non-obstruction. Why is this?
Because they take that which is apprehended as their means. "Furthermore, Kausika,
when Bodhisattvas Mahasattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should not abide in this."
This is one who follows by faith; this is one who follows by dharma; this is the eighth type of person (*pudgala*);
this is the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) who is reborn at most seven times; this is the "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*); this is the "one-interval" (*ekavicika*);
this is the "level-headed" (*samaśīrṣa*) person for whom afflictions are exhausted only at the end of their lifespan; and this is the stream-enterer.
This one is destined not to fall away; this one is of the nature to attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state;
this one is a once-returner who, having come to this world, will reach the end of suffering; this one is a non-returner candidate;
this one is a non-returner who attains parinirvāṇa upon going to that realm; this one is an arhat candidate; this one is an arhat fruit.
He will now certainly enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*; this one is a *pratyekabuddha*.

This one is a *bodhisattva*, who has transcended the stages of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas* and dwells securely in the stage of a *bodhisattva-mahāsattva*, cultivating all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Having awakened to all phenomena and all their aspects, he has forever severed the continuity of all afflictions, fetters, and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). He has realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, attained the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and possesses great majestic power. He turns the sublime wheel of Dharma, performs the deeds of a Buddha, and delivers immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings, causing them to attain the ultimate peace and bliss of *nirvāṇa*.
Why is this? Because they employ the attainment of something as their means. "Furthermore, Kausika!"
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should not dwell upon this thought:

"Having thoroughly cultivated the four bases of power, I shall abide in such a sublime samādhi; by the predominant power of this samādhi, may my lifespan endure for as many great kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges."
One should not dwell upon the thought:
"I shall attain an infinite lifespan.
One should not dwell upon such a thought.
One should not dwell on the thought: "I shall achieve the thirty-two marks, each mark adorned by a hundred merits, so that sentient beings who see them will obtain great benefit and happiness.
Nor should one dwell on the thought:
"I shall achieve the eighty secondary signs, each sign possessing immeasurable, rare, and supreme qualities, so that sentient beings who see them will obtain great benefit."
One should not dwell upon the thought:
"I shall abide in a single adorned and purified buddha-field, a land so vast that it equals the extent of worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions."
One should not dwell upon the thought:
"I shall sit peacefully upon a single vajra-throne, a throne so vast in extent that it equals the three-thousandfold world-system."
One should not dwell upon the thought:

"I shall establish myself beneath the Great Bodhi Tree, which is lofty and vast, adorned with all manner of jewels; from it issues a wondrous fragrance, dense and pervasive, which can cause those who hear it to eliminate all mental afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion, and even cure their immeasurable and boundless physical ailments."
"Any who hear the fragrance of this Bodhi tree will certainly attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, having abandoned all mental orientations of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
One should not dwell upon such thoughts as:
"May I attain a purified Buddha-field, a land that is pure and free from all defilement and evil."
Why is this? Because they employ the means of "attaining something. Furthermore, Kauśika!
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they should not dwell upon or form such thoughts as:
"May I, in my purified buddha-field, attain a state where there is no mention whatsoever of attachment to the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) up to the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha);
likewise, no mention of attachment to the sense-base of the eye (cakṣur-āyatana) up to the sense-base of the mind (manas-āyatana); and no mention of attachment..."
There is no attachment to the designations "form base" through to "phenomena base"; there is no attachment to the designations "eye element" through to "mind element";
there is no attachment to the designations "form element" through to "phenomena element";
there is no attachment to the designations "eye-consciousness element" through to "mind-consciousness element"; and there is no attachment to the designations "eye-contact" through to "mind-contact."

There is no attachment even to the designation "name and sound"; there is no attachment even to the designations for the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, up to and including those produced with mind-contact as condition;
there is no attachment even to the designations for the earth element, up to and including the consciousness element;
there is no attachment even to the designations for the causal condition, up to and including the sovereign condition; there is no attachment even to the designation "non-existence."
They have no attachment to the renown of [the links of dependent origination] from ignorance up to old age and death;
they have no attachment to the renown of the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
they have no attachment to the renown of inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature; and they have no attachment to the renown of suchness up to the inconceivable realm.
Furthermore, there is no attachment to the names or sounds of the realm of cessation up to the unconditioned realm;
there is no attachment to the names or sounds of the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;

there is no attachment to the names or sounds of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; and there is no attachment to the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four [formless attainments]...
There is no attachment to the names of the concentrations on form; there is no attachment to the names of the eight liberations or the nine successive meditative attainments;
there is no attachment to the names of the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
there is no attachment to the names of the stages from the Ground of Pure Observation up to the Ground of the Tathāgata; and there is no attachment to the names of the Ground of Utmost Joy...
At the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*), there is no attachment to the reputation of the five eyes or the six supernormal powers;
there is no attachment to the reputation of the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
there is no attachment to the reputation of the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; nor is there any attachment to the reputation of non-...

There is no attachment to the renown of the dharmas of forgetfulness or the state of constant equanimity; nor is there attachment to the renown of any of the gateways of dhāraṇī or the gateways of samādhi;
nor is there attachment to the renown of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);
nor is there attachment to the renown of the Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, or Mahāyāna vehicles.
"Nor is there attachment to the reputation of those in the stage of entering the stream, the fruit of stream-entry,
up to and including Bodhisattvas and Tathāgatas. Why is this?"
This is because they employ the method of "having something to be attained. Why is this so?

When all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they awaken to the fact that all phenomena are utterly non-existent; neither names nor sounds can be apprehended.
When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide on the stage of non-retrogression, they likewise see that all phenomena are utterly non-existent, and that names and sounds are entirely unobtainable.
“Kauśika! This is the manner in which a bodhisattva mahāsattva should dwell with respect to the profound perfection of wisdom, and the manner in which they should not dwell.”

Kauśika! Regarding the profound Prajñāpāramitā, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should train in this way: by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method, they should learn according to the characteristics of how one ought to abide and how one ought not to abide.
At that time, Śāriputra had this thought:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), should not abide in any phenomena at all, how then should they abide in the profound perfection of wisdom?"
The Venerable Subhūti, knowing the thoughts in the mind of Śāriputra, said to him:
"What do you think? In what does the mind of the Tathāgatas abide?"
Śāriputra said: “The minds of all Tathāgatas abide nowhere. Why is this? Because...”
The minds of all Buddhas do not abide in the aggregate of form, nor even in the aggregate of consciousness; they do not abide in the sense-base of the eye, nor even in the sense-base of the mind;
they do not abide in the sense-base of forms, nor even in the sense-base of mental phenomena; they do not abide in the element of the eye, nor even in the element of the mind;
they do not abide in the element of forms, nor even in the element of mental phenomena; they do not abide in the element of eye-consciousness, nor even in the element of mind-consciousness.

He does not dwell in eye-contact, nor even in mind-contact; he does not dwell in the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, nor even in the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition; he does not dwell in the earth element, nor even in the consciousness element;
he does not dwell in the causal condition, nor even in the dominant condition; he does not dwell in ignorance, nor even in old age and death.
They dwell in the realm of the conditioned and the realm of the unconditioned; they do not dwell in the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
they do not dwell in inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature;
they do not dwell in suchness up to the inconceivable realm; they do not dwell in the realm of cessation up to the realm of the unconditioned. They do not...
They abide in the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; they do not abide in the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
they do not abide in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the four formless absorptions;
they do not abide in the eight liberations or the nine successive attainments; and they do not abide in the liberations of emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness.
The gate does not abide in the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata;
it does not abide in the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma stage; it does not abide in the five eyes or the six supernormal powers;
it does not abide in the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and it does not abide in the thirty-two marks or the eighty minor characteristics.
He does not abide in the quality of non-forgetfulness, nor does he abide in the nature of equanimity;

he does not abide in any of the gateways of dhāraṇī or the gateways of samādhi; he does not abide in all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, or the knowledge of all aspects. Why is this?
Because all dharmas are unapprehendable. Thus it is, Subhūti!
The mind of the Tathāgata does not abide in any dharma whatsoever, nor does it not abide.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti said to Śāriputra:

“When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, it is likewise so: although they abide in the perfection of wisdom, they are just like the Tathāgata, whose mind abides in nothing among all phenomena, yet does not not abide.”

Why is this? When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, although they abide in the perfection of wisdom, they neither abide nor do they not abide in the aggregate of form; likewise, they neither abide nor do they not abide in the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

In this way, up to and including omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), he neither abides nor does he not abide; regarding the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), he likewise neither abides nor does he not abide.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
it is because dharmas such as form do not possess dual characteristics.

Śāriputra! Regarding the profound perfection of wisdom, bodhisattva mahāsattvas should train in this manner by means of non-apprehension, in accordance with this characteristic of neither abiding nor not abiding.
At that time, there were among the assembly certain sons of the gods who thought to themselves:
"Although the words and incantatory phrases of the yakṣas and others, with their various distinctions, are indeed obscure, we are still able to understand them;
yet although the Venerable Subhūti has revealed the profound Prajñāpāramitā through various expressions, we are ultimately unable to comprehend it!"
The Venerable Subhūti, knowing what was in the minds of the devaputras, addressed them, saying:
"Do you, O devaputras, not understand what I have said?"
The devaputras said: "So it is! So it is!"
“I am entirely unable to understand the profound meaning of the words of the *prajñāpāramitā* as spoken by the Venerable One.
The venerable Subhūti replied to him:
“I have never uttered a single word regarding the meaning associated with this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, nor have you heard anything; how then could there be anything to be understood?”
Why is this? O sons of the gods!

Within the meaning associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, all letters and verbal expressions are utterly transcended; for herein, neither speaker, listener, nor one who understands can be apprehended. It is likewise with the subtle, profound, and unsurpassed *samyaksaṃbodhi* realized by all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
“Son of Heaven, you should know!
It is as if a Buddha were to manifest a transformed Buddha-body, and this transformed Buddha-body were to manifest the fourfold assembly, all gathering together for him to preach the Dharma.”
"What do you think?
Within this, is there anyone who truly exists who can speak, who can listen, or who can understand?
The devaputras replied:
"No, Venerable Sir! Subhūti replied.

"So it is, O Devaputra! Since all phenomena are like illusions, within this profound meaning associated with the Prajñāpāramitā, neither the speaker, the listener, nor the one who understands can be apprehended."
“Son of Heaven, you should know!
It is like seeing a Buddha in a dream preaching the Dharma to the assembly.
What do you think?”
"In this, is there anyone who truly exists who can speak, who can listen,
or who can understand? The sons of the gods replied, "No!"
"Venerable One!
Subhūti replied, "So it is!"
O Devaputra!
Since all phenomena are like dreams, within this profound meaning associated with the *prajñāpāramitā*, neither the speaker, the listener, nor the one who understands can be apprehended.
“O Son of Heaven, you should know this!
Suppose there are two people situated in a single mountain valley, each dwelling on one side and praising the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, such that their voices resound simultaneously.
"What do you think?
Can these two echoes hear each other or understand one another?
The sons of the gods replied:
"No, Venerable Sir! Subhūti replied.

"So it is, O Devaputra! Since all phenomena are like echoes, within this profound meaning associated with the *prajñāpāramitā*, neither the speaker, the listener, nor the one who understands can be apprehended."
“O Son of Heaven, you should know this!
Suppose a master illusionist or his disciple were to create, at a crossroads, an illusory assembly of the four groups and a single Tathāgata preaching the Dharma to that assembly. What do you think?”
"In this matter, is there anyone who speaks, anyone who listens,
or anyone who understands? The sons of the gods replied, "No!"
"Venerable One!
Subhūti replied, "So it is!"
"O Son of Heaven!
Because all dharmas are like illusions, within this profound meaning associated with the *prajñāpāramitā*, neither the speaker, the listener, nor the one who understands can be apprehended."
“Son of Heaven, you should know!
For this reason, within this profound meaning associated with the *prajñāpāramitā*, I have never uttered a single word; you likewise have heard nothing—what, then, could there be to understand?”
At that time, the sons of the gods again had this thought:

"Although the Venerable Subhūti, through various skillful means, has explained the profound meaning of this *prajñāpāramitā* so as to make it easy to understand, its significance remains exceedingly deep, even more profound, subtle, and even more subtle, such that it is difficult to fathom."
The Venerable Subhūti, knowing their thoughts, addressed them, saying:
"Sons of the gods, you should know this:
the aggregate of form is neither profound nor subtle; the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise neither profound nor subtle."
Why is this? O sons of the gods!
Because the intrinsic nature of the aggregate of form, up to the intrinsic nature of the aggregate of consciousness, is neither profound nor subtle.

In this way, even up to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), it is neither profound nor subtle; the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are likewise neither profound nor subtle.
Why is this? O sons of the gods!
The intrinsic nature of all-knowledge, the intrinsic nature of the knowledge of the paths, and the intrinsic nature of the knowledge of all aspects are neither profound nor subtle.
Then, those sons of the gods again had this thought:
"In the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, no form-aggregate is established, nor are the feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness-aggregates established."
Why is this? Because the nature of the aggregate of form and so forth cannot be expressed.

In this same way, up to and including omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), one does not designate it, nor does one designate the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Why is this? Because the nature of all-knowledge and so forth is inexpressible.

Within the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, there is no designation for the stage of entering the stream or the fruit of stream-entry; the stage of entering once-returning or the fruit of once-returning; the stage of entering non-returning or the fruit of non-returning; the stage of entering arhatship or the fruit of arhatship; the stage of entering pratyekabuddhahood or the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood; nor is there any designation for the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas or the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas.
Why is this? Because the natures of those such as the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry are all inexpressible.
Within the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, neither written characters nor verbal expressions are established.
"Why is this? Because the nature of letters and language is such that they cannot be expressed.
The Venerable Subhūti, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the devaputras, addressed them, saying:
"So it is! So it is! It is just as you have reflected."

From the aggregate of form up to unsurpassed enlightenment, all words and speech are inexpressible; therefore, within this profound meaning associated with the *prajñāpāramitā*, there is no speaker, no listener, and no one who understands.
Therefore, among all phenomena, you should cultivate profound and firm patience in accordance with what has been taught.

O Son of Heaven, you should know that those who wish to realize or abide in the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship, as well as the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha or the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha, must rely upon this patience to be able to realize and abide therein.
In this way, O Devaputra!

From the first generation of the mind of awakening until the ultimate goal, all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should abide in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*—which is without speaking, without listening, and without understanding—and should constantly and diligently practice it without ever abandoning it for even a moment.
Then, those sons of the gods again had this thought:
"Venerable Subhūti, for what kind of sentient beings does he now wish to preach what Dharma?
The venerable Subhūti, knowing the thoughts in the minds of those sons of the gods, addressed them, saying:
“Son of Heaven, you should know!
I now wish to proclaim for sentient beings who are like illusions, like transformations, and like dreams, the Dharma that is likewise like illusions, like transformations, and like dreams.”
"Why is this? Because such listeners have neither heard, nor understood, nor realized the Dharma that was taught.
At that time, the sons of the gods again asked:
"Are the one who speaks, the one who listens, and the Dharma that is spoken, all like an illusion, a transformation,
or what is seen in a dream? Subhūti replied, "So it is!"
It is so! It is as you have said.

Just as illusory beings speak the illusory Dharma for illusory beings, as conjured beings speak the conjured Dharma for conjured beings, and as dream-like beings speak the dream-like Dharma for dream-like beings.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know!

From the self up to the perceiver, these are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream. The aggregate of form up to the aggregate of consciousness are likewise like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream. Even the fruit of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship; the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas are likewise like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream."
Then the sons of the gods asked Subhūti: "Venerable One!

Do you now teach only that from 'self' up to 'awakening' is like an illusion, like a transformation, and like what is seen in a dream; or do you also teach that nirvāṇa is like an illusion, like a transformation, and like what is seen in a dream?"

Subhūti replied, "At this moment, I do not merely say that from 'self' up to 'enlightenment' is like an illusion, like a transformation, or like what is seen in a dream; I also say that even nirvāṇa is like an illusion, like a transformation, or like what is seen in a dream."
"Son of Heaven, you should know this!
Even if there were another dharma that surpassed nirvāṇa, I would likewise declare it to be like an illusion, like a transformation, or like what is seen in a dream. Why is this?"
"O sons of the gods!
Illusion, transformation, and dream-phenomena are entirely non-dual and indivisible from all dharmas, even up to nirvāṇa.

At that time, the venerable Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākauṣṭhila, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Mahākātyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, and other great śrāvakas, together with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, simultaneously raised their voices and addressed the venerable Subhūti:

"This Prajñāpāramitā that has been taught is thus profound, difficult to see and difficult to realize, tranquil and subtle, beyond discursive thought, transcending the sphere of discursive thought, supreme and foremost—who could believe and accept it?"
At that time, Ānanda addressed the great śrāvakas and the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, saying:
"There are non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are able to receive this Prajñāpāramitā with deep faith."

Furthermore, there are immeasurable great arhats who have already seen the noble truths, who are able to fathom the very source and bottom of all profound dharmas, whose aspirations are fulfilled, and whose outflows are forever exhausted; they too are able to believe in and accept this Prajñāpāramitā.

Furthermore, there are immeasurable sons and daughters of good family who, in the past, have personally approached and made offerings to immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Buddhas; they have formed great vows, planted various roots of goodness, possess intelligence and wisdom, are sustained by virtuous friends, and are likewise able to believe in and accept this Prajñāpāramitā.
"Why is this? Because such persons are able to remain without discrimination regarding what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma.

That is to say, they do not discriminate between emptiness and non-emptiness with respect to form, up to and including consciousness; nor do they discriminate between form, up to and including consciousness, with respect to emptiness and non-emptiness."

One does not discriminate between form and so forth up to consciousness as being with signs or signless; nor does one discriminate between form and so forth up to consciousness as being with signs or signless.

One does not discriminate between form and so forth up to consciousness as being with aspiration or without aspiration; nor does one discriminate between form and so forth up to consciousness as being with aspiration or without aspiration.

One does not discriminate between form and so forth up to consciousness as being tranquil or non-tranquil, nor does one discriminate between form and so forth up to consciousness as tranquility or non-tranquility.

One does not discriminate form through to consciousness by means of "separation" or "non-separation," nor does one discriminate "separation" or "non-separation" by means of form through to consciousness.

One does not discriminate between form and so forth up to consciousness by way of arising or non-arising, nor does one discriminate between form and so forth up to consciousness by way of arising or non-arising.

One does not discriminate between form and so forth up to consciousness by way of cessation or non-cessation, nor does one discriminate between form and so forth up to consciousness by way of cessation or non-cessation.

In this way, one does not discriminate between the conditioned and unconditioned realms by means of "empty" or "not empty," nor does one discriminate between "empty" or "not empty" by means of the conditioned and unconditioned realms.

One does not discriminate between the conditioned and unconditioned realms by means of signs or signlessness, nor does one discriminate between signs and signlessness by means of the conditioned and unconditioned realms.

One does not differentiate the conditioned and unconditioned realms by means of wishing or wishlessness, nor does one differentiate wishing or wishlessness by means of the conditioned and unconditioned realms.

One does not differentiate the conditioned and unconditioned realms by means of tranquility or non-tranquility, nor does one differentiate tranquility and non-tranquility by means of the conditioned and unconditioned realms.

One does not discriminate between the conditioned and unconditioned realms by way of detachment or non-detachment, nor does one discriminate between detachment and non-detachment by way of the conditioned and unconditioned realms.

One does not discriminate between the conditioned and unconditioned realms by means of arising or non-arising, nor does one discriminate between arising and non-arising by means of the conditioned and unconditioned realms.

One does not discriminate between the conditioned and unconditioned realms by means of cessation or non-cessation, nor does one discriminate between cessation and non-cessation by means of the conditioned and unconditioned realms.
"For this reason, such persons as these are able to have faith in and accept this Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the devaputras, saying:

"This Prajñāpāramitā is indeed profound; it is difficult to see and difficult to realize. It is tranquil and subtle, beyond the scope of discursive thought, transcending the realm of conceptualization, supreme and foremost. Within it, there is truly no one who can have faith in and accept it."

Why is this so? Because within this there is no dharma that can be manifested or shown; since there is truly no dharma that can be manifested or shown, even those who believe and accept it cannot be found.
Then, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

"Is it not the case that within the profound teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā, the dharmas corresponding to the three vehicles are extensively expounded—namely, the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, and the unsurpassed vehicle?"

He extensively explains the bodhisattva path for the gathering and sustaining of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, from their initial generation of the mind of awakening through to the tenth generation of the mind;
that is to say, the perfections from the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom,
abiding in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, and abiding in suchness.
...up to the inconceivable realm; abiding in the realm of cessation up to the unconditioned realm;

abiding in the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; whether it be the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, or the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, or the eight liberations, the nine...
The successive meditative concentrations; the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
the stages from the Ground of Extreme Joy up to the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma; the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; the quality of non-forgetfulness; and the state of constant abiding in equanimity—if...
All dhāraṇī-doors and samādhi-doors, as well as all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)— to speak extensively,
these comprise the superior matters of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) acquired by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; that is to say, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva...
Because he diligently practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, wherever he is born, he always undergoes miraculous birth (*upapāduka*);
he is able to sport with mastery in non-regressive supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and can skillfully penetrate immeasurable dharma-gates;
from one buddha-field to another, he makes offerings, pays homage, respects, and praises [the Buddhas].
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in accordance with their vows and inclinations, have planted the roots of all virtues;
they have upheld the True Dharma from the presence of the Buddhas until the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, never forgetting it.
Constantly abiding in supreme meditative concentration and free from a distracted mind, by virtue of these causes and conditions, they have attained unimpeded eloquence and inexhaustible eloquence.
"Is it the eloquence free from error, the appropriate eloquence, the swift eloquence, the eloquence that abounds in profound meaning and flavor in all that is expounded,
and the most supreme and wondrous eloquence in all the world? Subhūti replied:
"So it is! So it is! It is exactly as you have said."

Within this profound teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā, by employing the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), there is extensively expounded the Dharma corresponding to the three vehicles, up to the extensive exposition of the superior matters of the bodhisattva’s supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and even leading to the attainment of the most excellent and sublime eloquence in all worlds.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

"In this profound teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā, regarding all that is taught by means of non-apprehension as the expedient, with respect to what phenomena is non-apprehension employed as the expedient?"
Subhūti replied: "This is by means of non-apprehension of everything from 'self' up to 'seer'; this is by means of non-apprehension of everything from 'form' up to 'consciousness';
this is by means of non-apprehension of everything from the 'eye base' up to the 'mind base'."
Taking non-apprehension as the skillful means: this is taking non-apprehension as the skillful means regarding the sphere of form up to the sphere of mental phenomena;
this is taking non-apprehension as the skillful means regarding the eye element up to the mind element;
this is taking non-apprehension as the skillful means regarding the form element up to the mental-phenomena element.
This takes non-apprehension as the means regarding the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element;
this takes non-apprehension as the means regarding eye-contact up to mind-contact;
and this takes non-apprehension regarding all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition up to all feelings produced with mind-contact as condition.
And as for skillful means: this is skillful means through non-apprehension regarding the element of earth, up to the element of consciousness;
this is skillful means through non-apprehension regarding the causal condition, up to the dominant condition;
this is skillful means through non-apprehension regarding ignorance, up to old age and death; this is [skillful means] regarding the laying out...
The perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom is practiced by means of non-apprehension;
this is practiced by means of non-apprehension within the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence;
this is practiced by means of non-apprehension within true suchness up to the inconceivable realm.
This [practice] takes non-apprehension as the means regarding the element of cessation up to the unconditioned element;
this takes non-apprehension as the means regarding the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
this takes non-apprehension as the means regarding the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path. This...
Regarding the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments, they take non-apprehension as their means;
regarding these eight liberations and nine successive concentrations, they take non-apprehension as their means;
regarding these doors of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—they take non-apprehension as their means.
This is the skillful means of non-apprehension regarding the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata;
this is the skillful means of non-apprehension regarding the Joyous Stage up to the Cloud of Dharma Stage;
this is the skillful means of non-apprehension regarding the five eyes and the six supernormal powers; this is, with respect to the Tathāgata...
To come [to mastery] regarding the ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha by means of non-apprehension as the expedient;
this regarding the thirty-two marks of a Great Being and the eighty minor characteristics by means of non-apprehension as the expedient;
this regarding the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity by means of non-apprehension as the expedient.
This is the skillful means of non-apprehension regarding all dharani-doors and samadhi-doors;
this is the skillful means of non-apprehension regarding all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects;
this is [the skillful means] regarding those who have entered the stream, the fruit of stream-entry, and so forth, up to the bodhisattva.
“The practice of the mahāsattva and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas are characterized by the expedient means of non-apprehension.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed Subhūti, saying:
"For what reason, within this profound teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā, is the Dharma corresponding to the three vehicles extensively expounded by taking non-apprehension as the means?"

For what reason, within this profound teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā*, is the path of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—from their first generation of the mind of awakening through to the tenth generation of the mind—extensively explained by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method?

For what reason, within this profound teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā*, is there such an extensive exposition on the superior matters of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) that sustain bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, even unto the attainment of the most excellent and sublime eloquence (*pratibhāna*) in all the world?
Subhūti replied, "Śāriputra!

Because of inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, within this profound teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā, one extensively expounds the dharmas associated with the three vehicles by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method."

Śāriputra! Because of the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, within this profound teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā, by means of the expedient of non-apprehension, the bodhisattva paths of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—from their initial generation of the mind of awakening through successive stages up to the tenth generation of the mind—are extensively explained and encompassed.

Śāriputra! Because of inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, within this profound teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā, by means of the expedient of non-apprehension, the superior matters of the supernormal powers of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are extensively explained and encompassed, even unto the attainment of the most supreme and wondrous eloquence in all the world.
