If good sons or good daughters were to teach and transform all sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in each of the ten directions, causing them all to dwell securely in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless absorptions, and the five supernormal powers—what do you think?
The rest is as explained above.
"Furthermore, Kauśika! Setting aside these sentient beings in each of the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River."

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to teach and transform all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions, causing them all to dwell securely in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers—what do you think?
The remainder is as explained above. "Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, with a sincere heart, hears, receives, upholds, recites, diligently studies, and reflects upon this profound sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā according to the principle, the mass of merit obtained by them surpasses that of one who teaches all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa, causing them to abide in the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers."

It is superior to teaching and transforming all sentient beings in a single four-continent world system; it is superior to teaching and transforming all sentient beings in a small thousand-world system; it is superior to teaching and transforming all sentient beings in a medium thousand-world system; it is superior to teaching and transforming all sentient beings in a great thousand-world system; it is superior to teaching and transforming all sentient beings in as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges in each of the ten directions; and it is superior to teaching and transforming all sentient beings throughout the entirety of the ten directions, causing them all to abide in the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless absorptions, and the five supernormal powers.

“Kauśika! In this context, ‘correct reflection’ means that for the sake of seeking unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, one reflects upon the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity by way of a practice that is neither dual nor non-dual; and likewise, up to that point, for the sake of seeking unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, one reflects upon all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) by way of a practice that is neither dual nor non-dual.”
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to extensively expound this profound sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom to others through immeasurable gateways—proclaiming, elucidating, clarifying, explaining, and analyzing its meaning and intent so that it may be easily understood—the mass of merit they would obtain would be infinitely greater than the merit obtained by oneself merely hearing, receiving, upholding, reciting, diligently practicing, and correctly contemplating this profound Perfection of Wisdom."
Kauśika! Regarding the meaning and intent of this Prajñāpāramitā, one should not contemplate the meaning and intent of this Prajñāpāramitā through dualistic characteristics,
nor should one contemplate it through non-dualistic characteristics.
Neither having marks nor lacking marks; neither entering nor exiting; neither increasing nor decreasing;
neither defiled nor pure; neither arising nor ceasing; neither grasping nor relinquishing; neither clinging nor non-clinging;
neither abiding nor non-abiding; neither real nor unreal; neither conjoined nor dispersed; neither associated nor...
It is not dissociated; it is neither a small portion nor not a small portion; it is neither the whole nor not the whole;
it is neither a causal condition nor not a causal condition; it is neither dharma nor non-dharma; it is neither suchness nor not suchness;
it is neither the limit of reality nor not the limit of reality. Such meanings and principles have immeasurable doors of entry.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, with a sincere heart, hears, receives, upholds, reads, recites, diligently practices, and reflects upon this profound sūtra of the *Prajñāpāramitā* according to the truth, and extensively explains it for others through immeasurable methods—proclaiming, expounding, elucidating, interpreting, and analyzing its meaning and intent so that it is easily understood—the mass of merit they obtain will surpass the previous mass of merit by an immeasurable and boundless amount."
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“These sons and daughters of good family should expound the profound *prajñāpāramitā* to others using various skillful words and meanings.”
At that time, the Buddha said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.
All sons and daughters of good family should, by means of various skillful words and meanings, expound this profound Prajñāpāramitā for others.

Kauśika! If sons or daughters of good family can expound the profound *prajñāpāramitā* for others using various skillful words and meanings, they will accomplish an immeasurable, incalculable, boundless, and inconceivable mass of great merit.

Kauśika! If good sons and good daughters, for as long as their lives last, were to offer, revere, respect, honor, and praise all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas in all the immeasurable and innumerable worlds of the ten directions, using immeasurable varieties of exquisite flower garlands, up to lamps and other ritual offerings;

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, with a sincere heart, hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently practice, and reflect upon this profound *prajñāpāramitā* sūtra according to the principle, and furthermore, relying on its various skillful words and meanings, extensively expound it to others through immeasurable approaches—proclaiming, elucidating, clarifying, explaining, and analyzing its significance so that it may be easily understood—the mass of merit they obtain will be far greater than the former.

Why is this? Because all Buddhas of the three periods of time have, by relying upon the Prajñāpāramitā, diligently practiced and studied it, thereby realizing unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters, for immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless great kalpas, diligently practice the perfections from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom by means of the apprehension of a basis, [they would not equal one who practices with non-apprehension]."

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, regarding this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, by means of the method of non-apprehension, listen with a sincere heart, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, diligently practice and study it, and reflect upon it according to the principle; and furthermore, using various skillful words and meanings, for even a brief moment explain it to others—proclaiming, expounding, clarifying, interpreting, and analyzing its significance so as to make it easy to understand—the mass of merit they obtain is far greater than the former.
“Kauśika! Those who have attainment refer to good sons and good daughters who, when practicing generosity, form such thoughts: ‘I am the one who gives;
he is the recipient; this is the fruit of giving; and these are the act of giving and the objects given.’”
When he practices giving, it is called abiding in generosity, but it is not called the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramitā).
When practicing pure ethical discipline, he forms this thought:
"I am able to maintain the precepts in order to protect that [giving]; this is the fruit of the precepts and the precepts themselves that are maintained."
"When he practices ethical discipline, it is called abiding in pure morality, but it is not yet called the perfection of morality (*śīlapāramitā*).
When practicing patience, he forms this thought:
'I am able to practice patience for the sake of protecting others'; this is the fruit of patience as well as its intrinsic nature."
When he cultivates patience, it is called abiding in patience, but it is not yet called the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
When he cultivates diligence, he forms this thought:
"I am able to exert diligence in order to cultivate the abandonment of those [defilements]; this is the fruit of diligence and the intrinsic nature of diligence."
When he practices diligence, it is called abiding in diligence, but it is not called the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā).
When practicing meditative concentration (dhyāna), he forms this thought:
"I am able to cultivate concentration; that is the object of concentration, and this is the fruit of concentration as well as its intrinsic nature."
"When he cultivates meditative concentration, it is called abiding in dhyāna, but it is not called the dhyāna-pāramitā.
When he cultivates prajñā, he forms this thought:
'I am able to cultivate wisdom; that is the object of wisdom, and this is the fruit of wisdom as well as the intrinsic nature of wisdom.'"
"When they cultivate wisdom at that time, it is called abiding in *prajñā*, but it is not called *prajñāpāramitā*.
Kausika! Because these sons and daughters of good family employ the method of 'having something to obtain,' they are unable to bring the six *pāramitās*, such as generosity, to fulfillment."
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice so as to be able to fulfill the six pāramitās, such as generosity?"
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices generosity, they do not apprehend the giver, the recipient, the fruit of giving, the act of giving, or the object given. In this way, up until the practice of wisdom, they do not apprehend the wise one, the object of wisdom, the fruit of wisdom, or the intrinsic nature of wisdom. By taking non-apprehension as their skillful means, they are able to bring the six perfections, beginning with generosity, to full completion."

“Kauśika! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should, by means of such wisdom of non-apprehension as well as various skillful expressions and meanings, proclaim the *prajñāpāramitā* and even the *dānapāramitā*.

Why is this? In future ages, there will be sons and daughters of good family who, employing the method of "attainment," shall proclaim a semblance of the *prajñāpāramitā* up to the *dānapāramitā* for others. When those who have first resolved upon unexcelled bodhicitta hear such a semblance of the *prajñāpāramitā* up to the *dānapāramitā*, their minds will become deluded and mistaken, and they will fall away from the Middle Way. Therefore, one should, by means of the wisdom of non-attainment and through various skillful words and meanings, proclaim the *prajñāpāramitā* up to the *dānapāramitā* for those who have resolved upon unexcelled bodhicitta.
Then, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What is meant by the teaching of counterfeit *prajñāpāramitā*, *dhyāna*, *vīrya*, *kṣānti*, *śīla*, and *dānapāramitā*?”
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of Devas, saying:

"If sons or daughters of good family speak of the six pāramitās—such as prajñā and the others—as being characterized by apprehension, this is called proclaiming counterfeit prajñā, dhyāna, vīrya, kṣānti, śīla, and dāna pāramitās."
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is it that sons and daughters of good family speak of the six pāramitās, such as prajñā, as being 'with attainment'?"

The Buddha said, “Kauśika! If good men and good women explain to those who have resolved upon unexcelled bodhicitta that form, up to and including consciousness, is either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure— and likewise, up to and including, they explain that omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure— speaking in this manner:”

"If there are those who are able to practice from the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity by relying on such dharmas as these, they are practicing from the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity."
Furthermore, it is said:

"One who practices the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity should seek whether form up to the knowledge of all aspects is permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure."

If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice from the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity, this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity.

"Kauśika! If there is one who thus seeks form, up to and including all-aspect omniscience (sarvākārajñatā), whether as permanent or impermanent, as pleasant or painful, as self or non-self, or as pure or impure."

I say that those who practice the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity by relying on such dharmas are practicing a semblance of the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.

Kauśika! If it is as previously described, you should know that all these are merely similitudes of the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity that involve apprehension. Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, proclaim the *prajñāpāramitā* and so forth up to the *dānapāramitā*, saying these words: "Come!..."
"Noble son! I shall instruct you in the practice and study of the *prajñāpāramitā* and the other perfections up to the *dānapāramitā*.
If you practice and study according to my instructions, you shall swiftly abide in the first bodhisattva stage (*bhūmi*) through to the tenth."

"Kauśika! Because they employ signs (*nimitta*) and the apprehension of objects (*upalambha*) as their means, and teach the cultivation of the *prajñāpāramitā* up to the *dānapāramitā* based on the perception of temporal divisions, this is called teaching a counterfeit *prajñāpāramitā* up to a counterfeit *dānapāramitā*."

"Furthermore, Kauśika! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family should proclaim the *prajñāpāramitā* and so forth, up to the *dānapāramitā*, for those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, saying: 'Come!'"
"Son of good family!
I shall instruct you in the practice and study of the *prajñāpāramitā* and the other *pāramitās*, up to and including the *dānapāramitā*.

If you practice and study according to my instructions, you will swiftly transcend the stages of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, swiftly enter the Bodhisattva’s state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), attain the Bodhisattvas’ endurance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and acquire the Bodhisattvas’ sublime supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). You will be able to travel to all Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions to make offerings, pay homage, revere, and praise the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, thereby swiftly realizing the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*)."

“Kauśika! Because they employ signs and the apprehension of objects as their skillful means, and teach the cultivation of the *prajñāpāramitā* up to the *dānapāramitā* based on the perception of temporal divisions, this is called the teaching of counterfeit *prajñāpāramitā* up to the *dānapāramitā*.”
"Furthermore, Kauśika! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family should say to one who belongs to the lineage of the bodhisattva vehicle:

'If you listen with a sincere heart to this profound sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, diligently practice and study it, and reflect upon it according to the principle, you will certainly obtain immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless merit.'"

"Kauśika! Because they employ signs and the apprehension of objects as their means, they speak in this way; this is called teaching a counterfeit perfection of wisdom, up to and including the perfection of generosity."
"Furthermore, Kauśika! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family should say to one belonging to the lineage of the bodhisattva vehicle:

'Regarding all the roots of goodness of the World-Honored Buddhas of the three periods of time—from their first generation of the mind of awakening until their ultimate perfection—you should rejoice in them all, collect them together, and dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening for the sake of all sentient beings.'"

“Kauśika! Because they employ signs and the apprehension of objects as their means, they speak in this way; this is called proclaiming a counterfeit perfection of wisdom, up to and including the perfection of generosity.”
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How should one proclaim the true and correct Prajñāpāramitā, up to and including the Dānapāramitā?
The Buddha said:

“Kauśika! If sons and daughters of good family, employing the method of non-apprehension, proclaim the *prajñāpāramitā* and so forth up to the *dānapāramitā*, this is called proclaiming the true and correct *prajñāpāramitā* and so forth up to the *dānapāramitā*.
Then, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How do sons and daughters of good family, by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method, proclaim the *prajñāpāramitā* and even the *dānapāramitā*?"
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!
If good sons and good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the Mahāyāna bodhicitta, proclaim the *prajñāpāramitā* and so forth up to the *dānapāramitā*, speaking as follows:”
"Come, son of good family!

You should cultivate the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity. While you are cultivating them correctly, you should not regard form up to the knowledge of all aspects as either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure."
Why is this? Son of good family!
Form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form, and so on, up to the knowledge of all aspects, which is empty of the intrinsic nature of the knowledge of all aspects.

The intrinsic nature of this form is itself the absence of intrinsic nature; likewise, the intrinsic nature of everything up to the knowledge of all aspects is itself the absence of intrinsic nature. That which is the absence of intrinsic nature is itself the perfection of wisdom, and so on, up to the perfection of generosity.

Within this Prajñāpāramitā, up to the Dānapāramitā, from form (*rūpa*) up to all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), nothing can be apprehended; neither permanence nor impermanence, neither pleasure nor suffering, neither self nor non-self, and neither purity nor impurity can be apprehended therein.

Why is this? Because herein even form and the other aggregates cannot be apprehended; how much less can there be the apprehension of such things as permanence or impermanence, pleasure or suffering, self or non-self, and purity or impurity!
"Noble son! If you can cultivate such perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity."
"Kauśika! When these sons of good family and daughters of good family speak in this manner, it is called proclaiming the authentic Prajñāpāramitā, up to and including the Dānapāramitā."

"Furthermore, Kauśika! If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have generated the bodhicitta of the Mahāyāna, proclaim the *prajñāpāramitā* up to the *dānapāramitā*, saying: 'Come!'"
"Noble son! I shall instruct you in the cultivation and study of the *pāramitās*, from *prajñā* down to *dāna*.

When you cultivate and study them, do not observe any phenomenon whatsoever as something in which one may abide, that may be transcended, that may be entered, that may be attained, that may be realized, or that may be heard; nor [observe] any merit obtained therefrom, nor anything that may be rejoiced in or dedicated toward enlightenment."
Why is this? Son of good family!

Within this *prajñāpāramitā* and even up to the *dānapāramitā*, there is ultimately not the slightest dharma that can be dwelled in, transcended, entered, attained, realized, heard, or any merit obtained that can be rejoiced in and dedicated toward awakening.

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty; if their intrinsic nature is empty, then they are non-existent. That which is non-existent is precisely the perfection of wisdom, and so on, up to the perfection of generosity.

Within this *prajñāpāramitā*, and even up to the *dānapāramitā*, not the slightest dharma can be found that enters or exits, arises or ceases, is annihilated or eternal, is identical or different, or comes or goes.

“Kauśika! When these sons and daughters of good family speak in this manner, they are in total opposition to all that belongs to the dark category; this is called proclaiming the true and correct Prajñāpāramitā, up to and including the Dānapāramitā.”

"For this reason, Kauśika, sons and daughters of good family should, regarding this profound sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā, by means of the method of non-apprehension, listen with a sincere heart, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, diligently practice and study it, and reflect upon it according to the principle. They should extensively explain it to others using various skillful words and meanings, proclaiming, expounding, clarifying, interpreting, and analyzing its significance so that it may be easily understood."

“Kauśika! For this reason, I say that if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, regarding this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, employs the skillful means of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) to listen with a sincere heart, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, diligently practice and study it, and reflect upon it according to the principle; and furthermore, using various skillful and elegant words and meanings, for even a brief moment explains it to others—proclaiming, expounding, clarifying, interpreting, and analyzing its significance so as to make it easy to understand—the merit they obtain is far greater than the former.”
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to instruct all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa, or all sentient beings in the four great continents, or all sentient beings in a small thousand-world system, or all sentient beings in a medium thousand-world system, or all sentient beings in a great trichiliocosm, or even all sentient beings in worlds throughout the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, or all sentient beings in the infinite worlds throughout the ten directions, and cause them all to abide in the fruit of a stream-enterer, or the fruit of a once-returner, or the fruit of a non-returner, or the fruit of an arhat, or in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha."
"What do you think?
By reason of this, would these sons and daughters of good family acquire much merit?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied:
“Very many, World-Honored One! Very many!”
“Excellent, Sugata! The Buddha told Kauśika:

“If sons or daughters of good family, regarding this profound sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā, should extensively expound it for others through immeasurable methods and skillful words and meanings—proclaiming, unfolding, clarifying, explaining, and analyzing its purport so that it may be easily understood—and further say these words:”
"Come, son of good family!

You should, with a sincere mind, hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, and master this profound *prajñāpāramitā*; you should contemplate it according to the principle and diligently practice and study in accordance with this Dharma-gate."
The merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family is far greater than that mentioned before.
Why is this? Kausika!
All the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship, as well as the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, are all that flow forth from the perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters were to instruct all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa, or all sentient beings in the four great continents, or all sentient beings in a small thousandfold world system, or all sentient beings in a medium thousandfold world system, or all sentient beings in a great trichiliocosm, or even all sentient beings in worlds throughout the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, to cause them all to resolve upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, or to abide in the stage of non-retrogression of a bodhisattva."
"What do you think?
By this cause and condition, would these sons and daughters of good family acquire much merit?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied:
“Very much so,
World-Honored One!
Very much so!”
“Excellent, Sugata!
The Buddha said to Kauśika:

“If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, by means of immeasurable gateways and skillful phrasing and meaning, should extensively expound this profound sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā for others—proclaiming, unfolding, clarifying, explaining, and analyzing its significance so that it is easily understood—and should further say these words:”
"Come, son of good family!

You should, with a sincere heart, listen to, receive, uphold, read, recite, and master this profound *prajñāpāramitā*; you should contemplate it according to the principle, and you should develop right faith and understanding in accordance with this Dharma-gate."
If one possesses correct faith and understanding, one will be able to practice and study the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
If one can practice and study the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one will be able to realize the dharma of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
If one can realize the dharma of omniscience, then the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom will increase and reach fulfillment.
If the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom increases and reaches fulfillment, one then realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Kauśika! The merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family is far greater than that previously mentioned. Why is this?"

Kauśika! Whether it be all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have first resolved upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, or all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwelling on the stage of non-retrogression, they all proceed until reaching unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment precisely because they flow forth from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

"Furthermore, Kauśika! Whether it be the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa, or the sentient beings of the four great continents, or the sentient beings of a small thousandfold world system, or the sentient beings of a medium thousandfold world system, or the sentient beings of a great trichiliocosm, or even the sentient beings of worlds in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River—if all these were to set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, regarding this profound sūtra of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, extensively explain it to others through immeasurable approaches and skillful words and meanings—proclaiming, expounding, clarifying, interpreting, and analyzing its significance so that it may be easily understood—and further say: "Come!..."

"Good son! You should, with a sincere mind, listen to, receive and uphold, read, recite, master thoroughly, and reflect upon this profound *prajñāpāramitā* according to the principle; you should develop right faith and understanding in accordance with this Dharma-gate.
If you develop right faith and understanding, you will be able to practice and study the profound *prajñāpāramitā*."
If one can practice and study the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, then one can realize the dharma of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*);
if one can realize the dharma of omniscience, then the cultivation of *prajñāpāramitā* will increase and reach fulfillment;
and if the cultivation of *prajñāpāramitā* increases and reaches fulfillment, one then realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

"If a son or daughter of good family should encounter a single non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva, and for that person, through immeasurable gateways of skillful phrasing and meaning, extensively expound this profound sūtra of the *prajñāpāramitā*, proclaiming, unfolding, clarifying, explaining, and analyzing its significance so as to make it easy to understand, and further say these words: 'Come!'"
"Good son! You should explain this extensively here as previously stated. "Kauśika! [he said.]
The merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family is far greater than the former.
Furthermore, Kausika, suppose all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa,

or all sentient beings in the four great continents, or all sentient beings in a small thousandfold world system, or all sentient beings in a medium thousandfold world system, or all sentient beings in a great trichiliocosm, or even all sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in each of the ten directions, were all to attain non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

There may be sons or daughters of good family who, regarding this profound sūtra of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, extensively expound it for others through immeasurable gateways of skillful phrasing and meaning; they proclaim, elaborate upon, clarify, explain, and analyze its significance so that it is easily understood. Among them, one might say:
"I now rejoice in swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, in order to deliver sentient beings from the manifold sufferings of birth and death."

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of accomplishing that matter, extensively expound the *prajñāpāramitā* through immeasurable gateways of skillful phrasing and meaning—proclaiming, unfolding, clarifying, explaining, and analyzing its significance so as to make it easy to understand.
“Kauśika! The merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family is far greater than that of the former.
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Bhagavān! To the extent that a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws closer to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, to that same extent they should be instructed and exhorted by means of the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom; and so on in detail until they should be instructed and exhorted by means of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); and they should be honored and sustained with offerings of excellent robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites, providing whatever various necessities they require.”

"Bhagavān! If good sons or good daughters are able to provide offerings and support to those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas through such gifts of Dharma and gifts of material wealth, the merit obtained by these good sons and good daughters will be far greater than the former."

Why is this? Because those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas must, through such offerings of the gift of Dharma and the gift of material wealth, be sustained and gathered in, so that they may swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"

That you are able to exhort those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, further able to sustain those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and also able to protect and assist those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—you have now performed what a noble disciple of the Buddha ought to do.
Why is this? Kauśika!

All Tathāgatas and their noble disciples, desiring to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, employ skillful means to encourage and exhort those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, causing them to swiftly realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek.

By means of the gifts of Dharma and material wealth, they provide offerings and support, diligently protecting and assisting those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas so that they may swiftly realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek.
Why is this? Because all the supreme worldly phenomena of the Tathāgatas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas appear by means of those Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas.
Why is this? Kauśika!

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas did not give rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, then there would be no bodhisattva-mahāsattvas capable of training in the six pāramitās, up to and including all-aspect omniscience.

If there were no bodhisattva mahāsattvas who train in the six pāramitās up to and including all-aspect omniscience, then there would be no bodhisattva mahāsattvas capable of realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas did not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, then there would be no such superior worldly phenomena as the Tathāgatas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.

“Kauśika! Because there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who give rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are able to train in the six pāramitās up to all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*);

because there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who train in the six pāramitās up to all-aspect omniscience, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.”

Because there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, they are able to sever the realms of hell, the animal kingdom, and the hungry ghosts; they are also able to diminish the hosts of asuras and increase the multitudes of devas and humans. Consequently, great kṣatriya clans and even great householder clans appear in the world; likewise, the Four Great Kings and the heavens up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception appear in the world. Furthermore, the six pāramitās and even all-aspect omniscience appear in the world; and furthermore, the vehicles of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the Unsurpassed Vehicle appear in the world.
Chapter Nine: Rejoicing and Dedication, Part Three, Section One. At that time, the Bodhisattva Maitreya addressed the Venerable Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, employing the method of non-apprehension, rejoices in all the meritorious deeds associated with the virtues of all sentient beings; and if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, employing the method of non-apprehension, takes these meritorious deeds associated with rejoicing and, sharing them equally with all sentient beings, dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;"

If other sentient beings rejoice in and dedicate various meritorious deeds—whether they be the meritorious deeds of ordinary worldlings, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas, namely the three types of meritorious deeds consisting of giving, ethical discipline, and cultivation, or the meritorious deeds such as the four foundations of mindfulness.

All the merit of this bodhisattva mahāsattva’s rejoicing and dedication surpasses all the meritorious deeds of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas; it is the most excellent, the most preeminent, the most honored, the highest, the most sublime, the most exquisite, the supreme, the unsurpassed, the peerless, and the equal to the unequaled.
Why is this? Because ordinary beings cultivate meritorious deeds merely for their own sovereignty and happiness;
whereas śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cultivate meritorious deeds merely for their own subduing, for their own tranquility, and for their own nirvāṇa.
All the merit of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas' rejoicing and dedication is universally for the sake of disciplining, pacifying, and bringing all sentient beings to nirvāṇa.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti asked the Bodhisattva Maitreya:

“This bodhisattva mahāsattva’s mind of sympathetic joy and dedication universally takes as its object the infinite, countless, and boundless worlds of the ten directions. Within each and every world, regarding all the Buddhas who have already entered parinirvāṇa—from their first generation of the mind of awakening until their unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and even further, from after they have entered the realm of nirvana without remainder until the final extinction of their True Dharma—in the interval between these times, there are roots of virtue associated with the six perfections, as well as roots of virtue associated with the infinite, countless, and boundless Buddha-dharmas, whether shared or unshared, belonging to śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and all sentient beings.”
Whatever meritorious deeds consisting of giving, ethical discipline, and cultivation performed by those ordinary disciples;
whatever untainted roots of virtue belonging to those śrāvaka disciples in the stages of training and beyond-training;

and the aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation achieved by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as well as the immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless Buddha-dharmas of great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity for the sake of benefiting and gladdening all sentient beings.

And as for the true Dharma taught by those Buddhas, if one diligently studies and practices in accordance with that Dharma, one may attain the fruit of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship; or attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; or enter the bodhisattva’s state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*); or cultivate the conduct of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Thus, all these roots of goodness, as well as the roots of goodness planted by other sentient beings toward the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, Śrāvakas, and Bodhisattvas—whether they currently dwell in the world or have entered parinirvāṇa—I now rejoice in them all collectively, bringing them before me.

Having thus rejoiced, he further dedicates all these meritorious deeds associated with such rejoicing to be shared equally with all sentient beings for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, wishing that these roots of virtue may together bring forth unsurpassed bodhi for all sentient beings.

This rejoicing and dedication thus generated is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the highest, the most sublime, the most exquisite, the superior, the unsurpassed, the peerless, and the equal to the unequaled among all other meritorious deeds that have been generated.
What do you think?

Regarding those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, based on such matters, give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy and dedication—can such objects of focus be apprehended in the same way as the characteristics grasped by those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?
The Bodhisattva Maitreya replied to Subhūti:

“When those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy and dedication based on such objects, there is in reality no such object to be apprehended as the mark grasped by those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.”
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti said to the Bodhisattva Maitreya:

"If there were no objective referent corresponding to the marks as they are grasped, then how could that bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of the mind of sympathetic joy and dedication—which employs the grasping of marks as its expedient—universally take as its object the infinite, countless, and boundless worlds of the ten directions; and within each world, all the roots of goodness of the infinite, countless, and boundless Buddhas who have already entered parinirvāṇa, from their first generation of the mind until the extinction of their Dharma, as well as all the roots of goodness of their disciples and others, and having gathered them all together, manifest before him sympathetic joy and dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
Is this rejoicing and dedication that has thus arisen not, in fact, a perversion?

Just as to regard the impermanent as permanent, suffering as pleasure, the non-self as self, and the impure as pure constitutes a perversion of perception, mind, and view—so too should it be understood for this taking of signs where there are no signs.

Just as the object of focus does not exist in reality, so too is the mind of sympathetic joy and dedication; so too are all roots of virtue; so too is unsurpassed enlightenment; and so too are the six perfections beginning with generosity, up to and including the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

If, as it is said, the objects of focus are in reality non-existent, and if the mind of sympathetic joy and dedication is likewise—extending even to the knowledge of all aspects—then what are these objects of focus?
What is this matter?
What is the mind of sympathetic joy and dedication?
To speak at length, up to: what is the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)?
"And how does that bodhisattva mahāsattva, taking such matters as an object, give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy and dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Maitreya replied to the Venerable Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva has long studied the six perfections, has already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, has long since made great vows and planted many roots of virtue, has been sustained by many spiritual friends, and has well studied that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty—then this bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding the objects of focus, the mind of sympathetic joy and the act of dedication, the various roots of virtue, unsurpassed enlightenment, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and all phenomena, does not grasp at their marks, yet is able to give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy and dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Such rejoicing and dedication as thus arisen are accomplished by means of that which is neither dual nor non-dual; by means of that which is neither with signs nor signless; by means of that which is neither obtainable nor unobtainable; by means of that which is neither defiled nor pure; and by means of that which is neither arising nor ceasing. Regarding the objects of focus, up to and including unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they are able not to grasp at signs; because they do not grasp at signs, they are not subsumed under perversion.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva has not yet long practiced the six perfections, has never made offerings to immeasurable buddhas, has not long since generated the great resolve, has not extensively planted roots of goodness, has not been sustained by many virtuous friends, and has not well studied the self-characteristic emptiness of all phenomena, then that bodhisattva mahāsattva—regarding the objects of focus, the activities, the mind of sympathetic joy and dedication, the various roots of goodness, unexcelled enlightenment, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and all phenomena—still grasps at their signs and gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy, dedicating it toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Such rejoicing and dedication as has arisen, because it involves grasping at signs, is still subsumed under perversion; it is not the mind of true rejoicing and dedication.
"Furthermore, Venerable Sir!

One should not, for the sake of those newly trained bodhisattvas of the Mahāyāna nor in their presence, proclaim the meaning of the emptiness of intrinsic characteristics regarding the perfections from *prajñā* down to *dāna*, as well as other Buddha-dharmas.

Why is this? Although those bodhisattvas who have newly set out in the Mahāyāna possess a small measure of faith, reverence, and affection for such teachings, upon hearing them they immediately forget them all; they become startled, terrified, and doubtful, and for the most part give rise to slander.

If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is non-retrogressive, who has made offerings to immeasurable buddhas in the past, who has long since made great vows, who has planted many roots of virtue, and who is sustained by many virtuous friends, one should, in their presence, extensively explain, analyze, and reveal for them the meaning of the self-characteristic emptiness (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) of all the perfections from *prajñāpāramitā* down to *dānapāramitā*, as well as other qualities of the Buddha.

Why is this? Because all bodhisattvas who have attained the stage of non-retrogression, upon hearing this Dharma, are able to receive and uphold it without ever forgetting it, nor do they feel alarm, fear, doubt, or slander.
“Virtuous One, you should know that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should dedicate these meritorious deeds accompanied by such sympathetic joy toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
At that time, one should form this thought:

"The mind that is employed for rejoicing and dedication—this mind is subject to exhaustion, cessation, detachment, and change. The objects of focus and all these roots of goodness are likewise, like the mind, subject to exhaustion, cessation, detachment, and change. Within this, what is the 'mind that is employed'?"
Furthermore, by means of what objects of focus and what roots of goodness does one speak of sympathetic joy and dedication toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment?

This mind cannot have sympathetic joy or dedication within the mind itself, because two minds do not arise simultaneously; nor can the mind itself be the object of sympathetic joy or dedication, because the intrinsic nature of the mind is empty.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they are able to know that all the *pāramitās*, from *prajñā* down to *dāna*, are non-existent, and so on extensively until one knows that even the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is non-existent. Although this bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are non-existent, they are nevertheless able to dedicate with the mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) all meritorious deeds to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). Such a mind of sympathetic joy and dedication is not subsumed by perversion, because it employs the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*); therefore, it is called true sympathetic joy and dedication to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 504; The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 505.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
The Ninth Chapter, Part Two: The Dedication of Rejoicing.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:
"When bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have newly set out in the Great Vehicle hear such a teaching as this, will their minds not be struck with alarm, fear, or doubt?"
How should the newly trained bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have set out in the Mahāyāna dedicate the roots of goodness they have cultivated toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
How should they embrace the various meritorious deeds accompanied by sympathetic joy and dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
Then, the Venerable Subhūti addressed Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, saying:

“Newly initiated bodhisattva mahāsattvas who practice the veneration of the perfection of wisdom, and so forth, up to all-aspect omniscience, should embrace the perfection of wisdom, and so forth, up to all-aspect omniscience, by means of the expedient of non-apprehension and the expedient of signlessness.”

By virtue of these causes and conditions, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to generate profound conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding the meaning of the emptiness of intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) of the *prajñāpāramitā*, up to and including the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). They are constantly sustained by spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), who, through immeasurable methods and skillful words and meanings, explain for them the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and the teachings associated with it, up to and including the knowledge of all aspects. Through such instructions and exhortations, they cause them to eventually enter the bodhisattva’s state of certainty (*samyaktvaniyāma*).

Even before entering the bodhisattva’s state of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*), they shall never be separated from the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, up to and including the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); furthermore, they shall explain the various deeds of Māra so that, upon hearing them, their minds will neither increase nor diminish in regard to those demonic activities.
Why is this? Because the nature of all demonic activities is non-existent and cannot be apprehended.

Furthermore, by instructing and admonishing them with these teachings, they are led to enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*), never being separated from the Buddhas. Having planted various roots of goodness in the presence of those Buddhas, and because they are sustained by those roots of goodness, they are always born into the family of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and until they reach unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they shall never be separated from those roots of goodness.

“Kauśika! If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have newly set out in the Mahāyāna can, by means of the expedient of non-apprehension and the expedient of signlessness, gather all merits and develop a profound resolute belief in those merits; if they are constantly sustained by virtuous friends and, upon hearing such a teaching, their minds are not startled, terrified, nor do they harbor doubt—[they shall attain this].”
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

All bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have newly set out in the Great Vehicle, in whatever they cultivate and accumulate—from the six perfections beginning with generosity, as explained at length, up to all-aspect omniscience—all should take non-apprehension as their means and signlessness as their means, and dedicate these together with all sentient beings equally toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Kauśika, all the Tathāgatas, Arhats,
and Samyaksaṃbuddhas throughout the infinite, innumerable, and boundless worlds of the ten directions—
those who have severed the paths of existence and cut off conceptual proliferation— for the sake of the newly trained Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas practicing the Great Vehicle..."
The Teacher— who has cast off all heavy burdens, destroyed the thorns of the village, exhausted all fetters of existence, is fully endowed with right knowledge, whose mind is well-liberated,
and who is skilled in expounding the Dharma— and his disciples’ accomplishment of the aggregate of morality,
the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation, as well as other [qualities].
Having performed various meritorious deeds and planted roots of goodness in these places— namely,
the roots of goodness planted by great kṣatriya clans up to great householder clans,
as well as the roots of goodness planted by the gods of the Four Great Kings up to the Śuddhāvāsa heavens— all such things are gathered together, weighed, and brought before him.
He generates a mind of sympathetic joy that, compared to other roots of goodness, is the most supreme, the most excellent,
the most honored, the highest, the most sublime, the most exquisite, the superior, the unsurpassed, the peerless, and the equal to the unequaled; furthermore,
he shares with all sentient beings equally all those meritorious deeds associated with such sympathetic joy.
"and dedicate it toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Maitreya asked the Venerable Subhūti:

"If newly initiated bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have set out in the Great Vehicle, recollecting all the merits of the Tathāgatas and their disciples, as well as the roots of goodness planted by humans, devas, and others—collecting and weighing all such things before them and generating a mind of sympathetic joy (anumodanā) that regards these as superior to other roots of goodness—and furthermore, sharing these roots of goodness born of sympathetic joy equally with all sentient beings and dedicating them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment: how does this bodhisattva mahāsattva avoid falling into errors of perception, mind, and view?"
The Venerable Subhūti replied, “Great Being!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva,
regarding the merits of the Buddhas they recollect and their disciples, does not give rise to the conceptualization of ‘Buddhas,’ ‘disciples,’ or ‘merits’;”
Regarding the roots of goodness planted among humans, devas, and others, they do not give rise to the notion of "roots of goodness," nor the notion of "humans," "devas," and so forth;

regarding the mind of great enlightenment that they initiate through sympathetic joy and dedication, they likewise do not give rise to the notion of "sympathetic joy" or "dedication toward enlightenment. Thus, the mind of sympathetic joy and dedication initiated by this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not fall into errors of notion, mind, or view.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding the merits of the Buddhas and their disciples whom they bring to mind, grasps at the marks of those Buddhas, disciples, and merits;
regarding the roots of goodness planted by humans, devas, and others, grasps at the marks of those roots of goodness, humans, devas, and so forth;

and regarding the mind of sympathetic joy and dedication toward great enlightenment that they have generated, grasps at the marks of that generated mind of sympathetic joy, dedication, and enlightenment—then the mind of sympathetic joy and dedication produced by this bodhisattva mahāsattva falls into the perversions of perception, mind, and view.
"Furthermore, Great Being!

If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, with such a mind, recollects the merits and roots of goodness of all Buddhas and their disciples, he correctly knows that this mind is subject to exhaustion, cessation, detachment, and transformation, and thus cannot be the agent of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*); he correctly knows that those dharmas are likewise by nature such that they are not the objects of sympathetic joy; furthermore, he correctly realizes that the nature of the mind capable of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) is also thus and cannot be the agent of dedication, and he correctly realizes that the nature of the dharmas to be dedicated is also thus and cannot be the object of dedication."
If there are those who can rely upon this aforementioned rejoicing and dedication, which is correct and not erroneous, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should likewise rejoice and dedicate in this manner.
"Furthermore, Great Being!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva universally [regards] all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, throughout the three periods of time—from their first generation of the mind of awakening until they attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and even until the extinction of the Dharma—with respect to all the merit therein; as well as the roots of goodness arising from that Buddha's Dharma by his disciples and the various pratyekabuddhas; the roots of goodness planted by ordinary beings upon hearing his teaching of the Dharma; the roots of goodness planted by nāgas, devas, asuras, and others upon hearing his teaching of the Dharma; and the roots of goodness planted by great kṣatriya clans, up to great householder clans, upon hearing his teaching of the Dharma;"

If those from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven hear that teaching of the Dharma and plant roots of goodness therein; or if sons and daughters of good family, upon hearing that teaching of the Dharma, resolve their minds toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and diligently cultivate the various practices of a bodhisattva.

Having thus gathered all these together and weighed them before one, one gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) that regards this as superior to other roots of goodness; furthermore, one dedicates these roots of goodness of sympathetic joy to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), sharing them equally with all sentient beings.

At such a time, if one correctly understands that all dharmas which can be rejoiced in and dedicated are subject to cessation, detachment, and transformation, and that the intrinsic nature of all dharmas of rejoicing and dedication is empty, then even while knowing this, one is able to rejoice in and dedicate [merit] toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, at that time, if one correctly understands that there is no dharma whatsoever that can be rejoiced in or dedicated toward a dharma.

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is empty; within emptiness, there is absolutely no dharma that can act as the agent of rejoicing or dedication, nor any dharma that is the object thereof.
Although they know this, they are able to rejoice in it and dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can thus rejoice and dedicate, practicing the perfection of wisdom—extensively explained up to the knowledge of all aspects—they will not fall into errors of perception, mind, or view.

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not give rise to attachment toward the mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) or the roots of merit and virtue that are the object of that joy; nor do they give rise to attachment toward the mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) or the unsurpassed awakening (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) to which it is dedicated. By being without attachment, they do not fall into error. Thus, the mind of sympathetic joy and dedication generated by such a bodhisattva is called "unsurpassed sympathetic joy and dedication," as it is far removed from all false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
"Furthermore, Great Being!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding the various meritorious deeds they perform, understands them as they truly are—being detached from the aggregates (*skandha*), sense bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), and likewise detached from the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) as extensively explained up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)—then that bodhisattva mahāsattva, having understood the various meritorious deeds they perform in this way, is able to correctly rejoice in them and dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Great Being! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva understands,
as it truly is, that the various meritorious deeds accompanied by sympathetic joy are devoid of a self-nature associated with those meritorious deeds accompanied by sympathetic joy,
and that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are devoid of [a self-nature associated with] the Buddhas..."
The intrinsic nature of the Bhagavat is devoid of the intrinsic nature of merit and roots of goodness;
the intrinsic nature of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and ordinary beings is devoid of the intrinsic nature of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and ordinary beings;
and the mind of sympathetic joy and dedication toward great enlightenment is devoid of the intrinsic nature of the mind of sympathetic joy and dedication toward great enlightenment.
Intrinsic nature: the bodhisattva mahāsattva is devoid of the intrinsic nature of a bodhisattva mahāsattva;
the perfection of wisdom up to the knowledge of all aspects is devoid of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom up to the knowledge of all aspects;
and all bodhisattva mahāsattva practices are devoid of all bodhisattvas.

The intrinsic nature of the practice of a mahāsattva is remote from the intrinsic nature of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas; when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way,
being detached from intrinsic nature, it is called the true practice of the profound perfection of wisdom.
One is able to correctly rejoice in and dedicate [these merits] toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Furthermore, Great Being!

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas wish to arouse a mind that rejoices in and dedicates toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment the roots of virtue and merit of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their disciples who have already entered parinirvāṇa, they should perform such rejoicing and dedication by forming this thought:

"Just as all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their disciples have already entered parinirvāṇa and are non-existent by nature, so too are their merits and roots of goodness. The mind of mine that has been generated for sympathetic joy and dedicated toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, and the unexcelled enlightenment toward which it is dedicated, are likewise of such a nature."

Having understood this, one gives rise to sympathetic joy toward all roots of goodness and dedicates them to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; thus, one will be able to avoid giving rise to errors of perception, thought, or view.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom by means of grasping at signs, and takes up signs regarding the meritorious roots of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, who have already entered parinirvāṇa, as well as their disciples, and rejoices in them and dedicates them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, this is not a wholesome rejoicing or dedication.

Because the merit and roots of goodness of the past Buddhas and their disciples are not objects to be grasped through signs or signlessness, yet this bodhisattva mahāsattva generates sympathetic joy and dedicates it toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment by grasping at signs; therefore, this is not a skillful dedication of sympathetic joy, and by means of this, they fall into the perversions of perception, mind, and view.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* by means of non-apprehension of signs, and rejoices in and dedicates toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment the roots of virtue and merit of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, who have already entered parinirvāṇa, as well as their disciples—doing so while remaining free from signs—this is called "skillful rejoicing and dedication. By this, one does not fall into perversions of perception, mind, or view.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Maitreya asked the Venerable Subhūti:

"How is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, without apprehending any signs regarding the meritorious roots and the bases of meritorious action associated with rejoicing in the qualities of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their assemblies of disciples, is nevertheless able to rejoice and dedicate [that merit] toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"

Subhūti replied, “One should know that the Prajñāpāramitā in which Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train possesses such skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) that, although they do not grasp at signs, their activities are accomplished. It is not apart from the Prajñāpāramitā that one is able to correctly initiate meritorious deeds accompanied by sympathetic joy (*anumodanā-sahagata*) and dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
Therefore, the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to accomplish what is to be done should study the perfection of wisdom.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva Maitreya said: “Venerable Subhūti!
Do not speak thus. Why is this?

Because within the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, their disciples, and the roots of merit and virtue they have accomplished are all non-existent and unapprehendable; likewise, the various meritorious deeds performed with sympathetic joy and the resolve for dedication toward unsurpassed enlightenment are also non-existent and unapprehendable.
In this regard, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they should contemplate in this way:

"The nature of the merits and roots of goodness of the past Buddhas and their assemblies of disciples has already ceased; the nature of the meritorious deeds performed with sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) and the resolve for dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) toward unsurpassed enlightenment is entirely quiescent. If I were to grasp at signs and engage in conceptual discrimination regarding those merits and roots of goodness of the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, and their disciples, or if I were to grasp at signs and engage in conceptual discrimination regarding the meritorious deeds accompanied by sympathetic joy and the resolve for dedication toward unsurpassed enlightenment, then by employing such means of grasping at signs and conceptual discrimination to generate sympathetic joy and dedication toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, it would be disapproved by all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones."

Why is this? To take up signs and engage in conceptual discrimination regarding the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, and their disciples who have already entered parinirvāṇa, and then to rejoice in and dedicate [the merit] toward unsurpassed bodhi—this is called having great attainment.

Therefore, when the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wishes to correctly generate sympathetic joy and dedicate toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment the merits and roots of goodness of the Tathāgatas and their disciples, they should not, within that process, give rise to conceptualizations of grasping at signs based on the apprehension of something obtainable. If they were to give rise to such conceptualizations of grasping at signs based on the apprehension of something obtainable while generating sympathetic joy and dedicating, the Buddha would say that they do not possess great benefit or profit.
Why is this? Because such a mind of sympathetic joy and dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) is called "mixed with poison" due to its conceptualization and discrimination.

It is like food and drink that, though endowed with excellent color, fragrance, and flavor, is mixed with poisonous medicine; a person of shallow understanding greedily takes it and eats it. Although it is pleasing at first, bringing joy and happiness, when the food is digested later, one undergoes manifold sufferings, or even dies, or nearly loses one's life.

In this way, a certain class of individuals does not properly uphold or properly examine the words and meanings of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*; they do not properly recite it nor properly penetrate its profound significance, yet they say to those of the Mahāyāna lineage: "Come!..."

"Good son! Regarding all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the three periods of time—from their first generation of the mind of awakening until they attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; from their turning of the sublime wheel of Dharma and their deliverance of the multitudes of sentient beings, through their entry into the realm of nirvana without remainder, up until the extinction of the Dharma—in the interval between these events, there are roots of goodness accumulated, yet to be accumulated, and currently being accumulated through the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom, and so forth, up to the knowledge of all aspects; as well as roots of goodness accumulated, yet to be accumulated, and currently being accumulated through the maturing of sentient beings and the purification of Buddha-fields."

Whatever aggregates of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation possessed by all Tathāgatas, as well as their other immeasurable and boundless qualities; whatever roots of merit, whether with outflows or without outflows, possessed by the disciples of the Buddha; whatever qualities of the awakening of a Pratyekabuddha possessed by gods, humans, and others who have been, are being, or will be predicted for parinirvāṇa by the Tathāgatas; and whatever roots of merit have been accumulated, will be accumulated, or are currently being accumulated by gods, nāgas, asuras, and others—if a son or daughter of good family generates sympathetic joy toward these qualities and dedicates those roots of merit, [they shall attain the supreme enlightenment].

Thus, having gathered all these together and weighed them before oneself, one rejoices and dedicates them equally and in common with all sentient beings toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"The rejoicing and dedication thus described employ the conceptualization of signs and the grasping of attainments as their means.
This is like worldly food mixed with poison, which brings benefit at first but harm later; therefore, this is not a wholesome rejoicing and dedication."

Why is this? Because if one generates a mind of sympathetic joy and dedication by apprehending signs through grasping at attainments, there will be causes, conditions, mental engagements, and conceptual proliferation; such is not in accordance with the perfection of wisdom.

Because it is mixed with poison, it constitutes a slander against the Buddha; it does not follow the Buddha’s teaching nor is it a discourse in accordance with the Dharma. A person belonging to the bodhisattva lineage should not study according to what such a person says.
"Therefore, Venerable One,

you should explain how sons of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva Vehicle should rejoice in and dedicate the roots of goodness and merits of all Buddhas and their disciples throughout the three times and the ten directions."

That is to say, from the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment until the extinction of the Dharma, whatever roots of goodness those Buddhas cultivated during that interval—ranging from the perfection of wisdom up to the knowledge of all aspects—and likewise, whatever roots of goodness sons and daughters of good family generate through sympathetic joy toward those merits and dedicate toward awakening: how do those sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle generate sympathetic joy toward those roots of goodness and merit and dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The Venerable Subhūti replied to the Bodhisattva Maitreya:

“Good sons and good daughters who abide in the vehicle of the bodhisattvas and practice the profound perfection of wisdom, wishing not to slander the Buddha but to generate a mind of sympathetic joy and dedication, should form this thought:

‘Just as the Tathāgatas, through their unsurpassed buddha-wisdom, have thoroughly realized and fully known that these roots of virtue and merits possess such a nature, such characteristics, and such qualities that they may be rejoiced in, so too should I now rejoice.’”

Just as the Tathāgatas, with their unsurpassed Buddha-wisdom, have thoroughly understood and fully known how these various meritorious deeds should be dedicated toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, so too shall I now dedicate them in this same way.

“Sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle should, regarding the roots of goodness and merit of all Tathāgatas and their disciples, perform such rejoicing and dedication. If they perform such rejoicing and dedication, they do not slander the Buddha; they follow the Buddha’s instructions and speak in accordance with the Dharma.”
This mind of sympathetic joy and dedication of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is unmixed with various poisons and is able to reach the ultimate.
"Furthermore, Great Being!

All sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle and practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* should, regarding the roots of virtue and merit of all Tathāgatas and their disciples, perform such rejoicing and dedication.
Just as the aggregates such as form do not fall within the three realms and are not subsumed by the three times, so too should one’s sympathetic joy and dedication be.

To speak at length, even up to omniscience, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects—which do not fall within the three realms and are not subsumed by the three times—so too should one’s sympathetic joy and dedication be.

Just as the aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation do not fall within the three realms and are not subsumed by the three times, so too should one’s sympathetic joy and dedication be.

Why is this? Because those dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*), they do not fall within the three realms and are not subsumed by the three times; sympathetic joy and dedication are likewise so. That is to say, because the intrinsic nature of all Tathāgatas is empty, they do not fall within the three realms and are not subsumed by the three times;
because the intrinsic nature of the merits of all Buddhas is empty, they do not fall within the three realms and are not subsumed by the three times.
Because the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, humans, devas, and so forth are empty of intrinsic nature, they do not fall within the three realms and are not subsumed by the three times;
because those roots of goodness are empty of intrinsic nature, they do not fall within the three realms and are not subsumed by the three times;
because the rejoicing in them is empty of intrinsic nature, it does not fall within the three realms and is not subsumed by the three times.
Because the dharmas to which one dedicates are empty of intrinsic nature, they do not fall within the three realms and are not subsumed by the three periods of time;
because the one who is able to dedicate is empty of intrinsic nature, they also do not fall within the three realms and are not subsumed by the three periods of time.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they understand as it truly is that the phenomena of the five aggregates and so forth do not fall within the three realms and are not subsumed by the three times. Since they do not fall within the three realms and are not subsumed by the three times, one cannot, by means of signs or by means of apprehension, generate rejoicing and dedicate [merit] toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Why is this? Because the dharmas such as the aggregates are unarisen by their own nature; if a dharma is unarisen, it is non-existent. Since one cannot rejoice in a non-existent dharma and dedicate that which is non-existent toward that which is non-existent, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva thus rejoices and dedicates toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, it is unmixed with any poisons and can reach the ultimate goal.

If sons or daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle employ the method of conceptual signs (*nimitta*) or the method of grasping at attainment (*upalambha*) to generate a mind of sympathetic joy and dedication toward the roots of goodness and merit of the Tathāgatas and their disciples, you should know that this is a perverted sympathetic joy and dedication. Such a perverted mind of sympathetic joy and dedication is not praised by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

Because such a mind of sympathetic joy and dedication is not praised by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, it cannot bring to fulfillment the six perfections, such as generosity, and so forth, up to and including the inability to fulfill all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Because their various merits are not yet perfected, they are unable to adorn and purify buddha-fields or bring sentient beings to maturity; because they are unable to adorn and purify buddha-fields or bring sentient beings to maturity, they do not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Why is this? Because the rejoicing and dedication arising from that are characterized by signs and grasping, being mixed with various poisons.
"Furthermore, Great Being!"
When all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they should form this thought:

"Just as all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas in the realms of the ten directions have, through their realization of reality, attained such dharmas of merit and roots of goodness that one may, by relying on these dharmas, generate unerring sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) and dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), so too should I now rely on such dharmas to generate sympathetic joy and dedicate [the merit] toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

"This is what constitutes the correct arousal of sympathetic joy and dedication; by means of this, one will certainly realize unsurpassed bodhi and be able to deliver the multitudes of sentient beings until the end of the future.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Subhūti, saying: "Excellent!"

Excellent! You have now performed a great Buddha-work for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; that is to say, you have skillfully taught the non-erroneous rejoicing and dedication for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. This teaching on rejoicing and dedication employs as its means the signless, the non-attainment, the unborn and undying, the unstained and unpurified, the absence of nature and intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of self-characteristic; it also employs as its means True Suchness, the Dharma-realm, the Dharma-nature, and so forth, up to the inconceivable realm.

“Subhūti, you should know that even if all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were to achieve the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless absorptions, and the five supernormal powers;”
"What do you think?
Is the merit of these sentient beings great or not? Subhūti replied:
“Very much so,
World-Honored One!
Very much so!”
“Excellent, Sugata! The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If good sons or good daughters give rise to unattached sympathetic joy toward the roots of virtue and merits of all Tathāgatas and their disciples, and dedicate them [toward enlightenment], the merit they obtain will be far greater than the former.”
