"Subhūti, you should know that this rejoicing and dedication generated by these sons and daughters of good family is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the most exalted, the most wondrous, the most subtle, the highest, and the unsurpassed among all other roots of virtue; it is peerless and equal to the unequaled."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose all sentient beings in a trichiliocosm were to attain the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, and pratyekabuddha-enlightenment. If some sons or daughters of good family were to provide all manner of offerings to those stream-enterers up to the pratyekabuddhas for as long as they lived, honoring, revering, respecting, and praising them."
"What do you think?
By reason of this, would those sons or daughters of good family acquire much merit? Subhūti replied:
“Very much so,
World-Honored One!
Very much so!”
“Excellent, Sugata! The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If a son of good family or a daughter of good family should give rise to a non-attached sympathetic joy and dedicate it toward the roots of virtue and merits of all Tathāgatas and their disciples, the merit obtained will be far greater than the former.”

"Subhūti, you should know that the rejoicing and dedication thus performed by these sons and daughters of good family is the most supreme and excellent among all other roots of virtue," and so forth, as extensively explained.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were to set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. And suppose there were as many sentient beings in each of the ten directions as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and one were to offer them all various articles of worship and provide them with gifts, for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, honoring, revering, respecting, and praising them. What do you think?"
“By this cause and condition, would those sentient beings acquire much merit? Subhūti replied, “Very much!”
"World-Honored One!
It is very much so! Sugata!"
“If this mass of merit were to have a physical form, the worlds of the ten directions, each as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, would not be able to contain it.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
"So it is! It is as you have said.
Subhūti, you should know this!"

If good sons and good daughters, regarding the roots of goodness and meritorious virtues of all Tathāgatas and their disciples, give rise to non-attached sympathetic joy and dedicate them toward enlightenment, the merit they obtain will be far greater than the former.

"Subhūti, you should know that the rejoicing and dedication thus performed by these sons and daughters of good family is the most supreme and excellent among all other roots of virtue," and so forth, as extensively explained.

Subhūti, you should know that if one were to compare the former mass of merit with this subsequent virtue, the former would not equal even a hundredth part of the latter; it would not equal a thousandth part, nor even a *upaniṣad* (fractional) part.

Why is this? Because those classes of sentient beings [practice] the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, and so forth, by employing the means of having signs (*sanimitta*) and apprehending something (*upalambha*).

Those sons and daughters of good family who offer various articles of worship to those ranging from stream-enterers up to those who have set out for great enlightenment do so by means of signs and the apprehension of objects.
At that time, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, each accompanied by thirty-two thousand sons of gods from their retinues, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined their palms in reverence, and said:
“World-Honored One!

Those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are indeed able to initiate such vast sympathetic joy and dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). That is to say, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, through their skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), employing the methods of signlessness (*animitta*), non-apprehensibility (*anupalambha*), non-attachment (*asaṅga*), and non-conceptualization (*anabhisaṃskāra*), initiate unerring sympathetic joy and dedication toward the roots of goodness and merits of all Tathāgatas and their disciples. Such sympathetic joy and dedication as they initiate does not fall into either duality (*dvaya-dharma*) or non-duality (*advaya-dharma*).

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, along with Suyāma, Santuṣita, Sunirmita, and Vaśavartin, each accompanied by hundreds of thousands of their retinues of devaputras, all carrying various celestial and exquisite flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses, robes, necklaces, jeweled banners, pennants, parasols, and many wonderful and rare treasures, played celestial music to make offerings to the Buddha.
Prostrating at his feet and joining their palms, they addressed him, saying:

"Those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are indeed able to initiate such vast sympathetic joy and dedication—that is to say, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, through skillful means, employing the methods of signlessness, non-apprehensibility, non-attachment, and non-conceptualization, initiate unerring sympathetic joy and dedication toward the roots of virtue and merit of all Tathāgatas and their disciples. This sympathetic joy and dedication thus initiated does not fall into either dualistic or non-dualistic phenomena."

At that time, the Great Brahmā King, along with the Ābhāsvara Heaven, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, the Bṛhatphala Heaven, and the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, each accompanied by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of celestial beings, approached the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated at his feet, and with palms joined in reverence, spoke in unison:
“How extraordinary! How rare!”

"Bhagavān! Because those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are embraced by the skillful means of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they surpass the roots of goodness cultivated by those sons of good family who previously lacked skillful means and who possessed signs and apprehension."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the gods of the Four Great Kings up to those of the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, saying:
"Suppose all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were to set out for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment;
and suppose they were to [serve] all Tathāgatas throughout the past, future, and present in all the worlds of the ten directions from their very first..."
From the initial generation of the mind of awakening until the endurance of the Dharma, all the roots of virtue associated with the perfection of generosity—
and so forth, up to the perfection of all-aspect wisdom— that are cultivated during that interval; as well as all the roots of virtue belonging to the disciples,
and the aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, and liberation belonging to the Tathāgatas.
The aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation, as well as the other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas; the true Dharma taught by the Tathāgatas;
the three types of meritorious action consisting of generosity, ethical discipline, and cultivation practiced in reliance upon that Dharma;
and the diligent training in accordance with that Dharma which results in the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning...
Furthermore, [the merit] of returning to the fruit of arhatship, the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha,
or entering the bodhisattva’s state of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*), as well as all the roots of virtue produced by sentient beings through practicing generosity,
pure ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom— if all these were gathered together and weighed, they would be surpassed by that which possesses—
With signs, with apprehension, with attachment, with volitional effort, and with duality and non-duality as skillful means, they manifest sympathetic joy;
having thus rejoiced, they dedicate [the merit] toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

“Suppose there are sons or daughters of good family who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Regarding all the roots of virtue associated with the perfection of giving cultivated by all Tathāgatas throughout the ten directions—in the past, future, and present—from their first generation of the mind of awakening until the endurance of the Dharma; and so on, as extensively explained, including all the roots of virtue produced by sentient beings through practicing generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—having gathered and weighed all such things together, they manifest sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) by means of the signless, the non-apprehensible, the unstained, the non-conceptual, and the non-dual and non-non-dual. Having thus rejoiced, they dedicate [the merit] toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

These sons and daughters of good family, through their sympathetic joy and dedication, are the most supreme and excellent among all other roots of virtue, and so forth, as extensively explained; they are a hundred times more excellent than the sympathetic joy and dedication previously directed toward sentient beings, a thousand times more excellent, and even up to an *upaniṣad*-fold more excellent.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

"As the Buddha has taught, the rejoicing and dedication performed by these sons and daughters of good family is the most supreme among all other roots of goodness," and so forth, as extensively described.
“For what reason is this rejoicing and dedication said to be the most excellent among all other roots of goodness?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“These sons of good family and daughters of good family, regarding all the roots of goodness of all Tathāgatas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and all other sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions in the past, future, and present—neither grasping nor rejecting them, neither being conceited nor disparaging them; neither having anything attained nor having nothing attained—they realize that all phenomena are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity, without increase and without decrease, without going and without coming, without accumulation and without dispersion, and without entering and without exiting. They form this thought:”

"Just as the true suchness, the dharma-realm, and so forth, up to the inconceivable realm of the dharmas of the three periods of time, I likewise, by means of non-apprehension, rejoice in and dedicate all wholesome dharmas."

"Subhūti! Regarding this arising of sympathetic joy and dedication, I declare it to be the most excellent and so forth among other roots of virtue. Such sympathetic joy and dedication is superior to other instances of sympathetic joy and dedication by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and even up to an *upaniṣad*-fold. Therefore, I declare that this arising of sympathetic joy and dedication is the most excellent and so forth among other roots of virtue."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Those sons of good family or daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle, and who wish to, with respect to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions throughout the three times—from their first production of the thought of awakening until the duration of the Dharma—[consider] the roots of goodness associated with the practice of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom during that interval; and so forth, including the immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless Buddha-dharmas; as well as the roots of goodness and merits of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas; and all other sentient beings' three types of meritorious actions consisting of giving, morality, and cultivation, along with their other roots of goodness—all such things, having collected and weighed them together, they should now give rise to a mind of unerring sympathetic joy and dedication, thinking thus:"
"Form through to consciousness are equal to liberation; as explained at length, even up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is equal to liberation;
the five aggregates beginning with the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*) are equal to liberation; the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding all phenomena is equal to liberation;
and the Buddhas of the three times are equal to liberation, as are all phenomena of the three times."
Liberation and so forth are equal to all rejoicings and dedications;
the maturation of the faculties of the Buddhas, their disciples, and the pratyekabuddhas is equal to liberation;
the nirvāṇa attained by the Buddhas, their disciples, and the pratyekabuddhas is equal to liberation; [and] the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, and śrāvakas...
One hears that the dharma-nature of all phenomena is equal to liberation; that all sentient beings, all phenomena, and their respective dharma-natures are equally equal to liberation;

and that, like the dharma-nature of all phenomena, there is neither bondage nor liberation, neither defilement nor purity, neither arising nor ceasing, neither birth nor extinction, and neither grasping nor relinquishing.

I rejoice in these roots of merit and virtuous qualities as they manifest before me; I take these roots of merit and share them equally with all sentient beings, dedicating them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Such rejoicing and dedication are not an act of rejoicing or dedication, because there is nothing to rejoice in and no object to which one dedicates. Thus, the rejoicing and dedication thus generated neither proceed nor cease, for they are without arising or ceasing.

"Subhūti! This rejoicing and dedication by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is the most supreme and excellent among all other rejoicings and dedications that have arisen," and so forth, as extensively explained.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such rejoicing and dedication, they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If sons or daughters of good family who have set out upon the Mahāyāna were to, by means of signs and the apprehension of objects, constantly provide various supreme and exquisite offerings, and pay homage, respect, honor, and praise for as long as they live, to all the Tathāgatas and their disciples throughout as many worlds in the ten directions as there are sands in the Ganges, currently existing at this time;

After those Tathāgatas and their assemblies of disciples have entered parinirvāṇa, one takes their śarīra relics and constructs high and vast stūpas made of the seven precious jewels; day and night, with diligent devotion, one prostrates, circumambulates to the right, and further offers worship, respect, honor, and praise with various kinds of exquisite flower garlands, up to lamps and illuminations.

Furthermore, there are sons of good family and daughters of good family who, by employing the means of signs and apprehension, diligently cultivate the perfections from generosity through wisdom, as well as other roots of virtue.

Yet others, having set out in the Great Vehicle, are able to employ the means of signlessness and non-apprehension; they practice the skillful means of roots of virtue associated with the six perfections and, generating sympathetic joy toward all other merits and roots of virtue, they hold these roots of virtue in common with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

These sons and daughters of good family, by means of their skillful means in relying upon the *prajñāpāramitā* for sympathetic rejoicing and dedication, surpass the merit performed by the aforementioned sons and daughters of good family who have set out in the Mahāyāna, by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and even up to an *upaniṣad*-fold.
Therefore, it is said that such rejoicing and dedication are the most supreme among all other roots of virtue.

"For this reason, Subhūti, bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have set out in the Great Vehicle should, by means of the signless and the non-apprehensible, diligently cultivate roots of virtue associated with the perfections from generosity through the perfection of wisdom; and by relying on the skillful means of the perfection of wisdom, they should generate unerring rejoicing and dedication toward the roots of virtue and merits of all Tathāgatas and their disciples."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to employ the signless and the non-apprehensible as skillful means for sympathetic joy and dedication, that bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and will be able to bring benefit and happiness to all beings throughout the future.
Chapter Ten: The Hell Section, Part Three, Section One of the Hell Section. At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is able to provide illumination because it is ultimately pure;
it should be paid homage to by all humans, devas, and others because it is revered by them;
it is without defilement or attachment because no worldly phenomena can pollute it.
It is far removed from all cataracts of the triple world, for it can eliminate the darkness of afflictions and false views;
it is the foremost leader, for it is most supreme among all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*);
and it can provide security, for it forever severs all terrors, oppressions, and calamities.
It is able to bestow radiance, for it gathers in all sentient beings so that they may attain the five eyes;
it is able to demonstrate the Middle Way, so that those who have lost their way may leave the two extremes behind;
and it is well able to give rise to the knowledge of all-knowledge, forever severing the continuity of all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies.

This is the mother of all these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, for all the Buddha-dharmas cultivated by bodhisattvas arise from her; she is characterized by non-arising and non-ceasing, being empty of intrinsic nature;
she liberates one from all birth and death, being neither permanent nor subject to destruction;
and she serves as a refuge, bestowing the jewels of the Dharma upon all sentient beings.
They are able to perfect the ten powers of a Tathāgata, for they cannot be defeated by any opposing arguments;
they are able to turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma with its three revolutions and twelve aspects, for they have realized that all phenomena are without turning or returning;
they are able to demonstrate the non-erroneous nature of all phenomena, for the self-nature of things is clearly manifest as the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
“Bhagavān! How should all sentient beings abide in this Prajñāpāramitā?
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:

"All classes of sentient beings should abide toward this Prajñāpāramitā as they would toward a Buddha; they should honor, pay homage to, and contemplate the Prajñāpāramitā just as they would honor, pay homage to, and contemplate the Blessed Buddha."
Why is this? Śāriputra!

The Buddha is not different from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and the perfection of wisdom is not different from the Buddha. The Buddha is itself the perfection of wisdom, and the perfection of wisdom is itself the Buddha.
Why is this so? Because all Buddhas, bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, and śrāvakas appear through the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

Furthermore, all the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers in the entire world also appear through the perfection of wisdom.
All the perfections, from the perfection of generosity up to the knowledge of all aspects, likewise appear by means of the perfection of wisdom.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had this thought to himself:
"For what reason and by what cause does Śāriputra now ask the Buddha about this matter?
Then, Śāriputra, knowing his thoughts, addressed him, saying:

“Kauśika! Because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are sustained by this perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they are able, through skillful means (upāya-kauśalya), to gather together and weigh all the merits of the Buddhas of the three times and ten directions—from their first generation of the mind until the endurance of the Dharma—including all the roots of goodness (kuśala-mūla) possessed by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and other sentient beings.

Taking these as a whole, they employ the expedient of signlessness (animitta) and non-apprehensibility (anupalambha) to rejoice in them as they manifest before them. Having rejoiced, they share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi). It is for this reason that you ask about this matter.”
"Furthermore, Kauśika! The perfection of wisdom in which the bodhisattva mahāsattvas train surpasses the perfections from generosity up to meditative concentration by infinite multiples."

Suppose there were a multitude of hundreds of thousands of people born blind, who lacked a pure-eyed guide to lead them well; they would still be unable to approach the right path, let alone reach the great city of abundant joy in the distance!

In this way, these groups of those born blind—the first five perfections—cannot even set out upon the right path of a bodhisattva without the guidance of the pure eye of the perfection of wisdom; how much less could they reach the distant city of omniscience!
"Furthermore, Kauśika, the five pāramitās,
beginning with generosity, must rely upon the prajñāpāramitā to be designated as 'possessing eyes.'"
"Furthermore, because it is embraced by the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), it is called 'reaching the other shore' (pāramitā).
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:
"Is it not the case that the first five perfections also take each other as their head, embracing the remaining five perfections and causing them to reach the other shore?"
"If that is so, for what reason do you alone praise the Prajñāpāramitā as being superior to the other five pāramitās?
Śāriputra replied, "The principle stated by the Lord of Devas should not be so."
Why is this so? It is not by means of the first five perfections that one leads the others to the further shore;

rather, it is through the great power and skillful means of the perfection of wisdom that the other five perfections are embraced, enabling them to reach the further shore swiftly and without attachment.

Therefore, among the aforementioned five types, the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the most exalted, the most sublime, the most subtle, the highest, the unsurpassed, the unequaled, and the equal to the unequaled.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how should bodhisattva-mahāsattvas bring forth the perfection of wisdom?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should bring forth the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of bringing forth form;
they should bring forth the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of bringing forth feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.”
To speak at length, up to: one should bring forth the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of bringing forth all-knowledge;
one should bring forth the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of bringing forth the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects;
one should bring forth the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of bringing forth any phenomena.
Śāriputra asked: "How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva bring forth the perfection of wisdom so as not to bring forth form, up to and including all phenomena?"
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"Because form and all phenomena up to the ultimate are without activity, without arising, without attainment, without destruction, and without intrinsic nature, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of producing form and all phenomena up to the ultimate."
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"With what phenomena do the bodhisattva mahāsattvas thus bring forth the perfection of wisdom in conjunction?"
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“When bodhisattva mahāsattvas thus bring forth the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do not conjoin with any phenomena; because they do not conjoin, it is named the perfection of wisdom.”
Śāriputra asked: “In this Prajñāpāramitā, with what dharmas is it not conjoined?
The Blessed One replied:
"In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not conjoin with wholesome dharmas, nor does it conjoin with unwholesome dharmas;
it does not conjoin with faulty dharmas, nor does it conjoin with faultless dharmas;
it does not conjoin with outflowing dharmas, nor does it conjoin with non-outflowing dharmas."
It does not conjoin with conditioned phenomena, nor does it conjoin with unconditioned phenomena;
it does not conjoin with defiled phenomena, nor does it conjoin with undefiled phenomena;
it does not conjoin with worldly phenomena, nor does it conjoin with supramundane phenomena.
It does not associate with defiled phenomena, nor does it associate with pure phenomena;
it does not associate with the phenomena of birth and death, nor does it associate with the phenomena of nirvāṇa. Why is this?
Śāriputra! Because the profound perfection of wisdom cannot be apprehended in any phenomenon, it cannot be said to be conjoined with such phenomena.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Does this profound perfection of wisdom not also accord with omniscience?"
The Buddha said: "So it is! It is just as you have said."
"The profound *prajñāpāramitā* also does not speak of being conjoined with all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), because therein nothing can be apprehended.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked:
"In what way is the *prajñāpāramitā* neither conjoined with nor apprehensive of all-knowledge?"
The World-Honored One replied:
“In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, there is no union with or attainment of all-knowledge by way of names, marks, or conditioned activities.”
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked:
"How is it that the perfection of wisdom also attains union with all-knowledge?
The Blessed One replied:

“By means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, regarding all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), there is neither receiving nor grasping, neither abiding nor ceasing, neither clinging nor relinquishing, according to its name and characteristics; thus it is attained through union, yet there is no attainment through union.

Regarding all phenomena (*dharmas*) as well, it is likewise: according to their names and characteristics, there is neither receiving nor grasping, neither abiding nor ceasing, neither clinging nor relinquishing; thus they are attained through union, yet there is no attainment through union.”
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How extraordinary!
World-Honored One!”
"How marvelous!
Well-Gone One!

It is because all phenomena are without arising and without cessation, without action and without accomplishment, without attainment and without destruction, and without intrinsic nature, that this Prajñāpāramitā appears in the world. Although there is union and attainment, there is no union and attainment; such a principle is inconceivable, and only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is able to awaken to it and to teach it."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they give rise to such a conception as this:”

"If the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is either conjoined with or not conjoined with all phenomena," such a bodhisattva-mahāsattva both abandons and remains far removed from the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Furthermore, there are causes and conditions by which bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abandon and distance themselves from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). That is to say, when they practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they give rise to this notion:
'The profound perfection of wisdom is non-existent, not real, not solid, and not autonomous.'"
"Such a bodhisattva mahāsattva abandons and distances himself from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva has faith in the profound perfection of wisdom, what dharmas does he not believe in?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva has faith in the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not have faith in form; they do not have faith in feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness; and so on, in detail, up to not having faith in all-knowledge, nor having faith in the knowledge of the paths, nor having faith in the knowledge of all aspects.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva has faith in the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not have faith in form, and so on, up to not having faith in the knowledge of all aspects?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, because they perceive that all form—and, as extensively explained, everything up to all-aspect omniscience—is unapprehendable, although they have faith in the perfection of wisdom, they do not have faith in form—and, as extensively explained, everything up to all-aspect omniscience.”
In this way, Subhūti,
when bodhisattva mahāsattvas place their faith in the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not place faith in form, nor indeed in anything up to all-aspect omniscience.

At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"The profound perfection of wisdom is itself the great perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Based on what intention do you speak thus?"
“Is this profound perfection of wisdom indeed the great perfection of wisdom? Subhūti replied,
“World-Honored One!”

By means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not conceive of form as great or small; nor does one conceive of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as great or small. In this way, up to and including the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, one does not conceive of it as great or small; nor does one conceive of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as great or small. One does not conceive of form as accumulating or dispersing;

nor does one conceive of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as accumulating or dispersing. In this way, up to and including the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, one does not conceive of it as accumulating or dispersing; nor does one conceive of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as accumulating or dispersing.

One does not conceive of form as finite nor as infinite; one likewise does not conceive of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as finite nor as infinite. In this manner, up to and including the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, one does not conceive of it as finite nor as infinite; and regarding all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, one likewise does not conceive of them as finite nor as infinite.

One does not conceive of form as broad nor as narrow; one likewise does not conceive of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as broad nor as narrow. In this manner, up to and including the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, one does not conceive of it as broad nor as narrow; and regarding all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, one likewise does not conceive of them as broad nor as narrow.

One does not regard form as having power nor as being powerless; one likewise does not regard feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as having power nor as being powerless. In this manner, up to and including unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, one does not regard it as having power nor as being powerless; and regarding the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, one likewise does not regard them as having power nor as being powerless.
"It is for this reason that I have made this statement:
'The profound Prajñāpāramitā is itself the Mahāpāramitā.
World-Honored One!"
If a newly trained bodhisattva mahāsattva, relying on the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity, gives rise to such a thought:

"The profound perfection of wisdom does not make form great or small, does not make it gathered or dispersed, does not make it finite or infinite, does not make it broad or narrow, and does not make it powerful or powerless; and likewise, it does not make the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas great or small, does not make them gathered or dispersed, does not make them finite or infinite, does not make them broad or narrow, and does not make them powerful or powerless."
“Such a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by giving rise to this thought, is not practicing the perfection of wisdom.
World-Honored One, if a newly trained bodhisattva mahāsattva, relying upon the perfections from wisdom down to generosity, gives rise to such a thought as this:”

"The profound *prajñāpāramitā* makes form large or small, gathered or dispersed, finite or infinite, broad or narrow, powerful or powerless; and so it continues, even unto making the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas large or small, gathered or dispersed, finite or infinite, broad or narrow, powerful or powerless."
“Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought, he is not practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Bhagavān, if a newly trained bodhisattva mahāsattva, not relying on the perfections from wisdom down to generosity, gives rise to such a thought as this:”

"The profound *prajñāpāramitā* does not make form great or small, does not make it gathered or dispersed, does not make it finite or infinite, does not make it broad or narrow, and does not make it powerful or powerless; likewise, it does not make the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas great or small, does not make them gathered or dispersed, does not make them finite or infinite, does not make them broad or narrow, and does not make them powerful or powerless."
“Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a conception, they are not practicing the perfection of wisdom.
World-Honored One,
if a newly trained bodhisattva mahāsattva who has set out in the Great Vehicle does not rely on the perfections from wisdom down to generosity, yet gives rise to such a conception as this:”

"The profound *prajñāpāramitā* makes form large or small, gathered or dispersed, finite or infinite, broad or narrow, powerful or powerless; and so it continues, even unto making the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas large or small, gathered or dispersed, finite or infinite, broad or narrow, powerful or powerless."
“World-Honored One, because this bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought, they are not practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? World-Honored One, [because...]"
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives rise to such a perception as this:

“If the profound *prajñāpāramitā* treats form as large or small, or does not treat it as large or small; treats it as accumulated or dispersed, or does not treat it as accumulated or dispersed; treats it as finite or infinite, or does not treat it as finite or infinite; treats it as broad or narrow, or does not treat it as broad or narrow; treats it as powerful or powerless, or does not treat it as powerful or powerless—and likewise, even unto the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, treats them as large or small, or does not treat them as large or small; treats them as accumulated or dispersed, or does not treat them as accumulated or dispersed; treats them as finite or infinite, or does not treat them as finite or infinite; treats them as broad or narrow, or does not treat them as broad or narrow; treats them as powerful or powerless, or does not treat them as powerful or powerless.”
"In this way, none of these are the natural outflow fruits (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
'World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a conceptualization as this:'"

"The profound *prajñāpāramitā* does not, with respect to form and so forth, up to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, effect greatness or smallness, nor effect accumulation or dispersion; it does not effect the finite or the infinite, nor effect breadth or narrowness; it does not effect power or powerlessness."
This bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to have a great attainment of something; he is not practicing the perfection of wisdom. Why is this?
Because a perception of attainment cannot realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Why is this? Because sentient beings are without arising, without intrinsic nature, non-existent, empty, signless, wishless, detached, quiescent, unapprehendable, inconceivable, indestructible, and without cognitive apprehension; and because their powers are not established, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise without arising—and so on, as extensively explained, up to its powers being not established.

Because form, up to and including all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, are without arising, without intrinsic nature, non-existent, empty, signless, wishless, secluded, quiescent, unapprehendable, inconceivable, indestructible, and without cognitive apprehension, and because their powers are not established, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise without arising, and so on, up to its powers not being established.
"It is for this reason that I have made this statement:
'The profound perfection of wisdom is itself the great perfection of wisdom.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to believe and understand this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, from where did they pass away to come and be born here?”
For how long has he set out toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment?
How many Buddhas has he personally attended and made offerings to?
For how long has he practiced the perfections, from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom?
"How does one have faith and resolve in such profound meaning and intent of this *prajñāpāramitā*?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to have faith and resolve in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they have passed away from the assemblies of Buddhas where they served the various Buddhas in the worlds of the ten directions and have come to be born here."
They have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and have already passed through immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas.
They have already personally approached, served, and made offerings to immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless, inconceivable, and unfathomable Buddhas, Bhagavāns.

From the first generation of the mind of enlightenment, they have constantly practiced the perfections from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom for immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon seeing or hearing this profound prajñāpāramitā, forms this thought:
"I am now seeing the Buddha and hearing what the Buddha has taught."

By means of signlessness, non-duality, and non-apprehension as their skillful means, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to correctly believe in and understand the profound meaning and intent of this Prajñāpāramitā.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Is there anyone who can hear or see this profound perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"In the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, there is truly no one who can hear or see it.
Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is truly not a dharma that can be heard or seen."
"Subhūti, you should know this!
Form is neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient."
To speak extensively, even the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient;
likewise, all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are also neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“For how long have those bodhisattva mahāsattvas already accumulated practice for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, such that they are able to diligently train in this profound perfection of wisdom?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"In this matter, one should explain by means of differentiation.
Subhūti, you should know this!"

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, from the very first production of the thought of enlightenment, are able to practice and study the profound perfection of wisdom, and are likewise able to practice and study the perfections of meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity.

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses skillful means, he does not slander any dharmas; he perceives no increase or decrease in any dharmas; he never departs from the correct practice associated with the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; and he never departs from the Buddhas and bodhisattvas.

From one buddha-field to another buddha-field, they are able to provide all manner of sublime and excellent offerings to honor, respect, revere, and praise the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as they wish; furthermore, they can plant various roots of goodness therein so that they may quickly reach fulfillment, and wherever they take birth, they do not fall into the womb of a mother’s belly to be born from a placenta.

Their minds never dwell in association with afflictions, nor have they ever given rise to the mind of the two vehicles; they are never separated from sublime supernormal powers as they travel through the buddha-fields to mature sentient beings and purify the buddha-lands—this is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva can diligently practice and study the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

“There may be sons and daughters of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva Vehicle who, although they have previously seen a hundred, a thousand, or even immeasurable Buddhas, and have extensively practiced generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom in the presence of those Buddhas and their disciples, yet—because they employ the means of ‘attainment’—are unable to cultivate and study the profound perfection of wisdom, up to the perfection of generosity.”

"Subhūti, you should know that when these sons and daughters of good family hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, they give rise to thoughts of contempt and, rising from their seats, depart from the assembly."
Since they treat this profound *prajñāpāramitā* with contempt, they also treat the Buddha with contempt; having abandoned such profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they have also abandoned all Buddhas.
Within this assembly there are also those of such a kind who, upon hearing me proclaim the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, will depart from the gathering with hearts lacking in respect.

Why is this? Because these sons and daughters of good family, having previously heard the teaching of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and having departed from it, now, by the power of their past habits, depart once again upon hearing me speak it.

"These sons and daughters of good family, being in disharmony with this profound *prajñāpāramitā* in body, speech, and mind, thereby create and increase the karmic offenses of delusion and impaired wisdom."

Because they have committed and increased sinful karma through their ignorance and impaired wisdom, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they immediately slander, obstruct, and abandon it. Since they have slandered, obstructed, and abandoned this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they have thereby slandered, obstructed, and abandoned the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*) of all Buddhas of the three times.
By slandering, obstructing, and abandoning the omniscient wisdom of all Buddhas of the three times, they thereby create and increase karma that leads to the deprivation of the true Dharma.

By having performed and accumulated karma that leads to the deprivation of the true Dharma, they fall into the great hells and remain there for many hundreds of years, even up to many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of years, undergoing various agonizing and intense sufferings.

Because their offenses are grave, they shall pass from one great hell to another within this world until the kalpas of fire, water, and wind have not yet arisen, during which time they will undergo various forms of agonizing and intense suffering.

If the fire, water, or wind kalpas arise in this world, because their karma of depleting the Dharma is not yet exhausted, after death they are reborn in a similar great hell in another world, where for many hundreds of years, even up to many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of years, they undergo various agonizing and intense sufferings.

Because their offenses are so grave, they pass from one great hell to another in other worlds, undergoing various forms of agonizing and intense suffering until the kalpas of fire, water, and wind have yet to arise.

If the fire, water, or wind kalpas arise in other worlds, because their karma of depriving others of the Dharma is not yet exhausted, after they die they are reborn in a great hell similar to this one in another region; there they undergo various agonizing and intense sufferings for many hundreds of years, even up to many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of years.

Because their offenses are so grave, they pass from one great hell to another in other worlds; until the kalpas of fire, water, and wind have arisen, they undergo various agonizing and intense sufferings. Thus, they wander successively through all the great hells of the other worlds throughout the ten directions, undergoing various agonizing and intense sufferings.

If, when the fire, water, and wind kalpas arise in those other worlds of the ten directions, because their karma of obstructing the Dharma is not yet exhausted, they die and are reborn again in the great hells of this Sahā world; from one great hell to another great hell, until the fire, water, and wind kalpas have arisen, they undergo various agonizing and intense sufferings.

If the fire, water, or wind kalpas arise in this world, because their karma of depleting the Dharma is not yet exhausted, they die here and are reborn again in other worlds throughout the ten directions, traversing the great hells and undergoing various agonizing and intense sufferings.

Thus they wander in saṃsāra for incalculable kalpas; once the force of their karmic offenses from the deprivation of the Dharma has slightly diminished, they emerge from hell and fall into the animal realm, where for many hundreds of years, even up to many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of years, they take birth in animal bodies and undergo all manner of suffering, including being slaughtered, harmed, and threatened.

Because their offenses are not yet exhausted, they wander from one perilous and evil place to another within this world; until the kalpas of fire, water, and wind have arisen, they undergo all manner of suffering, including being slaughtered and threatened.

If, when this world is destroyed by the three calamities, the residual force of their karma of lacking the Dharma has not yet been exhausted, they die and are reborn in another world within the animal realm (tiryagyoni) of a similar kind; there they undergo various sufferings of slaughter, intimidation, and so forth for many hundreds of years, even up to many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of years.

Because their offenses are not yet exhausted, they pass from one perilous and evil place to another in other worlds; until the fire, water, and wind kalpas have arisen, they undergo all manner of suffering, including being slaughtered and threatened.

If, at the time when the three calamities destroy another world-system, the residual force of their karma of deprivation of the Dharma has not yet been exhausted, they die and are reborn in other world-systems within the animal realm (*tiryagyoni*) of a similar class; there, for many hundreds of years, or even for many hundreds of thousands of *koṭi-nayuta* years, they undergo various sufferings such as being slaughtered and threatened.

Because their karma has not yet been exhausted, they pass from one perilous and evil place to another in other worlds; until the fire, water, and wind kalpas have arisen, they undergo all manner of suffering, including slaughter and intimidation. Thus, they travel successively throughout the various remaining worlds of the ten directions, taking birth in the bodies of animals and undergoing all manner of suffering, including slaughter and intimidation.

If, when the three calamities destroy those other worlds in the ten directions, the residual force of their karma of obstructing the Dharma has not yet been exhausted, they die and are reborn within this Sahā world among the realm of animals; from one perilous and evil place to another, they undergo all manner of suffering, such as being slaughtered and threatened, until the fire, water, or wind kalpas have arisen.

If, when this world is destroyed by the three calamities, the residual force of their karma of depriving others of the Dharma has not yet been exhausted, they will die and be reborn again in other worlds throughout the ten directions, undergoing manifold sufferings extensively within the realm of animals.

Thus they circulate through countless eons; eventually, the force of their karmic offenses from the sin of withholding the Dharma gradually diminishes, and they escape the realm of animals to fall into the realm of hungry ghosts, where for many hundreds of years, even up to many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of years, they undergo all manner of sufferings such as hunger, emaciation, and parching thirst.

Because their transgressions are not yet exhausted, they travel from one realm of hungry ghosts to another within this world; until the kalpas of fire, water, and wind have arisen, they undergo all manner of sufferings such as hunger, emaciation, and parching thirst.

If, when this world is destroyed by the three calamities, the residual force of their karma of lacking the Dharma has not yet been exhausted, they die and are reborn in another world system within the realm of hungry ghosts of a similar kind; there they undergo the sufferings of hunger, emaciation, and parching thirst for many hundreds of years, even up to many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of years.

Because their offenses are not yet exhausted, they travel from one realm of hungry ghosts to another in other worlds; until the kalpas of fire, water, and wind have arisen, they undergo all manner of sufferings such as hunger, emaciation, and parching thirst.

If, when the three calamities destroy another world-system, the residual force of their karma of deprivation regarding the Dharma has not yet been exhausted, they die and are reborn in a similar realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*) in another direction; there they undergo the sufferings of hunger, emaciation, parching thirst, and so forth for many hundreds of years, even up to many hundreds of thousands of *koṭi-nayuta* years.

Because their transgressions are not yet exhausted, they travel from one realm of hungry ghosts to another in other worlds; until the kalpas of fire, water, and wind have arisen, they undergo all manner of sufferings such as hunger, emaciation, parching, and thirst. Thus, they wander successively through all the remaining worlds of the ten directions, experiencing every kind of suffering—hunger, emaciation, parching, and thirst—within the realm of ghosts.

If, when the three calamities destroy those other worlds in the ten directions, the residual force of their karma of obstructing the Dharma has not yet been exhausted, they die and are reborn in this Sahā world within the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*). From one land of hungry ghosts to another, until the kalpas of fire, water, and wind have arisen, they undergo all manner of sufferings such as hunger, emaciation, and parching thirst.

When this world is destroyed by the three calamities, those whose karma of deprivation of the Dharma has not yet exhausted its residual force die and are reborn again in other worlds throughout the ten directions, where they undergo manifold sufferings extensively within the realm of hungry ghosts.

Thus they wander through countless kalpas until the residual force of their karma of obstructing the Dharma is nearly exhausted; emerging from the realm of hungry ghosts, they are reborn among humans. Although they obtain human form, they dwell in lowly and base conditions—namely, they may be born into families of those blind from birth, the deaf, or into families of caṇḍālas, or pulkasa families, or butchers, or fishermen and hunters, or craftsmen, or musicians, or families of wrong views, or other miscellaneous families of evil discipline.

Or they may receive a body that lacks eyes, ears, nose, tongue, hands, or feet; or one that is blind, deaf, mute, afflicted with abscesses, scabies, leprosy, insanity, epilepsy, lameness, or physical deformity; or one that is hunchbacked, short and ugly, crippled, or deficient in its sense faculties; or one that is dark-complexioned, emaciated, and wretched, or dull-witted and ignorant such that all people who encounter them treat them with contempt and ridicule. Or they may be born in places where they do not hear the names of the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, Bodhisattvas, or Pratyekabuddhas; or they may be born in worlds of perpetual darkness where day and night never exist and light is never seen, dwelling in perilous, obstructed, foul, and thorn-filled environments.

Why is this so? Because their karma of depriving others of the Dharma has been created, accumulated, and intensified to such an extreme degree that they experience such undesirable and complete fruits of suffering; these varieties are so numerous that they are difficult to describe in full, for were one to attempt to describe them exhaustively, it would not be finished even at the end of an eon.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Can the karma created and accumulated by those who cause the True Dharma to be depleted—which is capable of bringing about such a result—be said to be similar to the five deeds of immediate retribution?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"The karma that results in the deprivation of the Dharma is most extremely coarse and heavy; it cannot even be compared to the five deeds of immediate retribution.
This refers to those who, upon hearing the teaching of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, immediately resist, slander, and revile it, saying:"
"Such words were not spoken by the Buddha; they are not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not the teaching of the Great Master. We should not believe or study them.
Such a person who slanders the Dharma slanders the Prajñāpāramitā themselves and teaches others to slander it as well;
they destroy their own bodies and cause others to destroy theirs as well.
One drinks poison oneself and causes others to drink it as well;
one loses for oneself the blissful fruits of rebirth in heaven and liberation, and causes others to lose them as well;
one sustains one's own body with the fires of hell, and causes others to sustain theirs as well.
They themselves lack faith and understanding in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and they also teach others not to have faith and understanding;
they themselves sink into the ocean of suffering, and they also cause others to drown.
“Śāriputra! Regarding this profound perfection of wisdom, I do not even wish for those who would slander the true Dharma to hear its name, much less to teach it to them!”
Śāriputra! As for those who slander the true Dharma, I do not even permit sons of good family who have set out in the Bodhisattva vehicle to hear their names, let alone see them with their own eyes!
How could we permit co-residence? Why is this so, Śāriputra?

Those who revile this profound *prajñāpāramitā* should be known as destroyers of the True Dharma; they fall into the category of darkness like foul snails and slugs, defiling themselves and others like stinking, rotting excrement.
If there are those who place their trust in the words of one who corrupts the Dharma, they too shall undergo the great suffering previously described. Śāriputra!

You should know that all those who destroy the profound *prajñāpāramitā* are, in effect, hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts; they will certainly undergo extremely heavy, fierce, and boundless great suffering. Therefore, the wise should not slander the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
Then, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“For what reason does the Tathāgata speak only of those who destroy the true Dharma falling into the great hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts to suffer for a long time, yet does not describe their physical appearance or bodily dimensions?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Stop! You should not speak of the dimensions of the miserable realms that those who destroy the true Dharma will undergo in the future."

Why is this? If I were to describe in detail the dimensions and forms of those realms, those who hear it would be struck with terror and vomit hot blood, thereby meeting their end or suffering near-death agony; their minds would be suddenly overwhelmed by distress as if pierced by a poisoned arrow, and their bodies would gradually wither away like cut-down grain stalks. Fearing that those who hear of the great and loathsome bodies such as these—bodies to be endured by those who slander the True Dharma—would in vain be seized by panic and lose their lives, I have compassion for them and therefore do not speak of it to you.

Śāriputra said: "I only pray that the Buddha will describe the magnitude of that evil form, clearly warning those of the future so that they may know the great suffering one shall incur for slandering the Dharma, and thus refrain from committing such a sin."
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"What I have previously said is sufficient as a clear warning!

That is to say, when good sons and others in future ages hear my teaching regarding the karma of destroying the True Dharma—how its commission and growth reach full completion—and fall into the great hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts, suffering for a long time within each of these destinies, they will naturally be moved to tremble with apprehension and refrain from slandering the True Dharma."
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: “So be it,
World-Honored One!”
"So be it! Sugata!

When future sons of good family hear that the Buddha has previously declared that the karma of destroying the True Dharma brings about suffering for a long duration as a sufficient warning, they will surely sacrifice their own bodies and lives rather than ever slandering the Dharma, lest they themselves suffer such misery in the future."
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If there are intelligent sons of good family who hear the Buddha’s teaching that those who slander the true Dharma will undergo heavy suffering for a long time in future worlds, they should well-guard their actions of body, speech, and mind. They must not revile or destroy the true Dharma, lest they fall into the three evil realms and suffer for long kalpas; nor shall they fail to see the Buddhas, hear the true Dharma, or encounter the Saṅgha for a vast period of time; nor shall they be born in a land where a Buddha resides. Even if they are born in the human realm, they will be lowly, impoverished, ugly, dull-witted, and physically deformed, such that no one will believe or accept whatever they say.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Is it not by habituating oneself to the karma of evil speech that one creates and increases the karma for the deprivation of the Dharma?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"So it is! So it is! Indeed, because of the habitual practice of unwholesome verbal karma, they have created and increased the karma that results in the deprivation of the Dharma. Among my true Dharma and Vinaya, there will be certain foolish renunciants who, though they call me their Great Teacher, will slander and destroy the profound *prajñāpāramitā* that I have taught."
“Subhūti, you should know that whoever slanders this profound perfection of wisdom slanders the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas.”
If one slanders the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas, one thereby slanders the omniscient wisdom of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
If one slanders the omniscient wisdom of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, one thereby slanders the Jewels of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
If one slanders or reviles the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha Jewels, then one is slandering right view in the world.
If one slanders right view in the world, then one is slandering the six perfections, such as generosity, and so forth, up to and including the knowledge of all aspects.
By slandering and disparaging this collection of all virtues, one thereby incurs immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sinful karma.

By incurring such immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sinful karma, one thereby incurs all the immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless great sufferings within the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, and humans.
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By how many causes and conditions do those foolish people slander and revile such profound prajñāpāramitā?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"There are four causes and conditions. What are the four?
First, because they are instigated and deluded by various māras and evil spirits."
Second, because they lack faith and understanding regarding the profound Dharma;
third, because they do not apply themselves with diligence, are attached to the five aggregates, and are influenced by evil associates.
Fourth, they harbor much malice, delight in practicing unwholesome dharmas, and take pleasure in self-exaltation while disparaging others.

Because those deluded persons possess these four causes and conditions, they slander and revile this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and by virtue of this, they shall undergo great suffering in the future.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

Those foolish people who do not apply themselves with diligence, who are influenced by evil associates, who have not planted roots of goodness and are possessed of various evil deeds, will truly find it difficult to believe in and understand the profound *prajñāpāramitā* spoken by the Buddha."
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is as you have said.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In this way, how is it that this Prajñāpāramitā is so profound, difficult to believe, and difficult to understand?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Form, and so on up to consciousness, are neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?"
This is because the nature of non-existence of form, up to and including consciousness, constitutes the intrinsic nature of form and the others.

In this way, even up to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), they are neither bound nor liberated.

Why is this? Because all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) have the nature of non-existence as their own-being (*svabhāva*). Thus, all-knowledge and the others are characterized by such a self-nature.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
From form up to consciousness, the past, future, and present limits are neither bound nor liberated. Why is that?

Because the nature of non-existence regarding the past, future, and middle limits of form, up to consciousness, constitutes the intrinsic nature of the past, future, and middle limits of form and so forth.

In this way, up to all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), there is neither bondage nor liberation regarding their past, future, and middle limits.

Why is this? Because the non-existence of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) in the past, future, and present limits constitutes the very intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of those past, future, and present limits of all-knowledge and the others.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Those individuals who do not exert diligent effort, who have not planted roots of virtue, who possess unwholesome roots, who are influenced by evil friends, in whom indolence predominates, who follow the course of Māra’s power, whose diligence is feeble, and who lack mindfulness and possess faulty wisdom—such persons find it truly difficult to believe in and understand this profound perfection of wisdom spoken by the Buddha."
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said. Why is that? Subhūti!
The purity of form is the purity of the fruit, and the purity of the fruit is the purity of form. Why is this?
Because this purity of form and the purity of the fruit are non-dual, not divided into two, distinct, or separate.

In this way, up to the point that the purity of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is the purity of the fruit, and the purity of the fruit is the purity of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas.

Why is this? Because the purity of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of these Buddhas and the purity of the fruit are non-dual; they are not two, there is no division between them, they are not distinct, and they are not separate.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
The purity of form is the purity of the perfection of wisdom; the purity of the perfection of wisdom is the purity of form.
Why is this? Because the purity of form and the purity of the perfection of wisdom are non-dual, not divided into two, without distinction, and without interruption.
In this way, up to the point that the purity of all-aspect omniscience is the purity of the perfection of wisdom, and the purity of the perfection of wisdom is the purity of all-aspect omniscience.
Why is this? Because the purity of all-aspect omniscience and the purity of the perfection of wisdom are non-dual, not divided into two, distinct, or separate.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
The purity of form is the purity of the knowledge of all modes; the purity of the knowledge of all modes is the purity of form. Why is this?
This purity of form and the purity of the knowledge of all modes are non-dual, not divided into two, distinct, or separate.
Thus, up to the purity of the knowledge of all aspects is the purity of the knowledge of all modes, and the purity of the knowledge of all modes is the purity of the knowledge of all aspects.
Why is this? Because the purity of all-aspect omniscience and the purity of the knowledge of all aspects are non-dual, not divided into two, distinct, or separate.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Non-duality purity is the purity of form; the purity of form is non-duality purity. Why is this?
This non-dual purity and the purity of form are non-dual, not divided into two, without distinction, and without interruption.
Thus, up to and including the point that non-dual purity is the purity of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), and the purity of the knowledge of all aspects is non-dual purity.
Why is this? Because this purity of non-duality and the purity of the knowledge of all aspects are non-dual, not divided into two, without distinction, and without interruption.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
The purity of the self up to the perceiver is itself the purity of form; the purity of form is itself the purity of the self up to the perceiver."
Why is this? Because the purity of the self up to the purity of the seer and the purity of form are non-dual, not divided into two, distinct, and inseparable.

In this way, up to the point that the purity of the self and even the purity of the seer is the purity of the knowledge of all aspects, and the purity of the knowledge of all aspects is the purity of the self and even the purity of the seer.
Why is this? Because the purity of the self, up to and including the viewer, and the purity of the knowledge of all aspects are non-dual, not divided into two, distinct, or discontinuous.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
The purity of greed, hatred, and delusion is the purity of form; the purity of form is the purity of greed, hatred, and delusion."
Why is this? Because the purity of greed, hatred, and delusion and the purity of form are non-dual, not divided into two, distinct, or separate.

In this way, up to and including the purification of greed, hatred, and delusion, there is the purification of the knowledge of all aspects; the purification of the knowledge of all aspects is itself the purification of greed, hatred, and delusion.
Why is this? Because the purity of this greed, hatred, and delusion and the purity of the knowledge of all aspects are non-dual, not divided into two, without distinction, and without interruption.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Because form is pure, feeling is pure; because feeling is pure, form is pure. Why is this?
This purity of form and purity of feeling are non-dual, not divided into two, distinct, or separate. Thus, because feeling is pure, perception is pure;

because perception is pure, feeling is pure. Extending in this manner, up to the point that because the knowledge of the aspects of the path is pure, the knowledge of all aspects is pure; and because the knowledge of all aspects is pure, the knowledge of the aspects of the path is pure.
Why is this? Because the purity of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the purity of the knowledge of all aspects are non-dual, not divided into two, distinct, nor discontinuous.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Because the perfection of wisdom is pure, form is pure; because form is pure, the knowledge of all modes is pure."

Why is this? Because the purity of the perfection of wisdom, the purity of form, and the purity of the knowledge of all modes are non-dual, not divided into two, without distinction, and without interruption.

In this way, up to and including the purity of the perfection of wisdom, there is the purity of the knowledge of all aspects; because of the purity of the knowledge of all aspects, there is the purity of the knowledge of all-knowingness.

Why is this? Because the purity of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the purity of all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), and the purity of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvajñajñāna*) are non-dual, not divided into two, without distinction, and uninterrupted.

To speak at length, up until: because the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is pure, form (*rūpa*) is pure; because form is pure, the knowledge of all knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*) is pure. Why is this?
If the purity of the knowledge of all aspects, the purity of form, and the purity of the knowledge of all-knowledge are non-dual, not divided into two, without distinction, and without interruption.

In this way, up to and including the purification of all-aspect-knowledge, because of the purification of all-aspect-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths is purified; and because of the purification of the knowledge of the paths, the knowledge of all aspects is purified.

Why is this? Because the purity of the knowledge of all aspects, the purity of the knowledge of the paths, and the purity of the knowledge of all knowledge are non-dual, not divided into two, without distinction, and without interruption.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Because the knowledge of all modes is pure, form is pure; because form is pure, the perfection of wisdom is pure."

Why is this? Because the purity of the knowledge of all modes, the purity of form, and the purity of the perfection of wisdom are non-dual, not divided into two, without distinction, and not separate.
In this way, up to and including: because the knowledge of all modes is pure, the knowledge of all aspects is pure; because the knowledge of all aspects is pure, the perfection of wisdom is pure.

Why is this? Because the purity of the knowledge of all modes, the purity of the knowledge of all aspects, and the purity of the perfection of wisdom are non-dual, not divided into two, without distinction, and without interruption.

To speak extensively, up to: because the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) is pure, form (*rūpa*) is pure; because form is pure, the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is pure. Why is this?
If the purity of the knowledge of all modes, the purity of form, and the purity of the knowledge of all aspects are non-dual, not divided into two, without distinction, and without interruption.
In this way, up to the point that because the knowledge of all modes is pure, the knowledge of the paths is pure; and because the knowledge of the paths is pure, the knowledge of all aspects is pure.

Why is this? Because the purity of the knowledge of all modes, the purity of the knowledge of the paths, and the purity of the knowledge of all aspects are non-dual, not divided into two, distinct, or discontinuous.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Because the conditioned is pure, the unconditioned is pure; because the unconditioned is pure, the conditioned is pure. Why is this?
Whether it be the purity of the conditioned or the purity of the unconditioned, they are non-dual, not divided into two, without distinction, and without interruption.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Because the past is pure, the future and the present are pure; because the future is pure, the past and the present are pure; because the present is pure, the past and the future are pure.
Why is this? Whether it be purity of the past, purity of the future, or purity of the present, they are non-dual, not divided into two, without distinction, and without interruption.
11. Chapter Eleven: Praising Purity (Praise of Purity), Part Three, Section One. At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"Such purity is most profound.
The Buddha said,
"Because it is ultimately pure."
Śāriputra asked: “By the ultimate purity of what phenomena is this purity said to be most profound?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"Because form is ultimately pure, this purity is said to be most profound; because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are ultimately pure, this purity is said to be most profound. Thus, up to and including: because all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is ultimately pure, this purity is said to be most profound; because the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are ultimately pure, this purity is said to be most profound."
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Such purity is exceedingly clear.
The Buddha said:
“Because it is thus ultimately pure. Śāriputra asked:
“By the ultimate purity of what dharma is this purity said to be so very clear?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“Because the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is ultimately pure, it is said that its purity is most clearly manifest; even up to the point that because the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā) is ultimately pure, it is said that its purity is most clearly manifest.”

In this way, up to and including the fact that all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is ultimately pure, it is said to be extremely clear as purity; because the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are ultimately pure, it is said to be extremely clear as purity.
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In this way, it is pure, non-reverting, and non-continuing.
The Buddha said:
“Because it is thus ultimately pure.
Śāriputra asked: “By the ultimate purity of what dharma is it said that this purity does not turn back and does not continue?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"Because form does not transition and does not continue, being ultimately pure, it is said to be pure, non-transiting, and non-continuing. Thus, up to and including all-aspect omniscience, because it does not transition and does not continue, being ultimately pure, it is said to be pure, non-transiting, and non-continuing."
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In this way, it is pure and fundamentally free from defilement.
The Buddha said:
“Because it is thus ultimately pure. Śāriputra asked:
“By the ultimate purity of what dharma is it said to be pure, fundamentally free from defilement?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"Because form is ultimately pure, it is said to be pure by nature and fundamentally free from defilement; likewise, up to and including all-aspect omniscience, because it is ultimately pure, it is said to be pure by nature and fundamentally free from defilement."
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“In this way, its nature is pure and its essence is luminously radiant.
The Buddha said:
“Because it is thus ultimately pure. Śāriputra asked:
“By the ultimate purity of what dharma is this intrinsic nature said to be pure and luminously radiant?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"Because form is ultimately pure, it is said to be pure by nature and luminously radiant; likewise, up to and including all-aspect omniscience, because it is ultimately pure, it is said to be pure by nature and luminously radiant."
Then, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“In this way, purity is without attainment and without clear realization.
The Buddha said:
"Because it is thus ultimately pure. Śāriputra asked:
"Due to the ultimate purity of what dharma is it said that this purity is without attainment and without clear realization?"
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“Because the intrinsic nature of form is empty and ultimately pure, it is said to be pure, without attainment and without clear realization. Thus, up to and including the fact that the intrinsic nature of the knowledge of all aspects is empty and ultimately pure, it is said to be pure, without attainment and without clear realization.”
Then, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In this way, it is pure, without arising, and without manifestation.
The Buddha said:
"Because it is thus ultimately pure. Śāriputra asked:
