"By virtue of what dharma being ultimately pure is it said to be pure, unarisen, and non-manifesting?"
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“Form is without arising and without manifestation because it is ultimately pure; therefore, it is said to be pure, without arising, and without appearance. Thus, even up to all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), it is without arising and without manifestation because it is ultimately pure; therefore, it is said to be pure, without arising, and without appearance.”
Then, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Such purity does not arise in the desire realm, does not arise in the form realm, and does not arise in the formless realm.”
The Buddha said: "It is because it is ultimately pure. Śāriputra said:
“How is it that such purity does not arise in the desire realm, does not arise in the form realm, and does not arise in the formless realm?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“Because the intrinsic nature of the three realms cannot be apprehended, it is said that this purity does not arise in the desire realm, does not arise in the form realm, and does not arise in the formless realm.”
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In this way, the pure intrinsic nature is without cognition.
The Buddha said:
"Because it is thus ultimately pure.
Śāriputra asked: "In what way is this purity such that its intrinsic nature is without cognition?"
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“Because all phenomena are by nature dull, such pure nature is without cognition. Śāriputra said:
“Because what dharmas are by nature without cognition, are they said to be pure by nature without cognition?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“Form is by nature without cognition because it is empty of its own characteristics; therefore, it is said to be pure by nature without cognition. Thus, up to and including all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), it is by nature without cognition because it is empty of its own characteristics; therefore, it is said to be pure by nature without cognition.”
Then, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Because all dharmas are pure by their very nature, this is called purity.
The Buddha said:
"In this way, because all phenomena are ultimately pure.
Śāriputra asked: "In what sense is it said that they are pure because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is pure?"
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Because all phenomena are unattainable, their intrinsic nature is pure; this is what is called purity.
Then, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In this way, the perfection of wisdom neither benefits nor harms omniscience.
The Buddha said,
"Because it is ultimately pure."
Śāriputra asked: "In what way does the perfection of wisdom neither benefit nor harm omniscience?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“Because the dharma-realm is eternally abiding, this perfection of wisdom neither benefits nor harms omniscience.
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“This perfection of wisdom is pure by its very nature; it does not grasp at any phenomena.”
The Buddha said: "It is because all phenomena are ultimately pure. Śāriputra said:
“How is it that the *prajñāpāramitā* is pure by nature and does not grasp at any phenomena?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“Because the *dharmadhātu* is serene and unshakable, such is the *prajñāpāramitā*—pure by nature and not grasping at any phenomena.”
The Venerable Subhūti also addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Because I am pure, form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness—up to and including the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity—are pure.”
The Buddha said,
“It is so, because it is ultimately pure.
[He asked,] “World-Honored One!”

For what reason is it said that because the self is pure, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—up to and including the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity—are pure, being ultimately pure?

“Subhūti! Because the self does not exist, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness—even up to the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity—do not exist; this is ultimate purity.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Because I am pure, the fruit of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship; the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas are pure."
The Buddha said:
“It is so, because it is ultimately pure.
[He asked: “World-Honored One!”

“For what reason is it said that because the self is pure, the fruit of stream-entry up to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is pure—this being ultimate purity? “Subhūti!

“Because the self is empty of its own characteristics, the fruit of stream-entry up to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is also empty of its own characteristics; this is ultimate purity.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Because the self is pure, omniscience, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects are pure.”
The Buddha said,
"It is so, because it is ultimately pure.
[He asked,] "World-Honored One!"

"For what reason is it said that because the self is pure, omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are pure—this being ultimate purity?
"Subhūti! [The Blessed One replied:]

Because I am without marks, without attainment, without thought, and without cognition, all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are likewise without marks, without attainment, without thought, and without cognition; this is ultimate purity.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Because of the purity of both, there is neither attainment nor clear realization.
The Buddha said:
"It is because it is ultimately pure.
"World-Honored One,
for what reason do you say that because of these two purities, there is neither attainment nor clear realization, and this is ultimate purity?"
“Subhūti! Because there is neither defilement nor purification arising from inversion, there is no attainment and no clear realization; this is ultimate purity.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Because the self is infinite, form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness—even up to all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects—are also infinite.”
The Buddha said:
“It is so, because it is ultimately pure.
[He asked: “World-Honored One!”

For what reason is it said that because the self is infinite, form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness—even up to all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)—are also infinite and ultimately pure?
“Subhūti! Because of ultimate emptiness and boundless emptiness, this is ultimate purity.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can awaken in this way, this is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
The Buddha said,
“It is because it is ultimately pure.”
“World-Honored One!
For what reason do you say that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva can awaken in this way, this is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) which is ultimately pure?”
“Subhūti! It is because by means of this one can accomplish the knowledge of the aspects of the path.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, does not apprehend the far shore, does not apprehend this shore, and does not apprehend the middle stream, this is the profound perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva."
The Buddha said:
“It is so, because it is ultimately pure.
[He asked: “World-Honored One!”

For what reason is it said that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they do not apprehend the far shore, do not apprehend this shore, and do not apprehend the middle stream; and how is it that this profound *prajñāpāramitā* of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is ultimate purity?
“Subhūti! Because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is equal throughout the three periods of time.
*The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Fascicle 506.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 573.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Dharma Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Part Three: The Chapter Praising Purity, Number Eleven, Part Two.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Great Vehicle lack skillful means, and they give rise to the notion of ‘perfection of wisdom’ regarding the profound perfection of wisdom, these sons and daughters of good family, because they employ the method of apprehending something as real, will abandon and distance themselves from the profound perfection of wisdom.”
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “Excellent! Excellent!”
"So it is! So it is! It is just as you have said."
Those sons and daughters of good family who are attached to names and attached to signs will therefore abandon and distance themselves from this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how do those sons and daughters of good family become attached to names and attached to signs?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Those sons and daughters of good family who grasp at the name and grasp at the signs of this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and having grasped its name and signs, become attached to the *prajñāpāramitā* and give rise to arrogance, will be unable to realize the *prajñā* of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, such individuals abandon and distance themselves from the profound *prajñāpāramitā*."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! If sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Great Vehicle possess skillful means, they do not give rise to the thought of 'prajñāpāramitā' regarding the profound prajñāpāramitā, because they employ the method of non-apprehension. Thus, regarding the profound prajñāpāramitā, they do not grasp at names or signs, they do not give rise to attachment, and they do not produce arrogance; in this way, they are able to realize the prajñā of the true nature (bhūtārtha-prajñā)."
"You should know that such persons as these will neither abandon nor distance themselves from this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How extraordinary!"
“World-Honored One!
You have skillfully revealed and distinguished for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas the characteristics of attachment and non-attachment regarding the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
“What is the mark of attachment and non-attachment that a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to regarding the profound *prajñāpāramitā*? Subhūti replied:

“When sons or daughters of good family who abide in the Great Vehicle practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* without skillful means, they conceive of form as empty and give rise to the mark of attachment to emptiness; they conceive of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as empty and give rise to the mark of attachment to emptiness. In this way, up to conceiving of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) as empty, they give rise to the mark of attachment to emptiness; they conceive of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) and all-aspect knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) as empty and give rise to the mark of attachment to emptiness.”

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when sons or daughters of good family who abide in the Great Vehicle practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* without skillful means, they conceive of form as 'form' and give rise to the perception and attachment of form; and so on, up to: they conceive of all-aspect-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) as 'all-aspect-knowledge' and give rise to the perception and attachment of all-aspect-knowledge.

They conceive of past phenomena as 'past phenomena' and give rise to the perception and attachment of past phenomena; they conceive of future phenomena as 'future phenomena' and give rise to the perception and attachment of future phenomena; they conceive of present phenomena as 'present phenomena' and give rise to the perception and attachment of present phenomena."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva,

by means of the expedient of apprehending something as real, gives rise to conceptualizations and attachments regarding the practice of everything from the perfection of generosity up to the knowledge of all aspects, starting from the first production of the thought of enlightenment."

Śāriputra! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, if they lack skillful means and employ the notion of "attainment" as their means, giving rise to various such conceptualizations and attachments, this is called "attachment to signs."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, as to what you previously asked:
'How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva not become attached to signs regarding the profound perfection of wisdom?'"

"Thus it is said: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, because they possess skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), they do not give rise to the notion of emptiness or non-emptiness regarding form; they do not give rise to the notion of emptiness or non-emptiness regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. This is explained at length up to: they do not give rise to the notion of emptiness or non-emptiness regarding all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*); they do not give rise to the notion of emptiness or non-emptiness regarding the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
They do not give rise to the notion of emptiness or non-emptiness regarding past phenomena, nor do they give rise to the notion of emptiness or non-emptiness regarding future or present phenomena."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, because they possess skillful means, they do not form such thoughts as:
'I am able to practice giving; this is the giving I practice; in this manner I practice giving.'"
"I am able to maintain the precepts; these are the precepts I maintain, and this is how I maintain them.
I am able to cultivate patience; this is the patience I cultivate, and this is how I cultivate it.
I am able to exert diligence; this is diligence, and this is how I exert it."
"I am able to cultivate meditative concentration; this is the meditative concentration I cultivate, and this is how I cultivate it.
I am able to cultivate wisdom; this is the wisdom I cultivate, and this is how I cultivate it.
I am able to plant merit; this is the merit I plant, and this is how I plant it."
I am able to enter the bodhisattva’s state of certainty;
I am able to adorn and purify buddha-fields; I am able to bring sentient beings to maturity;
and I am able to realize the knowledge of all modes.

“Śāriputra! When these bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, because they possess skillful means, they are free from all such conceptual discriminations, due to their thorough realization of inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.”
“Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s non-attachment to signs regarding the profound perfection of wisdom.
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, asked Subhūti:
"How do sons and daughters of good family who are established in the Great Vehicle recognize the signs of attachment that arise when they practice the profound perfection of wisdom?"
Subhūti replied:

"When sons and daughters of good family who are established in the Great Vehicle practice the profound perfection of wisdom, if they lack skillful means and take 'attainment' as their means, they give rise to the perception of a self, the perception of giving, and so forth, up to the perception of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvajñajñāna*), the perception of the Buddhas, the perception of planting roots of virtue under the Buddhas, and the perception of collecting and weighing these planted roots of virtue and dedicating them equally in common with all sentient beings toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."
Kauśika! By this you should know the nature of the attachments that arise when sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Great Vehicle practice the profound perfection of wisdom.

Kauśika! Because these sons and daughters of good family are attached to signs, they are unable to practice the non-attached Prajñāpāramitā and dedicate it toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Why is this? Kausika!
It is because the intrinsic nature of form cannot be dedicated; and so on, in detail, up to the fact that the intrinsic nature of the knowledge of all aspects cannot be dedicated.

"Furthermore, Kauśika! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to manifest, exhort, encourage, and gladden other sentient beings regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should contemplate the equal, true nature of all phenomena. Following this mental engagement, they should manifest, exhort, encourage, and gladden those other sentient beings by saying:

'O sons of good family, when practicing generosity, you should not discriminate, thinking "I am able to practice generosity," and so on, up to: when practicing the knowledge of all aspects, you should not discriminate, thinking "I am able to practice the knowledge of all aspects"; and when cultivating the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas, you should not discriminate, thinking "I am able to cultivate the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas.'"

"Kauśika! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to manifest, exhort, encourage, and gladden other sentient beings regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should manifest, exhort, encourage, and gladden those other sentient beings in this manner."

If one can act in this way, one will neither harm oneself nor harm others, thereby manifesting, exhorting, encouraging, and gladdening all sentient beings in accordance with what is permitted by the Tathāgatas.

Kauśika! If sons of good family who abide in the Mahāyāna can thus manifest themselves to instruct, exhort, encourage, and gladden those sentient beings who are proceeding toward the Bodhisattva vehicle, they will be able to remain far removed from all attachments.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Subhūti, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!”

You have now skillfully explained the characteristics of attachment for the sake of all bodhisattvas; furthermore, there are other subtle attachments which I shall now explain to you. You should listen attentively and reflect upon them with great care.
Subhūti replied: "Indeed! I pray that you will speak."
“We would delight to hear it.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If sons of good family who abide in the Great Vehicle and wish to proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should apprehend signs and dwell upon the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, all of these are attachments.”

If one takes signs and recollects all roots of goodness—from the initial generation of the mind until the endurance of the Dharma—belonging to the World-Honored Buddhas of the three periods of time, and rejoices in them and dedicates them toward unsurpassed enlightenment, all of this is attachment.

If one takes signs and recollects the wholesome dharmas practiced by the disciples of the Tathāgata, and rejoices in them and dedicates them toward unsurpassed enlightenment, all of this is attachment.

Why is this? One should not grasp at signs, nor engage in recollection or conceptual discrimination regarding the roots of merit and virtues of the Tathāgatas and their disciples; for all grasping at signs is false and illusory.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"This Prajñāpāramitā is most profound.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because all phenomena are by their very nature detached.
Subhūti spoke again:
"One should pay homage to this Prajñāpāramitā in this way. The Buddha said, "So it is!"
"Because its merit is so great, this Prajñāpāramitā is without creation, without action, and there is no one who can realize it.
Subhūti spoke again:
"The nature of all dharmas cannot be realized or awakened to."
The Buddha said: "It is so!
Because all dharmas are of a single nature and not two."
"Subhūti, you should know that the single nature of all phenomena is itself the absence of nature; the absence of nature of all phenomena is itself their single nature.
Thus, this single nature and absence of nature of all phenomena is their fundamental, true nature; this fundamental, true nature is uncreated and unconditioned."

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can know, as it truly is, that there is neither a single nature nor a lack of nature, and that there is no creation and no action, they will be able to remain far removed from all attachments.
Subhūti spoke again:
"In this way, the Perfection of Wisdom is difficult to realize."
The Buddha said: "It is so!
Because of the profound Prajñāpāramitā, there is no one who can see, hear, perceive, or know it."
Subhūti spoke again:
"In this way, the Prajñāpāramitā is inconceivable.
The Buddha said:
"It is so! By means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, it cannot be grasped by the mind, because it is free from the characteristics of the mind;
it cannot be grasped by form, because it is free from the characteristics of form."
To speak at length, it cannot be apprehended by the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), because it is free from the characteristics of the knowledge of all aspects;
nor can it be apprehended by any phenomena (*sarvadharma*), because it is free from the characteristics of all phenomena.
Subhūti spoke again:
“In this way, the perfection of wisdom is without any conditioned activity.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! Because no agent can be apprehended.
Subhūti, you should know this!"

Because form (*rūpa*) cannot be apprehended, the agent cannot be apprehended; because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*) cannot be apprehended, the agent cannot be apprehended. To speak at length, up to the point that because all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) cannot be apprehended, the agent cannot be apprehended; and because all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) cannot be apprehended, the agent cannot be apprehended. Since both the agents and phenomena such as form cannot be apprehended, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is without creation and without activity.
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not practice with regard to form, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom;
does not practice with regard to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom;
and so on, in detail, up to: does not practice with regard to all-knowledge, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom."

Not practicing the knowledge of the characteristics of phenomena (*lakṣaṇa-jñāna*) or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), this is practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Furthermore, Subhūti,

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not practice with respect to form (*rūpa*) as being permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, detached or non-detached, or tranquil or non-tranquil, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

To speak at length, up to not practicing the knowledge of all aspects as either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, detached or non-detached, or tranquil or non-tranquil—this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Because from form up to the knowledge of all aspects, even these do not exist; how much less could there be permanence or impermanence, up to tranquility or non-tranquility!
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not practice for the fulfillment of form, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom;
if they do not practice for the non-fulfillment of form, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom."
To practice until one does not engage in the fulfillment of all-aspect omniscience is to practice the perfection of wisdom;
to practice such that one does not engage in the non-fulfillment of all-aspect omniscience is to practice the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Whether form (*rūpa*) is complete or incomplete, it is neither called "form" nor does one practice in such a manner; this is practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

This is explained at length until: whether the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is complete or incomplete, it is neither called "knowledge of all aspects" nor does one practice in such a manner; this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How extraordinary!
O Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha!”
“Excellent! You have well explained to the Bodhisattvas the various characteristics of attachment and non-attachment.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is!”

It is so! All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have skillfully proclaimed to Bodhisattvas the various characteristics of attachment and non-attachment, causing them to study the Prajñāpāramitā and swiftly reach the ultimate goal.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, if they do not practice by way of the signs of attachment or non-attachment regarding form, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom;
if they do not practice by way of the signs of attachment or non-attachment regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom."
To speak at length, up to and including: if one does not practice all the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices with attachment to or non-attachment to signs, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom;
if one does not practice the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas with attachment to or non-attachment to signs, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How extraordinary,
World-Honored One!"
"The profound nature of phenomena is extremely rare; whether it is explained or not, there is neither increase nor decrease.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "It is so!"
"So it is! This profound nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is exceedingly rare; whether it is spoken of or not, there is neither increase nor decrease.

It is like space: even if all Buddhas were to exhaust their lifespans in either praising or disparaging it, that space would neither increase nor decrease. The profound nature of phenomena is likewise; whether it is spoken of or not, there is neither increase nor decrease."

Furthermore, just as a conjured being feels neither joy nor sorrow when praised or reviled, and neither increases nor decreases, so too is the profound nature of phenomena (dharmatā): whether it is explained or not, it remains no different from its original state.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is a most difficult task for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to practice the profound perfection of wisdom.”

This refers to the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, which—whether practiced or not practiced—is without increase or decrease, without sorrow or joy, and without inclination or aversion; yet one diligently trains in this profound *prajñāpāramitā* until reaching unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, never regressing.
Why is this so? When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do so as if practicing that which is entirely non-existent, like empty space.

Just as in empty space there is no form to be perceived, nor are there feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness to be perceived—and as it is explained at length, up to and including the fact that there is no bodhisattva practice of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva to be perceived, nor is there any unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) of the Buddhas to be perceived—the perfection of wisdom being practiced is likewise so.

It means that within this profound Dharma of the *prajñāpāramitā*, form cannot be apprehended; as it is explained at length, up to and including the fact that the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas cannot be apprehended.

Although herein no phenomena whatsoever can be apprehended, bodhisattvas are nevertheless able to apply themselves with diligent vigor to the study of the perfection of wisdom, never regressing until they reach unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. For this reason, I say that it is an extremely difficult task for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to practice the profound perfection of wisdom.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
All sentient beings, including ourselves, should pay homage to these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are able to don such great armor of merit."

"Bhagavān! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dons the armor of merit and exerts diligent vigor for the sake of maturing and liberating all sentient beings, it is as if they don the armor of merit and exert diligent vigor for the sake of maturing and liberating space;
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva dons the armor of merit and exerts diligent vigor for the sake of all phenomena, it is as if they don the armor of merit and exert diligent vigor for the sake of space."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dons the armor of merit and exerts diligent vigor in order to uproot sentient beings from the suffering of birth and death, it is like donning the armor of merit and exerting diligent vigor in order to lift an empty space and place it upon a high and exalted location.

"Bhagavān! It is for the sake of securing great benefit and happiness for all sentient beings, who are like space, that the bodhisattva mahāsattvas attain the perfection of great diligence and set out toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

"Bhagavān! These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have attained inconceivable and peerless spiritual powers; donning the armor of merit for the sake of the ocean-like nature of all phenomena, which is like space, they set out toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

"Bhagavān! These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are most exceedingly courageous; for the sake of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas—which is like space—they don the armor of merit and exert diligent vigor."
“World-Honored One!

It is truly rare that the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, for the sake of all sentient beings who are like space, diligently practice asceticism with the desire to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment!”

Why is this? Suppose the great trichiliocosm were filled with Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as dense as a forest of bamboo, hemp, reeds, or sugarcane, who remained in the world for an eon or more than an eon, constantly preaching the sublime Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings and each delivering immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings, causing them to enter parinirvāṇa and attain ultimate peace and happiness; yet the realm of sentient beings would neither increase nor decrease.
Why is this? Because all sentient beings are non-existent and by nature remote from existence.
World-Honored One!

Suppose that all the worlds of the ten directions were filled with Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas—standing like forests of bamboo, hemp, reeds, or sugarcane—and they remained for an eon or more than an eon, constantly preaching the sublime Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, each delivering immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings and causing them to enter nirvāṇa, the ultimate peace and happiness; yet the realm of sentient beings would neither increase nor decrease.
Why is this so? Because all sentient beings are non-existent and by nature remote from existence.
World-Honored One!

For this reason, I say that it is truly rare for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to diligently practice asceticism for the sake of all sentient beings—who are like space—in order to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment!
At that time, a certain bhikṣu among the assembly had this thought to himself: "I should pay homage to the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

Although within it there is no arising or ceasing of any phenomena (*dharma*), there is the designation of the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*), the aggregate of concentration (*samādhiskandha*), the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñāskandha*), the aggregate of liberation (*vimuktiskandha*), and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśanaskandha*) which can be found; there is also the designation of the fruits of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), non-returning (*anāgāmin*), and arhatship, as well as the enlightenment of a solitary buddha (*pratyekabuddhabodhi*), the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas (*anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi*) which can be found; and there is also the designation of the Buddha-jewel (*buddharatna*), the Dharma-jewel (*dharmanatna*), and the Saṅgha-jewel (*saṅgharatna*), as well as the turning of the sublime wheel of Dharma to deliver the multitudes of sentient beings which can be found."
The Buddha, knowing his thought, addressed him, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have conceived:

Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked Subhūti:

"How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, although they realize that all phenomena are like an illusion, like a dream, like an echo, like a reflection, like a shadow, like a mirage, like a city of the gandharvas, and like a magical creation, yet this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not grasp at these illusions—and so on, as extensively explained—up to these magical creations; does not grasp at [arising] from illusions—and so on, up to—from magical creations; does not grasp at [belonging to] illusions—and so on, up to—to magical creations; and does not grasp at [relying upon] illusions—and so on, up to—relying upon magical creations?"

Subhūti replied: "When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not grasp at this form—this being explained in detail up to all-aspect-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā)—nor do they grasp by means of form, nor do they grasp as belonging to form, nor do they grasp based on form; and so on, up to all-aspect-knowledge."

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, although they realize that all phenomena are like illusions and even like conjured things, they are able to refrain from grasping at these as being illusions or even as being conjured things; nor do they grasp at them by way of illusion or even by way of conjured things; nor do they grasp at them as belonging to illusion or even as belonging to conjured things; nor do they grasp at them as depending upon illusion or even as depending upon conjured things; and so on, up to not grasping at them as being characteristics, by way of characteristics, belonging to characteristics, or depending upon characteristics.

At that time, by the power of the World-Honored One’s majestic spiritual authority, all the devas from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven within this trichiliocosm took celestial sandalwood powder and scattered it from afar over the World-Honored One; they then approached the Buddha’s presence, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, through the spiritual power of the Buddha, the various devas each saw one thousand Buddhas in the ten directions proclaiming the *Prajñāpāramitā*; the meaning, the chapters, and the names were all identical to those here.

Among the assemblies of bhikṣus who requested the teaching of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the leader of each was named Subhūti; among the assemblies of devas who posed questions regarding the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the leader of each was named Śakra.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed Subhūti, saying:
“When the Bodhisattva Maitreya realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, he too shall proclaim the perfection of wisdom in this very place;
likewise, all the Buddhas who will appear in this Bhadrakalpa shall also proclaim the perfection of wisdom in this very place.”
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“When the Bodhisattva Maitreya realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, by what dharmas, modes of activity, characteristics, and signs will he proclaim the perfection of wisdom?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When the Bodhisattva Maitreya realizes unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, he shall proclaim the perfection of wisdom by teaching that form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are neither permanent nor impermanent, neither pleasure nor suffering, neither self nor non-self, neither pure nor impure, neither distant nor not distant, neither tranquil nor not tranquil, neither bound nor liberated, neither existent nor empty, and neither past, nor future, nor present."

To speak at length, up to and including: one should proclaim the *prajñāpāramitā* by means of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*), and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) as being neither permanent nor impermanent, neither pleasure nor suffering, neither self nor non-self, neither pure nor impure, neither distant nor not distant, neither tranquil nor not tranquil, neither bound nor liberated, neither existent nor empty, and neither past, nor future, nor present.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When the Bodhisattva Maitreya attains unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, what dharmas will he realize?
What dharmas will he teach?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When the Bodhisattva Maitreya attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, he will realize the ultimate purity of form and proclaim the ultimate purity of form; and so on, in detail, until he realizes the ultimate purity of all-aspect omniscience and proclaims the ultimate purity of all-aspect omniscience."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“In what way is the profound perfection of wisdom pure?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Because form is pure, the profound perfection of wisdom is pure; and so on, up to: because the knowledge of all aspects is pure, the profound perfection of wisdom is pure.”
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In what way is the profound perfection of wisdom purified because form is purified?
To speak at length, in what way is the profound perfection of wisdom purified because everything up to all-aspect omniscience is purified?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Form is pure because it is without arising or cessation, and without defilement or purification; because form is pure, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is pure. This is explained at length up to: all-aspect-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) is pure because it is without arising or cessation, and without defilement or purification; because all-aspect-knowledge is pure, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is pure.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti, because space is pure, the perfection of profound wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is pure.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:

The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Furthermore, Subhūti!

To speak at length, up to: because all-aspect omniscience cannot be grasped, it is without defilement; because all-aspect omniscience is without defilement, the profound perfection of wisdom is pure.”

Chapter Twelve: Praising Virtues, Part Three. Chapter Twelve: Praising Virtues. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

If sons or daughters of good family can, with a sincere mind, hear, receive and uphold, read and recite, diligently study, reflect upon according to principle, copy, explain, and widely disseminate this profound *prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, these sons and daughters of good family will have no affliction of the sense faculties, their limbs will be complete, their bodies will not grow decrepit, nor will they die an untimely death; they will always be respectfully surrounded, followed, and protected by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas.
These sons and daughters of good family, on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of both the dark and light fortnights, shall read, recite, and proclaim this profound Prajñāpāramitā.

At that time, the gods from the Realm of the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven all gathered at the place where this Dharma teacher was, in order to listen to and receive the profound meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā. By virtue of these causes and conditions, these sons and daughters of good family shall obtain immeasurable, incalculable, boundless, inconceivable, and rare merit.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.
Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is a great treasury of jewels.

By virtue of this great jewel-treasury of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings are liberated from the sufferings of the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the miseries of poverty and illness among humans and devas. Furthermore, it can bestow wealth, honor, and peace upon immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings, from the great kṣatriya clans up to the great householder clans; it can bestow wealth, honor, and peace upon immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings, from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception; and it can bestow the sovereign peace and bliss of the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship, as well as the enlightenment of pratyekabuddhas and unsurpassed bodhi, upon immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings.

Why is this? Within the great jewel-treasury of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, there is an extensive exposition and revelation of the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and so on, up to all-aspect knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*). Within this, immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings practice and train, thereby attaining birth in great kṣatriya clans or even great householder clans; or they are born among the gods of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception; or they attain the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; or they enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from corruption (*samyaktvaniyāma*), cultivate the various stages of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
For this reason, the profound Prajñāpāramitā is called a great treasury of jewels, because all the precious virtues of both the mundane and supramundane realms appear in dependence upon it.

“Subhūti, you should know that within this great jewel-treasury of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, not even the slightest phenomenon is said to arise or cease, to be defiled or purified, or to be grasped or relinquished.”
Why is this? Because herein there is no dharma that can arise or cease, that can be defiled or purified, and that can be grasped or abandoned.
Subhūti, you should know this!

Within this great jewel treasury of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, it is not taught that any phenomenon is wholesome or unwholesome, with outflows or without outflows, blameworthy or blameless, defiled or pure, mundane or supramundane, conditioned or unconditioned.
For this reason, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is called the great dharma-treasury of non-apprehension.
Subhūti, you should know that within this great jewel-treasury of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, not even the slightest dharma is said to be either defiled or purified.
Why is this? Because within this there is no dharma that can be defiled or purified.
For this reason, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is called the great dharma-treasury of non-defilement and non-purification.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they have no such perception, no such discrimination, no such attainment, and no such conceptual proliferation as:
'I am able to practice the profound perfection of wisdom.'"

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in accordance with reality, is also able to draw near to and serve the Buddhas; they travel from one buddha-field to another to make offerings, pay respect, honor, and praise the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. Wandering through these buddha-fields, they skillfully grasp their characteristics, bringing sentient beings to maturity and adorning and purifying the buddha-fields, while cultivating the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva and swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

This profound prajñāpāramitā does not lean toward or away from any phenomena; it does not attract or repel, does not grasp or abandon, does not arise or cease, is neither defiled nor pure, and neither increases nor decreases."

The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is neither of the past, nor of the future, nor of the present; it does not transcend the desire realm, nor does it abide in the desire realm; it does not transcend the form realm, nor does it abide in the form realm; it does not transcend the formless realm, nor does it abide in the formless realm.
It neither bestows nor relinquishes the *dānapāramitā*, and so on, up to neither bestowing nor relinquishing the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

It neither bestows nor relinquishes the fruit of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), and so on, up to neither bestowing nor relinquishing the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha.

He does not bestow the dharmas of the noble ones, nor does he abandon the dharmas of ordinary beings; he does not bestow the dharmas of the Buddhas, nor does he abandon the dharmas of the Two Vehicles; he does not bestow the unconditioned realm, nor does he abandon the conditioned realm.
Why is this so? Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear in the world, these phenomena remain forever unchanging, abiding within the realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*).

All Tathāgatas realize and directly perceive them; having themselves realized and directly perceived them, they proclaim, reveal, analyze, and clarify them for all sentient beings, causing them to likewise awaken to and enter that which is free from all conceptual constructions, discriminations, and inversions.

At that time, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devaputras, dwelling in the midst of the sky, leaped for joy with great exultation. Each of them took celestial *utpala* flowers, *padma* flowers, *kumuda* flowers, *pundarika* flowers, and *sugandhika* flowers, as well as various powdered incenses, and scattered them over the Buddha. They congratulated one another and, with one voice, proclaimed:
"We now behold in Jambudvīpa the Buddha’s second turning of the sublime Wheel of Dharma."

"In this regard, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devaputras, having heard the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā*, all equally realized the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, the Blessed One addressed Subhūti, saying:
'Such a wheel of Dharma is neither the first turning nor the second.'"

Why is this? It is because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* appears in the world not for the sake of turning toward or returning from any phenomena, but solely because of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,

by virtue of the emptiness of what kind of non-existent intrinsic nature does the profound perfection of wisdom appear in the world so as not to cause any phenomenon to proceed forward, nor to cause it to return?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā*—indeed, because the *prajñāpāramitā* from the profound *prajñāpāramitā* down to the *dānapāramitā*—is empty of its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*); and so on, up to: because all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are empty of their own intrinsic nature;

and because the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*) is empty of the intrinsic nature of the fruit of stream-entry; and so on, up to: because the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*) is empty of the intrinsic nature of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas.”

Subhūti, you should know that because all such phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature by virtue of having no intrinsic nature, this profound perfection of wisdom appears in the world neither for the sake of proceeding nor for the sake of returning.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“This profound perfection of wisdom is a great perfection, because it realizes that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty.”

Although they realize that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, by relying on this prajñāpāramitā, realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment and turn the wondrous wheel of Dharma to deliver the multitudes of sentient beings;
yet, although they realize enlightenment, there is nothing realized, because the dharma of realization and non-realization cannot be apprehended;
and although they turn the wheel of Dharma, there is nothing turned, because the turning of dharmas and the returning of dharmas cannot be apprehended.
Although one delivers sentient beings, there is nothing delivered, because the dharma of seeing or not seeing cannot be apprehended.
World-Honored One!

Within this Great Prajñāpāramitā, the act of turning the wheel of Dharma is entirely unapprehendable, because all dharmas are eternally unborn and both the one who turns and that which is turned are unapprehendable.
Why is this? Within the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, how could there be any dharma that can turn forward or turn back?
This is because a dharma characterized by turning or returning cannot be apprehended.

“Bhagavān! If one can thus proclaim, reveal, analyze, and clarify the profound *prajñāpāramitā* so as to facilitate its easy comprehension, this is called the skillful and pure proclamation of the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Within this, there is absolutely no speaker, no hearer, no teaching, and no dharma received; since there is no speaker, no hearer, and no dharma, those who could realize it are likewise unattainable, and because there is no one to realize it, there is also no one who can attain nirvāṇa.

Within the well-expounded Dharma of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, there is likewise no field of merit; because the giver, the recipient, and the gift are all empty of intrinsic nature, and since the field of merit does not exist, the nature of merit is also empty.
"Because all designations and names are unapprehendable, it is therefore called the Great Pāramitā.
