Noble sons who train therein may only attain the fruit of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, but they do not attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; these are called "other sūtras that are like branches and leaves," which cannot give rise to the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is certainly able to bring forth the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*), possessing great power and function like the roots of a tree.
Those sons of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle who abandon the *prajñāpāramitā* to seek and study other sūtras will certainly be unable to attain the knowledge of all modes.
Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can give rise to all mundane and supramundane merits of the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, whereas other sūtras lack such efficacy.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and studies the perfection of wisdom, they are thereby practicing and studying all the mundane and supramundane treasures of merit belonging to the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

It is like a starving dog that abandons its own staple food and instead seeks it from a servant; likewise, there will be sons of good family who abide in the Mahāyāna and yet abandon the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, which is the root of all Buddha-dharmas, to seek and study sūtras associated with the two vehicles. You should know that this is a work of Māra for bodhisattvas."
"Furthermore, Subhūti! It is as if there were a person who, desiring to seek a fragrant elephant, having found this elephant, would abandon it to seek its tracks.
What do you think?"
"Is that person wise? Subhūti replied,
"That person is not wise."
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"In future ages, there will be sons of good family who abide in the Mahāyāna and yet abandon the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, which is the root of all Buddha-dharmas, to seek and study sūtras associated with the two vehicles; their condition shall be understood as an act of Māra for bodhisattvas."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
It is as if there were a person who wished to see the great ocean; having reached the shore, he instead looked back at a cow's footprint and thought to himself:
'How could the measure of the water in the great ocean—so deep and vast—possibly compare to this?'"
"What do you think? Is that person wise? Subhūti replied:
“That person is not wise.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“In a future age, there will be sons of good family who abide in the Mahāyāna; they will abandon the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, which is the root of all Buddha-dharmas, and instead seek to study sūtras associated with the two vehicles. Their condition will be just like that; you should know that this is the work of Māra for a bodhisattva.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose there were a skilled master builder or his apprentice who wished to construct a great palace equal in scale to the magnificent palace of Śakra, Lord of the Devas; yet, having seen that palace, he instead took the celestial palaces of the sun and moon as his model."
"What do you think?
Could such a master craftsman, or his disciple, construct a great palace equal in measure to the magnificent palace of Śakra? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Is that person wise? Subhūti replied:
"That person is not wise; he belongs to the class of the deluded. The Buddha told Subhūti:

"In future ages, there will be sons of good family who abide in the Mahāyāna and wish to proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, yet they abandon the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and seek to study scriptures associated with the two vehicles. Their condition is just like that [of the aforementioned person]; they will certainly not attain unsurpassed enlightenment. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! It is as if there were a person who wished to see a wheel-turning monarch; having seen him, they did not recognize him and left for another place. There, they saw a minor king and, observing his physical appearance, thought to themselves:
'How does the physical appearance and majestic power of a wheel-turning sage-king differ from this?'"
"What do you think? Is that person wise? Subhūti replied:
"That person is not wise.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"In a future age, there will likewise be sons of good family who abide in the Great Vehicle and seek to proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, yet they abandon the profound *prajñāpāramitā* to seek and study sūtras associated with the two vehicles, saying:"
"What difference is there between this sutra and that one? What use is that?
Because of such thoughts, they will certainly be unable to attain the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Suppose there were a hungry person who, having obtained food of a hundred flavors, cast it aside to seek and eat sixty-day-old rice.
What do you think?"
"Is that person wise? Subhūti replied,
"That person is not wise."
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"In a future age, there will be sons of good family who abide in the Mahāyāna and yet abandon the profound *prajñāpāramitā* to seek and study sūtras associated with the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*). Desiring to find the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) therein, they will labor in vain and ultimately be unable to attain it."
"What do you think?
Is that person wise? Subhūti replied:
"That person is not wise.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"It is so! It is thus!"
"It is so! You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!"
Suppose there were a poor man who obtained a priceless jewel, yet he cast it aside and instead took up a *kācamaṇi*.
What do you think? Is that person wise?
Subhūti replied, “That person is not wise.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"In future ages, there will be sons of good family who abide in the Mahāyāna, yet who abandon the profound *prajñāpāramitā* to seek and study sūtras associated with the two vehicles; desiring therein to find the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*), they will labor in vain and ultimately be unable to attain it."
"What do you think?
Is that person wise? Subhūti replied:
"That person is not wise.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"It is so! It is thus!"
"It is so! You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!"

When sons of good family who abide in the Mahāyāna are transcribing the profound *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, if various forms of eloquence suddenly arise and they take delight in expounding diverse and distinct Dharma-gates, such that the transcription of the sūtra cannot be brought to completion, you should know that this constitutes a demonic activity of a bodhisattva (*bodhisattva-mārakarma*).

What is meant by "various forms of eloquence"? It refers to delighting in speaking of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles; delighting in speaking of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*); delighting in speaking of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm; delighting in speaking of the merit of upholding, reciting, and reading [the scriptures]; delighting in speaking of tending to the sick and cultivating other meritorious deeds; delighting in speaking of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*); delighting in speaking of all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, and attainments (*samāpatti*); and delighting in speaking of inner emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) up to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). One should know that all such things are the works of Māra for a bodhisattva.

Why is this? Because in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the characteristics of dharmas that delight in being spoken of are entirely unattainable; for it is without vitarka and vicāra, difficult to conceive, beyond deliberation, without arising or ceasing, without defilement or purity, without concentration or distraction, free from names and phrases, ineffable, and unattainable.
Why is this? Because within the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, all the phenomena previously described are non-existent and utterly unapprehendable.

When sons of good family who abide in the Great Vehicle transcribe this profound *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, such phenomena disturb their minds and prevent them from reaching completion; therefore, these are called the deeds of Māra for a bodhisattva.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
can this profound perfection of wisdom be written down?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"It cannot be written down. Why is that?

In this profound *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, the six *pāramitās*, beginning with *prajñā*, all lack intrinsic nature and are entirely unapprehendable; as explained at length, even up to and including the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), they likewise lack intrinsic nature and are entirely unapprehendable.
"Subhūti, you should know that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is non-existent and entirely unapprehendable; this very absence of nature is the profound *prajñāpāramitā*."
It is not that a dharma lacking intrinsic nature can write down that which lacks intrinsic nature; therefore, I say that the profound *prajñāpāramitā* cannot be written down.
Subhūti, you should know this!
If sons of good family who abide in the Mahāyāna conceive the notion of non-existence regarding the Prajñāpāramitā, you should know that this is an act of Māra for a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If sons of good family and others who abide in the Great Vehicle, while copying the profound *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, should form this thought:
'I am writing down the *Prajñāpāramitā* with letters.'"
If one relies on words and becomes attached to the *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva. Why is this?

Within this profound sūtra of the *prajñāpāramitā*, all the *pāramitās* from *prajñā* down to *dāna* are without words; form (*rūpa*) through consciousness (*vijñāna*) are also without words; and so on, in detail, even up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), which is likewise without words. Therefore, one should not grasp at the notion that there are words capable of writing down the *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Subhūti, you should know this!
If sons of good family and others who abide in the Great Vehicle should form such an attachment as this:

'In this profound *prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, all perfections from *prajñāpāramitā* down to *dānapāramitā* are without syllables; from form (*rūpa*) down to consciousness (*vijñāna*), they too are without syllables; and so on, in detail, up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), which is also without syllables.'"
"You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva. Furthermore, Subhūti,
when sons of good family who abide in the Great Vehicle write down, receive, uphold, read, recite, and cultivate [this teaching]..."
...when contemplating, reflecting upon, or expounding this profound *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*,
if one should think of a land, or a city, or a royal capital,
or a region, or a preceptor, or a teacher, or fellow students, or friends; or...
Whether one thinks of one's parents, or one's wife and children, or one's brothers, or one's sisters,
or one's relatives, or one's friends, or one's king, or one's ministers, or one's thieves,
or one's fierce beasts, or one's wicked people, or one's evil spirits, or...
If one thinks of the assembly gathering, or of pastimes, or of seeking revenge, or of repaying kindness,
or of various other tasks to be performed, one should know that all these are the works of Māra for a bodhisattva.
"Māra uses these matters to disturb and vex the bodhisattva, so that the tasks they undertake are not accomplished.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when sons of good family who abide in the Great Vehicle write down, receive, uphold, read, recite, cultivate, contemplate, and expound this profound *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, they may obtain great fame, profit, offerings, and respect—namely, clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicinal requisites for illness, and other material wealth. If they become attached to such things and neglect their spiritual practice, you should know that this is a work of Māra for the bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When sons of good family and others who abide in the Great Vehicle are copying, upholding, reading, reciting, practicing, contemplating, and expounding this profound *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, there will be various evil Māras who hold various worldly treatises or even scriptures associated with the Two Vehicles, and falsely appearing as friends, they will offer them to the Bodhisattvas. These works extensively explain worldly superior matters, or else they extensively explain the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), truths (*satya*), dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*), the three doors of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*), the four meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), and so forth, saying: 'The meaning and flavor of these scriptures are profound; you should diligently practice and study them, and abandon the scriptures you have previously practiced.'"

These sons of good family who abide in the Mahāyāna possess skillful means; they should not accept or become attached to the worldly treatises bestowed by Māra, nor to the sūtras associated with the two vehicles.

Why is this so? Because worldly treatises and the scriptures of the two vehicles cannot give rise to the knowledge of all modes; they are not the unerring means for proceeding toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, but rather constitute a profound obstacle to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

"Subhūti, you should know that within this profound sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā, I have extensively explained the skillful means of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas' path. If one diligently practices and studies herein, one will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

If sons of good family who abide in the Mahāyāna, due to a lack of skillful means, abandon the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and instead study the mundane treatises of Māra or the sūtras of the two vehicles, you should know that this constitutes a demonic deed (*mārakarman*) for a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If those who are able to hear the Dharma delight in hearing, questioning, copying, receiving, upholding, reciting, and practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, yet those who are able to teach the Dharma become attached to pleasure and indolence, being unwilling to explain it or bestow this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is the work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma has a mind that is neither attached to pleasure nor indolent, and delights in preaching and bestowing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, skillfully encouraging [others] to copy, uphold, recite, and cultivate it; yet the one who listens to the Dharma is indolent and attached to pleasure, having no desire to listen, receive, or even cultivate it—know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If those who are able to hear the Dharma take delight in hearing it, taking delight in questioning about it, copying it, receiving and upholding it, reciting it, and practicing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, yet the one who can preach the Dharma intends to go to another region and is unable to provide instruction, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a teacher of the Dharma delights in speaking and delights in bestowing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and through skillful means encourages [others] to copy, uphold, read, recite, and cultivate it, yet a listener of the Dharma wishes to go to another region and fails to receive and hear it—know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma possesses great evil desires, being deeply attached to fame, profit, clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other material wealth, and never having enough in their heart regarding offerings and respect; while the one who listens to the Dharma has few desires, is easily contented, practices the life of seclusion, is courageous and diligent, is endowed with mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, and feels weary of and fears gain, honor, and reputation—because these two are not in harmony, they will fail to obtain the teaching, listening, copying, reciting, and cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose the one who preaches the Dharma has few desires and is content, practices seclusion, is courageous and diligent, possesses mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, and feels aversion toward and fear of gain, honor, and fame; yet the one who listens to the Dharma possesses great evil desires, craving and valuing reputation, profit, clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other material wealth, never being satisfied with offerings, honor, or respect. Because these two are not in harmony, they fail to obtain the teaching, listening, copying, upholding, reciting, and practicing of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma practices the twelve dhūta-guṇas—namely, dwelling in an araṇya up to possessing only three robes—and the one who listens to the Dharma does not practice the twelve dhūta-guṇas, they will lack mutual harmony. They shall fail to obtain the teaching, listening, writing, reciting, and cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who listens to the Dharma practices the twelve dhūta-guṇas, while the one who preaches the Dharma does not practice the twelve dhūta-guṇas, they will not be in harmony. Consequently, they will fail to obtain the teaching, listening, writing, upholding, reciting, and cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose the one who preaches the Dharma possesses faith and ethical discipline, and delights in explaining the profound *prajñāpāramitā* to others, skillfully encouraging them to copy, receive, uphold, recite, and cultivate it; yet the one who listens to the Dharma lacks faith and ethical discipline, and does not delight in listening or receiving it. Because these two are not in harmony, they fail to obtain the teaching, listening, copying, upholding, reciting, and cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! Suppose those who listen to the Dharma possess faith and ethical discipline, and delight in hearing and in questioning; they transcribe, receive, uphold, recite, and cultivate the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. Yet, the one who expounds the Dharma lacks faith and ethical discipline, and has no desire to instruct. Because these two are not in harmony, they fail to achieve the exposition and listening, the transcription, receiving, upholding, reciting, and cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma has a mind free from stinginess and is able to relinquish everything, while the one who listens to the Dharma has a mind possessed by stinginess and is unable to give or sacrifice, these two will not be in harmony. They shall fail to obtain the teaching, listening, copying, upholding, reciting, and practicing of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is an affair of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who listens to the Dharma has a mind free from stinginess and is able to relinquish everything, while the one who preaches the Dharma has a mind of stinginess and is unable to give, these two will not be in harmony. They shall fail to obtain the teaching, the listening and receiving, the copying and upholding, the reading and reciting, and the cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is an act of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If those who wish to listen to the Dharma desire to provide the Dharma-preacher with offerings of robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other requisites, yet the Dharma-preacher does not wish to accept them, and because of this lack of harmony between the two, they fail to receive instruction, listen to, write down, recite, and cultivate the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma seeks to provide the listener with robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other necessities, but the listener does not wish to accept them, and thus the two do not harmonize, failing to obtain the teaching, listening, copying, reciting, and practicing of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is the work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who can preach the Dharma possesses the wisdom of opening [the meaning] but does not delight in detailed exposition, while the one who can listen to the Dharma possesses the wisdom of unfolding [the words] but does not delight in concise summary, and the two are thus not in harmony, they will fail to obtain the teaching, the listening and receiving, the copying and upholding, the reading and reciting, and the cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who listens to the Dharma possesses the wisdom of opening [the meaning] yet does not delight in extensive explanation, and the one who explains the Dharma possesses the wisdom of unfolding [the words] yet does not delight in concise summary, and the two are thus not in harmony, they will fail to obtain the teaching, listening, receiving, writing, reciting, and practicing of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma is solely intent on extensively knowing the sequential meanings of the twelve branches of the teaching—namely, from the *sūtra* up to the *upadeśa*—while the one who listens to the Dharma does not take pleasure in extensively knowing the sequential meanings of the twelve branches of the teaching, and the two do not harmonize, such that they fail to obtain the instruction, listening, receiving, writing, reciting, and cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who listens to the Dharma takes sole delight in extensively knowing the sequential meanings of the twelvefold teachings, while the one who preaches the Dharma does not take delight in extensively knowing the sequential meanings of the twelvefold teachings, these two will not be in harmony. Consequently, they shall fail to obtain the teaching, listening, receiving, copying, reciting, and practicing of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma has accomplished the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) and possesses skillful means (upāya-kauśalya) regarding these six perfections, yet the one who listens to the Dharma lacks such virtues, and the two are not in harmony, they will fail to obtain the teaching, listening, copying, upholding, reciting, and practicing of the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If those who are able to listen to the Dharma have accomplished the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) and possess skillful means (upāya-kauśalya) regarding these six perfections, while those who are able to preach the Dharma lack such virtues, and the two do not harmonize, they will fail to obtain the teaching, listening, copying, upholding, reciting, and practicing of the profound Prajñāpāramitā. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma has attained dhāraṇī, while the one who listens to the Dharma has not attained dhāraṇī, they will not be in harmony. Consequently, they will fail to obtain the teaching, listening, receiving, writing, upholding, reciting, and practicing of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who listens to the Dharma has already attained dhāraṇī, while the one who preaches the Dharma has not yet attained dhāraṇī, and the two do not harmonize, they will fail to obtain the teaching, listening, receiving, writing, upholding, reciting, and practicing of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma wishes for others to respectfully copy, uphold, read, recite, and practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, yet the one who listens to the Dharma does not comply with their intention, and because the two are not in harmony, they do not obtain the teaching, listening, copying, upholding, reading, reciting, or practicing of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is the work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If those who wish to listen to the Dharma desire to respectfully transcribe, uphold, recite, and cultivate the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, yet the one who preaches the Dharma does not comply with their wishes, such that the two do not harmonize, and they fail to obtain instruction, listening, transcription, recitation, and cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma has already abandoned the stain of stinginess and the five hindrances, while the one who listens to the Dharma has not yet abandoned the stain of stinginess and the five hindrances, and the two are thus not in harmony, they will fail to obtain the teaching, listening, writing, upholding, reciting, and practicing of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who listens to the Dharma has already abandoned the stain of stinginess and abandoned the five hindrances, while the one who preaches the Dharma has not yet abandoned the stain of stinginess and has not yet abandoned the five hindrances, and the two are thus not in harmony, they will fail to obtain the teaching, listening, writing, upholding, reciting, and practicing of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is the work of Māra for a bodhisattva."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when sons of good family who abide in the Great Vehicle are copying, upholding, reading, reciting, practicing, contemplating, and expounding this profound *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, if someone should come and describe to them the various sufferings of the three miserable realms, they might further say to them:

'You should apply yourself with diligence in this very body to quickly reach the end of suffering and enter parinirvāṇa. Why do you linger in the great ocean of birth and death to undergo hundreds of thousands of kinds of unbearable sufferings in pursuit of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? "

"Because of these words, they will fail to reach the ultimate goal regarding the profound sūtras of the *prajñāpāramitā*—whether in writing them down, receiving and upholding them, reciting them, practicing them, contemplating them, or explaining them. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When sons of good family and others who abide in the Great Vehicle are copying, upholding, reading, reciting, practicing, contemplating, and expounding this profound *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, if someone comes and praises the various superior matters of the human realm, or praises the various sublime and wondrous matters of the gods from the Cāturmahārājika Heaven up to the Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana Heaven, and says to them: "

"Although you experience the pleasures of desire in the desire realm, the bliss of meditative concentration in the form realm, and the bliss of meditative absorption in the formless realm, all of these are impermanent, suffering, empty, non-self, impure, and subject to transformation; they are phenomena that pass away, depart, exhaust, and cease. Why, with respect to this body, do you not apply yourself with diligence to attain the fruit of a Stream-enterer, or a Once-returner, or a Non-returner, or the fruit of Arhatship; or why do you not enter Parinirvāṇa through the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha for the sake of ultimate peace and happiness? What is the use of dwelling long in the cycle of birth and death, undergoing various hardships on behalf of others for no purpose, when you could instead seek to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"

"Because of these words, one will fail to reach the ultimate goal regarding the profound sūtras of the *prajñāpāramitā*—whether in writing them down, receiving and upholding them, reading and reciting them, practicing them, contemplating them, or explaining them. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma has no personal attachments and is solely intent on his own affairs, unconcerned with the work of others, while the one who listens to the Dharma is fond of leading a retinue and delights in attending to the affairs of others, unconcerned with his own work—if these two are not in harmony and thus fail to obtain instruction, listening, writing, upholding, reciting, and practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a demonic deed of a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose the one who listens to the Dharma has no attachments in this life and devotes himself exclusively to his own affairs, showing no concern for the work of others; while the one who preaches the Dharma delights in leading a following and enjoys managing the affairs of others, showing no concern for his own work. Because these two are not in harmony, they fail to obtain the teaching and listening, the copying and upholding, the reciting and chanting, and the cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a demonic deed of a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma does not delight in clamor and bustle, while the one who listens to the Dharma delights in staying amidst clamor and bustle, and the two are thus not in harmony, they will fail to obtain the teaching, listening, writing, upholding, reciting, and practicing of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who listens to the Dharma does not delight in clamor and confusion, while the one who preaches the Dharma delights in dwelling amidst clamor and confusion, and the two are thus not in harmony, they will fail to obtain the teaching, listening, writing, upholding, reciting, and practicing of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who preaches the Dharma desires that the listener assist them in all their undertakings for my sake, yet the listener does not comply with that desire, and the two do not reach harmony, such that they fail to obtain the teaching, listening, copying, upholding, reciting, and practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If those who listen to the Dharma take pleasure in assisting the teacher in all their activities, yet the teacher who expounds the Dharma does not comply with their wishes, and because the two are thus not in harmony, they fail to obtain the teaching, listening, writing, upholding, reciting, and practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a teacher of the Dharma, for the sake of fame and profit, desires to preach it to others and further wishes to have them write down, receive, uphold, recite, and practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, yet the listener understands his motive and does not wish to receive it from him—so that the two do not harmonize and fail to obtain the teaching, the listening, the writing, the upholding, the reciting, and the practicing of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*—you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! Suppose there is a listener who, for the sake of fame and profit, desires to request another to preach, and further wishes to employ skillful means to copy, receive, uphold, recite, and cultivate the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. However, the preacher, knowing the listener's motives, does not comply with the request. Because the two do not harmonize, they fail to obtain instruction, nor to listen, receive, copy, uphold, recite, or cultivate the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the one who can preach the Dharma wishes to go to another region where life and limb are in danger, while the one who can listen to the Dharma fears for their life and does not wish to follow them, and thus the two are not in harmony, failing thereby to obtain the teaching, listening, receiving, copying, reciting, and practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, if the one who wishes to hear the Dharma intends to go to another region where life and limb are in danger, while the one who can preach the Dharma fears for their own life and does not wish to go with them, and because these two are not in harmony, they fail to obtain the teaching, the hearing and receiving, the copying and upholding, the reading and reciting, and the cultivation of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose a teacher of the Dharma wishes to go to another land that is beset by many bandits, epidemics, hunger, and thirst, while those who wish to hear the Dharma fear the hardships there and are unwilling to follow him. If these two do not harmonize and thus fail to obtain the teaching, listening, writing, upholding, reciting, and practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose a listener of the Dharma wishes to go to another land that is beset by many bandits, epidemics, hunger, and thirst, while the teacher of the Dharma, fearing such hardships, is unwilling to go with them. Because the two are not in harmony, they fail to receive instruction, listen to, write down, uphold, recite, or practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! Suppose a teacher of the Dharma wishes to go to another region that is peaceful, prosperous, and free from calamities, and a listener of the Dharma wishes to follow him. The teacher of the Dharma, employing skillful means, might say:
'Although you wish to follow me for the sake of profit, will you necessarily achieve your heart's desire upon reaching that place? You should reflect well and carefully before later feeling regret.'"
At that time, those listening to the Dharma, having heard this, thought to themselves:
"This is his sign of wishing for me to leave; even if I were to follow him firmly, would I necessarily hear the Dharma?"

For this reason, if one does not follow them away, and the two do not reach a harmonious accord, such that one fails to obtain instruction, listen to, write down, recite, or practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this constitutes a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose a teacher of the Dharma wishes to travel to another region, and the road he must traverse passes through a wilderness that is desolate and perilous, filled with many dangers from bandits, as well as fears of caṇḍālas, wild beasts, hunters, and venomous snakes. A listener of the Dharma wishes to follow him, but the teacher of the Dharma uses skillful means to test him, saying:

'For what reason do you now follow me without any business of your own, intending to pass through such places of great danger and hardship? You should reflect upon this carefully; do not later fall into grief or regret.'"
The one who is able to listen to the Dharma, having heard this, thinks to themselves:
"He likely does not wish for me to go along with him; even if I were to insist on going, how could I possibly hear the Dharma?

Due to these causes and conditions, they do not follow him. Because the two are not in harmony, they fail to receive instruction, to listen and accept it, to write it down and uphold it, to recite it, and to cultivate the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this constitutes a demonic deed (*mārakarman*) of a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a Dharma-preacher has many donors who constantly follow him, and a listener comes to request that he preach the *prajñāpāramitā*, or requests that it be written down, upheld, recited, or practiced according to the teaching, the preacher may have many obstacles and lack the leisure to provide instruction. Consequently, the listener gives rise to a mind of resentment; even if instruction is later provided, they do not listen or accept it. Because the two are not in harmony, they fail to obtain the teaching, listening, writing, upholding, reciting, and practicing of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

there are evil Māras who take the form of bhikṣus and approach bodhisattvas with skillful means to destroy them, so that they may not transcribe, uphold, read, recite, cultivate, contemplate, or explain to others the profound sūtras of the Prajñāpāramitā."
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:

“How is it that Māra, the Evil One, assuming the guise of a bhikṣu, approaches a bodhisattva and employs skillful means to obstruct them, so that they are unable to copy, or even to expound, the profound sūtras of the Prajñāpāramitā?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"There are certain evil Māras who take the form of bhikṣus and approach the bodhisattvas with skillful means to destroy them, causing them to disparage and become weary of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, saying:
'The formless sūtras you study and recite are not the true *prajñāpāramitā*; the sūtras with signs that I study and recite are the true *prajñāpāramitā*.'"

When these words were spoken, there were bodhisattvas who had not yet received their prediction [of enlightenment] and consequently gave rise to doubt and confusion regarding the *prajñāpāramitā*. Because of this doubt and confusion, they developed revulsion and disdain for the *prajñāpāramitā*. Due to this revulsion and disdain, they ultimately failed to write it down, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, cultivate and contemplate it, or explain the profound *prajñāpāramitā* to others; you should know that this constitutes a demonic activity (*mārakarman*) of a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! There are evil Māras who take the form of bhikṣus and approach a bodhisattva, saying to that bodhisattva:

'If a bodhisattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they will only realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and attain the fruit of a stream-enterer, up to and including the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; they will ultimately never be able to realize unsurpassed buddhahood. For what reason, then, do you exert yourself in vain in this? "

When a bodhisattva hears this, yet does not write it down, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, cultivate it, contemplate it, or explain it to others—the profound *prajñāpāramitā*—you should know that this is an act of Māra for the bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is being transcribed and so forth, many demonic activities (*mārakarman*) will arise; a bodhisattva should recognize them and remain far removed from them."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What are called the deeds of Māra that cause bodhisattvas to recognize them and remain far removed from them?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When transcribing and otherwise engaging with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, there will be many demonic deeds (*mārakarman*) that resemble the counterfeit *prajñā*, *dhyāna*, *vīrya*, *kṣānti*, *śīla*, and *dāna* pāramitās; there will be many demonic deeds that resemble the counterfeit internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, great emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, non-dispersal emptiness, essential nature emptiness, characteristic emptiness, emptiness of all phenomena, emptiness of non-existence, and emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence; there will be many demonic deeds that resemble the counterfeit *tathatā*, *dharmadhātu*, and so forth, up to the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*). A bodhisattva should recognize these and remain far removed from them."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When this profound *prajñāpāramitā* is being transcribed and so forth, many demonic obstacles (*mārakarman*) will arise to create hindrances. That is to say, an evil Māra may appear in the guise of a bhikṣu and approach the bodhisattva to proclaim teachings associated with the two vehicles, saying to the bodhisattva:
'This is what the Tathāgata has truly taught; those who study this dharma will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.'"

Furthermore, there may be an evil Māra who assumes the form of a bhikṣu and approaches the bodhisattva to proclaim the four foundations of mindfulness and other teachings of the two vehicles, saying to the bodhisattva:

"For now, rely on these dharmas and practice with diligent effort to attain the fruit of stream-entry, and so forth, up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, thereby remaining far removed from all birth, old age, sickness, and death. What need is there for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
"This is an evil Māra-activity regarding the perfection of wisdom; a bodhisattva should recognize it and remain far removed from it.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"

There are certain evil Māras who assume the form of a Buddha, with bodies of true golden color, a constant radiance extending one fathom, and fully adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics. They approach the Bodhisattva, and when the Bodhisattva sees them, he develops deep attachment. Because of this, his progress toward the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) declines, and he fails to hear, inquire about, write down, receive, uphold, recite, practice, contemplate, or explain the profound Prajñāpāramitā. One should know that this is a demonic deed of a Bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are evil Māras who take the form of bhikṣus, with dignified deportment and handsome appearance, and approach the bodhisattva. When the bodhisattva sees them, he develops deep attachment; because of this, his progress toward the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) declines, and he fails to hear, inquire about, write down, receive, uphold, recite, cultivate, contemplate, or explain the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. You should know that this is an activity of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are evil Māras who manifest in the form of a Buddha, surrounded by bhikṣus proclaiming the essentials of the Dharma. They come to where the bodhisattva is, and upon seeing them, the bodhisattva develops a deep attachment and thinks:
'May I, in the future, also be like this. "

Because of this, they regress from the knowledge of all modes; failing to obtain the opportunity to hear, inquire about, write down, receive and uphold, read and recite, practice, contemplate, and expound the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There may be various evil Māras who take the form of bodhisattvas—whether numbering in the hundreds, thousands, or even immeasurably many—and who practice either the perfection of generosity or the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom. When a bodhisattva sees them, they develop deep attachment; because of this, their progress toward all-knowledge (*sarvajñājñāna*) declines, and they fail to hear, inquire about, write down, receive, uphold, recite, cultivate, contemplate, or explain the profound perfection of wisdom. You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva."
"Why is this so, Subhūti?

Because within this profound teaching of the Great Perfection of Wisdom (Mahāprajñāpāramitā), form does not exist; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness also do not exist. To speak extensively, even up to all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not exist, and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas also does not exist."

If, in this context, form does not exist—and to speak at length, even the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas does not exist—then in this context, all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as well as the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and all classes of ordinary beings do not exist either.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature. "Furthermore, Subhūti!

When sons of good family and others who dwell securely in the Mahāyāna listen to, inquire about, write down, receive and uphold, recite, practice, contemplate, and explain to others this profound *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, many obstacles and hindering circumstances will arise, causing those of meager merit to fail in their endeavors.

Just as there are various precious jewels in Jambudvīpa, such as vaidūrya down to gold and so forth, which are beset by many thieves, harms, and obstacles, such that persons of meager merit cannot obtain them despite seeking them.
The priceless divine jewel of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise so: when those of meager merit listen to or inquire about it, many evil Māras create obstacles and hindrances.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying: “So it is,
World-Honored One!”

"So it is, Sugata! This profound perfection of wisdom is like the various precious gems of Jambudvīpa, such as vaidūrya and the like, for which there are many obstacles; those of meager merit are unable to obtain them even when seeking them."

Because those sons of good family who abide in the Mahāyāna possess little merit, they encounter many obstacles when listening to or inquiring about the teachings; thus, although they have the aspiration, they are unable to achieve their goal.

Why is this? There are those who are deluded and act under the influence of Māra; when sons of good family who dwell securely in the Great Vehicle listen to, inquire about, write down, receive and uphold, recite, practice, contemplate, and explain to others this profound *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, they create obstacles for them.

"Bhagavān! Those foolish ones possess dull and obscure wisdom; they are unable to conceive of the vast Buddha-dharma, and they themselves are incapable of writing down, receiving, upholding, reciting, practicing, contemplating, inquiring about, or explaining the Prajñāpāramitā. Furthermore, they take pleasure in obstructing others from performing such acts as writing it down."
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.

There are foolish persons who are incited by Māra; they have not planted roots of goodness, their merit and wisdom are meager and inferior, they have not yet made great vows before the Buddha, and they have not been taken into the care of virtuous friends. Such individuals are unable to listen to, inquire about, or even expound the Prajñāpāramitā themselves, yet they create obstacles when newly ordained sons of good family who study the Mahāyāna listen to, inquire about, transcribe, or even expound this profound Sūtra of the Great Prajñāpāramitā.

In future ages, there will be sons and daughters of good family whose merit and wisdom are meager, whose roots of goodness are slight, and who take no delight in the vast merits of the Tathāgatas. Being unable themselves to listen to, inquire about, or even expound the Prajñāpāramitā, they further take pleasure in obstructing others from listening to or inquiring about it. It should be known that such individuals shall incur immeasurable transgressions.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When sons of good family and others who abide in the Great Vehicle listen to, inquire about, write down, receive and uphold, read and recite, practice, contemplate, and explain to others this profound *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, many demonic obstacles (*mārakarma*) will arise to create hindrances, causing their listening, inquiry, and so forth, to fail to reach completion. Because of this, they will be unable to fulfill the *prajñāpāramitā* and the other perfections up to the *dānapāramitā*, and as explained at length, they will be unable to fulfill the *sarvākārajñatā*.

When sons of noble family who abide in the Mahāyāna listen to, inquire about, write down, receive and uphold, read and recite, practice, contemplate, and explain to others this profound *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, if they are free from demonic interference and are further able to fulfill the perfections of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*), diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*), patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), and generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*), up to and including the fulfillment of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), it should be known that this is entirely due to the Tathāgata’s supernatural power, compassion, and protective mindfulness; it is also due to the empowerment and protection of the supernatural powers of all present Tathāgatas in the worlds of the ten directions and the assembly of non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas, which prevents evil Māra hosts from obstructing such activities as listening and inquiring so that they may not be accomplished; and it is also due to the power of those individuals’ own roots of virtue.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle Five Hundred and Nine;
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle Five Hundred and Ten.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Fifteen: The Manifestation of the World, Part Three. Chapter Fifteen: The Manifestation of the World, Section One. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

Suppose there is a woman who has given birth to many sons—perhaps five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or even a hundred or a thousand—and that mother falls ill. Each of her sons diligently seeks out medical treatment, thinking to themselves:
"How may our mother recover from this illness, so that she may enjoy long life and peace, her body free from all suffering and her mind liberated from sorrow?"

At that time, the sons vied with one another to employ skillful means to seek out articles of comfort and protection for their mother’s body, so that she would not be afflicted by the touch of mosquitoes, gadflies, snakes, scorpions, wind, heat, hunger, or thirst. Furthermore, they honored and made offerings to her with various kinds of excellent and sublime articles of pleasure, saying:
"Our mother, through her compassion, gave birth to us and instructed us in the various worldly affairs; how could we fail to repay our mother's kindness!"
"Subhūti! In the same way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha likewise constantly observes and protects the profound Prajñāpāramitā with his Buddha-eye through various skillful means."
Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can give birth to all our Buddha-dharmas and can reveal the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena in the world.

All Tathāgatas throughout the worlds of the ten directions who are currently teaching the Dharma likewise constantly observe, protect, and keep in mind the profound Prajñāpāramitā with their Buddha-eye.
Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can give birth to all the merits of the Tathāgata and can reveal the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena in the world.
For this reason, we Buddhas constantly observe and protect the profound *prajñāpāramitā* with our Buddha-eye; to repay that kindness, we should not abandon it for even a moment.

Why is this? Because all the meditative concentrations of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, up to and including the perfection of generosity, and so forth, up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), are all produced by means of this profound perfection of wisdom;

and because the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship, as well as the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, are likewise produced by means of this profound perfection of wisdom.
All the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas arise from this very profound perfection of wisdom;
all those from stream-enterers up to the buddhas exist because of this very profound perfection of wisdom;
and all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who have attained, are attaining, or will attain unsurpassed enlightenment do so by means of this very profound perfection of wisdom.

For this reason, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* possesses great merit toward all Tathāgatas; therefore, the Buddhas constantly observe and protect it with their Buddha-eyes through various skillful means.

“Subhūti, you should know that if there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who are able to hear and inquire about, write down, receive and uphold, read and recite, practice, contemplate, and explain this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas will constantly observe and protect them with their Buddha-eye, causing their bodies and minds to always attain peace and happiness, and ensuring that no obstacles shall hinder the wholesome deeds they cultivate.”

"Subhūti, you should know that if sons or daughters of good family are able to listen to, inquire about, write down, receive and uphold, read and recite, practice, contemplate, and explain to others this *prajñāpāramitā*, all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the worlds of the ten directions will together protect and keep them in mind, causing them to attain non-retrogression from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As the Blessed One has said:
'The profound perfection of wisdom can give birth to all Buddhas and can reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world.'"
World-Honored One!
How is it that the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can give birth to all Buddhas and reveal the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena in the world?
And how is it that all Buddhas are born from *prajñā*?
"How does the Tathāgata speak of the characteristics of the world? The Buddha told Subhūti:

"The profound *prajñāpāramitā* can give birth to all the ten powers (*daśabala*) of the Buddhas, and so on, up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). All these immeasurable and boundless merits grow and develop from the *prajñāpāramitā*. Because they have attained such qualities of the Buddhas, they are called 'Buddhas'."

The profound *prajñāpāramitā* can give rise to such meritorious qualities of all Buddhas; for this reason, it is said that the profound *prajñāpāramitā* gives birth to all Buddhas, and it is also said that all Buddhas arise from it.

Subhūti, you should know that the profound perfection of wisdom is able to reveal the true nature of all phenomena in the world; that is to say, it reveals the true nature of the five aggregates of the world. All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas likewise teach the true nature of the five aggregates of the world.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, through the profound Prajñāpāramitā, reveal the true nature of the five aggregates of the world?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, in their profound Prajñāpāramitā, do not teach that the five aggregates—form and the rest—possess arising or ceasing, birth or extinction, defilement or purification, increase or decrease, entering or exiting, past, future, or present, wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate, or that they are bound to the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm.”

Why is this so? It is because the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness have no formation or destruction, no arising or cessation, and so forth; nor do the dharmas that are unconditioned, unarisen, unceasing, and without intrinsic nature have formation or destruction, arising or cessation, and so forth.

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas thus teach the true nature of the five aggregates through this profound Prajñāpāramitā; since these characteristics of the five aggregates are themselves the world, the world likewise possesses no such characteristics as formation, destruction, arising, or ceasing.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, by relying upon the Prajñāpāramitā, are able to universally realize and know the distinctions in the mental activities of immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings."

However, within this profound meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā*, neither sentient beings nor the designation of "sentient beings" can be apprehended; neither forms nor the designation of "forms" can be apprehended; neither feeling, perception, mental formations, nor consciousness, nor the designation of "feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness," can be apprehended; and so on, in detail, up to neither omniscience, the knowledge of the paths, nor the knowledge of all aspects, nor the designation of "omniscience, the knowledge of the paths, or the knowledge of all aspects," can be apprehended.
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have thus taught and revealed the characteristics of the world through this profound Prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."
The profound *prajñāpāramitā* does not manifest form, nor does it manifest anything up to and including all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). Why is this?

Within the profound meaning of this Great *prajñāpāramitā*, even the profound *prajñāpāramitā* itself does not exist and is utterly unattainable; how much less could form, or anything up to and including all-aspect omniscience, be found or manifested!
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Regarding all sentient beings designated by conventional expression—whether they possess form or are formless, whether they possess perception, lack perception, or are neither percipient nor non-percipient; whether they are in this world or in all other worlds throughout the ten directions—the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, by means of the profound Prajñāpāramitā, know them all as they truly are, whether their minds are contracted or distracted."
“World-Honored One!

How does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, relying on the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, know as they truly are the concentrated minds and distracted minds of those various classes of sentient beings?”

“Subhūti! All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, relying on the profound perfection of wisdom, know through the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) those classes of sentient beings as they truly are—whether their minds are contracted or distracted.”
“World-Honored One!

How does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā and through the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), know those classes of sentient beings as they truly are—whether their minds are contracted or distracted?”

“Subhūti! All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, know as it truly is that within the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), even that nature of phenomena does not exist and is entirely unattainable; how much less could there be sentient beings with either a concentrated or a distracted mind who could be found!”

In this way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by means of the profound perfection of wisdom and by virtue of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), knows as they truly are the concentrated minds and distracted minds of those various classes of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, relying on the profound perfection of wisdom, know those classes of sentient beings—whether their minds are contracted or distracted—as they truly are, by way of their exhaustion, detachment, cessation, abandonment, tranquility, and seclusion."
“World-Honored One!

How does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, through its exhaustion, detachment, cessation, abandonment, tranquility, and seclusion, know as they truly are the contracted minds and distracted minds of those various classes of sentient beings?”

“Subhūti! All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, know as they truly are that within exhaustion, detachment, cessation, abandonment, tranquility, and seclusion, even the nature of exhaustion and so forth does not exist and is entirely unobtainable; how much less could there be sentient beings with either a concentrated or a distracted mind who could be found!”

In this way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, through its exhaustion, freedom from passion, cessation, abandonment, tranquility, and detachment, knows as they truly are the concentrated minds and distracted minds of those various classes of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

By relying on the profound perfection of wisdom, all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas know, as they truly are, whether those classes of sentient beings have minds possessed of desire or minds free from desire; minds possessed of hatred or minds free from hatred; and minds possessed of delusion or minds free from delusion."
“World-Honored One!

How does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by relying on the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, know as they truly are those classes of sentient beings who possess minds of desire and those who are free from desire, who possess minds of hatred and those who are free from hatred, and who possess minds of delusion and those who are free from delusion?”

“Subhūti! All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, relying upon the profound Prajñāpāramitā, know, as they truly are, the suchness of the minds of those sentient beings that possess greed, hatred, and delusion; yet they are not minds possessed of greed, hatred, and delusion, nor are they minds separated from greed, hatred, and delusion.”

Why is this so? Within the nature of reality as it truly is (*yathābhūtatā*), even the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) do not exist and are entirely unfindable; how much less could there be a mind possessed of greed, hatred, and delusion, or a mind free from greed, hatred, and delusion that could be found!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, know as they truly are that the nature of the minds of those sentient beings—whether free from greed, hatred, and delusion, or not free from greed, hatred, and delusion—is neither a mind possessing greed, hatred, and delusion, nor is it a mind devoid of greed, hatred, and delusion.

Why is this so? Because within the nature of reality as it truly is (*yathābhūtatā*), even the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) do not exist and are entirely unobtainable; how much less could there be a mind free from greed, hatred, and delusion, or a mind possessed of greed, hatred, and delusion that can be found!

In this way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by relying on the profound perfection of wisdom, knows as they truly are those classes of sentient beings who possess minds of attachment and those whose minds are free from attachment; who possess minds of aversion and those whose minds are free from aversion; and who possess minds of delusion and those whose minds are free from delusion.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, know those classes of sentient beings as they truly are: whether their minds possess greed, hatred, and delusion; whether their minds do not possess greed, hatred, and delusion; and whether their minds are not free from greed, hatred, and delusion."
Why is this? Because these two minds do not harmonize.

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, know those classes of sentient beings as they truly are: their minds are neither free from greed, hatred, and delusion, nor are they not free from greed, hatred, and delusion, nor do they possess greed, hatred, and delusion.
Why is this? Because these two types of mind do not coalesce.

Thus, by means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha knows, as they truly are, those classes of sentient beings who possess minds of desire and those who are free from desire; who possess minds of hatred and those who are free from hatred; and who possess minds of delusion and those who are free from delusion.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, relying upon the profound Prajñāpāramitā, know as they truly are the expansive minds of all those classes of sentient beings."
“World-Honored One!
How does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, know as they truly are the expansive minds of those various classes of sentient beings?”

“Subhūti! All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, know as they truly are the vast minds of those various classes of sentient beings—minds that are neither vast nor narrow, neither increasing nor decreasing, neither departing nor arriving.”
Why is this so? Because the intrinsic nature of the mind is ultimately detached; it is entirely non-existent and ultimately unobtainable. Who is broad? Who is narrow?
Who increases? Who decreases?
Who goes? Who comes?
In this way, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, knows as they truly are the expansive minds of all those classes of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, relying on this profound prajñāpāramitā, know as they truly are the great minds possessed by those various classes of sentient beings."
“World-Honored One!
How does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, know, as they truly are, the great minds of those various classes of sentient beings?”

“Subhūti! All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, know as they truly are the great minds of those sentient beings—minds that are neither great nor small, neither departing nor arriving, neither arising nor ceasing, neither abiding nor changing, and neither defiled nor pure.”
Why is this so? Because the intrinsic nature of the mind is ultimately detached; it is entirely non-existent and ultimately unobtainable. Who is great?
Who is small? Who goes? Who comes?
Who arises? Who ceases?
Who abides? Who changes?
Who is defiled? Who is purified?
In this way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, relying on the profound perfection of wisdom, knows as they truly are all the great minds of those classes of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, relying upon the profound Prajñāpāramitā, know as they truly are all the immeasurable minds of those classes of sentient beings."
“World-Honored One!
How does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by relying on the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, know as they truly are all the immeasurable minds of those classes of sentient beings?”

“Subhūti! All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, know as they truly are all the immeasurable minds of those sentient beings—neither measurable nor immeasurable, neither abiding nor non-abiding, neither departing nor non-departing.”

Why is this so? Because the intrinsic nature of the mind is ultimately detached, it is without outflows and without dependence; how, then, can one speak of it as being finite or infinite, abiding or non-abiding, departing or not departing?
In this way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, knows as they truly are all the immeasurable minds of those sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, know as they truly are all those mental states of sentient beings that are invisible and non-obstructive."
“World-Honored One!

How does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by relying on the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, know as they truly are all those classes of sentient beings who possess minds that are invisible and non-obstructive?”

“Subhūti! All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, relying on the profound perfection of wisdom, know as they truly are that all those classes of sentient beings possess minds that are invisible, non-obstructive, and entirely devoid of the characteristics of mind.”
Why is this? Because all minds are empty of their own intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Thus, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, relying on the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, knows as they truly are all those states of mind belonging to sentient beings that are invisible and non-obstructive.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, know as they truly are all those classes of sentient beings' formless and invisible minds."
“World-Honored One!
How does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, know as they truly are all those classes of sentient beings’ formless and invisible minds?”

“Subhūti! All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, know as they truly are those mental states of sentient beings that are formless and invisible—minds which the five eyes of all Buddhas cannot perceive.”
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of all minds is empty.
Thus, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, by means of the profound Prajñāpāramitā, knows as they truly are the formless and invisible minds of those various classes of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, relying upon the profound Prajñāpāramitā, know as they truly are the minds and mental factors of those various classes of sentient beings—whether they are emerging or submerging, contracting or expanding."
“World-Honored One!

How does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by relying on the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, know as they truly are the minds and mental factors of those various classes of sentient beings—whether they emerge or submerge, whether they contract or expand?”

“Subhūti! All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, know as they truly are the arising and ceasing, the contraction and expansion of the minds and mental factors of those various classes of sentient beings—all of which arise in dependence upon form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.”

In this way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, knows as they truly are the minds and mental factors of those sentient beings—their emergence and subsidence, their contraction and expansion. That is to say, the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas, by means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, know as they truly are the emergence, subsidence, contraction, and expansion of the minds and mental factors of those sentient beings; they know that based on form up to consciousness, these beings grasp at a self and the world as either permanent or impermanent, both permanent and impermanent, or neither permanent nor impermanent, [claiming]: "This alone is the truth and reality; all else is foolish and false."

Based on form, and so forth up to consciousness, one clings to the self and the world as being either finite, or infinite, or both finite and infinite, or neither finite nor infinite, thinking: "This alone is the truth and reality; all else is foolish and false.

Based on form, and so forth up to consciousness, one clings to the Tathāgata after death as being either existent, or non-existent, or both existent and non-existent, or neither existent nor non-existent, thinking: "This alone is the truth and reality; all else is foolish and false.

Based on form, and so forth up to consciousness, one clings to the life-principle as being either identical to the body or different from the body, thinking: "This alone is the truth and reality; all else is foolish and false."

In this way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, knows as they truly are the minds and mental factors of those various classes of sentient beings—whether they emerge or submerge, whether they contract or expand.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, know form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as they truly are."
“World-Honored One!
How does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, know form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as they truly are?”

“Subhūti! All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, know form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as they truly are: as being like suchness—unchanging, non-conceptual, signless, unstartled, free from proliferation, and non-apprehendable.”

In this way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, relying on the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, knows form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as they truly are; he also knows the arising and passing away, the contraction and expansion of the minds and mental factors of all classes of sentient beings as being, in accordance with true suchness (*tathatā*), unchanging, non-conceptual, signless, without alarm, free from proliferation, and unapprehendable.
“Subhūti, you should know this!
The suchness of the mind and mental factors—the arising and ceasing, the bending and extending—of all sentient beings is the suchness of the five aggregates;
the suchness of the five aggregates is the suchness of the twelve bases; the suchness of the twelve bases is the suchness of the eighteen elements.”
The suchness of the elements; the suchness of the eighteen elements is the suchness of all phenomena,
the suchness of all phenomena is the suchness of the six perfections, the suchness of the six perfections is the suchness of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment,
and the suchness of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment is the sixteen...
The suchness of emptiness; the suchness of the sixteen kinds of emptiness is the suchness of the eight liberations;
the suchness of the eight liberations is the suchness of the nine successive attainments; the suchness of the nine successive attainments is the suchness of the three gates of liberation;
the suchness of the three gates of liberation is the suchness of the ten powers of the Tathāgata. The suchness of the Tathāgata’s ten...
The suchness of the powers is the suchness of the four fearlessnesses; the suchness of the four fearlessnesses is the suchness of the four analytical knowledges;
the suchness of the four analytical knowledges is the suchness of great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity;
the suchness of great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity is...
The suchness of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha is the suchness of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
the suchness of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha is the suchness of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*); the suchness of all-knowledge is the suchness of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*);

the suchness of the knowledge of the paths is the suchness of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); and the suchness of the knowledge of all aspects is that which is wholesome and unwholesome.
The suchness of indeterminate phenomena is the suchness of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena;
the suchness of mundane and supramundane phenomena is the suchness of tainted and untainted phenomena;
the suchness of tainted and untainted phenomena is the suchness of faulty and faultless phenomena.
The suchness of dharmas that are sinful; the suchness of dharmas that are sinful or non-sinful is the suchness of afflicted and purified dharmas;
the suchness of afflicted and purified dharmas is the suchness of conditioned and unconditioned dharmas;
the suchness of conditioned and unconditioned dharmas is the suchness of the three times; the suchness of the three times is...
The suchness of the three realms is the suchness of the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship;
the suchness of the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship is the suchness of the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
and the suchness of the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha is the suchness of all bodhisattvas.
The suchness of the practice of a mahāsattva is the suchness of the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
the suchness of the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is the suchness of the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas;

the suchness of the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas is the suchness of all tathāgatas, arhats, and perfectly enlightened ones; [the suchness] of all tathāgatas, arhats, and...
The suchness of the Truly Perfectly Enlightened One is the very suchness of all sentient beings.
"Subhūti, you should know this:
