the suchness of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Truly Perfectly Enlightened Ones; the suchness of all sentient beings; and the suchness of all phenomena—these are all inseparable."
Because they are inseparable, they are inexhaustible and non-dual, and cannot be differentiated. "Subhūti,

you should know that all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, by relying on the profound Prajñāpāramitā, realize the ultimate suchness of all phenomena and thereby attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
For this reason, it is said that the profound perfection of wisdom can give birth to all Buddhas; she is the mother of all Buddhas, capable of revealing to all Buddhas the true reality of the world.

“Subhūti, you should know that it is by relying on this profound perfection of wisdom that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is able to realize, as they truly are, the suchness of all phenomena— their non-falsity and their immutability.”
"Because he has awakened to the true nature of suchness (*tathatā*) as it truly is, he is called a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:

"The true nature of suchness of all phenomena realized by the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is extremely deep, difficult to see, and difficult to awaken to. All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas employ the true nature of suchness of all phenomena to manifest and distinguish the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) of the Buddhas."
Who is able to believe and understand such profound and subtle *tathatā*?

Only bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have reached the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*), as well as arhats who have exhausted their outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) and possess right view, can give rise to faith and understanding upon hearing the Buddha speak of this profound *tathatā*. For their sake, the Tathāgata reveals and distinguishes the characteristics of *tathatā* according to what he has personally realized.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said. Why is this?
Because true suchness (*tathatā*) is inexhaustible, it is profound; only the Tathāgata has attained manifest, perfect enlightenment regarding this inexhaustible true suchness.
“World-Honored One!
By means of what does the Buddha realize inexhaustible suchness? “Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
“The Buddha, by means of true thusness (*tathatā*), is able to realize such inexhaustible true thusness.
“World-Honored One,
whom does the Tathāgata realize as inexhaustible true thusness?”
“Subhūti! One realizes the inexhaustible suchness of all phenomena.
“World-Honored One!”
"Why is the suchness of all phenomena inexhaustible? "Subhūti, it is because all phenomena are inexhaustible;

because all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have realized the inexhaustible suchness of all phenomena, they have attained unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and reveal and distinguish the characteristics of the suchness of all phenomena for the sake of all sentient beings. For this reason, they are called those who speak according to reality."

At that time, all the devaputras of the desire realm and the form realm within this trichiliocosm each took various kinds of exquisite celestial flowers and incense and scattered them from afar over the World-Honored One as an offering. They approached the Buddha’s presence, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. Together they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What are the characteristics of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* spoken of by the Tathāgata?"
At that time, the Buddha addressed the sons of the gods, saying:
"Sons of the gods, you should know!

The profound *prajñāpāramitā* has emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) as its characteristics. The profound *prajñāpāramitā* has non-activity, neither arising nor ceasing, neither defilement nor purity, no intrinsic nature and no marks, neither annihilation nor permanence, neither identity nor difference, neither coming nor going, and space as its characteristic. The profound *prajñāpāramitā* possesses such immeasurable characteristics as these."
"O Son of Heaven, you should know that these various marks are all spoken by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas according to conventional truth, not according to ultimate truth."
"O Son of Heaven, you should know!
These characteristics of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* cannot be destroyed by any in the world—whether devas, humans, or asuras."
Why is this? Because the world’s devas, humans, asuras, and so forth are also characterized by signs.
O Son of Heaven, you should know this!

Characteristics cannot destroy characteristics, nor can characteristics fully know characteristics; characteristics cannot destroy the absence of characteristics, nor can characteristics fully know the absence of characteristics; the absence of characteristics cannot destroy characteristics, nor can the absence of characteristics fully know characteristics; the absence of characteristics cannot destroy the absence of characteristics, nor can the absence of characteristics fully know the absence of characteristics.

Why is this? Whether it be with marks, without marks, or both with and without marks, all are non-existent; for neither the one who destroys nor the one who knows, nor that which is destroyed, nor that which is known, nor the act of destroying or knowing can be apprehended.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know!

These marks are not produced by form; they are not produced by feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. To speak at length, they are not produced by anything up to and including omniscience, nor are they produced by the knowledge of the paths or the knowledge of all aspects."

"O Son of Heaven, you should know that these marks are not made by devas, nor are they made by non-devas; they are not made by humans, nor are they made by non-humans; they are neither with outflows (*sāsrava*) nor without outflows (*anāsrava*); they are neither mundane (*laukika*) nor supramundane (*lokottara*); they are neither conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); they are without attachment and cannot be described."
“O Son of Heaven, you should know!
The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is free from all marks; therefore, one should not ask by what marks the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is characterized.”
"O you sons of the gods!
What do you think?
If someone were to ask, 'What are the characteristics of space?', would such a question be a correct question?"
The devaputras said: “No, World-Honored One!”
"Why is this? Because space has no substance, no marks, and is unconditioned; it is not something that should be questioned.
The Buddha told the devaputra:
"The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise; it should not be the subject of such questioning.

Nevertheless, whether a Buddha exists or does not exist, the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are the very nature of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). Because the Buddha has realized these characteristics as they truly are, he is called the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
Then, the sons of the gods again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The various marks realized by the Tathāgata are exceedingly profound, difficult to see, and difficult to realize."
Because the Tathāgata has realized such characteristics through manifest awakening, unimpeded wisdom operates regarding all phenomena.

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas abide in such characteristics, analyzing and revealing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*; they gather the characteristics of all phenomena for the sake of sentient beings and skillfully reveal them, so that sentient beings may attain unimpeded wisdom regarding the *prajñāpāramitā*.
“Rare indeed, World-Honored One!
This profound *prajñāpāramitā* is the constant sphere of practice for all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.”

Because all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas practice this sphere, they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and for the sake of all sentient beings, they analytically reveal the characteristics of all phenomena—namely, they analytically reveal the characteristic of form; they analytically reveal the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; and so on, extensively explained up to analytically revealing the characteristic of all-knowledge, and analytically revealing the characteristics of the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the sons of the gods, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is as you have said.
Son of Heaven, you should know that the Tathāgata has awakened to the characteristics of all phenomena as being, in reality, signless (animitta). That is to say:"

Resistance and obstruction are the characteristic of form; experiencing is the characteristic of feeling; grasping signs is the characteristic of perception; conditioning is the characteristic of formations; and discerning is the characteristic of consciousness. The Tathāgata has realized them, as they truly are, to be signless.

The characteristic of the aggregates (*skandha*) is a mass of suffering; the characteristic of the sense bases (*āyatana*) is a gateway for growth; the characteristic of the elements (*dhātu*) is manifold toxicity. The Tathāgata has awakened to these, as they truly are, as being without characteristics (*animitta*).

The ability to give generously is the characteristic of generosity; the absence of feverish distress is the characteristic of ethical discipline; the absence of anger and resentment is the characteristic of patience; the inability to be overcome is the characteristic of diligence; the absence of distraction is the characteristic of meditative concentration; and the absence of attachment is the characteristic of wisdom. The Tathāgata has realized these, as they truly are, to be signless.

Non-existence is the characteristic of internal emptiness and so forth; non-perversion is the characteristic of suchness and so forth; non-falsity is the characteristic of the four noble truths; and the Tathāgata has awakened to these as they truly are as being signless.

The absence of agitation and affliction is the characteristic of the four dhyānas; the absence of obstruction is the characteristic of the four immeasurables; the absence of clamor and confusion is the characteristic of the four formless attainments; the Tathāgata has realized these, as they truly are, to be signless.

Being unbound is the characteristic of the eight liberations; being undistracted is the characteristic of the nine successive concentrations; and being able to transcend is the characteristic of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—all of which the Tathāgata has realized, as they truly are, to be signless.

Being able to remain far removed from the characteristics of this gate of liberation of emptiness is the characteristic of the gate of liberation of signlessness; being without grasping or attachment is the characteristic of the gate of liberation of signlessness; and wearying of all sufferings is the characteristic of the gate of liberation of wishlessness. The Tathāgata has awakened to these as they truly are as being signless.

Comprehending the pure stages is the characteristic of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of the three vehicles; tending toward great enlightenment is the characteristic of the ten stages of the bodhisattva; and the Tathāgata’s realization of them as they truly are is their signlessness (*animitta*).

Being able to observe and reflect is the characteristic of the five eyes; being free from obstruction is the characteristic of the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); and the Tathāgata’s realization of them as they truly are is their signlessness.

Being invincible is the characteristic of the Tathāgata’s ten powers; being free from timidity is the characteristic of the four fearlessnesses; being uninterrupted is the characteristic of the four analytical knowledges; bestowing benefit and happiness is the characteristic of great loving-kindness; uprooting decline and suffering is the characteristic of great compassion; rejoicing in virtuous matters is the characteristic of great sympathetic joy; abandoning clamor and distraction is the characteristic of great equanimity; being unassailable is the characteristic of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; that the Tathāgata awakens to these as they truly are as being signless (animitta) is the characteristic of the Tathāgata.

To be able to adorn these marks and signs is the characteristic of the dharma of non-forgetfulness; to have no attachment is the characteristic of the nature of constant equanimity; the Tathāgata awakens to these as they truly are as being signless.

The universal gathering and upholding of all dharanī-doors is the characteristic of these doors; the universal gathering and receiving of all samādhi-doors is the characteristic of these doors; the Tathāgata has awakened to them as they truly are, as being without characteristics.

Skillfully receiving the teaching is the mark of the fruit of the Śrāvaka vehicle; self-awakening is the mark of the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha; proceeding toward the great fruit is the mark of the practice of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva; and possessing the great function is the mark of the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas. The Tathāgata has realized these, as they truly are, to be signless.

Manifesting perfect enlightenment is the characteristic of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*); being thoroughly proficient in this is the characteristic of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*); manifesting the distinct realization of each phenomenon is the characteristic of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); and the Tathāgata’s awakening to these as they truly are is their characteristic of signlessness (*animitta*).
“Son of Heaven, you should know!
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are able to realize, in accordance with reality, that all such characteristics of phenomena are signless.”
"For this reason, I say that the Buddhas have attained unimpeded wisdom, and there is none who can equal them.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Subhūti:

"The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is the mother of all Buddhas; it is able to reveal the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena in the world. Therefore, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas abide in accordance with this Dharma. They honor, revere, respect, praise, and uphold the Dharma upon which they rely and abide—this Dharma is precisely the profound *prajñāpāramitā*."
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas do not fail to rely upon the profound Prajñāpāramitā, making offerings to it, honoring it, respecting it, praising it, and upholding it with care.

Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can give birth to all Buddhas, serves as the locus of reliance for all Buddhas, and can reveal the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena in the world.
“Subhūti, you should know that all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are those who recognize kindness and are able to repay kindness. If someone were to ask:
‘Who is it that recognizes kindness and is able to repay kindness?’”
One should answer correctly:
"The Buddha is one who knows gratitude and is able to repay it. Why is this so?
"In all the worlds, there is none who knows gratitude and repays kindness better than the Buddha.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In what way does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha know gratitude and repay kindness?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas mount this very vehicle and travel this very path to arrive at unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Having attained enlightenment, they have at all times made offerings, shown reverence, honored, praised, embraced, and protected this vehicle and this path, never ceasing for even a moment. You should know that this vehicle and this path are none other than the profound Prajñāpāramitā; this is what is called a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha knowing gratitude and repaying kindness."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are no Tathāgatas, Arhats, or Samyaksaṃbuddhas who do not rely upon the profound Prajñāpāramitā to realize perfect awakening regarding all phenomena—whether characterized by signs or signless—in which there is no actual activity, because there is no agent who acts."

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, without exception, rely upon the profound Prajñāpāramitā; regarding all phenomena characterized by signs as well as those without signs, they have realized perfect awakening without anything to be accomplished, because no physical form or substance can be apprehended.
"Subhūti, you should know this:

because the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, relying upon this profound Prajñāpāramitā, have realized and fully awakened to the fact that both phenomena with marks and phenomena without marks are devoid of activity and lack anything to be accomplished; and because they have at all times unceasingly made offerings, shown reverence, honored, praised, sustained, and protected it, they are therefore called those who truly know gratitude and repay their debt of gratitude."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are no Tathāgatas, Arhats, or Samyaksaṃbuddhas who do not rely upon this profound Prajñāpāramitā to turn the wheel of wisdom regarding all phenomena as being without action, without accomplishment, and without arising; furthermore, they are able to know the causes and conditions for this non-turning."

Therefore, one should know that the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is able to give birth to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and is also able to reveal the characteristics of the world as they truly are.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:

“The Tathāgata has always taught that the nature of all phenomena is without birth, without arising, without cognition, and without vision. How then can it be said that the profound *prajñāpāramitā* gives birth to all Buddhas, is the mother of all Buddhas, and can also reveal the characteristics of the world as they truly are?”
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.

The nature of all phenomena is without birth, without arising, without cognition, and without vision; yet, relying on worldly convention, it is said that the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can give birth to all Buddhas, is the mother of these Buddhas, and can also reveal the characteristics of the world as they truly are.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“In what way are all phenomena unborn, unarisen, unknowable, and unseen?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Because all phenomena are empty and non-existent, being entirely devoid of autonomy, deceptive, and unsubstantial, all phenomena are unborn, unarisen, unknowable, and invisible."
Furthermore, Subhūti, the nature of all phenomena has no basis of reliance and no point of attachment; for this reason, they are without birth, without arising, without cognition, and without vision.
“Subhūti, you should know that although the profound perfection of wisdom gives birth to the Buddhas and reveals the characteristics of the world, there is nothing born and nothing revealed.”

“Subhūti, you should know this: because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* does not perceive form, it is called the manifestation of the characteristic of form; because it does not perceive feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, it is called the manifestation of the characteristics of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. This is explained at length up to: because it does not perceive all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), it is called the manifestation of the characteristic of all-knowledge; because it does not perceive the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), it is called the manifestation of the characteristics of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects.”

Subhūti, you should know that by virtue of this meaning, the profound perfection of wisdom can reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world, can give birth to all Buddhas, and is thus named the Mother of all Buddhas.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“How is it that this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, by not seeing form (*rūpa*), is said to demonstrate the characteristic of form; by not seeing feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*), is said to demonstrate the characteristics of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness; and so on, in detail, until by not seeing all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), it is said to demonstrate the characteristic of all-knowledge; and by not seeing the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), it is said to demonstrate the characteristics of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* does not give rise to consciousness by taking form (*rūpa*) as its object, it is called 'indicating the characteristic of form' because form is not seen. This is explained at length until: because it does not give rise to consciousness by taking the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) as its object, it is called 'indicating the characteristic of the knowledge of all aspects' because the knowledge of all aspects is not seen."

Subhūti, you should know that by virtue of this meaning, the profound perfection of wisdom can reveal the true reality of all phenomena in the world, can give birth to all Buddhas, and is thus named the Mother of all Buddhas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

This profound perfection of wisdom can reveal the emptiness of the world for all Buddhas; therefore, it is called the Mother of Buddhas, as it can demonstrate to all Buddhas the true reality of the world."
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“In what way does the perfection of wisdom manifest the emptiness of the world for all Buddhas?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is able to reveal for all Buddhas the emptiness of the world of the five aggregates (*skandha*),

reveal the emptiness of the world of the twelve bases (*āyatana*), reveal the emptiness of the world of the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), reveal the emptiness of the world of the six contacts (*sparśa*),
reveal the emptiness of the world of the six feelings (*vedanā*), reveal the emptiness of the world of the six elements (*dhātu*), and reveal the four...”
By means of the emptiness of the world, it reveals the emptiness of the world of the twelve links of dependent origination;
it reveals the emptiness of the world of the sixty-two views rooted in the view of self; it reveals the emptiness of the world of the ten paths of wholesome action;
it reveals the emptiness of the world of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; and it reveals the emptiness of the six pāramitās.
The emptiness of the many worlds reveals the emptiness of the internal world up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;
it reveals the emptiness of the worlds of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; it reveals the emptiness of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;
and it reveals the emptiness of the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities.
The world is empty; it reveals the emptiness of the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
It reveals the emptiness of the worlds of the three vehicles and the ten stages. It reveals the emptiness of the worlds of the bodhisattva’s ten stages.
It reveals the emptiness of all doors of dhāraṇī and doors of samādhi. It reveals the emptiness of the five eyes and the six supernormal powers.
The world is empty; this reveals that the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four analytical knowledges, and eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are empty of the world.
The world is empty; this reveals that great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity are empty of the world.
The world is empty; this reveals that the thirty-two marks of a Great Being and the eighty secondary characteristics are empty of the world.

Emptiness reveals the emptiness of the world regarding the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity; it reveals the emptiness of the world regarding the fruit of stream-entry up to the awakening of a pratyekabuddha;
it reveals the emptiness of the world regarding all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening of all buddhas;
and it reveals the emptiness of the world regarding all-knowledge and the knowledge of the aspects of the path.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the knowledge of all aspects is empty of the world.

Thus, Subhūti, this profound perfection of wisdom can reveal the emptiness of the world for all Buddhas; therefore, it is called the Mother of Buddhas, for it can demonstrate to all Buddhas the true reality of the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

By means of the perfection of wisdom, the Buddha is able to reveal for the world that the world is empty of form, and so on, up to revealing that the world is empty of the knowledge of all aspects, causing all worlds to experience the emptiness of the world, perceive the emptiness of the world, conceive the emptiness of the world, and cognize the emptiness of the world."
Thus it is, Subhūti!

This profound perfection of wisdom can manifest the emptiness of the world for all Buddhas; therefore, she is named the Mother of Buddhas, capable of revealing to all Buddhas the true reality of the world.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can demonstrate to all Buddhas the empty characteristic of the world.
How does it demonstrate to all Buddhas the empty characteristic of the world?
That is to say, it causes the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha to see that the world of form is empty, up to and including seeing that the world of all-aspect omniscience is empty.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
The profound perfection of wisdom can demonstrate to all Buddhas the empty nature of the world. "Furthermore, Subhūti,
the profound perfection of wisdom can demonstrate to all Buddhas the inconceivable nature of the world."
How does one demonstrate the inconceivable characteristics of the world of all Buddhas?

It means demonstrating the inconceivable characteristics of the world of form of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, up to the inconceivable characteristics of the world of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Thus it is, Subhūti!
This profound prajñāpāramitā can reveal to all Buddhas the inconceivable characteristics of the world.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
The profound *prajñāpāramitā* can demonstrate to all Buddhas the characteristic of the world’s detachment.
How does it demonstrate to all Buddhas the characteristic of the world’s detachment?

This refers to demonstrating the world-transcending characteristic of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha’s form, up to the world-transcending characteristic of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Thus it is, Subhūti!
The profound *prajñāpāramitā* can demonstrate to all Buddhas the characteristic of the world’s detachment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! The profound *prajñāpāramitā* can demonstrate to all Buddhas the characteristic of the world’s tranquility."
How can one demonstrate the world’s aspect of tranquility for all Buddhas?

It means demonstrating the world’s aspect of tranquility regarding the physical form (*rūpa*) of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, up to and including the world’s aspect of tranquility regarding the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Thus it is, Subhūti!
This profound perfection of wisdom can demonstrate to all Buddhas the characteristic of the tranquility of the world.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The profound *prajñāpāramitā* can reveal to all Buddhas the ultimate mark of emptiness of the world.
How does it reveal to all Buddhas the ultimate mark of emptiness of the world?
That is to say, it demonstrates that the world of form of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is ultimately empty, up to and including the world of all-aspect-knowledge being ultimately empty.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
This profound perfection of wisdom can demonstrate to all Buddhas the ultimate mark of emptiness in the world.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The profound *prajñāpāramitā* can reveal to all Buddhas the mark of the emptiness of the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva-śūnyatā*) of the world.
How does it reveal to all Buddhas the mark of the emptiness of the lack of intrinsic nature of the world?

That is to say, it demonstrates that the world of form of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is empty of intrinsic nature, up to and including the world of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) being empty of intrinsic nature.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
This profound perfection of wisdom can demonstrate to all Buddhas the mark of the emptiness of the lack of intrinsic nature in the world.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The profound *prajñāpāramitā* can reveal to all Buddhas the characteristic of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of the world.
How does it reveal to all Buddhas the characteristic of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of the world?

That is to say, it demonstrates that the world of the form-body of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is empty of intrinsic nature, up to and including the world of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) being empty of intrinsic nature.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
This profound perfection of wisdom can demonstrate to all Buddhas the mark of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of the world.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The profound *prajñāpāramitā* can demonstrate to all Buddhas the mark of the emptiness of the self-nature of the lack of nature of the world.
How can it demonstrate to all Buddhas the mark of the emptiness of the self-nature of the lack of nature of the world?

That is to say, it demonstrates that the world of form of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is empty of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, up to and including the world of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) being empty of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
This profound perfection of wisdom can demonstrate to all Buddhas the mark of the emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence within the world.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The profound *prajñāpāramitā* can demonstrate to all Buddhas that the world is purely characterized by emptiness.
How does it demonstrate to all Buddhas that the world is purely characterized by emptiness?

That is to say, it demonstrates that the world of the form of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is purely empty in its characteristics, up to and including the world of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) being purely empty in its characteristics.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
The profound *prajñāpāramitā* can demonstrate to all Buddhas the purely empty characteristic of the world.
"Subhūti, you should know that by such a principle,
the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can demonstrate to all Buddhas the true characteristic of the world."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, the profound perfection of wisdom is that which can demonstrate the characteristics of the world to all Buddhas; that is to say, it causes one not to give rise to the notion of 'this world' or the notion of 'another world.'"
"Why is this? It is because, in reality, there is no dharma that can give rise to the notion of 'this world' or 'another world.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 513, translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Chapter 16: On the Inconceivable and Other Matters, Part Three. Chapter 16: On the Inconceivable and Other Matters. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One! This profound *prajñāpāramitā* appears in the world for the sake of a great matter; it appears in the world for the sake of an inconceivable matter; it appears in the world for the sake of an immeasurable matter; it appears in the world for the sake of an incalculable matter; it appears in the world for the sake of a matter that is unequaled.”
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
"It is as you have said,
Subhūti! How is it that the profound perfection of wisdom appears in the world for the sake of a great task?"

It is said that for all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, the great task consists in rescuing all sentient beings without ever abandoning them for even a moment; it is for this purpose that the profound Prajñāpāramitā appears in the world.
“Subhūti! How is it that the profound perfection of wisdom appears in the world for the sake of inconceivable matters?

It is because the buddha-nature, tathāgata-nature, self-awakened nature, and omniscient nature of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are all inconceivable; it is for this purpose that the profound perfection of wisdom appears in the world.”
“Subhūti! How is it that the profound perfection of wisdom appears in the world for the sake of an immeasurable matter?

It is because the Buddha-nature, Tathāgata-nature, self-awakened nature, and all-knowledge nature of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas cannot be measured by any sentient beings; it is for this purpose that the profound perfection of wisdom appears in the world.”
“Subhūti! How is it that the profound *prajñāpāramitā* appears in the world for the sake of immeasurable matters?

That is to say, regarding the Buddha-nature, Tathāgata-nature, self-awakened nature, and omniscient nature of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas—there is no one who can truly know their measure or number. It is for this purpose that the profound *prajñāpāramitā* appears in the world.”
“Subhūti! In what way does the profound perfection of wisdom appear in the world for the sake of that which is unequaled?
It is because the Buddha-nature, Tathāgata-nature, self-awakened nature, and omniscient nature of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have no equal, much less any superior!”
"It is for this purpose that the profound *prajñāpāramitā* appears in the world.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Is it only the Buddha-nature, Tathāgata-nature, self-awakened nature, and all-knowledge nature of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas that is inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled, or are there other dharmas as well?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“It is not only that the buddha-nature, tathāgata-nature, self-awakened nature, and all-knowledge nature of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled; there are also other dharmas that are inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled.”

That is to say, form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness—extensively explained up to the knowledge of all aspects—are likewise inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, and unequaled.
All such phenomena as these are likewise inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled; within the true nature of all phenomena, both the mind and its mental factors are unfindable.

Why is this? Because form, up to and including consciousness, cannot be designated, they are inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled; and so on, in detail, until: because all-aspect wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*) cannot be designated, it is inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:

"By what causes and conditions are form through consciousness—and, as explained at length, up to all-aspect omniscience—all inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and peerless, because they cannot be designated?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"From form up to consciousness, and so on extensively up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), because they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), they cannot be designated; because they cannot be designated, they are inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what causes and conditions are form, up to and including consciousness—and, as explained at length, up to and including all-aspect omniscience—all devoid of intrinsic nature?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“From form up to consciousness, and so on extensively up to the knowledge of all aspects, because their nature of being conceivable, measurable, quantifiable, equal, or unequal cannot be apprehended.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“By what causes and conditions are form through consciousness—and, as extensively explained, up to all-aspect omniscience—inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and such that their equality and inequality cannot be apprehended?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“From form up to consciousness, and so on extensively until the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), their intrinsic nature is inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled, because their intrinsic nature is empty.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

From form up to consciousness, and so forth in detail up to all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), because they are all unapprehendable, they are inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled."
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:

"By what causes and conditions are form through consciousness—and, as extensively explained, up to all-aspect omniscience—inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled, because they are all unapprehendable?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"From form up to consciousness, and so forth in detail up to all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), because they are all limitless, they cannot be apprehended; because they cannot be apprehended, they are inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled."
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what causes and conditions are form through consciousness—and, as explained at length, up to all-aspect omniscience—all immeasurable and thus unapprehendable?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"From form up to consciousness, and so forth in detail up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), they are all inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled; because they are without limit, they are all unattainable."
"Furthermore, Subhūti! What do you think?

Within that which is inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled—ranging from form through to consciousness, and as extensively explained up to the knowledge of all aspects—is form through to consciousness, and as extensively explained up to the knowledge of all aspects, to be apprehended?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
For this reason, all phenomena are inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled.
"Subhūti, you should know this!"

Because all phenomena are inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled, so too are all the Buddha-dharmas, Tathāgata-dharmas, self-awakened dharmas, and omniscient dharmas of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas—inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled.

"Subhūti, you should know that all the Buddha-dharmas, Tathāgata-dharmas, self-awakened dharmas, and all-knowledge dharmas of all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are inconceivable, because conceptualization has ceased;
they are immeasurable, because measurement has ceased."
It is immeasurable because all measure has ceased;
it is unequaled because all equality has ceased.
For these reasons, all phenomena are likewise inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, and unequaled.
"Subhūti, you should know that all the Buddha-dharmas, Tathāgata-dharmas, self-awakened dharmas, and omniscient dharmas of all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are inconceivable,
because they transcend the conceivable; they are immeasurable, because they transcend the measurable."
It is immeasurable because it transcends all measure;
it is unequaled because it transcends all that can be compared.
For these reasons, all dharmas are likewise inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, and unequaled.
“Subhūti, you should know this:
that which is inconceivable is merely a designation for the inconceivable;
that which is immeasurable is merely a designation for the immeasurable.”
"Immeasurable" is merely a designation for the immeasurable;
"unequaled" is merely a designation for the unequaled.

For this reason, all the Buddha-dharmas, Tathāgata-dharmas, self-awakened dharmas, and omniscient dharmas of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, and unequaled.

"Subhūti, you should know that 'inconceivable' is so called because it is inconceivable like space; and so on, up to 'unequaled with the unequaled,' which is so called because it is unequaled with the unequaled like space."

For this reason, all the Buddha-dharmas, Tathāgata-dharmas, self-awakened dharmas, and omniscient dharmas of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled.

“Subhūti, you should know that all the Buddha-dharmas, Tathāgata-dharmas, self-awakened dharmas, and omniscient dharmas of all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas cannot be conceived, measured, calculated, or equated by Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or any in the world— whether devas, humans, or asuras.”

For this reason, it is said that all the Buddha-dharmas of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—the dharmas of a Tathāgata, the dharmas of self-awakened realization, and the dharmas of omniscience—are inconceivable, immeasurable, incalculable, and unequaled.

When the Buddha had spoken this chapter on the inconceivable, the immeasurable, the incalculable, and the unequaled, five hundred bhikṣus among the assembly attained liberation of mind through the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*).
Furthermore, two thousand bhikṣuṇīs also attained liberation of mind through the exhaustion of all outflows;
and sixty thousand upāsakas, regarding all phenomena, became free from dust and defilement, giving rise to the pure Dharma-eye.
Furthermore, thirty thousand *upāsikās* likewise attained the pure Dharma-eye, free from dust and defilement regarding all phenomena;

additionally, twenty *bodhisattva-mahāsattvas* attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and received the prediction that they would become Buddhas within this Bhadrakalpa.
Chapter 17: The Chapter on Similes, Part Three. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

The profound perfection of wisdom appears in the world for a great purpose; it appears in the world for an inconceivable purpose; it appears in the world for an immeasurable purpose; it appears in the world for an incalculable purpose; it appears in the world for a purpose that is unequaled.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can bring to fulfillment the six *pāramitās*;

it can bring to fulfillment inner emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*); and it can bring to fulfillment suchness (*tathatā*) up to the inconceivable (*acintya*).
The elements can bring about the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
they can bring about the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; they can bring about the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path;
and they can bring about the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, and the nine successive meditative attainments.
The ten totalities can accomplish the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
they can accomplish the stage of pure observation up to the stage of a Tathāgata; they can accomplish the Joyful Stage up to the Cloud of Dharma Stage;
they can accomplish all doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of samādhi; they can accomplish...
The five eyes and six supernormal powers can accomplish the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they can accomplish great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity;
they can accomplish the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; they can accomplish the quality of non-forgetfulness and constancy...
Abiding in equanimity, one is able to accomplish the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
one is able to accomplish all the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva and the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas;
and one is able to accomplish all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
“Subhūti, you should know this!

Just as a Kṣatriya great king who has received the consecration, possessing majestic power and sovereignty, subdues all and entrusts all affairs of state to his ministers, remaining at ease with hands folded and free from action in peaceful happiness; so too is the Tathāgata, the Great Dharma King, who possesses majestic power and sovereignty and subdues all. He entrusts the teachings of the Śrāvakas, the teachings of the Pratyekabuddhas, the teachings of the Bodhisattvas, and the teachings of the Tathāgatas entirely to the profound Prajñāpāramitā, for it is through the profound Prajñāpāramitā that all undertakings are universally accomplished.”
Therefore, Subhūti, this profound perfection of wisdom appears in the world for a great purpose, and so on at length, appearing in the world for the purpose of that which is unequaled.
Why is this so? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* appears in the world and is able to accomplish its tasks by being without grasping or attachment toward form;
it appears in the world and is able to accomplish its tasks by being without grasping or attachment toward feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

To speak at length, up to and including the fact that because they have no grasping or attachment toward all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), they appear in the world and are able to accomplish their tasks; because they have no grasping or attachment toward the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), they appear in the world and are able to accomplish their tasks;

because they have no grasping or attachment toward the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*), they appear in the world and are able to accomplish their tasks; and so on, up to the fact that because they have no grasping or attachment toward the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), they appear in the world and are able to accomplish their tasks.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:

"How is it that this profound perfection of wisdom, by being without grasping or attachment toward anything from form up to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha, appears in the world and is able to accomplish its purpose?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Do you perceive form, or even the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas, as something that can be grasped or clung to?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
"No, Sugata! The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“Excellent! Excellent!

I, too, do not see form, nor do I see anything up to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as something that can be grasped or clung to; because I do not see them, I do not grasp them, and because I do not grasp them, I do not cling to them.”

For this reason, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* neither grasps nor clings to anything from form (*rūpa*) up to the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Subhūti, you should know this:

I do not perceive any Buddha-nature, Tathāgata-nature, self-awakened nature, or all-knowledge nature of all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas that can be grasped or clung to. Because I do not perceive them, I do not grasp them;

because I do not grasp them, I do not cling to them. It is the same with the profound Prajñāpāramitā: it does not perceive at all any Buddha-nature, Tathāgata-nature, self-awakened nature, or all-knowledge nature of all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas that can be clung to or grasped. For this reason, there is neither clinging nor grasping.

Therefore, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should neither grasp nor cling to form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness; and so on, up to and including all the buddha-nature, tathāgata-nature, self-awakened nature, and omniscient nature of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
At that time, the devaputras of the desire realm and the form realm together addressed the Buddha, saying:

"This Prajñāpāramitā is most profound; it is difficult to see and difficult to realize. It is beyond the reach of discursive thought, transcending the sphere of conceptualization; it is tranquil, subtle, precise, and deep-seated. Only those of supreme intelligence are able to comprehend it."

If any sentient beings are able to have deep faith and understanding in this Prajñāpāramitā, you should know that they have made offerings to many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas in the past, have made great vows before those Buddhas, have planted various roots of goodness, have served many spiritual friends, and have been sustained by immeasurable spiritual friends; only then can they believe and understand such Prajñāpāramitā.

If there are those who, upon hearing this Prajñāpāramitā, develop deep faith and understanding, you should know that such individuals are great bodhisattvas who will certainly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Even if all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were to become followers by faith, followers by dharma, those at the eighth stage, stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas, the wisdom and abandonment they have achieved would not equal that of a person who, for a single day, endures with joy, contemplates, weighs, and examines this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
The patience achieved by this person regarding this profound *prajñāpāramitā* surpasses that wisdom and abandonment [of others] immeasurably and boundlessly. Why is this?

“The wisdom and the abandonment of those who follow by faith and so forth are all but a small portion of the forbearance of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have already attained the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the devaputras, saying: “Excellent!”
Excellent! It is as you have said.
O Son of Heaven, you should know this!

If sons or daughters of good family are able to hear the *prajñāpāramitā* even for a brief moment, and having heard it, believe and understand it, write it down, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, practice it, contemplate it, and explain it to others—these sons and daughters of good family will swiftly emerge from birth and death and quickly realize *nirvāṇa*. They surpass those who seek the vehicles of the *śrāvaka* or *pratyekabuddha*, even if the latter remain far removed from the *prajñāpāramitā* while studying other sūtras for an entire kalpa or more than a kalpa.

Why is this so? Because within this profound *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, all subtle and supreme dharmas are extensively expounded; those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*) should all diligently practice and study herein. According to their respective aspirations, they shall all swiftly bring their undertakings to ultimate completion. All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have relied upon this training to realize, are realizing, and will realize unsurpassed bodhi.
Then, all the sons of the gods raised their voices together and said:
"Such is the perfection of wisdom: it is a great perfection, an inconceivable perfection, an immeasurable perfection, a countless perfection, and a perfection equal to the unequaled."
All those who follow by faith, up to the pratyekabuddhas, diligently train within this and swiftly realize nirvāṇa.
All the assemblies of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas diligently train within this and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
Although all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas rely on this training to each reach their ultimate goal, the profound perfection of wisdom neither increases nor decreases.

When the sons of the gods had spoken these words, they leaped for joy and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet. Circumambulating him three times to the right, they took their leave of the Buddha and returned to their palace. Not long after they had departed from the assembly, they simultaneously vanished and each returned to his own palace within his respective realm.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears this teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā* and gives rise to profound faith and understanding, from where did they pass away to be reborn here?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā*, gives rise to profound faith and understanding, neither sinking nor desponding, neither becoming confused nor distressed, being without delusion or doubt, without grasping or attachment, joyfully listening and receiving it, honoring and making offerings to it, and constantly following the Dharma teacher to inquire about its meaning and intent—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—never for a moment abandoning them, like a newborn calf that does not leave its mother; until they have attained the ultimate mastery of all the meanings and intents of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and are able to explain them to others, they shall never be separated from such profound *prajñāpāramitā* sūtras and the Dharma teacher who expounds them."
Subhūti, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has passed away from among humans and been reborn here in this world. Why is this?

These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having previously heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā* in former lives, and having heard it, upheld, recited, practiced, contemplated, expounded, and transcribed it with adornment; and having made offerings, shown reverence, honored, and praised it—by virtue of these roots of goodness, they have escaped the eight states of no-leisure (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*), passed away from the human realm, and were reborn among humans, whereupon hearing this sūtra briefly, they give rise to deep faith and understanding.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Is it possible that there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, having accomplished such sublime merits and having made offerings to and served Buddhas in other directions, pass away from those places and are reborn here, and upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, develop deep faith and understanding, and then write it down, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, practice and cultivate it, contemplate and explain it, and honor and revere it without weariness?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have accomplished such supreme merits that, having made offerings to and served Buddhas in other directions, they pass away from those places and are reborn here. Upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, they give rise to deep faith and understanding; they copy it down, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, practice it, contemplate it, and explain it to others; they honor and revere it with a mind free from weariness."

Why is this? It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have previously, in the presence of immeasurable Buddhas in other directions, heard the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā* and developed profound faith and understanding; they have copied it, received and upheld it, read and recited it, practiced and contemplated it, explained it to others, and made offerings and paid respect to it with a mind free from weariness. By virtue of these roots of goodness, they pass away from those places and are born here, whereupon hearing this sutra taught, they develop profound faith and understanding.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, passing away from the common assembly of the Tuṣita heaven, are reborn among human beings; they too have accomplished such meritorious qualities."

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, in previous lives, had already inquired about the profound meaning and intent of the *prajñāpāramitā* from the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya in Tuṣita Heaven. Carrying the roots of merit from that [existence], they passed away from there and were reborn among humans; upon hearing the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā*, they developed deep faith and understanding, and they transcribed, received, upheld, recited, practiced, contemplated, and explained it, honoring and revering it with a mind free from weariness.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! There are sons of good family and others who abide in the Great Vehicle, who, although they have in previous lives heard the Prajñāpāramitā up to the Dānapāramitā,
or heard the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature, or heard..."
From suchness up to the inconceivable realm; or hearing of the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
or hearing of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; or hearing of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
or hearing of the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, and the nine successive...
Furthermore, they may hear of the four dhyānas and the ten bases of totality; or hear of the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
or hear of the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata; or hear of the stages from the Ground of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma;
or hear of all the doors of dhāraṇī and the doors of samādhi; or hear of the five eyes.
the six supernormal powers; or hearing of the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
or hearing of great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity;
or hearing of the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; or hearing of the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant abiding in equanimity; or hearing...
Regarding all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas, or having heard of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*),
the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), they do not inquire about their profound meaning and intent.

Having now been born among humans, if they hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, their minds become confused and distressed, they fall into hesitation and cowardice, or they give rise to erroneous interpretations; it is difficult to awaken them.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

there may be sons of good family and others who abide in the Great Vehicle, who, although they have heard the *prajñāpāramitā* in previous lives and have also inquired about its profound meaning for as long as one day up to ten days, do not practice with diligence according to what was taught."

Having been born among humans and having heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, even if they practice it for only one day up to ten days, their minds will be firm and indestructible; yet, if they depart from the profound *prajñāpāramitā* they have heard, they will immediately fall back and their minds will become hesitant.

Why is this so? Because these sons of good family who abide in the Mahāyāna, having heard the *prajñāpāramitā* in previous lives, although they also inquired about its profound meaning and intent, did not practice with diligence according to what was taught. Therefore, in this present life, if they encounter virtuous friends who earnestly exhort them, they will delight in hearing and receiving the profound *prajñāpāramitā*; however, if they do not encounter virtuous friends who earnestly exhort them, they will have no delight in hearing and receiving this sūtra.

Regarding the perfection of wisdom, they may at times delight in hearing it and at other times not; at times they are steadfast and at other times they regress. Their minds are light and fickle, their progress and retreat being inconsistent, like cotton wool drifting and turning with the wind.

It should be known that such sons of good family who abide in the Great Vehicle have not long since set out upon the Great Vehicle; they have not yet extensively approached true spiritual friends, nor have they extensively made offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. They have not yet upheld, recited, copied, contemplated, or expounded the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, nor have they yet diligently practiced and studied the *prajñāpāramitā* through to the *dānapāramitā*, and so forth, up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

It should be known that such sons of good family who have newly entered the Great Vehicle and dwell thus in it possess only a small degree of faith, respect, and affection for the Dharma of the Great Vehicle; they are yet unable to write down, receive and uphold, read, recite, practice, contemplate, or explain to others this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If sons of good family who abide in the Great Vehicle do not write down, receive, uphold, read, recite, cultivate, contemplate, or explain to others this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and if they are unable to extensively teach and thereby gather in sentient beings through the profound *prajñāpāramitā* up to the *dānapāramitā*, and up to the *sarvākārajñatā*, then those sons of good family abiding in the Great Vehicle will not be protected by the *prajñāpāramitā* up to the *dānapāramitā*, and up to the *sarvākārajñatā*."

These sons of good family who abide in the Mahāyāna are unable to practice in accordance with the *prajñāpāramitā* and so forth, up to the *dānapāramitā*, and as extensively explained, up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); by reason of this, they fall to the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha.

Why is this? Because these sons of good family who abide in the Great Vehicle are unable to write down, receive, uphold, read, recite, cultivate, contemplate, or explain to others this profound *prajñāpāramitā*. Furthermore, they are unable to embrace sentient beings through this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, up to and including the *sarvākārajñatā* (knowledge of all aspects); they cannot practice in accordance with the *prajñāpāramitā*, up to and including the *sarvākārajñatā*; and they are not protected by the *prajñāpāramitā*, up to and including the *sarvākārajñatā*. Due to these causes and conditions, they fall to the level of a *śrāvaka* or the level of a *pratyekabuddha*.
“Subhūti, you should know this:

it is like a ship upon which people have embarked to cross the great ocean; if those on board do not take hold of wood, vessels, floats, planks, or even a corpse to rely upon, you may be certain they will drown and fail to reach the other shore.”

If one can take hold of wooden objects, a floating bag, a plank, or a corpse as something to rely upon, you should know that such a person will ultimately not drown or die; they will reach the safe shore on the other side of the great ocean, remaining unhurt and unharmed while experiencing all manner of happiness.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

Although sons of good family and others who abide in the Great Vehicle may achieve a small measure of faith, respect, and joyful devotion toward the Great Vehicle, if they do not write down, receive, uphold, read, recite, contemplate, cultivate, or explain to others the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and so forth, up to the sūtras associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) as their point of reliance, you should know that such sons of good family abiding in the Great Vehicle will decline midway and fail to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, falling back instead into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.

If sons of good family who abide in the Mahāyāna possess perfect faith, respect, and joyful devotion toward the Mahāyāna, and are further able to write down, receive, uphold, read, recite, contemplate, cultivate, and explain to others this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and even rely upon sūtras associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), it should be known that such sons of good family abiding in the Mahāyāna will never midway fall back into the stage of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, but will certainly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

It is as if a person wishing to cross a perilous and desolate wilderness were unable to reach a land of peace and happiness, and might instead encounter suffering and lose their life along the way, if they do not gather the necessary provisions and equipment."
Thus it is, Subhūti!

If sons of good family who abide in the Great Vehicle possess faith, patience, a pure mind, a superior intention, aspiration, resolute conviction, equanimity, and diligence regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, yet do not embrace the profound *prajñāpāramitā*—and so on, as extensively explained, up to the knowledge of all aspects—it should be known that such sons of good family abiding in the Great Vehicle will perish midway and fail to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, falling back instead into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.
“Subhūti, you should know this!

Just as a person who wishes to cross a perilous and treacherous wilderness will certainly reach a land of peace and happiness—if they can gather the necessary provisions and equipment—and will never encounter suffering or lose their life midway;”
Thus it is, Subhūti!

If sons of good family and others who abide in the Great Vehicle possess faith, patience, a pure mind, superior intention, desire, resolute conviction, equanimity, and diligence regarding unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; and if they further are able to embrace the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and so forth, up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), you should know that such sons of good family abiding in the Great Vehicle will never suffer decline or regression midway. They will transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, bring sentient beings to maturity, adorn and purify buddha-fields, and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Suppose there were a man or a woman who, carrying an unbaked clay jar, went to a river, a pond, a well, a spring, or a canal to fetch water; you should know that this jar will soon rot and break."
Why is this? Because this jar, being unrefined, is unfit to hold water and will ultimately return to the earth.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

If there are sons of good family who abide in the Great Vehicle and possess faith, patience, a pure mind, a superior intention, desire, resolute conviction, equanimity, and diligence toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, yet do not embrace the skillful means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*—and so on, as extensively explained, up to the knowledge of all aspects—it should be known that such sons of good family abiding in the Great Vehicle will fail midway and not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, but will instead fall back into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.
“Subhūti, you should know this:

suppose there were a man or a woman who, carrying a well-fired jar, went to a river, or a pond, or a well, or a spring, or a canal to fetch water; you should know that this jar would never break or perish.”
Why is this? Because this jar is well-fired, capable of holding water, and extremely durable.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

There are sons of good family who abide in the Great Vehicle; if they possess faith, patience, a pure mind, a superior intention, desire, resolute conviction, equanimity, and diligence regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and are further able to embrace the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and skillful means, up to and including the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), you should know that such sons of good family who abide in the Great Vehicle are always sustained and protected by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. They shall never suffer decline or regression midway, but will transcend the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, mature sentient beings, purify Buddha-fields, and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Suppose there is a merchant who lacks skillful wisdom;

he does not properly repair his ship while it is still at the shore, yet he places his goods upon it, hauls it into the water, and sets sail immediately. You should know that this ship will break apart and sink midway, and the people, the ship, and the goods will all be scattered to different places. Thus, because this merchant lacks skillful wisdom, he loses both his life and his great wealth."
Thus it is, Subhūti!

If sons of good family who abide in the Great Vehicle possess faith, patience, a pure mind, superior intention, aspiration, resolute conviction, equanimity, and diligence regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, yet do not embrace the skillful means of the profound perfection of wisdom—and so forth, as extensively explained, up to the knowledge of all aspects—then you should know that such sons of good family abiding in the Great Vehicle will perish midway; they will lose their lives and their great wealth. Losing one's life means falling to the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha; losing one's wealth means failing to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
“Subhūti, you should know this:

suppose there is a merchant possessed of skillful wisdom who first thoroughly repairs a boat on the seashore, then draws it into the water to ensure there are no leaks, and finally loads it with his goods before departing. You should know that this boat will certainly not break or sink; the people and their cargo will reach their destination in safety and security.”
Thus it is, Subhūti!

If sons of good family and others who abide in the Great Vehicle possess faith, patience, a pure mind, a superior intention, desire, resolute conviction, equanimity, and diligence regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and if they further are able to embrace the skillful means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, extending broadly even to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), you should know that such sons of good family who are established in the Great Vehicle are constantly sustained and protected by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. They shall never suffer decline or regression midway, but will transcend the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, mature sentient beings, purify Buddha-fields, and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

It is as if there were a person one hundred and twenty years old, decrepit and frail, further afflicted by various diseases—namely, wind-diseases, bile-diseases, phlegm-diseases, or combinations of these three."
"What do you think?
Would this old, sick man be able to rise from his bed by himself? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Even if someone were to support this person and help them stand up, they would still lack the strength to walk even one *krośa*, two *krośas*, or three *krośas*. Why is that? "
Because they are extremely old and sick. Thus it is, Subhūti!

If sons of good family who abide in the Great Vehicle possess faith, patience, a pure mind, superior intention, desire, resolute conviction, equanimity, and diligence regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, yet do not embrace the skillful means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*—and so on, as extensively explained, up to the knowledge of all aspects—it should be known that such sons of good family abiding in the Great Vehicle will decline midway; they will not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, but will regress into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.

Why is this? Because they do not embrace the skillful means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and so forth, up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); therefore, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not protect and mind them.
“Subhūti, you should know this!

For example, suppose there were a person one hundred and twenty years old, aged, decrepit, and frail, further afflicted by various diseases—namely, those of wind, heat, phlegm, or a combination of these three.”
This old, sick man wishes to rise from his bed and go elsewhere, yet he is unable to do so himself. Two strong men each support one of his armpits, slowly assisting him to stand up, and say to him:
"Do not be distressed; go wherever you wish. We two will never abandon you; we shall surely reach your destination safely and without harm."

"In this way, Subhūti, when sons of good family who abide in the Great Vehicle possess faith, patience, a pure mind, a superior intention, desire, resolute conviction, equanimity, and diligence regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and when they further are able to embrace the profound perfection of wisdom and skillful means, up to and including the knowledge of all aspects—it should be known that such sons of good family who are established in the Great Vehicle will never suffer decline or regression midway, but will transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, mature sentient beings, purify buddha-fields, and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Why is this? Because they are able to embrace the profound *prajñāpāramitā* through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), and because they are protected and mindful of by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, [extending] as far as the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

"How is it that sons of good family belonging to the Great Vehicle, by not embracing the profound perfection of wisdom and skillful means—extending in detail up to the knowledge of all aspects—fall back into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, rather than realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “Excellent! Excellent!”
"You have been able to ask the Tathāgata about such essential points; listen attentively now, and I shall explain them for you.

There are sons of good family who abide in the Mahāyāna, and from the first production of the thought of awakening, they grasp at 'self' and 'what belongs to self' while practicing the perfections from generosity up to wisdom. When these sons of good family abiding in the Mahāyāna practice generosity, they form this thought:
'I am the one who can give; I am giving this object; he is receiving my gift.'"
When practicing pure ethical discipline, one forms this thought:
"I am able to maintain the precepts; I maintain these precepts; I am endowed with these precepts.
When practicing patience, one forms this thought:
"I am able to practice patience; I am patient toward that [object]; I am endowed with this patience.
When practicing diligence, one forms such a thought:
"I am able to be diligent; I am diligent for this purpose; I am endowed with this diligence."
When practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one forms this thought:
"I am able to practice concentration; I am practicing concentration for this purpose; I possess this concentration.
When practicing wisdom (*prajñā*), one forms this thought:
"I am able to cultivate wisdom; I cultivate this wisdom for its own sake; I possess this wisdom.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when these sons of good family who abide in the Great Vehicle practice giving, they grasp at this giving, they grasp at it as being by means of this giving, and they grasp at giving as "mine."
When practicing pure ethical discipline, one clings to this pure ethical discipline, clings to it as originating from pure ethical discipline, and clings to pure ethical discipline as "mine";
when practicing patience, one clings to this patience, clings to it as originating from patience, and clings to patience as "mine";
when practicing diligence, one clings to this diligence, clings to it as originating from diligence, and clings to diligence as "mine."
When practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one clings to the existence of this concentration, clings to it as being derived from this concentration, and clings to concentration as "mine.
When practicing wisdom (*prajñā*), one clings to the existence of this wisdom, clings to it as being derived from this wisdom, and clings to wisdom as "mine."

Because these sons of good family who abide in the Great Vehicle are constantly pursued by the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self, the practice of their generosity up to the perfection of wisdom increases the cycle of birth and death, and they are unable to liberate themselves from the manifold sufferings of birth and so forth.
Why is this so? Because within the six pāramitās, such as giving, there is no such conceptual differentiation that could give rise to this attachment. Why?
Because the characteristic of the six pāramitās, such as giving, is the transcendence of this shore and the other shore.

“Subhūti, you should know that these sons of good family who abide in the Great Vehicle, because they do not understand the characteristics of this shore and the other shore, are unable to fully embrace the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of diligence, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom— and so on, as extensively explained, up to the knowledge of all aspects.”

Due to these causes and conditions, these sons of good family who abide in the Great Vehicle may fall back into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, and fail to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
