“How is it that sons of good family in the Great Vehicle, due to a lack of skillful means, although they practice the six perfections, fall into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, and do not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"There are sons of good family who abide in the Great Vehicle; because they lack skillful means from the time they first resolve their minds, when practicing generosity, they form such thoughts as:
'I am able to practice giving,' 'I possess generosity,' and 'This is generosity.'"
When practicing pure ethical discipline, one forms this thought:
"I am able to maintain the precepts; I am endowed with pure ethical discipline; this is pure ethical discipline.
When practicing patience, one forms this thought:
"I am able to practice patience; I possess patience; this is patience.
When practicing diligence, one forms this thought:
"I am able to be diligent; I possess diligence; this is diligence."
When practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one forms this thought:
"I am able to practice concentration; I possess meditative concentration; this is meditative concentration.
When practicing wisdom (*prajñā*), one forms this thought:
“I am able to cultivate wisdom; I possess prajñā; this is prajñā.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when these sons of good family who abide in the Great Vehicle practice giving, they grasp at this giving, grasp at the source from which this giving arises, and grasp at giving as "mine," thereby giving rise to arrogance and negligence.

When practicing pure ethical discipline, one clings to this pure ethical discipline, clings to it as being derived from pure ethical discipline, and clings to pure ethical discipline as "mine," thereby giving rise to arrogance and negligence;
when practicing patience, one clings to this patience, clings to it as being derived from patience, and clings to patience as "mine," thereby giving rise to arrogance and negligence;
when practicing diligence, one clings to this diligence, clings to it as being derived from diligence, and clings to diligence as "mine," thereby giving rise to arrogance and negligence.

When practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one clings to the existence of this concentration, clings to it as being derived from this [self], and clings to concentration as "mine," thereby giving rise to arrogance and negligence;

when practicing wisdom (*prajñā*), one clings to the existence of this wisdom, clings to it as being derived from this [self], and clings to wisdom as "mine," thereby giving rise to arrogance and negligence.

Because these sons of good family who abide in the Mahāyāna are constantly pursued by the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self, the practice of their generosity up to the perfection of wisdom increases the cycle of birth and death and cannot liberate them from the manifold sufferings of birth and so forth. Why is this so?
Within the six pāramitās, such as generosity, there is no such conceptual differentiation, nor are they as they are conceptually differentiated.
Why is this? Because the characteristics of the six pāramitās, such as generosity, do not consist in reaching this shore or the other shore.

“Subhūti, you should know that these sons of good family who abide in the Great Vehicle, because they do not understand the characteristics of this shore and the other shore, are unable to fully embrace the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of diligence, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom, and so on, up to and including all-aspect omniscience.”

For this reason, these sons of good family who abide in the Great Vehicle may fall back and descend to the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, and fail to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

Sons of good family and others who abide in the Great Vehicle, by not embracing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and other merits, and likewise by not embracing skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), although they practice the six *pāramitās*, fall into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, and do not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"How is it that sons of good family belonging to the Great Vehicle, by means of their skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) in embracing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*—and so forth, up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)—do not fall into the levels of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"There are sons of good family who abide in the Great Vehicle; from their first production of the thought of enlightenment, they practice giving up to the perfection of wisdom while remaining free from grasping at 'I' and 'mine. When these sons of good family who abide in the Great Vehicle practice giving, they do not form such thoughts as:
'I am able to give,' 'I am giving this object,' or 'that person is receiving my gift.'"
When practicing pure ethical discipline, one does not form such thoughts as:
"I am able to uphold the precepts," "I am upholding these precepts," or "I am endowed with these precepts.
When practicing patience, one does not form such thoughts:
"I am able to practice patience; I am patient toward that [object]; I possess this patience.
When practicing diligence, one does not form such thoughts:
"I am able to be diligent; I am diligent for this purpose; I possess this diligence."
When practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one does not form such thoughts as:
"I am able to practice concentration," "I am practicing concentration for this purpose," or "I possess this concentration.
When practicing wisdom (*prajñā*), one does not form such thoughts:
"I am able to cultivate wisdom; I cultivate this wisdom for this purpose; I possess this wisdom.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when these sons of good family who abide in the Great Vehicle practice giving, they do not grasp at the existence of this giving, they do not grasp at [the agent] by means of this giving, and they do not grasp at giving as "mine."

When practicing pure ethical discipline, one does not grasp at this pure ethical discipline as existing, does not grasp at it as arising from this [self], and does not grasp at pure ethical discipline as "mine.
When practicing patience, one does not grasp at this patience as existing, does not grasp at it as arising from this [self], and does not grasp at patience as "mine.
When practicing diligence, one does not grasp at this diligence as existing, does not grasp at it as arising from this [self], and does not grasp at diligence as "mine."

When practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one does not grasp at this concentration as being existent, does not grasp at it as arising from this [concentration], and does not grasp at concentration as "mine.
When practicing wisdom (*prajñā*), one does not grasp at this wisdom as being existent, does not grasp at it as arising from this [wisdom], and does not grasp at wisdom as "mine."

Because these sons of good family who abide in the Mahāyāna are not pursued by the grasping at a self or what belongs to a self, their cultivation of the perfections from generosity up to wisdom swiftly brings about liberation from the various sufferings of birth and so forth within saṃsāra.
Why is this so? Because within the six pāramitās, such as generosity, no such conceptual discrimination exists that could give rise to this attachment.
For what reason?
Because being far removed from this shore and the other shore is the characteristic of the six perfections,
such as generosity, Subhūti,

you should know that these sons of good family who abide in the Great Vehicle, by virtue of their skillful knowledge of the characteristics of this shore and the other shore, are able to embrace the six perfections, beginning with generosity, and so forth, up to the knowledge of all aspects.

By what causes and conditions do these sons of good family who dwell in the Mahāyāna not fall into the levels of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but instead swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“How is it that sons of good family belonging to the Great Vehicle, by virtue of their skillful means, practice the six perfections and do not fall into the levels of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“There are sons of good family who abide in the Great Vehicle; because they possess skillful means from the moment they first resolve their minds, when they practice giving, they do not form such thoughts as:
‘I am able to practice giving,’ ‘I possess giving,’ or ‘This is giving.’”
When practicing pure ethical discipline, one does not form such thoughts as:
"I am able to uphold the precepts," "I possess pure ethical discipline," or "This is pure ethical discipline.
When practicing patience, one does not form such thoughts:
"I am able to cultivate patience; I possess patience; this is patience.
When cultivating diligence, one does not form such thoughts:
"I am able to be diligent; I possess diligence; this is diligence."
When practicing meditative concentration, one does not form such thoughts as:
"I am able to practice concentration," "I possess meditative concentration," or "This is meditative concentration.
When practicing wisdom, one does not form such thoughts:
"I am able to cultivate wisdom; I possess prajñā; this is prajñā.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when these sons of good family who abide in the Mahāyāna practice giving, they do not grasp at this giving, they do not grasp at that by which they give, and they do not grasp at giving as "mine," nor do they give rise to arrogance or indolence.

When practicing pure ethical discipline, one does not grasp at this pure ethical discipline as existing, does not grasp at it as originating from this [self], and does not grasp at pure ethical discipline as "mine," thereby giving rise to no arrogance or negligence;

when practicing patience, one does not grasp at this patience as existing, does not grasp at it as originating from this [self], and does not grasp at patience as "mine," thereby giving rise to no arrogance or negligence;

when practicing diligence, one does not grasp at this diligence as existing, does not grasp at it as originating from this [self], and does not grasp at diligence as "mine," thereby giving rise to no arrogance or negligence.

When practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one does not grasp at the existence of this concentration, does not grasp at it as being from this [cause], and does not grasp at concentration as "mine," so as not to give rise to arrogance or negligence;

when practicing wisdom (*prajñā*), one does not grasp at the existence of this wisdom, does not grasp at it as being from this [cause], and does not grasp at wisdom as "mine," so as not to give rise to arrogance or negligence.

Because these sons of good family who abide in the Mahāyāna are not pursued by the grasping at a self or what belongs to a self, their cultivation of the perfections from generosity up to wisdom swiftly enables them to liberate themselves from the various sufferings of birth and so forth within saṃsāra.

Why is this so? Because within the six pāramitās, such as giving, there is no such conceptual differentiation, nor do they exist in the manner in which they are conceptually differentiated. Why is that?
It is not that reaching this shore or the other shore constitutes the characteristic of the six perfections,
such as generosity. "Subhūti,

you should know that these sons of good family who abide in the Great Vehicle, because they well understand the characteristics of this shore and the other shore, are able to embrace the six perfections, such as generosity, and so forth, up to the knowledge of all aspects."

By these causes and conditions, these sons of good family who dwell in the Great Vehicle do not fall into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"So it is, Subhūti! Sons of good family who abide in the Great Vehicle, by being able to embrace the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and other merits, and by also being able to embrace the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) for practicing the six *pāramitās*, do not fall into the levels of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 511. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Chapter 18: The Good Friend. Part Three, Chapter Eighteen: The Good Friend. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
How should the newly trained bodhisattva mahāsattvas train in the perfections of wisdom, meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have newly set out in the Great Vehicle and wish to train in the perfection of wisdom up to the perfection of generosity should first approach, serve, and make offerings to true spiritual friends who are able to skillfully explain and analyze the perfections of wisdom up to generosity."
That is to say, when the profound *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras are being taught, he instructs and exhorts the newly trained bodhisattvas of the Mahāyāna, saying:
"Come, noble son!..."
"You should diligently cultivate the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
When you practice diligently, you should do so by means of non-apprehension, dedicating [the merit] equally with all sentient beings toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."
Do not apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the aggregate of form up to the aggregate of consciousness;
nor do you apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the sense field of the eye up to the sense field of the mind;
nor do you apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the sense field of forms up to the sense field of phenomena; nor do you [apprehend it] by means of the eye element...
One should not grasp at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the element of mind;
nor should one grasp at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the element of form up to the element of phenomena;

nor should one grasp at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the element of eye-consciousness up to the element of mind-consciousness; nor should one [grasp it] by means of eye-contact up to mind-contact.

One should not grasp at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; nor should one grasp at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, up to and including the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition;
nor should one grasp at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the earth element, up to and including the consciousness element; nor should one grasp [at it] by means of causes.
One should not apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of conditions up to and including the dominant condition;
nor should one apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of ignorance up to and including old age and death;
nor should one apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the perfection of generosity up to and including the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore—
Do not grasp at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;
nor do you grasp at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of suchness up to the inconceivable realm;
nor do you grasp at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
Nor should one grasp unsurpassed perfect enlightenment by means of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
nor should one grasp unsurpassed perfect enlightenment by means of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments;
nor should one grasp it by means of the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, or the nine successive stages.
One should not attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment by means of the meditative concentrations or the ten spheres of totality;
nor should one attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment by means of the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
nor should one attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment by means of the stage of pure observation up to the stage of a Tathāgata; nor should one [attain it] by means of the ultimate...
One should not attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the Joyful Ground up to the Cloud of Dharma Ground;
nor should one attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of any of the gateways of dhāraṇī or the gateways of samādhi;
nor should one attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the five eyes or the six supernormal powers. Nor should one...
One should not apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
nor should one apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the thirty-two marks or the eighty minor characteristics;
nor should one apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the quality of non-forgetfulness or the state of constant equanimity.
Regarding bodhi, do not grasp at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the fruit of a stream-enterer up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;

nor do you grasp at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas or the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas; nor by means of omniscience.
They attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects. Why is this?
O son of good family!

If one does not grasp at form, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and so on, up to: if one does not grasp at the knowledge of all aspects, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
“O son of good family!
When practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, do not become attached to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, and so on, up to and including all-aspect omniscience.”
Why is this? Because form, up to and including all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), is not something to be attached to.
For what reason?
“Good son! Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature.
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas perform what is difficult; within the emptiness of intrinsic characteristics of all phenomena, they aspire to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, desiring to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”

These bodhisattva mahāsattvas are able to perform what is difficult: within all phenomena that are empty of their own intrinsic characteristics, they aspire for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and they desire to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti, you should know this:

although bodhisattva mahāsattvas know that all phenomena are like illusory things—and as has been explained at length, even like a city of gandharvas—being empty of their own characteristics, they nevertheless set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening for the sake of attaining benefit for the world;
they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening for the sake of bringing about the welfare of the world.
They set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to bring peace and happiness to the world;
they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment out of a desire to rescue and deliver all the worlds;
they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to serve as a refuge for the world.
They set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to act as a dwelling place for the world;
they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment because they wish to show the ultimate path to the world;
they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to act as an island for the world.
They set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to become the sun and moon for the world;
they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to become lamps and torches for the world;
they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to become guides for the world.
They set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to act as generals for the world;
they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to serve as the destination for the world.
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening so as to bring about the welfare and benefit of the world?

Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening by practicing generosity through to wisdom, desiring to liberate all sentient beings from their various sufferings and afflictions; this is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening so as to bring about the welfare and benefit of the world.”
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to bring benefit to the world? Subhūti!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to uproot sentient beings who are terrified by the five realms of existence and establish them on the fearless further shore of nirvāṇa; this is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to bring benefit to the world.”
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to the world?

Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to uproot sentient beings who are afflicted by grief, suffering, and distress, and establish them on the secure shore of nirvāṇa; this is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to the world."
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment out of a desire to rescue and deliver all the world? Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees sentient beings fallen into the three evil destinies, they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment with the desire to rescue them, lead them to cultivate wholesome karma, and gradually cause them to attain liberation by relying on the three vehicles. This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment out of a desire to rescue and deliver all the world."
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to become a refuge for the world?

Subhūti, it is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening so that all sentient beings who are oppressed by birth, old age, sickness, death, lamentation, grief, and suffering may swiftly attain liberation from these manifold sufferings and dwell in the realm of nirvana without remainder. This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to become a refuge for the world.”
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to act as a dwelling place for the world? Subhūti!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment with the desire to teach sentient beings that all phenomena are without conjunction; this is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to act as a dwelling place for the world."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
why are all dharmas entirely non-composite?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When all forms (*rūpa*) do not come together, they are not mutually connected; if forms are not mutually connected, they are unarisen; if forms are unarisen, they are unceasing; if forms are unceasing, they do not come together. This applies extensively to feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), and likewise to everything up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)."
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to teach sentient beings that all phenomena possess such a characteristic of non-concordance set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to demonstrate the ultimate path to the world?

Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening with the desire to teach sentient beings such a Dharma as this: that the 'other shore' of form is not form; the 'other shore' of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is not feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; and so on, in detail, up to the 'other shore' of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is not all-knowledge; and the 'other shore' of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is not the knowledge of the paths or the knowledge of all aspects."
"Subhūti, you should know that just as the characteristic of the 'other shore' (pāra) of form and so forth is, so it is with all phenomena.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If all dharmas are like the characteristic of the further shore, such as that of form and so forth, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva manifest complete awakening regarding all dharmas?"

Why is this? Within the perfection of form, there is no such discrimination as "this is form," "this is feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness," and so on, up to and including the knowledge of all aspects.

Within the perfection of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness—and so on, in detail, up to the perfection of all-aspect omniscience—there is no such discrimination as "this is form," "this is feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness," and so on, in detail, up to "this is all-aspect omniscience."
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"

In the transcendence of form, there is no such conceptual differentiation as "this is form," and so on, up to "this is the knowledge of all aspects"; likewise, in the transcendence of the knowledge of all aspects, there is no such conceptual differentiation as "this is form," and so on, up to "this is the knowledge of all aspects."
Because all phenomena are empty by their very nature, Subhūti,

you should know that it is a most difficult task for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: namely, that although they contemplate all phenomena as having the mark of total quiescence— profound and subtle— their minds do not sink into despondency, and they form this thought:

"Having attained manifest perfect enlightenment regarding this Dharma and realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, I proclaim and reveal such a profound and subtle Dharma of cessation for the sake of all sentient beings."
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to demonstrate the ultimate path to the world.
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to act as an island for the world?
"Subhūti! It is just as, for example, when there are great oceans, rivers, and ponds, a high ground that can be inhabited and is surrounded by water on all sides is called an island.
In the same way, Subhūti!"

From form up to consciousness, the prior and posterior limits are severed; this is explained in detail up to the fact that the prior and posterior limits of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are severed.

Because these prior and posterior limits are severed, all phenomena (*dharma*) are severed. This severance of the prior and posterior limits of all phenomena is itself the subtle, sublime, and suchness-like state of cessation (*śānta*); it is called emptiness, non-apprehension, the path of severance, the exhaustion of craving without remainder, the eternal extinction of all afflictions (*saṃkleśa*), and ultimate *nirvāṇa*.

"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva seeks to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, desiring to proclaim and reveal to sentient beings such dharmas as these—which are severed at their prior and subsequent limits, profoundly quiescent, subtle, and true to reality—it is for this reason that the bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to act as an island for the world."
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to act as the sun and moon for the world? Subhūti!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to shatter the heavy darkness of sentient beings covered by the eggshell of ignorance throughout the long night; in order to heal the cataracts of ignorance in sentient beings so that they may become clear-sighted; and in order to provide illumination for all sentient beings who are mired in folly and obscurity. This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to act as the sun and moon for the world.”
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to act as a lamp and torch for the world?

Subhūti, it is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to proclaim to sentient beings the true meaning and intent of the sūtras associated with the six perfections and the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*); they provide skillful instruction, leading them to apply themselves diligently to practice, thereby eliminating the various darknesses of ignorance and setting out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to act as a lamp and torch for the world."
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to act as a guide for the world?

Subhūti, it is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva—desiring to cause sentient beings who have entered onto wrong paths to abandon the four improper courses of action—sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to teach them the single path so they may return to the right way; in order that those who are defiled may attain purification; in order that those who are sorrowful and distressed may attain joy; in order that those who are troubled by grief and suffering may attain happiness; in order that those who act unreasonably may attain what is reasonable; and in order that those who wander in saṃsāra may attain cessation. This, Subhūti, is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to act as a guide for the world."
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to act as a general for the world?

Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva seeks unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening with the desire to proclaim and reveal to sentient beings that form is without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purification; that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purification; and so on, in detail, up to omniscience being without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purification, and the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects being without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purification.”
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to act as a general for the world.
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in order to act as a destination for the world?"

"Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who aspires for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening desires to proclaim and reveal to sentient beings that form has space as its destination; that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness have space as their destination; and so on, in detail, up to omniscience having space as its destination, and the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects having space as their destination."
Because all phenomena are like space and are non-existent, one wishes to proclaim and reveal to sentient beings that form is neither a destination nor a non-destination. Why is this?
Because the nature of form is empty, and within emptiness there is neither going nor not-going.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither going nor not-going. Why is this?
Because the nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is empty, and within emptiness there is neither going nor not-going.
This is explained at length until it reaches: omniscience is neither going nor not-going.
Why is this? Because the nature of all-knowledge is empty, and within emptiness there is neither going nor not-going.
Thus, the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects are neither going nor not-going.
Why is this? Because the nature of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects is empty; within emptiness, there is neither proceeding nor not proceeding.
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of providing a destination for the world, sets out toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
Why is that? "Subhūti!
All dharmas have emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness as their destination; Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination."
Why is this? Because within emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, neither going nor not-going can be apprehended. "Subhūti!..."
All dharmas have non-arising and non-action as their ultimate destination; the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination. Why is this?
Because within non-arising and non-activity, neither going nor not-going can be apprehended.
"Subhūti! All phenomena have non-arising and non-ceasing as their destination; bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination."
Why is this? Because within that which is neither arising nor ceasing, neither going nor not going can be apprehended. "Subhūti!..."
All phenomena have neither defilement nor purity as their ultimate destination; the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination. Why is this?
Within that which is neither defiled nor pure, neither going nor not-going is to be found.
"Subhūti! All phenomena have non-existence as their destination; Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination."
Why is this? Because within that which is non-existent, neither going nor not-going can be apprehended. "Subhūti!
All phenomena have the nature of being like a dream, up to and including being like a city of Gandharvas; Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a nature.
Why is this? Because, from dreams up to the city of Gandharvas, neither going nor not-going can be apprehended. "Subhūti!..."
All dharmas take the immeasurable and boundless as their ultimate destination, and the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination. Why is this?
Because within the immeasurable and boundless, neither going nor not-going can be apprehended. "Subhūti!
All dharmas take non-giving and non-taking as their destination; Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination."
Why is this? Because within non-giving and non-taking, neither going nor not-going can be apprehended. "Subhūti!..."
All dharmas have as their ultimate destination neither rising nor falling; the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination. Why is this?
Because neither going nor non-going can be apprehended, there is no rising, no falling, and no middle. "Subhūti!
All phenomena have non-going and non-coming as their destination; Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination."
Why is this? Because within that which is neither going nor coming, neither "going" nor "not going" can be apprehended.
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin!..."
All phenomena have non-increase and non-decrease as their ultimate destination; Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination. Why is this?
Because within that which neither increases nor decreases, going and not-going cannot be apprehended. "Subhūti!
All phenomena have non-entry and non-exit as their destination; Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination."
Why is this? Because within that which is without entering and without exiting, neither going nor not-going can be apprehended. "Subhūti!
All dharmas have non-accumulation and non-dispersion as their ultimate destination; the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination. Why is this?
Within that which is neither accumulated nor dispersed, neither going nor not going can be apprehended. "Subhūti!
All phenomena have non-union and non-separation as their destination; Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination."
Why is this? Because within the absence of conjunction and the absence of disjunction, neither going nor not-going can be apprehended. "Subhūti!..."
All phenomena have that which extends from the self to the viewer as their destination; the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination. Why is this?
Since even a self up to a "seer" is ultimately non-existent, how could there be any going or not-going to be found therein?
"Subhūti! All dharmas have non-self up to no-seer as their destination; bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination."

Why is this? Because from the absence of a self up to the absence of a seer, these do not ultimately exist at all; how much less could there be any attainment of a realm of existence or non-existence within them! "Subhūti!
All dharmas take permanence, bliss, self, and purity as their ultimate destination; all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.
Why is this? Since permanence, bliss, self, and purity are ultimately non-existent, how could there be any attainment of a realm of existence or a non-realm within them! "Subhūti!..."
All phenomena have impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity as their destination; the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.
Why is this? Since impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity are ultimately non-existent, how could there be any attainment of a realm of existence or a non-realm within them!
“Subhūti! All dharmas have as their objective the entities of greed, hatred, and delusion; bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such an objective.”
Why is this? Since even the phenomena of greed, hatred, and delusion ultimately do not exist, how could there be any attainment of a state of existence or a non-state of existence within them!
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
All phenomena have as their ultimate goal the performance of their respective functions; the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a goal. Why is this?
Since even the activities performed are ultimately non-existent, how could there be any attainment of a destination or a non-destination therein!
"Subhūti, all dharmas take True Suchness (tathatā), up to the inconceivable realm (acintyadhātu), as their destination; Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination."
Why is this? Since even suchness up to the inconceivable realm ultimately does not exist at all, how could there be any attainment of a "path of going" or a "non-path of going" within them!
“Subhūti! All dharmas have non-movement as their destination, and bodhisattva mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination. Why is this?
Since even immovability is ultimately non-existent, how could there be any attainment of a destination or a non-destination therein!
"Subhūti, all phenomena have the five aggregates as their destination; bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination."
Why is this? Because from form up to consciousness, these do not ultimately exist at all; how much less could there be any going or coming within them! "Subhūti!..."
All phenomena have the six internal sense bases as their destination, and the bodhisattva mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination. Why is this?
Since even the sense-base of the eye up to the sense-base of the mind ultimately do not exist, how could there be any going or non-going to be found therein!
"Subhūti, all dharmas take the six external sense-bases as their destination; bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination."

Why is this? Because from the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) up to the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), these do not ultimately exist at all; how much less could there be any going or coming within them! "Subhūti!..."
All phenomena have the six internal bases as their destination, and the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination. Why is this?
Since even the eye-element up to the mind-element ultimately do not exist, how could there be any going or non-going to be found therein!
"Subhūti, all phenomena take the six external elements as their destination; bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination."

Why is this? Because from the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) up to the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), there is ultimately nothing that exists; how much less could one find therein any going or not-going! "Subhūti!..."
All phenomena take the six consciousness elements as their destination; the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination. Why is this?
"Subhūti! Since even the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element ultimately do not exist at all, how could there be any going or non-going to be found therein?"
All phenomena have the six contacts as their destination, and the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.
Why is this? Since even eye-contact up to mind-contact ultimately do not exist, how could there be any "destination" or "non-destination" to be found therein!
“Subhūti! All dharmas have the six feelings as their destination, and bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination. Why is this?

Since even all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including all feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, are ultimately non-existent, how could there be any attainment of a realm of existence or a non-realm within them?
“Subhūti! All dharmas have the six elements as their destination, and bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination. Why is this?
"Since even the element of earth up to the element of consciousness ultimately do not exist, how could there be any going or non-going to be found therein!
'Subhūti, all phenomena take the four conditions as their destination; Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.'"

Why is this? Because even the causal conditions, up to and including the dominant conditions, are ultimately non-existent; how much less could there be any attainment of a "going" or a "not going" within them! "Subhūti!..."
All phenomena have the twelvefold dependent origination as their ultimate course, and the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend this course. Why is this?
Since ignorance up to old age and death are ultimately non-existent, how could there be any attainment of a "path" or a "non-path" within them!
"Subhūti, all dharmas take the six pāramitās as their path; bodhisattva mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a path."
Why is this? Since even the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom ultimately do not exist at all, how could there be any attainment of a state of going or non-going within them!
"Subhūti! All dharmas have the sixteen kinds of emptiness as their destination; bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination."

Why is this? Since even internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature is ultimately non-existent, how could there be any attainment of a path of going or not going within it!
"Subhūti! All phenomena have the four noble truths as their destination; Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination."

Why is this? Since even the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path are ultimately non-existent, how could there be any attainment of a realm of existence or a realm of non-existence within them!
“Subhūti! All dharmas have the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment as their destination; Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.”
Why is this? Since even the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path do not ultimately exist, how could there be any attainment of a "going" or a "not going" within them!
“Subhūti! All dharmas have the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions as their destination; bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.”

Why is this? Since the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments are ultimately non-existent, how could there be any attainment of a realm of existence or a non-realm within them!

“Subhūti! All dharmas have the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities as their destination; bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.”

Why is this? Since even the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities are ultimately non-existent, how could there be any attainment of a realm of existence or a non-realm within them!
"Subhūti! All dharmas have the three gates of liberation as their destination; bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination."

Why is this? Since even the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are ultimately non-existent, how could there be any attainment of a realm of existence or non-existence within them!
"Subhūti! All dharmas have the three vehicles and the ten stages as their destination; bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination."

Why is this? Since even the Stage of Pure Contemplation up to the Stage of the Tathāgata ultimately do not exist, how could there be any attainment of a realm of existence or non-existence within them!
“Subhūti! All dharmas have the ten stages of a bodhisattva as their destination; bodhisattva mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.”

Why is this? Since even the stages from the Ground of Utmost Joy up to the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma are ultimately non-existent, how could there be any attainment of a path of going or not-going within them!
"Subhūti! All dharmas have the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi as their destination; bodhisattva mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination."
Why is this? Since even the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi ultimately do not exist, how could there be any attainment of a realm of existence or non-existence within them!
"Subhūti! All dharmas have the five eyes and the six supernormal powers as their destination; bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination."

Why is this? Since even the five eyes and the six supernormal powers ultimately do not exist, how much less could there be any attainment of a realm of existence or non-existence within them! "Subhūti!..."

All dharmas take the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four analytical knowledges, and eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as their destination; bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.

Why is this? Since even the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are ultimately non-existent, how could there be any attainment of a path of going or not going within them!
“Subhūti! All dharmas have great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity as their destination; bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.”

Why is this? Since even great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity are ultimately non-existent, how could there be any attainment of a realm of existence or a non-realm within them!
“Subhūti! All dharmas have the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics as their destination; bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.”

Why is this? Since even the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics are ultimately non-existent, how much less could there be any attainment of a realm of existence or non-existence within them!
“Subhūti! All dharmas have the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity as their destination; bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.”

Why is this? Since even the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant abiding in equanimity are ultimately non-existent, how could there be any attainment of a realm of existence or a realm of non-existence within them!

“Subhūti! All dharmas have all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñā*) as their destination; bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.”

Why is this? Since even omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are ultimately non-existent, how could there be any attainment of a destination or a non-destination within them!
“Subhūti! All dharmas have as their destination the fruit of stream-entry up to and including the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; bodhisattva mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.”
Why is this? Since even the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha ultimately does not exist, how could there be any attainment of a "going" or a "not-going" within them!

“Subhūti! All dharmas have as their destination all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas; bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.”

Why is this? Because even all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas are ultimately non-existent; how much less could there be any attainment of a "going" or a "not-going" within them!
“Subhūti! All dharmas have the stream-enterer up to the Tathāgata as their destination; bodhisattva mahāsattvas cannot transcend such a destination.”
Why is this? Because even the stream-enterer up to the Tathāgata ultimately does not exist; how much less could there be any going or non-going to be found therein!
Thus it is, Subhūti!
“Because the bodhisattva mahāsattvas act as a destination for the world, they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Who will be able to give rise to deep faith and understanding in this profound perfection of wisdom?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva has long since set their mind upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and sought its diligent cultivation; if they have already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas and formed great vows in the presence of those Buddhas; if the roots of virtue they have planted have all reached full maturity; and if they have been embraced and protected by immeasurable spiritual friends—only then can they give rise to deep faith and understanding in this profound *prajñāpāramitā*."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Of what nature and what characteristics does this bodhisattva mahāsattva possess?"
Of what character and what appearance is one who is able to have deep faith and understanding in this Prajñāpāramitā?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva has as his nature the subduing of greed, hatred, and delusion; he has as his characteristic the distancing from the marks of greed, hatred, and delusion; he has as his aspect the distancing from the forms of greed, hatred, and delusion; he has as his appearance the distancing from the manifestations of greed, hatred, and delusion."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva takes as his nature the subduing of greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as the nature of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion; he takes as his characteristic the distancing from the marks of greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as the marks of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion; he takes as his aspect the distancing from the forms of greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as the forms of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion; he takes as his appearance the distancing from the manifestations of greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as the manifestations of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion."

Subhūti, you should know that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with such a nature, characteristics, features, and appearance, they will be able to give rise to deep faith and understanding in this profound prajñāpāramitā.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to have deep faith and understanding in this profound perfection of wisdom, where will that bodhisattva mahāsattva be headed?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva shall proceed toward the knowledge of all modes.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva proceeds toward omniscience, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to serve as a refuge for all sentient beings."
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can develop profound faith and understanding in this very profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they will be able to advance toward the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*); and if they can advance toward the knowledge of all modes, they will then be able to serve as a refuge for all sentient beings.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to perform a difficult task, in that he dons such firm armor as this:
'I shall deliver all sentient beings and cause them all to realize ultimate nirvāṇa.'"
"Although one performs such deeds for sentient beings, one does not perceive the conceptual designation of 'sentient being' at all.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "It is so!
It is just as you have said."
"So it is! It is just as you have said.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The armor donned by this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not belong to form, nor even to consciousness. Why is this?

Because from form through to consciousness, all are ultimately non-existent; since they are neither the bodhisattva nor the armor, it is said that the armor does not belong to form, nor even to consciousness.

In this way, even up to this point, the armor donned by this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not belong to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Why is that?

Because omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are ultimately non-existent—neither being the bodhisattva nor the armor—it is said that this armor does not belong to omniscience, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, or the knowledge of all aspects.
The armor donned by this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not belong to the self, nor even to the perceiver.

Why is this? Because from the self to the perceiver, all are ultimately non-existent; since they are neither the bodhisattva nor the armor, it is said that this armor does not belong to the self, nor even to the perceiver.
The armor donned by this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not belong to any phenomena. Why is this?
Because all phenomena are ultimately non-existent, being neither the bodhisattva nor the armor; therefore, it is said that his armor does not belong to any phenomena.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices this profound perfection of wisdom in this way, they are able to don such firm armor, thinking: ‘I shall deliver all sentient beings and cause them all to realize ultimate nirvāṇa.’”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can don such firm armor as this—vowing, ‘I shall deliver all sentient beings and cause them all to realize parinirvāṇa’—he will not fall into the levels of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.”
For this bodhisattva mahāsattva, there is no possibility or occasion for falling into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha. Why is that?
Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not establish limits regarding sentient beings when donning such firm armor.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Subhūti, based on what meaning do you say this:
'If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can don such firm armor, they will not fall into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha'?"
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not don such firm armor for the sake of liberating only a small portion of sentient beings, nor does he don such firm armor for the sake of seeking only a small portion of wisdom.”

Why is this? It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have donned such firm armor for the sake of universally rescuing and delivering all sentient beings to parinirvāṇa; they have donned such firm armor solely for the purpose of seeking to attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). By virtue of these causes and conditions, they do not fall into the levels of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva dons such firm armor solely for the purpose of seeking the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) in order to universally rescue and deliver all sentient beings and lead them to parinirvāṇa; by virtue of these causes and conditions, they do not fall into the levels of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This Prajñāpāramitā is most profound; there is no one who can practice it, no dharma to be practiced, no place for practice, and nothing by which it can be cultivated."

Why is this? Because within this profound meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there is not even the slightest real dharma that can be called the "one who practices," the "dharma practiced," the "place of practice," or that by which one practices.
“World-Honored One!
If one cultivates space, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
if one cultivates all dharmas, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.”
If one cultivates unreal phenomena, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
if one cultivates non-existence, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
if one cultivates non-appropriation, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
"If one cultivates the removal of phenomena, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"By removing what phenomena does one cultivate the perfection of wisdom?"
Subhūti replied: “To cultivate the elimination of the five aggregates is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the elimination of the six internal sense bases is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.”
To cultivate the removal of the six external bases is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the removal of the six internal elements is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the removal of the six external elements is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the elimination of the six consciousness elements is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the elimination of the six contacts is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the elimination of the six feelings is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the elimination of the six elements is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the elimination of the four conditions is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the elimination of the twelve links of dependent origination is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the elimination of [the notions of] a self up to a viewer is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the elimination of the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the elimination of internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the removal of conceptualization regarding suchness up to the inconceivable realm is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the removal of conceptualization regarding the four noble truths is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the removal of conceptualization regarding the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the elimination of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the elimination of the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the elimination of the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the removal of conceptualization regarding the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the removal of conceptualization regarding the stage of extreme joy up to the stage of the cloud of dharma is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the removal of conceptualization regarding all doors of dhāraṇī and doors of samādhi is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the removal of the five eyes and the six supernormal powers is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the removal of the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the removal of great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the removal of the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the removal of the qualities of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the removal of the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the relinquishment of all bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the relinquishment of all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the relinquishment of form, and so on extensively up to the knowledge of all aspects, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."
One should verify and recognize a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva by relying upon this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices from the *prajñāpāramitā* down to the *dānapāramitā* without attachment, one should know that he is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva; and so on, in detail, until: if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) without attachment, one should know that he is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not regard the words or instructions of others as essential truths; they do not act merely out of faith in others. They are not defiled by the faults of greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and so forth, nor are their minds led astray by them."
When any non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not depart from the perfections, ranging from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom.

When any non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, upon hearing this teaching of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, their minds are not startled, not terrified, not afraid, do not sink, and do not become despondent; nor do they ever abandon or retreat from the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening they seek. Regarding the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they joyfully delight in hearing it, receiving and upholding it, reading and reciting it, mastering it thoroughly, contemplating it with focused mindfulness, and practicing according to the teaching without ever becoming weary.

It should be known that such non-retrogressive Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas have, in previous lives, already heard the meaning and intent of this profound Prajñāpāramitā; they have upheld, recited, and reflected upon it according to reason, practicing with diligence and without weariness of mind.

Why is this? Because when these non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas hear such profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, their minds are not startled, not terrified, and not afraid; as it has been explained at length, they practice according to the teaching, remaining forever free from weariness.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, their mind is not startled, not terrified, not afraid, does not sink, and does not become despondent; and if they do not regress or abandon the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek, but instead joyfully delights in hearing, receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, thoroughly mastering, and reflecting upon this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, practicing as it has been taught without ever becoming weary."
"How should this bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the profound perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, whose mental continuum conforms to, inclines toward, and enters into the knowledge of all modes, should practice the profound perfection of wisdom in this manner."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How does this bodhisattva mahāsattva continuously accord with, incline toward, and enter into all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna), practicing the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva continuously accords with, inclines toward, and enters into emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, space, non-existence, non-arising, non-cessation, non-defilement, non-purity, suchness, up to the inconceivable realm, non-conditioning, non-action, and that which is like a dream up to like a city of gandharvas, practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva continuously accords with, inclines toward, and enters into all-knowledge (*sarvajñājñāna*), practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying: “As the Blessed One has said:

‘If a bodhisattva mahāsattva continuously accords with, inclines toward, and enters into emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—expounded at length up to being like a city of gandharvas—and practices the profound perfection of wisdom, this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva who continuously accords with, inclines toward, and enters into all-knowledge, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom.’”
When that bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, is he practicing the five aggregates, up to and including all-aspect omniscience?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not course in the five aggregates, nor even in the knowledge of all aspects. Why is that?

This bodhisattva mahāsattva accords with, inclines toward, and enters into the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), which has no creator and no destroyer; it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; it abides nowhere; it is without direction or domain, without number or measure, and without going or coming. Since neither number nor measure nor coming and going can be apprehended therein, there is likewise nothing that can realize it.

“Subhūti! This omniscience (sarvajñajñāna) cannot be realized by means of the five aggregates; as explained at length, it cannot even be realized by means of the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā).”
Why is this? The five aggregates are themselves the knowledge of all modes; to speak extensively, even up to the knowledge of all aspects is itself the knowledge of all modes. Why is this so?

Whether it be the suchness of the five aggregates, the suchness of the knowledge of all modes, or the suchness of all phenomena, they are all one single suchness, without duality or distinction. To speak at length, up to the suchness of the knowledge of all aspects, the suchness of the knowledge of all modes, and the suchness of all phenomena, they are all one single suchness, without duality or distinction.

"Therefore, the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) cannot be realized by means of the five aggregates; this is explained at length up to: it cannot be realized by means of the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā).

*The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Fascicle 512, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Chapter 19: Suchness (Tathatā), Part Three of the Nineteenth Chapter, "Suchness," Section One. At that time, the devaputras of the desire realm and the form realm each took various celestial powdered incenses and heavenly flowers, scattered them from afar over the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

Thus, this Prajñāpāramitā is most profound, difficult to see and difficult to realize; it is beyond the reach of discursive thought and transcends the sphere of conceptualization. Subtle, wondrous, and tranquil, it can be known by those who are wise and discerning, yet it cannot be readily believed or accepted by the world at large; it is indeed unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have declared in this profound Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom:
"The five aggregates are themselves the knowledge of all modes; the knowledge of all modes is itself the five aggregates."
To speak at length, even up to the point that all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) is the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), and the knowledge of all modes is all-aspect omniscience;
the Buddhas are the knowledge of all modes, and the knowledge of all modes is the Buddhas.

Why is this so? Whether it be the suchness of the five aggregates, the suchness of the knowledge of all modes, or the suchness of all phenomena, they are all a single suchness, without duality or distinction.

To speak at length, up to and including the suchness of all-aspect knowledge, the suchness of the knowledge of all modes, and the suchness of all phenomena—all are a single suchness, without duality and without distinction.
Whether it be the suchness of all Buddhas, the suchness of the knowledge of all-knowledge, or the suchness of all phenomena, they are all a single suchness, without duality or distinction.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the devaputras, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is as you have said.
O Son of Heaven, you should know that as I contemplate this meaning, my mind constantly inclines toward tranquility and does not delight in preaching the Dharma."

Why is this? Because this Dharma is extremely profound, difficult to see and difficult to realize; it is beyond the reach of discursive thought and transcends the sphere of conceptualization. Subtle, wondrous, and tranquil, it can be known only by those who are wise and of keen intelligence; it is not something that the world at large can readily believe or accept—that the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is itself the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment realized by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.

“O Son of Heaven, you should know that this unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment realized by all Buddhas is that which cannot be realized, is not something to be realized, has no place of realization, and no time of realization.”
"O Son of Heaven, you should know!
This Dharma is profound and subtle, its non-dual activity is not something that can be fathomed or compared by any in the world.
O Son of Heaven, you should know!"

Because space is profound, this Dharma is profound; because true suchness up to the inconceivable realm is profound, this Dharma is profound; because the immeasurable and boundless is profound, this Dharma is profound; because there is no going and no coming is profound, this Dharma is profound; because there is no arising and no ceasing is profound, this Dharma is profound; because there is no defilement and no purity is profound, this Dharma is profound; because there is no knowing and no attaining is profound, this Dharma is profound; because there is no creating and no acting is profound, this Dharma is profound; because the self up to the viewer is profound, this Dharma is profound; because the five aggregates are profound, this Dharma is profound; and so on, in detail, up to because all-aspect omniscience is profound, this Dharma is profound; because all Buddha-dharmas are profound, this Dharma is profound.
At that time, the sons of the gods again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This Dharma that has been taught is extremely profound and subtle; it is not something that those in the world can suddenly believe and accept."
Why is this? This profound and subtle Dharma is not taught for the sake of grasping the five aggregates, nor is it taught for the sake of abandoning the five aggregates.
To speak extensively, it is not taught even for the sake of grasping the knowledge of all aspects; [it is taught for the sake of realizing non-attachment].
It is not taught for the sake of abandoning all-aspect omniscience;
it is not taught for the sake of grasping all Buddha-dharmas, nor for the sake of abandoning all Buddha-dharmas.

Sentient beings in the world mostly engage in grasping at "I" and "mine," saying: "Form is I, form is mine; feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are I, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are mine. This is explained in detail up to: "Omniscience is I, omniscience is mine; the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects are I, the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects are mine."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the sons of the gods: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is as you have said. Son of Heaven,

you should know that if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices for the sake of grasping the five aggregates, or practices for the sake of relinquishing the five aggregates— and so on, in detail, until— practices for the sake of grasping all buddha-dharmas, or practices for the sake of relinquishing all buddha-dharmas."

This bodhisattva mahāsattva is unable to practice the perfection of wisdom, meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity; and so on, up to being unable to practice the knowledge of all aspects.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

This profound Dharma is able to accord with all dharmas; that is to say, it is able to accord with the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of meditative concentration, the perfection of diligence, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity, and so forth, up to and including the knowledge of all aspects.”
This profound Dharma is entirely without obstruction; that is to say, it does not obstruct form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, and so on, in detail, up to all-aspect omniscience.
This profound dharma has non-obstruction as its characteristic.
Why is this? Because space is equal;

because true thusness, up to the inconceivable realm, is equal; because emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are equal; because non-arising and non-ceasing are equal; because non-creation and non-action are equal; and because non-defilement and non-purity are equal—this profound dharma has non-obstruction as its characteristic.
This profound dharma is without arising and without cessation. Why is this?

Because form is without arising and without cessation; because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without arising and without cessation; and so on, in detail, up to omniscience being without arising and without cessation, and the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects being without arising and without cessation—this profound dharma is without arising and without cessation.
This profound Dharma is entirely without tracks. Why is this? Because the track of form cannot be apprehended;

because the tracks of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot be apprehended; and so on, in detail, up to the fact that the track of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) cannot be apprehended, and the tracks of the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) cannot be apprehended—therefore, this profound Dharma is entirely without tracks.
