At that time, the devaputras of the desire realm and the form realm again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Virtuous Subhūti is a true son of the Buddha, born after the manner of the Tathāgata.”
"Why is this? Because, Venerable Subhūti, all the teachings you have expounded are entirely in accord with emptiness.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the devaputras of the desire and form realms, saying:
"You all say that you are true sons of the Buddha, born after the Tathāgata; in what way, Subhūti, are you born after the Tathāgata?
It is because you are born after the *tathatā* (suchness) of the Tathāgata."

Why is this so? Because the Tathāgata’s suchness neither comes nor goes, and Subhūti’s suchness likewise neither comes nor goes; therefore it is said that Subhūti is born in accordance with the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata’s suchness is the suchness of all phenomena, and the suchness of all phenomena is the Tathāgata’s suchness. Such suchness has neither the nature of suchness nor the nature of non-suchness; Subhūti’s suchness is likewise so. Therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born in accordance with the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata has the characteristic of being eternally abiding in suchness; Subhūti’s suchness is likewise. Therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born after the manner of the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata’s suchness is without change, without discrimination, and pervades the transformation of all phenomena; Subhūti’s suchness is likewise. Therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born after the manner of the Tathāgata.

The *tathatā* of the Tathāgata is without obstruction, and the *tathatā* of all phenomena is likewise without obstruction. Whether it be the *tathatā* of the Tathāgata or the *tathatā* of all phenomena, they are one and the same *tathatā*, non-dual and undifferentiated, without creation and without fabrication.

Thus, true suchness is the constant characteristic of true suchness; there is no time when it is not the characteristic of true suchness. Because it is the constant characteristic of true suchness and there is no time when it is not the characteristic of true suchness, it is non-dual and without distinction. Subhūti, true suchness is likewise so; therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born after the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata’s suchness is without recollection and without conceptual discrimination in all places; Subhūti’s suchness is likewise. Therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born in accordance with the Tathāgata.
The *tathatā* (suchness) of the Tathāgata is undifferentiated and unapprehendable; the *tathatā* of Subhūti is likewise. Therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born in accordance with the Tathāgata.

The *tathatā* of the Tathāgata is not separate from the *tathatā* of all phenomena (*dharma*), and the *tathatā* of all phenomena is not separate from the *tathatā* of the Tathāgata. Such *tathatā* is the constant characteristic of *tathatā*; there is no time when it is not the characteristic of *tathatā*. The *tathatā* of Subhūti is likewise. Therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born in accordance with the Tathāgata.

Although it is said that he is born in accordance with [the Tathāgata], there is nothing with which he is born in accordance. This is because Subhūti’s *tathatā* (suchness) is not different from the Buddha’s; the *tathatā* of the Tathāgata is neither past, nor future, nor present, and the *tathatā* of all phenomena is likewise neither past, nor future, nor present. The *tathatā* of Subhūti is also thus; therefore, it is said that Subhūti is born in accordance with the Tathāgata.
Because the suchness of the past is equal, the suchness of the Tathāgata is equal; because the suchness of the Tathāgata is equal, the suchness of the past is equal.
Because the suchness of the future is equal, the suchness of the Tathāgata is equal; because the suchness of the Tathāgata is equal, the suchness of the future is equal.
Because the suchness of the present is equal, the suchness of the Tathāgata is equal; because the suchness of the Tathāgata is equal, the suchness of the present is equal.

Whether it be the suchness of the past, the suchness of the future, or the suchness of the present, they are equal; and whether it be the suchness of the Tathāgata, it is equal—this single suchness is equal, non-dual, and without distinction.
Because the suchness of form is equal, the suchness of the Tathāgata is equal; because the suchness of the Tathāgata is equal, the suchness of form is equal.

Because the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is equal, the suchness of the Tathāgata is equal; because the suchness of the Tathāgata is equal, the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is equal.

Whether it be the suchness of form, or the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—being equal—and whether it be the suchness of the Tathāgata—being equal—all are the same single suchness, equal, non-dual, and without distinction.

To speak at length, up to: because the *tathatā* (suchness) of all-knowledge is equal, the *tathatā* of the Tathāgata is equal; because the *tathatā* of the Tathāgata is equal, the *tathatā* of all-knowledge is equal.

Because the *tathatā* of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects is equal, the *tathatā* of the Tathāgata is equal; because the *tathatā* of the Tathāgata is equal, the *tathatā* of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects is equal.

Whether it be the suchness of all-knowledge, or the suchness of the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects, or the suchness of the Tathāgata—these are equal as a single suchness, non-dual and without distinction.
“O Son of Heaven, you should know!
Because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have directly realized the equality of the suchness (tathatā) of all these phenomena, they are called Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.”
"Because I have developed deep faith and understanding in the suchness (*tathatā*) of all these dharmas, I say that Subhūti is born after the Tathāgata.
When this characteristic of suchness was being spoken, this trichiliocosm shook in six ways:

it surged in the east and subsided in the west; it surged in the west and subsided in the east; it surged in the south and subsided in the north; it surged in the north and subsided in the south; it surged in the center and subsided at the edges; and it surged at the edges and subsided in the center.

At that time, the devaputras of the desire realm and the form realm again took various kinds of exquisite celestial powdered incense and celestial flowers, scattering them over the World-Honored One and Subhūti, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How extraordinary!
“World-Honored One!
This is unprecedented!
The Venerable Subhūti is born after the Tathāgata by virtue of suchness.”
At that time, Subhūti addressed the devaputras of the desire and form realms, saying:
"Devaputras, you should know this!
I, Subhūti, do not arise following the Tathāgata by way of form; I do not arise following the Tathāgata by way of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness."

One does not follow the Tathāgata’s birth by virtue of the suchness of form; one does not follow the Tathāgata’s birth by virtue of the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
One follows the Tathāgata’s birth without being separate from form; one follows the Tathāgata’s birth without being separate from feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

One follows the Tathāgata’s birth without being separate from the suchness of form; one follows the Tathāgata’s birth without being separate from the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

To speak at length, up to: it is not by virtue of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) that one follows the Tathāgata’s birth, nor is it by virtue of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) that one follows the Tathāgata’s birth;

it is not by virtue of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all-knowledge that one follows the Tathāgata’s birth, nor is it by virtue of the suchness of the knowledge of the paths or the knowledge of all aspects that one follows the Tathāgata’s birth;

it is not by being separate from all-knowledge that one follows the Tathāgata’s birth, nor is it by being separate from the knowledge of the paths or the knowledge of all aspects that one follows the Tathāgata’s birth.

Because they do not depart from the *tathatā* (suchness) of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), they are born following the Tathāgata; because they do not depart from the *tathatā* of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), they are born following the Tathāgata.
They are not born following the Tathāgata by virtue of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), nor are they born following the Tathāgata by virtue of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
They are not born following the Tathāgata by virtue of the *tathatā* of the conditioned, nor are they born following the Tathāgata by virtue of the *tathatā* of the unconditioned.
Because they do not depart from the conditioned, they are born following the Tathāgata; because they do not depart from the unconditioned, they are born following the Tathāgata.

Because they do not depart from the suchness of the conditioned, they are born following the Tathāgata; because they do not depart from the suchness of the unconditioned, they are born following the Tathāgata.

Why is this? Because all these phenomena (*dharma*) are utterly non-existent; those who follow along with arising, that which is followed in arising, the means by which one follows along with arising, and the place where one follows along with arising—all these are unattainable, because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*).
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The suchness of all phenomena, and so forth, up to the inconceivable realm, are all most profound; for herein form cannot be apprehended, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness likewise cannot be apprehended.”
The suchness of form is unapprehendable; the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is likewise unapprehendable. Why is this?
Because within this, even form up to consciousness cannot be apprehended, much less can the suchness of form up to the suchness of consciousness be apprehended!

To speak at length, up to this point: herein all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is unapprehendable; the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are also unapprehendable. The suchness (*tathatā*) of all-knowledge is unapprehendable; the suchness of the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects are also unapprehendable.

Why is this so? Because within this, even omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are not to be found; how much less could the suchness (*tathatā*) of omniscience, the suchness of the knowledge of the aspects of the path, or the suchness of the knowledge of all aspects be found!
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying: “So it is! So it is!”
"It is as you have said.
While these characteristics of suchness were being explained, the outflows of two hundred bhikṣus were forever exhausted; their minds attained liberation, and they became arhats.
Furthermore, a community of five hundred bhikṣuṇīs distanced themselves from dust and left behind defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.

At that same time, five thousand bodhisattvas simultaneously realized the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), and six thousand bodhisattvas exhausted all outflows (āsrava), their minds attained liberation, and they became arhats.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:

"In this assembly, there are six thousand bodhisattvas who, in the past, have personally approached and made offerings to five hundred buddhas, left the household life with right faith, and diligently practiced the holy life (*brahmacarya*). Although they have practiced generosity, pure ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration, they have not embraced the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), giving rise to notions of differentiation and engaging in differentiated practices."
When practicing generosity, one forms this thought:
"This is generosity; this is the object of giving; this is the recipient; I am able to practice giving."
When practicing pure ethical discipline, one forms this thought:
"This is pure ethical discipline; this is sinful karma; this is the object to be guarded; I am able to maintain the precepts."
When practicing patience, one should form this thought:
"This is patience; this is an obstacle to patience; this is the object of patience; I am capable of practicing patience."
When practicing diligence, one forms this thought:
"This is diligence; this is laziness; this is that which is to be done; I am capable of being diligent."
When practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one forms this thought:
"This is meditative concentration; this is distraction; this is that which is to be accomplished; I am able to cultivate concentration."

Lacking the skillful means of embracing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they practice the distinct acts of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration based on the perception of diversity.
Because of distinct perceptions and distinct practices, they fail to attain the bodhisattva’s non-distinct perception and lose the bodhisattva’s non-distinct practice.

Due to these causes and conditions, they fail to enter the bodhisattva stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*). Because they fail to enter the bodhisattva stage of right determination, they instead attain the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), proceeding gradually through the stages up to the fruit of arhatship.

Therefore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses the path of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, as well as the gates of liberation— emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness— but does not embrace the profound perfection of wisdom and skillful means, they will then realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and fall into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.
Then, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"By what causes and conditions do some bodhisattvas practice the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, yet, because they do not embrace the skillful means of profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and fall into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha;

whereas other bodhisattvas practice the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and furthermore, by embracing the skillful means of profound *prajñāpāramitā*, enter the bodhisattva’s state of right determination (*samyaktvaniyāma*), gradually cultivate all bodhisattva practices, and shall realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
At that time, the Blessed One addressed Śāriputra:

“If bodhisattvas distance themselves from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), do not take great compassion as their primary guide, and cultivate the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, yet—due to failing to embrace the skillful means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*—realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and fall into the stage of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha;

whereas if bodhisattvas do not depart from the mind of omniscience, take great compassion as their primary guide, cultivate the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and further embrace the skillful means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they will be able to enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*), gradually practice all the bodhisattva deeds, and shall attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
“Śāriputra! It is as if there were a bird whose body was vast, measuring one hundred yojanas, or perhaps two hundred, even up to five hundred yojanas, yet it had no wings.
Suppose this bird were to cast itself down from the Heaven of the Thirty-three, heading toward Jambudvīpa, and while on its way, it were to think again:
"I wish to return up to the Heaven of the Thirty-three."
"What do you think? Would this bird be able to return to the Heaven of the Thirty-three? Śāriputra said:
"No, World-Honored One! No!"
“Sugata! The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“Suppose this bird, midway on its journey, were to make this aspiration:”
"Upon reaching Jambudvīpa, may my body be without injury or affliction.
What do you think? Can this bird's wish be fulfilled?
Śāriputra said: “No, World-Honored One!”
"No, Sugata!
When this bird reaches this Jambudvīpa, its body will certainly suffer injury and affliction; it will either meet its end or experience suffering near death."
"Why is that? Because this bird's body is large and it falls from a great distance, yet it has no wings.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"So it is! So it is! It is just as you have said."

Śāriputra! It is the same with certain bodhisattvas: although they have spent immeasurable and incalculable great eons diligently practicing generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration, and have also cultivated the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—if they do not embrace the profound perfection of wisdom and skillful means, they will realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and fall into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas have distanced themselves from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), and do not take great compassion as their primary guide; although they pass through immeasurable and incalculable great eons, diligently cultivating generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration, and also practicing the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—they fail to embrace the profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), and consequently fall to the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.

Although these bodhisattvas recollect the aggregates of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present, and although they make offerings, pay respect, and practice in accordance with them, because they grasp at signs within those aggregates, they are unable to correctly understand the true merits of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones’ aggregates of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.

Because these bodhisattvas are unable to correctly understand the qualities of the Buddha, although they hear the sounds of the path of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, they grasp at their signs based on those sounds; having grasped at these signs, they dedicate [the merit] toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
If these bodhisattvas dedicate in this manner, they will not attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, but will instead fall to the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha. Why is that?

Śāriputra! Because these bodhisattvas do not embrace the skillful means of the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), although they take up various roots of goodness they have cultivated and dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, they nevertheless fall to the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, there are bodhisattvas who, from the first production of the thought of awakening, do not depart from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñājñāna*), always taking great compassion as their foremost guide. They diligently cultivate generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration; they also constantly embrace the profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*). Although they recollect the aggregates of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the past, future, and present, they do not grasp at their signs. Although they cultivate the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—they do not grasp at their signs. Although they recollect the various merits of themselves and others, they share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, yet they do not grasp at their signs."

“Śāriputra, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva proceeds directly toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and does not fall into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.”

Why is this? Because from the first generation of the mind of enlightenment until its ultimate consummation, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not depart from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*). They always take great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) as their primary guide. Although they cultivate generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration, they do not grasp at signs (*nimitta*). Although they recollect the aggregates of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present, they likewise do not grasp at signs. Although they cultivate the path of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, they also do not grasp at signs.

“Śāriputra! Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess skillful means, they practice from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom with a mind free from signs; and so on, in detail, until they practice all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) with a mind free from signs. By means of this, they will certainly realize the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).”
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:

"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first generation of the mind of awakening until the ultimate end, is always able to embrace the profound perfection of wisdom through skillful means, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is close to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening."

Why is this? Because from the first production of the thought of enlightenment until its ultimate consummation, this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive even the slightest dharma that can be apprehended—whether it be that which realizes, that which is realized, the locus of realization, the time of realization, or that by means of which one realizes. None of these can be apprehended; that is to say, form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, and so on, up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), are all unapprehendable.
"Furthermore, Blessed One,

there are sons of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who, being unable to embrace the profound perfection of wisdom through skillful means, seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
It should be known that regarding the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening they seek, they will harbor doubt and hesitation as to whether they will attain it or not. Why is this?

Because these sons of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle do not embrace the skillful means of profound *prajñāpāramitā*; they grasp at signs in the practice of the *pāramitās* of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and so on extensively, up to grasping at signs in the practice of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Due to these causes and conditions, these sons of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle will harbor doubts and hesitations regarding unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, wondering whether they will attain it or not.
"Therefore, World-Honored One,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they must certainly not distance themselves from the skillful means of the perfection of wisdom."

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom through skillful means, employing the method of non-apprehension, should cultivate the perfections from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom with a mind accompanied by the signless; and so on, in detail, until: with a mind accompanied by the signless, they should cultivate all-knowledge, the knowledge of paths, and the knowledge of all aspects.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in the perfection of wisdom through skillful means, employing the method of non-apprehension and with a mind accompanied by the signless, they cultivate and abide in all such buddha-dharmas and will certainly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, the devaputras of the desire realm and the form realm addressed the Buddha together, saying:
"The unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is extremely difficult to believe and understand, and exceedingly difficult to realize."

Why is this so? Because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas must realize and know both the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena (*dharma*) before they can attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) that they seek; yet, the characteristics of phenomena as known by bodhisattvas are entirely non-existent and utterly unobtainable.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the devaputras, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.
The unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is extremely difficult to believe and understand, and exceedingly difficult to realize.
O Son of Heaven, you should know this!

I too have directly awakened to the characteristics of all phenomena and realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; yet, in the ultimate sense, I do not apprehend any characteristic of a phenomenon that can be designated as "this is the realizer," "this is the realized," "this is the place of realization," "this is the time of realization," or "it is by means of this that one realizes."
Why is this? O sons of the gods!

Because all phenomena are ultimately pure, and because the conditioned and the unconditioned are ultimately empty, for this reason, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is extremely difficult to believe and understand, and exceedingly difficult to realize.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Regarding what the World-Honored One has said—that the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is extremely difficult to believe and understand, and exceedingly difficult to realize—according to my contemplation of the meaning of the Buddha’s words, the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is extremely easy to believe and understand, and exceedingly easy to realize.”

Why is this? If one can have faith and understanding that there is no dharma that can realize, no dharma that is realized, no place of realization, no time of realization, and furthermore, nothing by means of which realization occurs, then one is able to have faith and understanding in the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas.

If one realizes that there is no dharma that can realize, no dharma that is realized, no place of realization, no time of realization, and nothing by means of which realization occurs, then one is able to realize the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Why is this? Because all phenomena are ultimately empty; within ultimate emptiness, there is no phenomenon that can be called the "realizer," no phenomenon that can be called the "object realized," no phenomenon that can be called the "place of realization," no phenomenon that can be called the "time of realization," and no phenomenon by which anything is realized.
Why is this? Because the nature and characteristics of all phenomena are empty; whether increasing or decreasing, they are entirely non-existent and cannot be apprehended.

For this reason, the giving practiced by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, up to and including the perfection of wisdom, is entirely non-existent and cannot be apprehended; this is explained at length, extending even to omniscience (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), which are all entirely non-existent and cannot be apprehended.

Regarding all phenomena observed by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—whether they have form or are formless, visible or invisible, resistant or non-resistant, with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned—they are entirely non-existent and cannot be apprehended.

For this reason, as I contemplate the meaning and intent of what the Buddha has taught, the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is extremely easy to believe and understand, and very easy to realize; therefore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should not think that it is difficult to believe and understand, or difficult to realize.
Why is this? Form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form;

feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. To speak at length, up to omniscience is empty of the intrinsic nature of omniscience; the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects, are empty of the intrinsic nature of the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can give rise to deep faith and understanding regarding this meaning of the emptiness of intrinsic nature and realize it without error, they will attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"By virtue of this meaning, I say that unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is not difficult to believe and understand, nor is it difficult to realize.
At that time, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"For these reasons, the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is extremely difficult to believe and understand, and exceedingly difficult to realize."
Why is this so? Because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas contemplate all phenomena as being entirely devoid of intrinsic nature and identical to space.
For example, space does not form such a thought:
"I shall believe, resolve upon, and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
In this same way, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should not form such a thought as:
"I shall believe, resolve upon, and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Why is this? Because the nature and characteristics of all phenomena are empty and equal to space; it is only when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to believe and understand that all phenomena are empty and equal to space, and realize them without error, that they attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has faith and understanding that all phenomena are equal to space were to easily give rise to faith and understanding regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and were to easily realize it, then there should not be bodhisattva mahāsattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who don the great armor of merit and set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, only to experience retreat or discouragement along the way.
"Therefore, know that unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is extremely difficult to believe and understand, and exceedingly difficult to realize.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Śāriputra, saying: "What do you think?"
"Does form experience any retreat or discouragement regarding the Buddha's unsurpassed, perfect,
and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied, "No!"
"Subhūti! What do you think? Do feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness ever regress from the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti!”
“What do you think? Is there any phenomenon apart from form that could experience retreat or discouragement regarding the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied:
"No, Subhūti! What do you think?"
"Is there any dharma apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that could experience retreat or discouragement regarding the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect,
and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied, "No, indeed!"
"Subhūti! What do you think? Does the suchness of form recede or falter in the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti!”
“What do you think? Does the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness ever regress from the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied:
"No, Subhūti! What do you think?"
"Is there any dharma apart from the *tathatā* of form that could experience retreat or discouragement regarding the Buddha's unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied, "No!"

"Subhūti! What do you think? Apart from the true thusness (tathatā) of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, is there any dharma that could regress or be discouraged from the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti!”
“[The Buddha said: ‘To speak at length, even up to this point: what do you think?
Does the omniscience of a Buddha ever experience retreat or discouragement regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied:”
"No, Subhūti! Does the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects ever regress from the Buddha's unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti!”

“What do you think? Is there any phenomenon apart from omniscience that could experience retreat or discouragement regarding the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied:
"No, Subhūti! What do you think?"
"Is there any phenomenon that, apart from the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects, could cause one to regress from the Buddha's unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied, "No!"
"Subhūti! What do you think? Does the suchness of all-knowledge ever retreat or falter from the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti!”
"What do you think? Does the suchness of the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects ever regress from the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti!”

“What do you think? Apart from the *tathatā* (suchness) of omniscience, is there any dharma that could regress or be discouraged from the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied:
"No, Subhūti! What do you think?"

“Is there any phenomenon within the *tathatā* of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) that could regress from the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect,
and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied, “No, indeed not!”
"Excellent, Subhūti! Furthermore, Śāriputra,
what do you think?"
"Regarding the suchness of all phenomena, extensively explained up to the inconceivable realm, would there be any retreat or discouragement in the Buddha’s unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete enlightenment? Śāriputra replied, "No!"

"Subhūti! What do you think? Apart from the suchness of all phenomena—and as extensively explained up to the inconceivable realm—is there any phenomenon that would experience retreat or discouragement regarding the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti!”
Then, the Venerable Subhūti said to Śāriputra:

"If all phenomena, by virtue of their truth and their abiding nature, are entirely non-existent and cannot be apprehended, what phenomenon could there be that might regress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
Then, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:

"According to what you have said, within the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), there is no phenomenon whatsoever, nor is there any bodhisattva who could be said to experience retreat from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. If that is so, for what reason did the Buddha speak of three types of persons abiding in the vehicle of the bodhisattvas, rather than speaking of only one?"
"Furthermore, as you have said, there should be no distinction between the three vehicles of bodhisattvas; there should be only one vehicle, that of the perfectly awakened ones.
Then, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"One should ask Subhūti:"
Do you admit that there is a single Bodhisattvayāna?
Only then can it be challenged:
there should be no establishment of distinctions between three vehicles, but rather only a single vehicle of Perfect Enlightenment (samyaksambuddhayāna).
Then, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"Is it admitted that there exists a bodhisattva vehicle?
Then, the Venerable Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
"What do you think? Within the suchness (tathatā) of all phenomena, are there three distinct characteristics of individuals (pudgala) who abide in the vehicle of the bodhisattvas?"
"Is it that there are those who regress and abide in the Śrāvaka vehicle, or those who regress and abide in the Pratyekabuddha vehicle,
or those who realize the Unsurpassed Vehicle? Śāriputra replied, "No!"
"Subhūti! What do you think? Within the true suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena, are there any distinctions among the bodhisattvas of the three vehicles?"
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti!”
"What do you think? Within the suchness of all phenomena, does there truly exist a vehicle of the perfectly awakened ones for those bodhisattvas? Śāriputra replied:
"No, Subhūti! What do you think?"
"Does the suchness of all phenomena have one, two,
or three characteristics? Śāriputra replied, "No!"
"Subhūti! What do you think? Within the suchness of all phenomena, can any phenomenon or any bodhisattva be apprehended?"
Śāriputra said: “No, Subhūti!”

Then, the Venerable Subhūti said to Śāriputra: "If all phenomena, by virtue of their truth and their abiding, are utterly non-existent and cannot be apprehended, how can you, Śāriputra, entertain such thoughts as:

'This bodhisattva will certainly experience regression from the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha'; 'this bodhisattva will certainly not experience regression from the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha'; 'this bodhisattva is declared to be indeterminate regarding the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha'; 'this bodhisattva belongs to the vehicle of the śrāvakas'; 'this bodhisattva belongs to the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas'; 'this bodhisattva belongs to the unsurpassed vehicle'—thus making three, or thus making one?"

“Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva finds nothing to be apprehended in any phenomena whatsoever, and is likewise able to have correct faith and understanding that even the suchness of all phenomena is entirely unapprehendable; if they find nothing to be apprehended in other bodhisattvas, and find nothing to be apprehended in the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha—then you should know that this is a true bodhisattva mahāsattva.”

Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing it taught that such true thusness (tathatā) of all phenomena is characterized by non-apprehensibility, their mind is not startled, not terrified, not afraid, has no doubt, no regret, no retreat, and no despondency, then this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, remaining entirely free from retrogression or discouragement throughout that interval.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Subhūti, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
It is well that you are now able to skillfully expound the essential Dharma for the sake of all bodhisattvas; everything you have spoken is due to the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata.
Subhūti, you should know this!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to deep faith and understanding regarding the mark of the non-apprehensibility of the true suchness (*tathatā*) of phenomena, and knows that all phenomena possess no marks of differentiation; and upon hearing the teaching of this mark of the non-apprehensibility of the true suchness of all phenomena, their mind is not startled, not terrified, not afraid, has no doubt, no regret, no retreat, and no sinking—this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes this dharma, will they swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening?”
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes these dharmas, they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and will not fall into the levels of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to swiftly realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek, in what should they abide?"
"How should one dwell?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to swiftly realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek, they should dwell with a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings; they should not dwell with a mind of inequality."
One should give rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings and should not give rise to a mind of partiality;
one should address all sentient beings with a mind of equanimity and should not address them with a mind of partiality;
one should give rise to a mind of great loving-kindness toward all sentient beings and should not give rise to a mind of malice.
One should address all sentient beings with a mind of great loving-kindness, and not with a mind of anger;
one should give rise to a mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings, and not give rise to a mind of malice or harm;
one should address all sentient beings with a mind of great compassion, and not with a mind of malice or harm.
One should give rise to a mind of great joy toward all sentient beings and should not give rise to a mind of envy;
one should address all sentient beings with a mind of great joy and should not address them with a mind of envy;
one should give rise to a mind of great equanimity toward all sentient beings and should not give rise to a mind of partiality.
One should address all sentient beings with a mind of great equanimity, and not with a partisan mind;
one should give rise to a mind of reverence toward all sentient beings, and not give rise to a mind of arrogance;
one should address all sentient beings with a mind of reverence, and not with a mind of arrogance.
One should give rise to a mind of straightforwardness toward all sentient beings and should not give rise to a mind of flattery and deceit;
one should address all sentient beings with a mind of straightforwardness and should not address them with a mind of flattery and deceit;
one should give rise to a mind of gentleness and flexibility toward all sentient beings and should not give rise to a mind of rigidity and harshness.
One should address all sentient beings with a mind of gentleness and flexibility, and not with a harsh or rigid mind;
one should give rise to a mind of benefit toward all sentient beings, and not give rise to a mind of non-benefit;
one should address all sentient beings with a mind of benefit, and not with a mind of non-benefit.
One should give rise to a mind of peace and happiness toward all sentient beings, and not give rise to a mind of unease;
one should address all sentient beings with a mind of peace and happiness, and not address them with a mind of unease;
one should give rise to a mind free from obstruction toward all sentient beings, and not give rise to a mind of obstruction.
One should speak to all sentient beings with an unobstructed mind, and not with an obstructed mind.
One should regard all sentient beings as one would one's own father or mother, as one's brother or sister, as one's son or daughter, or as one's kinsmen; with such a mind, one should speak to them.
One should regard all sentient beings as friends, and with such a mind, one should speak to them.

One should give rise toward all sentient beings a mind as toward one’s preceptor, as toward one’s instructor, as toward a disciple, and as toward a fellow student, and one should address them with that very mind;

one should give rise toward all sentient beings a mind as toward a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, an arhat, a pratyekabuddha, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, a Tathāgata, an Arhat, and a Samyaksaṃbuddha, and one should address them with that very mind;
one should give rise toward all sentient beings a mind of worship, reverence, respect, and praise, and one should address them with that very mind.
One should give rise to a mind of rescue, compassion, and protection toward all sentient beings, and with that very mind, one should speak to them;
one should give rise to a mind that perceives all sentient beings as ultimately empty, non-existent, and ungraspable, and with that very mind, one should speak to them;
one should give rise to a mind of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness toward all sentient beings, and with that very mind, one should speak to them.

"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to swiftly realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek, they should abide in this dwelling by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to swiftly realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek, they should personally abstain from taking life and also exhort others to abstain from taking life; they should constantly and correctly praise the dharma of abstaining from taking life, and joyfully extol those who abstain from taking life. This should be explained in detail, up to and including: they should personally abstain from wrong views and also exhort others to abstain from wrong views; they should constantly and correctly praise the dharma of abstaining from wrong views, and joyfully extol those who abstain from wrong views."

One should personally cultivate the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; one should also encourage others to cultivate the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; one should constantly and correctly praise the practice of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; and one should joyfully extol those who cultivate the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments.

One should personally fulfill the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, and likewise encourage others to fulfill the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom; one should constantly and correctly praise the dharma of fulfilling the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, and joyfully extol those who have fulfilled the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom.

One should personally abide in inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, and likewise encourage others to abide in inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature; one should constantly and correctly praise the dharma of abiding in inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, and joyfully extol those who abide in inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.

One should abide oneself in true thusness (tathatā) up to the inconceivable realm (acintyadhātu), and likewise encourage others to abide in true thusness up to the inconceivable realm; one should constantly and correctly praise the Dharma of abiding in true thusness up to the inconceivable realm, and joyfully extol those who abide in true thusness up to the inconceivable realm.

One should abide oneself in the Four Noble Truths, and likewise encourage others to abide in the Four Noble Truths; one should constantly and correctly extol the practice of abiding in the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, and joyfully praise those who abide in the Four Noble Truths.

One should personally cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, and likewise encourage others to cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; one should constantly and correctly praise the practice of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, and joyfully extol those who cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path.

One should personally cultivate the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; likewise, one should encourage others to cultivate the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; one should constantly and correctly extol the practice of the dharmas of the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; and one should joyfully praise those who cultivate the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

One should personally cultivate the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality, and also encourage others to cultivate the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality; one should constantly and correctly praise the practice of the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality, and joyfully extol those who cultivate the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality.

One should personally fulfill all the bodhisattva stages, encourage others to fulfill all the bodhisattva stages, constantly and correctly praise the dharmas that fulfill all the bodhisattva stages, and joyfully extol those who fulfill all the bodhisattva stages.

One should personally fulfill the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi, and likewise encourage others to fulfill the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi; one should constantly and correctly extol the teachings on fulfilling the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi, and joyfully praise those who fulfill the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi.

One should personally fulfill the five eyes and six supernormal powers, and also encourage others to fulfill the five eyes and six supernormal powers; one should constantly and correctly praise the dharma of fulfilling the five eyes and six supernormal powers, and joyfully extol those who have fulfilled the five eyes and six supernormal powers.

One should personally fulfill the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and likewise encourage others to fulfill the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; one should constantly and correctly praise the dharma of fulfilling the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and joyfully extol those who have fulfilled the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

One should personally fulfill great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity; likewise, one should encourage others to fulfill great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity; one should constantly and correctly praise the dharmas of fulfilling great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity; and one should rejoice in and extol those who have fulfilled great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity.

One should personally fulfill the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, and likewise encourage others to fulfill the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; one should constantly and correctly praise the dharma of fulfilling the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, and joyfully extol those who have fulfilled the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.

One should personally fulfill the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity; one should also encourage others to fulfill the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity; one should always correctly praise the qualities of fulfilling non-forgetfulness and constant equanimity; and one should joyfully extol those who have fulfilled non-forgetfulness and constant equanimity.

One should personally contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination in both forward and reverse order, and likewise encourage others to contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination in both forward and reverse order; one should constantly and correctly praise the method of contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination in both forward and reverse order, and joyfully extol those who so contemplate them.

One should personally know suffering, abandon its origin, realize its cessation, and cultivate the path; likewise, one should encourage others to know suffering, abandon its origin, realize its cessation, and cultivate the path; one should constantly and correctly praise the Dharma of knowing suffering, abandoning its origin, realizing its cessation, and cultivating the path; and one should joyfully extol those who know suffering, abandon its origin, realize its cessation, and cultivate the path.

One should personally give rise to the wisdom for realizing the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, yet realize the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha without realizing the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). One should also encourage others to give rise to the wisdom for realizing the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha and to realize the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha without realizing the limit of reality. One should constantly and correctly praise the method of giving rise to the wisdom for realizing the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha and of realizing the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha without realizing the limit of reality, and one should joyfully extol those who give rise to the wisdom for realizing the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha and who realize the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha without realizing the limit of reality.

One should personally enter the bodhisattva stage of the certainty of rightness (*samyaktva-niyāma*), and likewise encourage others to enter the bodhisattva stage of the certainty of rightness; one should constantly and correctly praise the Dharma for entering the bodhisattva stage of the certainty of rightness, and joyfully extol those who have entered the bodhisattva stage of the certainty of rightness.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 513. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Three, Chapter Nineteen on Suchness (Tathatā), Section Two. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to swiftly realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek, they should personally bring sentient beings to maturity, encourage others to bring sentient beings to maturity, constantly and correctly praise the methods for bringing sentient beings to maturity, and joyfully extol those who bring sentient beings to maturity.

One should personally adorn and purify the Buddha-field, encourage others to adorn and purify the Buddha-field, constantly and correctly extol the methods for adorning and purifying the Buddha-field, and joyfully praise those who adorn and purify the Buddha-field.

One should personally give rise to the sublime supernatural powers of a bodhisattva, encourage others to give rise to the sublime supernatural powers of a bodhisattva, constantly and correctly praise the method of giving rise to the sublime supernatural powers of a bodhisattva, and joyfully extol those who have given rise to the sublime supernatural powers of a bodhisattva.

One should personally give rise to all-knowledge, encourage others to give rise to all-knowledge, constantly and correctly praise the dharma of giving rise to all-knowledge, and joyfully extol those who have given rise to all-knowledge.

One should personally give rise to the knowledge of the aspects of the path, encourage others to give rise to the knowledge of the aspects of the path, constantly and correctly praise the method of giving rise to the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and joyfully extol those who have given rise to the knowledge of the aspects of the path.

One should personally give rise to the knowledge of all aspects, encourage others to give rise to the knowledge of all aspects, constantly and correctly praise the dharma of giving rise to the knowledge of all aspects, and joyfully extol those who have given rise to the knowledge of all aspects.

One should personally and forever sever the continuity of all habitual tendencies of afflictions, and likewise exhort others to forever sever the continuity of all habitual tendencies of afflictions; one should constantly and correctly praise the dharma of forever severing the continuity of all habitual tendencies of afflictions, and joyfully extol those who have forever severed the continuity of all habitual tendencies of afflictions.

One should personally undertake the full attainment of the lifespan, encourage others to undertake the full attainment of the lifespan, constantly and correctly extol the Dharma for undertaking the full attainment of the lifespan, and joyfully praise those who undertake the full attainment of the lifespan.

One should personally turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, encourage others to turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, constantly and correctly extol the method of turning the sublime wheel of Dharma, and joyfully praise those who turn the sublime wheel of Dharma.

One should personally uphold and protect the True Dharma so that it endures, and likewise encourage others to uphold and protect the True Dharma so that it endures; one should constantly and correctly praise the practice of upholding and protecting the True Dharma so that it endures, and joyfully extol those who uphold and protect the True Dharma so that it endures.
"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to swiftly realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek, they should abide in these dharmas by means of non-apprehension."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All bodhisattva mahāsattvas should train in the skillful means of the profound perfection of wisdom in this way; by training thus, they will be able to abide securely in the dharmas in which they should abide."
If one trains in this way and abides thus, then one will attain non-obstruction regarding the five aggregates,
and likewise attain non-obstruction regarding the six internal bases, the six external bases, the six internal elements, and the six external elements.
They attain non-obstruction regarding the six consciousness elements;

they also attain non-obstruction regarding the six contacts, non-obstruction regarding the six feelings, non-obstruction regarding the six elements, non-obstruction regarding the four conditions, and non-obstruction regarding everything from ignorance up to old age and death. Furthermore, they attain...
They attain non-obstruction regarding the abstention from taking life up to the abandonment of wrong views;

they also attain non-obstruction regarding the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions; they also attain non-obstruction regarding the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
and they also attain non-obstruction regarding internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.
They attain non-obstruction; they also attain non-obstruction regarding suchness up to the inconceivable realm;
they also attain non-obstruction regarding the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;

they also attain non-obstruction regarding the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; they also [attain non-obstruction] regarding emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness...
May they attain unimpeded mastery over the gates of liberation; likewise, may they attain unimpeded mastery over the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality;
may they attain unimpeded mastery over the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata;
may they attain unimpeded mastery over the Joyous Stage up to the Cloud of Dharma Stage; and likewise, may they attain unimpeded mastery over the gates of dhāraṇī.
He attains unimpeded mastery over the doors of samādhi; he likewise attains unimpeded mastery over the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
he likewise attains unimpeded mastery over the ten powers of a Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
and he likewise attains unimpeded mastery over great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity.

They also attain unimpeded mastery regarding the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics; they also attain unimpeded mastery regarding the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity;
they also attain unimpeded mastery regarding the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination in both forward and reverse order;
and they also [attain unimpeded mastery] regarding the knowledge of suffering, the abandonment of its origin, the realization of its cessation, and the cultivation of the path.
They attain non-obstruction; they likewise attain non-obstruction regarding the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
they likewise attain non-obstruction regarding entering the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth;
and they likewise attain non-obstruction regarding maturing sentient beings, purifying buddha-fields, and manifesting the sublime supernormal powers of a bodhisattva.
They also attain unimpeded mastery regarding all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);
they also attain unimpeded mastery regarding the permanent severance of the continuity of all afflictions and their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*);
they also attain unimpeded mastery regarding the perfection of the lifespan; they also attain unimpeded mastery regarding the turning of the sublime wheel of Dharma; and furthermore, regarding...
They will dwell in the protection of the Dharma and attain freedom from obstacles.
Why is this, Subhūti?
From the very beginning, this bodhisattva mahāsattva has not grasped the aggregate of form up to the aggregate of consciousness;
has not grasped the sense-base of the eye up to the sense-base of the mind; has not grasped the sense-base of forms up to the sense-base of phenomena;
has not grasped the element of the eye up to the element of the mind; and has not grasped the element of forms up to the element of phenomena.
One does not grasp at the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element; one does not grasp at eye-contact up to mind-contact;
one does not grasp at the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition;
one does not grasp at the earth element up to the consciousness element; one does not grasp at causal conditions.
Up to and including the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), they do not grasp at ignorance up to old age and death;
they do not grasp at taking life up to wrong view; they do not grasp at the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments;
and they do not grasp at the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom.
To a great extent, they do not embrace inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature;
they do not embrace suchness up to the inconceivable realm; they do not embrace the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
they do not embrace the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; and they do not embrace emptiness and signlessness.
the wishless gate of liberation; it does not embrace the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality;
it does not embrace the stage of pure observation up to the stage of a Tathāgata; it does not embrace the stages from the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma;
it does not embrace the gates of dhāraṇī or the gates of samādhi; it does not embrace the five...
They do not grasp at the eye, the six supernormal powers, or the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they do not grasp at great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, or great equanimity;
they do not grasp at the thirty-two marks or the eighty minor characteristics; they do not grasp at the quality of non-forgetfulness or the state of constant abiding.
The nature of relinquishment does not involve the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination in either forward or reverse order;

it does not involve the knowledge of suffering, the abandonment of its origin, the realization of its cessation, or the cultivation of the path; it does not involve the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
it does not involve entering the bodhisattva’s stage of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*); and it does not involve maturation.
To purify the buddha-fields of sentient beings, yet not to embrace the sublime supernatural powers of a bodhisattva;
not to embrace the permanent severance of the continuity of all afflictive habitual tendencies; not to embrace the perfection of lifespan;
not to embrace the turning of the sublime wheel of Dharma and its long endurance; and not to embrace omniscience and the path.
The knowledge of characteristics (*lakṣaṇajñāna*) and the knowledge of all characteristics (*sarvākārajñatā*). Why is this?

Because the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) up to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) cannot be grasped; if they cannot be grasped, they are not the aggregate of form up to the aggregate of consciousness. This is explained at length up to the point that omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all characteristics cannot be grasped; if they cannot be grasped, they are not omniscience, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, or the knowledge of all characteristics.

When this teaching on the dharmas in which bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should abide was being spoken, two thousand bodhisattvas within the assembly simultaneously realized the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Chapter 20: Signs of Non-Retrogression, Part Three, Section One. At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what practices, characteristics, and signs shall we recognize a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is non-retrogressive?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can know, as they truly are, the stage of ordinary beings, the stage of śrāvakas, the stage of pratyekabuddhas, the stage of bodhisattvas, or the stage of tathāgatas—though these stages are said to be distinct, within the true suchness (tathatā) of all phenomena, there is no alteration and no differentiation; they are all non-dual and indivisible."

Although this bodhisattva mahāsattva truly awakens to and enters the suchness of all phenomena, they do not engage in any conceptual discrimination regarding that suchness, because they employ the method of non-apprehension.

Since this bodhisattva mahāsattva has truly realized and entered into the suchness of all phenomena, although they hear that suchness and all phenomena are non-dual and undifferentiated, they remain free from doubt or obstruction.
Why is this? Because true suchness and phenomena cannot be said to be identical, nor can they be said to be different, nor can they be said to be both or neither.

Therefore, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas never utter speech frivolously; whatever they say is drawn from what is meaningful and beneficial, and if it is not meaningful and beneficial, they do not speak at all.
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva never observes the likes or dislikes, the strengths or weaknesses of others, but preaches the Dharma out of impartial compassion;
this bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not observe whether the lineage of the Dharma-preacher is noble or base, seeking only the true and pure meaning of the Dharma being taught.

"Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who is non-retrogressive possesses such practices, tokens, and signs; one should recognize a bodhisattva mahāsattva as non-retrogressive by means of these very practices, tokens, and signs."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Furthermore, by what kinds of conduct, characteristics, and signs can one know that this is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to contemplate all dharmas as being without activity, form, or characteristics, you should know that this is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva."
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If all dharmas are without activity, characteristics, or marks, by means of what dharma does a bodhisattva mahāsattva proceed so that he is called 'non-retrogressive'?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva is called 'non-retrogressive' because he turns away from the aggregate of form up to the aggregate of consciousness;

he is called 'non-retrogressive' because he turns away from the sense-base of the eye up to the sense-base of the mind; [he is called non-retrogressive] because he turns away from the sense-base of form up to..."

They are called "non-retrogressive" because they turn toward the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*); they are called "non-retrogressive" because they turn toward the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) up to the mind-element (*manodhātu*);
they are called "non-retrogressive" because they turn toward the form-element (*rūpadhātu*) up to the phenomena-element (*dharmadhātu*);

they are called "non-retrogressive" because they turn toward the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) up to the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*); [and] they are called "non-retrogressive" because they turn toward eye-contact (*cakṣuḥsaṃsparśa*) up to mind-contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*).

Because they turn away, they are called "non-retrogressive"; because they turn away from all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including all feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, they are called "non-retrogressive";
because they turn away from the earth element, up to and including the consciousness element, they are called "non-retrogressive";
because they turn away from the causal condition, up to and including the sovereign condition, they are called "non-retrogressive."
It is called "non-retrogression" because it proceeds from ignorance through to old age and death;
it is called "non-retrogression" because it proceeds from the perfection of generosity through to the perfection of wisdom;

it is called "non-retrogression" because it proceeds from internal emptiness through to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature; and it is called "non-retrogression" because it proceeds from suchness through to...

They are called "non-retrogressive" because they have turned away from the inconceivable realm; they are called "non-retrogressive" because they have turned away from the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
they are called "non-retrogressive" because they have turned away from the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
and they are called "non-retrogressive" because they have turned away from the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path.
They are called "non-retrogressive" because they proceed through the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—and thus are called non-retrogressive;
because they proceed through the eight liberations up to the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*), and thus are called non-retrogressive;

because they proceed through the stage of pure observation (*śuddhadarśanabhūmi*) up to the stage of a Tathāgata, and thus are called non-retrogressive; [and] because they proceed through the Stage of Utmost Joy (*pramuditābhūmi*)...
Because they advance to the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), they are called "non-retrogressive";

because they advance through the gates of dhāraṇī and the gates of samādhi, they are called "non-retrogressive"; because they advance through the five eyes and the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they are called "non-retrogressive";
and because they advance through the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), they are called "non-retrogressive."
He is called "non-retrogressive" because he turns toward great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity;
he is called "non-retrogressive" because he turns toward the thirty-two marks of a Great Being and the eighty minor characteristics;

he is called "non-retrogressive" because he turns toward the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant abiding in equanimity; [and he is so called] regarding the stage of Stream-enterer...
They are called "irreversible" because they turn away from the fruits up to and including the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
they are called "irreversible" because they turn away from all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*), and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);

and they are called "irreversible" because they turn away from the stage of ordinary beings, the stage of śrāvakas, the stage of pratyekabuddhas, the stage of bodhisattvas, or the stage of tathāgatas.
They are called "non-retrogressive" because they proceed toward the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
they are called "non-retrogressive" because they proceed toward the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha.

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of form is non-existent, and so on up to the intrinsic nature of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas being non-existent; because the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not abide therein, it is called "turning."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can know in this way, they are called a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, all non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattvas never take pleasure in observing the physical appearances or verbal discourses of external path śramaṇas, brahmins, and the like."
It is absolutely impossible that those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas could truly know and truly see the phenomena that ought to be known, or that they could establish a gateway to the Dharma of right view.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, one should know that this is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas develop profound faith and understanding in the Buddha’s well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, giving rise to no doubt or uncertainty. Regarding worldly matters, they do not hold precept-and-vow grasping (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), do not fall into evil views, and do not cling to various worldly auspicious rites as being pure. They never pay homage to other celestial deities as those worldly non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) do, nor do they ever offer various flower garlands, unguents, powdered incense, clothing, necklaces, precious banners, pennants, canopies, music, or lamps to such deities or non-Buddhist practitioners.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, one should know that this is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."

All non-retrogressive Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas are not born in the hells, among animals, in the realm of hungry ghosts, or among the asuras; nor are they born into lowly castes, such as the Caṇḍālas or Pukkasas. Furthermore, they never take on the bodies of śaṇḍhas, paṇḍakas, those lacking sexual organs, or those with dual sexual organs, nor do they ever take the body of a woman. Moreover, they do not suffer from blindness, deafness, muteness, lameness, paralysis, epilepsy, or physical deformities, and they are never born in circumstances that lack leisure for practice.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, one should know that this is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas always delight in practicing the ten paths of wholesome action; they themselves abstain from taking life up to and including wrong views, and likewise exhort others to abstain from taking life up to and including wrong views. They constantly and correctly praise the dharmas of abstaining from taking life up to and including wrong views, and joyfully extol those who abstain from taking life up to and including wrong views.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not even manifestly engage in the ten unwholesome paths of action within a dream, much less do so while awake!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, one should know that this is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

All non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, for the universal benefit of all sentient beings, constantly practice the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension, never flagging or abandoning them.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such practices, characteristics, and signs, one should know that this is a non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
