there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā) and see sentient beings shrouded by the five hindrances (pañcanīvaraṇa), far removed from the meditative concentrations, the immeasurables (apramāṇa), and the formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti), being distracted and negligent, and failing to cultivate various virtues."
Having seen this, he reflects: "How shall I rescue and deliver these classes of sentient beings, causing them to remain far removed from the hindrances and mental distractions?"
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:

"I shall practice the perfection of meditative concentration with diligent effort and without regard for anything else, maturing sentient beings and purifying the Buddha-field, so that I may swiftly fulfill [the requirements] and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, may there be no such sentient beings who possess the five hindrances or mental distractions; may all sentient beings enter and emerge at will from the sublime concentrations of the dhyānas, the immeasurables, and the formless realms."

"Subhūti, you should know that by means of this perfection of meditative concentration, these bodhisattva mahāsattvas will swiftly bring it to fulfillment and draw near to the realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom who see that sentient beings are deluded and possess evil wisdom; they have lost both mundane and supramundane right views, denying the existence of wholesome and unwholesome karma as well as the fruits of such karma, and clinging to various false doctrines such as nihilism, eternalism, identity, difference, both, or neither."
Having seen this, he reflects: "How shall I rescue and deliver these classes of sentient beings, causing them to distance themselves from evil views and perverse attachments?"
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:

"I shall practice the *prajñāpāramitā* with diligent effort and without regard for anything else; I shall bring sentient beings to maturity and purify Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill all requirements and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. In my Buddha-field, there shall be no such sentient beings who engage in evil conduct or hold wrong views; all sentient beings shall achieve right view and be adorned with various sublime wisdoms."

"Subhūti, you should know that by means of this perfection of wisdom, these bodhisattva mahāsattvas will swiftly bring it to fulfillment and draw near to the realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, while fully practicing the six perfections, perceive the three categories of sentient beings:
first, the group of those fixed in rightness (samyaktva-niyata-rāśi)."
2. The group of those fixed in error.
3. The group of those who are undetermined.
Having seen these things, he reflects as follows:
"How shall I employ skillful means to rescue and deliver all classes of sentient beings, causing them to leave behind the categories of those fixed in wrongness and those of indeterminate destiny?
Having reflected thus, he made this vow:

"I shall practice the six perfections with diligent effort and without regard for anything else, maturing sentient beings and purifying Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill [the requirements] and rapidly realize the knowledge of all modes. In my Buddha-field, there shall be no sentient beings fixed in wrongness or of indeterminate destiny; even the very names of these two categories shall not exist, and all sentient beings shall abide in right determination."
"Subhūti, you should know that by means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to the realization of the knowledge of all modes."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see sentient beings fallen into the three evil destinies, undergoing various kinds of suffering— namely, those in the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts."
Having seen this, he reflected:
"By what skillful means shall I rescue and deliver them, so that they may forever be freed from the sufferings of the three evil realms?
Having thus reflected, he made this aspiration:

"I shall apply myself with diligent effort, free from all attachment, to practice the six perfections, ripen sentient beings, and purify the Buddha-fields, so that these may be swiftly perfected and I may quickly realize the knowledge of all modes. In my Buddha-field, there shall be no hells, no animal realms, and no realm of hungry ghosts; even the very names of such evil destinies shall not exist, for all sentient beings therein shall be comprised within the happy destinies."
"Subhūti, you should know that by means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to the realization of the knowledge of all modes."

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 516. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Three, Chapter Twenty-One on the Characteristics of Emptiness (III): "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see that, due to the karmic obstructions of sentient beings, the great earth upon which they dwell is uneven with highs and lows, mounds and ravines, foul grasses, stumps, and poisonous thorns, and is filled with impurities.
Having seen this, he reflected:

"By what skillful means should I rescue and deliver all classes of sentient beings, so that they may forever eliminate their various karmic obstructions, and their dwelling places become as level as the palm of a hand, free from all foul grass, stumps, and the like?"
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:

"I shall practice the six perfections with diligent effort and without regard for anything else, maturing sentient beings and purifying Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill [the requirements] and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes. In my Buddha-field, may there be no such various impure karmas; may the great earth where sentient beings dwell be level, and may it be adorned with groves, ponds, and various exquisite fragrant flowers interspersed together, being exceedingly delightful."

"Subhūti, you should know that by means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to full completion and draw near to the realization of the knowledge of all aspects."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see that because sentient beings have meager merit, the great earth they inhabit is devoid of precious jewels and consists only of various kinds of soil, stones, tiles, and rubble."
Having seen this, he reflects:
"How may I rescue and deliver these sentient beings who possess such great faults and little merit, so that the places where they dwell shall abound in precious treasures?"

Having reflected thus, he made this vow: "I shall practice with diligent effort, free from all attachment, cultivating the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) to mature sentient beings and purify Buddha-fields. May I swiftly fulfill [these requirements] and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*). In my Buddha-field, may there be no such sentient beings who possess little merit and much demerit. May golden sand be spread upon the ground, and everywhere may there be various wondrous and rare jewels such as lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*); though they constantly enjoy these things, may they remain free from defiled attachment."
"Subhūti, you should know that by means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to the realization of the knowledge of all modes."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see that sentient beings, being possessed by many attachments, give rise to various kinds of evil and unwholesome karma."
Having seen this, he reflects:

"How shall I rescue and deliver these sentient beings who have grasped so much and developed such deep attachment, so that they may forever be free from their grasping, their attachment, and the unwholesome karma arising from them?"
Having reflected thus, he made this vow:

"I shall practice with diligent effort, free from all attachment, cultivating the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) to bring sentient beings to maturity and purify the Buddha-field. May I swiftly fulfill these requirements and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*). In my Buddha-field, may there be no sentient beings who, through excessive grasping and deep-seated attachment, commit various evil deeds; may all sentient beings therein have no grasping for forms, sounds, and so forth, and may they feel no attachment toward material requisites."
"Subhūti, you should know that by means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to the realization of the knowledge of all modes."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and perceive that sentient beings are divided into four classes of high and low status, namely from the kṣatriyas down to the śūdras."
Having seen this, he reflected:
"By what skillful means shall I rescue and deliver all classes of sentient beings, so that there may be no such distinctions of noble and base?"
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:

"I shall practice the six perfections with diligent effort and without regard for anything else; I shall bring sentient beings to maturity and purify Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill all requirements and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes. In my Buddha-field, there shall be no such fourfold distinctions of high and low based on physical appearance; all sentient beings shall be of one uniform appearance, and all shall be noble, belonging to the human realm."
"Subhūti, you should know that by means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to the realization of the knowledge of all modes."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and perceive that sentient beings have distinctions of inferior, middling, and superior families.
Having seen this, he reflects:
"By what skillful means shall I rescue and deliver all classes of sentient beings, so that there may be no such distinctions of inferior, middling, or superior families?"
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:

"I shall practice the six perfections with diligent effort and without regard for anything else; I shall mature sentient beings and purify Buddha-fields so that I may swiftly fulfill them and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes. In my Buddha-field, there shall be no such distinctions of inferior, middling, or superior families; all sentient beings therein shall be equally of the superior class."
"Subhūti, you should know that by means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to the realization of the knowledge of all modes."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and perceive the distinctions in the physical forms and appearances of sentient beings, whether they are handsome or ugly.
Having seen this, he reflected:
"By what skillful means should I rescue and deliver all classes of sentient beings, so that there shall be no such distinctions of physical form between the handsome and the ugly?"
Having reflected thus, he made this vow:

"I shall practice with diligent effort and without regard for anything else, cultivating the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), maturing sentient beings, and purifying the Buddha-field, so that I may swiftly fulfill [the requirements] and rapidly realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). In my Buddha-field, there shall be no such distinctions among sentient beings regarding their physical forms as being handsome or ugly; all sentient beings shall be of a true golden color, dignified and exquisite, pleasing to behold by all, and endowed with the most supreme and perfect pure form."
"Subhūti, you should know that by means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to the realization of the knowledge of all modes."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see that sentient beings are bound to a sovereign, such that they lack autonomy in all their actions."
Having seen this, he reflected:
"By what skillful means shall I rescue and deliver all classes of sentient beings so that they may attain mastery?
Having thus reflected, he made this aspiration:

"I shall apply myself with diligent effort, free from all attachment, to practice the six perfections, to bring sentient beings to maturity, and to purify the Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill [these goals] and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes. In my Buddha-field, all classes of sentient beings shall be without a master; in all their activities they shall attain mastery, to the point that they do not even perceive the form of a master, nor hear the name of a master, except for the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who alone governs by means of the Dharma and is thus called the Dharma King."
"Subhūti, you should know that by means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to the realization of the knowledge of all modes."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and perceive that sentient beings have various distinctions among the realms of existence, such as the hells and so forth."

Having seen this, he reflects: "By what skillful means shall I rescue and deliver all classes of sentient beings, so that there are no longer distinctions between the various realms of existence based on good and evil?"
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:
"I shall practice with diligent effort and without regard for anything else, cultivating the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*),
maturing sentient beings, and purifying Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill them and quickly realize all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*)."
O Wisdom, within my buddha-field, there shall be no distinctions between the various realms of existence or between good and evil;

indeed, even the names of the evil destinies shall not exist. All sentient beings shall be of one kind and equally cultivate a single activity—namely, they shall all harmoniously practice from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, and abide in inner emptiness up to [the other forms of emptiness].
The emptiness of the nature of non-existence; abiding in true suchness up to the inconceivable realm;
abiding in the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; practicing the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
practicing the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; practicing emptiness...
The doors of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness; the cultivation of the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality;
the cultivation of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva stages; the cultivation of the doors of dhāraṇī and the doors of samādhi;
the cultivation of the five eyes and the six supernormal powers; and the cultivation of the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen [unique qualities].
The unique qualities of a Buddha: practicing great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity;
practicing the causes for the primary marks and secondary signs; practicing the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant dwelling in equanimity;
practicing all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and all-aspect knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*); practicing the bodhisattva...
“...the conduct of a bodhisattva mahāsattva and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha. Subhūti,
you should know that by means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to the realization of the knowledge of all aspects.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who,
while fully practicing the six perfections, perceive the distinctions among the four modes of birth of sentient beings."
Having seen this, he reflected:
"By what skillful means shall I rescue and deliver all classes of sentient beings so that they are no longer subject to these four distinctions of birth?"
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:

"I shall practice with diligent effort and without regard for anything else, cultivating the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), maturing sentient beings, and purifying Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill [these qualities] and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). In my Buddha-field, there shall be no such distinctions of the four types of birth; all classes of sentient beings shall equally undergo miraculous birth (upapāduka)."
"Subhūti, you should know that by means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to the realization of the knowledge of all modes."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see that sentient beings lack the five supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), such that they lack mastery over all their actions."
Having seen this, he reflects:
"By what skillful means shall I rescue and deliver all classes of sentient beings, causing them all to attain the wisdom of the five supernormal powers?"
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:

"I shall practice with diligent effort, free from all attachment, the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) to ripen sentient beings and purify Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill [the requirements] and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*). In my Buddha-field, all classes of sentient beings shall fully achieve the five supreme supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*)."

"Subhūti, you should know that by means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to full completion and draw near to the realization of the knowledge of all aspects."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see that sentient beings consume solid food, and that their bodies produce various forms of excrement and urine— pus, blood, and foul impurities so utterly loathsome as to be worthy of total renunciation."
Having seen this, he reflects:
"By what skillful means shall I rescue and deliver all classes of sentient beings, so that within their bodies there may be no such filth and evil?"
Having reflected thus, he made this vow:

"I shall practice with diligent effort, free from all attachment or longing, cultivating the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), maturing sentient beings, and purifying the Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill [the requirements] and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). In my Buddha-field, all classes of sentient beings shall partake solely of the sublime food of the joy of the Dharma; their bodies shall be fragrant and pure, free from all excrement or impurities."
"Subhūti, you should know that by means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to the realization of the knowledge of all modes."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see that sentient beings lack bodily radiance and must seek out lamps and torches for all their activities."
Having seen this, he reflects:
"By what skillful means shall I rescue and deliver all classes of sentient beings, so that they may be freed from such bodies lacking light?"
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:

"I shall practice with diligent effort, free from all attachment, the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), maturing sentient beings and purifying Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill [the requirements] and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). In my Buddha-field, all classes of sentient beings shall possess bodily radiance, rendering external illumination unnecessary."
"Subhūti, you should know that by means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to the realization of the knowledge of all modes."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and perceive that the lands where sentient beings dwell have days and nights, months and fortnights, and that the changes of seasons and years are not constant.
Having seen this, he reflects:
"By what skillful means shall I deliver all classes of sentient beings, so that their dwelling places are free from the shifting of time, such as day and night?"
Having reflected thus, he made this vow:

"I shall practice with diligent effort, free from all attachment, the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), maturing sentient beings and purifying the Buddha-field, so that I may swiftly fulfill [the requirements] and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*). In my Buddha-field, there shall be no names for such temporal divisions as day and night, month, or half-month."
"Subhūti, you should know that by means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to the realization of the knowledge of all modes."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see that the lifespan of sentient beings is short.
Having seen this, he reflected:
"By what skillful means shall I rescue and deliver all classes of sentient beings, so that they may be freed from such a short lifespan?"
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:

"I shall practice with diligent effort, free from all attachment, cultivating the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), maturing sentient beings, and purifying Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill [the requirements] and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*). In my Buddha-field, the lifespan of all sentient beings shall be so long that its duration in kalpas will be difficult to know."
"Subhūti, you should know that by means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to the realization of the knowledge of all modes."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see that sentient beings lack the primary and secondary marks of physical excellence.
Having seen this, he reflected:
"By what skillful means shall I rescue and deliver all classes of sentient beings so that they may attain the primary and secondary marks?
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:

"I shall apply myself with diligence and without attachment, practicing the six perfections to ripen sentient beings and purify Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill all requirements and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes. In my Buddha-field, all sentient beings shall possess the thirty-two marks of a great man and be fully adorned with the eighty secondary signs, such that when sentient beings see them, they will give rise to pure and sublime joy."
"Subhūti, you should know that by means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to the realization of the knowledge of all modes."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see that classes of sentient beings lack various roots of virtue."
Having seen this, he reflected:
"By what skillful means shall I rescue and deliver all classes of sentient beings so that they may be endowed with roots of goodness?
Having thus reflected, he made this vow:

"I shall apply myself with diligent effort, free from all attachment, to practice the six perfections, to bring sentient beings to maturity, and to purify the Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill [these goals] and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes. In my Buddha-field, all classes of sentient beings shall fully accomplish pure and superior roots of goodness; by virtue of these roots of goodness, they will be able to prepare various kinds of sublime offerings to worship the Buddhas, and by the power of this merit, wherever they are born, they will further be able to make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones."
"Subhūti, you should know that by means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to the realization of the knowledge of all modes."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see that sentient beings are afflicted by diseases of both body and mind.
There are four types of physical illnesses, namely: wind, heat, phlegm, and miscellaneous disorders.
There are likewise four types of mental illnesses, namely: greed, hatred, delusion, and the illness of pride, etc.
Having seen this, he reflected:
"By what skillful means shall I rescue and deliver all sentient beings from the suffering of physical and mental illness?
Having thus reflected, he made this vow:

"I shall apply myself with diligence and without attachment, practicing the six perfections to ripen sentient beings and purify Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill [these goals] and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes. In my Buddha-field, there shall be no sentient beings who experience such physical or mental suffering from illness, nor even the name of 'physical or mental illness' shall exist."
"Subhūti, you should know that by means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to the realization of the knowledge of all modes."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and perceive the various inclinations and the distinctions between the three vehicles among sentient beings."
Having seen this, he reflects:

"By what skillful means shall I rescue and deliver those sentient beings whose inclinations are narrow and inferior, causing them to abandon the inclinations of the two vehicles and lead them solely toward the unsurpassed Mahāyāna?"
Having reflected thus, he made this aspiration:

"I shall practice the six perfections with diligent effort and without regard for anything else; I shall bring sentient beings to maturity and purify Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill [the requirements] and quickly realize the knowledge of all aspects. In my Buddha-field, all classes of sentient beings shall seek only unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, taking no pleasure in the fruits of the vehicles of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, to the point that even the names of these two vehicles do not exist."

“Suvikrāntavikrāmin, you should know that by means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to the realization of the knowledge of all modes.”

"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see sentient beings harboring overweening pride— those who have not relinquished [what they should] claim to have relinquished, and those who have not attained [what they should] claim to have attained."
Having seen this, he reflects:
"By what skillful means shall I rescue and deliver all classes of sentient beings, causing them to abandon the fetter of overweening pride?"
Having reflected thus, he made this vow:

"I shall practice with diligent effort and without regard for anything else, cultivating the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) to ripen sentient beings and purify Buddha-fields, so that they may be swiftly perfected and I may quickly realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*). In my Buddha-field, there shall be no such persons of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), and all sentient beings shall know and see, exactly as it is, what is to be relinquished and what is to be attained."
"Subhūti, you should know that by means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to the realization of the knowledge of all modes."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and perceive that sentient beings have given rise to much attachment— namely, attachment to the aggregate of form, attachment to the aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, and so on, up to and including attachment to the conduct of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva and attachment to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Having seen this, he reflected:
"By what skillful means shall I rescue and deliver all classes of sentient beings so that they may be free from attachment?
Having thus reflected, he made this aspiration:

"I shall apply myself with diligence and without attachment, practicing the six perfections to mature sentient beings and purify buddha-fields, so that they may be swiftly perfected and I may quickly realize the knowledge of all modes. In my buddha-field, the various classes of sentient beings shall be free from such diverse attachments."
"Subhūti, you should know that by means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to the realization of the knowledge of all modes."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and see Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas whose lifespan, radiance, and number of disciples are all limitless."
Having seen this, he reflected:
"How may I obtain a lifespan and radiance, as well as a number of disciples, all of which are without limit?
Having thus reflected, he made this vow:

"I shall apply myself with diligence and without regard for anything, practicing the six perfections to mature sentient beings and purify buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill them and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes. At that time, my lifespan, my radiance, and the number of my disciples shall all be without limit."
"Subhūti, you should know that by means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to the realization of the knowledge of all modes."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who,
while fully practicing the six perfections, perceive the land where a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha dwells as having a finite circumference."
Having seen this, he reflected:
"How may I obtain a dwelling land that is immeasurable in circumference, peaceful, secure, and prosperous?
Having thus reflected, he made this vow:

"I shall apply myself with diligence and without attachment, practicing the six perfections to ripen sentient beings and purify Buddha-fields, so that I may swiftly fulfill [these goals] and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes. May the worlds of the ten directions, each as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, be merged into a single land—peaceful, prosperous, and joyful—and dwelling therein, I shall preach the Dharma to teach and transform immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings."
"Subhūti, you should know that by means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to the realization of the knowledge of all modes."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fully cultivate the six perfections and perceive that the limits of birth and death extend infinitely forward and backward, and that the realms of sentient beings are boundless in number."
Having seen this, he reflects:

"The limits of birth and death and the realm of sentient beings are all like space; although there is no real transmigrator in saṃsāra nor any who attains liberation, sentient beings nonetheless cling to false conceptions and wander through birth and death, suffering endlessly."
"How shall I employ skillful means to rescue and deliver them?
Having reflected thus, he made this vow:

"I shall practice with diligent effort, free from all attachment or longing, cultivating the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), maturing sentient beings, and purifying Buddha-fields. May I swiftly fulfill these and quickly realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). For the sake of all sentient beings, I shall preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma, causing them all to be liberated from the great suffering of birth and death, and leading them to realize and know that both birth and death and liberation are ultimately non-existent and entirely empty."
"Subhūti, you should know that by means of these six perfections, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly bring them to fulfillment and draw near to the realization of the knowledge of all modes."

Chapter 22: The Gaṅgā Devī. Part Three, Chapter Twenty-two: The Gaṅgā Devī. At that time, there was a goddess in the assembly named Gaṅgā Devī. She rose from her seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, bared her right shoulder while covering her left, knelt with her right knee on the ground, joined her palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

I am able to fulfill the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and I am able to encompass a buddha-field such as that which the Blessed One has described for the great assembly.

When the Gaṅgā goddess had spoken these words, she immediately took various golden flowers, silver flowers, and water- and land-born blossoms, as well as various ornaments and a pair of golden celestial robes, and with reverent sincerity scattered them over the Buddha. By the Buddha’s supernormal power, they leaped up into the air and circled to the right; above the Buddha’s crown, they transformed into a jeweled terrace with four pillars and four corners, exquisitely adorned and most delightful. Thereupon, the goddess held this jeweled terrace and dedicated it for the common enjoyment of all sentient beings, dedicating it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, the Tathāgata, knowing that the goddess’s resolve was profound and far-reaching, smiled.

It is the natural law of all Buddhas that when they smile, various colored lights issue from the gateway of their faces; now the Buddha did likewise, emitting from his face a variety of lights—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, purple, azure, and green—which illuminated the infinite and boundless Buddha-worlds of the ten directions. These lights returned to this land, manifested great spiritual transformations, and entered into the crown of the Buddha’s head.

At that time, having seen and heard this, Ānanda rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!
"For what cause and for what reason do you manifest this smile?
It is not without cause or condition that the Buddha manifests a smile.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, saying:

"In the future, this goddess shall become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—and so on, as extensively described—down to a Buddha-Bhagavān; the eon shall be named Star-Parable, and the Buddha’s name shall be Golden Flower."

Ānanda, you should know that this goddess has now received her final female body; after she casts off this body, she will receive a male body and shall never again be female for as long as the limits of the future endure.

After passing away from here, she will be reborn in the most delightful buddha-field of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Akṣobhya in the east; there, in the presence of that Buddha, she will diligently cultivate the holy life. In that realm, this woman shall be named Suvarṇapuṣpā, and she will practice the various deeds of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Ānanda, you should know this!

After the Bodhisattva Suvarṇapuṣpa has passed away from the world-system of Akṣobhya Buddha, he will be reborn in other directions, proceeding from one buddha-field to another. In every place where he is born, he shall never be separated from a Buddha. Just as a wheel-turning monarch proceeds from one jeweled palace to another, enjoying delights and pleasures, until his life ends without his feet ever touching the ground.

The Bodhisattva Suvarṇapuṣpa was likewise; from one buddha-field to another, until he attained unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, he constantly beheld all Buddhas in every place of rebirth, perpetually heard the true Dharma, and cultivated the practices of a bodhisattva.
At that time, Ānanda had this thought to himself:

"When the Bodhisattva Golden Flower attains Buddhahood, he too shall proclaim the profound Prajñāpāramitā; the number of the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in his gathering shall be equal to that of the present Buddha’s assembly of Bodhisattvas."
The Buddha, knowing his thought, addressed Ānanda, saying: “So it is! So it is!”

Just as you have reflected, when the Bodhisattva Golden Flower (Kanakavatsa) attains Buddhahood, he too shall proclaim this profound Prajñāpāramitā to a great assembly; the number of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in that assembly will be exactly like that of the present Buddha’s assembly of Bodhisattvas.

Ānanda, you should know that when the Bodhisattva Suvarṇapuṣpa attains Buddhahood, his ordained disciples will be so numerous as to be beyond calculation; they cannot be numbered by hundreds, thousands, or koṭis, but can only be described collectively as immeasurable and boundless.

Ānanda, you should know that when the Bodhisattva Suvarṇapuṣpa attains Buddhahood, his land will be free from all such various faults and afflictions as those I have described in this profound Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom.
At that time, Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“In the past, under which Buddha did this goddess first resolve her mind upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, plant various roots of goodness, and dedicate them through making vows, such that she has now encountered the Buddha, made offerings and paid him respect, and immediately received the prediction of non-retrogression?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"This goddess had already resolved her mind toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment under Dīpaṃkara Buddha; having planted various roots of goodness and dedicated them through making vows, she has now encountered me, and by making offerings and paying respect, she has immediately received the prediction of non-retrogression."
Ānanda, you should know!
In the past, at the time of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, I scattered five stalks of flowers over that Buddha and dedicated this toward the attainment of awakening.
Then the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara, knowing that my faculties were mature, conferred upon me the prediction of enlightenment:
"In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood; your name shall be Śāntamati (The Able One to Quiesce), the world-system shall be named Sahā, and the eon shall be called Bhadra.

When the goddess heard the Buddha bestow upon me this prediction of Great Bodhi, she leaped for joy and immediately scattered golden flowers over the Buddha. She then gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, planted various roots of goodness, and dedicated them toward this vow:

"In a future age, when I become a Buddha here as this Bodhisattva does, may I likewise receive a face-to-face prediction of Great Bodhi from that Buddha, just as the present Buddha has now bestowed it upon me."
"Therefore, I now bestow this prediction upon her.
At that time, Ānanda, hearing what the Buddha had said, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; he again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"This goddess has long since resolved her mind upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Having planted various roots of goodness and dedicated them through her vows, they have now reached maturity; it is for this reason that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha grants her this prediction."
The Buddha told Ānanda: “So it is! So it is!”
"It is as you have said.
Since those roots of goodness have ripened, I grant them the prediction [of enlightenment].
Chapter 23: Skillful Means (Upāyakauśalya), Part Three, Section One. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the profound perfection of wisdom train in the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness?”
How does one enter the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness?
How does one practice the four applications of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path?
How does one cultivate the four applications of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path?
"How does one practice the remaining factors of enlightenment?
How does one cultivate the remaining factors of enlightenment?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the profound perfection of wisdom should contemplate the emptiness of the aggregate of form up to the aggregate of consciousness;

they should contemplate the emptiness of the sense-base of the eye up to the sense-base of the mind; they should contemplate the emptiness of the sense-base of forms up to the sense-base of phenomena;
they should contemplate the emptiness of the element of the eye up to the element of the mind; they should contemplate the emptiness of the element of forms...”
Up to the emptiness of the dharma-realm, one should contemplate the emptiness of the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element;

one should contemplate the emptiness of eye-contact up to mind-contact; one should contemplate the emptiness of all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition up to all feelings produced with mind-contact as condition;
and one should contemplate the emptiness of the earth element up to the consciousness element.
One should contemplate that the causal conditions up to the dominant conditions are empty; one should contemplate that ignorance up to old age and death are empty;
one should contemplate that generosity up to the perfection of wisdom is empty;
one should contemplate that inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature is empty; and one should contemplate that suchness up to the inconceivable realm is empty.

One should contemplate the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path as empty; one should contemplate the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path as empty;
one should contemplate the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments as empty;
one should contemplate the eight liberations up to the ten totalities as empty; and one should contemplate emptiness and signlessness [as empty].
The emptiness of the door of liberation of wishlessness; one should contemplate the emptiness of the stage of pure vision up to the stage of the Tathāgata;
one should contemplate the emptiness of the Joyful Stage up to the Cloud of Dharma Stage; one should contemplate the emptiness of all doors of dhāraṇī and doors of samādhi;
one should contemplate the emptiness of the five eyes and the six supernormal powers; one should contemplate the emptiness of the Thusness...
One should contemplate the emptiness of the ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;

one should contemplate the emptiness of great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity; one should contemplate the emptiness of the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics;
one should contemplate the emptiness of the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant dwelling in equanimity; and one should contemplate the emptiness of all-knowledge.
The knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects are empty; one should contemplate the emptiness of the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
one should contemplate the emptiness of all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas;
one should contemplate the emptiness of contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena; one should contemplate the emptiness of the mundane and the supramundane.
The phenomena of the world are empty; one should contemplate the emptiness of conditioned and unconditioned phenomena,
one should contemplate the emptiness of past, future, and present phenomena, one should contemplate the emptiness of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena,
and one should contemplate the emptiness of phenomena belonging to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
"Subhūti, you should know that when this bodhisattva mahāsattva performs this contemplation, he does not allow the mind to become distracted.
If the mind is not distracted, one does not perceive dharmas; if one does not perceive dharmas, one does not realize [them]."

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have well studied that the self-characteristics of all phenomena are empty; since there is no phenomenon to be increased and no phenomenon to be diminished, they neither perceive nor realize any phenomena.

Why is this? Because within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) of all phenomena, the subject that realizes, the object realized, the locus of realization, the time of realization, and that by which one realizes—whether collectively or individually—are all unobtainable and invisible.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

"As the World-Honored One has said that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena without realizing it, how should a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena without realizing it?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena, they first form this thought:

'I should contemplate that all characteristics of phenomena are empty, yet I should not realize [this emptiness]. I contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena for the sake of training, not for the sake of realization. Now is the time for training; it is not the time for realization.'"
"When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva has not yet entered meditative absorption, he fixes his mind upon the object; it is not while in the state of absorption that he fixes his mind upon the object.
At such a time, this bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not fall back from any of the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma), nor does he realize the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya)."

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have accomplished such vast wisdom and are well-established in the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) as well as all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*); they constantly maintain this thought:
"At this time, I should practice; I should not realize [the fruit]."
"When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they constantly reflect:
'Regarding the perfections from generosity up to wisdom, at this time I should train in them, but I should not realize them.'"
Regarding inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, at this time I should train in them but not realize them.
Regarding suchness up to the inconceivable realm, at this time I should train in them but not realize them.
Regarding the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, at this time I should train in them but not yet realize them.
Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, at this time I should train in them but not yet realize them.
Regarding the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments, at this time I should train in them but not realize them.
Regarding the eight liberations up to the ten totalities, at this time I should train in them but not realize them.
Regarding the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—I should now train in them, but not realize them.
Regarding the stages from the Ground of Pure Observation up to the Ground of the Tathāgata, I should now train in them, but not realize them.
From the Ground of Extreme Joy up to the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma, I should now train and not realize them.
Regarding all the doors of dhāraṇī and the doors of samādhi, I should now train and not realize them.
Regarding the five eyes and the six supernormal powers, at this time I should train in them but not realize them.
Regarding the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, at this time I should train in them but not realize them.
Regarding great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity, at this time I should train in them but not realize them.
Regarding the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant dwelling in equanimity, at this time I should train in them but not realize them.

Regarding all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), I should now train in them but not realize them.
Regarding all the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, I should now train in them but not realize them.
Regarding the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas, I should now train in it rather than realize it.

For the sake of training in the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), I should train in the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a solitary realizer (*pratyekabuddha*), becoming skillful in them all without realizing them.

"Subhūti, you should know that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they should cultivate the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; they should abide in the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; and they should practice the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, yet they should not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)."

One should practice the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; one should abide in the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; one should cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, yet one should not realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

One should practice the other factors of enlightenment, abide in the other factors of enlightenment, and cultivate the other factors of enlightenment, yet one should not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
“Subhūti, you should know this:

although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—and likewise abide in and cultivate the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—they do not realize the fruit of stream-entry, nor do they realize up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.

Although they practice the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, and likewise abide in and cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, they do not realize the fruit of stream-entry, nor do they realize up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.”

Although they practice the other factors of enlightenment, abide in the other factors of enlightenment, and cultivate the other factors of enlightenment, they do not realize the fruit of stream-entry, nor do they realize up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.

By virtue of these causes and conditions, this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not fall into the levels of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but swiftly realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Subhūti, you should know this!"

For example, it is like a mighty warrior of handsome appearance, fierce and courageous, whom all who see him rejoice in; he possesses a superior, perfect, and pure retinue, has mastered the arts of war to their ultimate limit, and is skilled in wielding weapons with steady and unshakable composure. He is adept in all sixty-four arts and eighteen branches of knowledge, and is so dexterous in every craft that the multitude admires and bows down before him in reverence; because his undertakings are skillful, he achieves great results with little effort.

Because these people constantly provided him with offerings, respect, honor, and praise without ceasing for even a moment, he at that time felt redoubled joy and exultation, and he congratulated himself before his retinue.

Due to certain causes and conditions, he set out for another region with his parents, wife, children, and retinue; on the way, they passed through a perilous wilderness where there were many fearsome occurrences, such as predatory beasts, bandits, and enemies lying in ambush, so that none among the retinue, whether young or old, failed to be struck with alarm.

Relying on his many skills and arts, he was formidable and courageous, with a mind at ease; he comforted his parents and all his kinsmen, saying, "Do not have any anxiety or fear; I shall ensure that you suffer no distress."
By means of his skillful arts, that man led his retinue to a place of safety; having escaped the peril, they enjoyed themselves in joy and pleasure.
Yet, within that wilderness, the wild beasts and hostile bandits harbored no intention to harm them.
Why is this? Because they rely on their own majesty and prowess, possessing various arts and skills, and thus have no fear.
"Subhūti, you should know this!"

In the same way, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas likewise take pity on the classes of sentient beings suffering in saṃsāra and set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Universally taking sentient beings as their object, they give rise to the four immeasurables; abiding in a mind conjoined with these four immeasurables, they diligently cultivate the perfections from generosity up to wisdom so that they may be swiftly brought to fulfillment.

While these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have not yet perfected these six pāramitās, desiring to train in the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), they do not realize the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). Although they abide in the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—they do not turn according to their influence, nor are they led away or deprived by them; thus, they do not realize those gates of liberation [prematurely].
Because they do not realize [these stages], they do not fall into the levels of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but will certainly proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Subhūti, you should know this!

Just as a bird with strong wings soars through the void, flying freely and at ease for a long time without falling, though it sports within the sky, it does not rely upon the sky, nor is it obstructed by the sky."

“Subhūti, you should know that it is likewise for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: although they repeatedly practice, abide in, and cultivate the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—they are able not to realize them therein. Because they do not realize them, they do not fall into the levels of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.”

If they have not yet perfected the cultivation of the Buddha’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and other immeasurable Buddha-dharmas, they will never realize the exhaustion of outflows by relying on emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness.
"Subhūti, you should know this!

For example, suppose there were a strong man well-versed in the art of archery who, wishing to display his skill, shot an arrow upward into the air. To prevent the arrow from falling to the ground, he would shoot a subsequent arrow into the notch of the preceding arrow; in this manner, continuing for a long time, each arrow supported the next so that none would fall."
If one wishes to cause them to fall, one simply stops the final arrow; at that moment, all the arrows will suddenly drop to the ground.

"Subhūti, you should know that it is the same for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: because they are sustained by skillful means while practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, until their roots of goodness cultivated through practice have fully matured, they will never prematurely realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) midway."

When one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, all roots of goodness cultivated through practice have reached full maturity; at that time, the bodhisattva realizes the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and thereby attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"Therefore, Subhūti, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the profound perfection of wisdom should, in this manner, carefully and precisely observe the true nature of all phenomena as previously described, and thus cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva while proceeding toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are truly rare and perform what is difficult to do;

for although they constantly cultivate and study the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, although they constantly cultivate and study suchness (*tathatā*), the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and even the inconceivable realm; although they constantly cultivate and study internal emptiness, external emptiness, up to the emptiness of non-existence and intrinsic nature (*abhāvasvabhāvaśūnyatā*); although they constantly cultivate and study the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; although they constantly cultivate and study the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; and although they constantly cultivate and study the three doors of liberation and all other factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), they do not fall into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha midway, nor do they ever lose their unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening."
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas vow never to abandon sentient beings; that is to say, they make this aspiration:
'As long as sentient beings have not attained liberation from birth, old age, sickness, and death, I shall never relinquish my application of roots of virtue.'"
"Subhūti, you should know that the power of the vows of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is exceptionally sublime; they always maintain this thought:
'As long as any sentient being has not yet attained liberation, I shall never abandon them.'"
"Because they have given rise to such a vast and great mind, they will certainly not fall back along that path.
Subhūti, you should know that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constantly maintain this thought:"

"I must not abandon any sentient beings, but must certainly bring them to liberation; yet, since these sentient beings practice what is not the Right Dharma, I should repeatedly induce the liberations of tranquility, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness in order to deliver them, and though I repeatedly induce them, I shall not realize them as a final attainment."

"Subhūti, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has accomplished sublime skillful means; although they frequently manifest the three gates of liberation, they do not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) in the interim until they have attained the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna)."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas also delight in contemplating that the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, as well as the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are all empty of their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnya*), within the context of profound emptiness, dispersed emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-existence, and the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence."
"Subhūti, you should know that after this bodhisattva mahāsattva has made this observation, he gives rise to this thought:

'Beings of all classes, through the power of evil friends, give rise to the grasping at the notion of a self—and as it is extensively explained, up to the grasping at the notion of a viewer. Because of these graspings at notions, they act with apprehension, transmigrating through birth and death and undergoing various sufferings.'"

In order to sever sentient beings' such conceptual attachments, one should aspire to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and preach the profound and sublime Dharma for all sentient beings, so that they may sever their conceptual attachments and be freed from the suffering of birth and death.
"At that time, although this bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the three gates of liberation, he does not rely upon them to realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Because he does not proceed toward the realization of the limit of reality, he does not fall into the fruit of a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, an arhat, or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha."
By means of such mindfulness, this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, accomplishing roots of virtue without realizing the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Although they do not immediately realize the limit of reality, they do not fall away from the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments;
nor do they fall away from the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path.
Furthermore, they do not fall away from the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
nor do they fall away from the eight liberations up to the ten totalities; nor do they fall away from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;
nor do they fall away from suchness up to the inconceivable realm; nor do they fall away from suffering.
...the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; nor does one fall away from the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
nor does one fall away from the bodhisattva stages; nor does one fall away from the doors of dhāraṇī or the doors of samādhi;
nor does one fall away from the five eyes or the six supernormal powers; nor does one [fall away]...
They do not fall away from the ten powers of a Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
nor do they fall away from great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, or great equanimity;

nor do they fall away from the quality of non-forgetfulness or the nature of constant abiding in equanimity; nor do they fall away from all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, or the knowledge of all aspects.
Wisdom, as well as all other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas, will likewise not be lost or diminished.

"Subhūti, you should know that at that time, this bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*); until he realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, his various merits shall never decline."

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom and is sustained by skillful means, from moment to moment their pure qualities increase and their faculties become sharp and keen, such that they cannot be equaled by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly reflects thus:
'Throughout the long night, the minds of all sentient beings have always operated within four kinds of perversions.'"

That is to say: the perversion of perception, the perversion of mind, and the perversion of view regarding permanence; or the perversion of perception, the perversion of mind, and the perversion of view regarding pleasure; or the perversion of perception, the perversion of mind, and the perversion of view regarding self; or the perversion of perception, the perversion of mind, and the perversion of view regarding purity.

"For the sake of such sentient beings as these, I should proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, and upon realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, teach the unerring Dharma to all sentient beings. That is to say, I shall teach that saṃsāra is impermanent, without bliss, without self, and without purity; whereas only nirvāṇa is subtle, tranquil, and endowed with the various true merits of permanence, bliss, self, and purity."

"Subhūti, you should know that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes this mindfulness and practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, being sustained by skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), they will never enter the supreme meditative concentrations of the Buddhas until they have fully perfected the Tathāgata’s ten powers, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, as well as all other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas."

“Subhūti, you should know that although at that time this bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the three doors of liberation and enters and emerges from them with mastery, he does not yet realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi). This is because until the causal practices and merits for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment are fully perfected, he does not realize the limit of reality or those other merits; rather, he shall realize them only when he attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.”

Subhūti, you should know that although at that time this bodhisattva mahāsattva has not yet perfected the cultivation of other virtues, he has already perfected the cultivation of the door of the wishless samādhi.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 517. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Three, Chapter Twenty-three on Skillful Means (Upāyakauśalya), Section Two. "Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly reflects thus:
"All classes of sentient beings have for a long night practiced with the notion of attainment, namely, grasping at a self up to a 'seer';
or grasping at the aggregate of form up to the aggregate of consciousness; or grasping at the sense-base of the eye up to..."
Regarding the sphere of mind (*manāyatana*), one may either hold that there are spheres of form (*rūpāyatana*) up to the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*),
or hold that there are the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) up to the mind-element (*manodhātu*), or hold that there are the form-realm (*rūpadhātu*) up to the phenomena-realm (*dharmadhātu*),

or hold that there are the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) up to the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*), or hold that there is eye-contact (*cakṣuḥsaṃsparśa*) up to mind-contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*), or hold that there is eye-contact... [and so forth].
Regarding all feelings produced with conditions, up to and including those produced with mind-contact as condition;
or clinging to the existence of the earth element up to the consciousness element; or clinging to the existence of the causal condition up to the predominant condition;
or clinging to the existence of ignorance up to old age and death; or clinging to the existence of the ten paths of wholesome action; or clinging to the existence of the four [noble truths].

Whether they cling to the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), or the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), or whether they cling to other various superior wholesome dharmas—

for the sake of such sentient beings, I should proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, and upon realizing unsurpassed, perfect awakening, cause all sentient beings to forever sever such clinging to objective apprehension.

"Subhūti, you should know that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes this mindfulness and practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, being sustained by skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), they will never enter the supreme meditative concentrations of the Buddhas until they have fully perfected the Tathāgata’s ten powers, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, as well as all other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas."

"Subhūti, you should know that although at that time this bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the three doors of liberation and enters and emerges from them with mastery, they do not yet realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi). Until the causal practices and merits for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment are fully perfected, they do not realize the limit of reality or other such qualities; rather, it is only upon attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment that they may realize them."

Subhūti, you should know that although at that time this bodhisattva mahāsattva has not yet perfected the cultivation of other virtues, they have indeed perfected the cultivation of the gateway of the samādhi of emptiness.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly reflects thus:

'Beings of all kinds have for a long night always practiced upon various signs—namely, grasping at the sign of male, or grasping at the sign of female, or grasping at the sign of form, or grasping at the sign of sound, or grasping at the sign of odor, or grasping at the sign of taste, or grasping at the sign of tangibility, or grasping at the sign of phenomena, or grasping at various other signs of self and signs of phenomena.'"

For the sake of such sentient beings, I should proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, and upon realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, cause all sentient beings to forever sever their various attachments to signs.

"Subhūti, you should know that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes this mindfulness and practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, being sustained by skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), they will never enter the supreme meditative concentrations of the Buddhas until they have fully perfected the ten powers of a Tathāgata, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, as well as all other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas."

Subhūti, you should know that although at that time these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train in the three doors of liberation and enter and emerge from them with mastery, they do not immediately realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Until the causal practices and merits for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment are fully perfected, they do not realize the limit of reality or other such qualities; rather, they can only realize them upon attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

Subhūti, you should know that although at that time this bodhisattva mahāsattva has not yet perfected the cultivation of other merits, they have already perfected the cultivation of the gate of signless samādhi.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva has already well cultivated and studied the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
has already well established themselves in inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature; and has already..."
They are well-established in suchness up to the inconceivable realm; they are well-established in the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
they have well-practiced and studied the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
they have well-practiced and studied the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; they have well-practiced and studied the four...
Having well practiced the dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
having well practiced the eight liberations up to the ten totalities; having well practiced all the bodhisattva stages;
having well practiced the gates of dhāraṇī and the gates of samādhi; having well practiced the five eyes and the six supernormal powers; having...
They have well cultivated and studied the ten powers of a Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they have well cultivated and studied great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity;
and they have well cultivated and studied the quality of non-forgetfulness, the state of constant dwelling in equanimity, and other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas.

"Subhūti, you should know that for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has accomplished such sublime wisdom and vision, it is impossible that they would conceive a notion of pleasure regarding saṃsāra, or speak of there being pleasure, or dwell with attachment within the triple world."
“Subhūti, you should know this!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva has already well practiced the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma), all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their disciples should examine him with these questions:

‘If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, how should he practice the factors of enlightenment so that he does not realize emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, non-cessation, non-action, the unconditioned, the absence of intrinsic nature, or the reality limit (bhūtakoṭi)? And because he does not realize them, how does he not attain the fruit of a stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, or arhat, nor the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, while diligently practicing the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) and remaining forever without grasping?’”
"Subhūti, you should know that when this bodhisattva mahāsattva is asked such a question, if he were to answer: 'Bodhisattva mahāsattvas who wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect,

and complete enlightenment should only contemplate emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, non-cessation, non-action, the unconditioned, the absence of intrinsic nature, the limit of reality, and all other factors conducive to enlightenment, and they should not practice or train [in anything else].'"
This bodhisattva mahāsattva has not yet received from the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha the prediction of non-retrogression regarding unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Why is this? It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have not yet been able to reveal, predict, or clarify the characteristics of the dharmas practiced by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who abide in the stage of non-retrogression.
"Subhūti, you should know that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva receives this question, if they should answer thus:

'Bodhisattvas mahāsattvas who wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should correctly contemplate emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, non-cessation, non-action, the unconditioned, the absence of intrinsic nature, the reality limit, and all other factors conducive to enlightenment; furthermore, they should skillfully train in them through the aforementioned expedient means, yet not realize [these states] prematurely.'"
This bodhisattva mahāsattva has already received from the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the prediction of non-retrogression regarding unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Why is this? It is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva has already been able to reveal, predict, and clarify the characteristics of the dharmas practiced by bodhisattva mahāsattvas who abide in the stage of non-retrogression.

“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva has not yet been able to explain, predict, or clarify the characteristics of the dharmas practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva who dwells on the stage of non-retrogression, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has not yet skillfully trained in the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, nor in any other factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma). He has not yet entered the Stage of Thinness (tanubhūmi), and he has not yet explained, predicted, or clarified the characteristics of dwelling in non-retrogression in the same manner as other bodhisattva mahāsattvas who dwell on the stage of non-retrogression.”

"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to reveal, predict, and clarify the characteristics of the dharmas practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva who abides on the stage of non-retrogression, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has already well cultivated the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as all other factors conducive to awakening. He has entered the Stage of Thinness (tanutva-bhūmi) and, just like other bodhisattva mahāsattvas abiding on the stage of non-retrogression, he reveals, predicts, and clarifies the characteristics of abiding in non-retrogression."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
is there any bodhisattva mahāsattva who has not yet attained the stage of non-retrogression yet is able to provide such a true and accurate answer?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, although they have not yet attained the stage of non-retrogression, are nevertheless able to provide such a response as this.
Subhūti, you should know this!"

Although this bodhisattva mahāsattva has not yet attained the stage of non-retrogression, they are able to practice and train in the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as all other factors conducive to enlightenment. Having already attained a matured and sharp awakening-intelligence, whether they hear it or not, they are able to answer in accordance with reality just like a bodhisattva mahāsattva on the stage of non-retrogression.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
