“There are many bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who seek to train for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, but few are able to answer correctly as one who dwells having already well-cultivated the stages or not yet well-cultivated the stages of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva of the stage of non-retrogression.”
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"

Why is this? Because there are few bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have received such a prediction of the supreme wisdom of the stage of non-retrogression; and those who have received such a prediction are all able to provide a response to this in accordance with reality.

"Subhūti! If one can answer correctly in this manner, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has planted roots of goodness that are most extremely bright and sharp; the measure of the wisdom they have cultivated is profound and vast, such that the world with its gods, humans, and asuras cannot lead them astray or cause their destruction; they will certainly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, even in a dream, does not take pleasure in or praise the dharmas of the levels of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor gives rise to a mind that takes pleasure in or praises the dharmas of the three realms; and if they constantly contemplate all dharmas as being like a dream, like an echo—and so forth, as extensively explained, up to—like a city of gandharvas; and though they observe them in this way, do not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), it should be known that this bodhisattva possesses the marks of non-retrogression."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, in a dream, sees a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, surrounded by countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of beings who respectfully attend him as he teaches the Dharma; and having heard that Dharma, they well understand its meaning and intent; and having understood its meaning and intent, they practice with diligence; and practicing in accordance with the Dharma, they enter samādhi and arise from it having practiced in accordance with the Dharma—then one should know that this bodhisattva possesses the marks of non-retrogression."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, in a dream, sees a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—fully adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty secondary signs, with a constant light extending one fathom illuminating all around, leaping into the air with an immeasurable assembly, manifesting great supernormal powers and preaching the essentials of the True Dharma, and creating emanations who go to other boundless buddha-fields to perform the work of a Buddha—one should know that this bodhisattva possesses the signs of non-retrogression."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees in a dream mad bandits destroying a village or city; or sees a fire breaking out and burning down a settlement; or sees lions, tigers, wolves, fierce beasts, venomous snakes, or evil scorpions about to come and harm his body; or sees an enemy about to cut off his head; or sees his father, mother, brother, sister, wife, children, or kinsmen on the verge of death; or sees himself oppressed by cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and other such painful conditions.
Seeing such terrifying things as these, they are neither startled nor afraid, nor do they feel distress; having awakened from the dream, they are immediately able to reflect:

"The three realms are not real; they are all like what was seen in a dream. When I attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, I shall preach the Dharma of the three realms for the sake of sentient beings, explaining that everything is false and entirely like a dream."
"You should know that this bodhisattva possesses the signs of non-retrogression. Furthermore, Subhūti,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, even in a dream, sees sentient beings in the realms of hell, animals, or the hungry ghosts, and then forms this thought:"

"I shall diligently cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva and swiftly proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, so that in my buddha-field there shall not even be the names of the evil destinies of hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts."
Upon awakening from the dream, he likewise forms this thought:
"Subhūti, you should know that when this bodhisattva mahāsattva attains buddhahood, there shall certainly be no evil realms in the buddha-field where he dwells."
Why is this? Whether in a dream or while awake, all phenomena are non-dual and cannot be divided into two parts; one should know that this is the mark of a bodhisattva who is non-retrogressive.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while dreaming, sees fire burning sentient beings in the hells and other realms, or sees cities and villages being consumed by flames, he then makes this vow:
'If I have already received the prediction of non-retrogression and shall realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, may these great fires be instantly extinguished and transformed into coolness.'"
"If this bodhisattva, having made such a vow, sees fire in a dream that is immediately and suddenly extinguished, one should know that they have already received the prediction of non-retrogression.

If this bodhisattva, having made such a vow, sees fire in a dream that is not immediately and suddenly extinguished, one should know that they have not yet received the prediction of non-retrogression."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while awake, sees a great fire suddenly break out, burning various cities or villages, he then forms this thought:

'Whether in a dream or in the waking state, I have previously seen the practices, marks, and signs of my own non-retrogressive stage; I do not yet know whether they are real or false. If what I have seen is truly existent, may this great fire be instantly and completely extinguished and transformed into coolness. "

If this bodhisattva makes such a vow and utters these words of truth, at that moment the great fire will be instantly extinguished; one should know that he has already received the prediction of non-retrogression.

If this bodhisattva makes such a vow and utters these words of truth, yet the fire is not immediately extinguished, you should know that they have not yet received the prediction of non-retrogression.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while awake, sees fire burning various cities or villages, he then forms this thought:
"Whether in a dream or in the waking state, I have previously seen the practices, marks, and signs of my own stage of non-retrogression."
If what I have perceived is certainly real, and I am destined to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may this great fire be instantly extinguished and transformed into coolness.

After this bodhisattva-mahāsattva had uttered these words of solemn and truthful resolve, the great fire did not immediately go out; rather, it burned one house and then skipped over another, burning yet another house or a single lane, skipping over a lane and then burning another lane. In this manner, as it passed from one place to another, the fire was finally extinguished.
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva should know for himself that he has definitely received the prediction of non-retrogression.

As for those who are burned, it is because those sentient beings have created and accumulated karma that destroys the True Dharma; by virtue of this karma, they first fell into the evil destinies and underwent the full fruit of suffering for immeasurable kalpas. Now, having been born in the human realm, they undergo the remaining retribution of that karma. Alternatively, by virtue of this karma, they are destined to fall into the evil destinies and undergo the full fruit of suffering for immeasurable kalpas, yet now, while in the human realm, they first manifest a small portion of that retribution.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Based on the various causes and conditions previously explained, one knows a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is non-retrogressive.
Moreover, there are other practices, marks, and signs by which one knows a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is non-retrogressive; I shall analyze and explain them for you, so listen attentively!"
"Excellent, Subhūti! Subhūti replied, "Indeed, so it is!"
"Please speak!
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees a man or a woman who has been possessed by a non-human spirit and is undergoing various sufferings from which they cannot escape, he then forms this thought:"

"If the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas know that I have attained pure intention and have conferred upon me the prediction of non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;

and if I have long since generated pure mental attention seeking to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, remaining far removed from the mental attention of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and not seeking to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through the mental attention of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas."
If, in the future, I shall certainly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and bring benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings until the end of the future;

and if, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there currently exist immeasurable Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who proclaim the subtle and wondrous Dharma to benefit and gladden sentient beings—those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, who see nothing that is not seen, know nothing that is not known, understand nothing that is not understood, and realize nothing that is not realized, and who presently know, see, and awaken to the differences in the inclinations of all sentient beings—I pray that you will graciously examine my thoughts and these words of truth.

If I am truly able to cultivate the conduct of a bodhisattva and shall certainly attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment to rescue sentient beings from the suffering of birth and death, then may this man or this woman not be disturbed or harassed by non-human spirits; at my word, they shall immediately depart.
When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva speaks these words, if that non-human being does not depart, one should know that they have not yet received the prediction of non-retrogression.
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva speaks these words, if that non-human being immediately departs, you should know that they have already received the prediction of non-retrogression.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have not yet well cultivated and trained in the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom;

who have not yet well established themselves in inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; and who have not yet well established themselves in suchness up to the inconceivable realm.
While well-established in the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, they have not yet well-cultivated the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
they have not yet well-cultivated the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
and they have not yet well-cultivated the eight liberations up to the ten totalities. They have not yet well-cultivated...
They have studied the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—but have not yet skillfully trained in the gates of dhāraṇī or the gates of samādhi;
they have not yet entered the bodhisattva’s state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*); they have not yet fully practiced all Buddha-dharmas;
they are far removed from the bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), and they have not yet escaped the afflictions caused by evil Māras.

Being distracted, they fail to recognize the various works of Māra; without measuring the thickness of their own roots of goodness, they study the teachings of the bodhisattvas and utter words of solemn truth, only to be deceived and deluded by evil Māras.

If this bodhisattva mahāsattva sees a man or a woman who has been possessed by a non-human spirit, suffering various afflictions and unable to escape them, he immediately makes a sincere declaration of truth:

"If I have indeed received from the Buddhas of the past the prediction of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment as one who is irreversible, then let this man or this woman not be disturbed or tormented by the non-human spirit; let it depart quickly, following my words."
After this Bodhisattva-mahāsattva had spoken these words, at that time the evil Māra, for the sake of deception and delusion, immediately drove away and coerced the non-human beings to depart.
Why is this? Because the power of Māra is superior to that of the non-human beings; therefore, at Māra’s command, those non-human beings immediately depart.
When the bodhisattva-mahāsattva sees this occurrence, he leaps for joy and thinks to himself:
"The non-human has now departed because of my spiritual power. Why is this?
It is because the non-human released this man and woman in accordance with the vow I have made; there is no other cause."

This bodhisattva mahāsattva fails to recognize that this is the work of a wicked Māra; instead, he falsely gives rise to joy, thinking it to be his own power. Relying on this, he treats other bodhisattvas with contempt, saying:

"I have already received from the Buddhas of the past the prediction of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment and shall not fall back; the vows I have made will not be in vain. You, however, have not yet received such predictions from the Buddhas, so you should not emulate me by making solemn declarations of truth; even if you were to set such goals, they would surely be empty and bear no fruit."

Because this bodhisattva-mahāsattva treats other bodhisattvas with contempt and derision, falsely relying on their meager abilities and giving rise to many forms of overweening pride regarding their various merits, they distance themselves from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and are unable to realize the knowledge of all modes.

Because this bodhisattva-mahāsattva lacks the power of skillful means, because they give rise to many forms of overweening pride, and because they disparage and despise other bodhisattvas, they fall to the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha despite their diligent application of effort.
Because this bodhisattva-mahāsattva possesses meager merit, all the wholesome deeds he performs and the truthful words he utters are moved by the works of Māra.

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva is unable to approach, make offerings to, revere, respect, and praise true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); he is unable to inquire about the characteristics of the practice of non-retrogressive bodhisattvas; and he is unable to consult with or receive instruction regarding the activities of the various evil māra armies. Due to these factors, his bonds of Māra become increasingly firm and solid.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have not long practiced the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and because they lack skillful means, they are deceived and deluded by Māra.
Therefore, Subhūti, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should skillfully recognize all the deeds of Māra. Furthermore, Subhūti:

How should Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas correctly recognize those who, having not long practiced the perfections of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and who have even distanced themselves from skillful means, are deceived and deluded by Māra? How should they be made aware of this?
It refers to a wicked Māra who, for the sake of deception and delusion, employs skillful means to manifest various forms and approaches the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, saying: "Ho!..."
"Good son! Do you know this yourself?
The Buddhas of the past have already bestowed upon you the prophecy of great enlightenment; you shall certainly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening and shall never again fall back."

I fully know the names and distinctions of your parents, brothers, sisters, friends, and kinsmen, even down to seven generations; I know that you were born in such a direction, such a country, such a city, such a town, and such a village, and that you were born under such a year, such a month, such a day, such a time, and under the constellation of such a king.
If an evil Māra sees that a bodhisattva is by nature gentle and compliant, with dull faculties, he will falsely declare:
"In previous lives, the root-nature you have received was already like this."
If he sees that a bodhisattva is by nature firm and strong, with keen and sharp faculties, he then falsely predicts:
"In previous lives, the root-nature you received was also like this."
"If one sees a bodhisattva dwelling in an araṇya, or constantly begging for food, or accepting only one meal a day,
or eating in a single sitting, or eating from a single bowl, or dwelling among graves, or dwelling in the open air,
or dwelling at the foot of a tree, or wearing rag-robes, or possessing only the three robes, or constantly sitting without lying down."
Some may possess old bedding and requisites; some may have few desires, or be content, or delight in seclusion, or delight in meditative concentration;
some may possess right mindfulness, or possess sublime wisdom; some may not value gain and offerings, or prize fame and reputation;
some may prefer frugality and austerity, not even anointing their feet, or may minimize sleep.
Whether he is drowsy, or free from agitation, or fond of speaking little, or delights in gentle speech—
when the Evil Māra observes these various practices of the bodhisattva, he feigns a prophecy, saying:
"In previous lives as well, you were just like this."

Why is this? Because you have now accomplished such and such extraordinary merits, which are witnessed by all the world; it must be that in previous lives you also certainly possessed such extraordinary merits. You should rejoice and comfort yourself, and not disparage yourself.

“When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva hears this evil Māra describe his past and future merits, as well as the specific names of his current friends and himself, and further praises his various excellent roots of goodness, he will leap for joy and give rise to overweening pride, thereby despising, slandering, and reviling all other bodhisattvas.”
At that time, Māra, knowing that he was dull-witted and had given rise to overweening pride to despise others, spoke to him again, saying:

"You have certainly accomplished supreme merit; the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past have already bestowed upon you a prophecy. You shall certainly realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and never regress; such auspicious signs as these have already appeared before you."

At that time, for the sake of causing disturbance, Māra the Evil One may falsely manifest himself in the form of a renunciant, or falsely manifest himself in the form of a householder; or he may falsely manifest himself in various forms such as those of parents, brothers, sisters, friends, kinsmen, brahmins, preceptors, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, or non-humans, and approach this bodhisattva mahāsattva, saying these words:
"The Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past have long ago bestowed upon you the prophecy of great enlightenment."
"You shall certainly attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and never again regress. Why is this?
You possess all the marks and signs of the merit of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have reached the stage of non-regression; you should respect yourself and not give rise to doubt."
At that time, having heard those words, the bodhisattva’s mind of overweening pride became even more firmly entrenched.
"Subhūti, you should know that the practices, tokens,
and signs of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has truly attained non-retrogression, as described by me, do not exist at all for this bodhisattva mahāsattva."
"Subhūti, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is possessed by Māra and harassed by Māra,
such that they lack self-mastery. Why is this so?"

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva has not yet actually attained any of the practices, marks, or signs of a non-retrogressive bodhisattva-mahāsattva; yet, having merely heard an evil Māra falsely proclaiming their virtues, name, and so forth, they give rise to overweening pride and treat other bodhisattvas with contempt, slandering and reviling them.
Therefore, Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they should skillfully recognize all the deeds of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are possessed by Māra and bewitched by Māra; they merely hear the names [of these dharmas] and give rise to false attachments.

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva has not yet practiced the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, nor the other immeasurable and boundless buddha-dharmas; for these reasons, Māra gains an opportunity.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva is unable to fully comprehend the modes of activity of the māra of the aggregates, the modes of activity of the māra of death, the modes of activity of the celestial māra, and the modes of activity of the māra of afflictions; by reason of these causes and conditions, it allows the māras to gain an opportunity.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva is unable to fully comprehend the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness, nor the other immeasurable dharma-gates; furthermore, they do not understand the true reality of the names of all phenomena pertaining to sentient beings—that is to say, their signlessness (*animitta*).
Due to these causes and conditions, Māra gains an opportunity and, through skillful means, manifests various forms and addresses this bodhisattva mahāsattva, saying:
"The practices and vows you have cultivated are now fulfilled; you shall attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"When you attain Buddhahood, you shall obtain such supreme, wondrous merit and this noble title!
This was said because that evil Māra knew that this bodhisattva had long harbored the thought and aspiration:
"When I attain Buddhahood, I shall obtain such merit and a name!"
He then prophesies according to that person’s thoughts and aspirations.
At that time, because this bodhisattva is far removed from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) and lacks skillful means (upāyakauśalya), upon hearing the Māra’s prophecy, he thinks to himself:
"This person is truly marvelous!"
Please grant me a prophecy regarding the merit, name, and title I shall attain upon becoming a Buddha, so that it may correspond with the aspirations I have cherished throughout the long night.

By this, I know that the Buddhas of the past must have already granted me the prophecy of great enlightenment; I am certain that I shall attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening and shall never again fall back.
"When I attain Buddhahood, I shall certainly obtain such meritorious and noble titles.

As the evil Māra, or his retinue, or various śramaṇas possessed by Māra, prophesy the names by which this bodhisattva-mahāsattva will be known upon attaining future Buddhahood, so too does his pride increase:
"In the future, I shall certainly become a Buddha and obtain such meritorious titles; no other bodhisattvas are my equal."

"Subhūti, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has not yet accomplished any of the practices, tokens, or signs of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has attained non-retrogression as I have described them. Merely hearing the false reputation of attaining buddhahood spoken by Māra, he gives rise to arrogance and treats others with contempt, disparaging and belittling the entire assembly of other bodhisattva mahāsattvas."

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to arrogance and treats other bodhisattva mahāsattvas with contempt, derision, and disdain, he distances himself from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva is far removed from the perfection of wisdom, lacks skillful means, abandons virtuous friends, and is constantly influenced by evil associates, they will fall into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.

"Subhūti, you should know that such a bodhisattva mahāsattva may regain right mindfulness regarding this body, sincerely repent their transgressions, and abandon the mind of pride; they repeatedly draw near to, make offerings to, revere, respect, and praise true and pure spiritual friends."

Although they may wander through birth and death for a long time, they will subsequently rely on this profound *prajñāpāramitā* to train gradually and shall realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Subhūti, you should know that if such a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not attain right mindfulness regarding this body, is unable to repent their transgressions, does not relinquish their prideful mind, and does not delight in associating with, making offerings to, honoring, respecting, and praising true and pure spiritual friends;

That person will certainly wander through birth and death for a long time; although they may later apply themselves with diligence to cultivate various wholesome deeds, they will fall to the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.

For example, just as a bhikṣu seeking the state of a śrāvaka who commits even one of the four grave offenses is no longer a śramaṇa nor a son of the Śākya, so too that person will certainly be unable to attain the fruit of stream-entry or other such fruits in the present life.

The same applies to those who falsely cling to the empty title of "Bodhisattva": merely hearing the Māra’s discourse on the hollow name of "attaining Buddhahood," they give rise to arrogance and treat other Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas with contempt and derision. You should know that this transgression is infinitely many times greater than the four grave offenses committed by that bhikṣu.
Setting aside the four pārājika offenses committed by that bhikṣu, this bodhisattva’s transgression exceeds even the five ānantarya crimes by immeasurable multiples. Why is this?

Because this bodhisattva-mahāsattva has not actually accomplished any sublime merit; yet, hearing the evil Māra proclaim his false reputation for attaining Buddhahood, he becomes conceited and looks down upon other bodhisattvas. Therefore, this transgression exceeds the five ānantarya crimes.

From this, it should be understood that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should skillfully recognize such subtle demonic activities as the recording and proclaiming of false names and titles.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the conduct of seclusion; that is to say, they dwell in hidden mountain forests, empty marshes, and vast wildernesses, residing in *āraṇya* (forest hermitages) to sit in meditation and engage in contemplation."
At that time, an evil Māra came to where he was and, with respectful praise for the merit of seclusion, spoke these words:
"Excellent, Great Being!
One is able to cultivate such true practice of seclusion.

This practice of seclusion is praised by all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; it is protected, honored, and revered by Śakra, Lord of Devas, and all other celestial beings and ṛṣis. You should dwell constantly here and not go elsewhere.
"Subhūti, you should know this:

I do not praise those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who dwell in forest hermitages, wildernesses, or mountain groves, engaging in seated meditation and contemplation while practicing the conduct of seclusion."
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

“What other practices of seclusion (*viveka*) should bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate, such that the Buddha does not praise dwelling in *āraṇya*, wildernesses, or mountain forests, nor the merit of abandoning superior bedding and seats for the sake of meditative reflection and solitary sitting?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Whether bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell in mountain forests, empty marshes, wildernesses, or forest hermitages (āraṇya), or reside in cities, villages, or the bustle of royal capitals, as long as they can remain far removed from afflictions, evil karma, and the mental orientations of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and practice the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) along with cultivating other sublime and excellent merits, this is called the bodhisattva’s true practice of detachment."

This practice of seclusion is praised by all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and is authorized by all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. All bodhisattvas should constantly train in it; whether by day or by night, they should correctly contemplate and diligently practice this dharma of seclusion. This is called a bodhisattva’s cultivation of the practice of seclusion.

This practice of seclusion is unmixed with the mental orientations of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and unmixed with any afflictions or unwholesome karma; it is free from all clamor and utterly pure, causing bodhisattvas to swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and to constantly and inexhaustibly benefit and bring happiness to sentient beings.
"Subhūti, you should know that what Māra praises—
hiding away in mountain forests, empty marshes, wildernesses, and *āranyaka* dwellings to abandon superior bedding and sit in meditation— is not the true practice of seclusion for bodhisattvas."

Why is this? Because even that practice of seclusion may still involve distraction; that is to say, it may be interspersed with evil karma and afflictions, or interspersed with the mental orientations of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Consequently, one cannot diligently believe in, accept, and train in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, nor can one fulfill the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).
“Subhūti, you should know this!”

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, though they delight in practicing the dharmas of seclusion praised by Māra, give rise to a mind of pride and impurity, and treat other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas with contempt and derision. They say: "There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, although dwelling in cities, villages, and royal capitals, possess pure minds; they are unmixed with various afflictions, evil deeds, or the mental orientations of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Diligently training in the perfections of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—extending even to the knowledge of all aspects—they purify buddha-fields and mature sentient beings. Though they dwell amidst the clamor of the crowd, their minds are tranquil, and they constantly and diligently cultivate the practice of true seclusion."
"Subhūti, you should know that toward such a truly pure assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, they give rise to arrogance, treating them with contempt, disparaging them, slandering them,
and looking down upon them."

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva is far removed from the perfection of wisdom and lacks skillful means, even though he dwells in a wilderness extending for a hundred yojanas that is utterly devoid of all predatory beasts, snakes, scorpions, and bandits, there are only ghosts, spirits, and rākṣasas who roam and dwell therein.

While dwelling in such a forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*), even if they spend one year, or five, or ten, or even up to a hundred thousand *koṭis* of years practicing the conduct of seclusion (*viveka-caryā*) beyond such numbers, they do not understand true seclusion. This is because the assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, though dwelling in the midst of bustle and clamor, possess mental tranquility; they remain far removed from various afflictions (*kleśa*), evil karma, and the mental orientations (*manasikāra*) of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, as they set out toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

"Subhūti, you should know that although these bodhisattvas dwell in the wilderness for a long time, they harbor the mental orientations of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; they develop a deep attachment to those two stages, practice the conduct of seclusion based on the dharmas of those two stages, and furthermore, they become deeply addicted to and stained by this very conduct."
Although he practices such conduct of seclusion, it does not accord with the minds of the Buddhas.

"Subhūti, you should know that the true conduct of seclusion praised by me for bodhisattva mahāsattvas is entirely unaccomplished by him; furthermore, within that truly pure conduct of seclusion, he does not perceive even a semblance of its characteristics."

Why is this? It is because they do not find delight in such genuine practice of seclusion, but instead take pleasure only in diligently cultivating the empty practices of seclusion characteristic of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
"Subhūti, you should know that when this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the conduct of seclusion for the sake of non-perfect purity, Māra comes through the air and joyfully praises him, saying:
'O Great Being!'"
Excellent! Excellent!
You are able to diligently cultivate the practice of true seclusion; this practice of seclusion is praised by all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
"If you apply yourself with diligence to this practice, you will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Subhūti, you should know that such a bodhisattva mahāsattva clings to these dharmas of the practice of seclusion cultivated by the two vehicles as being supreme; they treat with contempt and derision those bhikṣus who abide in the vehicle of the bodhisattvas, whose minds are tranquil despite living in the midst of bustle, and who have accomplished the dharmas of discipline and goodness, saying: "Those people cannot cultivate the practice of seclusion; though they dwell in bustle, their minds are not tranquil, and they lack the dharmas of discipline and goodness."

“Subhūti, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva despises and disparages those bodhisattva mahāsattvas praised by the Buddha who dwell in genuine seclusion, saying: ‘They dwell in clamor and their minds are not tranquil; they are unable to diligently cultivate the practice of genuine seclusion.

Yet he honors and praises those bodhisattva mahāsattvas whom the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas do not praise, saying: ‘They are not in clamor; their minds are tranquil, and they are able to correctly practice the path of genuine seclusion.’”

Subhūti, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not approach, honor, or make offerings to those who are like World-Honored Ones— whom one ought to approach, honor, and make offerings to— but instead treats them with contempt; conversely, he approaches, honors,
and makes offerings to those who are like evil friends— whom one ought to avoid and not approach, honor, or make offerings to— as if serving a World-Honored One.

"Subhūti, you should know that because this bodhisattva mahāsattva is far removed from the perfection of wisdom and lacks skillful means, they falsely give rise to various forms of conceptual discrimination and attachment."
Why is this? He thinks to himself: "The practice I cultivate is true seclusion; therefore, non-human beings praise and protect me."
"Those who dwell in cities and towns have their bodies and minds in turmoil; who then would protect, mindfully attend to, revere, or praise these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?

Due to these causes and conditions, their minds become filled with arrogance, and they treat other assemblies of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas with contempt and disparagement, such that their afflictions and evil karma increase day and night.
"Subhūti, you should know that such a bodhisattva mahāsattva acts as a caṇḍāla toward the assembly of other bodhisattva mahāsattvas, defiling the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas."

Although they appear to possess the marks of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, they are in fact great thieves among gods and humans; they deceive and delude gods, humans, asuras, and others. Though their bodies are clad in the dharma-robes of śramaṇas, their minds constantly harbor the intentions of thieves.
Those who have set out upon the bodhisattva vehicle should not associate with, make offerings to, honor, revere, or praise such evil persons. Why is this?
"These people harbor overweening pride; though they appear outwardly to be bodhisattvas, they are inwardly full of afflictions.

Therefore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva truly does not abandon the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), does not forsake unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, and with a profound resolve desires to seek the knowledge of all modes and attain unsurpassed perfect enlightenment for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, he should not draw near to, make offerings to, honor, respect, or praise such evil persons."

“Subhūti, you should know that Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should always cultivate their own task with diligence: they should feel weary of and detached from birth and death, remain unattached to the triple world, and constantly generate loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity toward those evil, murderous Cāṇḍālas. They should think:

‘I must not give rise to the faults that such evil persons give rise to; even if I should momentarily lose mindfulness and such faults arise, I shall immediately recognize them and swiftly eliminate them.’”

"Therefore, Subhūti! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should skillfully recognize the deeds of Māra; they should diligently apply themselves to distance themselves from and eliminate those faults arising in such bodhisattvas, and strive earnestly to seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a superior intention, desires to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they should always draw near to, make offerings to, revere, respect, and praise true and pure spiritual friends."
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What are called the true, pure, and virtuous spiritual friends of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are the true, pure, and virtuous friends of all bodhisattvas; all the assemblies of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are also the true, pure, and virtuous friends of a bodhisattva. Furthermore, any śrāvakas or other noble beings who are able to proclaim, reveal, analyze, and clarify for the assemblies of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas the dharma-gates associated with the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, making them easy to understand, are likewise the true, pure, and virtuous friends of a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
The perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom are the true, pure, and virtuous friends of bodhisattvas;
the four applications of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path are also the true, pure, and virtuous friends of bodhisattvas."
The four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments are also the bodhisattva’s true, pure, and virtuous friends;
the eight liberations up to the ten totalities are also the bodhisattva’s true, pure, and virtuous friends;
and the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are also the bodhisattva’s true, pure, and virtuous friends. To the utmost...
The Joyful Ground (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) up to the Cloud of Dharma Ground (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*) are also the Bodhisattva’s true, pure, and virtuous friends;

the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi are also the Bodhisattva’s true, pure, and virtuous friends; the five eyes and the six supernormal powers are also the Bodhisattva’s true, pure, and virtuous friends;
and the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha [are likewise so].

The Dharma is also the Bodhisattva’s true, pure, and virtuous friend; great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity are also the Bodhisattva’s true, pure, and virtuous friends;
the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant dwelling in equanimity are also the Bodhisattva’s true, pure, and virtuous friends;
and all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects [are likewise].
Furthermore, the permanent severance of all continuities of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) is a true and pure spiritual friend for a bodhisattva;
all the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva are a true and pure spiritual friend for a bodhisattva;
and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas is also a true and pure spiritual friend for a bodhisattva.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! The noble truth of suffering up to the noble truth of the path are the true, pure, and virtuous friends of bodhisattvas. The nature of conditions of all phenomena is also the true, pure, and virtuous friend of bodhisattvas. The members of dependent origination are also the true, pure, and virtuous friends of bodhisattvas. Inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature are also the true, pure, and virtuous friends of bodhisattvas. True thusness up to the inconceivable realm are also the true, pure, and virtuous friends of bodhisattvas."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

From the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, these serve as teachers and guides for the bodhisattva mahāsattvas; they are the light and the torch, the lamp and the illumination, the understanding and the awakening, the knowledge and the insight, the rescue and the protection, the chamber and the dwelling, the island and the promontory, the refuge and the destination, and the father and the mother."

The four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including all-aspect omniscience, also serve as teachers and guides for the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas; they are the illumination, the torch, the lamp, and the light; they are the liberation, the awakening, the knowledge, and the wisdom; they are the rescue, the protection, the dwelling, and the home; they are the island, the peninsula, the refuge, and the destination; and they are the father and the mother.

Having forever severed all continuities of habitual tendencies, the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas likewise serve as teachers and guides for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; they serve as illumination and torches, as lamps and lights, as understanding and awakening, as knowledge and wisdom, as rescue and protection, as a chamber and a dwelling, as an island and a peninsula, as a refuge and a destination, and as fathers and mothers.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

The noble truth of suffering, up to and including the noble truth of the path, acts as the teacher and guide for the bodhisattva mahāsattvas; it serves as the light and the torch, the lamp and the illumination, the understanding and the awakening, the wisdom and the insight, the savior and the protector, the chamber and the dwelling, the island and the peninsula, the refuge and the destination, and the father and the mother."

The nature of conditions of all phenomena (*dharmāṇāṃ pratītyasamutpāda*) and the branches of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpādāṅga*) also serve as teachers and guides for the bodhisattva mahāsattvas; they serve as illumination and torches, as lamps and lights, as understanding and awakening, as knowledge and wisdom, as saviors and protectors, as dwellings and houses, as islands and peninsulas, as refuges and destinations, and as fathers and mothers.

From internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, these also serve as teachers and guides for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; they serve as illumination and torches, as lamps and lights, as understanding and awakening, as knowledge and wisdom, as rescue and protection, as a chamber and a dwelling, as an island and a shore, as a refuge and a destination, and as fathers and mothers.

From suchness up to the inconceivable realm, they likewise serve as teachers and guides for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; they serve as illumination and torches, as lamps and lights, as understanding and awakening, as knowledge and wisdom, as rescuers and protectors, as dwellings and homes, as islands and peninsulas, as refuges and destinations, and as fathers and mothers.

Why is this so? Because all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present, have all taken—from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, and broadly speaking, from suchness up to the inconceivable realm—as their teacher and guide, as their light and torch, as their lamp and illumination, as their liberation and awakening, as their knowledge and insight, as their salvation and protection, as their chamber and dwelling, as their island and continent, as their refuge and destination, and as their father and mother.

Why is this? Because all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present, have all grown and flourished from the perfection of giving up to the perfection of wisdom, and so forth, extensively explained, up to suchness and the inconceivable realm.

"Therefore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*), desires to realize unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, to bring sentient beings to maturity, and to purify a buddha-field, they should train in the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom; and so on, in detail, up to training in suchness (*tathatā*) up to the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*)."

Having trained in the perfection of generosity, and so forth up to the inconceivable realm, this bodhisattva mahāsattva should further gather all sentient beings by means of the four means of attraction.
What are the four? First, generosity;
second, pleasant speech.
Third is beneficial conduct;
fourth is cooperation.

It is with reference to this meaning that I have made this statement: all the perfections of giving, and so forth, up to the inconceivable realm, act as teachers and guides for the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and so forth, up to acting as fathers and mothers.

Therefore, Subhūti, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish not to act according to the instructions of others, who wish to abide on the stage of not following the instructions of others, who wish to sever the doubts of all sentient beings, who wish to fulfill the aspirations of all sentient beings, who wish to purify buddha-fields, and who wish to bring sentient beings to maturity, should study the perfection of wisdom.

Why is this? Because within this profound *prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, the dharmas that the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should study are extensively expounded; all members of the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should diligently practice and train therein.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll 518. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Three: Chapter Twenty-three on Skillful Means (III). At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“What are the characteristics of the profound perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“The profound perfection of wisdom has emptiness as its characteristic; it has non-attachment as its characteristic; it has signlessness as its characteristic; it has tranquility as its characteristic; and it has detachment as its characteristic.”
Why is this? Because within the profound characteristics of this Prajñāpāramitā, all phenomena and all marks are unattainable and non-existent.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Is there any basis by which one might say that whatever sublime characteristics belong to the Prajñāpāramitā, all other dharmas likewise possess such sublime characteristics?"
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
Because there are causes and conditions, one may speak of the sublime characteristics possessed by the *prajñāpāramitā*; other dharmas likewise possess such sublime characteristics. Why is this so?

The profound *prajñāpāramitā* has the characteristic of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), and other phenomena likewise have the characteristic of the emptiness of intrinsic nature;
the profound *prajñāpāramitā* has the characteristic of non-attachment, and other phenomena likewise have the characteristic of non-attachment;
the profound *prajñāpāramitā* has the characteristic of signlessness (*animitta*), and other phenomena likewise have the characteristic of signlessness.
The profound *prajñāpāramitā* has tranquility as its characteristic, and other phenomena likewise have tranquility as their characteristic;
the profound *prajñāpāramitā* has detachment as its characteristic, and other phenomena likewise have detachment as their characteristic.
For this reason, it can be said:

whatever sublime characteristics the profound *prajñāpāramitā* possesses, other dharmas likewise possess such sublime characteristics, because all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature and devoid of intrinsic nature.
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature and devoid of intrinsic nature, then all dharmas are empty of all dharmas, and all dharmas are devoid of all dharmas; how, then, can sentient beings be designated as having defilement or purity?”
It is not that there is defilement or purification within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, nor is there defilement or purification apart from phenomena;

it is not that the emptiness of intrinsic nature can realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, nor can anything apart from phenomena realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
it is not that any phenomenon can be apprehended within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, nor can any phenomenon be apprehended apart from [intrinsic nature].

In the emptiness of intrinsic nature, there is no bodhisattva mahāsattva who realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; nor is there any bodhisattva mahāsattva who realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment apart from it. How am I to understand the profound meaning and intent of what the Buddha has spoken?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? For a long night, have sentient beings harbored the notions of 'I' and 'mine,' and have they clung to 'I' and 'mine' with their minds?"
Subhūti replied, “So it is, World-Honored One!”
"So it is! Well-gone One!
For a long night, sentient beings have held to 'I' and 'mine,' and their minds have been attached to 'I' and 'mine.'"
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Are the 'self' and 'what belongs to the self' grasped by sentient beings empty and remote?"
Subhūti replied, “So it is, World-Honored One!”
"So it is! Sugata! The 'self' and 'what belongs to the self' grasped by sentient beings are all empty and utterly remote."
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Is it not the case that sentient beings transmigrate through birth and death due to the grasping at 'I' and 'mine'?"
Subhūti replied, “So it is, World-Honored One!”
"So it is! Well-gone One!
It is by means of the grasping at 'I' and 'mine' that all classes of sentient beings wander through birth and death."
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"In this way, sentient beings transmigrate through birth and death due to the existence of afflictions; therefore, sentient beings are designated as being defiled."
If sentient beings were free from mental attachment, then "I" and "mine" would be without defilement; if there were no defilement, there could be no wandering through birth and death.

Since the transmigration through birth and death cannot be apprehended, one should know that sentient beings are far removed from defilement; it is by virtue of the absence of defilement that purity is conventionally designated. Therefore, Subhūti!
"Although all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature and devoid of intrinsic nature, it is nevertheless possible to designate that sentient beings are subject to defilement and purification.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice the profound perfection of wisdom in this manner..."
Since the nature of all phenomena is empty and detached, this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not engage with the aggregate of form up to the aggregate of consciousness;
nor does he engage with the sense base of the eye up to the sense base of the mind; nor does he engage with the sense base of form up to the sense base of mental phenomena;
nor does he engage with the eye element up to the mind element; nor does he engage with the form element.
Even up to the dharma-realm, they do not practice; nor do they practice the eye-consciousness realm up to the mind-consciousness realm;

nor do they practice eye-contact up to mind-contact; nor do they practice the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition; nor do they practice the earth element up to the consciousness element. Nor...
One does not engage with the causal conditions up to the dominant conditions; nor does one engage with ignorance up to old age and death;
nor does one engage with the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
nor does one engage with inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature; nor does one engage with suchness up to the inconceivable.
They do not practice with respect to the sphere of discernment, nor do they practice with respect to the noble truth of suffering up to the noble truth of the path;

nor do they practice with respect to the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; nor do they practice with respect to the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments;
nor do they practice with respect to abstaining from taking life up to abstaining from wrong view; nor do they practice.
One does not practice the gateways of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; nor does one practice the eight liberations up to the ten totalities;
nor does one practice the stage of pure observation up to the stage of a Tathāgata;
nor does one practice the stages from the Ground of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma; nor does one practice the gateways of dhāraṇī or the gateways of samādhi.
Nor does one practice the five eyes or the six supernormal powers; nor does one practice the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
nor does one practice great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, or great equanimity;
nor does one practice the thirty-two marks of a Great Being or the eighty secondary signs; nor does one practice non-existence.
They do not practice the loss of dharmas or the state of constant equanimity; nor do they practice the fruit of a stream-enterer up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
nor do they practice any of the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva or the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas;
nor do they practice all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Why is this? Because all such phenomena are unapprehendable; the one who practices, that which is practiced, the time of practice, the place of practice, and that by means of which one practices—all these are non-existent.
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice in this way, they will not be overcome by any in the world—whether devas, humans, or asuras—but will instead be able to overcome them.”
"Bhagavān! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice in this way, they will not be overcome by any śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, but will instead be able to overcome them."
Why is that? Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva has already attained abiding in the state that cannot be overcome, namely, the bodhisattva’s stage of "separation from birth" (avivartika).
World-Honored One!
This bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly dwells in the mental engagement of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) and cannot be overcome.

World-Honored One, when this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this manner, they draw near to the knowledge of all modes, swiftly realize unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, and turn the sublime wheel of Dharma to deliver the multitudes of sentient beings.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to practice such profound *prajñāpāramitā* and the emptiness and signless nature of all phenomena, that bodhisattva mahāsattva does not practice the aggregate of form, and so forth, up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). In this way, they draw near to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), swiftly realize unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, and turn the sublime wheel of Dharma to deliver the multitudes of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, what do you think?

Suppose all sentient beings in this Jambudvīpa were to attain human bodies; having attained human bodies, they were to resolve their minds upon and practice the conduct of bodhisattvas, and all were to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, for as long as their life lasts, provide all manner of supreme and exquisite worldly articles of enjoyment to these Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, honoring, revering, respecting, and praising them; and furthermore, take these accumulated roots of goodness and, sharing them equally with all sentient beings, dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Would these sons and daughters of good family, by reason of this cause and condition,
obtain much merit? Subhūti replied, "Very much!"
"O Bhagavān,
it is very much so! O Sugata!"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If sons or daughters of good family, amidst a great assembly, proclaim this profound Prajñāpāramitā, establishing, defining, analyzing, and elucidating it so that it may be easily understood, and remain with a mental attention associated with this profound Prajñāpāramitā."
The merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family through these causes and conditions is far greater than the former—immeasurable, incalculable, and beyond all reckoning.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! What do you think?

Suppose that all sentient beings within this trichiliocosm were to obtain human bodies, and having obtained human bodies, they were to resolve their minds upon and practice the conduct of bodhisattvas, and all were to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, for as long as their life lasts, provide all manner of supreme and exquisite worldly comforts to these Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, honoring, revering, respecting, and praising them; and furthermore, take these accumulated roots of virtue and, sharing them equally with all sentient beings, dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Would these sons and daughters of good family obtain much merit by reason of this?
Subhūti replied, "Very much!"
“World-Honored One!
It is very much so! Sugata!”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If sons or daughters of good family, in the midst of a great assembly, proclaim this profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), establishing, defining, analyzing, and elucidating it so that it may be easily understood, and abide in a mental engagement (manasikāra) associated with this profound perfection of wisdom."
The merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family through these causes and conditions is far greater than the former—immeasurable, incalculable, and beyond all reckoning.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, what do you think?
Suppose all the sentient beings in this Jambudvīpa were to simultaneously, without one preceding another, attain human bodies."

There are sons and daughters of good family who, through skillful means, guide and transform others so that they all come to abide in the ten paths of wholesome action; or in the four dhyānas, or the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments; or in the five supernormal powers; or in the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship; or in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, or even in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, by taking these roots of goodness from such transformative guidance and sharing them equally with all sentient beings, dedicating them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment—
would those sons or daughters of good family, by reason of this cause and condition, acquire much merit?
Subhūti replied, “Very much so,
World-Honored One!”
"Very much so,
Sugata! The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"If good sons and good daughters, among the great assembly, proclaim such profound *prajñāpāramitā*, establishing, defining, analyzing, and elucidating it so that it is easily understood, and correctly abide in the mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñatājñāna*), then the merit obtained by these good sons and good daughters through these causes and conditions will be far greater than the former—immeasurable, incalculable, and beyond reckoning."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, what do you think?
Suppose that all sentient beings throughout a trichiliocosm, neither before nor after, were simultaneously to obtain human bodies."

There are sons and daughters of good family who, through skillful means, guide and transform others so that they all come to dwell securely in the ten paths of wholesome action; or in the four dhyānas, or the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments; or in the five supernormal powers; or in the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship; or in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, or even in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, by taking these roots of goodness from such transformative guidance and sharing them equally with all sentient beings, they dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Would these sons and daughters of good family, by reason of this cause and condition, acquire much merit?
Subhūti replied, “It would be very much,
World-Honored One!”
“Very much so,
Sugata! The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"If good sons and good daughters, within a great assembly, proclaim such profound *prajñāpāramitā*, establishing, formulating, analyzing, and elucidating it so that it may be easily understood, and correctly abide in the mental engagement associated with omniscience (*sarvajñājñāna*)."
The merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family through these causes and conditions is far greater than the former—immeasurable, incalculable, and beyond all reckoning.
"Subhūti, you should know that by the superior power of this diligence, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas reach the further shore of the field of merit for all sentient beings."

Why is this? Because the power of this bodhisattva mahāsattva’s superior diligence regarding the Dharma is such that no sentient being can equal it, with the sole exception of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.

Why is this? Because when these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they give rise to a mind of great loving-kindness (*maitrī*) upon seeing sentient beings who lack benefit and happiness; they give rise to a mind of great compassion (*karuṇā*) upon seeing sentient beings who undergo decline and suffering; they give rise to a mind of great sympathetic joy (*muditā*) upon seeing sentient beings who obtain benefit and happiness; and they give rise to a mind of great equanimity (*upekṣā*) upon seeing that sentient beings are devoid of intrinsic nature and devoid of marks—states that are not attained by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

Subhūti, you should know that although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas impartially give rise to great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity toward sentient beings, they remain unattached to anything whatsoever. They do not, like ordinary worldlings, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas, give rise to a mind of attachment following whatever arises.

“Subhūti, you should know that when these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they attain great illumination; that is to say, they attain the great illumination of the perfections from generosity up to wisdom.”

Subhūti, you should know that although these bodhisattva mahāsattvas have not yet realized the knowledge of all aspects, because they have attained non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they have reached the further shore of being a field of merit for sentient beings and are worthy of receiving all clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and all other necessities of life.

Subhūti, you should know that because this bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly dwells in mental attention associated with the perfection of wisdom, they are able to ultimately repay the kindness of their donors and also draw near to the knowledge of all modes.

Therefore, Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes not to receive in vain the faithful offerings of kings, ministers, and other sentient beings; if he wishes to show sentient beings the true and pure path; if he wishes to act as a great illumination for sentient beings; if he wishes to liberate sentient beings from the prison of the three realms; and if he wishes to bestow upon sentient beings the pure Dharma-eye, he should always dwell securely in the mental engagement associated with the profound perfection of wisdom.

“Subhūti, you should know that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly dwells in mental attention associated with the perfection of wisdom, there is no opportunity for any other mental attentions to arise in the interim.”

"Subhūti, you should know that these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are diligent day and night, constantly abiding in mental engagement associated with the perfection of wisdom, never abandoning it for even a moment."

For example, suppose there is a person who had never before possessed a mani-jewel, but later by chance obtained one; he rejoiced and congratulated himself. Then, having lost it due to some circumstance, he was overcome with great anguish and constant lamentation, never ceasing to dwell upon the thought of how he might devise a plan to recover that jewel.
Because of this associated mental attention, that person never for a moment abandons his focus on this precious gem.
In the same way, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should always abide in mental attention associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
If one does not abide in the mental engagement associated with the profound perfection of wisdom, then one loses the mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"All mental engagements are empty of intrinsic nature; all mental engagements are devoid of intrinsic nature; and all phenomena are likewise."

Within all phenomena, which are empty of intrinsic nature and devoid of intrinsic nature, neither the bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor the perfection of wisdom, nor the knowledge of all aspects, nor any mental engagements can be apprehended.

How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva remain without departing from the mental engagement associated with the perfection of wisdom, and likewise remain without departing from the mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena and all mental engagements is empty and devoid of intrinsic nature—and that such emptiness and lack of intrinsic nature were not made by śrāvakas, nor made by pratyekabuddhas, nor made by bodhisattvas, nor made by Tathāgatas, nor made by any other sentient beings; rather, that all phenomena are the fixed nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), non-falsity, non-alteration, equality, the state of being free from birth, suchness (*tathatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), and the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*)—which abide eternally as they naturally are.”

This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not depart from the mental engagement associated with the perfection of wisdom, nor does he depart from the mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes.

Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*), and all mental engagements (*manasikāra*) are by nature empty and by nature detached. Such emptiness and detachment neither increase nor decrease; to correctly penetrate them is what is called "non-detachment."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha again:

"If this profound perfection of wisdom is also empty of intrinsic nature and detached from intrinsic nature, how is it that the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, having cultivated and realized the equality of the perfection of wisdom, attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When bodhisattva mahāsattvas cultivate and realize the equality of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), there is neither increase nor decrease in the qualities of a buddha (buddhadharma). Nor is there increase or decrease in the fixed nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the stability of phenomena (dharmaniyāmatā), the nature of phenomena (dharmadhātu), the non-falsity of phenomena (avitathatā), the unchanging nature of phenomena (ananyathābhāvatā), equality, the state beyond birth (anupapatti), suchness (tathatā), the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), the realm of space (ākāśadhātu), or the inconceivable realm (acintyadhātu)."
Why is this? Because the profound perfection of wisdom is neither one, nor two, nor many.
Subhūti, you should know this!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing this teaching of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, their mind is not startled, not terrified, not afraid, does not sink, does not despair, and is free from hesitation, then that bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* to its ultimate conclusion, dwells securely on the stage of non-retrogression, and will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Is there any dharma that can be apprehended apart from the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—that is able to practice the profound perfection of wisdom?”
"No, World-Honored One! Subhūti, it is not so. "World-Honored One! [Subhūti replied.]
"Can one who abides in the stage of pure observation, up to and including the stage of a Tathāgata, practice this profound perfection of wisdom?
"No, Subhūti."
“World-Honored One!
Is there any dharma to be found that, being apart from the Stage of Pure Observation up to the Stage of the Tathāgata, is able to practice the profound perfection of wisdom?”
"No, World-Honored One! Subhūti, it is not so. "World-Honored One! [Subhūti replied.]
"Can those on the stages from the Very Joyful up to the Cloud of Dharma practice the profound perfection of wisdom?
"No, Subhūti!"
“World-Honored One!
Is there any dharma to be found—distinct from the stages beginning with the Ground of Utmost Joy and ending with the Cloud of Dharma—that can practice this profound perfection of wisdom?”
"No, World-Honored One! Subhūti, [it is not so]. "World-Honored One! [Subhūti replied.]
"Can the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi themselves practice the profound perfection of wisdom?
"No, Subhūti!"
“World-Honored One!
Is there any dharma that can be apprehended apart from the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi, which is able to practice the profound perfection of wisdom?”
"No, World-Honored One! Subhūti, it is not so. "World-Honored One! [Subhūti replied.]
“Are it the five eyes and the six supernormal powers that are able to practice the profound perfection of wisdom?
“No, Subhūti!”
“World-Honored One!
Is there any dharma apart from the five eyes and the six supernormal powers that can practice this profound *prajñāpāramitā*? “No, indeed.”
“Excellent, Subhūti!
“World-Honored One!
Is it that the Tathāgata’s ten powers, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are able to practice the profound perfection of wisdom?”
"No, World-Honored One! Subhūti, it is not so. "World-Honored One! [Subhūti replied.]
Can one who perceives any dharma as existing apart from the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha practice the profound perfection of wisdom?
"No, World-Honored One! Subhūti, [it is not so].
"World-Honored One! [Subhūti said:]
“Can great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity themselves practice the profound perfection of wisdom? “No, they cannot.”
“Subhūti! ‘World-Honored One!

Is there any dharma that can be apprehended apart from great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity, which is able to practice the profound perfection of wisdom?’”
"No, World-Honored One! Subhūti, it is not so. "World-Honored One! [Subhūti replied.]
“Can the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs themselves practice the profound perfection of wisdom? “No, they cannot.”
“Subhūti! ‘World-Honored One!
Is there any dharma that can be apprehended apart from the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs, which is able to practice the profound perfection of wisdom?’”
"No, World-Honored One! Subhūti, it is not so. "World-Honored One! [Subhūti replied.]
“Can one who possesses the quality of non-forgetfulness and abides in equanimity practice this profound perfection of wisdom?
“No, Subhūti.”
“World-Honored One!
Is there any dharma that can be apprehended—distinct from the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant abiding in equanimity—that is able to practice the profound perfection of wisdom?”
"No, World-Honored One! Subhūti, it is not so. "World-Honored One! [Subhūti replied.]
“Can one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry, up to and including the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, practice this profound perfection of wisdom?
“No, Subhūti!”
“World-Honored One!
Is there any dharma to be found—ranging from the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha—that can practice this profound perfection of wisdom?”
"No, World-Honored One! Subhūti, it is not so. "World-Honored One! [Subhūti replied.]
"Is it that all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to practice the profound perfection of wisdom?
"No, Subhūti!"
“World-Honored One!
Is there any dharma that can be apprehended apart from all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, which is able to practice the profound perfection of wisdom?”
"No, World-Honored One! Subhūti, it is not so. "World-Honored One! [Subhūti replied.]
"Is it that the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas itself can practice this profound perfection of wisdom?
"It is not so, Subhūti!"
“World-Honored One!
Is there any dharma that can be apprehended apart from the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas, which is able to practice the profound perfection of wisdom?”
“No, World-Honored One! Subhūti, it is not so. “World-Honored One! [Subhūti replied.]
"Can omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) themselves practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*? "No, they cannot."
"Subhūti! "World-Honored One!

Is there any dharma that can be apprehended apart from all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) that is able to practice the profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)?"
"No, World-Honored One! Subhūti, [it is not so]. "World-Honored One!"

Can one practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* by means of the emptiness, non-existence, lack of self-mastery, and lack of solidity of the aggregate of form, up to and including the aggregate of consciousness?
"No, World-Honored One!
[It is not so], Subhūti!
"World-Honored One!"

Is it possible for one to practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* by apprehending any dharma as having a nature that is empty, non-existent, lacking self-mastery, and unsubstantial, from the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) up to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*)?
"No, World-Honored One! Subhūti, [it is not so]. "World-Honored One! [Subhūti replied.]

In this way, up to and including whether one can practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* by means of the emptiness, non-existence, lack of self-mastery, and lack of solidity of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)?
"No, World-Honored One! Subhūti, it is not so. "World-Honored One! [Subhūti replied.]

Can one who perceives as a real entity any phenomenon that is characterized by the emptiness, non-existence, lack of sovereignty, and lack of solidity of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) practice the profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)?
"No, World-Honored One! Subhūti, [it is not so]. "World-Honored One! [Subhūti replied.]

Is it by means of the suchness of the aggregate of form up to the aggregate of consciousness—the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-falsity, the immutability, the equality, the state of being free from birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm—that one is able to practice the profound perfection of wisdom?
"No, World-Honored One! Subhūti, [it is not so]. "World-Honored One! [Subhūti replied.]

Apart from the suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-falsity, the non-alteration, the equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm of form-skandha up to consciousness-skandha, is there any dharma that can be apprehended which is able to practice the profound perfection of wisdom?
"No, World-Honored One!
"Subhūti, [is it so]?
"World-Honored One," [he replied].
