It is certainly not the case that one dwells in True Suchness and practices the bodhisattva path, thereby swiftly dwelling in the stage of non-retrogression and quickly realizing unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, in order to perform beneficial deeds for all sentient beings.
Why is this? Because the suchness of all phenomena is without arising and without cessation, nor can even the slightest portion of abiding or alteration be found. Subhūti!
If phenomena are without arising and without cessation, and not even the slightest portion of abiding or change can be found, who would abide therein to cultivate the bodhisattva practice?
Who would dwell in the stage of non-retrogression?
Who has realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
Who brings great benefit to sentient beings?
If these were truly existent, it would be impossible; they are merely provisionally designated within the conventional world.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:

"This Prajñāpāramitā is thus subtle, profound, and extremely difficult to believe and understand. Although Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the profound Prajñāpāramitā know that all dharmas are ungraspable, they nevertheless seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, desiring to bring great benefit to sentient beings; this is truly a most difficult task."

Why is this? It is because there is no one who, while dwelling in the cultivation of the bodhisattva path within *tathatā*, will not swiftly abide in the stage of non-retrogression, quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and perform beneficial deeds for all sentient beings. Yet, when these bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they contemplate that all phenomena are utterly non-existent; their minds do not sink into the profound nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and they are without confusion, without doubt, without alarm, without fear, and without bewilderment. Such matters are truly rare.
At that time, Subhūti said to Śakra: “Kauśika, it is as you have said.”

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they contemplate that all phenomena are utterly non-existent; yet their minds do not sink away from this profound nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). They are without confusion, without doubt, and are neither startled, nor terrified, nor bewildered. Such matters as these are truly rare and marvelous.

Kauśika! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they contemplate that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty; within this emptiness, nothing at all exists—so who could sink?
Who is submerged?
Who is deluded?
Who is in doubt?
Who is startled?
Who is afraid?
Who is deluded?
Who would be despondent?

Therefore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, it is not at all rare that their mind does not sink, has no confusion, no doubt, is not startled, is not terrified, and is not bewildered or despondent regarding the profound nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed Subhūti, saying:
"Whatever the Venerable One has spoken does not fail to rely upon emptiness; therefore, his words are always free from obstruction."
Just as when an arrow is shot upward into the sky, it meets no obstruction whether near or far, so too is it with what the Venerable One has spoken; who would dare to create an obstacle therein?
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:

“When I speak thus, praise thus, and declare thus, am I in accordance with the true words and the Dharma-words of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; am I in accord with the Dharma following the Dharma; is this a correct declaration?”
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, saying: “Kauśika!

That you speak thus, praise thus, and declare thus is entirely in accordance with the true words and the Dharma-words of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; it is a non-perverted declaration regarding the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma.”
Then, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying: “It is rare,
World-Honored One!”
Venerable Subhūti, everything that you say is without exception based upon emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;

it is also based upon the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, as well as the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the eight liberations up to the ten totalities. It is also based upon...
The perfections from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom also rely upon the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;
they also rely upon suchness up to the inconceivable realm; they also rely upon the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
they also rely upon the stages of the bodhisattva mahāsattva; and they also rely upon all dhāraṇīs.
They also rely on the doors of dhāraṇī and the doors of samādhi; they also rely on the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
they also rely on the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they also rely on great kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity; and they also rely on the thirty-two marks of a Great Being and the eighty secondary signs.
Furthermore, they rely on the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity;

they also rely on all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); and they rely on the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practice as well as the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed Śakra, the Lord of the Devas: “Kauśika!

The venerable Subhūti abides in the emptiness of all phenomena; he does not perceive even the perfection of giving, up to and including the perfection of wisdom, as something obtainable, much less one who practices the perfection of giving, up to and including the perfection of wisdom.”

When even the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path cannot be apprehended through contemplation, how much less can there be anyone who cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path who can be apprehended!

Since even the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments cannot be apprehended, how much less can there be anyone who cultivates the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments who can be apprehended!

If even the eight liberations up to the ten totalities cannot be apprehended when examined, how much less can there be anyone who cultivates the eight liberations up to the ten totalities who can be apprehended!

If even internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature cannot be apprehended when examined, how much less can there be anyone who dwells in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature who can be apprehended!
If even true thusness up to the inconceivable realm cannot be apprehended, how much less can one who dwells in true thusness up to the inconceivable realm be apprehended!

If even the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path cannot be apprehended, how much less can one who dwells in the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path be apprehended!

If even the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—cannot be apprehended, how much less can there be anyone who practices these gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—who could be apprehended!

When one contemplates the stages of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, even those stages themselves cannot be apprehended; how much less can there be anyone who cultivates the stages of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who can be apprehended!

When one contemplates the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi, even these cannot be apprehended; how much less can there be anyone who cultivates the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi who can be apprehended!
If one observes that even the five eyes and six supernormal powers are unobtainable, how much less can there be anyone who brings them forth!
If one observes that even the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are unobtainable, how much less can there be anyone who brings them forth!

If even great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity cannot be apprehended when contemplated, how much less can one who abides in great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity be apprehended!

If even the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs cannot be apprehended when examined, how much less can there be anyone who possesses a body adorned with such marks and signs!

Since even the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity cannot be apprehended, how much less can there be anyone who brings them forth or who could be apprehended as possessing them!

Since even omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) cannot be apprehended, how much less can there be the production or attainment of omniscience, the knowledge of the paths, or the knowledge of all aspects!

When one contemplates that even all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot be apprehended, how much less can there be anyone who can practice all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and be apprehended!

When one contemplates that even the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas cannot be apprehended, how much less can there be anyone who attains that unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas!
When one contemplates that even the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) is ultimately unattainable, how much more so could there be anyone who attains it!
When one contemplates that even the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are ultimately unattainable, how much more so could there be anyone who turns the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma!
Even the dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing cannot be apprehended when contemplated, let alone one who can realize that dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing!
Why is this? Kausika!

The Venerable Subhūti dwells in the dwelling of detachment regarding all phenomena; he dwells in the dwelling of tranquility, the dwelling of non-existence, the dwelling of non-apprehension, the dwelling of emptiness, the dwelling of signlessness, and the dwelling of wishlessness.

“Kauśika! Although the venerable Subhūti abides in such immeasurable and supreme states regarding all phenomena, compared to the profound and wondrous state of practice—the perfection of wisdom—in which the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas abides, it does not equal even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, or even a *upaniṣad* part thereof.”
Why is this? Kauśika!

With the exception of the dwelling of the Buddhas, this profound and wondrous dwelling in the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā* in which these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the most sublime, the most exquisite, the most subtle, the highest, and the unsurpassed among all the dwellings of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others.
For this reason, Kauśika,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to abide above all sentient beings, they should abide in the profound and subtle practice of the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Kauśika!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in this dwelling, they transcend the stages of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, enter the bodhisattva’s state of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*), and swiftly fulfill all Buddha-dharmas. They forever sever the continuity of the habitual tendencies of afflictions, quickly realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), and receive the names Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha. Ultimately, they bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, establishing them in the liberation of humans, devas, and the three vehicles.

At that time, immeasurable and innumerable gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven within the assembly rejoiced and leaped for joy; each took exquisite celestial flowers of subtle sound and scattered them as offerings over the Tathāgata and his disciples.

At that time, eight hundred bhikṣus within the assembly all rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, bared their right shoulders while covering the left, knelt with their right knees touching the ground, bowed with reverence, and joined their palms toward the Buddha; gazing up at his venerable countenance, they did not for a moment turn their eyes away.

By the spiritual power of the Buddha, exquisite *sūkṣmasvara* flowers spontaneously filled the palms of each member of the assembly of bhikṣus. Overjoyed and filled with unprecedented delight, they each took these flowers and scattered them over the Buddha and the various bodhisattvas.
Having scattered the flowers, they made this vow together:

"By the power of these supreme roots of goodness, may we always dwell securely in the subtle practice and abiding of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, which cannot be dwelt in by *śrāvakas* or *pratyekabuddhas*; may we swiftly proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and transcend all stages of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*."

At that time, the Tathāgata, knowing that the assembly of bhikṣus was pure in intention and firmly established in non-retrogression, smiled according to the constant custom of the Buddhas. From his face, he emitted various rays of light—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, purple, emerald, green, gold, silver, and crystal—which illuminated the entire trichiliocosm. These rays gradually withdrew and circled the Buddha’s body three times before entering through the crown of his head.
At that time, Ānanda, having beheld this auspicious omen, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness. He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated before the Buddha, joined his palms, and said:
"World-Honored One!
For what cause and for what reason do you manifest this smile?"
"The Buddhas do not manifest a smile without cause or condition; I only pray that the Tathāgata will, out of compassion, explain it for us!
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda, saying:
"In a future age known as the Nakṣatra-kalpa, all these bhikṣus shall become Buddhas, all sharing the same name, Puṣpavarṣa (Scattering Flowers), and fully possessing the ten titles."
The lifespan of those Buddhas, the lands in which they dwell, and their disciples—the bhikṣus—are all identical.

Each of these Tathāgatas abides for a thousand years; from their birth, their renunciation, and after their attainment of Buddhahood, wherever they may be, whether by day or by night, there constantly falls a rain of exquisite five-colored flowers that emit sublime sounds.
It is for this reason that I smile. Therefore, Ānanda,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to abide in the most excellent abiding, they should train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to dwell securely in the dwelling of the Tathāgata, they should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Ānanda, you should know this!”

If good sons or good daughters diligently practice and study this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, these good sons and good daughters have, in previous lives, either passed away from among humans and been reborn here, or passed away from the Tuṣita heaven and come to be born in the human world.

In previous lives, whether among humans or dwelling in the heavens, because they had extensively heard the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they are now able to diligently study and practice this profound *prajñāpāramitā* in their present life.
Ānanda, you should know this:

if a son of good family or a daughter of good family is able to diligently study and practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, without regard or attachment for body, life, or wealth, you should know that they are certainly a great bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

If sons or daughters of good family delight in hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and having heard it, they uphold, recite, master, diligently study, and contemplate it according to the principle, and then explain, reveal, instruct, and admonish it for sons or daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle; [they shall gain great merit]."

One should know that such a person is a great bodhisattva who, in the past, personally heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā* taught by a Tathāgata; having heard it, they upheld, recited, mastered, diligently practiced, and reflected upon it according to the principle. Furthermore, because they previously expounded, revealed, instructed, and advised others regarding this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they are able to accomplish these matters in their present life.

Ānanda, you should know that these sons and daughters of good family are able to perform such deeds in this present life because they have planted various roots of goodness under immeasurable Buddhas in the past.
These sons and daughters of good family should form this thought:
"I have not previously heard such a profound perfection of wisdom from śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; I must certainly have heard such a profound perfection of wisdom from the Buddhas."

I have not previously approached, made offerings to, or planted roots of virtue under Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; rather, I have certainly approached, made offerings to, and planted roots of virtue under Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

By virtue of these causes and conditions, I am now able to hear this profound Prajñāpāramitā, and with love and joy, I uphold it, read and recite it, master it, diligently practice and study it, contemplate it according to the principle, and extensively proclaim it for the sake of sentient beings without weariness.
"Ānanda, you should know this:

if sons or daughters of good family delight in hearing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and having heard it, they uphold, read, recite, master, diligently practice, and reflect upon it according to the truth—thoroughly penetrating and practicing in accordance with its phenomena (*dharma*), meaning (*artha*), phrasing (*vyañjana*), and intent—then these sons and daughters of good family are, for that very reason, seeing us Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas face to face."
“Ānanda, you should know that if sons or daughters of good family,

upon hearing the exposition of the meaning and intent of this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, develop deep faith and understanding, do not give rise to slander, and cannot be deterred or destroyed, these sons and daughters of good family have already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, have planted many roots of merit in the presence of those Buddhas, and have also been sustained by immeasurable virtuous friends.”
“Ānanda, you should know this!
If sons or daughters of good family are able to plant various roots of goodness in the presence of the Tathāgata, the Arhat,
the Samyaksaṃbuddha— the supreme field of merit— they will certainly attain either the fruit of a Śrāvaka or that of a [Pratyekabuddha].”

To realize the fruit of awakening, or the fruit of the Tathāgata, and thus attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, one must thoroughly master and remain unimpeded in the profound meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā*;
one must practice the *pāramitās* from generosity through wisdom, and abide in the emptinesses from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence. Abiding in...
From suchness up to the inconceivable realm, they abide securely in the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
they practice the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; they practice the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions;
and they practice the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
They practice the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality; they practice the stages of a bodhisattva mahāsattva;
they practice all doors of dhāraṇī and doors of samādhi; they practice the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
and they practice the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. They practice...
They practice great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity;

they cultivate the quality of non-forgetfulness and abide constantly in equanimity; and they cultivate all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects, bringing them to ultimate perfection.
“Ānanda, you should know this:

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to thoroughly master and remain unimpeded in the profound meaning and intent of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and practices the *dānapāramitā*—and so forth, as extensively explained, up to the *sarvākārajñatā*—bringing them to complete perfection, it is absolutely impossible that such a bodhisattva mahāsattva would fail to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and instead abide in the stage of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.”

Therefore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening should thoroughly master and remain unimpeded in the profound meaning and intent of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and should practice the perfection of generosity—and so forth, as extensively explained—up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) until they are fully perfected.
Therefore, Ānanda, I entrust this profound sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā to you; you should correctly receive, uphold, read, recite, and master it, so that it is never lost or forgotten.
"Ānanda, you should know this:
apart from this profound sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom, if one were to forget or lose any other teachings of mine that have been received and upheld, the fault would still be light."
If one does not properly uphold this profound sūtra of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and forgets even a single phrase, the transgression is extremely grave.
Ānanda, you should know that if one is able to properly receive, uphold, and not forget even a single verse from this profound sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā, the merit obtained will be immeasurable.
If one does not properly uphold this profound sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā, and should forget even a single verse, the grave sin incurred will be equal in measure to the aforementioned merit.

Therefore, Ānanda! I entrust this profound sūtra of the *prajñāpāramitā* to you with earnest care. You should correctly receive and uphold it, read and recite it until it is mastered, contemplate it according to the principle, explain it extensively to others, and analyze and reveal it, so that those who uphold it may ultimately understand its words, meanings, and underlying intent.
“Ānanda, you should know this!

If sons or daughters of good family receive, uphold, read, recite, master, reflect upon according to principle, extensively explain to others, analyze, and elucidate this profound *prajñāpāramitā* so that others may understand it, they will thereby receive, uphold, and grasp the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment realized by all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present.”
“Ānanda, you should know this!

If sons or daughters of good family give rise to a profound and pure mind and appear before me, desiring to offer various kinds of exquisite flower garlands up to lamps for the purpose of making offerings, honoring, respecting, and praising [the Tathāgata] without weariness, they should, with a sincere heart, listen to, receive, uphold, read, recite, master, reflect upon according to the principle, extensively explain to others, and analyze and reveal the *Prajñāpāramitā* so that others may understand it; or else, having transcribed it adorned with various jewels, they should constantly offer various kinds of exquisite flower garlands up to lamps to it, honoring, respecting, and praising it without ever becoming weary or ceasing.
Ānanda, you should know this:

if sons and daughters of good family offer worship, respect, honor, and praise to the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they are thereby offering worship, respect, honor, and praise to me and to all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Ānanda, you should know this:

if sons or daughters of good family, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, give rise to a heart of earnest purity, reverence, and love, they will immediately give rise to a heart of earnest purity, reverence, and love toward the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment realized by all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present.
Ānanda! If you love me and do not forsake me, you should likewise love and not forsake this profound sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā, ensuring that not even a single phrase is forgotten or lost.

“Ānanda! Even if one were to spend immeasurable hundreds of thousands of great kalpas explaining the causes and conditions for entrusting such profound sūtras as this Prajñāpāramitā, they could not be exhausted. To state the essentials: just as I am your teacher, you should know that the profound Prajñāpāramitā is also your teacher. Just as you revere and honor me, O gods and humans, you should likewise revere and honor the profound Prajñāpāramitā.”

Therefore, Ānanda! By means of immeasurable skillful means, I entrust to you this profound sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā; you should receive and uphold it so as not to let it be lost. Now, in the presence of this great assembly of devas, humans, asuras, and others, I hold this profound Prajñāpāramitā and entrust it to you; you should correctly receive and uphold it so as not to let it be lost.
"Ānanda! I now tell you this in truth:

those who possess pure faith and do not wish to forsake the Buddha, do not wish to forsake the Dharma, do not wish to forsake the Saṅgha, and furthermore do not wish to forsake the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment realized by the Buddhas of the three times, must certainly not forsake the profound Prajñāpāramitā. This is what we call the method of instruction and admonition for our disciples."

“Ānanda, you should know that if sons or daughters of good family delight in hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and if they receive, uphold, read, recite, master it thoroughly, and contemplate it according to the principle; and if they extensively explain it to others through immeasurable gateways, analyzing, revealing, establishing, and instituting it so that others may understand and practice it with diligence—then these sons and daughters of good family will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and will be able to draw near to the fulfillment of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).”

Why is this? Because the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas and the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) are both produced in dependence upon this profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Ānanda, you should know that all Buddhas of the three periods of time have given birth to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by relying upon this very profound perfection of wisdom."

Therefore, Ānanda! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should diligently apply themselves with vigor to study this profound perfection of wisdom.
Why is this so? Because this profound *prajñāpāramitā* is the mother of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, for it gives birth to all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
“Ānanda, you should know that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva diligently trains in the six perfections, they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
Therefore, Ānanda! I entrust these six pāramitās to you once again; you should receive and uphold them correctly so that they are not lost or forgotten. Why is this?
These six perfections are the inexhaustible treasury of the Dharma of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, for all the Buddha-dharmas arise from them.

“Ānanda, you should know that all the essential teachings spoken by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, flow forth from this inexhaustible Dharma-treasury of the six perfections.”
Ānanda, you should know that the Buddhas,

the World-Honored Ones, of the ten directions and the three periods of time, all diligently practiced and studied the inexhaustible Dharma-treasury of the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) and thereby realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).

Ānanda, you should know that the śrāvaka disciples of all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, have all diligently practiced and studied the inexhaustible Dharma-treasury of the six pāramitās, and have entered, are entering, or will enter nirvana without remainder.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

Even if you were to teach the Dharma of the Śrāvaka vehicle to those of the Śrāvaka vehicle, and by means of that Dharma all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were to attain the fruit of Arhatship, you would still not have performed what is required of a disciple of the Buddha."

If you can expound even a single verse of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in accordance with the Dharma for one who belongs to the Bodhisattva vehicle, that shall be called performing for me the duty of a disciple of the Buddha; I shall feel deep sympathetic joy regarding this matter, which is superior to your teaching all sentient beings in a trichiliocosm so that they all attain the fruit of Arhatship.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

Suppose all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm, through the power of another's instruction, were simultaneously to obtain human bodies and at once realize the fruit of arhatship; then consider all the meritorious deeds consisting of giving, morality, and cultivation belonging to those arhats."
"What do you think? Would that meritorious deed be great? Ānanda replied:
“Very much so,
World-Honored One!
Very much so!”
“Sugata! That meritorious deed is immeasurable and boundless.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If there were a śrāvaka who could proclaim for a bodhisattva the teachings associated with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), the mass of merit obtained by that [bodhisattva] in a single day and night would be far greater than that."

Ānanda, you should know this! Setting aside one day and night, let us consider just one day; setting aside one day, let us consider just half a day; setting aside half a day, let us consider just one watch (muhūrta); setting aside one watch, let us consider just the time it takes to eat a meal; setting aside the time for a meal, let us consider just a brief moment (kṣaṇa); setting aside a brief moment, let us consider just an instant (tatkṣaṇa); and setting aside an instant, let us consider just the snap of a finger. If a śrāvaka were to proclaim to a bodhisattva the Dharma associated with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) for even that duration, the mass of merit obtained would be far greater than the former.
Why is this? Because the mass of merit obtained by these śrāvakas surpasses all the roots of goodness of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva were to proclaim various Śrāvaka vehicles for the sake of śrāvakas, and if, by means of these teachings, all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm were to realize the fruit of arhatship and come to possess all manner of sublime qualities;
"What do you think?
Is the mass of merit obtained by this bodhisattva mahāsattva through these causes and conditions not great? Ānanda replied:
“Very much so,
World-Honored One!
Very much so!”
“Sugata! The mass of merit obtained by this bodhisattva mahāsattva is immeasurable and boundless.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva were to teach the Dharma associated with the perfection of wisdom to sons of good family belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas, or the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, or the unsurpassed vehicle, for a single day and night, the mass of merit obtained would be far greater than the former.”

Ānanda, you should know this! Setting aside one day and night, let us consider just one day; setting aside one day, let us consider just half a day; setting aside half a day, let us consider just one watch (muhūrta); setting aside one watch, let us consider just the time it takes to eat a meal; setting aside the time for a meal, let us consider just a brief moment; setting aside a brief moment, let us consider just a fleeting instant; and setting aside a fleeting instant, let us consider just the snap of a finger. If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can proclaim to sons of good family of the three vehicles the Dharma associated with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) during even that duration, the mass of merit they obtain will be infinitely and incalculably greater than the former.

Why is this? Because the gift of Dharma associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā* surpasses all gifts of Dharma associated with the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, as well as all the roots of goodness belonging to those two vehicles.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas seek unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment for themselves, and they also manifest, instruct, encourage, inspire, and gladden other sentient beings with dharmas corresponding to the Great Vehicle, causing them to attain non-retrogression from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

“Ānanda, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva personally cultivates the six perfections and also teaches others to cultivate the six perfections; and so on, in detail, up to personally cultivating the knowledge of all aspects and also teaching others to cultivate the knowledge of all aspects.”
"By this cause and condition, one's roots of virtue will increase; it is impossible that one would ever regress from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

At that time, the World-Honored One, surrounded by the fourfold assembly, having praised and expounded the Prajñāpāramitā and entrusted it to Ānanda for him to uphold, further [addressed] all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas...
Before the great assembly of Dāva and others, he manifested supernatural powers, causing everyone to see the Tathāgata,
Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Acalanātha, surrounded by a great multitude of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas,
preaching the sublime Dharma to the ocean-like assembly, as well as the signs of the pure adornments of that land; and [they saw] his śrāvaka-saṃgha.
They were all arhats whose outflows were exhausted and who were free from further afflictions, having attained true mastery;

their minds were well-liberated and their wisdom was well-liberated. Like well-trained intelligent horses or great dragons, they had done what was to be done and accomplished what was to be accomplished;
they had laid down the heavy burdens and achieved their own benefit, having completely severed the fetters of existence.
They possess knowledge of liberation, reaching the ultimate pinnacle of sovereign mastery of mind.
This assembly of Bodhisattvas is entirely renowned to all; they have attained *dhāraṇīs* and unimpeded eloquence, and have accomplished immeasurable, sublime merits.

The Buddha withdrew his supernormal power, causing the assembly of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others to no longer see that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Akṣobhya, nor the śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and the rest of the great multitude, along with the signs of the pure adornments of that buddha-field.
The assembly of that Buddha and his adorned pure land are not objects perceived by the visual faculty of this land.
Why is this? Because the Buddha has withdrawn his supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), and thus there is no causal condition for seeing those distant realms.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Do you see again the land and the assembly of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Akṣobhya?"
Ānanda said, “I no longer see it,
for that matter is not within the range of these eyes.
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:

"Just as the assembly and the land of that Tathāgata are not within the range of the eyes of this land, you should know that all phenomena are likewise not within the range of the eye-faculty and the other sense faculties."
“Ānanda, you should know this:
a dharma does not proceed toward a dharma; a dharma does not see a dharma; a dharma does not know a dharma; a dharma does not realize a dharma.
Ānanda, you should know this!”
The nature of all phenomena cannot be practiced, cannot be seen, cannot be known, and cannot be realized; it is without movement and without action.
Why is this so? Because all phenomena are devoid of functional activity, being far removed from the nature of grasper and grasped.
Because all phenomena are inconceivable, being far removed from the nature of that which conceives and that which is conceived.
Because all phenomena are like illusions and the like, appearing to exist through the convergence of various conditions;
and because all phenomena lack an agent or recipient, falsely manifesting as if they existed while lacking any solid reality.

Ānanda, you should know that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice in this way, see in this way, know in this way, and realize in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and yet they do not cling to the characteristics of these phenomena.
Ānanda, you should know that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they are training in the perfection of wisdom.
Ānanda, you should know!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to swiftly fulfill all the pāramitās and reach the ultimate further shore of all phenomena, they should study the prajñāpāramitā.

Why is this so? Because for those who train in this manner, among all forms of training, it is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the most exalted, the most sublime, the most subtle, the highest, and the unsurpassed; it brings benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, providing refuge and protection to those who are without refuge or protection. Thus, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have authorized, permitted, and praised the cultivation and study of the *prajñāpāramitā*.

“Ānanda, you should know that after all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have trained in this training and abided within this training, they are able to take up the trichiliocosm with their right hand or the tip of their right toe and cast it elsewhere or return it to its original place, such that the sentient beings therein are unaware and unperceiving, and suffer neither injury nor fear.”

Why is this? The merit and power of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* are inconceivable; the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present, by training in this *prajñāpāramitā*, have all attained unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding the dharmas of the past, future, present, and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Therefore, Ānanda, I declare that among all trainings,
the training in the profound perfection of wisdom is the foremost, the most excellent, the most venerable, the highest, the most sublime, the most exquisite, the supreme, and the unsurpassed.
“Ānanda, you should know this:
those who wish to grasp the measure or the limit of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* are like foolish people who wish to grasp the measure and the limit of space.”
Why is this? Because the merit of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is immeasurable and boundless.
"Ānanda, you should know this!"
I never say that the merit and excellence of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* have a measure or a limit, such as those possessed by names, bodies, and so forth. Why is this?

The collections of names, phrases, and syllables are phenomena that are finite; however, the meritorious benefits of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* are not finite phenomena. It is not by means of the collections of names and so forth that the meritorious benefits of the *prajñāpāramitā* can be measured, nor are those meritorious benefits of the *prajñāpāramitā* the objects measured by them.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what causes and conditions is the profound *prajñāpāramitā* said to be immeasurable?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“Because the nature of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is inexhaustible, because its nature is detached, because its nature is quiescent, because it is like the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and because it is like space, it is said to be immeasurable.”

Ānanda, you should know that all Buddhas of the three periods of time study the Prajñāpāramitā, ultimately perfecting it and realizing unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, which they then proclaim and reveal to all sentient beings; yet this Prajñāpāramitā is eternally inexhaustible.
Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is like space and cannot be exhausted.
Whoever wishes to exhaust the profound *prajñāpāramitā* would be wishing to exhaust the limits of space.
"Ānanda, you should know that because the six perfections,
beginning with giving, and so forth up to the knowledge of all modes, are inexhaustible, they have not been exhausted, are not being exhausted, and will not be exhausted."
"Why is this? Because such dharmas as these are without arising, without cessation, and without abiding or change; how could they be established as having an end?
At that time, the Tathāgata extended his broad and long tongue from his mouth, covering his entire face, and having manifested this tongue-mark, he withdrew it back into his mouth.
He addressed Ānanda, saying: "What do you think?
If one possessed such a tongue-mark as this in the world, would the speech uttered by them ever be false?"
Ānanda replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"From this day forward, you should extensively expound such profound *prajñāpāramitā* for the fourfold assembly; analyze, reveal, establish, and define it so that it may be easily understood."

Ānanda, you should know that within this profound and secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) and the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are extensively explained. Therefore, all sons of good family who seek the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, or the unsurpassed vehicle, should rely upon these dharma-gates taught in this profound *prajñāpāramitā* and constantly and diligently practice them without becoming weary.
If one can thus constantly and diligently practice and study, one shall swiftly realize the goal sought for oneself. "Furthermore, Ānanda!

This profound *prajñāpāramitā* is that which enables entry into the characteristics of all phenomena; it is that which enables entry into all syllables; it is that which enables entry into the gates of *dhāraṇī*. All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should constantly and diligently practice and study such gates of *dhāraṇī*."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva upholds such dharanī-gates, they will swiftly be able to realize all forms of eloquence and the analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid).
Ānanda, you should know this!

This profound *prajñāpāramitā* is the inexhaustible Dharma-treasury of all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present; it sustains and upholds all subtle and wondrous Buddha-dharmas.

Therefore, I now tell you clearly: if there are those who receive, uphold, read, recite, master, and correctly contemplate this profound Prajñāpāramitā, they are upholding the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment attained by all Buddhas of the three times.
Ānanda, you should know!

This profound *prajñāpāramitā* that I have taught is the firm foot for those who travel upon the path to enlightenment; it is also the great *dhāraṇī* of all unsurpassed Buddha-dharmas. If you are able to receive and uphold this profound *prajñāpāramitā* *dhāraṇī*, you will thereby maintain all Buddha-dharmas and bring benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 520–523. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Order. Chapter 26: Skill in Means (Upāyakauśalya), Part Three. Section One of Chapter Twenty-Six: Skill in Means. At that time, Subhūti thought to himself:

"This Prajñāpāramitā is most profound, and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is also most profound. I shall now question the Buddha regarding these two profound meanings."
Having formed this thought, he addressed the Buddha, saying:

"The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) of the Buddhas; the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas is the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. Since both this *prajñāpāramitā* and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas are equally most profound and inexhaustible, for what reason are these two said to be 'inexhaustible'?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha are both like space and cannot be exhausted, they are said to be inexhaustible."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva bring forth the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that form is inexhaustible;
they should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are inexhaustible;
and so on, in detail, until they bring forth the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that even the knowledge of all modes is inexhaustible.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that form is inexhaustible like space;
they should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are inexhaustible like space."

To speak extensively, up to: one should contemplate that the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) is like space and inexhaustible; thus one brings forth the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that formations conditioned by ignorance are as inexhaustible as space;
they should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that consciousness conditioned by formations is as inexhaustible as space;
they should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by contemplating that name-and-form conditioned by consciousness is as inexhaustible as space.
One should contemplate that name-and-form conditions the six sense bases as being inexhaustible like space, thereby eliciting the perfection of wisdom;
one should contemplate that the six sense bases condition contact as being inexhaustible like space, thereby eliciting the perfection of wisdom;
one should contemplate that contact conditions feeling as being inexhaustible like space, thereby eliciting the perfection of wisdom.
One should contemplate that feeling conditions craving as being inexhaustible like space, thereby giving rise to the perfection of wisdom;
one should contemplate that craving conditions grasping as being inexhaustible like space, thereby giving rise to the perfection of wisdom;
one should contemplate that grasping conditions becoming as being inexhaustible like space, thereby giving rise to the perfection of wisdom.
One should contemplate that birth conditioned by existence is as inexhaustible as space, and thereby bring forth the perfection of wisdom;
one should contemplate that old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair conditioned by birth are as inexhaustible as space, and thereby bring forth the perfection of wisdom.
"Subhūti, you should know that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should bring forth the perfection of wisdom in this manner.
Subhūti, you should know!"

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas observe the twelve links of dependent origination in this manner, they remain far removed from the two extremes; this is the sublime contemplation unique to the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

"Subhūti, you should know that when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas sit beneath the Bodhi tree upon the diamond throne, they observe the twelve links of dependent origination as being like space and inexhaustible; thus, they are able to realize the knowledge of all modes."

"Subhūti, you should know that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom with a mode of practice as inexhaustible as space, and observes dependent origination as it truly is, they will not fall into the levels of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

“Subhūti, you should know that if those sons of good family who abide in the vehicle of the bodhisattvas should regress from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, it is because they all fail to rely on the skillful mental engagement that brings forth the perfection of wisdom. This is due to their lack of understanding:

how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, can observe the twelve links of dependent origination in accordance with reality through an inexhaustible mode of activity like space, thereby bringing forth the perfection of wisdom.”

"Subhūti, you should know that if sons of good family who abide in the bodhisattva vehicle should regress from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, it is entirely due to their being far removed from the skillful means that induce the perfection of wisdom."

"Subhūti, you should know that all bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment do so by relying entirely upon the skillful means that induce the perfection of wisdom."

By relying on such skillful means, this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom and, through the mode of practice that is inexhaustible like space, brings forth the perfection of wisdom and observes the twelve links of dependent origination as they truly are.
By means of these causes and conditions, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly be able to fulfill the profound perfection of wisdom.
"Subhūti, you should know this!"

When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas thus contemplate the dharma of dependent origination, they do not perceive any dharma arising without a cause, nor do they perceive any dharma ceasing without a cause. They do not perceive any dharma whose nature and characteristics are eternally abiding, neither arising nor ceasing. They do not perceive any dharma that possesses a self, a sentient being—and so on, as extensively explained—up to a knower or a seer. They do not perceive any dharma that is either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or non-tranquil, or secluded or non-secluded.
"Subhūti, you should know that bodhisattva mahāsattvas should always observe dependent origination in this way and practice the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti, you should know!"

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva observes the dharma-gate of dependent origination as it truly is and practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), at that time the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) up to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) as either permanent or impermanent, as either pleasant or painful, as either self or non-self, as either pure or impure, as either tranquil or non-tranquil, or as either secluded or non-secluded; and so on, in detail, until he does not perceive even the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) as either permanent or impermanent, as either pleasant or painful, as either self or non-self, as either pure or impure, as either tranquil or non-tranquil, or as either secluded or non-secluded.
Subhūti, you should know this:

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, although at that time the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive any perfection of wisdom being practiced; nor do they perceive any dharma that can perceive the perfection of wisdom being practiced; nor do they perceive such non-perception itself.

Although they practice the perfections of dhyāna, vīrya, kṣānti, śīla, and dāna, they do not perceive any such thing as the practice of the perfection of dhyāna up to the perfection of dāna; nor do they perceive any dharma that can perceive the practice of the perfection of dhyāna up to the perfection of dāna; nor do they perceive even such non-perception.

To speak at length, even when cultivating the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), one does not perceive that there is a knowledge of all modes being cultivated; nor does one perceive any dharma that can perceive the knowledge of all modes being cultivated; nor does one perceive such non-perception itself.
"Subhūti, you should know that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension regarding all phenomena."
"Subhūti, you should know this!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension regarding all phenomena, at that time Māra the Evil One gives rise to great distress and affliction, as if pierced by a poisoned arrow; just as a person whose parents have suddenly passed away suffers physical and mental agony, so it is with Māra."
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Is it because a single evil Māra sees all bodhisattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom through the skillful means of non-apprehension regarding all phenomena that he gives rise to great anguish, as if pierced by a poisoned arrow?”
"Is it the case that all the evil Māras throughout the entire trichiliocosm are likewise so?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"All the evil Māras filling the entire trichiliocosm are likewise so; each is unable to remain at ease upon their own seats."

“Subhūti, you should know that all bodhisattva mahāsattvas should always abide in the true, pure conduct and dwelling of the profound perfection of wisdom. If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can always abide in the true, pure conduct and dwelling of the profound perfection of wisdom, then gods, humans, asuras, and others of the world will never be able to find any fault in them, nor will they be able to disturb or obstruct them.”

Therefore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they should diligently abide in the true and pure practice of the profound perfection of wisdom.

“Subhūti, you should know that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva can correctly abide in the true, pure practice and dwelling of profound prajñāpāramitā, they will be able to cultivate and fulfill the pāramitās of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom. If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can correctly practice profound prajñāpāramitā, they will be able to fully cultivate and fulfill all the pāramitās.”
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva correctly practice the profound perfection of wisdom, such that they are able to cultivate and fulfill the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom without error, they practice giving up to wisdom with a mind associated with the knowledge of all modes, and dedicate these merits together with all sentient beings toward the knowledge of all modes.”
Thus it is, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to practice the profound perfection of wisdom correctly, they are then able to cultivate and fulfill the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of generosity, attract and gather the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving with a mind free from attachment and free from stinginess, and dedicates this giving together with all sentient beings toward the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), and gives rise to compassionate bodily, verbal, and mental actions toward all sentient beings while remaining far removed from unwholesome precepts—this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva abiding in the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā) and thereby attracting and encompassing the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā)."

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving with a mind free from attachment and free from stinginess, and dedicates this gift together with all sentient beings toward omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), if the recipients or other sentient beings should unreasonably revile, resent, harm, or insult them, the bodhisattva does not give rise to any altered state of anger, resentment, or malice, nor does he retaliate through body or speech. Instead, he gives rise only to a heart of pity and compassion, responding with gentle words, shame, and humble apology. This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), draws forth and encompasses the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*)."

"When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices giving with a mind free from attachment and free from stinginess, he dedicates this gift together with all sentient beings toward the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). If the recipients or other sentient beings should unreasonably revile, disparage, harm, or insult him, the Bodhisattva then reflects:
'Those who perform such types of actions will themselves experience such types of results; I should not now take account of what they have done and thereby neglect my own practice.'"
Furthermore, he forms this thought:
"I should cause the mind of equanimity and the mind of giving toward those beings and other sentient beings to increase even more, without any sense of regret or attachment.

Having formed this thought, he initiates superior physical and mental diligence and constantly practices generous relinquishment; this is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s dwelling in the perfection of generosity while attracting and gathering the perfection of diligence.

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing generosity with a mind free from attachment and free from stinginess, takes this generosity and dedicates it together with all sentient beings toward omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*); if their mind remains undistracted regarding the recipients and other objects, seeking neither the desires of the triple world nor the vehicles of the two vehicles, but seeking only the fruit of Buddhahood—this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s abiding in the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) that draws forth and encompasses the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*)."

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving with a mind free from attachment and free from stinginess, and dedicates this giving together with all sentient beings toward omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*); if they contemplate the recipients, the giver, and the gift as all being like illusory phenomena; if they do not perceive this giving as either harmful or beneficial to sentient beings; and if they realize that all dharmas are ultimately empty and ungraspable—this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva abiding in the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) while drawing forth the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of ethical discipline, attract and gather the perfections from generosity up to wisdom?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), possessing restraint of body, restraint of speech, and restraint of mind, and performs various meritorious deeds—by virtue of which meritorious deeds they abstain from taking life up to and including wrong views—and seeks not the level of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, but seeks only unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi).”

At that time, the bodhisattva dwells securely in pure ethical discipline and extensively practices generosity: providing food to those sentient beings who need food, drink to those who need drink, and other necessities to those who need them. Furthermore, taking these roots of goodness from such giving, they share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, seeking neither the level of a śrāvaka nor that of a pratyekabuddha. This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of ethical discipline, draws forth and encompasses the perfection of generosity.

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā), even if sentient beings should come vying with one another to sever the limbs and joints of that bodhisattva, taking each part away, the bodhisattva would not give rise to even a single thought of anger or resentment toward them, but would instead think:
‘I have now obtained a vast and sublime benefit; namely, by relinquishing this foul-smelling, putrid, and fragile body, I shall attain the Buddha’s pure vajra-body.’”
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), draws forth and encompasses the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*).

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of ethical discipline, they apply physical and mental diligence constantly and without interruption, donning the armor of great compassion and making this vast vow:
'All sentient beings are submerged in the ocean of suffering; I shall pull them out and establish them in the nectar of nirvāṇa.'"
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), draws forth the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of ethical discipline, although they enter the first dhyāna up to the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*), they do not fall into the levels of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor do they realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Because they are sustained by the power of their original vows, they think:

"All classes of sentient beings are submerged in the ocean of suffering and cannot emerge on their own. Since I now abide in pure morality (*śīla*), I shall employ skillful means to bring forth supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), and shall certainly pull them out and establish them in the eternal bliss of nirvāṇa."
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of ethical discipline, draws forth and encompasses the perfection of meditative concentration.

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), they do not perceive any phenomenon—whether conditioned or unconditioned, falling into the realm of signs or the signless, falling into the realm of the numbered or the numberless—but observes only that all phenomena are not separate from suchness (*tathatā*), extending broadly even to the inconceivable realm (*acintya-dhātu*). Since these suchnesses and so forth are also unapprehendable, through this skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*), they do not fall into the levels of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but proceed solely toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of ethical discipline, draws forth and encompasses the perfection of wisdom."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of patience, attract and gather the perfections from generosity up to wisdom?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in the perfection of patience, from the first generation of the mind of awakening until sitting upon the seat of sublime enlightenment, should there arise various kinds of sentient beings who unreasonably revile, despise, or humiliate him, even going so far as to sever his limbs and carry them away, at that time the bodhisattva feels no anger whatsoever.

He thinks only this: ‘These sentient beings are deeply pitiable; their bodies and minds are disturbed by the poison of afflictions and they lack self-mastery. Having no refuge and no protector, they are oppressed by poverty and suffering. I shall give them whatever food, drink, clothing, and other requisites they desire.’”

Furthermore, taking these roots of goodness from such giving, they share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, employing the method of non-apprehension.
When dedicating in this manner toward great enlightenment, one remains free from three thoughts: namely, who is dedicating?
what is being dedicated? and by means of what is it being dedicated?
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of patience, draws forth the perfection of generosity.

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in the perfection of patience, from the first generation of the mind of awakening until sitting upon the seat of sublime enlightenment, throughout that interval, even for the sake of saving his own life, he never harms any sentient being, nor does he ever give rise to any evil or false views."

When a bodhisattva thus cultivates pure ethical discipline, they do not seek the levels of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; furthermore, they take these roots of virtue from such pure ethical discipline and, together with all sentient beings, dedicate them equally toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, employing the method of non-apprehension.
When dedicating in this manner toward great enlightenment, one remains free from the three thoughts: namely, who is dedicating?
What is being dedicated?
And by means of what is it dedicated?
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of patience, draws forth the perfection of ethical discipline.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of patience, initiates courageous and superior diligence, they constantly reflect:
"If even a single sentient being were located one *yojana* away, or ten, or a hundred, or even..."
Beyond the measure of *yojanas*, or outside a single world-system, or beyond ten, a hundred,
or even an infinite number of world-systems— whosoever is capable of being delivered, I shall certainly go to them and employ skillful means to teach and transform them,
causing them to receive and uphold either the eight precepts, the five precepts, or the ten precepts. Or...
Even if one were to cause them to possess the training rules, or cause them to abide in the fruit of stream-entry, or cause them to abide in the fruit of once-returning,
or cause them to abide in the fruit of non-returning, or cause them to abide in the fruit of arhatship, or cause them to abide in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha,
or cause them to dwell securely in the bodhisattva stages up to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, [they] would still not...

"How much less, then, should one become weary or indolent when acting for the sake of teaching and transforming immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings, so as to cause them all to obtain benefit and happiness!

Furthermore, he takes these roots of merit from such diligence and, through the skillful means of non-apprehension, dedicates them equally and in common with all sentient beings toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
When dedicating in this manner toward great enlightenment, one remains free from three thoughts: namely, who is dedicating?
What is being dedicated?
And by means of what is it dedicated?
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of patience, draws forth the perfection of diligence.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of patience, gathers the mind so that it is not distracted, and—free from desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion—enters the first dhyāna, and so on as extensively described until entering the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling; then, regarding all the minds, mental factors, and roots of goodness that arise within these various concentrations, he unites them all and, together with all sentient beings, dedicates them equally toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, employing the method of non-apprehension.
When dedicating in this way toward great enlightenment, one remains free from three thoughts: namely, who is dedicating?
What is being dedicated?
And by what means is it dedicated?
They do not apprehend any of the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) or their constituent factors (*dhyānāṅga*).
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*), brings forth and gathers the perfection of concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in the perfection of patience while practicing the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the contemplation of phenomena among all dharmas. Although they contemplate all dharmas through the aspect of detachment, or the aspect of tranquility, or the aspect of inexhaustibility, or the aspect of ultimate cessation, they do not realize the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). Thus, they are able to sit upon the sublime seat of enlightenment and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening; rising from that seat, they turn the sublime wheel of Dharma to benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings."

Furthermore, taking these roots of goodness of such sublime wisdom, they share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, employing the method of non-apprehension.
When dedicating in this manner toward great enlightenment, one remains free from three thoughts: namely, who is dedicating?
What is being dedicated?
And by means of what is it dedicated?
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of patience, draws forth the perfection of wisdom; such drawing forth is neither grasping nor abandoning.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of diligence, attract and gather the perfections from generosity up to wisdom?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of diligence, with physical and mental vigor never flagging or resting, seeking all wholesome dharmas without weariness, they should constantly think:
‘I must certainly attain the knowledge of all modes; it is not possible that I shall not attain it.’”
This bodhisattva mahāsattva, desiring to benefit all sentient beings, constantly makes this vow:

"If there is even a single sentient being beyond one *yojana*, or ten, or a hundred, or even an immeasurable number of *yojanas* away; or if there are those who should be delivered beyond a single world-system, or ten, or a hundred, or even an immeasurable number of world-systems—I shall certainly go to them and, through skillful means, teach and transform those sons of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva Vehicle, causing them to abide in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
and those sons of good family belonging to the Śrāvaka Vehicle, causing them to abide in the fruits of Stream-enterer, Once-returner, Non-returner, or Arhat."
If there are sons of good family belonging to the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, he causes them to dwell securely in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;

if there are other sentient beings, he causes them to dwell securely in the ten paths of wholesome action. In this way, he draws them in and sustains them through the skillful means of providing both the gift of Dharma and material gifts.

Furthermore, taking these roots of goodness from such giving, they share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, seeking neither the stage of a śrāvaka nor that of a pratyekabuddha, employing the method of non-apprehension.
When dedicating in this manner toward great enlightenment, one remains free from three thoughts: namely, who is it that dedicates?
What is it that is dedicated?
And by what means is it dedicated?
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of diligence, draws forth and encompasses the perfection of generosity.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of diligence, from the first generation of the mind of awakening until sitting upon the seat of sublime enlightenment, they personally abstain from taking life up to and including wrong views; they also encourage others to abstain from taking life up to and including wrong views; they correctly extol the dharmas of abstaining from taking life up to and including wrong views; and they joyfully praise those who abstain from taking life up to and including wrong views.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva maintains this perfection of pure ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) without seeking the fruits of the two vehicles or the three realms; rather, they take these roots of goodness from such pure ethical discipline and, together with all sentient beings, dedicate them equally toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), employing the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*).
When dedicating in this way toward great enlightenment, one remains free from three thoughts: namely, who is dedicating?
What is being dedicated?
And by means of what is it dedicated?
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of diligence, draws forth and encompasses the perfection of ethical discipline.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of diligence, from the first generation of the mind of awakening until sitting upon the seat of sublime enlightenment, during that interval, humans, non-humans, and others may come in competition to harass and provoke them; or they may hack, pierce, and cut off their limbs and members, taking them away as they please.
At that time, the bodhisattva does not form this thought:
"Who is hacking and piercing me?
Who is cutting and dismembering me?"
"Who else could take them away? He simply thought:
"I have now obtained vast and excellent benefit; those sentient beings have come to sever and cut my body limb from limb for my own sake."
"However, I originally took on this body for the sake of all sentient beings; since he has come here to take what belongs to himself, he is thereby accomplishing my purpose.

In this way, the bodhisattva reflects with precision upon the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) and cultivates patience (*kṣānti*). Taking these superior roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) of patience, they do not seek the levels of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, but rather, with the non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) as their skillful means, they share these roots of goodness of patience equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
When dedicating in this manner toward great enlightenment, one remains free from three thoughts: namely, who is it that dedicates?
What is it that is dedicated?
And by what means is it dedicated?
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of diligence, draws forth the perfection of patience.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of diligence, they diligently cultivate various meditative concentrations: namely, being free from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, they enter the first dhyāna; and so on, as extensively described, up to entering the fourth dhyāna.

Toward all sentient beings, they conceive the thought of bestowing happiness and enter the immeasurable state of loving-kindness (maitrī); and so on, as extensively described, up to entering the immeasurable state of equanimity (upekṣā).

Regarding all forms, they give rise to the perception of revulsion toward coarseness and enter the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space; as explained at length, they proceed even unto entering the meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling.

Although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter such dhyānas, immeasurables, formless attainments, and the absorption of cessation, they do not appropriate their karmic maturation. Rather, in accordance with where sentient beings may be ready for conversion, they take birth in those places to act for their benefit.
Once born there, they benefit sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) and the six perfections (*pāramitā*).

Relying upon these meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas manifest superior supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and travel from one buddha-field to another. There, they attend upon and make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, inquire about the profound nature and characteristics of all phenomena, and diligently cultivate and bring forth supreme roots of goodness.
Taking these roots of goodness as a means through non-apprehension, they share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
When dedicating in this manner toward great enlightenment, one remains free from three thoughts: namely, who is dedicating?
What is being dedicated?
And by what means is it dedicated?
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*), draws forth the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).
