If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of diligence, they do not perceive the names, entities, natures, or characteristics of anything from the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom; they do not perceive the names, entities, natures, or characteristics of anything from the four applications of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; they do not perceive the names, entities, natures, or characteristics of even the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvajñajñāna*); nor do they perceive the names, entities, natures, or characteristics of any phenomena (*dharmas*) at all. Within all phenomena, they give rise to no conceptualizations and remain without attachment, acting exactly as it is taught.

Furthermore, they take these roots of goodness of such sublime wisdom and, through the skillful means of non-apprehension, dedicate them equally and in common with all sentient beings toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
When dedicating in this manner toward great enlightenment, one remains free from three thoughts: namely, who is it that dedicates?
What is it that is dedicated?
And by what means is it dedicated?
"This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of diligence, draws forth and encompasses the perfection of wisdom.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again:
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration, draw forth and encompass the perfections from generosity up to wisdom?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā), he practices the giving of material goods and the Dharma to all sentient beings; that is to say, free from desire and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained investigation, born of seclusion, joyful and blissful, he enters the first dhyāna, and so on, as extensively described, up to entering the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling."
This bodhisattva mahāsattva, with an undistracted mind, proclaims the true Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings and practices the giving of material wealth and the Dharma.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly practices the giving of material wealth and the Dharma himself, and also constantly encourages others to practice the giving of material wealth and the Dharma; he always correctly extols the method of practicing the giving of material wealth and the Dharma, and always joyfully praises those who practice the giving of material wealth and the Dharma.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, upholding these roots of goodness, does not seek the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha; rather, taking these roots of goodness from such giving and sharing them equally with all sentient beings, they dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, employing the method of non-apprehension.
When dedicating in this manner toward great enlightenment, one remains free from three thoughts: namely, who is dedicating?
What is being dedicated?
And by what means is it dedicated?
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration, draws forth and encompasses the perfection of generosity.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in the perfection of meditative concentration, they uphold pure ethical discipline and never give rise to a mind associated with greed, hatred, delusion, or malice, nor do they give rise to a mind associated with stinginess, envy, or the breaking of precepts; rather, they constantly give rise to mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

Furthermore, taking these roots of goodness from maintaining such pure precepts, they do not seek the levels of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but dedicate them equally and in common with all sentient beings toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, employing the method of non-apprehension.
When dedicating in this way toward great enlightenment, one remains free from three thoughts: namely, who is dedicating?
What is being dedicated?
And by means of what is it dedicated?
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), draws forth and encompasses the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of meditative concentration, practices patience, they contemplate form as being like a mass of foam, feeling as being like a bubble, perception as being like a mirage, mental formations as being like a plantain tree, and consciousness as being like a magical illusion. When making such contemplations, the perception that the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) are not solid or substantial is constantly present before them.
Again, he reflects thus:
"All phenomena are empty and devoid of self and what belongs to self; whose form is it?
Whose feeling is it?"
Whose perception is this perception?
Whose volitional formations are these volitional formations?
Whose consciousness is this consciousness?
While observing in this way, he further reflects:
"All phenomena are empty, devoid of self and what belongs to a self; who is it that can cut?
Who is it that receives the cutting?"
Who is it that can revile?
Who is it that receives the reviling?
And who, moreover, should give rise to anger therein?

"When the Bodhisattva thus relies upon meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and observes with discernment, they are able to possess patience (*kṣānti*). Furthermore, they take these roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) of patience and, through the skillful means of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), dedicate them equally in common with all sentient beings toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*)."
When dedicating in this manner toward great enlightenment, one remains free from three thoughts: namely, who is dedicating?
What is being dedicated?
And by what means is it dedicated?
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā), draws forth the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of meditative concentration, exerts diligent effort, becomes detached from desires and unwholesome states, and—possessing applied and sustained thought, born of seclusion, joyful and blissful—enters the first dhyāna, and so on, up to entering the fourth dhyāna.

When a bodhisattva practices meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) in this manner, they do not grasp at the signs of the concentrations or their constituent factors (*dhyānāṅga*). They give rise to the supernormal knowledge of the power of transformation (*ṛddhividhi-jñānābhijñā*), thereby performing boundless great miraculous feats.

Alternatively, they may further develop the supernormal power of the divine ear, a clear and pure divine hearing that transcends that of humans and devas, enabling them to hear, as they truly are, the various sounds of both sentient and insentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions.

Alternatively, they may give rise to the supernormal power of knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna-abhijñā*), being able to know, as they truly are, the minds and mental factors of other sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions.

Alternatively, they may give rise to the supernormal power of knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna-abhijñā*), truly recollecting and knowing the various matters of the past lives of immeasurable sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions.

Alternatively, they may further develop the supernormal knowledge of the divine eye—a clear and pure divine eye that transcends that of humans—by which they are able to see, as they truly are, the various forms of sentient and non-sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions, and even know their karmic fruits exactly as they are.

Abiding in these five pure supernormal powers, this bodhisattva mahāsattva travels from one buddha-field to another, attending upon and making offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; he inquires about the profound meaning of the Tathāgata’s Dharma, plants immeasurable roots of true and pure goodness, brings sentient beings to maturity, purifies buddha-fields, and diligently cultivates the various sublime practices of a bodhisattva.

Taking these roots of goodness, they do not seek the fruits of the three realms or the two vehicles, but instead share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, employing the method of non-apprehension.
When dedicating in this way toward great enlightenment, one remains free from three thoughts: namely, who is dedicating?
What is being dedicated?
And by means of what is it dedicated?
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), draws forth and encompasses the perfection of diligence (*vīryapāramitā*).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in the perfection of meditative concentration, they perceive that the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) up to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) cannot be apprehended; as explained at length, they even perceive that the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) cannot be apprehended; they perceive that the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛtadhātu*) cannot be apprehended, and they perceive that the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*) likewise cannot be apprehended.

In this way, because the Bodhisattva perceives that all phenomena are unobtainable, they are without action and without creation; because there is no action or creation, there is neither arising nor ceasing; because there is no arising or ceasing, there is neither grasping nor abandoning; and because there is no grasping or abandoning, they are ultimately pure, eternally abiding, and immutable.

Why is this so? Because all phenomena—whether Buddhas appear in the world or do not appear—abide in the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), and the stability of phenomena (dharmaniyāmatā); they are without arising, without cessation, and eternally immutable.

The mind of this bodhisattva mahāsattva is never distracted; at all times they dwell securely in the mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes, observing that the nature of all phenomena is utterly non-existent.

Furthermore, taking these roots of goodness of such sublime wisdom, they share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, employing the method of non-apprehension.
When dedicating in this manner toward great enlightenment, one remains free from three thoughts: namely, who is dedicating?
What is being dedicated?
And by what means is it dedicated?
"This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration, draws forth and gathers the perfection of wisdom.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again:
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom, draw forth and gather the perfections from generosity up to meditative concentration?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of wisdom, they contemplate all phenomena as empty and non-existent."
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of wisdom, contemplate all phenomena as empty and non-existent?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"When bodhisattva mahāsattvas abide in the perfection of wisdom, they contemplate internal emptiness, yet the nature of internal emptiness is not apprehended;
they contemplate external emptiness, yet the nature of external emptiness is not apprehended."
One contemplates internal and external emptiness, yet the nature of internal and external emptiness cannot be apprehended;
one contemplates great emptiness, yet the nature of great emptiness cannot be apprehended;
one contemplates the emptiness of emptiness, yet the nature of the emptiness of emptiness cannot be apprehended.
Contemplating the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of the ultimate is unapprehendable;
contemplating the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the conditioned is unapprehendable;
contemplating the emptiness of the unconditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned is unapprehendable.
One contemplates ultimate emptiness, yet the nature of ultimate emptiness cannot be apprehended;
one contemplates boundless emptiness, yet the nature of boundless emptiness cannot be apprehended;
one contemplates non-dispersal emptiness, yet the nature of non-dispersal emptiness cannot be apprehended.
One contemplates the emptiness of intrinsic nature, yet the emptiness of intrinsic nature cannot be apprehended;
one contemplates the emptiness of characteristics, yet the emptiness of characteristics cannot be apprehended;
one contemplates the emptiness of all phenomena, yet the emptiness of all phenomena cannot be apprehended.

Abiding thus in these fourteen kinds of emptiness, this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend form as either empty or non-empty; he does not apprehend feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either empty or non-empty. To speak extensively, he does not apprehend even the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) as either empty or non-empty; he does not apprehend the conditioned realm (saṃskṛtadhātu) as either empty or non-empty, nor does he apprehend the unconditioned realm (asaṃskṛtadhātu) as either empty or non-empty.

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom, contemplates all the gifts given by sentient beings—whether food, drink, or other requisites—as empty. He likewise contemplates as empty the one who gives, the object given, the merit of giving, and the fruit of giving; indeed, he contemplates all such things as empty."
At that time, because the bodhisattva abides in emptiness, he observes that neither craving nor stinginess can possibly arise.

Why is this? Because when this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), from the first generation of the mind of awakening until sitting upon the seat of sublime enlightenment, no such conceptual discriminations arise at all.

Just as all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas never at any time give rise to a mind of attachment or a mind of stinginess, so too it is with this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva: while practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), minds of attachment and stinginess never arise at all.

Subhūti, you should know that this perfection of wisdom is the teacher of all bodhisattva mahāsattvas; it enables the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas to refrain from arising any conceptual constructions or discriminations, so that whatever generosity they practice is entirely free from attachment.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, taking these roots of goodness as a basis, employs the method of non-apprehension to share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
When dedicating in this manner toward great enlightenment, one remains free from three thoughts: namely, who is dedicating?
What is being dedicated?
And by means of what is it dedicated?
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom, draws forth and encompasses the perfection of generosity.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in the perfection of wisdom and upholds pure ethical discipline, there is no possibility for the minds of any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or others to arise [in opposition].

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are all unapprehendable; the mind that dedicates itself toward them is also unapprehendable; and even the physical and verbal discipline for dedicating oneself toward those stages is likewise unapprehendable.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom, from the first generation of the mind of awakening until sitting upon the seat of sublime enlightenment, personally abstains from taking life up to and including wrong view; he also encourages others to abstain from taking life up to and including wrong view; he unerringly extols the dharmas of abstaining from taking life up to and including wrong view; and he joyfully praises those who abstain from taking life up to and including wrong view.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva takes the roots of goodness produced by maintaining these pure precepts and, without seeking the fruits of the two vehicles or the triple world, dedicates them equally and in common with all sentient beings toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, employing the method of non-apprehension.
When dedicating in this manner toward great enlightenment, one remains free from three thoughts: namely, who is it that dedicates?
What is it that is dedicated?
And by what means is it dedicated?
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom, draws forth the perfection of ethical discipline.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in the perfection of wisdom and gives rise to conforming patience, having attained this patience, they constantly reflect:

"Among all phenomena, there is not a single phenomenon that arises or ceases, that is born, ages, falls ill, or dies; nor is there one who can revile, one who receives reviling, one who can slander, or one who receives slander."

Whether one performs acts of cutting, slicing, stabbing, striking, binding, or inflicting harm and pain, or whether one is subjected to such cutting, slicing, stabbing, striking, and binding—all such natures and characteristics are empty; one should not engage in false conceptualization or discrimination regarding them.

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva has attained this patience, from the first generation of the mind of awakening until sitting upon the seat of sublime enlightenment, during that interval, even if all classes of sentient beings were to come and revile, disparage, slander, and insult them, or were to harm, strike, slash, pierce, and hack at them with various swords, staves, tiles, stones, and clods of earth, even to the point of dismembering their limbs and joints.
At that time, the Bodhisattva’s mind remained unchanging, and he thought only this: "How truly strange!

Within the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), there are absolutely no matters of reviling, slandering, insulting, or harming; yet sentient beings, through their deluded conceptualizations, claim these to be real, thereby giving rise to various afflictions and evil karmas, and undergoing all manner of suffering in the present and the future."
This bodhisattva mahāsattva takes these roots of goodness and, sharing them equally with all sentient beings, dedicates them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
When dedicating in this manner toward great enlightenment, they remain far removed from three thoughts: namely, "Who is it that dedicates?"
What is it that is dedicated?
By what means is it dedicated?
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of wisdom, draws forth and encompasses the perfection of patience.

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom with courageous diligence, proclaims the sublime Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, causing them to abide in the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom; or causing them to abide in the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; or causing them to be established in other meritorious qualities.”

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, having accomplished various skillful means and possessing physical and mental diligence, travels by means of supernormal powers to beings in one world, or ten, or a hundred, up to immeasurable and boundless worlds. There, he proclaims the sublime Dharma and guides them through skillful means, causing them to dwell in the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship; or causing them to abide in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; or causing them to realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
Although this bodhisattva mahāsattva performs these deeds, they do not abide in the realm of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtadhātu*), nor do they abide in the realm of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*).

Furthermore, they take these roots of merit from such diligence and, through the skillful means of non-apprehension, dedicate them equally and in common with all sentient beings toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
When dedicating in this way toward great enlightenment, one remains free from three thoughts: namely, who is dedicating?
What is being dedicated?
And by means of what is it dedicated?
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of wisdom, draws forth and gathers the perfection of diligence.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom, with the exception of the meditative concentrations of the Buddhas, they are able to enter and emerge at will and with mastery in all other superior meditative concentrations of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in the supreme meditative concentration of a bodhisattva’s mastery, being able to enter into and emerge from the eight liberations in both forward and reverse order—namely, the liberation of one possessing form who perceives forms, up to the liberation of the cessation of perception and feeling.

Furthermore, this bodhisattva mahāsattva enters into and emerges from the nine successive attainments with mastery, whether in direct or reverse order—namely, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.

Having thoroughly mastered the entry into and emergence from the eight liberations and the nine successive attainments in both forward and reverse order, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to enter the bodhisattva mahāsattva samādhi known as the Lion’s Yawn.
What is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s *siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*?

It refers to the bodhisattva-mahāsattva who, detached from desires and unwholesome states, possessing applied and sustained thought, and experiencing the joy and happiness born of seclusion, enters the first dhyāna; proceeding in sequence through all stages up to transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and entering the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodha-samāpatti*); then, arising from the cessation of perception and feeling, returning to enter the concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; and proceeding in sequence back down to enter the first dhyāna. This is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s *siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*.
“After this bodhisattva mahāsattva has become well-ripened in the siṃhavijṛmbhita samādhi, he further enters the bodhisattva mahāsattva saṃcayavigata samādhi.”
What is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s Samādhi of the Collection and Dispersion?

It refers to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who, detached from desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of detachment, enters the first dhyāna;
and having arisen from the first dhyāna, proceeds in succession until entering the cessation of perception.
Having attained meditative absorption, he emerges from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling and enters the first dhyāna;

emerging from the first dhyāna, he enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling; emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, he enters the second dhyāna;

emerging from the second dhyāna, he enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling; emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, he enters the third dhyāna.

Emerging from the third dhyāna, he enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling; emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, he enters the fourth dhyāna;
emerging from the fourth dhyāna, he enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling;

emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, he enters the sphere of infinite space; emerging from the sphere of infinite space, he enters the attainment of the cessation of perception...
Having attained meditative absorption, he emerges from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling and enters the sphere of infinite consciousness;

emerging from the sphere of infinite consciousness, he enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling; emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, he enters the sphere of nothingness;
emerging from the sphere of nothingness, he enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling; emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling...

He arises and enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception he arises and enters the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling;
from the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling he arises and again enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception he arises and dwells in a non-concentrated state of mind; from that non-concentrated state of mind he returns.
Entering the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, arising from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling and abiding in a non-fixed mind;

from that non-fixed mind entering the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, arising from the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and abiding in a non-fixed mind;
from that non-fixed mind entering the attainment of the sphere of nothingness, from the sphere of nothingness...
Emerging from meditative absorption, he dwells in a state of non-concentrated mind; from that non-concentrated mind, he enters the concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness;

emerging from the concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness, he dwells in a state of non-concentrated mind; from that non-concentrated mind, he enters the concentration of the sphere of infinite space;
emerging from the concentration of the sphere of infinite space, he dwells in a state of non-concentrated mind; from that non-concentrated mind, he enters the fourth [dhyāna].
Regarding the dhyānas: arising from the fourth dhyāna, he abides in an unconcentrated mind; from that unconcentrated mind, he enters the third dhyāna;
arising from the third dhyāna, he abides in an unconcentrated mind; from that unconcentrated mind, he enters the second dhyāna;
arising from the second dhyāna, he abides in an unconcentrated mind; from that unconcentrated mind...
Entering the first dhyāna, arising from the first dhyāna, and abiding in a non-concentrated state of mind—
this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s samādhi of gathering and dispersing.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in this samādhi of gathering and dispersing, they attain the equal true nature of all phenomena.

Furthermore, this bodhisattva mahāsattva takes these roots of goodness from meditative concentration and, with the skillful means of non-apprehension, dedicates them equally and in common with all sentient beings toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
When dedicating in this way toward great enlightenment, one remains free from three thoughts: namely, who is dedicating?
What is being dedicated?
And by means of what is it dedicated?
"This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling in the perfection of wisdom, draws forth and encompasses the perfection of meditative concentration.

The Great Perfection of Wisdom Sūtra, Fascicle 523, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Three, Chapter Twenty-Six on Skillful Means, Section Two. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“After how long have these bodhisattva mahāsattvas, having accomplished such skillful means, set out toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“These bodhisattva mahāsattvas have already set out toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment for countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How many Buddhas have these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas already approached, served, and made offerings to, such that they have accomplished such skillful means?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“This bodhisattva mahāsattva has already personally attended upon and made offerings to as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What kind of subtle and wondrous roots of virtue have these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas planted, such that they have accomplished such skillful means?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Since these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas first resolved their minds [on awakening], there has been no root of virtue—ranging from the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom—that they have not diligently cultivated to completion. By virtue of this cause and condition, they have accomplished such skillful means.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is truly rare that bodhisattva mahāsattvas accomplish such skillful means!”
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is as you have said.
That these bodhisattva mahāsattvas accomplish such skillful means is truly rare!
Subhūti, you should know this!"

Just as the disks of the sun and moon revolve around and illuminate the four great continents, performing their various functions, all sentient and insentient beings therein proceed according to the power of that light, each accomplishing its own task.

In this way, the perfection of wisdom illuminates and touches the other five perfections to perform their various activities; the five perfections, such as generosity, proceed in accordance with the power of the perfection of wisdom, each accomplishing its own task.
“Subhūti, you should know that the five perfections, beginning with generosity, are only designated as ‘perfections’ because they are all embraced by the perfection of wisdom.”
Just as a wheel-turning monarch is not so called unless he possesses the seven treasures, but is only named a wheel-turning monarch when he is endowed with them;

so too it is with the five perfections, such as generosity: if they are separated from the perfection of wisdom, they cannot be called "perfections," but only because they are embraced by the perfection of wisdom do they receive the name "perfection."
“Subhūti, you should know this!

Suppose there is a woman who is beautiful and very wealthy; if she is not protected by a powerful husband, she is easily insulted and oppressed by wicked people, but if she is protected by a powerful husband, she will not be insulted or oppressed by wicked people.”

The same applies to the five perfections, such as generosity and the rest: if they are not sustained by the power of the perfection of wisdom, they are easily thwarted and destroyed by Māra and his retinue; however, if they are sustained by the power of the perfection of wisdom, no Māras or their retinues can thwart or destroy them.
“Subhūti, you should know this:

just as a valiant military general who is well-versed in the arts of war and has properly equipped himself with various kinds of firm armor and weapons cannot be harmed by the enemy forces of a neighboring kingdom.”

The same applies to the five perfections, such as generosity and the rest: when they are not separated from the perfection of wisdom, neither the hosts of celestial Māras, nor those of overweening pride, nor even the *caṇḍāla*-like bodhisattvas can destroy them.

“Subhūti, you should know that it is just as the minor kings of Jambudvīpa attend upon a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin) at all times, and by relying on the wheel-turning sage king, they are able to travel to superior places.”

The same applies to the five perfections, such as generosity and the rest; by assisting the perfection of wisdom and being guided by its power, they swiftly proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
“Subhūti, you should know this:
just as all the waters in the eastern regions of Jambudvīpa flow toward the great river Gaṅgā and, following the course of the Gaṅgā, enter the great ocean.”

The five perfections, beginning with generosity, are likewise so; because they are all gathered and led by the perfection of wisdom, they are able to reach unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
“Subhūti, you should know that just as a person’s right hand is capable of performing all manner of tasks, so too does the perfection of wisdom bring forth all supreme and wholesome dharmas.”
"Subhūti, you should know that just as a person's left hand is not dexterous for performing tasks, so too the first five perfections cannot induce the arising of sublime wholesome dharmas."
“Subhūti, you should know this!
Just as all rivers, regardless of their size, become of one salty taste once they enter the great ocean, so too it is with the five perfections, such as generosity:
they must enter the perfection of wisdom before they can realize the knowledge of all modes. It is for this reason that they are called ‘those who have reached the other shore.’”
“Subhūti, you should know this:

when a wheel-turning monarch wishes to go somewhere, his fourfold army follows him with the wheel-treasure leading the way. When the king and the fourfold army desire to eat and drink, the wheel immediately stops; once they have eaten and drunk, the king thinks of proceeding, and the wheel moves on ahead. That wheel goes or stops according to the king’s will, and only upon reaching its destination does it no longer move forward.”

The five perfections, beginning with generosity, are likewise thus: when they seek to proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment along with all wholesome dharmas, they must take the perfection of wisdom as their guide; they follow it in both advancing and halting, never departing from one another, and once the fruit of Buddhahood is reached, they no longer proceed further.
“Subhūti, you should know this:

it is like a wheel-turning monarch who possesses the seven treasures; when he wishes to go somewhere, his fourfold army and the seven treasures escort him from front and back. At that time, although the wheel-treasure is foremost, it does not discriminate between the characteristics of front and back.”

In this way, when the first five perfections (pāramitās) and all wholesome dharmas aspire toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they are invariably preceded by the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Yet, this perfection of wisdom does not form the thought:
"I am the foremost leader among the first five perfections, and they follow after me."
The five perfections, such as generosity and the rest, do not form this thought:
"The profound perfection of wisdom stands before us; we shall follow her."

Why is this so? Because these six perfections and all phenomena have a nature that is inherently dull and incapable of action; they lack a sovereign master, being false and unreal, empty and non-existent, characterized by a lack of self-mastery.
For example, like a mirage, a reflection, the moon in water, a magical illusion, a dream, and so forth, within these there is no real essence or characteristic that functions through discrimination.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, and entirely lack any real essence, characteristics, or activity, how can bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train in the six perfections, such as generosity, and thereby realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas diligently train in these six perfections, they constantly reflect: 'Sentient beings in the world have minds that are perpetually inverted;

they are submerged in the suffering of birth and death and cannot liberate themselves. If I do not cultivate skillful and superior practices, I will be unable to rescue them from the suffering of birth and death.'"

For the sake of those sentient beings, I shall diligently cultivate the skillful means of the perfections from generosity up to wisdom, swiftly attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, and uproot the great suffering of birth and death for all sentient beings.
"Having formed this thought, that bodhisattva mahāsattva relinquishes internal and external things for the sake of all sentient beings; having relinquished them, he further reflects:
'I have not relinquished anything at all regarding these things.'"
Why is this? Because these internal and external things are all empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and cannot be relinquished as gifts; they do not belong to me alone.

By means of this contemplation, the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) until it is swiftly fulfilled, and quickly realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
"This bodhisattva-mahāsattva never violates the precepts for the sake of sentient beings.
Why is this? Because this bodhisattva-mahāsattva constantly maintains this thought:"

"For the sake of sentient beings, I seek to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; I must certainly not take the life of any living being, nor even hold wrong views. Furthermore, I must certainly not seek the objects of exquisite sensual desire or the pleasures of the heavens, nor must I certainly seek the stage of the two vehicles for the sake of mere personal liberation."

By means of this contemplation, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of ethical discipline until it is swiftly brought to fulfillment, and they quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not give rise to anger toward sentient beings; even if they should constantly encounter slander, humiliation, the dismemberment of their limbs, or various forms of suffering, they do not give rise to a single thought of malice."
Why is this? Because this bodhisattva-mahāsattva observes all sounds as being like echoes and all forms as being like masses of foam; he should not give rise to false anger or resentment therein.
By means of this contemplation, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas swiftly bring the perfection of patience to fulfillment and rapidly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of all sentient beings, diligently seeks wholesome dharmas up until unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, remaining constantly free from indolence throughout that interval."
Why is this? It is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly reflects:

"If I am indolent, I shall be unable to rescue and deliver all sentient beings so that they may distance themselves from the great suffering of birth and death, nor shall I be able to attain the knowledge of all modes."

By means of this contemplation, that bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of diligence until it is swiftly brought to fulfillment, and quickly realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"For the sake of all sentient beings, this bodhisattva mahāsattva diligently cultivates supreme meditative concentration until reaching unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, never giving rise to a distracted mind characterized by greed, hatred, or delusion."
Why is this? It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constantly maintain this thought:

"If I give rise to a distracted mind characterized by greed, hatred, or delusion, I will be unable to accomplish the task of benefiting others, nor will I be able to realize the sought-after fruit of Buddhahood."

By means of this contemplation, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas swiftly bring the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā) to fulfillment and rapidly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of all sentient beings, never departs from the perfection of wisdom and constantly and diligently cultivates sublime, supreme insight until reaching unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Why is this? It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constantly maintain this thought:
"If one is separated from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), one cannot bring sentient beings to maturity, nor can one realize unsurpassed enlightenment."

By means of this contemplation, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas will swiftly bring the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) to fulfillment and rapidly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).

For this reason, although all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature and entirely devoid of any real essence, characteristics, or activity, the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas diligently cultivates the six perfections and realizes unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha again, saying:

"If these six perfections are without distinction, as they are all embraced by the perfection of wisdom, how can it be said that the perfection of wisdom is the foremost, the most excellent, the most honored, the highest, the sublime, the most subtle, the superior, and the unsurpassed among the five perfections?"
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said:
the six pāramitās, such as generosity and the rest, are without distinction because they are all subsumed within the prajñāpāramitā.
If there were no prajñāpāramitā, the five [perfections] such as dāna would not be called pāramitās;
it is only by relying on prajñāpāramitā that the five such as dāna are designated as pāramitās.
"Subhūti, you should know this:
just as various classes of sentient beings, despite having diverse differences in their physical forms and colors, all become of one single color when they approach Sumeru, the King of Mountains."

Thus, although these first five perfections have various distinctions of category, because they are embraced by the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), because they are all brought to fulfillment through the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom, and because they all enter into the perfection of wisdom, it is impossible to designate them with distinct names or identities.

Furthermore, it is only by relying upon the perfection of wisdom that the first five perfections can realize the knowledge of all modes; thus, they are called "those who have reached the other shore. Therefore, the six perfections are of a single flavor, their nature is without distinction, and one cannot designate them as "this is the perfection of generosity" up to "this is the perfection of wisdom."

Why is this so? Because these six kinds of pāramitās are all capable of realizing the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñājñāna) and reaching the further shore; their nature is without distinction. For this reason, it is impossible to designate different names or surnames for the six perfections, such as generosity and the rest.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If, according to their true meaning, the perfections and all phenomena are devoid of any distinction of 'this' or 'that,' or of superiority or inferiority, for what reason is it said that the *prajñāpāramitā* is the foremost, the most excellent, the most honored, the highest, the sublime, the most subtle, the superior, and the unsurpassed among the five perfections?"
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.

If one follows the ultimate meaning, the pāramitās and all phenomena are entirely devoid of such distinctions as "this" or "that," or superiority and inferiority; it is only in reliance upon conventional designations and functional activity that one speaks of these distinctions of "this" or "that," and of superiority and inferiority.

The establishment of the perfections, from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, is for the purpose of liberating all sentient beings from the worldly processes of birth, aging, sickness, and death; yet these births, aging, sickness, and deaths of sentient beings are not truly existent, but are merely conventional designations.

Why is this so? Because sentient beings do not exist, one should know that all phenomena likewise have no existence. The profound *prajñāpāramitā* realizes that all phenomena are entirely non-existent; it can extract sentient beings from the mundane functions of birth, old age, sickness, and death. For this reason, it is said that among the five *pāramitās*, the *prajñāpāramitā* is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most venerable, the highest, the most sublime, the most exquisite, the most superior, and the unsurpassed.
“Subhūti, you should know this:

just as the woman-jewel possessed by a wheel-turning monarch is the most excellent, the most superior, the most honored, the most sublime, the most exquisite, the most wondrous, the highest, and the unsurpassed among all women of the human realm, so too is this perfection of wisdom the most excellent, the most superior, the most honored, the most sublime, the most exquisite, the most wondrous, the highest, and the unsurpassed among the previous five perfections.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"For what reason does the Tathāgata repeatedly praise and speak of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* alone, declaring it to be the foremost, the most excellent, the most venerable, the highest, the sublime, the most subtle, the superior, and the unsurpassed among the *pāramitās* such as generosity?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Because this perfection of wisdom is able to universally encompass all wholesome dharmas, it brings them together to enter into the knowledge of all modes, abiding therein immovably by means of non-apprehension as its expedient.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Does this perfection of wisdom involve the grasping or abandoning of any wholesome dharmas?
The Buddha said:
"No, indeed! Thus, this Prajñāpāramitā neither grasps nor abandons any phenomena. Why is that?"
"Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, and thus can neither be grasped nor abandoned.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In this way, regarding what phenomena does the perfection of wisdom neither grasp nor abandon?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Is it thus that this perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor abandons anything from form up to the knowledge of all aspects?
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Regarding this perfection of wisdom, how is it that from form up to the knowledge of all modes there is neither grasping nor relinquishing?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“This perfection of wisdom does not conceptualize form, and so on up to the knowledge of all modes; therefore, from form up to the knowledge of all modes, there is neither grasping nor relinquishing.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is it that the perfection of wisdom does not contemplate form, nor [contemplate] anything up to and including the knowledge of all aspects?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Because this Prajñāpāramitā does not contemplate any marks regarding form up to the knowledge of all modes, nor does it contemplate any objects of focus, for this reason it does not contemplate form, and so on, up to the knowledge of all modes."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not contemplate form—and so on, as extensively explained, up to the knowledge of all modes—how do the roots of goodness they have planted increase?”
If one does not increase the roots of goodness that have been planted, how can one fulfill the perfections?
If one does not fulfill the perfections, how can one realize the knowledge of all modes?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not mentally engage with form—extending in detail up to the knowledge of all modes—then that bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to increase the roots of virtue they have planted.”

Because the roots of virtue they have planted increase, they are able to fulfill the perfections (pāramitās); because the perfections are fulfilled, they are able to realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

Why is this? Because it is only when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not engage in mental deliberation regarding form—and so forth, as extensively explained, up to and including omniscient wisdom—that they are able to fully cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"By what causes and conditions must Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas not conceptualize anything from form (*rūpa*) up to and including the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), before they can fully cultivate the practices of a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva and realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas contemplate form—and as extensively explained, up to the knowledge of all modes—then they have something apprehended. Because they have something apprehended, they become attached to the three realms. If they are attached to the three realms, they cannot fully cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, nor can they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not conceptualize form—and so on, as explained at length, up to the knowledge of all modes—then there is nothing to be apprehended. Because there is nothing to be apprehended, they do not cling to the triple world. Since they do not give rise to clinging within the triple world, they are able to fully cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Therefore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to be able to fully cultivate all the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should diligently study the profound perfection of wisdom and must not contemplate with attachment to any phenomena.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to diligently practice and study the profound perfection of wisdom, in what should they abide?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to diligently practice and study the profound perfection of wisdom, they should not dwell upon form, nor upon anything up to and including the knowledge of all modes."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"For what reason should bodhisattva mahāsattvas who wish to diligently practice and study the profound perfection of wisdom not abide in form—and as extensively explained, up to and including the knowledge of all aspects?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can diligently practice and study the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, because they have no attachment to any phenomena, they should not dwell upon form—and as it is explained at length—up to and including the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*)."
Why is this? Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive any dharma within which they might give rise to attachment or in which they might dwell.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by means of non-attachment and non-abiding as their skillful means, are able to diligently practice and study the profound perfection of wisdom.
“Subhūti, you should know this:

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva forms such a thought as this—‘If one can thus practice with non-attachment and non-abiding, diligently training in the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom’—then they are indeed practicing the perfection of wisdom.”
That I am thus able to practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* with non-attachment and no fixed abiding—this is the cultivation of *prajñāpāramitā*, this is the practice of *prajñāpāramitā*.
Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva grasps signs and clings through such reflections, they distance themselves from the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

If they distance themselves from the perfection of wisdom, they distance themselves from the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), and so on, up to and including the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* has no attachment toward any phenomena; the profound *prajñāpāramitā* possesses neither an agent of attachment nor the nature of attachment.
Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that could be grasped or attached to among any phenomena. Therefore, Subhūti!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they are entirely without attachment to all phenomena or to the profound perfection of wisdom itself.
“Subhūti, you should know that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they give rise to such a thought:
‘This is the perfection of wisdom; I am practicing the perfection of wisdom; this is the universal traversal of the true reality (dharmatā) of all phenomena.’”
Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought, they retreat from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If they retreat from the perfection of wisdom, they then retreat from the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā), and so on, as extensively explained, up to the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā).
Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is the root of all pure dharmas (*śukladharma*); if one regresses from the *prajñāpāramitā*, one thereby falls away from all pure dharmas.
“Subhūti, you should know that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva forms this thought:
‘The profound perfection of wisdom subsumes the perfection of giving, and so forth, up to the knowledge of all aspects.’”

This bodhisattva mahāsattva will fall away from the perfection of wisdom; if they fall away from the perfection of wisdom, they will be unable to embrace the perfection of giving, and so on, up to and including the knowledge of all aspects.

Why is this? It is because apart from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), one cannot fully embrace the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma), nor can one realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñājñāna).
“Subhūti, you should know that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva forms such a thought:
‘By abiding in the perfection of wisdom, one will certainly receive the prophecy of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment,’”
Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva forms such a thought, they fall away from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
If they fall away from the perfection of wisdom, they will not be fit to receive the prediction (vyākaraṇa) regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Why is this? Because it is not apart from the perfection of wisdom that one can receive the prediction of attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Subhūti, you should know this!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva forms this thought:

"By abiding in the perfection of wisdom, one is able to bring forth the perfection of generosity, and so on, up to bringing forth great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity."

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva harbors such a thought, they fall away from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). If they fall away from the perfection of wisdom, they will be unable to bring forth the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā), and so on, up to being unable to bring forth great loving-kindness (maitrī), great compassion (karuṇā), great sympathetic joy (muditā), and great equanimity (upekṣā).
Why is this? Because it is not apart from the perfection of wisdom that one can give rise to and abide in the supreme Dharma.
"Subhūti, you should know this!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva forms this thought:
"The Buddha, knowing that all phenomena have the characteristic of being without grasping, has personally realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Once I have attained awakening, I shall proclaim and reveal the true nature of all phenomena to all sentient beings.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva harbors such a thought, they will thereby fall away from the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has no knowledge of dharmas, no awakening, no speaking, and no demonstrating. Why is this?
The true nature of all phenomena is unknowable and cannot be designated; how, then, could there be one who knows and demonstrates all phenomena?
If it were said that there truly exists one who knows and demonstrates all phenomena, such a thing is impossible.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), how should they come to be free from these various kinds of faults?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the profound perfection of wisdom forms this thought:

'All phenomena are non-existent and ungraspable; if phenomena are non-existent and ungraspable, then there is no one who can realize perfect awakening, nor is there anyone who can proclaim or reveal them.'"
"If one can practice in this way, this is practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* free from all faults.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva becomes attached to dharmas that are non-existent and ungraspable, they then depart from the *prajñāpāramitā*."

Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* has no attachment to and no grasping of any phenomena (*dharma*). If one were to have attachment to or grasp at any phenomena, one would be separated from the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Is the perfection of wisdom distant from the perfection of wisdom, or is it not distant?"
Furthermore, is the perfection of generosity distant from the perfection of generosity, or is it not distant?
To speak at length, up to: is the knowledge of all aspects distant from the knowledge of all aspects, or is it not distant?

"Bhagavān! If the perfection of wisdom is either distant from or not distant from the perfection of wisdom, how can a bodhisattva mahāsattva, free from attachment, bring forth the perfection of wisdom?"

In this way, even up to the point that if the perfection of generosity is either distant from or not distant from the perfection of generosity, how can a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of generosity without attachment?

To speak at length, up to: if the knowledge of all modes is either distant from or not distant from the knowledge of all modes, how can a bodhisattva mahāsattva, free from attachment, bring forth the knowledge of all modes?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Prajñāpāramitā is neither distant from prajñāpāramitā nor not distant from it; therefore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to bring forth prajñāpāramitā without attachment."

In this way, up to the perfection of generosity, the perfection of generosity is neither distant from nor not distant from the perfection of generosity; therefore, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to unfurl the perfection of generosity without attachment.

To speak extensively, up to the point that the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) is neither distant from nor not distant from the knowledge of all modes; therefore, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to bring forth the knowledge of all modes without attachment.
Why is this? It is because it does not consist of intrinsic nature, nor is it apart from intrinsic nature, yet it can induce and establish one in intrinsic nature.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not cling to form, thinking, "This is form," or "This form belongs to that. This is explained at length until it is said that they likewise do not cling to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), thinking, "This is the knowledge of all modes," or "This knowledge of all modes belongs to that."
Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva has no attachment to any such phenomena, they are able to bring forth the perfection of wisdom, and even bring forth the knowledge of all modes.

Why is this? If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* has any attachment toward phenomena—thinking, "This is a phenomenon," or "This phenomenon belongs to that"—then they will be unable to spontaneously evoke and abide in supreme qualities at will.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do not observe form as either permanent or impermanent, as either pleasant or painful, as either self or non-self, as either pure or impure, as either empty or non-empty, or as either secluded or not secluded; and so on, up to not observing the knowledge of all aspects (sarvajñājñāna) as either permanent or impermanent, as either pleasant or painful, as either self or non-self, as either pure or impure, as either empty or non-empty, or as either secluded or not secluded. Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not observe any such phenomena, they thereby bring forth the perfection of wisdom, and even bring forth the knowledge of all aspects."

Why is this? If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* were to observe any phenomena as either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, empty or non-empty, or detached or non-detached, they would be unable to bring forth and abide in the sublime qualities at will.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they are thereby practicing the perfection of giving, and so on, up to and including practicing the knowledge of all modes."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Wherever the profound perfection of wisdom proceeds, all other perfections and all other factors conducive to enlightenment likewise proceed."
Wherever this profound perfection of wisdom goes, all other perfections and all other factors conducive to enlightenment follow it there.
Just as the fourfold army of the wheel-turning monarch follows wherever he travels, so too do the fourfold armies follow wherever the wheel-turning monarch arrives.

The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise: wherever it proceeds and wheresoever it reaches, the five *pāramitās* beginning with generosity, as well as all other factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣikadharma*), follow after it until they ultimately reach the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*).

Just as a skilled charioteer, driving a carriage drawn by four horses, causes it to avoid dangerous paths and travel upon the right road, so that it reaches its destination according to his original intent;

even so is the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. It skillfully guides all the *pāramitās* and all other factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), causing them to avoid the perilous paths of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, to travel upon the right path of benefiting oneself and others, and to reach the originally sought-after knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*).
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“In what way, World-Honored One, do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constitute the path?
In what way do they not constitute the path?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Whether it be the path of the śrāvakas, the path of the pratyekabuddhas, or the path of ordinary beings, these are not the paths of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, for by means of them one cannot proceed to all-knowledge (sarvajñatā).

All the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) induced by the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) are the paths of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, for by means of them one will certainly proceed to all-knowledge."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"The profound *prajñāpāramitā*, appearing in the world, is able to perform a great task; that is to say, it demonstrates the characteristics of the path and the non-path for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, enabling those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to know the path and the non-path, and swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*)."
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.

The appearance of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in the world is able to perform a great task; that is to say, it manifests the characteristics of the path and the non-path for all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, enabling them to know the path and the non-path, so that they may swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*).
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

The appearance of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in the world is capable of performing a great task; that is to say, it delivers immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings, causing them to obtain supreme benefit and peace."
"Subhūti, you should know that although the profound perfection of wisdom performs boundless deeds for the benefit and happiness of others, it remains without attachment to these deeds."
"Subhūti, you should know this!

Although the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can manifest all activities to be performed, it does not grasp at form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness; nor does it grasp at anything up to and including the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), nor does it grasp at the activities performed by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."

Subhūti, you should know that although the profound *prajñāpāramitā* leads all the hosts of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, causing them to remain far removed from the levels of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, it neither produces nor extinguishes any phenomena, for it takes the abiding nature of dharmas (*dharmasthititā*) as its definitive standard.
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is such that all phenomena are neither produced nor extinguished, how is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they should practice giving for the sake of sentient beings, should maintain pure ethical discipline, should arouse patience, should exert diligence, should enter meditative concentration, and should cultivate wisdom?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they take all-knowledge as their object and, for the sake of all sentient beings, should practice giving, maintain pure ethical discipline, arouse patience, exert diligence, enter meditative concentration, and cultivate wisdom.”
This bodhisattva mahāsattva takes these roots of virtue and, sharing them equally with all sentient beings, dedicates them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva dedicates these roots of virtue toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they swiftly bring the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) to fulfillment; they also swiftly bring the bodhisattva’s loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity to fulfillment. By means of this, they quickly attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), and until they sit upon the sublime seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*), they never remain apart from these six perfections.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is never separated from these six perfections, then they are not separated from the knowledge of all aspects. Therefore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes, they should diligently apply themselves to training in the six perfections and constantly and diligently practice the six perfections.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly and diligently applies themselves with vigor to study and practice these six perfections, all their roots of virtue will swiftly reach fulfillment, and they will quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Therefore, Subhūti, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should always remain in conjunction with the six perfections and must not abandon them even for a moment.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to remain constantly associated with the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), never abandoning them even for a moment?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates form as neither associated nor dissociated with reality; if they contemplate feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as neither associated nor dissociated with reality; and so on, in detail, until they contemplate the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) as neither associated nor dissociated with reality—then this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to remain constantly associated with the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), never abandoning them for even a moment."
Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly reflects:
"I should not abide in form, nor should I abide in non-form," and so on at length until: "I should not abide in the knowledge of all modes, nor should I abide in non-knowledge of all modes."

Why is this? Because form is neither that which abides nor that in which it abides; and so on, in detail, up to the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), which is likewise neither that which abides nor that in which it abides.
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to remain constantly in association with the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), never abandoning them for even a moment.
Subhūti, you should know this!"

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice the six perfections through such skillful means of non-abiding, that bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
“Subhūti, you should know this!

Suppose a person wishes to eat *āmra* fruits or *panasa* fruits; they first take their seeds and plant them in fertile soil, irrigating, guarding, and tending them at the proper times. Gradually, sprouts, stems, branches, and leaves grow, and when the seasons converge, flowers and fruits appear. Once the fruits have ripened, they harvest and eat them.”
Thus it is, Subhūti!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment first train in the six perfections, and furthermore, they gather in sentient beings through generosity, or through kind words, or through beneficial conduct, or through cooperation.

Having thus gathered them in, he instructs them to abide in the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and causes them to abide in the factors of enlightenment, such as the four applications of mindfulness.
Once firmly established therein, they are liberated from all the great sufferings of birth and death, and realize the eternal, quiescent peace and bliss.
In this way, the Bodhisattva shall attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and be able to benefit all beings throughout the future.

"Therefore, Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to awaken to all phenomena through self-realization without depending on others; wishes to bring all sentient beings to maturity; wishes to purify the Buddha-field he seeks; wishes to swiftly sit upon the sublime seat of awakening (bodhimanda); wishes to subdue the armies of all evil Māras; wishes to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñājñāna); and wishes to turn the wheel of Dharma to deliver the multitudes of sentient beings—he should train in the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā). Using the four means of attraction (saṃgrahavastu) as skillful means, he should gather in all classes of sentient beings and cause them to be liberated from the manifold sufferings of birth and death. When a bodhisattva thus trains with diligent effort, he should constantly and diligently train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Does the Buddha teach that a bodhisattva should diligently train in the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, Subhūti! It is so, it is so!”
I say that a bodhisattva should constantly and diligently train in the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti, you should know this:
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain great mastery over all phenomena, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* possesses great majestic power, enabling the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to attain great mastery over all phenomena.
"Subhūti, you should know that this profound perfection of wisdom is the gateway through which all wholesome dharmas proceed. It is,
for example, like the great ocean, which is the gateway through which all waters proceed."

Therefore, Subhūti! Whether they be sons of good family belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle, or sons of good family belonging to the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, or sons of good family belonging to the Unsurpassed Vehicle, all should constantly and diligently study this profound perfection of wisdom.

“Subhūti, you should know that when bodhisattva mahāsattvas diligently train in the profound perfection of wisdom, they should also constantly train in everything from the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, and even constantly train in the knowledge of all aspects.”
"Subhūti, you should know that just as a skilled archer,
clad in firm armor and wielding excellent bows and arrows, has no fear of enemies, so too it is with the bodhisattva mahāsattvas.

Having embraced the perfection of wisdom— and as extensively explained, even up to the skillful means of the knowledge of all modes— they cannot be overcome by any of the demonic armies, non-Buddhists, or opposing disputants."

Therefore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and turn the sublime wheel of Dharma to deliver the multitudes of sentient beings, they should diligently study and practice the profound perfection of wisdom.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly and diligently practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they will be constantly protected and mindful of by all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:

“In what way does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by constantly and diligently training in the profound perfection of wisdom, come to be constantly protected and remembered by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly and diligently practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they will be able to practice the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—extensively explained up to the knowledge of all aspects—and for this reason, they are always protected and remembered by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"How does this bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—extending even to the knowledge of all aspects—and thereby become constantly protected and remembered by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving, and so forth, up to the knowledge of all aspects, because they perceive that the perfection of giving, and so forth, up to the knowledge of all aspects, are all unapprehendable, they are constantly protected and remembered by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Although the Buddhas of the past, future, and present always protect and keep in mind these bodhisattva mahāsattvas, they do not do so by way of extensively teaching form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, up to and including the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), because form, up to and including the knowledge of all modes, cannot be apprehended."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Although bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train in many places, they have no place of training.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"So it is! So it is! Although bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train in many places, they have no place of training."
"Why is this? Because, in reality, there is no dharma whatsoever that can cause the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to train and study within it.
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Buddha, for the sake of the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, has taught, either briefly or extensively, the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) and the dharmas associated with them.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and turn the sublime wheel of Dharma to deliver the multitudes of sentient beings, they should—whether the teachings on these six perfections are brief or extensive—listen to, receive and uphold, read, recite, and master them thoroughly. Having mastered them, they should reflect upon them according to the principle; having reflected, they should examine them correctly; and having examined them, they should cause the mind and mental factors to no longer revolve toward the signs of their objects.”
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
"It is as you have said. Furthermore, Subhūti,

when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas diligently train in the teachings corresponding to the six perfections spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One— whether in brief or in detail— they should understand, in accordance with reality, the characteristics of brevity and detail regarding all phenomena."
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva correctly understand, in accordance with reality, the concise and detailed characteristics of all phenomena?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
