"Since neither the meaning nor the non-meaning of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* can be apprehended, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the *prajñāpāramitā* by way of practicing the profound significance of the *prajñāpāramitā*?"

The Buddha told Subhūti: “All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, practicing the profound meaning and purpose of the perfection of wisdom, should form this thought: ‘I should not practice that which is non-beneficial—the affliction of desire;

I should not practice that which is non-beneficial—the affliction of hatred; I should not practice that which is non-beneficial—the affliction of delusion; I should not practice that which is non-beneficial—arrogance; I should not practice that which is non-beneficial—false views; I should not practice that which is non-beneficial—even all manner of speculative views—and I should not practice the benefit of desire, hatred, delusion, arrogance, false views, speculative views, or any other dharmas.’”
Why is this so? Because greed, hatred, delusion, and so forth, as well as suchness and the limit of reality, do not constitute either benefit or harm in relation to all phenomena.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, practicing the profound meaning and intent of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), should form this thought:

"I should not practice the meaning or non-meaning of form; I should not practice the meaning or non-meaning of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; and so on, in detail, up to: I should not practice the meaning or non-meaning of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas; I should not practice the meaning or non-meaning of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna)."
Why is this? When the Buddha attained unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, he sought the meaning and non-meaning of all phenomena, yet found neither to be obtainable.
"Subhūti, you should know this!

Whether Buddhas appear in the world or do not appear, the dharma-realm of all phenomena, the stability of phenomena, and the fixed nature of phenomena remain eternally as they are; no phenomenon can be either beneficial or non-beneficial to another phenomenon.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should abandon all attachment to what is meaningful and what is meaningless, and they should practice the profound significance of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what causes and conditions does the profound perfection of wisdom not constitute either benefit or harm for any phenomena?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“The profound *prajñāpāramitā* performs no action toward conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) or unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*); it is neither a benefactor nor an adversary, neither beneficial nor harmful. For this reason, it does not constitute either the meaningful or the meaningless for any phenomena.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Is it not the case that all Buddhas, the disciples of the Buddhas, and all noble ones take the unconditioned as their ultimate goal?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said:
all noble ones and sages take the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as their ultimate goal; yet, the unconditioned dharma neither benefits nor harms any phenomena.

Just as space, suchness, and the limit of reality neither benefit nor harm any phenomena, so too is the profound *prajñāpāramitā* of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas: it neither benefits nor harms any phenomena. Therefore, the *prajñāpāramitā* does not constitute either benefit or non-benefit for any phenomena.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Do not all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas necessarily train in the unconditioned *prajñāpāramitā* before they are able to realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*)?"
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas must study the profound, unconditioned perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) in order to realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), employing the non-dual dharma as their skillful means (*upāya*).
Subhūti asked again:
"Is it by means of non-dual dharmas that one attains the non-dual dharma?
The Buddha said:
"No, it is not so. Subhūti asked again:
"Is the non-dual dharma attained by means of dual dharmas?"
The Buddha said, "It is not so. Subhūti replied:
"If neither duality nor non-duality can be attained by means of dualistic or non-dualistic dharmas, how then shall the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain the knowledge of all modes?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Both duality and non-duality are unattainable; therefore, the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) is not attained by means of dualistic dharmas nor by means of non-dualistic dharmas. Nevertheless, it is through the dharma of non-attainment that one can attain non-attainment."
Why is this? Because both the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*) are unattainable; to attain without attaining is what is called true attainment.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

“This Prajñāpāramitā is most exceedingly profound. It is a difficult feat that these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to perform, for they do not apprehend a sentient being, nor do they apprehend the designation of a sentient being, yet they seek to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of sentient beings.”
For example, it would be an exceedingly difficult task for someone to plant a tree in the air!

It is likewise with the bodhisattva mahāsattvas: to seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening for the sake of sentient beings, while neither apprehending sentient beings nor their designations, is an extremely difficult task!
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.

This perfection of wisdom is most exceedingly profound; it is a difficult feat that these bodhisattva mahāsattvas are able to perform, for they seek to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of sentient beings, yet they neither apprehend sentient beings nor even the designation of "sentient beings."

"Subhūti, you should know that although bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not perceive any truly existent sentient beings nor the designations for them, yet sentient beings—due to their ignorance and inverted views—cling to them as being real. Sinking into the cycle of birth and death, they undergo endless suffering. To pull them out from this state, the bodhisattvas seek to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening; having attained awakening, they deliver and liberate them through skillful means."

“Suppose, for example, there is a person who plants a tree in a fertile field; although this person does not recognize the roots, trunk, branches, leaves, flowers, or fruits of the tree, nor the one who would enjoy them, once the tree has been planted, they irrigate it at the proper times and diligently protect it.”
In time, this tree gradually grows, its roots, trunk, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits becoming lush and abundant, so that all people enjoy them and more swiftly attain peace.

It is the same with the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: although they do not perceive the existence of a Buddha-fruit or sentient beings, they seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of sentient beings. They gradually practice the six pāramitās and other immeasurable factors of enlightenment; once these are perfected, they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, enabling all sentient beings to enjoy the branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits of the Buddha-tree, each obtaining great benefit.
“Subhūti, you should know this!
The benefit of the branches and leaves is that all sentient beings rely upon this Buddha-tree to escape the sufferings of the evil realms.

The benefit of the flowers is that all sentient beings, relying upon this Buddha-tree, are born into great kṣatriya clans, or even up to great householder clans; or they are born among the gods of the Four Great Kings, or even up to the gods of the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception.”

The benefit of its fruit is that all sentient beings, relying upon this Buddha-tree, may realize the fruit of stream-entry, up to and including the realization of pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, or the realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Once these sentient beings have attained awakening, they in turn use the branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits of the Buddha-tree to benefit sentient beings, causing them to escape the suffering of the evil realms and attain the happiness of humans and devas, gradually establishing them so that they enter the realm of parinirvāṇa through the three vehicles.

“Subhūti, you should know that although bodhisattva-mahāsattvas perform such great deeds of benefit, they do not perceive at all any real sentient beings who attain nirvāṇa; rather, they see only the cessation of the manifold sufferings of conceptual construction.”
Thus it is, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not apprehend sentient beings nor their designations; yet, for the sake of eliminating those false conceptions and inversions, they seek to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. For this reason, it is an exceedingly difficult task.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It should be known that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are like the Buddha. Why is this so?”

By relying upon the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, one is able to forever sever all realms of hell, the animal realm, and the world of hungry ghosts; furthermore, one is able to forever sever all the manifold sufferings of the three realms, including the states of no-leisure, poverty, and inferior destinies.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should know that they are like the Buddhas.

If there were no assembly of bodhisattvas in the world who set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, then there would be no Buddhas of the ten directions and the three times, nor any pratyekabuddhas or śrāvakas; furthermore, there would be none capable of permanently severing the sufferings of the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, and other states of non-leisure, poverty, and inferior destinies within the three realms.
Therefore, Subhūti, as you have said,
bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should be known as being like Buddhas.
Furthermore, Subhūti, you should know this!
The assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is itself the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.

Why is this? If it is by means of this very suchness that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is designated, then it is by means of this very same suchness that the Pratyekabuddha is designated.
If by means of this suchness a pratyekabuddha is designated, then by that same suchness a śrāvaka is designated;
if by means of this suchness a śrāvaka is designated, then by that same suchness all noble ones (ārya) are designated;
if by means of this suchness all noble ones are designated, then by that same suchness the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is designated.
If by means of this suchness the aggregate of form is designated, then by means of that same suchness the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are designated;
if by means of this suchness the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are designated, then by means of that same suchness the sense-base of the eye is designated;
if by means of this suchness the sense-base of the eye is designated, then by means of that same suchness the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are designated.

Thus it is explained in detail through successive stages, up to: if by means of this suchness the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas is designated, then by means of that same suchness the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) is designated;
if by means of this suchness the knowledge of all modes is designated, then by means of that same suchness the realm of the conditioned (saṃskṛtadhātu) is designated;
and if by means of this suchness the realm of the conditioned is designated, then by means of that same suchness the unconditioned realm (asaṃskṛtadhātu) is designated.
If by means of this suchness one designates the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*), it is by means of this very same suchness that one designates all phenomena (*sarvadharma*);
if by means of this suchness one designates all phenomena, it is by means of this very same suchness that one designates all sentient beings (*sarvasattva*);
and if by means of this suchness one designates all sentient beings, it is by means of this very same suchness that one designates all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

Thus it is, Subhūti! Whether it be the suchness of a Tathāgata, the suchness of a Pratyekabuddha, the suchness of a Śrāvaka, the suchness of all noble ones, the suchness of all phenomena such as form, the suchness of sentient beings, or the suchness of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva—such suchnesses are in reality entirely without difference. Because they are without difference, they are called "suchness."

When all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have brought their training in this suchness to perfection and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they are therefore called Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

Therefore, Subhūti, you should know that the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is itself the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, because all phenomena and all sentient beings take true suchness as their definitive standard.
"In this way, Subhūti, bodhisattva mahāsattvas should train in the profound *prajñāpāramitā* of suchness;
if they train in the profound *prajñāpāramitā* of suchness, they are able to train in the suchness of all phenomena."
If one can study the suchness of all phenomena, then one can fulfill the suchness of all phenomena;
if one can fulfill the suchness of all phenomena, then one attains mastery over the suchness of all phenomena;
and if one attains mastery over the suchness of all phenomena, then one can skillfully know the superior or inferior faculties of all sentient beings.
If one can skillfully know the superior or inferior faculties of all sentient beings, then one can thoroughly know the differences in their inclinations;
if one can thoroughly know the differences in their inclinations, then one knows that all sentient beings experience the fruits of their own karma;
and if one knows that all sentient beings experience the fruits of their own karma, then...
May the wisdom of aspiration be perfected; if the wisdom of aspiration is perfected, one will be able to purify and cultivate the sublime wisdom of the three times;
if one can purify and cultivate the sublime wisdom of the three times, one will be able to perfect the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna);
if one can perfect the knowledge of all modes, one will be able to practice the bodhisattva conduct without error; if one can practice the bodhisattva conduct without error...
By practicing, one is able to bring sentient beings to maturity; by bringing sentient beings to maturity, one is able to purify Buddha-fields;
by purifying Buddha-fields, one is able to realize the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
and by realizing the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, one is able to turn the sublime wheel of Dharma in accordance with reality.
If one can thus turn the sublime wheel of Dharma in accordance with reality, then one can unerringly establish sentient beings upon the paths of the three vehicles;
if one can unerringly establish sentient beings upon the paths of the three vehicles, then one causes sentient beings to enter the realm of nirvana without remainder.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas see all such merits of both self-benefit and benefit for others, they should resolve to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and with courageous and correct diligence, practice the profound perfection of wisdom firmly and without retreat.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, desiring to benefit all sentient beings, is able to give rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and practices the profound perfection of wisdom as it has been taught, then all the world—including devas, humans, and asuras—should pay homage to them.”
The Buddha said, “So it is, Subhūti!”
"So it is! It is as you have said.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, is able to give rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* as it has been taught, they should be honored and revered by the world of gods, humans, and asuras."
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of universally benefiting all sentient beings, first generates the mind set on unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, how much merit does he obtain?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva shall obtain immeasurable merit, which cannot be reached by calculation or analogy.
Subhūti, you should know this!"
Suppose that all sentient beings throughout the entire trichiliocosm of a Buddha-world were to attain the stage of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha; what do you think?
"Would these sentient beings have much merit? Subhūti replied, "Very much!"
“World-Honored One!
The merit obtained by that person would be immeasurable and boundless.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"The merit obtained by that person does not equal even a hundredth part of the mass of merit obtained by a single bodhisattva mahāsattva who has first resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of universally benefiting all sentient beings as you have asked; it does not equal a thousandth part, nor even a hundred-thousand-koṭi-nayuta-th part."

Why is this? It is because śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas all exist in dependence upon bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, whereas bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not exist in dependence upon śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Setting aside the mass of merit obtained by all sentient beings filling a trichiliocosm who have all entered the stage of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.
Suppose that all sentient beings throughout a trichiliocosm were to abide on the stage of pure observation; what do you think?
Would the merit of these sentient beings be great?
Subhūti replied, “Very much so,
World-Honored One!”
“The merit obtained by that person would be immeasurable and boundless.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“The merit obtained by that person does not equal even a hundredth part of the mass of merit obtained by a single bodhisattva mahāsattva who, for the sake of universally benefiting all sentient beings, has first resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening; it does not equal a thousandth part, nor even a hundred-thousand-koṭi-nayuta-th part.”

Why is this? It is because śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas all exist in dependence upon bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, whereas bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not exist in dependence upon śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Setting aside the mass of merit obtained by all sentient beings filling a trichiliocosm who abide on the stage of pure observation,

suppose all sentient beings filling a trichiliocosm were to abide on the stage of the spiritual lineage, or the eighth stage, or the stage of having seen the truth, or the stage of refinement, or the stage of freedom from desire, or the stage of completion, or the stage of a pratyekabuddha— what do you think?"
"Would these sentient beings have much merit? Subhūti replied, "Very much!"
“World-Honored One!
The merit obtained by that person would be immeasurable and boundless.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"The merit obtained by him does not equal even one hundredth part of the mass of merit obtained by a single bodhisattva mahāsattva who has first resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening for the sake of universally benefiting all sentient beings as you have asked; it does not equal one thousandth part, nor even one part in a hundred-thousand-koṭi-nayuta."

Why is this? It is because śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas all exist in dependence upon bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, whereas bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not exist in dependence upon śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose all sentient beings throughout the entire trichiliocosm were to generate the mind set on unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of benefiting all classes of sentient beings."

The mass of merit obtained by all these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas does not equal even a hundredth part of the mass of merit obtained by a single bodhisattva-mahāsattva who has entered the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth; it does not equal a thousandth part, nor even a hundred-thousand-koṭi-nayuta-th part.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose all sentient beings throughout the three-thousandfold world-system of a Buddha were to enter the bodhisattva’s state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma). The mass of merit obtained by that assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas would not equal even a hundredth part of the mass of merit obtained by a single bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing for enlightenment; it would not equal a thousandth part, nor even a hundred-thousandth, a koṭi-thousandth, a nayuta-hundred-thousandth part."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose all sentient beings throughout the entire trichiliocosm were to practice toward awakening; the mass of merit obtained by that assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas would not equal even a hundredth part of the mass of merit possessed by a single Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. It would not equal a thousandth part, nor even a hundred-thousand-koṭi-nayuta-th part."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What do those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have first resolved upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening contemplate?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly and correctly contemplates all-aspect omniscience.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is the nature of the knowledge of all aspects?
What is its object?
What is its dominant influence?"
“What is its mode of activity?
What are its characteristics?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"All-aspect omniscience has non-existence as its nature; it is without marks, without causes, without that which is to be awakened to, and without arising or manifestation.
Furthermore, regarding what you asked: 'What is the object of focus for all-aspect omniscience?'"
What is its predominance?
What is its mode of activity?
What are its characteristics?
"Subhūti, you should know this:
omniscience (sarvākārajñatā) takes non-existence as its object, right mindfulness as its dominant influence, tranquility as its mode of activity, and signlessness as its characteristic."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Is it only that all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) has non-existence as its intrinsic nature, or do form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness also have non-existence as their intrinsic nature?"

To speak at length, even up to the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas has non-existence as its nature; does the realm of the conditioned and the realm of the unconditioned also have non-existence as their nature?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Not only is all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) characterized by the absence of intrinsic nature, but form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are also characterized by the absence of intrinsic nature; even the conditioned realm and the unconditioned realm are characterized by the absence of intrinsic nature.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“By what causes and conditions is the nature of all-aspect omniscience (sarvākārajñatā) non-existence by nature; why is form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness also non-existence by nature; and even why is the conditioned realm (saṃskṛtadhātu) and the unconditioned realm (asaṃskṛtadhātu) likewise non-existence by nature?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Because the intrinsic nature of all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) does not exist, whatever dharma lacks an intrinsic nature has non-existence as its nature;

because form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, up to the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛtadhātu*) and the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*), also lack an intrinsic nature, whatever dharma lacks an intrinsic nature has non-existence as its nature."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"By what causes and conditions is the intrinsic nature of all-aspect omniscience non-existent, and why is the intrinsic nature of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness—even up to the realm of the conditioned and the realm of the unconditioned—also non-existent?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Because all-aspect omniscience (sarvākārajñatā) has no nature of synthesis, if a phenomenon has no nature of synthesis, that phenomenon has non-existence as its nature.

Because form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, up to the realm of the conditioned and the realm of the unconditioned, also have no nature of synthesis, if a phenomenon has no nature of synthesis, that phenomenon has non-existence as its nature."
For this reason, Subhūti, bodhisattva mahāsattvas should know that all phenomena have the absence of intrinsic nature as their nature.

Furthermore, Subhūti, all phenomena have emptiness as their intrinsic nature, signlessness as their intrinsic nature, and wishlessness as their intrinsic nature; for this reason, bodhisattva mahāsattvas should know that all phenomena have the absence of intrinsic nature as their nature.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

All dharmas have true thusness as their intrinsic nature; to speak at length, they have even the inconceivable realm as their intrinsic nature. For this reason, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should know that all dharmas have "the absence of intrinsic nature" as their intrinsic nature.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, by what skillful means do those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have first resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening become able to practice the perfections from generosity up to wisdom, thereby maturing sentient beings and purifying buddha-fields?"

To speak extensively, up to: what kind of skillful means must one accomplish to be able to practice the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), to bring sentient beings to maturity, and to purify Buddha-fields?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva has accomplished subtle and wondrous skillful means; although he knows that all phenomena have non-existence as their very nature, he constantly exerts himself to mature sentient beings and purify buddha-fields.

Although he constantly exerts himself to mature sentient beings and purify buddha-fields, he always penetrates the fact that all sentient beings and all buddha-fields take non-existence as their intrinsic nature."

Subhūti, you should know that although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom while training in the path to enlightenment, they know that generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, as well as the path to enlightenment, all have non-existence as their intrinsic nature. To speak at length, even though they practice the knowledge of all aspects while training in the path to enlightenment, they know that the knowledge of all aspects and the path to enlightenment both have non-existence as their intrinsic nature.

“Subhūti, you should know that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva thus practices the six perfections to train in the path to enlightenment, and so forth, up to practicing all-knowledge (sarvajñājñāna) to train in the path to enlightenment— if they have not yet accomplished the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, the quality of non-forgetfulness, the state of constant abiding in equanimity, all-knowledge, the knowledge of paths, and all-aspect knowledge, as well as other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas— this is called training in the path to enlightenment without having attained its fulfillment.”
If one has already attained perfection in training in this path, then one has also attained perfection in all the pāramitās;
because the pāramitās have been perfected, one is able to realize the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) through the wisdom associated with a single moment.

At that time, because the continuity of all subtle habitual tendencies of afflictions never arises again, it is called "complete eradication without remainder," and one is then named a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.

Furthermore, with the unobstructed and pure Buddha-eye, he universally observes the dharmas of the ten directions and the three periods of time; since even "non-existence" cannot be apprehended, how much less could "existence" be found!
It is thus, Subhūti!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice the perfection of wisdom, contemplating that all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature. Subhūti!

This is called the accomplishment of subtle and skillful means by the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; that is to say, when practicing the perfection of wisdom and contemplating all phenomena, they do not even apprehend non-existence, much less existence!

“Subhūti, you should know that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom and cultivates generosity, they do not even perceive the non-existence of this gift, the giver, the recipient, the object given, and the mind of awakening; how much less would they perceive them as existing!

When practicing pure precepts, one does not even perceive the non-existence of these pure precepts, the basis for protecting pure precepts, the one who upholds pure precepts, or the mind that guards pure precepts; how much less could one perceive them as existing!

When practicing patience, one does not even perceive the non-existence of this patience, the locus where patience is practiced, the one who practices patience, or the mind that practices patience; how much less could one perceive them as existing!

When practicing diligence, one does not even perceive the non-existence of this diligence, the basis for practicing diligence, the one who practices diligence, or the mind that practices diligence; how much less could one perceive them as existing!

When practicing meditative concentration, one does not even perceive the non-existence of this concentration, the locus of its practice, the practitioner, or the mind that practices it; how much less could one perceive them as existing!

When practicing prajñā, one does not even perceive the non-existence of this prajñā, the locus where prajñā is practiced, the person who practices prajñā, or the mind that practices prajñā; how much less could one perceive them as existing!

To speak extensively, up until the time one attains the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), regarding this knowledge of all modes—whether it be that which is attained, that by which it is attained, or the time and place of its attainment—one does not even perceive it as non-existent, much less perceive it as existent!
Why is this? It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constantly maintain this thought:

"All phenomena have non-existence as their nature; such non-existence is the very nature of things, existing inherently from the beginning. It was not made by a Buddha, nor by a pratyekabuddha, nor by a śrāvaka, nor by anyone else, because all phenomena are devoid of an agent and are free from an agent."
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Are not all phenomena devoid of the nature of phenomena?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"So it is! So it is! Subhūti then asked again:

"If all phenomena were devoid of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), how could that which is devoid of phenomena know whether that which is devoid of phenomena exists or does not exist? Why is this so?

A non-existent phenomenon cannot know a non-existent phenomenon; an existent phenomenon cannot know an existent phenomenon; a non-existent phenomenon cannot know an existent phenomenon; and an existent phenomenon cannot know a non-existent phenomenon."

Since all these phenomena have non-cognition as their intrinsic nature, how can a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, manifest whether phenomena exist or do not exist?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they manifest whether phenomena exist or do not exist in accordance with worldly convention, but not in accordance with the ultimate truth."
Subhūti asked again:
"Are the conventional and the ultimate truth different?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"The ultimate truth does not exist separately from the conventional. Why is this?
Because the suchness of the conventional is itself the ultimate."

All classes of sentient beings, through their inverted and false attachments, neither know nor see this suchness (tathatā). To benefit them, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, in accordance with conventional signs, manifest that phenomena either exist or do not exist; this is not in accordance with the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Sentient beings give rise to the notion that the five aggregates and so forth are substantially existent, not knowing they are non-existent.

To benefit them, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas demonstrate whether the aggregates and so forth exist or do not exist, so that sentient beings may, by means of this, realize that all phenomena such as the aggregates are neither existent nor non-existent; it is not their desire to cause them to cling to the characteristics of substantial existence or non-existence."
Thus it is, Subhūti!

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should apply themselves with diligent vigor, free from the grasping at existence and non-existence, and practice the profound perfection of wisdom in order to bring great benefit to all sentient beings.
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Tathāgata has often spoken of the practices of bodhisattvas; what are these called ‘the practices of bodhisattvas’?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"The practice of a bodhisattva refers to practicing for the sake of unsurpassed enlightenment, or it is called the practice of a bodhisattva because it benefits all sentient beings."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“In what place should bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the bodhisattva conduct?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice the bodhisattva conduct within the emptiness of form; they should practice the bodhisattva conduct within the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;

and so on, in detail, up to practicing the bodhisattva conduct within the emptiness of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), and practicing the bodhisattva conduct within the emptiness of the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).”

One should practice the bodhisattva conduct within the emptiness of the purification of buddha-fields; one should practice the bodhisattva conduct within the emptiness of the maturation of sentient beings;
one should practice the bodhisattva conduct within the emptiness of the elicitation of eloquence and dhāraṇīs;
one should practice the bodhisattva conduct within the emptiness of the elicitation of dhāraṇīs of syllables; and one should enter into realization...
One should practice the bodhisattva conduct of the emptiness of the dhāraṇī of letters; one should practice the bodhisattva conduct of the emptiness of the dhāraṇī of non-letters;
one should practice the bodhisattva conduct of the emptiness of the conditioned realm; and one should practice the bodhisattva conduct of the emptiness of the unconditioned realm.

“Subhūti, you should know that when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the bodhisattva path in this way, they do not conceive of dualistic characteristics regarding any phenomena, just as the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment does not.

Subhūti, you should know that when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom in this manner, it is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and it constitutes their practice of the bodhisattva path for the sake of sentient beings.
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Tathāgata constantly speaks of 'Buddha' in various places; by what meaning is this name 'Buddha' spoken?"

The Buddha said to Subhūti: "One is called a Buddha because they are able to awaken to the true meaning; one is called a Buddha because they have perfectly awakened to the true dharmas; one is called a Buddha because they are able to correctly penetrate the ultimate reality; one is called a Buddha because they are able to manifest equal and perfect awakening regarding the nature of things as they are (*yathāvadbhāva*) and the extent of all phenomena (*yāvadbhāva*); and one is called a Buddha because they truly awaken all sentient beings, causing them to leave behind all inversions."
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Tathāgata constantly speaks of bodhi in various places; by what meaning is this term ‘bodhi’ spoken?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Awakening (bodhi) is the meaning of emptiness, the meaning of suchness, the meaning of the reality limit, the meaning of the dharma-realm, and the meaning of the nature of phenomena."
Furthermore, Subhūti!

Because it is able to truly awaken to that which is most supreme and most subtle through the provisional establishment of names and signs and the application of verbal designations, it is called bodhi.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
It is called *bodhi* because it is true, real, non-illusory, and unchanging.
Furthermore, Subhūti,
the meaning of *bodhi* is the sense of being indestructible and free from conceptual differentiation.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
That which all Buddhas have perfectly and purely awakened to is therefore called bodhi.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
Because the Buddhas, by means of this, manifest complete and perfect enlightenment regarding all phenomena in all their aspects,
it is called bodhi. Furthermore, Subhūti,
because it is merely a conventional designation and a worldly expression, with no real entity to be found, it is called bodhi.
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, for the sake of awakening, practice the six perfections—and as extensively explained, up to the knowledge of all aspects—accumulating roots of virtue, in what dharma do they find benefit or harm, increase or decrease, arising or ceasing, or defilement or purification?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When bodhisattva mahāsattvas, for the sake of awakening, practice the six perfections—and as it is extensively taught, up to the knowledge of all aspects—accumulating roots of virtue, they regard all phenomena as neither beneficial nor detrimental, neither increasing nor decreasing, neither arising nor ceasing, and neither defiled nor pure.”

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of awakening, practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, employing the skillful means of non-objectification toward all phenomena; thus, it manifests before them neither for benefit nor harm, neither for increase nor decrease, neither for arising nor ceasing, and neither for defilement nor purity.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of awakening, practices the profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), employing the skillful means of non-objectification toward all phenomena—neither benefiting nor harming, neither increasing nor decreasing, neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiling nor purifying—when such a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, how does he take up the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom?”
To speak at length, up until: How does one embrace the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)?

How is it possible to transcend the stages of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*), enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*), practice the stages of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, and gradually realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*)?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not, by way of duality, take up the perfections from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom; and so on, as explained at length, until they do not, by way of duality, gradually realize the knowledge of all aspects."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not, by way of duality, take up the perfections from generosity up to wisdom; and so on, as extensively explained, until: they do not, by way of duality, gradually realize the knowledge of all aspects.”
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly increase sublime wholesome dharmas from the first production of the thought of enlightenment until the final thought?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices by means of duality, then these wholesome dharmas will not increase.”
Why is this? Because foolish ordinary beings all rely on duality, the wholesome dharmas they produce do not increase.

Since the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not practice duality, from their first production of the thought of enlightenment until their final thought, they constantly increase their supreme wholesome dharmas.

Therefore, Subhūti, the roots of goodness of all bodhisattva mahāsattvas are firm and unyielding; the gods, humans, asuras, and others in the world cannot destroy them or cause them to fall to the levels of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

The various evil and unwholesome dharmas of the world cannot draw them away or cause them to practice the six perfections, nor can they prevent the increase of all wholesome dharmas, ranging extensively up to the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
"In this way, Subhūti,
all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice the profound perfection of wisdom that is non-dual.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“Do the bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom for the sake of their roots of goodness? The Buddha said, “No!”

Subhūti, you should know that bodhisattva mahāsattvas do not practice the profound perfection of wisdom for the sake of roots of virtue, nor do they practice the profound perfection of wisdom for the sake of unwholesome roots.

Why is this? It is because it is the natural law for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that they cannot attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) unless they have personally approached, made offerings to, and revered the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; unless their roots of goodness are fully perfected; and unless they have been extensively sustained by true spiritual friends.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva approach, serve, and make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, so that their roots of goodness become most perfectly fulfilled, they are extensively sustained by true spiritual friends, and they are able to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas draw near to and make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones;
from those Buddhas they hear the exposition of sūtras up to the *upadeśa* (treatises), and having heard them, they receive and uphold them, and further..."
Having read, recited, and mastered them thoroughly, one reflects upon them in accordance with the truth;
having reflected, one deeply perceives their underlying intent; having perceived the intent, one attains thorough penetration;
having attained thorough penetration, one acquires dhāraṇī, gives rise to the unimpeded analytical knowledges, and even realizes unsurpassed bodhi, accordingly...
In whatever place they are born, they never forget the teachings and meanings of the sublime Dharma that they have heard and retained;

they extensively plant roots of virtue in the presence of all Buddhas, and because they are sustained by the power of those roots of virtue, they do not fall into the evil destinies or take birth in the states of no leisure;
furthermore, because they are embraced by those roots of virtue, their aspirations are pure—this is the purity of aspiration.
Because they are sustained by power, they are always able to mature sentient beings without error and adorn and purify Buddha-fields;
furthermore, because they are embraced by roots of goodness, they never remain apart from true, pure spiritual friends—
namely, the Tathāgatas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and others who can praise the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
"Monks, it is thus, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas draw near to and make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, they bring their roots of goodness to ultimate perfection; being extensively sustained by true spiritual friends, they are able to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes."
Therefore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the profound perfection of wisdom wishes to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes, they should apply themselves with diligent vigor to attend upon and make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; they should gather and perfect sublime and excellent roots of goodness, and serve true spiritual friends without ever becoming weary.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not draw near to and make offerings to the Buddhas, cannot fulfill their supreme and wondrous roots of goodness, and do not extensively serve true and pure spiritual friends, would they not be unable to attain the knowledge of all modes?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If one does not draw near to and make offerings to the Buddhas, cannot fulfill sublime and excellent roots of virtue, and does not extensively serve true and pure spiritual friends, one should not even be called a 'Mahāsattva,' let alone be able to realize the knowledge of all modes."

Why is this? There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, having personally attended upon and made offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have extensively planted roots of goodness and served virtuous friends, yet even they cannot attain the knowledge of all modes; how much less so those who do not attend upon or make offerings to the Buddhas, do not plant roots of goodness, and do not serve virtuous friends—how could they possibly realize the knowledge of all modes!
It is simply impossible that they could attain the knowledge of all modes;
such a thing is absolutely out of the question.

Therefore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to receive the name of a bodhisattva mahāsattva and desires to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes, they should always draw near to and make offerings to the Buddhas, cultivate and plant supreme roots of goodness to perfection, and serve spiritual friends without ever becoming weary.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“For what reason do some bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, though they are able to draw near to and make offerings to the Buddhas, extensively plant roots of goodness, and attend upon many spiritual friends, yet fail to attain the knowledge of all modes?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are devoid of skillful means regarding the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), then even though they are able to draw near to and make offerings to the Buddhas, extensively plant roots of virtue, and serve many spiritual friends, they will nonetheless be unable to attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna)."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is called 'skillful means' (upāyakauśalya)?
By accomplishing such skillful means, how do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas certainly attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) in whatever they undertake?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first production of the thought of awakening, while practicing the perfection of giving, employs a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) to give to the Buddhas, or to bodhisattvas, or to pratyekabuddhas, or to śrāvakas, or to other humans and non-humans."

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, having accomplished such mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes, although practicing generosity, has no perception of giving, no perception of a recipient, and furthermore, no perception of a self or what belongs to a self.

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates that the nature and characteristics of all phenomena are empty—without arising, without formation, without transformation, and without cessation—and thus enters into the characteristics of all phenomena;
knowing that all phenomena are without agency and without capacity, he enters into the characteristics of all conditioned activities.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, having accomplished such skillful means, constantly increases superior and sublime roots of goodness; because these roots of goodness increase perpetually, they are able to practice the perfection of generosity, bringing sentient beings to maturity and purifying buddha-fields.

Although they practice generosity, they do not seek the fruits obtained from giving; that is, they do not crave the superior rewards of saṃsāra, but rather diligently cultivate the perfection of generosity solely for the sake of protecting those who lack protection and desiring to liberate those who are not yet liberated.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, practices the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), they maintain that ethical discipline with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*). Their mind never gives rise to the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) or fetters (*paryavasthāna*) such as greed, hatred, and delusion; nor does it give rise to other unwholesome states that obstruct enlightenment, namely: stinginess, immoral conduct, anger, laziness, inferiority of mind, distraction, faulty wisdom, and other forms of pride. Furthermore, they never give rise to mental orientations associated with the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas contemplate that the nature and characteristics of all dharmas are empty—without arising, without formation, without transformation, and without cessation—and thus enter into the characteristics of all dharmas;
they know that all dharmas are without agency and without capacity, and thus enter into the characteristics of all conditioned formations.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, having accomplished such skillful means, constantly increases superior and sublime roots of goodness; because these roots of goodness increase perpetually, they are able to practice the perfection of ethical discipline, bringing sentient beings to maturity and purifying buddha-fields.

Although they practice pure ethical discipline, they do not seek the fruits obtained from that discipline—meaning they do not crave the superior rewards of saṃsāra—but rather, for the sake of protecting those who lack protection and desiring to liberate those who are not yet liberated, they diligently cultivate the perfection of ethical discipline up to the perfection of wisdom; each of these should be explained in detail according to the preceding account.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first production of the thought of awakening, through skillful means and with mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes, enters the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments."

Although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain mastery in entering and emerging from the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), they do not grasp at their karmic maturation (*vipāka-phala*).

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have accomplished the most supreme skillful means; they contemplate that the nature and characteristics of all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*) are all empty—without arising, without formation, without transformation, and without cessation—and they enter into the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), knowing that all phenomena are without action and without agency, thereby entering into the characteristics of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, having accomplished such skillful means, constantly increases superior and sublime roots of goodness; because these roots of goodness increase perpetually, they are able to practice the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*). By practicing the meditative concentrations, the immeasurables, and the formless attainments, they are then able to spontaneously mature sentient beings and purify buddha-fields.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first production of the thought of awakening,

possesses skillful means and applies mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes, then although they practice the path that abandons through seeing and cultivation, they are able to refrain from grasping at the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, or the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha."

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates that the nature and characteristics of all phenomena are empty—without arising, without formation, without transformation, and without cessation—and enters into the characteristics of all phenomena, knowing that all phenomena are without action and without agency, thereby entering into the characteristics of all conditioned formations.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes the most excellent skill in means and constantly increases supreme and wondrous roots of goodness. Because these roots of goodness increase perpetually, they are able to practice all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth; this is called the bodhisattva’s acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*).
By virtue of this patience, they are always able to freely bring sentient beings to maturity and purify Buddha-fields.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom with skillful means, and with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), although they attain mastery in entering and emerging from the eight liberations and the nine successive absorptions in both forward and reverse order, they are nevertheless able to refrain from grasping at the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship, or at the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha."

Why is this? It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas contemplate that the nature and characteristics of all phenomena are empty—without arising, without formation, without transformation, and without cessation—and they enter into the characteristics of all phenomena, knowing that all phenomena are without action and without agency, thereby entering into the characteristics of all conditioned formations.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes the most supreme skillful means and constantly increases sublime and excellent roots of goodness. Because these roots of goodness increase perpetually, they are able to freely bring sentient beings to maturity and adorn and purify buddha-fields, entering the bodhisattva stage of non-retrogression and attaining the patience of receiving the prediction of enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom with skillful means, applying mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes, and diligently cultivates the ten powers of a Tathāgata as well as other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas, they will not yet realize the knowledge of all modes until they have fully matured sentient beings and purified the Buddha-field."

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates that the nature and characteristics of all dharmas are empty—without arising, without formation, without transformation, and without cessation—and enters into the characteristics of all dharmas; knowing that all dharmas are without action and without agency, he enters into the characteristics of all conditioned formations.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes the most excellent skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) and constantly increases supreme and sublime roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). Because these roots of goodness increase perpetually, he is able to fully mature sentient beings and purify buddha-fields, gradually realizing the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*); this is what is called skillful means.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such skillful means, whatever they undertake will certainly lead them to realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
This most supreme skillful means is entirely accomplished through the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Therefore, Subhūti, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should diligently train in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. The Great *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Fascicle 526.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Chapter 27: The Perfection of Wisdom (Part Three). Chapter Twenty-Seven: The Perfection of Wisdom. At that time, having heard these words, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess supreme awakening wisdom; although they are able to practice such profound dharmas, they do not grasp at the superior rewards of existence.”
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.
Although the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess superior wisdom and are able to practice such profound dharmas, they do not grasp at the superior retributions of existence.
"Why is this? It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to remain unshakable within their own nature.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"In what intrinsic nature does this bodhisattva mahāsattva remain unshakable?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva remains unshakable within the intrinsic nature of non-existence."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In what absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) does this bodhisattva mahāsattva remain immovable?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“This bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to remain unmoved in the intrinsic nature of the aggregate of form up to the aggregate of consciousness;

able to remain unmoved in the intrinsic nature of the sense base of the eye up to the sense base of the mind; able to remain unmoved in the intrinsic nature of the sense base of form up to the sense base of phenomena;
and able to remain unmoved in the intrinsic nature of the element of the eye up to the element of the mind.”
They are immovable in the intrinsic nature of the form realm up to the dharma-realm;
they are immovable in the intrinsic nature of the eye-consciousness realm up to the mind-consciousness realm; they are immovable in the intrinsic nature of eye-contact up to mind-contact;
and they are immovable in the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition.
Immovable in its intrinsic nature, it is immovable in the intrinsic nature of the element of earth up to the element of consciousness;
it is immovable in the intrinsic nature of the causal condition up to the dominant condition; it is immovable in the intrinsic nature of ignorance up to old age and death;
it is immovable in the intrinsic nature of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom.
Moving, they are immovable in their intrinsic nature within inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of self-nature;

they are immovable in their intrinsic nature within suchness up to the inconceivable realm; they are immovable in their intrinsic nature within the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
and they are [immovable] within the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path.
Immovable in their intrinsic nature, they are immovable in their intrinsic nature regarding the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
they are immovable in their intrinsic nature regarding the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
they are immovable in their intrinsic nature regarding the eight liberations up to the ten totalities; and they are immovable in their intrinsic nature regarding pure contemplation.
The nature of the stages from the Stage of the Earth up to the Stage of the Tathāgata is immovable;
it is immovable within the nature of the stages from the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma; it is immovable within the nature of all doors of dhāraṇī and doors of samādhi;
it is immovable within the nature of the five eyes and the six supernormal powers; it is immovable within the nature of the Tathāgata...
They are immovable in the intrinsic nature of the ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they are immovable in the intrinsic nature of great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity;

they are immovable in the intrinsic nature of the thirty-two marks of a Great Being and the eighty secondary characteristics; they are immovable in the intrinsic nature of the quality of non-forgetfulness, and always...

Abiding in the immovability of the intrinsic nature of equanimity, one is able to remain immovable within the intrinsic nature of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);
one is able to remain immovable within the intrinsic nature of the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
one is able to remain immovable within the intrinsic nature of all the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva; one is able to remain immovable within...
The unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas is immovable in its intrinsic nature;
it is immovable in the intrinsic nature of the knowledge of all modes, and it is immovable in the intrinsic nature of both the conditioned realm and the unconditioned realm.

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these phenomena is itself the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*). Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas do not waver from this absence of intrinsic nature; yet, that which is the absence of intrinsic nature cannot realize the absence of intrinsic nature.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Does that which has an intrinsic nature serve to realize that which lacks an intrinsic nature?
The Buddha said:
"Not so! Subhūti asked again: "Can that which is without intrinsic nature realize that which has intrinsic nature?"
The Buddha said,
"It is not so. Subhūti asked again:
"Does existence serve as the means to realize existence? The Buddha said: "No!"
Subhūti asked again:
"Can that which is without intrinsic nature realize that which is without intrinsic nature?
The Buddha said:
"Not so! The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If that is so, then there must also be a nature that cannot realize the absence of nature, an absence of nature that cannot realize the presence of nature, a presence of nature that cannot realize the presence of nature, and an absence of nature that cannot realize the absence of nature. Would it not then be the case, World-Honored One, that there is neither attainment nor realization?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Although I have attainment and realization, I am far removed from the four extremes.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How can there be attainment and clear realization apart from the four extremes?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Whether it be attainment or clear realization, they are neither existent nor non-existent; they are free from characteristics and names, transcending all conceptual proliferation. Therefore, I say that while there is attainment and clear realization, they remain far removed from the four extremes.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“By what dharma do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas engage in conceptual proliferation?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"For Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, to regard the aggregate of form up to the aggregate of consciousness as either permanent or impermanent, as either pleasant or painful, as either self or non-self, as either pure or impure, as either tranquil or non-tranquil, as either detached or non-detached, or as either that which is to be fully known or that which is not to be fully known—this is conceptual proliferation."

To speak at length, even to contemplate omniscience (sarvajñajñāna) as permanent or impermanent, as pleasure or suffering, as self or non-self, as pure or impure, as tranquil or not tranquil, as secluded or not secluded, or as that which is to be fully known or that which is not to be fully known—this is conceptual proliferation (prapañca).
"Furthermore, Subhūti! If bodhisattva mahāsattvas should form such a thought:

'The noble truth of suffering should be fully known; the noble truth of origination should be permanently abandoned; the noble truth of cessation should be realized; the noble truth of the path should be cultivated. "
This is frivolous conceptualization (*prapañca*). Furthermore, Subhūti,
if bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should form such a thought as this:
"To practice the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom" is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
If one forms such a thought:

"One should abide in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature; one should abide in suchness up to the inconceivable realm; one should abide in the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path."
This is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
If one forms such thoughts as:

"One should cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path; one should cultivate the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions; one should cultivate the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; and one should cultivate the eight liberations up to the ten totalities."
This is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
If one forms this thought:

"I should transcend the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, enter the bodhisattva's state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*), fulfill the correct practice of the ten bodhisattva stages, and bring sentient beings to maturity and adorn and purify buddha-fields."
This is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). If one should think:

"I should give rise to all doors of dhāraṇī and doors of samādhi; I should bring forth the five eyes and the six supernormal powers; I should bring forth the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; I should bring forth great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity; I should fulfill the thirty-two marks of a Great Being and the eighty minor marks; I should bring forth the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant dwelling in equanimity; I should bring forth all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)."
This is frivolous conceptualization (*prapañca*). If one should think:
"I ought to practice all the deeds of a bodhisattva mahāsattva; I ought to realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas."
This is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
If one forms this thought:
"I shall forever sever the continuity of all afflictions and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), and I shall realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*)."
"This is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Subhūti,
you should know that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas engage in conceptual proliferation through various such types of discrimination."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should contemplate the aggregate of form up to the aggregate of consciousness as either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or untranquil, detached or non-detached, and that which is to be fully known or that which is not to be fully known; because all these are beyond conceptual proliferation, they should not engage in such proliferation."

To speak at length, one should contemplate omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*) as either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure, tranquil or untranquil, detached or undetached, and as something to be fully known or not to be fully known; since all these are beyond conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), one should not engage in such proliferation.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should contemplate whether the noble truth of suffering is to be fully known or not to be fully known; they should contemplate whether the noble truth of origination is to be permanently abandoned or not to be permanently abandoned; they should contemplate whether the noble truth of cessation is to be realized or not to be realized; they should contemplate whether the noble truth of the path is to be cultivated or not to be cultivated. Because all these are beyond conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), they should not be conceptually proliferated. This is explained at length until: they should contemplate whether the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvajñajñāna*) is to be attained or not to be attained; because both are beyond conceptual proliferation, they should not be conceptually proliferated."

Subhūti, you should know that when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should contemplate all such phenomena and sentient beings as being beyond conceptual proliferation; therefore, they should not engage in conceptual proliferation regarding them.

Why is this so? Because regarding all phenomena and all sentient beings, that which possesses intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) cannot engage in conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) concerning that which lacks intrinsic nature (*asabhāva*); that which lacks intrinsic nature cannot engage in conceptual proliferation concerning that which possesses intrinsic nature; that which possesses intrinsic nature cannot engage in conceptual proliferation concerning that which possesses intrinsic nature; and that which lacks intrinsic nature cannot engage in conceptual proliferation concerning that which lacks intrinsic nature. Apart from existence and non-existence of intrinsic nature, neither the one who proliferates, nor the object of proliferation, nor the locus of proliferation, nor the time of proliferation can be apprehended.
Therefore, Subhūti, the aggregate of form is without conceptual proliferation;

the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without conceptual proliferation; and so on, in detail, up to the knowledge of all aspects, which is also without conceptual proliferation.
"In this way, Subhūti,
all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice the profound perfection of wisdom that is free from conceptual proliferation.
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, how do they contemplate the aggregate of form through to the aggregate of consciousness—and as explained at length, up to the knowledge of all modes—such that, because they are all beyond conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), they should not be conceptually proliferated?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should contemplate that the aggregate of form, up to and including the aggregate of consciousness, all lack intrinsic nature; as explained at length, even the knowledge of all modes lacks intrinsic nature. If a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, it cannot be the object of conceptual proliferation.”

Therefore, Subhūti, because the aggregate of form up to the aggregate of consciousness are all beyond conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), bodhisattva mahāsattvas should not engage in conceptual proliferation; and so on, in detail, until: because even the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*) is beyond conceptual proliferation, bodhisattva mahāsattvas should not engage in conceptual proliferation.

"Subhūti, you should know that if bodhisattva-mahāsattvas can thus practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful means, free from conceptual proliferation (*aprapañca*) regarding all phenomena, they will enter the bodhisattva’s state of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*), swiftly fulfill all the bodhisattva stages (*bhūmi*), quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), and be able to bring benefit and happiness to all beings throughout the future."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature and there is no conceptual proliferation to be found,
by what path do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth?"
"Is it for the path of the śrāvakas, the path of the pratyekabuddhas, or the path of the Buddhas?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not enter the bodhisattva’s state of certainty (samyaktva-niyāma) by means of the paths of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or Buddhas; rather, having first studied all paths exhaustively, they enter the bodhisattva’s state of certainty by means of the bodhisattva path."
Subhūti, you should know this:

just as one who is an eighth-rank practitioner first trains in all paths and later, by means of his own path, enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) of his own vehicle, yet until he has given rise to the path of the fruit of perfection, he is not yet able to realize the ultimate fruit of his own vehicle.

The bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are also like this: having first studied all paths universally, they enter the bodhisattva’s state of certainty beyond regression by means of the bodhisattva path; yet, until they have given rise to the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), they are still unable to attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek.
"If one enters this meditative absorption, by means of the sublime wisdom associated with a single moment, one is able to realize the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, desiring to fulfill the knowledge of all modes, first trains extensively in all paths and then enters the bodhisattva’s state of certainty through the bodhisattva path,"

If that is so, would it not follow that the paths of the eighth person, the stream-enterer, the once-returner, the non-returner, the arhat, the pratyekabuddha, and the Tathāgata—each directed toward their respective fruits—are distinct from one another?

Since these various paths are each distinct, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, desiring to fulfill the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), first study all paths universally and subsequently enter the bodhisattva’s state of right determination (samyaktvaniyāma) by means of his own path?

That is to say, when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas give rise to the eighth path, they should become those of the eighth stage; when they give rise to the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*), they should become stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*); when they give rise to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), they should become once-returners (*sakṛdāgāmin*) or non-returners (*anāgāmin*); when they give rise to the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*), they should become arhats; and when they give rise to the path of the solitary realizer (*pratyekabuddha*), they should become solitary realizers.
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having already become an eighth-rank [śrāvaka], were able to enter the bodhisattva’s certainty of the state free from outflows (samyaktvaniyāma), this is impossible.
And if one does not enter the bodhisattva’s certainty of the state free from outflows, yet realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, this too is impossible.”

"Bhagavān! If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has attained the fruit of a stream-enterer up to that of a pratyekabuddha, it is absolutely impossible for them to enter the bodhisattva’s state of certainty beyond regression."
It is impossible that one could realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without entering the bodhisattva’s state of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*).

How then can I truly understand how bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, desiring to fulfill the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), first train extensively in all paths before entering the bodhisattva’s state of certainty, without contradicting the principle of reality?
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, after having become an eighth-rank disciple, and so on up to having become a pratyekabuddha, were able to enter the bodhisattva’s state of certainty in the departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma), this is simply impossible; yet, without entering the bodhisattva’s state of certainty in the departure from birth, to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—this too is impossible.
