Nevertheless, it is not contrary to reason that Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having first studied all paths in their entirety, subsequently enter the Bodhisattva’s state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).

That is to say, from the moment they first resolve their minds [on awakening], Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice with courageous diligence the perfections from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom; by means of superior knowledge and vision, they transcend the eight stages, namely, from the Stage of Pure Observation (*śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi*) up to the Stage of the Pratyekabuddhas.

Although they universally cultivate and study all eight stages thus described, they are able to transcend them through superior wisdom and vision, and by means of the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), they enter the bodhisattva’s state of correct determination (*samyaktvaniyāma*).

Having entered the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth, they gradually further employ the knowledge of all aspects to forever sever the continuity of all habitual tendencies, thereby realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Subhūti, you should know that whatever wisdom or abandonment constitutes the eighth stage of training, up to and including the wisdom or abandonment of a pratyekabuddha— all these are the patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
After all bodhisattva mahāsattvas have first studied all paths universally, they subsequently enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth by means of their own path.

Having entered the bodhisattva’s state of correct determination and transcendence of birth, they gradually cultivate all bodhisattva practices and subsequently realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, benefiting all classes of sentient beings with its fruit.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

“As the Blessed One has taught, bodhisattva mahāsattvas should train in the thorough knowledge of all aspects of the paths—whether the path of śrāvakas, the path of pratyekabuddhas, the path of bodhisattvas, or the path of buddhas. Knowing all the aspects of these paths is called the ‘knowledge of the aspects of the path. How, then, should bodhisattva mahāsattvas give rise to the path of the knowledge of the aspects of the path?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should give rise to the knowledge of the aspects of all pure paths.
How should a bodhisattva-mahāsattva give rise to the knowledge of the aspects of all pure paths?”
This refers to those modes of conduct, characteristics, and signs that can correctly manifest the knowledge of signs regarding the pure path.

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas universally and perfectly awaken to all such modes of conduct, characteristics, and signs; having attained perfect awakening, they truthfully proclaim, reveal, designate, and establish them for others, enabling sentient beings to attain unerring understanding and to proceed accordingly toward benefit and happiness.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva should attain skillfulness in all sounds and languages; using this skillful mastery of sound and language, they should proclaim the true Dharma throughout the sentient beings of the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system, causing them to know that what is heard is like an echo—though there is understanding, there is no attachment.
“Subhūti, you should know that for this reason, bodhisattva mahāsattvas should train to perfect the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*).

Having trained to perfect the knowledge of the aspects of the path, they should know, as they truly are, the various differences in the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and dispositions (*āśaya*) of all sentient beings, and accordingly bring them benefit and happiness. That is to say, they should know, as they truly are, the latent tendencies, dispositions, and their causes and effects regarding sentient beings in the hells; having known these, they employ skillful means to block those paths.”

Furthermore, he knows as they truly are the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), dispositions, and their causes and effects regarding the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, the nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and so forth; having known them, he employs skillful means to obstruct those paths.

Likewise, he knows as they truly are the latent tendencies and dispositions of humans, the gods of the desire realm, up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; having known them, he employs skillful means to obstruct those paths.
Furthermore, he knows as they truly are the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path, as well as their causes and results;
he knows as they truly are the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, as well as their causes and results;
and he knows as they truly are the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—as well as their causes and results. Furthermore...
They truly know the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality, as well as their causes and results;
they also truly know the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, as well as their causes and results;
they also truly know the six perfections and their causes and results; and they also truly know inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature.
He also knows their causes and effects as they truly are; he also knows true thusness up to the inconceivable realm and their causes and effects as they truly are;
he also knows the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata and their causes and effects as they truly are;
he also knows the stage of extreme joy up to the stage of the cloud of dharma and their causes and effects as they truly are.
He knows, as they truly are, the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi, as well as their causes and results;
he knows, as they truly are, the purification of the five eyes and the six supernormal powers, as well as their causes and results;

he knows, as they truly are, the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, as well as their causes and results; and he knows, as they truly are, great loving-kindness and great compassion.
...great joy, great equanimity, and their causes and results; likewise, he knows as they truly are the quality of non-forgetfulness, the constant abiding in equanimity, and their causes and results;

likewise, he knows as they truly are the knowledge of all things, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects, along with their causes and results; and likewise, he knows as they truly are the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas...
"Bodhisattvas, Tathāgatas, and their causes and results. Subhūti,

you should know that once bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have, according to reality, understood the paths of the śrāvakas and so forth, along with their causes and results, they establish sentient beings in the paths of the three vehicles as appropriate, causing them to practice diligently so that each may attain the ultimate goal."
Subhūti, you should know that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should give rise to such knowledge of the characteristics of the true path.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva trains in this knowledge of the characteristics of the true path, they will thoroughly penetrate the various elements, latent tendencies, and inclinations of all sentient beings.
Having thus attained realization, he teaches the True Dharma to each according to their needs, ensuring that all obtain the supreme fruits they seek without fail. Why is this so?

This bodhisattva mahāsattva skillfully knows the superior and inferior faculties of sentient beings; they truly penetrate the distinctions in the mental states and mental factors of all sentient beings as they wander through birth and death, and thus, for the sake of teaching the Dharma, no one ever departs empty-handed.
Subhūti, you should know that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) as these various paths. Why is this so?
All the factors conducive to enlightenment—the path that all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas should study—are entirely subsumed within this profound perfection of wisdom.
"All śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas train diligently therein and all attain the ultimate.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) of every kind and all forms of enlightenment are such that they are neither associated nor dissociated, formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and of a single characteristic—namely, the characteristic of being signless (*animitta*)—"
How can such factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) grasp enlightenment?

They are all neither associated nor dissociated; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic—namely, the characteristic of signlessness (animitta). How can these dharma-s, which are signless, exercise grasping or relinquishing toward other dharmas?

For example, just as space neither grasps nor rejects any phenomena because its intrinsic nature is empty, so too all phenomena are likewise empty of intrinsic nature; there is no grasping or rejecting of other phenomena.
"How can it be said that the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharmas) are able to grasp enlightenment?
The Buddha told Subhūti: "It is so!"
"So it is! It is just as you have said.

Because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, there is neither grasping nor relinquishing; yet sentient beings are unable to comprehend the meaning of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena. For their benefit, I employ skillful means to proclaim the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma), which can lead to the attainment of bodhi."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Whether it be the aggregate of form up to the aggregate of consciousness, or as extensively explained up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), within this noble Dharma and Vinaya, they are neither associated nor dissociated; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics."

The Buddha, for the benefit of all sentient beings, so that they may attain correct understanding and enter into the true nature of phenomena, speaks in reliance upon conventional truth and not ultimate truth.
Subhūti, you should know this!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should train in wisdom and vision regarding all such phenomena.
Having trained in wisdom and vision, they should, through their observation according to reality, discern which of these phenomena are to be embraced and which phenomena are not to be embraced.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In which dharmas should bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train their wisdom and vision so that, having observed them as they truly are, they do not grasp at them?"
"In regard to what dharmas should one, having trained in knowledge and vision, observe them as they truly are and then accept them?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have trained in knowledge and vision regarding the dharmas of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and so forth, they should observe them as they truly are and not accept them."

Having studied the knowledge and vision regarding all phenomena associated with the knowledge of all modes, one should, as it truly is, observe that all aspects associated [with those phenomena] are worthy of being embraced.
Subhūti, you should know this!
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should train in this profound perfection of wisdom within this noble Dharma-Vinaya.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“When the Buddha speaks of the ‘noble Dharma-Vinaya,’ what is meant by the name ‘noble Dharma-Vinaya’?”
"For what reason is it called the 'Noble Dharma and Vinaya'?
The Buddha told Subhūti: "Whether they be śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or tathāgatas..."
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is, in all such respects, neither associated with nor dissociated from greed, hatred, and delusion;
he is neither associated with nor dissociated from the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*);
and he is neither associated with nor dissociated from sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) and ill will (*vyāpāda*).
It is neither associated nor dissociated with attachment to the realm of form, attachment to the formless realm, restlessness, pride, and ignorance;
it is neither associated nor dissociated with the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
and it is not associated with the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path.
It should not be dissociated; it is neither associated nor dissociated with the Noble Truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
it is neither associated nor dissociated with the doors of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
and it is neither associated nor dissociated with the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality.
They are neither associated nor dissociated with the six pāramitās;
they are neither associated nor dissociated with inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence;
they are neither associated nor dissociated with suchness up to the inconceivable realm; and [they are neither associated nor dissociated] with the stage of pure observation...
Up to the stage of a Tathāgata, they are neither associated nor dissociated; with the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma Stage, they are neither associated nor dissociated;
with the gates of dhāraṇī and the gates of samādhi, they are neither associated nor dissociated;
and with the five eyes and the six supernormal powers, they are neither associated...
It should not be dissociated; it is neither associated nor dissociated with the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
it is neither associated nor dissociated with great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity;
[it is neither associated nor dissociated] with the thirty-two marks of a Great Being and the eighty secondary characteristics...
All these are neither associated nor dissociated; they are neither associated nor dissociated with the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity;
they are neither associated nor dissociated with all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and all-aspect knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*);
[they are likewise] with the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha...

All these are neither associated nor dissociated; they are neither associated nor dissociated with the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha;

they are neither associated nor dissociated with the severance of the continuity of the habitual tendencies of afflictions and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*); [they are likewise] not associated with the conditioned...
The realms and the unconditioned realm are neither associated nor dissociated.
"Subhūti, you should know that they are called 'noble ones,' and this is their noble Dharma-Vinaya; therefore it is named the Noble Dharma-Vinaya."

Why is this? Because all these phenomena are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being signless; the noble ones perceive them as they truly are.

Subhūti, you should know this: all formless phenomena and formless phenomena are neither associated nor dissociated; all invisible phenomena and invisible phenomena are neither associated nor dissociated; all non-obstructive phenomena and non-obstructive phenomena are neither associated nor dissociated; all single-characteristic phenomena and single-characteristic phenomena are neither associated nor dissociated; and all signless phenomena and signless phenomena are neither associated nor dissociated.

Subhūti, you should know that bodhisattva mahāsattvas should constantly train in this profound perfection of wisdom— which is formless, invisible, non-resistant, of a single characteristic, and signless— and having so trained, they do not grasp at the characteristics of any phenomena.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Should Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas not train in the characteristics of form, up to and including consciousness?"
To speak at length, up to: "Should one not train in the various characteristics of the knowledge of all modes?
Should one not train in the various characteristics of knowing suffering, abandoning the origin, realizing cessation, and cultivating the path?"
Should one not train in observing the various characteristics of the twelve links of dependent origination in both forward and reverse order?
Should one not train in the various characteristics of the noble ones and the noble dharmas?
"Should one not train in the characteristics of the conditioned realm and the unconditioned realm? [The Blessed One replied:
"World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not train in the characteristics of such dharmas, they likewise should not train in the characteristics of conditioned formations."

"Bhagavān! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva cannot train in the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and the characteristics of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāralakṣaṇa*), how can they transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?"
If one cannot transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, how can one enter the bodhisattva’s state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma)?
If one cannot enter the bodhisattva’s state of right determination, how can one realize unsurpassed enlightenment?
If one cannot realize unsurpassed bodhi, how can one turn the subtle and wondrous wheel of Dharma?

If one cannot turn the subtle and wondrous wheel of Dharma, how can one establish sentient beings through the unsurpassed vehicles of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, causing them to escape the great suffering of boundless birth and death and to dwell securely in the pure, eternal bliss of nirvāṇa?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If all dharmas possessed real marks, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should train therein.

However, because all dharmas do not possess real marks—being formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and having a single mark, namely 'marklessness'—therefore the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas does not train in marks, nor do they train in the dharma of marklessness."

Why is this so? Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, the dharma-realm remains eternally abiding, and all phenomena possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (*animitta*). Since such signlessness is neither a characteristic of existence nor a characteristic of non-existence, it cannot be learned. Why is this so?
It is not that all dharmas first possess characteristics and later become characteristicless; rather, all dharmas are fundamentally characteristicless and remain so thereafter.

Therefore, the assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas does not train in what has characteristics, nor do they train in what is characteristicless, because the dharmas of characteristics and characteristiclessness are established in mutual dependence and are not ultimate.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If all dharmas neither possess the mark of existence nor the mark of non-existence, they should neither have a single mark nor different marks; how then can a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the perfection of wisdom?"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not cultivate the perfection of wisdom, they will be unable to transcend the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
If they cannot transcend the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, they will be unable to enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth.
If one cannot enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth, one should be unable to transcend the bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena.
If one cannot transcend the bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena, one should be unable to give rise to the bodhisattva’s supreme and wondrous supernormal powers.
If one cannot manifest the sublime and wondrous supernormal powers of a bodhisattva, one should be unable to purify buddha-fields and mature sentient beings.
If one cannot purify buddha-fields and mature sentient beings, one should be unable to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
If one cannot attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, one should be unable to turn the pure wheel of Dharma.

If one cannot turn the pure wheel of Dharma, then one should be unable to skillfully establish all classes of sentient beings, causing them to abide in the fruit of the Śrāvaka vehicle, or the fruit of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, or the fruit of the Unsurpassed Vehicle.

Furthermore, they would likewise be unable to skillfully establish sentient beings so that they might abide in meritorious actions consisting of generosity, or abide in meritorious actions consisting of ethical discipline, or abide in meritorious actions consisting of cultivation, thereby attaining the sovereign wealth and happiness of humans and devas.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said:
all dharmas have neither marks nor absence of marks, neither a single mark nor diverse marks.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that whether dharmas have marks or lack marks, or whether they have a single mark or diverse marks, they are all of one and the same mark—namely, the markless—and cultivates this marklessness, it is called cultivating the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In what way does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate this signlessness (animitta) such that it is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates the relinquishment of all phenomena, this is called cultivating the perfection of wisdom.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the removal of all phenomena, such that it is called cultivating the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates the removal of form and also removes this very cultivation, it is called cultivating the perfection of wisdom.”
To cultivate the removal of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, and also to remove that very cultivation—this is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the removal of the sense base of the eye up to the sense base of the mind, and also to remove that very cultivation—this is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the removal of the sense base of form up to the sense base of mental phenomena, and also to remove that very cultivation—this is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the removal of the eye-element up to and including the mind-element, and to remove even that cultivation itself, is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the removal of the form-element up to and including the phenomena-element, and to remove even that cultivation itself, is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;

to cultivate the removal of the eye-consciousness-element up to and including the mind-consciousness-element, and to remove even that cultivation itself, is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

To cultivate the relinquishment of eye-contact and so forth, up to and including mind-contact, and to relinquish even that cultivation itself, is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

To cultivate the relinquishment of all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, and so forth, up to and including all feelings produced with mind-contact as condition, and to relinquish even that cultivation itself, is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

To cultivate the relinquishment of the earth element and so forth, up to and including the consciousness element, and to relinquish even that cultivation itself, is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

To cultivate the relinquishment of the causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) up to and including the dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*), and to further relinquish that very cultivation—this is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

To cultivate the relinquishment of ignorance (*avidyā*) up to and including old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), and to further relinquish that very cultivation—this is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

To cultivate the relinquishment of entering and emerging from saṃsāra as well as the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), and to further relinquish that very cultivation—this is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

To cultivate the relinquishing of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments, while also relinquishing that very cultivation, is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;

to cultivate the relinquishing of the recollection of the Buddha up to the recollection of peace, while also relinquishing that very cultivation, is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;

to cultivate the relinquishing of the perception of impermanence up to the perception of cessation, while also relinquishing that very cultivation, is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the removal of the notion of a self, up to and including the notion of a "seer," and to remove them as well—this cultivation is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;

to cultivate the removal of the notion of dependent origination and the notion of non-dependent origination, and to remove them as well—this cultivation is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;

to cultivate the removal of the notions of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, as well as the notions of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity, and to remove them as well—this cultivation is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

To cultivate the relinquishing of the four applications of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, and furthermore to relinquish that very cultivation, is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;

to cultivate the relinquishing of the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—and furthermore to relinquish that very cultivation, is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the relinquishing of the eight liberations up to the ten totalities, and furthermore to relinquish that very cultivation, is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

To cultivate the removal of the notion of the noble truths as well as the notion of what are not noble truths, and furthermore to remove that very cultivation, is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;

to cultivate the removal of the samādhi with applied and sustained thought, the samādhi without applied thought but with sustained thought, and the samādhi without applied or sustained thought, and furthermore to remove that very cultivation, is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the removal of the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, and furthermore to remove that very cultivation, is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the elimination of the knowledge of suffering up to the knowledge as it is, and likewise to eliminate that very cultivation, is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the elimination of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, and likewise to eliminate that very cultivation, is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;

to cultivate the elimination of internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, and likewise to eliminate that very cultivation, is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the thorough removal of everything from suchness up to the inconceivable realm, while also removing that very cultivation itself, is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;

to cultivate the thorough removal of everything from the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata, while also removing that very cultivation itself, is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;

to cultivate the thorough removal of everything from the stage of extreme joy up to the stage of the cloud of dharma, while also removing that very cultivation itself, is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the removal of the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi, and yet to remove even this cultivation, is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the removal of the five eyes and the six supernormal powers, and yet to remove even this cultivation, is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;

to cultivate the removal of the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and yet to remove even this cultivation, is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

To cultivate the removal of great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity, while also removing that very cultivation, is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the removal of the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs, while also removing that very cultivation, is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the removal of the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity, while also removing that very cultivation, is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

To cultivate the removal of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), while also removing that very cultivation, is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

To cultivate the removal of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*) up to the awakening of a solitary buddha (*pratyekabuddhabodhi*), while also removing that very cultivation, is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the removal of all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, while also removing that very cultivation, is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
To cultivate the removal of the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas, while also removing that very cultivation, is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;

to cultivate the removal of the perpetual severance of the continuity of the habitual tendencies of afflictions, while also removing that very cultivation, is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
to cultivate the removal of the knowledge of all modes, while also removing that very cultivation, is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates the elimination of form and also eliminates this cultivation itself, it is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
and when they cultivate the elimination of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, and also eliminate this cultivation itself, it is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom?"

To speak at length, up to the point that the cultivation of the removal and permanent severance of the continuity of the habitual tendencies of the afflictions is itself removed—that is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
the cultivation of the removal of even the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) and the removal of this very cultivation—that is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), if they conceive of form and then cultivate its destruction, they are not eliminating form, nor are they practicing the perfection of wisdom.

If they conceive of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness and then cultivate their destruction, they are not eliminating feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor are they practicing the perfection of wisdom."

To speak at length, up to: if one thinks of the permanent severance of the continuity of the habitual tendencies of afflictions and the destruction of this cultivation, that is not the removal of the continuity of the habitual tendencies of afflictions, nor is it the cultivation of the *prajñāpāramitā*.

If one thinks of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*) and the destruction of its cultivation, that is not the removal of the knowledge of all modes, nor is it the cultivation of the *prajñāpāramitā*.

However, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do not conceive of form or the cultivation that destroys it; this elimination of form is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

They do not conceive of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor the cultivation that destroys them; this elimination of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

To speak at length, up to: not to conceive of the continuity of the habitual tendencies of afflictions (*kleśavāsanā*) being permanently severed, nor of the destruction of this cultivation, is to eliminate the continuity of the habitual tendencies of afflictions; this is the cultivation of the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Not to conceive of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*), nor of the destruction of this cultivation, is to eliminate the knowledge of all modes; this is the cultivation of the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Why is this? It is because one who possesses perceptions cannot sever the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), the active fetters (*paryavasthāna*), and the defilements (*mala*) of greed, hatred, and delusion, nor can such a person cultivate the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Therefore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the removal of form and also removes that very practice, it is called practicing the perfection of wisdom; if they practice the removal of feeling,
perception, mental formations, and consciousness, as well as the removal of that very practice, it is called practicing the perfection of wisdom.

To speak at length, up to: the cultivation of the removal of the continuity of the habitual tendencies of afflictions and the removal of that very cultivation is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom;
the cultivation of the removal of the knowledge of all modes and the removal of that very cultivation is called the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Those who dwell in the perception of existence cannot cultivate the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom; to speak extensively, those who dwell in the perception of existence also cannot permanently sever the continuity of the habitual tendencies of afflictions, nor can they cultivate the knowledge of all aspects."

Why is this so? Those who dwell in the perception of existence will certainly grasp at a self and what belongs to a self (*ātman* and *ātmīya*). Due to this grasping, they become attached to the two extremes; because of attachment to the two extremes, they are definitively unable to be liberated from birth and death. For them, there is no path and no nirvāṇa. How, then, could they practice the six *pāramitās* as they truly are, and—expanding on this—how could they ever sever the continuity of the habitual tendencies of afflictions, or cultivate the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*)?
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is existence? What is non-existence?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Duality is existence; non-duality is non-existence.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What are these two? What is non-duality?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"The perception of form up to the perception of consciousness constitutes duality; the emptiness of the perception of form up to the emptiness of the perception of consciousness constitutes non-duality.

The perception of the eye-base up to the perception of the mind-base constitutes duality; the emptiness of the perception of the eye-base up to the emptiness of the perception of the mind-base constitutes non-duality.

The perception of the form-base up to the perception of the phenomena-base constitutes duality; the emptiness of the perception of the form-base up to the emptiness of the perception of the phenomena-base constitutes non-duality."

The perception of the eye-element up to the perception of the mind-element constitutes duality; the emptiness of the perception of the eye-element up to the emptiness of the perception of the mind-element constitutes non-duality.

The perception of the form-element up to the perception of the phenomena-element constitutes duality; the emptiness of the perception of the form-element up to the emptiness of the perception of the phenomena-element constitutes non-duality.

The perception of the eye-consciousness-element up to the perception of the mind-consciousness-element constitutes duality; the emptiness of the perception of the eye-consciousness-element up to the emptiness of the perception of the mind-consciousness-element constitutes non-duality.

The perception of eye-contact up to the perception of mind-contact constitutes duality; the emptiness of the perception of eye-contact up to the emptiness of the perception of mind-contact constitutes non-duality.

The various feelings and perceptions produced with eye-contact as condition up to the various feelings and perceptions produced with mind-contact as condition constitute duality; the emptiness of the various feelings and perceptions produced with eye-contact as condition up to the emptiness of the various feelings and perceptions produced with mind-contact as condition constitutes non-duality.

The perception of the earth element up to the perception of the consciousness element constitutes duality; the emptiness of the perception of the earth element up to the emptiness of the perception of the consciousness element constitutes non-duality.

The perception of causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) up to the perception of dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) constitutes duality; the emptiness of the perception of causal conditions up to the emptiness of the perception of dominant conditions constitutes non-duality.

The perception of ignorance (*avidyā*) up to the perception of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) constitutes duality; the emptiness of the perception of ignorance up to the emptiness of the perception of old age and death constitutes non-duality.

The perception of the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*) up to the perception of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) constitutes duality; the emptiness of the perception of the perfection of generosity up to the emptiness of the perception of the perfection of wisdom constitutes non-duality.

The perception of internal emptiness up to the perception of the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature constitute duality; the emptiness of the perception of internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the perception of the non-existence of intrinsic nature constitutes non-duality.

The perception of suchness up to the perception of the inconceivable realm constitute duality; the emptiness of the perception of suchness up to the emptiness of the perception of the inconceivable realm constitutes non-duality.

The perception of the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path constitute duality; the emptiness of the perception of the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path constitutes non-duality.

The perception of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the perception of the eightfold noble path constitutes duality; the emptiness of the perception of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the emptiness of the perception of the eightfold noble path constitutes non-duality.

The perception of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments constitutes duality; the emptiness of the perception of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments constitutes non-duality.
The perception of the three gates of liberation constitutes duality; the emptiness of the perception of the three gates of liberation constitutes non-duality.

The perception of the eight liberations up to the perception of the ten totalities is duality; the emptiness of the perception of the eight liberations up to the emptiness of the perception of the ten totalities is non-duality.

The perception of the stage of pure observation up to the perception of the stage of the Tathāgata is duality; the emptiness of the perception of the stage of pure observation up to the emptiness of the perception of the stage of the Tathāgata is non-duality.

The perception of the stage of extreme joy up to the perception of the stage of the cloud of dharma is duality; the emptiness of the perception of the stage of extreme joy up to the emptiness of the perception of the stage of the cloud of dharma is non-duality.

To conceive of the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi as two is dualistic; to conceive of the emptiness of the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi as non-dual is non-dualistic.

To conceive of the five eyes and the six supernormal powers as two is dualistic; to conceive of the emptiness of the five eyes and the six supernormal powers as non-dual is non-dualistic. To conceive of the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as two is dualistic; to conceive of the emptiness of the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the emptiness of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as non-dual is non-dualistic.

To conceive of great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity as two is dualistic; to conceive of the emptiness of great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity as non-dual is non-dualistic.
The perception of the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics as dual, and the perception of the emptiness of the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics as non-dual;

the perception of the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity as dual, and the perception of the emptiness of the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity as non-dual;

the perception of all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects as dual, and the perception of the emptiness of all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects as non-dual.

The perception of the fruit of stream-entry up to the perception of pratyekabuddha-enlightenment constitutes duality; the emptiness of the perception of the fruit of stream-entry up to the emptiness of the perception of pratyekabuddha-enlightenment constitutes non-duality.

The perception of all bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices and the perception of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas constitute duality; the emptiness of the perception of all bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices and the perception of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas constitutes non-duality.

The perception of the conditioned realm and the perception of the unconditioned realm constitute duality; the emptiness of the perception of the conditioned realm and the perception of the unconditioned realm constitutes non-duality.

"Subhūti, you should know that all perceptions whatsoever constitute duality; all duality whatsoever constitutes existence; and all existence whatsoever involves birth and death. Those who possess birth and death cannot be liberated from birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair."
"Subhūti, you should know this!

All those for whom perceptions are empty are non-dual; all those who are non-dual are non-existent; all those who are non-existent have no birth-and-death; and those who have no birth-and-death are able to be liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair."

For this reason, you should know that for one who possesses the notion of duality, there is certainly no giving, nor even the perfection of wisdom; there is no path, no attainment, and no clear realization. Even the "patience in accordance with truth" (anulomikī kṣānti) does not exist for such a person, let alone the thorough knowledge of form—and so on, as extensively explained—up to the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
Since they are not even able to cultivate the various noble paths, how much less can they attain the fruit of stream-entry, up to and including the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha!

How much less can they forever sever the continuity of all afflictions and habitual tendencies, realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and turn the sublime wheel of Dharma to deliver the multitudes of sentient beings!

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Number Five Hundred Twenty-Seven. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Chapter 28: The Sublime Marks. Part Three, Chapter Twenty-Eight on the Sublime Marks, Section One. At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If those who dwell in the perception of existence lack compliant patience (*anulomikī kṣānti*), they likewise lack the cultivation of the path, the attainment of the fruit, and clear realization (*abhisamaya*). How could those who dwell in the perception of non-existence possess compliant patience?"

Whether it be the stage of pure observation, or as extensively explained up to the stage of a Tathāgata, if one cultivates the noble path and, by relying on that cultivation of the noble path, abandons all afflictions—yet because of being obscured and hindered by those very afflictions, one cannot even attain the stages corresponding to the dharmas of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, much less enter the Bodhisattva’s state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Without entering the bodhisattva’s state of right determination and transcendence of birth, how could one possibly realize the knowledge of all aspects?
If one cannot attain the knowledge of all aspects, how could one ever sever the continuity of all afflictions and their habitual tendencies?
“World-Honored One!

If all dharmas are ultimately non-existent, neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure—if such dharmas are in every way unarisen, how can one realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna)?”
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.

Those who abide in the state of non-conception likewise lack the patient acceptance that accords with truth (*anulomikī kṣānti*), and so forth, up to lacking the permanent severance of the continuity of the habitual tendencies of afflictions (*kleśavāsanā*), nor can they attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).

Nevertheless, by relying on the signless, one cultivates and attains the conforming patience (*anulomikī kṣānti*) regarding the fact that no real phenomena exist; eventually, one forever severs the continuity of all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), and is likewise able to realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, do they have the perception of existence, or the perception of non-existence?"
Is there the perception of the aggregate of form, and so on, up to the perception of the aggregate of consciousness?
To speak more extensively, is there even the perception of the perpetual severance of the continuity of all afflictions and their habitual tendencies?
"Do they have the notion that they have realized the knowledge of all modes?
World-Honored One!
Does this bodhisattva mahāsattva have the notion of form, or the notion of the abandonment of form?"
Is there a perception of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness? Is there a perception of the cessation of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness?

Is there a perception of the sense-base of the eye, up to and including the sense-base of the mind? Is there a perception of the cessation of the sense-base of the eye, up to and including the sense-base of the mind?
Is there a perception of the form base up to the mental-object base? Is there a perception of the abandonment of the form base up to the mental-object base?
Is there a perception of the eye element up to the mind element? Is there a perception of the abandonment of the eye element up to the mind element?
Is there a perception of the form realm up to the dharma realm? Is there a perception of the abandonment of the form realm up to the dharma realm?
Is there a perception of the eye-consciousness realm up to the mind-consciousness realm? Is there a perception of the abandonment of the eye-consciousness realm up to the mind-consciousness realm?
Is there the perception of eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact? Is there the perception of the cessation of eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact?

Is there the perception of the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, up to and including the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition? Is there the perception of the cessation of the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, up to and including the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition?
Is there a perception of the earth element up to the consciousness element, and is there a perception of the cessation of the earth element up to the consciousness element?
Is there a perception of the causal condition up to the dominant condition, and is there a perception of the cessation of the causal condition up to the dominant condition?
Is there the perception of greed, hatred, and delusion, and is there the perception of the abandonment of greed, hatred, and delusion?
Is there the perception of ignorance up to old age and death, and is there the perception of the abandonment of ignorance up to old age and death?
If one has the perception of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, does one also have the perception of the abandonment of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path?

To speak at length, up to: if one has the perception of all afflictions, their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), and their continuity as things to be abandoned, does one also have the perception of the abandonment of all afflictions, their habitual tendencies, and their continuity?
"Do they have the notion that there is the wisdom of omniscience, or the notion that there is the abandonment of the wisdom of omniscience?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they have no notion regarding any phenomena, nor do they have the notion of non-notion."

If there is neither perception nor non-perception, one should know that this is the Bodhisattva’s conformative patience (anulomikī-kṣānti), as well as the cultivation of the path, the attainment of the fruit, and clear realization (abhisamaya).
Subhūti, you should know that for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, non-existence is the noble path; non-existence is the attainment of the fruit; and non-existence is the clear realization.
"For this reason, you should know that there are no phenomena whatsoever whose nature is not the absence of intrinsic nature.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If all phenomena have as their nature the absence of intrinsic nature, how is it that the Blessed One has attained manifest, complete, and perfect enlightenment regarding the fact that all phenomena have as their nature the absence of intrinsic nature? Having attained manifest, complete, and perfect enlightenment, why is he called a 'Buddha,' and why does he exercise sovereign mastery over all phenomena and all objects?"
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
All phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature.

When I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, I cultivated the perfections from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom; by means of this, I became free from sensual desires and unwholesome states, and with directed thought and evaluation, born of seclusion, joy and happiness, I entered the first dhyāna. (The full account continues) until: having abandoned pleasure and abandoned pain, and with the prior disappearance of joy and grief, neither-painful-nor-pleasant, with equanimity and mindfulness purified, I entered and dwelt in the fourth dhyāna, fully accomplished.

At that time, although I skillfully grasped the signs of the various dhyānas and their constituent factors, I was without any attachment; I did not give rise to craving for the various dhyānas and their constituent factors, nor did I perceive any entity whatsoever within the various dhyānas and their constituent factors.
At that time, my practice of the four dhyānas was pure in its aspects and free from conceptual differentiation.

Although at that time I was thoroughly proficient in the various dhyānas and their constituent factors (*dhyānāṅga*), I did not experience the karmic fruition resulting from them. Rather, relying upon dhyāna, I brought forth the supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) of psychic power, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, and the divine eye. Although I skillfully grasped the signs of these five supernormal powers, I harbored no attachment, nor did I relish them; regarding the objects of these powers, I perceived nothing at all, remained without conceptual differentiation, and dwelt like space.

At that time, I contemplated all phenomena as perfectly equal and equal, having non-existence as their very nature. With a sublime wisdom corresponding to a single kṣaṇa, I realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; that is to say, I fully awakened to the fact that these are the Noble Truth of Suffering, the Noble Truth of its Origin, the Noble Truth of its Cessation, and the Noble Truth of the Path—all of which share one and the same characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (*animitta*). Furthermore, even this signlessness is not to be apprehended.

By means of this, one accomplishes the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four analytical knowledges, eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and other boundless merits; through the sublime wisdom of a Buddha, one establishes the distinctions among the three categories of sentient beings and guides them through skillful means according to their needs, enabling them to attain supreme benefit and peace.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"How does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, within the naturelessness of all phenomena, give rise to the four dhyānas, manifest the five supernormal powers, realize great bodhi, possess all merits, and establish the three groups of sentient beings in benefit and happiness?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If all those sensual desires, unwholesome states, and unvirtuous dharmas possessed even the slightest intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), or if they had another nature as their intrinsic nature, then when I was originally practicing and training in the bodhisattva path, I would not have realized that all sensual desires, unwholesome states, and unvirtuous dharmas take the absence of nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) as their intrinsic nature, thereby transcending sensual desires and the like to enter and dwell fully in the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*). This is because all sensual desires, unwholesome states, and unvirtuous dharmas lack both self-nature and other-nature, and thus take only the absence of nature as their intrinsic nature.”

When I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, I attained mastery over sensual desires, evil, and unwholesome dharmas, realizing that they all have non-existence as their intrinsic nature; thus, free from sensual desires and evil, I entered the various meditative concentrations (dhyāna) and dwelt therein in full perfection.
“Subhūti, you should know this!

If the five supernormal powers possessed even the slightest intrinsic nature, or if another nature were their intrinsic nature, then when I was originally practicing and training in the bodhisattva path, I would not have realized that all supernormal powers take the absence of nature as their intrinsic nature, thereby giving rise to various sovereign supernormal powers that function with wondrous mastery and unimpededness across all objective realms. This is because these supernormal powers possess neither an intrinsic nature nor an extrinsic nature, but rather take the absence of nature as their very essence.”

When I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, I attained mastery over the supernormal powers, all of which take non-substantiality as their intrinsic nature; I gave rise to various sovereign supernormal powers, which function with wondrous and unimpeded efficacy within all realms of experience.
“Subhūti, you should know this:

if the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha possessed even the slightest intrinsic nature, or if another nature were its intrinsic nature, then when I was originally training in the bodhisattva path, I would not have attained penetration into the fact that the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas and all their qualities have ‘non-existence’ as their intrinsic nature, nor would I have realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and become endowed with all those qualities. This is because the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha and all its qualities possess neither an intrinsic nature of self nor an intrinsic nature of other, but have only non-existence as their intrinsic nature.”

When I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, I realized that unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment has "absence of intrinsic nature" as its very essence; by means of a single moment of corresponding sublime wisdom, I attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, endowed with all meritorious qualities.
"Subhūti, you should know this!

If sentient beings possessed even a slight intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), or if they possessed another nature as their intrinsic nature, then after I had attained Buddhahood, I would not have realized that all sentient beings take the absence of nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) as their intrinsic nature, nor would I have established the distinctions among the three groups of sentient beings, nor guided them through skillful means according to their needs to enable them to obtain supreme benefit and happiness. This is because sentient beings possess neither an intrinsic nature of their own nor that of another, but take only the absence of nature as their intrinsic nature."

Once I have attained Buddhahood, I shall realize that all sentient beings take the absence of intrinsic nature as their own nature; I will establish the distinctions among the three categories of sentient beings and, according to what is appropriate for each, guide them through skillful means so that they may obtain supreme benefit and peace.
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that all phenomena have non-existence as their nature, yet within that state gives rise to the four dhyānas, manifests the five supernormal powers, realizes unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, possesses all merits, and establishes sentient beings in the three categories of those to be trained, skillfully guiding them according to their needs so that they may obtain benefit and happiness—how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has first resolved on enlightenment perform gradual karma, practice gradual training, and carry out gradual conduct within the nature of the non-existent nature of all phenomena; and by means of this gradual karma, training, and conduct, how does he realize unsurpassed perfect enlightenment and bring about the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas first produce the thought of enlightenment, they hear it either from a Buddha, or from those who have made extensive offerings to Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, Anāgāmins, Sakṛdāgāmins, and Srotāpannas—these noble ones. They hear that one who has realized that all phenomena have 'non-nature' as their nature (*abhāva-svabhāva*) to the ultimate degree of perfection is called a Buddha; one who gradually realizes that all phenomena have non-nature as their nature is called a Bodhisattva; and even one who, as a Srotāpanna, has deep faith that all phenomena have non-nature as their nature is called a virtuous person (*satpuruṣa*). Therefore, there are no phenomena or sentient beings whatsoever that do not take non-nature as their nature; among phenomena and sentient beings, not even so much as the tip of a hair can be found to possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)."
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva hears this matter, he reflects as follows:

"If all phenomena and all sentient beings have 'absence of intrinsic nature' as their very essence, then by realizing this, one is called a Buddha; and even those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry are called noble persons because they have deep faith in this."

Whether I shall realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment or not, since all phenomena and sentient beings always have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, I must certainly set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Having attained enlightenment, if there are sentient beings who act with conceptualization, I shall employ skillful means to establish them so that they may abide in non-conceptuality.

"Having thus reflected, this bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; for the sake of all sentient beings attaining nirvāṇa, he performs gradual karma, cultivates gradual training, and practices gradual conduct."

Just as the bodhisattva mahāsattvas of the past set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by first training in the gradual sequence of karma, training, and practice, thereby realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, so too this bodhisattva mahāsattva must first train in the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), next train in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), and so on in succession until finally training in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

“Subhūti, you should know that when these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, from their first production of the thought of awakening, practice the perfection of generosity, they should personally practice generosity, encourage others to practice generosity, constantly and correctly extol the merit of generosity, and joyfully praise those who practice generosity.”

By reason of these causes and conditions, their generosity is perfected, and they attain great wealth and status; they constantly practice giving, free from the mind of stinginess, bestowing upon all sentient beings whatever food, drink, and other requisites they require.
By means of giving, this bodhisattva mahāsattva upholds the aggregate of ethical discipline and is born among gods and humans, attaining great nobility;
by means of giving and ethical discipline, he further attains the aggregate of meditative concentration;
and by means of giving, ethical discipline, and meditative concentration, he further attains the aggregate of wisdom.
By means of generosity, ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom, one further attains the aggregate of liberation;
by means of generosity, ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, and liberation, one further attains the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation;

and by means of the perfection of the aggregates of generosity, ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, one transcends the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and enters the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth.
Having entered the Bodhisattva’s state of right determination free from birth, they bring sentient beings to maturity and purify Buddha-fields;

having performed these deeds, they are able to realize the knowledge of all modes, turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, and establish and deliver all classes of sentient beings by means of the three vehicles, causing them to transcend birth and death and realize nirvana.

By means of this giving, although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are thus able to perform gradual deeds, cultivate gradual training, and practice gradual conduct, they do not apprehend anything at all in any of these.
Why is this? Because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature. Furthermore, Subhūti!

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline from the first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment, they should personally practice ethical discipline, encourage others to practice ethical discipline, constantly and correctly extol the merits of ethical discipline, and joyfully praise those who practice ethical discipline.

By these causes and conditions, their aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*) becomes pure; they are born among gods and humans and attain great nobility. They bestow upon the poor whatever material goods are required.

Having practiced giving, they abide securely in the aggregates of ethical discipline, meditative concentration (*samādhiskandha*), wisdom (*prajñāskandha*), liberation (*vimuktiskandha*), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśanaskandha*).

Because these aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation are purified, they transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and realize entry into the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktvaniyāma*).
Having entered the bodhisattva’s state of right determination free from birth, they bring sentient beings to maturity and purify buddha-fields;

having performed these deeds, they are able to realize the knowledge of all modes, turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, and establish and deliver all classes of sentient beings by means of the three vehicles, causing them to transcend birth and death and realize nirvana.

Because of their pure ethical discipline, although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to perform gradual deeds, cultivate gradual training, and practice gradual conduct in this manner, they do not apprehend anything at all in any of these.
Why is this? Because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature. Furthermore, Subhūti!

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of patience from the first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment, they should personally practice patience, encourage others to practice patience, constantly and correctly extol the merits of patience, and joyfully praise those who practice patience.
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices patience, he is able to give material wealth to all sentient beings, bringing them all to satisfaction;

having practiced giving, he dwells securely in the aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation.

Because these aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation are purified, he transcends the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and enters the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth.
Having entered the Bodhisattva’s state of right determination free from birth, they bring sentient beings to maturity and purify Buddha-fields;

having performed these deeds, they are able to realize the knowledge of all modes, turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, and establish and deliver sentient beings by means of the three vehicles, causing them to transcend birth and death and realize nirvana.

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses patience, although they are able to perform gradual deeds, cultivate gradual training, and practice gradual conduct in this manner, they apprehend nothing whatsoever in all things.
Why is this? Because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature. Furthermore, Subhūti!

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of diligence from the first moment of generating the mind of awakening, they should personally practice diligence, encourage others to practice diligence, constantly and correctly extol the merits of diligence, and joyfully praise those who practice diligence.
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices diligence, he is able to bestow material wealth upon all sentient beings, bringing them all to full satisfaction;

having practiced giving, he dwells securely in the aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation.

Because these aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation are purified, he transcends the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and enters the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth.
Having entered the Bodhisattva’s state of rightness and freedom from birth, they bring sentient beings to maturity and purify Buddha-fields;

having performed these deeds, they are able to realize the knowledge of all modes, turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, and establish and deliver all classes of sentient beings by means of the three vehicles, causing them to transcend birth and death and realize nirvana.

By virtue of this diligence, although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to perform gradual activities, cultivate gradual training, and practice gradual conduct in this manner, they do not apprehend anything at all.
Why is this? Because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature. Furthermore, Subhūti!

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of meditative concentration from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, they should personally enter the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*); they should also encourage others to enter the meditative concentrations, the immeasurables, and the formless attainments; they should constantly and correctly extol the merits of the meditative concentrations, the immeasurables, and the formless attainments; and they should joyfully praise those who have entered the meditative concentrations, the immeasurables, and the formless attainments.
When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he is able to give material wealth to all sentient beings, bringing them all to full satisfaction;

having practiced giving, he dwells securely in the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīla-skandha*), the aggregate of concentration (*samādhi-skandha*), the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*), the aggregate of liberation (*vimukti-skandha*), and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana-skandha*).

Because these aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation are purified, he transcends the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and enters the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Having entered the bodhisattva’s state of certainty free from birth, they bring sentient beings to maturity and purify buddha-fields;

having performed these deeds, they are able to realize the knowledge of all modes, turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, and establish and deliver all classes of sentient beings by means of the three vehicles, causing them to transcend birth and death and realize nirvana.

Because of their meditative concentration, although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are thus able to perform gradual deeds, cultivate gradual training, and practice gradual conduct, they do not apprehend anything at all in any of these.
Why is this? Because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature. Furthermore, Subhūti!

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva first generates the mind of awakening and practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they establish sentient beings in ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, the sublime liberations, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; doing so by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method, they should personally practice the six perfections, encourage others to practice the six perfections, constantly and correctly extol the merits of the six perfections, and joyfully praise those who practice the six perfections.

By means of skillful means regarding the perfections from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, this bodhisattva mahāsattva transcends the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and enters the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Having entered the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth, they bring sentient beings to maturity and purify buddha-fields.

Having performed these deeds, they are able to realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, and establish and deliver all classes of sentient beings by means of the three vehicles, causing them to emerge from birth and death and realize nirvāṇa.

By means of this prajñā, although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to perform gradual deeds, cultivate gradual training, and practice gradual conduct in this manner, they do not apprehend anything at all in any respect.
Why is this? Because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature.
Subhūti, you should know this!

This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has first resolved upon awakening relies on training in the six perfections to perform gradual deeds, cultivate gradual training, and practice gradual conduct for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, from their first production of the thought of awakening, perform gradual deeds, cultivate gradual training, and practice gradual conduct, they do so with mental attention associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*). They should first train in the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*), next train in the recollection of the Dharma (*dharmānusmṛti*), and proceed successively until finally they should train in the recollection of the deities (*devatānusmṛti*). They resolve that all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature."
“Subhūti, you should know this!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the recollection of the Buddha?

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the recollection of the Buddha, they should not contemplate the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by way of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.”
Why is this? Because from form up to consciousness, all lack intrinsic nature.
If a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, then it is non-existent.
If there is nothing that exists, then it cannot be recollected and cannot be contemplated.
Why is this? Because when there is no recollection and no contemplation, this is the recollection of the Buddha.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the recollection of the Buddha, they should not contemplate the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by way of the thirty-two marks, the body of true golden color, the constant light extending one fathom, or the eighty secondary signs."
Why is this so? Because these marks and signs, as well as the golden-colored body, are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, then it is non-existent.
If there is nothing that exists, then it cannot be recollected and cannot be contemplated.
Why is this? Because when there is no recollection and no contemplation, this is the mindfulness of the Buddha.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the recollection of the Buddha, they should not contemplate the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by means of the aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of meditative concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, or the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation."
Why is this so? Because these aggregates are all devoid of intrinsic nature.
If a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, then it is non-existent.
If there is nothing that exists, then it cannot be recollected nor can it be contemplated. Why is this?
Because when there is neither recollection nor contemplation, this is the recollection of the Buddha.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the recollection of the Buddha, they should not contemplate the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha by means of the five eyes, the six supernormal powers, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity, the quality of non-forgetfulness, the state of constant dwelling in equanimity, all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, the knowledge of all aspects, or any other immeasurable and boundless buddha-qualities."
Why is this so? Because all such phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature.
If a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, then it is non-existent.
If there is nothing that exists, then it cannot be recollected and cannot be contemplated.
Why is this? Because when there is no recollection and no contemplation, this is the recollection of the Buddha.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the recollection of the Buddha, they should not contemplate the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by means of the principle of dependent origination."
Why is this so? All dependently originated phenomena lack intrinsic nature.
If a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, then it is non-existent.
If phenomena are non-existent, they cannot be recollected and cannot be contemplated.
