Why is this? Because when there is neither recollection nor contemplation, this is the recollection of the Buddha.
"Subhūti, you should know that when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should train in this way in the recollection of the Buddha;
if they train in the recollection of the Buddha in this manner, they are performing gradual karma, practicing gradual training, and engaging in gradual conduct."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to perform gradual karma in this way, cultivate gradual training, and practice gradual conduct, then they will be able to fulfill the four applications of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path, and so forth, extensively up to all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), thereby realizing the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).

By the power of skillful means, which takes the absence of intrinsic nature in all phenomena as their very nature, this bodhisattva mahāsattva awakens to the fact that all phenomena are devoid of self-nature; therein, there is neither conceptualization nor even non-conceptualization.

"Subhūti, you should know that bodhisattva mahāsattvas should train in the recollection of the Buddha in this way: therein, even the Buddha cannot be apprehended, much less the recollection of the Buddha."
"Furthermore, Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the recollection of the Dharma?

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the recollection of the Dharma, they should not contemplate whether dharmas are wholesome or unwholesome; whether they are determinate or indeterminate; whether they are mundane or supramundane; whether they are dharmas with relish or without relish; whether they are noble or non-noble; whether they are with outflows or without outflows; whether they are dharmas that fall within the three realms or do not fall within the three realms; or whether they are conditioned or unconditioned."
Why is this so? Because all such phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, then it is non-existent.
If there is nothing that exists, then it cannot be recollected and cannot be contemplated.
Why is this? Because when there is neither recollection nor contemplation, this is what constitutes the mindfulness of phenomena (dharmānusmṛti).
"Subhūti, you should know that when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should train in the recollection of the Dharma (dharmānusmṛti) in this way.
If they train in the recollection of the Dharma in this way, this constitutes performing gradual karma, practicing gradual training, and engaging in gradual conduct."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to perform such gradual karma, cultivate gradual training, and practice gradual conduct, they will then be able to fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path, and so on extensively up to all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), by means of which they realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).

By the power of skillful means, which takes the absence of intrinsic nature as the nature of all phenomena, this bodhisattva mahāsattva awakens to the fact that all phenomena are devoid of self-nature; therein, there is neither conceptualization nor non-conceptualization.

Subhūti, you should know that bodhisattva mahāsattvas should train in the recollection of the Dharma in this way: therein, even the Dharma itself cannot be apprehended, much less the recollection of the Dharma.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the recollection of the Saṃgha?
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the recollection of the Saṃgha, they should form this thought: "

“The assembly of the Buddha’s disciples, possessing all merits—the four pairs and eight classes of *pudgalas*—are all manifested through the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and take non-substantiality (*niḥsvabhāva*) as their intrinsic nature. For these reasons, they should not be objects of mental preoccupation.”
Why is this so? Because such virtuous persons are all devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, then it is non-existent.
If there is nothing that exists, then it cannot be recollected and cannot be contemplated.
Why is this? Because when there is neither recollection nor contemplation, this is the recollection of the Saṃgha.
Subhūti, you should know that when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should train in the recollection of the Saṅgha in this way.
If they train in the recollection of the Saṅgha in this manner, it constitutes performing gradual karma, practicing gradual training, and engaging in gradual conduct.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to perform gradual karma in this way, cultivate gradual training, and practice gradual conduct, then they will be able to fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, and so forth in detail up to all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), thereby realizing the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses the skillful means that takes the absence of intrinsic nature in all phenomena as their very nature, they realize that all phenomena are devoid of self-nature; therein, there is neither conceptualization nor even the absence of conceptualization.

Subhūti, you should know that bodhisattva mahāsattvas should train in the recollection of the Saṃgha in this way: therein, even the Saṃgha cannot be apprehended, much less the recollection of the Saṃgha.
“Furthermore, Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the recollection of ethical discipline (*śīlānusmṛti*)?

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the recollection of ethical discipline, from the first production of the thought of awakening (*prathamacittotpāda*), they should recollect the noble ethical discipline as being without deficiency, without breach, without flaw, without impurity, and without attachment; as being worthy of offerings, praised by the wise, excellently undertaken, excellently perfected, and conforming to supreme meditative concentration. By contemplating this ethical discipline as having non-substantiality as its nature, for these reasons, one should not engage in discursive recollection.”
Why is this so? Because such noble ethical discipline has no intrinsic nature at all.
If a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, then it does not exist.
If there is nothing that exists, then it cannot be recollected and cannot be contemplated.
Why is this? Because when there is neither recollection nor contemplation, this is the mindfulness of precepts (śīlānusmṛti).
Subhūti, you should know that when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should train in this way in the recollection of ethical discipline (*śīlānusmṛti*).
If they train in this way in the recollection of ethical discipline, this constitutes performing gradual karma, practicing gradual training, and engaging in gradual conduct.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to perform such gradual karma, cultivate gradual training, and practice gradual conduct, they will then be able to fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path, and so on extensively up to all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), by means of which they realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).

By the power of skillful means, which takes the absence of intrinsic nature as the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, this bodhisattva-mahāsattva awakens to the fact that all phenomena are devoid of self-nature; therein, there is neither conceptualization nor even the absence of conceptualization.

"Subhūti, you should know that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should train in the recollection of ethical discipline (*śīlānusmṛti*) in this way: therein, even ethical discipline itself cannot be apprehended, much less the recollection of ethical discipline."
"Furthermore, Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the recollection of relinquishment?

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the recollection of relinquishment, from the first production of the thought of awakening, they should, by means of the skillful method of taking non-existence as their nature, practice the recollection of relinquishment. That is to say, when relinquishing material wealth or relinquishing the Dharma, they do not form such a thought:"
"I can give away, or I may not give away.
Even when giving away parts of the body, such as limbs and joints, one does not give rise to the thought:
"I can give away, or I may not give away."
"Nor does one contemplate the merit or the fruit of the gift that has been relinquished or bestowed. Why is this?
Because all such phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature."
If phenomena lack intrinsic nature, then they do not exist;
if they do not exist, they cannot be recollected and cannot be contemplated. Why is this?
If there is no mindfulness and no mental engagement, this is the recollection of equanimity (*upekṣā-anusmṛti*). Subhūti,
you should know that when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they should train in the recollection of equanimity in this manner.
If one trains in this way in the recollection of equanimity, this constitutes performing gradual karma, practicing gradual training, and engaging in gradual conduct.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to perform gradual karma, practice gradual training, and engage in gradual conduct in this manner, they will then be able to fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path, and so on extensively up to all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), thereby realizing the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).

By the power of skillful means—taking the absence of intrinsic nature in all phenomena as their very nature—this bodhisattva mahāsattva realizes that all phenomena are devoid of self-nature; therein, there is neither conceptualization nor non-conceptualization.

"Subhūti, you should know that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should train in this way in the recollection of equanimity (*upekṣā-anusmṛti*); for within it, even equanimity itself is unapprehendable, let alone the recollection of equanimity."
"Furthermore, Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the recollection of the devas?

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the recollection of the devas, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, they should practice the recollection of the devas by means of the skillful method of taking non-existence as their nature, thinking thus: "
"Those who are stream-enterers and the like are born in the six heavens of the desire realm; those who are non-returners and the like are born in the two higher realms.
All such things are ultimately unattainable and should not be contemplated.
Why is this so? Because these devas and others all lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If a dharma lacks intrinsic nature, then it is non-existent.
If there is nothing that exists, then it cannot be recollected and cannot be contemplated.
Why is this? Because when there is neither recollection nor contemplation, this is what constitutes the recollection of the devas.
Subhūti, you should know that when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should train in this way in the recollection of the devas;
if they train in this way in the recollection of the devas, this constitutes performing gradual karma, practicing gradual training, and engaging in gradual conduct.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can thus perform gradual karma, cultivate gradual training, and practice gradual conduct, then they will be able to fulfill the four applications of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path, and so on extensively up to all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), by means of which they realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).

By the power of skillful means, which takes the absence of intrinsic nature as the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, this bodhisattva mahāsattva awakens to the fact that all phenomena are devoid of self-nature; therein, there is neither perception nor non-perception.

"Subhūti, you should know that bodhisattva mahāsattvas should train in the recollection of the devas in this way: therein, even a 'deva' cannot be apprehended, much less the recollection of the devas."

Subhūti, you should know that this is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has first resolved upon awakening relies on the training in the six recollections to perform gradual deeds, practice gradual training, and carry out gradual conduct for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, if they wish to fulfill the karma of gradual progression, cultivate gradual training, and engage in gradual conduct, they should—by means of the skillful power that takes the absence of intrinsic nature as the nature of all phenomena—study internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; they should study suchness up to the inconceivable realm; they should study the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; they should study the four applications of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; and, to speak extensively, they should study all-knowledge, the knowledge of paths, and all-aspect knowledge."

When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva thus trains in the path to enlightenment, they realize that all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature; therein, not even the slightest thought can be apprehended, much less thoughts of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, extending broadly to the knowledge of all modes.
In this way, it is impossible for these various thoughts and the phenomena that are their objects to exist as even the slightest reality.

Thus, Subhūti, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, although they perform gradual deeds, cultivate gradual training, and engage in gradual practices, their minds do not waver therein, because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, then there should be no form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, and so on, up to there being no 'knowledge of all aspects. In that case, there would be no Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; there would be no path, no fruits, no defilement, and no purity; furthermore, there would be no attainment and no clear realization. Thus, all phenomena should be non-existent."
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “What do you think?
Within the nature of the absence of nature in all phenomena, can a nature or an absence of nature be apprehended?”
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"If, within the naturelessness of all phenomena, both existence and non-existence are unapprehendable, how can you now make such a statement:

'If all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, then there should be no form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness,' and so on at length, up to 'then all phenomena should be non-existent'?"

Subhūti replied: "I have no doubt regarding this meaning myself; however, it is for the sake of future bhikṣus—whether they seek the state of a śrāvaka, a pratyekabuddha, or the fruit of Buddhahood—who might think:
'If all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, who is defiled and who is purified?'"
"Who binds and who liberates?

Because they do not understand the meaning of defilement and purification, bondage and liberation, they violate their precepts, their views, their decorum, and their pure livelihood; consequently, they shall fall into the three evil destinies, undergo various sufferings, and transmigrate through birth and death, finding it difficult to attain liberation.
"I observed that such terrifying events will occur in the future; therefore, I asked this question. However, regarding this matter, I truly have no doubt.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "Excellent!"

Excellent! That you are now able to pose such a question for the sake of future generations is truly commendable. However, within the naturelessness of all phenomena, both existence and non-existence are equally unapprehendable; one should not, therefore, cling to the notion of either existent or nonexistent nature therein.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, for what purpose do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, desiring to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, observe and seek to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Because all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas seek to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings."

Why is this? Because all classes of sentient beings possess the views of eternalism and nihilism, abide in grasping at objective existence, and are difficult to subdue; they are deluded and inverted, and thus difficult to liberate.
"Subhūti, you should know this:

for one who dwells in the apprehension of something, because of that perception of apprehending something, there is neither attainment nor clear realization, nor is there unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If there is something attained, would there be no attainment, no clear realization, and no unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
If there is nothing attained, would there be attainment, clear realization, and unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If there is no attainment, that itself is attainment; that itself is clear realization; that itself is unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Why is this so?
Because that dharma-realm is indestructible.
Subhūti, you should know this:

if anyone, within this state of non-apprehension, desires to apprehend something, desires to attain clear realization, or desires to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, you should know that such a person desires to destroy the dharma-realm.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If there is anything attained, there is no attainment, no clear realization, and no unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening;
if there is non-attainment, that itself is attainment, that itself is clear realization, and that itself is unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening."

Within non-apprehension, there is neither attainment nor clear realization, nor even unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; how then can bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have the first ground, the second ground, and so on up to the tenth ground?

How can there be the attainment of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti)? How can there be the attainment of supernormal powers born of maturation (vipākaja-abhijñā)?
How can there be the attainment of the perfections from generosity up to wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā) born of maturation?

How can there be such abiding in these dharmas born of maturation (*vipākaja*), whereby one matures sentient beings, purifies Buddha-fields, and obtains roots of goodness by approaching and making offerings with supreme requisites to the Buddhas—roots that remain inexhaustible until the fruit of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, and which continue even after final *parinirvāṇa*, so that one’s own relics and disciples still receive various offerings and respect, while the power of those roots of goodness remains undiminished?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Because all dharmas are non-apprehendable, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain the first bhūmi, the second bhūmi, and so on up to the tenth bhūmi."
It is precisely because of this that one attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti);
it is precisely because of this that one attains supernormal powers born of maturation (vipākaja-abhijñā);
and it is precisely because of this that one attains the perfections from generosity up to wisdom (dāna-pāramitā through prajñā-pāramitā) born of maturation.

Precisely because of this, one is able to abide in the dharmas born of maturation (*vipākaja*), to bring sentient beings to maturity, and to purify Buddha-fields. Regarding the roots of goodness obtained by approaching and making offerings with supreme and wondrous requisites to the Buddhas, these continue until the fruit of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment is inexhaustible; they extend even until after *parinirvāṇa*, when one's own *śarīra* relics and disciples still receive various forms of offering and veneration, the power of those roots of goodness remaining undiminished.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If all phenomena are non-apprehendable, what distinction is there between the six perfections, such as generosity, and the various supernormal powers?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"For those who have nothing to attain, there is no distinction between the six perfections, such as giving, and the various supernormal powers.

However, for the sake of causing those who perceive things as attainable to abandon all defiled attachments, he employs skillful means to proclaim that the six perfections, such as giving, and the various supernormal powers possess distinct characteristics."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what reason and by what causal conditions are the six perfections, such as giving, and the various supernormal powers said to be without distinction for one who has nothing to acquire?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not apprehend giving, they do not apprehend the giver,
they do not apprehend the recipient, they do not apprehend that which is given, and they do not apprehend the act of giving."
They practice giving without having attained the fruit; they maintain pure ethical discipline without having attained pure ethical discipline;
they cultivate patience without having attained patience; they exert diligence without having attained diligence; they enter meditative concentration without having attained meditative concentration;
they study wisdom without having attained wisdom; and they manifest supernormal powers without having attained supernormal powers.
One does not apprehend the four foundations of mindfulness while cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness, nor even the eight branches of the noble path;

this is explained in detail up to: one does not apprehend all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) while cultivating all-knowledge, knowledge of the paths, and knowledge of all aspects; nor does one apprehend any form of existence (*bhava*).
While maturing sentient beings through their passions, they do not attain the Buddha-fields, yet they purify the Buddha-fields;
they do not attain the Buddha-dharma, yet they realize bodhi. Thus it is, Subhūti!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice the profound perfection of wisdom that is non-apprehensible.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is able to practice this profound perfection of wisdom that is non-apprehensible, neither the celestial Māras nor the followers of external paths will be able to destroy them.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

“How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, by the single-minded arising of one thought-moment, they are able to fully encompass the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and so on extensively up to the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, the cultivation of the perfections from generosity up to wisdom—and so forth, extensively including the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks—is all embraced by the perfection of wisdom, whereby they attain fulfillment."
Thus it is, Subhūti!

When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, a single moment of focused attention can encompass all six perfections, and so on extensively up to the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, all that they do is embraced by the perfection of wisdom; thus, with a single moment of mind arising, they are able to embrace the six perfections, and so on extensively up to the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, the six perfections they cultivate, up to and including the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs that they bring forth, are all embraced by the perfection of wisdom; therefore, they remain far removed from dualistic conceptions."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, although they practice the six perfections, and even though they manifest the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs, they remain free from the notion of duality?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, in order to fulfill the perfection of giving, they encompass all perfections within that very perfection of giving. They practice giving extensively, even up to the eighty minor marks; by virtue of these causes and conditions, they maintain no dualistic conception.”

In this manner, up to and including the desire to fulfill the eighty minor marks (*anuvyañjana*), one embraces all the *pāramitās* within those very eighty minor marks; from the detailed exposition up to the eighty minor marks, one draws forth the eighty minor marks. By means of these causes and conditions, there is no dualistic conception.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
Because bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, when they practice the perfection of giving, they dwell in an untainted mind while practicing the perfection of giving;
and so on, in detail, until when they manifest the eighty minor marks, they dwell in an untainted mind while manifesting the eighty minor marks.
"Therefore, although they practice the perfection of generosity, and so on, up to manifesting the eighty minor marks, they maintain no notion of duality.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"How is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, when practicing the perfection of generosity, dwells in an untainted mind while practicing the perfection of generosity?"
"Furthermore, when manifesting the eighty minor marks, does one manifest them while abiding in an untainted mind?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they practice the perfection of giving with a mind free from signs, not perceiving any signs—namely, not perceiving who is able to give, what is the object given, who receives this gift, by means of this giving, for the sake of this giving, or how the giving is performed."

Abiding in this untainted mind that is free from signs, one practices the perfection of generosity while being free from craving and stinginess; at that time, one does not perceive the act of giving, nor does one perceive this untainted mind, nor even perceive any of the Buddha-dharmas. In this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the untainted mind and practices the perfection of generosity.

To speak at length, up until this point: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, with a mind free from signs (*animitta*), they do not perceive any signs as they bring forth the eighty minor marks (*anuvyañjana*). That is to say, they do not perceive who is the bringer-forth, what is brought forth, by means of what it is brought forth, for the sake of what it is brought forth, or in what manner the eighty minor marks are brought forth.

Abiding in this untainted mind that is free from signs, one is without defilement or attachment yet brings forth the eighty minor marks; at that time, one does not perceive the eighty minor marks being brought forth, nor does one perceive this untainted mind, nor even perceive all the Buddha-dharmas. In this way, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva abides in the untainted mind and brings forth the eighty minor marks.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll 528. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Three, Chapter Twenty-Eight: The Sublime Marks, Part Two. At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, knows that all phenomena are signless (*animitta*), unattainable (*anupalabdha*), and without activity (*akṛtya*), how can they fulfill the six *pāramitās*?”
How can one fulfill inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature?
How can one fulfill suchness up to the inconceivable realm?
How can one fulfill the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path?
How can one fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path?
How can one fulfill the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions?
How can one fulfill the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness?
How can one fulfill the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality?
How can one fulfill the stages from the Ground of Utmost Joy up to the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma?
How can one fulfill the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi?
How can one fulfill the five eyes and the six supernormal powers?
How can one fulfill the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha?
How can one fulfill great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity?
How can one fulfill the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity?
How can one fulfill all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)?
How can one fulfill all the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
How can one fulfill the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas?
How can one fulfill the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they are able to cultivate the perfection of generosity with a mind that is free from signs and untainted."

If there are sentient beings who require food, I give them food; those who require drink, I give them drink; and those who require other necessities, I give them those necessities. If there are sentient beings who require internal things—be they head, eyes, marrow, brain, skin, flesh, limbs, joints, tendons, bones, or even life itself—I bestow all these upon them as gifts. If there are sentient beings who require external things—be they kingdoms, cities, wives, children, beloved relatives, or various forms of adornment—I joyfully bestow all these upon them.
When a bodhisattva practices giving in this manner, suppose someone should come before them and rebuke them, saying:
"What is the use of practicing such unbeneficial giving?
For one who gives in this way, there will be much physical and mental exhaustion and many sufferings in both this life and future lives!"
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, although they hear these words, they do not retreat or become disheartened, but instead think:

"Even though that person comes to reproach me, I should not give rise to sorrow or regret in my mind; I shall courageously bestow upon all sentient beings whatever they require, without weariness of body or mind."
“This bodhisattva-mahāsattva takes this merit from giving and dedicates it equally to all sentient beings for the sake of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
When thus practicing giving and dedicating, they do not perceive any signs; that is to say, they do not perceive who is giving.”
Who receives?
What object is given?
To whom is it given?
From what and for what purpose?
How does one practice giving?
Furthermore, one does not perceive anyone who can perform dedication.
What is it that is dedicated?
To what is it dedicated?
By means of what, and for what purpose?
What is dedication?
It is that one does not perceive any of these things whatsoever. Why is this so?
In this way, there are no phenomena that are not empty by virtue of internal emptiness, and so on, up to being empty by virtue of the emptiness of marks.
Having observed that all phenomena are without exception empty, this bodhisattva mahāsattva further reflects:
"Who is it that can perform the dedication?"
What is it that is dedicated?
To what is it dedicated?
By means of what, and for the sake of what?
"What is dedication?
It is that all such phenomena are unattainable.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, through such contemplation and such mindfulness, gives rise to dedication, it is called "virtuous dedication."

By means of this, one is further able to bring sentient beings to maturity and purify Buddha-fields; one is also able to fulfill the practices ranging from the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, and so on extensively until one is also able to fulfill the eighty minor marks.
Although this bodhisattva mahāsattva is thus able to fulfill the perfection of generosity, they do not appropriate the karmic fruition of that generosity.
Although they do not appropriate the karmic fruition of generosity, because the perfection of generosity is thoroughly purified, they are able to provide all necessary requisites at will.

Just as for the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*), everything required appears in accordance with their minds, so it is likewise for this bodhisattva mahāsattva: whatever is required can be accomplished according to his will. By the superior power of this generosity, he is able to reverently make offerings of various supreme and exquisite articles of enjoyment to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and is also able to fully satisfy the multitudes of devas, humans, and others.

By means of this perfection of giving, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas employ skillful means to gather all sentient beings and establish them in the vehicles of the Three Vehicles, causing each to obtain benefit according to what is appropriate for them.

"So it is, Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, by the power of their untainted mind which is free from all signs, they are able to fulfill the perfection of generosity within all signless, ungraspable, and unconditioned phenomena, and they are likewise able to fulfill all other wholesome dharmas."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they cultivate the perfection of ethical discipline with a mind that is free from signs and untainted (*anāsrava*). That is to say, they cultivate the dharmas subsumed under the limbs of the noble, untainted path; the well-purified ethical discipline thus obtained is without deficiency, without flaw, without blemish, without impurity, and without attachment. It is worthy of offerings and praised by the wise."
By means of this pure ethical discipline, one grasps at nothing whatsoever among all phenomena;
that is, one does not grasp at form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, nor even at the thirty-two marks of a great man or the eighty secondary characteristics.
Furthermore, one does not grasp at the great kṣatriya clans, nor even the great householder clans.
Furthermore, they do not grasp at the states of the gods from the Realm of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception;
nor do they grasp at the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a solitary buddha (*pratyekabuddha*);

nor do they grasp at the position of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) or other positions such as minor kings, ministers, or officials. Rather, by means of the precepts thus received and upheld, they [bestow them] upon all...
One dedicates [merit] equally for all sentient beings toward the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
At the time of dedication, one employs the method of signlessness, non-apprehension, and non-duality, rather than employing the method of signs, apprehension, and duality;
this is done solely by relying on the conventional (saṃvṛti) and not on the ultimate (paramārtha). By these causes and conditions, all Buddhas...
All dharmas are thereby brought to perfection.

By means of this skillful means of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), this bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to the stages of further progress within the four dhyānas; because he employs non-attachment as his skillful means, he brings forth the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of the pure divine eye born of maturation, is able to see all the Buddhas of the present in the ten directions, up until the attainment of the knowledge of all modes; furthermore, they do not forget or lose what has been seen.

By means of the supramundane, purified divine ear, they are able to hear the Dharma teachings of the Buddhas of the ten directions; furthermore, until they realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), they do not forget what they have heard, and according to the teachings they have heard, they perform beneficial deeds for themselves and others without fail.

By means of the knowledge of others' minds, having known the minds and the objects of those minds of the Buddhas of the ten directions as well as of sentient beings, one is able to initiate all manner of beneficial activities for sentient beings according to what is appropriate for them.

Using the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), he knows the karma previously created by sentient beings; because that created karma does not perish, they are born in various places to experience various forms of suffering and happiness. Having known this, he explains for them the causal conditions of their original karma, causing them to remember and know it so as to perform acts of benefit.

Using the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows, they establish sentient beings, causing them to abide in the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, and so on in detail until causing them to abide in unsurpassed enlightenment.

In brief, wherever this bodhisattva-mahāsattva is born, he employs various skillful means according to the differing capacities of sentient beings, causing them to abide in all categories of wholesome qualities.
"In this way, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, by means of the power of their mind—which is free from all signs and untainted—they are able to fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline within all signless, non-apprehending, and unconditioned phenomena, and they are also able to fulfill all other wholesome dharmas."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they cultivate the perfection of patience with a mind that is free from signs and untainted."

"From the first generation of the mind of awakening until sitting upon the seat of sublime enlightenment, even if all sentient beings were to inflict various kinds of suffering and harm upon this bodhisattva mahāsattva, that bodhisattva mahāsattva would not give rise to a single thought associated with anger or resentment."
At that time, the bodhisattva should cultivate two kinds of patience:
first, one should endure all verbal abuse, insults, and physical harm inflicted by sentient beings, remaining free from anger and resentment through the patience of subduing hatred.
Second, they should give rise to the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

"If this bodhisattva mahāsattva encounters various insults and verbal abuse, or is subjected to various harms from blades and staves, they should carefully examine and investigate: 'Who is it that can insult and abuse? "
Who is it that receives abuse?
Who is able to inflict harm?
And who is it that receives the harm?
Who gives rise to anger?
Who should endure it?

Furthermore, one should carefully examine that the nature of all phenomena is ultimately empty; since even phenomena themselves cannot be apprehended, how much less could there be a "nature of phenomena"!
Since even the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) does not exist, how much less could there be sentient beings!

When observing in this way, if one can [endure] being reviled, or that which is reviled; if one can [endure] inflicting harm, or that which is harmed—all are seen as non-existent. Even when the limbs of the body are severed piece by piece, the mind remains patient and equanimous without any other thought. By thus observing the nature of all phenomena as it truly is, one is further able to realize the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
What is called the "patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena" (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti)?

It refers to causing all afflictions not to arise, maintaining a subtle and wondrous wisdom that is constantly uninterrupted, and observing that all phenomena are ultimately unarisen; therefore, it is called the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena.

“Abiding in these two kinds of patience, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to swiftly fulfill the six pāramitās, such as generosity, and so forth, up to and including the swift fulfillment of the eighty minor marks.”

“Having established themselves in these qualities of all Buddhas, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain perfection in the noble, untainted, supramundane, and unique superknowledges (abhijñā) that are not shared with any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.”

Having become established in such supreme supernormal powers, they constantly behold the Buddhas of the present in the ten directions with their purified divine eye, until they realize the knowledge of all modes; they give rise to the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti) without interruption.

With their purified divine ear, they constantly hear the Dharma teachings of the Buddhas of the ten directions, retaining them without forgetfulness and proclaiming them according to reality for the sake of all sentient beings.

With their knowledge of others' minds, they are able to correctly measure the minds and mental factors of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, as well as the minds and mental factors of other classes of sentient beings; accordingly, they preach the True Dharma to bring about resolute faith.

Using the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), they know the various distinctions among the roots of goodness planted by sentient beings in their past; having known these, they employ skillful means to manifest, exhort, encourage, and gladden them, thereby bringing them benefit.
Using the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*), they establish sentient beings in the vehicles of the Threefold Dharma according to what is appropriate for each.

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, through skillful means purifies buddha-fields and matures sentient beings; he is swiftly able to fulfill all-aspect knowledge, realize unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, and turn the sublime wheel of Dharma for the benefit of all."

"So it is, Subhūti! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, by means of the power of their mind—which is free from all signs and untainted—they are able to fulfill the perfection of patience within all signless, non-apprehending, and unconditioned phenomena, and they are also able to fulfill all other wholesome dharmas."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they are able to cultivate the perfection of diligence with a mind that is free from signs and untainted."

This bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes courageous physical and mental diligence, entering the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna; relying on these four dhyānas, they manifest various supernormal powers and transformations, even to the point of touching the sun and moon with their hand and turning them at will without finding it difficult.

Because they have accomplished the physical diligence of heroic valor, by means of their supernormal powers they are able to reach Buddha-worlds in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in a mere instant. Furthermore, they honor and make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, with various kinds of supreme and exquisite articles of enjoyment. Through the inexhaustible fruit and retribution of these roots of goodness, they gradually realize the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).

Having attained buddhahood through the predominant power of these roots of goodness, he will further be honored and venerated with immeasurable varieties of supreme and exquisite articles of pleasure by countless beings of the world—gods, humans, and asuras alike.

By virtue of these roots of goodness, even after his parinirvāṇa, his physical relics and his disciples will still be honored and revered by immeasurable multitudes of worldly devas, humans, and asuras.

"Furthermore, by means of their supernormal powers, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to travel to Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions. In the presence of those Buddhas, they listen to the sublime Dharma; having heard it, they receive and uphold it, never forgetting it until they attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Furthermore, by means of their supernormal powers, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to reach Buddha-worlds in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to ripen sentient beings and purify Buddha-fields. Having diligently cultivated and mastered the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) and attained its perfection, they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), turning the sublime wheel of Dharma to deliver the multitudes of sentient beings.
"In this way, Subhūti! Because bodhisattva mahāsattvas achieve courageous physical diligence, they are able to swiftly bring the perfection of diligence to full completion."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Because bodhisattva mahāsattvas have accomplished the vigor of a courageous mind, they are able to swiftly fulfill the perfection of vigor subsumed within the noble, untainted path and its branches; by means of this, they ensure that no unwholesome actions of body, speech, or mind can arise."

“This bodhisattva mahāsattva, among all phenomena, never grasps at or adheres to them as either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure; nor does he grasp at or adhere to the conditioned realm or the unconditioned realm, the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; nor the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments; nor the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; nor the three doors of liberation; nor any other infinite and boundless Buddha-dharmas—such as permanence, impermanence, and so forth—and he likewise does not grasp at or adhere to the fruit of a stream-enterer up to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

This bodhisattva mahāsattva likewise does not grasp at or adhere to the notion that "this one is a stream-enterer," "this one is a once-returner," up to "this one is a Buddha. Nor does he grasp at the view that a sentient being is called a "stream-enterer" because they are endowed with such a vision; nor that a sentient being is called a "once-returner" because their lower fetters have been attenuated; nor that a sentient being is called a "non-returner" because their lower fetters have been exhausted; nor that a sentient being is called an "arhat" because their higher fetters have been exhausted; nor that a sentient being is called a "pratyekabuddha" because they have attained the path of a pratyekabuddha; nor that a sentient being is called a "bodhisattva" because they have attained the knowledge of the aspects of the path; nor that a sentient being is called a "Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha" because they have attained all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).
This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not grasp at or become attached to such dharmas or sentient beings.
Why is this? Because all dharmas and all sentient beings lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and are thus incapable of being grasped or attached to.

“Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva has accomplished a courageous mind of diligence, although he performs deeds that benefit all sentient beings without regard for his own body or life, he apprehends no sentient beings at all;
although he is able to fulfill the perfection of diligence he practices, he apprehends no perfection of diligence at all;
although he is able to fulfill all Buddha-dharmas, he apprehends no Buddha-dharmas at all.”
Although they are able to adorn and purify all buddha-fields, they do not apprehend any buddha-field at all.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, having accomplished such physical and mental diligence, is able to remain far removed from all unwholesome dharmas and can also embrace all wholesome dharmas without any attachment.

Because they are free from grasping and attachment, they travel from one buddha-field to another buddha-field and from one world-system to another world-system. For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, whatever supernormal feats they wish to manifest, they are able to display them all with mastery and without obstruction.

That is to say, he may manifest the raining down of various exquisite flowers, the scattering of various famous incenses, and the performance of various musical instruments; he may manifest the sound of clouds and thunder that shakes the great earth.

Or again, he may manifest worlds adorned with various wonderful seven-jeweled treasures, emitting from his body a radiance by which sentient beings in blindness and darkness are all brought to enlightenment.
Or again, he may manifest his body emitting wondrous fragrances, causing all that is foul and impure to become fragrant and clean.

Or again, he may manifest the performance of great sacrificial rites, wherein he does not afflict any sentient beings; through this, he transforms and guides immeasurable sentient beings, leading them to enter the Right Path and to abstain from taking life, up to and including abandoning wrong views.

Or, by means of the perfections from generosity up to wisdom, they gather in all sentient beings; for the sake of benefiting them, they may relinquish wealth and treasures, or relinquish wife and children, or relinquish their royal throne, or relinquish their limbs and joints, or relinquish their very body and life. According to whatever skillful means are appropriate for each sentient being to obtain benefit and happiness, they provide that very same benefit and happiness through those respective skillful means.

"So it is, Subhūti! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, by means of the power of the mind that is free from all signs and untainted, they are able to fulfill the perfection of diligence within all signless, non-apprehending, and unconditioned phenomena, and they are also able to fulfill all other wholesome dharmas."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they cultivate the perfection of meditative concentration with a mind that is free from signs and untainted."
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, with the exception of the concentration of the Tathāgata, is able to bring all other concentrations to full perfection.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, detached from desires and unwholesome states, possessing applied and sustained thought, and experiencing the joy and happiness born of seclusion, enters the first dhyāna, and so on, up to entering the fourth dhyāna and dwelling therein in its full accomplishment."

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—and so on, as extensively explained, up to—a mind imbued with equanimity, dwells pervasively, taking the ten directions as his object."

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva transcends all perceptions of form, extinguishes perceptions of sensory resistance, and does not attend to perceptions of diversity; he enters and dwells, having fully attained, in the sphere of infinite space, up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception."

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration, is able to abide fully in the eight liberations and the nine successive attainments, both in forward and reverse order."

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells fully endowed with the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; he dwells fully endowed with the uninterrupted concentration, the lightning-flash concentration, the diamond-like concentration, the noble right concentration, and so forth."

“This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration, cultivates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the knowledge of the aspects of the path, bringing them all to full completion.”

Having embraced all samādhis by means of the knowledge of the characteristics of the path, one gradually cultivates the stages of transcendent tranquility and insight; having cultivated up to the stage of transcending the level of the pratyekabuddhas, one enters the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth. Once having entered the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth, one cultivates the practices of the various stages until the perfection of the Buddha-stage.

Although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas gradually cultivate and leap through the stages, they do not realize the fruit of fruition in the interim until they have attained the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration, travels from one buddha-field to another, attending upon and making offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. Under those Buddhas, they plant many roots of goodness, ripen sentient beings, and purify buddha-fields. Traveling from one world-system to another, they benefit and bring happiness to sentient beings with bodies and minds free from weariness."

They may gather sentient beings through the perfections from generosity up to wisdom; or they may gather sentient beings through the aggregates from ethical discipline up to the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; or they may instruct sentient beings to abide in the fruit of stream-entry, and so on in detail until they instruct sentient beings to dwell securely in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. According to the power of the roots of goodness of those sentient beings and the growth of their wholesome qualities, they cause them to abide securely through various skillful means.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration, is able to bring forth all doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of samādhi; they are able to attain the four supreme analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) and the supreme supernormal powers (abhijñā) born of karmic maturation.

“This bodhisattva mahāsattva, having accomplished the extraordinary supernormal powers of karmic maturation, will certainly never again enter a mother’s womb; will certainly never again experience the pleasure of sexual desire; will certainly never again take up rebirth in a vehicle; and will certainly not be defiled by the faults of birth.”

Why is this? It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas clearly perceive and thoroughly understand that the nature of all phenomena is entirely like an illusion or a magical transformation; yet, although they know that all conditioned formations are like illusions and transformations, they still ride upon the power of compassion and vows to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings.
Although one utilizes compassionate vows to benefit and bring happiness to sentient beings, one realizes that both sentient beings and their designations are unapprehendable.

Although one realizes that both sentient beings and their designations are unapprehendable, one is nevertheless able to establish all sentient beings, causing them to abide in the dharma of non-apprehensibility; this is based on the conventional, not the ultimate.

“This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of meditative concentration, practices all dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, and meditative attainments; until they fully realize unsurpassed awakening, they never abandon the perfection of meditative concentration they have cultivated.”

“This bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the knowledge of the aspects of the path, skillfully brings forth the knowledge of all aspects, and dwells therein, forever severing the continuity of the habitual tendencies of afflictions; thus they are able to perfectly benefit themselves and perfectly benefit others, serving as a pure field of merit for all the world—including devas, humans, and asuras—and being worthy of receiving the world’s offerings and respect.”

"So it is, Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, by means of the power of their untainted mind which is free from all signs, they are able to fulfill the perfection of meditative concentration within all signless, non-apprehending, and unconditioned phenomena, and they are also able to fulfill all other wholesome dharmas."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they cultivate the perfection of wisdom with a mind that is free from signs and untainted."

This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive even the slightest dharma as being truly established; that is to say, they do not perceive form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness—expounded at length up to all contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharmas—as being truly established. Furthermore, they do not perceive these various dharmas as arising or ceasing, as increasing or decreasing, or as accumulating or dispersing.

One contemplates form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as they truly are—extensively explained up to all contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena—as being entirely false, entirely lacking solidity, and entirely devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

"When this bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates in this manner, he does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of form; he does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; and so on, in detail, until he does not apprehend the intrinsic nature of contaminated phenomena, nor does he apprehend the intrinsic nature of uncontaminated phenomena."

"When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and contemplates in this manner, they develop deep faith and understanding toward all phenomena, realizing that their very nature is the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Having developed such faith and understanding, they are able to practice internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*), and so on, up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāva-śūnyatā*)."

When practicing in this way, one has no grasping or attachment toward any phenomena; that is to say, one does not grasp at or attach to form, nor does one grasp at or attach to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. This is explained in detail up to: one does not grasp at or attach to any of the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor does one grasp at or attach to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas.

"When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* of non-existence, they are able to fulfill the path to enlightenment; that is, they are able to fulfill the *pāramitās* of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and so on, up to the eighty minor marks."

“Once this bodhisattva mahāsattva is established in such a path to enlightenment, they are further able to fulfill the ripened Buddha-path; that is to say, they are able to fulfill the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as the other immeasurable factors conducive to enlightenment.”

“Abiding in this Buddha-way of maturation, this bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of the superior supernormal powers born of maturation, skillfully benefits all classes of sentient beings. To those who should be gathered through generosity up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), he gathers them with generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;

to those who should be gathered through the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*) up to the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśanaskandha*), he gathers them with the aggregate of ethical discipline up to the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation;

and to those who should be established in the fruit of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna-phala*), or the fruit of a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin-phala*), up to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), he uses skillful means to establish them in the fruit of a stream-enterer, the fruit of a once-returner, up to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.”
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to perform various supernatural transformations; if he wishes to go to worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he can go there at will.
If he wishes to manifest various kinds of precious jewels within those worlds he visits, he can manifest them at will.
If he wishes to cause the sentient beings in those worlds to enjoy various exquisite jewels, he causes them all to be satisfied according to their desires."

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva proceeds from one world to another world, benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings; seeing the signs of the adornment and purity of various worlds, they are able to personally take up and manifest a Buddha-land adorned according to their own wishes."

Just as the various articles of pleasure required by the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations appear according to their will, so too does this bodhisattva, according to his own inclination, take possession of various adornments for immeasurable buddha-fields; within these buddha-fields thus taken possession of, subtle and pure, free from all defiled phenomena, everything can be manifested exactly as he desires.

"Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom born of maturation, as well as the various sublime supernormal powers born of maturation and the path to enlightenment born of maturation, they practice the knowledge of the aspects of the paths; and by virtue of having brought that knowledge of the aspects of the paths to maturity, they are further able to realize the knowledge of all aspects."

By attaining this wisdom, one does not grasp at any phenomena; that is to say, one does not grasp at form, nor does one grasp at feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. To speak extensively, this extends even to not grasping at anything that is wholesome or unwholesome, mundane or supramundane, with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned.

Nor do they grasp at the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they have realized, nor do they grasp at any objects of enjoyment in any buddha-field; furthermore, the sentient beings therein likewise have no grasping toward any phenomena.

Why is this so? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have not previously grasped at any phenomena, because they find nothing to be apprehended in any phenomena, and because they correctly proclaim to all sentient beings that the nature of all phenomena is without grasping.

"So it is, Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, by means of the power of their mind—which is free from all signs and untainted—they are able to fulfill the perfection of wisdom within all signless, ungraspable, and unconditioned phenomena, and they are also able to fulfill all other wholesome dharmas."
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How can bodhisattva-mahāsattvas fulfill the perfections from generosity up to wisdom within phenomena that are unmixed, signless, and empty of intrinsic characteristics?"
How can one establish distinctions among all untainted (anāsrava) and undifferentiated dharmas?
How can one thoroughly understand the characteristics of the distinctions among such dharmas?
How is it that within the *prajñāpāramitā*, the six *pāramitās* and all other mundane and supramundane dharmas are subsumed?

How is it possible to designate a single characteristic—namely, the "characteristicless"—to phenomena that possess diverse characteristics, and to designate various distinct dharma-characteristics within those dharmas that are of a single characteristic or without characteristic?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they abide within the five aggregates of clinging—which are like a dream, an echo, an image, a reflection, a mirage, an illusion, a transformation, and a city of gandharvas—and for the sake of all sentient beings, they practice the perfections from generosity up to wisdom, while truly understanding that these five aggregates of clinging, from being like a dream up to being like a city of gandharvas, are all devoid of marks.”

Why is this? From dreams up to the city of Gandharvas, all are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). If a phenomenon lacks intrinsic nature, that phenomenon is without marks (*animitta*); if a phenomenon is without marks, that phenomenon has but a single mark, namely, the markless.
By this causal condition, one should know that the giver, the recipient, the gift, the nature of giving, the fruit of giving, and the conditions for giving are all equally signless (*animitta*).

"If one practices giving with such understanding, then one will be able to bring the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) to completion; if one brings the perfection of giving to completion, then one will never abandon the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom."

Abiding in these six perfections, one is able to fulfill the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions; one is also able to fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path, and, to speak at length, is also able to fulfill all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

"Abiding in these various dharmas born of maturation that are noble and untainted, this bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of supernormal powers, is able to travel to Buddha-worlds in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. There, he honors and makes offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, with immeasurable kinds of supreme and exquisite articles of pleasure. He performs beneficial deeds for all sentient beings: those who should be benefited through the perfections from generosity up to wisdom, he benefits them with those very perfections;
those who should be benefited by other various wholesome dharmas, he benefits them with those very various wholesome dharmas."

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, having accomplished such sublime roots of goodness, attains mastery over all phenomena; though they undergo birth and death, they are not defiled by the faults of birth and death."

For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, they assume the sovereignty of wealth and honor among gods and humans; by the power of this wealth and sovereignty, they are able to perform various acts of benefit for sentient beings, gathering them in through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that all phenomena are signless, although he knows the fruit of stream-entry, he does not abide in the fruit of stream-entry; and so on, up to: although he knows the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, he does not abide in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having understood all phenomena as they truly are, desire to realize the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā), which is not shared with any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

"So it is, Subhūti! Because all dharmas are signless, bodhisattva mahāsattvas understand, in accordance with reality, that the six perfections beginning with generosity, as well as all other immeasurable and boundless buddha-dharmas, are likewise identical in being signless."

By means of these causes and conditions, one is able to universally fulfill all Buddha-dharmas, thereby attaining the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (sarvajñajñāna), and benefiting and gladdening sentient beings until the end of the future.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they abide within the five aggregates of clinging— which are like a dream, like an echo, like a reflection, like a shadow, like a mirage, like a magical illusion, like a transformation, and like a city of gandharvas— and thereby fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline."

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva understands these five aggregates of clinging as they truly are—as being like a dream, and so forth, up to being like a city of gandharvas—he is then able to fulfill the perfection of pure ethical discipline that is signless.

Such pure ethical discipline is without deficiency or flaw, without blemish or impurity; it is free from attachment, worthy of offerings, praised by the wise, excellently undertaken, and excellently brought to completion. It is noble and untainted, and is subsumed within the factors of the supramundane path.

Abiding in this precept, one is able to properly receive and uphold the precepts of designation, the precepts acquired through the nature of phenomena, the precepts of restraint, manifest precepts, non-manifest precepts, active precepts, non-active precepts, the precepts of dignified conduct, and the precepts of non-dignified conduct.
"Although this bodhisattva mahāsattva is fully endowed with such precepts, he has no attachment to any phenomena and does not form the thought:
'By means of these precepts, I shall be born into a great kṣatriya clan, or even into a great householder clan, possessing wealth, nobility, and sovereignty.'"
He does not form such thoughts as:
"By means of this precept, I shall become a minor king, or a great king, or a universal monarch (cakravartin), or a high minister, wealthy, noble, and sovereign."
He does not form this thought:

"By means of this precept, I shall be born in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, or even up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception, where I shall possess wealth, nobility, and sovereignty."
One does not form this thought:
"By means of this precept, I shall attain the fruit of stream-entry, up to and including unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Why is that?

Thus all these dharmas share one and the same characteristic, namely: being without characteristics (*animitta*), without abiding, and without attainment. A dharma without characteristics cannot attain a dharma without characteristics; a dharma with characteristics cannot attain a dharma with characteristics; a dharma without characteristics cannot attain a dharma with characteristics; and a dharma with characteristics cannot attain a dharma without characteristics. For this reason, there is ultimately nothing to be attained.
"So it is, Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they are able to swiftly fulfill the signless perfection of pure ethical discipline;
having fulfilled the signless perfection of pure ethical discipline, they swiftly enter the bodhisattva’s state of certainty and transcendence."
Having entered the bodhisattva’s state of certainty beyond regression, they further attain the bodhisattva’s endurance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);

having attained the bodhisattva’s endurance of the non-arising of phenomena, they practice the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and, proceeding toward the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), they obtain the five superior supernormal powers born of maturation (*vipākaja*).

Furthermore, they attain five hundred dharanī-gates and also five hundred samādhi-gates; abiding therein, they further attain the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), traveling from one buddha-field to another, approaching and making offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, maturing sentient beings, and purifying buddha-fields.
"This bodhisattva-mahāsattva, for the sake of transforming sentient beings, although manifests the cycle of birth and death within the various realms of existence, is not defiled by their faults."
Just as a magically conjured person may manifest the acts of walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, yet lacks any real karma of coming and going;
and though they manifest various ways of benefiting and bringing happiness to sentient beings, they find no sentient beings nor any designations for them whatsoever.

Suppose there were a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Suśānta, who, having attained enlightenment, turned the sublime wheel of Dharma and delivered immeasurable multitudes, causing them to transcend birth and death and realize nirvāṇa.

At that time, as there was no sentient being capable of receiving the Buddha’s prediction, he manifested a transformation Buddha (nirmāṇa-buddha) to remain in the world for a long time, while he himself relinquished the formations of life and secretly entered nirvana.

After that transformation Buddha had remained for one kalpa, he bestowed the prediction of great enlightenment upon a bodhisattva, and subsequently demonstrated his entry into nirvana without remainder (anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa).

Although those emanated Buddha-bodies perform various deeds for the benefit of sentient beings, they have no attainment; that is, they do not attain form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, nor do they attain any phenomena—whether contaminated or uncontaminated—nor any sentient beings whatsoever.
So it is with the bodhisattva mahāsattvas: although they perform actions, they have no attainment. "Thus it is, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline. Because they fulfill this perfection of ethical discipline, they are able to embrace all the buddha-dharmas; by means of this, they realize the knowledge of all modes and bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings until the end of the future."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they abide within the five aggregates of grasping—which are like a dream, like an echo, like a reflection, like a shadow, like a mirage, like an illusion, like a transformation, and like a city of gandharvas—and thereby fulfill the perfection of patience."

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva understands, as they truly are, that the five aggregates of clinging are like a dream and so forth, even like a city of gandharvas, he is then able to fulfill the perfection of signless patience.

“Subhūti, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, truly understand that the five aggregates of clinging are like a dream and even like a city of gandharvas, and thereby fulfill the signless perfection of patience?”

"Subhūti! Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva understands, as they truly are, that the five aggregates of clinging lack any real characteristic, he cultivates two kinds of patience and is thus able to bring to perfection the perfection of patience characterized by signlessness."
What are these two?
First, the patience of acceptance;
second, the patience of discernment.

"Regarding 'patience through acceptance': this refers to when Bodhisattvas, from their first generation of the mind of awakening until they sit peacefully upon the seat of sublime enlightenment, should all classes of sentient beings come to revile them or inflict harm with swords and staves during that interval, the Bodhisattva—so as to fulfill the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā)—does not give rise to even a single thought of malice or resentment, nor does he conceive the intention to retaliate.

He thinks only this: 'These sentient beings are deeply to be pitied; their minds have been struck by such powerful afflictions that they lack self-mastery and thus initiate such evil karma toward me. I should not harbor malice or resentment toward them.'"
Again, he reflects:
"It is because I have grasped these aggregates, which are like enemies, that those sentient beings have initiated such evil karma against me; I should only reproach myself and not feel anger."
When that bodhisattva examines in this way, they give rise to deep compassion for those sentient beings; such categories as these are called "the patience of acceptance" (*anupālambha-kṣānti*).
Regarding "the patience of observation" (*pratyavekṣaṇā-kṣānti*), it means that bodhisattvas reflect as follows:

"All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are like illusions, false and unreal, and lack autonomy; they are also like space, devoid of self (*anātman*), even down to the knower and the seer, which arise solely from false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). All things are transformations of one's own mind; who then can reproach me?"
"Who is it that harms me?
And who, in turn, is subject to that censure and harm?

All this is but the false conceptualization of one's own mind; I should not now give rise to groundless attachment. Such phenomena are entirely non-existent because they are empty of intrinsic nature and empty of ultimate reality."
