"When a Bodhisattva thus examines with scrutiny, they understand all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as empty and quiescent according to reality, and do not give rise to divergent conceptions regarding any phenomena; such categories are called the patience of examination (*vicaya-kṣānti*)."

“Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and trains in these two kinds of patience, they are able to fulfill the perfection of signless patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), and by means of this, they attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).”
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What is meant by ‘the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena’ (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti)?
What is it that is abandoned by this?”
“Furthermore, what kind of wisdom is this?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“By the power of this, even the slightest portion of evil or unwholesome dharmas cannot arise; therefore, it is called the ‘patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas’ (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).”

This brings about the ultimate pacification of all afflictions, such as the conceit of "I" and "mine. One truly endures that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are like dreams, and so forth, up to being like a city of Gandharvas. This endurance is called wisdom; because one attains this wisdom, it is termed the attainment of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“What is the difference between the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena of bodhisattvas?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Whatever wisdom or abandonment belongs to those from stream-enterers up to pratyekabuddhas is also called the patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, there is another patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, namely, the patience that all phenomena are ultimately non-arising; this is the distinction."
“Subhūti, you should know that because bodhisattva mahāsattvas have accomplished such sublime patience, they surpass all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.”

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell securely in such maturation-patience (*vipāka-kṣānti*) and practice the bodhisattva path, they are able to fulfill the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*). Because they have accomplished this knowledge of the aspects of the path, they are never separated from the four applications of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; nor are they separated from the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; nor are they separated from the supernormal powers of maturation.

By not being separated from the supernormal powers of maturation, they travel from one buddha-field to another, attending upon and making offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, bringing sentient beings to maturity, and adorning and purifying buddha-fields.
Having performed these deeds, one is able to realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*). "In this way, Subhūti,
when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they are swiftly able to fulfill the signless perfection of patience (*animitkṣāntipāramitā*)."

Because this perfection of patience is brought to fulfillment, one is able to fulfill all Buddha-dharmas; thereby, one realizes the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) and brings benefit and happiness to sentient beings until the end of the future.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they abide within the five aggregates of clinging— which are like a dream, an echo, an image, a reflection, a mirage, an illusion, a transformation, and a city of Gandharvas— and having realized as they truly are that these five aggregates of clinging are without real characteristics, being like dreams up to like a city of Gandharvas, they arouse courageous physical and mental diligence."

"Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva has initiated courageous physical diligence, they manifest superior and swift supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). They are able to travel to the worlds of the Buddhas of the ten directions to attend upon and make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; there, at the presence of those Buddhas, they plant various roots of goodness, benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings, and are also able to adorn and purify various Buddha-fields."
"By means of physical diligence, this bodhisattva mahāsattva brings sentient beings to maturity and, through skillful means, causes them to abide in the three vehicles.
It is thus, Subhūti!"
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, through physical diligence they are able to swiftly fulfill the signless perfection of diligence.

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva has aroused a courageous mind and diligence, they bring forth the noble path comprised of the branches of the noble untainted path, thereby perfecting the perfection of diligence; therein they are fully able to encompass all wholesome dharmas, namely the four foundations of mindfulness, and so on, up to the knowledge of all aspects.

By means of mental diligence, this bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the perfection of all primary marks and secondary signs, and emits great radiance that illuminates boundless realms. Because his mental diligence is utterly perfected, he forever severs the continuity of the habitual tendencies of afflictions, realizes unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, turns the wondrous wheel of Dharma endowed with the thirty-two marks, and causes the great trichiliocosm to shake in six ways.

The sentient beings therein, touched by the light, beholding these transformations, and hearing the sound of the True Dharma, attain non-retrogression and even ultimate realization within the paths of the Three Vehicles, according to their respective capacities.

"In this way, Subhūti, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they fulfill the perfection of diligence. By means of this perfection of diligence, they are able to accomplish many beneficial deeds for both themselves and others, swiftly perfect all Buddha-dharmas, and thereby realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), benefiting and bringing happiness to sentient beings until the end of the future."

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 529. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Three, Chapter Twenty-Eight on the Sublime Marks, Section Three. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they abide within the five aggregates of clinging—which are like a dream, an echo, an image, a reflection, a mirage, a magical illusion, a transformation, and a city of gandharvas—and thereby fulfill the perfection of meditative concentration.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva,

when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, abide within the five aggregates of clinging— which are like a dream, as extensively explained, up to being like a city of gandharvas— and thereby fulfill the perfection of meditative concentration?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they understand as it truly is that the five aggregates of clinging are like a dream, and so forth, up to being like a city of gandharvas, lacking any real characteristic. Having done so, they enter the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; they cultivate the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; they cultivate the lightning-flash-like and diamond-like noble right samādhis. Abiding in the diamond-like samādhi—with the exception of the Tathāgata’s concentration—they are able to enter and fully abide in all other superior concentrations, whether shared with the two vehicles or otherwise; yet they do not give rise to attachment toward these samādhis, nor do they crave the fruits obtained therein.”

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva understands, as they truly are, that the meditative concentrations such as dhyāna and all phenomena are identical in being signless and having non-existence as their nature; he should not relish the signless through the signless, nor should he relish non-existence through non-existence.

Because they are free from attachment to flavors, they never follow the power of meditative concentrations to be born within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) or the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Why is this?

It is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva finds nothing at all to be apprehended in any realm; regarding the one who enters concentration, the concentration entered, the means by which, the purpose for which, and the time of entering concentration—all these are likewise unapprehendable.

“Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend any phenomena, they are able to swiftly fulfill the perfection of signless meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*). By virtue of fulfilling this perfection of meditative concentration, they transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.”
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How does this bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of the perfection of meditative concentration that is signless, become fulfilled and thereby transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva has well studied the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of non-essential nature, he is able to fulfill the perfection of signless meditative concentration and transcend the stages of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling within all these emptinesses, finds nothing at all to be apprehended among any phenomena; they do not perceive any phenomenon that is apart from emptiness.

Abiding therein, this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not attain the fruit of a stream-enterer, up to and including the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; nor do they attain any of the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor do they attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas.
Why is this? Because within emptiness there are no phenomena, nor is there emptiness itself.
By abiding in this emptiness, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and freedom from birth.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“By what are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas born?
By what are they separated from birth?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas take all that is apprehended as birth, and take all that is non-apprehended as freedom from birth."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have something to be apprehended?
By what do they have nothing to be apprehended?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas take all dharmas to be objects of apprehension.

That is to say, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas take the aggregate of form to be an object of apprehension; they take the aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness to be objects of apprehension; and so on, in detail, up to taking the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvajñājñāna*) to be an object of apprehension.”
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas take such various Dharma-gates as being objects of attainment, that very attainment is called "arising.
This is because, just as the arising of food and drink can become a source of affliction.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas take the fact that all dharmas are without activity, without attainment, without expression, and without demonstration as being non-apprehensible."

It means that a bodhisattva-mahāsattva regards form, up to and including the knowledge of all modes, as non-attainment because they are without activity, without acquisition, without explanation, and without demonstration.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of everything from form up to the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) is entirely non-practicable, unobtainable, inexpressible, and undemonstrable.

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by means of such various Dharma-gates as these—being without practice, without attainment, without speech, and without demonstration—regard them as non-apprehension; this very non-apprehension is termed ‘departure from birth.’”

Once the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have entered the stage of the certainty of rightness (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and perfected all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), they do not even take birth according to the power of those concentrations, much less according to afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion!
It is impossible that one would take birth through the power of secondary afflictions!

It is also impossible that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while dwelling in this state, would perform various karmas and, by the power of those karmas, transmigrate through the various realms of existence!

Although this bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells amidst the mass of conditioned phenomena that are like an illusion, performing what is beneficial and brings peace and happiness to all sentient beings, they do not apprehend either the illusion or those sentient beings.
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva finds nothing to be apprehended in such matters, they never weary or desist in maturing sentient beings and purifying buddha-fields.
"Thus it is, Subhūti!"
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they are swiftly able to fulfill the perfection of signless meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).

Because this perfection of meditative concentration is fulfilled, they are then able to fulfill all Buddha-dharmas; by means of this, they realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*), and until the end of the future, they turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, benefiting and gladdening sentient beings without interruption.
This unsurpassed wheel of Dharma thus turned, although it has a purpose, is without anything attained, because both the speaker and that which is spoken lack intrinsic nature.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they abide within the five aggregates of clinging—which are like a dream, like an echo, like an image, like a reflection, like a mirage, like a magical illusion, like a transformation, and like a city of gandharvas—and thereby fulfill the perfection of wisdom.

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva understands, as they truly are, that the nature of all phenomena is like a dream and even like a city of gandharvas—utterly devoid of reality—they are then able to fulfill the signless perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:

"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, truly understand that the nature of all phenomena is like a dream, and so forth, up to being like a city of gandharvas?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive dreams, nor do they perceive one who sees dreams;
they do not hear echoes, nor do they perceive one who hears echoes."
One does not see the image, nor does one see the one who sees the image;
one does not see the reflection, nor does one see the one who sees the reflection;
one does not see the mirage, nor does one see the one who sees the mirage.
One does not see the illusion, nor does one see the one who sees the illusion;
one does not see the transformation, nor does one see the one who sees the transformation;
one does not see the city of Gandharvas, nor does one see the one who sees the city of Gandharvas.

Why is this so? Dreams and those who see dreams, up to and including the city of Gandharvas and those who see the city of Gandharvas, are all attachments held by foolish ordinary beings through their inversions. All Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas do not see dreams or those who see dreams; as explained at length, they do not see the city of Gandharvas or those who see the city of Gandharvas.

Why is this so? Because all dharmas have non-existence as their nature; they are neither produced nor real, being signless and unconditioned, and lacking any truly existent nature, they are equal to nirvāṇa.

If all phenomena have non-existence as their nature, and so on, up to being equal to nirvāṇa, how is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they give rise to the notion of existence, the notion of formation, the notion of reality, the notion of being, and the notion of having a conditioned or real nature regarding all phenomena?
If one were to give rise to such a thought, it would be impossible. Why is this?

If all phenomena possessed even the slightest intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), were established or real, possessed characteristics or were conditioned, or if a real nature could be apprehended therein, then the practice of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* would not be *prajñāpāramitā*, for it would fail to apprehend the true nature and characteristics of all phenomena.

"In this way, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not cling to the aggregate of form, nor do they cling to the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, up to and including not clinging to the knowledge of all aspects."

"Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva is without attachment to all such dharma-gates, they are able to fulfill the first through the tenth bodhisattva stages, yet they do not give rise to craving or attachment toward them."

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not apprehend the perfection of the first stage through to the tenth stage, nor the agent or the object of that perfection; how then could they give rise to craving and attachment toward them?

Although this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not apprehend the perfection of wisdom; because they do not apprehend the perfection of wisdom, they likewise do not apprehend any phenomena.
Although this bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates that the perfection of wisdom subsumes all phenomena, they do not apprehend any phenomenon at all. Why is this?
Because all phenomena are non-dual and inseparable from this Prajñāpāramitā. Why is this?
Because the nature of all phenomena cannot be distinguished as being called "Suchness," "Dharmadhātu," or "Bhūtakoṭi"; for all phenomena are without admixture and without differentiation.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If all phenomena are by nature undifferentiated and without distinction, how can one speak of them as being wholesome or unwholesome, with outflows or without outflows, worldly or supramundane, conditioned or unconditioned, and so forth—of these and other such immeasurable distinctions?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Regarding the true nature of all phenomena, is there anything that can be said to be 'wholesome' and so forth?"
"Furthermore, can it be said that there is the fruit of a stream-enterer,
up to and including the Buddha's enlightenment? Subhūti replied, "No!"
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“For this reason, you should know that the nature of all phenomena is without mixture and without distinction; it is signless, unarisen, unceasing, unobstructed, ineffable, and undemonstrable.”
"Subhūti, you should know that when I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, I attained nothing at all regarding the nature of phenomena;
that is to say, I did not attain form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, nor did I attain the sense bases from the eye base up to the mind base."
One does not apprehend the sphere of form, up to and including the sphere of mental phenomena; one does not apprehend the eye element, up to and including the mind element;
one does not apprehend the form element, up to and including the mental-phenomena element; one does not apprehend the eye-consciousness element, up to and including the mind-consciousness element;

one does not apprehend eye-contact, up to and including mind-contact; one does not apprehend the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, up to and including [feelings produced with] mind-contact.
The various feelings produced with contact as a condition cannot be apprehended; from the earth element up to the consciousness element, they cannot be apprehended.
From the causal condition up to the dominant condition, they cannot be apprehended. The various phenomena produced from conditions cannot be apprehended.
Ignorance up to old age and death cannot be apprehended. The desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm cannot be apprehended. The wholesome cannot be apprehended.
...one does not apprehend non-virtuous dharmas; one does not apprehend tainted or untainted dharmas;
one does not apprehend mundane or supramundane dharmas; one does not apprehend conditioned or unconditioned dharmas;

and so on, in detail, up to not apprehending the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; one does not apprehend the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practice; one does not apprehend...
Unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. "In this way, Subhūti,

when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment until unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should always properly train in the intrinsic nature of all phenomena."

If one can skillfully study the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, one will be able to thoroughly purify the path to great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), and also fulfill the various practices of a bodhisattva, ripen sentient beings, and adorn and purify buddha-fields. Abiding in these dharmas, one will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), and through the skillful means of the three vehicles, tame all classes of sentient beings, causing them no longer to transmigrate within the three realms of existence and enabling them to attain the ultimate peace and happiness of parinirvāṇa.
"In this way, Subhūti, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should train in the perfection of wisdom by employing the method of signlessness, so that it may be swiftly perfected."

If one cultivates the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) and swiftly brings it to fulfillment, one will be able to encompass all Buddha-dharmas; by means of this, one realizes the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñājñāna) and brings benefit and happiness to sentient beings until the end of the future.
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If all dharmas are no different from dreams—and as has been explained at length, up to being like a city of Gandharvas—being devoid of any real entity, having non-existence as their nature, and being empty of self-characteristics, how can one establish that ‘this is wholesome’ and ‘this is unwholesome,’ ‘this is with outflows’ and ‘this is without outflows,’ ‘this is mundane’ and ‘this is supramundane,’ ‘this is conditioned’ and ‘this is unconditioned,’ and so on at length, up to ‘this is the fruit of stream-entry’ and ‘this is the dharma by which the fruit of stream-entry is realized,’ and likewise up to ‘this is the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha’ and ‘this is the dharma by which the enlightenment of a Buddha is realized’?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Worldly fools—uninstructed ordinary persons—perceive dreams within dreams and see those who dream; to speak extensively, they even perceive and see gandharva-cities within gandharva-cities.”

In this way, foolish worldlings who have not heard the Dharma, having experienced dreams and the like, engage in inverted attachments. They may perform unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind; or they may perform wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind; or they may perform indeterminate actions of body, speech, and mind; or they may perform non-meritorious actions of body, speech, and mind; or they may perform meritorious actions of body, speech, and mind; or they may perform immovable actions of body, speech, and mind. Due to these volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), they wander through birth and death, undergoing suffering without end.

"When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they abide in two kinds of emptiness to observe all phenomena, namely, the two emptinesses of ultimate limit and boundlessness."
Abiding thus in these two kinds of emptiness, this bodhisattva mahāsattva proclaims the sublime Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, saying:

"Form up to consciousness is empty and non-existent; the eye-base up to the mind-base is empty and non-existent; the form-base up to the phenomena-base is empty and non-existent; the eye-element up to the mind-element is empty and non-existent; the form-element up to the phenomena-element is empty and non-existent; the eye-consciousness-element up to the mind-consciousness-element is empty and non-existent; eye-contact up to mind-contact is empty and non-existent; all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition up to all feelings produced with mind-contact as condition are empty and non-existent; the earth-element up to the consciousness-element is empty and non-existent; the causal condition up to the sovereign condition is empty and non-existent; all phenomena produced from conditions are empty and non-existent; and the factors from ignorance up to old age and death are empty and non-existent."
Furthermore, he spoke these words:
"Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are like a dream, even up to being like a city of Gandharvas; they are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature.
The eye-base, even up to the mind-base, are like a dream, even up to being like a city of Gandharvas; they are entirely devoid of [intrinsic nature]."
Nature: from the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) up to the sense-base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), they are like a dream and even like a city of Gandharvas, entirely lacking intrinsic nature;
from the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) up to the mind-element (*manodhātu*), they are like a dream and even like a city of Gandharvas, entirely lacking intrinsic nature;

from the form-element (*rūpadhātu*) up to the phenomenon-element (*dharmadhātu*), they are like a dream and even like a city of Gandharvas, entirely lacking intrinsic nature; the eye... [and so forth].
The element of consciousness up to the element of mental consciousness is like a dream, even like a city of gandharvas, and is entirely devoid of intrinsic nature;
eye-contact up to mind-contact is like a dream, even like a city of gandharvas, and is entirely devoid of intrinsic nature;
the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition are like a dream... [and so forth].
Just as the city of Gandharvas has no intrinsic nature, so too do the earth element up to the consciousness element lack intrinsic nature, being like a dream and like a city of Gandharvas;
from causes and conditions up to dominant conditions, they lack intrinsic nature, being like a dream and like a city of Gandharvas;
and all phenomena produced from conditions lack intrinsic nature, being like a dream and like [a city of Gandharvas].
“The city of Gandharvas has no intrinsic nature; likewise, phenomena from ignorance up to old age and death are like dreams and like cities of Gandharvas, having no intrinsic nature. He further said:

"In this, there is no form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; no eye-base up to the mind-base; no form-base up to the phenomena-base; no eye-element up to the mind-element; no form-element up to the phenomena-element; no eye-consciousness-element up to the mind-consciousness-element; no eye-contact up to mind-contact; no feelings produced with eye-contact as condition up to feelings produced with mind-contact as condition; no earth-element up to the consciousness-element; no causal condition up to the sovereign condition; no phenomena produced from conditions; and no phenomena such as ignorance up to old age and death."
Furthermore, he spoke these words:
"In this, there is no dream and no one who sees a dream; to speak extensively, there is no city of Gandharvas and no one who sees a city of Gandharvas."
He further spoke these words:
"All such phenomena are devoid of substantial reality; their nature is to have no nature.

It is through the power of your false conceptualization that you perceive a form aggregate, up to and including a consciousness aggregate, within what is actually the non-existence of a form aggregate, up to and including the non-existence of a consciousness aggregate."
Regarding the absence of the eye-base up to the mind-base, they perceive the presence of the eye-base up to the mind-base;
regarding the absence of the form-base up to the mental-object-base, they perceive the presence of the form-base up to the mental-object-base;
regarding the absence of the eye-element up to the mind-element, they perceive the presence of the eye-element up to the mind-element.
Within the formless realm up to the dharma-realm, they perceive the existence of the form realm up to the dharma-realm;
within the absence of the eye-consciousness realm up to the mind-consciousness realm, they perceive the existence of the eye-consciousness realm up to the mind-consciousness realm;
within the absence of eye-contact up to mind-contact, they perceive the existence of eye-contact up to mind-contact.

Regarding those feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, up to those feelings produced with mind-contact as condition, they perceive feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, up to feelings produced with mind-contact as condition;
regarding the non-existent earth element, up to the consciousness element, they perceive the earth element, up to the consciousness element;
regarding the non-existent causal conditions, up to the sovereign condition, they perceive causal conditions, up to the sovereign condition.
Within phenomena that do not arise from conditions, one perceives phenomena that do arise from conditions;
within the absence of phenomena such as ignorance up to old age and death, one perceives phenomena such as ignorance up to old age and death.
Again, he spoke these words:

"The nature of all phenomena—the aggregates, bases, elements, and so forth—is established through the conjunction of various conditions, arises from perversion, and is governed by the maturation of various karmas."
"For what reason do you conceive the notion of a real entity regarding these phenomena that are false and devoid of reality?

At that time, the Bodhisattva, practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), employs expedient means to rescue and deliver those sentient beings who possess stinginess and greed, causing them to abandon such greed. Once these sentient beings have abandoned stinginess and greed, he exhorts them to cultivate the *dānapāramitā*.
By means of giving, these sentient beings obtain great wealth, status, and sovereign power.
Furthermore, from this state, he skillfully delivers them and exhorts them to cultivate the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).
By means of pure ethical discipline, these sentient beings attain rebirth in the higher realms with wealth, nobility, and mastery.
From those states, he further delivers them through skillful means, exhorting them to cultivate the perfection of meditative concentration.
By means of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), these sentient beings are born in the Brahma-world and dwell with mastery in the first *dhyāna*.

Through skillful means, they are rescued from the first *dhyāna* and further established in the second *dhyāna*; thus, by successive stages of skillful means, they are rescued until they are finally established in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

"These sentient beings, having attained superior karmic fruits through generosity, ethical discipline, and meditative concentration, become deeply attached to them. At that time, the Bodhisattva employs skillful means to rescue them from these inferior states and establishes them in the realm of nirvana without remainder."
That is to say, by means of skillful means appropriate to each case, they cause [beings] to diligently cultivate the noble path according to the three vehicles;
or cause them to abide in the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
or cause them to abide in the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; or cause them to abide in the eight liberations up to the ten totalities.
Or they cause them to dwell securely in the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
or they cause them to dwell securely in the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination in direct and reverse order; or they cause them to dwell securely in the six perfections;
or they cause them to dwell securely in inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature; or they cause them to dwell securely in suchness up to [the limit of reality].
The inconceivable realm, or causing them to dwell securely in the various bodhisattva stages,
or causing them to dwell securely in the gates of dhāraṇī and the gates of samādhi, or causing them to dwell securely in the five eyes and the six supernormal powers,
or causing them to dwell securely in the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or causing them to dwell securely in the Great...
They cause them to abide in loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity;

or they cause them to abide in the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity; or they cause them to abide in all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, through skillful means accomplishes the truly untainted dharmas that are formless, invisible, and non-obstructive, and abides therein."

If there are sentient beings who are destined to attain the fruit of a stream-enterer, he manifests, exhorts, encourages, gladdens, and employs skillful means to rescue them, causing them to attain the fruit of a stream-enterer; and so on, as extensively explained, up until: if there are sentient beings who are destined to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, he manifests, exhorts, encourages, gladdens, and employs skillful means to rescue them, causing them to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete bodhi.

"In this way, Subhūti! When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they contemplate the two kinds of emptiness. Although they know that all phenomena are like dreams and even like a city of *gandharvas*—that none are truly existent, that their nature is the absence of nature, and that their specific characteristics are all empty—they are nonetheless able to establish what is wholesome and what is unwholesome, what is with outflows and what is without outflows, what is mundane and what is supramundane, what is conditioned and what is unconditioned; and so on, in detail, up to: what is the fruit of a stream-enterer and what are the dharmas by which the fruit of a stream-enterer is realized, and so forth, up to: what is the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment of a Buddha and what are the dharmas by which the enlightenment of a Buddha is realized—all of these without any confusion."
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is most wonderful and marvelous that the bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom!”

They observe and dwell securely in the two kinds of emptiness—ultimate and boundless—and although they know that all phenomena are like dreams, up to like cities of Gandharvas, being neither truly existent nor having intrinsic nature as their nature, and that their own characteristics are fundamentally empty, they are nevertheless able to establish the immeasurable dharma-gates of the wholesome and the unwholesome without any confusion.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said. It is most wonderful and marvelous that when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*,

although they know that all phenomena are ultimately the emptiness of boundlessness and are not at all real— being like dreams, and even like cities of Gandharvas, empty of intrinsic characteristics from the very beginning, having non-existence as their nature— they are nevertheless able to establish various dharma-gates, such as the wholesome and the unwholesome, without any confusion between them.

If you were to know all the most marvelous and extraordinary qualities of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas who practice the profound perfection of wisdom—qualities which neither śrāvakas nor pratyekabuddhas have accomplished and cannot fathom.
You śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot even respond to the eloquence of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, let alone any other sentient beings!
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,

what are the marvelous and extraordinary dharmas of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas who practice the profound perfection of wisdom— dharmas that neither śrāvakas nor pratyekabuddhas have accomplished, nor can they fathom?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!"
Reflect upon this well!
I shall analyze and explain for you all the most marvelous and rare dharmas belonging to the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, so as to bring joy to your heart.

“Subhūti, you should know that when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they abide in the six perfections born of maturation, the five sublime supernormal powers, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, as well as dhāraṇīs, the analytical knowledges, and other immeasurable and innumerable truly pure merits; by means of their supernormal powers, they travel throughout the ten directions.”

If there are sentient beings who should be benefited by means of the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, he benefits them by means of the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
if they should be benefited by means of the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna, he benefits them by means of the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna;

if they should be benefited by means of the immeasurable of loving-kindness up to the immeasurable of equanimity, he benefits them by means of the immeasurable of loving-kindness up to the immeasurable of equanimity.

Those who should be benefited by the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space, up to the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he benefits them with the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space, up to the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
those who should be benefited by the four foundations of mindfulness, up to the eightfold noble path, he benefits them with the four foundations of mindfulness, up to the eightfold noble path;
those who should be benefited by the gateway of emptiness, up to the gateway of wishlessness, he benefits them with the gateway of emptiness, up to the gateway of wishlessness.
"Those who should be benefited by other superior wholesome dharmas, he shall benefit them with those other superior wholesome dharmas.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again, saying:

"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, abide in the truly pure merits of the six *pāramitās* and the five superknowledges (*abhijñā*) born of maturation, and thereby benefit sentient beings through giving and the other perfections?"

The Buddha told Subhūti: “When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they give to sentient beings whatever requisites they require. That is to say, if they require food and drink, they give them food and drink; if they require vehicles, they give them vehicles; if they require clothing, they give them clothing; if they require incense and flowers, they give them incense and flowers; and if they require any other various kinds of requisites, they give them all so that there is no lack. Or they may give various kinds of offerings to śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.”

When giving in this manner, one practices generosity with a mind of equanimity, free from discriminatory thoughts; as one gives to those who uphold the precepts, so too does one give to those who violate them;
as one gives to those of the human realm, so too does one give to non-humans;
as one gives to those of the inner path, so too does one give to those of the outer paths.
As one gives to the noble ones, so too does one give to ordinary beings;
as one gives to the honorable and noble, so too does one give to the lowly and base.
From the Buddhas above down to the animals below, one is equal and impartial, without making any distinctions, and does not regard the field of merit as superior or inferior.

Why is this? Because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas realize that the self-characteristics of all phenomena and all sentient beings are empty and entirely without distinction; thus, they practice giving without any notion of difference.

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving without any notion of difference, they shall obtain a fruit that is non-differentiated and free from conceptual construction—namely, the attainment of the omniscience of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*) and other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-qualities.
“Subhūti, you should know that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees a beggar approaching, he should form this thought:
‘If this beggar who has come here is a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, because he is a field of merit, I ought to give to him.’”
"If it were not for the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, but were instead an animal or the like, it would not be a field of merit, and therefore one should not give to it.
For a bodhisattva-mahāsattva to form such a thought is to contravene the bodhisattva dharma.
Why is this? Because it is only when the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have purified their own minds that the field of merit becomes pure.
Upon seeing beggars, they should not think:
If one thinks, "To such beings who come begging, I shall give; to such beings who come begging, I should not give," one violates the original aspiration of the Great Bodhicitta.
For all Bodhisattvas originally generate the mind of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment with this thought:
"I shall act as a refuge, an island, a dwelling, and a place of protection for sentient beings."
Upon seeing a beggar approach, one should form this thought:
"This sentient being is now impoverished, destitute, and exposed; I shall benefit and sustain them through giving.

By means of this cause and condition, they too will be able to practice giving, become moderate in desire and content, abstain from taking life—and as extensively explained, up to abstaining from frivolous speech—and further be able to subdue greed, hatred, and wrong views. Through these causes and conditions, after the end of their life, they will be reborn into a great kṣatriya clan, or even into a great householder clan, or be born in some other wealthy and noble place, possessing abundant riches and treasures while cultivating various wholesome deeds. Or, by virtue of the causes and conditions of sustaining them through this gift, they will gradually rely upon the Three Vehicles and attain liberation."
"Furthermore, Subhūti! If various enemies or other sentient beings should come to where a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells, seeking something for the sake of causing harm or out of destitution;
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva should not give rise to a discriminatory mind, thinking:
"This should be given; this should not be given.

Rather, they should give rise to a mind of equanimity and bestow as gifts whatever is requested—whether parts of their own body, other wealth and treasures, kingdoms and cities, or wives and children.

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva seeks to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings; yet, if they were to give rise to a discriminatory mind, thinking:
"This should be given as a gift; this should not be given."
Then all the Buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, devas, humans, asuras, and other assemblies of noble beings collectively rebuked him:

"Who requested you to resolve upon bodhicitta, vowing to universally benefit all classes of sentient beings—to be a refuge for those without refuge, a home for those without a home, a protector for those without protection, an island for those without an island, and to bring peace and happiness to those who lack it—and yet now do you discriminate between those who give and those who do not?"
"Furthermore, Subhūti! If a human or a non-human being comes to where a bodhisattva mahāsattva is and requests his body parts—his hands, feet, limbs, or joints—"
This bodhisattva mahāsattva should not give rise to the two discriminating thoughts:
"Should I give, or should I not give?
He should instead form this thought alone:
"Whatever they may seek, I shall bestow it all upon them. Why is this?
Because this bodhisattva-mahāsattva constantly reflects thus:
"I have taken up this body for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings; therefore, I must certainly grant whatever comes to me who seeks it, and I should not fail to give.
Upon seeing a beggar, he gives rise to this thought:
"This body of mine was originally received for the sake of others; even if they did not come to take it, I should still offer it myself, let alone when they come to request it—how could I not give!"
Having formed this thought, he leaped for joy; he dismembered his own limbs and gave them away, further exclaiming in celebration:
"Now I have attained a great benefit, in that by relinquishing this defiled body, I shall obtain a pure one."
"Subhūti, you should know that all bodhisattva mahāsattvas practicing the profound perfection of wisdom should train in this way when seeking great enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon seeing beggars, gives rise to this thought:
'Now, in this situation, who is it that gives?'"
Who receives?
What is the object given?
By what means and for what purpose?
What is giving? The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is entirely unapprehendable. Why is this so?
"In this way, all these phenomena are ultimately empty; within the emptiness of phenomena, there is no giving, no taking away, no bestowing, and no receiving.
Subhūti, you should know this!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should train in this way:
that all phenomena are empty—whether by virtue of being empty through internal emptiness, up to and including being empty through the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in this emptiness while practicing generosity without interruption, thereby perfecting the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).

Because this perfection of generosity has been brought to fulfillment, when others cut him or plunder all his internal and external possessions, his mind is entirely free from conceptualization or resentment; he thinks only this:
"Sentient beings and all phenomena are entirely empty. Who is it that cuts me?"
Who has robbed me?
Who, moreover, receives it?
And who is it that performs this contemplation of emptiness within this?
"Furthermore, Subhūti! With my Buddha-eye, I survey throughout the ten directions all the Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, desiring to benefit all classes of sentient beings, intentionally enter the great hells by means of their vows. Seeing sentient beings undergoing various sufferings, and having seen them, they initiate the three kinds of demonstrations."
What are the three?
First, miraculous transformations;
second, prophetic declarations.

Third is instruction. This bodhisattva mahāsattva first employs the power of the demonstration of miraculous transformations (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) to eliminate the various instruments of suffering in the hells, such as boiling water, fire, and blades. Next, he employs the power of the demonstration of telepathic reading (*ādeśanāprātihārya*), discerning the thoughts in the minds of those sentient beings to preach the Dharma for them. Finally, he employs the power of the demonstration of instruction (*anuśāsanīprātihārya*), engendering great loving-kindness (*maitrī*), great compassion (*karuṇā*), great sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and great equanimity (*upekṣā*) toward them while preaching the Dharma. This causes those sentient beings in the hells to conceive pure faith in the bodhisattva; by this cause and condition, they emerge from the hells and are reborn among the gods or among humans, gradually attaining liberation by relying on the three vehicles.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

With my Buddha-eye, I survey throughout the ten directions all the Buddha-worlds, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and see Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who draw near to and make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones."

When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva draws near to and makes offerings to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, he does so with a profound mind of joy, delight, and reverence; it is not that he lacks joy, delight, and reverence.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva reverently listens to, receives, upholds, reads, and recites the true Dharma taught by the Buddha, World-Honored One; they do not forget it until reaching unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. According to the Dharma they have heard, they are able to explain it correctly to sentient beings, enabling them to obtain supreme benefit and peace, never becoming weary until reaching unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

With my Buddha-eye, I survey throughout the ten directions all the Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and see Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, desiring to benefit sentient beings within the realm of animals, sacrifice their own bodies and lives."

When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva sees various animals oppressed by the fires of hunger and intent on harming one another, he gives rise to a heart of compassion and pity; he then cuts off his own body parts and severs his limbs and joints, scattering them in the ten directions so that they may eat and devour them at will.

Any among the various classes of animals who eat the flesh of this bodhisattva’s body will all give rise to a heart of deep affection, reverence, and shame toward the bodhisattva. By virtue of these causes and conditions, they will escape the realm of animals and be reborn in the heavens or among human beings; there they will encounter a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, hear the preaching of the True Dharma, practice according to the principle, and gradually attain liberation by relying on the three vehicles.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to perform for the world what is difficult to do and bring great benefit; that is to say, for the sake of the welfare, happiness, and liberation of all sentient beings, they themselves give rise to the unsurpassed mind of great bodhi, and they also cause others to give rise to it and to practice various kinds of correct conduct in accordance with reality, and they also cause others to practice so as to transcend the suffering of birth and death and attain the bliss of nirvāṇa.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! With my Buddha-eye, I survey the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River. There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, desiring to benefit the sentient beings within the realm of hungry ghosts, intentionally travel to those worlds by means of their vows and skillful means to pacify and eliminate their sufferings of hunger and thirst. Once the various sufferings of those hungry ghosts have been stilled, they develop deep feelings of love, respect, shame, and remorse toward these bodhisattvas. The bodhisattvas then proclaim for them the essential teachings on transcending stinginess, causing them to give rise to a mind of generosity upon hearing it. By virtue of these roots of goodness, they escape the realm of hungry ghosts and are reborn either in the heavens or among humans. There they encounter the Tathāgata, attend upon and make offerings to him, and hear the preaching of the True Dharma. They gradually practice the correct conduct of the three vehicles, until finally they enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder."
Thus it is, Subhūti!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in great compassion toward sentient beings, giving rise to boundless skillful means to rescue them and lead them into the nirvāṇa of the three vehicles.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

With my Buddha-eye, I survey the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and see Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, through their skill in means, proclaim the sublime Dharma for the gods of the Four Great Kings, and so on, up to proclaiming the sublime Dharma for the gods of the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations."

Having heard the sublime Dharma from the Bodhisattva, those hosts of devas gradually rely upon the three vehicles to diligently cultivate correct practice, and accordingly realize entry into ultimate nirvāṇa.

Among those devas, there were certain sons of gods who were deeply attached to the five kinds of exquisite sensual pleasures of the heavens and to the various jeweled palaces where they dwelt. This bodhisattva-mahāsattva manifested a fire that burned those palaces, causing them to feel revulsion and fear; he then preached the Dharma to them, saying:
"O sons of gods!..."

"One should carefully observe that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, and cannot be relied upon with confidence; what wise person would take pleasure in or become attached to them?

At that time, having heard this sound of the Dharma, the sons of the gods developed a profound sense of weary detachment from the pleasures of the five senses. They observed their own bodies and lives as false and impermanent, like plantain trees, flashes of lightning, or mirages, and they viewed the celestial palaces as if they were prisons.
Having made this contemplation, they gradually rely upon the three vehicles to diligently cultivate correct practice and proceed toward parinirvāṇa. "Furthermore, Subhūti!

With my Buddha-eye, I survey throughout the ten directions all Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, where there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, seeing the various Brahmā devas attached to their respective views, employ skillful means to transform and guide them, causing them to grow weary of and abandon those attachments, and say to them: "
“O celestial sages!
For what reason do you give rise to such evil views within this collection of conditioned phenomena—which are empty, signless, illusory, and unreal?”
"You should quickly abandon these and faithfully accept the True Dharma, so that you may obtain the unsurpassed nectar!
Thus, Subhūti, do all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
abiding in great compassion, proclaim the True Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
These are the most marvelous and extraordinary qualities of all bodhisattva mahāsattvas who practice the profound perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Suvikrāntavikrāmin!”

With my unobstructed and pure Buddha-eye, I survey throughout the ten directions all Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, where there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who gather in sentient beings by means of the four bases of sympathy.
What are the four? First, giving;
second, pleasant speech.
Third is beneficial conduct;
fourth is cooperation. "Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
How do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas gather in sentient beings through the practice of giving?
It is by means of two kinds of giving that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas gather in sentient beings:
first, the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*).
The second is the gift of Dharma.
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, use the gift of material wealth to gather in all sentient beings?"

This refers to a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), who is able to bestow upon sentient beings various kinds of food and drink, clothing, dwellings, bedding, vehicles, lamps, music, incense and flowers, gold, silver, precious jewels, ornaments, and so forth; or who bestows upon sentient beings wives and concubines, sons and daughters, male and female servants of all ages, attendants, elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, and medicines; or who bestows upon sentient beings treasuries, cities, towns, villages, and even royal thrones; or who bestows upon sentient beings the limbs and members of his body, such as hands, feet, head, eyes, marrow, and brain.
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva places various kinds of objects at the crossroads and ascends a high platform, proclaiming these words:

"All sentient beings who have any need, come and take as you please; do not harbor doubt or hesitation. Take them as if they were your own property and do not entertain thoughts of them as belonging to another. Even my own body, its limbs and members, hands, feet, head, eyes, marrow, and brain—take them as you wish; I have no stinginess toward you."
"Having given all necessary things to sentient beings, this bodhisattva mahāsattva further exhorts them to take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha;
or exhorts them to receive and uphold the five precepts of a lay follower (upāsaka); or exhorts them to receive and uphold the eight precepts of the one-day fast (upavāsa);
or exhorts them to receive and uphold the ten paths of wholesome action; or exhorts them to practice and study the four..."

They may encourage the cultivation of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), or encourage the cultivation of the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), or encourage the cultivation of the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*),
or encourage the cultivation of the six recollections (*anusmṛti*), or encourage the cultivation of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*) and mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*),
or encourage the cultivation of the ten wholesome perceptions (*daśakuśalasaṃjñā*), or encourage the cultivation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśadbodhipākṣikadharma*).
Regarding the Dharma, they may encourage the cultivation and study of the three gates of liberation;
or encourage the cultivation and study of the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality; or encourage the cultivation and study of the six perfections;
or encourage abiding in inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence; or encourage abiding in suchness up to the inconceivable realm.
Some were exhorted to abide securely in the four noble truths; some were exhorted to practice and study from the stage of pure observation (*śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi*) up to the stage of the Tathāgata;
some were exhorted to practice and study from the stage of extreme joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) up to the stage of the Dharma-cloud (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*);
some were exhorted to practice and study the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi; and some were exhorted to practice and study the five eyes and the six supernormal powers.
Some were exhorted to practice and study the ten powers of a Tathāgata, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
some were exhorted to practice and study great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity;
some were exhorted to practice and study the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty minor characteristics; and some were exhorted to practice and study the quality of non-forgetfulness.

They constantly abide in equanimity; or they exhort others to train in all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);
or they exhort them to train in the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
or they exhort them to train in all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; or they exhort them to train in the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas.
The Buddha said, “So it is, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom through skillful means, after they have bestowed material gifts upon sentient beings, they further skillfully establish those classes of sentient beings, causing them to abide in the unsurpassed, peaceful dharma, even unto the attainment of the knowledge of all modes.”
“Subhūti! These are the most marvelous and extraordinary qualities of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the profound perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Subhūti!”
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, gather in all sentient beings through the gift of Dharma?
It is said that there are two kinds of Dharma-gifts for a bodhisattva mahāsattva:
first, the worldly gift of Dharma.
Second is the supramundane gift of Dharma.
"What is the mundane gift of Dharma for a bodhisattva mahāsattva?

It refers to when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, proclaims, reveals, analyzes, and elucidates the sublime mundane dharmas for all sentient beings—namely, the contemplation of impurity, mindfulness of breathing, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the five supernormal powers, and other mundane dharmas shared with ordinary worldlings. This is called the mundane gift of Dharma."

"Having performed this sublime gift of Dharma in the world, this bodhisattva mahāsattva employs various skillful means to transform and guide sentient beings, causing them to abide in the noble Dharma and the fruits of the noble Dharma."
What are the noble dharmas and the fruit of the noble dharmas?
Subhūti, you should know that what are called the noble dharmas refer to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, as well as the concentrations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
The fruits of the noble Dharma refer to the fruit of stream-entry, and so forth, up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, the noble dharmas of bodhisattva mahāsattvas consist of the knowledge of the fruit of stream-entry up to the knowledge of the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; the knowledge of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas; the knowledge of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment up to the knowledge of the ten powers of a Tathāgata and so forth; the knowledge of great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity; the knowledge of other immeasurable Buddha-dharmas; the knowledge of all mundane and supramundane dharmas; and the knowledge of all conditioned and unconditioned dharmas."
All such forms of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) are called the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*).

As for the fruit of the noble dharmas, it refers to the permanent severance of the continuity of all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); this is called the fruit of the noble dharmas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

The noble dharmas of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas refer to the six pāramitās, and so forth, up to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), as well as all other untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas."
"The fruit of the noble Dharma refers to the realization of the *tathatā* (suchness), the *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm), and ultimate *nirvāṇa*; this is called the true fruit of the noble Dharma.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 533, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Third Division, Chapter on the Sublime Marks, Part 28-4. At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Can Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas also attain all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*)?"
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are also able to attain all-aspect omniscience.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are also able to attain all-aspect omniscience, what is the difference between them and the Tathāgatas?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“There is indeed a distinction; what are its characteristics?
It is that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to be ‘one who is about to attain all-aspect omniscience,’ whereas the Tathāgatas are said to be ‘those who have already attained all-aspect omniscience.’”

Why is this so? It is because the minds of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot be established as distinct from those of the Tathāgatas; that is to say, the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwells together with the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas in the non-differentiated nature of all phenomena. One who seeks complete and perfect enlightenment regarding the characteristics of all phenomena is called a bodhisattva, while upon reaching the ultimate state, one is called a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha.

When one possesses the complete, pure, and unobscured illumination of the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena, abiding in the causal stage, one is called a bodhisattva; if one reaches the resultant stage, one is called a Tathāgata.
Therefore, although both bodhisattvas and the Tathāgatas are said to have attained the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), there is a distinction between them. "Subhūti!

This is called the worldly gift of Dharma by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Relying upon and based on such a worldly gift of Dharma, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are further able to practice the supramundane gift of Dharma; that is to say, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, through their skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), they first bestow upon sentient beings the wholesome dharmas of the world, and subsequently cause them to become weary of and detached from those worldly wholesome dharmas, establishing them in the supramundane, untainted (*anāsrava*) noble dharmas, until they finally attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*)."
What are called the supramundane noble dharmas?
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas proclaim, reveal, analyze, and elucidate them for the sake of all sentient beings, this is termed the gift of Dharma.
"Subhūti, you should know that all the wholesome dharmas not shared with ordinary beings, when correctly cultivated and studied, cause sentient beings to transcend the world and abide in peace;
therefore, they are called 'transcendent. These are the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment."
The three gates of liberation, the eight liberations, the nine successive attainments, the knowledge of the four noble truths,
the wisdom of the perfections and all forms of emptiness, the ten stages of the bodhisattva, the five eyes and the six supernormal powers, and the Tathāgata’s ten powers,
four fearlessnesses, four analytical knowledges, and eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
The dharmas—great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity;
the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; the gates of dhāraṇī and the gates of samādhi;
and all such untainted wholesome dharmas as these are collectively termed supramundane noble dharmas.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva proclaims, reveals, analyzes, and elucidates such dharmas for the sake of all sentient beings, this is called the bodhisattva’s supramundane gift of Dharma.
“Subhūti! In this context, what are called the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment? They are:

the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path. These are called the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.”
“Subhūti! What are called the four foundations of mindfulness? They are:

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells contemplating the body in the internal body, or the external body, or both the internal and external body, possessing right effort, right knowledge, and right mindfulness, removing worldly greed and sorrow; dwelling in the contemplation of the origination of the body, and dwelling in the contemplation of the cessation of the body. Because he dwells contemplating the body in the body, dwelling in the contemplation of its origination, and dwelling in the contemplation of its cessation, he is without dependence and has no grasping toward any world. This is called the first.
It is the same for feelings, the mind, and phenomena; these are called the four foundations of mindfulness.
"Subhūti, what are called the four right endeavors?

It refers to when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, in order that unarisen evil and unwholesome dharmas may never arise, and in order that arisen evil and unwholesome dharmas may be permanently severed and extinguished;

and in order that unarisen wholesome dharmas may arise, and in order that arisen wholesome dharmas may remain firm, not be forgotten, be cultivated to fulfillment, increase, expand, and be realized through wisdom—gives rise to aspiration, exerts diligent effort, rouses the mind, and sustains the mind. These are called the four right endeavors (*samyakprahāṇa*).
“Subhūti! What are called the four bases of psychic power? They are:

the base of psychic power consisting in the cultivation of concentration of desire accompanied by the volition of abandonment; the base of psychic power consisting in the cultivation of concentration of effort accompanied by the volition of abandonment; the base of psychic power consisting in the cultivation of concentration of mind accompanied by the volition of abandonment; and the base of psychic power consisting in the cultivation of concentration of investigation accompanied by the volition of abandonment. These are called the four bases of psychic power.”
“Subhūti! What are called the five faculties?

They are the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s faculty of faith, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom; these are called the five faculties.”
“Subhūti! What are called the five powers?
They are the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s power of faith, power of diligence, power of mindfulness, power of concentration, and power of wisdom; these are called the five powers.”
“Subhūti! What are the seven factors of enlightenment? They are:

the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment of discrimination of phenomena, the factor of enlightenment of diligence, the factor of enlightenment of joy, the factor of enlightenment of pliancy, the factor of enlightenment of concentration, and the factor of enlightenment of equanimity. These are called the seven factors of enlightenment.”
“Subhūti! What are the eight branches of the noble path?

They are the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration; these are called the eight branches of the noble path.”
“Subhūti! What are the three gates of liberation?

They are the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, and the gate of liberation of wishlessness; these are called the three gates of liberation.”
“Subhūti! What is the liberation door of emptiness?
It refers to a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, by means of the mental aspects of emptiness and non-self, collects the mind into a single focus; this is called the liberation door of emptiness.”
"Subhūti! What is the gate of liberation of signlessness?
It refers to a bodhisattva mahāsattva gathering the mind into a single focus through the mode of activity of cessation; this is called the gate of liberation of signlessness."
Subhūti! What is the door of liberation of wishlessness?

It refers to a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, by means of the mental aspects of suffering and impermanence, collects the mind into a single point of focus; this is called the door of liberation of wishlessness.
“Subhūti! What are called the eight liberations? They are:
a bodhisattva mahāsattva who possesses form perceives forms; this is called the first liberation.
Perceiving external forms while having no internal perception of form is called the second liberation.
Realizing for oneself the body of purified resolve is called the third liberation.
Fully abiding in the meditative concentration of the sphere of infinite space is called the fourth liberation.
Fully dwelling in the meditative concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness is called the fifth liberation.
Fully dwelling in the meditative concentration of the sphere of nothingness is called the sixth liberation.
Abiding fully in the meditative attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is called the seventh liberation.
Abiding fully in the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling is called the eighth liberation.
These are called the eight liberations. "Subhūti!
What are the nine successive concentrations?

That is to say, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, detached from desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained thought, and possessing the joy and happiness born of seclusion, enters and dwells in the first dhyāna, this is called the first sequential concentration (anupūrva-samādhi).

To speak at length, up until transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters and dwells in the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling; this is called the ninth successive concentration.
These are called the nine successive meditative attainments. "Subhūti,
what is meant by the knowledge of the four noble truths?"
This refers to the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin, knowledge of cessation, and knowledge of the path; these are called the four noble truths’ knowledges.
“Subhūti! What are the perfections?”
That is to say, Subhūti, all the perfections of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the perfection of giving up to the perfection of wisdom, are what are called "perfections. Subhūti!
What are the knowledges of the various emptinesses and so forth?

They refer to the knowledge of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas regarding internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature, as well as the knowledge regarding suchness up to the inconceivable realm; these are called the knowledges of the various emptinesses and so forth.
“Subhūti! What are the ten stages of a bodhisattva?
They are the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Stage of the Dharma Cloud; these are called the ten stages of a bodhisattva.”
“Subhūti! What are called the five eyes?
They are the flesh eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the dharma eye, and the buddha eye, which are sought by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; these are called the five eyes.”
“Subhūti! What are called the six supernormal powers? They are:

the supernormal power of the realization of knowledge of psychic travel, the supernormal power of the realization of knowledge of the divine ear, the supernormal power of the realization of knowledge of others' minds, the supernormal power of the realization of knowledge of recollecting past lives, the supernormal power of the realization of knowledge of the divine eye, and the supernormal power of the realization of knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows. These are called the six supernormal powers.”
“Subhūti! What are the ten powers of a Tathāgata? They are as follows:
A Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, knows as it truly is what is possible as possible, and knows as it truly is what is impossible as impossible; this is called the first power.

If the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas know, as they truly are, the past, future, and present karmas of sentient beings, as well as the locations, causes, and maturations of their various experiences of phenomena, this is called the second power.
If the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as they truly know the various distinctions among the many and diverse elements within all worlds, this is called the third power.
If the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas know, as they truly are, the various and manifold differences in the inclinations of all sentient beings, this is called the fourth power.
If the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas know, as they truly are, the superior and inferior faculties of all sentient beings, this is called the fifth power.
If the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas know, as they truly are, the paths leading everywhere, this is called the sixth power.

If all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas truly know, in accordance with reality, the distinctions established regarding all meditative concentrations (dhyāna), liberations (vimokṣa), samādhis, and meditative attainments (samāpatti), as well as their defilement and purification, this is called the seventh power.

If the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, regarding the infinite past lives of sentient beings—whether one birth, ten births, a hundred births, a thousand births, or immeasurable births; or one eon, ten eons, a hundred eons, a thousand eons, or immeasurable eons—truly know all their conduct, speech, and characteristics as they really are, this is called the eighth power.

If the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, with the pure divine eye that transcends that of humans, see the various good and evil deeds of sentient beings at the time of death and at the time of birth—extensively explained up to their knowing, as it truly is, how sentient beings are born into good or evil realms according to the power of their karma—this is called the ninth power.

If the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas truly know, as it really is, the liberation of mind through the exhaustion of all outflows and the liberation by wisdom through the exhaustion of all outflows; and if they dwell, having personally realized through direct knowledge the true dharma of liberation from their own outflows, fully endowed [with these qualities], and so on at length until "no further existence is to be undergone"—this is called the tenth power.
