This is what is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva knowing the suchness of perception as it truly is.”
“Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva know the characteristics of formations as they truly are?

It means that a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows formations as they truly are to be like a plantain tree: when one strips away leaf by leaf, no core can be found. This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva knowing the characteristics of formations as they truly are.”
“Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva know the arising and ceasing of formations as they truly are?

It means that a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows as it truly is that when formations arise, they come from nowhere, and when they cease, they go nowhere; although there is no coming and no going, they are nonetheless associated with arising and ceasing. This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva knowing the arising and ceasing of formations as they truly are.”
“Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva know the suchness of phenomena as it truly is?

It means that a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows the suchness of phenomena as it truly is to be without arising and without cessation, without coming and without going, without defilement and without purity, without increase and without decrease; because it is always as its own nature, non-false, and immutable, it is called ‘suchness. This is what is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva knowing the suchness of phenomena as it truly is.”
“Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva know the characteristics of consciousness as they truly are?

It means that a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that consciousness is like a magical illusion: it exists through the conjunction of various conditions and is provisionally established by designation, yet in reality it cannot be apprehended. Just as a magician or his apprentice might, at a crossroads, conjure the fourfold army—namely, the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry—or conjure other various forms and appearances, which, though appearing to exist, have no reality; so too is consciousness: in reality it cannot be apprehended. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s knowledge of the characteristics of consciousness as they truly are.”
“Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva know the arising and ceasing of consciousness as it truly is?

It is this: a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that when consciousness arises, it comes from nowhere; when it ceases, it goes nowhere. Although there is no coming and no going, it is characterized by arising and ceasing. This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva knowing the arising and ceasing of consciousness as it truly is.”
“Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva know the suchness of consciousness as it truly is?

It is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that the suchness of consciousness is without arising and without cessation, without coming and without going, without defilement and without purity, and without increase and without decrease; it is eternally as it is by nature, non-false, and unchanging, and is therefore called ‘suchness. This is what is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva knowing the suchness of consciousness as it truly is.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, train in the twelve bases?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, knows as it truly is that the internal bases are empty of the intrinsic nature of the internal bases, and knows as it truly is that the external bases are empty of the intrinsic nature of the external bases, this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, while practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, is able to train in the twelve bases."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, train in the eighteen elements?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, knows as it truly is that the eye-element is empty of the intrinsic nature of the eye-element—and so on, in detail, until—he knows as it truly is that the mental-consciousness-element is empty of the intrinsic nature of the mental-consciousness-element, this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, when practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, is able to train in the eighteen elements."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, train in the four noble truths?”

The Buddha told Subhūti: "When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they know suffering as it truly is as the characteristic of oppression; they know origination as it truly is as the characteristic of arising; they know cessation as it truly is as the characteristic of tranquility; and they know the path as it truly is as the characteristic of detachment. Furthermore, they know that the intrinsic nature of suffering, origination, cessation, and the path is fundamentally empty, detached from dualistic phenomena, and is the Noble Truths.

These Four Noble Truths, such as suffering and so forth, are themselves *tathatā* (suchness), and *tathatā* is itself the Four Noble Truths. They are non-dual and without distinction, and only true noble ones can know them as they truly are. This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and being able to train in the Four Noble Truths."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, train in the twelve links of dependent origination?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, knows as it truly is that from ignorance up to old age and death there is neither arising nor ceasing, neither defilement nor purity, that their intrinsic nature is fundamentally empty, and that they are remote from dualistic dharmas—this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, while practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, is able to train in the twelve links of dependent origination."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, train in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

“If, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they know as it truly is that everything from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature is without self-nature and entirely unapprehendable, and yet are able to abide therein, this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the profound perfection of wisdom while training in everything from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, train in suchness up to the inconceivable realm?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they know that from suchness up to the inconceivable realm are all without conceptual proliferation and entirely without discrimination, and are thus able to dwell therein, this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the profound perfection of wisdom who is able to train in suchness up to the inconceivable realm."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, train in the perfection of giving up to the immeasurable and boundless buddha-dharmas?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they know, in accordance with reality, that from the perfection of giving up to the immeasurable and boundless buddha-dharmas there is neither increase nor decrease, neither defilement nor purity, no intrinsic nature, and that they are unapprehendable, yet are able to cultivate them—this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the profound perfection of wisdom who is able to train in the perfection of giving up to the immeasurable and boundless buddha-dharmas."
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they understand, in accordance with reality, that form and all other phenomena are each distinct and non-confused.”
Could it be that the World-Honored One destroys the true dharma-dhātu by means of dharmas such as form? Why is this so?
Because the dharma-dhātu is non-dual and without differentiation.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If any dharma other than the dharmadhātu could be apprehended, one could say that such a dharma could destroy the dharmadhātu.
However, since no dharma apart from the dharmadhātu can be apprehended, there is no other dharma capable of destroying the dharmadhātu."
Why is this so? Because Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas know that apart from the dharmadhātu, no dharma can be found.
Since they know that non-dharmas are not separate from the dharmadhātu, they do not establish or proclaim them for others; therefore, the dharmadhātu cannot be destroyed by anything.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should train in the dharmadhātu as having the characteristic of being non-dual, undifferentiated, and indestructible.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to train in the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), in what should they train?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to study the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), they should study all dharmas. Why is this?
Because all dharmas enter into the dharma-realm.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“By what causes and conditions is it said that all phenomena enter the dharmadhātu?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, all dharmas are by their very nature (dharmatā) such that they enter the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) as a state of non-differentiation; this does not depend upon the Buddha’s teaching. Why is this so? [Because...]"

Whether they be wholesome dharmas or unwholesome dharmas, with-outflows or without-outflows, mundane or supramundane, conditioned or unconditioned—all such dharmas without exception enter into the signless, unconditioned, and empty nature of the dharma-realm.

Therefore, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, those who wish to study the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) should study all phenomena; for if they study all phenomena, they are studying the dharma-realm.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If all dharmas enter the dharma-realm as non-dual and undifferentiated, how should bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train in the six pāramitās?”
How should one train in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments?
How should one train in the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path?
How should one train in inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature?
How should one train in suchness up to the inconceivable realm?
How should one train in the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path?
How should one train in the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness?
How should one train in the eight liberations up to the ten totalities?
How should one train in the stages from the Ground of Extreme Joy up to the Ground of the Dharma Cloud?
How should one train in the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi?
How should one train in the five eyes and the six supernormal powers?
How should one train in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha?
How should one train in great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity?
How should one train in the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant abiding in equanimity?
How should one train in all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)?
How should one train to bring to fulfillment the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics?
How should one train to become a great clan of Kṣatriyas, up to a great clan of householders?
How should one train to become a deva of the Four Great Kings, up to a deva of the Heaven of Control over Others' Emanations?
How should one train to be born among the Brahmakāyika devas up to the Bṛhatphala devas?
How should one train in the dharmas of the non-percipient sentient beings (asaṃjñisattva) without taking pleasure in being born there?
How should one train in the dharmas of the Śuddhāvāsa devas without delighting in being born there?
How should one train in the dharmas of the devas of the Sphere of Infinite Space up to the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception without delighting in being born there?
How should one train in the initial generation of the bodhicitta up to the tenth generation of the bodhicitta?
How should one train in entering the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth?
How should one train in all the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas without realizing them?
How should one train in maturing sentient beings and purifying buddha-fields?
How should one train in the various dhāraṇīs and unimpeded eloquence?
How should one train in the path of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and in the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha?
Having trained in this way, one knows all phenomena in all their aspects and is thus able to realize the knowledge of all modes.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!..."

Since there are no such various conceptual distinctions within the dharma-realm, will not the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by means of these conceptual distinctions, practice in inversion and give rise to various conceptual proliferations within that which is free from proliferation?
Why is this? Because within the true dharma-realm there are no phenomena of conceptual discrimination or discursive proliferation.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!"

The dharma-realm is not form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, yet it is not separate from form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Form through to consciousness is itself the dharma-realm, and the dharma-realm is itself form through to consciousness. This is explained at length until: the dharma-realm is neither conditioned nor unconditioned phenomena, yet it is not separate from conditioned or unconditioned phenomena; conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are themselves the dharma-realm, and the dharma-realm is itself conditioned and unconditioned phenomena.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”

It is as you have said. Within the true dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), there are no conceptual proliferations (prapañca) of any kind. The dharma-realm is not form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; yet it is not separate from form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. The dharma-realm is itself form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are themselves the dharma-realm. To speak at length, even up to this: the dharma-realm is neither conditioned nor unconditioned phenomena; yet it is not separate from conditioned or unconditioned phenomena. The dharma-realm is itself conditioned and unconditioned phenomena; conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are themselves the dharma-realm.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, if they perceive any phenomenon as being separate from the dharma-realm, they are not correctly proceeding toward the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek."
Therefore, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive any phenomena as being separate from the true dharma-realm.
“Subhūti, you should know that when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they realize that all phenomena are the true dharma-realm.
Through skillful means, they understand that there are no names or marks in phenomena, yet for the sake of sentient beings, they provisionally assign names.”
Designation refers to saying: "This is form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness;
this is the eye base up to the mind base; this is the form base up to the mental-object base; this is the eye element up to the mind element;
this is the form element up to the mental-object element; this is the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-..."
The element of consciousness; these are the contacts of the eye up to the contact of the mind;
these are the various feelings produced with the contact of the eye as condition up to the various feelings produced with the contact of the mind as condition;
these are the earth element up to the consciousness element; these are the causal conditions up to the predominant conditions; these are the phenomena produced from conditions.
"This is ignorance up to old age and death; this is wholesome phenomena and unwholesome phenomena;
this is contaminated phenomena and uncontaminated phenomena; this is mundane phenomena and supramundane phenomena;
this is conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena; this is from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom."
Maitreya, to speak extensively, it extends even to this: "This is unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
It is like a master illusionist or his apprentice who, holding a small object before a crowd, conjures various different forms and images—such as conjuring men and women, large and small;
or further conjuring various beasts such as elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, camels, donkeys, chickens, and so forth.
Or again, they may magically create cities, villages, gardens, and ponds, adorned in various ways and most delightful;
or again, they may magically create clothing, food and drink, houses, bedding, flowers, incense, necklaces, and all manner of rare treasures, grain, and treasuries;
or again, they may magically create immeasurable varieties of music and performers to bring joy and pleasure to countless people.

Alternatively, they may manifest various forms through illusion to cause others to practice giving, or to observe ethical discipline, or to cultivate patience, or to exert diligence, or to practice meditative concentration, or to study wisdom;
or they may manifest birth into great kṣatriya clans, up to great householder clans;
or they may further create illusions of mountains, great oceans, Sumeru the king of mountains, the Cakravāḍa mountains, and so forth.
Or again, they manifest birth in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception;
or again, they manifest as Stream-enterers, Once-returners, Non-returners, Arhats, or Pratyekabuddhas;
or again, they manifest as Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, practicing from the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment through to the perfection of generosity...
In the *prajñāpāramitā*, one practices the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
one practices the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; one practices the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
and one trains in abiding in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature. One trains...
Abiding in suchness up to the inconceivable realm, training in abiding by the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path,
entering the bodhisattva’s state of right determination free from birth, practicing the stages from the Ground of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma,
manifesting various sublime supernormal powers, and emitting great radiance that illuminates all worlds.

They purify Buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity; they sport in all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, and attainments (*samāpatti*); and they cultivate the various merits of all Buddhas.

Alternatively, they may manifest illusory forms of the Tathāgata, complete with the thirty-two marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*) and the eighty secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*), fully adorned and perfected, and endowed with the ten powers (*bala*), the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*), as well as great loving-kindness (*maitrī*), great compassion (*karuṇā*), great sympathetic joy (*muditā*), great equanimity (*upekṣā*), and other immeasurable and boundless merits.
"In this way, a magician or his apprentice, in order to delude others, performs such various illusory feats before a great multitude.
When the ignorant men and women there—both young and old—see these things, they all exclaim in wonder:
'How marvelous!'"

This person has skillfully mastered all arts and can perform various most rare feats, even to the point of manifesting the physical marks and signs of a Tathāgata’s body, adorned with all merits, thereby displaying his own artistic talents.
Among them, one who possessed wisdom and insight, having perceived this matter, reflected thus:
"This is truly marvelous; how is it that this person can manifest such a feat?"
"Although within it no real dharma can be found, it causes all people to be deluded and joyful, giving rise to the perception of real objects where there are no real objects.
Only the wise fully comprehend that all is empty; though they see and hear, they harbor no attachment."

"So too it is with the bodhisattva mahāsattvas: when practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, although they do not perceive a *dharmadhātu* existing apart from all phenomena, nor do they perceive all phenomena existing apart from the *dharmadhātu*; and although they do not perceive sentient beings or their designations as having any real existence that can be apprehended, they are nonetheless able to give rise to skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*). They personally practice the six *pāramitās*, encourage others to practice the six *pāramitās*, correctly extol the dharma of practicing the six *pāramitās*, and joyfully praise those who practice the six *pāramitās*."

To speak extensively, up to and including personally fulfilling all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) and also exhorting others to fulfill all-aspect omniscience; correctly praising the dharma of fulfilling all-aspect omniscience and joyfully extolling those who have fulfilled all-aspect omniscience;

personally fulfilling the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*), as well as exhorting others to fulfill the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; correctly praising the dharma of fulfilling the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics and joyfully extolling those who have fulfilled the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.
“Subhūti, you should know this:

if the true *dharmadhātu* were subject to distinctions between its beginning, middle, and end, then bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* would be unable to employ skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) to teach the true *dharmadhātu* for the sake of sentient beings, to adorn and purify buddha-fields, to bring sentient beings to maturity, to cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, to realize unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, and to turn the sublime wheel of Dharma to deliver the multitudes of sentient beings.”

Because the true dharma-realm is eternally without distinction throughout its beginning, middle, and end, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they employ various skillful means to teach the true dharma-realm to all sentient beings, purifying buddha-fields and maturing sentient beings, cultivating the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, realizing unexcelled perfect enlightenment, and turning the sublime wheel of Dharma to deliver the multitudes of sentient beings.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 532, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Three, Chapter Twenty-nine on Giving and so forth, Part Two. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
If all sentient beings and their designations are ultimately non-apprehensible, for whose sake do the bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Because they take the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) as their sole measure, bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom."
Subhūti, you should know that if the limit of sentient beings were different from the limit of reality, then bodhisattva mahāsattvas would not practice the profound perfection of wisdom.
Because the limit of sentient beings is not different from the limit of reality, for this reason the bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they establish sentient beings in the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) by means of the non-disruption of the reality-limit.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If the limit of sentient beings is itself the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), establish sentient beings in the limit of reality without destroying the nature of the limit of reality?"

"Bhagavān! If, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they establish sentient beings so that they abide in the *bhūtakoṭi*, then they would be establishing the *bhūtakoṭi* so that it abides in the *bhūtakoṭi*. If one establishes the *bhūtakoṭi* so that it abides in the *bhūtakoṭi*, then one would be establishing self-nature (*svabhāva*) so that it abides in self-nature. However, logically, it is not possible to establish self-nature so that it abides in self-nature. How, then, can it be said that when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they establish sentient beings so that they abide in the *bhūtakoṭi* without destroying the dharma of the *bhūtakoṭi*?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"In truth, one should not establish the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) so that it dwells in the limit of reality, nor should one establish self-nature (*svabhāva*) so that it dwells in self-nature. Nevertheless, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, because they possess skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), they are able to establish sentient beings so that they dwell in the limit of reality; yet the limit of sentient beings is not different from the limit of reality."
"In this way, Subhūti,
the limit of sentient beings and the limit of reality are non-dual and without distinction.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"What is called the skillful means of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas when they practice the profound perfection of wisdom? By the power of this skillful means, how do they establish sentient beings so that they abide in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), yet without destroying the characteristic of the limit of reality?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, from their first generation of the mind of awakening, they accomplish such skillful means; by the power of these skillful means, they establish sentient beings and cause them to abide in giving."

Once those sentient beings have established themselves in generosity, he explains to them the characteristic of non-differentiation between the prior, middle, and subsequent limits of generosity, saying:

"In this way, the prior, middle, and subsequent limits of generosity are all entirely empty; the giver, the receiver, and the fruit obtained from giving are likewise entirely empty. Thus, all these things do not exist within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and are utterly unobtainable."
Do not cling to the idea that the gift, the giver, the recipient, and the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) of the fruit of giving are each distinct.

If you can refrain from clinging to the gift, the giver, the recipient, and the reality-limit of the fruit of giving as being each different, then the merit of the giving you practice will lead to the Deathless (amṛta), attain the fruit of the Deathless, and will surely culminate in the Deathless.
Furthermore, he spoke these words:
"By means of the merit you have cultivated through this giving, do not grasp at the aggregate of form, nor even up to the aggregate of consciousness;

do not grasp at the sense base of the eye, nor even up to the sense base of the mind; do not grasp at the sense base of forms, nor even up to the sense base of mental phenomena; do not grasp at the eye..."
Do not grasp the element of the eye up to the element of the mind; do not grasp the element of visible forms up to the element of mental phenomena;
do not grasp the element of eye-consciousness up to the element of mind-consciousness; do not grasp eye-contact up to mind-contact;
do not grasp the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition; do not grasp the earth element.
Up to the element of consciousness, do not grasp at causes and conditions up to the dominant condition; do not grasp at the various phenomena produced from conditions;
do not grasp at ignorance up to old age and death; do not grasp at generosity up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*);
do not grasp at inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature; do not grasp at them.
Do not grasp at anything from suchness up to the inconceivable realm; do not grasp at the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
do not grasp at the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
do not grasp at the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the four formless absorptions; and do not grasp at the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Do not grasp at the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality; do not grasp at the stage of pure observation up to the stage of a Tathāgata;
do not grasp at the stage of extreme joy up to the stage of the cloud of dharma;
do not grasp at any of the doors of dhāraṇī or the doors of samādhi; do not grasp at the five eyes or the six supernormal powers; do not grasp at suchness...
Do not grasp at the ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; do not grasp at great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, or great equanimity;
do not grasp at the thirty-two marks of a Great Being or the eighty secondary signs;
do not grasp at the quality of non-forgetfulness or the nature of constant abiding in equanimity; do not grasp at all-knowledge or the knowledge of the aspects of the path.
Wisdom and the knowledge of all aspects; do not grasp at the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
do not grasp at the conduct of a bodhisattva mahāsattva; do not grasp at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
do not grasp at contaminated or uncontaminated phenomena; do not grasp at mundane or supramundane phenomena; and do not grasp at conditioned or...
Unconditioned phenomena. Why is this so?
Because all giving has the nature of emptiness.
All givers are empty of the nature of a giver;
all receivers are empty of the nature of a receiver;
all fruits of giving are empty of the nature of the fruit of giving.
In emptiness, the gift, the giver, the recipient, and the fruits of giving are all unapprehendable. Why is this?
Because the intrinsic nature of all such differentiated phenomena is ultimately empty.
Because such phenomena cannot be apprehended within ultimate emptiness, and because these phenomena cannot be apprehended, other objects of grasping likewise cannot be apprehended.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, from the first production of the thought of awakening they achieve such skillful means. By the power of these skillful means, they establish sentient beings and cause them to abide in pure ethical discipline."
Once those sentient beings have established themselves in pure ethical discipline, they further say:

"You all should now feel deep compassion for all sentient beings; you must abstain from taking life—and as has been explained at length—abstain from everything up to and including wrong views, and practice right view."
Why is this so? Because all such phenomena are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature; you should not engage in conceptual discrimination or attachment toward them.
Furthermore, you should investigate according to reality: what phenomenon is it that is called "arising of desire," by which one seeks to take another's life?
Furthermore, by what cause does one take their life?
To speak at length, up to: what phenomenon is called the object of wrong view from which wrong view arises?
And by what cause does wrong view arise?
"In this way, all intrinsic natures are empty.

"Subhūti, you should know that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they achieve such skillful means that they are well able to bring sentient beings to maturity. Through immeasurable gateways, they teach them regarding the fruits of generosity and pure ethical discipline, both of which are unapprehendable, causing them to realize that the intrinsic natures of the fruits of generosity and pure ethical discipline are both empty."

Having realized that the nature of the fruits of the practiced generosity and pure ethical discipline is empty, they are able to give rise to no attachment toward them. Because their minds are free from attachment, they are undistracted; being undistracted, they are able to generate sublime wisdom. Through this sublime wisdom, having forever severed the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the active fetters (*paryavasthāna*), they enter the realm of nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*).
“Subhūti, you should know that all that has been said relies upon conventional truth and does not rely upon ultimate truth. Why is this?

In space, not even the slightest dharma can be apprehended—whether it be that which has already entered nirvāṇa, that which is currently entering nirvāṇa, that which will enter nirvāṇa, the one who enters nirvāṇa, or the means by which nirvāṇa is attained. All such things are entirely non-existent and are ultimately empty; this very ultimate emptiness is nirvāṇa, and apart from this nirvāṇa, there is no other real dharma.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, from the very first production of the thought of enlightenment, they achieve such skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). By the power of these skillful means, seeing that the minds of sentient beings are largely filled with anger and resentment, they give rise to deep compassion and provide them with skillful instruction."
They spoke these words:
"You all should now cultivate patience and delight in the dharma of patience; you must subdue your minds and undertake the practice of patience.
Since the intrinsic nature of the phenomena toward which you feel anger is entirely empty, how can you give rise to wrath within them?"
You should further examine this according to principle:
by what dharma do I give rise to anger?
Who is it that can be angry?
At whom would one be angry?
Such phenomena are all empty by their very nature; that which is empty by nature has never been non-empty.

This emptiness was not created by the Tathāgata, nor by the Bodhisattvas, nor by the Pratyekabuddhas, nor by the Śrāvakas; it was not created by nāgas and spirits, and so on, up to humans and non-humans; nor was it created by the gods of the Four Great Kings, up to the gods of the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception.
Furthermore, you should investigate according to reason: from what does such anger arise?
To whom does it belong?
And toward whom does it arise?
What fruit shall one obtain?
What benefit shall one find in this life?
Since the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is emptiness, and within emptiness there can be no anger or resentment, one should practice patience to bring benefit to oneself.

"In this way, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they achieve the most excellent skill in means (upāyakauśalya). They establish sentient beings in the principle of the emptiness of nature and the causes and effects of the emptiness of nature; they gradually instruct, exhort, inspire, and gladden them with unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, causing them to dwell securely therein and swiftly attain realization."
“Subhūti, you should know that all that has been said relies upon the conventional and not upon the ultimate. Why is this?
Within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, that which attains, that which is attained, the time of attainment, and the place of attainment are all not truly existent.
"Subhūti, you should know! This is called the principle of the emptiness of intrinsic nature regarding the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)."

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, desiring to benefit all classes of sentient beings, practice the profound perfection of wisdom by relying on this principle of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), yet they do not apprehend sentient beings nor their designations.

Why is this? Because all phenomena are devoid of sentient beings; since sentient beings are absent, phenomena cannot be apprehended. Phenomena and sentient beings are established in mutual dependence, yet from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), all are empty.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, from the first generation of the mind of awakening, they accomplish such skillful means. By the power of these skillful means, seeing that sentient beings have become physically and mentally indolent and have fallen away from diligence, they employ skillful means to exhort and guide them so that they may initiate physical and mental diligence to cultivate all wholesome dharmas."
He spoke these words: "O noble sons!

You should with deep faith accept that within the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), there is no phenomenon of indolence, no indolent person, no place of indolence, no time of indolence, and no phenomenon by which indolence is produced; all such things are intrinsically empty and do not transcend the principle of emptiness."

You all should arouse physical and mental diligence, abandon all laziness, and zealously cultivate wholesome dharmas—namely, the cultivation of the perfections from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
or the cultivation of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
or the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; or the cultivation of...
The gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; whether abiding in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;
whether abiding in suchness up to the inconceivable realm; whether abiding in the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
whether practicing the eight liberations up to the ten totalities; or whether practicing the purifications...
Contemplating the stages from the Stage of the Earth up to the Stage of the Tathāgata; whether cultivating the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma Stage;
whether cultivating all the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi; whether cultivating the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
whether cultivating the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; or whether cultivating the Great...
If one cultivates loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity; if one cultivates the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary characteristics;
if one cultivates the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity;
if one cultivates all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects; or if one cultivates the fruit of stream-entry up to that of the solitary realizer...
To awaken to bodhi, whether practicing all the deeds of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva,
practicing the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas, or practicing any other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas,
you should apply yourself with diligent vigor and not give rise to indolence; for if indolence arises, one will suffer without end.
"O sons of good family!

The intrinsic nature of all these phenomena is entirely empty and free from all obstructions. You should contemplate this principle of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, wherein there is no phenomenon of indolence and no indolent person; even the conditions of place and time cannot be apprehended therein."

"In this way, Subhūti, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they achieve sublime skillful means and establish sentient beings so that they abide in the principle of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena; yet, while establishing them therein, they harbor no notion of duality."

Why is this? Because the principle of the emptiness of intrinsic nature is non-dual and without distinction; there is no duality among dharmas such that one could form dualistic conceptions regarding it.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, relies upon the teaching of the emptiness of intrinsic nature to instruct and admonish all classes of sentient beings, causing them to diligently practice and train.
That is to say, he speaks thus:
"O sons of good family!

You should diligently practice and study the wholesome dharmas. When practicing from the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, you should not contemplate these dharmas in terms of dualistic or non-dualistic characteristics. This is explained at length until: when practicing any other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas, you should not contemplate these dharmas in terms of dualistic or non-dualistic characteristics."
Why is this so? Sons of good family! All these phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature;
within the principle of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, one should not contemplate the characteristics of duality or non-duality.

"Thus it is, Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they achieve sublime skillful means and, while practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, bring sentient beings to maturity."

Once all classes of sentient beings have been matured, he gradually establishes them according to their respective capacities: some he causes to abide in the fruit of stream-entry; some he causes to abide in the fruit of once-returning; some he causes to abide in the fruit of non-returning; some he causes to abide in the fruit of arhatship; some he causes to abide in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; some he causes to abide in the various stages of a bodhisattva mahāsattva; and some he causes to abide in the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, from the very first production of the thought of enlightenment, they achieve such skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). By the power of these skillful means, they see that sentient beings have minds largely distracted, do not restrain their sense faculties regarding the objects of desire, and give rise to various kinds of non-quiescent actions."
Having seen this, he employs skillful means to instruct and exhort them,
leading them into superior concentration, saying: "Come!
"Good son! You should cultivate the supreme samādhi, and do not give rise to thoughts of distraction or even thoughts of 'supreme concentration. Why is this?
All such phenomena are empty by their very nature; within this emptiness of intrinsic nature, no phenomenon can be apprehended that might be called "distraction" or "one-pointedness of mind.

If you are able to abide in this sublime concentration, all the wholesome deeds you perform will swiftly reach fulfillment, and you will likewise dwell in the emptiness of intrinsic nature according to your wish.
What is meant by "wholesome deeds performed"?

It refers to the arousal of pure and superior actions of body, speech, and mind; whether it be the cultivation of the perfections from generosity up to wisdom; or, as explained at length, the cultivation of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices and unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of a Buddha; or the ripening of sentient beings and the purification of buddha-fields.

"In this way, all such pure, supreme, and wholesome dharmas are swiftly accomplished through the power of meditative concentration, and one abides in the emptiness of intrinsic nature according to one's aspirations. "Thus it is, Subhūti!"

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, seek to perform virtuous deeds from their first generation of the mind until the ultimate end, never ceasing for a moment.

For the sake of bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, they travel from one buddha-field to another, attending upon and making offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and receiving the true Dharma from those Buddhas. Even as they cast off one body and take up another through countless eons, until they reach unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they never forget or lose what they have learned during that interval.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the dhāraṇī of body, speech, and mental faculties, which are never subject to decline.

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly and perfectly cultivates the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā), and is thus able to exercise skillful deliberation in all that they do.

By virtue of having fully cultivated the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), they are able to deliberate well upon whatever actions they undertake and are capable of practicing all paths—namely, the path of the śrāvaka, the path of the pratyekabuddha, the path of the bodhisattva, the path of the Tathāgata, the superior path of gods, the superior path of humans, and the superior supernormal powers of bodhisattvas.

Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in the superior power of the superknowledges, they constantly perform all manner of beneficial deeds for sentient beings; although they pass through the cycle of birth and death across the various realms of existence, their superior superknowledges never diminish.
By means of the superknowledges of maturation, which are never subject to decline, they constantly perform supreme acts of benefit for themselves and others. Thus, Subhūti,

when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they abide in the skillful means of the emptiness of intrinsic nature and are able to effectively benefit all classes of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, from their first generation of the mind of awakening, they accomplish such skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). By the power of these skillful means, while abiding in the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), they perceive that sentient beings have meager wisdom, and being deluded and inverted, they commit various evil deeds; thus, they instruct and teach them, employing skillful means to lead them into the profound perfection of wisdom."
He spoke these words:
"O sons of noble family!
You should cultivate the perfection of wisdom and contemplate that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is emptiness."

If you are able to cultivate this Prajñāpāramitā and contemplate that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, then all the physical, verbal, and mental actions you practice will tend toward the deathless and attain the fruit of the deathless, with the deathless as their ultimate conclusion.
"O sons of good family!

The intrinsic nature of all these phenomena is emptiness. Within this emptiness of intrinsic nature, although sentient beings and phenomena cannot be apprehended, that which is practiced is likewise never lost."
Why is this? Son of good family!

The principle of the emptiness of intrinsic nature neither increases nor decreases; within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, there are no phenomena that increase or decrease, nor is there anyone who increases or decreases.

Why is this so? Because the principle of the emptiness of intrinsic nature has neither intrinsic existence nor non-intrinsic existence; it is free from all conceptual discrimination and transcends all proliferations of discourse.

In this regard, there is no phenomenon that increases or decreases, nor is there anyone who increases or decreases; because of this, what has been done will not be lost. Therefore, you should cultivate the perfection of wisdom and perform what is to be done by contemplating the emptiness of intrinsic nature.

“In this way, Subhūti, bodhisattva mahāsattvas practicing the profound perfection of wisdom with skillful means instruct and teach all sentient beings, causing them to enter the perfection of wisdom, abide in the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and cultivate all wholesome deeds.”

“Subhūti, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva thus instructs and exhorts sentient beings to cultivate all manner of wholesome deeds without ever becoming weary or negligent. That is to say, he himself constantly practices the ten paths of wholesome action and also encourages others to constantly practice the ten paths of wholesome action;
he himself constantly upholds the five precepts of a lay follower (*upāsaka*) and also encourages others to constantly uphold the five precepts of a lay follower.”
They themselves constantly observe the eight precepts of the upavāsa, and they also exhort others to constantly observe the eight precepts of the upavāsa;
they themselves constantly observe all the precepts of renunciation, and they also exhort others to constantly observe all the precepts of renunciation;

they themselves constantly practice the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments, and they also exhort others to constantly practice the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments.

They themselves constantly practice the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, and they also encourage others to constantly practice the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;

they themselves constantly practice the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—and they also encourage others to constantly practice the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
they themselves constantly practice the perfections from generosity up to wisdom, and they also encourage others to constantly practice the perfections from generosity up to wisdom.

They themselves constantly abide in the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, and they also exhort others to constantly abide in the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;
they themselves constantly abide in suchness up to the inconceivable realm, and they also exhort others to constantly abide in suchness up to the inconceivable realm;

they themselves constantly abide in the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, and they also exhort others to constantly abide in the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
They themselves constantly practice the eight liberations up to the ten totalities, and they also encourage others to constantly practice the eight liberations up to the ten totalities;
they themselves constantly practice the various bodhisattva stages, and they also encourage others to constantly practice the various bodhisattva stages;
they themselves constantly practice the gates of dhāraṇī and the gates of samādhi, and they also encourage others to constantly practice the gates of dhāraṇī and the gates of samādhi.

They themselves constantly cultivate and study the five eyes and the six supernormal powers, and they also exhort others to constantly cultivate and study the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;

they themselves constantly cultivate and study the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and they also exhort others to constantly cultivate and study the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;

they themselves constantly cultivate and study great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity, and they also exhort others to constantly cultivate and study great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity.

They themselves constantly practice and study the quality of non-forgetfulness and abide constantly in equanimity, and they also encourage others to constantly practice and study the quality of non-forgetfulness and abide constantly in equanimity;

they themselves constantly practice and study all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), and they also encourage others to constantly practice and study all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects;

they themselves constantly practice and study the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks, and they also encourage others to constantly practice and study the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks.

They themselves constantly initiate the wisdom of the fruit of stream-entry up to the wisdom of the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, yet they do not dwell in the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; furthermore, they encourage others to constantly initiate the wisdom of the fruit of stream-entry up to the wisdom of the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, or cause them to dwell in the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
They themselves constantly initiate all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and also encourage others to constantly initiate all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;

they themselves constantly initiate the path to the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas and also encourage others to constantly initiate the path to the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas.

"So it is, Subhūti! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they cultivate wholesome deeds themselves through skillful means, never becoming weary or negligent; they likewise instruct and admonish all sentient beings to cultivate wholesome deeds, never becoming weary or negligent."
Subhūti! This is called the skillful means of bodhisattva mahāsattvas when they practice the profound perfection of wisdom.

By the power of this skillful means, they establish sentient beings so that they abide in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), yet they are able to do so without destroying the characteristics of the limit of reality, swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, and within this emptiness of intrinsic nature neither sentient beings nor phenomena can be apprehended, then by virtue of this, there is likewise no non-phenomenon therein."
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva seek the swift realization of the knowledge of all modes for the sake of all sentient beings?
The Buddha told Subhūti: "It is thus!"
So it is! It is just as you have said.

All phenomena are empty by their very nature; within this emptiness of intrinsic nature, neither sentient beings nor phenomena can be apprehended, and for this reason, there is likewise no non-phenomenon therein.
Subhūti, you should know this:

if all phenomena were not empty by their very nature, then bodhisattva mahāsattvas, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, would not abide in the principle of the emptiness of intrinsic nature to seek the swift realization of the knowledge of all aspects, nor would they speak the Dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature for the benefit of sentient beings.

Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they abide in the principle that all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, seeking to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes, and for the benefit of sentient beings, they teach the dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature.

“What are those phenomena whose intrinsic nature is entirely empty, such that when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, having understood intrinsic emptiness as it truly is, they abide in intrinsic emptiness and teach the Dharma to others?”
Subhūti, you should know that from form up to consciousness, all are empty of intrinsic nature; from the eye-base up to the mind-base, all are empty of intrinsic nature;
from the form-base up to the phenomena-base, all are empty of intrinsic nature; and from the eye-element up to the mind-element, all are empty of intrinsic nature.
Emptiness: from the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) up to the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), all are empty of intrinsic nature;

from the eye-consciousness realm (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) up to the mind-consciousness realm (*manovijñānadhātu*), all are empty of intrinsic nature; from eye-contact (*cakṣuḥsaṃsparśa*) up to mind-contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*), all are empty of intrinsic nature;
and from all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition up to all feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, all are empty of intrinsic nature.
The earth element up to the consciousness element are all empty by their very nature; the causal conditions up to the dominant conditions are all empty by their very nature;
all phenomena produced from conditions are all empty by their very nature; ignorance up to old age and death are all empty by their very nature;
and generosity up to the perfection of wisdom are all empty by their very nature.
From internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the nature of non-existence, all are empty by their very nature;
from suchness up to the inconceivable realm, all are empty by their very nature; the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path are all empty by their very nature;
the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the four foundations of mindfulness are all empty by their very nature.
The stages from the dwelling [of the dry wisdom] up to the eight branches of the noble path are all empty by their very nature;
the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are all empty by their very nature; the eight liberations up to the ten totalities are all empty by their very nature;
the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata is all empty by its very nature; and the stage of extreme joy up to the cloud of dharma...
The earth is empty of intrinsic nature; the dhāraṇī-doors and samādhi-doors are all empty of intrinsic nature;
the five eyes and six supernormal powers are all empty of intrinsic nature; the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are all empty of intrinsic nature;
great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity are all...
The emptiness of intrinsic nature: the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant abiding in equanimity are all empty of intrinsic nature;
omniscience, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects are all empty of intrinsic nature;

the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks are all empty of intrinsic nature; and the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha [are all empty of intrinsic nature].
All are empty by their very nature; all practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are empty by their very nature;

the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas is empty by its very nature; the perpetual severance of the continuity of all afflictions, cognitive obstructions, and habitual tendencies is empty by its very nature; and the knowledge of all modes of knowledge is empty by its very nature.

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they understand, as it truly is, that the five aggregates beginning with form, and so forth up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*), are by nature empty. Having abided in this emptiness of intrinsic nature, they proclaim for the sake of all sentient beings this Dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If the intrinsic nature of internal emptiness were not empty of its own nature, up to and including the intrinsic nature of the emptiness of non-existence and self-nature were not empty of its own nature, then when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they would not teach sentient beings that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty; if they were to speak thus, it would be a subversion of the emptiness of intrinsic nature."
However, the principle of the emptiness of intrinsic nature is indestructible; it is neither eternal nor annihilated. Why is this so?
Because the principle of the emptiness of intrinsic nature has no direction and no location; it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.

This principle of emptiness is also called the "abiding nature of phenomena" (*dharmasthiti*). Within it, there are no phenomena; there is no aggregation and no dispersion, no decrease and no increase, no arising and no ceasing, and no defilement and no purification. This is the fundamental nature in which all phenomena abide.

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide therein, seeking to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes; yet they do not perceive any dharma that is sought or realized, nor do they perceive any dharma that is not sought or realized. Because all dharmas are entirely non-abiding, it is called the "abiding of dharmas" (dharmasthiti).

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide within this and practice the profound perfection of wisdom, having seen that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, they will certainly attain non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not perceive any dharma capable of acting as an obstruction;
seeing that all dharmas are without obstruction, they give rise to no doubt or hesitation regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and thus they do not regress.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
abiding in the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, contemplate that within this emptiness of intrinsic nature nothing at all can be apprehended—
namely, the self, sentient beings, and so forth, up to the knower and the seer, as well as those [phenomena]."
All designations are unattainable; from form up to consciousness, as well as their designations, they are unattainable.
From the eye-base up to the mind-base, as well as their designations, they are unattainable. From the form-base up to the mental-object-base, as well as their designations, they are unattainable.
From the eye-element up to the mind-element, as well as their designations, they are unattainable.
These also cannot be apprehended; from the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) up to the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), as well as their designations, cannot be apprehended;
from the realm of eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) up to the realm of mind-consciousness (*manovijñānadhātu*), as well as their designations, cannot be apprehended;

from eye-contact (*cakṣuḥsaṃsparśa*) up to mind-contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*), as well as their designations, cannot be apprehended; nor can the various sensations (*vedanā*) produced with eye-contact as a condition be apprehended.
Even the various feelings arising with mental contact as a condition, and their designation, cannot be apprehended;
the earth element up to the consciousness element, and their designations, cannot be apprehended;
the causal conditions up to the dominant condition, and their designations, cannot be apprehended; nor can the phenomena produced from conditions, and their designations, be apprehended.
They are also unapprehendable; from ignorance up to old age and death, as well as their designations, are unapprehendable;
from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, as well as their designations, are unapprehendable;
from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature, as well as their designations, are unapprehendable; and suchness...
One cannot find the inconceivable realm nor its designation; one cannot find the Noble Truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path nor their designations;
one cannot find the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path nor their designations;
the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four [formless attainments]...
The meditative concentration on form and its designation are both unattainable; the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—and their designations are also unattainable;
the eight liberations up to the ten totalities and their designations are also unattainable;
and the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata and their designations are also unattainable.
They are unapprehendable; from the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma Stage, as well as their designations, are unapprehendable;
the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi, as well as their designations, are unapprehendable;
the five eyes and the six supernormal powers, as well as their designations, are unapprehendable; and so on, up to the ten powers of the Tathāgata...
The eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) and their designation are also unapprehendable;
great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity, as well as their designations, are also unapprehendable;

the quality of non-forgetfulness, the state of constant abiding in equanimity, and their designations are also unapprehendable; and the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*) and the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*).
The knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) and its designation are both unapprehendable;
the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha and their designations are also unapprehendable;
the entire conduct of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment of the Buddhas, and their designations are also unapprehendable; [and likewise] the outflows (*āsrava*).
Neither the untainted dharmas nor their designations can be apprehended; neither mundane nor supramundane dharmas nor their designations can be apprehended;
neither conditioned nor unconditioned dharmas nor their designations can be apprehended;
and neither the thirty-two marks of a great man nor the eighty minor marks nor their designations can be apprehended.
It is unattainable.
"Subhūti, you should know this:
it is as if a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha were to emanate four assemblies—namely, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās."
Suppose an emanated Buddha were to preach the sublime Dharma for the sake of the fourfold assembly for an eon, or even more than an eon.
What do you think?

Could any among such an emanated assembly obtain the fruit of a stream-enterer, or the fruit of a once-returner, or the fruit of a non-returner, or the fruit of an arhat; or could they attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, or receive the prediction of non-retrogression regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”

Why is this? Because these manifested beings have no substantial reality; yet it is not that there can be no attainment of the fruit or the prediction of non-retrogression for those dharmas that lack substantial reality.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"All phenomena are likewise; they are all empty by their very nature and entirely devoid of substantial reality. Within this, what bodhisattva mahāsattva could teach what dharma to what sentient beings so that they might realize the fruit of stream-entry, or even receive the prediction of non-retrogression?"
“Subhūti, you should know that although bodhisattva mahāsattvas proclaim the dharma of emptiness for the sake of sentient beings, those sentient beings are in fact unapprehendable;
out of compassion for those who have fallen into inverted dharmas, they rescue them and cause them to abide in non-inverted dharmas.”
Non-inversion means non-conceptualization, because that which is non-conceptual is without inversion;
whereas if there is conceptualization, there is inversion, as it is the outflow thereof.
Subhūti, you should know this:

perversion itself is the dharma of non-perversion. Within non-perversion there is no self, no sentient being—and so on, as extensively explained, up to—no knower or seer; nor is there the aggregate of form, up to the aggregate of consciousness; and even up to, there is no mark of the thirty-two major characteristics or the eighty minor marks.
“Subhūti, you should know that this ‘non-existence’ is itself the emptiness of intrinsic nature.

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they abide therein and perceive sentient beings fallen into perverted perceptions; through skillful means, they cause them to attain liberation—namely, liberation from the notion of a self where there is no self, and so forth, up to liberation from the notion of a knower or seer where there is no knower or seer. They also cause them to be liberated from the notion of form where there is no form, and so forth, up to liberation from the notion of the eighty minor marks where there are no eighty minor marks. Furthermore, they cause them to be liberated from all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) such as the five aggregates of clinging, and they also cause them to be liberated from all uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) such as the four foundations of mindfulness.”

Why is this? Because the various untainted dharmas, such as the four foundations of mindfulness, are not like the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); they are subject to arising and ceasing, possess characteristics, are conditioned, involve conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and entail discrimination. Therefore, one must also be liberated from those dharmas. That which is the true ultimate truth is the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*); this emptiness of intrinsic nature is precisely the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) realized by all Buddhas.
"Subhūti, you should know that herein neither a self nor even a perceiver can be apprehended; likewise, neither the aggregate of form nor even the aggregate of consciousness can be apprehended;
neither the sense base of the eye nor even the sense base of the mind can be apprehended; and neither the sense base of forms nor even the sense base of phenomena [can be apprehended]."
No sphere can be apprehended, nor can the eye-element up to the mind-element be apprehended;
nor can the form-element up to the mental-object-element be apprehended; nor can the eye-consciousness-element up to the mind-consciousness-element be apprehended;
nor can eye-contact up to mind-contact be apprehended; nor can any feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition be apprehended.
Even up to the feelings produced with mental contact as a condition, none are to be found;
likewise, from the earth element up to the consciousness element, none are to be found; from causes and conditions up to the dominant condition, none are to be found;
from the phenomena produced from conditions, none are to be found; and from ignorance up to old age and death, none are to be found. Furthermore, there is nothing...
One cannot apprehend anything from the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
nor can one apprehend anything from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature; nor can one apprehend anything from suchness up to the inconceivable realm;
nor can one apprehend anything from the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; nor can one apprehend anything from the four applications of mindfulness...
One cannot find the eight branches of the noble path; nor can one find the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments.
Nor can one find the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Nor can one find the eight liberations up to the ten totalities. Nor can one find the stage of pure observation, and so forth.
The stage of the Tathāgata cannot be apprehended, nor can the stages from the Extremely Joyful up to the Cloud of Dharma be apprehended;
nor can the gateways of dhāraṇī or the gateways of samādhi be apprehended; nor can the five eyes or the six supernormal powers be apprehended;
nor can the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha be apprehended.
Furthermore, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity are not to be found;
the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant abiding in equanimity are not to be found; all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects are not to be found;
nor are the fruit of stream-entry up to and including the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha to be found.
There is nothing to be attained, nor is there anything to be attained regarding the practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva or the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas;
nor is there anything to be attained regarding the thirty-two marks of a great man or the eighty secondary signs.
“Subhūti, you should know this:

it is not for the sake of the path to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment that bodhisattva mahāsattvas seek to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; rather, it is solely for the sake of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena that they seek to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
This intrinsic nature is empty of its prior, middle, and posterior limits, and has never been anything other than empty.

Abiding in the perfection of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the knowledge of the aspects of the path for the sake of liberating all sentient beings, because they [otherwise] cling to the notion of a sentient being and the notion of phenomena.

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the knowledge of the aspects of the path, they practice all paths—namely, the path of the śrāvaka, the path of the pratyekabuddha, the path of the bodhisattva, and the path of the Tathāgata.

“Subhūti, you should know that once these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have attained perfection in all paths, they bring sentient beings to maturity and purify buddha-fields. They maintain their life-force (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*) until they proceed to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Having realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they are able to ensure that the Buddha-eye is never interrupted or destroyed.”
What is called the Buddha-eye?
It is the emptiness of intrinsic nature.

All Buddhas of the past, future, and present, dwelling in the worlds of the ten directions, proclaim the sublime Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings; there are none who do not employ this emptiness of intrinsic nature as their Buddha-eye.
“Subhūti, you should know this:

there are no Buddhas who appear in the world apart from the emptiness of intrinsic nature. There are no Buddhas appearing in the world who do not all teach the meaning of the emptiness of intrinsic nature. Sentient beings to be converted must hear the Buddhas teach the meaning of the emptiness of intrinsic nature before they can enter the Noble Path and attain the fruits of the Noble Path; apart from the emptiness of intrinsic nature, there is no other expedient means.”

"Therefore, Subhūti! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) should correctly abide in the principle of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (prakṛti-śūnyatā) and practice the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) as well as the other bodhisattva-mahāsattva deeds."

If one correctly abides in the principle of the emptiness of intrinsic nature and practices the six perfections as well as other bodhisattva-mahāsattva deeds, one will never fall away from the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñājñāna) and will always be able to benefit all sentient beings.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:

“It is most marvelous and extraordinary that although Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas practice all phenomena, which are by nature empty, they never lose or impair that emptiness of intrinsic nature. That is to say, they do not grasp at form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness as being different from the emptiness of intrinsic nature, up to and including not grasping at the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as being different from the emptiness of intrinsic nature.”

"Bhagavān! Form is itself the emptiness of intrinsic nature; the emptiness of intrinsic nature is itself form. This extends up to: the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is itself the emptiness of intrinsic nature; the emptiness of intrinsic nature is itself the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas."
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.

These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are most marvelous and extraordinary; although they practice all dharmas, which are all empty by their very nature, they never at any time lose or impair that emptiness of intrinsic nature.

"Subhūti, you should know this: form is not different from the emptiness of intrinsic nature; the emptiness of intrinsic nature is not different from form.
