Form itself is the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of intrinsic nature is itself form. This extends up to the point that the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas is not different from the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of intrinsic nature is not different from the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas. The unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas is itself the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of intrinsic nature is itself the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas."
“Subhūti, you should know this!

If form were different from the emptiness of its own nature, or if the emptiness of its own nature were different from form; if form were not the emptiness of its own nature, or if the emptiness of its own nature were not form—and if, up to and including, the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas were different from the emptiness of its own nature, or if the emptiness of its own nature were different from the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas; if the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas were not the emptiness of its own nature, or if the emptiness of its own nature were not the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas—then when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they would not observe that all phenomena are empty of their own nature, nor would they be able to realize the knowledge of all aspects.”
“Subhūti, you should know this:

because form is not different from the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of intrinsic nature is not different from form; form itself is the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of intrinsic nature itself is form—and so on, up to the point that the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas is not different from the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of intrinsic nature is not different from the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas; the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas itself is the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of intrinsic nature itself is the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas—therefore, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they contemplate all phenomena as being empty of intrinsic nature, and are thus able to realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*).”

Why is this? Apart from the emptiness of intrinsic nature, there is not a single dharma that is real, permanent, destructible, or subject to cessation; within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, likewise, there is not a single dharma that is real, permanent, destructible, or subject to cessation.

However, all foolish worldlings, deluded, mistaken, and inverted, give rise to the perception of difference, claiming that form is distinct from its intrinsic emptiness, and so on, up to claiming that the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of the Buddhas is distinct from its intrinsic emptiness.

Because these foolish people discriminate between phenomena and their intrinsic emptiness as being distinct, they do not know form as it truly is, nor do they know feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as they truly are.
Due to ignorance, one becomes attached to form, and attached to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
due to this attachment, one conceives of form as "I" or "mine," and conceives of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as "I" or "mine."

Due to false conceptualization, one becomes attached to internal and external things, thereby undergoing the aggregates of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness in future lives. Consequently, one is unable to attain liberation from birth, aging, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and distress within the various realms of existence, wandering endlessly through the cycle of the three realms of being.

"For this reason, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas abide in the perfection of the emptiness of intrinsic nature and practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not grasp at form, nor do they negate form as being either empty or non-empty;

and so on, up to not grasping at the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas, nor negating the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as being either empty or non-empty."

Why is this so? Form does not destroy emptiness, nor does emptiness destroy form; one cannot say, "This is form" and "This is emptiness. This extends even to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas, which does not destroy emptiness, nor does emptiness destroy the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas.
That is to say: this is the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas; this is emptiness.
For example, space does not destroy space; the internal realm of space does not destroy the external realm of space, nor does the external realm of space destroy the internal realm of space.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

Form does not destroy emptiness, and emptiness does not destroy form; even up to the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas, that does not destroy emptiness, and emptiness does not destroy the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas.

Why is this so? Because all such phenomena are equally devoid of intrinsic nature; one cannot distinguish them by saying "this is empty" and "this is not empty," for all phenomena are empty of their own inherent nature, and within the emptiness of inherent nature there is no differentiation.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 533. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Three: Chapter Twenty-nine on Giving, etc., Section Three. At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, and within the emptiness of intrinsic nature there is no distinction whatsoever, for what purpose do Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide and set out toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, making this vow:
‘I shall realize the vast, unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, and deliver the multitudes of sentient beings’?”
“World-Honored One!

Unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is vast and profound; it can be realized through a non-dual mode of activity and a mode of activity that is not dual. How, then, can bodhisattva-mahāsattvas realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek?”
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will take pity on us and explain it for us!
The Buddha told Subhūti: "It is so! It is so!"
"So it is! It is as you have said.
The unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is vast and profound; it can be realized through a non-dual mode of activity, a mode of activity that is not dual."

Why is this? Awakening is non-dual and without discrimination; if one practices with respect to awakening by means of dualistic characteristics or through discrimination, one will certainly be unable to realize the vast, unsurpassed, and perfectly complete awakening.

“Subhūti, you should know that bodhisattva mahāsattvas do not practice toward awakening by means of dualistic signs, nor do they engage in conceptual discrimination; remaining entirely without abiding, they set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas do not engage in dualistic characteristics regarding all phenomena, nor do they engage in conceptual discrimination, being entirely without any such engagement, they are then able to proceed toward and realize vast, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
“Subhūti, you should know that the unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete enlightenment sought by bodhisattva mahāsattvas cannot be realized by practicing with dualistic characteristics.”

The enlightenment of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas has no sphere of activity whatsoever; that is to say, they do not practice with respect to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
they do not practice with respect to the sense bases from the eye base up to the mind base; they do not practice with respect to the sense fields from the form field up to the phenomena field;
they do not practice with respect to the elements from the eye element up to the mind element; nor do they practice with respect to the form element... [and so forth].
Reaching the dharma-realm, one does not engage with the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element; one does not engage with eye-contact up to mind-contact;
one does not engage with the various feelings produced conditioned by eye-contact up to the various feelings produced conditioned by mind-contact;
one does not engage with the earth element up to the consciousness element; one does not engage with causes and conditions up to...
Regarding the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*): one does not engage with the phenomena produced from conditions; one does not engage with ignorance up to old age and death;

one does not engage with generosity up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); one does not engage with inner emptiness (*adhyātmaśūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāvaśūnyatā*);
one does not engage with suchness (*tathatā*) up to the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*). One does not engage...
They do not practice the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
they do not practice the four applications of mindfulness up to the eight branches of the noble path; they do not practice the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments;
they do not practice the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; and they do not practice the eight liberations up to the ten totalities.
One does not practice the Stage of Pure Observation up to the Stage of the Tathāgata; one does not practice the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Stage of the Dharma Cloud;
one does not practice the gateways of dhāraṇī or the gateways of samādhi; one does not practice the five eyes or the six supernormal powers;
one does not practice the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. One does not...
One practices great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity;
one does not practice the thirty-two marks of a great man or the eighty secondary signs; one does not practice the quality of non-forgetfulness or the nature of constant dwelling in equanimity;
one does not practice all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, or the knowledge of all aspects; nor does one practice the fruit of stream-entry... [and so forth].
Up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, one does not practice the conduct of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor does one practice for unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete enlightenment. Why is this?
The enlightenment of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas does not depend on names and reputations, nor does it grasp at a self or what belongs to a self.
That is to say, that enlightenment does not form such a thought:
"I am practicing with respect to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! The bodhi of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is not practiced for the sake of grasping, nor is it practiced for the sake of abandoning; it makes no conceptual distinctions regarding any phenomena."
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If the bodhi of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is practiced neither by way of grasping nor by way of relinquishing, and there is no conceptual differentiation regarding any phenomena, then where should the bodhi of all bodhisattva mahāsattvas be practiced?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Where should the bodhi of all the emanations of the Buddhas be practiced?"
"Is it for the sake of grasping that one practices,
or is it for the sake of relinquishing? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
Since the emanation bodies of the Buddhas do not truly exist, how could one speak of any bodhi being practiced in such a place, whether as something to be grasped or abandoned?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Where would the awakening of various arhats go within a dream?"
"Is it for the sake of grasping that one practices,
or is it for the sake of relinquishing? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One!

For all Arhats, afflictions are forever exhausted; torpor, drowsiness, and the fetters of the hindrances are all extinguished, and they ultimately have no dreams. How could there be any taking or rejecting while practicing the awakening within a dream?"
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
It is as you have said.

For all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, their awakening is likewise: they do not practice by way of grasping, nor do they practice by way of abandoning; there is no place of practice at all, because they have realized that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, all that constitutes awakening is practiced neither by way of grasping nor by way of relinquishing; there is no place of practice at all. That is to say, one does not practice form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, and so on, up to and including not practicing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, nor practicing the knowledge of all modes."

Could it be that the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas does not practice the ten stages; does not practice from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); does not practice the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; does not practice the sixteen kinds of emptiness; does not practice the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), meditative stabilizations (*samādhi*), and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*); and does not practice even the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four analytical knowledges, and eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; does not practice great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity—extensively including the eighty minor marks and other immeasurable, boundless Buddha-dharmas; and yet, without dwelling in the bodhisattva’s sublime supernormal powers to mature sentient beings and purify buddha-fields, they are nonetheless able to realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*)?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Although the bodhi of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas has no sphere of activity, nevertheless, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas must practice the ten stages and the perfection of giving, and so on extensively up to abiding in the sublime supernormal powers of a bodhisattva to mature sentient beings and purify buddha-fields; only then can they realize the knowledge of all aspects."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If the bodhi of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas has no sphere of activity, will it not be that the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, desiring to benefit all sentient beings, does not dwell for a long time in the ten stages until they have fully cultivated them, nor dwell for a long time in the perfections from generosity up to wisdom until they have fully cultivated them—and as explained at length, nor dwell for a long time in the maturation of sentient beings and the purification of buddha-fields through the bodhisattvas' sublime supernormal powers—yet still be able to realize the knowledge of all modes?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"Although the bodhi of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas has no locus of practice, nevertheless, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas must dwell in the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and cultivate them until they are perfected; they must dwell in the perfections from generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*) up to wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) and cultivate them until they are perfected; and so on, in detail, until they must dwell in the sublime supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of a bodhisattva to mature sentient beings and purify buddha-fields, cultivating them until they are perfected, before they can realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*)."
"Subhūti, you should know this!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva has not yet fully perfected all roots of goodness, they will ultimately be unable to attain the knowledge of all modes.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should dwell in the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of form; they should dwell in the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; and so on, in detail, up to dwelling in the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice, dwelling in the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and dwelling in the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all sentient beings. Having brought the ten stages to fulfillment through their cultivation, and having brought to fulfillment the cultivation of the perfections from generosity up to wisdom, and so on in detail, until having brought to fulfillment the cultivation of the bodhisattva’s sublime supernatural powers for the sake of maturing sentient beings and purifying buddha-fields, they shall then attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"Subhūti, you should know that the principle of the intrinsic emptiness of all these phenomena, as well as the principle of the intrinsic emptiness of all sentient beings, is utterly quiescent; there is not the slightest phenomenon capable of increasing or decreasing, arising or ceasing, being annihilated or eternal, being defiled or purified, or attaining fruit or realizing clear observation."

“Subhūti, you should know that bodhisattva mahāsattvas, relying on conventional truth, speak of the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom; having realized the emptiness of intrinsic nature as it truly is, they attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening—not by relying on ultimate truth.”

Why is this? Because within ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), form cannot be apprehended, nor can feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness be apprehended; and so on, in detail, up to the point that the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot be apprehended, nor can unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) be apprehended. Neither can one who practices the path of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva be apprehended, nor can one who realizes the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas be apprehended.
"Subhūti, you should know that these dharmas and all sentient beings are all provisionally designated based on conventional discourse, not based on the ultimate truth.
Subhūti, you should know this!"

When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, although from their first resolve they cultivate the conduct of enlightenment for the sake of all sentient beings with extreme vigor, they do not apprehend this mind at all; they do not apprehend sentient beings, nor do they apprehend great enlightenment, nor do they apprehend Buddhas or Bodhisattvas. This is because all phenomena and all sentient beings are by nature empty and unapprehendable.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If all dharmas are entirely non-existent, being by their very nature empty and unapprehendable, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the conduct of enlightenment?"
"How can one attain unsurpassed enlightenment?
The Buddha told Subhūti: "What do you think?"

In the past, by relying on the realm of abandonment, you severed the fetters of afflictions such as the view of a self-identity and attained the untainted faculties; you dwelt in the concentration of immediate succession and realized the fruit of stream-entry, followed by the fruit of once-returning, then the fruit of non-returning, and finally the fruit of arhatship.
"At that time, did you perceive any dream, or mind, or path, or fruit of the paths as being obtainable? Subhūti replied, "No!"
"World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If at that time you had not attained anything at all, how could you say that you have attained the fruit of arhatship?"
Subhūti replied, “It is spoken in accordance with conventional truth, not in accordance with ultimate truth.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"So it is! So it is! It is just as you have said."

So it is with the bodhisattva mahāsattvas as well: they practice the conduct of enlightenment and attain great enlightenment by relying on conventional discourse, not by relying on the ultimate truth.
"Subhūti, you should know this!"

Based on worldly convention (*saṃvṛti*), one designates the existence of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; and so on, in detail, up until based on worldly convention one designates the practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. Based on worldly convention, one designates sentient beings, bodhisattvas, and buddhas; it is not based on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

“Subhūti, you should know that bodhisattva mahāsattvas do not perceive any dharma that can increase or decrease, benefit or harm, in regard to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, because the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is empty.”

“Subhūti, you should know that for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, even the intrinsic emptiness of all phenomena cannot be apprehended; how much less can an initial resolve to attain awakening be apprehended!”

If even the initial generation of the mind of awakening cannot be apprehended, how much less can there be anything to be apprehended in the cultivation of the six perfections—such as generosity—from the first bhūmi up to the tenth, or in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the three gates of liberation, or even the infinite and boundless qualities of a Buddha!
If there were anything to be attained, such a thing would certainly be impossible. Thus it is, Subhūti!

By means of skillful means while practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the conduct of enlightenment and realize great enlightenment, continuously and without interruption delivering the multitudes of sentient beings.
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha,
saying: "If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, although diligently practicing from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom,
abides in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, and abides in suchness..."
Up to and including the inconceivable realm, they dwell securely in the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
they practice the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path; they practice the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
and they practice the gates of liberation: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. They cultivate...
They practice the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality; they practice the stages from the Ground of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma;
they practice all doors of dhāraṇī and doors of samādhi; they practice the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
they practice the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. They practice...
They practice great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity;
they cultivate the thirty-two marks of a Great Being and the eighty minor characteristics; they cultivate the quality of non-forgetfulness and the constant abiding in equanimity;
they cultivate all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); they cultivate the bodhisattva-mahāsattva...
Regarding the practice of the perfections (pāramitā), one cultivates unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

If the path to enlightenment has not been fully cultivated, one cannot realize unsurpassed enlightenment. How, then, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the path to enlightenment so that it becomes perfected and is able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom with skillful means, by the power of these skillful means, when practicing the perfection of giving, they do not apprehend the gift, they do not apprehend the giver, they do not apprehend the recipient, and they do not apprehend the purpose for which it is given; yet they do not practice the perfection of giving while remaining apart from such dharmas."
When this bodhisattva mahāsattva gives in this manner, they are able to fulfill the cultivation of the path to awakening and swiftly achieve its realization.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

All bodhisattva mahāsattvas, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom through skillful means, cultivate the path to enlightenment until it is brought to full completion, thereby enabling them to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

Regarding the perfections such as pure ethical discipline, up to the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of a Buddha, the detailed explanation should likewise be applied accordingly.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), cultivate the path to enlightenment with courageous and correct diligence?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom through skillful means, they do not conjoin form up to consciousness, nor do they disperse form up to consciousness;
they do not conjoin the eye base up to the mind base, nor do they disperse the eye base up to the mind base.”
The sense-field of form up to the sense-field of phenomena is neither conjoined nor dispersed;
the eye-element up to the mind-element is neither conjoined nor dispersed;
the form-element up to the phenomena-element is neither conjoined nor dispersed.
They do not combine with the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element, nor do they disperse from the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element;
they do not combine with eye-contact up to mind-contact, nor do they disperse from eye-contact up to mind-contact;

they do not combine with the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition, nor do they disperse from the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition.
The earth element is neither conjoined with nor dissociated from the consciousness element;
the causal conditions are neither conjoined with nor dissociated from the dominant conditions;
the phenomena arising from conditions are neither conjoined with nor dissociated from the phenomena arising from conditions.
Ignorance through old age and death are neither conjoined nor dispersed;
generosity through the perfection of wisdom are neither conjoined nor dispersed;
inner emptiness through the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature are neither conjoined nor dispersed.
The non-conjunction of true thusness up to the inconceivable realm, and the non-dispersion of true thusness up to the inconceivable realm;
the non-conjunction of the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, and the non-dispersion of the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
the non-conjunction of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, and the non-dispersion of the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path.

They do not combine with the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments, nor do they separate from the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments;
they do not combine with the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—nor do they separate from the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
they do not combine with the eight liberations up to the ten totalities, nor do they separate from the eight liberations up to the ten totalities.
They do not combine with the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata, nor do they disperse from the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata;
they do not combine with the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma, nor do they disperse from the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma;
they do not combine with the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi, nor do they disperse from the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi.
They do not combine with the five eyes and six supernormal powers, nor are they separated from the five eyes and six supernormal powers;

they do not combine with the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, nor are they separated from the Tathāgata’s ten powers up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;

they do not combine with great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity, nor are they separated from great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity.
They do not combine the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs, yet they do not separate from the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs;
they do not combine the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity, yet they do not separate from the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity;

they do not combine all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects, yet they do not separate from all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects.
They do not combine with the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, nor are they separated from the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;

they do not combine with all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas, nor are they separated from all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas.
Why is this? Because all such phenomena lack intrinsic nature (svabhāva), such that they can be brought together or separated. "Thus it is, Śāriputra!"
"When the bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they cultivate the path to enlightenment with courageous and correct diligence.
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If all phenomena are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature such that they can neither be joined together nor separated, how do bodhisattva mahāsattvas bring forth the perfection of wisdom and train within it?"
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not train in the perfection of wisdom, they will ultimately be unable to attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek.
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "It is so! It is so!"
So it is! It is as you have said.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they will ultimately be unable to attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) that they seek.
Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva seeks to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they must train in the perfection of wisdom in order to attain it.
Śāriputra! The unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment sought by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas can only be realized through skillful means; it cannot be realized without skillful means.

“Śāriputra! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, if they were to perceive any dharma whose intrinsic nature could be apprehended, then it would be something to be grasped; yet, since no dharma with an apprehendable intrinsic nature is perceived, what is there to be grasped?”
That is to say, not grasping at the thought: "This is the perfection of wisdom;
this is the perfection of meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity; these are the aggregate of form up to the aggregate of consciousness;
these are the sense base of the eye up to the sense base of the mind; and these are the sense base of form up to the sense base of phenomena."
This is the eye-element up to the mind-element; this is the form-element up to the mental-object-element;
this is the eye-consciousness-element up to the mind-consciousness-element; this is eye-contact up to mind-contact;
and these are the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition.
This is the earth element up to the consciousness element; this is the causal condition up to the dominant condition;
these are all phenomena produced from conditions; this is ignorance up to old age and death;
this is internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature; this is suchness up to the inconceivable realm.
These are the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; these are the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
these are the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
these are the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; these are the eight liberations up to the ten...
The spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*): these are the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata;
these are the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma stage; these are the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi;
these are the five eyes and the six supernormal powers; these are the ten powers of the Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
These are great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity;
these are the thirty-two marks of a Great Being and the eighty secondary characteristics; these are the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant abiding in equanimity;
these are the knowledge of all, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects; these are the stream-enterer.
The fruits up to and including the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha—this is the entire practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
this is the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas; this is an ordinary person (pṛthagjana);
this is a śrāvaka; this is a pratyekabuddha; this is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva; this is a Tathāgata, Arhat...
"Perfectly Enlightened One.
Śāriputra! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they understand as it truly is that one..."
The nature of all phenomena is entirely ungraspable; that is to say, from the perfection of wisdom down to the perfection of generosity, they are all ungraspable.
From the aggregate of form down to the aggregate of consciousness, they are all ungraspable. From the sense base of the eye down to the sense base of the mind, they are all ungraspable.
From the sense base of form down to the sense base of phenomena, they are all ungraspable. The eye element...
Even the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is ungraspable; the form-element (*rūpadhātu*) up to the phenomena-element (*dharmadhātu*) are all ungraspable;

the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) up to the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*) are all ungraspable; eye-contact (*cakṣuḥsaṃsparśa*) up to mind-contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*) are all ungraspable;
and the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with eye-contact as condition, up to those produced with mind-contact as condition, are likewise ungraspable.
All feelings are ungraspable; the earth element up to the consciousness element are all ungraspable;
the causal conditions up to the dominant condition are all ungraspable; all phenomena arising from conditions are ungraspable;
ignorance up to old age and death are all ungraspable; and the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path are likewise ungraspable.
All members [of the path] are ungraspable; from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature, all are ungraspable;
from suchness up to the inconceivable realm, all are ungraspable; the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path are all ungraspable;
the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments are all...
They cannot be grasped; the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—all cannot be grasped.
The eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality cannot be grasped. The stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata cannot be grasped.
The stage of extreme joy up to the stage of the Dharma-cloud cannot be grasped. The dhāraṇīs...
The doors of liberation and the doors of samādhi are all ungraspable; the five eyes and the six supernormal powers are all ungraspable;
the ten powers of a Tathāgata, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are all ungraspable;
great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity are all ungraspable; the thirty-two marks of a great man...
The marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs are all ungraspable; the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity are all ungraspable;
omniscience, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects are all ungraspable;
the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha are all ungraspable; and all [bodhi]...
The practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas are both ungraspable;
likewise, all ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas are ungraspable.

“Śāriputra! Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practicing the profound perfection of wisdom understand, as it truly is, that the nature of all phenomena is ungraspable, they attain non-obstruction regarding all phenomena.”

Śāriputra! This perfection that cannot be grasped is the perfection without obstruction; this perfection without obstruction is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should train within it.

Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can train in this way, they do not apprehend anything at all among all phenomena; since they do not even apprehend training, how much less could they apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment!
How much more so for attaining the *prajñāpāramitā*!
How much more so for attaining the dharmas of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and the Buddhas! Why is this?
Śāriputra! There is not even the slightest dharma that possesses an intrinsic nature.
Among all dharmas that lack intrinsic nature, what could possibly be a dharma of an ordinary person?
"What are these things, from the stream-enterer up to the qualities of all Buddhas? Śāriputra,
since such phenomena are ultimately unattainable, by means of what dharma could one conceptually designate a 'person' (pudgala)?"
Since a person (pudgala) cannot be apprehended, how can it be said that "this is an ordinary being," "this is a stream-enterer," and so on, up to "a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha"?
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If all phenomena are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature and none are truly existent, by virtue of what basis can one discern that 'this is an ordinary person' or 'these are the phenomena of an ordinary person'?"
"Extending this explanation even further: 'This is the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; these are the dharmas of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha'?
The Buddha said to Śāriputra: "What do you think?"
Is there truly a form that has existed or will exist in the way that foolish ordinary beings cling to it?
Is there truly feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that have existed or will exist in the way that foolish ordinary beings cling to them?

To speak at length, up to: do you think that the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the truly existent Buddhas has ever existed, or will it ever exist, in the manner that foolish ordinary beings cling to it?

Do ordinary beings, up to and including Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, truly exist as they are grasped by foolish ordinary beings—either having existed in the past or being destined to exist in the future?
Śāriputra said, “No, World-Honored One!”
"It is only because of their delusions and inversions that foolish ordinary beings harbor such attachments.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), although they observe that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature and are not truly existent, they nevertheless set out for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment by relying on worldly convention. For the sake of all sentient beings, they employ skillful means to teach them, enabling them to attain correct understanding and become free from all inversions."
Then, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, employ skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) such that, by the power of this skillful means, although he contemplates all phenomena as being entirely without intrinsic nature and as not truly existent, he nevertheless sets out toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment according to worldly convention, and skillfully proclaims it for the sake of all sentient beings, enabling them to attain correct understanding and become free from all perversions?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they achieve such skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) that they do not perceive even the slightest real dharma in which they might abide. Because they would abide therein, there would be obstruction; because of obstruction, there would be regression; because of regression, the mind becomes weak and inferior; and because the mind is weak and inferior, laziness arises.”

“Śāriputra! Because all phenomena are entirely devoid of substantial reality, being without self or what belongs to a self, they all take non-existence as their intrinsic nature; their fundamental nature is empty and quiescent, and their own characteristics are empty and quiescent.”
Only all foolish ordinary beings, through delusion and perversion, cling to the aggregate of form up to the aggregate of consciousness;
they cling to the sense base of the eye up to the sense base of the mind; they cling to the sense base of form up to the sense base of mental phenomena;
they cling to the eye element up to the mind element; they cling to the form element up to the mental-phenomena element; they cling...
The eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element; attachment to eye-contact up to mind-contact;
attachment to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition;
attachment to the earth element up to the consciousness element; attachment to the causal condition up to the dominant condition; attachment.
Regarding all phenomena produced from conditions, they cling to ignorance up to old age and death;
they cling to generosity up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); they cling to inner emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature;
they cling to suchness (*tathatā*) up to the inconceivable realm; they cling to suffering, its origin, its cessation, and...
The Noble Truth of the Path: attachment to the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
attachment to the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; attachment to the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
attachment to the eight liberations up to the ten totalities; and attachment to the stage of pure observation.
Up to and including the stage of a Tathāgata; attachment to the Stage of Extreme Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma stage;
attachment to the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi; attachment to the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
attachment to the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and attachment to great loving-kindness and great compassion.
...great joy, and great equanimity; clinging to the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks;
clinging to the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant abiding in equanimity;
clinging to all-knowledge, the knowledge of paths, and the knowledge of all aspects; and clinging to the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
They cling to the practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva; they cling to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
and they cling to ordinary beings, up to and including tathāgatas, arhats, and perfectly enlightened ones.

"For this reason, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas contemplate all phenomena as being entirely devoid of substantial reality; they are without self or what belongs to a self, taking non-existence as their intrinsic nature, and are by nature empty and quiescent, with their own characteristics being empty and quiescent."

Practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, he establishes himself as a master of illusions to preach the Dharma to sentient beings: for those who are stingy and greedy, he preaches generosity; for those who violate the precepts, he preaches pure morality; for those who are angry and resentful, he preaches patience; for those who are indolent, he preaches diligence; for those who are distracted, he preaches meditative concentration; and for those with impaired wisdom, he preaches wisdom.

Having established sentient beings in the perfections from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, this bodhisattva mahāsattva further proclaims for them the sublime noble dharmas capable of bringing about emergence from saṃsāra, so that those sentient beings may rely upon them in their practice and training, thereby attaining either the fruit of a stream-enterer, the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, or the fruit of arhatship; or attaining the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; or entering the stage of a bodhisattva mahāsattva; or abiding in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), why are they not called those who have something to obtain?”

That is to say, although sentient beings do not truly exist, one causes them to abide in the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; furthermore, one proclaims for them the sublime noble Dharma capable of bringing about transcendence from birth and death, thereby causing them to attain the fruit of stream-entry, or even to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not apprehend any sentient beings as having real existence.”

Why is this? Because when these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do not perceive even the slightest substantial reality of sentient beings; there are only sentient beings as conventional designations.
Śāriputra! When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they abide in the two truths and proclaim the sublime Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.
What are these two? First, the conventional; second, the ultimate.

Śāriputra! Although neither the two truths nor the designation of sentient beings can be apprehended, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they employ skillful means to proclaim the essential teachings of the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings. Having heard the true Dharma, these sentient beings do not even apprehend a self in the present life, let alone attain the sought-after noble fruits of the future!

In this way, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the profound perfection of wisdom with skillful means teaches the essential Dharma to sentient beings, causing them to cultivate correct practice and attain the fruits of realization; yet, his mind apprehends nothing at all regarding them, because he understands that all phenomena are unapprehendable.
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:

“These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are true bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; although they do not apprehend a single nature, nor a diverse nature, nor a collective nature, nor a distinct nature among all phenomena, they nevertheless don such great armor of merit.”

By donning such armor of great merit, one is not born in the desire realm, not born in the form realm, and not born in the formless realm; one does not perceive a conditioned realm, nor does one perceive an unconditioned realm.
Although one transforms sentient beings to enable them to transcend the three realms, one apprehends no sentient being whatsoever, nor does one apprehend even the designation "sentient being.

Because the designation "sentient being" cannot be apprehended, there is neither bondage nor liberation; because there is neither bondage nor liberation, there is neither defilement nor purity; because there is neither defilement nor purity, the distinctions between the various realms of existence (*gati*) cannot be discerned; because the distinctions between the various realms of existence cannot be discerned, there is neither karma nor affliction; and because there is neither karma nor affliction, there is also no fruition of maturation (*vipāka-phala*).

"If there is no ripening fruit (vipākaphala), how can there be the various distinctions such as the self (ātman) and sentient beings (sattva) transmigrating through the various realms of existence and being born within the three worlds?
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "It is so!"
"So it is! It is just as you have said, Śāriputra."

If sentient beings existed previously and later ceased to exist, the Bodhisattvas and Tathāgatas would incur fault; yet the principle that they were previously non-existent and later came to be is likewise untenable. The same applies to the existence and non-existence of the cyclic wandering through the various realms of existence.

Therefore, Śāriputra, whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, the nature of phenomena remains eternally abiding; suchness, the dharma-realm, and the non-false nature never undergo change.

Because the dharma-nature, dharma-realm, dharma-abiding, dharma-stability, suchness, and the limit of reality of all dharmas are like empty space, within them even a self cannot be apprehended, much less can any dharmas such as form be apprehended!
Since no phenomena such as form and so forth can be apprehended, how could there be the saṃsāra of the various realms of existence?
Since the saṃsāra of the various realms cannot be apprehended, how could there be the ripening of sentient beings for their liberation?
They exist only as conventional designations.
"Śāriputra, because the intrinsic nature of such phenomena is entirely empty."

After the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have heard this as it truly is from the Buddhas of the past, they seek to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in order to liberate sentient beings from their inverted attachments. While seeking that attainment, they do not form such thoughts:
"I have already attained or shall attain this Dharma, and I have already delivered or shall deliver those sentient beings from the manifold sufferings of birth and death in which they are attached."

“Śāriputra! This bodhisattva mahāsattva, in order to liberate sentient beings from their inverted attachments, dons the armor of merit and is adorned with great vows; with courageous and correct diligence, they are free from all longing and attachment, never retreating from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and never giving rise to doubt regarding enlightenment, thinking:
‘Shall I attain it, or shall I not attain it?’”
One should simply maintain right mindfulness, thinking:

"I shall certainly attain the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and bring true benefit to all sentient beings; that is to say, I shall cause them to be liberated from the suffering of birth and death within the cycle of rebirth in various realms, which is characterized by delusion, error, and perversion."

"Śāriputra! Although these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas liberate sentient beings from the births and deaths of the various realms of existence—those states of confusion, delusion, and inversion—they do so without apprehending anything at all; it is only by relying on worldly convention that they say such a thing exists."

“Śāriputra! Suppose a skilled illusionist or his disciple, relying on the art of Indra’s net, conjures forth immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of beings, and further conjures various kinds of exquisite food and drink to bestow upon these illusory beings, satisfying them all. Having performed this deed, he joyfully proclaims:
‘I have already attained a vast accumulation of merit.’”
"What do you think?
Does this skillful illusionist or his disciple actually cause sentient beings to become satiated?
Śāriputra replied:
"No, World-Honored One! The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“The bodhisattva mahāsattva is also like this: from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, for the sake of delivering all sentient beings, they practice the perfections from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
they abide in the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature; and they abide in suchness up to the inconceivable realm.”
Abiding securely in the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, they practice the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
they practice the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
they practice the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; and they practice the eight liberations up to...
The ten spheres of totality; the cultivation of the stages from the Ground of Utmost Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma;
the cultivation of the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi; the cultivation of the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
the cultivation of the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and the cultivation of great loving-kindness, great compassion, and great...
They cultivate joy and great equanimity; they cultivate the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs;
they cultivate the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant abiding in equanimity; they cultivate all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects;
they fulfill the great path to bodhi of a bodhisattva and bring sentient beings to maturity.
They purify the Buddha-fields.
"Śāriputra, although Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas perform these deeds, they apprehend neither sentient beings nor any phenomena whatsoever, and they do not form such thoughts:

"By means of this Dharma, I shall subdue such classes of sentient beings, causing them to distance themselves from inverted attachments and no longer undergo the suffering of birth and death through the cycle of coming and going."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
what is called the Great Path to Bodhi of a bodhisattva?"

By means of skillful means, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice this path bring sentient beings to maturity, purify buddha-fields, and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“From the first generation of the mind of awakening, all that Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice—ranging from the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, and extensively including everything up to omniscience (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), as well as other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas—is the great path to the awakening of a bodhisattva.”

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice this path, they employ skillful means to bring sentient beings to maturity and to adorn and purify buddha-fields, swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, yet without any conceptualization of "sentient beings," "buddha-fields," or the like.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of generosity, bring sentient beings to maturity through skillful means?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, when practicing the perfection of generosity, employ skillful means; they practice generosity themselves and also encourage others to practice generosity, earnestly instructing and exhorting them, saying: ‘O noble sons!’”
Do not be attached to giving; if you are attached to giving, you will undergo further rebirth, and through this succession of births, you will experience immeasurable and boundless great suffering.
"O sons of noble family!

Within ultimate truth, there is no giving whatsoever, nor is there a giver, a recipient, the object given, or the fruit of giving. Thus, the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is emptiness; within this emptiness of intrinsic nature, there is no phenomenon that can be grasped, and even the emptiness of phenomena cannot be grasped."

"In this way, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), although they themselves are able to practice giving toward sentient beings and also exhort others to give, they apprehend nothing at all regarding the act of giving, the giver, the recipient, the gift, or the fruit of giving. Such a perfection of generosity is called the 'perfection of non-apprehension' (*anupalambhapāramitā*)."

Subhūti, you should know that when these bodhisattva mahāsattvas do not apprehend any of these dharmas, they employ skillful means to lead sentient beings to abide in the fruit of a stream-enterer, and so on, up to and including leading them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
In this way, Subhūti,
when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of generosity, they bring sentient beings to maturity, causing them to obtain benefit and happiness.

"Subhūti, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving himself, encourages others to practice giving, constantly and correctly extols the dharma of practicing giving, and joyfully praises those who practice giving."

Having practiced such great giving as this, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are born into a great kṣatriya clan, or a great brāhmaṇa clan, or a great householder clan; or they are born into a great clan of lay devotees abundant in wealth and treasures; or they become minor kings with sovereign power and wealth over small territories; or they become great kings with sovereign power and wealth over large territories; or they become universal monarchs (cakravartin) with sovereign power and wealth over the four continents.

“Having been born in such noble and honorable states, this bodhisattva mahāsattva gathers sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*). First, he teaches sentient beings to abide in generosity; by means of this, he gradually causes them to abide in ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom. Furthermore, he causes them to abide in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; he further causes them to abide in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*), and finally causes them to abide in the three gates of liberation.”

Having established all sentient beings in such wholesome dharmas as these, this bodhisattva mahāsattva causes them to enter the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*), attaining the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) up to the fruit of arhatship; or he causes them to enter the state of rightness and departure from birth, gradually realizing the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; or he causes them to enter the state of rightness and departure from birth, gradually training in the stages of a bodhisattva (*bodhisattvabhūmi*) and swiftly proceeding toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
He further addressed them, saying:
"O sons of noble family!
You should conceive the great vow to swiftly proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and perform deeds of supreme benefit for all sentient beings."

All phenomena grasped by the false conceptualizations of sentient beings lack intrinsic nature; they are merely held to exist through inverted and deluded attachments. Therefore, you all should apply yourselves with diligent effort: sever your own inversions and encourage others to sever theirs; liberate yourselves from birth and death and cause others to be liberated as well; attain great benefit for yourselves and cause others to attain it too.

“Subhūti, you should know this! The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 534, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Three, Chapter on Giving and Other Virtues, Twenty-Nine, Section Four. “Subhūti, you should know this!”

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should constantly practice the perfection of generosity in this manner. By means of this perfection of generosity, from the first generation of the mind of awakening until its ultimate consummation, they do not fall into the miserable realms, nor into states of poverty, lowliness, or the borderlands. For the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, they are frequently reborn in the human realm as universal monarchs (cakravartin), possessing wealth, sovereignty, and great capacity for benefitting others.

Why is this? Because one experiences such fruits according to the power of the seeds sown; that is to say, when that bodhisattva becomes a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*), upon seeing a beggar approach, he reflects:
"For what purpose am I wandering through birth and death to become a wheel-turning monarch?"

"Could it be that I do not dwell within the cycle of birth and death for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to sentient beings, merely to receive this supreme fruit and for no other purpose?
Having had this thought, he said to the beggar:
"Whatever various wealth and treasures you require, I shall give them all to you; when you take these things, regard them as your own property and harbor no other thoughts."

Why is this? It is because I have taken up this body and accumulated these material goods for the sake of your peace and happiness. These goods belong to you; take them as you please. Whether you enjoy them yourself or bestow them upon others, do not harbor any doubt or hesitation.
When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva thus feels compassion for all sentient beings, his objectless great compassion (anālambana-mahākaruṇā) is swiftly brought to fulfillment.

Because this great compassion is swiftly fulfilled, although he constantly benefits and brings happiness to immeasurable sentient beings, he apprehends no sentient beings whatsoever, nor does he apprehend any superior fruit resulting therefrom.
One knows as it truly is:
"It is solely through conventional verbal expression that one designates the various affairs concerning the benefit and happiness of sentient beings.
Furthermore, one knows as it truly is:
"All phenomena that are designated are like echoes and reflections; though they appear to exist, they lack true reality.
For this reason, one grasps at nothing whatsoever regarding dharmas.
"Subhūti, you should know this!"

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should constantly practice the perfection of generosity in this manner: that is, they should have no attachment or regard for sentient beings, even to the point of being able to give away their own flesh and bones, let alone external material possessions which they cannot bear to relinquish!
"It means that all requisites sustain sentient beings, causing them to quickly attain liberation from birth, old age, sickness, and death.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What are the requisites that sustain sentient beings, causing them to quickly attain liberation from birth, old age, sickness, and death?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"It refers to all the requisites for cultivating the perfections from generosity up to wisdom;
or all the requisites for abiding in the emptinesses from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature; or [abiding] in suchness up to..."
Whatever requisites belong to the inconceivable realm; whatever requisites belong to abiding in the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
whatever requisites belong to cultivating the four applications of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
or whatever requisites belong to cultivating the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions—[all these are included therein].
Whether it be the requisites for cultivating the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
or the requisites for cultivating the eight liberations up to the ten totalities; or the requisites for cultivating the stage of pure observation up to the stage of a Tathāgata;
or the requisites for cultivating the stage of extreme joy up to the stage of the cloud of dharma.
...possessing all the requisites for cultivating all dharani-doors and samadhi-doors;
all the requisites for cultivating the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
all the requisites for cultivating the ten powers of a Tathagata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and all the requisites for cultivating great loving-kindness and great compassion...
The requisites for great joy and great equanimity; the requisites for cultivating the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant abiding in equanimity;
the requisites for cultivating all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and all-aspect knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*);
and the requisites for attaining the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
Whether it be the requisites for practicing the bodhisattva-mahāsattva path, or the requisites for realizing unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete enlightenment—
Subhūti, you should know this!
All such requisites of wholesome dharmas as these embrace sentient beings, causing them to swiftly attain liberation from birth, old age, sickness, and death.

By means of various such requisites and skillful means, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constantly embrace sentient beings, causing them to swiftly attain liberation from the manifold sufferings of saṃsāra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in the perfection of generosity, they personally practice the perfection of generosity and encourage all sentient beings to do so. If they see sentient beings who have violated the pure precepts, they give rise to deep compassion and say to them:
'You all should receive and uphold the pure precepts; I shall provide you with various kinds of material resources so that you will never lack anything throughout the long night.'"

"Because you lack the various necessities of life, you have violated the pure precepts and committed various evil deeds; I shall provide you with whatever necessities you lack, bestowing them all upon you so that you may have nothing in want."

Abiding securely in the discipline of pure ethical conduct, you shall gradually be able to bring an end to suffering; by relying on the Dharma of the Three Vehicles as appropriate for each, you will transcend the suffering of birth and death and attain the bliss of nirvana.
"Subhūti, you should know this:

this bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of generosity, personally upholds pure ethical discipline, encourages others to uphold pure ethical discipline, constantly and correctly extols the dharma of upholding pure ethical discipline, and joyfully praises those who uphold pure ethical discipline."
In this way, Subhūti,

bodhisattva mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of generosity exhort all sentient beings to abide in pure ethical discipline, so that they may be liberated from the suffering of birth and death and attain the bliss of nirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas abide in the perfection of generosity, they see sentient beings who are mutually angry and resentful toward one another; they give rise to deep compassion and address them, saying:
'For what reason do you all become mutually angry and resentful?'"

If you should find yourselves lacking in anything and consequently commit various evils against one another, you should request what you need from me; do not harbor doubts or difficulties, for I shall grant you whatever you require.
"You all should not harbor mutual anger or resentment; you should cultivate patience and together give rise to a mind of loving-kindness.

Subhūti, you should know that when these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, dwelling securely in the perfection of generosity, have exhorted sentient beings to practice patience, they desire to make it firm and further address them, saying:
"The causes and conditions of anger have no fixed reality at all; they all arise from false conceptualization, for the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty.
For what reason do you give rise to false anger toward these unreal phenomena and further injure one another?"

Do not, on account of false conceptualization, give rise to mutual anger and create various evil karmas, whereby you shall fall into the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, and other evil states to undergo various heavy sufferings. Those pains are agonizing, fierce, and sharp, piercing both body and mind to the point that they are most difficult to endure.

You all must not, out of attachment to unreal things, give rise to false anger and commit various sinful karmas. Because of such sinful karma, it is difficult even to obtain a human body of inferior status, let alone being born in the celestial realms or among humans, encountering a Buddha, hearing the Dharma, receiving it with deep faith and acceptance, and practicing according to the teachings!

"You should all know that a human body is difficult to obtain, the appearance of a Buddha is difficult to encounter, the arising of faith is further difficult, and hearing the Dharma and practicing it according to its meaning is yet more difficult.
Now that you have fulfilled these conditions, do not let this favorable opportunity be lost through anger; if this moment is lost, it will be difficult to remedy."
"Therefore, you should not give rise to anger toward sentient beings, but should instead cultivate patience. "Subhūti,

you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of generosity, personally practices patience, encourages others to practice patience, constantly and correctly extols the dharma of practicing patience, and joyfully praises those who practice patience."

In this way, Subhūti, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, abiding in the perfection of generosity, exhort all sentient beings to practice patience; through this, those sentient beings gradually attain liberation by relying on the three vehicles.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in the perfection of generosity, they see sentient beings who are physically and mentally indolent; they give rise to deep compassion and address them, saying:
'For what reason do you not diligently apply yourselves with vigor to cultivate the various wholesome dharmas, but instead give way to indolence?'"
He spoke thus: "I lack the necessary requisites and am unable to apply myself diligently to the wholesome dharmas.
The Bodhisattva said to him:

"I can provide you with whatever requisites you lack so that you may be fully supplied; you should diligently cultivate generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom."

At that time, all sentient beings, having obtained the requisites bestowed by this bodhisattva, were free from any lack; they were thus able to arouse physical and mental diligence to cultivate various wholesome dharmas, swiftly attaining their full perfection.

Because they have attained perfection through these various virtues, they gradually give rise to all untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas. By means of these untainted dharmas, some attain the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), non-returning (*anāgāmin*), or arhatship; others may attain the enlightenment of a solitary buddha (*pratyekabuddha-bodhi*), or enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*), gradually practicing the bodhisattva stages (*bodhisattvabhūmi*) until they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
"Subhūti, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva,

dwelling securely in the perfection of generosity, personally practices diligence, encourages others to practice diligence, constantly and correctly extols the practice of diligence, and joyfully praises those who practice diligence."
In this way, Subhūti, bodhisattva mahāsattvas,
abiding in the perfection of generosity, cause all sentient beings to distance themselves from indolence, diligently cultivate all that is wholesome, and swiftly attain liberation.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When bodhisattva mahāsattvas abide in the perfection of generosity, they see sentient beings whose bodies and minds are distracted; they give rise to deep compassion and address them, saying:
'For what reason do you not cultivate meditative concentration? Why do you wander through the cycle of birth and death with distracted minds and lost mindfulness?'"
He said this: "Because I lack the necessary requisites, I am unable to practice meditative concentration.
The Bodhisattva told him:

"I can provide you with whatever requisites you lack so that all are fully satisfied; from this day forward, you should no longer give rise to false conceptualizations, nor allow yourselves to be disturbed by various thoughts and investigations directed toward internal or external objects."

At that time, all sentient beings, having obtained the requisites bestowed by this bodhisattva, were free from any lack; they were thus able to subdue and sever false imagination, discursive thought, investigation, and deliberation, as well as sensual desire and ill will, and enter the first dhyāna, gradually proceeding to enter the second, third, and fourth dhyānas.

Based upon the various dhyānas, one can further induce the four sublime abodes (brahmavihāras) of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; with these dhyānas and immeasurables as their support, one can then gradually enter the four formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpattis).

Having made the mind supple through the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*), one cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), progressing successively up to the eight branches of the noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*). By means of this, one is further able to induce the dharmas of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) until they are all fulfilled, thereby attaining the fruits of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) as appropriate.
"Subhūti, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva,

abiding in the perfection of generosity, personally cultivates meditative concentration, encourages others to cultivate meditative concentration, constantly and correctly extols the practice of meditative concentration, and joyfully praises those who cultivate meditative concentration."
In this way, Subhūti, bodhisattva mahāsattvas,
abiding in the perfection of generosity, exhort sentient beings to distance themselves from distraction and cultivate the various meditative concentrations, thereby bringing them great benefit.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When bodhisattva mahāsattvas abide in the perfection of generosity, they see sentient beings who are deluded and inverted; they give rise to deep compassion for them and say to them:
'For what reason do you not cultivate wisdom, yet remain deluded and inverted, wandering through the cycle of birth and death?'"
He said this: "Because I lack the necessary requisites, I am unable to practice the Prajñāpāramitā.
The Bodhisattva replied:
"I can provide you with whatever requisites you lack so that they may all be fully supplied; you should accept them.

Once you have brought to perfection the practices of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration, you should carefully examine the true nature of all phenomena and practice the perfection of wisdom."
That is to say, at that time, one should carefully examine whether there is even the slightest dharma that can be apprehended;
namely, whether a self, a sentient being—and so forth, as extensively explained—up to a knower or a seer can be apprehended.
Form up to consciousness; the eye-base up to the mind-base; the form-base up to the phenomena-base; the eye-element up to the mind-element;
the form-element up to the phenomena-element; the eye-consciousness-element up to the mind-consciousness-element;
eye-contact up to mind-contact; and all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to [feelings produced with] mind-...
The various feelings produced with contact as their condition; the earth element up to the consciousness element;
the causal conditions up to the dominant condition; all phenomena produced from conditions; ignorance up to old age and death;
the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm; generosity up to the perfection of wisdom; and internal emptiness.
