Up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; from suchness up to the inconceivable realm;
the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path;
the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments; and the gates of liberation: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
The eight liberations up to the ten totalities; the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata;
the stage of extreme joy up to the stage of the Dharma-cloud; the doors of dhāraṇī and the doors of samādhi; the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and great compassion.
...great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity; the thirty-two marks of a Great Being and the eighty secondary characteristics;
the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant abiding in equanimity; all-knowledge, knowledge of the paths, and all-aspect knowledge;
the fruit of stream-entry up to the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha; and all Bodhisattvas...
“O Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, can the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas be attained by examining each of these one by one?

Once those sentient beings have obtained the necessities of life without deficiency and, following the Bodhisattva’s words, have first cultivated and brought to perfection generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration, they further examine the true reality of all phenomena and practice the *prajñāpāramitā*.

When examining them closely, as previously stated, the true nature of all phenomena is found to be unattainable; because it is unattainable, there is no attachment; and because there is no attachment, one does not perceive even the slightest phenomenon as arising or ceasing, or as being defiled or purified.

When they do not apprehend any phenomena, they give rise to no conceptual discrimination regarding anything whatsoever; that is to say, they do not discriminate, "This is hell, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the asuras, or humans, or devas"; nor do they discriminate between those who uphold the precepts and those who violate them; nor do they discriminate between ordinary beings and noble ones; nor do they discriminate, "This is a stream-enterer," up to "this is a bodhisattva or a buddha"; nor do they discriminate between the conditioned and the unconditioned.
Because they are thus free from conceptual discrimination, they gradually realize the noble fruits of the three vehicles as appropriate to their capacities.

"Subhūti, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of generosity, personally cultivates wisdom, encourages others to cultivate wisdom, constantly and correctly extols the practice of the dharma of wisdom, and joyfully praises those who cultivate wisdom."
In this way, Subhūti,
bodhisattva mahāsattvas, abiding in the perfection of generosity, exhort all sentient beings to diligently cultivate wisdom, causing them to attain supreme and ultimate peace and happiness.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, dwelling securely in the perfection of generosity, personally practice generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, and having also exhorted others to practice generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, they further see sentient beings transmigrating through the various realms, undergoing the suffering of birth and death without yet attaining liberation. Desiring to bring them liberation from the suffering of birth and death, they first benefit them with various material requisites, and subsequently sustain them with the supramundane, untainted dharmas through skillful means."
Once those sentient beings have obtained all necessary provisions without deficiency, their bodies and minds become courageous and vigorous;
they are able to abide in inner emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; they are able to abide in suchness up to the inconceivable realm;
they are able to abide in the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; and they are able to cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness up to—
The eight branches of the noble path can cultivate the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
they can cultivate the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; they can cultivate the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality;
they can cultivate the stage of pure observation up to the stage of a Tathāgata; and they can cultivate the Stage of Utmost Joy.
Up to the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), they are able to cultivate the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi;
they are able to cultivate the five eyes and the six supernormal powers; they are able to cultivate the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they are able to cultivate great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity; and they are able to cultivate non-forgetfulness.
The loss of dharmas and the nature of constant equanimity enable one to cultivate all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*),
and all-aspect knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), as well as to cultivate all other boundless Buddha-dharmas.

Because those sentient beings are sustained by untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*), they are liberated from birth and death and attain the bliss of nirvāṇa. "Subhūti, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva,

dwelling in the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*), personally practices various sublime untainted dharmas, encourages others to practice various sublime untainted dharmas, constantly and correctly extols the practice of various sublime untainted dharmas, and joyfully praises those who practice various sublime untainted dharmas."
In this way, Subhūti,
bodhisattva mahāsattvas abide in the perfection of generosity, gathering in sentient beings through untainted dharmas, causing them to escape birth and death and attain the bliss of nirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva mahāsattvas abide in the perfection of generosity, they see sentient beings who are without support or protection, undergoing various sufferings and lacking the necessities of life; they give rise to deep compassion and comfort them, saying:
'I can act as your support and protection, enabling you to be liberated from the suffering you endure.'"

Whatever robes, food and drink, or other requisites you may require, you should all ask for them as you wish; I shall grant you whatever you ask for, so that you may enjoy benefit and happiness throughout the long night.
When you receive the gifts I bestow, do not regard them as the property of another, but accept them as your own. Why is this?
It is because I have accumulated these wealth and goods over a long night of time solely for the sake of your benefit.
"You all should now, with a mind free from hesitation, accept these goods as you please.
Having accepted them, you should first properly utilize them yourselves to cultivate various virtuous deeds;

thereafter, you should give these things to all sentient beings so that they too may cultivate virtue—namely, by causing them to practice generosity, pure ethical discipline, patience, and diligence."
The dhyāna-pāramitā and prajñā-pāramitā also cause them to abide in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;
they also cause them to abide in suchness up to the inconceivable realm;
they also cause them to abide in the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; and they also cause them to practice the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
Furthermore, they cause them to practice the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
they cause them to practice the three gates of liberation; they cause them to practice the eight liberations up to the ten totalities;
they cause them to practice the stage of pure observation up to the stage of the Tathāgata; and they cause them to practice the ultimate...
From the Ground of Joy up to the Ground of Dharma Clouds, they also cause them to practice the gates of dhāraṇī and the gates of samādhi;
they also cause them to practice the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
they also cause them to practice the ten powers of a Tathāgata up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and they also cause them to practice great loving-kindness and great compassion.
They also cause them to practice great joy and great equanimity, as well as the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant abiding in equanimity;
they also cause them to practice all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);
and they also cause them to practice all other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas.

“Subhūti, you should know that after these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have thus instructed sentient beings, they further cause them to practice the various untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) as appropriate, so that they may abide in the fruit of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), or the fruit of a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), or even abide in the enlightenment of a solitary buddha (*pratyekabuddha-bodhi*), or abide in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).”

"In this way, Subhūti, bodhisattva mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of generosity mature sentient beings through skillful means, causing them to be liberated from the miserable destinies and the cycle of birth and death, so that they may realize the nirvāṇa of the three vehicles as appropriate."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) and the other paths to great enlightenment (*mahābodhimārga*), employing skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) to bring sentient beings to maturity?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"There is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, while practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), employs skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*). Seeing sentient beings lacking material resources, with afflictions (*kleśa*) raging intensely, and unable to cultivate wholesome qualities, he says to them out of compassion:
'If you are unable to cultivate wholesome qualities because you lack material resources, I shall bestow upon you various kinds of wealth.'"
"You all must not give rise to afflictions or evil karma; you should correctly practice and train in wholesome virtues such as generosity.

Thus, that bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), appropriately gathers in and sustains all classes of sentient beings: those who are stingy and greedy, he causes to practice generosity, becoming free from attachment to body, life, or wealth;

those who violate the precepts, he causes to practice pure ethical discipline, enabling them to correctly receive and carry out the ten paths of wholesome action, abiding in the morality of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*)—unbroken, unpierced, untainted, unadulterated, and free from grasping.
To those who harbor anger and resentment, they cause them to cultivate patience (*kṣānti*), so that their minds remain unchanging even when subjected to insults and harm;
to those who are indolent, they cause them to cultivate diligence (*vīrya*), practicing all wholesome dharmas as if their hair were on fire;
to those who are distracted, they cause them to cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), so that their minds are constantly tranquil and stable, free from all agitation and movement.
For those who are deluded, they cause them to cultivate sublime wisdom;
for those who are attached to phenomena, they cause them to contemplate the emptiness of phenomena;
and for those who lack other virtues, they cause them to apply diligent effort in cultivating those other virtues.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, dwelling securely in the perfection of ethical discipline, employ skillful means to bring sentient beings to maturity, either liberating them from the sufferings of the evil realms or enabling them to realize the nirvāṇa of the three vehicles.

“Subhūti, you should know that there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the other four pāramitās and the other paths to great enlightenment of a bodhisattva; each is able, through skillful means, to bring sentient beings to maturity by means of all wholesome qualities—either causing them to be liberated from the sufferings of the evil destinies, or causing them to realize the nirvāṇa of the three vehicles—just as was explained at length previously regarding generosity.”
Chapter 30: The Buddha-land (Buddhakṣetra), Part One. At that time, Subhūti had this thought:
"What is the path of the bodhisattva mahāsattva?"
How do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, dwelling therein, don the armor of merit to benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings, and swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes?
The Buddha, knowing his thought, addressed Subhūti, saying: "Subhūti,

you should know that the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of diligence, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom— extending broadly even to all-aspect omniscience and all other immeasurable and boundless buddha-qualities— are all the path of the bodhisattva mahāsattva."
Furthermore, Subhūti!
All phenomena in their entirety constitute the path of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!
What do you think?
Is there even the slightest dharma that Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should not study?
Without studying such dharmas, could Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possibly realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna)?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
There is certainly not even the slightest dharma that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should not study.
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not study these dharmas, they will certainly be unable to attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
Why is this? If a bodhisattva mahāsattva cannot fully know all phenomena, they will not achieve the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, how do the bodhisattva mahāsattvas train in all phenomena?"

Could it be that the Blessed One is engaging in conceptual proliferation where there is no proliferation, by asserting that there are various phenomena which are "this" or "that," "because of this" or "for the sake of this";
that "this phenomenon is mundane" and "this phenomenon is supramundane";
or that "this phenomenon is with outflows" and "this phenomenon is without outflows"?
"This dharma is conditioned; this dharma is unconditioned.
This is the dharma of ordinary beings; this is the dharma of stream-enterers," and so on in detail, "up to: this is the dharma of bodhisattvas; this is the dharma of all buddhas"?
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
All phenomena have a self-nature that is empty.

If all phenomena were not empty by their own nature, then bodhisattva-mahāsattvas would be unable to attain the knowledge of all modes; because all phenomena are empty by their own nature, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are certainly able to realize the knowledge of all modes.
Furthermore, as for what you have said: "If the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is entirely empty, how can bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train in all dharmas?
[This applies] extensively up to: 'How is this the dharma of bodhisattvas and the Buddhas?'"
"Subhūti, you should know this:

if sentient beings were to know that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, then bodhisattva mahāsattvas would not need to train in all phenomena, nor would they be able to attain the knowledge of all aspects (sarvajñajñāna) to proclaim and reveal it to sentient beings."

Because sentient beings do not know that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, the bodhisattva mahāsattva must certainly train in all phenomena and, having realized the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), proclaim and reveal it to all sentient beings.
"Subhūti, you should know that when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas first begin to train in the bodhisattva path, they should carefully examine: 'The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is unapprehendable;

it is produced solely by false conceptualization. I shall thoroughly investigate how the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is ultimately empty, and I should not have any attachment therein—meaning I should not be attached to form (*rūpa*), nor should I be attached to feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*); and so on, in detail, until I should not be attached to any of the practices of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, nor should I be attached to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) of the Buddhas.'"

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty; one should not cling to emptiness as being emptiness. Within emptiness, even emptiness itself cannot be apprehended, so how could there be an emptiness that can cling to emptiness!

"Subhūti, you should know that when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas observe all phenomena in this way, although they do not cling to the intrinsic nature of phenomena, they constantly and diligently train in all phenomena without ever becoming weary."

Abiding in this training, this bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the differences in the mental activities of sentient beings, specifically examining: "In what state do the mental activities of these sentient beings reside?"
Having observed this, he understands that mind as it truly is: it merely functions within the objects grasped by false conceptualization.
At that time, the bodhisattva thinks:
"Since that mind functions within the objects grasped by false conceptualization, it will not be difficult for me to bring about its liberation."
Having formed this thought, that bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells securely in the perfection of wisdom and, through skillful means, instructs and exhorts all sentient beings, saying:
"You all should now distance yourselves from the objects of attachment grasped through false conceptualization, and enter into the true Dharma to cultivate all wholesome practices."
He further spoke these words:
"You should now practice giving; you shall thereby obtain all necessary provisions without lack. However, do not rely on this and give rise to arrogance or negligence."
Why is this? Because herein there is absolutely nothing substantial to be found.

You should now practice pure ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; you shall thereby attain the fullness of various meritorious qualities, yet do not rely upon these to give rise to arrogance or negligence.
Why is this? Because herein there is absolutely nothing substantial to be found.

To speak at length, you should now practice for the fruit of stream-entry, up to and including unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, as well as the other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas; yet, do not rely upon these to give rise to arrogance or negligence.
Why is this? Because herein there is absolutely nothing substantial to be found.

When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell securely in the skillful means of the *prajñāpāramitā* and provide instruction and admonition to sentient beings, they practice the bodhisattva path without any attachment.

Why is this? Because the nature of all phenomena (dharmas) should not be clung to; whether it be that which clings or that which is clung to, both lack intrinsic nature (svabhāva), for the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty.

“Subhūti, you should know that when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the bodhisattva path in this way, they do not abide in any phenomena at all. Taking non-abiding as their skillful means, although they practice from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, they do not abide in any of them. To speak extensively, even though they practice the conduct of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment of the Buddhas, and other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas, they do not abide in any of them.”
Why is this? Because the nature of such practice and all its modes of activity are entirely empty; therein, there is absolutely nothing upon which to abide.
"Sudhana, you should know this!"
Although the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to attain the fruit of a stream-enterer, and so forth, up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, they do not wish to realize or abide therein.
Why is this so? It is because there are two conditions. What are these two?
First, that fruit is entirely devoid of intrinsic nature; both the abider and the abode are unobtainable.
Second, they do not give rise to contentment with those [attainments].
Therefore, they do not wish to realize and abide therein; that is to say, the assembly of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constantly reflects:

"I must certainly attain the fruit of a Stream-enterer up to the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha; it is not possible that I shall not attain them. However, I should not realize and abide within them."

Why is this? Since I first resolved upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, at all times I have had no other thought but to seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Since I am certain to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, how could I dwell in any other fruit in the interim?

“Subhūti, you should know that from the first generation of the mind of awakening until entering the bodhisattva’s correct state of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*), this bodhisattva mahāsattva never entertains any other thought, but seeks only unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.”

"Subhūti, you should know that from the time this bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the first bhūmi, continuing successively until they attain the tenth bhūmi, they never harbor any divergent thoughts, but seek only unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Subhūti, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva seeks exclusively for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; at all times their mind is undistracted, and every physical, verbal, and mental action they initiate is invariably accompanied by the mind of enlightenment.
“Subhūti, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the mind of enlightenment, gives rise to the path of enlightenment and does not allow his mind to be disturbed by other matters.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If all phenomena are ultimately unarisen, how do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas give rise to the path to enlightenment?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“It is so! It is thus!”
It is so! All dharmas are non-arising; furthermore, how is it that those who do nothing and go nowhere know that all dharmas are non-arising? It is because they know all dharmas are non-arising.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Whether the Buddhas appear in the world or do not appear in the world, is it not the case that the dharma-nature of all phenomena remains eternally constant by its very nature?"
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"

However, sentient beings are unable to comprehend that the *dharmatā* of all phenomena is eternally abiding by its very nature; thus, they transmigrate through birth and death, undergoing various sufferings and afflictions.

To benefit them, the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas give rise to the path to enlightenment (*bodhimārga*), and by means of this path to enlightenment, they cause all sentient beings to ultimately be liberated from the manifold sufferings of birth and death, realizing the eternal, blissful, and cool state of *nirvāṇa*.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain awakening by means of a path that has arisen?"
The Buddha said,
“It is not so. [He replied,] “World-Honored One!”
"Is it by means of the path of non-arising that one attains bodhi?
The Buddha said, "It is not so."
“World-Honored One!
Is bodhi attained by means of a path that is produced, or by one that is unproduced?
The Buddha said:
"Not so! "World-Honored One,
is awakening attained by means of a path that is neither arising nor non-arising?"
The Buddha said, “It is not so.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If that is so, how shall a bodhisattva mahāsattva attain awakening?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Awakening is not attained by means of the path, nor is it attained apart from the path."
"Why is this? Awakening is itself the path, and the path is itself awakening; therefore, it is not attained by means of either the path or what is not the path.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again, saying:

"If awakening is itself the path, and the path is itself awakening, then would it not be the case that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having already attained the path to awakening, should have already attained awakening?"

If that is so, for what reason did the Blessed One further teach the bodhisattvas the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, the thirty-two marks, the eighty minor characteristics, and other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas, commanding them to cultivate and realize them?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Do you suppose that the Buddha has attained awakening?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
Why is this? Because the Buddha is enlightenment and enlightenment is the Buddha; therefore, one should not say that the Buddha attains enlightenment.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"So it is! So it is! Nevertheless, as for what you have asked: 'Since a bodhisattva mahāsattva has already attained the path to awakening, should they not have already attained awakening?'"
"Subhūti, you should know this:
if the bodhisattva mahāsattvas have not yet perfected the cultivation of the path to enlightenment, how can it be said that they have already attained enlightenment?"

“Subhūti, you should know that when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have fully perfected the pāramitās of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—extending broadly even to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) and other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas—they immediately thereafter, by means of the wisdom associated with the vajra-like samādhi in a single moment, forever sever the continuity of the heavy habitual tendencies (*dausthulya-vāsanā*) of both the afflictive and cognitive obstructions. They then realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and are designated as Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, having attained great mastery over all phenomena.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva purify and adorn a buddha-field?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“From their first generation of the mind of awakening until they reach the ultimate goal, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constantly purify the three types of coarse burdens of their own body, speech, and mind, and also purify the three types of coarse burdens of the body, speech, and mind of others; thus, they are able to adorn and purify the Buddha-lands in which they dwell.”
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What are the three kinds of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) regarding the bodily, vocal, and mental actions of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If there is taking life, taking what is not given, or sexual misconduct—these three unwholesome acts are called the bodhisattva’s bodily karma of heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).
If there is false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, or idle chatter—these four unwholesome acts are called the bodhisattva’s vocal karma of heaviness.
If there is covetousness, malice, or wrong view—these three unwholesome acts are called the bodhisattva’s mental karma of heaviness."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Whatever mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is characterized by stinginess, immorality, anger, laziness, distraction, or corrupted wisdom is also called a 'gross heaviness' (dauṣṭhulya)."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s aggregate of ethical discipline, aggregate of concentration, aggregate of wisdom, aggregate of liberation, and aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation are all impure, these are also called 'gross heaviness' (dauṣṭhulya)."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is far removed from the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path—and so on, up to and including all the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening of all buddhas—this too is called a 'coarse heaviness' (dauṣṭhulya)."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes greedily attached to the fruit of a stream-enterer up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, this is also called a heavy burden (dauṣṭhulya)."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to the notion of the aggregate of form, up to the notion of the aggregate of consciousness, this is also called a heavy burden (*dauṣṭhulya*).

To speak at length, even if they give rise to the notion of all the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, as well as the notion of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas, this is also called a heavy burden."

To give rise to the notion of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), the notion of a śrāvaka, the notion of a pratyekabuddha, the notion of a bodhisattva, or the notion of a Tathāgata is also called *dausthulya* (coarseness/heaviness).

To give rise to the notion of hell-beings, the notion of animals, the notion of hungry ghosts, the notion of humans, the notion of devas, the notion of male, or the notion of female is also called *dausthulya*.
To give rise to the notion of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the notion of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), or the notion of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is also called *dausthulya*.
The perception of the wholesome, the unwholesome, the outflowing, the non-outflowing, the mundane, the supramundane, the conditioned, and the unconditioned is also termed "coarseness" (*dauṣṭhulya*).

“Subhūti, you should know that all such immeasurable and boundless attachments to phenomena, as well as the false conceptualizations of sentient beings, along with the physical, verbal, and mental karmas they initiate, and their corresponding lack of functional capacity— all these are termed *dausthulya* (coarseness).”
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should completely abandon these coarse and heavy impediments (*dauṣṭhulya*). "Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they distance themselves from such aforementioned coarse and heavy impediments; they personally practice the *dānapāramitā* and also encourage others to practice the *dānapāramitā*. If sentient beings require food, they give them food; if they require drink, they give them drink; if they require other necessities, they give them those other necessities. According to the place, the time, and the specific items required, they bestow everything upon them. Just as they themselves practice various forms of giving, they likewise encourage others to do so."

Having given in this manner, he takes these roots of goodness and shares them equally with all sentient beings, dedicating them toward the adornment and purification of the Buddha-land where he shall dwell, so that it may be swiftly perfected for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva personally practices the precepts up to the perfection of wisdom, and also encourages others to practice the precepts up to the perfection of wisdom.

Having performed these deeds, they take these roots of virtue and, sharing them equally with all sentient beings, dedicate them toward the adornment and purification of the Buddha-fields where they shall dwell, so that they may swiftly be perfected for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who,
by the power of his supernormal vows, fills the trichiliocosm with the most excellent seven treasures and offers them to the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the stūpas of the Buddha."
Having given the gift, he joyfully makes this great vow:

"By means of these roots of goodness I have planted, may I share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward the adornment of a pure Buddha-field; may my land be adorned with the seven treasures, and may all sentient beings enjoy various precious jewels as they wish, without any attachment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who,
by the power of their supernormal vows, play and strike countless sublime musical instruments among the devas and humans to make offerings to the Three Jewels and the stūpas of the Buddhas."
Having made the offering, he joyfully gave rise to this great vow:

"By means of these roots of goodness I have planted, I shall share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward the adornment of a pure Buddha-field. May music such as this be constantly performed in my land, so that sentient beings who hear it will experience joy in body and mind without falling into attachment."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who,

by the power of their supernormal vows, fill the three-thousandfold world system with all manner of exquisite incense and flowers from among humans and devas, and offer them to the Three Jewels and the stūpas of the Buddhas."
Having made these offerings, he joyfully gave rise to this great vow:

"By means of these roots of goodness I have planted, I shall share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward a pure and adorned buddha-field. May my land always possess such exquisite fragrant flowers, so that sentient beings, upon using them, experience physical and mental delight without any attachment."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, through the power of their supernormal vows, prepare exquisite foods of a hundred flavors to make offerings to the Buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, śrāvakas, and the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."
Having made this offering, he joyfully gave rise to this great vow:

"By means of these roots of goodness I have planted, I shall share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward the attainment of a pure and adorned buddha-field. When I attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may all sentient beings within my land partake of such food of a hundred flavors, which nourishes and gladdens their bodies and minds, yet leaves them free from craving and attachment."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, by the power of their supernormal vows, prepare various kinds of exquisite celestial and human unguents and fine, soft garments, and offer them to the Buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, śrāvakas, and the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; or they may give them to the Dharma and to the stūpas of the Buddha."
Having given these gifts, he joyfully makes this great vow:

"By means of these roots of virtue I have planted, I share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward the attainment of a pure and adorned Buddha-field. When I attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may all the sentient beings within my land always obtain such clothing and fragrant ointments, enjoying them as they wish without any attachment."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, by the power of their supernormal vows, prepare various objects of the five exquisite sensual pleasures among humans and gods—arising according to their wishes—to make offerings to the Buddhas, the shrines of the Buddhas, the pratyekabuddhas, the śrāvakas, and the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and to bestow them upon other sentient beings."
Having given the gift, he joyfully makes this great vow:

"By means of these roots of virtue I have planted, I share them equally with all sentient beings and dedicate them toward the attainment of a pure and adorned Buddha-field. When I attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, may all the sentient beings within my land have whatever sublime objects of form, sound, fragrance, flavor, and touch they desire appear to them the very moment they think of them, so that they may enjoy them with joy and without attachment."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the profound perfection of wisdom, exerting themselves with courageous diligence and making great vows; they themselves abide in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, and they also encourage others to abide in internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence; and so on, in detail, until they themselves cultivate unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and also encourage others to cultivate unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Having performed these deeds, he further made this vow:
"When I attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may all sentient beings within my buddha-field never be separated from such various merits as these."

"In this way, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, by means of this practice and vow they are able to adorn and purify the buddha-fields in which they dwell."

“Subhūti, you should know that for as long as these bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the path to awakening, they must fulfill the practices and vows they have undertaken; for that same duration, they must train themselves with diligent effort.”

By virtue of these causes and conditions, one is able to personally accomplish all wholesome dharmas and can also cause others to gradually accomplish all wholesome dharmas; one is able to personally cultivate and attain a body adorned with the most excellent marks and signs, and can also cause others to gradually cultivate and attain a body adorned with the most excellent marks and signs, because of being sustained by vast merit.

“Subhūti, you should know that once these bodhisattva mahāsattvas have brought their practices and vows to fulfillment, at the time they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening in their respective adorned and purified buddha-fields, the sentient beings they have transformed will also be born in those lands, where they shall together enjoy the great Dharma-joy of the pure lands.”
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 535. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Three: Chapter on the Buddha-lands, Number Thirty-Two. "Furthermore, Subhūti!

These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should cultivate such purification of buddha-fields as follows: that in those lands, one never hears of the three evil destinies; nor does one hear of various wrong views; nor does one hear of the poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion; nor does one hear of the physical forms of men and women; nor does one hear of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; nor does one hear of disagreeable matters such as impermanence and suffering; nor does one hear of the acquisition of material requisites; nor does one hear of the grasping at a self or what belongs to a self; nor does one hear of latent tendencies, obsessions, or fetters; nor does one hear of inverted attachments; nor does one hear of the conventional designations of the distinctions between the fruits of sentient beings.

One hears only sounds such as emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), non-arising (*anutpāda*), non-ceasing (*anirodha*), and the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).

That is to say, according to the diverse inclinations of sentient beings, within external and internal objects such as groves of trees, subtle winds constantly strike against one another, giving rise to various kinds of exquisite sounds.

Within all sounds it is said: "All phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature; because they lack intrinsic nature, they are empty; because they are empty, they are signless; because they are signless, they are wishless; because they are wishless, they are unarisen; because they are unarisen, they are unceasing."
Because these phenomena are primordially quiescent and by nature in nirvāṇa, whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, the dharmatā of phenomena remains eternally as it is.

That is to say, all phenomena are without intrinsic nature, empty, and so forth; within that buddha-field, all classes of sentient beings—whether by day or night, whether standing, walking, lying down, or sitting—constantly hear the sound of such sublime Dharma.

“Subhūti, you should know that when these bodhisattva mahāsattvas, each dwelling in their own adorned and purified buddha-fields, realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the ten directions will all together praise the names of those respective Buddhas. If any sentient beings hear such names of the Buddhas, they will certainly attain non-retrogression from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

When these bodhisattva mahāsattvas, each dwelling in their own adorned and purified buddha-fields, attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they shall proclaim the sublime Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.
Upon hearing this, sentient beings will certainly not give rise to doubt as to whether it is the Dharma or non-Dharma, and so forth.

Why is this? Because those classes of sentient beings realize that all phenomena are themselves suchness (*tathatā*), the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); everything is the Dharma, and there is nothing that is not the Dharma.
Thus it is, Subhūti! All these bodhisattva mahāsattvas are able to adorn and purify such buddha-fields.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have sentient beings as their objects of conversion who possess unwholesome roots; they have not planted roots of virtue under the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, or śrāvakas; because they are influenced by evil associates and separated from virtuous friends, they do not hear the true Dharma. They are constantly ensnared and concealed by various views of a self, a sentient being, and other dogmatic positions, falling into the biased attachments of the two extremes of nihilism and eternalism.

Those sentient beings give rise to false attachments on their own and constantly teach others to do the same; they conceive the notion of the Three Jewels regarding what is not the Three Jewels, and conversely, they claim that which is the Three Jewels is not the Three Jewels; they slander the True Dharma and praise false teachings.
Due to these causes and conditions, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, they fall into the various evil destinies and undergo manifold sufferings.

These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, each dwelling in their own land, realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; seeing those sentient beings wandering in saṃsāra and undergoing immeasurable suffering, they employ supernatural powers and skillful means to guide and transform them, causing them to abandon wrong views and abide in right view, and to emerge from the evil destinies to be born in the human realm.

Furthermore, by means of various supernatural powers and skillful expedients, they transform and guide them so that they abide within the assembly of those destined for right certainty (samyaktva-niyāma), never again falling into the various evil realms.

They further cause them to cultivate sublime roots of goodness, so that at the end of their lives they attain rebirth in a majestic and pure Buddha-land, where they enjoy the Mahāyāna Dharma-bliss of that pure land.
"So it is, Subhūti! These bodhisattva mahāsattvas are all able to thus adorn and purify buddha-fields.

Because the lands they inhabit are utterly pure, the sentient beings born there do not give rise to false conceptualizations or hesitations regarding any phenomena, such as: 'This is a wholesome dharma; this is an unwholesome dharma'; 'this is a determinate dharma; this is an indeterminate dharma'; 'this is a mundane dharma; this is a supramundane dharma'; 'this is a contaminated dharma; this is an uncontaminated dharma'; 'this is a conditioned dharma; this is an unconditioned dharma.'"
All such conceptualizations and hesitations will ultimately not arise.

By virtue of these causes and conditions, those sentient beings will certainly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and turn the sublime wheel of Dharma to deliver the multitudes of sentient beings.
“Subhūti, you should know that this is the mark of the merit of a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s purification of a buddha-field, which brings benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings.”
Chapter 31: Proclaiming the Transformation; Part Three of the Third Division; Chapter Thirty-One, Part One. At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Does this bodhisattva mahāsattva abide in the group of those destined for certainty (niyata-rāśi) or in the group of those not so destined (aniyata-rāśi)?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas all abide in the stage of certainty.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In which fixed destiny does this bodhisattva mahāsattva abide?
Is it that of the śrāvaka vehicle,
or that of the pratyekabuddha vehicle?"
"Is this the Unsurpassed Vehicle?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the Unsurpassed Vehicle."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"At what time is this bodhisattva mahāsattva said to abide in the fixed category [of those destined for enlightenment]?
Is it at the initial generation of the mind?"
"Is it the stage of non-retrogression?
Is it the final existence?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Whether these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have first generated the mind of awakening, are at the stage of non-retrogression, or are in their final existence, they all abide in the fixed assembly.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Do these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who abide in the fixed assembly fall into the evil destinies?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in the fixed category [of those destined for enlightenment], they will certainly not fall into the various evil destinies.
He further addressed Subhūti:
“What do you think?
Do those in the eighth stage, stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, or pratyekabuddhas fall into the evil destinies? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"So too, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, practice the perfections from generosity up to wisdom, as well as other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas, thereby subduing and severing all evil and unwholesome states."
For this reason, it is impossible that they would fall into the various evil realms;
nor is it possible that they would be reborn in the long-lived heavens, for in those places, the various supreme wholesome dharmas cannot be put into practice.

It is impossible for this bodhisattva-mahāsattva to be born in a remote borderland, or among the Dardas or Mlecchas; that is to say, it is impossible for him to be in such a place where he cannot practice sublime and wholesome dharmas, where he frequently gives rise to evil views and lacks faith in cause and effect, where he constantly delights in practicing various defiled and evil deeds, and where he hears not of the Triple Gem nor encounters the fourfold assembly.

It is impossible for a bodhisattva-mahāsattva to be born into a family of wrong views—that is, to be born into such a family where one clings to various evil perspectives, denies the existence of wholesome and unwholesome actions as well as their results, fails to cultivate virtues, and delights in committing various evils; therefore, bodhisattvas are not born into such families.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

It is impossible for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who have first resolved upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment to undertake the practice of the ten unwholesome paths of action with a superior intention.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, accomplishes such roots of goodness and merit, they will not be reborn in an evil realm.”

For what reason does the World-Honored One frequently recount for the assembly his own past lives in hundreds of thousands of various ways, including those in which he was born in evil realms; at such times, where were his roots of goodness?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not receive bodies in evil realms due to defiled karma; rather, for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, they intentionally and by means of their vows receive those bodies. Therefore, one should not cite this as a difficulty."
He further addressed Subhūti: "What do you think?

Are there any pratyekabuddhas or arhats who, like the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, possess such skillful means—having accomplished such superior skillful means—that when they take birth in the bodies of animals and a hunter comes wishing to harm them, they give rise to unsurpassed patience and compassion, and for the sake of bringing that person benefit and happiness, they sacrifice their own life rather than harming him?"
Subhūti replied, “The Pratyekabuddhas do not possess such things.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"By this causal condition, it should be known that because a bodhisattva desires to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, to swiftly fulfill great compassion, and to rapidly realize great enlightenment, although they may undergo various forms of animal existence, they are not defiled by the faults of such animals."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In which roots of goodness do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide when they assume bodies in evil realms for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"What roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) are there that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should not bring to fulfillment?

Indeed, for the sake of attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, all roots of goodness must be brought to fulfillment by the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. That is to say, from the first generation of the mind of awakening until sitting upon the seat of sublime enlightenment, there is no root of goodness that a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should not fulfill."

One must fully perfect all wholesome dharmas to attain unsurpassed, right, and complete enlightenment; it is absolutely impossible to attain unsurpassed, right, and complete enlightenment if even a single wholesome dharma has not been perfected.

Therefore, Subhūti, from the first generation of the mind of awakening until sitting upon the seat of sublime enlightenment, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas constantly train to perfect all wholesome dharmas. Having so trained, they shall attain the knowledge of all aspects, forever severing the continuity of all habitual tendencies, and thereby realize the knowledge of all modes.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is it that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having accomplished various kinds of pure, noble, and untainted dharmas, are born in evil destinies and receive the bodies of animals?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Is the Tathāgata endowed with all pure, noble, and untainted [qualities]?"
Subhūti replied, “The Tathāgata has accomplished all pure, noble, and untainted dharmas.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“What do you think? If the Tathāgata were to manifest a body belonging to the realm of animals, would he not perform the work of a Buddha for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings? Subhūti replied:
“The Tathāgata manifests a body belonging to the animal realm to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings and perform the works of a Buddha.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “What do you think?”
"When the Tathāgata manifests in the form of an animal, is he truly an animal that experiences that suffering? Subhūti replied,
"When the Tathāgata manifests in the form of an animal, he is not truly an animal and does not experience that suffering."
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"It is the same for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; although they have fully accomplished various kinds of pure, noble, and untainted dharmas, they intentionally take birth in the bodies of animals through their vows and aspirations in order to bring sentient beings to maturity, maturing those beings as is appropriate."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, what do you think?
Is there an Arhat whose outflows are forever exhausted who can manifest a transformation body to perform various activities, and by means of those activities, produce joy in others?"

Subhūti replied, “There are arhats whose outflows are forever exhausted who can manifest emanated bodies to perform various activities, and through those activities, they cause others to give rise to joy.”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"It is likewise for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; although they have fully accomplished various pure, noble, and untainted dharmas, for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, they intentionally and by vow take on the bodies of animals to perform the works of Buddhas."
"Although he assumes such a body, he does not undergo the various sufferings and afflictions experienced by them,
nor is he defiled by their faults. Furthermore,
Subhūti, what do you think?"

Suppose there were a skilled illusionist or his disciple who conjured various things such as elephants and horses by means of illusion, causing a great multitude to see them and rejoice with leaping joy; would there be any real elephants, horses, or the like therein?
Subhūti replied, “In that regard,
there are no real elephants, horses, or such things.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"So too it is with the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: although they have fully accomplished various pure, noble, and untainted dharmas, for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, they intentionally take on the bodies of animals through their vows."
"Although they take on those bodies, they are in reality not those [beings], nor are they defiled by the faults of those [beings].
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess such vast skillful means that, although they have fully accomplished various pure, noble, and untainted dharmas, for the sake of sentient beings, they intentionally and through the skillful means of their vows assume various bodies, manifesting whatever benefit is appropriate according to the needs of each."
“World-Honored One!

In what dharmas do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide so that they are able to exercise such skillful means that, although they assume various bodies among animals and other realms, they are not defiled by their faults?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"All bodhisattva mahāsattvas, dwelling in profound prajñāpāramitā, are able to exercise such skillful means."

By the power of such skillful means, although they travel to Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions and manifest various bodies to benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings, they do not give rise to any defiled attachment therein.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not apprehend anything at all among all phenomena; that is, they do not apprehend the defiler, the defiled, nor the causes and conditions of defilement.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature.
"Sudhana, you should know this!
Emptiness cannot defile emptiness; emptiness cannot defile other phenomena, nor can any other phenomenon defile emptiness. Why is this so?
Even emptiness itself cannot be apprehended within emptiness, let alone any other phenomenon that could be apprehended!

This is called the emptiness of the unapprehendable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*). Abiding therein, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas are able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and turn the sublime wheel of Dharma to deliver the multitudes of sentient beings.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Do Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas perform such skillful means by abiding solely in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, or do they also abide in other dharmas?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Is there any other dharma not encompassed by the profound perfection of wisdom, such that you now ask this question again?"
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Since the intrinsic nature of the profound perfection of wisdom is itself empty, how can it be said that the profound perfection of wisdom encompasses all phenomena?"
"In the state where dharmas are empty, it cannot be said that there are dharmas that are either included or not included.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Is it not the case that the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is empty?"
Subhūti replied: “So it is! So it is!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"If all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, would it not be the case that within emptiness all phenomena are subsumed? Subhūti replied:
"So it is! So it is! the Buddha told Subhūti.

"For this reason, one should know that the profound *prajñāpāramitā* encompasses all phenomena; thus, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they are able to bring about the benefit of sentient beings through such skillful means."
At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, abide in the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena and thereby elicit the perfection of supernormal powers? Abiding in this perfection of supernormal powers, how is he able to travel to the buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, to make offerings and pay respect to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and to hear and receive the true Dharma from those Buddhas, planting various roots of goodness?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they thoroughly observe that the self-nature of all the buddha-fields in the ten directions—as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—as well as the assemblies of those buddhas and the teachings they proclaim, is entirely empty. There are only conventional designations and names spoken of as ‘buddha-fields,’ ‘assemblies of buddhas,’ and ‘teachings. Furthermore, the self-nature of these conventional designations and names is also empty.”
“Subhūti, you should know this!

If the worlds of the ten directions, the assemblies of Buddhas, and the names and intrinsic natures of the teachings they have established were not empty, then the emptiness spoken of would be only partial. Since the emptiness spoken of does not become merely partial, the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is entirely empty; this principle is all-encompassing, non-dual, and without distinction.”

"Subhūti, you should know that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, by means of skillful means through the universal contemplation of emptiness, they are able to bring forth the sublime perfection of supernormal powers."

Abiding in this perfection of supernormal powers, one is further able to evoke the subtle and sublime superknowledges of the divine eye, the divine ear, the power of transformation, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, and the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows.

“Subhūti, you should know that it is not apart from the perfection of supernormal powers (abhijñā-pāramitā) that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to spontaneously mature sentient beings, purify buddha-fields, and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

Therefore, this perfection of supernormal powers is the path to enlightenment; all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas rely upon this path to seek and proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. While seeking and proceeding, they are able to personally fulfill all wholesome dharmas and also encourage others to cultivate various wholesome dharmas; yet, although they perform these deeds, they remain without attachment to them.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas know that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all wholesome dharmas is empty; they do not have any attachment to that which is empty of intrinsic nature. If there were attachment, there would be a relish for it; because there is no attachment, there is also no relish.
Because there is no relishing within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the taster, the tasted, and the causal conditions for tasting are all unfindable within the dharma of emptiness.
"Subhūti, you should know this!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the profound perfection of wisdom and dwelling securely in the perfection of supernormal powers, brings forth the pure divine eye that transcends that of humans; with this divine eye, they contemplate how the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty.

Because they perceive that all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, they do not engage in the fabrication of various karmas based on the characteristics of phenomena; yet, although they teach such a Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, they do not apprehend the characteristics of sentient beings nor the conceptual designations applied to them.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of non-apprehension as a skillful method, brings forth the sublime supernormal powers of a bodhisattva, and employs these supernormal powers to perform all the deeds that ought to be done.

“Subhūti, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva, with the utterly pure divine eye that transcends that of humans, surveys throughout the ten directions all Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
having seen them, he manifests the supernormal power of the knowledge of traveling through space and proceeds to benefit those [beings].”
For all classes of sentient beings, he may bring benefit through the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom;
or he may bring benefit through the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;
or he may bring benefit through the meditative concentrations, the immeasurables, and the formless attainments; or he may bring benefit through the liberations, the samādhis, and so forth.

They bring benefit by entering meditative attainments (*samāpatti*); or they bring benefit by means of the gates of liberation—emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*);
or they bring benefit by means of various other sublime and wholesome dharmas;
or they bring benefit by means of the dharmas of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and all buddhas.

"This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, wandering through the worlds of the ten directions, if he sees sentient beings who are largely characterized by stinginess and greed, gives rise to deep compassion and teaches them this Dharma:
'You sentient beings should practice generosity.'"
Those who are stingy and greedy undergo the suffering of poverty; because of their poverty, they lack majesty and virtue, and are unable to benefit themselves, let alone others!

Therefore, you all should diligently practice giving; thus you will bring peace and happiness to yourselves as well as to others. Do not, out of poverty, devour one another, for in so doing, neither of you will be liberated from the sufferings of the evil realms.
"If he sees sentient beings who have violated the pure precepts, he gives rise to deep compassion and teaches them this Dharma:

'You sentient beings should maintain the pure precepts. Those who break the precepts undergo the suffering of the evil realms; a person who breaks the precepts has no majestic virtue and cannot benefit themselves, much less others!'"

Due to the causes and conditions of breaking the precepts, one falls into the various evil realms, where the ripening of suffering is so agonizing and unbearable that one cannot even save oneself, let alone others!
Therefore, you all should maintain pure precepts; you should not allow a mind that violates the precepts to remain for even a single thought-moment, much less for a long period of time!
"Do not give rein to your own minds, lest you later feel sorrow and regret.

"If he sees sentient beings who are further inflamed with mutual anger and resentment, harboring grudges against one another and harming each other, he generates deep compassion and teaches them this Dharma:
'You sentient beings should cultivate patience; do not harbor mutual anger, resentment, or harm one another.'"
All states of anger and resentment are contrary to wholesome dharmas; they increase unwholesome dharmas and bring about present ruin.

Because of this anger and resentment, when your bodies perish and your lives end, you shall fall into the evil realms and undergo intense suffering from which there will be no prospect of escape for a long time. Therefore, you should not allow anger and resentment to remain within you for even a single moment of thought, much less permit them to continue in succession for a long duration!
"You all should now take one another as objects of mutual concern, giving rise to loving-kindness and compassion to perform deeds of benefit.
"If he sees sentient beings who are indolent and lazy, he gives rise to deep pity and preaches this Dharma to them:

'You sentient beings should be diligent and energetic; do not be indolent and lazy regarding wholesome dharmas. Those who are indolent cannot accomplish any wholesome dharmas or any sublime matters.'"

Because of this, you will fall into the various evil destinies and undergo boundless suffering; therefore, you should not allow a lazy mind to persist for even a single moment, much less let it continue for a long duration!
"If he sees sentient beings who have lost mindfulness, whose minds are distracted, and whose hearts are not at peace, he gives rise to deep compassion and teaches them this Dharma:

'You sentient beings should cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Do not give rise to thoughts of lost mindfulness or distraction; such states of mind do not accord with wholesome dharmas, but increase unwholesome dharmas and bring about present decline and loss.'"

Because of this, when your bodies perish and your lives end, you will fall into the evil realms and undergo boundless suffering; therefore, you should not allow a mind associated with forgetfulness and distraction to remain for even a single moment, much less for a long duration in continuous succession!
"If he sees sentient beings who are foolish and possess evil wisdom, he gives rise to deep compassion and teaches them this Dharma:

'You sentient beings should cultivate superior wisdom and not give rise to evil wisdom; for those who give rise to evil wisdom cannot even proceed to the various happy realms, much less attain liberation!'"

By reason of this evil wisdom, you shall fall into the miserable realms and undergo boundless suffering; therefore, you should not allow a mind associated with such foolish and evil wisdom to remain for even a single moment, much less permit it to continue for a long duration.
"If he sees sentient beings who have much greed, he gives rise to deep compassion and employs skillful means to lead them to practice the contemplation of impurity.
If he sees sentient beings who have much anger, he gives rise to deep compassion and employs skillful means to lead them to practice the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion."
If he sees sentient beings who are full of delusion, he gives rise to deep compassion and employs skillful means to lead them to practice the contemplation of dependent origination.
If he sees sentient beings who are full of pride, he gives rise to deep compassion and employs skillful means to lead them to practice the contemplation of the elements.

If he sees sentient beings who are full of discursive thought and investigation, he gives rise to deep compassion and employs skillful means to lead them to practice mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).

If he sees sentient beings who have lost the right path, he gives rise to deep compassion and employs skillful means to cause them to enter the right path—whether it be the path of the Śrāvaka, the path of the Pratyekabuddha, the path of the Bodhisattva, or the path of the Tathāgata—and employs skillful means to teach them this Dharma:
"The intrinsic nature you grasp at is entirely empty; within the dharma of emptiness there can be nothing to grasp, for the characteristic of emptiness consists in the absence of grasping."

"Thus it is, Subhūti! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they must abide in the perfection of supernormal powers (abhijñā-pāramitā) before they can freely proclaim the true Dharma to benefit, bring peace, and happiness to all sentient beings."

Subhūti, you should know that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva is far removed from the perfection of supernormal powers (abhijñā-pāramitā), they will be unable to freely proclaim the true Dharma and bring about the welfare and happiness of sentient beings.

Subhūti, you should know that just as a bird without wings cannot fly freely through the sky to reach distant places, so it is with bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: if they lack the perfection of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-pāramitā*), they cannot freely proclaim the sublime Dharma or perform deeds for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings.

Therefore, Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they should bring forth the perfection of supernormal powers. If they bring forth the perfection of supernormal powers, they will be able to freely proclaim the true Dharma, benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings according to their wishes.
“Subhūti, you should know that bodhisattva mahāsattvas,
with their most pure divine eye that transcends that of humans, survey all the Buddha-worlds in the ten directions,
as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and observe the sentient beings born therein; having seen them, they lead [them]...”
He manifests the supernormal power of the knowledge of miraculous feats and, in the space of a mere moment, travels to that realm. There, with the knowledge of others' minds,
he understands as they truly are the minds and mental factors of those sentient beings, and according to what is appropriate for them, he teaches the essentials of the Dharma— namely,
the teachings on generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, or the four foundations of mindfulness.
Up to and including the eight branches of the noble path; or it speaks of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions;
or it speaks of the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
or it speaks of the eight liberations up to the ten totalities; or it speaks of the gates of dhāraṇī and the gates of samādhi; or it speaks of...
From internal emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature;
or speaking of suchness up to the inconceivable realm; or speaking of the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
or speaking of conditions from causal conditions up to dominant conditions; or speaking of all phenomena produced from conditions; or speaking of ignorance up to old age and death.
He may teach various doors of the aggregates, bases, and elements;
he may teach the path of the śrāvakas, the path of the pratyekabuddhas, or the path of the bodhisattvas;
he may teach awakening or nirvāṇa, so that those sentient beings, having heard these teachings, all obtain supreme benefit and peace.
“Subhūti, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of the most pure divine ear that transcends that of humans and gods, is able to hear the voices of all humans and non-humans.”

By means of this divine ear, they hear everywhere throughout the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions—as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—all the true Dharma spoken by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas. Having heard it, they receive and uphold it, contemplate its meaning and intent, and according to the Dharma they have heard, they are able to proclaim it to sentient beings as it truly is. They may speak of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom; speaking extensively, they may even speak of bodhi or nirvāṇa, causing those sentient beings to obtain supreme benefit and peace and happiness upon hearing this Dharma.

“Subhūti, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of the most pure supernormal power of knowing the minds of others, truly understands the minds and mental factors of all classes of sentient beings. According to what is appropriate for them, he teaches the essentials of the Dharma—namely, from the discourse on generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, and so forth, even up to awakening or nirvāṇa—so that once those sentient beings have heard this Dharma, they all obtain supreme benefit and peace.”

“Subhūti, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives with purified wisdom, truly recalls and knows the distinctions in the names and so forth of the Buddhas of the past and their assemblies of disciples. If there are sentient beings who would benefit from hearing accounts of past lives, he then proclaims those accounts of past lives for them. By means of this skillful method, he teaches the True Dharma—namely, teaching from the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, and so on extensively, even teaching about awakening or nirvāṇa—so that when those sentient beings have heard this Dharma, they all obtain supreme benefit and peace.”

"Subhūti, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of the extremely swift superknowledge of the power of spiritual travel (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna-abhijñā*), goes to the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, to attend upon and make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. Having planted roots of goodness under those Buddhas, he returns to his own land to speak of the matters of the various Buddha-fields for the sake of sentient beings. By these skillful means, he preaches the True Dharma—namely, preaching from *dāna-pāramitā* up to *prajñā-pāramitā*, and so forth extensively up to either preaching about bodhi or preaching about nirvāṇa—so that once those sentient beings have heard this Dharma, they all obtain supreme benefit and peace."

“Subhūti, you should know that by means of the supernormal power of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows as it has been attained, this bodhisattva mahāsattva understands, in accordance with reality, which sentient beings have exhausted their outflows and which have not; he also understands, in accordance with reality, the skillful means for the exhaustion of outflows. For those who have not yet exhausted them, he proclaims the essentials of the Dharma—namely, the teachings on giving up to the perfection of wisdom, and so forth, extensively up to either awakening or nirvāṇa—so that once those sentient beings have heard this Dharma, they all obtain supreme benefit and happiness.”
"In this way, Subhūti, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the profound perfection of wisdom should bring forth the perfection of supernormal powers."

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva has cultivated the perfection of supernormal powers (abhijñāpāramitā) to fulfillment, he assumes various bodies according to his wishes, yet remains unstained by the faults of suffering or pleasure; just as a transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) of a Buddha can perform various activities without being defiled by the faults of suffering or pleasure.

"In this way, Subhūti, bodhisattva mahāsattvas practicing the profound perfection of wisdom should sport in the perfection of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). If they sport in the perfection of the supernormal powers, they will be able to bring sentient beings to maturity, purify buddha-fields, and swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*)."
Subhūti, you should know that if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not bring sentient beings to maturity and purify buddha-fields, they will ultimately never be able to attain the knowledge of all modes.
"Why is this? Because if the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have not yet perfected the provisions for awakening, they will certainly be unable to attain the knowledge of all modes.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What are called the provisions for enlightenment of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
by fulfilling such provisions for enlightenment, how do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas then realize the knowledge of all modes?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“All wholesome dharmas are the provisions for a bodhisattva’s enlightenment. Only when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have perfected such provisions for enlightenment can they realize the knowledge of all modes.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha,
saying, “What are called all wholesome dharmas?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"From the first generation of the mind of awakening, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfections from generosity up to wisdom; throughout this process, they are entirely without conceptualization or attachment, such that they do not form thoughts like:
'This is generosity... up to wisdom; for this reason and for this purpose, I am practicing generosity... up to wisdom.'"

Since these three types of conceptualization and clinging are entirely absent—because one knows that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is empty—the six perfections (*pāramitās*), such as generosity (*dāna*) and the rest, which are cultivated thereby, can benefit oneself and also benefit all sentient beings by causing them to transcend birth and death and attain *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, they are called "wholesome dharmas" (*kuśala-dharma*), are also termed the "provisions for enlightenment" (*bodhi-sambhāra*) of a bodhisattva, and are further termed the "path" (*mārga*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
