Because the multitudes of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the past, future, and present practice this path, they have already attained, are now attaining, and will attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; furthermore, they cause sentient beings to have already crossed, to cross, and to be crossing the great ocean of birth and death, thereby realizing the bliss of nirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! From the first production of the thought of awakening, bodhisattva mahāsattvas cultivate the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
they cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, and abide in internal emptiness..."
They reach the emptiness of the nature of non-nature, abide in true suchness up to the inconceivable realm, abide in the noble truths of suffering,
origin, cessation, and the path, cultivate the gates of liberation— emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—
cultivate the eight liberations up to the ten totalities, and cultivate the stages of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
They cultivate the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi; they cultivate the ten powers of a Buddha up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they cultivate great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity;
they cultivate the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant abiding in equanimity; they cultivate all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and all-...
Regarding the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), they have no conceptual discrimination or attachment therein, such that they think:
"This is the four dhyānas, and so forth, up to the knowledge of all aspects; for this reason and for this purpose, I cultivate the four dhyānas, and so forth, up to the knowledge of all aspects."
In this state, these three kinds of conceptualization and attachment are entirely absent, because one knows that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is empty.

Because the four dhyānas and other practices cultivated through this can benefit oneself and also benefit all sentient beings by causing them to transcend birth and death and attain nirvāṇa, they are called "wholesome dharmas" (*kuśala-dharma*); they are also termed the "requisites for a bodhisattva’s enlightenment" (*bodhisambhāra*), and are also termed the "path of a bodhisattva mahāsattva."

Because the assemblies of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the past, future, and present practice this path, they have already attained, will attain, and are now attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening; furthermore, they have already, are now, and will cause sentient beings to cross the great ocean of birth and death and realize the bliss of nirvāṇa.

"Subhūti, you should know that there are further immeasurable collections of merit cultivated by the assembly of bodhisattvas; these are all called wholesome dharmas, are also called the bodhisattva’s provisions for enlightenment, and are also called the path of the bodhisattva mahāsattva."

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas must cultivate such supreme wholesome dharmas until they are perfectly fulfilled before they can realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna); only after having realized the knowledge of all modes can they turn the wheel of the sublime Dharma without error, enabling all sentient beings to escape the suffering of birth and death and realize ultimate, eternal bliss in nirvāṇa.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If these dharmas are the dharmas of a bodhisattva, what then are called the dharmas of a buddha?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“The very dharma of a bodhisattva is also called the dharma of a buddha.

This means that all bodhisattvas awaken to all aspects of all phenomena; by this, they shall attain the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) and forever sever the continuity of all habitual tendencies.”

If all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, having attained manifest complete enlightenment regarding all phenomena through the wisdom associated with a single moment, realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
This is what is meant by the distinction between a bodhisattva and a Buddha.

Just as two noble ones, though both are noble, differ in their status as those "progressing toward" [the fruit] versus those "abiding in" the fruit, so too the dharmas they have accomplished are not without difference.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

When one practices among all dharmas within the path of uninterrupted continuity (*ānantarya-mārga*), yet has not yet abandoned the obscuration of darkness, has not yet reached the further shore, has not yet attained mastery, and has not yet attained the fruit—at that time, one is called a bodhisattva.

When one practices among all phenomena within the path of liberation, having already departed from the obscuration of darkness, having reached the further shore, having attained mastery, and having realized the fruit, one is then called a Buddha.

"This constitutes the difference between a bodhisattva and a Buddha; while there is no lack of distinction due to the difference in their stages, one cannot say that there is a difference in their *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena).
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If all phenomena are empty of intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnya*), how can there be various distinctions within this emptiness of intrinsic characteristics—namely, 'this is hell' up to 'this is heaven,' 'this is the spiritual lineage,' and so forth, up to 'this is a Tathāgata'?"

Since the person (pudgala) thus described cannot be found, the karma performed by him cannot be found; and since the karma performed cannot be found, its ripening fruit (vipāka-phala) also cannot be found.
"How can there be various distinctions?
The Buddha told Subhūti: "It is so!
"So it is! It is just as you have said.

All phenomena are empty of intrinsic characteristics. Within the emptiness of intrinsic characteristics, since the person (pudgala) does not exist, the maturation of the results of karma also does not exist; within that which does not exist, there are no differentiated characteristics."

However, sentient beings are unable to fully comprehend the principle that all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature; they perform various actions—whether virtuous, non-virtuous, or untainted—and by the performance and accumulation of virtuous actions, they are born among gods and humans, while by the performance and accumulation of non-virtuous actions, they fall into the three miserable realms.

Among wholesome karmas, through the performance and accumulation of determinate karma, one is born in the form realm or the formless realm; furthermore, due to the preparatory and fundamental stages of untainted karma, there are distinctions among the noble ones such as their spiritual lineage (*gotra*).

For this reason, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfections from generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, and even practice all-aspect omniscience as well as other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas.
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates these aforementioned factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) continuously and without interruption until they are perfected.

Once they have reached perfection, he is able to induce the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*), which closely assists awakening, and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. He brings great benefit to all sentient beings, remaining forever indestructible; because he is indestructible, he causes all sentient beings to be liberated from birth and death and to realize the eternal, blissful, and cool state of nirvāṇa."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"After the Buddha has realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, have you attained the dharmas of birth and death within the various realms of existence?
The Buddha said:
"Not so! The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"After the Buddha has realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, has he attained black karma, white karma, black-and-white karma, or neither-black-nor-white karma?"
The Buddha said, “It is not so.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If the Buddha does not perceive the various realms of birth and death, nor the distinctions among karmas, how could he designate these as 'this is hell' up to 'these are humans and devas,' or these as the distinctions in stages from the spiritual lineage (gotra) up to the stage of a Tathāgata?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Do sentient beings know for themselves that the specific characteristics of all phenomena are empty? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"If sentient beings were to know for themselves that all phenomena are empty of their own intrinsic characteristics, then Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas would have no need to seek the realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through skillful means in order to extract sentient beings from the cycle of birth and death in the evil realms."
Because sentient beings do not know that the intrinsic characteristics of all phenomena are empty, they transmigrate through the various realms of existence and undergo boundless suffering.

Therefore, having heard from the Buddhas that all phenomena are empty of intrinsic characteristics, the Bodhisattva seeks to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, employing skillful means to extract them from the cycle of birth and death within the evil realms.
“Subhūti, you should know that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas always maintain this thought:
‘All phenomena do not possess intrinsic characteristics as they are grasped by foolish, ordinary worldlings.’”

However, due to the power of that distorted discrimination, one conceives the notion of real existence regarding what is not truly existent; one conceives the notion of a self regarding what is selfless; and so on, as explained at length, until one conceives the notion of a seer regarding what is not a seer.

Furthermore, within the formless [realms], one gives rise to the perception of form; within that which is without feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, one gives rise to the perceptions of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness; and so on, in detail, up to giving rise to the perception of the unconditioned within that which is without the unconditioned.

Thus, through the power of such inverted discrimination, they give rise to the perception of real existence toward what is not truly existent; their minds are deluded by false attachments, and they perform wholesome and unwholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind, unable to escape the cycle of birth and death in the evil realms. I shall rescue them and cause them to attain liberation.

Having formed this thought, that bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom; subsuming all wholesome dharmas within it, they practice the various bodhisattva deeds without error, gradually bringing the provisions for enlightenment to full completion.
Having brought the accumulations for awakening to full completion, he realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

Having attained awakening, he proclaims, reveals, analyzes, and establishes the meaning of the Four Noble Truths for all sentient beings, saying: "This is the noble truth of suffering; this is the noble truth of the origin of suffering; this is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering; this is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering."
Furthermore, all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) are subsumed within these Four Noble Truths.

Moreover, based upon all factors conducive to enlightenment, the Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha are established and designated; through the appearance of these Three Jewels in the world, all classes of sentient beings are liberated from birth and death.

Since sentient beings who fail to take refuge in and place faith in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha create various karmas and undergo endless suffering within the various realms of saṃsāra, they should take refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, and diligently seek the benefit and happiness of both themselves and others.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Is it by means of the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path that sentient beings realize parinirvāṇa?"
"Is it by means of the noble wisdom regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path that sentient beings realize parinirvāṇa?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"It is not by means of the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path that sentient beings realize parinirvāṇa."
It is not by means of the noble wisdom regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path that sentient beings realize parinirvāṇa.

Subhūti! I say that the sameness of the four noble truths is itself nirvāṇa. Such nirvāṇa is not realized through the truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, nor is it realized through the wisdom of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; rather, it is by means of the perfection of wisdom that one realizes this sameness, which is called realizing nirvāṇa.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What is called the equality of the four noble truths?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If, in this state, there is no truth of suffering, origin, cessation, or path, and no knowledge of suffering, origin, cessation, or path, it is called the nature of the equality of the four noble truths; this very equality is itself the four noble truths."

All suchness, extensively explained up to the inconceivable realm, whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, remains eternally constant in its essential nature and characteristics, without loss or destruction and without change; this is called the equality of the four noble truths.

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they do so because they wish to fully awaken to the equality of these four noble truths; thus they practice the profound perfection of wisdom.
If one can realize the equality of these four noble truths, it is called truly realizing all noble truths, and one will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they practice the profound perfection of wisdom for the sake of wishing to realize the equality of these four noble truths?"

If one can realize the equality of these four noble truths, is this called truly realizing all noble truths, such that one does not fall into the levels of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but enters the Bodhisattva’s state of certainty beyond regression?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, there is not the slightest dharma that they do not see as it truly is."
When one sees all phenomena as they truly are, one apprehends nothing at all within all phenomena.

When one apprehends nothing within all phenomena, one then sees all phenomena as empty as they truly are; that is, one sees as they truly are that all phenomena—both those subsumed within and those not subsumed within the Four Noble Truths—are empty.
When one perceives in this manner, one is able to enter the bodhisattva’s state of correct determination and departure from birth (*samyaktvaniyāma*).
Because one is able to enter the bodhisattva’s state of correct determination and departure from birth, one then abides within the bodhisattva’s stage of the lineage (*gotrabhūmi*).

Once one dwells within the stage of the bodhisattva lineage-ground, one is then certain not to fall from the summit; for were one to fall from the summit, one would necessarily fall into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely within the stage of the bodhisattva lineage, gives rise to the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments.
Abiding thus in the stage of śamatha, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is then able to discern the nature of all phenomena and to realize the principles of the Four Noble Truths accordingly.

At that time, although the Bodhisattva fully understands suffering, he does not give rise to a mind that clings to suffering as an object; although he has forever severed the origin of suffering, he does not give rise to a mind that clings to the origin as an object; although he is able to realize cessation, he does not give rise to a mind that clings to cessation as an object; and although he is able to cultivate the path, he does not give rise to a mind that clings to the path as an object.
"Simply give rise to a mind that accords with, inclines toward, and enters into bodhi, and realize the true nature of all phenomena as they truly are.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 536, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Three, Chapter on Teaching and Transforming, Number Thirty-one, Section Two. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“How do the bodhisattva mahāsattvas realize the true nature of all phenomena?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“When bodhisattva mahāsattvas contemplate that all phenomena are without exception empty, this is what it means to realize the true nature of all phenomena.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplate all phenomena as being without exception empty?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas contemplate all phenomena as empty of their own specific characteristics, this is what it means for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to contemplate that there are no phenomena whatsoever that are not empty."

“Subhūti, you should know that bodhisattva mahāsattvas, through the insight of vipaśyanā observing the characteristic of emptiness, contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena; they do not perceive any intrinsic nature of phenomena within which they might abide, yet they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

Why is this so? Because the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas and all phenomena have "lack of intrinsic nature" as their own nature. That is to say, from the aggregate of form up to the aggregate of consciousness, they all have "lack of intrinsic nature" as their own nature; and to speak at length, even all the practices of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas and the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas likewise have "lack of intrinsic nature" as their own nature.

Thus, this absence of intrinsic nature is not something produced by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, or Śrāvakas who are progressing toward their respective fruits, nor is it produced by anything else; rather, it is solely because sentient beings do not know and do not see that all phenomena are, in reality, entirely empty.

Therefore, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, through the skillful means of practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, proclaim and reveal it to all sentient beings according to what they have realized themselves, causing them to abandon attachment, escape the suffering of birth and death, and attain the ultimate peace and happiness of parinirvāṇa.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If all dharmas take non-existence as their intrinsic nature, and such non-existence was not created by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, or Śrāvakas, how can there be any differentiation established among these dharmas?"

This refers to the various distinctions among the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, humans, and the various classes of devas—ranging from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception—as well as the distinctions between the stages of the three vehicles. By such karma are the hells established; by such karma are the animal realm established; by such karma is the realm of hungry ghosts established; by such karma is the human destiny established with its various distinctions, such as Jambudvīpa, Pūrvavideha, Aparagoyānī, and Uttarakuru; by such karma is the celestial destiny established with its various distinctions, ranging from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception; by such karma are the stages from Stream-enterer up to Pratyekabuddha established; and by such karma are the Bodhisattvas and all Tathāgatas established?
“World-Honored One!

Since dharmas that lack intrinsic nature necessarily possess no functional activity, how can it be said that by means of this karma one is born in the hells, and so on, up to being born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; that by means of this karma one attains the fruit of stream-entry, and so forth, up to the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; that by means of this karma one enters the stage of a bodhisattva and practices the bodhisattva path; and that by means of this karma one is able to realize the knowledge of all modes, being designated as a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings?”
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.
Within phenomena that lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), it is impossible to designate any differentiation among phenomena; there is no karma, no fruit, and no functional activity.

It is only because foolish worldlings do not understand the Noble Dharma and Vinaya that they fail to know, as it truly is, that all phenomena have the absence of intrinsic nature as their very nature. Out of delusion and inversion, they initiate various karmas, and according to the distinctions of those karmas, they undergo various bodies.

Based on such distinctions in the categories of bodies, there are designated the realms of hell beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and the various devas, up to and including the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

In order to deliver such foolish and deluded beings who undergo the suffering of birth and death due to their inverted views, one establishes the various stages of the Noble Dharma and the Vinaya; based on these stages, one designates the categories from Stream-enterer up to Pratyekabuddha, Bodhisattva, and Tathāgata.

However, all phenomena are such that there is none whose nature is not the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Within the state of phenomena devoid of intrinsic nature, there are truly no distinct phenomena; there is no karma, no fruit, and no functional activity, because phenomena lacking intrinsic nature are eternally without intrinsic nature.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, it is as you have said.
Since dharmas that lack intrinsic nature necessarily possess no functional activity, how can one say:..."

By means of such karma, one attains the fruit of stream-entry, up until the realization of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), and is called a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who brings benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings?
"Subhūti! What do you think?
Is that which constitutes the path cultivated devoid of intrinsic nature?"

Are the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship; the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; the paths of the bodhisattvas; and the knowledge of all modes devoid of intrinsic nature?
Subhūti replied, “So it is! So it is!”
"All paths of cultivation, extensively explained up to the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), are devoid of intrinsic nature.
The Buddha addressed Subhūti: "What do you think?"
"Can a dharma that lacks intrinsic nature attain a dharma that lacks intrinsic nature? Subhūti replied, "No!"
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Non-existence and the Path—all these dharmas are neither associated nor dissociated; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and of a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness.”

Foolish ordinary beings falsely discriminate regarding phenomena that are signless, giving rise to perceptions of signs; they cling to the aggregates, the sense bases, and the elements. Within the impermanent, they falsely conceive of permanence; within suffering, they falsely conceive of pleasure; within the non-self, they falsely conceive of a self; and within the impure, they falsely conceive of purity. Thus, through delusion and inversion, they cling to an intrinsic nature in phenomena that are devoid of intrinsic nature.

By means of these causes and conditions, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* achieve sublime skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), thereby rescuing such sentient beings, causing them to abandon inverted and false conceptualization, and through skillful means establishing them within the signless (*animitta*) Dharma, so that they may diligently practice and study to liberate themselves from birth and death and realize the ultimate peace and bliss of *nirvāṇa*.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Is there even the slightest thing that is true, real, non-illusory, and non-false, wherein foolish ordinary beings might cling and perform various karmas, by reason of which they wander through the various realms of existence and are unable to liberate themselves from the suffering of birth and death?"

It would be better to have no small thing that is true, real, non-illusory, and non-false; why then do foolish people cling to such things, performing various karmas and wandering through the various realms of rebirth?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"As for the objects to which foolish common beings are attached, there is not even as much as the tip of a fine hair that is true, real, non-illusory, or non-false."

Because of clinging to those [objects], one performs various karmas; by means of these causes and conditions, one wanders through the various realms of existence and cannot liberate oneself from the manifold sufferings of birth and death, possessing nothing but inverted, false, and deluded attachments.

I shall now provide you with an extensive analogy to further clarify this meaning so that it may be easily understood; for those who possess wisdom attain a correct understanding of the explained meaning by means of analogies.
“Subhūti, what do you think?
When one sees a person in a dream experiencing the pleasures of the five senses, is there therein even the slightest real thing that could cause that person to experience those sensual pleasures?”
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”

"If even the person seen in a dream does not truly exist, how much less could there be a real entity that could cause that person to dwell within the dream and experience the pleasures of the five senses!
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?"
Are there not any phenomena that are either with outflows or without outflows, either mundane or supramundane, or conditioned or unconditioned, which are not like things seen in a dream?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
There is certainly no dharma—whether it be with outflows or without outflows, mundane or supramundane, conditioned or unconditioned—that is not like the things seen in a dream.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Within a dream, are there any truly real realms of existence in which one undergoes the process of birth and death by wandering to and fro?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Is there, within a dream, any truly real cultivation of the path, by means of which cultivation one might become free from defilement and attain purity?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”

Why is this so? Because the phenomena seen in a dream have no reality whatsoever; they are neither that which can be designated nor that which is designated. If even the cultivation of the path does not exist, how much less could there be the departure from defilement and the attainment of purity based upon the cultivation of the path!
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “What do you think?

Do the various images seen in a bright mirror and such have any substantial reality upon which one could rely to create karma, such that by virtue of the karma created, one would fall into the evil destinies or be born among humans or gods to experience suffering or pleasure?”
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”

The various images seen in a bright mirror and the like have no substantial reality whatsoever; they merely deceive ignorant children. How could one rely upon them to perform karmic actions, such that by those performed actions one might fall into the evil destinies or be born among humans or devas to experience various sufferings and pleasures?
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “What do you think?

Do those various images manifested in a bright mirror and the like possess any real cultivation of the path? By relying on such cultivation of the path, could one become free from defilement and attain purity?”
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”

Why is this so? Because those manifested images lack any substantial reality; they are neither the agent of designation nor the object of designation. If even the cultivation of the path does not exist, how much less could there be freedom from defilement or the attainment of purity based upon that cultivation!
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?

Do the various echoes produced within valleys and the like possess any substantial reality upon which one could rely to perform karma, such that by virtue of the karma performed, one would fall into the evil destinies or be born among humans or gods to experience suffering or pleasure?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”

The various echoes produced within mountain valleys and the like have no substantial reality whatsoever; they merely deceive the ignorant and childish. How could one rely upon them to perform karmic actions, such that by virtue of those performed actions one might fall into the evil realms or be born among humans or devas to experience various sufferings and pleasures?
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Does an echo possess any real path of cultivation? By means of such a path of cultivation, could one become free from defilement and attain purity?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”

Why is this so? Because echoes in mountain valleys and the like possess no substantial reality; they are neither the agent of designation nor the object of designation. If even the cultivation of the path does not exist, how much less could there be the departure from defilement or the attainment of purity based upon that cultivation of the path!
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?

Within a mirage or the like, there appears something resembling water. Does that have any real substance upon which one could rely to perform karma, such that by virtue of the karma performed, one would fall into the evil destinies or be born among humans or devas to experience suffering or pleasure?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”

All the waters and such things manifested within a mirage are entirely devoid of substantial reality and merely deceive the ignorant; how could they serve as a basis for performing various karmic actions, by which—due to those performed actions—one might fall into the evil destinies or be born among humans or gods to experience various forms of suffering and pleasure?
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Within those mirages, is there any water that is real? Is there any genuine path of cultivation therein, by relying upon which path one might become free from defilement and attain purity?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”

Why is this so? Because a mirage, water, and the like possess no substantial reality whatsoever; they are neither the agent of designation nor the object of designation. If even the path of cultivation does not exist, how much less could there be the departure from defilement or the attainment of purity based upon that path of cultivation!
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?

Do the forms and appearances manifested within various reflections and shadows possess any substantial reality upon which one could rely to create karma, such that by virtue of the karma created, one would fall into the evil destinies or be born among humans or devas to experience suffering or pleasure?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”

The forms and appearances manifested within all those reflections have no substantial reality whatsoever; they merely deceive the foolish and ignorant. How could one rely upon them to perform various karmic actions, such that by virtue of those performed actions one might fall into the evil realms or be born among humans or devas to experience various sufferings and pleasures?
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?

Within the forms and appearances of all reflected images, is there any truly real cultivation of the path? By relying on such cultivation of the path, could one become free from defilement and attain purity?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”

Why is this? Because reflections, shadows, colors, and forms have no substantial reality whatsoever; they are neither that which can designate nor that which is designated. If even the cultivation of the path does not exist, how much less could there be the departure from defilement or the attainment of purity based upon the cultivation of the path!
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?

If a magician were to conjure various forms such as elephant or cavalry troops, would there be any real entity therein that could serve as a basis for performing karma, such that by virtue of the karma performed one might fall into the evil destinies or be born among humans or gods to experience suffering or pleasure?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”

Since illusions, horses, and so forth have no reality and merely deceive the ignorant, how can one rely upon them to perform various karmic actions? And by virtue of the karma thus performed, how could one fall into the evil realms or be born among humans or devas to experience various sufferings and pleasures?
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Does an illusory being possess a genuine path of cultivation, such that by relying on that path of cultivation, one could become free from defilement and attain purity?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”

Why is this so? Illusions such as elephants and horses have no reality whatsoever; they are neither the agents of designation nor the objects of designation. If even the cultivation of the path does not exist, how much less could there be the departure from defilement and the attainment of purity based upon that cultivation of the path!
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?

Regarding the emanations created by those who possess the power of transformation, is there any substantial reality upon which they can rely to perform karma, such that by virtue of the karma thus performed, they would fall into the evil destinies or be born among humans or gods to experience suffering or pleasure?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”

Since all transformation bodies (nirmāṇakāya) are entirely devoid of substantial reality, how can they serve as a basis for performing various karmas? And by virtue of the karma thus performed, how could one fall into the evil destinies or be born among humans or devas to experience various sufferings and pleasures?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Does an emanation body possess a real path of cultivation? By means of that path of cultivation, is there any departure from defilement and attainment of purity?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”

Why is this so? All transformation bodies (nirmāṇakāya) are entirely devoid of substantial reality; they are neither the agents of designation nor the objects of designation. If even the cultivation of the path does not exist, how much less could there be freedom from defilement or the attainment of purity based upon the cultivation of the path!
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?

Regarding the various things manifested within the city of Gandhavatī, is there any substantial reality upon which one could rely to perform karma, such that by virtue of the karma performed, one would fall into the evil destinies or be born among humans or gods to experience suffering or pleasure?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”

Since the various phenomena appearing within the City of Fragrance possess no substantial reality whatsoever, how could they serve as a basis for performing karmic actions? And by virtue of those performed actions, how could one fall into the evil realms or be born among humans or devas to experience various forms of suffering and pleasure?
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?

Among the things and phenomena in the city of Gandhavatī, is there any genuine path of cultivation such that, by relying on that path of cultivation, one might become free from defilement and attain purity?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”

Why is this so? Because the entities within that city have no substantial reality; they are neither the agents of designation nor the objects of designation. Since even the cultivation of the path does not exist, how much less could there be the departure from defilement or the attainment of purity based upon the cultivation of the path!
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?

Are there any phenomena—whether they be with outflows or without outflows, whether worldly or supramundane, whether conditioned or unconditioned—that are not like a reflection, an echo, a mirage, a shadow, a magical illusion, a transformation, or the objects within a city of Gandharvas?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
There is certainly no dharma—whether it be with outflows or without outflows, mundane or supramundane, conditioned or unconditioned—that is not like a reflection and so forth.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Within this, is there any real entity that is defiled or purified?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
"In this, there is absolutely no real agent of defilement nor any agent of purification.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Just as the agent of defilement and the agent of purification do not truly exist, for this reason, defilement and purification are also not truly existent."

Why is this? Because sentient beings who dwell in the notions of "self" and "what belongs to self" engage in false conceptualization, asserting that there is defilement and purification; it is by reason of this that they speak of defilement and purification.

Those who do not see reality are said to have defilement and purification; however, as those who see reality know that there is neither defilement nor purification, so too there is neither defilement nor purification, because all phenomena are empty of their own intrinsic characteristics.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For those who see reality, there is neither defilement nor purification; for those who do not see reality, there is likewise neither defilement nor purification."
Why is this? Because all dharmas take the absence of intrinsic nature as their own nature.
World-Honored One!
For those who speak of reality, there is neither defilement nor purity; for those who speak of unreality, there is likewise neither defilement nor purity. Why is this?
Because all phenomena take the absence of intrinsic nature as their very essence.
“World-Honored One!

Phenomena that lack intrinsic nature are neither defiled nor pure; phenomena that possess intrinsic nature are likewise neither defiled nor pure; and all phenomena, whether lacking or possessing intrinsic nature, are also neither defiled nor pure.”
Why is this? Because all phenomena take the absence of intrinsic nature as their very self-nature.
World-Honored One!

If for one who sees reality and speaks of reality there is neither defilement nor purification, and for one who does not see reality and does not speak of reality there is likewise neither defilement nor purification, why did the World-Honored One at times say that there are dharmas of purification?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“I declare that the equality of all phenomena is the pure dharma.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is meant by the equality of all phenomena?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"The suchness of all phenomena—ranging from the detailed exposition up to the inconceivable realm—remains eternally constant in its essential nature whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear; this is called the equality of all phenomena."
This equality is called the pure dharma; it is designated as "pure" based on conventional truth, not ultimate truth. Why is this so?

Because within the ultimate truth there is neither conceptual differentiation nor discursive proliferation; all paths of names and language are severed, such that it cannot be described as either defiled or pure.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If all phenomena are like dream-visions—and as has been explained at length, even like a city of Gandharvas—appearing to exist while lacking any substantial reality, how can a bodhisattva mahāsattva rely upon such non-substantial phenomena to resolve upon the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, making this vow:..."

"I shall fulfill the six perfections, such as generosity, and so forth, up to and including the fulfillment of the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs; I shall produce immeasurable light that illuminates the infinite worlds of the ten directions; I shall produce a single sublime voice that pervades the infinite worlds of the ten directions, and according to the differences in the inclinations of the minds and mental factors of sentient beings, I shall preach various subtle and wondrous Dharma gates, causing them to diligently practice and train so that each may obtain their respective benefits."
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Is it not the case that all the dharmas you have spoken of are like a dream, and so forth, up to a city of gandharvas?"
Subhūti replied: “So it is! So it is!”

However, I have a doubt: if all phenomena are like dreams and even like cities of Gandharvas, such that they all lack any substantial reality, how can a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, utter words of solemn truth, saying:
"I shall fulfill all the buddha-dharmas and bring benefit, peace, and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings"?

The objects seen in a dream, and so forth, up to those manifested within the City of Fragrance, cannot practice the perfection of giving, nor even the perfection of wisdom; how much less could they fulfill [the marks], and so forth, up to the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs!
It is likewise said:
"The objects seen in dreams, and so forth, up to those manifested within the city of Gandharvas, are capable of accomplishing all desired undertakings."
"All other dharmas should also be understood in this way, for they are all equally not real.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "It is so!"
"So it is! It is as you have said.

Since even a non-existent dharma cannot practice the six pāramitās, such as giving, let alone fully perfect them—extending through the detailed exposition up to the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics."
A phenomenon that is not truly existent cannot accomplish its intended purpose, nor can it attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*). "Furthermore, Subhūti,
because the six perfections beginning with generosity, as well as the other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas, are not truly existent, one cannot realize the knowledge of all modes."

"Subhūti, you should know that all such dharmas are merely conceptual constructions and volitional formations. Whatever is a dharma produced through conceptualization and volition cannot attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā)."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Although these dharmas can induce the path to enlightenment, they lack the capacity to assist in its fruition, because these dharmas are unarisen, unoriginated, and devoid of any real characteristic."

From the first generation of the mind of enlightenment, although bodhisattva-mahāsattvas give rise to various kinds of sublime and wholesome dharmas—ranging from the cultivation of the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, and as extensively explained, up to all-aspect omniscience—they know that all these are like dream-visions, and as extensively explained, up to being like a city of gandharvas, truly non-existent.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Although these dharmas are not substantially existent, if they are not perfected and established with certainty, one cannot bring sentient beings to maturity, purify buddha-fields, nor attain the knowledge of all modes."

That is to say, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not fulfill the six pāramitās, beginning with generosity and extending through the detailed exposition up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), they will certainly be unable to bring sentient beings to maturity or to purify a buddha-field, nor will they be able to attain the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When these bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they know all the wholesome dharmas in which they dwell and practice as they truly are—like dreams, and so forth, up to like a city of gandharvas. That is to say, when they practice the six *pāramitās* such as generosity, and so on, up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), they are able to know them as they truly are—like dreams, and so forth, up to like a city of gandharvas.

Whether it be maturing sentient beings, purifying buddha-fields, or seeking to realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*), they are also able to know these as they truly are—like dreams, and so forth, up to like a city of gandharvas—and they likewise know the distinctions in the mental activities of sentient beings as they truly are—like dreams, and so forth, up to like a city of gandharvas."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When these bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not apprehend any phenomena as existing, nor do they apprehend them as non-existing."

If, by means of such grasping, one realizes the knowledge of all modes, one also knows that those phenomena are like a dream, even up to being like a city of Gandharvas; one does not grasp them as existent, nor does one grasp them as non-existent.

Why is this? Because the six perfections, beginning with generosity and extending up to all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), are all ungraspable; likewise, whether they be contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharmas, mundane (*laukika*) or supramundane (*lokottara*) dharmas, conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas, these too are ungraspable.
Having realized that all phenomena are ungraspable, this bodhisattva mahāsattva seeks to proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Why is this?
Because all phenomena are ungraspable and entirely devoid of substantial reality.

Just as things such as dreams, up to and including the city of Gandharvas, are ungraspable dharmas that cannot realize ungraspable dharmas, yet sentient beings do not know or see these dharmas in this way.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva seeks to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of benefiting those sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

From the first generation of the mind of awakening, this bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, practices the perfections from generosity up to wisdom, not for his own sake nor for any other purpose.
It is for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings that one seeks to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, not for one's own sake nor for any other purpose.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."

When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound perfection of wisdom, they see that foolish commoners dwell upon the notion of a self amidst what is not-self, and so on, up to dwelling upon the notion of a seer amidst what is not a seer.

Having seen this, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives rise to deep compassion and provides skillful instruction, causing them to abandon inverted conceptualizations and attachments, and establishing them within the signless nectar-realm (*amṛta-dhātu*). Abiding in this realm, they no longer manifest the notion of a self (*ātma-saṃjñā*) up to and including the notion of a viewer (*draṣṭṛ-saṃjñā*). At that time, all agitation, distraction, proliferation (*prapañca*), and discrimination no longer function; the mind predominantly dwells in a realm that is tranquil, detached, and free from proliferation.

“Subhūti, you should know that by means of this skillful method, this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom; he himself has no attachment to any phenomena, and he is also able to teach others to have no attachment to all phenomena. This is based on conventional truth, not on ultimate truth.”
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:

"When the Buddha realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, was that which he attained as the Buddha-dharma attained in reliance upon the conventional truth, or was it attained in reliance upon the ultimate truth?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"This is based on conventional truth, not on ultimate truth.
If one relies on ultimate truth, both the attainer and that which is attained are unapprehendable."

Why is this? If one were to say that this person attains such a dharma, they would then have something attained; and having something attained, they would then cling to duality. One who clings to duality cannot attain the fruit, nor can they achieve clear realization.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"If grasping at duality cannot lead to the attainment of the fruit nor to clear realization, does grasping at non-duality enable one to attain the fruit and achieve clear realization?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"One who clings to duality cannot attain the fruit nor realize clear observation (abhisamaya); one who clings to non-duality is likewise so, because there is clinging, just as in the case of clinging to duality."
If one does not grasp at duality, nor grasp at non-duality, this is called attaining the fruit and is also called clear observation (*abhisamaya*). Why is this so?

If one grasps that by means of this one can attain the fruit and possess clear observation, or if one grasps that by means of that one cannot attain the fruit and lacks clear observation—both are conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*).
"In the equality of all phenomena, there are no conceptual proliferations; only when one is free from conceptual proliferation can it be called the equality of phenomena.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If all phenomena take non-existence as their intrinsic nature, what therein is meant by the equality of phenomena?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If, in a certain place, there is neither existence nor non-existence, and it cannot even be described as a state of equality—it is precisely this that is called the equality of phenomena."

"Subhūti, you should know that the equality of phenomena (dharmasamatā) is neither expressible nor cognizable; apart from this equality, no phenomenon can be apprehended, and apart from all phenomena, there is no equality."
"Subhūti, you should know that the equality of phenomena cannot be traversed by either ordinary beings or noble ones, for it is not their domain.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Is the equality of phenomena (*dharma-samatā*) not also the objective range of the Buddha’s activity?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“The equality of phenomena cannot be traversed nor realized by any noble ones—namely, from those who have entered the stream (*srotāpanna*) up to the solitary realizers (*pratyekabuddha*), as well as the bodhisattvas and the Tathāgatas. None of them can take the equality of phenomena as an objective range of activity, because within it, all conceptual proliferations and discriminations do not operate.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Tathāgata has attained mastery over all dharmas; how can it be said that the equality of dharmas is not even within the range of the Tathāgata’s activity?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Although the Tathāgata has attained mastery over all phenomena, if the nature of equality were different from the Buddha, one could say it is the sphere of the Buddha's activity; however, since the nature of equality is not different from the Buddha, how can it be said that the Buddha travels within that sphere?"

“Subhūti, you should know that the sameness of all phenomena of ordinary beings, up to the sameness of the phenomena of the Tathāgata, are all of one single characteristic—namely, the absence of characteristics (animitta). Because this single sameness is non-dual and undifferentiated, it cannot be said that ‘this is the sameness of the phenomena of ordinary beings,’ and so on, up to ‘this is the sameness of the phenomena of the Tathāgata.’”
Within this equality of all phenomena, since no forms of equality can be apprehended, the distinguishing characteristics between ordinary beings and noble ones are likewise unapprehendable therein.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If, within the equality of all phenomena, no distinct characteristics can be apprehended, then there would be no distinction between ordinary beings, stream-enterers, and so forth, regarding their phenomena or their sentient nature."
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is! So it is!”
"It is as you have said.
Within the equality of all phenomena, there is no distinction between ordinary beings and noble ones, nor between phenomena and sentient beings.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"If, within the equality of all phenomena, there is no distinction between ordinary beings and noble ones, nor between phenomena and sentient beings, how do the Three Jewels appear in the world?"
"Furthermore, would there not be no distinction between the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha?
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?"
“Are the Jewels of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha distinct from the nature of equality? Subhūti replied,
“As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is no difference between the Jewels of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha and the nature of equality.”

Why is this so? Because the Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, along with the nature of equality—all such things as these are neither associated nor dissociated; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.

Nevertheless, the Tathāgatas, through their skillful means regarding the signless dharma, establish various distinctions of names and characteristics for phenomena and sentient beings, such as "this is an ordinary person and their phenomena," up to "this is a Tathāgata and their phenomena."
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is as you have said.
The Buddhas are skillful in means regarding the Dharma; they establish various distinctions of names and characteristics for dharmas and sentient beings.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"
What do you think?

If a Buddha did not realize unsurpassed awakening, or even if he did, were he not to establish for sentient beings the various distinctions of names and characteristics of phenomena, would these classes of sentient beings be able to know for themselves: "This is hell," and so on, up to "this is the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception"; "This is the aggregate of form," and so on, up to "the aggregate of consciousness"; "This is the knowledge of all aspects," and so on, up to "the knowledge of all modes"; "This is the wondrously vowed knowledge of all modes"; "This is the knowledge of all modes"; "These are the Three Jewels"; and "These are the Three Vehicles"?
"Can sentient beings themselves know such distinctions of names and characteristics? Subhūti replied, "No!"
“World-Honored One!
If the Buddha did not establish such various designations and characteristics for sentient beings, these classes of sentient beings would be unable to know them for themselves.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Therefore, the Buddhas possess skillful means regarding the signless Dharma; although they provisionally establish various differentiated names and signs for the sake of sentient beings, they do not waver at all from the equality of all phenomena."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Just as the Buddha does not move at all within the equality of phenomena, do ordinary beings and even bodhisattvas likewise not move within the equality of phenomena?"
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
Because all phenomena and all sentient beings do not transcend the nature of equality.

Just as it is with the nature of equality, one should know that it is likewise for true suchness (*tathatā*), and so forth, up to the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*); for there is no differentiation among phenomena, ordinary beings, and noble ones regarding true suchness and the rest.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If the nature of equality of all ordinary beings, all noble ones, and all phenomena is without distinction, then because the characteristics of all phenomena and all sentient beings are each different, their natures should also be distinct; thus, the nature of phenomena would also be individually distinct. That is to say, because the characteristics of the aggregates such as form are each different, their natures should also be distinct; and so on, in detail, until: because the characteristics of the conditioned and the unconditioned are each different, their natures should also be distinct.”
“World-Honored One!

If the dharmas and their suchness were each distinct, then the dharma-nature would also have to be distinct. How, then, could one establish a single characteristic for the dharma-nature across all these dharmas that possess diverse characteristics?”
How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not discriminate between phenomena and sentient beings as having various natures?
If one does not differentiate between the various natures of phenomena and sentient beings, then one would be unable to practice the profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
If one cannot practice the profound perfection of wisdom, then one would be unable to proceed from one bodhisattva stage to another.

If one were certainly unable to proceed from one bodhisattva stage to another bodhisattva stage, then one would be unable to enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
If one were certainly unable to enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth, then one would be unable to transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
If one were certainly unable to transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, then one would be unable to fulfill the perfection of supernormal powers (ṛddhipāramitā).
If one were certainly unable to fulfill the perfection of supernormal powers, then one would be unable to exercise mastery in sporting with the various supernormal powers.

If one is not able to exercise mastery and play with the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) through meditative concentration, then one will be unable to fulfill the perfections (*pāramitā*), from generosity up to wisdom.

If one cannot perfect the pāramitās from generosity up to wisdom through meditative concentration, then one will be unable to travel from one buddha-field to another to attend upon and make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

If one were unable, through meditative concentration, to travel from one buddha-field to another to attend upon and make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, then one would be unable to hear and receive the true Dharma from those Buddhas and plant various roots of goodness.

If one is unable, while in meditative concentration, to hear and receive the true Dharma from the Buddhas and plant various roots of goodness, then one will be unable to mature sentient beings or purify Buddha-fields.

If meditative concentration cannot mature sentient beings and purify Buddha-fields, it should not be possible to attain the knowledge of all modes, turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, and deliver the multitudes of sentient beings.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "As you have said:

'If the nature of equality of all ordinary beings, all noble ones, and all phenomena is without distinction, then because the characteristics of all phenomena and sentient beings are each different, their natures should also be distinct; thus, the dharma-nature itself should also be distinct. How then can one establish a single characteristic for the dharma-nature within these variously characterized phenomena?'"
How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not discriminate among phenomena and sentient beings as having various natures and so forth?
Regarding this, what do you think?
Is the dharma-nature of the aggregate of form emptiness?
Is the dharma-nature of the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness emptiness?
"Extending this in detail, up to: Is the nature of conditioned phenomena emptiness?
Is the nature of unconditioned phenomena emptiness? Subhūti replied:
"So it is! So it is! The nature of all phenomena is emptiness."
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
Within emptiness, can one perceive any distinct characteristics of phenomena?"
That is to say: can the distinct characteristic of the aggregate of form be apprehended?
Can the distinct characteristics of the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness be apprehended?
To speak at length, up to: can the distinct characteristic of conditioned phenomena be apprehended?
"Can a distinct characteristic of unconditioned phenomena be apprehended? Subhūti replied, "No!"
“World-Honored One!
Within emptiness, all distinct characteristics are unapprehendable.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"From this, one should know that the equality of phenomena is neither identical to ordinary beings nor separate from ordinary beings; as explained at length, it is neither identical to the Buddhas nor separate from the Buddhas."

The equality of phenomena is not identical to the aggregate of form, nor is it separate from the aggregate of form; it is not identical to the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor is it separate from the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. This is explained at length until: it is not identical to conditioned phenomena, nor is it separate from conditioned phenomena; it is not identical to unconditioned phenomena, nor is it separate from unconditioned phenomena.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Is the equality of phenomena conditioned or unconditioned?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"The equality of phenomena is neither conditioned nor unconditioned; yet, apart from conditioned phenomena, unconditioned phenomena cannot be found, and apart from unconditioned phenomena, conditioned phenomena likewise cannot be found."
"Subhūti, you should know this:

whether it be the realm of the conditioned or the realm of the unconditioned, these two kinds are neither associated nor dissociated; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness. The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, speak of these based on conventional truth, not based on ultimate truth."

Why is this? Because within the ultimate truth (paramārtha), bodily activity, verbal activity, and mental activity cannot be apprehended; nor can the ultimate truth be apprehended apart from bodily, verbal, and mental activity.

The equality of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), which is their true nature (*dharmatā*), is designated as the ultimate (*paramārtha*); it is not that the ultimate exists separately, apart from all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena.

Therefore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound perfection of wisdom, they practice the conduct of a bodhisattva mahāsattva without wavering from the ultimate truth; they bring sentient beings to maturity, purify buddha-fields, are able to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes, and provide benefit and happiness to sentient beings until the end of the future.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If the nature of equality of all phenomena is such that their intrinsic nature is emptiness, and this intrinsic emptiness is neither an agent nor an object among all phenomena, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, benefit sentient beings by means of the four means of attraction (saṃgrahavastu) without wavering from the ultimate truth?"
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.

The nature of equality of all phenomena is that their intrinsic nature is emptiness; this intrinsic emptiness is neither an agent nor an object with respect to existence or non-existence. Nevertheless, bodhisattvas are able to bring great benefit to sentient beings by means of the four bases of sympathy.
If sentient beings were to know for themselves that all phenomena are empty by their very nature,

then Buddhas and Bodhisattvas would not manifest supernatural powers or perform rare and wondrous deeds; that is to say, while remaining unmoved within the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena,
they cause sentient beings to distance themselves from various false conceptualizations, to abide in the emptiness of all phenomena, and to be liberated from birth.
The suffering of death means causing sentient beings to be separated from the notion of a self, and so forth, up to causing them to be separated from the notion of a perceiver;
it also causes sentient beings to be separated from the notion of form, up to the notion of consciousness;

it also causes sentient beings to be separated from the notion of the eye-base, up to the notion of the mind-base; and it also causes sentient beings to be separated from the notion of the form-base, up to the notion of mental phenomena (*dharma*).
He causes sentient beings to distance themselves from the perception of the sense bases, and also causes them to distance themselves from the perception of the eye element up to the mind element;
he causes them to distance themselves from the perception of the form element up to the phenomena element;

he causes them to distance themselves from the perception of the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element; and he causes them to distance themselves from the perception of eye-contact...

With resolute intent, he causes sentient beings to distance themselves from all perceptions arising from the condition of eye-contact, up to and including all perceptions arising from the condition of mind-contact;
he causes sentient beings to distance themselves from the perception of the earth element, up to and including the perception of the consciousness element;
and he causes sentient beings to distance themselves from the perception of causes and conditions, up to and including the perception of predominance.
It causes sentient beings to distance themselves from the perception of phenomena arising from conditions;

it causes sentient beings to distance themselves from the perception of ignorance up to the perception of old age and death; it causes sentient beings to distance themselves from the perception of contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena;
and it causes sentient beings to distance themselves from the perception of mundane and supramundane phenomena.
Furthermore, they cause sentient beings to distance themselves from the conceptualization of conditioned and unconditioned phenomena;
having caused sentient beings to distance themselves from all such conceptualizations, they cause them to abide in the unconditioned realm, liberated from all birth, old age, sickness, and death.
"The unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛta-dhātu*) is the emptiness of all phenomena; it is designated as the 'unconditioned realm' by way of conventional designation.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By virtue of being empty of what are all phenomena said to be empty?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Because form, up to and including the knowledge of all aspects, are all empty by nature, I say that all phenomena are empty. Furthermore, Subhūti!"
"What do you think?
If an emanated body were to further emanate another entity, would that [emanation] possess a substantial reality and not be empty? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
All that is conjured by illusion has no substantial reality; it is entirely empty."
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"The emanated being and emptiness—these two dharmas are neither joined nor dispersed; both are empty because they are empty of emptiness. One should not make the discrimination that 'this is emptiness' and 'this is an emanation.'"
Why is this? Because within emptiness, neither the two things of "emptiness" nor "transformation" can be found, for all phenomena are ultimately empty.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."
From the formless realms up to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas, there is nothing that is not an emanation;
and whatever is an emanation is entirely empty. Furthermore, Subhūti!

Based on such dharmas, various types of persons (*pudgala*) are designated—namely, ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas—and none of these are not transformations. All that are transformations are without exception empty.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If all worldly phenomena such as the aggregates, bases, and elements, as well as all sentient beings, are indeed transformations, then how could supramundane phenomena such as the four foundations of mindfulness, as well as sentient beings, also be transformations?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"All phenomena, whether mundane or supramundane, are without exception transformations. Within them, there are transformations of śrāvakas, transformations of pratyekabuddhas, transformations of bodhisattvas, transformations of tathāgatas, transformations of afflictions, and transformations of karma."
"For this reason, I say that all things are without distinction, being like illusions and transformations.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"As for the fruits of abandonment—namely, the fruit of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship—and the permanent severance of the continuity of afflictions and habitual tendencies by pratyekabuddhas and tathāgatas—are these also transformations?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“In this way, all these dharmas that are associated with the two characteristics of arising and ceasing are also all transformations.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What dharmas are not transformations?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“If a dharma is not associated with arising and ceasing, that dharma is not a transformation.”
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Which phenomena do not correspond with arising and ceasing?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"The dharma of non-deceptiveness is itself nirvāṇa; this dharma does not correspond with arising or ceasing.
The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying:

"As the World-Honored One has taught, the equal nature of dharmas is entirely empty and cannot be moved; no duality can be apprehended, and there is not even the slightest dharma that is not empty of its own nature. How then can it be said that nirvāṇa is not an emanation?"
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said:
there is not even the slightest dharma that is not empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*).

This emptiness of intrinsic nature was not made by śrāvakas, nor by pratyekabuddhas, nor by bodhisattvas, nor by buddhas, nor was it made by anyone else; whether a buddha appears or does not appear, intrinsic nature is eternally empty. This is itself nirvāṇa.
Therefore, I say that nirvāṇa is not an emanation. There is no truly existent dharma called nirvāṇa that can be described as unarisen, unceasing, and non-emanated.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When newly initiated bodhisattvas hear that all phenomena are ultimately empty—even Nirvana itself is like a magical illusion—their minds become terrified and they are unable to cultivate wholesome qualities. Therefore, I teach them: "If a phenomenon does not correspond with arising and ceasing, this phenomenon is not a magical illusion; it is not something else, truly existent, or an emptiness-less Nirvana."
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

"By what skillful means should one instruct and admonish those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have newly resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, so that they may understand that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is eternally empty, and upon hearing of ultimate emptiness, they do not give rise to fear?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Is it not the case that all phenomena, having previously existed and subsequently ceased to exist, are empty of intrinsic nature?
Yet, since all phenomena neither previously existed nor subsequently cease to exist, their intrinsic nature is eternally empty and free from fear."

One should provide such instruction and guidance to those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have newly resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, so that they may understand that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is eternally empty, and upon hearing of ultimate emptiness, receive it with joy and faith.

When the Bhagavān had finished speaking this sutra, the immeasurable assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as all the great multitude—including the śrāvakas, humans, non-humans, and others—having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle Five Hundred and Thirty-Seven.
